## Multi Tenancy using Accounts
- path: running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/accounts.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/accounts
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [SEC][PATTERN] Accounts are "securely isolated communication contexts that allow multi-tenancy"; "data silos are created by design, not software limitations", with controlled exchange between them.
- [SEC][MYTH] With traditional authorization "all clients can publish and subscribe to anything unless explicitly configured otherwise"; accounts make the subject space non-global so "clients can use short subjects without explicit authorization rules."
- [SEC][PATTERN][ANTI] "think of one account as a messaging container for one application ... more accounts with few (even one) clients is a better design topology than a large account with many users with complex authorization configuration."
- [SEC] Exports: streams (messages you publish; importers can consume but not request) and services (requests fulfilled by your account). Export `accounts` list makes it private; unspecified = public. `response_type` `single` or `stream`.
- [SEC][MYTH] The term "stream" in import/export "does not refer to ... a JetStream stream"; it predates JetStream and means a stream of Core NATS messages.
- [SEC] Imports need a matching export; "Accounts cannot do self-imports." `prefix` remaps stream imports (wildcards allowed, so only a prefix can be applied); `to` remaps service imports ("Currently, a service import can not make use of wildcards").
- [SEC][PATTERN] "Typically an account will export a wildcard service but then coordinate with a client account on specific subjects where requests will be answered."
- [SEC] `no_auth_user` maps unauthenticated clients to a user; "will not work with nkeys or bcrypted passwords"; the auth timeout still applies to the no-credentials handshake and slow links may hit "Authentication Timeout".
- [SEC][STRM][PATTERN] Cross-account JetStream: "in most use cases people want a setup where a stream in one account is mirrored or sourced in another account ... as this is a more 'locked-down' way to share messages", rather than letting apps use a stream in another account directly. References synadia-labs/cross-account-jetstream-sourcing (static security, "probably the best one to start with") and jetstream-leaf-nodes-demo (operator mode).

## Authorization
- path: running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/authorization.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/authorization
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [SEC] Per-user `publish`/`subscribe` permissions; `subscribe` entries may carry a queue name (`<subject> <queue>`) with wildcards; `default_permissions` applies to users without explicit permissions.
- [SEC] Permission map `allow`/`deny`; "In case of overlap deny has priority."
- [SEC][ANTI] "It is important to not break request-reply patterns": add `_INBOX.>` rules, or use `allow_responses`. Unauthorized pub/sub fails, is logged, and errors back to the client.
- [SEC] `allow_responses: true` = `{max: 1}` with no time limit; a map allows `max` and `expires`. It "implicitly denies publish to other subjects" except explicit publish allows.
- [SEC][ANTI] With `allow_responses` "the reply subject is not constrained to the publish allow or deny list"; for explicit control "do not use allow_responses and instead define allow/deny lists under the publish permission map."
- [SEC][ANTI] Any client allowed to subscribe to `_INBOX.>` "can receive all responses published"; sensitive installs should narrow the inbox prefix or use accounts for isolation.
- [SEC][CORE] Queue permissions: allow `"foo queue"` restricts subscribing to foo only inside that queue; `deny: ["> *.prod"]` blocks prod queue groups; `"foo *.dev"` limits queue names by wildcard.

## Authentication (intro), timeout, tokens, username/password, NKeys, TLS auth
- path: running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/auth_intro/*.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/auth_intro
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [SEC] Auth is multi-level: accounts with users; JWT mode adds an operator. Each account is an independent subject namespace; users share it but can be restricted.
- [SEC] Auth methods: token, plain or bcrypted username/password, TLS certificate, NKEY challenge, decentralized JWT; all but JWT are configured in `authorization`.
- [SEC][SIZE] Auth `timeout` default is 1 second more than `tls_timeout`; invalid values default to 1s; numeric seconds only (fractional ok). "long timeouts can be an opportunity for abuse"; must exceed the TLS timeout since it includes the TLS upgrade.
- [SEC] Tokens can be bcrypted (`nats server passwd`) so clear-text isn't in the config; clients still send the clear token. Token auth also works for clusters.
- [SEC] Bcrypted passwords supported; reload with `nats-server --signal reload` without disconnecting clients.
- [SEC] NKeys (Ed25519): server never stores private keys; random challenge per connection makes it "immune to playback attacks". "NKey is an excellent replacement for token authentication". Seeds start with `S`, user public keys with `U`.
- [SEC] TLS `verify` checks the client cert against `ca_file` (system trust store if absent) and requires extended key usage "TLS Web Client Authentication". `verify` and `verify_and_map` do not apply to the monitoring port.
- [SEC] `verify_and_map` searches SAN emails first, then DNS names, then the certificate subject (RFC 2253 DN, attribute order matters); "This mechanism will pick the user it finds first. There is no configuration to restrict this."

## Enabling TLS
- path: running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/tls.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/tls
- version context: TLS-first 2.10.4; connection_rate_limit 2.7.0

### Claims
- [SEC][SIZE] TLS defaults: `min_version "1.2"`, handshake `timeout` 2 seconds; `ca_file` absent = system trust store; `insecure` skips verification for outgoing connections only and is "NOT Recommended".
- [SEC][TOPO] `verify_cert_and_check_known_urls` (cluster/gateway only) matches cert SAN DNS entries against configured route/gateway URLs; "dynamic cluster growth may require config changes in other clusters where this flag is true"; wildcard SANs keep growth flexible.
- [SEC] `pinned_certs` restricts accepted certs to listed SHA256 public-key fingerprints.
- [SEC][OPS] Root `tls` also applies to the monitoring port when `https_port` is set; cluster/gateway/leaf blocks can have their own.
- [SEC][OPS] Certificate rotation: "Make sure that the ca_file contains both old and new root or intermediate CAs"; reload config to apply file changes.
- [SEC] TLS-first handshake (2.10.4) `handshake_first: true|auto|<duration>`; `auto` falls back to INFO after 50 milliseconds; only `true` guarantees no plaintext, and requires upgraded client libraries. TLS-first clients are marked in Connz.
- [SEC][SIZE][ANTI] TLS `timeout`: increase if clients disconnect during handshake, but "an extended timeout exposes your server to attacks where a client doesn't upgrade to TLS and thus consumes resources."
- [SEC][SIZE][OPS] `connection_rate_limit` (2.7.0) caps new TLS client connections per second server-wide (example 1000); excess get "Connection throttling is active. Please try again later."; default 0 disables; not applied to cluster/gateway/leaf/websocket/MQTT listeners. Rationale: "TLS handshakes are expensive, and a burst of reconnecting clients can keep the server busy".
- [SEC][PATTERN] Trust both active and standby intermediates in `ca_file` "to be prepared for such a day" when the CA switches.
- [SEC][ANTI] Self-signed certs: "DO NOT USE these certificates in production!!!" Use a public CA if outsiders connect, in-house CA for internal apps, environment CA (e.g. Kubernetes) for a single environment.
- [SEC][TOPO][ANTI] Cluster advertises IPs by default, which "may result in a failed TLS hostname verification with an IP SANs error"; set `advertise`/`cluster_advertise` to verifiable names.
- [SEC] The connecting IP/DNS must match a SAN or the handshake fails.
- [SEC][TOPO] Key usage: server needs "TLS WWW server authentication"; clients need "TLS WWW client authentication" when verify is on. "Cluster connections always have verify enabled ... Certificates containing both values are a must." Gateways always verify but may use a separate outgoing cert.
- [SEC][CLNT] Behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy configure `tls {}` plus `allow_non_tls: true`; minimum client versions: nats.go v1.31.0, nats.js 2024.1.2, nats.java 2.18.0, nats.rs 0.33, nats.net.v2 2.0.0, nats.net v1 1.1.5.

## OCSP Stapling
- path: running-a-nats-service/configuration/ocsp.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/ocsp
- version context: 2.3

### Claims
- [SEC] OCSP stapling is honored by default (`auto` mode) for Must-Staple certs; modes `auto`, `must` (shutdown on revoked), `always` (all certs, shutdown on revoked), `never`. `url` overrides the responder in the cert.
- [SEC][OPS] Staples are cached on disk in `store_dir` (shared with JetStream if enabled) so restarts don't refetch.

## Decentralized JWT Authentication/Authorization
- path: running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/jwt/README.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/jwt
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [SEC] JWT auth moves user/account config out of server files into signed tokens: "Users are not directly tracked by the server, but rather verified as and belonging to an Account", enabling user management "without requiring server configuration updates."
- [SEC] Isolation and import/export of accounts remain; JWT adds expiration and revocation.
- [SEC] NATS JWTs must be Ed25519-signed; Issuer and Subject are public NKEYs; roles Operator -> Account -> User form a chain of trust; servers trust specific operators.
- [SEC] Authentication: user presents account-issued JWT, signs a server nonce, server fetches account JWT, checks issuer chain to a trusted operator.
- [SEC][MYTH] "NATS JWTs are only used as configuration", not as sessions or proof of authentication; identity proof is the nonce signature.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Fully decentralized: operator admins issue account JWTs to prod/dev teams who issue their own users; "Neither entity has to be aware of the other's private Nkey."
- [SEC] JWT and NKEY/account-config auth can be mixed.

## Account lookup using Resolver / Memory Resolver
- path: running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/jwt/resolver.md, mem_resolver.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/jwt/resolver
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [SEC][OPS] Three resolvers: NATS-based ("the preferred option and should be your default selection"), `MEMORY` (static accounts in config), `URL` (build your own account service; standalone nats-account-server "is now legacy").
- [SEC][OPS][ANTI] NATS-based resolver stores JWTs in a local, not shared, directory ("you can't have more than one nats-servers using the same directory"); all servers in the cluster/super-cluster must use it; sync is eventually consistent via the system account.
- [SEC][SIZE] `full` resolver: `allow_delete` (default false; deletes rename to `.delete`), `interval "2m"` state comparison with one random peer, `limit 1000` JWTs. "Not every server in a cluster needs to be set to full. You need enough to still serve your workload adequately, while some servers are offline."
- [SEC][SIZE][ANTI] `cache` resolver: LRU subset, `limit 1000`, `ttl "2m"`; "does NOT accept account push messages from nsc and therefore is not suitable for stand-alone operation without a full resolver present."
- [SEC][OPS] Integration subjects: `$SYS.REQ.CLAIMS.UPDATE` to push a JWT; subscribe `$SYS.REQ.ACCOUNT.*.CLAIMS.LOOKUP` to implement an account server.
- [SEC][OPS] Migration from REST account server: `nsc pull`, reconfigure to nats resolver, `nsc edit operator --account-jwt-server-url nats://...`, `nsc push -A`.
- [SEC][PATTERN] "The MEMORY resolver is recommended when the server has a small number of accounts that don't change very often"; supports config reload of preloads; `nsc generate config --mem-resolver` generates it.

- path: running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/jwt/jwt_nkey_auth.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/jwt/jwt_nkey_auth
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [SEC][PATTERN] To mix static NKEY config and operator JWT auth: first prepare the trusted-operator setup, reuse the same account public NKEYs in the static config, and bridge the two servers via cluster routes during transition.
- [SEC][TOPO] "Even though they have different authorization mechanisms, these two servers are able to route account messages because they share the same NKEY."

## Auth Callout
- path: running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/auth_callout.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/securing_nats/auth_callout
- version context: 2.10.0

### Claims
- [SEC] Auth callout delegates client authentication/authorization to an application-defined NATS service, for external IAM (LDAP, SAML, OAuth, a database, or a file).
- [SEC][OPS][ANTI] Order: implement the service, plan migration, then configure; "enabling the configuration before deploying a service could cause issues for existing systems."
- [SEC][ANTI] In centralized mode "existing users defined in the config file will be ignored"; the auth service must authenticate all users including system account users and the implicit no-auth user, so port users first.
- [SEC] Config: `authorization { auth_callout { issuer, auth_users, account (default $G), xkey } }`.
- [SEC][PATTERN] "For new setups, it is recommended to use explicit accounts": an `AUTH` account for callout users, `APP` accounts for applications instead of `$G`, and `SYS` as system account.
- [SEC] `xkey` (x25519) encryption of payloads "is recommended as a security best practice, but not required"; the server generates a one-time XKey per connection which "prevents replay attacks".
- [SEC][STALE?] "Decentralized Auth: Coming soon!"
- [SEC] Response claims carry a user JWT used "for the duration of the client connection"; `issuer_account` indicates a signing key was used.

- [OPS][SIZE] "The support policy for the server is the current release as well as one patch version release prior" (e.g. 2.8.4 -> 2.8.3 downgrade supported); earlier downgrades "may work, but is not recommended." Downgrade path = same rolling procedure.

## Lame Duck Mode
- path: running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/lame_duck_mode.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/lame_duck_mode
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [OPS][PATTERN] "In production we recommend that a server is shut down with lame duck mode as a graceful way to slowly evict clients"; it "mitigates the 'thundering herd' situation that will place CPU pressure on servers as TLS enabled clients reconnect."
- [OPS][SIZE] LDM: stop accepting new connections, 10 second grace period, then evict clients over `lame_duck_duration` (default 2 minutes).
- [CLNT] The server notifies clients on LDM; some clients invoke an optional callback so apps can prepare for the short outage before reconnecting elsewhere.

## Slow Consumers
- path: running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/slow_consumers.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/slow_consumers
- version context: 2017 log sample

### Claims
- [CORE][CLNT][MYTH] "NATS favors the approach of protecting the system as a whole over accommodating a particular consumer to ensure message delivery." Slow consumers are cut off; clients not answering pings are disconnected and need reconnect logic.
- [CLNT] Client-detected slow consumer: app notified via async error callback and messages dropped; "It is better to catch a slow consumer locally in the client rather than to allow the server to detect this condition."
- [OPS] Server-detected: server buffers outbound, then designates "slow consumer" and may drop the connection; logged "Slow Consumer Detected"; counted in `varz` `slow_consumers`.
- [PATTERN] Handling options: JetStream, optimize consumer, scale with queue subscribers ("ideal if you do not rely on message order"), design a scalable subject namespace ("useful if you need to preserve message order": publish deep, subscribe with wildcards, later split `Sensors.>` into `Sensors.North|South|East|West` without touching publishers), meter the publisher ("less favorable"), tune NATS.
- [OPS][SIZE][ANTI] `write_deadline` can be raised (example `2s`) for bursts, but "Be sure you are not just postponing a slow consumer error." "Increasing buffer sizes is not typically recommended unless you are handling temporary bursts of data. Often, increasing buffer capacity will only postpone slow consumer problems."
- [CLNT][SIZE] Default subscriber pending limits: `65536` messages and `65536*1024` bytes; on reaching them the client drops messages and continues ("aligned with NATS at most once delivery"); the app must detect and recover. A local error doesn't mean the server flagged the subscription.

- [OPS] `--signal ldm`=SIGUSR2 (graceful, evict gradually), `quit`=SIGINT, `term`=SIGTERM, `stop`=SIGKILL, `reload`=SIGHUP, `reopen`=SIGUSR1 (log rotation); SIGQUIT kills with stack dump.

- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [STRM][SUBJ] Stream, consumer (durable) and account names appear in both the JetStream subject namespace and the filesystem, so they must follow subject rules and be file-system friendly.
- [STRM][SIZE][ANTI] Guidelines: alphanumeric; no spaces/tabs/`.`/`>`/`*`; no path separators; "keep names under 32 characters"; avoid reserved file names (NUL, LPT1); "some file systems are case insensitive so do not use stream or account names that would collide" (`Foo` vs `foo` on Windows/macOS).

## Data Replication (mirrors/sources admin)
- path: running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/jetstream_admin/replication.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/jetstream_admin/replication
- version context: 2022 CLI output; "In future builds ... between accounts" [STALE?]

### Claims
- [STRM][PATTERN] Tiered example: ORDERS and RETURNS are memory-based, short-retention, R3; ARCHIVE sources both, file-based, long retention, R3, and accepts direct publishes; REPORT mirrors ARCHIVE, unclustered (R1), one-month retention, no listen subjects.
- [STRM] A mirror copies from exactly one stream, "as far as possible IDs and ordering will match exactly the source"; a mirror has no listen subjects; a stream with a mirror cannot also have sources; mirrors support filter, start sequence, start time.
- [STRM][MYTH] With sources "We can therefore not maintain absolute ordering, but data from 1 single source will be in the correct order but mixed in with other streams"; timestamps may appear out of order.
- [OPS] `nats stream info` shows per-source Lag and Last Seen; `nats stream report --dot` emits a GraphViz replication map.

## Disaster Recovery
- path: running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/jetstream_admin/disaster_recovery.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/jetstream_admin/disaster_recovery
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [STRM][OPS][ANTI] "For R1 streams, data is persisted on one server node only. If that server node is unrecoverable then recovery from backup is the sole option."
- [STRM][OPS] Automatic recovery conditions: stream is R3 or greater; remaining replicas meet quorum floor(R/2)+1; a free node exists in the stream's cluster; impacted nodes are peer-removed from the meta group.
- [OPS] Backups (`nats stream backup`) include stream config and state, durable consumer config and state, and all messages with timestamps and headers. `nats account backup` covers all streams in an account.
- [OPS][ANTI] "Memory storage streams do not support snapshots. Only file-based storage streams can be backed up."
- [OPS] During backup the stream's configuration is frozen and "no data will be evicted based on stream retention policies."
- [OPS][SIZE] Example backup: 813 MiB uncompressed became 13 MiB compressed in 3368 chunks.
- [OPS][ANTI] Administering interactively with the CLI leaves no desired state to recreate from: "This is not the ideal way to administer the server, we recommend Configuration Management".
- [OPS] `nats account restore` supports `--cluster` and `--tag` placement; it "will fail if a stream with the same name already exists."

## Encryption at Rest
- path: running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/jetstream_admin/encryption_at_rest.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/jetstream_admin/encryption_at_rest
- version context: 2.3.0; TPM Windows 2.11.0

### Claims
- [SEC][STRM][PATTERN] "although encryption at rest by the NATS server is fully supported, we recommend using file system encryption where available" because it is throughput-optimized, adds no server burden, and removes secret management from NATS.
- [SEC] Ciphers: `chachapoly` (ChaCha20-Poly1305) and `aes` (AES-GCM); encrypts message blocks (headers+payloads) and stream/consumer metadata files.
- [SEC][OPS] Provide the key via an environment variable (e.g. `$JS_KEY`) "so it will not be persisted in a file."
- [SEC][OPS] Enabling on existing data encrypts only new blocks; back up and restore to re-encrypt old blocks. Restarting with a different or no key fails decryption ("message authentication failed") and breaks JetStream but core NATS still works. Cipher can change if the key stays the same.
- [SEC][SIZE] Performance cost observed from "as little as 1% decrease to more than 30%" on a MacBook Pro test; encrypted files may be larger.

## Streams / Consumers (JetStream admin CLI walkthrough)
- path: running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/jetstream_admin/streams.md, consumers.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/jetstream_admin/streams
- version context: 2021 CLI output [STALE? push examples]

### Claims
- [OPS] Every `nats` JetStream action can run non-interactively "making it usable as a CLI API"; `-j` gives JSON; config JSON matches `nats str info X -j | jq .config`.
- [STRM] `nats pub` to a stream subject is unacknowledged; `nats req` shows the `+OK` publish ack "if you want to be sure your messages got to JetStream and were persisted."
- [STRM] After `nats str purge`, sequence numbers keep advancing (FirstSeq 1,000,001 / LastSeq 1,000,000 in example), i.e. purge does not reset sequences.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Pull consumers let you "easily scale your services up by adding more workers and the messages will get spread across the workers based on their availability."
- [CONS] Pull vs push is decided by the presence of a delivery target. Example NEW/DISPATCH: explicit ack, ack wait 30s, max deliver 20, sample 100.
- [CONS][MYTH] "Stream vs Consumer sequence numbers ... are not directly related": stream sequence points to the message; consumer sequence is an ever-increasing counter of deliveries (10 redeliveries of one message -> consumer seq 10 or 11).
- [CONS] Pull is a `Request()` to `$JS.API.CONSUMER.MSG.NEXT.<stream>.<consumer>`; ack by responding with an empty payload.
- [CONS] Push consumer messages preserve the original subject (e.g. `ORDERS.processed`) so wildcard-stream consumers can distinguish them.

## Monitoring (endpoints reference)
- path: running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/monitoring/README.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/monitoring
- version context: 2.0.0 sample output

### Claims
- [OPS] Endpoints: `/varz`, `/connz`, `/routez`, `/gatewayz`, `/leafz`, `/subsz`, `/accountz`, `/accstatz`, `/jsz`, `/healthz`; all also reachable as system services. Conventional port 8222.
- [OPS][SEC][ANTI] Monitoring has no auth and binds `0.0.0.0` by default; don't expose it to the internet.
- [OPS][SIZE] `/connz` pages 1024 connections by default; "The server will default to holding the last 10,000 closed connections."
- [OPS][SIZE] Sample `/varz` shows defaults: max_connections 65536, ping_interval 120s, ping_max 2, auth_timeout 1, max_control_line 4096, max_payload 1048576, max_pending 67108864, tls_timeout 0.5 (older default), write_deadline 2s (older default; config page says 10s). Records: contradicts running-a-nats-service/configuration/README.md (`write_deadline` 10s) and tls.md (timeout 2s).
- [OPS][STRM] `/jsz`: "If you're in a clustered environment, it is recommended to retrieve the information from the stream's leader in order to get the most accurate and up-to-date data" (`leader-only=true`); `raft=true` includes RAFT details.
- [OPS] `/healthz` returns OK when the server accepts connections; `js-enabled-only` errors if JetStream is disabled; `js-server-only` skips account/stream/consumer checks; `js-enabled` is deprecated.
- [OPS] Prometheus NATS Exporter + Grafana walkthrough are the standard monitoring stack.

### Claims

- [TOPO] Leaf nodes extend NATS and JetStream to "a VPC, a VLAN, a remote office, a single machine at home or even an edge location with partial connectivity."

## Environmental considerations
- path: running-a-nats-service/environment.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/environment
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [TOPO][CLNT][ANTI] Load balancers are possible "but you don't need to": NATS balances across seed URLs (clients randomize DNS A records) and reconnects automatically. "If you have a cluster with 3 seed nodes you often get more network throughput than going through a load balancer".
- [SEC][ANTI] "if you want to use TLS for authentication you do not want the load balancer to be the TLS termination point."
- [TOPO][ANTI][MYTH] "Client connections and routes are permanent. Therefore a load balancer will not distribute messages from one client connections between servers"; a common failure is "redundant, but disconnected (non-clustered) servers to which the clients will randomly connect." Advertising must be off or point at the LB address.
- [TOPO][ANTI] Load balancers can cause idle-detection, packet-inspection protocol, and ephemeral-port problems at scale; routes or gateways through LBs "could results in JetStream lost quorum periods and create undue re-synchronization and protocol overhead traffic."
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Sensible LB use: a single entry point for clustered servers, or auto-connecting to the geographically closest cluster node.
- [OPS][PATTERN] "Think of Core NATS servers as a software equivalent of network switches. Enable JetStream, and they also become a new kind of DB server as well."
- [OPS][SIZE][ANTI] In public clouds "you get what you pay for": non-network-optimized instances may give 10 Gb/s for ~30 minutes then drop (e.g. to 5 Gb/s); choose network-optimized instances for sustained bandwidth. Local SSD gives best latency; network block storage (EBS) can give highest throughput but general-purpose tiers burst then drop IOPS; choose IO-optimized storage for sustained IOPS.
- [OPS][ANTI] Container resource limits: nats-server uses resources in proportion to traffic and bursts; set limits accordingly or the orchestrator kills it. It "will try to use all host memory, not the resource limits set for the container, unless you specify GOMEMLIMIT" (available in the official Helm charts).

## Installing (hardware requirements)
- path: running-a-nats-service/installation.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/installation
- version context: 2.11.6 example; tests on 2021-era CPU

### Claims
- [OPS][SIZE] "The NATS server itself has minimal hardware requirements to support small edge devices".
- [OPS][CLNT][PATTERN] TLS CPU: "After a network partition, every disconnected client will attempt to connect to a NATS server in the cluster simultaneously, so CPU on those servers will momentarily spike." Mitigate with reconnect jitter, longer TLS timeouts, and larger clusters.
- [OPS][ANTI] "We highly recommend testing to see if smaller, cheaper machines suffice for your workload - often they do!" Start small and adjust after load testing; ensure a sufficient NIC.
- [OPS][SIZE] "For high throughput use cases, the network interface card (NIC) or the available bandwidth are often the bottleneck".
- [OPS][SIZE] Core NATS minimums (containers, GOMEMLIMIT at 90%): 1 core / 32 MiB handles 100 publishers at 1000 msg/s each (100,000 msg/s total) on a single server; 3-node cluster 1 core / 32-64 MiB at 100,000 msg/s total.
- [OPS][SIZE][STRM] JetStream minimums (file storage, R3 on 3 nodes, pull consumers): 1 core / 32 MiB for 1,000 msg/s; 1 core / 64 MiB for 10,000 msg/s; 3 nodes 1 core / 256 MiB for 100,000 msg/s. "these are minimum configurations".
- [OPS][SIZE][STRM] "For production deployment of JetStream, we recommend starting with at least 4 CPU cores and 8 GiB of memory".

## WebSocket Configuration
- path: running-a-nats-service/configuration/websocket/websocket_conf.md

### Claims
- [SEC][CLNT] WebSocket "TLS configuration is required by default"; `no_tls: true` only for test environments.
- [SEC] `same_origin` (default false) and `allowed_origins` only apply when the request carries an Origin header (browsers).
- [SIZE] WebSocket `handshake_timeout` example `2s` includes the TLS handshake; `compression` requires both sides to support it.
- [SEC][PATTERN] `jwt_cookie`: an HTTP server can set a NATS Bearer user JWT in a secure cookie after its own authentication, so browser clients authenticate without embedding credentials.
- [SEC] WebSocket-level `no_auth_user` overrides the main one for websocket clients; "not compatible with running the server in operator mode."
- [SEC][PATTERN] `allowed_connection_types` (aliases `connection_types`, `clients`) restricts a user to `STANDARD`, `WEBSOCKET`, `LEAFNODE`, `MQTT`; absence allows all.
- [OPS] WebSocket is not enabled by default in Docker; add a `websocket { port, no_tls }` config.

## MQTT
- path: running-a-nats-service/configuration/mqtt/README.md, mqtt_config.md, mqtt_conf.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/configuration/mqtt
- version context: 2.2 (MQTT support); `.` translation 2.10.0

### Claims
- [MIG] NATS follows MQTT v3.1.1 and supports QoS 0, 1 and 2.
- [MIG][PATTERN] MQTT support "is intended to be an enabling technology allowing users to leverage existing investments in their IoT deployments"; "In greenfield IoT deployments, when possible, we prefer NATS extended out to endpoints and devices" for security and observability; NATS is "nearly as lightweight in terms of protocol bandwidth" as MQTT.
- [MIG][USECASE] Use NATS as a drop-in MQTT server to connect existing MQTT endpoints to a remote NATS cluster/supercluster.
- [MIG][STRM] "For an MQTT client to connect to the NATS server, the user's account must be JetStream enabled" because sessions and retained messages (even QoS 0) are persisted.
- [MIG][SUBJ] Topic mapping: `/` -> `.`; leading `/` -> `/.`; trailing `/` -> `./`; `.` -> `//` (2.10+; rejected before); space not supported (connection closed on publish, SUBACK failure on subscribe). `#` -> `>` (server creates two subscriptions `foo.>` and `foo`); `+` -> `*`. `*` and `>` inside topics become NATS wildcards if they form a whole token.
- [MIG][SEC] Permissions for MQTT users are written as NATS subjects (conversion happens before authz); QoS 1 subscriptions need subscribe permission on `$MQTT.sub.>`.
- [MIG][SIZE] QoS 1/2 redelivery after `ack_wait` (default 30 seconds); `max_ack_pending` valid 0..65535, session total cannot exceed 65535, `#` subscriptions count double; changes apply only to new subscriptions.
- [MIG] All sessions are persisted even with "clean session". Duplicate client IDs: the server accepts the new session and delays closing the old to reduce flapping; across servers "Users should avoid this situation".
- [MIG][ANTI] Clustered retained messages are best-effort: "applications that rely on the presence of a retained message should connect on the server that produced them." Replication factor is set automatically from cluster size.
- [MIG] Limitations: NATS-published messages reach MQTT subscribers as QoS 0 only.
- [MIG][SEC] MQTT requires a unique `server_name`. In operator mode MQTT clients cannot sign the nonce, so pass a Bearer user JWT (`nsc edit user --bearer`) as the MQTT password with any non-empty username.

## FAQ
- path: reference/faq.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/reference/faq
- version context: 2.2 (JetStream recommended, STAN deprecated)

### Claims
- [MIG][STALE?] "As of NATS Server 2.2, NATS JetStream is the recommended option for persistence ... NATS Streaming a.k.a. 'STAN' is now deprecated."
- [CORE] Request() is "a convenience API" over Publish with an INBOX subject unique to the requestor plus a timeout.
- [CORE][MYTH] Multiple subscribers can receive a request; with a queue group only one is picked; "the requestor does not know or control this information"; it only asks for one answer and NATS prunes interest after it.
- [CORE][MYTH] "NATS implements non-persistent distributed queuing via subscriber queue groups"; queue groups are "a form of message-distribution load balancing"; distribution is "controlled entirely by nats-server", not a publisher operation; messages "are not persisted to secondary storage."
- [SUBJ][MYTH] You cannot list subjects: "Do not think of it as a 'directory' that is aggregated over time. The interest graph is dynamic"; it can be derived at an instant by polling `/connz` and `/routez`.
- [CONS][PATTERN][STALE?] Consumer choice: shared pull consumer to horizontally scale or process high-throughput streams ("batching is in practice key to achieving high throughput"); ordered push consumer when each instance needs its own on-demand replay; durable push consumer with a queue group for "scalable low latency real time processing".
- [CLNT] Verbose mode acks every protocol command with +OK/-ERR and "is ON by default for new connections; most client implementations disable verbose mode by default"; pedantic adds subject checking.
- [CORE][MYTH] "NATS implements source ordered delivery per publisher ... There are no guarantees of message delivery order amongst multiple publishers."
- [CORE][SIZE] `max_payload` default 1 MB, max 64 MB, "we recommend keeping the max message size to something more reasonable like 8 MB."
- [SUBJ][SIZE] "As of nats-server v0.8.0, there is no hard limit on the maximum number of subjects."
- [CORE][MYTH] Core NATS is at-most-once: "messages are guaranteed to arrive intact, in order from a given publisher, but not across different publishers"; "offers only TCP reliability"; problematic or offline subscribers miss messages. JetStream (2.2+) adds at-least-once and "exactly-once (within a time window)".
- [CLNT] Graceful async subscriber shutdown: call `sub.Unsubscribe()` so outstanding handlers finish; one goroutine per subscription (Go).
- [SUBJ] "a subject does not exist in a NATS cluster until a client subscribes to it, and the subject goes away after the last subscribing client unsubscribes".
- [OPS][SIZE] Default max connections per server is 65,536; "Most systems can handle several thousand NATS connections per server without any changes" but OS limits (e.g. macOS) and TCP buffer sizes may need tuning.
- [OPS][SEC][PATTERN] TLS negotiation CPU during a thundering herd "is usually the constraint limiting the number of connections a single server should support"; mitigate with TLS-accelerated cipher suites (AES on x86) and reconnect jitter/delay ranges.
- [TOPO][SIZE] With clusters, superclusters and leaf nodes "one can build a NATS deployment supporting many millions of connections."

## Anatomy of a NATS Client Application
- path: using-nats/developing-with-nats/anatomy.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/developing-with-nats/anatomy
- version context: unstated (Object Store marked "Technology Preview" [STALE?])

### Claims
- [CLNT][MYTH] With NATS the developer never worries about who sends/receives, where services are or how many instances, "How many partitions or servers there are in the cluster", fault tolerance, or topology.
- [CLNT] Apps can open many independent connections (e.g. as two users) but "typically most applications only make a single NATS connection."
- [CLNT][PATTERN] "It is recommended that the application use connection event listeners" to log connects/reconnects/disconnects.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] "The recommended way to disconnect is to use Drain()"; use `close()` only when immediate close is needed.
- [CLNT] Flush after publishing if latency-sensitive; flush uses PING/PONG and those pings don't count toward max outgoing pings.
- [CLNT][MYTH] "A client will receive a message for each matching subscription" so overlapping subscriptions (`foo` and `>`) deliver the same message multiple times.
- [CORE] Multiple queue groups may exist on one subject, each an independent queue getting its own copy.
- [CLNT][ANTI] Core subscribers "must be able to keep up with the flow of messages ... or it will otherwise become a slow consumer".
- [CORE][PATTERN] "unless there's a specific reason not to, application servicing requests should subscribe to the request subject using the same queue group name"; a second queue group can do logging/monitoring of the same requests.
- [CLNT][STRM] JetStream contexts are lightweight: "while it is safe to share a JS context between threads, for best performance do not be afraid to have a context per thread."
- [STRM] Two stream use cases: temporal decoupling (replay) and queuing (distributed work queue).
- [STRM] "Streams can be (and often are) administratively defined ahead of time".
- [STRM][CLNT] Core publish to a stream subject is stored but unacknowledged; "you will get higher quality of service by publishing using the JetStream Context's publish call" because it is acknowledged after storage; hence sync and async variants.
- [CONS] Consumers are like database views: subject filter, ack policy (explicit acks "are required for some types of streams and consumer"), deliver policy, replay policy; "You can have as many consumers as you need per stream."
- [CONS][PATTERN] "Applications typically use ephemeral ordered push consumers to get they own copy of the messages" [STALE? push]; "Applications typically use durable pull consumers to distribute and scale horizontally the processing".
- [CONS] Ephemeral consumers are cleaned up when the creating instance shuts down and used only by it; durables are "always on" and shared or reused across restarts.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Ack semantics: `ack()` success; `term()` "when the request is invalid" (never redeliver); `nack()` "when the request is valid but you are unable to process it" and if temporary "you should also close your subscription temporarily until you are able to process again"; `inProgress()` to extend.
- [STRM][MYTH] At-least-once corner cases: double publication, ack loss, or crash after processing before ack; dedup plus double-ack give exactly-once.
- [OBJ][STALE?] "Object Store ... NOTICE: Technology Preview".

## Automatic Reconnections
- path: using-nats/developing-with-nats/reconnect/README.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/developing-with-nats/reconnect
- version context: nats.go option names

### Claims
- [CLNT] All nats-io clients auto-reconnect and re-establish all subscriptions; they use URLs from connect plus URLs gossiped by the servers; "This feature allows NATS applications and the NATS system itself to self-heal".
- [CLNT] Callbacks: ClosedCB, DisconnectedErrCB (DisconnectedCB deprecated), ReconnectedCB, DiscoveredServersCB, AsyncErrorCB (e.g. slow consumer).
- [CLNT][SIZE] Go defaults: `Timeout` 2s dial; `PingInterval` 2 minutes; `MaxPingsOut` 2 (then ErrStaleConnection); `AllowReconnect` true; `MaxReconnect` 60 (negative = forever); `ReconnectWait` 2s; `ReconnectJitter` 100ms (no TLS); `ReconnectJitterTLS` 1s; `ReconnectBufSize` 8 MiB ("Once this has been exhausted publish operations will return an error"); `RetryOnFailedConnect` false.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] `CustomReconnectDelayCB`: "It is strongly recommended that this value contains some jitter to prevent all connections to attempt reconnecting at the same time."

## Connecting to a Cluster / timeouts / misc / name / noecho / ping-pong / security
- path: using-nats/developing-with-nats/connecting/*.md, connecting/security/*.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/developing-with-nats/connecting/cluster (etc.)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [CLNT] Connect URLs "are usually checked in random order as to not have every client connect to the same server"; first success wins; randomization can be disabled.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] "your code should include a list of reasonable front line or seed servers"; you don't need every member, the server gossips the rest; "the mesh created by a cluster can grow and change organically while the clients are running."
- [CLNT] Connect timeout applies to each cluster member URL individually (example 10 seconds).
- [CLNT] Clients can read the server's `max_payload` after connect to chunk or limit data.
- [CLNT] Pedantic mode is off by default; publishing to a subject containing a wildcard is not checked unless pedantic is on.
- [CLNT][ANTI] `max_control_line` limits combined subject + queue group length; "It is not recommended to set this to a value that is higher than the one of other clients or the nats-server."
- [CLNT] Verbose mode "is only used for debugging the client library or the nats-server themselves. By default the server sets it to on, but every client turns it off."
- [CLNT][OPS] A connection name "is highly recommended as a friendly connection name will help in monitoring, error reporting, debugging, and testing."
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Echo is on by default (a connection's own subscribers get its publishes). NoEcho "can be useful in BUS patterns where all applications subscribe and publish to the same subject." It is per connection, and toggling it "can result in a major change to your applications communications protocol".
- [CLNT][SIZE][PATTERN] Ping interval x max pings outstanding sets how fast a stale connection is detected, including partitions the OS doesn't notice; default interval "is typically on the order of minutes"; example: interval 20s and 5 max pings closes after 100s. The server doesn't initiate PING/PONG while traffic flows.
- [SEC][CLNT] A credentials file bundles the user JWT and NKey seed and "should be protected because it contains a private key."
- [SEC][CLNT] NKey challenge-response "protects the private key from the server, which never has access to it!"
- [SEC][CLNT] A TLS-mode server requires TLS from all clients; a TLS-configured client fails against a non-TLS server. Using just a `tls://` URL "is very likely to fail" unless the language's TLS defaults find the CA.
- [SEC][ANTI] Tokens "are only as safe as they are secret ... It is highly recommended to use one of the other NATS authentication mechanisms."
- [SEC] Bcrypted passwords in server config; client still sends plain text; `nats://user:password@server:port` URL form.

## Receiving: async, sync, drain, queues, unsubscribe, wildcards, structure
- path: using-nats/developing-with-nats/receiving/*.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/developing-with-nats/receiving/drain (etc.)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [CLNT][MYTH] "For a given subscription, messages are dispatched serially, one message at a time." Concurrent processing requires the app to move messages to its own queue/worker pool.
- [CLNT] Async subscriptions cost library resources (threads); sync subscriptions suit single-expected-message cases.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Drain vs close: close/unsubscribe are immediate and halt pending messages; drain "will process any inflight and cached/pending messages before closing." Connection drain: drain all subs, stop publishing, flush, close. Subscription drain: unsubscribe, process cached/inflight, clean up.
- [CLNT][CORE][PATTERN] "Drain provides clients that use queue subscriptions with a way to bring down applications without losing any messages": bring up a new queue member, drain the old, shut down. "Without drain, there is the possibility of lost messages due to delivery timing."
- [CLNT][SIZE] "the timeout for drain should generally be higher than the timeout for a simple message request-reply".
- [CORE] Queue groups are dynamic, no server config; "In a cluster setup, every member has the same chance of receiving a particular message."
- [CORE][CLNT] The server never processes payloads; structured data (JSON etc.) is encoded by the app or library helpers.
- [CLNT][MYTH] Auto-unsubscribe after N counts total messages ever sent to that subscription, not new ones; "If the subscriber has already received one or more messages, the unsubscribe will be immediate." Libraries resend the updated total on reconnect.
- [CLNT] Unsubscribe requires a server round trip, so an async subscription may still receive a message during the window.
- [CLNT][SUBJ][PATTERN] With wildcard subscriptions "it is a common technique to use the subject provided with the incoming message to determine what to do with the message."

## Sending: caches/flush, reply-to, request-reply, structured data
- path: using-nats/developing-with-nats/sending/*.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/developing-with-nats/sending/request_reply (etc.)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [CLNT] Libraries buffer outgoing data for throughput while keeping low latency at low rates; use flush when a message must have "hit the wire"; flush is implemented with PING/PONG.
- [CORE][CLNT] Newer libraries use one wildcard inbox subscription with unique child subjects per request instead of a new subscription per request.
- [CORE] Request = publish with unique reply-to, accept only one response, usually synchronous with a timeout; conceptually "subscribe, get one message, unsubscribe".
- [CORE][PATTERN] Scatter-gather: subscribe to the reply inbox, publish the request, loop collecting responses bounded by time (e.g. 100ms) or "at least N responses" with a timeout (e.g. 500ms).

## Reconnect: buffer, disable, events, max, random, wait
- path: using-nats/developing-with-nats/reconnect/*.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/developing-with-nats/reconnect/buffer (etc.)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [CLNT][ANTI] "The Core NATS client libraries try as much as possible to be fire and forget, and you should use JetStream functionalities to get higher qualities of service" when connection interruptions drop messages.
- [CLNT][MYTH] The reconnect buffer caches publishes while disconnected and sends them on reconnect; when full, publishes error. "while the message appears to be sent to the application it is possible that it is never sent because the connection is never remade." Use acks or JetStream publish to ensure delivery.
- [CLNT] Max reconnect attempts are counted per server (including discovered ones); a server exceeding the count in a row is removed from the list, reset on success or rediscovery; running out of servers closes the connection with an error.
- [CLNT][ANTI][PATTERN] Thundering herd: "all of the clients try to reconnect immediately, thus creating a denial of service attack"; libraries randomize server order so "no one server bears the brunt"; randomization can be disabled.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Reconnect wait avoids thrashing the same server "especially when using TLS" and eases thundering herd when no other servers are available.
- [CLNT] Reconnect event listeners are "especially important for applications sending a lot of messages."

### Claims
- [CLNT] Listen for closed/disconnected/reconnected events, discovered servers, and errors; reconnecting may involve multiple disconnects while searching for a server.
- [CLNT][CORE] "NATS depends on the applications to consider and respond to changing message rates. The server will do a bit of impedance matching, but if a client is too slow the server will eventually cut them off".
- [CLNT] Library-side pending buffers absorb bursts (e.g. app handles 10 msg/s, receives 20); the server sees a healthy connection; on overflow the library raises SlowConsumer and discards messages.
- [PATTERN] Patterns for slow consumers: request-reply to throttle the sender, queue with multiple subscribers, persist with streaming ([STALE?] "something like NATS streaming").
- [CLNT][ANTI] Pending limits (count and bytes, e.g. 1,000 messages or 5mb) help with bursty publishers, not continuous mismatch; "Disabling these limits can be dangerous in production" and setting them to 0 "is also a dangerous proposition in production."
- [CLNT] Some libraries (Java) notify once per time the subscriber falls behind, not per dropped message; a dropped-message count may be available.

## Developing with JetStream
- path: using-nats/jetstream/develop_jetstream.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/jetstream/develop_jetstream
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [STRM][SIZE][ANTI] "Using streaming and its associated higher qualities of service is the facet of messaging with the highest cost in terms of compute and storage."
- [STRM][USECASE] Streaming is ideal when: producers/consumers are highly decoupled and may be online at different times; a historical record/replay is required; the last message is needed for initialization while the producer may be offline; consumers are unknown a priori "This is often a false assumption"; data outlives the application; consumers need their own pace; decoupled flow control; exactly-once.
- [STRM][ANTI] "no assumptions should ever be made of who will receive and process data in the future, or for what purpose."
- [CORE][USECASE] Core NATS is ideal as "the fast request path for scalable services where there is tolerance for message loss or when applications themselves handle message delivery guarantees": tightly coupled request-reply with app-handled timeouts; last-value-only data with frequent updates (stock ticker, control plane, telemetry); low message TTL; consumer set known and live; control plane messages.
- [CORE][ANTI] For request-reply, "Relying on a messaging system to resend here is considered an anti-pattern."
- [STRM][MYTH] Core publish to a stream subject is stored, "but that's not really the intent ... look at it more as a convenience that you can use to help ease the migration ... rather the desired end state or ideal design."
- [STRM][CLNT] JetStream publish acks mean the publisher "can safely discard any state it has for that publication"; sync and async both imply flow control; exactly-once needs a unique publication ID header.
- [CONS][PATTERN][STALE?] "Push consumers (specifically ordered push consumers) are the best way for an application to receive its own complete copy"; "Pull consumers are the best way to scale horizontally ... and allow for the processing of messages in batches."
- [CONS] Ack kinds: Ack, Nak (retried), InProgress (extends by another AckWait), Term (stop redelivery without success).
- [CLNT] Newer clients have "a more ergonomic API to work with Consumers" than the original Subscribe/QueueSubscribe/PullSubscribe calls.

## JetStream Concepts (functionalities)
- path: using-nats/jetstream/concepts/README.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/jetstream/concepts
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [STRM][PATTERN] Retention: `WorkQueue` deletes as consumed; `Limits` provides on-demand individual or distributed replay from the beginning or a point in time.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Mirror/source topology example: a short-retention capture stream feeds "any number of other streams configured for message consumption in a queue" so consumers work "without impacting that original stream and at their own pace."
- [CORE][MYTH] Core NATS message-loss scenarios: disconnections long enough to drop/reset TCP lose buffered messages; slow consumers get their connection reset and buffer purged; "from the client application's point of view it simply looks like the application experienced temporary server disconnection".
- [STRM] JetStream at-least-once/exactly-once make clients "automatically recover from getting disconnected ... without any message loss"; for slow consumers "the 'buffering' of the messages ... happen in a stream (which can be much larger than a server buffer)".
- [CORE][MYTH] Core NATS "does not implement any kind of end-to-end flow control" because 1-to-N flow control would throttle publishers "to the lowest common denominator of all the current subscribers" and pub/sub is for real-time distribution. You could build it with request-reply but JetStream's decoupled flow control is "much easier (and better)".

## JetStream Model Deep Dive
- path: using-nats/jetstream/model_deep_dive.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/jetstream/model_deep_dive
- version context: 2020 CLI output; AckFlowControl 2.14

### Claims
- [STRM][CONS] WorkQueuePolicy: "you can not have any overlapping consumers defined on the Stream - each subject captured by the stream can only have one consumer at a time".
- [STRM] MaxMsgs/MaxBytes/MaxAge "apply as upper bounds" in every retention policy; WorkQueue removes on ack by the consumer, Interest when all consumers for the subject acked.
- [STRM][SIZE] `MaxMsgSize` can cap stream messages below the server's 1 MiB default (e.g. 1024 bytes).
- [STRM] Dedup via `Nats-Msg-Id` consults "only the message ID not the body"; default window 2 minutes; "we would caution against large windows."
- [STRM] Stream publish acks only for `Request()`; `NoAck: true` disables stream acks.
- [CONS] Ack modes: AckExplicit ("the only supported option for pull-based Consumers"), AckAll ("good for processing batches and to reduce ack overhead"), AckNone, AckFlowControl (2.14).
- [CONS] Consumer sequence increments on every delivery attempt; ack floor stays at the last acked; Pending and Redelivered counts show unacked/redelivered messages.
- [CONS] Ack protocol bodies: `+ACK`/nil, `-NAK`, `+WPI` (progress, extends by AckWait), `+NXT` (pull only; `+NXT 10`, `+NXT {"no_wait": true}`), `+TERM`. All except `+NXT` support double ack via a reply subject.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Exactly-once consumption: `AckSync()` sets a reply subject on the ack and waits; on success "you can be sure that the message will never be re-delivered by the consumer (due to a loss of your acknowledgement)."
- [CONS][MYTH] DeliverPolicy "is only the starting point. Once started it will always give you what you have not seen or acknowledged."
- [CONS] Ephemeral consumer "exists as long as any subscription is active on its delivery subject" and is removed "after a short grace period to handle restarts" [STALE? push-only description].
- [CONS][STALE?] "You can only set ReplayPolicy on push-based Consumers" (contradicts nats-concepts/jetstream/consumers.md which lists ReplayPolicy as a general option).
- [OPS] Ack sampling (`--sample 80`) publishes redelivery counts and ack latency for monitoring; planned for NATS Surveyor.
- [STRM][SIZE] File storage per-message overhead without headers: record length 4 + seq 8 + ts 8 + subj_len 2 + subject + payload + hash 8; "A 5 byte hello message without headers will take 39 bytes." With headers add hdr_len 4 + headers.
- [STRM][SIZE][PATTERN] "if you are publishing many small messages the overhead will be, relatively speaking, quite large ... it's worth trying to optimize the subject length."

- [STRM][PATTERN] Streams and durable consumers "can be defined administratively outside the application ... in which case the application only needs to know about the well-known names of the durable consumers".

## JetStream Consumers (developer guide)
- path: using-nats/developing-with-nats/js/consumers.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/developing-with-nats/js/consumers
- version context: mixes legacy js.Subscribe API and newer API

### Claims
- [CONS] Durable consumers persist delivery progress server-side, can be shared for load balancing, and "can be made highly available through replicas"; ephemeral consumers are deleted when no client instances remain.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Durables "are typically created and deleted administratively rather than by the application code, which only needs to specify the durable consumer's well-known name".
- [CONS] Ephemeral consumers are for a single instance's own replay; `Drain()` on the subscription deletes the underlying ephemeral consumer.
- [CONS] Push consumers: server-controlled flow, load balancing via core queue groups. Pull consumers: explicit batch requests, "giving the client full control over dispatching, flow control, pending (unacknowledged) messages and load balancing."
- [CONS] "We recommend using pull consumers for new projects. In particular when scalability, detailed flow control or error handling are a design focus."
- [CONS][SIZE] "Pull consumers create less CPU load on the NATS servers and therefore scale better"; the difference shows "if you have sustained high message rates."
- [CONS] Ordered consumers: ephemeral, single-threaded in-sequence dispatch, client checks sequence to prevent gaps, recovers from server failure but not client failure.
- [CONS] AckWait timer starts on delivery, is deleted on Ack or Term, reset on inProgress; on expiry the message is redelivered and "there is no guarantee that the re-delivery would be to any particular client instance."
- [CONS] Redelivery timing: `AckWait` or `BackOff` (overrides AckWait); `NakWithDelay()` for delayed nak, else immediate.
- [CONS][PATTERN] "Dead Letter Queue" functionality: use `MaxDeliver`; advisories `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<STREAM>.<CONSUMER>` and `...MSG_TERMINATED...` carry `stream_seq`; fetch the message by sequence if needed. "If a message reaches its maximum level of delivery attempts, it will still stay in the stream until it is manually deleted or manually acknowledged."

## NATS API Reference (JetStream wire API)
- path: using-nats/jetstream/nats_api_reference.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/jetstream/nats_api_reference
- version context: consumer-based sourcing 2.14; CreateEx 2.9+

### Claims
- [STRM][TOPO] JetStream is a set of services over core NATS; with a domain the API prefix is `$JS.{domain}.API`.
- [OPS] Admin APIs respond with typed JSON (`type` -> JSON Schema in nats-io/jsm.go/schemas); `nats events` shows an API audit log; `$JS.API.STREAM.MSG.DELETE.*` is "useful for GDPR compliance".
- [SEC][STRM] Subject patterns are designed so ACLs can "limit users to a specific Stream or Consumer and to specific verbs"; response permissions ensure only the receiver of a message can Ack it.
- [SEC][STRM] Classic source/mirror uses 5 subjects: `$JS.API.CONSUMER.CREATE.<stream>[.<consumer>.<filter>]` (outbound), `$JS.FC.<stream>.>` (outbound), `$JSC.R.<uid>` (inbound reply), `$JS.S.<uid>`/`$JS.M.<uid>`/custom deliver (inbound). "all 5 subjects may need to be considered" for permissions/imports.
- [STRM][ANTI] "If this subject [`$JS.FC.<stream>.>`] is not forwarded, the consumer my stall under high load." If `$JS.ACK.<stream>.>` is not forwarded, pull consumers with ack `all`/`explicit` fail.
- [STRM][SIZE] Source/mirror retries consumer creation "every 10s to 60s" when the origin is unreachable; active consumers heartbeat at 1/s.
- [STRM][ANTI] "Do not delete and recreate the original stream! Please flush/purge the stream instead. The target stream remembers the last sequence id to be delivered. A delete will reset the sequence ID."
- [STRM][ANTI][SUBJ] `$JS.FC` is not domain-prefixed, so "identically named streams in different domains cannot be reliably sourced/mirrored into the same account. Please create unique stream names".
- [STRM] 2.14 consumer-based sourcing: origin consumer must be `flow_control` type, supports WorkQueue/Interest streams; "It is strongly recommended ... pre-creating consumers"; auto-creation exists for backwards compatibility but "Please avoid relying on this feature." Uses `$JS.API.CONSUMER.RESET`.
- [CONS] Ack reply subject format: `$JS.ACK.<stream>.<consumer>.<delivered count>.<stream sequence>.<consumer sequence>.<timestamp>.<pending messages>`.
- [CONS][ANTI] Flow control messages (`NATS/1.0 100 FlowControl Request`) "must be replied to, otherwise the consumer may stall"; Synadia clients handle it (`msg.Respond(nil)`).
- [CONS][MYTH] Plain pull requests accumulate on the server while the client is connected: "if you ask for 1 message 100 times and 1000 messages arrive you'll get sent 100 messages not 1." Use `{"expires": ns, "batch": n}` ("Set the expire time to now + your poll frequency") or `{"batch": n, "no_wait": true}` (404 status when empty, 409 when MaxAckPending reached).
- [CONS] Batch pulls "combine well with the AckAll Ack policy."
- [CONS] `$JS.API.CONSUMER.RESET` resets a consumer to a sequence/timestamp or original start; "The effective reset floor will never be earlier than the one set when the consumer was created." `CONSUMER.PAUSE` pauses until a timestamp.

## nats bench (benchmarking guide)
- path: using-nats/nats-tools/nats_cli/natsbench.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/nats-tools/nats_cli/natsbench
- version context: nats-server 2.12.1 on MacBook Pro M4 (numbers are illustrative)

### Claims
- [SIZE][CORE] Example numbers (single laptop, 2.12.1): core publish with no subscriber 14.8M msgs/s at 16 bytes; sync request-reply latency ~50.87 microseconds; larger messages lower msg/s but raise byte throughput.
- [PATTERN] To measure service throughput, run several synchronous requesters and several service instances load-balanced via queue groups "as you would in production".
- [STRM][SIZE][PATTERN] `nats bench js pub sync` is for latency, "not good to measure throughput"; `async` batches with acks measures throughput; `batch` (atomic) "has the side effect of potentially helping throughout, especially for smaller messages."
- [STRM][MYTH] "by default JetStream flushes disk writes synchronously, meaning that even if the nats-server process is killed suddenly no messages will be lost as the OS already has them in it's buffer"; only a whole-host crash needs sync-after-every-write (at a latency cost). `--persistasync` on R1 gives memory-like throughput.
- [CONS][SIZE] Example replay: ordered ephemeral consumer 1.2M msgs/s (128 B); durable fetch with 2 clients 1.13M msgs/s aggregate; sync direct get ~33k/s at ~30 microseconds; KV put ~30k/s, KV get 16 clients ~103k/s aggregate.
- [OPS][ANTI] Benchmarks can fill streams quickly; purge or delete `benchstream` afterwards to reclaim memory and files. Changing stream attributes between runs requires deleting the stream.
- [OPS] `--sleep` turns `nats bench` into a steady-rate traffic generator or simulates processing time.

## nsc (basics, streams, services, signing keys, revocation, managed operators), NATS tools overview
- path: using-nats/nats-tools/nsc/*.md, using-nats/nats-tools/README.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/using-nats/nats-tools/nsc
- version context: nsc 2.2.0 note; template functions 2.9.0

### Claims
- [SEC] Hierarchy: Operators run servers and issue account JWTs and set account limits (connections, data); Accounts issue user JWTs and define exports/imports; Users encode limits and authorization over the account's subject space.
- [SEC][OPS] nsc directories: `~/.nsc` home, `~/.nkeys` (private keys and creds; "should be treated as secrets"), stores in `$NSC_HOME/nats` ("can stored under revision control. The JWTs themselves do not contain any secrets").
- [SEC][PATTERN] Stream exports forward messages published on the exported subject to importers; stream imports can be prefixed with `--local-subject`; "Self-imports are not valid".
- [SEC][OPS] With the built-in NATS resolver you must `nsc push` local account changes for them to take effect.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Private exports (`--private`) require an activation token (a JWT signed by the exporting account) per importing account; the token can also "subset the exported stream's subject" and be hosted at a stable URL so updates propagate.
- [SEC] Service import: local subject may differ; the request is forwarded on the remote subject.
- [SEC][ANTI] "if someone gets a hold of an account or operator nkey they can do everything you can do as you."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Signing keys are "the first and most important line of defense": a JWT is valid if signed by the issuer's subject or one of its signing keys, so the operator/account identity key can be guarded more closely. On compromise: remove the signing key, reissue the entity, and reissue every JWT it signed ("effectively a large hammer"); mitigate by having many signing keys and rotating them.
- [SEC][OPS] "On a production environment private keys should be saved to a file and always referenced from the secured file." nsc doesn't track private signing keys; you must manage them.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Scoped signing keys attach a permission set to a signing key; users signed with it "must not have any permissions assigned"; updating the key's permissions "will immediately update permissions for users signed with that key."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Template functions (2.9.0) `{{name()}}`, `{{subject()}}`, `{{account-name()}}`, `{{account-subject()}}`, `{{tag(key)}}` give per-user subjects (e.g. `pam.>`) from one scoped key.
- [SEC] Revocations live in the account JWT; users are revoked by public key and time, activations per account and time: JWTs issued before T are invalid, later ones valid, so you can "revoke a user and renew their access at the same time." Deleting a revocation is permanent and should only happen if the tokens expired. Pushing a revocation immediately terminates matching connections.
- [SEC][OPS] Managed operators (e.g. NGS) hold the operator key; they may add limits or imports to your account JWT ("the operator gets the final call on all Account edits"); `nsc push`/`pull` keep local and server JWTs in sync.
- [SEC][OPS] "most should use the NATS account resolver built-in to 'nats-server'"; nats-account-server is "legacy, replaced by the built-in NATS resolver" but usable as a reference implementation; nsc "is the preferred tools to create security configuration unless you are using Synadia Control Plane."

## In Depth JWT Guide
- path: running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/jwt.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/running-a-nats-service/nats_admin/jwt
- version context: unstated (references nats-account-server as legacy)

### Claims
- [SEC][PATTERN] Motivation: "Accounts do NOT correspond to infrastructure, they correspond to teams or applications." "Infrastructure and its topology have nothing to do with Accounts and where an Account's User connects from." Users of one account can connect anywhere in the same authentication domain.
- [SEC] Operator = "operator of a set of NATS servers in the same authentication domain (entire topology, crossing gateways and leaf nodes)".
- [SEC][MYTH] JWT names "are only used by tooling, nats-server does not read this value"; names may collide, so keep them unique in nsc. "JWT content can be viewed as public, although it's content may reveal which subjects/limits/permissions exist."
- [SEC] Clients present only the User JWT; the server fetches the Account JWT itself and verifies the three-level chain. Changing the operator JWT needs a restart or reload.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Resolver choice: mem-resolver for "Very few or very static accounts"; url-resolver for "Very large volume of accounts" (needs a web server, nats-account-server legacy); nats-resolver = same over NATS, "No separate binary", "Easier clustering", needs an exclusive directory per server ("it can be on a shared Network File System, but the directories themselves can not be shared"). "Between nats-resolver and url-resolver, the nats-resolver is the clear recommendation." "JWT nats-resolver is recommended to use in production".
- [SEC][PATTERN] Deployment models: centralized (admins hold all keys); decentralized (admins hold operator keys and enforce limits by signing accounts; teams hold account keys and issue users); self-service (teams also hold an operator signing key; "there should be at least one organizational mechanism to prevent unchecked usage"); mixed. "pick the simplest deployment model that enables what you need ... NOT the most complicated one".
- [SEC][PATTERN] "Our official suggestion is to scope accounts by application/service"; accounts "can be arbitrarily scoped, from Application to Team".
- [SEC] User JWTs depend only on the issuing Account NKEY, not on a particular Account JWT version; a newer Account JWT causes existing connections to be re-evaluated.
- [SEC][ANTI] NKEY backups "should therefore best be offline and access to them should be severely restricted"; identity NKEYs "should be archived and then removed" from the nsc store once signing keys exist, so a breach doesn't force "a flag-day change-over of identities."
- [SEC][OPS] JWT store directory contains no private keys and may go in git, but restoring an old version may undo revocations and restore expired JWTs; keep NKEYs in tandem.
- [SEC][PATTERN] "We always recommend using signing keys for an operator" and likewise for accounts; nsc never updates the operator installed on servers automatically.
- [SEC][OPS][ANTI] After `nsc push`, if fewer servers respond than exist "it is best practice to resolve this issue and retry"; if only one server holds a new account and dies, "the pushed account is not available to the network at large" so "make sure that initially, more servers respond than what you are comfortable with losing".
- [SEC][PATTERN] Exchange only public NKEYs when generating users for another entity (`nsc generate nkey -u` without `--store`, then `nsc add user -k <pub>`).
- [SEC][PATTERN] Automated sign-up services: use NKEY+JWT libraries; "Dynamically provision user and integrate that process with your existing infrastructure, say LDAP, is the most common use case"; signing keys "highly recommended". "it becomes YOUR RESPONSIBILITY to properly authenticate incoming requests"; "For sign up service issued JWTs, ALWAYS set the SHORTEST POSSIBLE EXPIRATION".
- [SEC][ANTI] Sign-up requestor credentials: "Do not use this JWT/NKEY for anything else but contacting the sign up service"; allow publish only to the well-known subject; back up the account signing NKEY so requestors need not be replaced.
- [SEC][ANTI] System account: "It is NOT recommended to use this account to facilitate communication between your own applications. Its sole purpose is to facilitate communication with and between nats-server."
- [OPS][MYTH] System events: "you MUST NOT rely on a particular ordering or due to the possibility of loss, events matching" (a CONNECT may not have a matching DISCONNECT); periodic aggregate messages compensate for misses. Prefer `$SYS.ACCOUNT.<id>.SERVER.CONNS` over the old `$SYS.SERVER.ACCOUNT.<id>.CONNS`.
- [TOPO][SEC][MYTH] "leaf nodes do not multiplex between accounts. Every account that you wish to connect across a leaf node connection needs to be explicitly listed." The system account is not connected automatically even when both sides share it; add it as a separate `remote` with heavily restricted credentials, also when only needed for the NATS resolver or centralized monitoring.
- [SEC][OPS] `nsc generate diagram component` produces a plantuml diagram of account import/export relationships.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Key importance: operator keys > account keys; identity keys > signing keys. For huge deployments (IoT) where regenerating identities is infeasible, back up identity keys offline and use exchangeable signing keys; "prepare and try this out beforehand and not wait until disaster strikes."
- [SEC][OPS] Identity NKEY is the only key that can add/remove signing keys, so create signing keys before taking the identity key offline; delete user keys/creds from nsc after distribution.
- [SEC][PATTERN] "for user NKEYs and JWT, generating and distributing new ones to affected applications is the best option" when compromised.

## Legacy: NATS Streaming (STAN) and nats-account-server
- path: legacy/stan/README.md, legacy/stan/nats-streaming-concepts/relation-to-nats.md, legacy/stan/nats-streaming-concepts/clustering/README.md, legacy/nas/README.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/legacy/stan
- version context: deprecated; fixes until June 2023 [STALE]

### Claims
- [MIG][STALE] "The NATS Streaming Server is being deprecated. Critical bug fixes and security fixes will be applied until June of 2023." Persistence users should use JetStream.
- [MIG][MYTH][STALE] STAN is a client of a NATS server, not a server; NATS clients and STAN clients cannot exchange messages on the same subject (STAN payloads are protobuf with acks). Clients must close connections explicitly or the server keeps them until heartbeats fail.
- [MIG][SIZE][STALE] STAN clustering is not horizontally scalable (single leader); "The cluster size should probably be limited to 3 to 5 nodes"; odd number, minimum three "to avoid split-brain".
- [SEC][STALE] nats-account-server: "If you are creating a new NATS deployment we highly recommend using the internal NATS Resolver"; it remains "a good reference to build upon for custom account resolution" and also speaks the NATS resolver protocol.

## Coverage

**Repo state:** nats-io/nats.docs main @ f115becf (2026-08-24), 240 markdown files total in the five priority trees (nats-concepts 30, running-a-nats-service 78, using-nats 69, reference 7, legacy 56).

**Files read in full (169):** all 30 of nats-concepts/; 73 of running-a-nats-service/ (everything under configuration/, nats_admin/, running/nats_docker README + jetstream_docker + ngs-leafnodes, installation, environment, clients, introduction, nats-on-kubernetes); 64 of using-nats/ (all developing-with-nats/ pages read as prose with code tabs stripped, all jetstream/ pages, nsc/*, natsbench, nk); reference/faq.md and reference/roadmap.md.

**Files skimmed via grep only (16):** running-a-nats-service/running/flags.md, windows_srv.md, nats_docker/docker_swarm.md, nats-docker-tutorial.md, ngs-docker-python.md (pure CLI/tutorial content); using-nats/developing-with-nats/js/publish.md (only code tabs), tutorials/README.md, nats-tools/nats_cli/README.md, nats_top/README.md, nats_top/nats-top-tutorial.md (tool usage); reference/nats-protocol/nats-protocol/README.md and nats-client-dev.md, nats-server-protocol.md (protocol listings; grep'd for guidance); legacy/stan/README.md, legacy/stan/nats-streaming-concepts/relation-to-nats.md, clustering/README.md, legacy/nas/README.md (only the deprecation/migration statements captured).

**Files skipped (55):** reference/contributing.md, reference/nats-protocol/nats-protocol-demo.md (no design guidance); 52 remaining legacy/stan and legacy/nas pages (deprecated NATS Streaming and standalone account server configuration; no current design guidance).

**Total claims:** 794 across 108 page sections.

**Contradictions recorded between pages:**
- Replication factor: nats-concepts/jetstream/README.md says "Replication (1 (none), 2, 3)" in one list but "R=5, the replication factor limit" later on the same page; streams.md says maximum 5.
- Consumer MaxAckPending default: 1,000 (nats-concepts/jetstream/consumers.md, js_walkthrough.md) vs 20,000 shown in 2021 CLI output in leafnodes/jetstream_leafnodes.md.
- write_deadline default: 10s (configuration/README.md) vs 2s in the 2019 /varz sample (nats_admin/monitoring/README.md); tls timeout 2s (tls.md) vs 0.5 in that same sample.
- ReplayPolicy: "only on push-based Consumers" (using-nats/jetstream/model_deep_dive.md) vs general consumer option (nats-concepts/jetstream/consumers.md).
- Push-consumer guidance ("ordered push consumer is best for own replay", "durable push with queue group for low latency") in faq.md, develop_jetstream.md, anatomy.md vs "We recommend pull consumers for new projects" in consumers.md (both nats-concepts and js/consumers.md).

**10 most important claims for someone designing a large NATS system:**
1. Replica guidance: R=1 no fault tolerance, R=2 "No significant benefit ... We recommend using Replicas=3 instead", R=3 ideal balance, R=4 marginal, R=5 max; pick per use case rather than defaulting to max (nats-concepts/jetstream/README.md).
2. Durability model: file streams fsync every `sync_interval` (default 2m); replication is the primary durability mechanism; `sync_interval: always` costs "a few hundred msg/s"; hybrid pattern of a `sync:always` tagged cluster with placement tags; avoid NAS/NFS and shared store directories (nats-concepts/jetstream/README.md, configuration/README.md).
3. Cluster sizing and placement: recommend 3 or 5 JetStream servers per cluster, 2+2+1 across zones, quorum = 1/2 N + 1, `unique_tag` for AZ spreading, mixing JetStream and non-JetStream servers is recommended for cost; production JetStream start at 4 cores / 8 GiB (jetstream_clustering/README.md, installation.md).
4. Stream leader bottleneck and partitioning: one RAFT leader per stream limits ingest, so partition subjects deterministically (`partition(n, ...)`) into multiple streams and consumers to keep per-subject ordering while scaling (nats-concepts/subject_mapping.md).
5. Retention semantics: limits always apply on top of WorkQueue/Interest; Interest streams with no consumers drop messages immediately; WorkQueue needs non-overlapping consumer filters; MaxDeliver-exhausted messages stay in the stream and must be deleted manually (streams.md, model_deep_dive.md).
6. Consumer choice: pull consumers recommended for new projects, shared like queue groups, less server CPU; MaxAckPending is the only flow control for push; tune MaxAckPending high for throughput and low with longer AckWait for slow external calls (consumers.md).
7. Topology rules: gateways need the same name on all cluster servers and full reachability; leaf nodes bind one account per remote and do not multiplex accounts (system account needs its own remote); domains must be uniform within a cluster/super-cluster and only change across leaf links; source/mirror is "the recommended way to exchange persistent data across domains" (gateways, leafnodes, jetstream_leafnodes, jwt.md).
8. Security design: accounts scope to applications/teams, not infrastructure; "more accounts with few (even one) clients is a better design"; use signing keys for operator and account, keep identity keys offline; nats-resolver in production; system account only for server communication; `allow_responses` bypasses publish deny lists (accounts.md, jwt.md, authorization.md).
9. Core NATS limits and defaults: max_payload 1MB (recommend <= 8MB, max 64MB), max_pending 64MB, max_connections 64K, ping 2m/2, write_deadline 10s; slow consumers are disconnected to protect the server; >1M subscriptions needs >1GB RAM growing linearly; subject tokens <= 16 and length < 256 recommended (configuration/README.md, subjects.md, slow_consumers.md).
10. Operations: rolling upgrade one node at a time via lame duck mode + `/healthz` 200; LDM default 2m eviction mitigates thundering herd; clients must use reconnect jitter; no load balancers in front of routes/gateways; JetStream API drops requests past 10K in-flight (`request_queue_limit`) and `max_ha_assets` caps R3/R5 assets per server (upgrading_cluster.md, lame_duck_mode.md, environment.md, resource_management.md).

# Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design)

Local clone: /Users/tomaszpietrek/coding/nats-architecture-and-design (HEAD 279548d, 2026-08-27 "Merge pull request #427 from nats-io/maurice/desired-state").
Repo README states purpose: "captures Architecture, Design Specifications and Feature Guidance for the NATS ecosystem."
