# Source class: Blog posts and articles

## JetStream Anti-Patterns: Avoid these pitfalls to scale more efficiently
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/jetstream-design-patterns-for-scale
- author: Andrew Connolly | date: 2026-06-06 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.10 (multiple filter subjects), 2.11 (batch direct get)

### Claims
- [CONS][ANTI][OPS] Consumer info is a monitoring/debugging call, not for operational decision-making. "intended to provide insights for monitoring or debugging"
- [CONS][OPS] Consumer info requests go to the meta-leader and involve expensive state calculation; repeated calls "become very expensive across ten of thousands of clients."
- [CONS][PATTERN] Consumer create is idempotent: if a consumer with matching config exists the call succeeds without change; if configs differ it updates, unless a non-editable field (e.g., start sequence) is changed. Use create instead of info to check existence.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Get pending counts from message metadata rather than consumer info.
- [CONS][SIZE][ANTI] "Beyond 100,000 consumers, the potential for issues increases significantly." Consumers cost state management and cluster replication (Raft traffic, meta-leader load).
- [CONS][MYTH] "Too many consumers" often reflects "overstated persistence and delivery guarantee requirements."
- [STRM][PATTERN] Republish combines core NATS and JetStream: "ideal for use cases where subscribers can handle messages in real time and do not require strict delivery guarantees"; gives filtering without consumer state.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Direct Get API is "even faster and more lightweight than consumers, making it ideal for getting specific messages from streams"; suited for mobile/IoT fetching latest data per subject. Batch Get (2.11) returns multiple messages across multiple subject filters.
- [CONS][SIZE][ANTI] Multiple disjoint subject filters per consumer arrived in 2.10, but "More than a few hundred disjoint subject filters will likely lead to slowness and instability." Cost: more subject indexing/matching and scanning more message blocks.
- [CONS][SUBJ][PATTERN] Alternatives to many disjoint filters: split into separate consumers each with fewer filters, or "re-evaluate your subject name hierarchy so you can better leverage wildcard filters."
- [OPS] "There is no single ideal configuration"; anti-patterns are easier to enumerate than universal scaling patterns.

## How to Design NATS Subject Hierarchies (Patterns, Pitfalls & Best Practices)
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/designing-nats-subject-hierarchies
- author: Andrew Connolly | date: 2026-06-17 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [SUBJ] Subject design is the most expensive decision to reverse: "Publishers and subscribers both encode your subject schema into their code; changing it later means coordinating every service."
- [SUBJ] Subjects are case-sensitive, dot-separated tokens; "Orders.Created" and "orders.created" are different subjects. Tokens should be lowercase alphanumeric with hyphens, not underscores.
- [SUBJ] `*` matches exactly one token; `>` matches one or more and must be last. Wildcards are valid in subscriptions and server-side mappings, never in publishes.
- [SUBJ][SIZE] Practical guidance: at or below 16 tokens and 256 characters per subject.
- [SUBJ][SIZE] The subscription matcher uses a stack-allocated array sized for 32 tokens; "beyond that, matching spills to the heap and pays a small per-message allocation cost." Exceeding is a soft cliff, not a rejection.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Three patterns: namespace-first `{namespace}.{entity}.{action}` (service-oriented, team-owned domains); identifier-first `{identifier}.{namespace}.{action}` (per-tenant, per-entity audit); multi-dimensional `{env}.{region}.{service}.{entity}.{action}` (only with genuine routing dependencies).
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] "If two patterns look equally good, default to namespace-first." A tenant token can be prepended later; identifier-first "cannot easily un-prepend one."
- [SUBJ][ANTI] Multi-dimensional patterns are "powerful but expensive"; don't adopt speculatively.
- [SUBJ] Reserved prefixes: `$SYS.`, `$JS.`, `$JSC.`, `$KV.`, `$OBJ.`, `$NRG.`, `_INBOX.`. Never publish to `$`/`_` prefixes; subscribing to `$SYS.>` for monitoring is fine.
- [SUBJ][ANTI] Never put high-cardinality per-message data (correlation IDs, request IDs) in subjects; it burns the subject cache. "The right place for a correlation ID is a message header."
- [SUBJ][ANTI] Don't reuse `Nats-Msg-Id` as a correlation header; JetStream reserves it for dedup.
- [SUBJ] Entity IDs as tokens are fine: `customer-123` is "bounded by your customer count."
- [STRM][SUBJ][PATTERN] One stream per top-level namespace is the common default; splitting at namespace boundaries avoids coupling retention and storage budgets.
- [STRM][SIZE] JetStream subject-detail listings cap at 100,000 subject entries per request; high-cardinality schemas make them "unusable."
- [SEC][SUBJ] "your subject hierarchy is your authorization model"; there is no separate ACL layer. Namespace-first gives team-aligned permissions; identifier-first gives tenant-aligned permissions.
- [SEC][SUBJ][PATTERN] Hard multi-tenant isolation = "identifier-first subjects combined with separate NATS Accounts."
- [SUBJ][ANTI] Anti-patterns: flat subjects (no wildcards, no clean permissions, no filters); payload data in subjects; inconsistent casing/separators; no evolution plan. "Schemas change. If you haven't decided how, you've decided to break things."
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Routing-affecting version changes go in the subject (`orders.v1.customer.created`) so v1 and v2 subscribers run side by side; payload-only schema changes can use headers. Counter-position (header-only versioning) avoids subject churn but loses routing clarity.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Server-side subject mappings allow parallel publisher/subscriber migration; "they're the one place wildcards appear on the publish side."
- [SUBJ][OPS] Schema evolution order: stream filters, then consumer filters, then permissions; skipping any "turns migrations into incidents."

## Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS JetStream: Ordered, Scalable Processing
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/partitioned-consumer-groups
- author: Peter Humulock | date: 2026-07-15 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.10 (deterministic subject partitioning), 2.11+ (pinned_client priority groups; required by pcgroups)

### Claims
- [CONS][PATTERN] Most workloads need ordering only among related keys (customer/account/device), not across the whole stream. Standard consumers load-balance and break per-key order.
- [CONS][ANTI] `max_ack_pending = 1` restores strict order but serializes the whole stream: no throughput, single point of failure.
- [CONS][MIG] Design mirrors Kafka consumer groups: "Split the stream into buckets by key, assign each bucket to exactly one worker, and you get ordering within a bucket while running many buckets in parallel."
- [SUBJ][CONS] Partitioning uses the `{{partition(N, token...)}}` mapping function: "an FNV-1a 32-bit hash modulo the partition count", prepended as a leading token; same key always lands in the same partition.
- [CONS] With `pinned_client`, delivered messages carry `Nats-Pin-Id`; the client must echo it on every pull; a mismatch is rejected with status 423. After `PinnedTTL` silence or unpin, the server re-pins a standby: failover "with no external leader-election."
- [CONS][SIZE] Effective parallelism = `min(partitions, members)`. Partition count is fixed at creation and immutable; members are cheap to add/remove up to that ceiling. A 5th member on 4 partitions idles as standby.
- [CONS][ANTI] A member drains all its partitions serially through one consumer; "piling more partitions onto a member is parked ownership, not added throughput."
- [CONS][PATTERN] Static flavor: consumers directly on a partition-stamped stream, durable `<group>-<member>`, frozen membership; lower latency, fewer server resources, any ack policy.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Elastic flavor: sources the origin stream into a hidden work-queue stream `<stream>-<group>` with partitioning applied during copy; live membership changes via KV config watched by members; requires explicit ack.
- [CONS] Neither flavor changes partition count live; both require delete and recreate. Elastic = "elastic members over a fixed number of partitions."
- [CONS][ANTI][MYTH] Pinning is affinity plus failover, not a distributed lock; windows exist where a client believes it is pinned after the server re-pinned, and buffered messages cannot be revoked. Handlers must be idempotent.
- [CONS][SIZE][ANTI] Size partitions for peak future parallelism; raising later requires deleting the group and re-hashing every key.
- [CONS][SIZE][ANTI] Cap the elastic work-queue buffer above one second of throughput; hitting `max_buffered_msgs`/`max_buffered_bytes` pauses sourcing for at least a second, causing periodic stalls.
- [SUBJ][SEC] `{{partition(...)}}` "cannot cross accounts"; only `{{wildcard(x)}}` is allowed in inter-account import transforms.
- [CONS][PATTERN] For a hot key at 10x volume, hand-assign partitions so that key gets its own member.
- [CONS][USECASE] Use cases: ordered per-key processing at scale; single-active-worker with hot standby replacing leader-election machinery.

## Pull Consumer Priority Groups in NATS JetStream: Overflow, Pinned, and Prioritized Routing
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/pull-consumer-priority-groups
- author: Peter Humulock | date: 2026-06-22 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.11 (overflow, pinned_client), 2.12 (prioritized); nats.go v1.41.0+ / v1.46.0+

### Claims
- [CONS] "Pull consumer priority groups, introduced in NATS Server 2.11, add a routing layer directly to the consumer." Server-side policy replaces round-robin; "no leader election, no external lock, and no coordination code."
- [CONS] Pull-only; requires explicit ack policy (shipped validation does not currently reject other ack policies); rejected on push consumers. Exactly one priority group per consumer today; group names capped at 16 characters from a restricted alphabet.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Overflow policy serves a pull only when backlog crosses a threshold: "num_pending ... is at least min_pending, or num_ack_pending ... is at least min_pending." Designed for latency/cost-aware regional routing: local workers drain first; remote workers wake past the threshold.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Pinned client: one designated client gets all messages; others stand by. `PinnedTTL` defaults to 2 minutes (wire 0 = default). Advisories `consumer_group_pinned` and `consumer_group_unpinned` (reason admin or timeout) are published on every change.
- [CONS][OPS] Operators can force a hand-off with `nats consumer unpin <stream> <consumer> <group>` for clean deployment rotation.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Prioritized (2.12+) serves pulls by priority 0-9 (lower first); secondary pool picks up immediately when primary is not pulling. Trade-off: "some flip-flopping, where work bounces between clients more readily because there is no deliberate threshold."
- [CONS][ANTI][MYTH] Pinning is "not a hard guarantee"; an old client may believe it's pinned after the server moved on. Handler "must be idempotent."
- [CONS][MYTH] Fetch(N) is not an atomic reservation; the server may spread N messages across concurrent pulls.
- [CONS][OPS] Keep priority_timeout comfortably above pull expires; the 2-minute default pairs with pulls expiring in one minute or less. A 423 `Nats-Pin-Id` mismatch means clear the id and re-pull without one.
- [CLNT] `priority_policy` fields exist across Python, Rust, JS, Java, .NET, C clients.
- [CONS][USECASE] Use cases: active/standby exclusive processing; regional routing; tiered worker pools stacked by priority for zero-delay escalation.

## Mirror, Merge, or Consume: How to Choose Your Edge-to-Core Streaming Pattern
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/nats-edge-event-architecture-8-mirror-merge-or-consume
- author: Bruno Baloi | date: 2026-05-18 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Consume, mirror, and merge (source) "represent three different relationships between producers and consumers, with different tradeoffs"; teams "default to whichever pattern is easiest" and then "spend months working around its limitations."
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Consume: a core consumer reads an edge stream directly and selectively; puts "the selection logic where it belongs: at the consumer, at the point of ingest." Dependency: "A consumer pulling directly from an edge stream depends on the edge node being reachable."
- [STRM][TOPO] Mirror "creates an exact 1:1 replica of an edge stream in the core. Sequence numbers are preserved"; catches up automatically after reconnect; "clients cannot write to a mirror directly. It is read-only by design."
- [STRM][USECASE] Mirror for compliance/audit, backup/DR, distributing read load, consumers needing the complete unaltered sequence. "Consume applies logic and filters. Mirror preserves everything."
- [STRM][ANTI] Mirror is a full-copy operation: storage "scale[s] with edge volume rather than with actual consumption."
- [STRM][TOPO] Merge (sourcing) aggregates multiple edge streams into one core stream; "A sourced stream does not preserve origin sequence numbers — messages from different sources are interleaved"; per-source ordering is preserved, global ordering is not.
- [STRM][SUBJ] Subject transforms in the source configuration normalize edge naming into a global taxonomy; "the normalization lives in topology."
- [STRM][ANTI] Most common failure: "defaulting to mirror when consume would be more appropriate, because mirror feels safer." Result: a firehose where "downstream consumers ... end up doing in application code the filtering that should have happened at the ingest boundary."
- [STRM][ANTI] Inverse failure: consume when merge is needed, turning a unified query into "a distributed coordination problem that the application has to solve."
- [STRM][PATTERN] "In a mature edge-to-core architecture, all three patterns often appear simultaneously on different data paths."
- [STRM][MIG] "JetStream implements mirrors and sources natively — without external connector processes, without separate mirror-maker jobs"; pattern selection "is a configuration decision, not a development project."

## The Hidden Cost of Active-Passive Clustering (And What to Do Instead)
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/nats-edge-event-architecture-6-hidden-cost-of-active-passive-clustering
- author: Bruno Baloi | date: 2026-05-06 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [TOPO][MIG] Active-passive clustering means "paying for N nodes but only using one of them for productive work"; it forces vertical scaling and needs a load balancer tier that is itself a single point of failure.
- [TOPO] Active-passive failover has a latency spike between failure detection and promotion; at the edge "downstream consumers have their own backlogs and time-sensitive operations."
- [TOPO] Full-mesh: "Every node in the cluster is active. Every node handles traffic"; "no load balancer tier required for basic operation"; "Adding a node to a full-mesh cluster adds proportional throughput capacity."
- [TOPO][SIZE] "cost of handling twice the traffic is approximately twice the nodes"; on node failure "capacity decreases proportionally, but the cluster remains operational and observable."
- [TOPO][STRM] Clustering and Raft are different layers: clustering handles client connectivity; Raft handles replicated state. JetStream's default is "full-mesh: all nodes active" with "Raft for replication"; per-stream leaders are elected automatically; writes are acknowledged only after quorum commit.
- [SIZE][USECASE] Example edge scale: 500 machines x 10 events/s = 5,000 events/s per site; 50 sites = 250,000 events/s total.
- [OPS] Test: "if adding a node doesn't add proportional throughput capacity, you're not running a truly active-active cluster."

## Stop Building Firehoses: Flow Control Isn't a Performance Optimization — It's an Architectural Decision
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/nats-edge-event-architecture-4-flow-control-is-an-architectural-decision
- author: Bruno Baloi | date: 2026-04-16 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [PATTERN] "Flow control is the difference between a useful event stream and a firehose"; "By the time flow control becomes an obvious operational problem, the architectural window to fix it cleanly has already closed."
- [SUBJ][ANTI] "Publish everything, let consumers filter" bakes routing into application code: "Each consumer receives the full stream and discards most of it"; the system is "Decoupled on the surface but is actually tightly coupled at the routing layer."
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] "Filtering is declarative. It lives in the subscription, not in the application." Example hierarchy `sensors.<plant>.<line>.<machine>.<metric>`.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Subject mapping puts translation "in the topology. No additional service. No additional failure mode." Translation microservices add deployment, monitoring, scaling overhead.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Weighted subject mapping enables canaries: "route 90% of events to the stable consumer version and 10% to the new one" without external load balancers.
- [CONS][TOPO] "At the edge, 'consumers that can't keep up' is a routine condition, not a failure mode." Push delivery replays backlogs as spikes after reconnect.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Pull consumption: "Catch-up happens at a rate the consumer declares — not at whatever rate the producer decides." At the edge, consumers should control ingestion rate.
- [ANTI][OPS] Struggling edge systems share: client-side filtering, translation microservices, manual canaries, untested reconnection behavior after multi-hour disconnects.
- [USECASE] Intelecy: sub-second ML insights from tens of thousands of sensors; "That kind of performance with that data volume doesn't happen by accident."

## Why "Just Retry" Will Kill Your Edge System
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/nats-edge-event-architecture-2-retry-will-fail-your-edge-system
- author: Bruno Baloi | date: 2026-04-01 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [ANTI][TOPO] Retry assumes "the service was temporarily unavailable"; at the edge the failure mode is "the network doesn't exist right now and won't for… unknown hours." Retrying "burns CPU. It piles up in-memory state."
- [ANTI] Retry storms on reconnect: "every backed-up message hitting the core at once, overwhelming consumers who had no idea the edge was disconnected." "They're the predictable outcome of applying online-system thinking to offline-tolerant problems."
- [TOPO] Disconnection "is a first-class operating condition. It's not an exception."
- [STRM][PATTERN] Store-and-forward: collect locally, forward when connected, keep collecting while disconnected, catch up at a controlled rate. "Catch up" must mean "resume forwarding at a rate the core can absorb", which needs flow control and pull consumers.
- [STRM] Local durability: "Events get written locally before anything else happens." Survives process crash, network drop, upstream throttling.
- [USECASE] Rivitt (oil/gas) store-and-forward on NATS+JetStream: "continuous data capture possible even when the network isn't." PowerFlex (EV charging): JetStream buffers locally, syncs through intermittent connectivity.
- [ANTI] "If you're pushing directly to an upstream queue or API without local durability, you have data degradation and loss risk."
- [OPS][ANTI] Tests must include disconnection; testing only always-on networks means "testing the happy path and shipping the edge case."
- [TOPO] Treat edge and core as "separate operational realms connected by controlled paths, not assumed ones."

## The Edge Talks Back: Building Bidirectional Control Into Your Architecture
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/nats-edge-event-architecture-9-the-edge-talks-back
- author: Bruno Baloi | date: 2026-05-21 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [TOPO][PATTERN] "An architecture that can only receive from the edge is an architecture that can observe problems but not respond to them."
- [CORE][TOPO] "The same fabric that carries telemetry from edge to core carries commands from core to edge"; leaf nodes carry both without separate protocols.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Command targeting uses the same hierarchy as telemetry, e.g. `cmd.<site>.<device-class>.<device-id>.stream.pause`.
- [CORE][PATTERN] "Request-reply — NATS's native mechanism for synchronous-style communication over an asynchronous backbone — is what makes the edge interactive." Scatter-gather to wildcard subjects gives a live device census without a registry or heartbeats; timeouts distinguish offline devices from error responses.
- [KV][PATTERN] "The KV store is built on JetStream — which means it's persistent, replicated, and designed to survive connectivity gaps." Watchers propagate config immediately; disconnected nodes catch up on reconnect; KV history gives an audit trail per device; eliminates separate OTA/polling infrastructure.
- [KV][PATTERN] Fleet firmware upgrades: KV for artifacts, subjects for status, request-reply for confirmation; rollback targets specific failed devices.
- [SEC][PATTERN] "A credential issued to a core operations service can be scoped to publish only to `cmd.<site>.*.*.*` subjects"; compromised credentials cannot command outside their namespace; device credentials cannot impersonate other devices.
- [PATTERN] "The difference between an edge architecture that supports bidirectional control and one that doesn't isn't a feature you add later." Subjects need three layers: telemetry publish, command subscribe, status publish-response.

## You Don't Need Two Platforms: The Case for Hybrid Eventing
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/nats-edge-event-architecture-5-you-dont-need-two-platforms
- author: Bruno Baloi | date: 2026-04-30 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [CORE][STRM] Pub/sub is stateless: "if a subscriber is offline when the message arrives, it misses it." Streaming is stateful: replay from time, sequence, or last position; new consumers catch up from the beginning.
- [TOPO] Edge needs both: real-time commands need pub/sub; telemetry surviving disconnects needs streaming.
- [MIG] Kafka "requires JVM, substantial memory, careful partition planning, and coordination layer (ZooKeeper or KRaft mode)", incompatible with constrained edge gateways; teams end up bridging core Kafka and edge brokers.
- [STRM] JetStream feature list quoted: "durable streams, configurable retention, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery, consumer replay, and pull-based consumption for backpressure management"; same binary, no separate process, cluster, or client library.
- [SIZE] "NATS's server binary runs under 20MB" with JetStream enabled; runs on hardware "as constrained as a Raspberry Pi." Clients in 40+ languages.
- [TOPO] Same binary on edge leaf nodes, core hub clusters, and cloud with identical operational model.
- [ANTI] Bridge services between pub/sub and streaming platforms are a single point of failure and a "coordination seam"; the cost includes "deployment scripts, monitoring dashboards, credential configurations, client library versions."
- [USECASE][SIZE] Eviny: zero data loss across 39 hydropower plants with millisecond delivery on a single platform.
- [PATTERN] Hybrid eventing from a single deployable is the "minimum viable architecture" at the edge, not a "nice-to-have."

## NATS and Kafka Compared
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/nats-and-kafka-compared
- author: Synadia (unsigned) | date: 2024-11-08 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [MIG][CORE] "Core NATS alone is sufficient and optimal for fast request paths in scalable services with reliable but not guaranteed quality of service."
- [MIG] Kafka is log-based with topics; "The architectural tradeoff for Kafka's durability and scalability is additional complexity often encountered when scaling."
- [MIG][SIZE] "Kafka can process millions of records per second at a rate of over 500 MB per second." "Kafka has higher latency than NATS due to its batching and compression of messages." NATS positioned at "millions of messages per second" low-latency.
- [TOPO] NATS full-mesh cluster; "one-hop message routing" so messages don't loop; super-clusters connect clusters.
- [MIG] Many NATS built-in features "would require additional processes or JVMs in Kafka"; "While Kafka has moved away from requiring Zookeeper, many deployments still rely on it."
- [CORE][MYTH] Core NATS at-most-once delivers messages from a given publisher intact and in order, but "Core NATS's 'at-most-once' guarantee does not extend across different publishers."
- [STRM][CONS] JetStream offers at-least-once and exactly-once options; individual ack, double ack, nak with backoff.
- [MIG][CONS] Kafka order is guaranteed only within a partition; "Maintaining global order can be difficult across multiple partitions." In JetStream strict in-order delivery is "affected only by acknowledgment settings"; parallelism without partition planning.
- [MIG][CORE] Kafka is pub/sub-only; "Implementing any messaging pattern outside of unidirectional streaming with Kafka can be complex." Fan-out needs multiple consumer groups; request/reply needs manual correlation across topics. "While Kafka is developing similar queue functionality, this capability remains in the proposal stage."
- [MIG][USECASE] NATS fits microservices, IoT, embedded, edge; Kafka fits high-throughput, complex event processing, big data, log aggregation.
- [SEC][MIG] NATS claims more security options: multi-tenancy and distributed authentication.

## NATS vs RabbitMQ: How to Choose the Right Messaging System
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/nats-and-rabbitmq-compared
- author: Andrew Connolly | date: 2026-05-22 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [MIG] NATS is "minimal, lightweight, and subject-oriented"; RabbitMQ routes through "exchanges, queues, bindings, routing keys, queue types, channels, and plugins."
- [MIG][OPS] NATS is "a single binary with no language VM"; RabbitMQ "requires a compatible version of Erlang on each target machine."
- [CORE][STRM] Rule: use "Core NATS when losing an occasional message is acceptable" and "JetStream when messages need to be stored, replayed, or acknowledged."
- [MIG] RabbitMQ classic queues offer "exclusivity, TTL settings, queue length limits, message priority, consumer priority, dead-letter exchanges, prefetch, and lazy queue behavior"; quorum queues are "durable, replicated FIFO queues."
- [TOPO][MIG] NATS topology is "opaque to clients"; RabbitMQ clustering needs "external peer discovery infrastructure, such as DNS, Consul, etcd."
- [MIG][PATTERN] Choose RabbitMQ "when the broker should encode a significant amount of messaging policy"; choose NATS for "simplicity, low latency, and flexible service communication."
- [SIZE][MYTH] "A clean-room benchmark may not predict production behavior"; test under production-like conditions with `nats bench` and `nats-top`.
- [PATTERN] "Distributed systems are usually easier to maintain when message flow stays as simple as the application allows."

## MQTT vs. NATS for Fleet Management: Hub-and-Spoke vs. Distributed Mesh
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/nats-vs-mqtt-technical-comparison-iot-fleet-management
- author: Andrew Connolly | date: 2026-02-17 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [MIG][TOPO] "MQTT is built around a central broker. NATS is built as a distributed mesh." "Every MQTT message from a field device travels to a central broker before routing anywhere else — the network trombone effect."
- [MIG][ANTI] "Deploying a local MQTT broker solves the latency problem but creates a separate instance with its own configuration, ACLs, and monitoring." Federation risks "message loops, duplicates, and inconsistent topic namespaces"; bridges "can lose messages during disruptions or restarts."
- [MIG] MQTT has "no native concept of a message stream"; "MQTT expects clients to acknowledge receipt, not processing completion"; "QoS 1 can also deliver duplicates after network interruptions."
- [TOPO] "Any edge device can run its own local NATS server as a leaf node"; "When connectivity drops, local operations continue. Messages destined for the cloud queue up and sync automatically."
- [SEC][MIG] MQTT ACLs are centralized per broker; "Revoking credentials in one region requires propagation to every other broker." NATS: "The private key never leaves the device"; "Identity is proven through cryptographic challenge-response, not credential transmission"; revocation reaches "the entire cluster — including leaf nodes — within seconds."
- [SEC] JWTs encode permissions directly, e.g. publish to `telemetry.deviceA.*`; no external DB lookup.
- [SIZE] "NATS single-server throughput exceeds 10 million messages per second, with sub-millisecond p99 latency in production." "NATS is a single binary under 20MB. It runs on a Raspberry Pi or an industrial gateway."
- [CORE][MIG] MQTT 5.0 request/reply: "developers still manage response routing and timeout logic themselves." NATS creates a temporary inbox automatically.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Offline commands: "If a device loses connectivity when a command is sent, the command sits in a stream. When the device reconnects" it's delivered; no per-device sender state.
- [TOPO][OPS] "NATS servers discover each other through gossip protocols and form clusters automatically"; on failure "clients reconnect to another cluster member without message loss (with JetStream persistence)."
- [MIG] "The NATS server speaks MQTT natively"; "MQTT semantics — retained messages, sessions, QoS delivery guarantees — are implemented on top of JetStream"; MQTT clients get "clustering, leaf nodes, security, multi-tenancy, and subject mapping."

## Multi-Region Consistency: Have Your Cake and Eat it Too!
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/multi-cluster-consistency-models
- author: Jean-Noël Moyne | date: 2024-04-17 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.10 (stream-level subject transforms, cluster-scoped mappings)

### Claims
- [STRM][TOPO] Clustered JetStream is immediately consistent within a cluster via RAFT: "When a client application receives the publication acknowledgement it is assured that the message has been safely replicated to (and persisted by) the majority of the servers."
- [STRM][SIZE] Replicas are a subset: in a 9-server cluster only 3 servers participate in an R3 stream. Placement tags control AZ placement. Replication degree can be changed at any time without interruption.
- [TOPO] Super-clusters connect regional clusters via gateways; "A client application can be connected to any server in any cluster and still transparently be able to publish and consume from the streams." Streams can be moved between clusters without interruption.
- [STRM] Mirroring preserves sequence numbers; sourcing does not. Both are reliable store-and-forward that catches up after disconnect.
- [STRM][MYTH] Read mirrors give "eventual coherency" not true eventual consistency: writes serialize at the origin; mirrors don't help write scaling or availability if the origin region fails.
- [TOPO][STRM] Stretch clusters need at least 3 regions; "Stretched streams will be immediately consistent between regions, at the expense of much higher latency of synchronous operations." R5 across 5 regions survives two region failures. At least 2 of 3 nodes must be reachable for RAFT votes.
- [SIZE] Async publish keeps throughput up despite RTT; "If the RTT latencies between regions are high then operations will take much longer to complete and some client applications may start timing out." A production stretch cluster across cloud providers showed P99 write latency < 20ms (Derek Collison demo).
- [STRM][PATTERN] Virtual streams (2.10): per region a 'write' stream on region-prefixed subjects plus a 'read' stream sourcing all write streams and stripping the region token via transform (`foo.*.>` to `foo.>`); cluster-scoped mappings route local publishes transparently. "all read streams eventually contain all published messages, though not necessarily in same order."
- [STRM][ANTI] Virtual stream limits: no work-queue or interest retention (limits only); not for KV if the same key is modified from different regions; consumers are per-region (no global durable); message deletes are not propagated; no compare-and-set because read/write sequences differ.
- [SIZE][OPS] Example write stream max-age 1 hour; that is the maximum regional outage/split-brain window without message loss.
- [TOPO] If one region fails publishes continue; if two or three fail, no new consumer/stream creation but publishes and gets still work.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Global ordering can be kept with a stretch-cluster 'ordering' stream sourced from write streams and mirrored locally: lower write latency than direct stretched writes, but no compare-and-set.
- [TOPO] Leaf nodes are recommended for edge without guaranteed connectivity (vehicles, mobile).
- [KV][TOPO] KV direct gets go to local cluster replicas; needs cluster-scoped API subject mappings for transparency.

## Understanding JetStream Memory Usage Patterns
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/nats-jetstream-high-ram-usage
- author: Andrew Connolly | date: 2025-08-08 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [OPS][STRM] JetStream memory comes from: dedup IDs kept for the window "(default: 2 minutes)"; file-store caching of recently accessed messages; metadata and subject tracking for streams/consumers/subjects; extra overhead on meta-leader nodes.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Disable or shrink the dedup window per stream if deduplicating externally (example: 30s "Reduced from default 2 minutes").
- [OPS][ANTI] "Use fewer subjects per stream when possible"; "Long-lived consumers are more memory-efficient than short-lived ones"; separate meta leadership from nodes handling high-volume streams.
- [OPS][MYTH] Message count and size affect disk, not memory, "unless consumers perform full stream scans or create many short-lived consumers." 300M+ messages across a few streams with single consumers "shouldn't inherently cause high memory usage."
- [OPS] "Memory usage in JetStream clusters is more influenced by architectural patterns (meta leadership, deduplication settings, consumer lifecycle) than by raw message counts."
- [OPS][SIZE] Case: 13GB of a 16GB GOMEMLIMIT on stream/consumer leaders and meta leaders, elevated after all clients stopped, while other nodes sat at 2-3GB. Use Go pprof for definitive allocation data.

## NATS for Retail: Manage Thousands of Nodes at the Edge by Reducing East-West Traffic
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/east-west-vs-north-south-in-nats
- author: Andrew Connolly | date: 2024-10-29 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.11 (leaf-node cluster-name optimization "will be formalized")

### Claims
- [TOPO] North-south = "communication between different layers or network boundaries" (clients<->servers, leaf nodes<->servers); east-west = within a layer (servers in a cluster, clusters in a super-cluster, leaf servers in the same cluster).
- [TOPO][ANTI] Leaf nodes "generally do not communicate directly with one another unless there's legitimate interest," but with JetStream subscription propagation creates overhead "particularly noticeable during startup": "when the Nth leaf node starts, it receives N-1 leaf subscriptions."
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Give all leaf nodes the same cluster name to prevent "interest graph propagation between individual leaf nodes"; "will be formalized in the 2.11 release."
- [TOPO][USECASE] Hub-and-spoke: stores talk to the hub; JetStream source/mirror syncs store data; leaf nodes buffer locally while disconnected and sync on reconnect. Suits "point of sale applications, automated manufacturing, IoT devices, autonomous vehicles."
- [CLNT][SIZE] Client libraries in "more than 45 languages."

## Rethinking Microservices: Using NATS to Dramatically Simplify Your Microservices
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/rethinking-microservices
- author: Rahul Rai | date: 2024-07-11 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [MIG][PATTERN] Typical microservice stacks need load balancer, API gateway, cache, service registry, logging, sync/async transports, database-per-service; Netflix used "Zuul for API gateway, Eureka for service discovery, Hystrix for fault tolerance, Ribbon for load balancing" which "introduces a significant level of complexity."
- [CORE][PATTERN] NATS replaces API gateway (location abstraction), service discovery, and load balancing; "distributed load balancing by distributing messages across multiple queue group subscribers randomly."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Services deployed "without requiring inbound network access" are "watertight and secure"; they need no protocol other than NATS.
- [CORE][PATTERN] The services framework "places all subscriptions into queue groups automatically, enabling built-in load-balancing and geo-affinity"; provides discovery and monitoring; Prometheus exporter feeds Grafana.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Subject conventions segregate applications and separate north-south (client-service) from east-west (service-service) traffic. Canary deployments via subject mapping.
- [KV][OBJ] KV and object stores "are abstractions over streams"; the example uses KV for candidates and Object Store for vote counts.
- [OPS][ANTI] Production code should use cancellation tokens and "distributed locks or NATS optimistic concurrency control" for concurrency.

## Why NATS
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/why-nats
- author: Byron Ruth | date: 2025-12-16 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.0 (2019), 2.2 (2021)

### Claims
- [PATTERN] NATS consolidates messaging (pub/sub, request/reply), streaming, KV, and object storage rather than adding another tool; "Platform coherence has value."
- [CORE] Location independence: "no load balancers, DNS, or sidecars"; "The service API (built into official client SDKs), you get a discoverable registry for free."
- [CORE][MIG] HTTP and gRPC are 1:1 only, preventing passive observation without extra infrastructure; in NATS "M:N is the default", adding subscribers requires no publisher change, enabling audit/debug/analytics taps.
- [CORE][STRM] Spatial decoupling via pub/sub, request/reply, request/reply-many; temporal decoupling via JetStream where clients consume at their own rate.
- [SEC][TOPO] NATS 2.0 (2019): multi-tenancy, decentralized auth, superclusters, leaf nodes. NATS 2.2 (2021): JetStream (at-least-once delivery, exactly-once processing), WebSocket, MQTT 3.1.1.
- [MYTH] Evaluate NATS against the combination of tools it replaces, not just brokers; tradeoff stated: "NATS may not be the most optimized for any single narrow use case" but covers 80% via one API and one operational surface.
- [TOPO] Leaf nodes, async replication, and small footprint are "natural extensions" of async-first design, not bolted-on edge features.
- [CORE][STALE?] Original NATS (2011) was single-tenant at-most-once broker powering Cloud Foundry; modern NATS differs substantially.

## Total cost of ownership: NATS vs Kafka

## NATS and Decentralized Security: A Modern Approach to Scalable Authentication
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/decentralized-security-webinar
- author: Peter Humulock | date: 2025-07-07 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [SEC] Centralized auth "reaching their limits" at "millions per second" of auth requests; "The bottleneck isn't just technical; it's architectural." Regional security domains distribute the load.
- [SEC][TOPO] "Authentication and authorization aren't dictated by your topology. They're overlays on top of your topology."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Operator model suits "high connection churn environments"; hierarchical signing scales; config-based auth is "Better suited for less dynamic environments or deployments with lower volumes of authentication traffic"; hybrid (operator keys managed via config) is possible.
- [SEC] "Accounts define natural security boundaries." Exports/imports: streams (read-only subjects for other accounts) and services (request/reply across accounts).
- [SEC][MIG] Auth callout delegates to "IBM DC, LDAP, OAuth, OIDC" and allows gradual migration.
- [SEC][OPS] Resolvers: memory (dev), file, URL. File-based auth needs files updated on every node and "each node must be restarted"; operator-based "updating an account on one node will automatically synchronize the changes with the other two."
- [SEC] Resolver-based JWT auth and config-based auth "are different authentication models" and typically cannot be mixed within one; a cluster can support multiple operators; JWT verification needs only the public signing key; accounts can add signing keys for delegation or rotation.
- [SEC][TOPO] "Authentication works the same for leaf nodes and regular nodes"; cross-account service imports "must be authorized at the hub/root as well"; leaf tenants can run their own auth callout per account.
- [SEC] "you can't mix Auth Callout and JWT auth within the same Account", but one server can host accounts with different mechanisms (static, callout, resolver). Rotation disconnects clients; reconnect triggers a new callout.
- [SEC][MYTH] Publisher identity is "not part of NATS's core design, as publishers and subscribers are decoupled"; workaround: put a source_id in the payload.

## Per-Message TTL: Unlocking Ephemeral State Patterns in NATS
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/per-message-ttl-nats-2-11
- author: Peter Humulock | date: 2026-03-09 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.11+

### Claims
- [STRM] Before 2.11 all messages in a stream shared `MaxAge`. Per-message TTL needs `allow_msg_ttl: true` on the stream and a `Nats-TTL` header at publish. "Messages without a `Nats-TTL` header fall back to the stream's `MaxAge`." `Nats-TTL: never` ignores `MaxAge`.
- [KV] KV buckets expose per-key TTL (Go: `KeyTTL()`); expiry creates a short-lived delete marker for watchers whose lifetime is `LimitMarkerTTL`; watchers get real-time expiry notifications.
- [KV][PATTERN] Patterns: session + token stores in one bucket with different TTLs; "A lock can expire automatically if the holder dies"; job claims with 20-second `KeyTTL` renewed on heartbeat; IoT presence with 15-second refreshed keys so device-offline events fire without polling.
- [ANTI] Pre-2.11 alternatives were "One stream/bucket per TTL tier" (fragmented), client-side expiry (error-prone, duplicated), or an extra datastore.
- [MIG][KV] "Per-message TTL makes NATS a natural fit for ephemeral state and cache patterns"; positioned as a Redis alternative for some cache/ephemeral uses. Expired data remains replayable until the server deletes it.

## Mirror Streams in NATS JetStream: One-Way Replication Made Simple
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/mirror-streams-jetstream
- author: Peter Humulock | date: 2026-02-18 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.12 (mirror promotion)

### Claims
- [STRM] Mirrors are "one-way, asynchronous replication"; "Your origin stream doesn't need any special setup—it won't even see a consumer created." One origin per mirror; mirrors are read-only; consumers on mirrors have full capabilities.
- [STRM] Mirror config: name (required), start sequence, start time, filter subject, subject transforms, domain. Filter subject and subject transforms cannot be combined. Domain supports hub/leaf JetStream domains.
- [STRM][MYTH] "Delete a message from the origin, the mirror still has it. Delete from the mirror, the origin is unaffected." Deletes never replicate in either direction, which makes mirrors independent backups.
- [STRM][ANTI] Work-queue retention has only partial mirror support and is "not resilient over intermittent connections"; interest retention with mirrors is unsupported and undefined.
- [STRM][SIZE] On origin unavailability the mirror retries "about 10–20 seconds" before reconnecting.
- [STRM][USECASE] Uses: geographic distribution ("One origin can feed multiple mirrors"), cross-account/domain replication, load distribution via `mirror_direct` so clients read from mirrors instead of the origin.
- [STRM][OPS] Mirror promotion (2.12): unbind subjects from the old primary (use `$devnull` placeholder), remove mirror config, bind subjects to the promoted mirror. "the server won't verify if the mirror is fully caught up, so any unreplicated messages will be lost." Publishes fail briefly during the switch; clients need retries.

## JetStream Expected Sequence Headers: Optimistic Concurrency Without Locks
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/understanding-jetstream-expected-sequence-headers
- author: Peter Humulock | date: 2026-01-20 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.12 (atomic batch interaction)

### Claims
- [STRM][PATTERN] Expected-sequence headers detect conflicts rather than prevent them: "Only one succeeds, advancing the stream to sequence 5. The other is rejected because by the time it arrives, the stream has already moved to 5."
- [STRM][MYTH] There is one sequence counter per stream; per-subject expected values "are still stream sequence numbers, not independent counters starting from zero."
- [STRM] Headers: `NATS-Expected-Last-Sequence` (global, single-writer strict ordering), `NATS-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` (per subject, concurrent writers on different subjects), plus `NATS-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence-Subject` for per-pattern grouping (e.g. `order.1.*` shares tracking while `order.2.*` is independent), suited to event sourcing.
- [CLNT] Go: `WithExpectLastSequence(0)`, `WithExpectLastSequencePerSubject(0)`, `WithExpectLastSequenceForSubject(1, "events.order.1.*")`. Failure error text: "wrong last sequence: 1".
- [STRM][PATTERN] Applications must handle retries; capture sequences from PubAcks for the next attempt. Atomic batches use `NATS-Expected-Last-Sequence` on the first message to detect stream changes during batch construction.

## Atomic Batch Publishing in NATS 2.12: All-or-Nothing Message Guarantees
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/atomic-batch-publishing-nats-2-12
- author: Peter Humulock | date: 2025-12-17 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.12, 2.12.1

### Claims
- [STRM] Atomic batches stage messages invisibly and commit all-or-nothing; consumers never see partial batches. Headers: `NATS-Batch-ID` (max 64 chars), `NATS-Batch-Sequence` (incrementing), `NATS-Batch-Commit`.
- [STRM][USECASE] Use cases quoted: "Consistent multi-consumer fan-out", "Idempotent full-state replacement", "Snapshot + delta bootstrapping", multi-event commits ("Consumers should see all three or none"). Event sourcing is the primary use case.
- [STRM][ANTI] Batches rejected if: ID > 64 chars; sequence gaps; stream uses async persist mode; duplicate messages present (as of 2.12.1). Batches cannot cross streams.
- [STRM] `NATS-Expected-Last-Sequence` is "only allowed on the first message of a batch"; `NATS-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` gives subject-scoped checks.
- [STRM][SIZE] Defaults (configurable): 1,000 messages per batch; 50 batches in flight per stream; 1,000 batches per server; 10 seconds inactivity before abandonment.
- [STRM][OPS] Streams need `--allow-batch`. Orbit's `BatchPublisher` manages IDs and sequence numbers.

## Jepsen: NATS 2.12.1
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/jepsen-nats-2-12-1
- author: Neil Twigg | date: 2025-12-22 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.10.20-2.10.23, 2.11, 2.12.1, 2.12.3

### Claims
- [OPS][STRM] Bug in 2.10.20-2.10.22: "a stream could be unexpectedly deleted after process kills"; fixed in 2.10.23.
- [STRM] JetStream verifies message checksums on each load by design; known limitation: nodes may not auto-recover corrupted data from peers when corruption hits the beginning or middle of a stream; filestore struggles with corrupted blocks/metadata from bitflips or truncation.
- [TOPO][OPS] Multiple peer-removal fixes landed in 2.12.3; Synadia contributed membership-change safety fixes to Jepsen's library.
- [OPS][SIZE] Default `sync_interval` is two minutes: "the server will sync data every two minutes"; can be set to `always` to fsync every write at a performance cost. Power loss can lose unsynced page-cache writes up to that window.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Replicated/ephemeral/lossy data tolerates higher sync intervals; strict durability wants lower; "Single-server deployments should consider `sync_interval: always`."
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Multi-AZ clusters resist simultaneous power/storage failures and reconcile lost minority nodes over the network; single nodes can replicate via leaf-node sourcing/mirroring.
- [MYTH] "We did not observe data loss with simple network partitions, process pauses, or crashes in version 2.12.1." Antithesis partnership credited; future work: detect lost data and recover from peers automatically.

## Distributed Counters in NATS JetStream: A CRDT-Based Approach to Global Counting
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/distributed-counter-crdt
- author: Peter Humulock | date: 2026-04-29 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.12+ (JetStream API level 2)

### Claims
- [STRM][PATTERN] Counter streams are CRDTs: "multiple servers can update their own copies independently and still arrive at the same result when they merge." Enable with `AllowMsgCounter: true` plus `AllowDirect: true` (to batch-read).
- [STRM] Increment via `Nats-Incr` header matching `^[+-]\d+$`; server uses `big.Int` for "arbitrary precision by default"; values serialize as JSON strings so "JavaScript clients, capped at 53-bit safe integers" don't lose precision; PubAck `val` returns the post-increment value.
- [STRM] Sources rewrite deltas: "the server does not replay the sourced message's `Nats-Incr` verbatim"; `Nats-Counter-Sources` tracks per-source last values as `{stream name}#{original subject}` and entries are "never removed, even if you later drop a source."
- [STRM][ANTI] Incompatible with counters: mirrors ("would replay raw deltas and double-count"), `DiscardNew`, Interest/WorkQueue retention, per-message TTL, `Nats-Rollup`, `Nats-Expected-*` headers. `AllowMsgCounter` "cannot be turned off." Subject purge does not replicate across sourced counters; reset by publishing a negative delta then purging.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Hierarchical aggregation: "regional counters feed continental counters feed a global counter"; pattern is "write locally, tolerate divergence, merge when the network heals."
- [SIZE][MIG] Netflix's Distributed Counter Abstraction handled "75,000 increments per second, single-digit millisecond latency"; regional Redis/Kafka/sharded solutions all implement the same pattern.
- [USECASE] View/impression counts, edge rate limiting (increments stay local), per-region metrics via cascading sources, billing meters/leaderboards where "retries never double-charge a customer."
- [OPS][ANTI] `Nats-Counter-Sources` grows with every source ever attached; subject transforms during sourcing may hide leaf subjects, so "mirror-then-source if you need both views." Typed Go API is in `orbit.go/counters`.

## Delayed Message Scheduling in NATS JetStream
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/delayed-message-scheduling-nats-jetstream
- author: Peter Humulock | date: 2026-04-09 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.12 (`@at`), 2.14 (cron, `@every`, sampling, time zones)

### Claims
- [STRM][ANTI] The `NakWithDelay` retry workaround "does not scale well when you have thousands of pending scheduled messages" because it ties up consumer state.
- [STRM] `Nats-Schedule` header formats: `@at <timestamp>`, six-field cron (seconds first), `@every <interval>`, aliases `@hourly`/`@daily`/`@weekly`. `Nats-Schedule-Target` "must differ from the schedule subject." `Nats-Schedule-Source` (2.14) samples the latest message from another subject. `Nats-Schedule-TTL` needs `AllowMsgTTL`. `Nats-Schedule-Time-Zone` (2.14) applies to cron only; default UTC.
- [STRM] Each schedule is one subject; the latest message on the subject is the active schedule; publishing replaces it. Delivered messages carry `Nats-Scheduler` and `Nats-Schedule-Next` (or `"purge"`). `@at` schedules purge after delivery.
- [STRM][ANTI] `AllowMsgSchedules: true` "cannot be reverted" and cannot be enabled on source or mirror streams. Put `schedules.>` and delivery subjects in the same stream.
- [STRM][OPS] "Past-dated schedules fire immediately"; after a restart all past-due schedules fire at once; "Use `Nats-Schedule-TTL` so consumers can detect and discard stale deliveries." DST can skip or duplicate cron jobs; stay on UTC.
- [PATTERN] For many independent delays use unique subjects, e.g. `schedules.orders.<uuid>`.
- [MIG] SQS has native delay queues; RabbitMQ needs a plugin; "Kafka has no built-in per-message delay."
- [USECASE] Deferred order processing, periodic reports without cron daemons, sensor downsampling via `@every 5m` sampling, retry-with-backoff that "handles far more concurrent schedules than consumer-based retry patterns."

## Consumer Pausing in NATS 2.11: Hit Pause Without Losing Messages
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/consumer-pausing-nats-2-11
- author: Peter Humulock | date: 2026-01-06 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.11

### Claims
- [CONS] Pausing halts delivery until a deadline for push and pull consumers alike; messages keep accumulating in the stream; clients see "No errors, no disconnects" and heartbeats continue.
- [CONS] In-flight batches are not revoked; the server waits for them to complete. Deadlines can be extended/shortened by re-issuing; consumers can be created paused (`--pause=1h`, `--pause-until=<ISO8601>`).
- [CONS][USECASE] Uses: deployments/migrations, emergency maintenance, freezing flow for debugging, giving overwhelmed downstreams time to recover; removes the need for custom backpressure logic.
- [CLNT][OPS] Go: `consumer.Pause(ctx, deadline)` / `consumer.Resume(ctx)`; CLI `nats consumer pause events worker 10h` and `nats consumer resume events worker`; state visible in `nats consumer info`.

## Message Tracing in NATS 2.11: Debug Your Entire System with One Command
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/message-tracing-nats
- author: Peter Humulock | date: 2026-01-29 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.11

### Claims
- [OPS] "The `nats trace` command sends a message through your system and shows you exactly where it goes"; "No external tools, no code instrumentation." It creates a temporary inbox to receive trace events from each server.
- [OPS] Headers added: `Nats-Trace-Dest`, `Nats-Trace-Only`, `Accept-Encoding`. With `Nats-Trace-Only` the "message is traced but never actually delivered or stored in JetStream."
- [OPS] Event types: `IN`, `EG`, `JS`, `SE` (stream export), `SI` (stream import), `SM` (subject mapping). Connection kinds: 0 client, 1 router, 2 gateway, 3 system, 4 leaf, 5 JetStream, 6 account. `Nats-Trace-Hop` builds the routing tree (1, 1.1, 1.2.1).
- [SEC][OPS] Tracing stops at account boundaries by default; cross-account needs `allow_trace: true`: "For stream imports, the importer sets it. For service imports, the exporter sets it."
- [MIG] Positioned against Jaeger/Zipkin-style external tracing integrations.

## Monitoring NATS: From HTTP Scrapes to System Events
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/monitoring-nats-from-http-scrapes-to-system-events
- author: Andrew Connolly | date: 2026-01-24 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.10+ (remote reload)

### Claims
- [OPS] HTTP endpoints (`/varz`, `/connz`, `/jsz`) are point-in-time snapshots that miss transient events between scrapes; system-account events are delivered as NATS subjects.
- [OPS][MYTH] "The system account isolates subjects and permissions, not CPU, memory, or I/O. A severely overloaded server can still impact all traffic."
- [OPS][SEC] `$SYS` must be explicitly enabled (`system_account: SYS` or the account public NKey in operator mode) and users authorized; it uses existing client ports and full NATS auth, while HTTP monitoring needs an extra port and has no built-in auth.
- [OPS] Subjects: `$SYS.ACCOUNT.<account>.CONNECT`/`DISCONNECT`; auth failures on `$SYS.SERVER.<server>.CLIENT.AUTH.ERR` (structured: client IP, user/account, reason; SIEM-ready); periodic `$SYS.SERVER.<server>.STATSZ` ("periodic snapshots, not strict liveness guarantees"); request/reply `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.<server-id>.<ENDPOINT>` for VARZ/CONNZ/ROUTEZ/LEAFZ/GATEWAYZ/SUBSZ/JSZ/ACCOUNTZ/HEALTHZ; `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.PING` discovers all servers; `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.<id>.RELOAD` (2.10+).
- [OPS][STRM] JetStream advisories under `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.*` (lifecycle, leader elections, delivery failures), API audit at `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.API`, metrics under `$JS.EVENT.METRIC.*` (e.g. ack latency).
- [OPS][PATTERN] Use HTTP for k8s probes (`/healthz`), Prometheus, `nats-top`, LB checks; use the system account for real-time connection tracking, auth-error alerting, JetStream audit logs, and where HTTP ports can't be exposed. "For liveness checks, continue using `/healthz` via HTTP." Both are "complementary."
- [OPS][ANTI] `nats sub '$SYS.>'` is fine for exploration; narrow subscriptions in production to avoid volume. Persist system events in JetStream for audit/replay. Surveyor collects system-account data into Prometheus without per-server HTTP ports or sidecars.

## NATS Server 2.14 Release
- url: https://nats.io/blog/nats-server-2.14-release/
- author: Maurice van Veen, Neil Twigg, Daniele Sciascia | date: 2026-04-30 | publisher: nats.io
- version context: 2.14

### Claims
- [STRM] Fast batch publish persists messages continuously as they arrive with inline per-message consistency checks, "effectively unbounded batch sizes" unlike atomic batch, multiple acks in flight for pipelined batches, and gap detection.
- [STRM][SIZE] Fast batch "can almost double throughput compared to async publish depending on settings" and allows hundreds of concurrent publishers into one stream with flow control.
- [STRM] "Atomic batch rejects the entire batch if any message fails a check (including deduplication), fast batch behaves like traditional async publish." Modes `gap:fail` (hard fail) and `gap:ok` (report gaps without failing).
- [OBJ][ANTI] Object store "currently uses async publish underneath and lacks proper flow control for concurrent uploads."
- [STRM] Recurring schedules (`@every 5s`, cron) move periodic work server-side; can combine with TTL to stop scheduling. Scheduled subject sampling reads the latest value on a source subject each fire, falling back to the schedule payload; primary use is server-side downsampling.
- [STRM][MYTH] Before 2.14 mirrors/sources used internal ephemeral consumers; now WorkQueue and Interest retention sources use durable consumers, "visible in consumer listings, carries metadata showing the source domain, account, and stream", holding state across disconnects. Users can pre-create the consumer used for sourcing/mirroring.
- [TOPO][OPS] Leaf node remotes can be added/removed via config reload without restart.
- [STRM] Streams with sources no longer need a 100ms minimum dedup window when dedup is disabled; dedup can be disabled entirely for mirrors/sourced streams; sourced streams now dedup to avoid stalling when sourcing overlapping streams.
- [STRM] EOB (end of batch) lets a batch commit without persisting the final message, for atomic and fast batch.

## NATS Server 2.12 Release
- url: https://nats.io/blog/nats-server-2.12-release/
- author: Neil Twigg & Maurice van Veen | date: 2025-09-22 | publisher: nats.io
- version context: 2.12

### Claims
- [OPS] 6-month release cycle from 2.11 (March 2025); 2.10.x had 26 patch releases.
- [STRM] Atomic batch publish: "atomically write a batch of messages into a stream" with staging and per-message checks; "there can be no partially committed batches"; combinable with scheduling and counters. ADR-50.
- [STRM] Delayed Message Scheduling (ADR-51): single delayed messages only in 2.12, no repeats.
- [STRM] Distributed Counters (ADR-49) use `big.Int`; limit is what "is allowed to be stored in the payload of a single message"; support mirroring/sourcing via CRDT composition.
- [CONS] Prioritized pull policy (ADR-42) prefers local clients but lets remote clients pull immediately when no local client is pulling; Overflow (2.11) "may delay remote client message delivery if local clients are inactive."
- [STRM][OPS] Mirror promotion: remove mirror config to make it primary; delete the previous primary first.
- [OPS] Offline assets (ADR-44): on downgrade to 2.11.9+ unsupported-feature assets answer info/list only, preserve data unchanged, can be deleted, stay offline until upgrade.

## NATS Server 2.11 Release
- url: https://nats.io/blog/nats-server-2.11-release/
- author: Tomasz Pietrek | date: 2025-03-20 | publisher: nats.io
- version context: 2.11

### Claims
- [OPS] 2.10.26 called "the most stable and reliable release to date"; Antithesis partnership; nightly chaos tests.
- [STRM][KV] Single Message TTL: "set a TTL for individual messages"; delete markers on MaxAge expiry; improves KV expired-key notifications.
- [CONS] Consumer pinning (on priority groups) with standby clients for HA; Overflow spills to remote clients based on pending acks or messages; Consumer Pause until a deadline.
- [OPS] Distributed message tracing across gateways, leaf nodes, imports, exports, activated by a header.
- [STRM] Message Get existed since 2.8; Multi Message Get batches retrieval, "vastly more efficient approach to processing streams without the overhead" of dedicated consumers.

## NATS Server 2.10 Release
- url: https://nats.io/blog/nats-server-2.10-release/
- author: Byron Ruth | date: 2023-10-03 | publisher: nats.io
- version context: 2.10.0

### Claims
- [OPS][SIZE] 2.9.x: just over a year, 22 patches; 76% of 32.7k net lines were tests/benchmarks. 2.10.0: 62% of 20.8k net lines were tests; coverage 85% (from 68%). Burn-in, fault-injection, stress testing.
- [STRM][SIZE] New filestore reduces lock contention; "P99 stream publish times reduced and stabilized considerably"; large/encrypted streams "will now typically take less than a second to recover" at startup (no linear scan of blocks).
- [TOPO] Dedicated system-account route by default plus a pool of routes shared across accounts; opt-in account pinning for dedicated routes. Previously "single TCP connection between server pairs" with system traffic interleaved.
- [TOPO] Route compression modes incl. auto-compression that adapts ratio to inter-server latency; no upfront config.
- [SEC] Auth Callout: extension point implemented as a NATS service to integrate "existing identity and access management (IAM) providers", for users preferring centralized IAM.

## NATS Server 2.9 Release
- url: https://nats.io/blog/nats-server-29-release/
- author: Byron Ruth | date: 2022-09-16 | publisher: nats.io
- version context: 2.9.0

### Claims
- [STRM][OPS] Catch-up replication traffic is compressed; `max_outstanding_catchup` "limits the total bytes that are in-flight during stream catch-up."
- [CONS] Pull consumer distribution became round-robin across subscriptions; `InactiveThreshold` (default five seconds) now also applies to durable consumers.
- [OPS] Built with Go 1.19 for `GOMEMLIMIT` in memory-constrained containers.
- [STRM][KV] `AllowDirect` serves gets from any replica (auto-on for KV, opt-in for streams); `MirrorDirect` lets mirrors serve gets. Direct get headers: `Nats-Stream`, `Nats-Sequence`, `Nats-Time-Stamp`, `Nats-Subject`.
- [STRM][SIZE] Republish graduated from experimental; supports "millions of concurrent subscriptions"; `HeadersOnly` republish enables lazy fetch via direct get; `Nats-Last-Sequence` header for gap detection.
- [CONS][STRM] Consumer `Replicas`, `MemoryStorage`, `FilterSubject` editable after creation; stream `Placement` editable to move streams transparently.
- [SEC] AES-GCM added for file encryption (`cipher: aes`) alongside ChaCha20-Poly1305; `$JS.API.ACCOUNT.PURGE.<account>` purges an account's resources.
- [SUBJ] Mapping functions: `{{wildcard(x)}}` (replaces `$x`), `{{partition(x,a,b,c...)}}` deterministic hash to 0..x-1, `{{split}}`, `{{splitFromLeft}}`, `{{splitFromRight}}`, `{{sliceFromLeft}}`, `{{sliceFromRight}}`.
- [SEC] Templated scoped signing keys: `{{name()}}`, `{{subject()}}`, `{{account-name()}}`, `{{account-subject()}}`, `{{tag(key)}}`.

## Building a Wallet Event Backbone with NATS JetStream: Lessons from BroSettlement's Staging Tests
- url: https://nats.io/blog/brosettlement-building-a-wallet-event-backbone-with-nats-jetstream/
- author: Vadym Rozov | date: 2026-08-17 | publisher: nats.io (guest)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [USECASE][PATTERN] NATS chosen "not as a replacement for another broker, but to avoid coupling every service through synchronous calls" across wallet stages (policy, MPC signing, broadcast, confirmation, ledger, notification).
- [PATTERN] PostgreSQL is the source of truth; transactional outbox: business rows and outbox event in one transaction, published to JetStream only after commit. Prevents publishing rolled-back events and losing events when the broker is down; failed publish leaves the outbox row as a retry point.
- [STRM][MYTH] Delivery is "at-least-once, not magical exactly-once"; duplicates are a "normal recovery condition"; consumers dedup by globally unique eventId (plus chain tx identity for blockchain data); handlers idempotent via unique constraints; client requests carry Idempotency-Key.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Versioned subjects like `deposit.account.created.v1`; envelope separates transport metadata from domain data; version field "allows additive evolution without silently changing an existing consumer contract"; correlationId spans the whole workflow.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Durable consumers with queue-based processing for horizontal scale; retries with backoff; no assumption of "single global order across unrelated subjects."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Internal bus separate from public stream; TLS, service credentials, subject-level permissions; payloads "never private key material or signing shares"; WebSocket gateway authenticates with API keys, binds to one org, filters event families, translates internal events to a stable client contract; gateway uses filtered JetStream consumers with explicit ack and redelivery backoff.
- [SIZE][USECASE] Staging: 400 attempts (100 concurrent then 30 waves of 10 over 5 minutes) produced 926 business events with 926 unique event IDs (222 created, 484 updated, 220 failed), covering all 214 HTTP 201s, six 503s, two 500s. "Synchronous error response did not erase the asynchronous operational record."
- [PATTERN] Client recovers via REST reconciliation when the listener disconnects; future: explicit resume contract with durable consumer sequence/cursor. Ledger journal, not the event stream, is the rebuildable financial source; reconciliation jobs compare ledger to chain.

## Delegate with trust
- url: https://nats.io/blog/jetstream-eventual-consistency/
- author: Vincent Vermersch | date: 2024-05-21 | publisher: nats.io (guest)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [SIZE][PATTERN] Messaging latency: "happy path around 30ms, but arbitrarily long if flow interruptions occur"; CRUD lets you read-after-write immediately, messaging requires waiting for processing.
- [STRM][PATTERN] One subject per order plus publish expectation `lastSubjectSequence: 0` enforces "there will be only one subject per order payment" (first-writer-wins single withdrawal).
- [STRM][SIZE] Dedup window is per-stream in nanoseconds; example `duplicate_window: 5_000_000_000` (5s); duplicates in the window are rejected.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Query the order subject "like a database" to rebuild aggregate state from prior events; `lastSubjectSequence: 2` forces the message into exactly 3rd position or fails.
- [STRM][MYTH] Sequence numbering is stream-wide; per-subject ordering requires tracking the last subject sequence (from subscription metadata, fetching the last event, or in-memory).
- [STRM][SIZE][PATTERN] For high-frequency events (10ms intervals = 360,000 events/hour) publish snapshot/aggregate events (e.g. hourly average) to a separate subject to avoid reading the full history.

## Recovering Quorum After Renaming Servers
- url: https://nats.io/blog/nats-recover-quorum/
- author: John Weldon | date: 2024-01-20 | publisher: nats.io
- version context: 2.10, 2.11, 2.12+

### Claims
- [OPS][ANTI] Rename servers one at a time; remove the stale offline record before the next rename. Changing Helm `serverNamePrefix` during an upgrade renames all servers at once, doubling the recorded peer set and losing quorum. "This setting should only be changed before the first installation."
- [OPS] Symptoms: warning "JetStream has not established contact with a meta leader"; readiness probe 503; `nats server report jetstream` shows half offline; error "The cluster expects 6 nodes but only 3 responded. JetStream requires at least 4 up nodes."
- [OPS] On 2.12+ a fresh empty node cannot force itself into the peer set, so scale-up recovery doesn't work; bring nodes back under original names (all originally-named nodes needed simultaneously if disks are empty); reverting the prefix alone doesn't fix a bricked cluster. If original hosts are destroyed, "no in-product recovery exists on 2.12+; restore from backup."
- [OPS] On 2.10/2.11 add a fourth server (`kubectl scale --replicas=4`) to regain quorum, peer-remove stale entries (`nats server cluster peer-remove -f <peer ID>` or `$JS.API.SERVER.REMOVE`), then scale back down.

## Infinite message deduplication in JetStream
- url: https://nats.io/blog/new-per-subject-discard-policy/
- author: Jean-Noël Moyne | date: 2022-11-14 | publisher: nats.io
- version context: 2.9.0

### Claims
- [STRM][MYTH] Exactly-once needs two parts: publish-side dedup and ack-based consumption. Time-window dedup (Nats-Msg-Id) "cannot guarantee restart timeframes"; Kafka's connection-scoped producer idempotence "guarantees only single-session idempotence" and can't cover a client crash before ack.
- [STRM][PATTERN] `DiscardNewPerSubject` + max-msgs-per-subject 1 + discard `new` yields infinite BYOID dedup: a duplicate subject fails with "maximum messages per subject exceeded". Without it, per-subject limits with discard `new` behave as `old` (last-value cache).
- [STRM][MIG] JetStream "enforces exactly n maximum messages per subject; Kafka log compaction ensures at least one." Distributed WAL systems lack a `new` discard policy because they're designed to always accept or block.
- [STRM][PATTERN] "compare-and-append" via `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` gives SQL-update-like semantics.
- [STRM][SIZE][OPS] Per-subject limits need indexing; more subjects means more server memory. Subject filter needs at least one `*` or `>` where the unique ID token sits. Default "Duplicate Window: 2m0s".
- [USECASE] N workers acting at-most-once per period; concurrency/access control.

## Building Event-Driven Banking as a Service (BaaS) with NATS
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/event-driven-banking-as-a-service-with-nats
- author: Synadia | date: 2025-10-27 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [PATTERN][MIG] API-led BaaS (System/Process/Experience APIs) is "inherently synchronous and tightly coupled"; event-driven BaaS puts "an event fabric at the core" and APIs "become edges of the system rather than its core."
- [CORE][STRM] Core: "fire-and-forget ultra-low-latency delivery"; JetStream: "at-least-once or exactly-once semantics"; single supercluster spans "data center, AWS, or branch edge."
- [KV][OBJ][MYTH] KV/Object stores "complement, rather than fully replace, transactional databases."
- [SEC] "built-in TLS and mutual TLS (mTLS), nkey-based authentication, and fine-grained authorization via accounts and leaf nodes"; "no system component ever has access to private keys or passwords."
- [MIG] Legacy stacks split "IBM MQ or Solace for messaging, Kafka for streaming."

## Scaling Global AI Inference with NATS JetStream

### Claims

- [CONS][PATTERN] GPU workers use "pull-based JetStream consumers with explicit acknowledgements"; workers pull only when they have capacity, making GPU capacity "a first-class control signal"; crash mid-inference means no ack and redelivery to another GPU; no custom retry or DLQ plumbing.
