## Event-Driven Systems with NATS and Jetstream
- url: https://james-carr.org/posts/2026-01-21-nats-jetstream-building-reliable-messaging/
- author: James Carr | date: 2026-01-20 | publisher: third-party (james-carr.org)
- version context: 2.12.1 (via Jepsen reference)

### Claims
- [CORE][STRM][MIG] Core NATS is fire-and-forget, "comparable to Redis Pub/Sub"; JetStream "is closer to Kafka in persistence model."
- [STRM][SIZE] Example stream: `Limits` retention, file storage, max_bytes 100MB, max_age 7 days (nanoseconds), num_replicas 1.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Same durable name across instances = competing consumers "analogous to Kafka consumer groups"; separate durables on one stream = fan-out with independent positions; server-side subject filters plus app-level content routing can combine.
- [CONS][MYTH] Ack after processing gives at-least-once: "Messages may be delivered multiple times (if your service crashes mid-processing), but they won't be lost." `nak()` triggers redelivery.
- [OPS] Cites Jepsen finding real durability issues under failure modes while the system is "genuinely trying to provide strong guarantees while remaining performant."

## How to Build NATS Consumers
- url: https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-02-nats-consumers/view
- author: Nawaz Dhandala | date: 2026-02-02 | publisher: third-party (OneUptime)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [CONS] "Streams store messages persistently, while consumers track delivery state for subscriber groups. A single stream can have multiple consumers, each maintaining independent delivery positions."
- [CONS][PATTERN] Push for real-time low-latency; pull "when backpressure control or batch processing is needed." [DUBIOUS] Push-first framing contradicts current official guidance favoring pull.
- [STRM][SIZE] Example stream: file storage, `MaxAge: 7 * 24 * time.Hour`, `Replicas: 3`.
- [CONS] Deliver policies: All (full history), New (post-creation only), Last, ByStartSequence, ByStartTime. Explicit ack required in production; `NakWithDelay` (5s example) "useful for rate limiting or waiting for external services"; `Term` stops redelivery.
- [CONS][SIZE] Examples: AckWait 30s push / 60s pull ("Longer wait for batch processing"); MaxDeliver 5 push / 3 pull; MaxAckPending 1000; fetch batch 100 with 5s timeout; `DeliverGroup: "order-workers"` for push queue groups.
- [CONS][PATTERN] DLQ pattern: stream with 30-day MaxAge, subject `dlq.<original subject>`, publish when MaxDeliver reached then Term.
- [OPS][SIZE] Health heuristics: pending > 10,000 = falling behind; ack pending > 500 = slow/stuck; redelivery ratio > 10% = processing issues.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Set AckWait "based on your actual processing time, plus a safety margin": if p95 is 5 seconds "set AckWait to 15-30 seconds"; MaxAckPending trades throughput for memory; graceful shutdown drains in-flight with a timeout.

## NATS JetStream: Streams, Consumers, and Durable Messaging
- url: https://luismori.dev/article/nats-jetstream-persistence-streams-consumers/
- author: Luis Mori Guerra | date: 2026-07-06 | publisher: third-party (luismori.dev)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [STRM][CONS] JetStream adds "at-least-once delivery (exactly-once is opt-in)"; a consumer is "a stateful view of a stream — it tracks which messages were delivered and acknowledged."
- [CONS][PATTERN] Durable pull consumers are "the recommended default for new projects: explicit ack, flow control, scalable batch fetching." Push: "`MaxAckPending` is the only flow-control mechanism."
- [CONS][MYTH] "`MaxDeliver` is not a dead-letter queue — after max attempts, NATS stops redelivering but the message remains in the stream." Plan explicit poison-message handling.
- [STRM] Retention: `limits` (default), `workqueue` (delete on ack), `interest`; storage file (default) or memory; replicas 1-5; discard old (default) or new. "Prefer JetStream publish APIs over plain Core NATS publish — the server returns an acknowledgment."
- [KV] KV buckets "implemented as streams named `KV_<bucket>`" and inherit stream limits/replication/storage.
- [CONS] `BackOff` "Overrides `AckWait` when configured"; raise AckWait "for slow external APIs (e.g. OpenSearch bulk)"; "One consumer per downstream concern keeps projectors independent."
- [OPS][MYTH] Default `sync_interval` "2 minutes — ack does not always mean immediately on disk in all failure modes." Don't treat ack as "job done on disk"; understand replication and sync_interval for RPO.
- [ANTI] Don'ts: assume MaxDeliver = DLQ; push by default; "one consumer for everything"; skip idempotency. "still plan for rare duplicates" even with Nats-Msg-Id dedup.

## Bridging the Edge: Using NATS Leaf Nodes to Build Hybrid and Multi-Cloud Systems
- url: https://thinhdanggroup.github.io/nats-left-nodes/
- author: Thinh Dang | date: 2025-12-01 | publisher: third-party (thinhdanggroup)
- version context: 2.10 (TLS-first for leaf nodes)

### Claims
- [TOPO] Leaf nodes "accept client connections locally, dial out to a remote NATS system, forward only allowed/necessary traffic, and keep working locally if upstream connection fails"; "dial-out only ... great for NAT and strict firewalls"; hub sees one account-owned connection per leaf.
- [TOPO][CORE] Queue groups prefer local: "the leaf will route that request to a local member if any exist, and only go upstream if none available." Interest-pruned: hub delivers only over leaf connections "whose remote side expressed interest."
- [SEC][TOPO] Only subjects the leaf user may publish are exported; only subjects it may subscribe to are imported. Sidecar pattern: leaf next to the app, apps connect to localhost without credentials, leaf holds the real credentials.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Rule: "clusters for same region/LAN with low latency; gateways for peer regions/clouds; leaf nodes for crossing network ownership/security boundaries." Stretched clusters "get chatty and fragile." Keep leaf graphs acyclic: "trees and forests, not arbitrary meshes."
- [STRM][TOPO] JetStream domains (`hub` vs `branch-1`, API `$JS.hub.API.>`) separate instances; store-and-forward = persist locally, mirror/source into hub streams when connectivity returns.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Use "more accounts with simple rules" than one account with complex authorization; accounts are "messaging containers." Subject layout: `site.<site-id>.local.>`, `site.<site-id>.telemetry.>`, `site.<site-id>.control.>`.
- [SIZE] Cites GitHub discussion #5974: thousands of leaves "proven to work at scale, but it still requires capacity planning."

## Deploying a scalable NATS cluster part 1: core architecture and considerations
- url: https://one2n.io/blog/deploying-a-scalable-nats-cluster-part-1-core-architecture-and-considerations
- author: Barun Debnath | date: 2025-06-04 | publisher: third-party (One2N)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [TOPO][SIZE] Quorum "(Cluster Size / 2) + 1"; "deploy Jetstream cluster with 3 or 5 servers. The maximum replication factor per stream is 5"; odd sizes avoid split-brain; R3 balances cost/fault tolerance; R5 tolerates two failures.
- [STRM][TOPO] Meta group leader handles API and placement; each stream and each consumer is its own RAFT group; leadership churn hurts performance. [DUBIOUS] "NATS core servers form their own RAFT group for cluster synchronization" (core routing is not RAFT-based).
- [CONS][PATTERN] No native DLQ; implement via advisory streams capturing max-delivery advisories.
- [OPS][SIZE] Production: at least 2 cores, at least 8 GiB RAM, SSD with at least 3000 IOPS; `GOMEMLIMIT` at "80-90% of the instance's memory limit" (8 GiB machine: `GOMEMLIMIT=6GiB`).
- [SIZE][ANTI] Default max payload 1 MB; keep below 1 MB; 64 MB configurable but "generally advised against"; chunk or use external storage instead.
- [CONS][SIZE] Batch 100-1000 for throughput; max-ack-pending 1000-10,000; [DUBIOUS] "Prefer AckAll acknowledgment strategy for bulk processing."

## NATS Cluster Architectures: Multiregional Clusters - Connecting the Globe
- url: https://concurrentflows.com/nats-cluster-architectures-multiregional-clusters
- author: unknown | date: unknown | publisher: third-party (concurrentflows.com)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [TOPO] Gateways form a full mesh between clusters, on a dedicated port; connections are unidirectional though discovery makes them appear bidirectional; client connection info is not gossiped across gateways.
- [TOPO][SIZE] Three 3-node clusters: 36 full-mesh routed connections vs 18 gateway connections.
- [TOPO][CORE] Gateways use interest-only mode and queue-subscription optimization; "messages are delivered to a single subscriber in a queue group across the Supercluster, prioritizing local queue subscribers."
- [STRM][TOPO] Streams/consumers are placed within one cluster and replicate only over routes, not gateways; the meta group spans the whole supercluster and quorum loss blocks new resources; cross-region is eventual via mirrors (read-only) and sources (writable); regional loss can lose data within the replication window.
- [TOPO] All gateways in a cluster must share the cluster name. Leaf nodes are account-scoped point-to-point connections, not part of the routing mesh, presenting "a discrete NATS context distinct from that of the remote"; JetStream domain is "an independent namespace within JetStream that disambiguates requests between NATS deployments"; hub and leaf should use different domains.
- [OPS] Superclusters "demand careful, thorough design and configuration with a high level of operational observability."

## Building Distributed State Stores with NATS JetStream: KV and Object Storage Patterns
- url: https://timderzhavets.com/blog/building-distributed-state-stores-with-nats-jetstream/
- author: Tim Derzhavets | date: 2026-02-21 | publisher: third-party (timderzhavets.com)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [KV][SIZE][DUBIOUS] KV operations "typically land in the 1-5ms range for local deployments, while Redis serves requests in microseconds" (contradicts Synadia's 40µs in-cache figure).
- [OBJ][SIZE] Object Store throughput "measured in hundreds of MB/s"; default chunk 128KB ("Each file gets split into 128KB chunks by default"); a 1GB file is ~8,000 messages; SHA-256 digest verification.
- [KV][DUBIOUS] "TTL is applied at the bucket level to all entries" (per-key TTL exists since 2.11); advice to "create multiple buckets rather than fighting the single-TTL constraint."
- [KV] Revision is bucket-scoped: "Each new write to any key increments the bucket's global sequence." CAS: update succeeds "only if the current revision matches"; "revision 0 means key must not exist."
- [KV][SIZE] Watcher case: 50 instances in three regions, "12ms average latency" vs "45-180ms with Redis polling at one-second intervals"; local evaluation "100,000+ flag evaluations per second per instance"; eliminated "50,000 unnecessary Redis queries per second."
- [KV][OBJ][PATTERN] Use KV for "feature flags, service discovery metadata, or circuit breaker state"; Object Store for workflow artifacts and pipeline uploads; avoid for "high-frequency trading data, session storage with millions of writes per second, or multi-terabyte datasets." Keep S3 for multi-TB files, CDN delivery, compliance certifications.
- [KV][ANTI] Don't embed volatile data in key names (`cache.response.{hash}.expires-{timestamp}`); use dots for hierarchy; watch with `*`/`>`.
- [KV][SIZE] Examples: sessions ttl 1h history 1; feature flags ttl 0 history 64; locks ttl 30s history 1 replicas 3. `replicas: 3` "survives two simultaneous node failures" [DUBIOUS: R3 tolerates one failure for writes].
- [OPS][SIZE][DUBIOUS] "A 100GB object bucket with RF=3 takes approximately 30-45 minutes to rebuild on a replacement node over 10Gbps networking" (no methodology).
- [TOPO] Partition behavior: "Only the partition containing the Raft leader accepts writes"; 2+1 split keeps the majority writable while the isolated node "serves stale reads."
- [MIG] Migration via dual writes; "Start with JetStream stores for new features in existing NATS deployments."

## Replace Redis with NATS: Atomic Counters and Microsecond Key-Value
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/replace-redis-with-nats-atomic-counters-and-microsecond-key-value
- author: Andrew Connolly | date: 2026-07-01 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.12.0+ (API level 2)

### Claims
- [KV][SIZE] "in-cache get is around 40 microseconds plus the network round trip" on low-end cloud hardware; "within roughly 5–10 microseconds of Redis on the same hardware, and faster than Redis for writes" in those tests; on-disk reads "around 1 to 1.5 milliseconds depending on the disk, with NVMe at the lower end." Figures are "representative test results, not a guarantee."
- [STRM][KV] Counters (ADR-49): `Nats-Incr` header `+N`/`-N`, big-integer precision, server serializes updates per subject (no client read-modify-write, no retries under contention); "sourcing-compatible" across streams/accounts/regions.
- [STRM][ANTI] Counter streams need `AllowMsgCounter: true`, `AllowDirect: true`, Limits retention set at creation only; cannot be mirrors; incompatible with per-message TTL; every subject becomes a counter.
- [KV][PATTERN] CAS is optimistic and best when "writers rarely collide"; counters when "many writers hit the same key." Uses: "rate limiters, quotas, view/like/vote tallies, and inventory decrements."
- [KV][MYTH][ANTI] "The working set must fit in memory" for microsecond figures; "NATS is optimized for streaming, not random access"; high-churn random updates are slow because "overwriting a KV key deletes the previous message in the backing stream."
- [MIG] Keep Redis for sorted sets, hashes, set intersections, Lua scripting; choose NATS KV "when your hot working set fits in memory and you want one fewer system to run."
- [CLNT] Orbit is "the recommended way to work with counters" (Go, Java, .NET, JS, Python, Rust, C); async persist mode (creation-time) avoids per-write flush for single-replica KV/streams.

## From Solace to NATS: One Platform for Messaging, Streaming, and the Edge
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/solace-to-nats-migration
- author: Andrew Connolly | date: 2026-07-09 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [MIG][SUBJ] Solace `orders/state/city/store` maps to `orders.state.city.store`; wildcards `*` and `>` are the same; "Replacing `/` with `.` covers most cases." Prefix wildcards like `red*`, reserved namespaces (`$`, `#P2P`), and literal `.` in topic levels need explicit handling.
- [MIG][TOPO] Solace DMR interest propagation maps to NATS subject-interest propagation across clusters/superclusters; "DMR clusters become NATS clusters. Cross-region bridging becomes a supercluster with gateway connections"; "Edge sites that used to be broker clients become leaf nodes."
- [MIG][TOPO] Solace "typically pair[s] brokers in active-passive configurations, with a monitoring node to arbitrate failover"; NATS clusters are "full meshes of active nodes. There is no standby broker sitting idle"; "Adding capacity means adding nodes to the mesh."
- [MIG][STRM] Solace guaranteed delivery maps to "explicit JetStream stream and consumer designs"; "A consumer can be a pub/sub subscriber today and a durable, replayable stream consumer tomorrow without changing brokers"; Solace shops typically add Kafka for log semantics.
- [MIG][ANTI] Solace "exclusive queues with active/standby consumption and partitioned ordering require separate designs"; "Request-reply in NATS uses ephemeral inboxes."
- [MIG][SEC] "Solace's ACL model is broker-scoped"; NATS accounts are "designed for tenancy that spans a mesh"; Auth Callout for IdP delegation; "Security domains isolate edge tenancy from cloud tenancy."
- [MIG][ANTI] "NATS is a runtime platform. It does not ship a bundled event design environment"; plan for Event Portal replacement (AsyncAPI). Coexist via bridging; migrate "project by project rather than as a big-bang cutover."

## Migrating from TIBCO to NATS: A Modernization Guide for Financial Services
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/tibco-to-nats-migration-financial-services
- author: Andrew Connolly | date: 2026-07-09 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [MIG][SUBJ] "`TRADES.US.EQUITY.>` in RV is `TRADES.US.EQUITY.>` in NATS. Wildcards work the same way." Inboxes mirror RV `_INBOX` request-reply. JetStream covers RVCM (certified messaging): durable subs, at-least-once, acks, replay.
- [MIG][TOPO] RV is UDP multicast; NATS is TCP so it crosses cloud networks, meshes, WANs. A NATS cluster replaces an RVRD mesh with all nodes active.
- [MIG][ANTI] "Do not deploy NATS the way you deployed RV daemons. It technically works to run a local NATS server per host and treat it as an `rvd`, but you forfeit most of the operational benefits."
- [MIG] "Migrating EMS applications to NATS is more involved than migrating RV, and any post that pretends otherwise is not worth reading." No drop-in JMS bridge. Non-durable JMS topics map to Core subjects; durable topic subs need a stream plus durable consumer each; JMS queues map to a stream with a shared durable, often work-queue retention and explicit acks.
- [MIG][SUBJ] EMS selectors filter SQL-like predicates at the broker; NATS "pushes filtering into the subject itself", free at the routing layer; selector-heavy apps and FT pairs need redesign.
- [MIG][TOPO] EMS HA is primary plus hot standby with shared storage, "half the HA hardware idle by design"; a three-replica stream across failure domains tolerates one server failure.
- [MIG][OPS] Inventory every RV subject tree and EMS topic/queue (certified delivery, selectors, FT pairs, fire-and-forget); "Bridge selectively between TIBCO and NATS for flows in transition. Producers and consumers move independently. Nothing forces a synchronized cutover"; retire TIBCO capacity as flows move.

## Connecting distributed SCADA with NATS.io (part two)
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/connecting-distributed-scada-with-natsio-part-two
- author: David Gee | date: 2026-05-15 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [TOPO][PATTERN] "Level 1.5" zero-trust substrate with two components: Data Fabric Client (initiates connections to PLCs and NATS, easing firewalls) and Data Fabric Node (local NATS leaf node with local streams sourced from published subjects, surviving WAN loss).
- [TOPO] "NATS leaf nodes initiate a connection to a server (just like NATS client code)"; "NATS servers when clustered initiate full mesh unicast connections to each other"; "Islands of NATS clusters connect to each other through gateways, in which one gateway connection per cluster is made"; unicast IPv4/IPv6, no multicast/IGMP.
- [MIG] Core NATS replaces MQTT as the broker (request/reply + pub/sub); JetStream replaces Kafka for persistence; built-in MQTT lets Level 1 MQTT devices connect unchanged; built-in TLS removes VPN tunnels.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Decentralized auth: each application/process is a NATS account, each connection a user; operator mints account tokens; accounts have explicit import/export; users carry subject-level authorization. Clients need only one or two seed URLs and discover the rest via gossip.
- [SEC][OPS] Fabric components rate-limit and permit-list control messages to protect Level 1 devices; NAC by known MAC, alert on unknown MACs, shut ports disconnected outside maintenance windows.

## Orbit.go: A Guide to NATS Client-Side Abstractions for Go
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/orbit-go-guide
- author: Piotr Piotrowski | date: 2025-10-08 | publisher: synadia
- version context: 2.12

### Claims
- [CLNT] Orbit is "the umbrella project for client-side abstractions which are above the NATS protocol level or need incubation before being incorporated"; modules independently versioned; some may "graduate to main clients."
- [CLNT][CORE][PATTERN] natsext RequestMany: iterator over multiple responses with termination by "timeout, maximum number of responses or even a custom predicate"; for scatter-gather/discovery; not for single-responder request-reply.
- [CLNT][STRM] jetstreamext atomic batch publish: all-or-nothing, fewer round-trips; [ANTI] avoid when "message deduplication is required" as it is "not compatible with batch publishing." Batch get: N messages from a sequence or last per subject set; "often simpler and more efficient than using a consumer for ad-hoc retrieval"; not for real-time, work-queue, interest, or very large datasets.
- [CLNT][OPS] natscontext reuses NATS CLI contexts ("eliminates configuration drift"); natssysclient queries monitoring endpoints per server or cluster-wide (not full coverage yet; skip if using Prometheus/Surveyor).
- [CLNT][CONS] pcgroups "brings Kafka-style consumer groups to NATS, leveraging the server's consumer priority policies"; static vs elastic membership; avoid when needing "strict global ordering across all messages on stream" or for "relatively low-throughput streams."
- [CLNT][KV] kvcodec encodes keys with special characters (dots, spaces) and encrypts/compresses values transparently.
- [CLNT][STRM] counters module needs `AllowMsgCounter: true` and `AllowDirect: true`; works across sources and mirrors [note: contradicts later counter post which says mirrors are incompatible]; source tracking shows "exactly which service instances contributed."

## Orbit: NATS Extensions and the Future of the Clients

- [CLNT] Orbit libraries at the time: Java, Go, Rust, JavaScript.

## 14 factors of adaptive edge (part one)
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/adaptive-edge-1
- author: Synadia | date: 2022-06-20 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [TOPO][ANTI] Legacy brokers give "high-latency and inconsistent delivery of key data to or between edge clients"; apps are forced to "trombone" data to cloud data centers.
- [TOPO] Adaptive Edge is "a flexible deployment topology overlaid atop of legacy architectures"; supports one-to-many, many-to-many, "sharding of the connection fabric into local clusters" that keep working "even with eventual and discontinued connectivity."
- [KV][OBJ] Requires "not only persistence but a lightweight attached data store (such as a key/value or object store)" to reduce round trips.
- [SEC] Needs a "multi-tenant security model" with "tightly partitioned namespaces"; fabric should "behave more like a graph" of nodes "just as comfortable in a small Windows PC as in a cloud server."

## 14 factors of adaptive edge (part two)

- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [PATTERN] 14 factors: performant; easy to deploy/maintain ("If a team or dedicated engineer is required to maintain a solution, then it is not suitable"); lightweight anywhere (sensors, Raspberry Pis to cloud); resilient/self-healing ("Other nodes in the cluster should instantly absorb any traffic"); language agnostic; multi-cloud; location independent; tolerates disruptions (batch and stream); persists intelligently (KV/object); aggregates/distributes intelligently; secure by default ("The connection fabric never stores or accesses private keys. Security is bifurcated from connectivity"); multi-tenant; scales horizontally and vertically; client simplicity ("Clients should remain simple and stateless").

## NATS HTTP Monitoring Endpoints: A Complete Guide
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/nats-http-monitoring-endpoints
- author: Andrew Connolly | date: 2026-01-24 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [OPS] "no sampling, no asynchronous exporters inside the server, and no continuously running probes"; responses are live state. Monitoring is off by default; enable with `nats-server -m 8222` or `http_port`/`https_port`. No HTTP auth: treat the port as internal-only, bind to localhost/private network, use `https_port` in production, reverse-proxy for external auth.
- [OPS] Endpoints: `/healthz` (k8s probes), `/varz`, `/connz`, `/routez`, `/leafz`, `/gatewayz`, `/subsz` (can be very large), `/jsz` (`?accounts=1`).
- [OPS] `/varz`: `mem` growth from slow consumers, JetStream caching, route/leaf buffers, high subscription counts; `cpu` may exceed 100% on multi-core; `slow_consumers` increments when clients can't drain; `in_msgs`/`out_msgs`/bytes need deltas for rates.
- [OPS] `/connz`: pending bytes growth means a client is falling behind; `msgs_to`/`msgs_from` find hot producers/consumers; `?state=closed` shows exit reasons; `?sort=pending`, `?subs=1`, `?limit=100&offset=0`. `/routez` `pending_size` high means congestion or slow peers. `/jsz` `reserved_mem`/`reserved_store` are logical reservations.
- [OPS] Prometheus exporter converts JSON; Surveyor gives one Prometheus endpoint per cluster over NATS; `nats-top -s https://localhost:8222`.

## Your Perimeter Is Already Gone — Edge Security Isn't a Checkbox
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/nats-edge-event-architecture-3-your-perimeter-is-already-gone
- author: Bruno Baloi | date: 2026-04-13 | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [SEC] "The edge doesn't have a perimeter. It has exposure." Edge is "adversarial by nature, not by exception"; encryption "addresses only part of the edge security problem."
- [SEC][ANTI] Default/hardcoded and shared, unrotated credentials; compromised devices injecting plausible bad data for months; lateral movement via over-scoped credentials; supply-chain (BadBox 2.0 on "more than 10 million devices").
- [SEC][PATTERN] Realm-based security: "Each edge device gets credentials that authorize only what that device legitimately needs to publish and subscribe to, nothing more"; "A compromised edge node can't suddenly start publishing to a core command channel; the topology simply doesn't permit it."
- [SEC] Decentralized, cryptographically scoped credentials remove a single credential-store target; constraints must be "built into the topology" not layered on. The question is "what can this device actually reach, and what happens if it's compromised?"

- [SEC][ANTI] "Encrypt everything and trust the network" is perimeter thinking.

- [KV][MIG] ripienaar: use memory storage for a fair cache comparison ("Redis stores its data in memory. So can nats"); "I don't really think a cache is what our KV is going to be the best at." derekcollison disagrees: "no reason it can not be very fast IMO"; "We can be on par with Redis when there is a real network"; enable direct get; cache a KV subset in-app via watchers.
- [KV][SIZE] jnmoyne benchmark on M1 Ultra: NATS KV ~24,000 sync ops/s (~41.7 µs) vs Redis ~18 µs locally; LAN latency (hundreds of µs) makes the 20 µs gap negligible. User magicprinc: file-store KV 15,656 put/s and 16,720 get/s (1M keys, 128B); NATS in Docker much slower than bare metal.
- [OPS][MYTH] ripienaar: small-dataset cache tests are misleading because OS block cache makes disk-backed queries look RAM-fast; test with large random-read datasets.

## NATS Over-Replicated Inactive Streams: What They Mean and How to Fix Them (Synadia Insights check)
- url: https://www.synadia.com/insights/checks/nats-over-replicated-inactive-stream
- author: Synadia | date: unknown | publisher: synadia
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [STRM][OPS] Idle R3 streams still cost storage on three nodes, Raft heartbeats, and meta-cluster entries "that slow cluster-wide operations"; causes: decommissioned services, staging copies of prod templates, seasonal workloads, blanket R3 policies.
- [STRM][OPS] Find with `nats stream report` or `nats stream list --json | jq` on `num_replicas >= 3`; fix with `nats stream edit <stream> --replicas 1` (non-destructive, reversible, dissolves the Raft group).
- [STRM][PATTERN] "Ephemeral, test, and archival streams should default to R1"; keep replication for streams receiving "a few messages per day" where loss is unacceptable; 50+ idle R3 streams "meaningfully reduces capacity."

## NATS Weekly #32
- url: https://www.synadia.com/newsletter/nats-weekly-32
- author: Synadia | date: 2022-06-27 | publisher: synadia
- version context: nats.net v0.14.8, k8s/nats v0.17.1

### Claims
- [STRM] Default R1 on any JetStream-enabled server; R1 memory loses data on restart; R1 file is unavailable until recovery; "At least three replicas (R3) are required" for fault tolerance; R3 tolerates one down, R5 two; max five replicas.
- [STRM][MYTH] Even replica counts (R2, R4) are "generally not useful from an availability standpoint"; R2 adds a storage copy but cannot progress if the leader fails.
- [TOPO][STRM] Tags place replicas across AZs; mirrors are lightweight eventually consistent async replication that can use different configs (memory, R1); sourcing aggregates streams so one consumer replaces many; DR ladder: regional mirrors (most real-time), consumer-to-object-storage batches, offline backups.
- [SEC][OPS] nsc is "the primary and recommended method" for account/user JWTs; use signing keys with operators.

## Kafka vs NATS: A Comparison for Message Processing (DZone)

- [MIG] Kafka lacks at-most-once; NATS Core is at-most-once with JetStream adding at-least/exactly-once; Kafka orders per partition only; Kafka has log compaction and Beam/Flink integration.

## Coordinating Teams of AI Agents in Real Time on NATS and JetStream
- url: https://nats.io/blog/coordinating-ai-agent-teams-on-nats/

### Claims
- [PATTERN][SUBJ] Three addressing modes map to NATS primitives: multicast = subject fan-out on `cotal.<space>.chat.>`; unicast = per-agent durable consumers on `inst.>`; anycast = work-queue streams on `svc.>` for exactly-once handoff across roles.
- [KV][PATTERN] Presence = per-space KV bucket with TTL and heartbeats; channel registry in KV for late joiners.
- [SEC][SUBJ][PATTERN] Sender identity is the last subject token (`cotal.<space>.inst.<target>.<sender>`) enforced against the agent's JWT so "one agent cannot impersonate another"; account-as-space, user-as-agent; deny-by-default ACLs; inboxes are pre-created bind-only durables.
- [SIZE] Runs five agents today, designed for five thousand; each agent costs one subscription and one KV entry.
- [PATTERN] "Reach for the NATS primitive before you build your own"; "presence became a KV bucket, inboxes became durable consumers, roles became work queues."

## What's old is new: A NATS-native protocol for AI agents
- url: https://nats.io/blog/nats-native-protocol-for-ai-agents/
- author: Andrew Connolly | date: 2026-05-25 | publisher: nats.io
- version context: protocol v0.3

### Claims
- [PATTERN][CORE] Agents register as NATS micro services named `agents`; discovery via `$SRV.PING.agents` / `$SRV.INFO.agents`; endpoints `agents.{verb}.{agent}.{owner}.{name}` with verbs `prompt`, `hb`, `status`, `attachments`; `prompt`/`status` use queue group `"agents"` for load balancing.
- [PATTERN] Exactly one `ack` status chunk first; every response stream ends with a zero-byte, header-less terminator; heartbeat every 30 seconds, offline after 3 missed; per-stream inactivity timeout of 60 seconds recommended; delivery is at-most-once (core) with JetStream at-least-once deferred.
- [SEC] Security "delegated entirely to NATS accounts, users, and subject permissions"; callers must read subjects from `$SRV.INFO`, not construct them.

## Client-side Partitioned Consumer Groups for JetStream
- url: https://nats.io/blog/orbit-partitioned-consumer-groups/
- author: Jean-Noël Moyne | date: 2025-06-05 | publisher: nats.io
- version context: 2.11+, Orbit.go

### Claims
- [CONS][MIG][MYTH] "NATS JetStream does not require Stream partitioning to parallelize consumption, unlike Kafka"; standard consumption is elastic and on-demand; strict order needs max-ack-pending 1 which serializes the whole stream.
- [CONS] Pinned consumers give fault tolerance: only one instance of a member delivers at a time. Partition = consistent hash of subject token(s); users see member names and max members, partition numbers are "basically invisible."
- [CONS][SIZE] Elastic groups are a materialized view (work-queue stream sourced from the origin, partition token inserted during sourcing); lag observable via work-queue size; size caps cause a ~1 second sourcing pause when hit. Static: lower latency, fewer resources, any ack mode (explicit needed for strict order); elastic: explicit ack, live membership changes. Multiple elastic groups can exist per stream. `cg` CLI tool provided.

## NATS JetStream Explained: Streams, Consumers, and Durable Messaging (NATS Explorer)
- url: https://voltrus.id/nats-explorer/blog/nats-jetstream-explained/
- author: unknown (Voltrus) | date: 2026-08-16 | publisher: third-party (voltrus.id)

## The Real-Time Problem Hiding Inside Your AI Data Problem
- url: https://www.synadia.com/blog/real-time-problem-inside-your-ai-data-problem

- [USECASE] NVIDIA Cloud Functions routes GPU inference across regions on Synadia NATS; Rivian fleet connectivity.

## NATS JetStream as a Durable Job Queue in .NET
- url: https://milanjovanovic.tech/blog/nats-jetstream-job-queue-dotnet
- author: Milan Jovanović | date: 2026-07-10 | publisher: third-party (milanjovanovic.tech)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [STRM][CONS][PATTERN] Work-queue retention makes the stream a queue; one shared durable pull consumer gives competing consumers; adding a worker is "starting another process with zero configuration."
- [PATTERN][ANTI] "Publish the result FIRST, then ack the job." Crash before publish = redelivery; crash between publish and ack = harmless duplicate if processing is idempotent by job ID. Never ack before publishing results.
- [CONS][SIZE] Consumer `AckWait = 60s`, `MaxDeliver = 4`; poison jobs drop after bounded redelivery with a `MAX_DELIVERIES` advisory. Results stream: limits retention, `MaxAge = 5 minutes`, file storage; persist long-lived results to Postgres instead.
- [MIG] Redis-list queues lose jobs silently (no ack on LPOP, no persistence); NATS chosen over RabbitMQ for "single lightweight binary" ops on a VPS; single node is a SPOF, cluster with RAFT replicas for HA.
- [MYTH] "At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing beats exactly-once delivery promises."

## RPC vs NATS: It's Not About Sync vs Async — It's About Who Owns Completion
- url: https://dev.to/harrisonsec/rpc-vs-nats-its-not-about-sync-vs-async-its-about-who-owns-completion-1fi5
- author: Harrison Guo | date: 2026-04-17 | publisher: third-party (dev.to / harrisonsec.com)
- version context: unstated

### Claims
- [MIG][PATTERN] In RPC "the caller owns knowing the work finished"; in messaging "the receiver owns" completion. Sync/async is orthogonal: "synchronous messaging (request-reply over NATS)" and "asynchronous RPC (fire-and-forget gRPC)" both exist.
- [MIG] RPC: "Retry is a caller decision"; errors "propagate naturally"; "Backpressure is immediate." Messaging: "Retry is a consumer decision"; "Errors are silent on the publisher side"; "Backpressure is decoupled. Publishers can happily overwhelm consumers"; observability "splits in two."
- [ANTI][PATTERN] Publisher-side retry created duplicate orders "when the first publish actually succeeded but the ack was slow"; a consumer that partially committed then crashed had redelivery rejected by dedup, losing the order. Dedup check "has to be in the same transaction as the actual work."
- [ANTI] Don't use "Request-reply where the reply is supposed to happen later, via a different message." Failed messages need a DLQ; track lag, processing time, error rate, redelivery rate.
- [PATTERN] Decision rule: "who is responsible if the work doesn't happen?" caller = RPC (auth check, balance read, inventory reservation); receiver = messaging ("Order was placed", idempotent, delay-tolerant work).

## Grokking NATS Consumers: Push-based queue groups
- url: https://www.byronruth.com/grokking-nats-consumers-part-2/
- author: Byron Ruth | date: 2022-01-21 | publisher: third-party (byronruth.com) [STALE? pre-2.10 push-consumer era]
- version context: unstated (2.7-era)

### Claims
- [CORE][CONS] Core queue groups give HA ("Members can cleanly disconnect and reconnect or new members can join without interrupting") but "concurrent message processing gives up message order" and in-flight messages "may be dropped" on abrupt disconnect; slow consumers are disconnected.
- [CONS][SIZE] JetStream push queue groups: `DeliverGroup` in ConsumerConfig; ack wait default 30s; `MaxDeliver -1` = unlimited; default max ack pending 65536; `MaxAckPending(1)` means "only one message will ever be in-flight at a given time across the queue group" (ordered + HA).
- [CONS][MYTH] Redelivery can happen even when processing succeeded but the ack was lost; publisher dedup is windowed so consumers still need idempotency.
- [PATTERN] Core queue groups for request-reply services (latency, HA); JetStream queue groups for queuing/streaming needing persistence.

## Grokking NATS Consumers: Intro and push-based
- url: https://www.byronruth.com/grokking-nats-consumers-part-1/
- author: Byron Ruth | date: 2022-01-10 | publisher: third-party (byronruth.com) [STALE? pre-2.10 push-consumer era]
- version context: 2.2.0+

### Claims
- [CONS] Consumers are "stateful views" with their own sequence numbers; push consumers deliver "without waiting to be asked"; ephemeral consumers are auto-named and deleted on unsubscribe; durables need `nats.Durable()`.
- [CONS][SIZE] Defaults: `DeliverPolicy all`; `AckPolicy explicit` requires Ack/Nak; `AckWait` 30s; `MaxDeliver -1` retries forever; `MaxAckPending 65536` (1 forces serial); `ReplayPolicy instant` vs `original`.
- [STRM][MYTH] Limits streams are consumer-stateless; work-queue and interest retention are consumer-influenced. "Streams cannot have overlapping subject spaces."
- [CONS][OPS] `AckFloor` is the highest contiguous acked sequence (gaps block it); `NumRedelivered` can rise and fall; `NumWaiting` is pull-only; `PushBound` shows a live deliver subscription; delivery happens on the deliver subject, not the filter subject.

## NATS Weekly #13
- url: https://www.synadia.com/newsletter/nats-weekly-13
- author: Synadia | date: 2022-02-14 | publisher: synadia
- version context: nats.rs v0.18.1, k8s v0.13.0, nats-account-server v1.0.1

### Claims
- [STRM][MYTH] Interest retention: with zero consumers messages are discarded immediately; with one consumer messages are retained even without an active subscription; with several, "the message is not removed until all consumers consume the message (ack or term)"; consumers must exist before messages to see them.
- [MIG][CORE] NATS "qualifies as a replacement for gRPC for intra-service communication"; gRPC's main value is protobuf codegen; "NATS as the basis for microservice communication is significantly more robust and extensible than the point-to-point interactions that gRPC offers"; nats-rpc org offers protobuf codegen over NATS.

### Total claims: 634 (lines tagged with [TAG])

### 15 most valuable design claims
1. Consumer info is a monitoring call, not an operational one; consumer create is idempotent and is the way to "check existence"; trouble grows past ~100,000 consumers and past "a few hundred" disjoint filter subjects per consumer (Synadia anti-patterns, 2026-06).
2. Subject design rules: lowercase hyphenated tokens, at or below 16 tokens / 256 chars (32-token stack matcher cliff), default to namespace-first, never put high-cardinality per-message IDs in subjects, "your subject hierarchy is your authorization model", route-affecting versions go in the subject (Synadia subject hierarchies, 2026-06).
3. Edge-to-core stream pattern rules: consume = selective at ingest, mirror = exact read-only 1:1 with sequence numbers preserved, source/merge = interleaved with per-source order only; the common failure is defaulting to mirror-everywhere; deletes never replicate; mirror promotion drops unreplicated messages (Synadia, 2026).
4. Replica semantics: R1 = one copy, R3 required for fault tolerance, R5 max, even counts "generally not useful"; idle R3 streams still pay Raft and meta costs so "ephemeral, test, and archival streams should default to R1" (NATS Weekly #32, Synadia Insights).
5. Durability caveat: default `sync_interval` is two minutes, so a JetStream ack is not an fsync; single-node deployments "should consider `sync_interval: always`"; 2.10.20-2.10.22 could delete a stream after process kills, fixed in 2.10.23 (Jepsen post, 2025-12).
6. Consumer defaults for new work: durable pull consumers with explicit ack; `MaxDeliver` is not a DLQ, the message stays in the stream; build a DLQ from the `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES` advisory; handlers must be idempotent because acks can be lost (luismori, job-queue posts, Byron Ruth).
7. Priority groups (2.11/2.12): overflow (min_pending threshold), pinned_client (`Nats-Pin-Id`, 2-minute default TTL, 423 on mismatch), prioritized (0-9); pinning is affinity plus failover, "not a distributed lock"; Fetch(N) is not an atomic reservation; keep priority timeout above pull expires.
8. Partitioned consumer groups: FNV-1a hash of subject tokens, parallelism = min(partitions, members), partition count is frozen forever, extra members become standbys, elastic groups need explicit ack and a work-queue buffer above one second of throughput, `{{partition}}` cannot cross accounts.
9. Multi-region consistency ladder: mirrors give "eventual coherency" (writes still serialize at origin); stretch clusters need at least 3 regions and give immediate consistency at RTT cost (P99 < 20 ms demo); 2.10 virtual streams give eventual consistency but only with limits retention, no KV same-key writes, no global durables, no compare-and-set (Moyne, 2024-04).
10. JetStream memory is driven by architecture (dedup window default 2 min, file-store cache, meta-leader role, short-lived consumer churn, subjects per stream), not by message count; separate the meta leader from hot streams (Synadia, 2025-08).
11. Leaf-node topology rules: leaves dial out, queue groups serve local members first, give all leaves the same cluster name to avoid N-1 subscription propagation at startup, keep leaf graphs acyclic, use clusters for LAN, gateways for regions, leaf nodes for ownership/security boundaries (Synadia retail post, thinhdang, glossary).
12. Edge operating rules: replace retry with store-and-forward and controlled-rate catch-up via pull consumers; make filtering declarative in subjects and mappings rather than client-side; prefer full-mesh active-active over active-passive; scope credentials per device because "The edge doesn't have a perimeter. It has exposure" (Baloi series, 2026).
13. Counter streams are CRDTs with hard incompatibilities: no mirrors, no DiscardNew, limits retention only, no per-message TTL, no `Nats-Rollup`, no `Nats-Expected-*`; `AllowMsgCounter` is one-way; `Nats-Counter-Sources` entries are never removed; use counters when many writers collide, CAS when they rarely do.
14. Batch publishing: atomic batch defaults 1,000 msgs/batch, 50 in flight per stream, 1,000 per server, 10 s abandon; rejected with async persist mode or duplicates, and incompatible with dedup per Orbit; fast batch (2.14) "can almost double throughput compared to async publish" and is unbounded; Object Store still lacks flow control for concurrent uploads.
15. KV vs Redis: in-cache get ~40 µs plus RTT and "faster than Redis for writes" in Synadia's test, but "The working set must fit in memory" and overwriting keys is slow because the old message is deleted; maintainers disagreed on KV as a cache (ripienaar skeptical, Collison and Moyne on par with Redis on a real network); keep Redis for sorted sets, hashes, Lua.
