# Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives

<!-- Assembled 2026-09-07 from six extraction passes. Sources: NATS by Example (github.com/bruth/nats-by-example, shallow clone; the nats-io/nats.by.example URL 404s) and the local new-nats.docs repo: learn/**/*.md + docs/concepts/*.md. -->


## Topologies (category)
- path: examples/topologies/meta.yaml
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/topologies

### Claims
- [TOPO] NATS supports three deployment topology building blocks: clusters, superclusters, and leaf nodes. "various deployment topologies NATS supports including clusters, superclusters, and leaf nodes"

## Simple Leafnode
- path: examples/topologies/simple-leafnode
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/topologies/simple-leafnode/cli

### Claims
- [TOPO][PATTERN] The most minimal leafnode setup is a main server with only a `leafnodes.port` and a leaf server with only `leafnodes.remotes` pointing at the main server's leafnode port; no other configuration is required. "Create the most basic server config which enables leaf node connections."
- [TOPO] The leaf node's `leafnodes.remotes` list names the main server(s) the leaf will dial; the leaf initiates the connection, using the `nats-leaf://` URL scheme. "This needs to define the leaf node _remotes_ which is the main server it will be connecting to."
- [TOPO][CORE] A request published by a client connected to the leaf node is transparently routed to a responder connected to the main server; the client needs no knowledge of where the service lives. "As expected, this will get routed to the service connected to the main server."
- [TOPO][CORE][PATTERN] When the same request subject has responders on both the leaf and the main server, NATS delivers requests from leaf-connected clients to the closest responder (the one on the leaf). "NATS is smart enough to route messages to _closest_ service relative to where the client request comes from."
- [TOPO][CORE] Observed output: with a responder on both sides, three consecutive requests from the leaf-connected client were all answered by "hello from leaf"; the leaf-local responder wins over the remote one.
- [TOPO][CORE][PATTERN] If the leaf-local responder is removed, requests from the leaf fall back automatically to the responder connected to the main server. "If we remove the leaf-base service, it will fallback to the main service."
- [OPS] Start the main (hub) server before the leaf so the leaf's remote is reachable when it comes up. "Start the main server first."

## Leafnode with JWT Auth
- path: examples/topologies/leafnode-jwt
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/topologies/leafnode-jwt/cli
- version context: nsc output says "When running your own nats-server, make sure they run at least version 2.2.0"

### Claims
- [SEC][PATTERN] When bootstrapping an operator with nsc, generate an operator signing key; the text calls this a best practice. "Create the operator, generate a signing key (which is a best practice), and initialize the default SYS account and sys user."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Edit the operator to require signing keys so that accounts must also be signed with signing keys rather than identity keys. "A follow-up edit of the operator enforces signing keys are used for accounts as well."
- [SEC][OPS] Setting `account-jwt-server-url` on the operator is only a convenience so `nsc push` does not need the server URL each time. "Setting the server URL is a convenience so that it does not need to be specified with call `nsc push`."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Keep application traffic in a dedicated account (here `APP`) and reserve the `SYS` account for operational purposes. "The `SYS` account should be used for operational purposes."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Give the application account its own signing key (`nsc edit account APP --sk generate`) and create users under it, following the operator/account/user hierarchy.
- [SEC][TOPO] The main server enables JWT auth by including the nsc-generated NATS resolver config (`nsc generate config --nats-resolver --sys-account SYS`) alongside its `leafnodes.port`. "generates the bit of configuration to be used by the server to setup the embedded JWT resolver."
- [SEC][TOPO] With the full NATS resolver, an account JWT must be pushed to the main server (`nsc push -a APP`) before users of that account (and the leaf's remote credentials) are trusted. "We need to put up the `APP` account JWT we created previously to the main server so that the user credentials file ... is trusted."
- [SEC][TOPO][PATTERN] In a JWT setup, the leaf node authenticates to the hub by placing a user `.creds` file in `leafnodes.remotes[].credentials`; the leaf server itself can then have no client authentication configured. "no credentials file is specified since the leaf server does not have authentication setup. Instead the `leafnodes.remotes` section of the config defines the main server and provides the credentials so that the leaf node is authenticated for forwarding messaging."
- [SEC][TOPO] The leaf's remote credentials bind the leaf connection into the `APP` account on the hub, so unauthenticated clients on the leaf transparently reach a service connected to the hub under APP. "This request will be transparently fullfilled by the service connected to the main server."
- [OPS] Order matters: start the main server, push the account JWT, then start the leaf node (the leaf's remote creds are validated against the pushed account).

## Supercluster
- path: examples/topologies/supercluster
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/topologies/supercluster/cli
- version context: recorded output shows nats-server 2.10.1

### Claims
- [TOPO] A supercluster is a set of clusters joined by gateway connections; the gateway bridges communication by propagating the subject-interest graph across clusters. "A gateway connection bridges communication, specifically by propagating the subject-interest graph across clusters."
- [TOPO][CORE] A client on cluster A can use a service hosted by a client on cluster B; messages flow across clusters transparently and the client has no knowledge of physical location. "messages will transparently flow across clusters without the client needing to have any knowledge of physical location."
- [TOPO][PATTERN] If JetStream is in play, do not follow the plain supercluster example; use the dedicated Supercluster with JetStream layout (it has extra requirements). "if you are using JetStream, please refer to the dedicated Supercluster with JetStream example."
- [TOPO][SEC][PATTERN] Every server in a supercluster includes a shared `$SYS` account definition; the example factors it into a `sys.conf` included by all configs. "Define the system account to be included by all configurations."
- [TOPO] If the `cluster` block is omitted, the gateway name is used as the cluster name by default. "By default, the gateway name will be used as the cluster name even if the cluster block is not specified."
- [TOPO] A real multi-node cluster in a supercluster must still define its `cluster` block with routes; the single-node-per-cluster layout in the example is a simplification. "if this were a real cluster with routes defined, this would need to be defined as well."
- [TOPO] Each server's `gateway.gateways` list enumerates every cluster in the supercluster, including its own gateway name and URL. (Both east.conf and west.conf list both `east` and `west` entries.)
- [OPS] Use the monitoring endpoint `/healthz` (via `http_port`) to wait for servers to be healthy before using them. "Wait until the servers are healthy."
- [OPS][SEC] `nats server list` requires a system-account user; it reports per-server cluster membership and the count of gateway connections (GWs), plus a Cluster Overview of outgoing/incoming gateways. "Show the server list which will indicate the clusters and gateway connections."
- [TOPO] Observed output: with two single-node clusters, each server shows `Routes 0`, `GWs 1`, and each cluster shows 1 outgoing and 1 incoming gateway.

## Supercluster with JetStream
- path: examples/topologies/supercluster-jetstream
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/topologies/supercluster-jetstream/cli
- version context: recorded output shows nats-server 2.10.1

### Claims
- [TOPO][STRM] In a JetStream-enabled supercluster, one server across the entire supercluster is elected leader of the meta/API layer and handles JetStream API requests for placing streams and consumers. "one server across the entire supercluster is elected to handle JetStream API requests specifically for the placement of streams and consumers."
- [TOPO][STRM][SIZE] The meta layer is a Raft group, so electing its leader needs a quorum; in practice the supercluster needs an odd number of servers in total. "Since this is a Raft group as well, electing a leader requires a quorum across servers. What this means in practice is that there needs to be an odd number of servers across the supercluster."
- [TOPO][STRM][PATTERN][SIZE] JetStream superclusters should have at least three clusters, or use the arbiter pattern to reach an odd server count. "Supercluster deployments with JetStream-enabled servers should include at least three clusters or use the arbiter pattern."
- [TOPO][STRM][PATTERN][SIZE] For production, run three nodes per cluster so that R3 streams can be created. "for a production deployment it is recommended to have three nodes per cluster to support R3 streams."
- [TOPO][STRM] JetStream requires a `cluster` block with `routes` defined even for a single-node cluster. "A requirement of JetStream is to have a cluster block with routes defined, even for single node clusters."
- [TOPO][STRM][SIZE] Stream replicas never cross gateway connections; with one node per cluster only R1 streams can be created. "In this test setup, only R1 streams can be created since streams replicas do not cross gateway connections."
- [TOPO][STRM] An odd number of servers across the supercluster is required to reach consensus for the meta group leader. "across a supercluster, an odd number of servers must exist to support reaching consensus for the meta group leader."
- [TOPO][STRM] Each JetStream server in the supercluster needs its own `jetstream.store_dir` and a `server_name`; the gateway block lists all three clusters including its own.
- [OPS] `nats server report jetstream` (system account) shows the JetStream summary and the RAFT Meta Group with the current leader marked; observed output shows 3 servers, one leader, `Current true` for all.
- [TOPO][CORE] Observed output: a request from a client on west was served by a responder on east across the gateway with sub-millisecond rtt in the local test.

- [TOPO][STRM][PATTERN] An arbiter is a single-node cluster with JetStream disabled that has gateway connections to each of the JetStream-hosting clusters. "a single node cluster that is not JetStream-enabled can be deployed which connects to both clusters that are hosting the JetStream-enabled servers."

- [TOPO][STRM][PATTERN] Place JetStream nodes across availability zones with `server_tags: [az:N]` and set `jetstream.unique_tag: "az:"` so replicas of a stream are spread over distinct zones. "JetStream enabled with the unique tag as well as basic accounts."
- [TOPO][STRM] Two clusters with three nodes each plus the arbiter gives 7 servers total (6 JetStream-enabled), an odd count for meta-group quorum.
- [TOPO][STRM][PATTERN] A client connected to one cluster (east) can request that a stream be placed in another cluster by passing `--cluster=west` on stream creation; placement is a JetStream API concern, not a connection concern. "Connect to east (port 4222), but request that a stream be added to the west."
- [TOPO][STRM][ANTI] Observed output (unexplained in narrative): in the recorded run the cross-cluster `stream add --cluster=west --replicas=3` failed with `nats: error: could not create Stream: raft: corrupt peer state (10049)`; the meta table at that moment showed `east-az3` with `Current false`, `Active 2.35s`, `Lag 3`, i.e. one peer not yet caught up shortly after startup. The narrative does not comment on this, so treat it as an observed timing artifact, not documented behaviour.
- [SEC][STRM] The application account must have `jetstream: true` (here `APP`) for its users to create streams; the `$SYS` account is separate and used only for `server list`/`server report`.

## Regional and Cross Region Streams (Supercluster)
- path: examples/use-cases/cross-region-streams-supercluster
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/use-cases/cross-region-streams-supercluster/cli
- version context: recorded output shows nats-server 2.10.1

### Claims
- [USECASE][STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Use a supercluster of three regional clusters plus one dedicated cross-region cluster when you need streams that survive a regional failure by spreading replicas across three regions. "The use case is for streams that are resilient to regional failures by having replicas spread out across three different regions."
- [STRM][TOPO][ANTI] Cross-region replication costs latency; accept the trade-off only for streams that are critical for availability and can tolerate somewhat higher latency. "This of course comes at a cost of latency, but this trade-off may be appropriate for streams that are critical for availability, but can tolerate slightly higher latencies."
- [STRM][TOPO] `jetstream.unique_tag` forces all replicas of a given stream or consumer onto nodes whose value for that tag prefix differs; regional clusters use `unique_tag: "az:"` so replicas land in different availability zones. "the `unique_tag` option which enforces all replicas for a given stream or consumer to be placed on nodes with different availability zones (AZ)."
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] The cross-region cluster (`xr`) sets `unique_tag: "rg:"` so each replica lands in a different region; which AZ each of its nodes lives in does not matter as long as the region is unique. "The cross-region cluster defines a unique_tag on the cluster. Any AZ can be chosen as long as the region is unique."
- [STRM][TOPO] Nodes in the cross-region cluster carry both tags (`server_tags: [rg:1, az:1]`), one node per region chosen from an arbitrary AZ.
- [STRM][TOPO][SIZE][PATTERN] A three-node cross-region cluster has one node per region; if more AZs per region are wanted, a six- or nine-node cross-region cluster may be desirable. "If may be desirable to have a six or nine node cross-region cluster if more AZs per region are desired."
- [TOPO] The full gateway list (all four clusters, all nodes) is factored into one `gateway-routes.conf` included by every server's `gateway` block; each server still declares its own `gateway.name` and `port`.
- [TOPO][OPS] Every server needs a unique `server_name`, its own `jetstream.store_dir`, `server_tags`, a `cluster` block with the routes of its own cluster, and a `gateway` block naming its cluster.
- [OPS] Start servers one at a time with a short delay so the seed routes can come up and become healthy before the next node joins. "sleep a second in between so the seeds can startup and get healthy."
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Placement is chosen at stream creation: `--cluster=xr` places a stream on the cross-region cluster; `--cluster=rg2` places a regional stream in region 2. The stream is created from a client connected to rg1, so placement is independent of where the client is connected.
- [STRM][TOPO] Observed output: EVENTS (cluster xr, R3) got replicas `rg1-az1-x, rg2-az2-x, rg3-az3-x` (one per region); ORDERS (cluster rg2, R3) got replicas `rg2-az1, rg2-az2, rg2-az3` (one per AZ within the region).
- [TOPO][OPS] Observed output: `nats server info` on a supercluster member shows a `Super Cluster` section listing all gateway-connected cluster names (rg1, rg2, rg3, xr); each server shows `GWs 3` (one gateway to each other cluster) and `Routes 8`.
- [OPS][SIZE] Observed defaults in `nats server info` output (2.10.1): Max Payload 1.0 MiB, Max Conn 65,536, TLS Timeout 2.00s, Write Deadline 10.00s, JetStream "Always sync writes to disk: false", "Write sync Frequency: 2m0s".

## Regional and Cross Region Streams (Cluster)
- path: examples/use-cases/cross-region-streams-cluster
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/use-cases/cross-region-streams-cluster/cli
- version context: recorded output shows nats-server 2.10.1

### Claims
- [USECASE][STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] An alternative to the supercluster layout is a single nine-node cluster stretched across three regions with three AZs each; regional and cross-region placement is then done with tags rather than clusters. "Rather than a supercluster, this relies on a nine node cluster spread out across three regions and three availability zones each."
- [STRM][TOPO][SIZE] NATS placement tags cannot express logical OR or exclusive OR, so valid replica combinations must be precomputed and encoded as tags on the servers. "NATS does not currently support declaring tags with logical OR (or exclusive OR), so valid combinations can be precomputed as tags and then used when creating streams."
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Encode each valid cross-region combination as an `xr:` tag whose digit positions are regions and digit values are AZs; `xr:231` means one replica in region 1 AZ 2, one in region 2 AZ 3, one in region 3 AZ 1. "a tag `xr:231` can be read as a cross-region stream where one replica is placed in region 1 in AZ 2, another in region 2 in AZ 3, and the third replica in region 3 in AZ 1."
- [STRM][TOPO] The `xr:` scheme still satisfies `unique_tag: "az:"`, because each precomputed combination uses a different AZ in each region. "the `xr:` tag encodes the cluster/AZ combination while still adhering to the `unique_tag` requirement."
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Each server carries the plain `rg:` and `az:` tags in addition to its `xr:` tags so that regional streams can be placed with `--tag=rg:N`; `unique_tag: "az:"` then spreads the three replicas over the region's three AZs. "the standard `rg:` (region) and `az:` (AZ) tags are set to support _regional_ streams."
- [STRM][TOPO][SIZE] Each of the nine servers carries exactly two `xr:` tags (e.g. `rg1-az1` has `xr:123, xr:132`), so that every `xr:` combination matches exactly three servers, one per region.
- [STRM][TOPO] Observed output: `--tag=xr:123` placed EVENTS on `rg1-az1, rg2-az2, rg3-az3`; `--tag=rg:2` placed ORDERS on `rg2-az1, rg2-az2, rg2-az3`. The stream info reports these as `Placement Tags` rather than `Placement Cluster`.
- [TOPO][SIZE] Observed output: in a nine-node full-mesh cluster each server shows `Routes 32` and `GWs 0`; the seed routes list only three nodes and the rest discover each other.
- [TOPO][OPS] Only the three seed servers' route URLs are listed in the shared `cluster.conf`; every node includes the same routes and cluster name.

## Replace cluster nodes
- path: examples/operations/replace-cluster-nodes
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/operations/replace-cluster-nodes/shell

### Claims
- [OPS][USECASE] The rotate-nodes procedure exists to replace the underlying hardware of existing cluster nodes with minimal or no downtime. "The original use case was to replace the underlying hardware of existing nodes in a cluster. The goal is to minimize or remove the need for downtime."
- [OPS][PATTERN] Node replacement algorithm for a 3-node JetStream cluster: add a new node, put the old node in lame duck mode, then remove the old node as a Raft peer, which forces its replicas to be rescheduled onto the new node. "Remove `n0` which forces replicas to be scheduled on `n3`"
- [OPS][PATTERN] Replace one node at a time, in pairs: n3 replaces n0, n4 replaces n1, then reuse the original names/ports (n0, n1, n2 on new hardware) to replace n2, n3, n4 in turn.
- [OPS][CLNT][PATTERN] The reason to cycle back to the original names/ports is so the connection URLs clients already have stay addressable for reconnects; if every replacement had a new hostname or port, every client would need a config change. "This cycle is required so that the original connection URLs used by the clients remain addressable for if/when they need to reconnect. Otherwise if they were all new hostnames or ports, clients would need to update their local configuration."
- [OPS][STRM] Removing a peer is done with `nats server raft peer-remove --force <name>` using a system-account user; lame duck is signalled with `nats-server --signal ldm=<pidfile>`.
- [OPS][SIZE][ANTI] The demo waits only 60 s after lame-ducking and another 60 s after peer removal before the next node; this is described as aggressive and demo-only. In practice the wait depends on how much data must be migrated. "This script choose a fairly aggressive wait time (for demo purpsoes) of only 60 seconds ... In practice, the wait time would be dependent on how much data needs to be migrated."
- [OPS][CLNT] Expected client behaviour during rotation: some clients disconnect and reconnect automatically, and consumption may slow down. "Some will disconnect and reconnect automatically. There may be some slow down on consumption"
- [OPS][CLNT][PATTERN] Clients in the demo are given the full list of cluster URLs (`-s localhost:4222,localhost:4223,localhost:4224`) so they can fail over to another node when their current server goes lame duck.
- [OPS][TOPO] The new nodes n3 and n4 are configured with only a single seed route (n3 -> n2's route port, n4 -> n3's route port), showing that a joining node needs only one reachable existing peer to join the cluster.
- [OPS][STRM] Node configs set `pid_file` (used for signalling lame duck / stop) and per-node `jetstream.store_dir`, `max_memory_store` and `max_file_store` (1 GiB each in the demo).
- [OPS][SEC] The shared config declares `system_account: SYS`, a `USERS` account with `jetstream: enabled`, and `no_auth_user: user` so unauthenticated clients land in the application account while operations use the sys user.
- [STRM][OPS] The demo uses one R3 file stream (unlimited) and one R3 memory stream capped at 100k messages so that both storage types are exercised by the migration; both are watched via `nats stream report` and `nats consumer report` during migration.

## NATS Streaming to JetStream Migration
- path: examples/operations/stan2js
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/operations/stan2js/cli
- version context: docker-compose pins nats:2.10.3 and nats-streaming:0.25.3; Dockerfile pins stan2js v0.1.0, natscli v0.0.35

### Claims
- [MIG][STRM][CONS] The stan2js tool migrates NATS Streaming channels to JetStream streams and STAN subscriptions to JetStream consumers; it is a one-time exercise run once per set of channels. "This is a one time exercise and stan2js only needs to be run once for each set of STAN channels that require migration to JetStream streams."
- [MIG][SEC][PATTERN] The migration config names a NATS CLI context for the STAN side and one for the NATS side; if channels or subscriptions must go to different accounts, use multiple contexts. "if channels and/or subscriptions need to be migrated to different accounts, then multiple contexts can be used."
- [MIG][STRM] The stan2js config declares which channels and subscriptions to migrate plus a subset of stream/consumer options; the options are not exhaustive because many stream and consumer options can be changed after the migration. "These options are not exhaustive since many options on streams and consumers can be changed after the migration."
- [MIG][STRM] Per channel the config can set the target stream name and options such as `replicas`, `max_consumers`, `max_bytes`, `max_age`; per client subscription it can set the consumer name, whether to convert to pull (`pull: true`), and a queue name.
- [MIG][CONS] Observed output: a STAN durable subscription can be converted to a JetStream pull consumer (`CONVERTED TO PULL? true`), otherwise it becomes a push consumer; a STAN queue subscription becomes a queue (deliver-group) push consumer.
- [MIG][STRM] Observed output: STAN channel sequence numbers are re-based in JetStream (foo `501 -> 1`, `1000 -> 500`); the migrated streams contain only the messages the channel still held under its STAN `max_msgs` limit (500 for foo, 700 for bar, 1000 for baz).
- [MIG][STRM] Observed output: each migrated message carries headers `Nats-Streaming-Channel`, `Nats-Streaming-Sequence` and `Nats-Streaming-Timestamp` preserving the original STAN channel, sequence and publish time.
- [MIG][CONS] Observed output: subscription progress is preserved by mapping the STAN next sequence to the corresponding JetStream sequence (e.g. sub-foo `601 -> 101`, sub-bar `701 -> 401`); migrated consumers report Ack Policy Explicit and Ack Wait 30.00s.
- [MIG][OPS] After migration, verify with the NATS CLI: `stream report`, `stream view` to check headers and payloads, and `consumer report` to check consumer state. "Since the NATS CLI supports introspecting JetStream assets, we can use it to verify that the migration was successful."

- [SEC][OPS] A server always has an implicit system account, but by default it has no users, so no client can run administrative commands until one is defined. "Although there is an implicit system account created on the server, there are no _users_ associated with it, by default."

- [SEC][OPS] Adding or changing the `accounts` block can be applied with `nats-server --signal reload`, no restart required. "Simply reload the server with the `--signal` option."
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] You may use a differently named system account by defining any account and pointing `system_account:` at it; this is required for decentralized JWT auth. ## Private Inbox
- path: examples/auth/private-inbox
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/auth/private-inbox/cli

### Claims
- [CORE][SEC] All replies using the built-in request-reply pattern share the subject pattern `_INBOX.>`. "Replies to a request using the built-in request-reply pattern all share the same subject pattern `_INBOX.>`."
- [SEC][PATTERN] For multi-user applications needing isolation of messages inside one account, have each client connect with an explicit inbox prefix and combine it with explicit permissions so users cannot snoop on each other's service replies. "an explicit **inbox prefix** can be used when a client connects to the server. This combined with explicit permissions prevents users from _snooping_ on service replies."
- [SEC][CORE] A requesting user needs subscribe permission on its inbox subjects (`_INBOX.>` by default) or it cannot receive replies. "The `_INBOX.>` subscription permission is required in order to receive replies from a requester."
- [SEC][PATTERN] A service user can be limited to `sub.allow: [services.greet]` plus `allow_responses: true`, so it can only reply to requests it received rather than publish freely.
- [SEC] Declaring an explicit `sub.allow` list is an implicit deny of everything else: joe cannot subscribe to `pam.>` and vice versa. "A nice side effect of this is that now, joe and pam can't subscribe to each other's subjects (since an explicit allow has been declared)"
- [SEC][MYTH] Observed output: with `sub.allow: [_INBOX.>]`, pam subscribing to `_INBOX.>` receives the reply to joe's request. The text says this is expected: accounts are the isolation boundary; per-user granular permissions become necessary at scale. "This is actually expected and generally fine since _accounts_ are expected to be the isolation boundary, at a certain level of scale, creating users with granular permissions becomes increasingly necessary."
- [SEC][CORE] Inbox subjects are randomly generated, so by default there is no fixed set of subjects to grant per user; the client-side option is to choose an explicit inbox prefix other than `_INBOX`. "Sinces inboxes are randomly generated by the server, by default we can't pin down the specific set of subjects to provide permission to. However, as a client, there is the option of defining an explicit *inbox prefix* other than `_INBOX`."
- [SEC][ANTI] Observed output: connecting with `--inbox-prefix _INBOX_joe` while the user is only allowed `_INBOX.>` fails with `Permissions Violation for Subscription to "_INBOX_joe.<random>"`; the custom prefix must be in the user's subscribe allow list.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Per-user private inbox pattern: set each user's `sub.allow` to only `_INBOX_<user>.>` and have that user's client connect with the matching inbox prefix; then a user can subscribe neither to `_INBOX.>` nor to another user's prefix. "Now pam cannot subscribe to the general `_INBOX` nor joe's specific one since it does not have an explicit allow."
- [SEC][OPS] Permission changes in the config file are applied with `nats-server --signal reload=<pid>`; observed output shows subsequent subscribe attempts to `_INBOX.>` and `_INBOX_joe.>` by pam rejected with Permissions Violation while requests with the correct prefix succeed.

## Private Inbox using JWT
- path: examples/auth/private-inbox-jwt
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/auth/private-inbox-jwt/cli
- version context: nsc output says "make sure they run at least version 2.2.0"

### Claims
- [SEC] With nsc the service user is given `--allow-sub services.greet --allow-pub-response`; observed nsc output confirms `--allow-pub-response` sets `max responses to 1` (one reply per request).
- [SEC][ANTI] A JWT user with only publish allows and no explicit subscribe allow can still subscribe to `>`, so joe could subscribe to `pam.>`; add an explicit `--allow-sub` to close this. "Since we didn't set an explicit allow for subscriptions, these users can still subscribe to `>` which means joe could subscribe to `pam.>` and vice versa."
- [SEC][PATTERN] JWT version of the private-inbox fix: `nsc edit user --deny-sub '_INBOX.>' --allow-sub '_INBOX_<user>.>'`, i.e. explicitly deny the shared default prefix and allow only the user's own prefix. "we can deny the default one and allow for the custom one."
- [SEC][OPS] Every `nsc edit user` regenerates that user's `.creds` file; in the recorded run no server reload was needed for the new user permissions to take effect on the next connection (observed).
- [SEC] Creating an account with nsc is a two-step process: `nsc add account` then `nsc edit account --sk generate` to add a signing key. "It is currently a two-step process to create the account, followed by generating the signing key."

## Auth Callout - Centralized
- path: examples/auth/callout
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/auth/callout/cli
- version context: "Auth callout is a new feature in NATS v2.10.0"; recorded output nats-server 2.10.1

### Claims
- [SEC][MIG] Auth callout was introduced in nats-server v2.10.0 as an extension point for integrating alternative identity and access management (IAM) backends. "Auth callout is a new feature in NATS v2.10.0 providing an extension point for integrating with alternative identity and access management (IAM) backends."
- [SEC] Centralized (config-file) auth callout is configured under `authorization.auth_callout` with `issuer` (public account nkey that signs responses), `users` (the users in the auth account allowed to answer callouts), `account` (the account the callout service connects with), and optional `xkey` (public curve key enabling encryption).
- [SEC][PATTERN] The issuer nkey and xkey are normally generated with `nsc generate nkey --account` and `nsc generate nkey --curve`, or programmatically with an nkeys library; the example hardcodes them only for demonstration.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Use a dedicated `AUTH` account whose only user is the callout service; application users get bound into separate accounts (`APP`, `SYS`) by the service's response.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Implement the callout responder as a NATS micro service with endpoint `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH` so several instances can share load, expose stats, and give high availability. "This allows for running multiple instances to distribute the load, observe stats, and provide high availability."
- [SEC] When `xkey` is configured the server includes a `Nats-Server-Xkey` header and encrypts the request; the service must decrypt with its curve keypair and seal the response to the server's xkey. A service without a curve key should respond with an error ("xkey not supported").
- [SEC] The authorization response is an AuthorizationResponseClaims for the requesting user nkey, with `Audience` set to the server ID, containing either an error string or the issued user JWT, signed by the issuer keypair.
- [SEC] In non-operator (config) mode the issued user JWT sets `Audience` to the target account name and is signed with the issuer key. "Audience contains the account in non-operator mode." / "Sign it with the issuer key since this is non-operator mode."
- [SEC] The callout service can attach per-user permissions (pub/sub allow lists, `resp.max`) in the user JWT; the server enforces them. Observed output: bob publishing to `test` gets `Permissions Violation for Publish to "test"` while `bob.test` succeeds.
- [SEC] Observed output: an unknown user is rejected at connect with `Authorization Violation`; a callout-authorized user bound to the `SYS` account can run `nats server list`.
- [SEC] The Java variant of this example runs auth callout without the `xkey`, showing encryption is optional. "Encryption is not enabled in this example."

## Auth Callout - Decentralized
- path: examples/auth/callout-decentralized
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/auth/callout-decentralized/cli
- version context: "Auth callout is a new feature in NATS v2.10.0"

### Claims
- [SEC] In an existing JWT environment the operator/resolver bootstrapping step can be skipped; only the AUTH account and service need adding. "if this is an existing environment, this bootstrapping can be skipped."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Decentralized auth callout is enabled on an account with `nsc edit authcallout --account AUTH --curve <xkey> --auth-user <user pubkey> --allowed-account <...>`, then pushed to the server.
- [SEC][PATTERN] `--allowed-account` lists which accounts the callout service may bind authorized users to; `*` means any account, otherwise list account public nkeys. "The `--allowed-account` option is used to define which accounts this account is allowed to bind authorized users to. In this case, `*` indicates that any account can be bound."
- [SEC] Enabling auth callout does not break existing JWT users: observed output shows app1/app2 creds still publish after the AUTH account is pushed. "Confirm existing creds still work even with auth callout enabled."
- [SEC] The decentralized callout service needs three kinds of keys: creds for its own auth user, the AUTH account signing key to sign responses, and the signing key of every application account it is allowed to create users in. "we need the signing keys for the application accounts that the auth callout service is *allowed* to create and bind users to."
- [SEC] In operator mode the issued user JWT is signed with the target account's signing key and `IssuerAccount` is set to that account's public key (in non-operator mode the service instead sets `Audience` to the account name).
- [SEC][PATTERN] Clients must present a "sentinel" credential of the AUTH account (a user with `--deny-pubsub ">"`) together with their real username/password; the server uses the sentinel creds to delegate to the correct callout service. "The final requirement for clients to be able to connect is having a set of credentials of the AUTH acount which will be used to by the server to delegate to the correct auth callout service."
- [SEC][CLNT] The client connects with both `nats.UserCredentials(sentinel.creds)` and `nats.UserInfo(user, pass)`; the sentinel proves which account's callout to use and the user/pass are forwarded to the service.
- [SEC][OPS] Observed output: the service logs one "responding to authorization request" per connect and alice (bound to APP1) and bob (bound to APP2) both connect through the same AUTH account.

## Programmatic NKeys and JWTs
- path: examples/auth/nkeys-jwts
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/auth/nkeys-jwts/go

### Claims
- [SEC][PATTERN] nsc is the primary and recommended way to create and manage accounts and users; programmatic creation is for on-demand, application-level account/user workflows, and shelling out to nsc is another option. "The primary (and recommended) way to create and manage accounts and users is using the nsc command-line tool."
- [SEC] Not all client languages have standalone NKeys or JWT libraries. "not all languages currently implement standalone NKeys or JWT libraries."
- [SEC] The operator must exist ahead of time to configure the resolver in the server config; signing keys are technically optional but a best practice. "Signing keys are technically optional, but a best practice."
- [SEC] Public keys are prefixed O (operator), A (account), U (user); seeds (private keys) are prefixed S.
- [SEC][STRM][SIZE] The only requirement to enable JetStream for an account is setting its disk and memory storage limits to non-zero; -1 means unlimited. "The only requirement to "enable" JetStream is setting the disk and memory limits to anything other than zero. -1 indicates "unlimited"."
- [SEC] In an account JWT the `sub` field is the account public key and `iss` is the operator public key; in a user JWT `iss` is the account key.
- [SEC][OPS] A dynamically created account is activated by pushing its JWT to the server via a request to `$SYS.REQ.CLAIMS.UPDATE` from a connection authenticated as a SYS-account user.
- [SEC][ANTI] nsc stores and organizes every nkey and JWT for you; if you create accounts or users dynamically you must store and manage the keypairs and JWTs yourself. "If you opt to create accounts or users dynamically, keep in mind you need to store and manage the keypairs and JWTs yourself."
- [SEC] A creds file is the user JWT decorated with the user seed; the seed can sign and prove identity and must be treated as a secret (observed creds file banner).
- [SEC][SIZE] Observed default account claim limits: subs -1, data -1, payload -1, imports -1, exports -1, wildcards true, conn -1, leaf -1; user claims default subs -1 and payload -1, with `Limits.Data` settable (1 GiB in the example).

## Change Data Capture via Debezium
- path: examples/integrations/debezium
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/integrations/debezium/cli
- version context: docker-compose pins nats:2.10.5 and debezium/server:2.4.0.Final, debezium/postgres:16-alpine

### Claims
- [USECASE][STRM] Change data capture on a database streams granular change events to other parts of the system as data changes; Debezium handles the database-specific capture and Debezium Server can sink directly into a NATS stream. "stream granular change events to other parts of the system as data changes."
- [USECASE][STRM] For Postgres, Debezium registers itself as a logical-replication target, converts the raw change to a standard event model, and publishes to a NATS stream named `DebeziumStream` by default. "it publishes to the configured NATS stream, by default, called `DebeziumStream`."
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Each change event is published to a subject of the form `<prefix>.<schema>.<table>` (e.g. `postgres.public.test`), where the first token is the optional `debezium.source.topic.prefix`. "Each event is published to a subject corresponding to the Postgres schema and table, for example, `postgres.public.test`. The first token is an optional prefix specified in the Debezium configuration."
- [STRM] Sink configuration uses `debezium.sink.type=nats-jetstream`, `create-stream=true` (Debezium creates the stream itself) and `subjects=postgres.*.*` to match the prefix/schema/table subject shape.
- [STRM] Observed output: `nats stream subjects DebeziumStream` lists one subject per schema/table pair (`postgres.public.profile` 5 events, `postgres.public.books` 1 event), and each event payload carries `before`, `after`, `source` (db, schema, table, txId, lsn) and `op` (`c`, `u`, `d`).
- [STRM] Observed output: update events had `before: null` and delete events had `before` with only the id and null columns (the narrative does not comment on this; it is what the default Postgres setup produced).

## Mutual TLS

### Claims
- [SEC][OPS] An embedded server enforces mTLS by building its TLS config with `server.GenTLSConfig` from a server cert, key and CA file with `Verify: true`, so clients must present a certificate signed by that CA.
- [SEC][SIZE] The example sets the TLS handshake `Timeout` to 2 (seconds) in the embedded server's TLS options.

- [SEC][PATTERN] Development certs for mTLS can be produced with mkcert: a server cert for `localhost`, a client cert with `mkcert -client`, and the mkcert root CA used as the CA file for both sides. "This example relies on the mkcert tool ... to generate the necessary server and client certs."


## JetStream (category)
- path: examples/jetstream/meta.yaml
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream

### Claims
- [STRM] JetStream is "An integrated subsystem providing distributed persistence."

## Limits-based Stream
- path: examples/jetstream/limits-stream
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/limits-stream/go

### Claims
- [STRM][SUBJ] A stream binds a set of subjects; messages published to those subjects are persisted. "The mental model for a stream is that it binds a set of subjects for which messages published to those subjects will be persisted."
- [STRM][CORE] A stream is implemented as an implicit server-side service: the published message is the request and the reply comes once the message has been persisted. JetStream publish is therefore "a convenience for sending a `nc.Request` and waiting for the acknowledgement."
- [STRM][SIZE] Limits-based retention is the default retention policy, and limits still apply to streams with other retention policies. "This policy is the default, however, limits still apply to streams with other retention policies."
- [STRM][SIZE] The stream limit choices are: maximum number of messages, maximum total size in bytes, maximum age of a message.
- [STRM][SIZE] There is a separate per-subject maximum-messages limit ("a specialized maximum messages limit that can be applied at the subject level").
- [STRM][SIZE][ANTI] By default no limits are set, "which would require manually managing the ever-growing stream." Turn limits on and let the server truncate if any of them fit.
- [STRM] Stream configuration can be changed dynamically on demand; JetStream supports "dynamically changing the stream configuration on-demand."
- [STRM][PATTERN] Stream names are commonly uppercased to visually differentiate them from subjects, but this is not required.
- [STRM][SUBJ] A stream binds one or more subjects which "almost always include wildcards."
- [STRM][SUBJ][ANTI] No two streams can have overlapping subjects, "otherwise the primary messages would be persisted twice."
- [STRM][SIZE] JetStream offers file and in-memory storage; file storage is the default and is required for data to survive crashes and restarts. "For durability of the stream data, file storage must be chosen to survive crashes and restarts."
- [STRM][SIZE] By default a stream has one replica and uses file storage (deno narrative). "By default, a stream will have one replica and use file storage."
- [STRM][CLNT] Async publish batches messages to the server and receives acknowledgements asynchronously; a batch is awaited via PublishAsyncComplete.
- [STRM][SIZE] Setting MaxMsgs to 10 on a 12-message stream truncates the two oldest messages; first sequence and first timestamp then reflect the third message.
- [STRM][SIZE] Limits combine: "Limits can be combined and whichever one is reached, it will be applied to truncate the stream."
- [STRM][SIZE] Max age truncation is not instantaneous on config update; messages remain visible until the age elapses ("we still see all the messages.. until a second passes").
- [STRM][SIZE] Max age is expressed in nanoseconds in the JS client (deno narrative): "the age is in nanoseconds, so 1000 milliseconds (1 second) converted to nanos."
- [CLNT] Drain "is a safe way to ensure all buffered messages that were published are sent and all buffered messages received on a subscription are processed before closing the connection."

## Interest-based Stream
- path: examples/jetstream/interest-stream
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/interest-stream/go

### Claims
- [STRM] Interest retention "retains messages for as long as there are consumers which have interest in a particular message."
- [STRM][ANTI] With no consumers, published messages are immediately deleted from an interest stream. "By definition, they are immediately deleted from the stream since there are no consumers."
- [STRM][PATTERN][CORE] An interest stream is a middle ground between core NATS at-most-once QoS (all subscribers must be connected to receive) and a pure limits-based stream.
- [STRM][CONS] A message stays in an interest stream until, for each consumer whose filter overlaps it, a subscription bound to that consumer "successfully acks the message, terminates it, or the max redelivery has been reached."
- [STRM][SIZE][ANTI] Interest retention is additive to stream limits; with `max-msgs` = 1 and discard-old, each new message deletes the prior one "regardless if any of the consumer subscriptions were available to process the message."
- [STRM][PATTERN] If you need a stream that behaves as a queue, use a work-queue stream instead of an interest stream.
- [STRM][SIZE] Stream info on an empty interest stream after 3 publishes shows 0 messages, `last_seq` 3, and `first_seq` one greater than `last_seq`; first_seq "behaves as a sentinel value indicating the stream is empty."
- [STRM][CONS] Interest is established by the existence of a consumer, not by active consumption. "it is not required to be actively consuming messages to show interest, but it is the presence of a consumer which the stream cares about."
- [STRM][CONS] Each consumer is a separate view over the stream; if one consumer acked but another did not, the message is retained.
- [STRM][CONS][ANTI] A late consumer cannot retroactively show interest; messages deleted before it was created are gone. "this reinforces that a late consumer cannot retroactively show interest."
- [STRM][CONS] Interest respects the consumer's FilterSubject: a consumer filtered to `events.mouse_clicked` is not interested in `events.input_focused`, so that message's retention depends only on consumers whose filter overlaps.
- [CONS] Term (terminate) counts the same as ack for releasing interest. "Fetch and term (also works) and ack from the first consumers that do have interest."
- [CONS][CLNT] DoubleAck/AckSync is used "to ensure the stream state has been synced up for this subsequent retrieval" before reading stream info.

## Work-queue Stream
- path: examples/jetstream/workqueue-stream
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/workqueue-stream/go

### Claims
- [STRM][USECASE] Work-queue retention is for "queuing up messages that are intended to be processed once and only once."
- [STRM] Work-queue retention decouples queuing from consumption: it "supports queuing up messages from publishers independent of consummption."
- [STRM][CONS][ANTI] Consumers on a work-queue stream must have non-overlapping (disjoint) filter subjects, unlike limits- and interest-based streams which support overlapping consumers. "if multiple consumers are bound to a work-queue stream, they must have disjoint filter subjects."
- [STRM][SIZE][ANTI] Work-queue retention is additive to limits: with `max-msgs` = 1 and discard-old, every new message deletes the prior one regardless of whether any subscription processed it.
- [STRM] Messages in a work-queue stream are removed once acked; after fetching and acking all queued messages, stream info shows no messages.
- [STRM][CONS][ANTI] A work-queue stream allows "at most one consumer with interest on a subject at any given time"; creating a second unfiltered consumer fails until the first is deleted.
- [STRM][CONS][PATTERN] To run multiple consumers on a work-queue stream, give each a subject filter scoping it to a disjoint subset (example: `events.us.>` and `events.eu.>` per geo).

## Pull Consumers
- path: examples/jetstream/pull-consumer
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/pull-consumer/go

### Claims
- [CONS][PATTERN] A pull consumer lets the application fetch messages on demand, so "the application [can] control the flow of the messages coming in so it can process and ack them in an appropriate amount of time."
- [CONS] A durable consumer has its state tracked on the server, "most importantly, the last acknowledged message from the client."
- [CONS][PATTERN] Ephemeral consumers are "useful as one-off needs and are a bit cheaper in terms of resources and management"; they do not persist after the primary subscriber unsubscribes and the server auto-deletes them after a period of time.
- [CONS][SIZE] Without a durable name a consumer is removed after InactiveThreshold, which defaults to 5 seconds, when not actively consuming. "consumer will be removed after InactiveThreshold (defaults to 5 seconds) is reached when not actively consuming messages."
- [CONS] Consumer `Name` is optional; if not provided it is auto-generated.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Multiple subscriptions can bind to the same pull consumer without additional configuration; each subscriber fetches batches and processes them concurrently.
- [CONS][ANTI] Messages within one batch are ordered relative to each other, but each subscriber handles its batch independently, so cross-subscriber order is not guaranteed. For deterministic partitioning "for scalable order processing" the text points to deterministic subject token partitioning (subject mapping).
- [CONS][SIZE] The fetch batch size is the maximum number of messages that may be returned, not a guaranteed count.
- [CONS][CLNT] Fetch's Messages() channel closes only when the requested number of messages has been received or the operation times out; FetchNoWait returns whatever is available up to the batch size without waiting.
- [CONS][SIZE] A fetch at the end of the stream blocks until the max wait, "which is 5 seconds by default, but this can be set explicitly as an option."
- [CONS] Durable consumers are never removed automatically regardless of InactiveThreshold; they must be deleted explicitly with DeleteConsumer.
- [CONS] Ack after processing "so they are not redelivered."
- [CONS] (deno narrative) The new consumer API is pull-based; an ordered consumer is an ephemeral consumer "that guarantees that messages are delivered in order" and is managed under the covers given only the stream name.

## Pull Consumer - Applying Limits
- path: examples/jetstream/pull-consumer-limits
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/pull-consumer-limits/go

### Claims
- [CONS][SIZE] Server-enforced pull consumer limits include: max non-acked in-flight messages, max in-flight pull requests (across subscribers), max pull batch size per request, max timeout on a pull request, and max total bytes of a pulled batch.
- [CONS] Batch size and timeout can be set and changed per fetch request and can differ across subscribers.
- [CONS][ANTI] Consumer configuration can be changed on demand, with one exception: `MaxWaiting` "cannot be updated on a consumer as of now. This must be set up front when the consumer is created."
- [CONS][SIZE] MaxAckPending limits un-acked in-flight messages across all subscriptions bound to the consumer; with MaxAckPending=1 a fetch for 3 returns 1 and the next fetch times out with nothing until that message is acked. "This essentially forces serial processing messages for a pull consumer."
- [CONS][SIZE][PATTERN] MaxRequestBatch caps the batch size of any one fetch; requesting more than the limit is an error. "This can be used to keep the fetches to a reasonable size."
- [CONS][SIZE][PATTERN] MaxWaiting limits the number of fetch requests waiting in parallel; "This prevents building up too many requests that the server will have to distribute to for a given consumer." Extra concurrent fetches beyond the limit error.
- [CONS][SIZE][PATTERN] MaxRequestExpires caps the per-fetch max wait "to prevent requests waiting too long for messages"; a fetch with a longer timeout returns immediately with an error, while one equal or less works.
- [CONS][SIZE] MaxRequestMaxBytes caps the total bytes of a pulled batch; a FetchBytes over the limit errors.

## Push Consumers (legacy)
- path: examples/jetstream/push-consumer
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/push-consumer/go

### Claims
- [CONS] With a push consumer the server proactively pushes messages to the active subscription "up to the consumer's max ack pending limit," rather than the client fetching sized batches.
- [CONS] Happy path: the subscription keeps up and acks before ack wait elapses.
- [CONS][ANTI] Push consumers "can get unwieldy and confusing" when the subscriber cannot keep up, processing errors occur, or the subscription is interrupted: redeliveries interleave with newly pushed messages.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Ephemeral push consumers are "a lightweight and useful way to do one-off consumption of a subset of messages in a stream."
- [CONS][PATTERN] For durable use cases, "it is recommended to access pull consumers first which provides more control and implicit support for scaling out consumption."
- [CONS][SIZE] The maximum number of messages a push subscription buffers is set by `MaxAckPending`; "The default is 1,000."
- [CONS][CLNT] Push subscription messages are pre-buffered asynchronously, so the client-side pending count "may or may not be" the number published.
- [CONS] By default the underlying consumer requires explicit acks, "otherwise messages will get redelivered."
- [CONS][CLNT] Unsubscribing an ephemeral push subscription deletes the consumer; even if omitted, the server eventually cleans up the ephemeral when it determines the subscription is no longer active.
- [CONS][ANTI][CLNT] Helper-created durables (SubscribeSync with nats.Durable) are deleted when `Unsubscribe` or `Drain` is called: "these helpers should only be used if neither of those methods are called."
- [CONS][PATTERN] "A more explicit and safer way to create durables is using `js.AddConsumer`"; push consumers require a `DeliverSubject`.
- [CONS][ANTI] Subscriptions bound to a consumer "cannot independently define their own subject to filter on"; the filter lives on the consumer.
- [CONS][CLNT] On unsubscribe (or client crash), pending buffered messages are effectively dropped client-side; the server waits `AckWait` before redelivering, and "will only re-deliver if there is an active subscription."
- [CONS][MYTH] Consumer info tracks the last stream sequence a delivery was attempted for and a separate consumer sequence per delivery attempt; "These should not be treated as correlated since the consumer sequence for a given message will increment on each delivery attempt."
- [CONS] "num ack pending" counts delivered messages awaiting ack; "num redelivered" is zero while each message has been delivered only once.
- [CONS] A new subscription bound before AckWait expires gets a timeout because messages are still pending; after AckWait the message is redelivered with delivery attempt 2.

## Queue Push Consumers (legacy)
- path: examples/jetstream/queue-push-consumer
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/queue-push-consumer/go

### Claims
- [CONS][CORE] A queue push consumer is analogous to a core NATS queue group but for streams; a standard push consumer "only supports a single bound subscription at any time," while a queue push consumer supports multiple bound subscriptions.
- [CONS] Messages are "distributed randomly among active subscribers which can freely come and go."
- [CONS][MIG][ANTI] As of NATS server v2.8.4, ephemeral queue push consumers are not supported; the server does not track them and auto-cleans up when no subscriptions are bound. If you create a durable and your program crashes before deleting it, check for it on startup.
- [CONS][CORE] Internally the `DeliverGroup` corresponds to a core NATS queue group name; a plain core NATS queue subscription on the DeliverSubject + DeliverGroup can join the group.
- [CONS] `DeliverSubject` is randomly generated by default but can be set explicitly in the consumer config.
- [CONS][ANTI] With a group of subscriptions each receives a different subset; messages can be processed out of order, there is no correlation between message order and subscription creation order, and "it is possible that not all subscriptions will necessarily get a message."
- [CONS][ANTI] Helper-created queue push consumers are deleted when any subscription unsubscribes or drains.
- [CONS] With AddConsumer, both a durable name and a deliver group must be defined: the durable name is used for all consumer types while the deliver group is exclusive to queue push consumers; using the same name for both is a convention.
- [CONS][CLNT] Core NATS subscriptions are JetStream-unaware, so `msg.Ack` must be called explicitly; a `js.QueueSubscribe` handler auto-acks by default unless `nats.ManualAck` is supplied.

## Multi-Stream Consumption (legacy)
- path: examples/jetstream/multi-stream-consumption
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/multi-stream-consumption/go

### Claims
- [CONS][STRM][PATTERN] To fan in messages across multiple streams, create a push consumer per stream with the same `DeliverSubject` and optionally the same `DeliverGroup`; each consumer then delivers to the clients subscribed to that subject and/or queue group.
- [CONS][SEC][PATTERN] Sharing one deliver subject across streams is "a straightforward way to do this in a single account. It is recommended a user is created with specific permissions to subscribe to this subject."
- [CONS][CORE] A plain core NATS queue subscription on the shared deliver subject receives messages from both streams and can ack them; each stream's consumer state updates independently.

## Migration to new JetStream API
- path: examples/jetstream/api-migration
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/api-migration/go

### Claims
- [MIG][CONS] The new JetStream API "removes the complexity of `Subscribe()` in favor of more explicit separation of creating consumers and consuming messages."
- [MIG][CONS][PATTERN] The new API "focuses on using Pull Consumers as the primary means of consuming messages from a stream."
- [MIG][CONS] The legacy API supported pull consumers only in limited capacity: "it was not possible to retrieve messages from a stream in a continuous fashion."
- [MIG][CONS] With `Consume`, `Fetch` and `Next`, users choose how to consume depending on use case.
- [MIG][CONS][ANTI] In the legacy API the only way to continuously receive messages is push consumers; `Subscribe()` "leads to complications because it implicitly creates and manages underlying consumers."
- [MIG][CONS][ANTI] Unsubscribing a legacy `Subscribe()` subscription deletes the underlying consumer it created; `AddConsumer` "is the only way to create a consumer in the legacy API which will not be deleted when the subscription is unsubscribed."
- [MIG][CONS] Legacy `Subscribe()` performs stream lookup by subject by default; `BindStream` skips that lookup.
- [MIG][CONS][ANTI] Legacy push subscriptions hide complexity and need many options; "when using push consumers, there is no simple way to rate limit the message delivery, which leads to slow consumer errors."
- [MIG][CONS][ANTI] Legacy pull consumers "are greatly limited in functionality since it is only possible to pull a specific number of messages, without any optimization or coordination between pulls," making them inefficient versus push.
- [MIG][CLNT][ANTI] Because all legacy `Subscribe*` methods return the same `Subscription` interface, "it is very easy to encounter runtime errors by e.g. calling `NextMsg` on a subscription created with `PullSubscribe` or `Subscribe`."
- [MIG][CONS] The new API "does not auto-create consumers"; consumers must be created or retrieved explicitly, giving control over the consumer lifecycle and removing the hidden logic of `Subscribe()`.
- [MIG][CONS] Pull consumers do not need a `DeliverSubject`.
- [MIG][CONS] Stopping `Consume()`/`Messages()` in the new API does not delete the consumer, unlike legacy `Unsubscribe()`; the server deletes it when `InactiveThreshold` is reached.
- [CONS] An ephemeral short-lived consumer is made by setting a low `InactiveThreshold` and no name; `InactiveThreshold` "can be omitted for durable consumers."
- [CONS] `FilterSubject` on a consumer "is equivalent to providing a subject to `Subscribe` in the legacy API."
- [CONS][CLNT] `Messages()` still pre-fetches messages but returns them on `Next` instead of a handler.
- [CONS] `Next` works like `Fetch(1)`.
- [STRM][CONS][ANTI] "deleting a stream will also delete all consumers on that stream."
- [MIG][CONS] (deno narrative) Legacy `subscribe()` created the consumer if it did not exist and updated it if options differed; the new API only supports pull consumers, so an existing push consumer "will have to [be] recreate[d] as a pull consumer."
- [CONS][ANTI] (deno) "Durable consumers are not deleted, will consume resources forever if not managed."
- [CONS][ANTI] (deno) With legacy push on streams with huge message counts, missing options caused "slow consumers, or ... a consumer that cannot be horizontally scaled."
- [CONS][PATTERN] (deno) The different consumption methods exist "to help you align the buffering requirements of your application with what the client is doing"; consume defaults "are safe," but "you can ask for as many messages as you will be able to process within your ack window."
- [CONS][PATTERN] (deno) Delete a consumer preemptively "only if you know you are not going to need that consumer to resume processing."
- [CONS][PATTERN] (deno) Services typically process one message at a time; "instead of optimizing a client to pull many messages for processing, you can horizontally scale the number of process that work on just one message."

## Consumer - Fetch Messages
- path: examples/jetstream/consumer-fetch-messages
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/consumer-fetch-messages/java

### Claims
- [CONS][PATTERN] "Although you can make consumers on the fly, typically consumers will be created ahead of time."
- [CONS][CLNT] A FetchConsumer has no stop; "the fetch stops by itself." The new fetch "does not block before returning the entire batch," and returns null once there are no more messages to consume.
- [CONS] A consumer with `filterSubject` `events.1` on a stream with 4 messages reports 2 pending; the filter determines what the consumer sees.

## Subject-Mapped Partitions
- path: examples/jetstream/partitions
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/partitions/cli

### Claims
- [STRM][TOPO] "A stream provides total order over the set of messages it stores." With replicas, each stream has a dedicated Raft group that replicates every published message to a majority of the replica servers.
- [STRM] On a successful publish every replica has the same order of messages, and consumers always receive messages in stored order.
- [STRM][PATTERN][SIZE] A single serialized stream is highly performant; to scale out publishing or consumption, create N streams each representing a partition. "The trade-off introduced here is the ability to support concurrent publishes to N streams, while giving up total order across streams."
- [SUBJ][STRM][PATTERN] Deterministic distribution of messages to a partition stream uses subject mapping with `partition(N, token)` (deterministic subject token partitioning); `events.*` mapped to `events.{{wildcard(1)}}.{{partition(5,1)}}` maps `events.1` to `events.1.4`, a partition number in 0..4.
- [SUBJ] More than one token can feed the partition function; if a `>` wildcard is needed, at least one `*` token is required for partitioning, e.g. `"events.*.>": "events.{{partition(5,1)}}.{{wildcard(1)}}.>"`.
- [SUBJ][SEC] Mappings are defined per account in server config; with decentralized auth, mappings can be defined on account JWTs via `nsc`.
- [SUBJ][OPS] The CLI `nats server mapping` command tests a mapping against sample subjects before deploying it.
- [STRM][SIZE] Each partition stream binds `events.*.<i>`; published messages are transparently routed and written to the partition stream, and `nats stream report` shows them spread across all streams.
- [STRM][SIZE][ANTI] Synchronous publish (one ack per message) gives quite low throughput; async batch of 100 raises it; 5 concurrent publishers raise it a bit more. "throughput and latency will highly depend on the quality of the network, and the resources available on the servers."
- [OPS][SIZE] The NBE benchmark numbers came from a GitHub Actions runner with 2 CPU cores and 7GB memory hosting 3 servers and 5 R3 streams plus the CLI; "true performance will suffer in comparison to a production setup."

## List Subjects for a Specific Stream
- path: examples/jetstream/list-subjects
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/list-subjects/go

### Claims
- [STRM][SUBJ] Stream state includes a map of subjects to message counts, "but the server only collects and returns that information if WithSubjectFilter is set with a non-empty subject filter." Use `>` to get all subjects.
- [STRM][SUBJ] The subject map lists actual published subjects, not the wildcard templates the stream was configured with. "Wildcard subjects show the actual subject, not the template."
- [STRM][SUBJ] A subject only appears in state once it has messages (deno: "there are no subjects in the state unless there are messages in the subject").
- [STRM][SUBJ] The subject filter narrows the map to matching entries (e.g. `greater.>` or `greater.A.>`).

## Confirmed Message Ack
- path: examples/jetstream/ack-ack
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/jetstream/ack-ack/go

### Claims
- [CONS] A confirmed ack "means that the client waits for an ack from the server to ensure that the ack was received and processed."
- [CONS][CLNT] Client naming: "ack ack" (JavaScript), "double ack" (Rust, C# .NET V2), "ack sync" (Go, Python, Java, C).
- [CONS] "Any stream can work with confirmed acks."
- [CONS][ANTI] A standard ack does not wait for server confirmation; "If server is experiencing high load, or the connection is severed before the ack is received, the ack can be lost, leading to a redelivery."
- [CONS][CLNT][MYTH] An error from a plain Ack "only means that the client failed to send the ack message. There will be no error if the client published the ack, but the server did not receive (or process) it."
- [CONS][PATTERN] A confirmed ack "allows us to react to the ack being lost by sending it again, potentially avoiding redelivery"; its error can mean the ack failed to send or the server failed to confirm.
- [CONS] Consumer info shows NumPending decrease on receive and NumAckPending go to 1 until the ack; after ack, NumAckPending returns to 0.

## Key-Value (category)
- path: examples/kv/meta.yaml
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/kv

### Claims
- [KV][STRM] Key-Value is "A layer on top of JetStream for utilizing a stream as a key-value store."

## Key-Value Intro
- path: examples/kv/intro
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/kv/intro/go

### Claims
- [KV][STRM] KV "is an abstraction over a stream which models message subjects as keys. It uses a standard set of stream configuration to be optimized for KV workloads."
- [KV] Unlike most KV stores, a revision number of each entry is tracked.
- [KV][PATTERN] Revisions enable optimistic concurrency control: with multiple concurrent writers, `Update` with an expected revision prevents non-deterministic "last writer wins"; the value is updated only if the revision matches on the server.
- [KV][STRM] A KV bucket is "light abstraction over a standard stream. This is by design since it enables some powerful features." Internally a stream is created with the `KV_` prefix by convention.
- [KV][SUBJ] KV subjects are: a reserved first token, the bucket name as second token, then the key as the suffix. "The bucket name is inherently a namespace for all keys and thus there is no concern for conflict across buckets," unlike a stream binding public subjects.
- [KV][STRM] Because a bucket is a normal stream, a consumer can be created on it and each Put arrives as a stream message.
- [KV] A Delete produces a new message and a new revision; delete messages carry a `KV-Operation: DEL` header to distinguish deletion from a nil value.
- [KV][PATTERN] Use a `KeyWatcher` rather than subscribing to the stream directly; it yields `KeyValueEntry` values "which exposes more KV-specific information than the raw stream message ... (so this API is recommended)." Watch supports wildcards on keys.
- [KV] A watcher first delivers existing values (deno: "the watcher by default shows the last value for all the keys"), then a nil entry marking that it has "caught up with the current updates before tracking the new ones."
- [KV][MYTH] The revision of a new key is not 1: revisions are the underlying stream sequence, "always monotonically increasing, but numbers will be shared across keys (like subjects) rather than sequence numbers relative to each key."

## Object-Store (category)
- path: examples/os/meta.yaml
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/os

### Claims
- [OBJ][STRM] Object-Store is "A layer on top of JetStream for utilizing a stream as an object store."

## Object-Store Intro
- path: examples/os/intro
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/os/intro/deno

### Claims
- [OBJ][STRM] Object store is "an abstraction over a stream which models message subjects as keys similar to KV, but with payloads that span multiple chunks," for larger assets "typically loaded and read as readable/writable streams."
- [OBJ][SIZE] The server's default max payload is "about 1MiB"; a 10MiB object works because the client "automatically splits data into multiple chunks and stores it" as multiple stream messages and reassembles on read.
- [OBJ] Entries consist of metadata (name, description) plus payload, so information about the object is stored separately from the raw data; metadata can be updated directly.
- [OBJ][PATTERN] Because assets may be large, the object store "normally presents a 'Stream' based API" (readable streams) rather than whole-blob calls.
- [OBJ][ANTI] When reading via a readable stream, an error can occur mid-read, so "when you think you are done reading, you must check if there was an error" and discard staged data on error.
- [OBJ][ANTI] Destroying an object store means "the data is gone forever."
- [OBJ][SIZE] (java narrative) Chunk size defaults to 128K and is configurable (32K shown); "Setting chunk size is important to consider ... if you know you are on a connection with limited bandwidth or your server has been configured to only accept smaller messages."
- [OBJ][CLNT] (java narrative) Object store watch "currently uses a push consumer under the covers," so large objects may generate flow-control warnings; "These are just warnings."

## Services Framework (category)
- path: examples/services/meta.yaml
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/services

### Claims
- [CORE][PATTERN] The Services Framework is "A layer on top of core NATS for building services in a simple and consistent way."

## Services Intro
- path: examples/services/intro
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/services/intro/go

### Claims
- [CORE][PATTERN] The services framework "automatically places all subscriptions in a queue group and provides functionality for building subject hierarchies and their handlers."
- [CORE][OPS] The framework enables automatic service discovery and status reporting without extra effort; `nats micro` queries and reports all framework services.
- [CORE] A service definition is name (no whitespace), version, and description; "Even with no running endpoints, this service is discoverable via the micro protocol." Default background handlers for discovery, PING, and stats start at creation.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Each service instance gets a unique ID; multiple copies with the same name are treated as instances of one service, and because endpoint subscriptions are queue-subscribed "requests will only be sent to one endpoint instance at a time."
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Groups are namespaces used as subject prefixes for endpoints; (deno) reserving a root subject like `minmax` "will prevent polluting the subject space," and groups can be nested and mixed with endpoints.
- [CORE] Each endpoint is a subscription; requests to service endpoints are ordinary NATS requests, "nothing special about this request."
- [OPS] Per-endpoint statistics (e.g. request counts) are tracked by the framework with no application code.
- [OPS][SUBJ] (deno) Service APIs live on `$SRV.PING`, `$SRV.INFO`, `$SRV.STATS`; appending the service name narrows scope (`$SRV.PING.minmax`) and appending the ID targets one instance. `info` is a superset of `ping` (adds endpoints); `stats` reports per endpoint.

## Messaging (category)
- path: examples/messaging/meta.yaml
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/messaging

### Claims
- [CORE] Core messaging comprises pub-sub, request-reply, and queue groups.

## Core Publish-Subscribe
- path: examples/messaging/pub-sub
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/messaging/pub-sub/cli

### Claims
- [CORE] Publish-subscribe "is the fundamental pattern that all other NATS patterns and higher-level APIs build upon."
- [CORE] Core delivery is at-most-once; "For MQTT users, this is referred to as Quality of Service (QoS) 0."
- [CORE][ANTI] A published message is not delivered when the subscriber has no active connection (temporarily offline) or when a network interruption drops the message.
- [SUBJ] Messages are published to subjects of one or more concrete tokens (e.g. `greet.bob`); subscribers use wildcards to express interest in a set of subjects.
- [CORE] Publishing with no subscriber succeeds but nothing is delivered; a subscription created after a publish does not receive that earlier message.
- [CLNT] (go narrative) Once a subscription is established, published messages are immediately broadcast to all subscriptions and land in their buffer for subsequent NextMsg calls.
- [OPS] The `nats` CLI uses `NATS_URL` if set; `nats context` manages named connection/auth contexts.

## Request-Reply
- path: examples/messaging/request-reply
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/messaging/request-reply/go

### Claims
- [CORE][PATTERN] A request is either a command ("an intention for service to carry out some work that results in a state change") or a query ("a request for information").
- [CORE][MYTH] "Unlike request-reply constrained protocols like HTTP, NATS is not limited to a strict point-to-point interaction"; request-reply is built on publish-subscribe.
- [CORE] By default any one subscriber can be the responder; the client can also indicate to NATS that multiple replies should be allowed.
- [CORE] If no subscribers are available to handle the request, the standard "no responders" error is returned.
- [CORE] Request-reply "is just an optimized pair of publish-subscribe operations"; a request handler is a subscription that responds, called a service.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] A request must specify a timeout "since with a request we are waiting for the reply and we likely don't want to wait forever."

## JSON for Message Payloads
- path: examples/messaging/json
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/messaging/json/go

### Claims
- [CORE] A NATS message is the subject, an application-defined payload, optional headers, and for requests a reply-to subject. "The payload is a sequence of bytes, so it is up to the application to define how to serialize and deserialize the payload."
- [CORE][PATTERN] JSON is a ubiquitous, simple interchange format supported in virtually all languages.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] If deserialization into the expected type fails, handle it by discarding or decoding into a more general type (e.g. a map/empty interface).

## Protobuf for Message Payloads
- path: examples/messaging/protobuf
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/messaging/protobuf/go

### Claims
- [CORE] "NATS message payloads are byte slices, so any kind of serialization strategy can be applied."
- [CORE][PATTERN] Message types can be defined in the Protocol Buffers IDL, code-generated per language, and used as request/reply payloads over NATS.

## Concurrent Message Processing
- path: examples/messaging/concurrent
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/messaging/concurrent/java

### Claims
- [CLNT] "By default, when a subscription is created, each message that is received it process sequentially."
- [CORE][PATTERN] Multiple subscriptions in a queue group let the server distribute messages across group members.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Even within a single subscription, messages can be handled concurrently in clients that support it (Java: multiple dispatchers each on its own thread joined to one queue group; Rust/Python: concurrent iteration with a limit of 25 in-flight operations so a slow message does not block receiving the next).

## Iterating Over Multiple Subscriptions
- path: examples/messaging/iterating-multiple-subscriptions
- url: https://natsbyexample.com/examples/messaging/iterating-multiple-subscriptions/java

### Claims
- [SUBJ][CORE] Wildcards cannot express an arbitrary subset of subjects (e.g. `transport.cars`, `transport.planes`, `transport.ships` but not `transport.spaceships`); separate subscriptions are needed. (rust) A core subscribe covers many subjects via `>`/`*` "but not to two or more distinct subjects."
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Separate subscriptions are "performant, but not very convenient when reading"; merge them into one message stream client-side (Java: one dispatcher with several subjects; Rust: stream select/merge).
- [CLNT] (java) A Dispatcher runs on its own thread, receives messages via a FIFO queue for its registered subjects, and makes a blocking call to the handler for each message.


## JetStream Deep Dive
- path: learn/jetstream/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream

### Claims
- [STRM][CONS] JetStream is the part of NATS that stores messages; stored messages can be read again later and replayed as many times as needed. "Once a message is stored, you can read it again later, and replay it as many times as you need."
- [CONS] Delivery is tracked per reader; a message counts as handled only once it is acknowledged. "Delivery is tracked per reader: a message counts as handled once it's acknowledged."
- [OPS] JetStream must be enabled on the server (`nats-server -js`) before any stream can be created.

## Your first stream
- path: learn/jetstream/your-first-stream.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/your-first-stream

### Claims
- [CORE][STRM][MYTH] Plain core NATS drops a message the moment no service is listening; a stream saves it instead. "Plain core NATS drops any of these messages the moment no service is listening. A stream saves them instead."
- [STRM] A stream is a server-side store that keeps every message on the subjects you choose, readable minutes or a month later.
- [STRM][SIZE] Stream names are case-sensitive and cannot contain dots, `*`, `>`, spaces, or slashes. "They can't contain dots, `*`, `>`, spaces, or slashes, so a subject like `orders.created` won't work as a name."
- [STRM][SUBJ] A stream bound to a wildcard such as `orders.>` captures any current or future subject under that prefix with no stream change. "So would `orders.refunded` next month, with no change to the stream."
