- [OPS][MYTH] A `no responders available for request` error on stream creation means the server was started without `-js`; JetStream isn't running.
- [STRM][SIZE] Default stream config: Replicas 1, Storage File, Retention Limits, Discard Policy Old, Duplicate Window 2m0s, all Maximum limits (Messages, Per Subject, Bytes, Age, Message Size, Consumers) unlimited.
- [STRM][CLNT] The CLI turns Direct Get on by default when creating a stream; client libraries leave it off unless you set it. "The CLI turns direct get on by default, so that line shows here; client libraries leave it off unless you set it."
- [STRM][SIZE] A new stream is empty and the first message published gets sequence 1.
- [STRM][TOPO][ANTI] Replicas 1 means the stream lives on one server and goes down with it; fine on a laptop, risky in production. "If that server goes down, the stream goes down with it."
- [STRM] Storage File writes messages to disk; memory storage is faster but lost on restart. "The other option is memory, which is faster but lost on restart."
- [STRM] Retention Limits keeps messages until a size, age, or count limit is hit; Interest and WorkQueue delete messages once a consumer has read them.
- [STRM] Discard Policy Old deletes the oldest messages to make room when a limit is hit; Discard New turns away new messages when the stream is full.
- [STRM][PATTERN] On a real cluster you'd always set at least one of Maximum Messages / Bytes / Age / Message Size. "On a real cluster you'd always set at least one of these."
- [STRM][SIZE] Duplicate Window default is 2 minutes: for that long after a message is stored, the server turns away a second message carrying the same `Nats-Msg-Id` header.
- [STRM][SUBJ] Only one stream can keep a given subject; creating a second stream whose subjects overlap is rejected with error 10065 "subjects overlap with an existing stream".
- [STRM][SUBJ] The overlap check covers any overlap, not just an identical filter: with `orders.>` taken, `orders.*` or even the single subject `orders.created` is rejected the same way.
- [STRM][SUBJ] The single-stream-per-subject rule exists so JetStream always knows which stream a message on a subject goes into.
- [STRM][PATTERN] To keep overlapping subjects in more than one stream, use mirrors (copy of one other stream) and sources (pull from several streams into one).
- [ANTI][STRM][OPS] Unlimited defaults grow forever: with `--defaults` the stream keeps every message until the disk fills, and a full disk takes the server down. "a production stream needs at least one limit so old orders age out before the disk does."
- [ANTI][STRM] A stream name is permanent; there is no rename, and the server rejects any update that changes the name with `stream configuration name must match original`. "The only way to 'rename' `ORDERS` is to delete it and create a new stream, which loses every order already stored."
- [STRM][PATTERN] If you outgrow a stream name, add a new stream on new subjects and let the old one age out rather than delete-and-recreate.

## Publishing
- path: learn/jetstream/publishing.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/publishing
- version context: atomic batch publish server 2.12+; fast-ingest batch publish server 2.14+

### Claims
- [STRM][CLNT] Publishing into a stream works like a normal NATS publish except the server sends back a `PubAck` confirmation that it stored the message.
- [CLNT][MYTH] A plain `nats pub` is a core NATS publish and the server returns nothing; use `--jetstream` to get the confirmation.
- [STRM][SIZE] Stream sequence numbers start at 1, only increase, and are never reused. "Sequence numbers start at `1` and only increase. The server gives each new message the next number and never reuses one."
- [CLNT][STRM] You publish to a subject, not to a stream; the server finds the stream that captures the subject. "Your code doesn't need to know which stream is bound to which subject."
- [STRM] A `PubAck` has three regularly-used fields: stream, sequence, duplicate; it may also carry situational fields such as `domain` for multi-tenant or leaf-node setups.
- [PATTERN][STRM] Saving the PubAck sequence next to your business record lets you replay the stream from that point later.
- [STRM][CLNT] The `PubAck` is your only proof that the message was stored. "The rule: the `PubAck` is your only proof that the message was stored."
- [CLNT][STRM] A publish to a subject no stream captures fails immediately with "no responders" and nothing was stored; a network timeout means no confirmation, not no write. "the server may have stored the message and the ack got lost on the way back."
- [PATTERN][CLNT] Handle a failed publish by retrying it or reporting the failure, and make the retry safe with the `Nats-Msg-Id` header.
- [STRM][CONS][MYTH] A `PubAck` confirms storage, not delivery; storage and delivery are separate and can be minutes, hours, or days apart. "It does not confirm that any consumer has received it."
- [CONS] A message is considered handled only after the client acknowledges it, after processing.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Tag retryable publishes with a `Nats-Msg-Id` header; the server refuses to store the same ID twice within the stream's duplicate-tracking window and returns `duplicate: true` with the original sequence.
- [PATTERN][STRM] Give every publish you might retry a stable `Nats-Msg-Id` the producer can recompute, such as an order ID, a request ID, or a hash of the payload.
- [STRM] The duplicate-tracking window is a stream setting (`Duplicate Window`), not a header.
- [STRM][MIG] Atomic batch publish (all-or-nothing group store) requires server 2.12+; fast-ingest batch publish (flow-controlled, no atomicity) requires server 2.14+.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Expected-stream and expected-sequence headers fail a publish unless the stream is in a specific state, for optimistic concurrency.
- [ANTI][CLNT][STRM] Ignoring the `PubAck`: code that discards it can't tell a stored message from a lost one; plain `nats pub` prints `Published N bytes` whether or not a stream captured the subject. "That line doesn't prove the message was stored."
- [ANTI][STRM][SIZE] Retrying without a `Nats-Msg-Id` can store the message twice; the duplicate window is two minutes by default, so a retry arriving after that also stores a second copy. "Don't retry a bare publish."
- [ANTI][STRM][CONS] Treating "published" as "delivered": a `PubAck` means the stream stored the message, not that a consumer processed it. "Keep business outcomes separate from the publish."

## Reading back the stream
- path: learn/jetstream/reading-back.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/reading-back

### Claims
- [STRM][CONS] Three pieces move a message through JetStream: a producer (publishes, reads PubAck, retries), a stream (stores in order, assigns stream sequence), and a consumer (server-side cursor a client connects to).
- [CONS] A consumer sequence is bumped on every delivery, redeliveries included, so it counts deliveries, not distinct messages. "so it counts deliveries, not distinct messages."
- [STRM][CONS] A stream can feed many consumers at once, each reading at its own pace and each with its own position.
- [STRM][MYTH] Stream messages are durable records with fixed sequences; reading does not remove or move them. "Reading message 1 leaves message 1 where it was, available to the next reader."
- [STRM] A new consumer created a month later starts at the same sequence 1 as one created today.
- [CONS][CLNT] A consumer is an object on the server, not part of the application; stored messages and read position stay server-side so a client can disconnect and reconnect without losing its place. "The stored messages and the read position both stay on the server"
- [CONS] Deliver All starts the consumer at sequence 1 and reads the whole log.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Pull is the default for new consumers; an older push model exists. "Pull is the default for new consumers; an older push model exists"
- [CONS] Ack explicit is the default for a pull consumer; the consumer's position advances only as acks arrive.
- [CONS][SIZE] Default consumer limits: Outstanding Acks maximum 1,000 (MaxAckPending); Waiting Pulls maximum 512.
- [CONS] `Unprocessed Messages` is how many stored messages the consumer hasn't delivered yet.
- [CONS] Messages are delivered oldest first, each with its stream sequence; the `pending` count is how many stored messages are still waiting.
- [CONS][STRM] Stream sequence is the message's fixed position in the log, assigned at publish and never changed; consumer sequence is the consumer's own delivery counter.
- [CONS] Stream and consumer sequences drift apart when a consumer starts partway through, filters to a subset, or has a message redelivered.
- [CONS][PATTERN][CLNT] Every delivered message carries metadata (stream/consumer sequence, pending, delivery count); read state off the message in handlers rather than calling `nats consumer info` per message. "fine for a one-off check, too costly to call for every message."
- [CONS] A durable consumer's position is durable on disk and tied to the consumer name; a disconnect or server restart doesn't change it.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Create a durable consumer when a reader comes back; for a throwaway look at a stream, an ephemeral consumer suffices.
- [CONS][ANTI] An ephemeral consumer keeps no position you can return to; it is removed once it goes idle, and a reconnect then starts over from the beginning. "an ephemeral one is removed once it goes idle, and a reconnect then starts over from the beginning."
- [STRM][MYTH] Reading a stream doesn't remove its data; unlike taking an item off a queue, the messages stay in place for the next reader.
- [ANTI][CONS][CLNT] Re-running a caught-up reader waits: with nothing new to deliver, the read command waits for the next message instead of returning.
- [ANTI][CONS][OPS] Replaying a huge stream from the beginning: Deliver All on a stream holding millions of messages takes time and moves a lot of data. "Read the whole history only when you want it."
- [CONS][PATTERN] Delivery policy alternatives to All: most recent (`--deliver last`), a time window back (`--deliver 1h`), or a known sequence (`--deliver 1000`).
- [CONS] Delivery policy sets where a consumer starts; replay policy sets the pace. Default replay `instant` hands messages over as fast as the client reads; `original` spaces deliveries to match the original timestamp gaps.
- [ANTI][CONS] Reusing a durable name with a different config returns "consumer already exists"; the server won't silently reconfigure a consumer a reader is using. Edit the consumer or pick a new name.

## Filtering what you consume
- path: learn/jetstream/filtering.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/filtering

### Claims
- [CONS][SUBJ] A filter is a subject pattern attached to a consumer; the consumer receives only matching messages and the rest of the stream is skipped. The `*` and `>` wildcards behave as in a core subscription.
- [CONS][STRM] The filter lives on the consumer; nothing about the stream changes. "The stream still captures all of `orders.>`; nothing about the stream changes."
- [CONS] A consumer with no `Filter Subject` line receives every subject in the stream.
- [CONS][SIZE] Default consumer config shown: Pull Mode true, Deliver Policy All, Ack Policy Explicit, Ack Wait 30.00s, Replay Policy Instant, Max Ack Pending 1,000, Max Waiting Pulls 512.
- [CONS] Each consumer keeps its own cursor, stored alongside its config and ack state, separate from the stream's messages; advancing one consumer's cursor does not move another's.
- [CONS][PATTERN] A consumer is an independent view over the stored messages with its own filter, cursor, and ack state; the stream holds the one shared copy.
- [CONS][PATTERN] A filter is a cheap way to send the same messages to more than one reader: it copies no data, doesn't slow other consumers, and one consumer can start, stop, or fall behind without affecting others.
- [CONS][CORE][MYTH] A consumer differs from a core queue group: a queue group splits one subject's live traffic across workers; each JetStream consumer gets its own full (filtered) view of the stored stream.
- [CONS][SUBJ] A consumer can filter on several subjects at once (multiple filter subjects).
- [ANTI][CONS][SUBJ] A filter that matches nothing is accepted silently: a typo like `orders.shiped` creates a valid consumer that never receives anything, with no error and no warning. "Don't assume an empty pull means the stream is empty"
- [ANTI][CONS][STRM] Expecting a filter to delete from the stream: a filter narrows one consumer's view and never removes messages. "Don't use a filter to prune a stream."
- [CONS][STRM] Filter overlap between consumers is fine on limits and interest streams; on work-queue retention, consumers' filters must not overlap each other.
- [ANTI][CONS][SUBJ] Overlapping filters inside one consumer fail: if one filter subject covers another (e.g. `orders.>` next to `orders.shipped`), create fails with `consumer subject filters cannot overlap`; partial overlap where neither covers the other is accepted.

## Delivery and acknowledgment
- path: learn/jetstream/delivery-and-acknowledgment.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/delivery-and-acknowledgment

### Claims
- [CONS] The ack/redeliver loop gives JetStream at-least-once delivery: a message stays available and is redelivered until a reader confirms it. "so it's handled at least once even when things fail."
- [CONS][STRM] At-least-once relies on both the durable stream and the consumer's ack loop.
- [CONS] Delivery lifecycle: delivered/in flight (ack floor not past it), acked (floor advances), redelivered (no ack within Ack Wait, so the server delivers again to the same or another reader on the same consumer).
- [CONS] The gap between what's been delivered and what's been acked is the set of in-flight messages.
- [CONS] The delivery count (`tries`) rides along on each delivered message.
- [CONS][CLNT] A plain ack is fire-and-forget; if the ack is lost in transit the server never advances the floor, Ack Wait elapses, and the message is redelivered.
- [CONS][PATTERN] A double ack waits for the server to confirm the ack; use it when reprocessing would be harmful and the handler can't be made idempotent (e.g. a payment capture). "It costs a round-trip per message, so it's a deliberate choice, not the default."
- [CONS][CLNT] Double ack is a client-library call with no CLI flag (DoubleAck in Go, ackAck in JS, ack_sync in Python, ackSync in Java, AckAsync with double-ack option in .NET, double_ack in Rust).
- [CONS][SIZE] Ack Wait default is 30 seconds; an unacked message is redelivered after it with an incremented delivery count.
- [CONS][SIZE] MaxAckPending (default 1,000) caps how many messages a consumer delivers before they're acked.
- [CONS] A redelivery doesn't slot back into stream order: while one message waits for redelivery the consumer keeps handing out later ones, so the repeat can arrive after higher-sequence messages.
- [CONS][PATTERN][SIZE] For strict in-order processing set MaxAckPending to 1: the consumer delivers one message at a time and a redelivery always comes back before anything new. "That ordering guarantee costs throughput ... so use it only when order actually matters."
- [ANTI][CONS] Forgetting to ack looks identical to a crashed reader: the message is redelivered after Ack Wait, and with the default unlimited delivery limit that repeats forever. "Always ack on the success path."
- [ANTI][CONS][CLNT] Acking the same message twice does nothing useful; some clients (Go, Python) reject it locally with "message was already acknowledged", others ignore or resend it, and the server ignores the duplicate. "Ack each delivery exactly once, in one place in your handler."

## Ack responses and redelivery
- path: learn/jetstream/acknowledgment.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/acknowledgment

### Claims
- [CONS] With `AckPolicy=explicit` every delivered message must be answered; a message is not done until the client says so.
- [CONS] A message stays in flight from delivery until the consumer answers; the server keeps a copy on the pending list and starts a timer.
- [CONS][SIZE] AckWait is the redelivery timer and defaults to 30 seconds.
- [CONS] A client answers a delivered message in exactly one of four ways: ack (done, never redelivered), nak (failed, redeliver), term (never deliver again to anyone), in-progress (reset AckWait, not final).
- [CONS] ack, nak, and term are final and close out a delivery; in-progress only extends the timer.
- [CONS][ANTI] A plain nak redelivers immediately, which is rarely what you want for a temporary failure. "A plain nak redelivers immediately. That's rarely what you want."
- [CONS][PATTERN] Nak with a delay for temporary failures (dependent service down, locked row, rate limit); the server holds the message for the delay and then puts it back. This is a client-library call; the CLI `--nak` only does immediate redelivery.
- [CONS] A nak returns the message to the consumer, not to the worker that nak'd it; with several workers the redelivery can land on a different worker.
- [CONS][OPS] Each nak raises an advisory on `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MSG_NAKED.<stream>.<consumer>`.
- [CONS] A consumer backoff only shapes redeliveries that fire when the AckWait timer runs out; it doesn't slow a nak. "it only shapes redeliveries that fire when the AckWait timer runs out — it doesn't slow a nak."
- [CONS][PATTERN] Use term for poison messages (broken payload, a check that will never pass); the message leaves the pending list and is never delivered again no matter how many attempts remain.
- [CONS][STRM] After a term the message is gone from this consumer but not from the stream under Limits retention; on WorkQueue or Interest a term removes it just as an ack would.
- [CONS] Term runs through the same path as an ack: pending entry clears and the ack floor moves past the message.
- [CONS][OPS] A term publishes a terminated advisory on `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MSG_TERMINATED.<stream>.<consumer>` carrying stream/consumer sequence, delivery count, and an optional reason.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Use term only when the code can tell no future attempt will succeed; when in doubt, nak with a delay and let the delivery limit decide. "Use term only when the code can tell that no future attempt will succeed."
- [CONS][PATTERN] AckWait: shorten it for fast work, lengthen it for slow work.
- [CONS][SIZE] MaxDeliver caps delivery attempts per message; default is -1 meaning no limit, so a message can be redelivered forever.
- [CONS] AckWait handles the case where no answer arrives; MaxDeliver caps the case where a worker keeps nak'ing the same message.
- [CONS][SIZE] With `--max-deliver=5`, a message that fails five times stops being delivered; without a term path it's dropped after the fifth attempt.
- [CONS] A backoff is a list of delays, one per attempt (e.g. 1s before the second delivery, 5s before the third, 30s before the fourth); if the list is shorter than MaxDeliver the server reuses the last entry.
- [CONS][ANTI] Setting a backoff replaces AckWait: the first entry becomes the ack deadline for the first delivery. "Pick a `--backoff-min` at least as long as normal processing takes, or a slow job trips redelivery while it's still running."
- [CONS][PATTERN] AckPolicy `explicit` is the right default for work that must not be lost.
- [CONS] AckPolicy `none` requires no answer: a message is done the moment it's delivered, so no pending list, no Ack Wait, no redelivery.
- [CONS][ANTI] AckPolicy `all` lets one ack retire every earlier message; it only fits a consumer that processes strictly in order (MaxAckPending 1), otherwise acking message 10 also retires a failed message 7 waiting for redelivery. "silent data loss."
- [CONS] AckPolicy `flow_control` is for the push consumers the server creates for durable mirrors and sources; acks ride flow-control responses and behave like `all`.
- [ANTI][CONS] A plain nak retries with no delay, tying up one worker on one message. "Don't send a bare nak for a temporary failure." A consumer backoff won't help; it spaces AckWait timeouts, not naks.
- [ANTI][CONS] A poison message with no term path uses every attempt until MaxDeliver gives up, holding up the messages behind it.
- [ANTI][CONS][OPS] MaxDeliver drops a message with no dead-letter: the message stays in the stream but leaves the consumer's pending list silently. "JetStream has no built-in dead-letter queue." Catch it via the `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<stream>.<consumer>` advisory.
- [ANTI][CONS] AckWait shorter than real processing time causes double work: the server redelivers a message still being handled, so two workers run the same order. Raise AckWait or send in-progress during long jobs.

## Pull consumers in depth
- path: learn/jetstream/pull-consumers.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/pull-consumers

### Claims
- [CONS][CLNT] Two pull patterns exist in every client library: fetch (batch of up to N, returns when full or on timeout) and consume (continuous flow, library keeps pull requests open, runs until stopped).
- [CONS][PATTERN] Use fetch when your code wants control over each round (a cron job draining a queue, a request handler); use consume for a long-running worker. "Most services use consume."
- [CONS][CLNT] A fetch timeout is a ceiling: the call always returns within it, with whatever messages it has.
- [CONS][CLNT] The CLI has no single batch fetch; `nats consumer next --count N` issues N single-message pulls in a row.
- [CONS][PATTERN] A long-running worker shouldn't loop on fetch by hand; consume keeps pull requests open so a new message is delivered as soon as it's stored.
- [CONS][SIZE] Two pull request fields bound a pull: `batch` (max messages returned) and `expires` (how long the server holds the pull open).
- [CONS][PATTERN] A bigger batch means fewer round trips and higher throughput; a smaller batch means lower per-message latency and less work lost if the worker dies mid-batch.
- [CONS][CLNT] Client libraries set defaults for batch and expires, so a plain consume loop behaves well without tuning.
- [ANTI][CONS][CLNT] An empty fetch is normal: after `expires` the server replies `408 Request Timeout` (a no-wait fetch with no messages gets `404 No Messages`), and clients report an empty batch (CLI exits non-zero). "A worker that treats an empty fetch as a failure fails on a quiet stream."
- [ANTI][CONS][SIZE] A raw fetch with `expires` zero never times out; the server holds it until the batch fills. Client libraries default to about 30 seconds.
- [ANTI][CONS][SIZE] MaxAckPending set too low limits throughput: a limit of 10 against a batch of 100 delivers ten then stops until acks arrive. "Keep it at or above your batch size. The default is 1000; lower it only when you know the in-flight count you want."
- [ANTI][CONS][SIZE] A batch set too large uses more memory than expected because `batch` counts messages, not bytes; most clients offer a `max_bytes` option to bound a pull by size, and whichever limit is hit first ends the pull.

## Scaling a consumer
- path: learn/jetstream/worker-pool.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/worker-pool

### Claims
- [CONS][PATTERN] Point several processes at the same pull consumer to share load; the server hands each stored message to exactly one worker, serving pull requests in arrival order.
- [CONS] A worker only takes a turn while it has a pull request open; distribution follows demand, so a faster worker pulls more often.
- [CONS] The consumer tracks a single position regardless of worker count; the position belongs to the consumer, not each worker.
- [CONS][STRM] Sharing is a property of the consumer, not the stream; workers share a position, not the messages, and an ack advances the position without removing the message under Limits retention.
- [CONS][CORE][MYTH] A queue group splits live messages with no storage; an offline subscriber misses them for good. Workers sharing a consumer split stored messages, so an offline worker just leaves its share for the others. "Only the stream-backed split survives a worker dropping out or a restart."
- [CONS][SIZE] When a worker dies before acking, the server hands the message to another worker after AckWait (30 seconds by default).
- [CONS] If a dead worker had already completed the side effect before crashing, the work runs twice on redelivery.
- [CONS][SIZE] MaxAckPending (default 1000) is the ceiling on delivered-but-unacked messages across the whole consumer, shared by all workers: five workers get 1000 between them, not 1000 each. "The cap is shared across the whole consumer, not per worker"
- [CONS][ANTI] MaxAckPending too low leaves workers idle; too high leaves a big in-progress backlog that all redelivers at once if many workers die together.
- [ANTI][CONS][PATTERN] A redelivered order can arrive at a second worker and run twice; key side effects by a business ID such as `order_id`. A redelivery shows in the message's delivery count.
- [CONS][PATTERN] The pool shares work by demand, so you don't choose which worker gets a message; for that control use priority groups.
- [ANTI][CONS][SIZE] A low MaxAckPending starves a large set of workers: set to 3, ten workers leave seven idle. "Set the cap to at least your worker count, with room to spare."
- [ANTI][CONS][SIZE] A crashed worker holds its message until AckWait (30s default) because the server can't tell a crash from slow work. "Set `AckWait` to your normal processing time: too short redelivers while a healthy worker is still working, too long leaves real failures stuck."

## Ordered consumers
- path: learn/jetstream/ordered-consumer.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/ordered-consumer

### Claims
- [CONS][PATTERN] An ordered consumer is for a fast, in-order, one-pass read of a stream that cleans up after itself: no name to pick, no ack to send, no consumer to delete.
- [CONS][CLNT] The ordered consumer is a client-library construct; there is no CLI form.
- [CONS][CLNT] The library creates a consumer with a short inactivity threshold, tracks the stream sequence of each delivery, and on a missing sequence or lost heartbeats throws the consumer away and creates a fresh one at the next expected sequence (named `prefix_1`, `prefix_2`, ...). "the recovery is invisible."
- [CONS][MYTH] Without acks a plain no-ack consumer that missed a message would skip it with a gap; the ordered consumer spots the gap and rebuilds from the missing sequence, so order holds with no acks.
- [CONS][SIZE] An ordered consumer is an ordinary server consumer configured as: AckPolicy none, memory storage, one replica, inactivity threshold of five minutes, start at the requested point.
- [CONS] After a recovery the library pins the replacement consumer to the next sequence it expected.
- [CONS][ANTI] Ordered consumers give up per-message acks (not for exactly-once work), sharing (each reader creates its own), and parallelism (single-threaded, in order).
- [KV][OBJ][CONS] A Key-Value watch and an Object Store read are both ordered consumers under the cover.
- [ANTI][CONS] Using an ordered consumer for work that must be processed once: it can't mark individual messages handled. "use a named consumer with explicit ack and let redelivery cover failures."
- [ANTI][CONS] Expecting to share progress across processes: two processes reading with ordered consumers both read the whole stream; they don't split it.
- [ANTI][CONS] Counting on the position to survive: memory storage, one replica, and a short inactivity threshold make the cursor disposable; after a crash a long-running job starts over.

## Priority groups
- path: learn/jetstream/priority-groups.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/priority-groups
- version context: natscli v0.4.x `--overflow-groups` bug (error 10159); one group per consumer today, multiple planned for a future server release

### Claims
- [CONS][PATTERN] Priority groups (ADR-42) let a pull consumer steer which client gets messages: overflow, pinned_client, or prioritized policy.
- [CONS][SIZE] A consumer uses exactly one priority group today; naming more than one is accepted but only the first takes effect.
- [CONS] Overflow and pinned_client need the consumer to acknowledge messages (`--ack explicit`) because the server keeps per-client counts only when the consumer acks; prioritized needs no acks.
- [CONS] Once a consumer has a priority policy, every pull must name its group; a pull without one is rejected with `Bad Request - Priority Group missing`, and the group on the pull and consumer must match.
- [CONS][PATTERN][TOPO] Overflow policy: near workers pull with no threshold; far workers pull with `min_pending` so the server answers only when at least that many messages are waiting. "You want `us-west` to stay idle unless `us-east` falls behind."
- [CONS] Overflow thresholds go on the pull request, not on the consumer; `min_ack_pending` is a related threshold counted against unacknowledged messages, and meeting either triggers delivery.
- [CONS][CLNT] `nats consumer next` issues a plain pull with no flag for overflow thresholds or priority; those pulls must come from a client library.
- [CONS][PATTERN] pinned_client policy: the server pins one waiting pull as the active client and every other pull waits as standby; if the pinned client stops pulling past the pin timeout, the server pins a standby. Use it for strictly ordered pipelines with one active and one standby.
- [CONS][SIZE] The pin timeout (`--pinned-ttl`) must sit comfortably above the pull's `expires`; the server's default pin timeout is two minutes, so keep `expires` under a minute. "The server's default timeout is two minutes; keep `expires` under a minute and the whole cycle fits."
- [CONS][CLNT] Pinning is agreed via the `Nats-Pin-Id` header on the first delivered message; the client sends it back on every later pull. A stale ID gets a `423` status; the client clears its ID and rejoins the standby pool.
- [CONS][CLNT] The pinned-client loop (store `Nats-Pin-Id`, send it back, handle `423`) runs in Go, Java, JavaScript/TypeScript, and .NET; Rust and Python let you set config fields but don't run the client-side pinning loop.
- [CONS][PATTERN] prioritized policy: each pull carries a `priority` from 0 to 9; the server serves the lowest number present first, and pulls at the same priority share round-robin.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Overflow waits for a backlog to cross a threshold before a standby gets anything (avoids churn, far regions wait); prioritized shifts work the moment a higher-priority puller goes quiet, at the cost of some flip-flop.
- [CONS] The server lets you switch a live consumer's priority policy (via a full `--config`), though `nats consumer edit` has no flag for it.
- [ANTI][CONS] One group per consumer: passing two groups is accepted but only the first is used. "To split work by region or tier now, run separate consumers on the same stream, each with its own group."
- [ANTI][CONS] The pin does not give one client sole ownership: the server can switch the pinned client while it still believes it holds the pin. "If the same message must never be processed twice, use explicit acks and handlers that are safe to run more than once, not the pin alone."
- [ANTI][CONS] A quiet pinned client keeps the pin until the timeout, parking every other client; keep each pull's `expires` comfortably under the pin timeout so the client renews in time.

## Pausing a consumer
- path: learn/jetstream/pausing.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/pausing
- version context: pausing consumers needs NATS Server 2.11 or later

### Claims
- [CONS] A paused consumer stops receiving messages until a deadline and keeps all progress: cursor, acked state, and redelivery counts don't change; delivery resumes from the stopped position.
- [CONS][MYTH] Pausing differs from deleting and recreating a consumer, which throws away how far it read and which messages it acked.
- [CONS] Pause is until a fixed moment; when it arrives the consumer resumes on its own with no second command.
- [CONS] Clients can create a consumer already paused by setting `PauseUntil` in the consumer config.
- [CONS][STRM] While a consumer is paused the stream keeps accepting messages; pause stops delivery, not storage.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Pause for a maintenance window (downstream planned offline) or backpressure (downstream overloaded). "nothing is lost and nothing is handled twice."
- [CONS][TOPO] Pause runs on the consumer's leader; if the leader changes while paused, the new leader takes over the deadline and resumes on time.
- [CONS][MIG] Pausing consumers needs NATS Server 2.11 or later; an older server rejects the command.
- [ANTI][CONS] A deadline in the past does nothing: the server leaves the consumer running. Pause with a duration like `1h` instead.
- [ANTI][CONS][STRM] Pausing does not stop publishers: new messages count toward the stream's limits, and a long pause on a tight `MaxMsgs`/`MaxBytes` stream can drop the oldest messages before the consumer reads them. "Size the stream for the longest pause you expect, or keep pauses short."

## Shaping the stream
- path: learn/jetstream/shaping-the-stream.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/shaping-the-stream

### Claims
- [STRM][OPS][ANTI] Without a limit, a stream grows until it fills the disk and takes the server down with it.
- [STRM] Under Limits retention, three independent caps are all active at once: MaxAge (age), MaxBytes (disk), MaxMsgs (count); whichever is reached first triggers a discard. "You don't have to set all three."
- [STRM][PATTERN] MaxAge fits when only recent events matter; MaxBytes protects the server itself; MaxMsgs fits when message count is what you reason about.
- [STRM] `nats stream edit` changes limits in place; messages already stored stay where they are (editing limits doesn't discard messages already within them).
- [STRM] Maximum Message Size is a cap on a single message, not the whole stream.
- [STRM] Discard Old (default): when a limit is hit the server discards the oldest messages; the publish always succeeds.
- [STRM] Discard New: when a size or count limit (`MaxMsgs`, `MaxBytes`, or a per-subject cap) is hit the server rejects the publish with an error and nothing stored is dropped.
- [STRM] MaxAge is not a Discard-policy choice; it expires stored messages on its own timer under either policy. "the first limit to hit applies."
- [STRM][PATTERN] Use Discard Old for a rolling window of recent events; use Discard New when discarding an old message would lose data you're required to keep and you'd rather slow the publisher. Discard New is the less common choice because the publisher must handle rejected publishes.
- [STRM][CONS] A limit discards a message for everyone; a consumer's position or filter doesn't protect a message from the stream's limits. "If a consumer is too slow and a message ages out before that consumer reads it, the message is gone."
- [STRM][SUBJ] `MaxMsgsPerSubject` limits messages per subject rather than across the whole stream (e.g. last hundred per subject).
- [ANTI][STRM] Discard Old discards the oldest message silently with no warning to the publisher; switch to Discard New to reject the publish (`maximum bytes exceeded` / `maximum messages exceeded`) instead. Discard New still leaves MaxAge in force, so remove or raise the age limit too if you must keep history.
- [ANTI][STRM][SIZE] A seven-day MaxAge does not guarantee seven days of history: a traffic spike can hit MaxBytes first and discard messages only hours old. "Set MaxBytes for your busiest traffic, not your average, if the age window matters to you."
- [ANTI][STRM][SUBJ] Whole-stream limits don't balance across subjects: a high-volume subject counts toward the same ceiling, so Discard Old can discard a shipped order to make room for a created one. Add `MaxMsgsPerSubject` when each subject needs its own limit.
- [STRM][SUBJ] Under Discard New a per-subject limit still rolls by default (discards the subject's oldest); rejecting requires `DiscardNewPerSubject` (`discard_new_per_subject`) on top of Discard New, which fails the publish with `maximum messages per subject exceeded`.

## Retention policies
- path: learn/jetstream/retention-policies.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/retention-policies

### Claims
- [STRM] Limits decide when a message leaves because the stream ran out of room; the retention policy decides whether a message leaves because a consumer finished with it. "A message capped only by age or size stays until its limit hits, read or unread, acked or not."
- [STRM] A stream has exactly one retention policy: Limits (default), Interest, or WorkQueue.
- [STRM] Limits: messages stay until MaxMsgs, MaxBytes, or MaxAge is reached; consumers reading and acking has no effect on what the stream keeps.
- [STRM][CONS] Interest: a message is removed once every consumer whose filter covers it has acked it; if no consumer is interested in a subject, a message on that subject is removed right away.
- [STRM][CONS] WorkQueue: a message is kept only until one consumer acks it; the first ack removes it for everyone, so each message is delivered once and then removed.
- [STRM] Limits still apply under all three policies; on Interest or WorkQueue streams the limits are the backstop when consumers fall behind. "retention doesn't replace limits, it adds a second way a message can leave."
- [STRM][PATTERN] Audit log or event history → Limits (replay from any point, late consumers, re-reads). "Limits is the only policy that allows that"
- [STRM][PATTERN] Fan-out where every consumer must process each message → Interest (fan-out delivery without an ever-growing log).
- [STRM][PATTERN] Job queue where each message is work for one worker → WorkQueue (task removed on ack so no one does it twice).
- [STRM][PATTERN] Keep the record log (Limits) and the work queue (WorkQueue) as separate streams; a worker publishes the completion event back to the log as it finishes.
- [STRM][CONS][PATTERN] On a WorkQueue stream scale by adding workers to one consumer, not by adding consumers.
- [STRM][ANTI] Set retention at creation and leave it there; the server allows exactly one live change, swapping Limits and Interest in either direction; anything involving WorkQueue is locked.
- [STRM][ANTI] Even the allowed Limits→Interest swap applies to stored messages immediately: the server removes any message every consumer has acked and any message on a subject no consumer is interested in, including history you meant to keep.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Treat the retention policy as fixed at creation; to change it, create a new stream with the right policy rather than editing the running one.
- [STRM][CONS][ANTI] Interest can fill the disk: a stalled consumer holds up cleanup for every message it owes an ack on, so the stream grows until its limits. "Interest retention still needs limits set, and it makes watching consumer health more important."
- [STRM][CONS] WorkQueue allows more than one consumer only if their filters partition the subjects; each then handles only its slice. For several consumers that each see every message, use Interest or Limits.
- [ANTI][STRM] Retention to or from WorkQueue is locked after creation; the edit is rejected with `stream configuration update can not change retention policy to/from workqueue`. "Create a new stream with the policy you want and move the data."
- [ANTI][STRM][CONS] WorkQueue rejects consumers that overlap: a second unfiltered consumer fails with `multiple non-filtered consumers not allowed on workqueue stream`; overlapping filters fail with `filtered consumer not unique on workqueue stream`.

## Altering stream state
- path: learn/jetstream/altering-stream-state.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/altering-stream-state

### Claims
- [STRM] Delete-message and purge change what the stream holds without touching its config or consumers, and both leave sequence numbers alone.
- [STRM][SEC] `nats stream rmm` securely removes a message: the server overwrites the stored bytes so the old contents can't be read back; right for a message that held data it shouldn't have (e.g. a card number).
- [STRM][CLNT] From a client library, `DeleteMsg(seq)` marks the message erased but leaves bytes until later overwritten (cheap); `SecureDeleteMsg(seq)` overwrites right away (slower). The server sees only a `no_erase` flag.
- [STRM] Purge removes every message but keeps the stream: same config, same consumers, same name. `nats stream rm` deletes the whole stream, config and consumers included.
- [STRM][SUBJ] Purge can be narrowed by `--subject`, `--seq` (drop everything older than a sequence), or `--keep` (retain a number of newest); `--seq` and `--keep` can't be combined, but either can pair with `--subject`.
- [STRM] Sequence numbers never backfill: deleting sequence 2 leaves a hole, the server doesn't renumber 3, and never reuses 2. "sequence numbers only ever climb."
- [STRM] After a full purge the next message gets the number after the last one the stream ever held, because purge sets the stream's first sequence to one past its last.
- [STRM][CONS] Consumers skip deleted sequences; a consumer never blocks waiting for a deleted message, and a missing sequence is not redelivered.
- [STRM][PATTERN] A stored sequence is a stable address: a saved pointer either still points at the same message or at nothing, never at a different message.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Use delete and purge for one-off removals; use limits and TTL for the steady state.
- [ANTI][STRM][OPS] `purge` empties the stream; `rm` destroys it including config and every consumer. "don't type `rm` for that, and read the confirmation prompt before answering it."
- [ANTI][STRM] A deleted sequence is gone, not renumbered: code that assumes messages run 1..N with no holes breaks. "don't work out 'the next message' as `count + 1`, and don't read a message count as the highest sequence."
- [ANTI][STRM][OPS] A purge can't be undone: on a stream that matters set `DenyPurge` so a stray call can't wipe it, and keep a mirror if the data is worth recovering.
- [STRM] Setting `DenyPurge` is permanent: the server refuses any later update that turns it off; the only way to purge again is delete and recreate the stream.

## Surviving node loss
- path: learn/jetstream/surviving-node-loss.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/surviving-node-loss

### Claims
- [STRM][TOPO][ANTI] R=1 means the stream exists on exactly one server with no fault tolerance: lose that server and you lose every message and every consumer's position.
- [STRM][TOPO][SIZE][PATTERN] R=3 is the production floor: three copies across three servers tolerate one server failure with no data loss and no manual recovery. "This is R=3, and it's the production floor."
- [STRM][TOPO] Replicas agree on message order by majority vote (Raft); the group keeps working as long as more than half its members are reachable.
- [STRM][TOPO][SIZE] R=5 tolerates two simultaneous failures and is the maximum a stream supports. "Most production streams run R=3; R=5 is for state you can't afford to re-derive."
- [STRM][TOPO] Every write goes through the stream leader, which assigns the sequence, stores the message, and returns the `PubAck` only once a majority of replicas have it. "That's what makes the `PubAck` on an R=3 stream a real durability promise"
- [STRM][CONS][TOPO] Each consumer has its own leader that can sit on any of the stream's replicas, so delivery spreads across replica servers; a Direct Get can be answered by any replica, leader or not.
- [STRM][TOPO] On leader loss the remaining replicas elect a new leader automatically; writes pause for the election window, then resume. No acked message is lost because every acked message was already on a majority.
- [STRM][CLNT] A publish in flight when the leader crashed, not yet on a majority, is lost and never acked; the client must treat a missing `PubAck` as failed and resend. "The durability promise covers acked messages, not ones that were still on their way"
- [STRM][TOPO] If no majority remains (two of three gone), no leader can be elected and writes are blocked until enough replicas return. "The stream would rather stop than accept writes it couldn't safely copy to a majority."
- [STRM] File storage is the default and the durable one; Memory storage keeps messages in RAM only and loses its copy on restart. "It's not suitable for an order log."
- [STRM] Storage type is a property of the whole stream, not individual replicas; an R=3 stream is all file or all memory.
- [STRM][TOPO] R=3 memory storage survives a single server crash through replicas but loses everything if the whole group restarts at once.
- [STRM][OPS] File storage doesn't sync every write to disk right away; a write can sit unsynced after its `PubAck` long enough that an OS crash could lose it.
- [CONS][TOPO] Consumer state (read position, pending acks) replicates on an R=3 stream; by default a durable consumer takes its stream's replica count.
- [CONS][STRM] On a limits-retention stream a consumer may have fewer replicas than its stream (never more); on interest and work-queue streams the consumer replica count must match the stream's.
- [STRM][TOPO][MYTH] Replicas are a durability control, not a throughput control; adding replicas is not how you scale throughput.
- [STRM][SIZE] R=3 is roughly three times the storage and write traffic of R=1; every write still goes through one leader, so a higher count lowers peak write throughput.
- [CONS][TOPO] Consumer replicas don't scale delivery: one consumer leader does all the work, followers only stand by.
- [PATTERN][CONS][STRM] To scale a consumer add workers; to scale writes past one leader split subjects across streams; to spread streams across servers use clustering.
- [STRM][TOPO] A single server rejects `--replicas=3` because there aren't three servers to hold the copies.
- [ANTI][STRM][TOPO] Trusting R=1 in production: no recovery after disk loss because there was no second copy. "Before you trust a stream with real orders, check its replica count rather than assuming it."
- [ANTI][STRM][TOPO][SIZE] Setting an even replica count: R=2 still has a single point of failure (one of two can't form a majority, writes block); R=4 tolerates only one loss like R=3 while paying for a fourth copy. "Use odd counts: R=3 for the production floor, R=5 for state you can't re-derive."
- [ANTI][STRM][OPS] Reading failover from a single-server demo proves nothing about fault tolerance; prove failover on a real cluster.

## Advanced publishing
- path: learn/jetstream/advanced-publishing.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/advanced-publishing
- version context: atomic batch added in server 2.12; fast-ingest added in server 2.14

### Claims
- [STRM][PATTERN] One-at-a-time publish with a `PubAck` wait per message is the right default; most services never need anything else. "That's the right default, and most services never need anything else."
- [STRM][CLNT] Async publish fires each publish without waiting and collects acks later; the contract is unchanged (one `PubAck` per message, at-least-once storage), so you still check every ack.
- [STRM][CLNT][ANTI] The async order trap: a failed publish is re-sent after later messages were stored, so the retry takes a higher sequence and lands after messages you sent next.
- [STRM][PATTERN] If the ack was lost but the message stored, a stable `Nats-Msg-Id` makes the server drop the repeat; if order matters, set `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` so an out-of-order retry fails fast instead of silently landing in the wrong place.
- [STRM][ANTI] An async publish you never check is a lost write. "Firing publishes without reading the acks gives up the only guarantee a JetStream publish offers."
- [STRM][CLNT] Async publish is a client-library feature with no stream setting; Go, Java, .NET, Rust have a dedicated call returning a future; nats.js gathers un-awaited promises; nats.py has no first-class async publish (approximate with `asyncio.gather` plus your own concurrency limit); CLI async path is only `nats bench`.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Atomic batch stores a group all-or-nothing; use it when several messages only make sense together (e.g. line items of one order).
- [STRM] Atomic batch requires the stream to opt in with `AllowAtomicPublish`; the client uses `Nats-Batch-Id`, increasing `Nats-Batch-Sequence`, and `Nats-Batch-Commit` on the last message; the server stages and writes on commit; the committing `PubAck` carries `batch` and `count`.
- [STRM][SIZE] Atomic batch defaults: capped at 1,000 messages per batch and at most 50 batches in flight per stream; both are operator-configurable server limits, not fixed protocol caps.
- [STRM][SIZE] A sequence gap or over-limit atomic batch is rejected with an error `PubAck`; a batch that goes ten seconds without a message is dropped with no error reply, only a `stream_batch_abandoned` advisory. "Treat the final `PubAck` as the only proof the batch committed."
- [STRM][CLNT] Atomic batch client support: CLI and nats.js in the core client; Go, Java, Rust, .NET via Synadia Orbit; nats.py via raw `Nats-Batch-*` headers.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Fast-ingest batch publish is built to replace async publish: the client opens one channel and the server runs flow control, acking in batches and telling each publisher how fast it may go.
- [STRM] Fast-ingest trades away atomicity; a batch can run unbounded; per-batch gap handling: `gap: fail` abandons on the first gap (ordered data like object chunks), `gap: ok` reports and continues (e.g. metrics).
- [STRM][CLNT] Fast-ingest requires stream opt-in `AllowBatchPublish`; client support: CLI benchmark only, Go/Rust/nats.js via Synadia Orbit, Python/Java/.NET only the stream flag so far.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Mode choice: one-at-a-time by default; async when one-at-a-time is too slow at volume; atomic batch when a group must land together; fast-ingest for maximum sustained throughput tolerating (or failing on) gaps.
- [ANTI][STRM] An async publish you never check is a lost write; collect and check every ack, and add `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` if order matters.
- [ANTI][STRM][SIZE] An atomic batch can be abandoned: a gap or over-size (1,000 default) batch errors; ten seconds idle drops it silently with only an advisory. "don't assume a half-sent batch landed."
- [ANTI][STRM] `AllowAtomicPublish` and async persistence don't mix: a stream with `PersistMode: async` rejects atomic publishing because atomicity depends on the synchronous write path; fast-ingest batches are fine on such a stream.
- [ANTI][STRM] Fast-ingest `gap: ok` loses data on purpose; use it only when a hole is acceptable, otherwise `gap: fail` or an atomic batch.

## Mirrors and sources
- path: learn/jetstream/mirrors-and-sources.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/mirrors-and-sources

### Claims
- [STRM][TOPO] A mirror is a read-only stream that continuously copies every message from exactly one upstream stream; behavior is specified in ADR-59.
- [STRM] A mirror's copy is exact: same sequence number, same timestamp, same subject as upstream.
- [STRM] A mirror listens on no subjects of its own, so it can't be published to directly; a publish lands in whatever stream owns the subject.
- [STRM] A mirror keeps its own retention, independent of the upstream's limits (e.g. upstream seven days, mirror forever).
- [STRM] A mirror's configuration is fixed at creation: you can't re-point it or add a filter later; delete and recreate, which is cheap because the new mirror catches up from the upstream.
- [STRM] A source-fed stream pulls from one or many upstreams and merges them; messages from one upstream keep their order, but across upstreams there's no ordering guarantee and the aggregate assigns fresh sequence numbers.
- [STRM] A sourced stream may also listen on its own subjects and accept direct publishes alongside sourced messages.
- [STRM] Sources can change after creation: add, drop, or adjust a filter by updating the stream config.
- [STRM][PATTERN][TOPO] Use a mirror for a second copy of one stream: a read replica near a remote region, a stream that survives loss of the upstream's cluster, or a long-retention archive of a short-retention stream.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Use sources to combine many streams: merging per-region or per-tenant streams for reporting, or a derived view from several streams.
- [STRM][OPS] Mirror/source info: `Lag` is how many messages behind (0 = caught up; climbing and staying high means it can't keep pace); `Last Seen` is time since last message or heartbeat (small, steady is healthy).
- [STRM] A mirror catches up on its own with no consumer and no client code; each source replicates independently with its own Lag and Last Seen.
- [STRM][SUBJ][SEC] A mirror or source can filter subjects, rewrite subjects with a subject transform, or reach a stream in another account or JetStream domain via the `external` field.
- [ANTI][STRM] Treating a mirror as writable: a publish routes to the origin stream; forcing with `Nats-Expected-Stream: <mirror>` is rejected with `expected stream does not match` (error 10060). "publish to the upstream `ORDERS` and let the mirror copy the message on its own."
- [ANTI][STRM] Treating mirror contents as real-time: a mirror is eventually consistent and `Lag` climbs during write bursts. "Don't assume a message in `ORDERS` is already in `ORDERS-ARCHIVE` the instant it lands."
- [ANTI][STRM][SUBJ] Combining `filter_subject` and `subject_transforms` on one source or mirror entry is rejected; a transform filters and renames in one step, so pick one.
- [ANTI][STRM][SEC][TOPO] Cross-domain config fails silently: the consumer API and flow-control subjects must be service exports, the delivery subject a stream export; a wrong type doesn't error, the mirror just never catches up.

## Reading messages directly
- path: learn/jetstream/get-direct.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/get-direct

### Claims
- [STRM][PATTERN] A stream-get (by sequence or last-for-subject) is a lighter read than a consumer for a point read: no consumer to create, no position to track.
- [KV][STRM] "Get the last message on this subject" is the read a key-value lookup is built on; a KV bucket is a stream keyed by subject.
- [STRM][TOPO] `nats stream get` asks the stream's leader, the one server with the latest write, so a get right after a publish always sees it.
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Direct Get answers the same reads from any server holding a copy of the stream, not only the leader; use it for reads you run often or from far away.
- [STRM] Direct Get is the stream's `allow_direct` setting; `nats stream info` shows `Direct Get: true` when on and no line when off. The CLI enables it for new streams.
- [STRM][TOPO] When a mirror sets `mirror_direct`, the mirror's servers also answer Direct Get requests for the origin, so a reader can be served by a nearby mirror.
- [STRM][ANTI] Direct Get is not read-after-write coherent: a replica or mirror can trail the leader, so a just-published message may not appear on a direct read for a beat. "When you must see your own most recent write, read the leader with `nats stream get`."
- [STRM][PATTERN] Direct Get suits latest-value lookups that tolerate a little staleness (a cache, a dashboard) in exchange for spreading load.
- [STRM][SIZE] A batched Direct Get streams matching messages over one request; each carries a `Nats-Num-Pending` header that reaches 0 on the last message. A batch is bounded by a count or byte budget (`batch`, `max_bytes`, `multi_last`).
- [STRM][CLNT] nats.js sends batched Direct Get natively; Go, Rust, Java, and C# reach it through Synadia Orbit helper libraries.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Direct Get for point reads (one by sequence, latest on a subject, bounded batch snapshot: nothing acked, no position, any replica answers); a consumer to work through the log (in order, durable position, ack, follow new messages).
- [STRM][CONS] A direct read never moves a consumer's position and never removes a message.
- [ANTI][STRM] Direct Get off makes the read hang: with `allow_direct` unset no server answers and the request times out with nothing returned.
- [ANTI][STRM] A direct read can be stale; don't use it for read-after-write checks such as confirming a publish landed. "keep Direct Get for high-volume or far-away reads that tolerate a little lag."
- [ANTI][STRM] A direct batch isn't a subscription: it returns matching stored messages and stops; use a consumer to follow the stream as it grows.

## Subject mapping and transforms
- path: learn/jetstream/subject-mapping.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/subject-mapping

### Claims
- [SUBJ][STRM] Subject mapping rewrites a subject in three places: a stream subject transform on the way in, republish on the way out, and per-source/mirror transforms while copying; all use the same transform language.
- [SUBJ] Transform language: `{{wildcard(n)}}` (older `$n` form equivalent), `{{partition(n, 1)}}` hashes a token into one of n buckets 0..n-1 with the same value always landing in the same bucket, a trailing `>` carries across, and `split`/`splitfromleft`/`splitfromright`/`slicefromleft`/`slicefromright` reshape a single token (ADR-30).
- [SUBJ] A split delimiter is written without quotes and can't be `.`, which already separates tokens.
- [SUBJ][STRM] A stream subject transform rewrites the stored subject for matching messages; non-matching messages keep their original subject. "A transform rewrites subjects; it never drops a message."
- [SUBJ][STRM][PATTERN] A common transform use is deterministic partitioning: hash a token into a fixed set of buckets so consumers filtered to one bucket always read the same share.
- [SUBJ][STRM] A transform affects only messages stored from the moment it's set; it doesn't touch messages already in the stream.
- [SUBJ][STRM][CORE][PATTERN] Republish re-emits every stored message onto a second subject in real time so core subscribers can watch a stream without a consumer; a low-cost way to feed a dashboard or monitor.
- [SUBJ][STRM] Republished messages carry `Nats-Stream`, `Nats-Subject`, `Nats-Sequence`, `Nats-Time-Stamp`, and `Nats-Last-Sequence` (previous sequence on the same subject, or 0), plus any publisher headers; `--republish-headers` sends headers only with a `Nats-Msg-Size` header.
- [SUBJ][MYTH] Stream subject transforms differ from account-level subject mapping, which is server configuration that reroutes core subjects before they reach a stream.
- [ANTI][SUBJ][CONS] A transform that drops a token a consumer filters on collapses distinct subjects into one, so a consumer can no longer filter by type. "Keep every token a downstream filter needs in the destination."
- [ANTI][SUBJ][CORE] Republish is not a consumer: it's plain core NATS, fire-and-forget, no storage, no acks, no replay; a subscriber that's down misses what was republished. "use a consumer when a reader has to catch up on what it missed."
- [ANTI][SUBJ][STRM] A republish destination that overlaps the stream's own subjects is rejected as a cycle (error 10052); use a separate subject space, and watch for loops spanning two streams in one account, which the server can't always catch.
- [ANTI][SUBJ][STRM] Editing a transform doesn't rewrite what's already stored; to re-namespace existing data, copy it into a new stream that sources from the old one with the transform applied.
- [ANTI][SUBJ][CONS] A partition count is fixed once consumers depend on it: changing `partition(3, …)` to `partition(4, …)` can hash the same key to a different bucket and silently change a consumer's coverage. "Pick the bucket count up front"

## Per-message TTL
- path: learn/jetstream/message-ttl.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/message-ttl
- version context: per-message TTL needs server 2.11 or newer

### Claims
- [STRM] `MaxAge` applies one deadline to every message in the stream; a per-message TTL attaches a lifespan to one message so the server deletes it after a stated time even when `MaxAge` would keep it longer.
- [STRM] TTL is set with the `Nats-TTL` publish header (duration like `1h`, `5s`, `30m`), counted from when the message was stored.
- [STRM] Per-message TTL is off by default; the stream must opt in with `AllowMsgTTL`, and a stream rejects a `Nats-TTL` header until then.
- [STRM][ANTI] Turning `AllowMsgTTL` on cannot be reversed; the server refuses to turn it back off.
- [STRM][MIG] Per-message TTL needs server 2.11 or newer; on older servers the setting doesn't exist and the edit has no effect.
- [STRM] A message lives until the first deadline that arrives: the earlier of per-message TTL and stream `MaxAge` applies. "A per-message TTL only ever makes a message expire sooner than `MaxAge` would, never later, with one exception"
- [STRM][PATTERN] `Nats-TTL: never` makes a message permanent: it never expires, not even at the stream's `MaxAge`, until something deletes it on purpose (e.g. a schema definition or baseline snapshot).
- [STRM][CONS] A TTL is a deadline on the stored copy and says nothing about delivery; if no consumer reads and acks before the deadline the message expires unread.
- [STRM][SIZE] `SubjectDeleteMarkerTTL` can leave a delete marker in place of an expired message, but only when the expired message was the last one on its subject; on an active subject with newer messages no marker is placed.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Size the TTL shorter than the time in which the message still matters but long enough for a healthy consumer to keep up.
- [STRM][SIZE] The TTL must be at least one second; a sub-second or zero `Nats-TTL` is rejected with invalid-TTL error (`err_code` 10165) and nothing is stored.
- [STRM][SIZE] A valid `Nats-TTL` on a stream that hasn't opted in is rejected with TTL-disabled error (`err_code` 10166); no message stored. The server never quietly drops the header.
- [ANTI][STRM] A TTL header on a stream that never opted in fails the publish; it does not store the message without a TTL instead. "Don't publish a TTL message and walk away on a stream you haven't confirmed opted in."
- [ANTI][STRM][CONS] A short TTL deletes the message whether or not a consumer read it; a consumer holding a message doesn't pause its TTL. "Do size the TTL to outlast the lag of your slowest healthy consumer."
- [ANTI][STRM] Turning `AllowMsgTTL` on can't be undone; the stream keeps the feature for life. "Don't flip it on to test something and expect to undo it."

## Stream and consumer policies
- path: learn/jetstream/policies.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/policies

### Claims
- [STRM][CONS] There are nine policies (five stream, four consumer); each has a safe default, and five of the nine are fixed the moment the stream or consumer exists.
- [STRM] Retention: `limits` keeps until a cap removes; `interest` and `workqueue` remove once consumers have acked.
- [STRM] Discard: `old` deletes the oldest messages to make room; `new` refuses the publish.
- [STRM] Storage: `file` survives restart; `memory` is faster and gone on restart; the choice applies to the whole stream, replicas included.
- [STRM][OPS] Compression `s2` (default `none`) makes a file-storage stream compress message blocks on disk, spending CPU for disk; JSON compresses well, images don't. Editing later is allowed but takes effect only after the stream's store restarts (server restart or leader change), and blocks already on disk stay as they are.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Persist mode: default flushes to storage before the `PubAck`; `async` acks first and flushes in the background, buying ingest rate for a window in which a crash can lose acked messages. "it fits data that arrives in volume and tolerates a lost tail, such as metrics — not an order log."
- [STRM][SIZE] `async` persist mode is only accepted on a file-storage stream with a single replica, and an `async` stream refuses atomic batch publishing.
- [CONS] Deliver policy values: `all` (default, first message), `last` (newest then live), `new` (only messages after creation), `by_start_sequence`, `by_start_time`, `last_per_subject` (newest per matched subject, what KV watches are built on).
- [CONS][KV][MYTH] Deliver policy `last_per_subject` and the Direct Get `--last-per-subject` flag are different features sharing a name: one is a consumer start position, the other a one-shot read.
- [CONS] Ack policy values: `explicit`, `none`, `all`, `flow_control`.
- [CONS] Replay policy: `instant` (default, as fast as the reader takes them) or `original` (spaces deliveries to match original timestamp gaps).
- [CONS] Priority policy default `none` applies no steering; `overflow`, `pinned_client`, `prioritized` steer.
- [STRM] Live-stream changeability: Retention `limits`↔`interest` allowed (re-applies to stored messages), to/from `workqueue` refused; Discard can change; Storage fixed at creation; Compression can change (effective after restart); Persist mode fixed at creation.
- [CONS] Live-consumer changeability: Deliver policy, Ack policy, and Replay policy fixed at creation; Priority policy can change via `--config`.
- [ANTI][STRM][CONS] Changing a fixed policy means recreating the object: storage edit fails with `stream configuration update can not change storage type`; deliver policy update fails with `deliver policy can not be updated`. Recreating a consumer loses the saved position.
- [ANTI][CONS] Expecting `new` to skip the backlog on every restart: a deliver policy applies once at creation; a durable created with `new` keeps a saved position and resumes from it, backlog included. "Don't use it hoping each reconnect jumps to live traffic."
- [ANTI][CONS][STRM] Two features answer to "last per subject"; check which feature a flag or value belongs to before copying it.

## Where to go next
- path: learn/jetstream/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/jetstream/where-next

### Claims
- [STRM][CONS] Core model: a stream is a server-side log; a consumer is a position marker tracked separately from every other consumer; an ack is how a reader says a message is handled, and until then the server resends it after a timeout. "A stored message has not yet been processed."
- [KV][STRM] A key-value bucket is a stream underneath: keys become subjects, history becomes sequence numbers, a watch is a consumer; retention and limits apply directly.
- [OBJ][STRM] An object store splits an object across many messages in a stream and reassembles it on read.
- [PATTERN][CORE][STRM] Checklist: Stay on plain pub-sub when the next message supersedes the last; reach for a stream only when a missed message has consequences.
- [STRM][OPS] Checklist: Set at least one limit (`MaxAge`, `MaxBytes`, or `MaxMsgs`) so an unbounded stream never fills the disk.
- [STRM] Checklist: Pick the stream name deliberately the first time; there's no rename, only delete-and-recreate.
- [STRM] Checklist: Choose the retention policy before messages flow; switching to or from WorkQueue on a live stream is rejected.
- [STRM][CLNT] Checklist: Read the `PubAck` back; a plain `nats pub` line isn't proof the message was stored.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Checklist: Give every retryable publish a stable `Nats-Msg-Id` so a retry doesn't double-store.
- [STRM][CONS] Checklist: Wait for delivery and ack before acting on a business outcome; a `PubAck` means stored, not processed.
- [CONS] Checklist: Reach for `--all` only when you want the whole history; sample the tail with `--last`, `--since`, or `--start-sequence`.
- [CONS] Checklist: Use a named, durable consumer for any read you must resume after a disconnect; an ephemeral one restarts from sequence 1.
- [CONS] Checklist: Edit a durable consumer to change it; recreating with a new config is rejected as already-exists.
- [CONS] Checklist: Confirm `--all` versus `--new` matches the question (backlog or live traffic) before you run the command.
- [CONS][CLNT] Checklist: Pair `--all` with `--terminate-at-end` for a one-shot replay; on its own it drains the backlog then blocks waiting for more.
- [CONS][SIZE] Checklist: Set Ack Wait longer than your slowest handler, with headroom, to avoid a redelivery storm.
- [CONS] Checklist: Ack on every success path, and term a genuinely unprocessable message so it stops coming back.
- [CONS] Checklist: Ack each delivery exactly once, in one place in your handler; a second ack is a no-op the server ignores.
- [CONS][SUBJ] Checklist: Confirm the filter matches a subject the stream stores before assuming an empty pull means an empty stream.
- [CONS][STRM] Checklist: Decide retention through stream limits, not filters; a filter narrows a view, it never deletes messages.
- [CONS][SUBJ] Checklist: Keep multiple filter subjects on one consumer disjoint; the server rejects overlap inside a single consumer.
- [CONS] Checklist: Nak a transient failure with a delay, or set a backoff, instead of a bare nak that loops at network speed.
- [CONS] Checklist: Term a poison message the moment the code knows no attempt will succeed, rather than burning the delivery budget.
- [CONS][OPS] Checklist: Subscribe to the max-deliveries advisory so a dropped message doesn't vanish unnoticed; JetStream has no dead-letter queue.
- [CONS] Checklist: Raise AckWait or send in-progress for long jobs so a slow handler doesn't trigger double work.
- [CONS][CLNT] Checklist: Treat an empty fetch as "nothing right now" and loop; never as an error that crashes the worker.
- [CONS][CLNT] Checklist: Always set an `expires` on a fetch so a quiet stream returns control instead of stalling.
- [CONS][SIZE] Checklist: Keep `MaxAckPending` at or above your batch size so it doesn't throttle throughput.
- [CONS][SIZE] Checklist: Pair `batch` with `max_bytes` so a single pull is bounded by size as well as count.
- [CONS][PATTERN] Checklist: Key every side effect by `order_id` so a redelivered message is a no-op, not a double shipment.
- [CONS][SIZE] Checklist: Size `MaxAckPending` to at least your worker count, with headroom; the cap is shared across the whole pool.
- [CONS][SIZE] Checklist: Tune `AckWait` to real processing time so a crashed worker's message recovers without redelivering honest work.
- [CONS] Checklist: Reach for an ordered consumer only for a read you can restart from the top; for work that must land once, use a named consumer with explicit ack.
- [CONS] Checklist: Split work across processes with a named consumer and a worker pool; two ordered consumers each read the whole stream instead of sharing it.
- [CONS] Checklist: Don't build a resumable job on an ordered consumer; its cursor is disposable by design and starts over after a crash.
- [CONS] Checklist: Run one priority group per consumer; passing more than one silently uses only the first.
- [CONS][MIG] Checklist: Drive failover with `min_pending` or `min_ack_pending`; the ADR-42 `failover` timer isn't shipped yet.
- [CONS] Checklist: Lean on explicit acks and idempotent handlers, not the pin, to keep work from doubling up; the pin is not a lock.
- [CONS][SIZE] Checklist: Keep each pull's `expires` comfortably under `--pinned-ttl` so a pinned client renews in time.
- [CONS] Checklist: Pause with a duration like `1h` so the deadline can never land in the past and no-op.
- [CONS][STRM] Checklist: Size the stream for the longest pause you expect; publishes keep landing and count against the limits while a consumer sleeps.
- [STRM] Checklist: Switch to Discard New when you need backpressure; Discard Old drops the oldest message silently.
- [STRM][SIZE] Checklist: Size `MaxBytes` for your peak, not your average, when the age window matters; either limit can fire first.
- [STRM][SUBJ] Checklist: Add `MaxMsgsPerSubject` when each subject deserves its own retention; whole-stream limits let one noisy subject starve a quiet one.
- [STRM] Checklist: Create a new stream to move to or from WorkQueue; the server locks that change on a live stream.
- [STRM][CONS] Checklist: Give each WorkQueue consumer a disjoint filter, or share one consumer as a pool; overlapping consumers are rejected.
- [STRM][OPS] Checklist: Watch disk on an Interest stream with a stopped consumer; interest means messages wait for every registered consumer's ack.
- [STRM] Checklist: Treat a live switch from Limits to Interest as destructive; it re-applies to stored messages and can drop already-acked history.
- [STRM] Checklist: Confirm `Allows Per-Message TTL` is on before relying on `Nats-TTL`; a header on an opted-out stream fails the publish.
- [STRM][CONS] Checklist: Size a TTL to outlast the slowest healthy consumer's lag; the clock deletes the stored copy whether or not it was read.
- [STRM][SIZE] Checklist: Set `SubjectDeleteMarkerTTL` only when consumers must learn a value expired, and keep it at or below your shortest TTL.
- [STRM][OPS] Checklist: Use `nats stream purge` to clear messages and `nats stream rm` to delete the stream; don't swap the two.
- [STRM] Checklist: Treat a sequence as a stable address that may hold no message; never assume messages run `1..N` without gaps.
- [STRM][OPS] Checklist: Set `DenyPurge` on a stream that matters, and keep a mirror; a purge can't be undone.
- [STRM][TOPO] Checklist: Confirm the replica count before trusting a stream with real orders; R=1 has no copy to recover from.
- [STRM][TOPO][SIZE] Checklist: Use odd replica counts: R=3 for the production floor, R=5 for state you can't re-derive.
- [STRM][TOPO][OPS] Checklist: Prove failover on a real cluster; a green single-node run can't show leader election or a node loss.
- [STRM] Checklist: Collect and check every `PubAck` on an async publish; add `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` when order matters so a retry fails fast.
- [STRM][SIZE] Checklist: Treat the final `PubAck` as the only proof an atomic batch committed; a sequence gap, an oversized batch, or a ten-second idle drops the whole batch.
- [STRM] Checklist: Keep atomic publishing off a stream set to `PersistMode: async`; the server rejects it, though fast-ingest batches are fine there.
- [STRM] Checklist: Choose `gap: ok` only when a lost message is acceptable; use `gap: fail` or an atomic batch for anything you can't lose.
- [STRM] Checklist: Publish to the upstream stream, not the mirror; a mirror captures no subjects, and forcing it by name errors with `expected stream does not match`.
- [STRM] Checklist: Read the `Lag` field before assuming a mirror is current; a mirror is eventually consistent, not synchronous.
- [STRM][SUBJ] Checklist: Pick `filter_subject` or `subject_transforms` on one entry, never both; the server rejects a config that sets both.
- [STRM][SEC][TOPO] Checklist: Verify each export type for cross-domain sourcing; a wrong type lets the mirror silently never catch up.
- [STRM] Checklist: Confirm `Direct Get: true`, or set `--allow-direct`, before a direct read; without it the request just times out.
- [STRM] Checklist: Keep direct reads off read-after-write checks; they can answer from a trailing replica, so read with `nats stream get` against the leader there.
- [STRM][CONS] Checklist: Use a consumer, not a direct batch, when you need to follow the stream; a batch reads the backlog once and stops.
- [SUBJ][CONS] Checklist: Keep every token a downstream consumer filters on in the transform's destination; dropping a `{{wildcard}}` collapses messages under one subject.
- [SUBJ][CORE] Checklist: Use a consumer when a reader has to catch up on what it missed; republish is fire-and-forget core NATS with no storage or replay.
- [SUBJ][STRM] Checklist: Point a republish destination at a separate subject space, not one under the stream's own subjects; an overlap is rejected as a cycle (`10052`).
- [SUBJ][STRM] Checklist: Re-namespace existing data by sourcing it into a new stream with the transform; editing a transform leaves already-stored messages untouched.
- [SUBJ][CONS] Checklist: Pick the partition count up front; raising it later re-hashes keys, so a consumer's filter quietly starts covering a different set.
- [STRM][CONS] Checklist: Settle the fixed policies (storage, persist mode, deliver, ack, and replay) before creating anything durable; `stream edit` and `consumer edit` can't change them.
- [STRM][CONS] Checklist: Plan the data move when a fixed policy must change; recreating a stream needs a mirror or a re-publish, and a recreated consumer starts fresh.
- [CONS] Checklist: Treat `--deliver new` as a one-time start position, not a per-restart skip; a durable resumes from its saved position on reconnect.
- [CONS][STRM] Checklist: Check whether "last per subject" means the deliver policy or the Direct Get flag before copying a command.



## Core NATS Deep Dive
- path: learn/core-nats/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/core-nats

### Claims
- [CORE] Core NATS is publish-subscribe with no broker queue, no storage, and no acknowledgment; the message goes only to whoever is listening at publish time. "There's no broker queue, no storage, and no acknowledgment."
- [CORE][PATTERN] Core NATS is at-most-once: a message reaches every interested subscriber connected at the moment of publish, at most once; offline, restarting, or not-yet-subscribed subscribers never see it. "core NATS is at-most-once"
- [CORE][USECASE] At-most-once is the right fit when each message is superseded by the next: a live price, a current temperature, a cache invalidation.
- [CORE][STRM][PATTERN] When messages must wait for a subscriber, survive a restart, or be replayed, add a stream (JetStream) on top of core NATS.
- [OPS] Core NATS requires no server flags; the default nats-server build is all you need.

## Subjects & wildcards
- path: learn/core-nats/subjects-and-wildcards.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/core-nats/subjects-and-wildcards

### Claims
- [SUBJ] The dot splits a subject into tokens, and the server treats each token as a separate unit when matching; hierarchy meaning lives entirely in the names the application chooses.
- [SUBJ] Subjects are case-sensitive: `Orders.created` and `orders.created` are two different subjects.
- [SUBJ][ANTI] Spaces, tabs, and line breaks are never allowed in a subject; stick to letters, digits, `-`, and `_` inside a token.
- [SUBJ][SIZE] Subjects cost almost nothing: the interest graph holds an entry only once something subscribes, so a system can use millions of subjects without slowing the server. "a system can use millions of them without slowing the server down, because matching walks the token tree rather than scanning every subscription."
- [SUBJ] Wildcards are a subscriber-only tool; a publisher always names one full subject.
- [SUBJ] The single-token wildcard `*` matches exactly one token, not zero and not two; `orders.*.created` does not match `orders.created` or `orders.us.west.created`.
- [SUBJ] The multi-token wildcard `>` matches one or more tokens and must be the last token in the pattern; `orders.>.created` is invalid and the server rejects it with an Invalid Subject error.
- [SUBJ][CORE] A wildcard subscriber is just another interested subscriber; delivery is still at-most-once, and a wildcard subscriber that joins now sees only what's published from now on.
- [SUBJ][ANTI] Subjects beginning with `$` belong to the server (`$SYS`, `$JS`, `$KV`, `$O`, `$SRV`); don't publish application messages under `$`.
- [SUBJ][ANTI] The `_INBOX` prefix is reserved for client-generated reply subjects; don't pick `_INBOX` names or publish business messages there.
- [SUBJ][ANTI] `>` only works as the last token; use `*` for a free token in the middle. "`>` only works as the last token."
