- [SUBJ][ANTI][MYTH] Publishing "to a wildcard" produces no error: the `*` is taken as a literal character and the message lands on the literal subject `orders.*.created`, reaching wildcard subscribers but not exact-subject subscribers. "Publishers can't publish \"to a wildcard.\""
- [SUBJ][ANTI][PATTERN] An over-broad `orders.>` pulls every message at every depth including subjects created later; subscribe to the narrowest pattern that covers your need so unwanted traffic stays off the wire. "An over-broad `orders.>` pulls more than you want."
- [SUBJ][ANTI] Whitespace in a subject is read as a wire boundary; a client that skips the check (nats.py's `publish`) writes the space into the PUB line and the server silently misroutes. "Whitespace is never allowed in a subject."

## Publish-subscribe
- path: learn/core-nats/publish-subscribe.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/core-nats/publish-subscribe

### Claims
- [CORE] Publish is fire-and-forget: the call returns immediately, doesn't wait for a subscriber, and doesn't tell you how many subscribers received the message.
- [CORE] Each subscriber gets an independent copy; subscribing isn't taking from a queue.
- [CORE] Unsubscribe removes interest as soon as the server processes it, with nothing to clean up server-side; auto-unsubscribe ends a subscription after N messages server-side.
- [CORE] The interest graph is an in-memory structure; fan-out happens entirely on the server, and the publisher holds no list of subscribers.
- [CORE][MYTH] A publish with no interest is a silent no-op: no error, no stored backlog, and the publisher can't tell "delivered to three" from "delivered to nobody".
- [CORE] Core NATS doesn't retry a missed message, doesn't detect or suppress duplicates, and doesn't guarantee two subscribers see messages in the same order under load; each is a JetStream property.
- [CORE][USECASE] At-most-once suits telemetry you sample, cache invalidations, and live dashboard feeds; it is not enough for an order that must be packed exactly once.
- [SIZE][CORE] Default max payload is 1 MB (`max_payload`, 1048576 bytes), announced to every client on connect. "By default the server caps it at **1 MB**"
- [CLNT][SIZE] An official client checks the payload against `max_payload` before sending and fails the call with `nats: maximum payload exceeded`, leaving the connection up; the server backstops with `-ERR 'Maximum Payload Violation'` and closes the connection.
- [PATTERN][OBJ] For large data, publish a reference (an object-store key or a URL) and let the receiver fetch the bytes out of band.
- [ANTI][SIZE] Publishing over the limit fails the publish; keep payloads under the limit and pass a reference for anything large. "Publishing over the limit fails the publish."
- [ANTI][CLNT] A short-lived publisher that exits right after publish can quit before the buffered message reaches the server; flush (or drain) before exit. "Exiting before the publish leaves the client drops it."
- [ANTI][CLNT] Echo is on by default, so a connection that both publishes and subscribes to the same subject receives its own messages and can loop. "A connection receives the messages it publishes."
- [ANTI][CLNT][OPS] A subscriber that can't keep up builds a server-side backlog; past a threshold the server logs `Slow Consumer Detected` and closes its connection, other subscribers unaffected. "A slow subscriber gets cut off."

## Request-reply
- path: learn/core-nats/request-reply.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/core-nats/request-reply

### Claims
- [CORE] Request-reply is pub/sub used twice: the client subscribes to a fresh unique subject, publishes the request with that reply subject attached, and the responder publishes its answer there.
- [CORE][SUBJ] Clients generate inboxes under the reserved `_INBOX.` prefix with a random unique tail; each request uses a fresh inbox so in-flight requests never get each other's replies.
- [CLNT][SIZE] A client doesn't open a subscription per request: it subscribes once to `_INBOX.<connection>.*` and reuses it, so thousands of concurrent requests cost one subscription. "thousands of concurrent requests cost one subscription, not thousands"
- [SIZE] The server limits a single protocol line (subject plus reply subject) to 4 KB by default (`max_control_line`).
- [SEC][PATTERN] The `_INBOX.` prefix is configurable per connection so an operator can grant each application its own reply-subject namespace instead of a shared `_INBOX.>`.
- [CORE] The CLI's `nats reply` joins the default queue group `NATS-RPLY-22`.
- [CORE][SIZE] Replies are at-most-once; every request carries a timeout (CLI default five seconds), sized to cover the responder's work plus the network round-trip.
- [CORE] When a request goes to a subject with zero subscribers, the server sends back a no-responders signal immediately, a reply with a `503` status (`NATS/1.0 503` header), surfaced as a distinct error rather than a timeout.
- [PATTERN] No responders distinguishes "the service isn't running at all" (a deployment problem) from a timeout meaning "the service is slow" (a latency problem).
- [ANTI] A request without a timeout can wait forever; pass a deadline on every `request()`. "A request without a timeout can wait forever."
- [ANTI] Don't treat no responders as a hang; branch on it separately: no responders means nothing is deployed, a timeout means deployed but slow. "Treating no responders as a hang."
- [ANTI] A plain `request()` returns the first reply and silently discards the rest; when more than one service may answer, gather explicitly by count or deadline. "Assuming exactly one reply."
- [ANTI][PATTERN] Slow work inside a responder serializes every request behind it; keep the reply path fast or run several instances in a queue group. "Doing slow work inside the responder."
- [PATTERN] When request-reply services grow endpoints, discovery, and stats, that's the Services framework, built on request-reply and queue-group primitives.

## Queue groups
- path: learn/core-nats/queue-groups.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/core-nats/queue-groups

### Claims
- [CORE][PATTERN] A queue group is a set of subscribers on the same subject sharing a name; the server treats it as one logical subscriber and delivers each message to exactly one member.
- [CORE] Nothing is configured on the server for queue groups; the application picks the name and the server learns of the group when its first member subscribes.
- [CORE] On a single server, member selection is uniform-random per message, not round-robin; the same member can be chosen twice in a row and a short burst can look lopsided.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Queue-group membership is dynamic (join by subscribe, leave by unsubscribe or disconnect), which makes it a good fit for an autoscaler with no broker reconfiguration.
- [CORE][ANTI] Core NATS is at-most-once: if the picked member dies after delivery, the message is gone and the server won't retry with another member; work that must survive a worker crash belongs in a JetStream work queue.
- [CORE] Queue members and plain subscribers coexist on the same subject: plain subscribers always get every message while the group gets one shared copy.
- [CORE] Group membership is evaluated after subject matching; the same group name across different subjects does not share load. A queue group on a wildcard load-balances across everything the wildcard matches.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] When a queue group has members in several clusters, the server prefers a member in the publisher's own cluster before reaching across regions (geo-affinity).
- [ANTI] A typo in the queue group name makes a second group with no warning, and each message goes to one member of each group, double-handling the work. "A typo in the queue group name makes a second group."
- [ANTI] Don't expect ordering or an even split from a queue group; work that must be strictly ordered for a customer belongs on a single subscriber. "Don't expect ordering or an even split."
- [ANTI][PATTERN] Make a member's work safe to repeat (idempotent by `order_id`), because a slow or briefly cut-off member can still be doing work the publisher assumes was lost. "Make a packer's work safe to repeat."

## Scatter-gather
- path: learn/core-nats/scatter-gather.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/core-nats/scatter-gather

### Claims
- [CORE][PATTERN] Scatter-gather fans one request to every responder and gathers the replies; nothing in the inbox mechanism limits the number of responders.
- [CORE][ANTI] Scatter-gather works only when responders are not in a queue group; every responder must subscribe plainly.
- [CORE] The CLI's `nats reply` defaults to queue group `NATS-RPLY-22`, so multiple instances form one group and only one answers; a queue group of one member behaves like a plain subscriber.
- [CLNT] A plain `request()` never returns a list; gather helpers exist in nats.js (`requestMany`), orbit.go (`RequestMany`), and .NET (`RequestManyAsync`), following ADR-47 with count, stall, and sentinel stop conditions.
- [PATTERN] Gathering by a fixed count blocks forever if fewer responders answer; gather by deadline instead, collecting whatever arrives within a time budget. "The safer approach gathers by **deadline** instead."
- [CORE] With `--replies 0`, the CLI holds for the full timeout window even if all replies arrive early; with no subscribers at all it returns immediately with no responders.
- [PATTERN] A sentinel (empty payload reply) is a third way to end a gather, with `--reply-timeout` bounding the gap between replies if the sentinel never comes.
- [CORE] Scatter-gather is at-most-once: a dropped reply is simply absent from the set, and arrival order carries no meaning.
- [ANTI] Taking only the first reply: `nats request` defaults to `--replies 1`, discarding the other quotes silently. "Taking only the first reply."
- [ANTI] A hand-rolled gather with no deadline blocks forever if a provider is down; bound the wait. "No deadline, so you wait for replies that never come."
- [ANTI] Don't read the gathered set as ranked; arrival order isn't priority and a short set isn't an error. "Reading the gathered set as ranked."

## Message headers
- path: learn/core-nats/headers.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/core-nats/headers

### Claims
- [CORE] Headers are key/value metadata riding beside the payload in an HTTP-like `NATS/1.0` block; a key can appear on multiple lines to carry several values.
- [CORE] Header keys are case-sensitive and NATS keeps their case exactly; `Content-Type` and `content-type` are two different keys, unlike many HTTP libraries.
- [CORE][ANTI] Keep the `Nats-` prefix out of your own header keys; NATS reserves it for system headers.
- [PATTERN] Use a correlation ID header (e.g. a trace ID) that every message in one logical operation carries, and have responders copy it from request to reply.
- [CORE] The server signals status in-band with a code on the header version line (`NATS/1.0 503`) and no payload; that's how no-responders reaches the client.
- [CLNT] Header support is negotiated at connect (server INFO `headers` field, on by default; client declares in CONNECT); against a server with `no_header_support` or one too old, a headered publish fails client-side with `headers not supported by this server`.
- [CLNT] A connection without header support can't receive the no-responders signal either.
- [ANTI] Reading a header key with the wrong case returns an empty value and no error; settle on one spelling convention across services. "Reading a key with the wrong case."
- [ANTI][SIZE] The server checks header block plus body combined against `max_payload` (the same 1 MB ceiling); a large header block leaves less room for the body. "Headers count against the payload limit."
- [ANTI][PATTERN] Headers are for small metadata (an ID, a content type, a flag); large or structured data belongs in the payload. "Putting real data in headers."

## Subject mapping
- path: learn/core-nats/subject-mapping.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/core-nats/subject-mapping

### Claims
- [SUBJ] Subject mapping rewrites a message's subject in the server, from server config, before interest is checked; the publisher sends the same command and never sees the change.
- [SUBJ][STRM] Account-level (server-config) mapping runs on plain core subjects before any stream is involved; a stream's subject transform or republish is a different, stream-configured mechanism.
- [SUBJ][SEC] Mapping is always scoped to an account; with several accounts each has its own mappings and they never cross the account boundary. The top-level `mappings` block belongs to the built-in account.
- [SUBJ][OPS] The `mappings` block is reloadable with `nats-server --signal reload`; open connections stay up.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Preview a mapping with `nats server mappings` (runs the server's transform code with no server needed) before applying it.
- [SUBJ][SIZE] A weighted mapping lists destinations with weights 0 to 100; the server picks one per message at random in proportion. Weights totaling less than 100 leave the remainder on the original subject.
- [SUBJ][SIZE] Each weight must be 100 or less and the weights for one source must total 100 or less, or the server rejects the config.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] To drop the leftover share rather than keep it, list the source subject itself as a destination (only works for a literal source).
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Partitioning (`{{partition(n, 1)}}`) hashes a token into one of n buckets numbered 0 to n-1, deterministically, so the same token value always lands in the same bucket; queue groups share work inside a bucket, the partition decides the bucket.
- [SUBJ][ANTI] A subscriber still on the pre-map subject receives nothing, because the server moved the message before matching interest.
- [SUBJ][TOPO] A destination can carry a `cluster` field so the mapping applies only to messages published through a server in that cluster, with fallback to the unscoped mapping.
- [ANTI][SUBJ] A mapping quietly changes who receives what; before mapping a subject services already use, check what subscribes to it and keep a share on the original if needed. "A mapping quietly changes who receives what."
- [ANTI][MYTH] Weights under 100 keep the rest on the source subject; they don't drop it. "Weights under 100 keep the rest, they don't drop it."
- [ANTI][PATTERN] A partition count is part of the subject contract: raising `partition(3, ...)` to `partition(4, ...)` reshuffles which bucket an id hashes to; pick the bucket count once, up front. "A partition count is part of the subject contract."

## Connecting
- path: learn/core-nats/connecting.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/core-nats/connecting

### Claims
- [CLNT][PATTERN] A connection is a single long-lived TCP connection opened once at application start and kept for the application's lifetime; every publish and subscription is multiplexed onto it. "A single connection handles thousands of subscriptions and a high message rate"
- [SIZE] Servers listen on port 4222 by default; the default connect URL is `nats://127.0.0.1:4222`.
- [CLNT][TOPO] `ws://`/`wss://` carries the protocol over WebSocket, the transport a browser has to use and the one that gets through a network allowing only outbound 443.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] A production client usually passes several URLs so it can fail over when one server is unreachable.
- [CLNT] The server sends `INFO` first (announcing `max_payload`, 1 MB by default, and header support); the client replies with `CONNECT` declaring name, features, and credentials.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Set a connection name after the service that owns it; it surfaces in `nats server report connections` and the monitoring endpoint.
- [OPS] `nats server report connections` answers fully only with system-account credentials; the monitoring endpoint (`nats-server -m 8222`) is the no-credentials alternative.
- [CLNT] Echo is on by default; `NoEcho` at connect makes the server skip the originating connection. Name and echo are fixed for the life of the connection.
- [CLNT][SIZE] PING/PONG defaults match on both sides: a PING every two minutes, and the connection is declared dead after two unanswered PINGs. "a PING every two minutes, and the connection is declared dead after two unanswered PINGs."
- [ANTI][CLNT] Opening a new connection per message repeats the whole handshake each time; open one connection at service start and reuse it. "Opening a new connection per message."
- [ANTI][CLNT] A client that publishes and subscribes on one subject receives its own messages with echo on (the default). "A client that publishes and subscribes on one subject receives its own messages."
- [ANTI][CLNT] A short-lived program that exits immediately after publish can quit before the write buffer reaches the server; flush before exit. "Exiting before buffered publishes are sent."

## Connection lifecycle
- path: learn/core-nats/connection-lifecycle.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/core-nats/connection-lifecycle

### Claims
- [CLNT] The client owns reconnection: it re-dials, replays the handshake, and re-sends every subscription, on by default in every client library.
- [CLNT] The server keeps no per-client memory; a subscription exists only as an interest-graph entry tied to one socket, so a reconnecting client is a brand-new connection to the server.
- [CLNT][SIZE] Publishes made while disconnected go into a bounded reconnect buffer, 8 MB by default, flushed in order on reconnect; a publish that would overflow it returns an error. "That buffer is bounded (8 MB by default)"
- [CLNT][CORE] Messages other publishers send while you're disconnected are gone; no client-side buffer can change that.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Register the disconnect, reconnect, closed, and async error handlers before publishing or subscribing anything; the closed handler is the one that matters (client gave up or you closed deliberately).
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Wire the async error handler in every real service; without it, errors with no call to attach to (e.g. a subscription rejected by permissions) are invisible.
- [CLNT][OPS][PATTERN] Force reconnect (nats.go `Conn.ForceReconnect()`) is how you spread clients onto a newly added server after scaling out, or leave a server you know is about to go down on your schedule.
- [OPS][CLNT] Lame-duck mode stops accepting new connections, announces to connected clients, and closes existing connections gradually rather than all at once; a client watching for the notice can reconnect to another pool server before its socket is cut.
- [TOPO][OPS] Lame-duck mode matters most across a cluster, where the client has another server to move to.
- [ANTI][CLNT] The reconnect buffer lives in client memory and dies with the process; treat it as a short-term hold over a brief outage, not durable storage. "Trusting the reconnect buffer as a delivery guarantee."
- [ANTI][CLNT] Connection callbacks run on the client's own thread; blocking one with a database write or slow HTTP call stalls other callbacks and in some clients the connection's processing. Keep handlers to a log line or a channel signal. "Doing real work inside a connection callback."
- [ANTI][CLNT][OPS] Infinite reconnect can hide a wrong address or auth refusal as silent healthy-looking retries; log the drop and every failed attempt. "Letting infinite reconnect hide a dead configuration."

## Debugging delivery
- path: learn/core-nats/debugging-delivery.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/core-nats/debugging-delivery
- version context: `nats trace` needs NATS Server 2.11 or newer

### Claims
- [CORE][OPS] A published message that never arrived has one of three causes: no subscriber at publish time, a subscription on a different subject (typo/extra token), or the subscriber's connection had dropped so its interest was gone.
- [OPS][PATTERN] A `>` subscription used to observe traffic is a wire tap; narrow it to the family you're debugging (e.g. `orders.>`) on a busy account or it gets cut as a slow consumer.
- [OPS] The `/subsz` monitoring endpoint with `subs=1`, `acc=$G`, and `test=<subject>` returns only the subscriptions a publish to that literal subject would match, wildcards included; `/connz?subs=true` shows each connection's subscriptions.
- [OPS][SEC] `nats server request subscriptions` rides `$SYS` system-account requests; a default `nats-server` has the `$SYS` account but no user in it, so it fails on a plain local server. Production and clustered servers are run with system-account credentials.
- [OPS] `nats trace` publishes a special traced message and reports the computed route; without `--deliver` the traced message is not handed to matching subscribers, so it won't fire side effects.
- [CORE] If `test=` and `nats trace` both show a matching subscriber but the message still didn't arrive, the subscriber was absent at the instant of publish: at-most-once, never retried.
- [ANTI][OPS] A `>` tap on a production account receives every message and can get cut as a slow consumer; scope it and don't leave it running. "A `>` tap on a production account receives every message in it."
- [ANTI][OPS] A trace is its own fresh message, not proof about a past publish. "A trace is its own message, not proof about a past publish."
- [ANTI][SEC][OPS] The monitoring port is unauthenticated by default; anyone reaching `:8222` can read subjects and connections. Don't expose it on a shared or public network. "The monitoring port is unauthenticated by default."

## Where to go next (Core NATS)
- path: learn/core-nats/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/core-nats/where-next

### Claims
- [CORE] The four core ideas are subject, interest, reply subject, and queue group; scatter-gather is a reply subject with the first-answer-wins step removed, not a fifth idea.
- [CORE] Core NATS does not store messages; at-most-once is a deliberate choice that keeps a publisher from blocking on slow or offline subscribers.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Checklist: Open one connection per process and share it; don't connect per message or per request.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Checklist: Decide about echo up front; a service that publishes and subscribes on the same subject receives its own messages unless it connects with echo off.
- [SIZE][PATTERN] Checklist: Ask the server for `max_payload` and keep payloads under it; pass a reference for anything large.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Checklist: Flush or drain before a short-lived publisher exits, so buffered messages reach the server.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Checklist: Process messages fast enough (or hand off to a worker) so a slow subscriber isn't cut off.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Checklist: Put `>` only as the last token; use `*` for a free token in the middle.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Checklist: Publish a fully-qualified subject; never publish "to a wildcard."
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Checklist: Subscribe to the narrowest pattern that covers your need, not a catch-all `orders.>`.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Checklist: Keep whitespace out of subjects, and stay clear of `$` and `_INBOX` prefixes.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Checklist: Pass a timeout on every request, sized to the responder's work plus the round-trip.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Checklist: Branch on no responders separately from a timeout.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Checklist: Gather explicitly when more than one service may answer; don't assume exactly one reply.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Checklist: Keep the reply path fast, or spread responders across a queue group.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Checklist: Give every queue-group member the byte-for-byte identical queue group name.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Checklist: Don't expect ordering or an even split from a queue group; keep strictly-ordered work on a single subscriber.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Checklist: Make a queue member's work safe to repeat, since core NATS does not send a message again after a hand-off.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Checklist: Gather replies in a loop instead of taking the first reply.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Checklist: Bound the scatter-gather wait with a deadline so a missing responder costs only the timeout.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Checklist: Treat the gathered set as unordered; compare every reply on its merits, never by arrival order.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Checklist: Treat header keys as case-sensitive; read them back with the exact case you set.
- [SIZE][PATTERN] Checklist: Budget headers into `max_payload`; keep bulk data in the payload, not the headers.
- [SUBJ][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Dry-run every mapping with `nats server mappings` before you deploy it.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Checklist: Make weighted destinations sum to 100 unless you intend to drop a share.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Checklist: Treat the partition count as part of the subject contract; changing it reshuffles every key.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Checklist: Wire the disconnect, reconnect, and async error callbacks first, and keep them to a log line or a signal.
- [CLNT][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Log the drop from the disconnect handler and every failed attempt from the reconnect-error callback.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Checklist: Treat the reconnect buffer as best-effort client memory, not a delivery guarantee.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Don't leave a `>` wire tap running against production traffic.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Remember `nats trace` publishes its own test message; it doesn't prove an earlier publish arrived.
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Keep the monitoring port off the public network; it answers without authentication.

## Clustering & Replication Deep Dive
- path: learn/clustering/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/clustering

### Claims
- [TOPO] A cluster's five moving parts: routes form the mesh, RAFT groups agree, a quorum commits each write, placement decides where replicas live, and peer management grows or shrinks the set safely.
- [TOPO][SIZE] A single server isn't enough to see the replication mechanism: RAFT needs a majority, so it only appears once three servers are talking. "RAFT needs a majority, so the mechanism only appears once three servers are talking."
- [TOPO] Replication within one cluster is the clustering mechanism; replication across clusters (gateways, geo-affinity, super-cluster traffic) is a separate super-cluster concern.
- [OPS][SEC] Running `nats server` operator commands (`list`, `info`, `report`) needs a system account (`$SYS`) user and its credentials.

## Forming a cluster
- path: learn/clustering/forming-a-cluster.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/clustering/forming-a-cluster

### Claims
- [TOPO] A route is a server-to-server connection on a separate route port (6222), never the client port (4222); the two never share a port. "half of cluster-formation bugs are a route pointed at the client port."
- [TOPO] A route is bidirectional once open: subscription interest flows one way, matching messages the other; in a fully connected cluster each server is exactly one hop from all the rest.
- [TOPO] Explicit routes are configured seeds in the `routes` list; implicit routes are opened by the server on its own from gossip (INFO redistribution), completing the mesh.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Each server only needs one seed address; gossip discovers the rest. Adding a fourth server means giving it one route to a seed.
- [TOPO][ANTI] Every server that should join must set the exact same `cluster.name`; a mismatched name is rejected with `Rejecting connection, cluster name ... does not match ...` and the odd server forms a separate cluster.
- [TOPO][SIZE] The `Routes` count in `nats server list` counts route connections, not peers: each link to a peer is a pool of connections (three by default) plus a dedicated system-account route. "each link to a peer is a small pool of connections (three by default) plus a dedicated system-account route"
- [TOPO][OPS] The mesh is confirmed when every row of `nats server list` shows the same cluster name and the same non-zero route count.
- [ANTI][TOPO] A mismatched `cluster.name` forms two clusters that look like one until a message fails to cross; confirm all rows show the same name before trusting the cluster. "A mismatched `cluster.name` forms two clusters."
- [ANTI][TOPO] Pointing `routes` at the client port (4222) never forms the mesh; always point at a peer's route port. "Pointing `routes` at the client port (4222) never forms the mesh."
- [ANTI][TOPO][PATTERN] One seed is enough for gossip, but list two or three seed routes so formation survives any one seed being down at boot; don't rely on a single seed in production. "One seed is enough, but list two or three anyway."

## Raft and leaders
- path: learn/clustering/raft-and-leaders.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/clustering/raft-and-leaders
- version context: `nats stream cluster step-down --preferred` needs NATS Server 2.11+

### Claims
- [TOPO][STRM] Plain core traffic needs no agreement; stored data does: the servers holding a replicated stream's copies must agree on which messages exist and in what order.
- [TOPO] A RAFT group is a fixed set of peers keeping one shared log; the leader is the only peer that accepts new entries and copies each to followers.
- [TOPO] The meta group is one cluster-wide RAFT group whose peers are all servers; its log holds assignments (which streams exist, replica counts, which servers hold them) and its leader, the meta leader, decides where new streams and consumers are placed.
- [TOPO][STRM][CONS] Every replicated stream and every replicated consumer gets its own RAFT group; the stream leader is the server that accepts writes to the stream.
- [TOPO] The meta leader and a stream leader are independent; they may be the same or different servers and a change to one doesn't move the other.
- [TOPO][SIZE] The leader sends a heartbeat to followers by default about once a second; followers stay followers as long as it arrives. "by default about once a second"
- [TOPO] A term counts elections and only goes up; every entry and vote is stamped with it, so a leader from an older term is obsolete the moment a newer term exists.
- [TOPO] A peer votes for at most one candidate per term, granting the vote only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date as its own; this is what stops two leaders from emerging.
- [TOPO][SIZE] A candidate becomes leader on a quorum of votes, a majority `(N+1)/2`; for three peers that's two.
- [TOPO][SIZE][PATTERN] A three-peer group keeps a leader as long as two peers are up; lose two and the survivor can't reach a majority and the group goes leaderless. This is the consensus math behind odd server counts: an even count buys no extra majority. "an even count buys no extra majority."
- [OPS] A stepdown is a leader voluntarily yielding so the group elects a new one; use the stream form to move a single stream, the server form (`nats server cluster step-down`) to move cluster-wide meta assignment duty.
- [ANTI][SIZE][CLNT] An election takes seconds: the election timer fires between four and nine seconds after the last heartbeat, deliberately staggered. Don't build a client that treats a brief "no leader" as fatal; retry the write. "An election takes seconds, not milliseconds."
- [ANTI][OPS] Stepdown moves leadership off the current server but the election still picks the successor; `--preferred` is a request, not a guarantee. Read `nats stream info` afterward to learn who won. "Stepdown moves leadership, but the election still picks the successor."
- [ANTI][TOPO] The meta leader and a stream leader are different groups; losing one doesn't lose the other. Check `nats server report jetstream` for meta, `nats stream info` for the stream. "The meta leader and a stream leader are different groups."

## Replication and R=3
- path: learn/clustering/replication-and-r3.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/clustering/replication-and-r3

### Claims
- [STRM][TOPO] A stream's replica count is the number of copies; each copy lives on a different server and the servers holding them form one RAFT group. Every write goes through the leader; followers never take writes directly.
- [STRM][SIZE][PATTERN] Three is the minimum replica count for production, and a stream supports at most R=5. "Three is the minimum for production, and a stream supports at most `R=5`."
- [STRM][OPS] Raising R=1 to R=3 is done in place with `nats stream edit --replicas=3`; application code doesn't change.
- [STRM][TOPO] The leader appends a write locally, sends an append entry to each follower, and counts acks; the write is committed once a quorum (majority) holds it. For R=3 that's two of three, so one follower ack suffices.
- [STRM][TOPO] Commit is the point at which durability is reached: a committed entry survives the loss of any single server. The leader returns `PubAck` only after commit.
- [STRM][TOPO] The third peer isn't on the critical path; the group makes progress as long as a majority is reachable.
- [STRM][TOPO] Apply copies a committed entry from the log into the stream store; the leader's commit index rides on the next append entry or heartbeat. Every peer applies the same entries in the same order, so copies converge; a follower can lag but never reorders or skips.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Reads from the leader are read-after-write; reads from a follower can lag (correct but slightly behind). For read-after-write, read from the leader.
- [STRM][OPS][SIZE] JetStream doesn't `fsync` every write; it batches disk syncs on `sync_interval`, which defaults to 2 minutes. Until the next sync an applied write can sit in the OS write cache. "`sync_interval`, which defaults to 2 minutes."
- [STRM][OPS] A `PubAck` only confirms quorum; quorum commit protects against losing a server, not against losing a server's disk. Two peers can hold a write in memory and still lose it if hardware fails before either syncs.
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] `sync_interval: always` closes the window entirely (every write syncs before `PubAck`) at the cost of the slowest writes; combined with peers spread across availability zones it gives the strongest durability available.
- [STRM][OPS] The 2-minute default balances risk against performance for a typical production deployment spread across multiple availability zones; log divergence needs several independent faults landing in a specific order.
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] Mitigation after a crash: wait until `nats stream info` shows the remaining peers fully caught up before restarting the crashed server, or remove the crashed peer and let it rejoin wiped and resync over the network.
- [STRM][OPS][ANTI] `sync_interval: always` costs performance cluster-wide, even for streams that don't need it; weigh before turning it on everywhere.
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] Run most clusters on the default `sync_interval` and add a separate cluster tagged (e.g. `server_tags: ["sync:always"]`) with `sync_interval: always`; place only the streams needing strongest durability there via placement tags.
- [ANTI][STRM] R=1 has no copy: no second peer, no quorum; if that server's disk is lost the data is lost with no failover. Only R>=3 survives a node loss; don't run real orders at R=1. "`R=1` has no copy."
- [ANTI][STRM] A follower read can be stale; don't assume any peer is current just because the write was acked. "A follower may lag, so a follower read can be stale."
- [ANTI][STRM][OPS] A `PubAck` proves quorum, not full replication; if you need every copy current (before taking a server down), verify each replica shows `current` in `nats stream info` first. "A `PubAck` proves quorum, not full replication."

## Placement
- path: learn/clustering/placement.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/clustering/placement
- version context: `--preferred` needs NATS Server 2.11 or newer

### Claims
- [STRM][TOPO] Without placement the meta leader puts replicas on any servers in the cluster with capacity; with placement it must honor the constraint or refuse to create the stream.
- [STRM][TOPO] Placement has two levers: a cluster name (every replica must live there; a no-op in a single cluster, useful to pin a stream to one region) and server tags.
- [OPS] Tags are freeform labels set with `server_tags` in each server's config (region, disk class, hardware tier) and advertised to the cluster; read them back with `nats server info <name>` rather than assuming the config took.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Tag matching is an intersection: a server qualifies only if it carries every tag in the list, never either-or.
- [STRM] Tag matching folds case (`disk:ssd` equals `disk:SSD`) but spelling is exact; an unmatched tag fails with `no suitable peers for placement, tags not matched [...] (10005)`.
- [STRM][SIZE] Asking for three replicas when only two servers carry the required tags fails the same way; placement doesn't relax the constraint to fit the replica count.
- [STRM][MYTH] Placement cannot name a leader: a `preferred` server in placement is rejected with `preferred server not permitted in placement`, and no client library exposes such a field.
- [OPS] To put leadership on a chosen server after creation, use `nats stream cluster step-down --preferred <server>`; it's a request the election can still overrule.
- [ANTI][STRM] Tags are an intersection; a missing tag fails the placement rather than falling back to any server. Read tags back from servers first, then place against exactly what they advertise. "Tags are an intersection; a missing tag fails the placement."
- [ANTI][OPS] Don't build an operational assumption like "the leader is always n1-east" on where the group first landed; after a leader dies the next election picks from survivors. "You can't name a leader at placement time."

## Scaling and peer management
- path: learn/clustering/scaling-and-peers.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/clustering/scaling-and-peers

### Claims
- [STRM][OPS] You grow a stream's group by raising its replica count; the meta leader assigns the extra replica to a server qualifying under the stream's placement. The new server must already be a cluster member.
- [STRM][TOPO] A new peer catches up by streaming the entries it's missing from the leader; lag is a count of entries behind.
- [STRM][TOPO][SIZE] Adding a peer changes the quorum right away: an R=4 group commits once three peers hold a write, not two. A new empty peer can't win an election until the leader's first entries reach it.
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] Don't lean on a new peer as a data-bearing replica until `stream info` shows it `current`.
- [STRM][OPS] `peer-remove` doesn't shrink the stream: it evicts the replica from the named server and the meta leader re-places it elsewhere, keeping the replica count. If the evicted peer held leadership, the group elects a new leader first.
- [STRM][OPS] If placement leaves nowhere to re-place the replica, an R>1 stream still loses the peer and returns `peer remap failed`, leaving the group a replica short; only a single-replica stream is spared.
- [STRM][OPS] `peer-remove` moves a replica between servers; `nats stream edit --replicas` sets how many replicas there are.
- [OPS] Removing a server from the meta group (`nats server cluster peer-remove`) allows only one change at a time; a second in flight answers `cluster member change is in progress`.
- [ANTI][STRM][OPS] Don't stack membership changes before the replacement catches up; a second change can drop the peers holding the data below the majority and the group stops committing. Make one change, wait for a named leader and a caught-up replacement, then the next. "Don't stack membership changes before the replacement catches up."
- [ANTI][STRM][OPS] If `stream info` shows `no leader` after a change, stop: you've lost quorum and the fix is to restore a peer, not make another change.
- [ANTI][STRM] A freshly added peer isn't safe until its lag is zero; it can't win an election or serve a read while catching up, and killing another server mid-catchup can stall the group. "A freshly added peer isn't safe until its lag is zero."
- [ANTI][STRM] Removing the only peer needs `--force` (`removing the only peer on a stream will result in data loss`), and even forced the server answers `peer remap failed`; change the count with `nats stream edit --replicas` instead. "Removing the only peer needs `--force`, and forcing it doesn't move the data."
- [OPS][PATTERN] Take a backup before a risky resize, so a lost replica is recoverable.

## Where to go next (Clustering)
- path: learn/clustering/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/clustering/where-next

### Claims
- [TOPO] The five core ideas of clustering are routes, RAFT, quorum, placement, and peers; terms, elections, append entries, apply, preferred leader, and migration are refinements.
- [TOPO] Quorum is what lets a group make progress while a minority is down, and lose nothing when it returns.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: Give every server the same `cluster.name`; a mismatch silently forms two clusters that look like one until a message fails to cross.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: Point `routes` at the route port (6222), not the client port (4222).
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: List two or three seed routes so the cluster still forms if one seed server is down at boot.
- [TOPO][CLNT][SIZE][PATTERN] Checklist: Treat a brief "no leader" window during failover as normal; the election timer is 4–9s, so let the client retry instead of failing the write.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Use `nats stream cluster step-down` to move leadership off a server, not to pick its successor; read `nats stream info` to learn who won.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: Track the meta leader and a stream leader as different RAFT groups; losing one is not losing the other.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Checklist: Run real orders at R>=3, never R=1; a single copy is gone with its server's disk.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Checklist: Read from the leader when you need read-after-write; a follower can lag, so a Direct Get from one returns data that's correct but not the newest.
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Read a `PubAck` as quorum held, not full replication; before deliberately taking a server down, verify each replica shows `current`.
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Read a server's tags back before placing against them; tags are an intersection and a missing one fails rather than falling back.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Checklist: Spell tags exactly; matching folds case but a misspelling matches nothing.
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Placement can't name a leader; to move leadership to a specific server use `step-down --preferred` (NATS Server 2.11+) and treat it as a request the election can overrule.
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Make one membership change at a time; stacking a second before the replacement is `current` can drop the data-holding peers below a majority and the stream stops committing.
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Wait for a freshly added peer to show `current` with zero lag before trusting it; don't kill another server mid-catchup.
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Change the replica count with `nats stream edit --replicas`, not by removing the last peer.

## Topologies Deep Dive
- path: learn/topologies/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/topologies

### Claims
- [TOPO] NATS scales by composing servers; growing a deployment means building bigger topologies (single server, cluster, super-cluster, leaf nodes) out of smaller ones.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] The application never changes across shapes: the same server binary and the same client code run on every topology, so you change the deployment rather than the code.
- [TOPO][USECASE] The growth path: single server for a developer laptop; a cluster (three servers joined by routes) to survive a server outage; a super-cluster joined by gateways when traffic arrives from a second region; a leaf node when a site needs NATS on-site with only outbound network access.
- [TOPO][STRM] Every shape does two separate jobs: core messaging (routes, gateways, leaf connections carry messages to matching interest) and JetStream (stores and replicates across the servers the topology provides).

## Single server
- path: learn/topologies/single-server.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/topologies/single-server

### Claims
- [OPS][PATTERN] Even a single server should set `server_name`, an explicit `port`, `http_port` for monitoring (off by default; enable it at 8222 from the start), and a `jetstream` block with `store_dir`.
- [TOPO][USECASE] One server is the right tool for development (a laptop or a CI run), for NATS on the device itself (edge hardware or embedded in-process), and for a small single-instance service.
- [TOPO][USECASE] A device server often later dials out to a central system as a leaf node, but on its own it's still a single server.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Clustering NATS behind a single-instance service raises the broker's uptime but not the feature's, because the service still fails first; lifting availability means a second copy of the service too. "one server is the correct amount of infrastructure rather than a compromise."
- [TOPO] A single server is a single point of failure: if the process dies every client loses its connection at once and routing stops until it returns; not fine for production where a reboot during a deploy drops every order in flight.
- [TOPO][STRM] On one server JetStream gives durability against a crash (messages survive a process restart) but never against loss of the server itself; lose that disk and you lose the stream.
- [TOPO][OPS] A single server scales vertically (bigger CPU, more RAM, faster disk), sometimes the right fix, but every machine has a ceiling; past it the way forward is more servers.
- [ANTI][STRM][TOPO] A single server can't hold a replicated stream: asking for three replicas answers `replicas > 1 not supported in non-clustered mode`; redundancy is a cluster's job, don't treat the error as a config typo to override. "Reaching for redundancy too late."

## Your first cluster
- path: learn/topologies/your-first-cluster.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/topologies/your-first-cluster

### Claims
- [TOPO] A cluster is a set of servers that act as one logical NATS system; a client on any server can reach a subscriber on any other server.
- [TOPO] Clients connect on the client port (4222 default); servers connect to each other on a separate cluster port (6222 in the configs).
- [TOPO] Every server holds a route to every other, so each is one hop from all the rest; there's no central coordinator. A message received over a route is delivered to that server's own clients and forwarded no further, because one hop is always enough.
- [TOPO][SIZE] With three servers the full mesh is three routes.
- [TOPO] A mismatched cluster name (a typo like `eats`) gets that server's route refused (`cluster name "eats" does not match "east"`) and it ends up a cluster of its own.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Each server needs only one route entry; servers discover the rest from their peers and dial them (gossip). Hand-writing the full mesh is valid (extras dropped as `Duplicate Route`) but every new server then means editing every config; the trade-off is that a single-seed setup depends on the seed being up first.
- [TOPO][CLNT] On connect a server sends an INFO message including the other servers' client URLs, so a client knows all cluster members even if configured with one; this discovery is what enables failover to a server the client never named.
- [TOPO][CLNT] Loss of one server is a reconnect, not an outage.
- [TOPO][CLNT] `no_advertise: true` stops a server advertising its peers, so a client only knows the URLs given by hand; leave it off (the default) and failover spans the whole cluster.
- [ANTI][TOPO] Misspelling a cluster name raises no error; the odd server forms its own cluster. Catch it with the rejection line in the log or a cross-server publish test. "Misspell a cluster name."
- [ANTI][SEC][TOPO] The cluster port accepts routes, which are trusted links carrying every account's traffic plus the system account; left reachable with no authorization, anyone with the cluster name can join as a server and read or inject messages across accounts. Bind it to a private interface, firewall it, and in production require route credentials or TLS. "Expose the cluster port to the world."
- [ANTI][TOPO][SIZE][PATTERN] Plan for an odd server count once you replicate: two servers lose their majority as soon as one is down, and four tolerate only one loss, the same as three, so the extra server adds cost without failure tolerance. For a pure routing cluster any count is fine. "Plan for an even server count."

## JetStream in a cluster
- path: learn/topologies/jetstream-in-a-cluster.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/topologies/jetstream-in-a-cluster

### Claims
- [TOPO][STRM] A JetStream cluster elects one meta leader that owns every decision about where streams and consumers live; every JetStream-enabled server belongs to the meta group. You don't choose which server wins.
- [TOPO][STRM] The meta leader decides where a stream lives but doesn't handle writes to it; writes go through the stream's own replication.
- [TOPO][SIZE][PATTERN] The meta group decides by majority vote, so a JetStream cluster wants an odd number of servers. Three servers form a majority of two; lose one and streams keep serving; lose a second and no write can reach a majority, so the stream stops accepting messages until a server returns.
- [STRM] A write is never stored on a single copy that a majority hasn't confirmed.
- [TOPO][SIZE][PATTERN] Production clusters run an odd count, typically three or five; a stream keeps at most five copies, so more servers add capacity, not more copies of one stream. "typically three or five — a stream keeps at most five copies"
- [STRM][SIZE] R1 is the default replica factor unless you ask for more; R3 is the production floor, and a three-server cluster is exactly enough to hold it. "Three copies is `R3`, the production floor"
- [STRM][TOPO] Replication stays inside one cluster; the cluster is the unit a stream is replicated across. Each stream gets its own Raft group separate from the meta group.
- [STRM] The stream leader takes every write first, sends it to the replicas, and the write is acknowledged only once a majority hold it; `current` means a replica has recently checked in and holds the same data.
- [STRM][TOPO] The stream leader is chosen independently of the meta leader; you configure neither.
- [CONS][STRM] Consumers replicate too: each consumer gets its own Raft group and leader, chosen independently of the stream's, so a consumer can lead on one server while its stream leads on another.
- [CONS][SIZE][ANTI] By default a consumer takes its stream's replica count; an R1 consumer on an R3 stream is its own single point of failure, since its position lives on one server and losing it loses the reader's place even though the stream survives.
- [ANTI][STRM] An R1 stream on a cluster still has no HA; the cluster around it changes nothing. Audit replica counts (`nats stream find --replicas=1`) and raise the streams that matter to R3; `nats server check stream --peer-expect=3` exits non-zero when under-replicated. "An R1 stream on a cluster still has no HA."
- [ANTI][TOPO][SIZE] An even server count gives no extra protection: four tolerate the same single loss as three at the cost of an extra server; run an odd number, never four or six. "An even server count gives you no extra protection."
- [ANTI][STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] All three replicas in one failure domain defeat R3: three copies survive one loss only if the servers can fail independently; spread across one rack or one availability zone a single power or network event takes all three. "All three replicas in one failure domain defeat R3."
- [STRM][TOPO] Joining clusters into a super-cluster doesn't stretch one stream across them; the stream's replicas stay inside its cluster.

## Super-clusters
- path: learn/topologies/super-clusters.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/topologies/super-clusters

### Claims
- [TOPO][PATTERN] A super-cluster joins independent clusters into one logical system without combining them into a single mesh; it is the shape for a second region. "A full mesh assumes the members are close together."
- [TOPO][ANTI] Stretching one cluster across regions works but every server holds a route to every other and route traffic flows freely across the slow, expensive link.
- [TOPO] A route ties two servers and assumes they're close; a gateway ties two clusters and assumes they're far apart. Each server opens just one gateway connection to each other cluster, never one to every remote server.
- [TOPO] A gateway forwards a message to another cluster only when that cluster has a subscriber for it (interest-based forwarding); no interest on the far side means no traffic across the gateway. "no interest on the far side means no traffic across the gateway."
- [TOPO][SIZE] The gateway `name` identifies the cluster, not the server, and must match the `cluster {}` name exactly; otherwise the server refuses to start with `cluster name conflicts between cluster and gateway definitions`. A server's own entry in `gateways` is ignored automatically.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] List all remote gateway URLs so the connection has somewhere to land if one remote server is down; on separate hosts every server in a cluster can use the identical gateway block, port included.
- [TOPO] Gateways gossip like routes: point a server at a few remote gateways and it discovers the rest, including clusters it was never told about. URLs are a seed for discovery and a fallback, not a list you must keep complete.
- [TOPO] The `gateway {}` block is additive; each cluster keeps its `cluster {}` block and client port.
- [TOPO][CORE][PATTERN] Geo-affinity: NATS prefers a local queue subscriber first; a message published in a region goes to a worker in that region even though a remote worker is subscribed, so it never crosses the gateway.
- [TOPO][CORE] The gateway carries a queue-group message only when the local side can't serve; if all local workers are down the message crosses to a remote cluster with an interested worker. When more than one remote cluster has a worker, NATS picks one and sends across that single gateway, so it still reaches exactly one worker.
- [ANTI][TOPO] Don't grow a cluster across regions with routes; join two independent clusters with a `gateway {}` block so only interested traffic crosses. "Reaching for routes to span regions."
- [ANTI][TOPO] A typo in a `gateways` entry name never connects and logs `Failing connection to gateway "wset", remote gateway name is "west"` on every retry, but the super-cluster still forms through the other side's reverse connection and gossip, so a working cross-region publish doesn't prove the config is right. "Mismatched gateway names."
- [ANTI][TOPO][PATTERN] Geo-affinity only keeps traffic home when a local queue subscriber exists; centralize all workers in one region and every other region's messages cross the gateway as steady-state load. Place a queue subscriber for each workload in every region that produces that work. "Chatty cross-region traffic without local workers."
- [TOPO][STRM] A gateway carries interest across regions, not stream copies.

## Leaf nodes
- path: learn/topologies/leaf-nodes.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/topologies/leaf-nodes

### Claims
- [TOPO][PATTERN] A gateway joins two clusters that can both accept connections from each other; a site behind a firewall that can only reach out needs a leaf node instead. "A gateway won't help here."
- [TOPO] A leaf node is a server that opens an outbound connection to a remote NATS system (the hub) and bridges subject interest across it; the hub never dials the leaf, so no inbound firewall rule or public address is needed on the leaf side.
- [TOPO][CLNT] To local clients the leaf is a regular NATS server; a machine needs no leaf-specific configuration.
- [TOPO] The leaf carries only subjects that have interest on the other side, the same interest propagation clusters use internally, extended across one outbound hop.
- [TOPO][SIZE] The default leaf node port is 7422, a fourth kind of listener separate from the client port (4222), route port (6222), and gateway port (7222). "one port per kind of connection."
- [TOPO][PATTERN] A leaf can dial any hub server; listing several hub URLs in the remote gives it somewhere to reconnect if one is down.
- [TOPO] A leaf has no `cluster {}` or `gateway {}` block; it's a standalone server reaching the rest through one outbound link.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] `remotes` is a list: a leaf can dial several different NATS systems and bridge them all; a leaf can also run its own `leafnodes { listen }` and become a hub for leaves further out, so leaf links compose into trees.
- [SEC][TOPO][PATTERN] In production a remote carries `credentials` (a `.creds` file proving the leaf's identity) and `account` (which local account the bridged interest joins); point both ends at the same account and the leaf and cloud share one isolated subject space.
- [TOPO][SIZE] Local clients stay hidden behind the leaf: the hub sees one leaf link no matter how many machines connect to the leaf. "Add a thousand more machines and the hub still sees one leaf link."
- [TOPO][SEC] Address-space isolation (only subjects the account imports and exports cross the link) is an account decision, not something the leaf link gives for free; in the default account there is no subject boundary.
- [TOPO][STRM] If a leaf runs its own JetStream, it needs a JetStream domain; without distinct domains a leaf's JetStream and its hub's JetStream collide.
- [ANTI][TOPO] A leaf dials out: put the `remotes` block on the egress-only side and `leafnodes { listen }` on the side that accepts connections; reversing them means nothing connects. "Treating the leaf like an inbound connection."
- [ANTI][TOPO][STRM] A leaf enabling JetStream while sharing the hub's system account extends the hub's JetStream rather than running its own, so a stream created on the leaf may land on the hub; give the leaf its own JetStream domain for a distinct local store. "Expecting JetStream to span the leaf without a domain."

## Putting it together
- path: learn/topologies/putting-it-together.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/topologies/putting-it-together

### Claims
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Shapes are layers you combine, not options you choose between; each layer is added when the current one runs out of room and the layer below keeps working unchanged.
- [TOPO] Wiring stays local to each layer: routes wire servers inside a cluster, gateways wire clusters, leaf remotes wire a leaf to a hub; no config block has to know the whole picture.
- [TOPO] One server can take part in several layers at once (`cluster`, `gateway`, and `leafnodes` blocks in one config file).
- [TOPO][SEC] Stacking shapes gives one address space by default: routes carry an account's full interest across a cluster and a gateway forwards any subject the far side wants; neither partitions anything. Only a leaf bound to its own account draws a boundary. "stacking shapes adds reach, not boundaries."
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Layer selection: one server until a single point of failure is unacceptable or one server can't carry the load, then a cluster; one cluster until you need a second region or a failure domain a single mesh can't give, then a gateway; a super-cluster reaches every region but not every site, so attach a leaf when a factory, ship, or laptop needs NATS locally with only outbound access.
- [TOPO] Each step is reversible: the layer below never changed, so removing the layer above leaves a working deployment.
- [OPS][SEC] Surveying the whole fabric (`nats server list`, `report routes`, `report gateways`, `report leafnodes`) needs the system account (`$SYS`).
- [OPS] In `nats server report leafnodes`, `Account: $G` means the leaf landed in the default global account with no boundary; `Spoke` is `true` only on the leaf's own report.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] The topology is an operations concern, not an application one; you can start on a laptop and grow to multi-region edge without rewriting business logic.
- [ANTI][TOPO][OPS] Each layer adds operational cost; a super-cluster stood up "to be safe" is two regions to keep healthy before you have a second region's traffic. Add the next layer only when the current one runs out of room; adding early gives no benefit. "Building the whole stack before a limit forces it."

## Where to go next (Topologies)
- path: learn/topologies/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/topologies/where-next

### Claims
- [TOPO][USECASE] A single server is for development and small workloads; in production it's a single point of failure. A cluster is the shape you run in production. A super-cluster is how a deployment spans regions. A leaf node is how NATS reaches the edge.
- [OPS] Once live, watch routes on `/routez`, gateways on `/gatewayz`, and leaf connections on `/leafz`.
- [SEC][TOPO] A leaf opens a connection across a trust boundary, often the public internet, so authenticating it and scoping what it can publish and subscribe is not optional in production.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: Move production workloads off a single server before a reboot can drop orders in flight.
- [TOPO][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Plan for horizontal growth, not a bigger box; vertical scaling has a ceiling.
- [TOPO][STRM][PATTERN] Checklist: Add redundancy before an outage, not after; one server can't hold a replicated stream, so R1 survives a restart but never the loss of the box.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: Set the same `name` on all servers, then confirm they joined as one cluster.
- [SEC][TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: Bind the cluster port to a private interface and firewall it off the open internet.
- [TOPO][SIZE][PATTERN] Checklist: Run an odd server count once you replicate a stream.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Checklist: Audit replica counts and raise the streams that matter to R3; a cluster alone is not HA.
- [TOPO][SIZE][PATTERN] Checklist: Run an odd count (three or five), never an even count; a stream replicates across at most five servers.
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: Spread R3 replicas across independent failure domains, not one rack or zone.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: Join regions with a `gateway {}` block, never a `cluster {}` stretched across them.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: Match the local gateway `name` to the `cluster {}` name (the server won't start otherwise), and each `gateways` entry to the remote cluster's exact name; a remote typo fails silently, so confirm a publish crosses regions.
- [TOPO][CORE][PATTERN] Checklist: Place a queue subscriber for each workload in every region that produces it.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: Put `remotes` on the egress-only side and `leafnodes { listen }` on the hub.
- [TOPO][STRM][PATTERN] Checklist: Give a leaf its own JetStream `domain` when it needs a distinct local store.
- [TOPO][SEC][PATTERN] Checklist: Reach for accounts (with a leaf where the boundary follows a network edge) when you need an isolation wall, not another route or gateway.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: Add each layer only when the current one runs out of room.

## Deployment & Upgrades Deep Dive
- path: learn/deployment/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/deployment

### Claims
- [OPS] Production operations for a cluster are: sizing the resources a node needs, the manifests that stand it up, SIGHUP config reload without dropping a connection, lame-duck mode for upgrades without losing the stream, and systemd flags restricting access.
- [OPS] A node spends four resources (CPU, memory, disk, file descriptors), and an R3 stream counts against account limits.
- [OPS][PATTERN] On Kubernetes, the NATS Helm chart and the NACK controller (streams and consumers declared as CRDs) are the canonical path.
- [OPS][SEC] A hardened cluster has TLS on every link, credentials mounted, a locked-down systemd unit, and the monitor port closed to the internet.

## Sizing & resources
- path: learn/deployment/sizing-and-resources.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/deployment/sizing-and-resources

### Claims
- [OPS][SIZE] CPU: core NATS routing is cheap; TLS handshakes and JetStream replication are where cycles go. Overprovision CPU by 20–30% above steady state so a node has spare cycles for a rebalance when a peer leaves. "overprovision CPU by 20–30% above steady state"
- [OPS][SIZE] Memory holds connections, subscriptions, and memory-storage stream data; file-storage streams live on disk, not RAM. A few hundred light client connections fit in a few hundred megabytes; budget a light publisher at roughly 128 MiB.
- [OPS][SIZE] Disk holds file-storage streams and is the resource most likely to run out.
- [OPS][SIZE] JetStream spends roughly two file descriptors per stream; the default per-process FD limit is plenty on a small cluster and not on a large one, where the hardened unit raises it to `LimitNOFILE=800000`. "JetStream spends roughly two FDs per stream."
- [OPS][SIZE] JetStream memory storage defaults to 75% of system RAM (capped by `GOMEMLIMIT` if set), falling back to 256 MB only when the server can't read system memory. "**Memory storage** defaults to 75% of system RAM"
- [OPS][SIZE] JetStream file storage defaults to 75% of disk space available under `store_dir`, falling back to 1 TB only when the platform can't report disk size; on a 10 GiB container volume the default is about 7.5 GiB, not 1 TB.
- [OPS][ANTI] The container hazard is setting `max_file_store` larger than the volume, or a shared/thin-provisioned volume where "available" overstates safe use: the node accepts writes it can't store and the publish crossing the real boundary fails. Pin `max_file_store` to what the volume can hold.
- [OPS][STRM][SIZE] At R3 each node stores the full stream once (one copy per node). The Helm chart defaults `max_file_store` to the PVC size.
- [OPS][SEC][SIZE] Server config sizes the node; account limits (`MaxMemory`, `MaxStore`, `MaxStreams`, `MaxConsumers`) size the tenant, enforced regardless of node disk. Read them live with `nats account info` before sizing.
- [OPS][STRM][SIZE] On an un-tiered account an R3 stream counts as `replicas × bytes` against `MaxStore`: a 10 GiB R3 stream spends 30 GiB. Forget the multiplier and the third replica fails to place. "a 10 GiB ORDERS stream at R3 spends 30 GiB of the account's `MaxStore`"
- [OPS][STRM][SIZE] On a tiered account replication is baked into the tier: the reported bytes are usable bytes, so a 10 GiB tier holds a 10 GiB R3 stream.
- [OPS][SIZE] `max_connections` defaults to 64K (65,536), is reloadable, and overflow disconnects immediately. `max_subscriptions` per connection defaults to unlimited. `max_payload` defaults to 1 MB and must stay `<= max_pending`.
- [ANTI][OPS][SIZE] Setting `max_file_store` beyond the real disk fails as a publish error mid-stream, not a startup warning; set it to the volume size and watch the real disk with `df -h`. "Setting `max_file_store` beyond the real disk."
- [ANTI][OPS][SIZE] If `max_payload` exceeds `max_pending` the server refuses to start; keep `max_pending >= 10× peak message size` so a burst of large messages can't stall a connection; don't raise `max_payload` in isolation. "`max_payload` larger than `max_pending`."
- [ANTI][OPS][SIZE] FD exhaustion on a big cluster shows as connection refusals that look like a network fault; raise the limit (`ulimit -n 800000`) before the process starts. "File-descriptor exhaustion on a big cluster."
- [ANTI][OPS][SEC] Operator-mode account limits live in the account JWT the resolver holds; raising `MaxStore` or `MaxStreams` means editing and pushing the JWT, not a server reload or restart. "JWT account limits change only when the account JWT does."
- [OPS][MIG] Keep the cluster's server versions aligned as you roll upgrades so every node reads the same JWT limit fields (tiered R1/R3 limits need servers new enough to understand them).

## Config management
- path: learn/deployment/config-management.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/deployment/config-management

### Claims
- [OPS][PATTERN] Prefer reload over restart: apply new config to the running server through SIGHUP without dropping a connection, after a dry-run validates it.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Split a large config with `include`; the path is relative to the directory of the config file containing it, not the launch directory.
- [OPS] A JetStream cluster won't boot without both `server_name` and `routes`; a dry-run that reports the file valid still can't start without them.
- [OPS][SEC] An unquoted `$NAME` token resolves a config variable then an environment variable, and an unset one is a parse error; quoting stores the literal string, which is why bcrypt hashes (full of `$`) are the values you quote.
- [OPS] Reloadable keys: account, user, and permission definitions; `max_connections`, `max_payload`, `max_control_line` (not `max_subscriptions`, which a reload rejects); most JetStream account limits and the `jetstream` enable flag; TLS cert and key paths; cluster routes and logging settings. Gateway routes are not reloadable beyond refreshing TLS material.
- [OPS] Non-reloadable keys define identity and need a restart: `port`/`listen`, the cluster's listen host and port, and the JetStream `store_dir`. "A reload can change *policy* ... but it can't change *identity*"
- [OPS] Changing a non-reloadable key requires a rolling upgrade rather than a reload.
- [OPS] Reload is atomic: the server validates first and on a parse or validation failure the old config stays active; either the new config applies cleanly or nothing changes.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Validate with `nats-server -c <file> -t` before signaling; it exits non-zero on a broken config so a script can gate the reload. It checks syntax and validation, not whether the server can start.
- [OPS] A reload keeps open connections up and no client reconnects; the server logs `Reloaded server configuration`.
- [OPS] On Kubernetes the config reloader sidecar (enabled by default in the Helm chart) watches the mounted config with inotify and SIGHUPs the server PID from `/var/run/nats/nats.pid`; it retries 30 times by default, four seconds apart; use `--force-poll` where inotify events don't arrive. "30 retries by default, four seconds apart"
- [OPS][SEC][PATTERN] Credentials and TLS material never belong inline in the config; mount them as files (a Kubernetes Secret or a creds file on disk) and reference the path.
- [OPS][SEC] Rotating a certificate is replacing the files behind `cert_file`/`key_file` then reloading; new handshakes present the new certificate while open connections keep their session.
- [ANTI][OPS] Include paths are relative to the config file, not your shell; use absolute paths when in doubt and validate before trusting. "Include paths are relative to the config file, not your shell."
- [ANTI][OPS][STRM] Don't SIGHUP a node while JetStream is moving replicas or handing off Raft leadership; wait for the cluster to settle. "A reload during a rebalance can interrupt a leadership transfer."
- [ANTI][OPS][STRM] Lowering a store limit on reload changes the ceiling, not the contents: existing messages stay but new writes fail until an admin trims the stream under the limit. Raise limits freely; lower them only after checking current storage. "Lowering a store limit on reload does not evict data already stored."
- [ANTI][OPS][SEC] An expired certificate fails every new connection and every client reconnect at the TLS handshake; rotate well before expiry and track the expiry date. "Rotating a TLS certificate late fails every new handshake."
- [OPS][PATTERN] Never SIGHUP an unvalidated config; even if a bad reload slips past the dry-run, the server keeps the old config, so the worst case is no change, not a half-applied one.

## Hardening
- path: learn/deployment/hardening.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/deployment/hardening

### Claims
- [SEC][TOPO] There are three independent TLS blocks: top-level `tls {}` for clients, `cluster { tls {} }` for routes, `gateway { tls {} }` for supercluster links; turning on client TLS leaves routes plaintext until the cluster block is configured too. "These blocks are independent."
- [SEC][ANTI] A common hardening mistake is securing clients and shipping a cluster whose inter-node Raft traffic, including replicated stream data, is still unencrypted.
- [SEC] In the client `tls {}` block, `verify: true` makes the link mTLS (every client must present a certificate chaining to `ca_file`); without it the server never checks the client's certificate.
- [SEC][TOPO] Cluster and gateway routes force mutual verification whether or not `verify` is set, because each end acts as both client and server; a node can't join just by knowing the route address, it must present a certificate chaining to `ca_file`.
- [SEC] `verify_and_map: true` on the client block makes the client certificate's subject the NATS user.
- [SEC][OPS] Certificate rotation is drop-in-new-files plus a SIGHUP, not a restart; existing connections keep their session and new handshakes get the new cert.
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] Mount `.creds` files as a Kubernetes Secret or under a path only the `nats` user can read; one authenticated TLS publish distinguishes a TLS misconfiguration (handshake failure) from wrong or unmounted credentials (authorization error).
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] The NATS distribution ships a hardened systemd unit (`nats-server-hardened.service`); adapt it (only `ExecStart`, `ReadWritePaths`, `LimitNOFILE`) rather than writing from scratch.
- [OPS][SIZE] The hardened unit sets `LimitNOFILE=800000`, far above the default 1024; each stream costs roughly two FDs and gossip plus client sockets add many more. "A large cluster exhausts the default 1024 quickly."
- [SEC][OPS] `ProtectSystem=strict` mounts the entire filesystem read-only except `ReadWritePaths`, so TLS certs and the JetStream store live under `/var/lib/nats`; the unit also sets `MemoryDenyWriteExecute`, `ProtectKernelTunables`, `ProtectProc=invisible`, `PrivateDevices`, empty `CapabilityBoundingSet`, and `SystemCallFilter=@system-service ~@privileged ~@resources`.
- [SEC][SIZE] The server listens on four ports: 4222 clients, 6222 cluster routes, 7222 gateways, 8222 HTTP monitor. The first three carry TLS once configured; the monitor port serves `/varz`, `/healthz` in plaintext and leaks server version, client count, and memory usage.
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] On a host, bind the monitor to `127.0.0.1:8222` and firewall the rest (allow 4222 to clients, 6222 only from the cluster subnet, deny 8222).
- [SEC][OPS][ANTI] On Kubernetes don't bind the monitor to `127.0.0.1`: kubelet probes connect to the pod IP, so the pods never go ready. Keep the chart's default bind and restrict with a NetworkPolicy.
- [ANTI][SEC][OPS] `ProtectSystem=strict` blocks writes outside `ReadWritePaths`, not reads; the JetStream `store_dir` (and pid/ports-file directories) must sit inside `ReadWritePaths` or the server can't come up. "`ProtectSystem=strict` blocks writes outside `ReadWritePaths`, not reads."
- [ANTI][OPS][SIZE] `MemoryMax` and `GOMEMLIMIT` don't reserve memory; `max_memory_store` is an accounting limit and `GOMEMLIMIT` a soft GC target. Set `MemoryMax` above expected use (memory-store data plus connection and route buffers plus GC headroom) and `GOMEMLIMIT` somewhat below `MemoryMax`. Example: `max_memory_store: 4Gi`, `MemoryMax=6G`, `GOMEMLIMIT=5500MiB`. "A memory cap set below the working set gets the process OOM-killed under load."
- [ANTI][SEC] The monitor port exposed to the internet leaks operational detail useful for reconnaissance; don't leave `http:` bound to `0.0.0.0`. "The monitor port exposed to the internet leaks operational detail."
- [ANTI][SEC][TOPO] Denying cluster port 6222 globally without allowing it between nodes means route handshakes never complete and each node comes up as an orphan; allow 6222 explicitly from the cluster subnet, then deny elsewhere. "A firewall blocking cluster port 6222 leaves nodes unable to form quorum."
- [OPS][SEC] If a node still shows as an orphan after allowing 6222, its route handshake is failing on the firewall or on a missing or mismatched cluster certificate.

## Rolling upgrades
- path: learn/deployment/rolling-upgrades.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/deployment/rolling-upgrades

### Claims
- [OPS][MIG] A careless restart drops every client on that node and can leave the stream a node short of quorum; a new server version means the process must restart, so roll one node at a time.
- [OPS][MIG] Lame-duck mode (specified in ADR-5) is entered with `SIGUSR2` (or `nats-server -sl=ldm=<pidfile>`); the node closes its client listener, transfers any Raft leadership it holds, shuts JetStream assets down cleanly flushing to disk, broadcasts `INFO ldm:true` to routes and clients, then after a grace period closes remaining client connections spread over the lame-duck duration.
- [CLNT][OPS] The `INFO ldm:true` update drops the node from each client's server pool so the next reconnect lands elsewhere; the client takes no other action on the INFO itself.
- [OPS][SIZE] `lame_duck_grace_period` defaults to `10s` (how long before it starts kicking clients); `lame_duck_duration` defaults to `2m`, minimum `30s` (total window over which kicks are spread). The grace period must be shorter than the duration. "`lame_duck_duration` (default `2m`, minimum `30s`)"
- [OPS][PATTERN] Set `lame_duck_duration` to comfortably cover how long clients take to reconnect and how long JetStream needs to move leadership off the node.
- [OPS] The NATS Helm chart wires lame-duck mode into the pod `preStop` hook so `kubectl rollout restart` triggers it; the server ignores SIGTERM while draining, so the drain is protected only by `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`.
- [OPS][SIZE] The Helm chart defaults `lame_duck_duration` to `30s` and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to `60s`; if you raise the duration, raise the grace period above `lame_duck_duration` plus shutdown overhead or the kubelet SIGKILLs the node mid-drain.
- [OPS][SIZE][MIG] Stepping the meta-leader down forces a metadata election during which stream and consumer operations (create, update, leadership moves) pause: typically about 5 to 10 seconds with default timeouts if killed outright, or roughly a second if it handed leadership off first. "typically about 5 to 10 seconds with default timeouts if the node was killed outright, or roughly a second if it handed leadership off first."
- [OPS][MIG][PATTERN] Upgrade order rule: upgrade the non-leaders first and the meta-leader last, so the one unavoidable metadata election is short and happens once. "upgrade the non-leaders first, and the meta-leader last."
- [OPS][MIG] Find the meta-leader with `nats server report jetstream`; it's a separate Raft group from the stream leader and may sit on a different node.
- [OPS][MIG][PATTERN] Per-node procedure: enter lame-duck and let it drain, restart on the new binary, then wait until the stream reports the node as a `current` replica before moving to the next node; taking the next node down while this one is syncing leaves the stream one healthy replica short.
- [OPS][SIZE][PATTERN] On Kubernetes a `PodDisruptionBudget` with `minAvailable: 2` stops Kubernetes voluntarily evicting two of three pods together, so a node drain can never cost the R3 stream its quorum.
- [OPS] `lame_duck_duration` and `lame_duck_grace_period` are the only two keys you must set for a safe roll.
- [CLNT][OPS] A node leaving in lame-duck mode requires no action from a correctly configured client; it keeps its existing connection, no client dials the node again, and on the staggered close the normal reconnect logic dials another node, resubscribes, and resumes.
