- [ANTI][OPS][SIZE] A `lame_duck_duration` shorter than the rebalance kicks clients and exits while the stream is still catching up; measure a real drain first, then set the duration above it with margin rather than the minimum. "A `lame_duck_duration` shorter than the rebalance drops clients early."
- [ANTI][OPS][MIG] Restarting the meta-leader without draining leaves no metadata leader until the election timeout fires (about 5 to 10 seconds) and every stream and consumer operation stalls; draining transfers leadership in roughly a second. Always enter lame-duck first and always do non-leaders first. "Upgrading the meta-leader without draining it stalls stream ops until a new leader is elected."
- [ANTI][OPS] A node drain, cluster autoscaler, or careless `kubectl delete` can take two or three pods together; set a PDB with `minAvailable: 2` and don't rely on doing steps slowly by hand. "Evicting pods without a PDB can drain all three at once."
- [ANTI][OPS][CLNT] A reconnect storm comes from abrupt kills or a duration so short the spread collapses, not from lame-duck mode, which staggers closes precisely to spread reconnects. Roll one node at a time and let it rejoin before starting the next. "A reconnect storm comes from abrupt kills, not from lame-duck."

## Kubernetes
- path: learn/deployment/kubernetes.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/deployment/kubernetes

### Claims
- [OPS][PATTERN] A NATS cluster is stateful: each node owns a slice of the R3 stream on its own disk and identity must survive restart, which rules out a Deployment and calls for a StatefulSet (stable name, network identity, and volume).
- [OPS] The NATS Helm chart renders the StatefulSet, headless service, ConfigMap, and probes; the release name `nats` gives the pods their `nats-N` names.
- [OPS] The chart sets `podManagementPolicy: Parallel` because the ordered default (wait for each pod to be ready before the next) deadlocks a NATS cluster: no single node is ready until it can see its peers. "the ordered default ... deadlocks a NATS cluster, because no single node is ready until it can see its peers."
- [OPS] Nodes route to each other via headless-service DNS names (`nats-0.nats-headless.default.svc.cluster.local`); clients connect to the regular ClusterIP service `nats`, which readiness pulls a not-ready pod out of.
- [OPS][SIZE] The chart wires three probes to `/healthz` on 8222: a startup probe on plain `/healthz` with `failureThreshold: 90` (~900s window for boot plus sync), a readiness probe on `/healthz?js-server-only=true`, and a liveness probe on `/healthz?js-enabled-only=true`.
- [OPS] The startup probe guards the boot window because a rejoining node may need minutes to catch replicas up; readiness takes a not-ready pod out of rotation; liveness asks only whether JetStream is enabled and is the last resort for a wedged process.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Prefer declarative streams: the NACK controller reconciles `Stream` and `Consumer` CRDs (`jetstream.nats.io/v1beta2`) against the cluster, so desired state lives in version control. If someone deletes the stream by hand, the controller recreates it from the CRD.
- [ANTI][OPS] A pod stuck Pending is usually an unbound volume (no default storage class); the fix is to confirm a storage class exists, not delete and retry the pod. "A pod stuck Pending is usually an unbound volume."
- [ANTI][OPS] A ConfigMap edit does not reload the server by itself; the chart's `nats-server-config-reloader` sidecar (enabled by default) sends the SIGHUP, and without it a change sits inert until the pod restarts. "A ConfigMap edit does not reload the server by itself."
- [ANTI][OPS] Readiness (`js-server-only=true`) deliberately skips stream, consumer, and meta-assignment checks, so a pod catching replicas up still reports ready and serves clients; plain `/healthz` (startup probe) is the strict one, hence `failureThreshold: 90`. Override via the chart's container `merge`/`patch`; there's no named `failureThreshold` value. "Replica catch-up shows up in the startup probe, not readiness."
- [ANTI][OPS][SIZE] Never mix CLI and CRD management of the same stream: by default NACK re-creates a deleted stream on its ~30-second resync but does not revert a manual `nats stream edit`; in `--control-loop` mode it also reverts config drift on about a one-minute cycle. Pick one owner per stream. "Never mix CLI and CRD management of the same stream."
- [OPS][PATTERN] Verify the CRD-created stream reads `Replicas: 3`; if it reads `1`, the CRD spec is missing `replicas: 3` or reconciling hasn't finished; check `.status` first.

## Where to go next (Deployment)
- path: learn/deployment/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/deployment/where-next

### Claims
- [OPS][PATTERN] The five operational steps run in order: size, deploy, configure, upgrade, harden.
- [OPS][SIZE] Sizing means reading account limits before committing to a PVC, rather than estimating after the disk fills; an R3 stream counts three times against account limits.
- [OPS][SIZE][PATTERN] Checklist: Set `max_file_store` to a size the disk can actually hold; test small (`10GB`) and watch `df -h`.
- [OPS][SIZE][PATTERN] Checklist: Keep `max_payload` at or below `max_pending`; hold `max_pending` at `>= 10×` peak message size.
- [OPS][SIZE][PATTERN] Checklist: Raise the file-descriptor limit before the process starts (`ulimit -n 800000`); a big cluster spends about two FDs per stream plus routes and gossip.
- [OPS][MIG][SEC][PATTERN] Checklist: Keep server versions aligned as you roll operator-mode upgrades so every node reads the same JWT limit fields; account limits change only when you edit and push the account JWT.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Read the live limits with `nats account info` before sizing.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Use `volumeClaimTemplates` (the Helm default) so each PVC binds before its StatefulSet replica starts.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Run the config reloader sidecar; a ConfigMap edit does not reload the server on its own.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Raise the readiness failure threshold so the probe doesn't flap not-ready during a healthy JetStream rebalance.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Never mix `nats` CLI mutations with a CRD-owned stream.
- [OPS][STRM][PATTERN] Checklist: Confirm the CRD-created stream is R3 with `nats stream info` before trusting the declarative path.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Write include paths as absolute paths.
- [OPS][STRM][PATTERN] Checklist: Fit a SIGHUP inside the graceful window; a reload during a rebalance can interrupt leadership transfer.
- [OPS][SEC][PATTERN] Checklist: Monitor TLS cert expiry as you rotate it.
- [OPS][STRM][PATTERN] Checklist: Trim oversized streams by hand after lowering `max_file`; a reload changes the ceiling, not the contents.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Dry-run every config change with `nats-server -c nats.conf -t` before you reload it.
- [OPS][MIG][PATTERN] Checklist: Measure rebalance time before setting `lame_duck_duration`.
- [OPS][MIG][SIZE][PATTERN] Checklist: Transfer leadership before killing the meta-leader (upgrading it directly stalls stream ops for about 5 to 10 seconds); do non-leaders first.
- [OPS][SIZE][PATTERN] Checklist: Set a PodDisruptionBudget with `minAvailable: 2`; without it an eviction can drain all three pods and lose quorum.
- [OPS][CLNT][PATTERN] Checklist: Stagger lame-duck start across ordinals; firing it on every node at once triggers a reconnect storm.
- [OPS][STRM][PATTERN] Checklist: Read replicas and leader with `nats stream info` before and after the upgrade to confirm the stream stayed R3.
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Keep the JetStream `store_dir` (and pid/ports-file dirs) inside `ReadWritePaths`.
- [OPS][SIZE][PATTERN] Checklist: Set `MemoryMax` above the node's real peak usage (memory store plus buffers plus GC headroom).
- [SEC][TOPO][PATTERN] Checklist: Open cluster port 6222 between nodes; a firewall that blocks it leaves nodes unable to form quorum.
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Bind the monitor port 8222 to localhost; exposed it leaks version, client count, and memory.
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: Connect with `--creds` and `--tlsca` and publish one order to prove auth and TLS are live before calling the cluster hardened.



## Security Deep Dive
- path: learn/security/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/security

### Claims
- [SEC][PATTERN] Security in NATS is three questions per connection: authentication (who you are), authorization (what you may do), encryption (is the wire safe). "who are you, what are you allowed to do, and is the wire safe"
- [SEC] Authentication proof can be a password, a token, a bearer JWT, or a signature using a secret (mTLS or NKeys, possibly with non-bearer JWTs).
- [SEC][SUBJ] Authorization is always expressed as subjects: a user can publish and subscribe only to the subjects granted; the server denies everything else.
- [SEC] TLS protects each connection from eavesdropping and tampering, and a client certificate can serve as the identity itself.
- [SEC][PATTERN] An account is an isolated tenant with its own users and subject space; two accounts never see each other's messages unless deliberately connected. "Two accounts never see each other's messages unless you deliberately connect them."
- [SEC] If a server configuration does not configure accounts, connections use the implicit global account `$G`.
- [SEC][PATTERN] The layered model: a user authenticates into an account, permissions decide what it may do, TLS keeps the connection safe.
- [SEC][PATTERN] The chapter's reference design: two accounts (`ORDERS`, `ANALYTICS`) isolated by default, a publisher user scoped to `orders.>` only, a reader user in a separate account, and a deliberate export/import bridge for exactly one subject (`orders.shipped`).

## Authentication basics
- path: learn/security/authentication-basics.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/security/authentication-basics

### Claims
- [SEC] Centralized authentication means the server holds the full user list in its own config file and never consults an external service.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Use centralized (config-file) authentication when one team owns the server config and the user list is small and slow to change. "the right tool when one team owns the server config and the user list is small and slow to change"
- [SEC][ANTI] Splitting auth data into separate files with `include` buys only a little headroom; treat it as buying time before moving away from centralized configuration. "treat it only as buying time before you move away from centralized configuration"
- [SEC] Users with no `accounts` block share the global account `$G`.
- [SEC][SIZE] The `authorization.timeout` field is how long the server gives a client to finish authenticating; default 2 seconds. Plain numbers are seconds; duration strings need quotes (unquoted `1m` parses as a number, not a minute).
- [SEC][MYTH] The server returns the same `Authorization Violation` for a wrong password and an unknown user, so a failed login does not reveal which half was wrong.
- [SEC][CLNT] Credentials are offered once per connection at connect time; authentication decides the user for the whole life of that connection. On reconnect, authentication happens again for the new connection.
- [SEC] Config auth offers three credential styles: user/password, NKey, and token; the model doesn't change, only the field differs.
- [SEC] An NKey user entry holds only a public key and replaces the whole user/password pair; the server rejects an entry that mixes them. The client proves ownership by signing a server-issued nonce, so nothing secret crosses the wire.
- [SEC] A seed whose public key the server doesn't know fails with the same `Authorization Violation` as a wrong password.
- [SEC][ANTI] Token auth is a single shared secret with no username, set server-wide on the `authorization` block; it can't be per-user, making it usable for quick internal setups but little else. "usable for quick internal setups but little else"
- [SEC][ANTI] CLI trap: `--user` doubles as a token field; a lone `--user` with no `--password` is sent as a token and can mask a misconfiguration against a token-configured server.
- [SEC][OPS] The server logs `[WRN] Plaintext passwords detected, use nkeys or bcrypt` on startup if any config password is plaintext.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Store passwords as bcrypt hashes: the server keeps the hash, the client still sends plaintext, and the stored value reveals nothing usable if the config leaks.
- [SEC][SIZE] `nats server passwd` defaults to bcrypt cost 11 (`$2a$11$` prefix) and refuses passwords shorter than 10 characters.
- [SEC][ANTI] The server treats strings starting with `$` as potential hash indicators; don't use plaintext passwords starting with a dollar sign. "don't use plaintext starting with a dollar sign"
- [SEC] Tokens can be stored as bcrypt hashes the same way as passwords.
- [SEC][ANTI] bcrypt protects only the config file at rest because the client still sends plaintext over the wire; pair it with TLS. "bcrypt protects only the config file at rest. Pair it with TLS"
- [SEC][MIG] Centralized auth breaks down when many tenants manage their own users or the user set needs to be dynamic; operator mode is built for that.
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: Running with no authentication in production. A server with no `authorization` block admits every connection; give every server at least one user list. "on a shared network anyone who can reach the port can publish and subscribe, so don't ship it"
- [SEC][ANTI] `no_auth_user` admits unauthenticated connects as a named user even when a user list exists; set it only on purpose.
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: Leaving plaintext passwords in a deployed config. Don't treat the startup warning as noise; store the bcrypt hash on any server someone else can read.
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: Committing credentials to git. A `nats.conf` with a password (even a bcrypt hash) is a secret; once in history, rotating is the only real fix. Reference an env var or secret store and gitignore the real config. "rotating the password is the only real fix, because the old value lives in every clone"
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: Putting the password in the connection URL. `nats://user:pass@host` leaks into shell history, process listings, and logs; store it in a named context instead.
- [SEC][OPS] If `NATS_PASSWORD` is exported, the CLI prints `WARNING: Shell environment overrides in place using NATS_PASSWORD`; don't export it or unset it once the context is saved.
- [SEC] A client certificate can be a credential: the server can map a certificate identity straight to a user with mTLS.

## Authorization
- path: learn/security/authorization.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/security/authorization

### Claims
- [SEC][SUBJ] A permission is a grant to publish to, or subscribe to, a set of subjects; there is no separate admin role or resource type. "There's no separate notion of an admin role or a resource type."
- [SEC][SUBJ] Everything a client does travels over a subject (a request/reply is a publish plus a subscribe on a reply subject), so controlling subjects controls everything.
- [SEC] A user's publish and subscribe lists are independent; a user can publish to a subject it can't subscribe to, or the reverse.
- [SEC][SUBJ] Permissions use the same wildcards as subjects: `*` matches one token, `>` matches one or more trailing tokens.
- [SEC][PATTERN] A publisher's minimal footprint is: publish allow on its own prefix (`orders.>`), subscribe allow on `_INBOX.>` so it can receive request replies. The inbox prefix is configurable but `_INBOX.` is the default.
- [SEC][PATTERN] The moment you write an `allow` list, every subject not on it is denied — including the JetStream API under `$JS.API.>`. "The moment you write an `allow` list, every subject not on it is denied."
- [SEC][MYTH] A user with no `permissions` block (no allow, no deny) is unrestricted and can do anything on the server.
- [SEC][ANTI][MYTH] An empty allow list is not a lock-down: `publish: []` parses as no list, so the user can publish anywhere. To block all publishes write `publish: { deny: [">"] }`.
- [SEC] `default_permissions` inside `authorization {}` applies to every user with no `permissions` block of its own; a user with its own block ignores the defaults entirely — never merged.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Deny beats allow: when a subject matches both lists, the server checks allow first, then deny, and a match in deny overrides. "When a subject matches both lists, deny wins."
- [SEC][PATTERN] To express "all of `orders.>` except one subject", allow the broad pattern and deny the exception rather than enumerating an allow-list.
- [SEC][CLNT] A permissions violation is reported, not silent: the server sends an async error and drops the message; the connection stays open. Clients surface it differently (log, raise on next op, async error handler).
- [SEC][CORE][ANTI] A denied request looks silent: the publish is denied, no responder sees it, and the requester just times out. Every JetStream API call is a request, so a locked-down user running `nats stream info` fails with `context deadline exceeded` rather than a permission error.
- [SEC][OPS] Every permission violation is recorded in the server log with user, account, and subject (`Publish Violation - Subject "..."`); check the log when a request times out for no clear reason.
- [SEC][ANTI] With `nats auth user edit`, each `--pub-allow`/`--sub-allow` flag replaces the entire list, so always pass the complete set of subjects.
- [SEC][PATTERN] With scoped signing keys (the recommended setup), the user's JWT carries empty publish/subscribe lists and the permissions live in the account's signing-key scope.
- [SEC][CORE][PATTERN] `allow_responses` lets a service reply to requests without a broad publish allow; the server tracks each reply subject and permits exactly that one reply.
- [SEC][CORE] Queue-group permissions: a subscribe entry `"orders.created billing-workers"` permits subscribing to that subject only as a member of that queue group; a plain subscribe stays denied.
- [SEC] Import and export permissions are a property of an account, not a user.
- [SEC][ANTI][CORE] Pitfall: A subscribe deny silently breaks request-reply. `subscribe: { deny: [">"] }` blocks the inbox subscription; adding `allow: ["_INBOX.>"]` next to it doesn't help because deny beats allow. Replace the deny with the allow. "Adding `allow: ["_INBOX.>"]` next to the deny doesn't help — deny beats allow"
- [SEC][ANTI] In the broken subscribe-deny state the CLI request waits out its timeout and exits 0 with no error; the denial shows only in the server log as `Subscription Violation`.
- [SEC][PATTERN] A service that answers requests must be able to publish to the reply subject it was handed; `allow_responses` is the clean way to grant that.
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: An allow-list that forgets a needed subject closes it off too; a missing entry is a silent block. Prefer the wildcard matching the user's real subject space over an enumerated list you must remember to grow. "Prefer the wildcard that matches the user's real subject space over an enumerated list"
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: An over-broad `>` grants every subject on the server, including the `$JS.API.>` control plane when JetStream is on. Scope each user to the subject prefix it actually uses. "`orders.>` for `order-svc`, never `>`"
- [SEC][ANTI][SUBJ] Pitfall: A deny can be invisible under a wildcard subscription. A literal subscribe to a denied subject is rejected loudly, but a wildcard subscription overlapping the deny is accepted and the server filters denied subjects out at delivery time with no error, no gap marker, and no server-log line. "If a subscriber seems to miss messages, check its deny lists before suspecting the publisher."

## Accounts and multitenancy
- path: learn/security/accounts-and-multitenancy.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/security/accounts-and-multitenancy

### Claims
- [SEC][PATTERN] Separate teams structurally with accounts instead of ever-longer permission lists; every new subject otherwise means another allow-list edit.
- [SEC] An account is an isolated tenant with its own subject space; the same subject string in two accounts is two different subjects.
- [SEC][PATTERN] An account boundary is absolute (the message doesn't cross it), which is stronger than permissions, which only narrow what one user may do inside its account. "An account boundary is absolute: the message doesn't cross it."
- [SEC] Every server already runs two accounts: `$G` (global; every connection on a server with no `accounts` block lands here) and `$SYS` (system; the server publishes monitoring and management events on `$SYS.SERVER.>`).
- [SEC][MYTH] `$SYS.>` subjects aren't blocked for other accounts; a subscription from an ordinary account is accepted and simply never receives anything, because responders exist only inside the system account.
- [SEC] Only `$G` is a reserved account name (declaring your own `$G` is a config error). Declaring `$SYS` yourself makes it the system account; the system account can be renamed with the top-level `system_account` directive. Avoid the `$` prefix for your own names.
- [SEC] Declaring a top-level `accounts` block takes over from the top-level `authorization` block; users left in `authorization` stay in `$G`.
- [SEC] A user lives in exactly one account; the username selects the account, so it must be unique across all accounts. A duplicate is a startup error: `Duplicate user "order-svc" detected`.
- [SEC][STRM] On a server running JetStream, declaring an `accounts` block makes JetStream opt-in per account (`jetstream: enabled`); an account without it gets `JetStream not enabled for account (10039)` on every JetStream call.
- [SEC][STRM] Each account gets its own JetStream store; a stream created in `$G` before accounts existed doesn't follow a user into its new account.
- [SEC] Once tenant accounts are defined, connections no longer land in `$G` by default; an unauthenticated connect is rejected with `Authorization Violation`.
- [SEC][MYTH] The lockdown comes from tenant accounts, not the `accounts` block itself: a config whose only account is the system account still admits unauthenticated clients into `$G`.
- [SEC][CORE] A request across an account boundary returns `No responders are available` immediately, not a permissions error; when a request that "should" work reports no responders, check which account each side is in.
- [SEC][OPS] An account can set limits (connections, JetStream storage) and can export subjects for another account to import.
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: `no_auth_user` can reopen access you intended to close. Pointing it at a user in `$G` lands every anonymous client in the global account again. Name a deliberately narrow user, never a wide-open account. "Do name a deliberately narrow user, and don't point it at a wide-open account."
- [SEC][OPS][ANTI] `no_auth_user` can't be introduced or changed by config reload (`config reload not supported for NoAuthUser`; old config stays active), `nats-server -t` doesn't catch a `no_auth_user` naming a missing user, and the server rejects `no_auth_user` together with a trusted operator.
- [SEC][ANTI][OPS] Pitfall: The system account has no user, so server events are unreachable. Declaring your own `accounts` block still creates `$SYS` but with no user; declare a `SYS` account with a user and set `system_account: SYS`. "with no user inside it you can't connect there"
- [SEC][OPS] A tenant user with a restricted publish allow list can't even query its own account info, because the CLI asks over `$SYS.REQ.USER.INFO` and the publish allow blocks that request.
- [SEC][ANTI][MYTH] Pitfall: A shared subject name doesn't mean shared delivery. Two accounts using `orders.shipped` never exchange a message; connecting tenants is a deliberate export/import act. "Don't reach for a matching name to connect tenants."

## Cross-account
- path: learn/security/cross-account.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/security/cross-account

### Claims
- [SEC][PATTERN] Account isolation is the right default; share across it deliberately for exactly the subjects you need and leave every other subject isolated. "That isolation is the right default, but sometimes you need to share across it."
- [SEC] Sharing a subject across accounts takes a matching pair: an export (the owning account offers a subject) and an import (the receiving account names the same subject and the exporting account). Neither half works alone.
- [SEC][OPS] An export with no matching import shares nothing (no error); an import with no matching export is refused — the server rejects the configuration at startup.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Export type follows the messaging pattern: a stream export is one-way publish/subscribe (exporter publishes, importers subscribe); a service export mirrors request/reply and flows both ways.
- [SEC][MYTH] A stream export has nothing to do with JetStream streams; it only means a one-way flow across the account boundary. "a stream export has nothing to do with JetStream streams"
- [SEC] An export with no further options is a public export any account may import; list `accounts: [...]` on the export entry to restrict it to named accounts.
- [SEC] An import lands at the same subject name by default; it may rename on the way in (`prefix:` or `to:`) to avoid colliding with local subjects.
- [SEC] Neither publisher nor subscriber observes the cross-account wiring; it lives entirely in the server's account configuration.
- [SEC][PATTERN] The boundary stays closed by default and opens one named subject at a time; an account's `exports` array is the complete list of what leaves it. "you can read an account's `exports` array and know the complete list of what leaves it"
- [SEC] A third account won't see exported messages unless it too imports the subject; it can import on a distinct name without impacting existing importers.
- [SEC][OPS][ANTI] In operator mode, both changed account JWTs must be pushed after adding an export/import; until then the share silently doesn't exist, because JWT mode has no startup check to catch a mismatch.
- [SEC] `nats auth` (v0.4.0) has no activation tokens for private exports; its substitute is `--token-position`, which keys a wildcard export so each importing account can only import the subject carrying its own account key.
- [SEC][ANTI][OPS] Pitfall: An export with no import is silent; an import with no export stops the server. Config-mode error: `Error adding stream import "orders.shipped": stream import not authorized`. In operator mode the failure is silent instead. "An export nobody imports isn't an error ... An import with no matching export is loud"
- [SEC][ANTI][CORE] Pitfall: Service and stream are not interchangeable. A service import with no responder running in the exporting account returns `No responders are available` immediately (exit 0, no timeout).
- [SEC][CORE] `No responders` on a service import means the import matched the export but nothing answered; a request with no import at all gets the same immediate answer because it never leaves the local account.
- [SEC][ANTI][SUBJ] Pitfall: A renamed import is not the original subject. Subscribe to the name the import lands on (after `prefix:`/`to:`), not the name the exporter published.

## Operator mode
- path: learn/security/operator-mode.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/security/operator-mode

### Claims
- [SEC][PATTERN] Operator mode removes the user list from the server: an operator signs each account, an account signs its users, and the server (trusting only the operator) verifies signatures at connect time. "No user lives in the server config."
- [SEC][ANTI] Building the trust chain by hand is error-prone; one wrong seed produces a JWT the server silently rejects at connect time. Use `nats auth` (or nsc).
- [SEC][ANTI] The `nats auth` store holds every private key in the trust chain (JWTs under `stores`, seeds under `keys` in `$XDG_DATA_HOME/nats`); run the tool on a trusted machine and never on the server. "which is why you run the tool on a trusted machine and never on the server"
- [SEC] The `nats auth` store is nsc-compatible on disk; both tools read the same tree. `nats auth` v0.4.0 lacks activation tokens and importing a single account into an existing operator; keep using `nsc` for those.
- [SEC] `nats auth operator add` always creates two extras: a `SYSTEM` account and one operator signing key. The server uses `SYSTEM` to answer its own internal JWT-lookup requests.
- [SEC][SIZE] `--defaults` on user add bakes a 1 MiB (1,048,576) max payload limit into each user JWT and no permissions (the user can publish/subscribe anywhere in its account).
- [SEC][PATTERN] NKey IDs start with `O` (operator), `A` (account), `U` (user); anything starting with `S` (`SO`, `SA`, `SU`) is a seed — roughly the private key — so be very careful. "If you ever see an ID which starts with an `S` ... then _be very careful_"
- [SEC] A user JWT alone can't connect; the client also needs the private NKey seed to sign the server's challenge. That's why a creds file packages both.
- [SEC][ANTI] Bearer JWTs are an explicit opt-in exception; avoid them unless needed for WebSocket connections. "You should avoid them unless you need them for WebSockets connections."
- [SEC][ANTI] A credentials file is a secret: treat it like a password, readable by the one client that uses it and nothing more.
- [SEC] The account resolver tells the server where to find account JWTs at connect time; without it the server can't complete the chain and the connection fails.
- [SEC][PATTERN] The recommended resolver type is the full nats-based resolver (server keeps every account JWT in a local directory; new ones delivered over NATS). Memory, cache, and URL resolvers also exist, but `nats auth` can only push to a full resolver.
- [SEC][SIZE] Generated full resolver config uses `allow_delete: true`, `interval: "2m"`, `limit: 1000`.
- [SEC] `operator` in server config is the full operator JWT, not a bare key. `resolver_preload` bakes the SYSTEM account JWT into the config so a system user can connect before anything is pushed.
- [SEC][OPS] Account push is per account (once per account); `Success 1 Failed 0 Expected 1` means the single server confirmed. `nats auth account query` reads back what the resolver holds.
- [SEC] User JWTs are never pushed to the server; user definitions do not live in the server. The client presents its user JWT at connect time and the server remembers it for the life of the connection.
- [SEC][PATTERN] The shift from config mode: the server holds one trusted key, not a list of users.
- [SEC][ANTI][OPS] Pitfall: Editing an account without pushing it. `nats auth account edit` changes only the local JWT; the server keeps validating against its copy so the edit silently has no effect. Push after every account change and confirm with `account query`. "Push after every account change"
- [SEC][ANTI][OPS] Pitfall: System account missing under a nats-based resolver. The server exits at boot with `using nats based account resolver - the system account needs to be specified in configuration or the operator jwt`; bites when the operator JWT was built by hand or by a tool that didn't set one.
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: Leaking the `.creds` file. It carries the private seed; anyone holding it can connect, with no password to guess and no list to revoke against. Never bake it into an image, log it, or commit it; give it `0600` and mount it to the one client that needs it. To cut off a leak, revoke the user and re-push the account.
- [SEC][ANTI][OPS] Pitfall: Credential expiration. Expiring credentials reduce compromise impact without a signing-key rotation, but you then have a set of objects to monitor for expiration.

## Decentralized authentication
- path: learn/security/decentralized-auth.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/security/decentralized-auth

### Claims
- [SEC][PATTERN] Use decentralized auth when each team should manage its own users without touching the server; the server needs only a way to tell a real user from a forged one (a signature check), not knowledge of every user in advance.
- [SEC] The trust chain has three links: operator (root of trust, one per deployment, the single identity the server trusts), account (tenant, vouched for by the operator), user (auth identity, vouched for by its account). "Vouches for" means signs.
- [SEC] NKeys are Ed25519 keypairs; the server only ever handles public NKeys and signatures, never anyone's seed.
- [SEC] An account can hold extra signing keys that count as valid issuers for its users; the operator can hold signing keys for accounts the same way. A user signed by an account signing key carries `issuer_account` in its JWT.
- [SEC][MYTH] A user JWT isn't the config "token": the token is a password-style secret compared against config, while a JWT is a signed document anyone can inspect but only the right account key can produce.
- [SEC] The server sends a fresh random nonce per connection; the client signs it with the user seed and returns the signature with the user JWT.
- [SEC] The server checks three things: (1) nonce signature verifies against the user public key in the JWT (proves the client holds the seed now), (2) user JWT signed by the issuing account's identity or signing key, (3) account JWT from the resolver signed by a key in the operator JWT.
- [SEC][MYTH] A stolen user JWT alone is useless: without the seed it can't sign the nonce (fails check 1). That's why the creds file has two sections.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Decentralized auth scales because a signature check works for a user the server has never seen; no config entry has to exist before the user connects.
- [SEC][PATTERN] The clean way to assign permissions in operator mode is a scoped signing key: an account signing key with a role name and a fixed permission set; every user issued by that key gets exactly those permissions. "the clean way to assign them is a **scoped signing key**"
- [SEC] A scoped user's own JWT carries an empty permission set (`"pub": {}, "sub": {}`); the server applies the key's template at connect time, so a template change reaches every user signed by that key on the next account push, with no creds re-issued.
- [SEC][OPS] After adding a scoped signing key, the account must be pushed before new credentials are accepted; until then connects fail with `Authorization Violation`.
- [SEC][SIZE] Expiry belongs to the minted credential, not the stored user; `--expire 720h` on `nats auth user credential` makes the user JWT lapse after 30 days.
- [SEC][OPS] `nats auth user rm` without `--revoke` only deletes from the local store; handed-out credentials keep working because the server never consults your store. With `--revoke` a `revocations` map entry (public key to timestamp) is written into the account JWT; any user JWT for that key issued at or before that time is rejected.
- [SEC][OPS] Revocation takes effect on the next account push, and the push also disconnects clients currently connected as the revoked user.
- [SEC] Revocation pins the old user's public key; a re-issued user with a new key under the same name connects fine after the next push.
- [SEC] Bearer users connect with no seed and no nonce signature, so anyone holding the JWT can connect. Accounts disallow bearer tokens by default (`Bearer Tokens Allowed: false`); both account and user must be marked `--bearer`.
- [SEC][PATTERN][ANTI] Bearer tokens are a convenience for browser and websocket clients that have nowhere safe to keep a seed; they reduce the credential to a single document that must never leak.
- [SEC][TOPO] The server supports multiple operators; they are equivalent and the account namespace is flat across all operators.
- [SEC][ANTI][OPS] Rotating operators (after operator key compromise) is technically possible by adopting accounts into the new operator gradually, but it is not easy and there are no tooling affordances for it.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Use operator signing keys, keep at least one offline, and expose only one operator signing key to risk; then migrate between signing keys of the existing operator instead of between operators. "keep at least one off-line, and only keep one operator signing key exposed to risk"
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: Losing the operator seed. It is the only thing that can sign accounts; back the operator up before building on it (`nats auth operator backup`), encrypt with `--key`, store offline. An unencrypted backup holds the operator seed in cleartext.
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: Pasting a seed where a public key belongs. Config and JWT fields only take public NKeys (`O...`, `A...`, `U...`); a pasted `S...` seed must be rotated. "Treat every `S`-prefixed string like a password."
- [SEC][ANTI][PATTERN] Pitfall: Signing users with the account's identity key. It works, but permissions then live on each user and whoever holds the account seed can issue a user with any permissions; a scoped key pins permissions up front so a leaked signing key can only issue users with the chosen scope (ADR-14).
- [SEC][ANTI][OPS] The CLI (v0.4.0) can't edit a scope in place; the only way is to remove the key and re-add the role, which creates a new key and locks out every user signed by the old one at the next push. "Treat key removal as mass revocation, not as an edit."
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: Not planning for credential expiry. A user JWT minted by `nats auth user add` never expires, so a leaked creds file is valid until revoked. The only expiry control in v0.4.0 is on the credentials file (`--expire`). Pair a short expiry with a renewal step.
- [SEC][OPS] A lapsed client is rejected with plain `Authorization Violation`; the server's default log records only `authentication error`, and `claim is expired` appears only in the debug log.

## Auth callout
- path: learn/security/auth-callout.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/security/auth-callout
- version context: NATS Server 2.10.0+ required for auth callout; `allowed_accounts` is 2.11+

### Claims
- [SEC][PATTERN] Auth callout delegates the authentication decision to an external NATS service when the source of truth for identity lives in a system NATS can't read (OIDC, LDAP, custom credential service).
- [SEC] The hand-off happens over one subject, `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH`: the server publishes a request describing the connection attempt; the auth service replies with a user identity or a rejection. The protocol is fixed (ADR-26); the logic in the middle is yours.
- [SEC] The client has no indication that a callout happened.
- [SEC] `issuer` is the public account NKey allowed to sign the response; the server admits a client only if the reply was signed by this key.
- [SEC] `auth_users` lists users that skip the callout; the auth service itself must be listed or it could never connect to receive requests.
- [SEC] The account the callout places a client into must exist in the config.
- [SEC][SIZE] Auth callout requires NATS Server 2.10.0 or later; it is disabled in FIPS-140 mode and can't be configured there.
- [SEC][ANTI] `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH` carries every connection attempt with whatever the client presented (token, password, NKey) readable — base64 is encoding, not encryption — so anything that can read the subject can harvest credentials. "Anything that can read this subject can harvest other clients' credentials."
- [SEC] On the account where auth callout runs, publishing to `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH` is denied for every user (including the auth service), which stops forged requests and verdicts but not eavesdropping.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Run the auth service in its own dedicated account (the `account` field) holding nothing else, so no other user can subscribe to request traffic; the callout service can bind clients to any authorized account, so it should be isolated anyway (ADR-26 recommendation). "run `auth-svc` in its own dedicated account"
- [SEC] The `account` field defaults to the global account `$G` when unset; production setups override it.
- [SEC] The server signs each request with an NKey generated fresh at startup (issuer = server ID, audience `nats-authorization-request`); the real protection against provoked verdicts is the publish deny, since the request key isn't a pre-trusted identity.
- [SEC] Each request pins a one-time `user_nkey`; the reply is valid only if it names that exact NKey as subject, so a captured old reply can't be replayed against a new connection.
- [SEC] The response is two JWTs nested: an outer verdict (subject = `user_nkey`, audience = asking server's ID, so it's useless at another server) wrapping a user JWT whose audience is the target account name, which is what places the client in that account. Both must be signed by the `issuer` key; in config mode the server rejects a user JWT naming an `issuer_account`.
- [SEC] Rejection shapes: the service replies with an error (client gets `Authorization Violation` immediately; error text goes only to the server log) or drops the request (client waits out the callout timeout, typically reporting `i/o timeout`).
- [SEC][PATTERN] The callout libraries recommend dropping requests for bad credentials, because the added delay slows brute-force guessing. "The callout libraries recommend dropping for bad credentials"
- [SEC][PATTERN] Auth mode selection: static config list → centralized authentication; a trust chain you control with `nats auth` → operator mode; verdict must come from a system NATS doesn't own → auth callout. "Auth callout is for when the verdict must come from a system NATS doesn't own."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Use the x25519 `xkey` option to encrypt the request and response so credentials on `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH` are sealed even from a leaked subscription; reach for it whenever the wire carries secrets.
- [SEC][MIG] `allowed_accounts` (2.11+) limits delegation to listed config-defined accounts so you can move one account at a time; without it, once `auth_callout` is on every connection except `auth_users` goes through it, including config users with correct passwords. Connections matching no config user land in `$G` and always go through the callout.
- [SEC] In operator mode, auth callout is configured on the account's JWT, and the account declares which other accounts the auth service may bind clients to.
- [SEC][ANTI][OPS] Pitfall: The auth service is a single point of failure. If it's down or slow, the server waits out `authorization.timeout` (default two seconds) and rejects the client. Set `timeout` deliberately, run more than one instance, keep OIDC/LDAP lookups fast. "Run more than one instance so a single slow one doesn't stall logins"
- [SEC][SIZE][CLNT] A client's own connect deadline also defaults to about two seconds, so with both defaults the client usually reports `i/o timeout` rather than an auth error; if the callout timeout is shorter than the client deadline, the client sees `Authorization Violation`. The reason lives only in the server log.
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: Adding application users to `auth_users`. Every user there skips the callout and connects with no external check; list only the auth service. "Adding an application user here to 'save a round trip' silently exempts it from authentication."
- [SEC][ANTI] Two more mistakes: leaving the callout in the global account `$G`, and skipping `xkey` so credentials cross `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH` in the clear.

## Encryption & TLS
- path: learn/security/encryption.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/security/encryption

### Claims
- [SEC][TOPO] TLS is per connection type: the top-level `tls {}` block secures only client connections; monitoring, websocket, mqtt, leafnode, cluster, and gateway each have their own nested `tls {}` sub-block. "Turning on TLS for clients leaves cluster routes plaintext until you configure the cluster block too."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Per-link TLS independence is deliberate: a laptop client and an inter-datacenter gateway have different threat models, so each link gets its own configuration.
- [SEC] Server-side TLS needs three files: `cert_file` (server identity), `key_file` (its private key), `ca_file` (the authority trusted to have signed peer certificates).
- [SEC][SIZE] `tls.timeout` is the handshake budget in seconds; default `2`, enough for a healthy network. Too short and a slow client can't finish; too long and a stalled handshake holds a slot open.
- [SEC] With TLS on, a plaintext client is refused at the handshake and never reaches authentication.
- [SEC][CLNT] A TLS client verifies the server certificate before sending a single byte of credentials; it needs a CA certificate in its pool valid for the signing path to the server certificate.
- [SEC][TOPO] The server you connect to is the TLS endpoint and sees plaintext; routed copies of the traffic happen outside your TLS connection and depend on whatever TLS exists on those onward links.
- [SEC][CLNT] TLS verification checks the dialed hostname against names in the certificate; a cert for `nats.acme.internal` rejects a client dialing `127.0.0.1` unless the address is listed. Match the connection address to a name the certificate covers.
- [SEC][CLNT] If a client sees an IP address in the advertised server list (`client_advertise`), it treats it like an updated DNS entry and on reconnect should use the original DNS hostname as the identity to verify even while connecting to a different IP.
- [SEC] mTLS demands a certificate from every client and rejects any that doesn't chain to the server's `ca_file`; that proves the client holds a valid certificate but doesn't say who it is.
- [SEC][PATTERN] `verify_and_map: true` requires and verifies the client certificate, then reads an identity out of it as the NATS user: email SANs first, then DNS SANs, then URI SANs, then the subject DN (RFC 2253). A SAN is used only if it matches a user; otherwise it falls back to the subject.
- [SEC] With `verify_and_map`, the certificate is the credential: no password, no creds file. The DN match is DN-aware, not a plain string compare, so attribute spacing and ordering don't matter.
- [SEC][PATTERN] `verify_and_map` includes everything `verify: true` does plus the mapping, so don't set both. Use plain `verify` only when an external system already maps certificates to users. "Reach for plain `verify` only when an external system already maps certificates to users"
- [SEC] By default NATS starts every connection in plaintext: the server sends `INFO` first (server version, connect URLs, unencrypted), then both sides upgrade to TLS before credentials flow.
- [SEC] `handshake_first: true` makes the TLS handshake happen before any protocol byte, like HTTPS; the server warns `Clients that are not using "TLS Handshake First" option will fail to connect`.
- [SEC][CLNT] A client expecting plaintext `INFO` against a `handshake_first` server hangs until its read timeout and fails with `i/o timeout`.
- [SEC][SIZE][MIG] For migration, `handshake_first` accepts `"auto"`/`"auto_fallback"` (fall back to plaintext `INFO` if no TLS bytes arrive within 50 ms) or a duration like `"300ms"` for a custom fallback delay.
- [SEC][OPS][MYTH] `openssl s_client` fails with `wrong version number` against a default NATS TLS port because the first bytes are the plaintext `INFO` line; that error doesn't mean TLS is broken. Use `gnutls-cli --starttls` or turn on `handshake_first`.
- [SEC][STRM] Encryption at rest is a server-wide `jetstream {}` setting that encrypts stream data and metadata on disk with an AEAD cipher; it's global, not per account, and independent of TLS.
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] Some disk controllers handle encryption at rest at the block layer at high performance without server CPU cost; evaluate carefully whether having nats-server do the encryption is right for your deployment. "carefully evaluate if having the nats-server do the encryption itself is the right solution"
- [SEC][PATTERN] Keep the at-rest key out of the config file via an environment variable (`key: $JS_KEY`).
- [SEC] ChaCha20-Poly1305 is the default at-rest cipher; `cipher: aes` switches to AES-GCM.
- [SEC][OPS] To rotate the master key, restart once with the new key in `key` and the old in `prev_key`; the server re-wraps per-stream keys and persists the result. `prev_key` is transitional — drop it after the rotation restart.
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: TLS on without `verify` is encryption, not authentication. Any client that trusts your CA connects without presenting a certificate until you add `verify: true` or `verify_and_map: true`. "TLS on without `verify` is encryption, not authentication."
- [SEC][OPS] Confirm `verify` works by pointing a certificate-less client at the server: expect `remote error: tls: certificate required`; if the publish succeeds, the server isn't checking client certificates.
- [SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: `verify_and_map` needs the certificate subject to name a real user. A typo or wrong attribute fails with `Authorization Violation`. Don't hand-type the DN; read it with `openssl x509 -noout -subject` and paste it.
- [SEC][ANTI][TOPO] Pitfall: Cluster and gateway certificates need both `serverAuth` and `clientAuth` key usages. Route/gateway TLS is always mutual and each node presents its one cert as both server and client; a `serverAuth`-only cert fails the route handshake — the most common cluster-TLS failure. "the most common cluster-TLS failure"
- [SEC][OPS][TOPO] The route key-usage rejection is logged on the peer, not the misconfigured node (`TLS route handshake error: ... certificate specifies an incompatible key usage`); the cluster can still come up through the one working direction, leaving a mesh that works but logs the error on every reconnect.
- [SEC][ANTI][OPS] Pitfall: Certificates rotate on disk, not in the server. Cert/key/CA files are read once at startup; overwriting does nothing until `nats-server --signal reload` (or SIGHUP), and even then existing connections keep the certificate they handshook with; only new connections get the rotated one.
- [SEC][OPS] An expired certificate fails as a handshake rejection, not an auth error; monitor validity dates and pair renewal with the reload signal.
- [SEC][ANTI][MIG] Pitfall: `handshake_first: true` locks out every legacy client. Migrate with a duration value (`handshake_first: "300ms"`) that accepts both kinds of client, and flip to `true` only after the last client has opted in.
- [SEC][ANTI][STRM] Pitfall: A wrong at-rest key hides streams; it doesn't destroy them. `Error decrypting our stream metafile: unable to recover keys` means the wrong key; restart with the right one and the stream returns.
- [SEC][ANTI] Don't keep running with `prev_key` set after rotation; leaving the old key in place keeps a retired secret live.

## Where to go next (Security)
- path: learn/security/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/security/where-next

### Claims
- [SEC][PATTERN] Four questions define a connection's security posture: account (whose traffic), user (who are you), permissions (which subjects), TLS (is the wire protected). "If you can answer those four questions for a connection, you understand its security posture."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Centralized auth: user list in server config, change via config reload (`nats-server --signal reload`, no restart); right for one server and a handful of users. "It's the right tool for one server and a handful of users."
- [SEC][PATTERN] Decentralized auth: operator signs accounts, accounts sign users, server trusts only the operator; adding a user touches no server config; right for many tenants or when teams issue their own credentials.
- [SEC] Both auth styles produce the same runtime model (authenticated user, scoped to an account, bound by permissions); they differ only in where the identity lives and who signs it.
- [SEC][TOPO] A cluster, a leaf node, and a gateway are each a connection type carrying its own TLS and authentication.
- [SEC][TOPO] A leaf node authenticates to the hub with the same accounts and credentials; the credentials attach in the hub's `leafnodes {}` block.
- [SEC][STRM][MYTH] Whether a stream survives losing its server is replication, not security: security decides who may access a stream; replication decides whether it's still there.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Give every server a user list so an unauthenticated connect is rejected.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Store bcrypt hashes, not plaintext passwords, in any deployed config.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Keep credentials out of committed config: reference a secret store and `.gitignore` the real file.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Put credentials in a named context, never in the connection URL.
- [SEC][CORE] Checklist: Allow `_INBOX.>` on the subscribe side for any user that makes requests.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Checklist: Prefer a wildcard matching the user's real subject space over an enumerated allow-list.
- [SEC][ANTI] Checklist: Scope each user to its actual subject prefix — never grant `>`.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Check the subscriber's deny lists when messages silently go missing; a wildcard subscription overlapping a deny is accepted and filtered at delivery with no error.
- [SEC][ANTI] Checklist: Point `no_auth_user` at a deliberately narrow user, never a wide-open account.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Declare a `SYS` account with a user and set `system_account: SYS` so server events stay reachable.
- [SEC][ANTI] Checklist: Never rely on a shared subject name to bridge accounts; use an explicit export/import.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Pair every export with its import; in config mode an unmatched import stops the server at boot, and an unmatched export silently moves nothing.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Checklist: Match the export type to the data flow: `stream` for one-way, `service` for request/reply.
- [SEC][SUBJ] Checklist: Subscribe to the remapped subject when an import adds a `prefix:` or `to:`.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Run `nats auth account push` after every account change, including user revocations and signing-key changes, which live in the account JWT.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Keep the system account configured; the nats-based resolver refuses to start without it.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Give `.creds` files `0600` permissions; never bake, log, or commit them.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Consider monitoring issues if using credentials with baked-in expiration times.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Back up the operator offline before building anything on it.
- [SEC][ANTI] Checklist: Configure the server with the operator JWT (public material only), never a private seed.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Checklist: Sign users with a scoped signing key, not the account root seed.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Mint credentials with a deliberate expiry (`--expire 720h`) and pair it with a re-issue plan.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Run more than one auth-callout service instance and set `timeout` deliberately; the service is on the connection path.
- [SEC][ANTI] Checklist: List only the auth service in `auth_users`; every other user must go through the callout.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Checklist: Run the auth service in its own account, and reach for `xkey` when the wire carries secrets.
- [SEC][ANTI] Checklist: Add `verify` (or `verify_and_map`); TLS alone encrypts but doesn't authenticate the client.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Match the `verify_and_map` user string to the certificate identity (read it with `openssl x509 -noout -subject`).
- [SEC][TOPO] Checklist: Configure TLS on cluster, leafnode, and gateway blocks too, not just clients.
- [SEC][TOPO] Checklist: Give each cluster node's certificate both `serverAuth` and `clientAuth` extended key usage; the same cert acts as server and client on routes.
- [SEC][MIG] Checklist: Migrate to TLS-first with a duration value (`handshake_first: "300ms"`) before setting it to `true`, so legacy clients keep connecting during the rollout.
- [SEC][OPS] Checklist: Rotate certificates ahead of expiry and send `nats-server --signal reload` afterwards; certificate files are read once at startup.
- [SEC][STRM][OPS] Checklist: Keep the JetStream encryption key out of the config file (`key: $JS_KEY`), and carry `prev_key` for one rotation restart only.

## Resilient Clients Deep Dive
- path: learn/resilient-clients/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/resilient-clients

### Claims
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Resilience isn't new application code; it's the connection configured to survive faults: detect a break, buffer while broken, recover without losing the application's place, shut down without losing in-flight work.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] The connection is a state machine: DISCONNECTED, CONNECTING, CONNECTED, RECONNECTING, DRAINING, CLOSED; every fault is a transition. A server dying moves CONNECTED to RECONNECTING; a clean shutdown moves to DRAINING then CLOSED.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] A resilient client: opens with a name, a server pool, and a sane connect timeout; reconnects with backoff and jitter and flushes buffered publishes on rejoin; wires all events to one place and feeds state to a readiness probe; drains on SIGTERM; bounds subscriber memory with pending limits; distinguishes absent responder from slow responder; presents credentials over CA-validated TLS.
- [CLNT] Server-side faults (why a server went away) live in Topologies; consumer acknowledgment position across reconnect lives in JetStream; issuing credentials lives in Security — the client chapter covers only what the client does.

## Connecting
- path: learn/resilient-clients/connecting.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/resilient-clients/connecting

### Claims
- [CLNT] A connection option is fixed for the life of the connection: chosen at open time, not while messages flow.
- [CLNT][OPS][PATTERN] Name every connection (e.g. `order-svc`) so it's identifiable in `nats server report connections` and server logs; by default a connection is anonymous.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] The server pool is the list of URLs the client may connect to; with several URLs the client tries them until one answers — failover at connect time.
- [CLNT] By default the client randomizes the pool before dialing, spreading connections evenly across servers instead of concentrating on the first URL.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Turn randomization off (`NoRandomize`/`dont_randomize`/`retain_servers_order`) only when you deliberately want a preferred-server order; most applications should leave it on so a restart of every instance doesn't overload one server. "Most applications should leave it on"
- [CLNT][TOPO] The `INFO` message carries `connect_urls` listing cluster members' client addresses, and the server sends a fresh `INFO` whenever the list changes (gossip); the client merges each list into its pool as discovered servers.
- [CLNT] Discovered URLs follow the same randomization rule and are reconnect candidates; a configured URL stays in the pool for the life of the connection, while a discovered one can be dropped once the cluster stops advertising it.
- [CLNT] Discovery merging is on by default in every client; Go/Java/Rust/JS can opt out (`IgnoreDiscoveredServers`, `ignoreClusterUpdates`), Python and C# always merge. The usual reason to opt out is that advertised addresses may not be dialable from the client's network.
- [CLNT][TOPO] With `no_advertise` set in cluster configuration, `INFO` carries no `connect_urls` and the pool stays exactly what you configured.
- [CLNT][SIZE] The connect timeout caps how long a single dial may block before trying the next URL; default two seconds in most clients, five in Rust, twenty in JavaScript. "Two seconds is enough for a healthy network"
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Pool and timeout complement each other: one unreachable server costs one timeout, then the client moves to the next URL.
- [CLNT] The connect handshake: TCP dial (bounded by connect timeout) → server `INFO` (`server_id`, `max_payload`, `auth_required`, `tls_required`) → client `CONNECT` + `PING` → server `PONG` (CONNECTED) or `-ERR` and socket close. Clients turn verbose off by default, so `PONG` is what confirms the connection.
- [CLNT][SIZE] `max_payload` is the largest single message the server accepts, one megabyte by default; the client enforces it locally so an oversized publish fails before it leaves the client.
- [CLNT][ANTI] A failed connect isn't always a dead socket: the server can accept TCP and then reject with `-ERR` (e.g. `maximum connections exceeded`), so a retry loop around connect needs a wait between attempts.
- [CLNT][ANTI] Pitfall: One URL is a single point of failure at connect time. Don't hardcode one URL for a production client; pass the whole pool. "Don't hardcode one URL for a production client."
- [CLNT][ANTI][TOPO] Pitfall: A one-URL configuration that depends on discovery fails where discovery is off (`no_advertise`) or where advertised addresses aren't reachable. Configure every server you want the client to rely on, and treat discovered servers as additions.
- [CLNT][ANTI] Pitfall: A blocked dial with no timeout hangs the startup; a service hanging on startup looks dead rather than slow. Set a deliberate connect timeout and pair it with a pool.
- [CLNT][ANTI][SIZE] Pitfall: An oversized message fails the publish, not the connect. Don't treat that error as a connection problem; keep messages under `max_payload` (1 MB default), and for large bodies store the blob elsewhere and publish a reference. "for large bodies store the blob elsewhere and publish a reference"
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Handle connect failures at the boundary, branching on whether the client could reach any server in the pool, instead of letting them surface deep in the application.

## Reconnection
- path: learn/resilient-clients/reconnection.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/resilient-clients/reconnection

### Claims
- [CLNT] A disconnect is when the client notices the link is gone (socket close or unanswered keepalive PING); it fires a disconnect callback but doesn't close — it moves to RECONNECTING and walks the pool.
- [CLNT] State transitions: CONNECTED → (disconnect) RECONNECTING → (PONG) CONNECTED; RECONNECTING → (pool exhausted, retries spent) CLOSED.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Reconnect is on by default in every client; leave it on. Turning it off makes the connection close on the first disconnect, which is rarely what a service wants. "Leave reconnect on"
- [CLNT] By default most clients try each URL once on the first connect, return an error, and never enter RECONNECTING; a bad address fails loudly at startup.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] In production the common reason no server answers at startup is ordering after a deploy (the client restarts faster than servers); opt in to retry-on-failed-first-connect (`RetryOnFailedConnect`, `waitOnFirstConnect`, `retry_on_initial_connect`, `RetryOnInitialConnect`, Java `connectReconnectOnConnect`) so the service sits in RECONNECTING instead of crash-looping.
- [CLNT] Go's `RetryOnFailedConnect(true)` makes `Connect` return immediately in RECONNECTING; the `ConnectHandler` callback is how you learn it actually came up. JS `waitOnFirstConnect` keeps the promise pending and the attempt limit doesn't apply until first success. Python's `connect()` already retries and raises `NoServersError` only when every server's budget is spent.
- [CLNT] The CLI has no retry-on-first-connect flag; a `nats` command started while the pool is down fails immediately.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Backoff: after trying every URL once with none answering, the client pauses before the next sweep; without it a client would spin a tight dial loop against a pool that isn't ready.
- [CLNT][SIZE] Base reconnect wait (`ReconnectWait`) defaults to two seconds. Go, Java, Python, JS use the same wait every sweep by default; Rust and .NET grow the wait each attempt by default.
- [CLNT][SIZE] Default jitter: up to 100 ms on plaintext and up to 1 s on TLS in Go, Java, and JavaScript (TLS handshakes cost more, so spread retries wider); C# up to 100 ms regardless of TLS; Python and Rust add no jitter.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Jitter exists so a thousand clients that lost the same server don't retry in lockstep and overload the remaining server.
- [CLNT] In Go and JavaScript a custom reconnect-delay callback's return value is the entire sleep — no jitter is added on top — so include your own.
- [CLNT][SIZE] The `nats` CLI connects with unlimited retries and a delay that starts at 500 ms and grows to a 20-second cap, each step randomized between half and one-and-a-half times its value.
- [CLNT][SIZE] `MaxReconnect` is tracked per server, not per outage (Go, Java, JS, Python): a server that uses up its count is dropped from the pool and the connection gives up once none are left; Go and Python reset a server's count on successful connect. Defaults: 60 in Go/Java/Python, 10 in JavaScript, unlimited in Rust and C#.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] For a long-lived service set `MaxReconnect` to `-1` (unlimited) in clients that default to a bounded count so a long outage never closes the connection. "For a long-lived service, unlimited is what you want."
- [CLNT] Subscriptions are re-sent automatically on the new connection after reconnect.
- [CLNT][SIZE] The reconnect buffer holds outbound publishes during RECONNECTING and flushes them in order on reconnect; default 8 MB in Go and Java, 2 MB in Python; Rust applies backpressure on a bounded queue instead.
- [CLNT][MYTH] Flush is not a delivery guarantee: buffered publishes are still plain core publishes with at-most-once semantics; the buffer doesn't turn a publish into a durable acknowledged write. "Flush is not a delivery guarantee."
- [CLNT] On reconnect the client first restores subscriptions, then re-sends buffered publishes in the order they were made.
- [CLNT] When the reconnect buffer overflows, Go/Java/Python fail the next publish (Go: `ErrReconnectBufExceeded`); Rust blocks under backpressure. An overflowing buffer is a signal to slow down; don't ignore it.
- [CLNT][CONS][MYTH] The reconnect buffer does not restore a JetStream consumer's place in the stream; acknowledgment position is the JetStream layer's bookkeeping, not the connection's.
- [CLNT][ANTI] Pitfall: A bounded retry limit gives up on a long outage (rolling upgrade, long partition) and moves to CLOSED, never returning. Set `MaxReconnect` to `-1` and watch the reconnect-error callback so the outage is visible.
- [CLNT][ANTI] Pitfall: Retry on a failed first connect hides a bad address; the service sits in RECONNECTING forever. Keep the reconnect-error callback wired and alert on a service still RECONNECTING after the deploy finishes.
- [CLNT][ANTI] Pitfall: A zero wait or a jitter-free delay overloads the remaining server: zero spins a CPU loop; no jitter makes a fleet retry in lockstep. Keep a non-zero wait and keep the jitter. "Keep a non-zero wait, and keep the jitter"
- [CLNT][ANTI][SIZE] Pitfall: A full reconnect buffer stalls or drops your next publish (8 MB Go/Java, 2 MB Python). Back off publishing and let the buffer drain once the link returns instead of hammering publish in a loop.
- [CLNT][ANTI][SIZE] Pitfall: A stale connection on an overloaded server can go undetected for minutes. The client declares the link stale once outstanding pings exceed `MaxPingsOut`; with defaults (two-minute ping interval, one minute in Rust; two allowed outstanding pings) detection waits for the third unanswered ping, up to about six minutes (three in Rust).
- [CLNT] Go sends its keepalive PING on the interval regardless of traffic (only a PONG clears the outstanding count); Rust resets its ping interval every time it receives anything, so it pings only after a minute with nothing inbound. Rust fixes the ping budget at two.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Under heavy load, lower the ping interval (and `MaxPingsOut` where exposed) so a wedged link is detected in seconds instead of minutes.

## Connection Events
- path: learn/resilient-clients/connection-events.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/resilient-clients/connection-events

### Claims
- [CLNT] Six connection events cover the lifecycle: disconnect, reconnect, reconnect error (per failed attempt), closed (final, fires once), discovered servers, lame duck. Discovered servers and lame duck aren't state-machine transitions; they arrive over a healthy connection.
- [CLNT] The closed event fires on both edges into CLOSED (app `Close()` or retries spent), fires once, and is the last event the connection delivers.
- [CLNT] Rust and C# don't report a discovered-servers event; C# has no closed event at all (its terminal signal is the `ConnectionState` property).
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Disconnect is recoverable: log it, count it in a metric, let the reconnect loop work. Closed is final: no further events, no publish succeeds; the process must exit for a supervisor to restart it, or an alert must reach an operator. "Closed — exit or alert."
- [CLNT] CLOSED can arrive even with unlimited retries: on app `Close()`, after a drain, or on errors where retrying can't help — in Go, receiving the same authentication error twice aborts reconnecting regardless of policy, unless `IgnoreAuthErrorAbort` is set.
- [CLNT] JavaScript's `nc.closed()` promise resolves (never rejects) to the error that caused the close, so a `main` can end by awaiting it.
- [CLNT][ANTI][PATTERN] A status poll is a snapshot that races the state machine. Poll to report state (dashboards, metrics, readiness probes); react through events. "Poll to report state; react through events."
- [CLNT] Publishing after a stale `CONNECTED` poll is fine because the reconnect buffer holds the publish.
- [CLNT][OPS][PATTERN] Readiness check mapping: Ready while CONNECTED; Not ready while RECONNECTING (route work elsewhere, keep the process up — killing it throws away the reconnect buffer); Dead on CLOSED (closed observer exits, supervisor replaces). "RECONNECTING heals on its own; killing the process over it throws away the reconnect buffer."
- [OPS] `nats server check connection` measures connect time, server RTT, and a full pub/sub round trip against warning and critical thresholds, exiting with Nagios codes (0 OK, 1 warning, 2 critical, 3 unknown); an external probe can't read your process's connection state.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Force reconnect drops the current connection on purpose and runs the normal reconnect path; use it to rebalance long-lived connections that piled onto the server that stayed up longest after a rolling restart.
- [CLNT][ANTI] Treat a force reconnect as a real disconnect (in-flight requests may be rejected; the reconnect buffer covers the gap with the same limits), and don't fire it across a whole fleet at once — stagger it. "a synchronized mass reconnect is the load spike that reconnect jitter exists to prevent"
- [CLNT][ANTI] Pitfall: A status poll used as a trigger races the state machine. Recovery logic gated on polling acts on stale state and re-implements what events deliver in order.
- [CLNT][ANTI] Pitfall: No closed observer means permanent failure goes unnoticed; the service sits with a dead connection while its process reports healthy. Wire the closed event everywhere, even with unlimited retries. "The closed event is the one that demands an action, and it's the one most often left unwired."
- [CLNT][ANTI][OPS] Pitfall: Connection events and async errors are different signals. Events report state transitions; the async error callback reports problems while CONNECTED (e.g. slow consumer). Count them separately: rising disconnects point at network/servers, rising async errors point at your application.

## Drain & Shutdown
- path: learn/resilient-clients/drain-and-shutdown.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/resilient-clients/drain-and-shutdown

### Claims
- [CLNT] Close is an abrupt teardown: shuts the TCP socket immediately, sends no UNSUB, doesn't wait for in-flight work; it flushes the write buffer on the way out but stops delivering buffered inbound messages and drops the reconnect buffer. SIGKILL loses the write buffer too.
- [CLNT] Two kinds of in-flight work at shutdown: an in-flight message (delivered by the server, sitting in the subscription buffer, handler not finished) is dropped by close; a pending publish (in the client write buffer) is usually flushed by a library `Close()` but lost on crash/SIGKILL.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Close is right only for a connection you no longer care about (failed health check, test, error path where work is already lost); for a planned shutdown use drain. "For a planned shutdown, use drain instead."
- [CLNT] Drain runs in two phases: DRAINING_SUBS (UNSUB every subscription so the server stops delivering, let handlers finish buffered messages), then DRAINING_PUBS (flush every pending publish), then close. Go and Python expose the phases as states; other clients keep them internal.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Call drain from the process's SIGTERM handler and wait for the connection to report CLOSED before exiting.
- [CLNT][ANTI] In Go, `Drain()` returns immediately and drains in the background; returning from `Drain()` is not the signal that draining finished. Register a `ClosedHandler` and wait on it; exiting on `Drain()`'s return loses the work drain was meant to save.
- [CLNT] The `nats reply` CLI calls `Drain()` on Ctrl-C but exits as soon as it returns, without waiting for the background drain; `nats sub` just exits on Ctrl-C, abandoning in-flight messages.
- [CLNT] While DRAINING_SUBS most clients still accept a publish (so a handler can send its reply); once in DRAINING_PUBS new publishes are refused with a draining error (`ErrConnectionDraining` in nats.go). A publish right after `Drain()` races the phase change.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Drain is the last thing your shutdown does, after the application has stopped producing. "drain is the last thing your shutdown does, after the application has stopped producing"
- [CLNT][SIZE] The drain timeout bounds the subscription phase; if handlers don't finish in time, drain discards the remaining messages and proceeds to flush and close, surfacing `ErrDrainTimeout` (nats.go). The pending-publish flush has its own hardcoded five-second bound in nats.go; in nats.java the `drain()` timeout covers the final flush too.
- [CLNT][SIZE][PATTERN] The default drain timeout is 30 seconds in nats.go, but size it to your slowest handler's latency rather than a round number. "Size the timeout to your handler latency rather than to a round number."
- [CLNT][CORE][PATTERN] Draining a single subscription unsubscribes, lets the handler finish that subscription's buffered messages, and leaves the connection and other subscriptions open; the canonical use is rotating one queue-group member out while the group keeps consuming.
- [CLNT][ANTI] C# has no per-subscription drain; disposing a subscription drops messages still on their way. Set `DrainSubscriptionsOnDispose` (default `false`; bounded by `DrainPingTimeout`, five seconds default) on any C# service whose subscriptions do real work.
- [CLNT] A flush sends a PING and waits for the PONG; because the server processes a connection's sends in order, the PONG confirms the server received everything written before the PING, including buffered publishes. For a fire-and-forget publish, that round trip is the only confirmation there is.
- [CLNT][MYTH] Flush confirms receipt by the server only: it doesn't say any subscriber saw the message, and it isn't a storage acknowledgment (that's a JetStream publish ack).
- [CLNT][SIZE] Go `Flush()` has a fixed ten-second timeout; `FlushTimeout()` takes a bound you pick. C# has no flush (`PingAsync()` is the same round trip). Rust's `client.flush()` resolves when buffered writes reach the socket, without waiting for PONG, so it confirms bytes left the client, not server receipt.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Drain already ends with a flush, so a drained shutdown needs no flush of its own; call flush at checkpoints drain doesn't cover (after a burst of publishes before treating the batch as sent; before a close on an error path).
- [CLNT][TOPO] A server entering graceful shutdown signals lame duck via an `ldm` flag in `INFO`; a client watching for it can stop publishing and reconnect to another server before the link is cut. The departing server's `connect_urls` omits its own address so a reconnecting client won't pick it.
- [CLNT][ANTI] Pitfall: Publishing after you call drain. Drain can't be reversed; a "shutting down" event emitted after `Drain()` either slips through or fails with a draining error, and you can't count on either. Drain last.
- [CLNT][ANTI] Pitfall: A drain timeout shorter than your slowest handler discards in-flight work every deploy. Measure the slowest handler and set the timeout above it with margin.
- [CLNT][CONS][ANTI][MYTH] Pitfall: Assuming a core drain acks your JetStream messages. Drain winds down the connection; it does not acknowledge a consumer's messages. Ack explicitly before the connection closes or JetStream redelivers to the next client. "It does not acknowledge a JetStream consumer's messages for you."

## Slow Consumers
- path: learn/resilient-clients/slow-consumers.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/resilient-clients/slow-consumers

### Claims
- [CLNT] The subscription pending buffer is a per-subscription queue holding messages that arrived but the handler hasn't processed; it exists so a brief burst doesn't block the read loop.
- [CLNT][SIZE] Default pending limits are generous: 500,000 messages and 64 MB in Go (similar in Python and Java); Rust defaults to 65,536 messages; C# to a 1,024-message channel; JavaScript leaves the buffer unbounded and never drops client-side (its slow-consumer option only raises a status).
- [CLNT][ANTI] The default caps are sized for a typical workload, not yours; a high-rate subject or large messages can fill 64 MB in seconds. "The defaults serve as a backstop rather than a workload-specific tuning."
- [CLNT] C# overflow differs by API: low-level `NatsConnection` drops the newest queued message and raises `MessageDropped`; the `NatsClient` wrapper waits, blocking the read loop instead of dropping.
- [CLNT] A slow consumer is a subscriber whose pending buffer fills faster than the handler drains it.
- [CLNT] Pending limits cap messages and bytes per subscription; whichever limit is hit first applies. Rust sets a single `subscription_capacity` on connection options for every subscription; Rust and C# cap message count only.
- [CLNT][SIZE][PATTERN] Size the pending limit to roughly the handler's latency times the subject's peak rate. Too tight drops messages the handler could have caught up on; too loose wastes memory on a backlog it never catches up on. "A limit sized to roughly the handler's latency times the subject's peak rate"
- [CLNT] On overflow most clients drop the arriving message and fire the async error callback with a slow-consumer error (`ErrSlowConsumer` in Go) rather than blocking the read loop; the subscription stays active and resumes once the handler catches up.
- [CLNT] Go exposes `SubscriptionSlowConsumer` status, `Pending()` (current msgs/bytes) vs `PendingLimits()`, and `Dropped()` (running count) for a health check that watches how close a subscription runs to its limits.
- [CLNT][ANTI] The async error callback is the single place the client reports asynchronous problems not tied to one API call (slow consumer, permission violation, protocol error). In Go a connection with no callback discards these reports; Rust, JS, C# likewise unless wired; Java and Python fall back to a default logger.
- [CLNT][OPS][MYTH] Two different "slow consumers": a local slow consumer drops individual messages and keeps the connection (fix with pending limits + callback); a server-side slow consumer is the server closing the whole connection because the client reads its socket too slowly to meet the server's per-client write deadline (looks like a disconnect with a read error; fix by reading faster or spreading load).
