The server's view is the `slow_consumers` counter on `/varz`.
- [CLNT][CORE][PATTERN] When one subscriber genuinely can't keep up, the real answer is usually more subscribers sharing the load via a queue group, not a bigger buffer; pending limits protect each member. "the real answer is usually not a bigger buffer but more subscribers sharing the load"
- [CLNT][ANTI][SIZE] Pitfall: The default limits are a backstop rather than a workload-specific tuning. Always set pending limits on a subscription that does real per-message work, sized to handler latency and peak rate.
- [CLNT][ANTI] Pitfall: An unwatched async error callback hides every dropped message. Always set one and log the slow-consumer error visibly. "a quiet drop is worse than a crash because you don't even know it happened"
- [CLNT] The slow-consumer callback fires when the subscription enters the slow-consumer state, not once per dropped message; read `Dropped()` for the running count.
- [CLNT][ANTI][OPS] Pitfall: Don't confuse the local drop with the server-side disconnect; watch the async-error rate and the disconnect rate separately, since each points at a different fix.

## Request-Reply Resilience
- path: learn/resilient-clients/request-reply-resilience.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/resilient-clients/request-reply-resilience

### Claims
- [CORE][SEC][PATTERN] The `_INBOX` prefix is configurable (`inboxPrefix`, `CustomInboxPrefix`); when a user's subscribe permissions don't cover `_INBOX.>`, grant subscribe on a dedicated prefix and have the client set it.
- [CORE][CLNT] A request has three outcomes: a reply within the deadline; a timeout (the responder may be up but slow — no answer arrived in time); or no responders (the server knows no subscription is listening and sends an immediate 503 with no body, returning at once).
- [CORE] No responder means the service isn't running, isn't registered, or its account can't see the subject. "Rather than a slow answer, this means there is no one to answer."
- [CORE][PATTERN] No-responders is the most useful failure NATS gives you because it's fast and certain; without it a request to an unlistened subject would block for the full timeout. "the no-responders signal is the most useful failure NATS gives you, because it's fast and certain"
- [CORE] The no-responders signal needs a server new enough to send the 503 and a client that advertised support in the connect handshake; both have been the default for years.
- [CORE][CLNT][PATTERN] Retry differently per failure: a timeout means someone is there, so a short bounded fast retry; no responders means nothing is listening, so exponential backoff to give the responder time to register. "Use a short, bounded retry for a timeout and an exponential backoff for no responders."
- [CORE][SIZE][PATTERN] The retry loop must be bounded: cap the attempts (five is a reasonable default) and add jitter so a fleet of requesters doesn't retry in lockstep. "five is a reasonable default"
- [CORE][PATTERN] A retried request is a duplicate; make it idempotent by keying every request by a business ID (e.g. `order_id`) and having the responder remember recently seen IDs and return the cached reply. It's a discipline on both ends, not a new message.
- [CORE][CLNT] A request in flight when the connection drops is lost outright; NATS doesn't persist it. The inbox re-subscribes on reconnect, so an idempotent retry after the link returns is safe.
- [CORE][ANTI] Pitfall: Treating a timeout and no-responders as the same failure wastes a fast-retry opportunity on a slow responder and floods an unlistened subject. Branch on the error.
- [CORE][ANTI][SIZE] Pitfall: A timeout shorter than the responder's real latency makes every busy moment look like a failure. Measure the responder's latency and set the timeout to two or three times its p99. "set the timeout to two or three times its p99"
- [CORE][ANTI] Pitfall: An unbounded retry loop pins a CPU and never reports the problem. Cap attempts, add jitter, and stop with a clear signal (log and let the caller decide).
- [CORE][ANTI] Pitfall: A non-idempotent retry that double-acts (e.g. reserves stock twice when only the reply was lost). Key every request by `order_id` and de-dupe on the responder.

## TLS & Auth
- path: learn/resilient-clients/tls-and-auth.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/resilient-clients/tls-and-auth

### Claims
- [CLNT][SEC] A credentials file holds a user JWT and an nkey seed; the client reads both itself from a path. The `.creds` file is the form production deployments use.
- [CLNT][SEC] With nkey/JWT auth, `INFO` says `auth_required` and carries a one-time nonce; the client signs it with the seed and sends signature plus JWT in `CONNECT`; no password is ever sent over the wire.
- [CLNT][SEC][ANTI] The creds file is the whole identity and a secret: anyone holding it can connect as that user; load it from disk or an environment variable, never paste it into source.
- [CLNT][SEC] For the client, TLS is one input: the CA certificate. If the server certificate doesn't chain to it, the client aborts before sending any credentials.
- [CLNT][SEC] Default secure handshake order: TCP dial → plaintext `INFO` (where `tls_required` appears) → TLS upgrade and CA validation → `CONNECT` with creds over the encrypted link → `PONG`. No credential is sent before TLS is established.
- [CLNT][SEC] `handshake_first` / `--tlsfirst` must be opted into on both sides: a `--tlsfirst` client fails its TLS handshake against a plaintext-`INFO` server, and a plaintext-expecting client gets nothing from a handshake-first server until it fails with a timeout or EOF.
- [CLNT][SEC] For WebSocket, `wss://` is the encrypted equivalent of `tls://`.
- [CLNT][SEC] An auth error doesn't fit the transient-retry model: the server answered and rejected the credentials, so the same credentials get the same rejection. Most clients allow one rejection and stop on a repeat.
- [CLNT][SIZE] nats.go, nats.js, nats.net, and nats.java close the connection when the same auth error repeats twice in a row (opt-out `IgnoreAuthErrorAbort`/`ignoreAuthErrorAbort`); the abort applies regardless of the retry budget. nats.py and nats.rs have no abort rule and keep cycling until `max_reconnect_attempts` (60 default) / `max_reconnects` (unlimited default) runs out.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] An expired or revoked credential ends in CLOSED (nats.net: `Failed`) in the abort-rule clients; the closed handler is what tells the application it needs fresh credentials or a restart.
- [CLNT] The `nats` CLI sets `IgnoreAuthErrorAbort` and unlimited reconnects, so a CLI command keeps retrying where a library client closes.
- [CLNT][SEC][PATTERN] The dependable way to pick up rotated credentials is a credential callback invoked on every connect and reconnect attempt (`UserJWT(userCB, sigCB)`, JS authenticator function, `user_jwt_cb`/`signature_cb`, Java `AuthHandler`, Rust `with_auth_callback`, .NET `AuthCredCallback`).
- [CLNT][SEC] nats.go, nats.java, and nats.py re-read a `.creds` path on every attempt, so file rotation works without extra code; nats.js, nats.rs, and nats.net load once and need the callback form for a rotation to reach a reconnect at all.
- [CLNT][SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: Do not hardcode credentials in source. A pasted JWT or password gets committed and can't be rotated without a redeploy; load from a path or env var and never commit a `.creds` file.
- [CLNT][SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: Do not skip server verification in production. Skip-verify/insecure TLS accepts an impostor server with a self-signed certificate. Always supply the CA. "An encrypted link provides no protection if the server on the other end can't be trusted."
- [CLNT][SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: An unmonitored credential expiry drops a live connection. The server arms a timer at the JWT's expiry, sends `-ERR 'User Authentication Expired'`, closes the connection, and rejects each reconnect; most clients then abort and land in CLOSED. Refresh credentials ahead of expiry via callback or rotated file.
- [CLNT][SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: Rotate the creds file by opening a fresh connection, not in place. A live connection keeps the identity it authenticated with; overwriting the file changes nothing until the next connection cycle. Open a new connection with new creds and drain the old one.
- [CLNT][SEC] nats.go re-reads on reconnect and can read a half-written file mid-rotation (a client-side parse error, retried as transient); write the new file to a temp path and rename it into place so a reader never sees a partial file.
- [CLNT][SEC][PATTERN] A secure connect fails two distinct ways — CA validation (untrusted server cert) and authorization (wrong/expired/revoked creds) — handle them as separate cases at the connect boundary.

## Where Next (Resilient Clients)
- path: learn/resilient-clients/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/resilient-clients/where-next

### Claims
- [CLNT][PATTERN] The one model: a connection is a state machine (DISCONNECTED, CONNECTING, CONNECTED, RECONNECTING, DRAINING, CLOSED), every fault is a transition, and each option shapes one edge. "That model is the floor for running any NATS client in production."
- [CLNT] The chapter is unversioned and concept-first; the wire protocol, `-ERR` strings, and server config are in versioned Reference; exact client option names/defaults are in each client library's API reference.
- [CLNT] Checklist: Pass the whole server pool (several URLs, or several IPs behind one name) so a single unreachable server isn't fatal at connect time.
- [CLNT][TOPO] Checklist: Configure every server the client must rely on and treat discovered servers as additions; a one-URL setup that leans on gossip loses failover where `no_advertise` is set or addresses aren't reachable.
- [CLNT] Checklist: Set a deliberate connect timeout so a blocked dial costs one timeout, not a hung startup.
- [CLNT][SIZE] Checklist: Keep messages under the server's `max_payload` and store large bodies elsewhere; an oversized publish fails before it's sent and isn't a connection problem.
- [CLNT][SIZE] Checklist: Set `MaxReconnect` to `-1` on a long-lived service in Go, Java, Python, and JavaScript (bounded defaults); Rust and C# already retry forever.
- [CLNT][OPS] Checklist: Watch the reconnect-error callback so a long outage is loud in logs, not a silent give-up.
- [CLNT][OPS] Checklist: If retry on a failed first connect is on, keep the reconnect-error callback wired and alert on a service still in RECONNECTING after a deploy.
- [CLNT] Checklist: Keep a non-zero wait and always keep jitter; a zero or fixed delay spins the CPU or makes a fleet retry the one remaining server at the same instant.
- [CLNT][SIZE] Checklist: Handle a full reconnect buffer and back off publishing; the buffer is bounded (8 MB Go/Java, 2 MB Python) and the overflowing publish fails (Go `ErrReconnectBufExceeded`) or blocks (Rust).
- [CLNT][SIZE] Checklist: Lower the ping interval under heavy load to catch a wedged connection in seconds, not the ~six minutes the defaults take (two-minute interval, third unanswered ping closes; Rust pings every minute, so ~three).
- [CLNT] Checklist: Poll connection state for dashboards, metrics, and readiness probes; drive reactions through events.
- [CLNT] Checklist: Wire a closed observer on every long-lived service, even with unlimited retries.
- [CLNT][OPS] Checklist: Count connection events and async errors separately; disconnects point at network/servers, async errors at your application.
- [CLNT] Checklist: Drain last, not first; a publish after `Drain()` may come back with a draining error.
- [CLNT] Checklist: Size the drain timeout to your slowest handler's latency.
- [CLNT][CONS] Checklist: Ack JetStream in-flight messages before a core drain; a connection drain does not handle a consumer's ack position.
- [CLNT][SIZE] Checklist: Always set pending limits on a subscription that does real per-message work; the defaults (500,000 messages, 64 MB in Go) are a backstop.
- [CLNT] Checklist: Size the pending limit to the handler's latency and the subject's peak rate.
- [CLNT] Checklist: Always set the async-error callback and log the slow-consumer error loudly; a nil one drops every overflow message silently.
- [CLNT][OPS] Checklist: Tell a local drop apart from a server-side disconnect; watch async-error rate and disconnect rate separately.
- [CORE][SIZE] Checklist: Measure the responder's p99 and set the request timeout to two or three times it.
- [CORE] Checklist: Handle no-responders and a timeout separately; absent responder warrants backoff, slow one warrants fast retry.
- [CORE] Checklist: Key retries by `order_id` and de-dupe on the responder so a re-sent request is a no-op.
- [CORE] Checklist: Cap the retry count and add jitter.
- [CLNT][SEC] Checklist: Load credentials from a file or environment and never commit a `.creds` to source.
- [CLNT][SEC] Checklist: Always supply the CA certificate in production; skip-verify TLS encrypts the link but authenticates nothing.
- [CLNT][SEC] Checklist: Refresh a credentials JWT before it expires and watch the auth-error rate; at expiry the server closes the live connection and most clients abort the reconnect into CLOSED.
- [CLNT][SEC] Checklist: Rotate credentials with a fresh connection and drain the old one; reloading a creds file mid-connection races the live link.

## Services
- path: learn/services/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/services

### Claims
- [CORE][PATTERN] The Services framework (`micro` in Go/Python, `service`/`services` in JS/Java/Rust/C#) formalizes a request-reply responder into a named, versioned handler the server can discover, that reports stats, and that load-balances across copies. No new infrastructure: a service is still request-reply underneath.
- [CORE][MYTH] A service stores nothing; it answers a request and retains no record of it (at-most-once request-reply). Work that must survive a restart or be retried belongs to JetStream. "A service stores nothing; it answers a request and retains no record of it."
- [CORE][OPS] The Services framework needs nothing special enabled on the server; a plain `nats-server` is enough.

## Your first service
- path: learn/services/your-first-service.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/services/your-first-service

### Claims
- [CORE] A service is created with `Name` (shared by every copy), `Version` (SemVer), and `Description`; the framework generates a unique per-instance service ID (a NUID). The name identifies the kind of service; the ID identifies one instance.
- [CORE] A service needs an endpoint (a named handler bound to a subject) to answer anything.
- [CORE] An endpoint joins the default queue group `"q"` automatically, so running more copies gives load balancing for free.
- [CORE] Creating a service subscribes it to discovery subjects under `$SRV` the moment it starts.
- [CORE] The handler contract is `Data()` to read and `Respond()` to answer; the framework handles subscribing, the queue group, reading the reply subject, and publishing the answer.
- [CORE][ANTI] Pitfall: Validate the request body; never let bad input crash the handler. The framework doesn't validate payloads; on parse failure respond with a service error (`Nats-Service-Error` + `Nats-Service-Error-Code` headers, code always safe to parse as a number, `400` for bad input) so the caller sees "bad request" rather than a hang. "Don't assume the payload is well-formed."
- [CORE][ANTI] Pitfall: A service `Name` and `Version` are validated at creation. `Name` allows letters, digits, hyphens, underscores (no dots or spaces); `Version` must be valid SemVer; an invalid value fails `AddService` outright.
- [CORE] Service `Metadata` is immutable once set; to change it you stop the service and start a new one.

## Endpoints and groups
- path: learn/services/endpoints-and-groups.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/services/endpoints-and-groups

### Claims
- [CORE][SUBJ] A service can hold multiple endpoints; an endpoint's subject defaults to its name, and you set it explicitly only when the wire subject and endpoint name differ (the common case once subjects carry structure).
- [CORE][SUBJ] A group is a subject prefix: an endpoint added to group `orders.inventory` answers on `{group}.{endpoint}`. There's no separate routing layer; the wire looks identical whether the endpoint was added directly or through a group. Groups nest (`{outer}.{inner}.{endpoint}`).
- [CORE] The queue group is set at three levels, each overriding the one above: service default, group override, endpoint override; if none set, the endpoint falls back to `"q"`.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Most services never need a queue-group override; the default `"q"` already load-balances all instances of a service. Reach for an override only when a subset of endpoints should load-balance separately. "Most services never need this."
- [CORE][ANTI] Pitfall: Disabling the queue group turns an endpoint into broadcast — every instance receives every request and the caller gets one reply per instance. Never disable it on an endpoint that responds; do not disable it to "make sure a request is handled". "never disable it on an endpoint that responds"
- [CORE][ANTI] Pitfall: Endpoints are immutable once added: no remove, rename, or subject change on a running service; metadata is fixed at creation. Decide endpoint names and subjects deliberately before going live, the way you pick a stream name. To change shape, stop and start a replacement.

## Discovery
- path: learn/services/discovery.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/services/discovery

### Claims
- [CORE] Every service answers three discovery verbs under `$SRV`: PING (presence: name, instance id, version; use to find services and measure RTT), INFO (adds description and endpoint list with subject and queue group), STATS (per-endpoint counters).
- [CORE] A service doesn't publish to `$SRV`; it subscribes there and replies to requests.
- [CORE][SUBJ] Each verb answers at three address levels: `$SRV.INFO` (every service in the account), `$SRV.INFO.<Name>` (every instance of that name), `$SRV.INFO.<Name>.<id>` (one instance).
- [CORE][PATTERN] Discovery is broadcast, not load-balanced: the discovery verbs are not in a queue group, so a `$SRV.INFO.<Name>` request reaches every instance and every one replies. A caller waits a short deadline and collects however many responses arrive. "Discovery is broadcast, not load-balanced"
- [CORE][PATTERN] When you know an instance id, address the third level to get exactly one reply with no deadline loop.
- [CORE][ANTI] Pitfall: Discovery is broadcast: a single reply is not the whole answer. A plain request returns the first response and silently hides the rest, so five instances appear as one. Wait a deadline and collect every reply, as the CLI does.
- [CORE][ANTI][SUBJ] Pitfall: `$SRV` is a reserved subject prefix; do not publish to it yourself. Publishing under `$SRV` collides with the framework's machinery and corrupts what callers discover. Keep your subjects under your own prefixes.
- [CORE][SEC] Who may see `$SRV` across account boundaries is a security/account question.

## Observability
- path: learn/services/observability.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/services/observability

### Claims
- [CORE][OPS] Every endpoint carries a counter set the framework updates on each request under the service lock: `num_requests`, `num_errors`, `last_error`, `processing_time` (total handler time, ns), `average_processing_time` (ns). No metrics code needed.
- [CORE][OPS] Stats are per endpoint, not per service; that's the level for reasoning about load — which handler is busy and which is slow.
- [CORE] A service error is a reply carrying `Nats-Service-Error` (description) and `Nats-Service-Error-Code` (short code string like `"400"`); `req.Error(code, description, data)` attaches both headers, sends the response, and bumps `num_errors` and `last_error` in one step.
- [CORE][MYTH] A service error is a delivered reply, not a transport failure; it differs from no-responders, where nothing is listening at all.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Return a service error for bad input, an unavailable downstream dependency, or a business rule rejecting the request; a handler that responds normally instead leaves `num_errors` at zero and hides the problem.
- [CORE][ANTI] Pitfall: A service error arrives as headers, not as a failed call. A caller that only checks "did I get a reply" reads every service error as success. Check `Nats-Service-Error-Code` on every response; do not treat a returned message as proof the request succeeded.
- [CORE][ANTI][OPS] Pitfall: Stats are per instance, and `Reset()` zeroes them. `$SRV.STATS.<Name>` returns one `stats_response` per instance; sum across IDs yourself (the server keeps no aggregate), and don't assume counters only ever grow — `Reset()` zeroes them and resets `started`.
- [CORE][OPS] A custom `StatsHandler` can attach your own `data` blob per endpoint, and the server can emit service-latency advisories measuring round-trip time from outside the service.

## Scaling
- path: learn/services/scaling.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/services/scaling

### Claims
- [CORE][PATTERN] Horizontal scaling means running more instances with the same `Name`, `Version`, and endpoint; you don't register instances or configure a load balancer. The default queue group `"q"` is the entire scaling story. "That queue group is the entire scaling story."
- [CORE] The split across instances isn't a round-robin you control; the server delivers each request to whichever queue-group member is ready, with no coordinator.
- [CORE][ANTI] Disabling the queue group (`WithEndpointQueueGroupDisabled`) is broadcast, not scaling: useful for fan-out work, wrong for load balancing. Keep it on when you want to scale.
- [CORE][CLNT] `Stop()` drains each endpoint subscription: it removes queue-group interest immediately (so the server stops routing new requests there), then unsubscribes the `$SRV` verbs; accepted requests keep processing in the background.
- [CORE][CLNT][ANTI] `Stop()` returns before background processing finishes; don't exit the process the moment it returns — drain the connection or wait on the `DoneHandler` until in-flight work completes. "don't exit the process the moment it returns"
- [CORE][PATTERN] Because the endpoint leaves the queue group as part of the stop, there's no window where a request lands on a queue group whose only member vanished; roll a new version by starting fresh instances then stopping old ones one at a time.
- [CORE][STRM][PATTERN] Durable state (a count that must not reset, a queue of work that outlives the process) doesn't belong in the instance; put it behind JetStream.
- [CORE][ANTI] Pitfall: Instances don't share memory — protect external state. Each instance keeps its own counter/cache/"remaining stock" and they drift. Keep handlers stateless; push shared state into a database or a JetStream stream/KV bucket. "Keep handlers stateless"
- [CORE][ANTI] Pitfall: A blocking handler stops its instance from serving other requests; handlers run synchronously on the service's connection. The queue group masks it by routing to peers, but if every instance blocks the whole service stalls. Keep handlers fast, move long work off the request path, add instances.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Instances are disposable; make stopping one safe with a graceful stop that drains in-flight work and hands new requests to survivors.

## Where to go next (Services)
- path: learn/services/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/services/where-next

### Claims
- [CORE][PATTERN] Four pieces: the service (named, versioned, auto-ID, discovery subscribed, stats tracked), endpoints and groups (`{prefix}.{endpoint}`), the `$SRV` discovery verbs, and the default queue group `"q"` that scales it with no coordinator and no config.
- [CORE][STRM] A service is at-most-once request-reply; when an instance stops, its in-flight work is gone. State that must survive a restart belongs in a stream, not the service.
- [CORE] Checklist: Unmarshal `req.Data()` inside the handler and respond with a service error on bad input.
- [CORE] Checklist: Pick a `Name` matching the allowed character set and a valid SemVer `Version`; an invalid value fails service creation outright.
- [CORE] Checklist: Override an endpoint's queue group only when you mean to change who load-balances with whom; the change is silent and easy to get wrong.
- [CORE] Checklist: Disabling the queue group turns an endpoint into broadcast (every instance answers) instead of load balancing.
- [CORE] Checklist: Treat endpoints and metadata as immutable once added; name and shape them deliberately the first time.
- [CORE] Checklist: Collect discovery responses with a deadline-or-count loop; a single request returns only one instance.
- [CORE][SUBJ] Checklist: Treat `$SRV` as a reserved subject prefix; never publish to it yourself.
- [CORE] Checklist: Check `Nats-Service-Error-Code` on every reply; an unchecked failed call looks like success.
- [CORE][OPS] Checklist: Aggregate stats across instance IDs yourself; counters are per-instance and `Reset()` zeroes them.
- [CORE] Checklist: Protect any external state instances share (a database or a stream); the framework holds no shared memory across instances.
- [CORE] Checklist: Keep handlers non-blocking, or run more instances; a blocking handler stalls every other request on that instance.

## Monitoring & Observability Deep Dive
- path: learn/monitoring/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/monitoring

### Claims
- [OPS][PATTERN] Monitoring is observation: where the numbers live, which ones say something's wrong, and how to put them in front of a person before a customer notices; the fix belongs to the Operate chapters.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Four lenses: numbers come from the monitoring endpoints (`:8222`), lag comes from consumer state, surprises come from advisories, history comes from the exporter; profiling is the escalation when all four agree a node is unhealthy but none says why.
- [OPS][SIZE] The monitoring port listens on `:8222` by default once enabled.

## Monitoring endpoints
- path: learn/monitoring/monitoring-endpoints.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/monitoring/monitoring-endpoints

### Claims
- [OPS] The monitoring port is separate from `:4222`, off until enabled (`http_port: 8222` or `-m 8222`), speaks plain HTTP, and answers only on request with a JSON snapshot; nothing is pushed.
- [OPS] The four most-used endpoints: `/varz` (the server), `/connz` (its clients), `/routez` (its cluster routes), `/jsz` (its JetStream).
- [OPS][PATTERN] On `/varz`, `connections` is the live client count, `total_connections` is the count since start (only goes up), and `slow_consumers` is the number of clients the server has disconnected for not keeping up — on a healthy node it stays at `0`.
- [OPS] Every endpoint takes query parameters to filter, page, and sort; `/connz?acc=` scopes to an account, `?subs=true` lists subscriptions, `?auth=true` fills in the account and user each connection authenticated as.
- [OPS] In `/connz`, `num_connections` is how many the response returned; `total` is how many matched the query; with `?limit`/`?offset` paging, `total` stays put while `num_connections` shrinks.
- [OPS][PATTERN] `/connz?sort=pending&limit=10` returns the ten connections with the most data queued — the clients most likely to fall behind.
- [OPS][TOPO][SIZE] Since 2.10 routes are pooled: each peer contributes several route entries (a pool of three plus a dedicated system-account route), so a default three-node cluster shows eight entries on one node, four per peer.
- [OPS][TOPO][PATTERN] Route health is presence, not raw count: group `/routez` by `remote_name` and confirm each peer is still there; a vanished peer or a climbing `rtt` is the first sign a node dropped off the mesh.
- [OPS][STRM] `/jsz` reports JetStream state on a node: stream and consumer counts, the meta leader, and per-stream/per-consumer numbers; `last_seq` there is raw material for lag.
- [OPS] `/healthz` returns `200` when healthy and `503` when not; built for orchestrator liveness probes and load balancers. Its parameters narrow what "healthy" means (JetStream-only, this-server-only, a specific stream or consumer).
- [OPS][ANTI] Pitfall: Alert on `connections`, not `total_connections`. A client in a reconnect loop barely moves `connections` but inflates `total_connections`; alerting on the lifetime counter pages someone for a number that was always going to grow. Alert on `connections` for capacity, watch `slow_consumers` for dropped clients.
- [OPS] A large gap between live and lifetime connection counts, especially with `slow_consumers` above zero, is connection flapping, not load.
- [OPS][ANTI][SIZE] Pitfall: An unscoped `/jsz` is slow at scale. `/jsz?accounts=true&streams=true&consumers=true` walks every entity and can time out a scrape on a node with thousands of consumers, yielding no data. Don't fetch the whole tree on a schedule; scope with `?acc=` and page with `?offset`/`?limit`.
- [OPS][SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: The monitoring port is unauthenticated by default. Anyone who can reach `:8222` can read `/connz` and see users, subjects, and traffic; don't expose it to the open internet. "The monitoring port is unauthenticated by default."

## JetStream health
- path: learn/monitoring/jetstream-health.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/monitoring/jetstream-health

### Claims
- [OPS][STRM] Stream state (separate from configuration) is what's actually in the stream now: `messages`, `bytes`, first/last sequence, `num_subjects`, active consumers. `last_seq` only ever climbs.
- [OPS][CONS] Consumer state fields: `delivered.stream_seq` (last order handed to a worker), `ack_floor.stream_seq` (sequence below which everything is acked), `num_ack_pending` (in-flight: delivered but not acked), `num_redelivered` (currently tracked as delivered more than once — not a lifetime tally; it drops when the message is finally acked), `num_waiting` (waiting pulls).
- [OPS][CONS][PATTERN] Lag is a computed number: `lag = stream.last_seq − consumer.delivered.stream_seq`; a pull consumer reports the same value directly as `num_pending` (Unprocessed Messages). "lag = stream.last_seq − consumer.delivered.stream_seq"
- [OPS][CONS] Three numbers describe a consumer's full state: lag (`num_pending`), in-flight (`num_ack_pending`), redelivered (`num_redelivered`).
- [OPS][CONS][PATTERN] A healthy consumer keeps lag near zero and `num_redelivered` near zero. Lag climbing while `last_seq` climbs means orders arrive faster than they're processed; `num_redelivered` staying high or growing means workers keep taking orders and failing to ack. "A healthy consumer keeps lag near zero and `num_redelivered` near zero."
- [OPS][CONS] A redelivery happens when a worker takes a message and never acks it, or naks it, so the server hands it to another worker.
- [OPS][CONS][ANTI] Pitfall: Crashed workers show up as rising lag with nobody fetching. `num_pending` climbs whether or not any client fetches, so it's ambiguous alone; the signature of crashed workers is lag rising while `num_waiting` is `0` and `delivered.stream_seq` stops advancing. Read all three together.
- [OPS][CONS][ANTI][MYTH] Pitfall: In-flight is not lag. `num_ack_pending` counts messages a worker holds; `num_pending` counts messages no worker has taken. Rising in-flight means a stuck handler; rising lag means not enough handlers. "rising in-flight means a stuck handler, rising lag means not enough handlers"
- [OPS][CONS][ANTI] Pitfall: A filtered consumer's lag counts only its subjects. Empty pending on a filtered consumer doesn't mean the stream is empty; compare it against the stream's per-subject counts, not `last_seq`.

## Advisories & events
- path: learn/monitoring/advisories-and-events.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/monitoring/advisories-and-events

### Claims
- [OPS] Polling reads levels; it does nothing for events that happen between two polls. Advisories (`$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.>`) and system events (`$SYS.*`) are pushed by the server as ordinary messages you subscribe to.
- [OPS][STRM] An advisory is a transient JSON message JetStream publishes once, the moment something noteworthy happens to a stream or consumer, on a well-known subject under `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.>`; stream and consumer names are baked into the subject so wildcards can narrow to exactly the events you care about.
- [OPS][CONS] When a message exhausts its delivery attempts, the server publishes `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<stream>.<consumer>` with body `{type: io.nats.jetstream.advisory.v1.max_deliver, stream, consumer, stream_seq, deliveries}`. The message stays in the stream under its retention policy; only delivery to that consumer stops.
- [OPS][CONS][MYTH] The `max_deliver` advisory is the only built-in signal that a message stopped being delivered. There's no dead-letter queue, and the advisory is published once; if no one is subscribed when it fires, you never learn it happened. "There's no dead-letter queue, and the advisory is published once."
- [OPS] Other advisory types: `consumer_action` (consumer created/deleted), `nak` (handler negative-acked), `terminated` (message removed from delivery), and a leader-elected advisory when a replicated stream/consumer leader changes.
- [OPS][TOPO][PATTERN] A flapping leader showing up as repeated leader-elected advisories is worth watching; the advisory reports the fact, not the election mechanics.
- [OPS] System events on `$SYS.*` report server- and account-level activity: `$SYS.ACCOUNT.<account>.CONNECT` / `.DISCONNECT` per client, and a `STATSZ` heartbeat per server on `$SYS.SERVER.<id>.STATSZ` on a fixed interval carrying the same summary numbers as `/varz`, pushed instead of pulled.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Subscribe to `$SYS.ACCOUNT.*.CONNECT` to watch clients across every account come and go without polling `/connz` on a timer.
- [OPS][SEC] System events are published into the system account; subscribing to `$SYS.*` requires connecting as a system user, a separate privilege from application accounts.
- [OPS] A subscriber attached before an advisory fires receives it; one that connects after receives nothing.
- [OPS][ANTI] Pitfall: Advisories are transient — published exactly once and not stored in any stream. Don't rely on a watching human or ad-hoc subscription; capture advisories in a durable destination that is always subscribed.
- [OPS][STRM][PATTERN] The fix for transient advisories is to point a stream at the advisory subjects; a stream is always subscribed and stores what it captures. "point a stream at the advisory subjects"
- [OPS][CONS][ANTI] Pitfall: A `max_deliver` advisory is the only built-in signal a message was dropped. Subscribe to `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.>` or capture it in a stream; otherwise poison messages disappear silently.
- [OPS][TOPO][ANTI] Pitfall: A leader-elected advisory reports a flap, not its cause. Treat it as a symptom; don't diagnose the election from the advisory body alone.

## Prometheus & dashboards
- path: learn/monitoring/prometheus-and-dashboards.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/monitoring/prometheus-and-dashboards

### Claims
- [OPS] prometheus-nats-exporter runs outside NATS, scrapes a node's monitoring port `:8222`, and re-exposes the numbers as Prometheus metrics on its own `/metrics` endpoint on `:7777`. It holds no history; each scrape is a fresh read.
- [OPS] The exporter's `-jsz=all` flag turns on the JetStream collector (streams and consumers); `-prefix nats` renames metrics from the exporter's default `jetstream_` prefix to `nats_` (the same rename the NATS Helm chart applies).
- [OPS][CONS] JetStream collector series: `num_pending` becomes `nats_consumer_num_pending`, redeliveries `nats_consumer_num_redelivered`, in-flight `nats_consumer_num_ack_pending`, stream message count `nats_stream_total_messages`; labeled by `account`, `stream_name`, `consumer_name`.
- [OPS][SIZE] Example Prometheus scrape config uses `scrape_interval: 15s` against the exporter target.
- [OPS] Grafana publishes community dashboards for NATS that read a Prometheus data source out of the box.
- [OPS][PATTERN] `nats server check` is the alerting side: it compares a metric to a threshold you set and returns OK / WARNING / CRITICAL in a format Prometheus, Nagios, or a script can read; a dashboard needs a person watching, a check fires on its own.
- [OPS][TOPO] nats-surveyor connects to the system account, polls every server for its `Statz`, and exposes combined metrics on one `/metrics` endpoint; it needs a system-account credential and is an alternative to running the exporter against one node at a time.
- [OPS][TOPO][ANTI] Pitfall: A node-local health check passes even with no quorum. `/healthz?js-enabled-only=true` returns `200` even when the cluster has lost the quorum that keeps a stream writable, because it never looks past the local server. Don't wire it as your only JetStream alert; add `/healthz?js-meta-only=true`, which turns `503` when the cluster loses quorum. "Do not wire a node-local check as your only JetStream alert."
- [OPS][ANTI] Pitfall: A check with no threshold never fires. `nats server check consumer` defaults don't know your SLA; without `--unprocessed-critical` it sits at OK while lag climbs. Always set explicit thresholds (the example pins `--unprocessed-critical 100`). "A silent check looks like coverage while providing none, which makes it worse than having no check."
- [OPS][ANTI] Pitfall: The exporter keeps no time series. It only converts format; Prometheus stores history. Don't treat the exporter alone as monitoring; run both.

## Profiling the server
- path: learn/monitoring/profiling.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/monitoring/profiling

### Claims
- [OPS][PATTERN] Reach for a profile when `/varz` shows a heap growing with no matching traffic change or a pinned core with nothing on the dashboards explaining it; profiling is a development and support tool, not day-to-day monitoring.
- [OPS] Profile kinds: `heap` (live objects; memory growing), `allocs` (every allocation since startup; churn), `goroutine` (stack per goroutine; server looks stuck or goroutine count climbing), `cpu` (stacks sampled over a window; pinned core). `block`, `mutex`, `threadcreate` also exist; `block` needs sampling turned on first.
- [OPS] Memory and goroutine profiles return immediately; a CPU profile blocks for the sampling window.
- [OPS][SEC] `nats server request profile` travels on `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.PING.PROFILEZ`, so the context must be connected to the system account; a normal account gets no replies. It changes no config and needs no restart.
- [OPS][PATTERN] `--name`, `--host`, `--cluster`, and `--tags` limit which servers answer a profile request; asking the whole system is wasteful on a large cluster.
- [OPS][SIZE] For CPU profiles over the system account, the CLI's `--timeout` is the sampling window (default `5s`); the server rejects a window longer than 15 seconds. A longer capture must come from `prof_port`.
- [OPS] `prof_port` serves Go's `net/http/pprof` handlers; it's off until set and is not reloadable (SIGHUP won't pick it up; the node must restart). The 15-second cap is a limit of the system-account handler, not pprof, so `?seconds=` accepts longer on the port.
- [OPS][SEC][ANTI] Pitfall: The profiling port has no authentication; anyone who can reach it can pull a goroutine dump showing subjects and internal state. It binds to the same `host` as the client port (default `0.0.0.0`, every interface) with no separate profiling host. Leave `prof_port` unset in production or restrict it by firewall/network policy; prefer the authenticated system-account route. "Leave `prof_port` unset in production"
- [OPS][ANTI] Pitfall: Turning on `prof_port` costs a restart (not reloadable), meaning a rolling restart mid-incident that may lose the state you're chasing. Reach for `nats server request profile` first.
- [OPS][ANTI] Pitfall: Block profiling is empty until you enable it; `prof_block_rate` must be above zero. It is reloadable, so raise it with SIGHUP, take the profile, and drop it back to zero — block sampling slows the server down.

## Where to go next (Monitoring)
- path: learn/monitoring/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/monitoring/where-next

### Claims
- [OPS][PATTERN] The four lenses: numbers come from endpoints (`:8222`, no history, no subscription); lag comes from consumer state (`LastSeq` − `delivered.stream_seq`, plus `num_ack_pending` and `num_redelivered`); surprises come from advisories (transient, learned only if subscribed when fired); history comes from the exporter (`:7777`) with Prometheus storing, Grafana charting, and `nats server check` alerting.
- [OPS] Checklist: Alert on `connections` (active), not `total_connections` (lifetime); connection flapping inflates the lifetime count without anything being wrong.
- [OPS] Checklist: Watch `slow_consumers` on `/varz`; a rising count is a reader that can't keep up.
- [OPS] Checklist: Scope a `/jsz` scrape with `?acc=` and page it with `offset`/`limit`; the full `?accounts=true&streams=true&consumers=true` query is slow at scale and will time out.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: Restrict the monitoring port; it's unauthenticated by default.
- [OPS][CONS] Checklist: Read crashed workers as rising `num_pending` with `num_waiting` at `0` and `delivered.stream_seq` stalled; watch those three fields together.
- [OPS][CONS] Checklist: Read in-flight (`num_ack_pending`) and lag (`num_pending`) as two separate numbers; confusing them hides a stuck handler.
- [OPS][CONS] Checklist: A filtered consumer's `num_pending` counts only matching subjects; empty pending does not mean an empty stream.
- [OPS][STRM] Checklist: Persist advisories to a stream subscribed to `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.>`; advisories are transient.
- [OPS][CONS] Checklist: Treat the `max_deliver` advisory as the only built-in signal a message was dropped; JetStream has no dead-letter queue, so subscribe or lose poison messages silently.
- [OPS][TOPO] Checklist: Read a leader-elected advisory as a flap report only.
- [OPS][TOPO] Checklist: Use `/healthz?js-meta-only=true` to check cluster quorum; `?js-enabled-only=true` returns 200 even with no quorum.
- [OPS] Checklist: Set explicit `nats server check` thresholds like `--unprocessed-critical`; a check with no threshold never fires.
- [OPS] Checklist: Put Prometheus behind the exporter; the exporter stores no history.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: Leave `prof_port` unset in production, or restrict it with firewall rules; it has no authentication and binds to the same interfaces as the client port.
- [OPS] Checklist: Reach for `nats server request profile` before `prof_port`; it needs no config change and no restart, and `prof_port` isn't reloadable.
- [OPS] Checklist: Set `prof_block_rate` above zero before asking for a `block` profile, and drop it back to zero afterwards.



## Key-Value Store
- path: learn/key-value/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/key-value

### Claims
- [KV][STRM] A KV bucket is not a separate database; it is a JetStream stream named `KV_<bucket>` whose subjects are `$KV.<bucket>.>`. "a key is the last token of that subject, and a value is a message on it"
- [KV][STRM] A `put` appends a message, a `get` reads the last message for a subject, and a `watch` opens a consumer.
- [KV][OPS] The key-value store requires JetStream to be enabled on the server. "The key-value store is built on JetStream, so JetStream must be on."
- [KV][PATTERN] Compare-and-swap is the mechanism for safe concurrent decrements so "two concurrent sales never lose a write".
- [KV][PATTERN] A watch delivers the current value of every key as a snapshot, then live updates as values change.

## Your first bucket
- path: learn/key-value/your-first-bucket.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/key-value/your-first-bucket

### Claims
- [KV][STRM] A bucket is a JetStream stream the key-value API creates and configures for you; the bucket `INVENTORY` becomes the stream `KV_INVENTORY`.
- [KV][SUBJ] Bucket names are case-sensitive identifiers.
- [KV][SIZE] History is how many prior values the bucket keeps per key; the default is 1 (only the current value). "One means the bucket holds only the current value of a key and forgets the rest. That's the default"
- [KV][SIZE] History depth can go as high as 64 and no higher. "The depth can go as high as 64, but no higher"
- [KV] A put is an unconditional write that stores the value whether or not the key already exists.
- [KV][MYTH] The revision counter is bucket-wide, not per key. "a number the bucket assigns from a single counter it keeps across every key, not a per-key count"
- [KV] A get returns an entry (value, revision, write time), not a bare value.
- [KV] The entry timestamp records when the value was written, not when it was read.
- [KV][ANTI][CLNT] A get returns an entry rather than a value, and a missing key is signaled distinctly from an empty one; don't treat a missing key as "the count is zero". "an empty value is a value, and a missing key is the absence of one"
- [KV][CLNT] Client behaviour on a missing key differs: the CLI, Go, Python, and C# fail with a key-not-found error; JavaScript, Rust, and Java return null/None.
- [KV][ANTI][SUBJ] Bucket and key names are validated. A bucket name may contain only letters, digits, dash, and underscore, and can't be empty.
- [KV][SUBJ][SIZE] A key may contain only letters, digits, and `-`, `/`, `_`, `=`, and `.`, with no leading or trailing dot and no two dots in a row. "`a..b` is rejected even though `a.b` is fine"
- [KV][ANTI][SUBJ] A colon is not allowed in a key (`ord:8w2k` is rejected client-side before sending); use an underscore or dash instead.

## Watching
- path: learn/key-value/watching.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/key-value/watching

### Claims
- [KV][CONS][PATTERN] A watch delivers the current value of every matching key as an initial snapshot, then streams every later change. "One call gives you both halves: the state of the bucket now, and the changes from now on."
- [KV][CONS] Underneath, a watch is an ephemeral ordered consumer on the backing stream, replaying the last value per key then following new writes; opening the watch creates it and closing removes it.
- [KV][CLNT] After the last snapshot entry and before the first live change, the watch delivers one end-of-initial-data signal: a single nil entry with no key and no value.
- [KV][CLNT] The end-of-initial-data signal differs per client: Go and Python deliver a nil/None entry in-stream; JavaScript sets an `isUpdate` flag; Java calls `endOfData()`; C# takes an `OnNoData` option; Rust has no marker and you choose snapshot-plus-live or live-only at open time.
- [KV][PATTERN] Use the end-of-initial-data signal to hold a "loading" state until the snapshot is complete, or to mark a cache as warm before switching to incremental updates.
- [KV][SUBJ] A watch key filter is matched like a subject: keys are dot-separated tokens, `*` matches exactly one whole token, `>` matches one or more tokens at the end.
- [KV][SUBJ][MYTH] `widget-*` is not a wildcard; `*` is only special as a whole token, so a hyphenated prefix filter matches nothing. "To split keys with a wildcard you'd design them with dots, such as `widget.blue` and `widget.red`, so that `widget.*` matches both."
- [KV][CONS] A watch filter applies to both snapshot and live halves, so a filtered watch is a smaller, cheaper view rather than every change filtered client-side.
- [KV][CLNT] Watch options: `IncludeHistory` replays full history per key, `IgnoreDeletes` skips deleted keys, `UpdatesOnly` drops the snapshot, `MetaOnly` sends metadata without values.
- [KV][CLNT] `IncludeHistory` and `UpdatesOnly` conflict and a client rejects the pair.
- [KV][ANTI][CLNT] Don't stop reading at the boundary signal; a loop that treats the nil entry as end-of-stream quits before every live change. "when an entry is nil, skip it and keep looping. Do not break."
- [KV][ANTI][PATTERN] A watch is live state, not a point read; don't open a watch, read the first entry, and close it to fake a get. "you pay for a consumer and a snapshot to get one value get would have handed you directly"

## History and revisions
- path: learn/key-value/history-and-revisions.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/key-value/history-and-revisions

### Claims
- [KV] A revision always increases when you write a key, but not by one each time, because writes to other keys advance the shared counter in between.
- [KV][SIZE] History depth caps at 64; values written before a history-depth raise are already gone because depth 1 dropped each prior write.
- [KV][PATTERN] Optimistic concurrency via compare-and-swap uses no locks: read the revision, write on the condition the revision hasn't changed, retry on rejection.
- [KV] `create` writes a key only if it doesn't exist (CAS against revision 0); `update` writes only if the key is at the revision you name.
- [KV][PATTERN] Use the read-modify-write with update whenever the new value depends on the old one (decrement, increment, status transition).
- [KV][SIZE] History holds the prior revisions of a single key up to the depth; it's not an audit log of the whole bucket and doesn't grow without bound. "once a key has more revisions than the depth allows, the oldest one is removed"
- [KV][ANTI][CLNT] A rejected update is dropped rather than queued, and you must retry; a fire-and-forget update silently loses the write on conflict. "Don't assume an update succeeded; check the result, and on a revision mismatch, re-get the key and try again"
- [KV][ANTI][PATTERN] Do not use put for a read-modify-write; put is unconditional and overwrites a concurrent writer's value. "Use put to set a key to a given value, and update to change it from the value it currently holds."

## TTL and limits
- path: learn/key-value/ttl-and-limits.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/key-value/ttl-and-limits
- version context: nats-server 2.11 or newer for per-key TTL

### Claims
- [KV][USECASE] Per-key TTL suits values that should clean themselves up: a flash-sale price, a short-lived session token, a time-boxed lock flag.
- [KV] Per-key TTL is set at create time, and only at create time; the countdown starts the moment the value lands. "a TTL belongs to the value you're writing now, not to a value that might be put over it later"
- [KV][OPS] Per-key TTLs require the bucket feature "limit markers" enabled; a bucket needs limit markers on before any key can carry a TTL.
- [KV][MIG][SIZE] Per-key TTL needs nats-server 2.11 or newer, the release that added limit markers; on an older server enabling markers is rejected and the timed create fails.
- [KV][SIZE] Three bucket limits matter most: max bucket size (total bytes across all keys and kept revisions), max value size (largest single value), and history depth.
- [KV][SIZE] History depth caps at 64 and doubles as a per-key cap: the most messages any single key may hold.
- [KV][OBJ][PATTERN] Key-value values are meant to be small; large values belong in the Object Store.
- [KV][STRM] A bucket-wide TTL (`--ttl`) is the stream's `MaxAge` limit applied to every value; a per-key TTL expires one value and is built on JetStream per-message TTL.
- [KV][CONS] When a per-key TTL fires, the server leaves a marker with reason `MaxAge` rather than silently dropping the value; watchers receive it as a purge (CLI prints `PURGE`).
- [KV][ANTI] A per-key TTL is set at create, and only at create; neither put nor update takes a TTL, and rewriting the key appends a value with no TTL so the key stops expiring. "Use delete-then-create to change a TTL, not put or update."
- [KV][ANTI][SIZE] Limits reject, they do not make room for an oversized value; a put over max value size or that would exceed max bucket size returns an error and leaves existing values in place.
- [KV][OPS][PATTERN] Size the bucket for the working set you need to hold, not the average, and cap max value size above the largest value you legitimately store.

## Under the hood
- path: learn/key-value/under-the-hood.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/key-value/under-the-hood

### Claims
- [KV][STRM] Backing stream config for a bucket: `Maximum Per Subject` is the history depth; `Discard Policy: New`; `Direct Get: true`; `Allows Rollups: true`; `Allows Msg Delete: false` (`deny_delete`).
- [KV][STRM] Discard policy `New` is why limits reject: once the bucket hits a limit it rejects the newest write rather than dropping older messages.
- [KV][STRM] `deny_delete` makes the stream refuse the JetStream message-delete API so raw stream ops can't remove entries behind the KV API.
- [KV][STRM] A get uses direct get: the server returns the last message on a subject straight from storage via `$JS.API.DIRECT.GET.<stream>.<subject>`, with no consumer, no position, and no ack.
- [KV] The last message's sequence is the revision and its store time is the entry timestamp.
- [KV] A delete leaves a non-destructive marker with a `KV-Operation: DEL` header; prior revisions up to history depth stay readable through history.
- [KV] A purge writes a marker with `KV-Operation: PURGE` and `Nats-Rollup: sub` headers; the rollup drops every earlier message on the subject, collapsing history to one marker.
- [KV][PATTERN] Reach for purge when you must actually remove old values (for size, or because they were sensitive), not just hide them.
- [KV][ANTI] Delete does not remove history; only purge does. "If you delete `widget-blue` to scrub a wrong count and assume the bad value is unrecoverable, it's sitting one `nats kv history` away."
- [KV][ANTI][STRM] Do not operate the backing stream directly: don't hand-edit `KV_INVENTORY` config and don't publish to `$KV.INVENTORY.>` with raw `nats pub`, because raw publishes lack the CAS, `KV-Operation`, and `Nats-Rollup` headers.
- [KV][STRM] `deny_delete` does not stop a raw publish to the bucket's subjects.
- [KV][ANTI][SUBJ] A key has to be a legal subject token because it becomes the last token of `$KV.INVENTORY.<key>`; a colon or double dot is rejected.
- [KV][TOPO] A bucket's `Replicas` field is the number of servers holding a copy; replication and placement belong to the Clustering chapter.

## Where to go next (Key-Value)
- path: learn/key-value/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/key-value/where-next

### Claims
- [KV][STRM] Mapping: a bucket is a stream, a key is a subject token, a put is a message, a revision is a sequence, a watch is an ephemeral ordered consumer; every bucket limit is a stream limit.
- [KV][OBJ][PATTERN] Key-value values are small and capped; the object store is for large values reassembled from multiple messages on read (a file, a build artifact, anything multi-megabyte).
- [KV][STRM][PATTERN] A bucket can be sourced from or mirrored into another bucket via a subject transform from `$KV.SRC.>` to `$KV.DST.>` (e.g. regional `EU_INVENTORY` sourcing `INVENTORY`).
- [KV][OPS] Checklist: check that an entry exists before reading its value; key-not-found is not an empty value.
- [KV][OPS][SUBJ] Checklist: keep bucket names to alphanumerics, dashes, and underscores.
- [KV][OPS][SUBJ] Checklist: keep keys to alphanumerics and `-/_=.` with no leading or trailing dot; a `:` or leading dot is rejected.
- [KV][OPS][CLNT] Checklist: consume the end-of-initial-data nil entry; stopping at the snapshot boundary misses every live update.
- [KV][OPS] Checklist: treat a watch as live state, not a query; use get or history for a point read.
- [KV][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: wrap every update in a re-get-and-retry loop; a stale-revision update is rejected, not queued.
- [KV][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: use update (CAS), not put, for any read-modify-write like a decrement.
- [KV][OPS] Checklist: set a per-key TTL at create time only; delete then create to change a key's TTL.
- [KV][OPS][SIZE] Checklist: size the bucket for the working set, not the average; at its byte limit the bucket rejects the next put instead of dropping old values.
- [KV][OPS] Checklist: reach for purge, not delete, when you must drop prior revisions.
- [KV][OPS][ANTI] Checklist: use the key-value API, never raw `nats pub` to `$KV.INVENTORY.>` or hand edits to `KV_INVENTORY` config.
- [KV][OPS][SUBJ] Checklist: keep keys to legal subject tokens; `:` or two dots in a row is rejected.

## Object Store
- path: learn/object-store/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/object-store

### Claims
- [OBJ][STRM] An object is a stored file too large or too binary to ride on a plain message; a bucket is the named store, and both live inside a single JetStream stream named `OBJ_<bucket>`.
- [OBJ] On put the store splits bytes into chunks, writes each chunk as a message, then writes one metadata message; on get it reads the metadata, replays chunks in order, and verifies them.
- [OBJ][KV][PATTERN] Key-Value keeps small structured values with full revision history per key; Object Store keeps large chunked files and only the latest metadata per object. "Use key-value when you want many small values that you read, overwrite, and audit; use the object store when you want whole files that you put and fetch."
- [OBJ][OPS] The object store is built on JetStream, so JetStream must be enabled.
- [OBJ][CLNT] Some operations, like creating a link, are client-library only (not in the `nats` CLI).

## Your first object
- path: learn/object-store/your-first-object.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/object-store/your-first-object

### Claims
- [OBJ][SUBJ] Bucket name follows the same rule as a stream name: letters, digits, underscores, and dashes only.
- [OBJ] Put computes a running SHA-256 digest over the exact bytes and writes a final metadata record holding name, size, chunk count, and digest.
- [OBJ] Get recomputes the SHA-256 over the reassembled bytes and returns them only if the digest matches; otherwise it returns an error. "what you get is byte-for-byte what you put, or you get an error. The store does not return a quietly truncated file."
- [OBJ] Put writes the pieces then the metadata; get reads the metadata then the pieces then verifies.
- [OBJ][ANTI] A digest mismatch means do not use the bytes; `ErrDigestMismatch` means retry the get, and a repeated mismatch means the object is damaged and should be put again.
- [OBJ] An interrupted put leaves no gettable object at all because the metadata record is written last; a get reports not-found, not a corrupt file.
- [OBJ][ANTI] Getting a missing object is an error, not empty bytes; treat "not found" as a real branch. "don't ship the order on the assumption that an absent invoice is an empty one"
- [OBJ][ANTI] Don't assume a put "worked" without a get confirming it round-trips.

## Chunking
- path: learn/object-store/chunking.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/object-store/chunking

### Claims
- [OBJ][SIZE] The default chunk size is 128 KB. "The default chunk size is **128 KB**."
- [OBJ][SIZE] At the 128 KB default, a 3 MB file lands in roughly 24 chunks.
- [OBJ] Chunks are an implementation detail; you never ask for them or see them separately after the fact.
- [OBJ] The digest is computed over the whole object, so a single missing or reordered chunk changes it and the get refuses to return.
- [OBJ] The metadata message is written last, so an interrupted put never produces a gettable object; a surviving client also purges the partial chunks it already wrote.
- [OBJ][OPS] A hard crash mid-put runs no cleanup; already-written chunks stay in the stream as orphans, invisible to get but holding storage until the bucket's limits or age reclaim them.
- [OBJ] Each put gets a fresh NUID separate from the object name, so a re-put's chunks never overlap the previous put's; a re-put replaces the object cleanly rather than merging bytes.
- [OBJ][SIZE] Chunk size is configurable per put; the 128 KB default is "a reasonable middle for most files, and most of the time you leave it alone."
- [OBJ][ANTI][SIZE] A chunk size at the extremes causes problems: too small wastes storage on per-message framing overhead and slows puts/gets; too large exceeds the server's `max_payload` (1 MB by default) or a smaller stream max message size and the put fails outright.
- [OBJ][PATTERN][SIZE] Don't tune chunk size to chase a benchmark; if you must raise it, keep each chunk under `max_payload`. "the 128 KB default fits almost every file and stays well under the default payload limit"
- [OBJ][ANTI] Always check the get result before you use the bytes; re-put from the source on failure rather than shipping a partial file.

## Metadata and links
- path: learn/object-store/metadata-and-links.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/object-store/metadata-and-links

### Claims
- [OBJ] The `ObjectInfo` record has store-computed fields (size, chunk count, SHA-256 digest, modification time, deleted flag) and three user-set fields: description, headers (HTTP-style), and a free-form metadata map.
- [OBJ][SIZE] Metadata is held in the one trailing metadata message, so it adds no extra storage cost and no extra read cost.
- [OBJ][PATTERN] Reading metadata (`info`) doesn't fetch the bytes; use it as a low-cost index over the bucket and read bytes only when needed.
- [OBJ][KV][PATTERN] Metadata describes only the current object; each re-put replaces it. For a full revision history per name use the Key-Value store.
- [OBJ] A link is an object whose target is another object; get on the link returns the target's bytes; a link stores no chunks, only the target's bucket and name.
- [OBJ][USECASE] Links are useful when two names should resolve to the same bytes, or a stable name serves as an entry point for a changing set of files.
- [OBJ] A bucket link has an empty target name and records only a reference to another bucket; get on it returns an error (`ErrCantGetBucket` in Go).
- [OBJ] Two link rules the store enforces: a link can't point at a deleted object, and a link can't point at another link.
- [OBJ][ANTI] A link is a snapshot rather than a live reference; deleting the target leaves the link dangling (`ErrObjectNotFound`), and renaming the target breaks it too. "Do verify the target exists with `info` before you depend on the link, and re-create the link after you delete or rename its target."
- [OBJ][ANTI] `UpdateMeta` changes name, description, headers, and metadata, not chunk size or link; a new chunk size or link target is silently discarded. "To change the chunk size, delete the object and put it again. To change a link target, delete the link and add a new one."
- [OBJ] Renaming onto an existing, non-deleted name fails with `ErrObjectAlreadyExists`; renaming onto a deleted name reclaims it.

## Watching and listing
- path: learn/object-store/watching-and-listing.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/object-store/watching-and-listing

### Claims
- [OBJ] A list returns every non-deleted object as a one-time snapshot of metadata; it reads metadata, never chunks, so listing is cheap regardless of object size.
- [OBJ] A list skips soft-deleted objects; the deletion leaves a lingering metadata record that list filters out.
- [OBJ] Listing an empty bucket returns an empty result ("no objects found"), not a failure.
- [OBJ][CONS] A watch streams metadata updates in the order the bucket recorded them, then delivers a single nil sentinel when it has caught up; the CLI consumes the sentinel, client code must recognize it and keep reading.
- [OBJ][KV][PATTERN] An object watch delivers only `ObjectInfo` metadata, never chunk bytes; the KV watch delivers values directly because values are small. "the rule for objects is that watch tells you what changed and get returns the bytes"
- [OBJ][PATTERN] The two-step pattern: watch to learn what changed, then get the bytes you actually want.
- [OBJ][ANTI] Watch delivers metadata, not the bytes; a service that tries to read a large payload off the watch finds only metadata and breaks.
- [OBJ][ANTI] An empty bucket is an empty result, not an error; don't conflate "no objects" with "the bucket is missing".

## Under the hood (Object Store)
- path: learn/object-store/under-the-hood.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/object-store/under-the-hood

### Claims
- [OBJ][SUBJ][STRM] The backing stream `OBJ_<bucket>` captures two subject spaces: `$O.<bucket>.C.>` for chunk messages and `$O.<bucket>.M.>` for metadata messages.
- [OBJ][SUBJ] The chunk subject ends in a per-put NUID (`$O.INVOICES.C.<object-nuid>`) so a re-put never collides with old chunks; the metadata subject ends in the base64url-encoded object name (`$O.INVOICES.M.<base64url(name)>`) so any name, spaces and slashes included, is a safe subject.
- [OBJ] The digest is stored as `SHA-256=<base64url(hash)>`.
- [OBJ][STRM] Every metadata publish carries `Nats-Rollup: sub`, which purges every earlier message on the same subject; this keeps exactly one current `ObjectInfo` per name and makes the store rollup-latest, not multi-revision.
- [OBJ][STRM] Backing stream config: `AllowRollup` true, discard policy `new` (reject writes when full rather than dropping old chunks), `AllowDirect` true, `max_age: 0`, `max_bytes: -1`, `storage: file`, `num_replicas: 1`.
- [OBJ] A soft delete writes one more metadata message with `Deleted=true`, `Size` and `Chunks` zero, and a cleared digest, carrying the rollup header; the chunk messages are then purged.
- [OBJ] After a soft delete the name still has one metadata message (the marker), which is what lets `watch` report an object disappeared.
- [OBJ][SEC] Securing `$O.<bucket>.C.>` / `$O.<bucket>.M.>` or exporting a bucket to another account is an account/permission concern.
- [OBJ][ANTI][OPS] A soft delete does not reclaim disk the instant you call it; the purge frees bytes as the stream cleans up. "Don't delete a large object and immediately assert the disk is smaller."
- [OBJ][CLNT] The soft-delete tombstone is hidden by default; reading it requires the client show-deleted option (`GetObjectInfoShowDeleted` / `ListObjectsShowDeleted` in Go), which the `nats` CLI doesn't expose.
- [OBJ][ANTI][KV] A re-put after a delete is a new object identity, not a restored history. "Don't reach for the object store when you need the *previous* version after an overwrite; that history lives in the Key-Value Store."

## Where to go next (Object Store)
- path: learn/object-store/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/object-store/where-next

### Claims
- [OBJ] Three core ideas: a bucket is an API over one stream `OBJ_<bucket>`; a chunk is one slice written as a message with a whole-object SHA-256 digest; a rollup keeps only the latest metadata per name.
- [OBJ][KV][PATTERN] Key-value is the sibling store for "small structured values and a full revision history per key"; go there when you need versioning of a value, and for the per-key watch the object store doesn't have.
- [OBJ][TOPO] `replicas` on the backing stream (e.g. `R=3`) is what lets a bucket survive node loss.
- [OBJ][OPS] Checklist: check the result and error of every get before using the bytes.
- [OBJ][OPS] Checklist: retry a failed get or put with backoff; a put isn't done until you confirm it.
- [OBJ][OPS] Checklist: treat `ErrObjectNotFound` as a normal outcome on a missing or deleted name, not a crash.
- [OBJ][OPS][SIZE] Checklist: leave chunk size at its default unless you have a reason; too small floods the stream, too large can exceed the stream's max message size.
- [OBJ][OPS] Checklist: check the get result; an unchecked async put failure can leave an object that fails its digest check.
- [OBJ][OPS] Checklist: re-put from the source on a failed get rather than shipping a partial file.
- [OBJ][OPS] Checklist: verify a link's target still exists before relying on get-via-link.
- [OBJ][OPS] Checklist: re-create a link after deleting or renaming its target; a get on a bucket link returns `ErrCantGetBucket`.
- [OBJ][OPS] Checklist: delete and re-put to change chunk size, delete and re-add to change a link target; `UpdateMeta` silently keeps the old ones.
- [OBJ][OPS] Checklist: don't rename onto a name already in use (`ErrObjectAlreadyExists`).
- [OBJ][OPS][PATTERN] Checklist: use watch to learn what changed, then a separate get for bytes.
- [OBJ][OPS] Checklist: never try to read a large payload off the watch channel.
- [OBJ][OPS] Checklist: treat an empty bucket as an empty result; list returns `ErrNoObjectsFound`.
- [OBJ][OPS][SIZE] Checklist: expect a soft delete to mark deleted and purge chunks but not reclaim disk until the purge completes; size the backing stream accordingly.
- [OBJ][OPS] Checklist: treat a re-put after a delete as a new object identity, not a restored history.

## Backup & Recovery Deep Dive
- path: learn/backup-recovery/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/backup-recovery

### Claims
- [OPS][PATTERN] Protecting a NATS platform means protecting three things, none of which protects the others: a snapshot (recovery point), a mirror (recovery time), and identity (JWTs, nkeys, creds, server config).
- [OPS][STRM] A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a stream (messages, config, optionally consumer state) written off-site; it answers "how much data can I afford to lose" (recovery point).
- [OPS][STRM][TOPO] A mirror is a live, read-only copy of a stream at a second site kept current by replication; it answers "how long can recovery take" (recovery time).
- [OPS][SEC] Identity is the set of files that are your security layer: operator and account JWTs, the nkeys that sign them, user creds, and server config. "Without these, a restored stream is data nobody is allowed to read."
- [OPS][MYTH] A mirror won't save you from bad data: a corrupt write replicates to the mirror and a mirror keeps no earlier state to rewind to.
- [OPS][MYTH][STRM] R3 replication is high availability, not a backup; a bad write (accidental delete, corrupt message) is applied to every replica. "R3 keeps the stream *available*; only a snapshot lets you go *back* to before the mistake."
- [OPS][STRM][SIZE] Memory streams can't be snapshotted, so file storage is required for any stream you want to back up.
- [OPS][TOPO] A DR mirror needs a second site: a separate cluster reachable over a gateway or leaf-node link.

## Stream backup and restore
- path: learn/backup-recovery/stream-backup-restore.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/backup-recovery/stream-backup-restore

### Claims
- [OPS][STRM] Replication doesn't protect from a mistake (accidental purge, bad migration, logic bug); recovering from those needs a copy the cluster can't touch.
- [OPS][STRM] A snapshot is a complete copy of a stream at one instant: every message, the stream config, and optionally consumer state; the server streams it in chunks to a directory.
- [OPS][STRM] A snapshot directory holds `backup.json` (config and state: subjects, retention, limits, sequence range) and `stream.tar.s2` (messages packed in a tarball compressed with S2).
- [OPS][PATTERN] Name snapshot directories by date; a snapshot is a point in time.
- [OPS][CONS] By default a snapshot records each durable consumer's config and delivery position, so restored consumers resume where they left off; `--no-consumers` drops that. "keep the default when you back up a production stream"
- [OPS][SIZE] The server keeps a window of unacknowledged snapshot chunks in flight: 8 MiB by default, which is 64 of the default 128 KiB chunks.
- [OPS][SIZE] If no chunk ack arrives for about five seconds the backup aborts; windowed backpressure keeps a large stream from overwhelming a slow disk or high-latency link.
- [OPS][STRM] Restore recreates the stream from a snapshot: same messages, same sequence numbers, same configuration, plus consumers if the snapshot included them.
- [OPS][STRM] The stream name cannot change on restore; the server rejects a restore under a different name. "A snapshot of `ORDERS` restores as `ORDERS`, never as `ORDERS_COPY`."
- [OPS][PATTERN] If you need a second copy under a new name, restore to the original name first, then mirror or source it.
- [OPS][STRM] Restore expects the stream not to already exist; it recreates, it doesn't merge into a live stream. "confirm the broken stream is gone (or remove it), then restore"
- [OPS] A restore you didn't check is unverified: `Messages` and `Last Sequence` must match the snapshotted stream. "the backup command exiting zero does not prove it on its own"
- [OPS][ANTI][STRM] Memory streams cannot be snapshotted; the backup fails with `memory streams do not support snapshots`. Set `Storage: File` on any stream you want to back up.
- [OPS][ANTI][STRM] The stream name cannot change on restore; the server rejects with `stream name may not be changed during restore`.
- [OPS][ANTI][SIZE] Flow control can time out on slow disks or distant links (`408 No Flow Response`); the fix is smaller chunks and a smaller window (e.g. `--chunk-size 64k --window-size 1m`).
- [OPS][ANTI][CONS] `--no-consumers` silently drops consumer state; the restore rebuilds the stream with no consumers and nothing warns you.

## Mirrors as a DR tool
- path: learn/backup-recovery/mirrors-and-sources.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/backup-recovery/mirrors-and-sources

### Claims
- [OPS][STRM][TOPO] R3 replication protects against losing one node; it does nothing when you lose the whole cluster. A mirror lives at a separate site reachable over a gateway or leaf-node link.
- [OPS][STRM] A DR mirror accepts no direct writes; the copy flows one way, upstream to mirror, never back.
- [OPS][STRM][ANTI] A mirror's configuration is fixed once the stream exists; you can't re-point a running mirror or change what it copies. Changing it means delete and recreate, after which messages re-replicate.
- [OPS][STRM] Replication is asynchronous: the upstream acks the publisher before the mirror has the message; the gap is lag, the count of messages the mirror trails behind.
- [OPS][STRM] Mirror info fields: `Stream Name` (upstream), `Lag` (messages upstream has that the mirror doesn't), `Last Seen` (time since the mirror last heard from upstream; in monitoring JSON the field is `active`).
- [OPS][SIZE] `Lag: 0` means the mirror holds every upstream message; any number above zero is the data you'd lose if the primary vanished now.
- [OPS] A growing `Last Seen` means the mirror is no longer keeping up and the `Lag` you read is already stale.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Lag and Last Seen are your RPO; a mirror at `Lag: 0` gives RPO of zero messages. Read them before you trust a mirror in a failover, and watch `Lag` continuously rather than once.
- [OPS][MYTH][STRM] A mirror is not a backup. "A mirror follows the upstream's live writes, so a corrupt write lands in the mirror too — and a mirror keeps no earlier state to rewind to."
- [OPS][STRM] A mirror gives availability (short RTO because the data is already there) but no recovery point; its own retention limits can age messages out on their own schedule.
- [OPS][STRM] Deleting the upstream does not delete the mirror: it keeps every message already copied, stops receiving, and records the fault in the `Error` field of its Mirror Information.
- [OPS][STRM] Purging a range on the upstream leaves the mirror's already-stored messages in place; the mirror detects the sequence gap and skips missing messages.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Mirror is for site failure (promote, short RTO, no loss if lag was zero); snapshot is for wrong data (deleted, purged, corrupted; bounded RPO, restore-length RTO). You need both.
- [OPS][ANTI] Don't let a healthy mirror be your reason to stop taking snapshots.
- [OPS][ANTI][STRM] Don't reach for R3 as DR: a corrupt write replicates across all three R3 replicas just as it lands in a mirror.
- [OPS][ANTI][STRM] A mirror is not a backup; don't run a mirror instead of snapshots. "Pair them: the mirror for site failure, the snapshot for bad data."
- [OPS][ANTI] Read `Lag` before you trust the copy; replication is eventually consistent, not synchronous. "Diagnose the link before a failover, never during one."
- [OPS][ANTI][STRM] A mirror's config is effectively locked after creation; settle upstream, site, and subjects upfront.
- [OPS][ANTI][STRM][CONS] Avoid a Work Queue upstream under a mirror: the mirror's hidden internal consumer is a direct consumer that bypasses the work queue's subject-overlap check, so a worker and the mirror can both receive the same message. Use a `Limits` upstream instead.

## Disaster recovery
- path: learn/backup-recovery/disaster-recovery.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/backup-recovery/disaster-recovery

### Claims
- [OPS][PATTERN] Decide which tool per failure class ahead of time, not under pressure during an outage.
- [OPS][PATTERN][TOPO] Whole cluster gone: promote the mirror. "promotion is minutes, a restore is hours."
- [OPS][PATTERN] Accidental delete or purge: recover from the mirror (usually the freshest intact copy since it survives an upstream delete) or restore the snapshot as the older fallback.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Corrupt or wrong messages (bad publisher): restore a known-good snapshot or purge the bad range; the bad data replicated to the mirror too.
- [OPS][PATTERN][CONS] Consumer lost its position: restore a `--consumers` snapshot; only the snapshot captured the saved delivery position.
- [OPS][STRM] A snapshot is the only copy that predates a mistake; a mirror survives an upstream delete only as a copy frozen at the break.
- [OPS][MYTH] R3 is on neither recovery row: "replicating a bad write three times doesn't undo it."
- [OPS][STRM] Promotion step 1: verify lag is zero. If the site is unreachable, lag stalls at the last successful copy; that stalled number is your real recovery point. "Waiting for a lag that will never move to zero only extends the outage."
- [OPS][STRM] A mirror is read-only by design and rejects direct publishes; promotion removes the mirror relationship (`--no-mirror`), which doesn't touch the data.
- [OPS][STRM] Promotion must clear the lost stream's assignment first (`stream rm --force`) or the subject bind fails with `subjects overlap with an existing stream (10065)`; losing the site doesn't remove the dead stream from JetStream metadata.
- [OPS][STRM][SUBJ] A mirror has no subjects of its own; a promoted primary needs the subjects bound to it so publishers can reach it.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Official promotion order: free the mirrored stream's subjects, drop the mirror config, bind subjects to the promoted stream, then redirect publishers and consumers.
- [OPS][TOPO] Promotion edits go through the JetStream metadata group, which must keep quorum after the site is lost; if the failed site held the meta majority, no edit succeeds until the cluster recovers.
- [OPS][TOPO][PATTERN] A DR mirror is normally placed in its own JetStream domain (a leaf node) or an independent cluster, rather than sharing one meta group that spans both sites.
- [OPS][STRM] For an accidental delete, restore straight from the snapshot; don't recreate an empty stream first because restore creates it and an existing stream makes it fail.
- [OPS][PATTERN] For logical corruption, stop the publishers first so no new bad data races in, then purge the corrupt range or restore a snapshot that predates it.
- [OPS][ANTI][STRM] Never promote a mirror before lag reaches zero, or with a stalled lag you've consciously accepted; tail messages in flight are lost and new writes land on top of the gap.
- [OPS][ANTI][STRM] R3 replication will not save you from a mistake; an accidental delete or bad publish replicates to all three copies at once.
- [OPS][ANTI] Stop publishers before purging corrupted messages; otherwise new corrupt data arrives behind you and you keep purging against a growing tail.
