- [OPS][ANTI] An untested snapshot is unverified; a healthy `nats stream info` on the live stream proves nothing about the archive. "Rehearse the restore on a schedule (quarterly is a reasonable minimum)"

## Config and JWT backup
- path: learn/backup-recovery/config-and-jwt-backup.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/backup-recovery/config-and-jwt-backup

### Claims
- [SEC][OPS] Identity reduces to three groups of files: the `nats auth` store (JWTs and `.nk` seeds under `$XDG_DATA_HOME/nats`, default `~/.local/share/nats`), the creds files, and the server config.
- [SEC] A JWT is the signed identity token; a seed (`.nk`) is the private half of the nkey pair whose public key the JWT names; each JWT is signed by the key one level up (operator signs accounts, accounts sign users).
- [SEC] The `stores` half holds only JWTs, which are public; the `keys` half is secret. A leaked operator or account seed lets identity be forged; a leaked user seed lets an attacker connect as that user; a lost seed means that identity is lost. "Protect the `keys` subtree with the same controls you apply to stored passwords."
- [SEC][CLNT] A `.creds` file is a user's JWT and seed concatenated; creds files aren't inside the store, they sit wherever they were written, on client machines.
- [SEC][OPS] The server config anchors identity: the trusted operator JWT, the `SYSTEM` account preload, and the resolver directory. "Restore the keys without the config and the server doesn't know to trust them."
- [SEC][OPS] The account resolver `dir` holds the server's own copy of every pushed account JWT; that copy matters at restore time.
- [SEC][OPS] `nats auth operator backup` writes a single JSON document holding every JWT and every private seed (operator, signing keys, accounts, users); treat it as an opaque blob. "Whoever holds this one file *is* the `ACME` operator. Never ship it anywhere unencrypted."
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] Encrypt the backup with `--key` pointing at a curve seed file (`nats auth nkey gen curve`); store the curve seed somewhere other than the backups. "keeping an archive and its key in the same place is a single point of failure"
- [SEC][OPS] The operator backup contains no creds files (re-minted from the restored store) and nothing server-side; back up `server.conf` alongside it. The resolver directory needs no backup because re-pushing accounts rebuilds it.
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] Date each identity backup: an older backup restores the previous operator after a key rotation, and a server rebuilt from it trusts a chain nobody signs anymore.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Run the identity backup on a schedule like the snapshot (a daily cron line).
- [SEC][OPS] Restore brings back the original keys, not new ones, so every creds file handed out before the disaster keeps working.
- [SEC][OPS] Restore refuses to run if the operator already exists in the store (`operator ACME already exist`); to restore over a corrupted store, move the old store directory aside first.
- [SEC][OPS] A restored workstation store does not refill the server's resolver directory; a server that lost it rejects users with `Authorization Violation` until each account is pushed again.
- [SEC][OPS] The account push authenticates with `SYSTEM` creds and gets in despite an empty resolver because `server.conf` preloads the `SYSTEM` account JWT; that preload is the bootstrap path for recovery.
- [SEC][ANTI][OPS] The backup file is the whole authority; always pass `--key` and keep the curve seed away from the backups. Restore without the key fails with no recovery path. "Test-restore on a spare machine once so you know the file and the key actually pair up."
- [SEC][ANTI][OPS] A restored store doesn't refill the server's resolver; the fix is one `nats auth account push` per account, which works only while you still have `server.conf`.
- [SEC][ANTI][OPS] An un-backed-up operator rotation orphans the archive; tag every backup with the operator version or timestamp and take a fresh backup right after any rotation.

## Where to go next (Backup & Recovery)
- path: learn/backup-recovery/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/backup-recovery/where-next

### Claims
- [OPS][MYTH] R3 is availability, not a backup. "Three replicas keep a stream alive through a node loss, but a bad write replicates to all three just as a good one does."
- [OPS][SEC] A restored stream that nobody is allowed to read is not a recovery.
- [OPS][STRM] Checklist: use file storage for any stream you must snapshot; a memory stream cannot be backed up.
- [OPS][STRM] Checklist: restore to the original stream name; mirror or source afterward if you need a copy under a new name.
- [OPS][SIZE] Checklist: reduce `--chunk-size` and `--window-size` on a slow disk or high-latency link before the flow-control timeout aborts the snapshot.
- [OPS][CONS] Checklist: keep consumer state in the snapshot; `--no-consumers` silently drops durable consumer config and delivery position.
- [OPS][STRM] Checklist: pair every mirror with snapshots; a mirror is not a backup.
- [OPS][STRM] Checklist: plan the mirror topology upfront; config is effectively locked after creation.
- [OPS][STRM] Checklist: read the `Lag` field before trusting a mirror; replication is eventually consistent, not synchronous.
- [OPS][STRM][CONS] Checklist: avoid Work Queue retention on a mirrored upstream; use Limits.
- [OPS][STRM] Checklist: verify lag has reached 0 before promoting a mirror.
- [OPS][STRM] Checklist: reach for a snapshot, not R3, against an accidental delete or logical error.
- [OPS] Checklist: test restore on a schedule, quarterly at least.
- [OPS] Checklist: stop publishers before purging corrupted messages.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: seal every `nats auth operator backup` with `--key` and store the curve seed apart from the backups.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: re-push each account after an identity restore if the server lost its resolver directory; back up `server.conf` too because its `SYSTEM` preload lets the push in.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: tag each identity backup with the operator version or timestamp.

## Connect MQTT devices to NATS
- path: learn/mqtt/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/mqtt
- version context: nats-server 2.10 or later (MQTT landed in 2.2; `.`-in-topic conversion and QoS 2 arrived in 2.10)

### Claims
- [TOPO][PATTERN] `nats-server` speaks MQTT natively on its own listener; there's no bridge process and no second broker to run.
- [SUBJ] The server converts each MQTT topic to a NATS subject: `sensors/warehouse/cold-1/temp` reaches a NATS subscriber on `sensors.warehouse.cold-1.temp`.
- [SIZE][CLNT] NATS implements MQTT v3.1.1 and supports QoS 0, 1, and 2; a device requesting MQTT v5 is rejected at connect with CONNACK return code 1, "unacceptable protocol version".
- [USECASE][PATTERN] MQTT support exists to keep an existing device investment; use it when endpoints already speak MQTT or can only ever speak MQTT.
- [PATTERN] For a greenfield deployment, prefer NATS end to end. "One technology from device to cloud gives you a single security model and one set of observability tools. The NATS clients are efficient enough for constrained hardware."
- [TOPO][PATTERN] A standalone MQTT broker scales by making one node bigger; `nats-server` scales by adding servers (clusters, superclusters, leaf nodes), which carry MQTT traffic like everything else.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Where a broker's persistence stops at a last-value cache per topic, device traffic on NATS lands in JetStream streams with retention limits, replay, and consumers written later.
- [MIG][SIZE] Before 2.10, a `.` in an MQTT topic was rejected; the `//` encoding was added in 2.10.

## Your first MQTT client
- path: learn/mqtt/your-first-mqtt-client.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/mqtt/your-first-mqtt-client

### Claims
- [STRM][OPS] MQTT needs state that outlives a connection (session subscriptions, unacked QoS 1/2 messages, retained messages); the server keeps all of it in JetStream streams, so JetStream must be reachable.
- [OPS] Configuring `mqtt {}` without JetStream on a standalone server refuses to start: `mqtt requires JetStream to be enabled if running in standalone mode`. A server with a `cluster`, `gateway`, or `leafnode` config can reach JetStream elsewhere, so the check doesn't apply there.
- [OPS][ANTI] An `mqtt {}` block with no `listen` or `port` disables MQTT silently, with no error and no log line, so always set one.
- [SIZE] MQTT gets its own listener on port 1883 (the conventional MQTT port), separate from the client port 4222.
- [SUBJ] The MQTT payload crosses untouched; the server adds an `Nmqtt-Pub` header marking the message MQTT-originated with the QoS it was published at.
- [CORE] Nothing on the NATS side is MQTT-aware; any NATS subscriber, JetStream stream, or service consumes device traffic as normal messages.
- [CLNT][SIZE] A message published by a NATS client always arrives at an MQTT subscriber as QoS 0, whatever QoS the subscription asked for, because a NATS publish carries no QoS.
- [CORE][TOPO] An MQTT subscription is a real NATS subscription on the converted subject, so it propagates across a cluster like any other; publishers on other servers reach the device without knowing about MQTT.
- [STRM][PATTERN] Capture device traffic in a normal stream (e.g. `DEVICES` on `sensors.>,fleet.>`) so a QoS 0 reading, gone once delivered, and a QoS 1 reading, which only reaches subscribers that exist at the time, are still readable by a consumer written later.
- [ANTI][OPS] Starting without JetStream fails at startup; the requirement applies per account too: an MQTT user whose account has no JetStream is refused at connect. "Enable JetStream on the server, and on the account your MQTT users bind to."
- [ANTI][CLNT] Pointing an MQTT-over-WebSocket client at 1883 is rejected with `MQTT clients over websocket must connect to the Websocket port, not the MQTT port`; plain MQTT goes to 1883, MQTT over WebSocket goes to the WebSocket listener.

## Topics and subjects
- path: learn/mqtt/topics-and-subjects.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/mqtt/topics-and-subjects
- version context: `.`-in-topic conversion added in NATS Server 2.10

### Claims
- [SUBJ] Conversion rules: `/` between two levels becomes `.`; a leading `/` becomes `/.`; a trailing `/` becomes `./`; a `/` next to another `/` becomes `./`; a `.` in the topic becomes `//`.
- [SUBJ] Examples: `/sensors/temp` -> `/.sensors.temp`; `sensors/temp/` -> `sensors.temp./`; `sensors//temp` -> `sensors./.temp`; `//sensors/temp` -> `/./.sensors.temp`; `cold-1.temp` -> `cold-1//temp`.
- [SUBJ] The `/` and `.` characters swap roles in conversion, and the escaping keeps the mapping reversible.
- [SUBJ][MIG] Converting `.` was added in NATS Server 2.10; before that a `.` in a topic was rejected the way whitespace still is.
- [SUBJ][SIZE] Characters the server refuses in topics: space, tab, newline, carriage return, form feed, and DEL. The space has never been accepted on any version because it would break the NATS wire protocol control line.
- [SUBJ][CLNT] Publishing to a topic with a refused character closes the connection; subscribing with one returns a failure code in the SUBACK and the connection survives.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Treat anything that isn't printable as unusable in topics; strip whitespace from free-text fields before they reach a topic.
- [SUBJ] Wildcards map directly: MQTT `+` -> NATS `*` (exactly one level); MQTT `#` -> NATS `>` (one or more levels). Wildcards are allowed only in subscriptions; publishing to a topic containing `+` or `#` is rejected.
- [SUBJ][SIZE] MQTT `sensors/#` also matches the parent `sensors` while NATS `sensors.>` doesn't, so the server creates two NATS subscriptions (`sensors.>` and `sensors`) for that filter. A filter of just `#` converts to `>` and needs only one.
- [SUBJ][SIZE] A subscription ending in `#` counts twice against `max_ack_pending`.
- [SUBJ][ANTI] `*` and `>` are ordinary characters in MQTT and pass through unescaped; if one becomes a whole token in the subject NATS reads it as a wildcard. `fleet/*/telemetry` subscribes to `fleet.*.telemetry`. "Keep `*` and `>` out of topic names unless you mean the NATS behavior."
- [SEC][SUBJ] Authorization runs on the converted subject, not the MQTT topic; the server converts first, then checks permissions. Write permissions as NATS subjects with NATS wildcards; `sensors/#` as a rule never matches anything.
- [SEC][SUBJ] A device subscribing to `sensors/#` needs subscribe permission on both `sensors.>` and `sensors`; allow only the first and the whole filter fails.
- [SUBJ][OPS] The server's own MQTT-management traffic runs on `$JS.>` and `$MQTT.>` subjects; device messages are the ones carrying an `Nmqtt-Pub` header.
- [PATTERN][SUBJ] To learn the subject a topic lands on, publish one message and read the subject off a `nats sub ">"` rather than working it out by hand.
- [ANTI][SEC][SUBJ] Writing permissions as MQTT topics never matches; it fails late: the device connects fine, then its publishes are rejected.
- [ANTI][SEC][SUBJ] Granting only `sensors.>` for a `#` subscription: the server returns `0x80` in the SUBACK and tears down the `sensors.>` subscription it had already created, so the device receives nothing at all.
- [ANTI][SUBJ] Assuming a leading or trailing slash is cosmetic: `sensors/temp` and `/sensors/temp` are different subjects. "If some devices in a fleet emit a leading slash and others don't, you have two subject trees, not one."
- [ANTI][SUBJ] Letting free text into a topic: a space closes the connection on publish and fails the SUBACK on subscribe. "Sanitize anything interpolated into a topic."

## QoS, sessions, and retained messages
- path: learn/mqtt/qos-sessions-and-retained.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/mqtt/qos-sessions-and-retained

### Claims
- [SIZE] QoS 0: at most once, nothing stored, no ack. QoS 1: at least once, stored until PUBACK, duplicates possible. QoS 2: exactly once via a four-packet handshake, most round trips and most state.
- [CLNT] The effective QoS for a delivery is the lower of publish and subscription QoS; a QoS 0 publish to a QoS 1 subscriber is delivered at QoS 0.
- [CLNT][MYTH] QoS is an MQTT-side contract; NATS has no equivalent, so the guarantees hold end to end only when both ends are MQTT.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] A message published by a NATS client and delivered to an MQTT subscriber is always QoS 0. "When a device genuinely needs the delivery guarantee, the message has to originate from an MQTT publisher at QoS 1 or 2."
- [STRM][PATTERN] If traffic starts on the NATS side and delivery matters, keep the durability on the NATS side in a stream rather than expecting MQTT redelivery.
- [SIZE] `ack_wait` (redelivery timeout for unacked QoS 1/2 messages) defaults to 30 seconds; redelivered messages are flagged as duplicates (DUP).
- [OPS] A change to `ack_wait` applies only to subscriptions created after the change; existing subscriptions keep the old value until recreated.
- [PATTERN] A redelivered message is a genuine duplicate; handlers that matter should be idempotent.
- [SIZE] `max_ack_pending` caps in-flight QoS 1 and 2 messages per subscription; it defaults to 1024 with valid range 0 to 65535, and `0` means "use the default" (1024).
- [SIZE] The total `max_ack_pending` across all of a session's subscriptions can't exceed 65535; a subscription that would exceed it is refused with `0x80` in the SUBACK. A `#` subscription counts twice.
- [SIZE] At the default 1024, a session has room for 63 plain subscriptions, or 31 if they all end in `#`; the check is strict, so the subscription that would reach the cap exactly is refused.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Lower `max_ack_pending` if you need more subscriptions per session; like `ack_wait`, a change applies only to new subscriptions.
- [CLNT] A session (subscription state and in-flight delivery state) is keyed by the client ID from CONNECT, not the connection, which is what lets it survive a reconnect.
- [STRM][CLNT] Sessions are stored in JetStream, so they outlive both the connection and a server restart; a reconnecting device with the same client ID finds subscriptions still in place and unacked QoS 1/2 messages pending.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] The clean session flag clears stored state and makes the session last only as long as the connection. "A device with no durable subscriptions should set it; one that wants messages buffered while it's offline shouldn't."
- [CLNT][SUBJ] A client ID must be a valid name with the same character restrictions as NATS subject tokens; an invalid one is refused with an identifier-rejected code. An empty client ID is allowed only with clean session, and the server generates one.
- [CLNT] Client IDs must be unique; when a second connection presents a client ID in use, the server closes the first and accepts the newcomer.
- [CLNT][SIZE] Duplicate client IDs with reconnect logic evict each other in a loop; the server records the client ID as flapping and refuses to hand the session over again for about a second, which slows the cycle without stopping it.
- [CLNT][TOPO] Client-ID eviction across a cluster is less immediate because it travels between servers; the server sometimes refuses the new connection instead of closing the old one.
- [CLNT] A will message registered at CONNECT (topic, payload, optional QoS and RETAIN) is published only if the connection ends without a clean DISCONNECT; a clean DISCONNECT discards it silently.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] The will topic converts to a subject by the same rules, so device liveness is visible to NATS subscribers too.
- [PATTERN] Pair the will with RETAIN so the "offline" marker persists as the topic's retained value for dashboards that subscribe later.
- [SIZE] Only one message is retained per topic; a new retained publish replaces the previous one. Retention is per topic name, not per filter, so a wildcard subscriber receives the retained message for every matching topic.
- [STRM][OPS] Retained messages are stored regardless of QoS; a retained QoS 0 message is still persisted, which is part of why the account needs JetStream even for a fleet that never uses QoS 1.
- [CLNT] To clear a retained message, publish an empty payload to the same topic with RETAIN set; the zero-byte message is delivered to current subscribers, then the stored value is removed.
- [ANTI][CLNT] Expecting QoS 1 to cover NATS-originated messages: they arrive at QoS 0 with no redelivery. "put it in a JetStream stream and have something replay it, rather than relying on the MQTT subscription"
- [ANTI][CLNT] Sharing a client ID across devices looks like a flaky network. "Give every device its own client ID, and prefer one derived from hardware rather than baked into an image."
- [ANTI][SIZE] Raising `max_ack_pending` without counting subscriptions: the per-session total is capped at 65535 and every `#` subscription costs double; new subscriptions fail with `0x80`, easy to misread as a permissions problem.
- [ANTI][MYTH] Assuming a retained message is a message queue: only the last retained value per topic is kept. "Use JetStream when you need the history."
- [ANTI][OPS] Testing a will with a clean shutdown discards the will; test with a hard kill or by cutting the network.

## Auth and clustering (MQTT)
- path: learn/mqtt/auth-and-clustering.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/mqtt/auth-and-clustering
- version context: `$MQTT.sub.>` implicit allow from server 2.12.3; explicit allow needed on 2.10 and 2.11

### Claims
- [SEC] Users are shared across connection types by default; a username/password works from MQTT, NATS, or WebSocket unless `allowed_connection_types` pins it.
- [SEC][SIZE] `allowed_connection_types` values: `STANDARD`, `WEBSOCKET`, `LEAFNODE`, `LEAFNODE_WS`, `MQTT`, `MQTT_WS`, `IN_PROCESS`; a browser-based MQTT client needs `MQTT_WS` rather than `MQTT`. Omitting the option allows every type (the default). Aliases: `connection_types`, `clients`.
- [SEC][SUBJ][PATTERN] Permissions for MQTT users are written against converted subjects; a subscribe list for a device using `fleet/#` carries both `fleet.>` and `fleet`.
- [SEC][OPS] The `mqtt {}` block takes its own `tls {}` map separate from the client port's; add `ca_file` and `verify: true` for mutual TLS.
- [SEC] The `mqtt {}` block can carry its own `authorization {}` (username, password, or token scoped to the MQTT listener) and its own `no_auth_user` overriding the top-level one for MQTT connections.
- [SEC][PATTERN] `no_auth_user` on the MQTT listener is the answer when device firmware can't send credentials: it maps credential-less MQTT connections onto one top-level user's permissions.
- [SEC][SIZE] Two limits: a listener-scoped username or token can't be combined with a top-level `users` list, and `no_auth_user` doesn't work in operator mode.
- [SEC][STRM] A QoS 1 or 2 subscription is backed by a JetStream durable delivered over an internal subject under `$MQTT.sub.`.
- [SEC][MIG] From server 2.12.3 an MQTT connection is implicitly allowed to subscribe to `$MQTT.sub.` and `$MQTT.deliver.pubrel.` subjects; before 2.12.3 (including 2.10 and 2.11) you must allow `$MQTT.sub.>` in the user's subscribe list or every QoS 1/2 subscription fails with `0x80`.
- [SEC][ANTI] An explicit deny on `$MQTT.sub.>` is still enforced and breaks QoS 1 and 2 subscriptions. "leave those subjects out of your permission lists entirely: don't allow them (unnecessary) and don't deny them (breaks QoS 1)"
- [SEC][CLNT] MQTT clients can't sign the operator-mode nonce challenge; in operator mode the device sends the user JWT as the MQTT password with any non-empty username, and the server authenticates on the JWT alone.
- [SEC] The user must be a bearer user, which takes two steps because accounts disallow bearer tokens by default: enable bearer on the account and mark the user bearer. Missing either refuses with CONNACK return code 5, "not authorized".
- [SEC][CLNT] MQTT clients never receive the `Authorization Violation` string a NATS client would; check the CONNACK code instead.
- [SEC][PATTERN] A bearer JWT lets anyone holding it connect as that user; treat it like a password and put TLS in front of it.
- [SEC] `no_auth_user` isn't compatible with operator mode at all; every connection needs a JWT there.
- [TOPO][OPS] Once a server has a `cluster` or `gateway` block, MQTT requires `server_name` and startup fails otherwise: `mqtt requires server name to be explicitly set`. Server names must be unique across the cluster or super-cluster.
- [TOPO][STRM][SIZE] MQTT state streams are replicated automatically once JetStream is clustered; the replica count is derived from the number of addresses in the server's own `routes` list, clamped between 1 and 3, not from how many servers the cluster has.
- [TOPO][STRM][SIZE] A server listing two routes brings its MQTT streams up at `R=2`, not `R=3`; list all peers in `routes` or set `stream_replicas: 3` explicitly. Asking for more replicas than the cluster can satisfy makes the streams fail to create, surfacing as MQTT clients unable to connect.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] A leaf node close to devices can serve MQTT without running JetStream itself; the standalone JetStream check doesn't apply once the server has a `leafnodes` configuration.
- [TOPO][STRM][PATTERN] `js_domain` selects the JetStream domain MQTT stores its state in; set it to the leaf's local domain so sessions and retained messages stay on the leaf and local devices keep working when the hub link is down. The domain is part of the session's storage identity, keeping sessions in different domains from colliding.
- [TOPO][CLNT] Retained messages are best-effort in a cluster: propagation isn't instant, so a subscriber on a different server microseconds later may see nothing. "When an application depends on reading a retained value immediately, have it connect to the server that produced it."
- [TOPO][CLNT] Client-ID collision detection is slower in a cluster; both connections can be briefly alive at once.
- [OPS] With `http: 8222`, `/connz?mqtt_client=<id>` filters connections by MQTT client ID; each record carries `mqtt_client`, and `/varz` has an `mqtt` section including the JetStream domain in use.
- [ANTI][SEC] Leaving credentials off the MQTT listener lets any device that can reach port 1883 connect. "Devices sit on networks you control least, so put credentials and TLS on the MQTT listener before it leaves a lab."
- [ANTI][SEC] Denying `$MQTT.sub.>` silently breaks QoS 1 and 2 subscriptions while QoS 0 keeps working, so the fleet looks half-broken.
- [ANTI][SEC] Forgetting `--bearer` in operator mode: a valid JWT is refused with CONNACK return code 5; both the user and the account must be bearer-enabled.
- [ANTI][TOPO] Adding a cluster block without `server_name` makes the server refuse to start; set `server_name` on every server from the beginning.

## Where to go next (MQTT)
- path: learn/mqtt/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/mqtt/where-next

### Claims
- [SUBJ] Everything downstream (subscriptions, permissions, streams) is written against the converted subject, not the topic the device sent.
- [CLNT] QoS is an MQTT-side contract the server honors between MQTT clients; it can't extend to NATS publishes, which arrive as QoS 0.
- [STRM] Sessions, retained messages, and in-flight QoS 1/2 deliveries are all stored in streams the server manages; that's why the account needs JetStream and why sessions survive reconnect and restart.
- [SIZE] Only MQTT v3.1.1 is supported; a client requesting v5 is rejected at connect.
- [CLNT] Browser-based MQTT clients connect through the `websocket {}` listener with `MQTT_WS` as their connection type.
- [USECASE] Sparkplug B is ordinary MQTT traffic to the server; nothing in NATS interprets it.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Leaf nodes suit devices well: a leaf on a factory floor or in a vehicle gives local MQTT clients a nearby server that needs only outbound connectivity to the hub, so they keep working when the cloud link is down.
- [OPS] Checklist: enable JetStream on the server and on the account your MQTT users bind to.
- [OPS][CLNT] Checklist: point plain MQTT clients at the MQTT port and MQTT-over-WebSocket clients at the WebSocket listener.
- [OPS][SEC][SUBJ] Checklist: write every permission as a NATS subject with NATS wildcards.
- [OPS][SEC][SUBJ] Checklist: grant both `sensors.>` and `sensors` for a device subscribing to `sensors/#`.
- [OPS][SUBJ] Checklist: normalize leading and trailing slashes across the fleet, or account for both subject trees.
- [OPS][SUBJ] Checklist: sanitize anything interpolated into a topic.
- [OPS][STRM] Checklist: don't rely on a QoS 1 subscription to make NATS-originated traffic durable; put that data in a stream.
- [OPS][CLNT] Checklist: give every device its own client ID, ideally derived from hardware.
- [OPS][SIZE] Checklist: count subscriptions against `max_ack_pending`; at the default of 1024 a session fits 63 subscriptions (31 if they end in `#`) before the 65535 per-session cap.
- [OPS][STRM] Checklist: use JetStream where you need history; only the last retained value per topic is kept.
- [OPS] Checklist: test wills with a hard kill or a cut network, not a clean shutdown.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: put credentials and TLS on the MQTT listener before it leaves a lab.
- [OPS][SEC][MIG] Checklist: keep `$MQTT.sub.>` out of permission lists on 2.12.3 and later; on 2.10 and 2.11, allow it explicitly.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: set `--bearer` on both the account and the user for operator-mode devices.
- [OPS][TOPO] Checklist: set `server_name` on every server; MQTT requires it as soon as a cluster or gateway block exists.

## Connect over WebSocket
- path: learn/websocket/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/websocket

### Claims
- [CLNT] `nats-server` speaks the NATS protocol over WebSocket on a listener of its own; nothing above the transport changes, only the URL scheme (`ws://` or `wss://` instead of `nats://`).
- [USECASE][CLNT] A browser can't open a TCP socket, so WebSocket is the only way a page reaches NATS at all.
- [USECASE][TOPO] The other case is infrastructure that only speaks HTTP: a cloud HTTP load balancer or CDN routes HTTP only, so exposing NATS behind one means exposing the WebSocket listener; the same applies to a leaf node reaching a hub behind that edge.
- [PATTERN][CLNT] If neither the browser nor the HTTP-only-edge case applies, keep using `nats://`. "It's one less moving part, and a plain TCP connection avoids the WebSocket framing overhead."
- [CLNT][SIZE] Six of the seven Tier 1 clients implement WebSocket (Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Java, Rust, C#/.NET); the C client has no WebSocket transport.
- [CLNT] The `nats` CLI is built on the Go client and accepts `ws://` URLs, making it the quickest way to prove a listener works.

## Your first WebSocket connection
- path: learn/websocket/your-first-websocket-connection.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/websocket/your-first-websocket-connection

### Claims
- [SEC][OPS] The WebSocket listener requires TLS by default; leaving out both a `tls {}` block and `no_tls: true` stops the server at startup: `websocket requires TLS configuration`.
- [SEC][OPS] With `no_tls: true` the server logs `Websocket not configured with TLS. DO NOT USE IN PRODUCTION!`; a WebSocket client sending a bearer token over `ws://` sends it in the clear.
- [OPS][ANTI] There is no default WebSocket port; a `websocket {}` block without `port` or `listen` starts the server with no WebSocket listener, no error, and no warning.
- [CLNT][CORE] The WebSocket listener is another door into the same server; there's no bridging step and no separate subject space, so a `nats://` publisher and a `ws://` subscriber share subjects.
- [CLNT] Python's `nats-core` client keeps its WebSocket transport behind an optional extra: install `nats-core[websocket]`; it needs Python 3.13 or later.
- [CLNT] Subjects, queue groups, request-reply, JetStream, and headers all behave the same over WebSocket because the protocol above the transport is unchanged.
- [SEC] By default the server accepts any origin, which is why a page loaded from disk can connect.
- [CLNT][SIZE] nats.js `wsconnect()` fills in a port you leave out and never picks 4222: `ws://host` -> port 80; `wss://host` -> port 443; bare `host` -> `wss://host:443`; `nats://host:4222` -> `ws://host:4222` (scheme dropped, port kept). "Write the scheme and the port every time."
- [CLNT] NATS uses WebSocket data frames in binary; the server always sends binary and clients are expected to do the same.
- [CLNT] A WebSocket frame is not guaranteed to contain a whole NATS protocol message; one frame can carry part of a `MSG` or several messages, so a client parser must handle partial protocol rather than assuming frame boundaries mean anything.
- [ANTI][CLNT] Pointing a client at the wrong listener: `nats://` to the WebSocket port and `ws://` to 4222 both fail, and neither failure names the real problem.
- [ANTI][OPS] A `websocket {}` block with no port: the server starts and the listener doesn't exist; check the log for `Listening for websocket clients`.
- [ANTI][SEC] A `websocket {}` block with neither `tls {}` nor `no_tls: true` exits at startup.
- [ANTI][CLNT] A client URL without an explicit port: nats.js fills one in and never picks 4222.
- [ANTI][SEC] Shipping `no_tls: true`: it's a development flag, and the `DO NOT USE IN PRODUCTION!` warning is printed once at startup.
- [ANTI][OPS][MIG] A FIPS-140 build made with Go 1.25 or earlier refuses the whole WebSocket listener (and `ws://`/`wss://` leafnode remotes) because the handshake computes SHA-1 over `Sec-WebSocket-Key`; build with Go 1.26 or later.

## Browsers and origins
- path: learn/websocket/browsers-and-origins.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/websocket/browsers-and-origins
- version context: `user_cookie`, `pass_cookie`, `token_cookie` arrived in nats-server 2.11; `jwt_cookie` has always been available

### Claims
- [SEC] A browser attaches an `Origin` header to the WebSocket handshake naming the site the page was served from; `allowed_origins` requires it to match.
- [SEC][SIZE] The origin match is exact on scheme, host, and port and is a string comparison, not name resolution: `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` are different origins; a mismatch yields `403 Forbidden`.
- [SEC][SIZE] A URL with no port means port 80 for `http://` and 443 for `https://`, so `https://ops.acme.example` and `https://ops.acme.example:8443` are different origins; serving on both means listing both.
- [SEC] `allowed_origins` aliases: `origins`, `origin`, `allowed_origin`, `allow_origins`, `allow_origin`.
- [SEC][PATTERN] `same_origin: true` requires the `Origin` to match the host the request arrived on; it suits page and NATS endpoint on one hostname and gets in the way as soon as they differ. Set both options and a request must pass both; leave both unset (default) and any origin is accepted.
- [SEC][MYTH] The origin check is skipped when there's no `Origin` header; the CLI connects regardless because it sends none. "That is not a bug, and it isn't something you can configure away."
- [SEC][PATTERN] `allowed_origins` answers "may this web page open a connection using a visitor's browser?", not "may this connection reach my subjects?"; permissions do the latter and apply to browser and non-browser connections alike. Configure both.
- [SEC][ANTI] A browser has no filesystem; putting an account seed in front-end code hands it to anyone who opens developer tools.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Browser credential approach 1: in operator mode, the browser presents a bearer-user JWT (no nonce signature required); the page holds only a token that expires, never a signing key.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Browser credential approach 2: the HTTP server sets an `HttpOnly` cookie the page's scripts can't read; the browser attaches it to the handshake and the NATS server reads it via `jwt_cookie`.
- [SEC] `jwt_cookie` only works in operator mode; the server refuses to start when the cookie is set and no trusted operator or key is configured.
- [SEC][MIG] Four cookie settings: `jwt_cookie` (user JWT), `user_cookie` (user name), `pass_cookie` (password), `token_cookie` (auth token); the last three arrived in nats-server 2.11.
- [SEC] Each cookie is consulted only when the client didn't supply that field itself; a JWT or user name in `CONNECT` wins over the cookie.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Use the cookie pattern when your web application already has a login; the session cookie is a credential the browser transmits automatically and JavaScript can't exfiltrate.
- [SEC][PATTERN] For a genuinely public, read-only dashboard, `no_auth_user` names a user unauthenticated WebSocket connections bind to; give it subscribe permission on exactly the subjects shown. It doesn't work in operator mode.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Restrict browser credentials with `allowed_connection_types: ["WEBSOCKET"]` so they don't also work from a shell on 4222; a WebSocket leaf node uses `LEAFNODE_WS`.
- [CLNT][SIZE] `compress: true` (alias `compression`) offers the `permessage-deflate` extension, negotiated per connection; clients that don't ask get uncompressed connections at no cost.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Compression trades CPU on both ends for bytes on the wire; "it's a measurement rather than a default — compare CPU and throughput on your own traffic before turning it on broadly."
- [ANTI][SEC] Treating `allowed_origins` as access control: it's evaluated only when an `Origin` header is present, so it constrains browsers and nothing else.
- [ANTI][SEC] Setting `same_origin: true` when the page and the endpoint are on different hostnames fails, which is the normal case behind an ingress.
- [ANTI][SEC] Serving the page from a host you didn't list breaks the handshake for every user with a `403` until the list is updated.
- [ANTI][SEC] Putting a seed or credentials file in front-end code: "Anything the page can read, a visitor can read."
- [ANTI][SEC] Giving the dashboard user publish permission: a display-only page needs subscribe on `orders.>`; publish rights on a credential that ships to browsers is a much larger surface than needed.

## TLS and proxies
- path: learn/websocket/tls-and-proxies.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/websocket/tls-and-proxies
- version context: `ping_interval` in the `websocket {}` block from 2.12

### Claims
- [SEC][OPS] Two ways to get TLS: a certificate on the NATS WebSocket listener, or terminate TLS at an ingress in front; which depends on whether NATS sits behind the same edge as your web traffic.
- [SEC] The `websocket {}` block takes the same `tls {}` fields as every other listener.
- [OPS] Certificate material is the only part of the `websocket {}` block that reloads; `cert_file`/`key_file` changes apply to new connections while existing ones keep the negotiated certificate.
- [OPS][ANTI] Any other `websocket {}` change on reload (`verify_and_map`, `pinned_certs`, `allowed_origins`, timeouts) is rejected, and a rejected field aborts the entire reload, including otherwise-valid changes in the same edit.
- [SEC][PATTERN] The more common shape behind an existing edge: the ingress holds the certificate and the NATS listener runs plaintext (`no_tls: true`) on an internal network.
- [SEC][SIZE] `no_tls: true` is correct only when the proxy-to-server hop is a network you trust: a private subnet, a service mesh, or the same host.
- [TOPO][CLNT] `advertise` is what the server tells clients about itself; without it a server behind NAT or a proxy hands out the address it sees locally, which clients can't reach.
- [SEC][MYTH] `no_tls` and the client's URL scheme are separate questions; the client uses `wss://` because the proxy presents a certificate, while the listener's TLS is decided by its own config.
- [OPS] A proxy must pass the `Upgrade` and `Connection` headers through (HTTP/1.1); a proxy that strips them fails silently as a connection that never establishes.
- [OPS][SIZE] A NATS connection is idle between messages; a proxy that closes idle connections after 60 seconds will close a working subscription. Set the proxy idle timeout longer than the server's WebSocket ping interval (`ping_interval` in `websocket {}` from 2.12, server-wide ping interval before).
- [OPS][TOPO] If NATS is published under a path prefix, the prefix must appear in the client URL; for leaf nodes the server appends `/leafnode`, so a `location /nats` rule must also match `/nats/leafnode`.
- [OPS][SIZE] `handshake_timeout` bounds reading the request, the TLS handshake, and writing the response; a value tuned on a laptop can reject real clients behind a slow proxy under load.
- [SEC] `headers` adds fixed HTTP headers to the upgrade response, e.g. `Strict-Transport-Security` when no proxy is in front to add it.
- [ANTI][OPS] A proxy that drops `Upgrade` and `Connection`: the client reports a connection error, not a protocol error; if `ws://` works directly and fails through the proxy, check this first.
- [ANTI][OPS] A proxy idle timeout shorter than the ping interval: connections drop on a timer with no error on either side. "The pattern to look for is disconnects at a suspiciously round interval."
- [ANTI][SEC] `no_tls: true` on a hop that isn't private: correct behind a terminating proxy on a trusted network and wrong the moment traffic crosses anything else; there's no warning distinguishing the two.
- [ANTI][TOPO] Forgetting `advertise` behind NAT: connections succeed and then fail on a later reconnect to an unreachable advertised URL.
- [ANTI][SEC] Expecting `wss://` to configure the server: the client scheme and the server `tls {}` block are set independently, and a mismatch fails at the handshake.

## Leaf nodes over WebSocket
- path: learn/websocket/leaf-nodes-over-websocket.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/websocket/leaf-nodes-over-websocket

### Claims
- [TOPO] A leaf node can dial its hub over WebSocket instead of the leafnode port; account, subject interest, and link-down behaviour are unchanged, only the transport differs.
- [TOPO][USECASE] The reason is usually on the hub side: the leafnode port isn't published through an HTTPS ingress but the WebSocket listener is.
- [TOPO] Leaf nodes and browser clients share the WebSocket listener; the upgrade path tells them apart (`/leafnode` for a leaf, `/` for a client). The server appends `/leafnode` itself; you never write it.
- [TOPO][OPS] The hub needs both blocks: `leafnodes { port: ... }` is the switch that makes the server accept leaf nodes at all, and `websocket {}` is the door they arrive through. Without a `leafnodes` block (or with an empty one) the WebSocket listener accepts the connection and then closes it.
- [TOPO][SEC] The leafnode port (7422) is a real listener open to whatever can reach it even when no WebSocket leaf uses it; restrict it to the peers that need it.
- [TOPO] On the branch side the only change from a leafnode-port remote is the URL: `wss://` scheme and port 443.
- [SEC][TOPO] Either the `wss://` scheme or a `tls {}` block on the remote turns TLS on; you don't need both. `ws://` alone against a TLS hub fails; `ws://` with `tls {}` connects; `wss://` alone connects if the hub certificate is publicly trusted.
- [SEC] A `tls {}` block has two jobs: turning TLS on where the scheme hasn't, and supplying what verification needs (a CA for an untrusted certificate, or a client certificate when the hub verifies leaves). With a public-CA certificate no `tls {}` block is needed.
- [SEC][MYTH] The URL scheme doesn't tell you whether a link is encrypted: `ws://` with a `tls {}` block beside it is a TLS connection. "If you want that to be obvious to whoever reads the config next, write `wss://` and let the scheme say so."
- [TOPO][ANTI] Every URL in a single remote must use the same kind of scheme; mixing `wss://` and `nats://` stops the server at startup (`cannot have a mix of websocket and non-websocket urls`). You can't list the ingress and a direct leafnode port as alternatives.
- [TOPO][SIZE][ANTI] A leafnode URL without a port gets `:7422` appended whatever its scheme, so `wss://nats.acme.example` quietly dials the leafnode port and fails; write the port explicitly on every remote URL.
- [TOPO][CLNT] `ws_compression` (alias `websocket_compression`) asks the hub to negotiate compression on the link with the same CPU-versus-bytes trade as for clients; measure rather than assume.
- [TOPO][CLNT] `ws_no_masking` (alias `websocket_no_masking`) asks the hub to accept unmasked frames; masking exists to stop browsers poisoning intermediary caches, a concern that doesn't apply to server-to-server links. Both are requests the hub may decline, and the link works either way.
- [SEC][TOPO] The connection type for a leaf arriving over WebSocket is `LEAFNODE_WS`, not `LEAFNODE`; granting `LEAFNODE` refuses the branch.
- [ANTI][SEC] Reading the scheme as the encryption status: neither the scheme nor the block alone tells you what a link is doing; check both.
- [ANTI][TOPO] Mixing schemes in one `urls` list refuses to start.
- [ANTI][TOPO] Pointing the remote at the leafnode port: 7422 speaks the leafnode protocol directly and will not complete a WebSocket handshake.
- [ANTI][SEC] Granting `LEAFNODE` to a WebSocket leaf: the value has to match the transport.
- [ANTI][OPS] A path-routing proxy that doesn't forward `/leafnode`: route `/` or give the remote the proxy's prefix so the path becomes `/nats/leafnode`.
- [ANTI][TOPO] Reaching a hub that isn't running a WebSocket listener: a hub with only a leafnode port has nothing for a `wss://` remote to connect to.

## Where to go next (WebSocket)
- path: learn/websocket/where-next.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn/websocket/where-next

### Claims
- [CLNT] A WebSocket connection is a NATS connection: same clients, subjects, queue groups, request-reply, and JetStream; the URL scheme is most of the difference.
- [SEC] A browser is a different security situation, not a different NATS; origin checking and cookie settings address it, but neither replaces authorization, "which is still what protects the port."
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Reaching for WebSocket is often nothing to do with browsers: where an HTTP ingress or load balancer is the only path into the network, the WebSocket listener is what gets published, and a leaf node uses it exactly as a client does.
- [CLNT] Reconnection and drain behave the same over WebSocket as over TCP.
- [OPS] Checklist: set `port` or `listen` in `websocket {}`; there is no default.
- [OPS] Checklist: confirm `Listening for websocket clients` appears in the log before debugging the client.
- [OPS][CLNT] Checklist: point WebSocket clients at the WebSocket port and everything else at the client port.
- [OPS][CLNT] Checklist: give every client URL an explicit port; nats.js fills in 443 for a bare host and 80 for `ws://` without one.
- [OPS][MIG] Checklist: a FIPS-140 build must be built with Go 1.26 or later.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: set `allowed_origins` to the exact scheme, host, and port, or `same_origin: true` when page and endpoint share one hostname.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: treat origin checking as protection against other web pages, not access control; it's skipped when no `Origin` header is present.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: keep seeds and credentials files out of front-end code; use a bearer JWT or an `HttpOnly` cookie.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: give the browser user subscribe permission on the subjects it displays and no publish rights it doesn't need.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: restrict browser credentials with `allowed_connection_types: ["WEBSOCKET"]`.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: use `no_tls: true` only behind a TLS-terminating proxy on a trusted network.
- [OPS] Checklist: make the proxy forward `Upgrade` and `Connection`.
- [OPS][SIZE] Checklist: set the proxy's idle timeout longer than the server's WebSocket ping interval.
- [OPS][TOPO] Checklist: set `advertise` behind NAT or a proxy.
- [OPS][SIZE] Checklist: size `handshake_timeout` against the proxy's latency under load.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: configure TLS on the listener or terminate at the proxy; `wss://` in a client URL only says what the client will do.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: write `wss://` when the link is encrypted; `ws://` beside a `tls {}` block is encrypted too.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: add a `tls {}` block with `ca_file` only when the hub's certificate isn't publicly trusted.
- [OPS][TOPO] Checklist: keep every URL in a remote on the same kind of scheme.
- [OPS][TOPO] Checklist: point the remote at the hub's WebSocket listener, not the leafnode port.
- [OPS][TOPO][SEC] Checklist: keep a `leafnodes { port: ... }` block on the hub even when every leaf arrives over WebSocket, and firewall that port like any other.
- [OPS][TOPO] Checklist: give the hub a `websocket {}` listener as well.
- [OPS][SEC] Checklist: grant `LEAFNODE_WS`, not `LEAFNODE`, to a leaf that arrives over WebSocket.
- [OPS][TOPO] Checklist: write an explicit port on every leafnode remote URL; without one the server appends `:7422`.
- [OPS] Checklist: if a proxy routes on path, make sure it forwards `/leafnode`.

## Learn
- path: learn/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/learn

### Claims
- [PATTERN] The docs have three layers: Concepts (short primers, read first if new), Learn deep dives (one subsystem each, one running scenario, at most two new concepts per page), and Reference (exhaustive, versioned catalog, not a teaching resource).
- [CORE][PATTERN] Core NATS is the foundation every other chapter builds on; if you're new to NATS start there, and go straight to JetStream if you're here for persistence.
- [KV] Key-Value Store: buckets, watches, history and revisions, TTLs, and how KV sits on top of a stream.
- [OBJ] Object Store: chunked blobs over JetStream, with metadata, links, and listing.
- [OPS] Backup & Recovery: stream snapshots, mirrors for disaster recovery, a recovery runbook, and backing up identity.
- [TOPO] Clustering & Replication covers the mechanism under a cluster: routes and gossip, RAFT and leaders, `R=3` quorum, placement, and peer management.

## What is NATS?
- path: docs/concepts/what-is-nats.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/concepts/what-is-nats

### Claims
- [CORE] NATS is an open source messaging system; applications connect to a server and exchange messages by subject without knowing each other's network addresses.
- [CORE][SIZE] NATS optimizes for a small single binary, low latency at high message rates, and secure defaults; it runs from one server on a laptop up to clusters spanning regions.
- [CORE] Core components: the NATS server (broker that routes messages), publishers, subscribers, and subjects (named channels).
- [TOPO][OPS] Clustering, JetStream, leaf nodes, MQTT, and WebSocket are all configuration on the same single `nats-server` process.
- [CLNT] Official Tier 1 clients: Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Java, Rust, C#/.NET, and C. Tier 2 clients (may lag on new server features): Zig, Swift, Ruby, Elixir.
- [CLNT] Orbit is optional per-language extension libraries with higher-level utilities and experimental features built on top of the core client.
- [SIZE] Performance: millions of messages per second, sub-millisecond latency, small memory footprint (typically ~15MB).
- [CORE][PATTERN] Location transparency: applications don't need to know where other services are; NATS handles service discovery, load balancing, and fault tolerance.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Accounts isolate messaging domains within one server or cluster, supporting secure multi-tenant deployments, team isolation, and SaaS platforms.
- [USECASE] Use cases: agentic AI (agent-to-agent communication, event streams for LLM inference, multi-region GPU inference routing with scale-to-zero), real-time data streaming (IoT telemetry, market data, log/metrics aggregation), microservices (service mesh data plane, event-driven, CQRS/event sourcing), edge computing (edge-to-cloud, intermittent networks, constrained environments), command and control (RPC, config management, orchestration).

## Welcome to NATS
- path: docs/concepts/intro.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/concepts/intro

### Claims
- [USECASE] NATS is described as "a simple, secure and high-performance open source messaging system for cloud native applications, IoT messaging, and microservices architectures."

## Subjects
- path: docs/concepts/subjects.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/concepts/subjects

### Claims
- [SUBJ][CORE] NATS is a subject-based messaging system: publishers and subscribers communicate through named channels, giving a location-transparent, interest-based pattern that routes across distributed servers.
- [SUBJ] Subjects are case-sensitive and can contain any UTF-8 characters except whitespace, tabs, and line breaks.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Good practice is alphanumeric characters plus `-` and `_` for readability.
- [SUBJ] The `.` character creates a subject hierarchy for logical grouping.
- [SUBJ] Publishers always send to a fully specified subject; only subscribers use wildcards.
- [SUBJ] `*` matches exactly one token; `>` matches one or more tokens and can only appear at the end of a subject.
- [SUBJ] Reserved characters: `.` (hierarchy, cannot be part of a token), `*` and `>` (wildcards, cannot be in subject names), whitespace (not allowed).
- [SUBJ] Subjects starting with `$` are reserved for system use: `$SYS` (system), `$JS` (JetStream API), `$KV` (Key-Value), `$O` (Object Store), `$SRV` (Service API); `_INBOX` is for auto-generated reply subjects.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Hierarchy design: start general and get specific (`app.region.service.entity.action`, e.g. `myapp.us-east.users.profile.update`).
- [SUBJ][SIZE][PATTERN] Keep subjects reasonable: limit to ~16 tokens and under 256 characters total.
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Establish naming conventions early and stick to them; design hierarchies that work well with wildcard subscriptions.
- [SUBJ][SIZE] The subject interest graph is in-memory and dynamic: NATS builds a routing table only for subjects with active subscribers, kept entirely in RAM.
- [SUBJ][SIZE] Subjects are essentially free: creating new subjects has virtually no overhead and NATS handles millions of unique subjects.
- [SUBJ][SIZE] Wildcard subscriptions use efficient trie-based matching.
- [SUBJ][SEC][PATTERN] Well-designed hierarchies enable fine-grained access control per user/account, efficient JetStream stream filtering, clean import/export between accounts, and logical organization for monitoring.
- [SUBJ][TOPO] Subscriptions automatically propagate across the cluster; messages route to all interested subscribers regardless of location with no routing configuration.
- [SUBJ][OPS][PATTERN] The `>` wildcard enables wire taps and monitoring of everything under a prefix.

## Publish-Subscribe
- path: docs/concepts/pub-sub-basics.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/concepts/pub-sub-basics

### Claims
- [CORE] A publisher sends a message to a subject and every subscriber listening on that subject gets a copy; this is the foundation everything else builds on.
- [CORE] Publishers don't know about subscribers and subscribers don't know about publishers; services can be added, removed, or restarted without coordinating.
- [CORE] Publishers don't wait for acknowledgments (fire-and-forget); if no subscribers exist, the message is simply discarded.
- [CORE][USECASE][PATTERN] Pub/sub is ideal when multiple services need to react to the same event: event broadcasting, data distribution, fan-out notifications, audit logging.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Fan-out is one publisher to multiple subscribers (event notification); fan-in is multiple publishers to one subscriber (aggregation).
- [CORE][SIZE] Core NATS is at-most-once delivery without persistence; for guaranteed delivery use JetStream.
- [CORE] Only subscribers connected when the message is published receive it; messages aren't stored for later.
- [CORE] Every subscriber gets a copy; subscribing doesn't consume or remove messages.
- [SIZE][CORE] NATS has a default max message size of 1MB (configurable). "For large data, consider using object stores or passing references."
- [SIZE][PATTERN] NATS handles millions of subscriptions efficiently; use wildcards to reduce subscription overhead when possible.

## Request-Reply
- path: docs/concepts/request-reply.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/concepts/request-reply

### Claims
- [CORE] Request-reply brings synchronous, RPC-style interaction on top of pub/sub: the client creates a unique reply subject (inbox), subscribes to it, publishes the request with the reply subject, and the service publishes the response to it.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Timeouts are crucial in request-reply to prevent indefinite waiting; all clients support configurable timeouts.
- [CORE][PATTERN] With multiple responders and no queue group, all services receive the request and all can respond (scatter-gather), useful for gathering data from multiple sources, aggregating results, or querying replicas for consensus.
- [CORE][PATTERN] With queue groups, only one service receives the request and responds, giving automatic load distribution, horizontal scalability, and built-in failover.
- [CORE][CLNT] By default `request()` returns the first response and drops the rest; to gather every response, subscribe to a reply inbox directly and read until a timeout.
- [CORE] When no subscribers exist for the request subject, the server returns a "no responders" error immediately.
- [CORE] Headers are supported in request-reply for metadata exchange.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Timeout strategy: too short may miss valid responses, too long blocks unnecessarily; add buffer for network round-trip; implement retry logic for transient failures.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Error handling: always handle timeouts, check for no responders, validate responses before processing.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Service design: idempotent operations (requests might be retried), lightweight processing (long operations should be async), health checks, graceful shutdown (drain pending requests).
- [CORE][CLNT][PATTERN] Performance: reuse connections for multiple requests; modern clients reuse inbox subjects; batch related requests when possible.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Choose request-reply for synchronous communication, service discovery via no-responders detection, load balancing with queue groups, and RPC-style APIs. Use pub/sub for fire-and-forget, multiple consumers, event streaming, and decoupled systems.

## Queue Groups
- path: docs/concepts/queue-groups.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/concepts/queue-groups

### Claims
- [CORE] When subscribers share a queue name, NATS delivers each message to only one randomly chosen member of that group.
- [CORE] A lone subscriber in a queue group receives all messages; with multiple members NATS randomly selects one per message; distribution adjusts automatically as members join and leave.
- [CORE] The queue name is application-defined, not server-configured.
- [CORE][MYTH] Selection is random per message and does not account for how busy a member is.
- [CORE][CLNT] A member stops receiving only when its subscription or connection goes away, including when the server disconnects it as a slow consumer.
- [CORE][USECASE] Common uses: background job processing, API request handling across service instances, event processing pipelines, batch operations.
- [CORE][SIZE] When a worker leaves, NATS stops routing to it within milliseconds.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Queue groups enable horizontally scalable services without a service mesh or API gateway; service code needs no knowledge of other instances, leader election, or coordination.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Queue groups coexist with regular subscribers on the same subject. "Use queue groups for operational work that needs to happen exactly once, and regular subscribers for observational tasks (audit logging, monitoring, analytics)."
- [CORE][TOPO] In super-clusters queue groups exhibit geo-affinity: messages go to workers in the same cluster/region as the publisher, with automatic failover to other regions if no local workers are available, with no configuration.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Queue group naming follows subject-like conventions: service-based (`api.auth.workers`), environment-based (`prod.order-processors`), version-based (`service.v1.workers`).
- [CORE][ANTI][STRM] Core queue groups never redeliver: a message sent to a worker that crashes mid-processing is lost. For redelivery and durability, use JetStream worker pools.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Duplicates come only from publisher retries, so make processing idempotent if the publisher may resend.
- [CORE][PATTERN] Worker design: drain messages before stopping, handle failed messages, monitor worker health.
- [OPS][PATTERN] Scaling: start small, monitor metrics (queue depth with JetStream, processing time), scale based on load, then automate.

## JetStream
- path: docs/concepts/jetstream.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/concepts/jetstream

### Claims
- [STRM][CORE] Core NATS delivers only to subscribers connected at publication (at most once, never replayed); JetStream adds a persistence layer giving at-least-once delivery, with messages surviving restarts and replayable.
- [STRM][PATTERN] JetStream extends decoupling to time: publisher and subscriber no longer need to be online at the same moment.
- [STRM][CONS] Three pieces: a stream (server-side store bound to one or more subjects), a consumer (server-side stateful view tracking client progress), and a client (application that receives and acknowledges messages).
- [CONS] A consumer can be shared by multiple clients to divide the work; each acknowledgment advances the consumer's position.
- [STRM] A stream is bound to one or more subject patterns; a matching publish is appended and assigned a sequence number. Streams are configurable for storage (memory or disk), retention (limits or consumer acks), replication, and more.
- [CONS] Multiple consumers can read the same stream independently, each with its own position, maintained by the server.
- [CONS] If a message isn't acknowledged in time, the server redelivers it, which is what gives at-least-once delivery.
- [CONS] A consumer can start from the beginning of the stream, the latest message, a specific sequence number, or a specific time.
- [KV][OBJ] Higher-level abstractions on streams and consumers: Key Value Store (replication and durability built in) and Object Store (objects larger than a single message, split into chunks, with per-object metadata).

## Security
- path: docs/concepts/security.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/concepts/security

### Claims
- [SEC] NATS security rests on three independent pillars: authentication, authorization, and encryption.
- [SEC] NATS is multi-tenant by design: each user belongs to an account, a self-contained tenant with its own isolated subject space, users, and permissions; unrelated tenants can use the same subject names without collision.
- [SEC] Cross-account communication is possible but requires explicit configuration.
- [SEC][ANTI] NATS doesn't require authentication by default, so production deployments should always configure one of: config-based auth, decentralized auth (operator mode), or auth callouts.
- [SEC] Config-based authentication defines accounts, users, and credentials in the server config; credential types include username/password, token, NKeys, and TLS client certificates; simplest for development and smaller deployments.
- [SEC] Operator mode is a hierarchical trust chain: an operator signs accounts, each account signs its own users; credentials are JWTs signed with NKey (Ed25519) keypairs; the server needs only the operator's public key, with no server-side user list.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Operator mode scales to multi-tenant or large deployments because accounts issue and revoke their own users independently; you choose a resolver model for the server to locate account information.
- [SEC][PATTERN] Auth callouts delegate the authentication decision to an application-defined NATS service returning a signed JWT; useful for external identity providers (OIDC, LDAP) or custom logic.
- [SEC][SUBJ] Authorization is a subject-based permissions model: which subjects a user can publish to, subscribe to, or both, with the same wildcards as subjects; permissions are per user, in config or embedded in the user's JWT.
- [SEC] The presence of an allow list closes off everything else; deny takes precedence over allow.
- [SEC][TOPO] Each connection type can have TLS configured independently: client-server, server-server routes, leaf nodes, and gateways; with certificate pinning, CA pools, custom cipher suites, and mTLS.
- [SEC] mTLS proves the client holds a certificate signed by a trusted CA; `verify_and_map` maps the certificate's SAN or DN to a configured user, tying encryption into authentication.
- [SEC][STRM] JetStream streams can be encrypted on disk using AES or ChaCha20-Poly1305, protecting persisted data against attackers with filesystem or physical access.

## Topologies
- path: docs/concepts/topologies.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/concepts/topologies

### Claims
- [TOPO][PATTERN] NATS scales by composing servers; the same binary and client APIs work across every shape, so you change the deployment topology, not your application.
- [TOPO][USECASE] Use a single server for local development and demos, embedded use inside another application, small services where one node is enough, and quick experiments.
- [TOPO] A cluster is a group of servers connected by routes in a full mesh; clients connect to any server, messages flow across routes, and clients reconnect to another server if one goes down.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Reach for a cluster for high availability, more throughput than one server, production deployments, rolling upgrades without downtime, and JetStream replication.
- [TOPO] A super-cluster connects multiple clusters with gateways; each cluster operates independently (usually its own region or cloud), and gateways carry only traffic that has interest on the other side.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Super-clusters fit multi-region or multi-cloud deployments and global services with regional locality; queue groups prefer local workers automatically (geo-affinity).
- [TOPO] A leaf node initiates an outbound connection to a remote NATS system and bridges subject interest; because the connection is from the leaf side, it can run anywhere with outbound access. Clients on the leaf see a regular NATS server.
- [TOPO][STRM] JetStream streams can be mirrored or sourced across a leaf link for local copies of data.
- [TOPO][USECASE] Leaf nodes suit edge and IoT deployments, on-prem services bridging to a cloud cluster, hub-and-spoke architectures, and multi-tenant isolation where each tenant runs its own leaf.
- [TOPO][SEC] The hub sees one leaf connection rather than the individual clients, which the leaf authenticates on its own; the leaf still bridges subject interest into the account it binds to, so the subject namespace is shared unless you bind each leaf to its own account.
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Real deployments combine all shapes: clusters across regions via gateways, each fanning out to leaf nodes at edge sites, with the same client code everywhere.

## The NATS Ecosystem
- path: docs/concepts/ecosystem.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/concepts/ecosystem

### Claims
- [OPS] Clustering, JetStream, leaf nodes, MQTT, and WebSocket are enabled through configuration on the same `nats-server`; there are no separate components to install.
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Clients come in three tiers: Tier 1 (Synadia-maintained, track new server features at release), Tier 2 (Synadia-maintained, may lag), community (third-party). "If a tier 1 client is available for your language, prefer it."
- [CLNT] Tier 1: Go (`nats.go`, reference implementation), JavaScript/TypeScript (`nats.js`, supersedes archived `nats.node`/`nats.deno`/`nats.ws`/`nats.ts`), Python (`nats.py`, asyncio), Java (`nats.java`), Rust (`async-nats`), C#/.NET (`nats.net`, .NET 6+), C (`nats.c`, embedded and FFI).
- [CLNT] Tier 2: Zig, Swift, Ruby (`nats-pure.rb` preferred; `nats.rb` legacy EventMachine-based), Elixir (`nats.ex`, replaces archived `elixir-nats`).
- [CLNT] Community clients exist for Crystal, Dart, Kotlin, PHP; feature coverage and maintenance vary; the docs don't cover them.
- [CLNT] Orbit repos under `synadia-io` contain optional higher-level utilities and experimental features per tier 1 client: extra JetStream helpers (request-many, batch publish, scheduled messages), partitioned consumer groups, encoded KV/KV codecs, distributed counters, retry/chaos utilities. Successful patterns may graduate into the core client.
- [OPS] `nsc` is a standalone CLI for operators, accounts, and users; an alternative to `nats auth`, reads the same on-disk store, and covers operations `nats auth` doesn't yet.
- [OPS] Kubernetes tooling: official Helm charts (`k8s`) and NACK controllers/CRDs for declarative streams, consumers, and KV/Object stores.
- [OPS] Observability: `prometheus-nats-exporter` (varz, connz, routez, JetStream stats) and `nats-surveyor` (cluster-wide aggregation), which pair for full-cluster observability.
- [OPS] `jsm.go` is the canonical source of JetStream API JSON schemas used by tooling and the reference docs.
- [OPS] Bridges and integrations: Kafka bridge, Spark connector, Flink connector, Vert.x client, Terraform provider for JetStream resources.

## Getting Started
- path: docs/concepts/getting-started/index.md
- url: https://docs.nats.io/concepts/getting-started

### Claims
- [SIZE][OPS] The default NATS client port is 4222 and the HTTP monitoring port is 8222.
- [OPS] `nats-server -m 8222` enables monitoring; `nats-server -js` enables JetStream persistence.
- [CLNT] Official clients: Go, Java, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Rust, C, .NET.

### Learn / Concepts pages read

- Concepts pages: 11 (docs/concepts/*.md + getting-started/index.md)
- Total docs in this dump: 49 + 123 + 11 = 183

### Claim totals
- NBE: 157 + 190 = 347
- Learn + Concepts: 430 + 454 + 536 + 595 = 2,015
- Total claims: 2,362
- Every bolded `## Pitfalls` sentence was captured as an [ANTI] claim and every `## Production checklist` checkbox as a claim (prefixed "Pitfall:" / "Checklist:" in the secops and infra parts).

### 15 most valuable design claims
1. [STRM][TOPO][SIZE] R=3 is the production floor and R=5 the maximum; even counts buy nothing (R=2 blocks writes on one loss, R=4 tolerates one loss like R=3). Replicas are a durability knob, not throughput: every write funnels through one leader. (learn/clustering/replication-and-r3, learn/topologies/jetstream-in-a-cluster)
2. [STRM][OPS][SIZE] A `PubAck` proves quorum, not disk sync: `sync_interval` defaults to 2 minutes. `sync_interval: always` closes the window at cluster-wide cost, so put only the streams that need it on a separate tagged cluster via placement. (learn/clustering/replication-and-r3)
3. [STRM][PATTERN][ANTI] `PubAck` is the only proof of storage; a publish timeout means "no confirmation", not "no write". Every retryable publish needs a stable `Nats-Msg-Id`, and the dedup window is only 2 minutes by default, so a later retry double-stores. (learn/jetstream/publishing, advanced-publishing)
4. [CONS][ANTI] AckPolicy `all` without MaxAckPending=1 is silent data loss (acking 10 retires a failed 7 awaiting redelivery); strict ordering needs MaxAckPending=1; MaxDeliver has no dead-letter queue, only the once-published MAX_DELIVERIES advisory. (learn/jetstream/acknowledgment, learn/monitoring/advisories-and-events)
5. [STRM][CONS][ANTI] Interest and work-queue retention are additive to limits: with `max-msgs=1` + discard-old a new message deletes the prior one regardless of consumption. Interest exists by consumer existence, not consumption; a late consumer cannot retroactively hold interest; Term releases interest like Ack. (NBE interest-stream, workqueue-stream)
6. [STRM][CONS] Work-queue streams allow at most one consumer with interest per subject; multiple consumers need disjoint filter subjects, unlike limits/interest streams where overlap is fine. (NBE workqueue-stream, learn/jetstream/worker-pool)
7. [TOPO][STRM][SIZE] The JetStream meta layer is one Raft group across the whole supercluster, so total server count must be odd: use at least three clusters or a JetStream-disabled arbiter cluster gatewayed to both. Stream replicas never cross gateways, so one node per cluster caps you at R1. (NBE supercluster-jetstream, supercluster-arbiter)
8. [TOPO][PATTERN] Routes assume peers are close (full mesh); gateways join far-apart clusters and forward only on remote interest; leaf nodes are for egress-only sites with `remotes` on the leaf side. Stacking shapes adds reach, not boundaries; only a leaf bound to its own account partitions the address space. (learn/topologies/super-clusters, leaf-nodes, putting-it-together)
9. [OPS][MIG][SIZE] Rolling upgrade order: non-leaders first, meta-leader last, gated on each node returning `current`; an undrained meta-leader restart stalls all stream/consumer ops ~5-10 s versus ~1 s with lame-duck handoff (`lame_duck_duration` default 2m, min 30s; Helm 30s + `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` 60s, PDB `minAvailable: 2`). (learn/deployment/rolling-upgrades)
10. [OPS][MYTH][STRM] R3 is availability, not a backup, and a mirror is not a backup: a bad write replicates to every replica and every mirror. Mirror = site failure (short RTO), snapshot = bad data (recovery point); you need both. A DR mirror belongs in its own JetStream domain or independent cluster, never a meta group spanning both sites. (learn/backup-recovery/*)
11. [SEC][ANTI][MYTH] Permission traps: any `allow` list denies everything else including `$JS.API.>`; `publish: []` is NOT a lockdown (parses as unrestricted); deny beats allow; a wildcard subscription overlapping a deny is silently filtered with no error; a subscribe deny silently breaks request-reply and adding `allow: ["_INBOX.>"]` next to it doesn't help. (learn/security/authorization)
12. [SEC][PATTERN] Accounts are the isolation boundary; inside one account any user allowed `_INBOX.>` can read every other user's replies. Per-user isolation needs a client-side inbox prefix (`_INBOX_<user>`) plus `sub.allow` restricted to that prefix. (NBE private-inbox, private-inbox-jwt)
13. [SEC][PATTERN] Auth mode selection: static user list = centralized config (right for one server and a handful of users, treat as buying time); a trust chain you control = operator mode with scoped signing keys (user JWT carries empty perms; every account change is invisible until `account push`); verdict from a system NATS doesn't own = auth callout, which needs a dedicated AUTH account and a sentinel credential. (learn/security/auth-callout, decentralized-auth; NBE callout-decentralized)
14. [CLNT][SIZE][PATTERN] Client resilience numbers: set `MaxReconnect=-1` (defaults 60 Go/Java/Python, 10 JS); reconnect buffer 8 MB Go/Java, 2 MB Python and flush is not delivery; stale-link detection ~6 min at defaults; request timeout = 2-3x responder p99, cap retries ~5 with jitter, exponential backoff on no-responders, key retries by business ID. (learn/resilient-clients/*)
15. [OPS][CONS][PATTERN] Monitor `lag = last_seq - delivered.stream_seq` (= `num_pending`) separately from in-flight (`num_ack_pending`): rising in-flight = stuck handler, rising lag = not enough handlers, lag rising with `num_waiting`=0 and `delivered` stalled = crashed pool. `/healthz?js-enabled-only=true` returns 200 with no quorum; use `?js-meta-only=true`. (learn/monitoring/jetstream-health, monitoring-endpoints)

(EJJ2SG-cKyM) the presenter's on-air definitions of work-queue and interest retention are reversed relative to his later Episode 11; the claim text flags this.
