## Achieve MASSIVE Scale with NATS Clustering | Rethink Connectivity Episode 4
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=srARy0m9SdI
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz | date: unknown (Rethink Connectivity ep 4, ~2022) | duration: 13:52
- version context: 2.8/2.9 era (uses `nats server list`, cluster gossip, pre-2.10 tooling)

### Claims
- [CORE][SUBJ] NATS is location independent: clients address each other only by subject and never need the peer's address or DNS name; the server mediates message flow. "we just use subjects... they just connect to the NATS server and the server is the one that mediates all those messages" (~00:30)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Clustering is the answer when you need more scalability or redundancy than a single server gives; a super cluster is a "cluster of clusters" that can live in different regions and clouds. "clusters of clusters called super clusters... these clusters can live in different locations and regions and clouds" (~01:40)
- [OPS][SEC] To observe cluster state you need a user in the built-in `$SYS` system account, which has extended admin privileges and exposes server metrics via system events. "a special account called dollar sign sys and this account already has extended admin privileges so you can get all of the metrics" (~03:06)
- [SEC][ANTI] Username/password in the config file is the simplest but least secure auth flow because the credentials sit in plain text. "this one isn't the most secure because the username and password is in plain text on your config file" (~03:40)
- [OPS] The `nats server list` command (run with a $SYS user) shows each server's IP, version, whether JetStream is enabled and its connection count; the episode uses it inside `watch` sorted by name to monitor the cluster. "it will give us a list of the actual server, his ip address, version, whether it's using JetStream, its number of connections" (~05:50)
- [OPS] Set an explicit short server `name` in the config; otherwise the generated server name is long. "this server name is really long, if we wanted to change it... we could say name equals north america one" (~05:40)
- [TOPO][OPS] A cluster is configured with a `cluster` block containing a cluster name, a dedicated cluster port (6222 by convention, any free port works) and a `routes` list acting as seed servers. "we give this cluster a connection port which is 6222... routes, this is kind of like your list of seed servers" (~08:40)
- [TOPO] Routes use a gossip protocol: a server only needs to reach one seed server; it then learns about all its neighbours and the full mesh forms automatically. "once one of these servers connects to the seed server it will gossip about all of its neighbors and everything will get connected... automatically" (~09:30)
- [CLNT][OPS] Give clients (and the CLI context) the URLs of all cluster servers; the client randomly picks one and moves on if a server is offline, which spreads connections evenly across the cluster. "NATS will be smart about randomly selecting one of these... if it doesn't detect that a server is online it will move on to another one" (~11:20)
- [CLNT][TOPO] When a cluster server is killed, its client connections automatically fail over to the remaining servers and traffic continues. "I can kill one of these servers... and it will automatically move those connections over to either na1 or na3 and everything still works" (~12:50)
- [OPS] `nats bench` with subscribers plus a periodic `nats pub` is a quick way to simulate load and watch connection distribution across a cluster. "nats bench, I'm going to create 10 subscribers to this hello subject so we can actually create some simulation" (~12:20)

## How to build a NATS Supercluster | Rethink Connectivity Episode 5
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6O_sNSJ2p70
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz | date: unknown (Rethink Connectivity ep 5, ~2022) | duration: 16:09
- version context: 2.8/2.9 era (gateways, JetStream R3 KV, config-file accounts)

### Claims
- [TOPO] A cluster behaves as one logical system: a client connected to any node talks transparently to clients on other nodes, while the nodes give redundancy. "it operates as one singular system like it's one server that you connect to but in fact we have the redundancy of multiple nodes" (~00:40)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Nodes of a single cluster are assumed to live in the same data center or availability zone; a super cluster spans geographies and even different public clouds (e.g. GCP, AWS, Azure mixed). "nodes in a single cluster are kind of assumed that they live in the same data center or the same availability zone... a super cluster spans not only different geographies but different public clouds" (~01:10)
- [TOPO][OPS] Routes gossip so one seed route suffices to form a mesh, but in practice you should list two or three seed servers (and likewise for gateways) so that losing the single seed does not strand new nodes. "in practice you're probably going to want to maybe double or triple up for these connections... so if na1 goes down you're not out of luck" (~02:40)
- [STRM][SIZE] Replicated JetStream assets (R3, even R5) survive node loss; the replica count is a trade-off against the performance characteristics you want. "you can make an R3 or even an R5 and it's just going to be dependent on your performance characteristics that you want for your system" (~03:50)
- [SEC][STRM] The system account should not have JetStream enabled; create a separate account for a business use case and set `jetstream: enabled` on that account. "we don't want to enable JetStream here, in fact we want to create an account that can utilize JetStream for maybe a particular business case" (~04:20)
- [SEC][ANTI] Defining accounts and users inline in the server config is not ideal; decentralized JWT auth is the recommended construct for secure clusters and super clusters. "we're defining all of our accounts and all of our users inside of our server config and this might not be ideal" (~04:50)
- [STRM][OPS] Enabling JetStream on a cluster only requires the `jetstream` directive (no config needed) on each server plus a JetStream-enabled account. "you edit the config to enable JetStream and then you work with a JetStream enabled account" (~07:40)
- [KV][STRM] A KV bucket created without replicas lives on one node (the leader) and all access is served from that node; recreate with `--replicas 3` to place a replica on each node. "any time I talk to this cluster about this kv store it's actually going to be polling from north america 2... if I wanted redundancy here I would use what are called replicas" (~07:00)
- [TOPO][OPS] Use one config file per cluster: most content is shared, but cluster name, cluster seed routes and gateway name differ. "split this into multiple configurations one for each cluster... most of the stuff will be the same but some of it will have to change" (~08:30)
- [TOPO][OPS] A `gateway` block mirrors the `cluster` block: a name (matching the cluster), a port (7222 by convention) and a `gateways` list of the other clusters' name plus URL; gateways also gossip so a single seed per remote cluster works. "instead of route we're actually going to call this gateways... these also gossip between each other so we can also just have single seeds" (~10:10)
- [TOPO] The gateway block must be present in every cluster's config, each naming its own cluster, so connections are mutual. "we'll need this gateway also inside of our NA cluster" (~11:00)
- [OPS] Remote-cluster nodes need no client port published when they are only reached through gateways. "it doesn't need to have a port declaration and we're not going to be exporting any ports because we don't need to connect directly to them" (~11:40)
- [TOPO][SIZE] Three clusters is the recommended shape for the redundancy you need; a 3x3 super cluster shows 6 outgoing and 6 incoming gateway connections per cluster (18 total), meaning a full gateway mesh. "in order to achieve the amount of redundancy that we need it would be good to have three clusters... six outgoing gateway six incoming gateways there's a total of 18" (~13:00)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Clients connect to the geographically nearest cluster and still reach clients on other clusters transparently. "you can have clients connect to different clusters based on where they are geographically and they can start talking with clients that are connected to other clusters" (~14:40)

## How to set up Decentralized Authentication/Authorization in NATS | Rethink Connectivity Episode 6
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5pQVjN0ym5w
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz | date: unknown (Rethink Connectivity ep 6, ~2022) | duration: 28:32
- version context: 2.8/2.9 era (nsc + NATS resolver, no `nats auth`)

### Claims
- [SEC] NATS deliberately splits authentication ("I am who I say I am") from authorization ("what I'm allowed to do") because combining them causes problems. "we've split those two things apart, some systems put them together and it causes all sorts of problems" (~01:10)
- [SEC] Authentication uses NKeys: an ed25519 public/private key pair where the public key is the identity and the private key proves it by signing nonces; keys can be used hierarchically. "n keys which is just basically an ed25519 based public private key pair" (~01:40)
- [SEC] Authorization is expressed in a JWT that carries limits on messages, connections and allowed publish/subscribe subjects. "here are my limits on the amount of messages I could send or the amount of connections I can have or what kind of subjects I can publish to or subscribe to" (~02:10)
- [SEC][TOPO] The operator model is a hierarchy operator → accounts → users; a "NATS system" (single node, leaf node, cluster or super cluster) treats itself as one system with one operator. "a NATS system can be a single NATS node, it can be a leaf node, but it can also be a cluster or a super cluster... one operator operating it" (~02:40)
- [SEC][PATTERN] The operator is the entity running the system at the infrastructure level, e.g. a platform team or the company running NATS as a utility across an organization. "you're operating a NATS cluster across an entire organization as a utility and so your company name Acme Corp would be your operator" (~03:10)
- [SEC][SUBJ] Accounts are completely segregated messaging namespaces; by default messages never cross accounts unless explicitly shared via imports and exports. "by default you can't really cross accounts via messaging unless you explicitly describe it in imports and exports" (~03:40)
- [SEC][USECASE] Accounts give multi-tenancy: Synadia's global network runs multiple companies on one NATS system, separated only by accounts. "we have a global network that we have multiple companies using one NATS system and they're all separated via accounts" (~04:07)
- [SEC] Users are the end identities used by programs (microservices, producers, consumers); fine-grained pub/sub permissions and limits are defined at the user level. "these are the programs that are using them and this is really where you can get into some fine-grained permissions" (~04:30)
- [SEC] Each level (operator, account, user) has both an NKey pair and a JWT; JWTs are minted and signed with the parent's key so a user JWT is verifiable up the trust chain to the operator. "I can verify that it's signed by an account that I know and that that account was actually signed by my operator" (~05:09)
- [SEC] The server stores only the operator JWT and account JWTs; it stores no user JWTs and no private keys. "all that we really store are the account and the operator JWTs... we don't store any user JWTs... and then we store no private keys" (~05:40)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Because user JWTs are not stored server-side, users can be minted without updating the system, and creation of accounts/users happens entirely out of band of NATS (only account JWTs must be pushed). "you could actually mint user JWTs without having to update it in the system... the creation process actually happens outside of NATS" (~06:09)
- [SEC][CLNT] Connect flow: server INFO carries a nonce; the client signs it with the user private key, sends the signature plus its JWT in CONNECT; the server validates the signature against the public key in the JWT, checks expiry/revocation, checks the signing account is known and was signed by the operator. "is the JWT expired or has it been revoked, was the JWT signed by an account that I know about, and was this account... did I sign it" (~08:13)
- [SEC][OPS] nsc is the recommended way to start managing operators/accounts/users, but it is not required; the design is intentionally open so organizations can build their own issuance flow without sharing private keys. "you don't necessarily have to use nsc but this is the best way to get started... it's a very open design and that's on purpose" (~09:40)
- [SEC][OPS] Always generate signing keys and never use root keys operationally: signing keys can be rotated if compromised, root keys cannot be recovered from compromise. "root keys are great for printing out putting in a safe... if your root key gets compromised you're kind of out of luck" (~10:40)
- [SEC][OPS] Edit the operator to require signing keys on all accounts (strict signing key usage) and set the account JWT server URL so nsc knows where to push account JWTs. "we want to require all of our accounts to have signing keys as well... set up an account JWT server URL" (~12:16)
- [SEC][OPS] The memory resolver holds account JWTs in memory and suits small systems; the NATS resolver is needed when you want to push accounts dynamically to servers. "a memory resolver... that's great for smaller systems but if we want things more dynamic where we can actually push accounts to servers we'll want to use a NATS resolver" (~15:20)
- [SEC][OPS] `nsc generate config --nats-resolver --sys-account SYS` produces a server config containing the operator JWT, system account, resolver settings and a preloaded system account JWT; `nsc push -A` pushes accounts to the running server. "here's my operator's JWT, here's also the account that I want to use for system accounts, and we want to use a NATS resolver" (~16:00)
- [SEC][CLNT] A creds file is just the user JWT plus the NKey seed (private key), everything a client needs to connect; treat it as sensitive. "all a creds file is is it's a combination of the JWT and the private key" (~19:22)
- [SEC][SUBJ] A request from a user in another account to a service gets "no responders" because accounts are isolated; sharing requires an export from the serving account and an import in the consuming account. "it's going to say no responders are available because these two users actually exist in completely different accounts" (~21:40)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Exports are typed as either a service (request/response) or a stream (access to data); the import can alias the subject locally so the importer chooses its own naming. "there's either a service or a stream, a service is kind of a request response... a stream is access to data" (~22:50)
- [SEC] Adding the first `allow-pub` clamps the user down so it can publish only to the listed subjects; deny lists are an alternative when it is easier to exclude a few subjects. "once I put in my very first allow pub we really clamp down all of the permissions" (~26:00)
- [SEC][CLNT] A user that must do request/reply needs subscribe permission on its inbox (`_INBOX.>`) in addition to publish permission on the service subject. "allow it to subscribe to its inbox which happens to be inbox dot wildcard, this allows us to have request response" (~25:50)
- [SEC] Publishing to a subject outside the user's permissions yields a "permissions violation for publish" authorization error. "we get an authorization error which is great, permissions violation for publish" (~27:29)

## Extend your NATS Cluster with Leaf Nodes | Rethink Connectivity Episode 7
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WH55czo1BNk
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz | date: unknown (Rethink Connectivity ep 7, ~2022/2023) | duration: 26:45
- version context: 2.9 era (JetStream domains, stream sourcing across domains, NGS)

### Claims
- [TOPO] A leaf node is a second, separate NATS system (single server, cluster or super cluster) that connects into another NATS system, with its own auth model, its own JetStream assets and its own local interest. "a leaf node is a second NATS system that gets to connect into another NATS system" (~00:50)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Hub-and-spoke: cloud cluster as hub, each store/factory/site as a leaf node running local services, which gives better performance and isolation than having every site connect straight to the cloud. "instead of everything connecting to the cloud we actually get better performance and better isolation by separating these two things out" (~03:00)
- [TOPO][SEC] Run sites you don't fully control (partner sites, factories, retail) as their own NATS systems because they may need a different security model than the hub. "they might have some different use cases for what they need out of a security model so it's better to operate these things as separate NATS systems" (~02:20)
- [TOPO][USECASE] Three things leaf nodes are good for: extending a hub in hub-and-spoke, bridging two NATS systems that must stay separate but exchange some data, and edge connectivity over unreliable links such as 5G. "extending a hub in a hub and spoke topology... bridging two NATS systems... connectivity at the edge" (~03:30)
- [TOPO][USECASE] Good leaf-node candidates: location-based communication (factories, retail stores, planes/trains/automobiles) that operates independently and syncs with the cloud, plus inter-organization sharing (partners, OEMs, multi-prem deployments). "planes trains automobiles things that move around these are all really good candidates" (~04:40)
- [TOPO][SUBJ] Leaf node links carry explicit interest propagation: no traffic crosses the link unless it is authorized and there is actual interest on the other side, which cuts chattiness. "there's not going to be any traffic that goes over this leaf node connection unless one it's authorized and two there's actual interest" (~05:50)
- [TOPO][SEC] Hub and leaf have separate operational models: the hub can use decentralized auth while the leaf runs with no auth behind a firewall; what crosses the link is bounded by the hub-side user the leaf connects with. "the authorization of what kind of goes over the wire is bound to this user from the operational model of the hub" (~06:40)
- [TOPO] Leaf nodes are daisy-chainable into a constellation without strange performance issues, because they behave like cluster/super-cluster links but with explicit rather than optimistic interest propagation. "these leaf nodes are naturally daisy chainable... only with explicit interest propagation instead of any optimistic" (~07:00)
- [TOPO][OPS] Leaf node connections are self-healing: they fail over to gossiped hub servers, keep retrying while disconnected, keep operating locally in the meantime, and resync when the link returns. "I could turn off my internet... the leaf node will still operate as is because it's a separate NATS system... when it comes back up it'll sync back up" (~07:40)
- [STRM][TOPO] JetStream domains identify which JetStream (hub or leaf) a command such as stream/consumer creation targets. "JetStream domains which is a way to identify... where you want to operate that actual command" (~08:00)
- [TOPO][OPS] A leaf node into NGS needs only a `leafnodes { remotes [...] }` block with the hub URL and credentials, plus `jetstream` enabled; the JetStream domain may be left default or named explicitly. "I only need two things here, I need the url... and then we'll also grab these credentials" (~13:00)
- [CLNT][OPS] Requests through an already-connected leaf link can return faster than a fresh direct connection to the hub because the direct path pays the TLS handshake each time. "that's actually the TLS delay making that TLS connection... via the leaf node connection we actually get much faster responses" (~16:00)
- [PATTERN][TOPO] Running a responder locally on the leaf lets requests be served locally with sub-millisecond latency and never leave for the hub; kill it and requests transparently fall back to the hub responder. "it didn't actually ever hit the NGS cloud because it can see that there's somebody who's able to respond... if I kill this service... it's just going to go back to Oregon" (~17:40)
- [STRM][ANTI] With one giant cloud stream and many (e.g. 2000) stores, having every store fetch messages from the cloud hammers the hub; instead build filtered local read replicas. "everybody's going to be hammering the cloud with requests for orders and you might not want that" (~19:30)
- [STRM][OPS] From a leaf node, viewing or getting from a hub stream requires specifying the hub's JetStream domain (e.g. `--js-domain NGS`); without it the leaf's own (empty) domain is used. "there are no streams in our leaf node right now there's only a stream on NGS... that's where we need to specify a JS domain" (~20:20)
- [STRM][PATTERN] A leaf-local stream that sources the hub stream with a subject filter (e.g. `orders.store1.*`) yields a real read replica with sequences, not just a cache, and local gets become much faster. "it's not just a cache, it's a real read replica of a stream" (~22:00)
- [STRM] A sourced stream need not follow the source's storage rules: it can be memory instead of file, with its own replication and its own start position. "I don't have to follow the rules of the source stream... if this original order stream is file based I could say I just want this thing in memory" (~23:00)
- [STRM][SEC][PATTERN] Layer decentralized auth on top so a leaf node's credentials only permit sourcing specific subjects from the hub stream, giving partners scoped access to a global data store. "you can only source from this subject on this stream... a global data store that can only be accessed in certain ways" (~24:40)
- [STRM][TOPO] If the leaf goes down while messages are added at the hub, the sourced stream catches up automatically and in order when the leaf returns. "I can take down this leaf node and add messages to it and then pull a leaf node back up and NATS is automatically going to be syncing all that data in order" (~25:20)
- [SIZE] NGS round-trip from California measured ~41–45 ms to the nearest NGS server. "look at, I have a 45 millisecond RTT to the cluster" (~11:30)

## Dynamic Permissions with Scoped Signing Keys | Rethink Connectivity Episode 8
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KmGtnFxHnVA
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz | date: unknown (Rethink Connectivity ep 8, ~2023) | duration: 17:20
- version context: 2.9 era (scoped signing keys with templates; hints that auth callout is "coming in a future release")

### Claims
- [SIZE][TOPO] NGS, Synadia's global super cluster, ran about 72 NATS servers across geos and clouds at the time. "we have about 72 different NATS servers at play in various geos and clouds" (~01:03)
- [SEC] Signing keys are basic hygiene: if the account root key is compromised you are stuck, whereas a compromised signing key can be revoked and replaced and users reissued. "if that signing key gets compromised your whole system's not compromised... you can revoke that key, issue another one and reissue all of your users" (~02:40)
- [SEC][PATTERN] A scoped signing key is a signing key given a role and a permission template; every user signed with it inherits those permissions, which acts as role-based authorization inside an account. "you give it a role and then you can give it a template and every time a user is signed with that signing key they get those permissions out of the box" (~04:40)
- [SEC][SUBJ] Permission templates can interpolate the user's name, user tags, account name/tags or public keys, e.g. `chat.post.{{tag(org)}}.{{name}}`, so one template yields per-user subject permissions. "we can use templates to insert dynamic content in here based on user's tags or the user's name, the account tags or name, or even the actual public keys" (~06:11)
- [SEC][USECASE] Scoped keys suit fleets of edge devices where re-minting and redistributing user JWTs is impractical; permissions are updated centrally instead. "you have a lot of devices at the edge and it's not very convenient to update permissions to them and re-mint user JWTs" (~07:00)
- [SEC][CLNT] Include `allow-pub-response` on the scoped key so users can reply to requests later. "just for good hygiene in case we want to put in request reply at some point we should probably say allow pub response" (~08:00)
- [SEC] A user created with `-K <scoped key>` and tags has no explicit pub/sub permissions in its JWT JSON; all permissions are inferred from the issuer key at connect time. "if I look at the JSON output here it doesn't actually have any pub or sub permissions assigned to it, all of this is inferred from the key that signed it" (~09:40)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Because permissions live on the signing key, updating the key changes permissions for already-issued users without reconnecting or reissuing credentials. "they don't have to reload, they don't have to reconnect, they don't have to get new user JWTs" (~10:00)
- [SEC][SUBJ] Subject permissions are strict per token: a user permitted `chat.post.synadia.jeremy` cannot subscribe to `chat.post.*.*` or publish under another user's name. "if Liz tries to post into the Jeremy subject... she's going to get a permission denied" (~11:50)
- [SEC][ANTI] Minting users with permissions baked into the JWT means adding a new feature later requires re-minting and redistributing JWTs, which may be infeasible; scoped signing keys avoid this. "we would have no way of expanding the subjects they're allowed to use unless we re-minted the JWT... that might not be feasible" (~12:50)
- [SEC][SUBJ][PATTERN] A DM subject design `chat.dm.{org}.{receiver}.{sender}` with allow-pub on `chat.dm.{org}.*.{name}` and allow-sub on `chat.dm.{org}.{name}.*` lets users send to anyone but only read DMs addressed to them. "they can listen in on any DMs directed to them... but they can only publish on things that they should be able to send" (~14:19)
- [SEC][TOPO] Scoped signing keys work across leaf nodes and edge devices as well as the core cluster. "especially in the case of either leaf nodes or edge devices... this all works across all of it" (~16:00)

## Connect ANY Auth System to NATS.io with Auth Callout
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VvGxrT-jv64
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz | date: unknown (~2024; says auth callout "came out maybe about a year ago") | duration: 31:44
- version context: 2.10 era (auth callout, micro framework, KV/stream-backed chat app)

### Claims
- [SEC][CORE] On connect the server authenticates the client, assigns a connection ID (CID), binds it to an account (the `$G` global account if not multi-tenant) and attaches permissions and limits. "it creates a connection ID or a CID for that client, it then binds that client to a particular account... if you're not using multi-tenancy it's just going to be the dollar sign G account" (~02:30)
- [SEC][ANTI] Users defined in the server config are the easiest option but do not scale; decentralized JWT auth scales far, needs no config updates and keeps secrets out of config files, but is more complex and cumbersome. "put your users defined inside of a NATS server config which is the easiest approach but isn't super scalable" (~03:00)
- [SEC] Auth callout is a third option: on CONNECT the server delegates authentication to a request/reply service you write and run instead of using its own knowledge. "the server instead of with its knowledge trying to authenticate the user, it's actually going to delegate that to an auth service that you create and maintain" (~03:50)
- [SEC] The callout request carries client info, a server-generated NKey that is the user's temporary identity for the life of the connection, the server ID (anti-spoofing), and the full connect options including any mTLS certificate, token, JWT or username/password. "it's going to pass an NKey that it generates, this is going to be the user's temporary identity while it maintains connection to the server" (~04:20)
- [SEC] The auth service returns a signed user JWT, reusing the decentralized-auth toolset, but without minting and distributing JWTs to clients or restarting them when permissions change. "it's using all the same tool set except that you don't have to mint that JWT and hand it to another client" (~05:10)
- [SEC] Auth callout payloads can optionally be end-to-end encrypted between server and auth service using an XKey (curve key), so privileged operators cannot snoop the exchange. "the auth callout mechanism is end-to-end encrypted, or you actually have the option to do that... with an encryption key called an X key" (~05:40)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Any external system (Active Directory, OAuth, OIDC, your own database) can be plugged in; the auth service is a normal NATS connection, so it can also use KV/object store as its user database with no separate backend. "you might not even need to have your own database, you could have a database powered by KV that has all of your user permissions in it" (~06:30)
- [SEC] Auth callout can run in mixed mode alongside config-defined users or decentralized JWT auth. "you can support mix mode auth... some users defined in the config plus auth callout or you want to do the decentralized auth plus auth callout" (~07:05)
- [SEC][ANTI] A chat app using a single all-powerful shared NATS user lets anyone impersonate anyone; that is the anti-pattern the callout replaces. "I have a single NATS user that just has permissions to do anything that they want which obviously isn't great" (~09:00)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Pattern: client does Google OIDC first, passes the Google-signed JWT unchanged as the NATS token; the auth service verifies Google's signature and mints NATS user claims from the Google claims. "it's not a NATS JWT... it's exactly what Google handed back to us, we're just going to give that to the NATS server when we connect" (~10:00)
- [SEC][OPS] Server config: an `authorization { auth_callout { ... } }` block with `issuer` (public account NKey generated via `nsc generate nkey --account`, so the server can verify signed responses), `auth_users` (users that bypass callout, including the auth service itself), and the `account` in which callout users live. "we want to pass an issuer and this issuer is going to be the public key of the NKey that we just generated" (~12:40)
- [SEC][OPS] The auth service's own user should use NKeys or decentralized JWTs rather than a plaintext username/password in config. "I recommend that you use something like NKeys or even the decentralized JWT auth for a lot of these users" (~13:20)
- [SEC][OPS] Inject the auth service's NKey seed via environment or secrets in production, never hard-coded. "you likely want to inject this in via the environment or via secrets in some way shape or form when you're actually deploying" (~15:20)
- [SEC][CLNT] In the handler, create user claims with subject = the request's user NKey, set the audience to the target account name, and return the claims; the server signs and binds them. "the subject is actually going to be coming from our request... request.user_nkey" and "we do that by configuring the claim audience" (~19:20)
- [SEC] Returning an error from the handler surfaces to the client as an authorization error. "if there was an error here we want to make sure we return it and that will result in an authorization error" (~20:20)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Emails are not subject-safe, so base64-encode them into a user ID before using them as a subject token or KV key. "we don't want to use the email just as it is but what we can do is we could base64 encode this email so it's safe enough for subjects" (~21:00)
- [SEC][SUBJ][PATTERN] Permissions minted per user: read JetStream API info, chat-messages stream info, create/operate consumers on it, read the workspace KV, but publish only to `chat.<channel>.<own user id>`, which makes authorship verifiable. "they can only post on behalf of their own user ID... we kind of use this as a mechanism to verify who has posted what" (~24:00)
- [SEC][OPS] The auth service subscribes to the fixed subject `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH`; the example uses the micro framework with that as the endpoint subject. "the NATS server is going to send an $SYS request user auth, this is the subject that NATS is going to be using the callout for" (~26:29)
- [SEC][KV][PATTERN] The auth service also upserts the user's profile (name, email, photo) into a KV bucket on each login; clients watching that bucket update instantly, giving zero-touch onboarding. "all the chat applications were watching that key value store so they also updated their profile info before I even jumped into chat" (~28:40)
- [SEC] A client holding only a Google JWT gets an authentication error on `nats stream list` but can subscribe to the stream and publish only under its own user id; impersonation attempts fail with a permissions violation. "if I want to just throw some gobbledygook in here or try to impersonate somebody it's going to result in a permissions violation" (~30:20)
- [SIZE] An auth callout service is small: the OIDC+KV example is about 100 lines of Go. "in about 100 lines of code that we just wrote we're able to do an auth callout service" (~27:40)

## NATS Superclusters in Kubernetes: Cross-Cloud Geo-Affinity for High Availability and Low Latency
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tHQObmUxQWk
- speaker: Colin Lacy | date: unknown (~2025; uses services framework, nats micro CLI) | duration: 14:03
- version context: 2.10/2.11 era (micro services framework, Helm chart, gateways)

### Claims
- [OPS][TOPO] A three-server JetStream-enabled cluster in EKS was deployed with the maintainers' Helm chart and a values file; the options map straight onto standard NATS config documentation. "all I had to do was create this values.yaml file... they all point back to the NATS documentation" (~01:20)
- [OPS] In Kubernetes, application clients reach the servers through the Kubernetes Service the Helm chart exposes in front of the NATS pods. "they all interact through this service exposed by the Helm chart that fronts my NATS servers" (~01:50)
- [CORE] Request/reply does not use JetStream under the hood. "we're talking about request reply and that doesn't really use JetStream under the hood" (~01:00)
- [PATTERN][CLNT] A service in the services framework is declared with a name, version/description and endpoints that bind a handler to a full subject such as `math.numbers.add`; the Python `nats micro` module is one of many language implementations. "I'm using the NATS micro module and I'm going to add a service... declare the service name... and then add an endpoint" (~03:30)
- [OPS] `nats micro stats <service>` shows per-instance request counts; requests spread evenly across instances of a service (max 5 of 10 landed on any one instance in the demo). "you can see they pretty evenly distributed, right, no major spikes here" (~06:30)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] With a super cluster spanning AWS us-east-1 (EKS) and Azure (AKS), requests from the east were served by an adder service running only in the west when the east instance was removed, giving cross-cloud failover with no noticeable delay to the caller. "the NATS cluster in US East 1 is talking to a NATS cluster in Azure running on the other side of the country and that has an adder service deployed" (~08:00)
- [TOPO][OPS] Cross-cloud gateway connectivity was done by exposing each cluster's gateway port through a Kubernetes LoadBalancer Service mapped to a cloud NLB / Azure LB; each gateway block advertises its own LB hostname on 7222 and lists the other cluster's LB address on 7222. "this Kubernetes service, I deployed it as a load balancer type... it's advertising the NLB hostname on port 7222" (~10:00)
- [SEC][OPS] Gateway connections were authenticated with username/password for the demo; production should use something stronger like JWT. "in a production environment you might want something more like JWT" (~11:10)
- [TOPO][SIZE] Once a local responder reappears, super cluster geo-affinity routes all local requests to the local instance rather than the remote cluster, reducing latency (all 10 subsequent requests hit the east instance). "NATS clusters have geo affinity to make sure your traffic is handled as closely to the requester as possible" (~13:00)

## Building an Interactive Whiteboard with NATS Websockets | Rethink Connectivity Episode 3
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=As5FojxWViI
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz | date: unknown (Rethink Connectivity ep 3, ~2022) | duration: 18:38
- version context: 2.8/2.9 era (nats.ws with JsonCodec, `jetstream.subscribe` with ordered consumer option — legacy nats.js API)

### Claims
- [OPS][CLNT] WebSocket support is off by default; enable it with a `websocket` block giving a listen port, and `no_tls: true` only for local dev — the server warns that non-TLS websockets should not be used in production. "websocket isn't turned on by default inside of NATS, you have to turn it on yourself" (~01:50)
- [OPS][CLNT] Turning websocket `compression` on is recommended for better performance. "I'll turn compression on just for better performance" (~02:20)
- [PATTERN][USECASE] A browser app can use NATS as its whole backend: pub/sub for multiplayer and JetStream for persistence, with only front-end code written. "I'm just writing front end code and I'm using NATS for all the back end stuff" (~01:00)
- [CLNT][CORE] NATS is payload agnostic, so browser code needs a codec (here JSON) to encode objects to a byte array before publish and decode on receive. "remember that NATS is payload agnostic so we have to use some sort of codec to encode and decode the message" (~05:08)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Rooms map to subject tokens (`whiteboard.<roomId>`), giving simple multi-tenancy per whiteboard. "I can create a subject like whiteboard dot room id... we're kind of multi-tenant" (~06:50)
- [PATTERN][CLNT] Draw locally first for responsiveness, tag each message with a random per-player id, and on receipt ignore your own messages so only other players' strokes are applied. "if the data's id is not equal to this id then we can call draw raw" (~11:00)
- [CLNT] The nats.ws subscription is consumed as an async iterator (`for await (const m of sub)`). "we want to use an async iterator for this subscription" (~10:12)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Persistence is added by creating a stream on `whiteboard.*` and switching the subscription to a JetStream ordered consumer; each page load creates a fresh ephemeral consumer and replays the whole stream. "every time this thing refreshes it creates a new consumer and pulls in all the data via the stream" (~14:00)
- [CONS] An ordered consumer is an ephemeral consumer that guarantees ordered delivery and, on detecting a gap, restarts by creating a new consumer. "as soon as we find that there's gaps we kind of restart and create a new consumer" (~12:50)
- [STRM][PATTERN] The stream is created with `--allow-rollup` and `--no-deny-purge` so a "clear" message published with the `Nats-Rollup: sub` header replaces all prior messages on that subject, keeping replay cheap for new consumers. "when I send this message clear all of the messages before them so next time a consumer connects it's not getting all of those messages" (~15:30)
- [STRM] Rollup can be per subject or for the entire stream. "you could roll up the subject or you could roll up the entire stream" (~16:00)

## Mutually Trusted NGS Credentials
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zvcb3sM6SaI
- speaker: Matthias Hanel (Synadia) | date: unknown (~2020/2021) | duration: 15:19
- version context: 2.1/2.2 era (NGS developer plans, nsc memory/NATS resolver, leaf nodes); [STALE?] for plan/limit details

### Claims
- [SEC][TOPO] Running your own JWT-auth servers alongside NGS normally forces dual management: two sets of accounts and two sets of credentials. "dual management of accounts, you have one set of accounts in NGS and you have a corresponding set of accounts in your local environment" (~00:30)
- [SEC][PATTERN] One credential set can work in NGS and self-hosted servers if you accept that the account configuration is identical in both environments. "you are okay with your account configuration in either environment be identical, then this video is for you" (~01:10)
- [SEC] JWT identity chain: each JWT references a public NKey; the operator JWT is self-signed by the operator NKey, which also signs account JWTs; the account NKey signs user JWTs; the user NKey proves possession via challenge/response. "the operator JWT in a sense is self-signed, it also signs the account JWT, the account NKey signs and therefore authorizes the user JWT" (~02:30)
- [SEC] Permissions come both explicitly from the user JWT and implicitly from the account that signed it; the server verifies by downloading the account JWT via the resolver, checking its operator signature, then checking the user JWT was signed by an NKey referenced in the account JWT. "it verifies the user JWT was signed by an NKey referenced in the account JWT" (~03:20)
- [SEC][OPS] To trust NGS credentials on your own server: configure the server with the NGS operator, set up an account resolver (memory or NATS), and create a dedicated system account for your own servers. "we configure our NATS server with the NGS operator and we configure an account resolver" (~03:50)
- [OPS] Your own servers need their own system account because NGS servers use a different system account; `nats server list` against them with NGS's system creds returns nothing. "the only servers involved so far are NGS servers that are using a different system account, so failed without results as expected" (~05:40)
- [SIZE][STALE?] NGS free accounts had limits too low for the setup, specifically message size and leaf node connection count; developer plans allow leaf node connections and a decent payload size. "the limits of the free accounts are too low, specifically the message size and the number of allowed leaf node connections" (~06:00)
- [OPS] Unresolved-import warnings on connect are harmless: NGS accounts import services that do not exist on your servers; the imports can be removed. "these are imports NGS adds for services that do not exist on our end... they're harmless" (~07:50)
- [TOPO][SEC] With a leaf node config that connects each local account to its NGS counterpart, the import resolution moves from subscribe time to server startup, and the same creds subscribe locally and publish via NGS. "what used to be done with the connect during subscribe now is done during server startup because the server connects to NGS" (~09:13)
- [OPS] The memory resolver is fine for static accounts; the NATS resolver is more appropriate when accounts change dynamically, and needs an initial `nsc push` (errors until then) plus a push to your own resolver after every change. "NGS the push happens automatically on every change but to make your changes visible you need to push to your resolver as well" (~11:10)
- [OPS][TOPO] A NATS resolver in full mode holds all account JWTs and answers lookups; with at least one full-mode server, other servers (e.g. leaf nodes) can run in cache mode, downloading only locally used account JWTs and caching them for offline use for the resolver TTL. "as long as you have at least one server running with a NATS resolver in full mode you can start others in cache mode" (~12:00)
- [OPS] A cache-mode resolver still needs a leaf node remote for the system account for resolution to work. "I'm only setting one remote, the remote for the system account, that is needed in order to make the NATS resolver work even in cache mode" (~13:00)
- [OPS] The first connect through a cache-mode resolver for an unseen account may fail due to compounding import-resolution timeouts; the retry succeeds. "this command will fail at first, it does so because of compounding timeouts to resolve the imports" (~13:50)
- [TOPO][OPS] A cache-mode server keeps serving cached accounts while the full-mode server is offline. "we can still access it despite the NATS server with the full resolver being offline" (~14:40)

## NATS Connect Live! | Bearer Tokens in NATS
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PBPCwumaspE
- speaker: Kyle Thomas (Provide), closing remarks by Colin Sullivan | date: 2020 (NATS Connect Live) | duration: 19:12
- version context: [STALE?] 2.1 era (pre-official websockets, NATS Streaming still in use, custom fork of nats-server)

### Claims
- [SEC][USECASE][STALE?] Provide used NATS as a fault-tolerant backplane for a blockchain-oriented orchestration platform and wanted decentralized, private messaging with no central authority. "our requirements are obviously no central authority, we wanted to allow organizations to be self sovereign" (~02:50)
- [SEC][PATTERN][STALE?] Their model: organizations sign bearer JWTs to delegate authorization; a verified token creates an ephemeral in-memory user for the duration of the connection, with no operator/account/user configuration on the server. "if the token is verified an ephemeral user is created in memory for the duration of the connection" (~03:20)
- [SEC][STALE?] They needed RS256 and ed25519 signing/verification and did not want to depend on nsc for key material, to keep infra complexity low. "we wanted to support RS256 and ed25519 signing and verification and we didn't want to depend on NSC" (~03:40)
- [SEC] JWT fields that matter to the server: `exp` (server sets a timeout and drops the connection when it expires), `alg`, and `kid` to pick the verification key when multiple keys sign. "the server actually will set a timeout given this header and... when the expiration occurs then the connection will be dropped" (~04:40)
- [SEC] The NATS permissions claim in a token lists allowed publish subjects, allowed subscribe subjects and an allow-responses flag (false by default); on valid signature these permissions are applied in memory. "a list of publish subjects, subscribe subjects that are allowed for the connection, allow responses you can set it to true or false" (~05:30)
- [SEC][PATTERN] One JWT can carry both application permissions and the NATS permissions claim, so a single token serves the app and NATS. "if you generate and sign a JWT that has other application permissions... it's very nicely in line with a single token" (~06:20)
- [SEC][STALE?] Their fork honored the plain auth token as a fallback when no JWT was present, because NATS Streaming still connected with a token. "if no JWT is provided but an auth token is provided then that will still be honored" (~07:20)
- [SEC][STALE?] Verification keys were supplied through an environment variable; a WebSocket server was embedded in the fork ahead of official websocket support. "currently it's just done with an environment variable" (~08:10)
- [TOPO][SEC] Synadia's guidance to a project needing a non-standard auth model: run your own servers as leaf nodes with your model and let the core catch up, because leaf nodes allow mixing operator and security models. "with leaf nodes you can run your own servers for endpoints using the bearer tokens, don't wait on us, run ahead" (~17:50)

## NATS Connect Live! | NATS Leafnodes
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=01VPY86f78w
- speaker: Derek Collison (Synadia) | date: 2020 (NATS Connect Live) | duration: 28:36
- version context: 2.1 era (leaf nodes 3–6 months old, JetStream preview, websockets/MQTT just arriving); [STALE?] for JetStream-preview statements

### Claims
- [TOPO] Leaf nodes were born to amortize the cost of NATS 2.0 security setup (TLS to dynamic DNS, nonce challenge, JWT exchange) for short-lived utilities; they then became "the missing topology link". "leaf nodes were kind of born out of hey I want to try to solve this one specific problem of amortization of the security and TLS constructs" (~01:20)
- [TOPO][SIZE] Routes (clusters) assume good signal-to-noise, low RTT and decent bandwidth, i.e. a single region or availability zone; stretching a cluster coast-to-coast or across continents does not work well, and NATS was originally the same as Kubernetes or Kafka in this respect. "they don't like to be stretched from east coast to west coast or to Asia Pacific to Europe, and to be frank NATS was the same way with its initial clustering algorithms" (~02:50)
- [TOPO] Gateways (NATS 2.0) are the second topology and are extremely tolerant of long RTT, low bandwidth and spotty connections; leaf nodes add a hub-and-spoke third topology where the hub can be a server, cluster or super cluster and spokes can be daisy chained. "gateways which are extremely tolerant of very long RTT, low bandwidth, spotty connections" (~03:20)
- [TOPO][SEC] Leaf nodes bridge operator and security domains: a shared utility (inside a company or NGS) can be extended by servers that people own, operate and secure differently, e.g. WebSocket and MQTT each have their own security model. "they allow us to bridge operator and security domains, and this one is very subtle and nuanced but it's extremely important" (~04:00)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Architecture endorsed: a central server/cluster/super cluster with many leaf-node spokes that absorb inbound web/mobile client connections. "a very legitimate architecture of a single server cluster or super cluster that then has lots of hub and spokes to actually take on all of the inbound clients" (~06:00)
- [TOPO][USECASE] Almost every large proof of concept at the time used leaf nodes. "most of the large POCs we've been doing today, we're using them in almost every single one" (~06:20)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Run leaf spokes as a small cluster rather than a singleton; each server solicits its own connection to the hub and self-heals independently, so there is no leader election or single point of failure. "every single one of those NATS servers has configured it exactly the same way to solicit a connection to the NATS super cluster... there is no single point of failure" (~08:00)
- [SEC][TOPO] Clients on a leaf node need not be aware of hub accounts: a leaf can use the global account with its own security domain while the hub side binds the connection to account A/B/C, and any client bound to the same hub account anywhere in the super cluster can talk transparently. "they can actually not even expose accounts at all... but once it's inside of here it's bound to let's say account A, B or C" (~09:10)
- [SEC][TOPO] A leaf node into NGS requires no auth, TLS or user/password locally if you trust the machine; the hub side still sees strong NATS 2.0 security, and NGS never holds your private keys. "everything that's coming and going looks like Derek's account and everything over here is just, there's no authentication authorization TLS, it's just open port" (~15:10)
- [SIZE][TOPO] Requests via a local leaf node returned noticeably faster than direct requests to NGS because TLS and key-exchange costs are amortized once on the leaf connection. "it seemed very fast, right, because we've amortized all of the cost of TLS and all of the complexities around the key exchange" (~16:00)
- [TOPO][SUBJ] Purely local traffic between clients on the leaf never leaves for the hub. "if I started talking amongst myself just on my local computer here no traffic would ever move to NGS whatsoever" (~16:20)
- [SEC][TOPO] A leaf server can be multi-account locally: a remote can bind local account A to a hub account, while local account B (with no remote) stays isolated and requests to hub services from B simply time out. "if it's on account B it does not... it'll stall and just time out because there's no rule to propagate that information to NGS through that leaf node" (~17:20)
- [TOPO][SEC] Multiple leaf remotes can run from one server, each binding a different local account to a different hub account. "I'm actually going to create multiple leaf node connections bound to the different local accounts" (~18:40)
- [OPS] Add `-DV` to the server to see the leaf node handshake, credentials exchange and interest propagation in the logs. "you can always add -DV and it'll start showing you lots of stuff, interaction with the leaf node" (~19:00)
- [TOPO][SUBJ] Leaf nodes are the only NATS topology that is interest-only in both directions: unlike clients, whose publishes always go to the connected server, a leaf link sends nothing either way without explicit interest. "leaf nodes are the only network topology that NATS has that is interest only both ways" (~19:20)
- [TOPO][OPS] Leaf connections self-heal like everything else: if the hub server disappears the leaf re-solicits and rehooks automatically. "if all of a sudden the server that I was connected to inside of NGS went away the system would automatically try to reseal itself, re-solicit the connection" (~23:20)
- [STRM][TOPO][STALE?] JetStream enabled on a leaf's global account becomes JetStream for the bound hub account across NGS worldwide; leaf nodes with JetStream can extend a core cluster's storage (e.g. add a petabyte for one account) without touching the core. "you can utilize these leaf nodes that are running JetStream just to be extensions to your storage" (~24:30)
- [SEC][USECASE] NATS permissions cover what you can send/receive, where you may connect from and at what times, giving building blocks (not packaged solutions) for data-residency needs like GDPR. "we also have the notion of where are you allowed to connect from, what times can you connect from" (~26:30)
- [CLNT][TOPO] Client applications are unaffected by topology: connecting to a route server, leaf node or super cluster server works exactly the same. "it doesn't matter if it's connecting to a route server or a leaf node server, a super cluster server, it all works exactly the same" (~28:10)

## Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Andrew Gracey on Two Node K3S
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hZE93ld-O18
- speaker: Andrew Gracey (SUSE product manager) with a Synadia host (David Gee) | date: 2024 (RethinkConn 2024) | duration: 08:16
- version context: 2.10 era (two-node election engine announced, not yet GA)

### Claims
- [TOPO][USECASE] Synadia built a two-node leadership election engine (taking Raft out of the equation, borrowing telecom floating-IP/first-hop-redundancy ideas) and bound it to k3s so k3s can run on two nodes backed by NATS. "we've taken raft out of the equation to allow us to have two nodes and then we've bound that to k3s" (~01:50)
- [TOPO][OPS] NATS already underpins k3s for multi-node (3/5/7 node) systems; the two-node k3s option was targeted for later in 2024 and was not yet available. "we can actually underpin k3s now with NATS for multi node systems... at some point we're going to have a two node k3s system" (~02:10)
- [USECASE][SIZE] Edge customers demand two-node systems for three reasons: reusing existing active/passive hardware, physical constraints (space, power, cooling), and economics where a third node adds ~50% cost, especially with GPUs. "that additional 50% cost all of a sudden prices you out of the hardware refresh" (~03:50)
- [ANTI][OPS] Adding a third "witness" node at the edge increases operational complexity and is an extra point of failure, defeating the cost goal; the risk-versus-TCO balance kills the project for many customers. "now you just increase your cost again and increase the complexity of your solution by adding a third different node" (~04:30)
- [ANTI][TOPO] Moving the edge control loop to the cloud fails on latency and bandwidth (5G, satellite, DSL downstream links) and on cloud outages; companies that moved control loops to the cloud are moving them back. "imagine trying to run Kubernetes over DSL right, it's not going to happen, there's just not enough bandwidth" (~06:20)
