## Replace Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis and more w/NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity Ep 10
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_CN1OO7yN0I
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz (Synadia) | date: 2023 (mentions "new JetStream API rewritten earlier this year" and metadata "new in 2.10") | duration: 27:04
- version context: 2.10 era (new nats.go `jetstream` package, message metadata "new in 2.10")

### Claims
- [CORE][PATTERN] Core NATS is a pub/sub model where the cluster brokers communication between two live clients; this covers pub/sub, request/reply, fan-in and fan-out. "a NATS cluster is really brokering communication between two live clients" (~01:03)
- [CORE][ANTI] In core NATS, if a subscriber is offline when a message is published, the server drops it or delivers only to online subscribers; the offline one never gets it. "there's no subscribers so I'm just going to drop the message" (~02:03)
- [CORE][PATTERN] This behaviour is called temporal coupling: both parties must be online for the logic to work. "they are coupled in the sense that they both need to be online for them to work" (~02:03)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Core NATS is recommended for RPC and microservices; stream processing and distributing large datasets for one-at-a-time processing need temporal decoupling, which is JetStream. "fantastic for RPCs and for microservices ... stream processing ... that's when we start getting into temporal decoupling" (~02:03)
- [STRM] JetStream is a subsystem bundled into the NATS server that can be turned on or off, and it is built on top of core NATS using the same protocol. "it's not like it uses a different protocol or anything like that it's all still NATS under the hood" (~03:05)
- [STRM][CLNT] A JetStream publish is a request to the subject; the server responds with a publish acknowledgement (pub ack) that means the message has been saved. "we call a pub ack or a publish acknowledgement ... telling the publisher that the NATS server has saved that message" (~04:07)
- [STRM][SUBJ] A stream ingests every message whose subject matches its configured patterns (e.g. hello.*) and orders them globally. "it's going to order each of these globally which is actually a very important topic" (~05:07)
- [STRM][TOPO] Streams can optionally be replicated across cluster nodes; with R1 the stream lives on one node and if that node goes down you cannot read or write to it. "you can't write to it you can't read to it or anything like that" (~05:07)
- [STRM][TOPO] JetStream replication is built on an implementation of the Raft consensus protocol. "JetStream is built on top of an implementation of the Raft protocol" (~05:07)
- [STRM][TOPO][SIZE] With R3, JetStream picks three available nodes; losing one node still allows reads and writes, losing two still allows reads, losing all three is disaster-recovery territory. "if a second node goes down you can actually still read from that stream" (~06:08)
- [CONS][CLNT] The JetStream consumer API is built on core NATS request/reply on `$JS` subjects, so it can technically be used by hand, though the subjects are long and fiddly. "JetStream is actually built on top of core NATS request reply" (~07:10)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Consumers are described as windows into a stream; a consumer may take all data or a filtered subset by subject. "consumers are like windows into a stream" (~07:10)
- [CONS][MYTH] Unlike Kafka, where you'd have to deliver the whole stream, NATS filters at the consumer level by subject. "instead of having to whip through an entire stream ... NATS can actually filter on a consumer level" (~08:10)
- [STRM][SUBJ][KV][OBJ] Streams are indexed on a per-subject level, which lets you reach a particular message by subject without scanning; this indexing underpins the KV and Object Store implementations. "streams are indexed on a subject level ... this is actually what under the hood drives a lot of our KV and Object Store" (~08:10)
- [CONS][TOPO] Consumers are stored on the server and replicated across nodes, so clients can stay stateless. "consumers are also stored on the server and replicated ... so your clients can stay stateless" (~09:10)
- [CONS] A consumer must acknowledge messages; it can also signal it has not processed one or that it is in a bad state and wants no more messages for now. "I've not processed it or I'm in a really bad state don't send more messages to me right now" (~09:10)
- [OPS][SIZE] Synadia Cloud requires max bytes to be set on every stream so a tenant cannot exhaust the service. "it does require that I set max bytes on all of my streams" (~15:21)
- [CLNT] The new JetStream Go API uses `jetstream.New(nc)` instead of `nc.JetStream()`, `CreateOrUpdateStream` instead of `AddStream`, and accepts `context.Context` for deadlines and cancellation. "a lot of these functions now support the context package ... hugely requested feature" (~14:20)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Use create-or-update for streams so re-running the program keeps the server config matching the code. "we want to be able to run through it and make sure if we make any updates to the config of the stream that it matches" (~14:20)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Consumers live server-side; many clients can consume from one consumer and are naturally load balanced, unlike Kafka where partitioning and consumer groups are needed. "I could have a lot of clients consuming from one consumer and they're naturally load balanced" (~20:28)
- [CONS] Consumers are ephemeral by default: after the client dies there is a timeout, then the server cleans the consumer up; setting a durable name keeps it around. "they are ephemeral by default ... eventually clean up that consumer" (~21:30)
- [CLNT] The new API's `consumer.Consume(callback)` replaces the old mix of push/pull, ephemeral/durable options; messages expose data, subject, headers and metadata (metadata new in 2.10). "now it's just so much more simple to consume from" (~22:30)
- [CLNT][OPS] Stop the consume context on graceful shutdown (signal handling) to clean up. "it does return a consume context which we will want to stop when we gracefully shut down" (~23:31)
- [CONS] A restarted durable consumer resumes exactly where it left off. "it's going to pick up right where it left off" (~24:33)
- [OPS] Zero "pending" on a consumer means it is fully caught up. "it has zero pending which means it's up to date" (~25:34)

## How to configure NATS JetStream streams | Rethink Connectivity Ep 11
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ChSVWDW-874
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz (Synadia) | date: 2023 (follows Ep 10; subject transforms "pretty new") | duration: 28:03
- version context: 2.10 era (new nats.go jetstream API, stream subject transforms described as new)

### Claims
- [STRM][PATTERN] A stream is a single primitive that can be configured to express many distributed-systems patterns: distributed queue, key-value store, object store, append-only log. "you can have multiple different kind of patterns supported ... replace a whole swath of different tools" (~01:02)
- [STRM] Name, description, subjects and storage are the baseline options every stream uses; the name is the identifier used to look up the stream and create consumers. "these are kind of your primary bread and butter" (~04:05)
- [STRM][OPS] Description is not used by any JetStream machinery; it is a human-readable label that shows in `nats stream list`. "description isn't really used in any kind of infrastructure portion" (~05:06)
- [STRM][SUBJ] A stream can have multiple subjects, including wildcards like orders.*, which it "slurps up" from core NATS and persists to disk. "you can have multiple subjects that the stream is essentially slurping up from core NATS" (~05:06)
- [STRM][ANTI] Memory storage is ephemeral: if the server goes offline those messages are lost; it is niche and suited to caches or hosts without fast disk writes. "if that server goes offline those messages are going to be lost" (~06:07)
- [STRM][SIZE] Limits drive stream behaviour: max messages, max bytes (required on Synadia Cloud), max age (per-message TTL for retention like 30 or 365 days), max messages per subject, max message size, max consumers. "limits drives a lot of behavior inside of the stream" (~07:08)
- [STRM][KV][PATTERN] Max messages per subject set to 1 keeps only the last message per subject; the KV store's history setting is driven by this option. "this is actually in use inside of our key value store where you can set a history" (~08:09)
- [STRM] Keep the default retention policy (limits) in most cases; the other policies build on it. "for the most part you can keep it at the default which is limit" (~09:10)
- [STRM] With limits retention and discard old, when a limit is hit the oldest messages are deleted so the stream stays within limits. "it's going to start deleting the older messages to make sure that the stream stays within those limits" (~10:10)
- [STRM][CONS] Interest retention is a superset of limits: it still enforces limits but also deletes a message once every interested consumer has acknowledged it. "it will delete messages once they have been consumed by every consumer that's interested in it" (~11:11)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Interest retention suits multiple consumers each picking messages for different reasons where persistence after processing does not matter. "you have kind of multiple consumers that are using ... but you also want to keep this acting very much like a queue" (~11:11)
- [STRM][CONS] Work-queue retention behaves like interest retention but restricts the stream to one consumer; that one consumer can still be shared by many clients for load balancing. "just because I have one consumer it means I can't load balance between them ... that's actually not true" (~12:13)
- [STRM][PATTERN] A work-queue stream behaves like RabbitMQ or any durable queue: message goes in, gets processed, gets deleted. "works very similar to like a RabbitMQ or any other kind of durable queue system" (~12:13)
- [STRM] Discard policy chooses between dropping old messages and rejecting new publishes when a limit is hit; discard new rejects publishes until the condition changes; default is discard old. "start rejecting API calls or publishes to that stream until the limit is lifted" (~13:15)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Choose discard new when you absolutely must not lose data and would rather fail publishes at the limit. "you would rather start rejecting API calls in order to not lose data" (~13:15)
- [STRM][SIZE] Deduplication uses the Nats-Msg-Id header with a sliding window that defaults to two minutes and is configurable. "by default this duplicate window is going to be two minutes" (~14:15)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Republish is for cases needing millions of consumers, where consumer machinery costs hardware; the stream republishes a core NATS notification when a message is persisted. "once you get into the use case where you might need like millions of consumers ... might not be worth the added cost" (~15:15)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Republish can be configured headers-only to minimise bytes on the wire; suited to monitoring and logging that is not mission critical. "you could also make this very performant over the wire where it's just sending the bare minimum" (~16:17)
- [STRM][TOPO] Data must live somewhere; Raft-based immediate consistency constrains where replication can happen. "we have to abide by the laws of physics" (~17:17)
- [STRM][TOPO][SIZE] Use replication factors of 3, 5 or 7; with R3, one node offline still handles writes and two nodes offline still handles reads; default is R1. "you're going to want to use multiples of like three five seven" (~18:19)
- [STRM][TOPO] Replication-factor replicas are immediately consistent but must stay inside one cluster; they cannot span clusters. "I can't go outside the cluster with this version of replication" (~19:21)
- [STRM][TOPO][OPS] Placement selects the cluster and server tags; tag servers when building a supercluster (e.g. region, cloud, SSD) so stream creators can express affinity. "we recommend when you're building the NATS supercluster that you tag things appropriately" (~19:21)
- [STRM][TOPO] Mirrors and sources are the way to replicate outside a cluster. "if you want to go outside of your cluster for replication then you need to start looking to mirrors or sources" (~20:22)
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] A mirror is a one-to-one twin of a stream in another cluster; reads are served from the mirror while writes are forwarded to the origin stream to keep global consistency. "all reads will be served from this mirror but all writes will actually be forwarded to the source" (~21:22)
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Sources aggregate and filter many streams into one, and the sourcing stream may also ingest its own subjects; a good use is aggregating leaf-node edge streams into one cloud stream. "aggregate them all into one mega stream in the cloud" (~22:23)
- [STRM] A sourced stream is a brand new stream with its own sequence numbers, not a one-to-one mapping. "sequence IDs are going to be unique and different ... specifically unique to this stream" (~22:23)
- [STRM] Compression is only available for file-based stores, not memory stores. "it's only limited to the file based stores of streams" (~23:24)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Allow rollup lets a specially-headed message replace everything before it on the whole stream or one subject, useful for derived or computable state. "it will persist that message that just came through and it will delete everything before it" (~24:25)
- [STRM][SEC] Deny delete and deny purge flags control whether individual message deletes (e.g. GDPR) or subject/stream purges are allowed. "deleting messages is being able to pick out a particular message and delete it great for like GDPR purposes" (~24:25)
- [STRM][CONS] Consumer limits on a stream set default limits for consumers created on it. "configure default consumer limits for consumers that are created on this stream" (~24:25)
- [STRM][SUBJ] Stream subject transforms rewrite a message's subject before it is stored; useful when aggregating via sources into a mega stream. "transform the message's subject before it gets saved to disk" (~25:26)
- [STRM][OPS] Almost all stream options, including placement, can be changed at runtime; the server moves a replicated stream live while consumers and publishers keep working. "we actually take the stream we replicate it we move it in flight while consumers are consuming from it" (~26:27)

## Build Priority Background Jobs & Dead Letter Queues with NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity ep 12
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7Jp3tyCGMZs
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz (Synadia) | date: late 2023 (promotes RethinkConn 2024 "right after the new year") | duration: 33:01
- version context: 2.10 era (multiple filter subjects "in the newer version", stream metadata "brand new feature")

### Claims
- [STRM][PATTERN][USECASE] A worker/job queue is one of the most common queuing patterns (RabbitMQ, Sidekiq, Celery); JetStream can be shaped into this durable-queue form. "Jet Stream can kind of be molded and shaped into all kinds of different expressions of distributed systems" (~00:00)
- [STRM][SUBJ][PATTERN] JetStream has no built-in priority semantics; priorities are expressed through subject-based addressing (e.g. jobs.high.*, jobs.low.*) with separate worker pools sized differently. "NATS JetStream doesn't have priority semantics built in ... you can have priority semantics by using our subject based addressing" (~02:03)
- [STRM][CONS][MYTH] Correction to the previous episode: a work-queue stream can have multiple consumers as long as their filter subjects do not overlap. "you can actually have multiple consumers in a work queue stream as long as the subjects that they're interested in don't overlap" (~04:05)
- [STRM][OPS] In a work-queue stream, processed messages are deleted, so the stream size represents in-progress work. "you can look at the size of the queue as kind of your in progress work" (~04:05)
- [CONS] JetStream retries failed or unacknowledged deliveries automatically; the number of attempts and the backoff schedule are configurable. "that's a configurable setting to set how many times we want to retry as well as what the back off policy looks like" (~04:05)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Dead-letter queues are deliberately not a first-class JetStream feature; they are a specific pattern expressible through configuration without code. "we wanted to be able to express it but not necessarily bake it into JetStream as a core thing" (~05:05)
- [STRM][CONS][ANTI] In a work-queue stream, a message that exhausted max deliveries stays in the stream until manually acknowledged or deleted, so failures stack up the queue size. "it will stay there in the stream until you either manually acknowledge it or manually delete it" (~05:05)
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] JetStream advisories report which messages hit max failed deliveries; you can capture these into a stream to build your own dead-letter queue. "we have some JetStream advisories that you could listen to and actually insert into a queue" (~06:06)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Suggested job subject hierarchy: jobs.<priority>.<job-type>, e.g. jobs.high.send-welcome-email. "the first token is going to be the priority ... the second one will be kind of like the job's ID" (~07:07)
- [STRM][PATTERN] For a work queue, use discard policy "new" so a backed-up queue rejects new jobs rather than deleting old ones. "if my queue gets backed up I don't want to start deleting old messages ... I want to start actually rejecting" (~08:08)
- [STRM][OPS][SIZE] Put a message-count cap on queues (example 20,000) for monitoring and SLA purposes. "these queues have some sort of limit on them ... you might want to set kind of a cap on this" (~08:08)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Set a max age (example 7 days) on the work-queue stream so dead messages that exhausted retries eventually expire rather than backing up forever. "I'm okay having a sort of lifetime to my dead messages" (~09:10)
- [OPS] `nats stream subjects <stream>` shows per-subject message counts, useful to see how much of each priority is queued. "I have 5,000 of the clean old upload and low priority queue and 5,000 of the send email" (~10:11)
- [CONS][OPS] Name the connection and the consumer after the worker role and instance so monitoring and logging can identify each worker. "use these to create the name for our JetStream consumer as well as kind of just a worker name to use for both logging and for monitoring" (~11:14)
- [CONS] Max deliver (example 4) plus a backoff list (example 5s, 10s, 15s) controls redelivery; each backoff entry is how long to wait for an ack before redelivering. "this is how long it's waiting for an acknowledgement so if the job doesn't get back to you in 5 seconds then it's going to attempt to redeliver" (~17:25)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Exponential-backoff retry logic like a webhook system is pure JetStream consumer configuration, not code. "you could do all of this straight inside of JetStream without really having to write much code" (~18:26)
- [CONS][STRM] Creating two consumers with overlapping filter subjects on a work-queue stream errors; newer servers allow multiple filter subjects per consumer. "I'm actually going to get an error because I'm going to try to create two consumers that overlap" (~18:26)
- [CONS][CLNT] Every consumed JetStream message carries metadata including the stream sequence and consumer sequence. "every single message in JetStream as you're consuming it has metadata about the message" (~19:27)
- [CONS][CLNT] Nak retries immediately; nak-with-delay schedules redelivery later; simply not acking lets the ack wait expire so the server detects hung or dead workers and retries. "what if one of these workers cannot respond and it needs to shut down or it's hanging ... I want JetStream to pick up on that fact" (~24:32)
- [STRM][OPS] The max-deliveries advisory subject is $JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<stream>.<consumer>; wildcard the consumer so new priorities do not require DLQ changes. "I want to add a medium priority and I don't want to have to change the dead letter queue semantics" (~26:34)
- [OPS] All JetStream advisory events can be listed with the CLI schema command. "you can see all these through the NATS CLI via the schema command" (~26:34)
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] The advisory includes stream, consumer and stream sequence; use `nats stream get <stream> <seq>` to fetch the original failed message, which stays in the stream until its max age. "we also get the stream sequence which is really important here" (~28:36)
- [PATTERN] DLQ handling can be automated (delete known-safe failures) or human-in-the-loop, including a UI over the DLQ stream. "we can have kind of a human in the loop kind of intervention" (~29:38)
- [STRM][OPS] Stream metadata (new feature) can label a stream, e.g. dead-letter-queue=true, so tooling can discover DLQ streams. "I could look through all my streams and I could find the ones that are dead letter queues" (~30:38)
- [PATTERN][USECASE] The whole priority job queue with DLQ was about 80 lines, mostly configuration, positioned as a replacement for RabbitMQ, Celery or Sidekiq. "we had like 80 lines of code and most of that was configuration too" (~31:39)

## NATS & Kafka Compared: Part 1 | Rethink Connectivity
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C4BnJ5QLeTY
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz and Jean-Noël Moyne (Synadia) | date: 2023 (era: precedes the "simplified JetStream API" mention in Part 2) | duration: 38:47
- version context: 2.9/2.10 era (subject-based addressing, per-subject limits, CAS headers, rollups all described as current)

### Claims
- [MYTH][STRM] Kafka was designed as a streaming/distributed-log processing platform; NATS was first a messaging system and JetStream was a persistence layer added on top. "NATS historically came as being first and foremost a messaging system and then later on a persistence layer was added" (~02:02)
- [MYTH][CORE] Kafka is "semi-real time but not real real time" by its own admission and was not designed as a messaging system, although people use it for pub/sub and queues. "it really is not initially meant or designed to be a messaging system" (~03:03)
- [CORE][SUBJ] NATS was designed as a low-latency, high-throughput, high-fan-out messaging system with subject-based addressing, proper interactive request/reply and proper message queues. "low latency high throughput high fan out messaging system implementing publish subscribe with subject-based addressing" (~05:05)
- [MYTH][SUBJ] Kafka has no subject-based addressing; a topic is a plain string, regex topic matching requires the client to keep re-fetching the topic list, and a stream is one topic. "the topic is just a string" (~07:07)
- [SUBJ] Subjects are multi-token dotted hierarchies; `*` matches one token, `>` matches one or more trailing tokens, so foo.bar.*.> matches foo.bar.x.y but not foo.bar.x. "foo.bar.x will not match in this particular case because it's missing the dot and more tokens after that" (~09:08)
- [STRM][SUBJ][PATTERN] Subject-based addressing lets you address individual messages or ranges in a stream directly, e.g. get orders.eu.12345 or query orders.us.*. "you can address individual messages or series of messages directly in the stream" (~10:09)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] A sensor taxonomy like sensor.<type>.<id>.<event> or with region tokens supports queries like "all temperature sensors" or "all sensors in us-east". "give me all the sensor data for sensors located in region us-east" (~11:12)
- [MYTH][STRM] Kafka can only address messages by offset (partition number plus sequence); the publish key is used solely to hash onto partitions and cannot be queried. "the key ... is purely used for one thing and one thing only which is distribution over the partitions" (~12:13)
- [MYTH][SIZE][ANTI] For market data with ~100,000 instruments you would not create 100,000 Kafka topics; you use one topic per exchange with the instrument as key, and then filtering for one instrument means the broker sends everything to a client that discards most of it. "you're transferring all the data over the network to somewhere else where you are discarding most of it" (~15:16)
- [STRM][SUBJ][SIZE] JetStream maintains indexes on subject names inside streams, so getting the first or last message for nasdaq.microsoft is a single fast operation, not a scan; filtering happens server-side and only matching messages are transmitted. "internally JetStream maintains indexes on those subject names that are contained into the streams" (~16:16)
- [CONS][MYTH] Terminology mapping: a Kafka consumer group is what JetStream calls a consumer; Kafka's consumers are JetStream's client applications. "Kafka's concept of consumer groups is what in JetStream we call just consumers" (~17:17)
- [CONS][PATTERN] A JetStream consumer is like a database view on a stream: it can filter and can be shared by many client applications. "you can look at a consumer ... as essentially like a view on a stream" (~18:19)
- [CONS][CLNT] JetStream consumers hold state on the server (position, pending acks); Kafka consumer groups leave offset persistence to client applications, so NATS clients are purely stateless. "there's nothing for the client application to persist ever" (~19:21)
- [CONS][MYTH] Kafka is designed for one client application at a time per topic partition; distributing a topic across clients requires partitioning, whereas JetStream needs no partitions by default. "if you want to distribute messages in a topic amongst a set of client applications ... you must use partitioning" (~20:22)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Deterministic partitioning can be added in JetStream via server-side subject mapping that hashes chosen subject tokens and inserts a partition-number token, so foo.bar always lands on the same partition. "inserts a token in the subject that has a partition number" (~21:23)
- [MYTH][STRM] Kafka stores data in a write-ahead log where you can only append at the head and compact the tail; individual messages cannot be deleted. "there's no ability to delete individual messages in a Kafka stream" (~22:25)
- [STRM] JetStream behaves like a NoSQL-style data store, including deleting individual messages. "it has a functionality that you expect of a form of database ... that includes the ability to delete individual messages" (~23:25)
- [STRM][MYTH] Kafka always wants to accept writes; the only limit is stream size or time; JetStream lets you choose what happens at a limit, including per-subject limits Kafka cannot express. "you can also have limits on a per subject basis ... you can't do that with Kafka" (~24:25)
- [STRM][KV] Kafka's compaction keeps "at least" one message per key; a JetStream per-subject limit of 1 is exactly one. "it's a limit of exactly one right not an at least" (~25:26)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Discard-new plus max-messages-per-subject gives database-like constraints usable for distributed locking or gating: a second publish to a subject at its limit fails in the ack. "using a stream for distributed locking logic gating things like that" (~26:26)
- [KV][OBJ][STRM] KV and Object Store are possible only because streams combine subject-based addressing with enforced limits (e.g. keep last 5 per subject). "this is only possible because both you have subject-based addressing in streams and you have this ability to have constraints" (~27:27)
- [STRM][PATTERN] JetStream supports CRUD-style concurrency control: insert only if no message exists on the subject, and compare-and-set updates by expecting the last sequence on the subject. "I'm expecting the current last message on that subject to be sequence number 37 ... if it has been changed then that operation fails" (~29:29)
- [MYTH] Kafka has only upsert semantics with no concurrency control for two publishers on the same key. "you don't have the concept of being able to have concurrency access control in Kafka" (~30:31)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Rollup is an atomic controlled update that replaces all prior messages on a subject with one summarising message. "replace them with just one message ... that's one atomic operation in JetStream" (~32:35)
- [SIZE][MYTH] Kafka's throughput comes from batching and a deliberately simple write path aimed at throughput, not latency; Kafka latencies are measured in milliseconds. "latencies in Kafka typically measures in milliseconds" (~34:41)
- [CORE][STRM][SIZE] Core NATS and even JetStream latencies are measured in microseconds: one-way or two-way in the 100–200 µs range over a network, under 100 µs one-way on a fast network. "over this network you're talking 1 to 200 microsecond ranges ... with fast network below 100 microseconds" (~34:41)
- [STRM][CLNT][PATTERN] JetStream can also batch via asynchronous publishes for much higher write throughput; batching trades away real-time latency, and NATS leaves that trade-off to the engineer. "you can use asynchronous operations to get much higher write throughputs by doing batching" (~33:38)
- [MYTH] The speakers admit Kafka scales beautifully horizontally for accepting writes thanks to hard partitions, at the cost of having to deal with partitions. "Kafka scales beautifully horizontally because of partitions ... which is another issue" (~36:44)

## NATS & Kafka Compared Pt 2: Consumers | Rethink Connectivity
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TpMBo-rRAGQ
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz and Jean-Noël Moyne (Synadia) | date: 2023 (mentions the just-released simplified JetStream API) | duration: 27:09
- version context: 2.10 era (simplified JetStream client API "just came out")

### Claims
- [CONS][MYTH] Kafka consumer group = JetStream consumer; JetStream consumers can be shared by any number of client applications without partitions. "consumers in JetStream can be shared by any number of client applications at any given time without having to have partitioning" (~02:02)
- [CONS][MYTH] In Kafka only one consuming application at a time can read a topic partition, because of how (the lack of) acknowledgments work. "you can only have one consuming application at a time per partition of a topic" (~03:03)
- [CONS][PATTERN] JetStream distributes messages among client applications attached to a consumer evenly and according to demand, so you can scale clients up and down freely. "the consumer will automatically evenly and according to demand distribute the messages between those consuming applications" (~04:06)
- [ANTI][MYTH] Changing Kafka partition counts does not rebalance data, so teams over-partition up front (e.g. 100 partitions as a high-water mark for max consumers). "you cannot have more than just one single client application per topic partition ... so you over partition" (~05:07)
- [CONS][CLNT] Kafka client applications must persist their own offset; JetStream client applications persist no state. "the consuming applications in JetStream do not need to persist any state at all" (~07:10)
- [CONS] Kafka replay options are start, end, or a specific offset; JetStream adds last-per-subject, first-per-subject, by-time (e.g. last 2 hours), and rate-limited original-timing replay. "play back everything for the last two hours 10 minutes whatever it is" (~09:11)
- [CONS][OPS] Original-rate replay (metered at the ingest rate) is useful for debugging real-time applications. "only replay it at the same rate that it was initially put into the stream" (~10:13)
- [CONS][SUBJ] A consumer subject filter (explicit or wildcard) acts like a non-materialized SQL view: no copy of messages, only a little iteration state. "it's not materialized ... the stream doesn't create another copy of the messages" (~11:14)
- [CONS][USECASE][PATTERN] For edge devices on flaky 5G, deliver-last-per-subject avoids replaying five stale "beep" commands after reconnect; the consumer policy encodes business intent. "it probably doesn't want to beep five times ... give me the last message per this particular subject" (~13:16)
- [MYTH] Kafka gives no filtering: you pick a start position and get a fire hose the application must sift. "there's no filtering right it's all or nothing" (~14:16)
- [STRM][KV][SIZE] Direct get of the last or first message for an exact subject is how KV works; it is a get, not a query, and over loopback runs in the tens of microseconds. "the order of magnitude is tens of microseconds when going over loopback" (~15:17)
- [CONS] Durable consumers are long-lived and typically created administratively; use them to distribute messages across clients, or for a single transient application that must resume where it left off without client state. "it picks up automatically from that consumer where it was" (~18:21)
- [CONS] An ephemeral consumer is auto-deleted after a configurable inactivity period; it suits an application wanting its own copy of the messages and willing to re-read from the start on restart. "if there's no client application connected to it for a certain amount of time ... it automatically gets cleared up" (~18:21)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Analogy: a durable is a view on a table; an ephemeral is a query whose result set you iterate again on restart. "ephemeral it's just simply a query over which you iterate the result set" (~19:22)
- [CONS][USECASE] A browser whiteboard used ephemeral consumers per JavaScript client (start at beginning, then live updates), cleaned up when the browser closes; a web service or data pipeline should use a durable. "somebody closes their browser and we want that to be cleaned up" (~20:23)
- [STRM][CONS] A stream has exactly one order for all messages and every consumer, ephemeral or durable, delivers in that order; the tricky part is preserving order under errors. "there's just one order of all the messages into your stream" (~20:23)
- [CONS] JetStream consumers are flow controlled with two forms: one-to-many via max ack pending across all clients on a consumer, and one-to-one via pull batch sizes. "the maximum number of acknowledgments pending at any given time that you can control" (~23:25)
- [CONS] Push consumers send ahead using pub/sub underneath; pull consumers send only on fetch demand (next message or batch of N). "pull the messages are only sent on demand when the application says fetch me the next message" (~23:25)
- [CONS][MYTH] Kafka is pull-only with one-to-one flow control and has no one-to-many flow control. "in the case of Kafka it's only pull so you only have one to one flow control" (~24:27)
- [CLNT] The new simplified JetStream API hides push-versus-pull; you just create consumers and choose how to iterate. "it totally hides those subtleties" (~25:29)
- [CONS] You can create as many consumers as you want on a stream; each iterates its own view of all messages, and a deletion in the stream is reflected in every consumer. "each consumer will iterate through its own set of all the messages in the stream" (~26:29)

## Move over Kafka! Let's try NATS JetStream
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EJJ2SG-cKyM
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz (Synadia) | date: 2022 (early Rethink Connectivity, follows the core NATS episode) | duration: 13:36
- version context: 2.8/2.9 era (nats-server run dev context, push consumers default, old CLI flows)

### Claims
- [STRM] JetStream is a persistence layer on top of core NATS: same pub/sub APIs, with opt-in persistence for certain messages so they can be delivered later. "you get to use all of the same NATS pub sub APIs but you get to opt in to have certain messages persisted" (~00:01)
- [TOPO][OPS] NATS runs a hybrid model: in a cluster some servers can be core-only and some JetStream-enabled, mixed to match required scale, and stream placement is chosen deliberately. "you can run some of them as NATS core servers or you can run some of them as JetStream servers" (~01:03)
- [OPS] The CLI is only one way to create streams; Terraform and client SDKs can create them too. "you can also create streams through terraform or you can create them directly in the client libraries" (~02:03)
- [STRM] Retention policies: limits (default), interest and work queue; the latter two still obey limits but add rules. The speaker's description of work queue as "discard after all consumers acknowledged" and interest as "throw away messages no consumer is interested in" is the reverse of the definitions given in later episodes. "the work queue policy will discard the message after all of the consumers have acknowledged it whereas the interest policy will actually throw away any messages that no consumers are interested in" (~03:04)
- [STRM][CLNT] Publishers can keep using plain core NATS publish with no JetStream knowledge; the server decides whether a message needs persisting. "publishers can continue to use NATS core they actually don't have to have any knowledge of JetStream" (~04:04)
- [CONS][OPS] `nats sub --stream` reads from a stream with start options: all, new, last, last-per-subject (with a subject), or from a specific sequence number. "if i wanted to read a last message from a certain subject i can just say last per subject" (~05:05)
- [CONS] CLI subscriptions so far were ephemeral consumers, created on the fly and cleaned up on disconnect; a durable consumer remembers what has been consumed across runs. "when the client disconnects they get cleaned up" (~06:05)
- [CONS] Consumer state (cursor, last consumed) is stored server-side, so clients need no cursor handling. "the clients don't have to have any sort of special handling of cursors" (~06:05)
- [CONS] Push consumers receive messages as fast as the server can send; pull consumers fetch one at a time or in batches. "the server pushes messages to this consumer as fast as it possibly can" (~07:06)
- [CONS] Pull consumers require the explicit ack policy; replay policy can be instant or original (same spacing as first published). "since we're using a pull consumer we actually have to choose the explicit policy" (~07:06)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Pull fetches with timeouts let you scale down workers when the queue drains. "it allows you to essentially scale down workers as they time out and there's no messages left in the queue" (~08:07)
- [KV][STRM] KV buckets are streams underneath: you configure history depth and, because it is a stream, placement in the cluster. "because this is just a stream underneath you also get to choose where in the cluster you want to put your store" (~09:07)
- [KV][PATTERN] KV watch notifies on key updates, a powerful primitive for distributed systems. "being able to know when certain values get updated" (~10:08)
- [OBJ] Object store splits large files into chunks and relies on ordered replay to reassemble them. "large files are broken up into multiple chunks and because NATS JetStream messages can be replayed in order you can reassemble" (~10:08)
- [OPS][KV][OBJ] KV and object store streams are hidden from normal stream commands; use the `-a` flag to list them. "you can fix this by using the a flag to list all the streams" (~10:08)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Stream sourcing builds a stream from one or more other streams, with its own ownership, location and retention rules, including per-source start sequence and subject filters (e.g. orders.eu plus returns.eu into archive-eu). "a stream that gets its data from one or more other streams with all of its own rules around ownership location and retention" (~11:11)

## Comparing and contrasting NATS and Kafka | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=F2wutVP733c
- speaker: Jean-Noël Moyne (Synadia), introduced by Jeremy Saenz | date: 2022 (RethinkConn '22) | duration: 20:01
- version context: 2.9 era (RethinkConn 2022; mentions Benthos as ecosystem)

### Claims
- [MYTH][STRM] Kafka is a distributed append-only commit log; NATS with JetStream is a distributed messaging platform with added persistent storage. "Kafka is a distributed append-only commit log ... NATS and JetStream which is a distributed messaging platform with added persistent storage" (~01:00)
- [STRM] Kafka only compacts logs; JetStream is an immediately consistent messaging store where individual messages can be deleted, which changes which use cases are feasible. "JetStream which is actually an immediately consistent messaging store ... you can delete individual messages" (~02:03)
- [SUBJ][MYTH] Subject-based addressing is not the same as topics; Kafka doing pub/sub on topics does not equal subject-based addressing. "people think because Kafka says we do pub sub with topics that they do proper pub sub with subject-based addressing that's not the case" (~03:04)
- [SUBJ][STRM] Stream subjects do not need to be created ahead of time; streams capture by wildcard. "the subjects do not need to be created ahead of time" (~04:06)
- [MYTH][ANTI] Kafka topics usually need predefinition; auto-created topics default to one partition and topic creation can trigger re-partitioning across servers. "the default number of partition is one and that's not very useful in Kafka for many cases" (~05:06)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] With subject-based addressing the key or unique ID is naturally part of the subject, can be a composite of many tokens, and can include fields you will filter on when consuming. "you can use as many tokens as you need for making up the key so like a composite key" (~06:06)
- [SUBJ] Subjects can also be mapped, split and sliced by server-side subject mapping. "subjects can also in NATS always be mapped using subject-based addressing mapping and they can be split and sliced" (~06:06)
- [MYTH][ANTI] Filtering in Kafka requires a Kafka Streams process that reads everything and writes filtered sub-streams, storing messages more than once. "so you end up storing the message actually more than once" (~07:07)
- [CONS][STRM] JetStream consumer filters are pushed to the server, which uses indexing rather than a full scan and sends only matching records; filters support `*` and `>` and can combine with a start time. "it doesn't normally do a full table scan over the stream ... it uses indexing" (~08:10)
- [CONS][MYTH] JetStream consumers (Kafka consumer groups) are partition-less, stateful, and their state is persisted and replicated along with the stream. "they also are stateful and the state can be persisted and replicated along with the stream of the data" (~10:13)
- [CONS][MYTH] JetStream has push and pull delivery with one-to-one and one-to-many flow control; Kafka has pull only with one-to-one flow control. "Kafka only has the one to one flow control using pull" (~11:14)
- [CONS] JetStream cursor positioning: start, new, sequence, last, last-per-subject, or a time in the past; Kafka can only seek start, end or offset. "there's no ability to say give me the last hour or give me the last message on this subject" (~11:14)
- [CORE][STRM] Core NATS is at-most-once; JetStream and Kafka default to at-least-once, redelivering to subscribers that were absent at publish time. "core NATS is at most once ... JetStream and Kafka give you by default at least once" (~12:17)
- [CONS] JetStream acknowledgments are per individual message with ack, term (do not redeliver), nak (reprocess later) and in-progress (extend the deadline), plus nak backoff timing and DLQ-style functionality. "term a message saying don't try to redeliver it, nak saying I cannot process this message reprocess it later, or in progress" (~13:18)
- [MYTH][CONS] Kafka consumer groups only support cumulative offset acks; there is no individual acknowledgment and redelivery means the application seeks manually. "there's no concept of acknowledging individual messages" (~13:18)
- [STRM] Exactly-once has two parts; the publishing half is deduplication, needed when a pub ack is lost or the client crashes between publish and ack and republishes. "you end up having that message twice in the stream" (~14:19)
- [STRM][MYTH] JetStream has a built-in deduplication window over a configurable time that works across client sessions; Kafka's built-in dedup is per session, so a crash-and-resend still duplicates unless you use Kafka Streams. "the built-in deduplication feature of Kafka is only per session" (~15:22)
- [CONS] JetStream provides double acknowledgments for reliable consumption. "JetStream gives you double acknowledgements" (~16:23)
- [STRM] JetStream streams are read-write: usable as queues, safe deletion of individual messages, encryption, limits and discard policies richer than Kafka's. "JetStream streams are actually read write which means you can use them as queues" (~16:23)
- [OPS][MYTH] Matching JetStream's functionality with Kafka means brokers, ZooKeeper, Kafka Streams JVMs, MirrorMaker for cross-cluster replication, Redis for KV, a separate message broker, and Kafka Connect JVMs; NATS covers most of it in one binary, plus Benthos for stream processing apps. "compare the number of JVMs as far as the eye can see ... to a single binary that runs all of these at once" (~18:27)
- [MYTH] The speaker explicitly does not claim NATS replaces all Kafka; the pitch is fewer moving parts for many use cases. "we're not saying replace all your Kafka with NATS right we're just saying consider NATS" (~19:30)

## NATS Connect Live! | JetStream
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AJN0ZbFL0co
- speaker: R.I. Pienaar (Synadia) | date: 2020 (NATS Connect Live; JetStream tech preview, "release 2.2" upcoming) | duration: 22:12
- version context: 2.1 / JetStream tech preview era, pre-2.2 (single-server only, clustering in design) — [STALE?] throughout

### Claims
- [STALE?][MIG][STRM] JetStream is the next generation of NATS streaming technology, replacing the separate NATS Streaming server binary with one server binary. "we've made it into a single server binary so anyone who has NATS will have JetStream" (~01:03)
- [STALE?][MIG] NATS 2.0 changed the security and deployment model, forcing a revisit of how streaming worked. "NATS 2.0 has changed basically security model and deployment model of NATS and so we have to revisit how we handle streaming" (~01:03)
- [STRM][CORE] JetStream brings at-least-once delivery only to specific subjects; core publish to no listeners is gone, at-least-once means the server holds it for later consumers. "brings at least once delivery model only to specific subjects" (~01:03)
- [STALE?][MIG][CLNT] Any standard NATS client in any of the 40+ languages can interact with JetStream, unlike Streaming server which needed dedicated clients. "you can use any standard NATS client that you have" (~02:06)
- [STRM][SEC][TOPO] JetStream plugs into NATS routing, security and multi-tenancy: one compute set can serve completely isolated data stores per account, sharing data only when required. "completely isolated data stores streaming services from completely isolated subject namespaces on top of NATS" (~03:07)
- [CONS] JetStream supports push (messages as soon as available) and pull (good for horizontal scale-out of workers), plus a work-queue style where a message is removed once all interested parties have consumed it. "pull base model which is really good for scaling out horizontally" (~03:07)
- [STRM][CLNT] JetStream administration is an API over the NATS wire: publish JSON to well-known subjects, so no custom client is required. "you just publish a JSON message on to a well-known subject and that's how you access the API" (~04:09)
- [STRM][SUBJ][MIG] Streams listen on wildcard subjects, a key difference from NATS Streaming; order.received, order.processed and order.completed can all land in one stream. "we support wildcards ... this is a key difference from NATS streaming server to JetStream" (~07:13)
- [CONS][PATTERN] A stream is a log; multiple services consume it with each having a unique view (position, ack state, push or pull, acks or not); a consumer describes how a set of related services consumes. "each have a unique view over that data that can be in different places within the data" (~07:13)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Pull consumers let 20–40 worker services each ask for the next message when ready, replacing round-robin or least-weighted routing; a worker can ack, refuse work, or ask for more time. "you can scale up horizontally by having 20 or 30 or 40 of these worker services" (~09:15)
- [CONS][OPS] For observability the key metrics are how many times a message had to be redelivered and how long processing took; JetStream emits advisory events (e.g. "took ten milliseconds, tried four times") usable for dashboards and alerting without extra logic in services. "how many times has this message had to be redelivered ... and how long did it take for that message to be processed" (~11:17)
- [OPS] The new `nats` CLI consolidated scattered utilities (nats-pub, nats-sub, nats-bench, nats-box) into one tool that also configures JetStream, backed by a Go library for building your own tooling. "I pulled them all into one standard CLI that supports benchmarking ... it is the same utility that you use to configure the entire JetStream system" (~13:20)
- [OPS][PATTERN] Streams can be created by the microservice on startup, by CI/CD via the CLI's unattended mode, or by the Terraform provider for teams using a remote JetStream. "stand up a JetStream just for the purpose of that single CI run" (~14:21)
- [OPS][SEC] JetStream publishes a full ordered log of API interactions (who created streams, changed config, tried to consume), and all APIs fit into normal NATS authorization so you can restrict who may create or only view. "we have a full ordered log of all the API interactions" (~15:25)
- [STRM][PATTERN] A dead-letter-queue equivalent: configure max delivery attempts (e.g. 10) and JetStream publishes an event with the message content when exceeded. "configure messages only let me try ten times ... then we will publish an event saying that message's bad" (~16:27)
- [STALE?][OPS] At the time JetStream was a single-server tech preview not in the release binary; it would ship in 2.2 behind a feature flag, still single-server, with clustering across three servers targeted for around Q3. "by release 2.2 of NATS server you will get JetStream delivered to you ... behind a feature flag" (~17:27)
- [STALE?][OPS] Planned: server introspection APIs and event streams so administrators learn about problems (e.g. JetStream unable to write to disk) without log-file access. "we don't want only the people who have access to the log file to be aware of that" (~18:30)
- [STALE?][MIG] NATS Streaming server would be supported as a production platform, with security fixes, through mid-2023 but with no major new feature development; migration guides and a data migration tool were promised. "we will continue to support it as production platform ... we don't anticipate major new feature development" (~20:35)

## Getting Started with NATS JetStream: Streams, Storage, and Data Lifecycle
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6THUHpvtY4
- speaker: Colin Lacy (Synadia) | date: 2025 (Synadia channel, OpenTofu-era tutorial series) | duration: 15:51
- version context: 2.11 era (Synadia 2025 tutorial series; supercluster on EKS + Azure)

### Claims
- [STRM] A stream is dedicated data storage for a named set of subjects; with clustering you add replication so one server or disk failure leaves a copy. "if one of these NATS servers goes down, one of these discs get corrupted, you have a backup copy for high availability" (~02:03)
- [STRM][CONS] A stream retains data even with no consumers, so a consumer created later still receives it (at-least-once). "Even if you don't have any consumers, the stream will retain that data for you" (~03:04)
- [OPS][SEC] JetStream must be enabled at the server level and separately at the account level; without both it is not usable by that account. "you also have to activate it at the account level" (~04:04)
- [OPS] On Kubernetes, JetStream needs a persistent storage mechanism such as a PVC. "As long as your underlying infrastructure has a storage mechanism that JetStream can use, a PVC in Kubernetes world" (~04:04)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Route a response to different subjects by classification (answers.significant vs answers.throwaway) so consumers can filter per subject later. "If it's less than one, I will publish it to answers.throwaway" (~06:06)
- [OPS] Streams and consumers can be managed with the CLI, Terraform/OpenTofu provider, GitHub Actions, or the Kubernetes JetStream controller. "You can use Terraform or Open Tofu ... You can use GitHub actions. And you can also use a Kubernetes JetStream controller" (~07:08)
- [STRM][ANTI] Memory storage works but is not durable; use file storage for disk durability. "If you used the storage memory mechanism ... it would store data in memory. I don't want that" (~08:08)
- [STRM][OPS][ANTI] Default limits are unlimited, meaning data piles up with no cleanup; set limits so NATS cleans up automatically. "my maximums are all set to be unlimited, which means I'm just going to keep on piling data on without any data cleanup. That's not great" (~09:09)
- [STRM] Lowering max bytes (46 KB to 1 KB) or max messages on a live stream immediately truncates to the newest messages that fit. "I have eight messages left. It all has to sit under this 1 kilobyte limit" (~11:11)
- [STRM][OPS] When setting max age, the duplicate window must be set lower than the max age. "I also have to decrease the duplicate window to less than the max age, a configuration setting you just have to be aware of" (~12:11)
- [STRM] Setting max age below the age of existing messages deletes them on apply. "they're gone. Why are they gone? Because they were older than 20 seconds" (~13:12)
- [OPS] `nats stream subjects <stream>` breaks down message counts per subject. "92 of the responses that I got were throwaway and 308 were significant" (~15:14)

## Why NATS Consumers Just Work (And How to Use Them in 15 Minutes)
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANt_OCpcvk0
- speaker: Colin Lacy (Synadia) | date: 2025 (follow-up to the streams video) | duration: 16:53
- version context: 2.11 era (Synadia 2025 tutorial series; Python client pull_subscribe API)

### Claims
- [CONS] A consumer is how you get data out of a stream; it can pull a filtered subset or everything from the beginning, and multiple consumers can share a stream to build fan-out, fan-in and saga patterns. "you can follow all the standard event-driven patterns like fan out, fan in, saga" (~01:01)
- [CONS] Consumers are filters on a specific stream and must be bound to one at creation. "consumers are filters on a specific stream. So when you set up a consumer, it has to be tied to a stream" (~03:05)
- [CONS][SEC] A client must be authorized to subscribe on subjects matching the consumer's filter (a broader wildcard is fine); otherwise the subscription is rejected. "Without this block, any service that tries to subscribe to this consumer will get rejected because it hasn't been authorized" (~04:07)
- [OPS] `nats consumer info` shows where the consumer runs and its unprocessed count, which matches the per-subject count in the stream. "It's got 308 unprocessed messages ... It matches" (~06:10)
- [CLNT][CONS] Pull fetches need a timeout so the process can leave the fetch, re-evaluate and run other work; the speaker uses 5 seconds, not 500 ms or 1 s. "You have to pass in a timeout ... 5 seconds is good" (~08:11)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Three pods pulling on one durable consumer were load balanced automatically and roughly evenly, with variance explained by node speed or distance from the data. "that's automatic load balancing built in because each pod is pulling whenever it's ready" (~10:13)
- [CONS] A durable consumer is stateful: after draining it reports zero unprocessed and will only deliver the next new messages. "My answers consumer is now aware that it has no unprocessed messages. So, it's stateful" (~12:14)
- [CONS][ANTI] An ephemeral consumer does not track progress: it is created with a generated name, disappears when done, and re-running re-delivers everything (92 rows became 184). "I'm creating a new consumer that isn't tracking state ... 92 throwaway answers twice" (~15:18)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Ephemeral consumers suit one-off fire-hose reads of a stream or subject. "useful if you ever want to just pull fire hose of all the data that's stored in a stream" (~15:18)

## NATS JetStream for Key-Value Store Tech Preview
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yYL0ZGTNomE
- speaker: R.I. Pienaar (Synadia) | date: 2021 (KV experimental preview, pre-2.6) | duration: 09:44
- version context: 2.3–2.5 era, KV experimental — [STALE?] for API details, the semantics largely persist

### Claims
- [STRM][SIZE] Max-messages-per-subject limits keep N historical values per subject (e.g. 100 per device) instead of a global total, so busy writers do not push out idle ones. "keep a hundred historical values per device rather than keep a thousand messages in total" (~00:00)
- [KV][STRM] Storing every key as a subject and values as messages, with per-subject limits, is what makes a KV store on JetStream possible. "if you store every key as a subject and the value as values in the stream you have a kv store" (~01:02)
- [KV] A bucket is created with replicas (e.g. 3), placement (e.g. London cluster), a history depth (e.g. 5 values per key), and optional TTL that expires keys regardless of access. "we want to keep five historical values for every key so if you make a mistake you can just go back" (~01:02)
- [KV] KV supports watchers on the whole bucket or a single key, and per-key history shows how a value changed over time. "we support watchers so i can say watch cfg so we'll watch the entire bucket for all writes" (~03:06)
- [KV] Deleting a key writes a delete marker into history rather than removing data; a get then reports unknown key while history remains for recovery. "we're actually writing a delete operation into the history rather than deleting the data" (~04:07)
- [KV][SIZE] KV workloads are read-heavy; APIs were added to make reads in that scenario very fast. "kv tend to be very read heavy operations so you will write few times but very often read" (~05:08)
- [KV][TOPO][PATTERN] The backing stream can be replicated to other clusters in a supercluster as read replicas; read-only workers read locally and never talk to the origin, while writes go to the origin with a small replication delay. "if they know they're only ever going to read they never have to communicate to london" (~06:09)
- [KV][CLNT][PATTERN] The Go client offers an in-memory bucket cache: it starts a watcher, loads the whole bucket, marks ready, serves reads from memory, and writes invalidate the key until the watcher refreshes it. "before you need it even your cache will already be up to date" (~07:10)
- [KV][SEC] Encoders and decoders allow encrypting keys and values for end-to-end zero-trust storage. "you can encrypt your keys and your values to have completely end-to-end zero trust storage" (~07:10)
- [STALE?][KV] KV design is documented in an ADR (architecture design record); at the time the API and model might still change. "we'll be tweaking the api a little bit we'll be maybe changing the model a little bit" (~08:12)
- [STALE?][PATTERN] Leader election and concurrency control (e.g. only 10 of 1,000 instances allowed to run) were flagged as upcoming JetStream capabilities. "out of a thousand possible instances that needs to run only 10 at a time are allowed to run" (~09:13)

## NATS JetStream Mirror Streams Explained — One-Way Replication Made Simple
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rGT6DlQkyEY
- speaker: unknown (Synadia channel presenter) | date: 2025 (mentions mirror promotion "landed in NATS 2.12") | duration: 10:00
- version context: 2.12 (mirror promotion is a 2.12 feature)

### Claims
- [STRM][TOPO] A mirror is a replica that automatically and asynchronously syncs from exactly one origin stream; the relationship is strictly one-to-one. "each mirror can only replicate from a single origin stream. It's a strict one-to-one relationship" (~00:00)
- [STRM] Mirrors are read-only for publishing, but you can delete messages on demand and consumers have full capabilities. "mirrors are read only. Your clients can't directly publish to them ... you can still delete messages on demand" (~00:00)
- [STRM] Mirrors preserve origin sequence numbers and timestamps: sequence 42 at the origin is 42 in the mirror. "if a message was sequence number 42 in the origin, it'll be 42 in the mirror also" (~01:00)
- [STRM][OPS] Mirror configuration lives entirely on the receiving side; the origin needs no setup and does not even see a consumer created. "It won't even see a consumer created for the replication" (~01:00)
- [STRM] Mirror options: name (required), start sequence, start time, filter subject, subject transforms, and domain for hub-and-leaf topologies. "domain specifies which JetStream domain the origin stream lives in. Useful for hub and leaf topologies" (~01:00)
- [STRM][ANTI] Filter subject and subject transform cannot be combined on a mirror. "you can't use filter subject and subject transform together. You got to pick one" (~02:00)
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Use mirrors for geographic distribution, fan-out from one origin to many mirrors serving millions of clients, and cross-account or cross-domain replication. "One origin stream can feed multiple mirrors, perfect for fan-out topologies that serve millions of client connections" (~02:00)
- [STRM][PATTERN] With the mirror direct attribute, clients read directly from mirror replicas instead of being routed to the origin, spreading read load. "With mirror direct clients can read directly from the mirror replicas instead of being routed back to the origin" (~02:00)
- [STRM] Changes never flow backward: deleting from a mirror leaves the origin untouched, and origin deletes are not replicated to the mirror. "deletes in the origin stream are not replicated" (~03:02)
- [STRM][ANTI] Mirroring a work-queue origin is only partially supported and not resilient over intermittent links like leaf nodes; interest-based origins are unsupported with undefined behaviour. "if you're using interest-based retention, don't try it. Mirror streams don't officially support that" (~03:02)
- [STRM][SIZE] Mirrors tolerate a temporarily unreachable origin and retry after roughly 10 to 20 seconds. "the mirror waits about 10 to 20 seconds before retrying" (~03:02)
- [STRM] Publishing to a mirror fails with an "expected stream does not match" error. "it says expected stream does not match because mirrors only pull from the origin" (~05:06)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Because deletes are independent on each side, mirrors can serve as independent backups. "Deletes on one side don't affect the other. This makes mirrors useful as independent backups" (~06:06)
- [STRM][OPS] Mirror promotion (2.12): unbind subjects from the old primary (e.g. set subjects to a dev-null placeholder), remove the mirror config and bind the subjects to it, then clean up the old stream. "first unbind subjects from the old primary so you don't have two streams competing for the same subjects" (~07:07)
- [STRM][ANTI] The server does not verify the mirror is caught up before promotion, so unreplicated messages are lost. "the server won't verify if the mirror is fully caught up, so any unreplicated messages will be lost" (~07:07)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Mirrors are the tool for one-way replication across regions and unreliable networks without full synchronisation; they work best with standard (limits) retention. "they work best with standard retention policies" (~09:10)
