## EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jDBwS-FuRG8
- speaker: David (host, NATS.fm) and Byron Ruth (Synadia) | date: unknown (autumn after the 2.10 release; pumpkin-carving season, so likely Oct 2023) | duration: 81:34
- version context: 2.10 era (speaker cites "with 2.10 we added multiple filters" and the 2.10 subject-transform partitioning feature)

### Claims
- [SUBJ][STRM][PATTERN] Put the discriminating data (e.g. dwelling ID, room) in the subject, not buried in the payload or header, because consumer filtering works only on subjects. "definitely expose that bit of data in the subject so you can discriminate ... the degree of subscription filtering on the consumer side is all based on the subject" (~06:30)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Design the subject hierarchy for the consumption side: publishers can publish anywhere, but subscribers must be able to differentiate with wildcards. "when you're modeling your subject hierarchy it's really frankly for the consumption side" (~07:06)
- [STRM][TOPO][SIZE] Co-locating a stream near the data source (per region/neighbourhood) reduces collection latency and improves availability compared with publishing across the country. "whatever the granularity ... to make a stream accessible to that's going to obviously reduce latency of collection ... provide availability" (~10:11)
- [STRM][CORE] A NATS stream provides a total ordering on ingest; consumers always observe the same order regardless of how many publishers there are. "a stream in NATS provides a total ordering on ingest ... from a consumption side it's always going to observe the same order" (~11:14)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Choose one stream vs many based on access patterns: how much ordering you need across entities, how co-located streams should be, and ingest rate. "the choice of one stream versus many streams really kind of comes down to how collocated do you want those streams to be and also frankly the rate of ingest" (~12:16)
- [STRM][SIZE] A single stream cannot exceed the throughput of the disk it writes to, so ingest rate alone may force you to split into multiple streams. "you can't obviously exceed past the throughput of your disk ... it might be necessary from a purely physical technical perspective that you actually have to break up the ingestion" (~13:17)
- [SUBJ][STRM] Even with N streams, consumers still address data by subject filter, so you can drill down to a dwelling or zip code across a region-partitioned layout. "you can have n number of streams and you can still say I define a consumer I'm still interested in these particular subjects" (~13:17)
- [SUBJ][STRM][PATTERN] Publishers only care about the subject, not the physical stream; subject mapping and stream sourcing let you route to the right underlying stream and change the stream topology over time. "on the publisher side all you care about is what subject you're publishing to not concretely the stream behind the scenes" (~16:23)
- [STRM] The stream ingest timestamp is storage time when the server received the message, not the time the data was collected at the source; carry a source timestamp in the message if you need it. "it gives you a time stamp but that's really storage time when the server gets it not necessarily the time that the data was actually collected" (~18:24)
- [CONS][STRM] Consumers must know which physical stream they bind to; this is the asymmetry with the publisher side. "you do have to know which physical stream you're consuming from" (~19:26)
- [SEC][SUBJ][PATTERN] A sensor should be authorized to publish only to its own dwelling-ID-prefixed subject pattern, which doubles as a sort key over the data. "it should only in theory be authorized to publish to say a guid dot something or a pattern" (~20:30)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Stream sourcing multiplexes many origin streams into one aggregate stream asynchronously, like a materialized view; origin streams stay lightweight and highly available while the sourcing stream can have different retention. "I'm going to multiplex all of the data from all of these source streams ... and I'm going to funnel it all into one stream" (~22:32)
- [STRM][SIZE] A sourcing stream that aggregates tens, hundreds or thousands of origin streams needs correspondingly large disk. "if you're sourcing data from tens hundreds thousands of streams ... you're probably going to need a fairly beefy amount of disk space" (~23:32)
- [CONS][STRM] 2.10 added multiple, possibly disjoint, subject filters on a single consumer. "with 2.10 we added the ability to define multiple filters now which is really nice that can be disjoint" (~24:34)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Split workflows with two consumers on the same stream: one for real-time analytics and one archiving to external object storage; the aggregate can be short-retention while origins retain. "I have two consumers one for the real-time analytics and one for persisting out to stable object storage" (~25:35)
- [ANTI][STRM] Avoid the design where everything must synchronously deluge into one single stream; prefer origin streams plus async sourcing. "rather than saying I have this one single stream that everything basically has to deluge into synchronously" (~25:35)
- [STRM][SIZE][OPS] Every R3 stream adds load; a per-dwelling stream model multiplies replication cost, so size streams to hardware I/O limits rather than administrative units. "once you say let's have an R3 ... immediately the load on the system increases with each and every stream" (~27:36)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Start with the simplest setup, a single stream, if throughput, reachability and latency allow; only add streams when requirements force it. "if we can get by with a single stream that can handle everything that's the simplest thing to operate" (~28:37)
- [STRM][MYTH] Unlike topic/partition systems where the partition is the unit of total order and replication, a NATS stream is itself totally ordered in storage and messages are addressable by subject. "NATS is different in that we have a single stream which is totally ordered on ingest ... versus other systems that are more like topic and partition based" (~29:40)
- [SUBJ][STRM] Partition-based systems cannot filter by a subject hierarchy or tell you which partition holds a given key; NATS can address by known subject. "I can't address it by a subject that's known" (~30:42)
- [STRM][SUBJ] A single stream can hold heterogeneous message types, discriminated by subject. "you can have heterogeneous types of data in a single stream and you can discriminate them again based on subject" (~31:42)
- [SUBJ][STRM] A stream capturing foo.> stores foo.1, foo.10, foo.42 in one ordered log; subjects sort data within the stream, they do not route it elsewhere unless configured. "it's not going to break the ordering either so the subject names really give us a means of sorting data" (~33:46)
- [STRM][CORE] A stream is an internal server-side subscriber on the configured subjects whose job is to persist messages to disk or memory; it decouples time as core NATS decouples space. "the job of the stream is literally an internal subscriber in the server ... my job is literally to persist this on your behalf" (~34:46)
- [STRM][TOPO] In a replicated stream the leader receives the message, stores it, sends it to replicas, and the ack chain completes; consumption is fully decoupled from that. "the leader's job is to say I'm subscribed to this subject ... stores it to disk ... sends it off to its other replicas they store it you get your ack chain" (~35:49)
- [CONS][MYTH] You do not subscribe to a stream; you consume from it via a consumer, which is a server-side construct you attach to from the client. "you don't subscribe to the stream you consume from the stream this is where we see this a lot" (~39:53)
- [CONS] A consumer tracks delivered, in-flight and acknowledged messages; on ack it advances its offset. "it has all this internal state to keep track of which messages have I delivered which messages are in flight" (~41:55)
- [CONS] Consumers give at-least-once delivery by default and redeliver unacked messages after the ack wait timer as long as client interest exists. "I have this at least once guarantee of delivery by default with a consumer and so it's just going to redeliver until the client says otherwise" (~42:57)
- [CONS][TOPO] Consumer state is replicated; by default a consumer inherits the replication factor of its stream and is co-located on the same servers. "if it's an R3 stream you create a consumer if you don't change the replication factor it's actually going to inherit the replication factor of the stream" (~43:58)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Use an R1 consumer for short-lived, one-off, process-lifetime consumption to avoid replication overhead; use replicated durables for resumable long-running work. "you can opt for saying I only want a single replica consumer ... if it's not going to be a long lived durable consumer" (~43:58)
- [CONS][CLNT][PATTERN] An ordered consumer is a bundle of defaults: R1, no acks, client-side reset/retry on gaps, minimal server state, more work on the client. "ordered consumer ... an R1 no acknowledgement it handles if there are dropped messages it actually retries and resets itself internally" (~47:03)
- [CLNT][OPS][ANTI] A client that processes too slowly on a fast delivery path becomes a slow consumer and the server disconnects it. "the server is not going to be happy ... you're a slow consumer of this data so I'm going to disconnect you" (~48:05)
- [CONS][CLNT] In-progress acks extend the ack wait window (30s mentioned as the window) to stop redelivery while still working on a message; nack and no-ack modes also exist. "within a 30 second time window send it in progress to stop redelivery attempts" (~50:08)
- [CONS][CLNT] The new JetStream client API removes the push/pull distinction; internally everything is pull-based. "there's actually no distinction anymore of a push versus pull consumer internally it actually is all pull-based now" (~51:10)
- [CONS][ANTI] Push consumers deliver to an inbox subscription as fast as the publish side sends, which can overwhelm applications and forced developers to think about flow control and max ack pending. "that can overwhelm applications ... that whole push-based model even though it sounded nice in theory I think actually confused quite a few people" (~53:11)
- [CONS][CLNT][MYTH] Pull consumers with batching are not slower than push; clients interleave pull requests so latency between batches is minimized and it is on par or faster. "on par if not in some cases faster than a push consumer model" (~54:13)
- [CONS][CLNT][PATTERN] Batch fetching amortizes network overhead: one round trip for ten messages beats ten round trips. "you lose the network overhead of fetching one at a time pack a load of stuff together" (~56:14)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Two application instances bound to the same consumer get different batches (load balancing), not copies of the same data. "they're getting individual batches because now the server is assuming okay you're trying to actually parallelize the work" (~59:16)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Any number of workers can bind to one consumer for Lambda-style fan-out parallelism. "the consumer will happily basically load balance across and deliver across any number of instances" (~60:19)
- [CONS][SUBJ][PATTERN] To retain order per entity, create a filtered consumer at the granularity you need (e.g. per dwelling subject). "you apply a subject filter and then that consumer will basically only deliver the relevant data" (~61:20)
- [CONS][ANTI][SIZE] Do not plan on 100k or a million consumers, one per entity; you will never deploy that many client applications, so pick a wildcard granularity your app can handle in order. "nobody's running 100,000 a million containers ... the middle ground can be having a client application that can apply a wild card at the level of granularity" (~63:23)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Max ack pending of 1 has historically been the recommended way to retain perfect order with a shared consumer. "you can define this max ack pending ... you probably should do this if you want to truly retain perfect order" (~64:26)
- [STRM][SUBJ][PATTERN] 2.10 logical partitioning: on ingest the stream deterministically appends a partition-number token derived from the subject; consumers filter with wildcards plus a concrete partition ID to get total order within a bucket. "it's deterministic so given the same input subject it's going to derive the same partition ID" (~66:30)
- [STRM][MYTH] 2.10 partitions are logical tokens in the subject, not physical partitions like other systems. "this is not a physical partition like we talked about with the other systems this is a logical partition ID" (~66:30)
- [CONS] NATS (at 2.10) has no native exclusive consumer with automatic failover between two client instances; it is discussed for the roadmap. "we don't yet have this ability to define an exclusive consumer" (~68:34)
- [KV][PATTERN] Emulate exclusive consumption today with a KV-based lease/lock: multiple instances, one acquires the lock with a TTL and is the active participant. "I have a KV bucket ... leasing ... only one basically acquires a lock ... you can have a TTL" (~72:38)
- [OPS][STRM] CLI backup/restore is out of band and never incremental or real time; the general recommendation is a mirror stream, possibly in another region, plus backups. "you're never going to with this mechanism it's never going to be incremental in real time ... you could very simply have a mirror stream" (~74:43)
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] A mirror can live on slower disks with compression and long retention as an archive while the origin is pruned or compacted. "your mirror stream that is literally for archival ... on slower disks you could apply compression to that stream" (~75:43)
- [OPS] The defaults are generally fine; beginners get hung up on retention policies and ack modes that they usually do not need to change. "generally the default should be perfectly fine ... retention policies people get hung up on and the ack modes" (~77:46)
- [TOPO][PATTERN][USECASE] For latency-sensitive alerting, co-locate the workload with the origin stream (even on a Raspberry Pi at the edge) rather than on the async sourced/mirrored copy, because sourcing and mirroring are asynchronous with retries and partitions. "collocate your application workload to where the origin stream is ... sourcing things mirroring things that's all asynchronous" (~79:48)

## NATS 2.10 Webinar
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ds71axJRFm0
- speaker: Byron Ruth (Synadia; presenter, with David Gee and Jean-Noël Moyne in chat) | date: 2023 (October; "2.10 was released roughly a month ago in September") | duration: 57:44
- version context: 2.10 (2.10.3 recommended as current patch; 2.9.22 mentioned as the storage-format-aware 2.9 release)

### Claims
- [STRM][OPS] 2.10 adds opt-in per-stream compression using S2 (a Snappy variant), trading storage for CPU. "this is using S2 compression which is a variation on top of Snappy compression ... you're trading off storage and CPU" (~01:00)
- [OPS][CLNT] The NATS CLI `--defaults` flag skips the interactive stream-creation prompts. "there's this really nice new feature ... dash dash defaults so you don't have to fill out all this other stuff" (~02:01)
- [STRM][OPS] Compression is editable on an existing stream; the server compresses existing message blocks in real time after the edit. "this field is editable you define compression to S2 and then it will effectively rip through all the message blocks in real time" (~02:01)
- [STRM][SIZE] Compression does not degrade ingest throughput because the active block being appended to is left uncompressed; a block is compressed asynchronously only once it is full. "the active block that is actually being written to appended to is basically not compressed and only once the message block is done and filled up then it actually gets asynchronously compressed" (~03:03)
- [STRM][SEC] Storage-level encryption and compression compose correctly because data is compressed before it is encrypted. "the data actually gets compressed prior to being encrypted so you actually get that benefit of compression" (~04:03)
- [STRM][MIG][OPS] The 2.10 stream storage format is not backward compatible with 2.9 except that 2.9.22 and later patch releases understand it; downgrading is not recommended. "we did release 2.9.22 and then any patch release after that ... are aware of this new format" (~04:03)
- [STRM][SIZE][OPS] The new storage format cut restart/recovery of a 2.1 TB, 300-million-message stream from roughly 15 minutes on 2.9 to 1.1 seconds on 2.10, because 2.9 scanned and checksummed every block. "2.1 terabytes in size with 300 million messages ... roughly 15 minutes to actually restart the stream ... with 2.10 it takes 1.1 seconds" (~05:05)
- [OPS][STRM] Fast stream recovery matters for rolling upgrades, Kubernetes restarts, and placing replicas on new nodes, and the 15-minute figure was for one stream; many streams multiply the wait. "this is just for one stream mind you so for people who have a lot of streams this time can add up" (~06:05)
- [CORE][STRM] Native MQTT support requires JetStream because MQTT QoS relies on it, but no streams need to be defined by hand; the server translates between MQTT topics and NATS subjects. "it does require JetStream because of the quality of service mechanisms ... but beyond that you don't have to define any streams" (~08:11)
- [CORE][MIG] Before 2.10 MQTT supported QoS 0 (at most once, like fire-and-forget) and QoS 1 (at least once); 2.10 adds QoS 2 (exactly once) and from 2.10.3 the server runs an external MQTT compliance test suite. "with 2.10 QoS 2 has been implemented ... as of 2.10.3 we actually introduced a proper external MQTT compliance test suite" (~09:12)
- [OPS] Community contributions added NetBSD (following the OpenBSD build) and a stub IBM z/OS build target in 2.10. "for people wanting to run NATS on NetBSD now you can actually build for that platform and then IBM z/OS ... more of a stub implementation" (~10:14)
- [SEC][CLNT] By default the initial CONNECT/INFO exchange happens in clear text before the TLS handshake, even with TLS configured; it carries minimal client metadata. "that first initial message is basically in clear text and it has minimal metadata ... and then the TLS connection handshake actually occurs after that" (~12:16)
- [SEC][TOPO] 2.10 adds opt-in TLS-first for leaf nodes: `handshake_first: true` must be set on both hub and remote or the connection is rejected; rollout to other connection types follows later. "you can say handshake first true and then on the remote ... you would also define handshake first true and those have to be in agreement" (~13:18)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Auth callout exists so identity and permissions can be managed in an external IdP (SAML, Active Directory, OAuth) while NATS still enforces per-connection permissions and limits. "where you manage those permissions where you manage how those users are defined don't necessarily need to be in NATS itself" (~15:19)
- [SEC] Auth callout is an extension point: the server delegates connection credentials and metadata to your service, which validates identity and returns a user JWT with permissions and limits; the server verifies it and accepts or rejects. "generate a user JWT which has permissions and limits ... that service returns that user JWT to NATS ... it does a couple extra checks" (~16:20)
- [TOPO][CORE] NATS has four connection types: client, route (server-to-server within a cluster), gateway (cluster-to-cluster forming a supercluster), and leaf node. "you have a client connection ... route connections ... gateway connections ... leaf node connections" (~17:21)
- [TOPO][CORE] Traffic between servers in a cluster is always a single hop before landing on a subscriber. "it's always a single hop before it actually lands to a subscriber" (~18:21)
- [TOPO][ANTI][SIZE] Before 2.10 any two servers shared one TCP route connection, so a very active account could cause head-of-line blocking for other accounts sharing it. "any two pairs of servers only had a single TCP connection between them ... there can be some unintentional unfairness or head of line blocking" (~19:22)
- [TOPO][OPS] 2.10 "v2 routes" use multiple TCP connections per server pair out of the box: the system account is pinned to a dedicated connection and other accounts are spread over a pool of three. "you're going to get a pinned account for the system account ... and then there's going to be a pool size of three TCP connections" (~20:22)
- [TOPO][OPS] You can list specific accounts in the route config to pin each to its own dedicated TCP connection; throughput goes up "basically for free" but you should test in your environment. "there's going to be an additional TCP connection that actually gets pinned for that explicit account ... the throughput goes up significantly" (~21:22)
- [STRM][TOPO] Stream replicas must be placed within a single cluster; they cannot be spread across a supercluster. "when you define a stream the replicas have to be placed within the same cluster you can't spread replicas across a super cluster" (~22:23)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] The recommended scope of a cluster is a region (AZ-level fault tolerance); a supercluster spans regions. A "stretch cluster" spreads one cluster (e.g. 9 or 13 nodes) across regions to get multi-region stream replicas. "the scope of a cluster is typically regional a super cluster can span multiple regions ... we've been calling it the pattern as a stretch cluster" (~23:25)
- [TOPO][OPS] Route (and leaf node) compression is off by default; with `s2_auto` the server picks a compression level from measured round-trip time using RTT thresholds, and it adapts rather than pinning heavy compression after one bad RTT sample. "based on the round trip time between any two servers it's going to choose a level of compression that is appropriate" (~25:29)
- [STRM][SIZE] Max stream replicas remain five in 2.10; in a stretch cluster those replicas can sit in different regions. "the max stream replicas continue to be five yep but now you can place those replicas in servers that go across completely different regions" (~26:30)
- [CONS] 2.10 multi-filter consumers take an array of disjoint filter subjects instead of one, avoiding over-subscribing to a common root and dropping the rest client-side. "you don't have to over subscribe to the common root token in your subject hierarchy and then basically drop everything else" (~28:32)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Because a multi-filter consumer is a single server-side source, relative delivery order across the filtered subjects matches stream order, unlike the old workaround of two unsynchronized consumers. "the relative order for all messages being delivered by that consumer are now in the order that you would expect from the original stream" (~29:34)
- [CONS][STRM] All filter subjects of a consumer must belong to the same stream; to consume across streams, create a stream that sources from multiple origins and consume from that. "the pattern would be to create a stream that is actually sourcing from multiple origin streams and then create a consumer on that stream" (~29:34)
- [STRM][SUBJ][KV] Stream-level subject transforms (implemented by Jean-Noël Moyne) generalize server-config subject mapping and remove the pre-2.10 limitation that KV mirrors could not be created within the same account and cluster. "there was a limitation that you couldn't do that previously unless you were spanning a JetStream domain or cross accounts" (~31:36)
- [STRM][SUBJ][PATTERN] A stream subject transform can append a deterministic partition token computed from a wildcard token, e.g. events.* -> events.{{wildcard(1)}}.{{partition(5,1)}}; ordered pull consumers then bind to events.*.0 through events.*.4. "give me five partitions and compute that relative to the first wild card" (~32:37)
- [STRM][ANTI] Partition mapping stays stable unless you edit the partition count; changing it moves subjects between buckets, though strategies exist to handle that. "unless you're messing around with the partition count and editing those things" (~34:41)
- [SEC][OPS] Centralized auth callout config has only four options: issuer NKey, the auth account's users allowed to run the callout service, the auth account, and an optional XKey. "these are literally the only four config options that you can define for auth callout in this centralized mode" (~39:50)
- [SEC] The optional XKey encrypts the authorization request to the callout service, which decrypts it and re-encrypts the response with a one-time server key to prevent replay attacks. "it's able to re-encrypt it back with a public key that the server gives and that's a one-time key to prevent replay attacks" (~40:51)
- [SEC][KV][PATTERN] An OAuth-to-NATS bridge can store the IdP user claims in a KV bucket keyed by session ID; the client presents the session ID as its token and the callout service looks it up to mint the user JWT. "the key value bucket is the link between setting a token through my auth callout callback flow and then your auth callout service being able to observe this token" (~51:00)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Put NATS permissions and target account in IdP app metadata claims so users are managed in one place and the callout service maps them to a NATS user JWT. "you can define permissions anything that is relevant for your NATS user ... and you can manage it in one place" (~45:57)
- [SEC][CLNT] The server respects an expiry on the callout-issued user JWT; today it disconnects the client at expiry and the client must reconnect, and retaining connection state across credential renewal was future work. "once the JWT has expired the user JWT it will effectively today disconnect the client and the client would just have to reconnect" (~53:04)
- [SEC][OPS] Decentralized auth callout needs a few extra config options and a "sentinel" credential; both modes are walked through end to end on NATS by Example. "you need to work with a sentinel credential and there's a reason for that" (~56:08)
- [SEC][OPS] Auth callout is deliberately an extension point and is harder to set up than most NATS features. "it's not going to be as trivial to set up as some of the other NATS features" (~56:08)

## EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9J4pRzHSc2k
- speaker: Byron Ruth (host), Tomasz Pietrek and Neil Twigg (NATS server engineers, Synadia) | date: 2023 (recorded just after the 2.10 release; "2.9 was released back in September of 2022 so we have crossed the year mark") | duration: 70:40
- version context: 2.10 release (comparisons to the 2.9 series)

### Claims
- [OPS] 2.10 took over a year after 2.9 (Sept 2022) because effort went into stabilizing 2.9 patch releases for customers and building test infrastructure. "we've spent an awful lot of time focused on quality ... also we had a very big backlog of features going into 2.10" (~02:04)
- [OPS] Edge conditions that were once rare became common as adoption grew, so Synadia built chaos-test environments to catch them before users do. "edge conditions that we never seen start to be almost common ... we would love to catch those before others do" (~04:06)
- [OPS] Synadia has a dedicated DevX team running chaos testing and distributed-systems testing beyond the server and client teams. "we also have this sort of DevX team ... they're doing chaos testing and all sorts of crazy distributed systems testing" (~07:09)
- [OPS][SIZE] The NATS unit-test suite ran 117 hours of tests in a single day through parallel jobs; "unit" tests spin up whole clusters and dozens of servers. "the NATS test suite ran 117 hours worth of unit tests in a single day" (~10:11)
- [OPS] Consensus-based systems surface a new class of bugs under high or low latency and jitter, so each scenario must be tested across many variable inputs; perfect conditions do not reveal the most bugs. "if you start working with consensus ... suddenly a whole new set of problems appears that can surface if you have high latency or low latency" (~11:12)
- [OPS] The hardest part of a distributed bug is correlating which set of inputs reproduces it; once reproducible, fixing is simple. "the hardest part is to actually reproduce the error not to see the error but to then correlate it which set of inputs causes it" (~13:14)
- [OPS][TOPO] Even a three-node cluster can have asymmetric latency (A-B fast, A-C slow), and consensus must cope with that. "traffic between nodes A and B is significantly quicker than traffic that goes from A to C" (~14:14)
- [TOPO][OPS] NATS is deployed in heterogeneous environments (leaf nodes in cars, factories, oil rigs), unlike databases that assume sub-millisecond cloud links; this makes debugging dropped messages much harder. "we have leaf nodes running in cars ... on random edge devices in factories on oil rigs" (~15:16)
- [TOPO][USECASE] Leaf nodes were not designed for IoT use cases, but that became their main purpose. "the leaf nodes being used for those IoT use cases in the first place because they were not designed for it and now it is their main purpose" (~17:18)
- [OPS] Daily benchmark runs on every commit have "rescued more than once" by revealing performance regressions; performance is the number-one question users ask. "the number one thing that most customers and most users come to us asking is how do I squeeze the best performance out of this system" (~19:22)
- [OPS][CLNT] Chaos tests showed that when servers go down, problems are often on the client side: clients reconnect too aggressively while "trying to be smart". "sometimes it's the clients ... they try to be smart and reconnect but we see they end up doing it quick enough we found also those issues" (~20:24)
- [OPS] The first support question on an incident is whether anything happened on the network or VMs that day, because those are the usual triggers. "one of the first thing we ask when something breaks is did something happen on your network that day" (~21:25)
- [OPS] 2.10's three themes are scalability, a new extension point (auth callout), and predictability/stability, with tail-latency and storage work driven by the "millions of interior deletes" problem in KV buckets. "we have increased scalability ... a new point of extensibility ... and then we have predictability" (~22:26)
- [STRM][KV][SIZE] Users put and delete hundreds of millions of KV keys, producing streams with data at the head and tail and a huge deleted gap in the middle; this "interior deletes" state dominated Raft snapshots. "the state snapshot for the messages we're retaining and deleting ends up being really big because it's tracking more information about things that we no longer want to keep" (~26:29)
- [STRM][OPS] Marshalling large delete-state snapshots for replication consumed increasing CPU and backed up the server, so 2.10 reworked the file store; most 2.10 performance gains come from that work. "more and more CPU time was going into this process and the server is backing up behind that work" (~27:30)
- [STRM][KV][MYTH] Unlike append-only logs with only tail compaction, a NATS stream supports explicit deletion of an arbitrary interior message; that is how KV tombstoning works. "you can actually explicitly delete an arbitrary interior message within a stream ... this is how frankly the KV abstraction actually works" (~28:31)
- [STRM][KV][OBJ] KV buckets and object stores are streams, so file-store improvements benefit all of them. "KV buckets are streams object stores are streams so everything benefits from this" (~29:33)
- [STRM][OPS] 2.10 stores deleted-message state as AVL trees for sparse deletes and run-length encoding for large deleted ranges, and the server picks whichever structure fits the pattern. "we've tried to use AVL trees for what is effectively quite a sparse set of deletions and then we also use run length encoding for ... large blocks" (~29:33)
- [KV][SIZE][USECASE] KV was released as a convenience API and a year later a user ran a 10 TB KV store spanning the globe; it worked but needed to work better. "how about 10 terabytes key value store span across the whole globe will it work too yeah the thing is it worked it's just we needed it to work better" (~30:33)
- [OPS] Users adopt NATS as the connectivity layer for their entire infrastructure, so new APIs hit terabyte-scale global use almost immediately. "the new API just blows up almost immediately to the level where our other APIs are used" (~33:36)
- [TOPO][ANTI] Raft consensus traffic is itself carried over NATS between cluster nodes; with a single TCP route per server pair, application traffic and consensus traffic could block each other, and one account could effectively deny service to another. "what we don't want to happen is that application traffic gets stuck behind consensus traffic ... you don't want one to be able to cause a denial of service effectively to another" (~34:36)
- [TOPO][OPS] V2 routes give multiple connections per server pair; the server assigns accounts to routes automatically or an administrator can reserve a dedicated route for a latency-sensitive account. "the administrator can make that decision explicitly and say look this specific account is one that we care very deeply about having low latency for" (~35:38)
- [TOPO][OPS] Route head-of-line blocking is worse over the public internet or between cloud regions because of TCP congestion control; with V2 routes consensus stays up to date faster and application traffic moves faster, with no config required. "consensus stays up to date more quickly that application traffic makes around the cluster faster ... it works out of the box" (~36:38)
- [TOPO][OPS] Route and leaf compression uses fast algorithms with low CPU cost to gain network headroom; it is automatic on route and leaf connections in 2.10 and on by default for leaf nodes because they are assumed to be over longer, less reliable links. "it's by default for leaf nodes because it's the assumption that you're going to be over a longer distance" (~39:41)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] A stretch cluster is the regular clustering mechanism pushed across zones, regions or data centers (e.g. one nine-node cluster instead of three three-node clusters joined as a supercluster). "the alternative is that you just have a nine node cluster and it's the fact that it scales out of a specific location is what we refer to as the stretch clustering" (~42:42)
- [TOPO][STRM][PATTERN] In a supercluster each JetStream Raft group is bounded to one cluster, so persistence performance does not suffer from inter-region latency while global connectivity remains. "each JetStream group is only bounded to this specific cluster in a super cluster so ... persistence with JetStream does not suffer because you have more regions" (~43:43)
- [TOPO][STRM][PATTERN] Choose a stretch cluster when regulation requires data replicated consistently across regions and you accept higher-latency persistence; mirroring/sourcing across a supercluster gives similar reach but with secondary, eventually available copies. "you can achieve something similar with super clusters but then you need to include some mirroring and sourcing ... the guarantees around when the data will be available its consistency is a little different" (~44:45)
- [TOPO][STRM][OPS] Server tags let you dictate where stream replicas land, including anti-affinity across regions or providers, or you can let NATS place them. "you can actually tag the servers and say where the data lands ... or you can just say to NATS just do how you think" (~45:45)
- [SEC] Auth callout is the first built-in server extension point; it lets the server ask an external service whether a connecting client is allowed and what it may access, replacing large static configs. "the call out is basically a way of a NATS server reaching out to an external service to say hey I've got this client connecting should it be allowed what should it be allowed access to" (~51:52)
- [SEC][PATTERN] The callout service can consult LDAP, OIDC, a file or SQLite and can generate permissions dynamically per session, e.g. by time of day. "maybe at this time of day for this particular user ... they have this degree of permission at this time" (~52:52)
- [SEC][CORE] The auth callout service is just a NATS subscriber on a predefined subject that responds; there is no new protocol. "it's literally just another NATS subscriber right and then it just responds so it's not like a new protocol" (~53:55)
- [STRM][SEC] Enabling JetStream encryption destroys file-system block-level compressibility, so 2.10 compresses in the file store before encryption. "if you enable encryption in JetStream today pretty much all of your compressibility on the disk ... goes completely out of the window" (~55:58)
- [CORE][USECASE] MQTT QoS 2 was added because applications such as Home Assistant rely on it, making MQTT an entry point for moving workloads onto NATS. "one of the big projects that comes to mind is Home Assistant that uses MQTT integration relies on QoS 2" (~56:58)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Built-in MQTT lets embedded or industrial devices that will never speak anything else join a NATS backend without extra bridging infrastructure. "those clients might be embedded or they might be industrial and they don't ever stand a chance of talking anything that's not MQTT" (~57:58)
- [CONS][ANTI] Before 2.10 users needing several non-wildcard subsets (e.g. factories 1-5 of 10) had to create many consumers, which costs the server and forces the client to re-order across consumers. "people needed to create many consumers to get this one specific stream of data which is not only not perfect from optimization point of view for the server ... you have to handle the order" (~60:00)
- [SUBJ][STRM] Subject mapping existed since 2.9 at server level and was heavily used for cross-account imports/exports; 2.10 moves it to stream, source and mirror level. "you can have subject mapping on stream level sources and mirrors level" (~64:06)
- [SUBJ][STRM][PATTERN] Stream-level transforms let you change subjects for API changes without breaking clients, and aggregate identical subjects from many factories or leaf nodes without compromising your subject architecture. "it allows you to even handle switching subjects for API changes without any breaking changes" (~62:02)
- [SUBJ][STRM][PATTERN] Transforms on sources/mirrors solve subject-namespace collisions when bridging systems by rewriting subjects on the fly. "subject namespace collisions ... you can now just rewrite these on the fly so that you don't have to worry about whether you're polluting one namespace with another" (~65:08)
- [OPS][SIZE] Users who learn a system scales to 2 TB then "put one more zero at the end"; supporting that is the ongoing 2.11 focus over new features. "it's so easy to just put one more zero at the end not so easy to support that one more zero" (~68:11)

## EP07: Going off piste; KV patterns with NATS.io (pt1)
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-WHjEYLWo6c
- speaker: David Gee (host) and Byron Ruth (Synadia) | date: 2023 (recorded shortly after the 2.10 release, "a year and a week" after 2.9) | duration: 48:07
- version context: 2.10 era (follows the 2.10 release episode)

### Claims
- [KV][STRM][PATTERN] Byron's first NATS use was pub/sub fan-out to notify many things instead of HTTP hacks, then NATS Streaming for ETL pipelines: extract, transform, publish to a stream, fan out to consumers that load other systems. "taking data out transforming it throwing it into a stream and then I was able to fan out effectively consume from that stream and plop it in other systems" (~04:09)
- [STRM][MYTH][STALE?] NATS Streaming had only a handful of stream knobs, mostly limits like max messages; JetStream, KV and Object Store have many more options that can overwhelm newcomers, and each exists for a reason. "NATS Streaming had a handful of knobs ... fairly limited it was mostly around limits" (~04:09)
- [USECASE][PATTERN] David's first NATS use (2015) was connecting distributed syslog-ingestion instances east-west so they funnelled through one head-end, to avoid ten systems each hammering core internet infrastructure, with failover if one machine died. "the last thing I want is 10 systems basically doing a denial of service attack onto core internet infrastructure" (~08:14)
- [USECASE][ANTI] Relying on real-time clocks and NTP for synchronizing events across VMs with time-sliced CPUs fails; David used NATS signals and then Streaming so a system that missed a signal could catch up. "NTP would fail me sometimes ... it really is important when events needed to be synchronized" (~10:17)
- [KV][OBJ][CLNT] KV and Object Store are client-side abstractions layered on a stream, with a deliberately smaller set of knobs. "KV and Object Store are client abstractions that lay on top of the stream and these abstractions are very convenient to use because the amount of knobs that they have are smaller" (~11:20)
- [KV] KV supports optimistic concurrency control via a revision (sequence) number, with create and update operations distinct from put. "KV buckets support optimistic concurrency control you can have a sequence number" (~11:20)
- [KV][PATTERN] Because a KV bucket is a stream, watchers let you subscribe to puts, updates and deletes as a change stream over time. "it's inherently a stream under the hood so ... you can watch changes over time" (~12:23)
- [KV][PATTERN] The server can reject one of two concurrent writes to the same key, which gives you a distributed mutex across processes without slapping a local mutex on. "the server has the ability to basically prevent both concurrent writes to happen at the same time" (~12:23)
- [PATTERN][ANTI] If you are protecting one resource from more than a couple of workers, reconsider the design slightly. "if you're protecting one resource from more than maybe a couple of worker systems maybe you want to readdress your design ever so slightly" (~13:25)
- [KV][PATTERN] A lease adds a time element: set a TTL on the lock key so competitors retry until it expires and someone else acquires it; the TTL bounds how long any holder can own the resource. "you can set a TTL on keys ... this key will eventually expire after a certain number of seconds" (~15:29)
- [KV][PATTERN] Simplest distributed lock: every worker races to create the key with its node ID as the value, then reads back to see who won; losers stand down. "there's a race all of the machines try and write the key and the one that writes it ... they all go and do a read and go oh I'm not the one that won" (~17:32)
- [KV][ANTI] A KV lock is advisory: nothing locks the data out, so correctness depends on workers honouring the lock in code; NATS is not a magic firewall. "it's down to the developer to adhere to the lock nothing's going to actually lock the data out ... NATS isn't some kind of magic firewall" (~18:34)
- [KV][PATTERN] The lock holder can use the revision of its last write to update the key, extend the TTL or record progress for a long-lived job. "the one that won now has a revision of the last write so we can go back and even update it maybe increment the TTL" (~18:34)
- [KV][PATTERN] A "witness" process watches the lock key and heartbeats; when the worker's heartbeat disappears it deletes the key and signals a job restart. "as soon as the heartbeat disappears ... they go back and actually delete the key and then maybe issue another signal saying restart job" (~19:36)
- [KV][PATTERN] A semaphore generalizes the mutex: a pool of N resources that workers acquire and release, depleting and refilling over time. "more generalized from a mutex is a semaphore where you can have maybe a pool of resources that everyone is trying to compete for" (~20:37)
- [USECASE][PATTERN] Gaming use case: limited video-render farm capacity for ghost-lap replays, SAN write cycles and CDN upload rate/connection limits are all natural semaphore gates. "you'd only have limited resources to generate those videos ... there would be a queue" (~22:40)
- [KV][PATTERN] Batch data pipelines need a shared, distributed record of the last processed offset; store it as a KV key so a pool of workers can grab a job and its offset instead of using a local file or SAN. "you could maintain a key the last offset ... you just have a pool of workers just grab a job grab the last offset" (~28:46)
- [PATTERN] For multi-patient analytics, relative order of events per patient is the unit of parallelism. "as long as you keep the relative order of events that occur to a patient that's your unit of parallelism" (~28:46)
- [KV][PATTERN] A lock key need not be boolean: store a state-machine value (acquired, in progress, next state) so a witness can detect a stalled transition, reset it and let another worker retry. "it doesn't have to be a binary true false mutex you can have a state machine almost in a way" (~29:49)
- [PATTERN] Retry-on-stall requires idempotent downstream processing; rely on natural or primary keys across systems to model it. "there's many downstream things like idempotency you have to be aware of" (~30:49)
- [KV][PATTERN] Storing job state in KV rather than a database gives you real-time watching of state changes and an external witness that can intervene. "you don't have that benefit of really watching the state changes over time" (~31:50)
- [KV][SUBJ][PATTERN] Keys are subjects with a token hierarchy, so you can model a DAG of job states as a key hierarchy and watch a subtree; the watch history doubles as a write-ahead log for free. "because keys are under the hood just subjects and you have a token hierarchy you can model a DAG as a hierarchy naturally and then you can watch a sub tree" (~33:53)
- [KV][PATTERN][USECASE] Distribute policy (e.g. firewall rules) by having each host run a local agent that watches a KV bucket and realises its own desired state, instead of a central orchestration pool. "there's a local agent running you watch the KV store and then it programmed its own IP tables stuff" (~34:55)
- [PATTERN][SIZE] Distributed leaky-token-bucket rate limiting: claim tokens in batches (e.g. 100), not one at a time, because per-token round trips cost more than the work being gated. "there's no point going to a token bucket going give me one token give me one token ... it's like give me a 100 tokens" (~38:59)
- [PATTERN] Batch token claims can starve one worker; fairness systems sometimes have to be unfair to some participant. "you might starve one system out but that's the problem with fair systems" (~38:59)
- [KV][USECASE] Kine (the k3s etcd-replacement layer) gained a community-contributed NATS KV backend, so k3s can run with NATS instead of etcd or SQLite; the original was single-node, and HA three-node k3s over NATS was later built. "somebody contributed NATS as an alternate backend within the Kine abstraction layer" (~40:00)
- [KV][PATTERN] Three k3s servers continuously try to acquire a lease on a KV key for leader election; that is the same mechanism they use with etcd. "these three k3s servers that at a minimum all trying to acquire a lease on the KV bucket" (~42:02)
- [KV][PATTERN] Application-level leader election, quorum and leasing can be built on NATS KV even though the bucket has its own Raft leader underneath. "I need a leader election I need quorum I need leasing and unleasing you can use NATS KV to do that" (~44:05)
- [KV][MYTH] KV is more than a cache; locks, leases, semaphores, job state, policy distribution and leader election are all valid uses. "people go well great I can use it as a cache but there's so many other areas that you can apply this thing to" (~44:05)
