<!-- Group C: NATS.fm: HTTP mindset, modular monolith, service mesh pattern, client-side abstractions; services API -->

## EP03: Escaping the HTTP Mindset with NATS.io
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XTl87Fx1WLE
- speaker: David Gee (host) and Byron Ruth (Synadia) | date: 2023 (host says "we're in 2023") | duration: 37:50
- version context: 2.9 era (host jokes about "2.9.17 to 2.9.18" version bumps)

### Claims
- [PATTERN][ANTI] HTTP was designed to serve web pages, not for inter-service or intra-process communication, and most teams adopt it for services without questioning whether its semantics fit. "HTTP was designed as a protocol to serve the web... it was never designed to be inter-process communication" (~03:06)
- [PATTERN] HTTP is appropriate as a well-understood "sentinel" mechanism at the edge (browser, front door), with NATS used for the component-to-component middle. "HTTP is great as like a sentinel mechanism that everyone understands at the edge" (~04:08)
- [ANTI] Sticking an HTTP proxy in front of every decomposed component is the default reflex and the wrong one for service-to-service traffic. "what do people do? oh well we'll stick a HTTP proxy in front of everything" (~02:05)
- [PATTERN][CORE] Using NATS as the communication mechanism between modules from the start gives location transparency: modules can live in one monolith or be split and distributed without changing how they talk. "those modules all connect to NATS... you don't have to know physically where they're located" (~09:14)
- [ANTI][MIG] Starting with in-process function calls and later distributing means rewriting all the communication logic; that rewrite is the pain NATS-first design avoids. "now you have to completely rewrite all of your logic, all of your communication mechanisms, so it's very painful" (~10:16)
- [PATTERN] Microservice "size" should be defined by DDD bounded context, not lines of code; a bounded context is a starting deployable unit but does not have to equal a single deployable. "bounded context does not equate to a single deployable unit either" (~14:21)
- [PATTERN] Keep business capabilities and deployment units as separate dimensions of thought; only split further when part of a system must scale or ship on a different cadence. "decoupling the business logic... from the deployment unit and keeping those as separate dimensions of thought" (~15:23)
- [PATTERN] Data and schema are the real contract regardless of transport; everything else is an implementation detail, and an orchestrating service only needs the data contract of what it calls. "data and schema at the end of the day are king and queen" (~16:23)
- [PATTERN] The Enterprise Integration Patterns "routing slip" (a predetermined multi-step workflow carried with the message) is a way to make orchestration implicit over NATS, including parallel steps. "he has this message slip pattern... you basically have a predetermined workflow" (~18:25)
- [ANTI][MYTH] Programs embrace async primitives internally, then fall back to synchronous HTTP between components; NATS lets you break that synchronous point-to-point mindset. "we think about HTTP and service calls between components and then we're right back into synchrony land" (~19:27)
- [PATTERN] Choreography (event-driven: publish an event, interested components react and may raise further events) and orchestration are a spectrum, not an either/or, chosen per component. "there's a spectrum and I think it depends on what your component is needing to do" (~26:34)
- [PATTERN][MYTH] Choreography decouples function invocation but not data: changing an event schema still breaks downstream subscribers, so data contracts must still be coordinated. "it still couples on the data side going back to schema and data, you can't get around that" (~27:34)
- [CORE][PATTERN] HTTP cannot broadcast or publish to unknown receivers, which is why teams add a broker or SQS; NATS natively supports request-reply, request-reply-many (scatter/gather), fire-and-forget pub/sub, and persistent streams. "you can do request reply, request reply many... you can publish fire and forget... and then you also have persistent streams" (~28:36)
- [CORE] Fire-and-forget delivery goes to whoever is connected at that moment, which is right for time-sensitive events you do not want stored; persistent streams let consumers dequeue later when online. "whoever is connected at that time will receive that message, maybe it's a time sensitive event" (~28:36)
- [PATTERN][SUBJ] Versioning/AB testing pattern: publish to a liberal subject, put the required version in a header, and let responders filter on headers; a new version just subscribes to the same subject. "put the required version in the header on a subject... you literally just pub it to a subject and then you do a scatter-gather response" (~30:37)
- [CORE] NATS headers are just arbitrary key/value metadata on a message; HTTP-style content-type/encoding/schema semantics can be carried the same way. "headers aren't anything special, it's just an arbitrary bunch of data you can send into a message" (~30:37)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Version can be placed either as a subject token (v1/v2, strict: only responders on that version answer) or in a header (permissive); both are available and the choice sets granularity. "you can even apply a v1 v2 in the subject itself... or you can say I'm going to be a little bit more permissive" (~32:41)
- [PATTERN] Scatter-gather and "talk to many instances" come for free in NATS, whereas service discovery still limits HTTP callers to one component at a time. "you still are limited to talking to one component at a time... that just kind of comes for free for NATS" (~31:38)
- [PATTERN] Design principle from the host: remove lookups and coordination steps (service catalogs, version tables) because each lookup adds fragility; let the system self-organize via subjects and headers. "remove the fragility by removing choice, allow the system to self-organize" (~36:45)
- [PATTERN][CLNT] NATS can be taken all the way to the front end (browser NATS client with its own auth), so HTTP is only needed at the authentication step. "the only time you use REST or HTTP... is maybe at the point of authentication" (~34:44)
- [PATTERN] Observed call graphs in microservice systems are wide but shallow (hub-and-spoke), with few independent east-west calls beyond one or two hops. "the call stack's quite shallow, it might be wide but it's really quite shallow" (~22:31)

## EP02: Monolith to Modular Monolith with NATS.io
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=32emYRAwjY4
- speaker: David Gee (host) and Byron Ruth (Synadia) | date: 2023 (opens with "in 2023") | duration: 31:30
- version context: 2.9 era (2023, no version named)

### Claims
- [PATTERN] For a certain scale of application and team, a monolith is the right deployment unit; microservices are not an end goal but a response to organizational coordination pain or a component needing to scale differently. "for a certain scale of application and a certain scale of team monolithic applications are the right choice" (~02:02)
- [ANTI][OPS] A load balancer or proxy is another software component to deploy, manage, and learn, separate from the application, and it drags in network, firewall, and TLS-offload concerns. "it's another thing that you would have to manage and deploy and learn... independent of your actual application" (~07:06)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Load balancing is a native server primitive in NATS: subscribers forming a queue group get messages distributed at random across members with no extra software or external dependency. "the NATS server will distribute those messages across at random to those various members in that group without any additional software" (~07:06)
- [PATTERN][CORE] Define a subscription as a queue group from day one even if it has a single member; adding instances later scales out transparently because new members just join the group. "you might only have one member of that group right now... from day one you can design this knowing that this is a potential point of distribution" (~11:13)
- [TOPO][CORE] Because queue-group routing in a multi-region NATS system is RTT-aware, the closest responder answers without extra logic; one data fabric can stretch across EMEA and US regions instead of per-region load balancer pairs. "it also does RTT so round trip time responses... you could have the closest NATS service respond without any further logic" (~10:10)
- [PATTERN] Modular monolith path: divide functionality inside one monolith along boundaries and route the internal calls over NATS, so a second monolith instance can be stood up with the right subscriptions to scale horizontally. "internal communication for your monolith can begin to be over NATS" (~13:14)
- [PATTERN] Use DDD bounded contexts as the boundaries; within a bounded context keep direct function calls, and put NATS only across boundaries that may be deployed separately later. "within a bounded context you can do function calls all day... but across boundaries those are potentially going to be deployed separately" (~15:18)
- [PATTERN] The trade-off of NATS across module boundaries is a small added latency versus in-process calls, accepted in exchange for the ability to split, distribute, and scale later without rewriting. "if you can incur a tiny tiny extra little bit of latency... especially between the service boundaries" (~15:18)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] In Go the NATS server can be embedded directly in the application with no exposed TCP port, or an external server can broker the internal communication as a starting point. "you can even embed the NATS server directly into your application... you don't have to even expose any TCP connection" (~16:19)
- [PATTERN] Hot paths in a monolith are the early candidates for extraction; a less-busy instance can serve them and they often have a different development cadence from stable integration components. "it's a good way of identifying early candidates of what can be extracted and removed" (~17:21)
- [PATTERN][TOPO] Embedding NATS in each modular-monolith instance and connecting instances effectively builds a cluster gradually. "connecting that instance to another modular monolith, you build a cluster out effectively in slow-mo" (~18:21)
- [ANTI][MIG] Starting with in-process method calls and later distributing pushes teams to add RabbitMQ for queues and Kafka for streaming, each a new technology, dependency, and operational burden. "you start bringing in all these things and it's like more technologies to learn more dependencies... more operational overhead" (~19:23)
- [PATTERN] NATS used from day one covers messaging, streaming, and KV, acting as a framework for connectivity needs rather than a point tool. "if you just started with NATS from day one it'll serve all your application needs... you can do streaming and KV" (~20:25)
- [PATTERN][CLNT] Agreeing on a payload schema (protobuf, JSON schema) over NATS lets teams with different skills (C++ game engine vs. .NET monetization) keep their own language; NATS's client coverage makes polyglot splits natural. "each team gets to use their beloved language" (~22:29)
- [KV][PATTERN] Inventory example: the game watches a KV bucket key for the player, the transaction service updates that key, and the game gets the change notification without polling the database. "watching the KV inventory from the game with the C++ client... no database dips required" (~24:33)
- [KV][STRM][PATTERN] Polling a database for updates can be inverted into streaming state transitions or KV watchers, which is more responsive and optimized for that use. "if you invert that and you can just stream it out and you can model your state transitions in that way, that can be very powerful" (~26:36)
- [KV][SIZE] KV buckets can be placed in memory or on disk depending on need; a hot player inventory can be loaded from disk once at login into a memory bucket for speed. "you could put some things in memory, some things on disk" (~26:36)
- [PATTERN] Even without a distributed-systems problem, NATS is a useful lightweight starting point because it keeps the option to break off components open. "if you don't have that problem NATS can still be very very useful to you as a starting point" (~27:37)

## EP04: A Service Mesh Pattern for NATS.io
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xjobWTUVLw8
- speaker: Byron Ruth (Synadia) and David Gee (host) | date: 2023 (NATS.fm season 1) | duration: 51:17
- version context: 2.9/2.10 era (subject mapping with weights, hot reload, account JWT mappings)

### Claims
- [PATTERN][MYTH] Networking "service function chaining" (steering packets sequentially through IDS, proxy, WAF via VLANs) is not what an application-level service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) does; the host retracts the conflation from the prior episode. "I completely conflated all of that with service meshes" (~04:05)
- [PATTERN] What an application service mesh provides today: mTLS with certificate rotation, sidecar injection, service discovery, load balancing, circuit breaking, and black-box tracing. "TLS cert rotation, sidecar injection, service automatic service discovery, a little bit of tracing" (~10:11)
- [OPS][ANTI] Service meshes inject a sidecar container per pod (Envoy for Istio); it is convenient for the developer but adds compute, cost, and complexity for operators as the fleet scales. "the people that actually are paying the bills to run extra compute... that's where it gets a little interesting" (~09:11)
- [ANTI][OPS] Automation and mesh layers make an application's operational behaviour opaque because logic is split between code and layer-specific DSLs and config files. "you begin to lose insight as to how your application runs because the logic and the know-how is split" (~17:20)
- [ANTI][TOPO] Service meshes fall apart in heterogeneous estates (Kubernetes plus VMware, Hyper-V, bare Linux, mainframes, telco packet-centric environments) because they are Kubernetes-centric. "is it Kubernetes centric at that point and is everything else a satellite" (~18:21)
- [PATTERN] Service mesh exists mainly because HTTP/gRPC systems have no built-in load balancing or service discovery; those are point-to-point protocols. "HTTP and gRPC based systems... there is no inherent load balancing that is built in" (~15:18)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Canary / A-B traffic split (80/20) is done in NATS with weighted subject mapping: the public subject maps to .v1 and .v2 subjects by weight and versioned handlers subscribe to those. "a weighted mapping of saying this is the input subject... it gets mapped to a .v1 and a .v2" (~20:24)
- [PATTERN] HTTP ingress pattern: a thin proxy maps HTTP method + path to a subject, carries HTTP headers as NATS headers, and does a NATS request on the caller's behalf. "you map basically the method and the path to a subject and then you can encode anything in the body or... in the headers" (~22:29)
- [SUBJ][OPS] Subject mapping is enforced transparently by the server when it receives the message; it is configured either statically in server config (hot-reloadable without downtime) or in the account JWT claims under decentralized auth. "you can hot reload that without any downtime" (~23:32)
- [SEC][SUBJ] Under decentralized auth, subject mappings are per account, so each tenant (account = the application; user = the connection) can have its own mappings, pushed live via JWT update. "you can define subject mapping on an account by account basis which is our multi-tenancy mechanism" (~23:32)
- [CORE] Request/reply works transparently through mapping: the requester attaches a unique reply subject, whichever versioned responder receives the message replies to it, and the requester waits with a configurable timeout on that temporary subscription. "it actually supplies a reply subject that is unique... the responder is basically just waiting for a set timeout" (~25:35)
- [CORE][SIZE] Capacity example: 100 concurrent users, 20 per responder, 80/20 split, plus headroom gives 5 V1 and 2 V2 responders, all in queue groups, with no L4 load balancer. "we would basically have five... for the eighty percent case and two for the V2 case" (~28:37)
- [CORE] A queue group is identified by queue name plus subject; the server randomly distributes each request to one member of the group. "the queue name with the subject... makes that unique identifier for that particular group" (~30:40)
- [KV][PATTERN] A KV bucket can act as a scheduler substitute: keys hold a minimum service count and workers on VMware, Hyper-V, or Kubernetes claim keys semaphore-style. "we could be using a KV bucket on NATS to say minimum number of services five and you could have some keys that can be claimed" (~30:40)
- [TOPO][CORE] Request/reply across regions: several queue groups in different regions can subscribe to the same subject; the request is broadcast, each group picks one member, and the fastest reply wins. "whoever is the fastest responder on that subject that's the one that's actually going to come back" (~33:41)
- [TOPO][CORE] NATS sends requests to the closest responders relative to the ingress point on a region-by-region basis, giving geographic distribution for free. "it's going to transparently send it to the closest responders wherever that ingress point is" (~33:41)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Anycast HTTP gateways in multiple regions all bridging to one NATS system yields one globally deployed service set where the nearest responder answers. "one set of services running globally and the nearest one responds to that gateway" (~36:45)
- [TOPO] If a region is down, routing fails over transparently; traffic stays local when it can and is routed remotely only when the responder exists elsewhere. "everything that can be local will be local and everything that needs to get routed... it will do that" (~38:47)
- [TOPO][MYTH] Multi-region service mesh and multi-cluster Kubernetes are non-trivial and not out-of-the-box, in contrast to NATS's transparent cross-region routing. "how do you do a multi-cluster setup, it's non-trivial as far as I know" (~37:46)
- [PATTERN] All of this (global availability, canary, load balancing) needs no network overlay, VXLAN, or encapsulation; it runs over plain IP via NATS. "there's no network mesh required underneath, there's no encapsulation, there's no VXLAN" (~38:47)
- [PATTERN][OPS] Autoscaling can be self-organizing: when a gateway times out with no responder it can publish on an infrastructure subject and a listener claims and adds a responder; idle gateways can trigger scale-down. "nothing on Bob's responded, increase the license count maybe and then something listening says... I'm going to make that claim" (~39:48)
- [PATTERN] Service chaining (responder hands the payload to the next responder, only the gateway waits for the final reply on its inbox) is possible with NATS subjects, relevant mainly for telco and industrial IoT. "handing a payload off to a system and just forgetting about it... only the proxy waits for the response from the last responder" (~43:51)
- [PATTERN][ANTI] Chained handoffs need strong contracts between teams and probably a write-ahead log to track where the baton is. "I think you need a write ahead log just to keep a track of... passing a baton around different services" (~42:51)
- [PATTERN] Webhooks and HTTP-only integrations are the key use case for a declarative HTTP-to-NATS proxy; Byron hints a supported one is in progress and it would also support streaming, not just request/reply. "as long as you can configure this declaratively to make an HTTP call for an integration then I'm good" (~48:57)
- [CLNT] WebSocket support and the JavaScript client already extend NATS to the browser without an HTTP proxy. "we have the WebSocket interfaces... if you're a JavaScript junkie then we also have the JS library" (~49:59)

## EP05: Exploring Powerful Client-side Features and Abstractions in NATS.io
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kbJTuk2qr4U
- speaker: Tomasz Pietrek (Synadia client team tech lead), Byron Ruth, David Gee (host) | date: 2023 (recorded while 2.10 was being finalized) | duration: 72:30
- version context: 2.9 → 2.10 release-candidate era; JetStream "simplification" API, micro/services API, KV, Object Store still experimental

### Claims
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Client design goal: shared orientation points (same verbs and nouns, same structure) across languages, but each client stays idiomatic; identical APIs everywhere is only something NATS engineers think users want. "we don't also want to fall into the trap to make each client the same" (~04:05)
- [CLNT][ANTI] The original JetStream API mimicked core NATS Subscribe so closely that users jumped into JetStream without learning it and did not realize a consumer is a server-side construct, producing surprises. "people didn't even realize that the consumer's a server-side construct" (~06:07)
- [CLNT][CONS] The "simplification" API deliberately requires more explicit calls (create stream, create consumer, then consume) so the server-side resources and their behaviour are visible to the developer. "you explicitly have to do those things... oh I have to create some stream, oh I have to create some consumer" (~07:09)
- [CLNT] The JetStream API rewrite was treated as a once-in-a-long-time opportunity to fix the API, because the team otherwise avoids breaking changes and that makes iteration hard. "that's probably the only opportunity we have in quite a long time to in general improve the JetStream API" (~08:10)
- [CLNT][ANTI] Historically the Go client was the role model that other clients copied (callbacks everywhere even where iterators are idiomatic); the new approach decides per language how close to stay. "we have this role model Go client and then others are following it and we never discussed how close they should be" (~09:10)
- [CONS][CLNT] Ephemeral vs durable was reduced to a simpler concept: a consumer is ephemeral when it is cleaned up after an inactivity threshold; otherwise you delete it explicitly. "it's ephemeral based on some inactivity thresholds... or you say don't clean it up server for me" (~13:16)
- [CONS][ANTI] Auto-ack in the old subscribe-style API looked simpler but raised cognitive load because users could not tell whether messages were acked, and behaviour differed between clients. "even if the code looks simpler the cognitive load was bigger" (~14:18)
- [CONS] Push and pull consumers' capabilities overlapped more with each server release until "when should I use pull vs push" had no single answer; simplification leans on pull consumers. "with every single server release it was harder to answer in one way" (~15:18)
- [CONS][CLNT] Old fetch-loop pull consumption left gaps in network utilization between one fetch finishing and the next; the new consume method interleaves fetches under the hood so delivery never pauses. "the client will under the hood optimize the fetches, meaning it will interleave the fetches so there is never a pause" (~17:22)
- [CONS][SIZE] Pull consumers now match or beat push performance (use-case dependent) with better client resource utilization because the client controls flow, so client buffers can be much smaller at the same throughput. "the buffer on the client side can be much smaller while having the same throughput" (~16:19)
- [CONS][USECASE] For IoT or CPU/memory-constrained devices, pull with a low pending limit avoids being flooded by a push consumer until flow control kicks in. "you can just lower how many things can be pending... without this compromise of now the server can flood me with messages" (~17:22)
- [CONS] A consumer cannot be rewound; it is a pointer/view into the stream with its own sequence, so to go back you delete it and create a new consumer starting at the desired stream sequence (consumers are lightweight). "you cannot go back with this specific consumer but as consumers being pretty lightweight it's really pretty easy to just remove this consumer" (~20:25)
- [OPS] The 2.10 release was delayed by intensified distributed-systems and chaos testing of RAFT traffic and recovery; every miss led to a new test or tool so it could not slip again. "every single time we missed something we try to add a new tool, a new test" (~23:30)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] The services (micro) API is a purely client-side abstraction combining three server capabilities: the interest graph, subject-based routing, and queue groups; no server changes and no JetStream involved. "interest graph with subject based routing and the queue groups, those are the three elements" (~33:45)
- [PATTERN] Services get discovery, ping, stats, per-instance addressing, and load balancing out of the box; service instances are stateless and scale by simply running more instances. "you get more instances by just running more instances of the service, you don't need anything to manage it" (~65:19)
- [PATTERN][MYTH] Service discovery via the services API is not a static registry: an instance is discoverable while connected and disappears immediately when offline, with no de-registration or timeout. "it's not a static register either... the second it goes offline then... it's not there" (~31:43)
- [CLNT] Because the services API is a thin layer, code outside the framework can talk to services written with it and vice versa; using it never cuts you off from low-level NATS. "there's no cutting out of capabilities because of using the service API" (~34:46)
- [KV][STRM] KV is a client-side abstraction over a stream; the server does not know a stream is a KV bucket. The `max messages per subject` stream option was added specifically because KV history needed it. "that max message per subject stream configuration option was created purely because it was needed for key value" (~37:48)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Setting max messages per subject to 1 yields a stream that keeps only the latest message per subject, which spawned new non-KV use cases. "thanks to that you can have infinite application of messages if you set it to one" (~37:48)
- [KV][USECASE] KV was pitched (KubeCon Valencia, ~2.8) as "for simple use cases", but within 18 months it was in use as a Kubernetes persistence layer replacing etcd and for large key counts. "key value being able to be used as a Kubernetes persistence layer instead of etcd" (~39:51)
- [KV][USECASE] KV was motivated by leaf-node and factory-floor topologies where you want as little extra infrastructure as possible; JetStream users get a KV for free. "factory floor where you want to have as little infrastructure and tools installed as possible" (~39:51)
- [CLNT][ANTI] For client-side abstractions (KV, Object Store, services) the server cannot validate compatibility, so a bucket written from Rust can silently not work from Go unless the clients are cross-tested. "server will not help you here because it's just an abstraction layer" (~40:51)
- [OBJ][CLNT] Object Store stayed "experimental" until a cross-language compatibility test tool asserted put/get/update across Go, Rust, JavaScript, .NET, and Java, because a later fix would require migrating existing buckets. "we created... a tool that tests and asserts the results across all the languages" (~41:52)
- [CLNT] Client behaviour is specified in public ADR documents in the nats-io org, used as the spec for client maintainers; the team is moving toward test-driven specs where each ADR feature ships with a compatibility test. "use this testing tool to do something like test driven spec" (~44:55)
- [KV][ANTI] Transactional multi-key updates in KV were requested; the team says it is a wide change across the ecosystem and especially the server, not a workaround, and not coming soon. "don't expect it to be very soon but that's something you would love to have but it has to be done right" (~49:58)
- [SIZE][OBJ] Max payload can be raised but that hurts server performance and responsiveness; going beyond a few megabytes per message is not advised, which is why Object Store chunks. "it's not advised to go beyond some few megabytes of the max payload size of each message" (~50:59)
- [OBJ] Object Store exists because chunking large blobs correctly is tedious and error-prone and every user was re-implementing it; it is an opinion on how to store a large blob, not a full storage framework. "anybody who dealt with chunking some bytes know how easy it is to mess this up" (~50:59)
- [OBJ][KV] Object Store adds no new server API; it is a specific stream and consumer configuration on top of JetStream, and watch is just a consumer with a particular configuration. "consumers just can be treated as a watcher with different configurations" (~55:03)
- [OBJ][KV][TOPO] Because KV and Object Store are streams, they inherit mirroring and replication: read-only mirrors can be pushed to edge locations and data flows per mirror definitions with no extra dependencies. "you can create mirrors, read-only mirrors and push it down to edge locations" (~57:07)
- [OBJ] Object Store API was kept deliberately tiny rather than S3-compatible from day one, because it is easier to liberalize an API later than to shrink it. "it's much easier to become liberal over time and expand it" (~57:07)
- [KV][TOPO][MYTH] KV data does not have to be local to be accessible: if the NATS system is JetStream-enabled, a client in another region can still read the bucket where the data is not present. "you can still access the key value store from a different location where the data isn't" (~64:17)
- [KV][PATTERN] The underlying KV/Object stream can be used directly with normal stream operations if the abstraction's API is not enough; recurring workarounds become API candidates. "if this workaround looks like a pattern in the whole community then it will be considered as part of the API" (~59:09)
- [PATTERN] The services API doubles as an on-ramp: users who know HTTP handlers can write a request/reply service without understanding asynchronous messaging, then learn NATS top-down. "you don't have to grasp the whole asynchronous messaging stuff, it allows you to slowly get into it" (~66:19)

## Micro-services with auto discovery, observability and load balancing. | Rethink Connectivity Ep 9
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=byHGNUqIONw
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz (Synadia) | date: 2023 (Slack community "over five thousand, almost six thousand") | duration: 20:25
- version context: 2.9 era; services (micro) API newly available in Go, JS/TS, Rust, Java

### Claims
- [PATTERN][CLNT] The NATS services API is a set of conventions baked into client libraries (Go `micro` package, JS/TS, Rust, Java) rather than a framework, proxy, or extra tooling. "the NATS service API is a set of conventions that is baked into a lot of our client libraries" (~01:01)
- [PATTERN] A service declared with the API is instantly discoverable, observable via per-instance stats, load-balanced across instances, and can publish its request/reply schemas for client code generation. "you can also get the request and the reply schemas directly from these services just by talking to them" (~00:00)
- [CLNT] Service config carries name, version, description, optional API URL (e.g. an OpenAPI spec), a default endpoint or multiple endpoints; an endpoint is a schema coupled with a handler on a subject (wildcards allowed). "an endpoint is really a schema coupled with an actual handler" (~06:05)
- [CLNT] The stats, done, and error handlers are optional extension points; stats come out of the box and custom metrics can be pushed via the stats handler. "we actually bring stats out of the box with this services API" (~07:05)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Handler errors are returned with a code and description carried as headers (a 400-style code for malformed input); a payload can optionally be attached. "return a 400... I'm okay just having the error be embedded as a header" (~10:11)
- [OPS] The CLI `nats micro list` / `nats micro stats` commands discover and inspect services; `--trace` shows the underlying requests on the `$SRV.STATS.<name>` control subjects. "it's sending a request to this what we call a control channel around services, $SRV.STATS.sentiment" (~15:16)
- [PATTERN][CORE] Discovery is a one-to-many request: one request on the control subject gets a reply from every running instance, so no stateful service registry exists; the query reaches the services themselves. "these services aren't necessarily registering themselves with some stateful service discovery engine" (~16:17)
- [CORE] Ten requests to two instances were split five and five, showing queue-group load balancing between service instances with no configuration. "they got load balanced between the two, five and five" (~17:19)
- [CLNT] The schema field is an opaque string: JSON Schema, protobuf, or anything encodable (base64 if needed), so tooling can generate clients in any language. "these are all just a string so... you could really use whatever kind of schema that you want" (~18:19)

## NATS Connect Live! | NATS as a ServiceMesh
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E1eAvmCkIhQ
- speaker: Dale (OpenRMF open-source maintainer; community speaker, not Synadia), closing remarks by Derek Collison | date: 2020 (NATS Connect Live; "when 2.0 was coming out") | duration: 25:32
- version context: NATS 2.0/2.1 era, pre-JetStream GA (nats-io/not.go open-tracing reference; nats exporter)

### Claims
- [STALE?][PATTERN][ANTI] If you are asking whether you need a service mesh, you probably do not; meshes carry a lot of complexity and the team must be able to support it. "if you're asking that question you probably don't need one" (~03:03)
- [STALE?][PATTERN] Service-mesh feature list to compare against: discovery, distributed caching, load balancing, retry/timeout, circuit breaking, authn/authz, canary/blue-green rollouts, traffic shifting, mirroring, mTLS, metrics, tracing. "discovery, distributed caching, load balancing, retry timeout circuit break, there's authentication" (~02:03)
- [STALE?][SUBJ][PATTERN] With NATS you do not need to know where a service is or its name; you need to know the subject hierarchy and whether a subscriber exists for request/reply. "I don't need the name of the service, I need to know what subject" (~07:09)
- [STALE?][SEC] NATS 2.0 security (JWT operator/account/user model, decentralized, TLS with your own certs) replaces mesh-managed mTLS, but you have to manage certificate lifecycle yourself. "the caveat being for NATS... you have to manage it, you have to make sure that you maintain the certificate" (~09:09)
- [STALE?][OPS] Server metrics come from the Prometheus NATS exporter (CPU, memory, messages/bytes in/out, connections, subscriptions) with a Grafana dashboard; the speaker built per-client metrics on top for connection-level visibility. "I can have that kind of information on a per connection level, per client level" (~12:13)
- [STALE?][OPS][PATTERN] Tracing is not built into the server; the nats-io "not.go" reference shows carrying an OpenTracing span as a binary prefix on the message payload, stripped by the receiver (worked C# → Go). "you basically shove that on the front of your message data... you chop that piece off" (~15:18)
- [STALE?][OPS][ANTI] Do not use constant sampling for tracing; it locked the speaker's machine up. "make sure... that you don't do constant sampling like I did and lock your machine up" (~16:18)
- [STALE?][CORE][PATTERN] Load balancing in NATS is queue subscriptions (register the client with a queue name, effectively round-robin); locality-aware balancing comes from gateways, superclusters, and leaf nodes where closer subscribers get the message. "register your client with the queue name, that's how you load balance" (~17:20)
- [STALE?][PATTERN] Weighted load balancing was on the NATS roadmap at the time (later shipped as weighted subject mapping). "does a roadmap on a weighted load balancer" (~18:21)
- [STALE?][PATTERN] Traffic mirroring/shadowing in NATS is done by deploying the new version subscribing to the same subject (or wildcard) so it receives the same requests; permissions and accounts must allow it. "deploy a newer version and then listen for the same subject" (~20:24)
- [STALE?][TOPO][MYTH] Mesh-like functionality via NATS is not tied to Kubernetes; the speaker ran the same setup with Docker Compose, Kubernetes, and plain servers. "you can create a service mesh without Kubernetes as the basis" (~22:27)
- [STALE?][ANTI] Circuit breaking is the one mesh feature the speaker had not found in NATS. "circuit breaker, I haven't seen that in NATS yet" (~23:27)
- [STALE?][PATTERN] Derek Collison: NATS covers both services (request/reply) and streaming; the constraint of meshes being built inside a deployment platform like Kubernetes is what NATS considers too restricting. "the constraint that it has to be built inside of a deployment platform like Kubernetes sometimes can be too restricting" (~25:28)
