## EP01S3: Going back to basics with core NATS!
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mGzqEnIs7sk
- speaker: David Gee (host), Maurice van Veen, Tomasz Pietrek (Synadia) | date: unknown (NATS.fm season 3, Orbit being introduced → late 2024/2025) | duration: 52:33
- version context: 2.10 era; Orbit extensions just starting to land (episode 2 covers Orbit)

### Claims
- [CORE][PATTERN] Understanding core NATS is the foundation; JetStream, KV, Object Store and the service API are all layered on it, so learn core first. "if you understand core NATS you will be fine with JetStream, Object, Key Value and whatever other abstractions we built on top of it" (~03:20)
- [CORE][ANTI] People skip core NATS and go straight to JetStream "because we need persistence"; the speakers consider this a mistake. "sometimes people don't know where to start or they even skip core NATS entirely and go straight to JetStream" (~03:20)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Everything in NATS is pub/sub: request/reply is pub/sub with a reply inbox, JetStream is request/reply, KV is JetStream. "request reply is pub sub with reply subject, JetStream is request reply which is pub sub, key value is JetStream which is again pub sub" (~22:40)
- [CORE][SIZE] Host reports an early bench on an M1 Mac at roughly 48 gigabits per second for the simplest single-server pub/sub setup (unverified anecdote). "I think I was getting ridiculous numbers like 48 gigabits per second or something crazy" (~07:23)
- [CORE][SIZE] A single client can push on the order of 10 million messages per second if you try very hard, somewhat less on the subscriber side; persistent layers cannot match this. "you can get like 10 million messages per second if you try very hard on single client, a little bit less on subscriber side" (~20:37)
- [CORE][MYTH] Engineers reflexively demand maximum guarantees ("at most once? no, I need guarantees") but core NATS without persistence already gives useful guarantees, e.g. no-responders in request/reply. "core NATS even without any persistence can give you quite some guarantees" (~10:26)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Request/reply solves a whole class of timeout ambiguity: if the network is functional, NATS tells you immediately that nobody is listening instead of a timeout of unknown meaning. "you very quickly get an answer that nobody is there, maybe the service is down" (~11:27)
- [CORE][ANTI] A persistence layer (JetStream) is heavyweight and "stores everything"; with core NATS you can be selective about what gets stored. "every persistence layer is pretty heavy, it just stores everything if you use JetStream, while here you can be way more selective" (~11:27)
- [CORE][PATTERN] For publisher-side reliability in core NATS, assume anything can fail and require an acknowledgement/response; use request/reply plus timeouts and retries where you need to know the message arrived. "you always need to retry and hopefully be prepared for the worst cases" (~14:31)
- [CORE][USECASE] Some publishers (e.g. a temperature sensor broadcasting every half second) legitimately do not care whether anyone is listening; that is a valid core-NATS design. "if I'm a temperature sensor ... do I care that anybody's listening" (~16:32)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Periodic signalling (an aggregate or heartbeat every 10 seconds) is a lightweight core-NATS way to know a system is alive without JetStream. "you might want a response back every 10 seconds to say here's an aggregate or here's the last thing that we received" (~16:32)
- [CORE][STRM] JetStream, including its Raft layer, is built purely on core NATS publish/subscribe and request/reply with heartbeats; its reliability patterns can be borrowed selectively. "JetStream is actually built on top of core NATS, it's just using publish subscribe request reply and that's all it is, even the Raft layer" (~17:33)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Pull consumers already use heartbeats; a core-NATS app can adopt just the heartbeat idea ("once in 10 seconds let me know you're alive") without the rest of the guarantees. "in your specific use case you might not need all of those guarantees ... just one in 10 seconds just let me know" (~18:34)
- [STRM][CORE] JetStream is described as core NATS with the server subscribing to your messages to store them. "JetStream is just core NATS with server subscribing to your messages to store them" (~21:38)
- [PATTERN][ANTI] Start with core NATS; move to JetStream only when you find yourself reinventing consensus or replicated persistence. "at the moment you start feeling that you're reinventing the wheel of consensus or persistence ... then probably JetStream" (~21:38)
- [PATTERN] It is easier to add guarantees incrementally (core → JetStream for specific subjects) than to start with JetStream everywhere and later remove guarantees. "it's much easier to just start adding this than do everything for JetStream and then say okay when I can resign from the guarantees" (~23:41)
- [PATTERN][MIG] Because subjects decouple producers from storage, an app publishing sensor updates over core NATS can later have those subjects captured by a stream without changing the app. "you can just seamlessly switch to those subjects being captured by JetStream and the app doesn't even need to know" (~24:42)
- [CLNT][ANTI] The clients deliberately do not add generic request retry logic: a built-in retry is an opinion that suits ~90% of use cases but is wrong for the other 10% (e.g. transactional systems needing immediate failure). "for 90% of use cases yeah it should retry but it will then make very bad user experience for those 10%" (~29:46)
- [CLNT][ANTI] Stacked retries across layers (front end retries, back end retries, next back end retries) can bring a whole system down; a single enforced retry opinion is dangerous. "based on timing it would just bring the whole system down" (~30:50)
- [CLNT] Clients do reconnect automatically and resubscribe to prior subscriptions, and surface disconnect/reconnect events, because the network is usually the weakest link (e.g. clients in vehicles). "our clients do reconnect automatically and resubscribe to the subjects that they were subscribed before the connection was lost" (~28:45)
- [CLNT] Maintainers keep feature parity across clients while staying idiomatic per language; language-specific feature requests create a domino effect on every client. "we try to keep parity across the clients and this feature makes zero sense in like Rust or Go" (~31:51)
- [CLNT] Breaking changes to APIs like Object Store are avoided because honoring semver would force a major release across every client; this is why the API is hard to improve in place. "we are stuck with this API which we couldn't improve because we don't want to break any of our users" (~33:54)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Strategy shift: core clients focus on reliability and low-level protocol bindings with unopinionated patterns; opinionated/experimental abstractions go to the separately versioned Orbit umbrella project. "switch the focus and the client to focus on reliability, basically low-level NATS protocol binding ... and then to create separately versioned libraries elsewhere" (~32:52)
- [CLNT][ANTI] Connection pooling is a frequent request from database-minded users; the answer is to start with one connection and keep it unless you have a very specific reason. "you should start with one connection and unless you are something very specific use case you should keep that one connection" (~37:58)
- [CLNT] Considerable effort has gone into removing head-of-line blocking in the clients; a single TCP connection should not slow you down unless the network itself is misbehaving. "we did a really hard effort ... to remove the head of line blocking problems in NATS" (~37:58)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] One connection preserves publish ordering across all publishers in the application, and subscribers see that same ordering. "with one connection you also preserve publish ordering" (~38:59)
- [CLNT] You do not need separate connections per stream, consumer, or publisher; all of them multiplex over one connection. "you don't need a new connection for a consumer then also a new one for a publisher and then you maybe have five streams" (~40:02)
- [CLNT] A reason for a second connection is client-implementation specific, e.g. Java client internal queue sizes when one publisher saturates the queue. "in the Java client there are some triggers to do with queue sizes" (~41:03)
- [CLNT][TOPO] Some customers with unusual cloud network setups do get an improvement from multiple connections; creating two client instances works fine for that. "some customers who have very specific network setups over the cloud providers ... for them it actually makes an improvement to have more connections" (~41:03)
- [CLNT][ANTI] Pooling is deliberately not provided because users would default to it out of habit and then be confused by lost ordering. "if we give pooling to the users everybody would start with pooled connections and half of the people will be confused why I lost the order" (~42:05)
- [SIZE][CLNT] The ~10 million msgs/s a single client can publish goes over one connection; the speaker doubts two connections from the same client would exceed it. "they can go for one connection and I don't think you can get more if you do over two the same client" (~44:06)
- [PATTERN][TOPO][SEC] NATS has three "planes" (API: core/JetStream; security; topology); starting with all of them at once (JetStream over clustered leaf nodes with auth callout) piles on complexity, so start with a single server, one connection, and add features as they solve problems. "start with probably simple single server ... run an app with one connection ... make it use more features from there on" (~45:08)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] The scale path is incremental: core → JetStream, single server → cluster → leaf nodes/edge, unsecured → multi-tenancy with accounts. "you can scale it really easily from core NATS to JetStream, from single server to cluster, from cluster to leaf nodes" (~46:10)
- [OPS][SIZE] You will hit network limits before NATS limits: the host saturated a 100 Mbit home link while running a bench against a bare-metal cluster in Germany and mistook it for poor NATS performance. "turns out I just saturated 100 megabit link and that's all I'd done" (~48:12)
- [OPS][ANTI] Cloud I/O is often burstable: things look fine for hours and then throughput drops with no change in NATS; network/IO is usually the first bottleneck. "in the cloud environment when the I/O is burstable quite often, it looks fine for a few hours and then suddenly drops" (~49:14)
- [USECASE][CORE] Presence-style features (which page each user is viewing, Google-Docs-like) were built in a few hours with plain pub/sub request/reply: open page, request everyone on the page, they respond. "I opened the page and I request everyone that on the page and they respond" (~51:16)

## EP02S3: Orbit - The NATS Client Extensions
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o4rmeqfE5HE
- speaker: David Gee (host), Tomasz Pietrek (Synadia) | date: 2025 (recorded 4 February 2025 per host) | duration: 49:11
- version context: 2.10 era, 2.11 imminent (priority groups, batch get referenced as upcoming)

### Claims
- [CLNT] Tier-one clients (Go, Java, JavaScript, Rust, Python, C, Ruby, .NET) get every new server feature and promise parity; tier-two clients such as Swift are maintained by Synadia but may lag behind. "tier one clients are always in parity, that they have feature coverage ... each of them is idiomatic to their own language" (~04:06)
- [CLNT] Tier-one status is decided mostly by user, customer and community demand; Swift was not considered until interest from edge devices grew quickly. "that's how we mostly decide what's tier one what's not" (~05:08)
- [CLNT][ANTI] In the past, features were merged into individual clients as users asked; every such feature soon triggered "why is it not in the other language", so now every new tier-one feature must pass a parity check agreed by all maintainers. "every new feature added to tier one client has to go through the parity check" (~09:15)
- [CLNT][ANTI] Language-agnostic client APIs that look identical across languages end up feeling foreign in every language; NATS prefers idiomatic clients and steers users to per-language examples. "it felt very weird for me as a Gopher, like it didn't feel like Go" (~12:16)
- [CLNT] The ADR and design process was strengthened because parity failures were often about how a feature works, not just whether it exists. "we didn't have always the parity ... not just parity of features but parity in terms of how a given feature works" (~15:18)
- [CLNT][ANTI] Bundling JetStream, KV and Object Store in one client with a single version makes breaking changes practically impossible under semver, even for APIs marked experimental. "it feels like we never can break anything, we can mark a specific API experimental but how does it matter" (~16:20)
- [CORE][SIZE] The server keeps core, JetStream, KV and Object Store in one process on purpose: splitting into services would add operational complexity and inter-service latency that would make current performance unreachable. "it would be impossible to reach the current performance limits of NATS JetStream and KV and Object Store if it was not all in one package" (~17:20)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Orbit is a line in the sand: existing client features stay, and every new client-side abstraction built on streams/consumers (like KV, Object Store and the service API are) lands in Orbit instead of the client. "every new abstraction built on top of ... will land in Orbit, so it's like a line in the sand to not break the clients" (~19:21)
- [CLNT] Server APIs are performance-oriented (one struct for many operations), so clients do not expose them one-to-one; Orbit also serves as an incubator for new server-feature APIs whose client shape is not yet settled. "Orbit ... as an incubator for the new features and new APIs which we are not confident the shape of yet" (~21:23)
- [CLNT] Orbit is one umbrella repository per language containing many independently versioned modules, so each can evolve, be released weekly, be stabilized, or be deprecated without a client breaking change. "each client has their own umbrella repository with many crates, modules ... each having separate versioning" (~22:24)
- [CLNT] Orbit does not promise parity: request-many is expected in every tier-one Orbit library, but Go-specific utilities (context helpers) and Java-specific ones (publisher factory) stay language-local. "we also don't promise parity in Orbit" (~24:29)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Contributing to Orbit only requires knowing the public client API, not client internals, which lowers the barrier compared with the large client codebases. "the only knowledge necessary being I know how to use the client, not the machinery of the client itself" (~25:29)
- [CLNT] Orbit modules use only public client APIs (dogfooding), which exposed several internals that SDK builders need and that the clients had not exposed. "we learn along the way that we didn't expose some really important bit to be able to write really flexible SDKs on top of it" (~29:35)
- [CLNT][ANTI] Maintainers are conservative about exposing client internals because each exposed piece becomes something that can break during client evolution; needs are now justified by concrete Orbit usage. "we are always very careful with exposing any internals because it makes evolving the client even harder" (~31:36)
- [CLNT][STRM] Batch (direct) get is a 2.12 feature that will be implemented in Orbit rather than the client, not because the server side is unstable but because the client API shape could not be agreed within a few weeks. "batch get which will be the 2.12 feature ... we decided to get it into Orbit instead of the client" (~32:37)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Orbit never talks the wire protocol directly; it builds on the highest available client abstraction and drops at most one layer down to publish/subscribe. "never wire protocol ... we try to use as high level abstraction from the client in Orbit as possible" (~34:41)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Typed JetStream request helpers (with typed errors and success responses) are being exposed in Go so users can build their own admin APIs on top. "allow people to build their own additional like admin API ... which is actually now exposed in the Orbit of Go" (~34:41)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Request-many sends one request and collects multiple responses with pluggable stop strategies: expected message count, stall/jitter timeout since the last message, and others; it is a core-NATS extension built on pub/sub. "one of them being how many messages you expect, the other being the jitter, how long you expect to wait for the next message" (~35:41)
- [CLNT] Orbit coverage in early 2025: Go has the most modules, followed by Java, Rust and JavaScript; .NET, C and Ruby are following; Rust had only request-many at the time. "the most amount of modules are in Go and then it's followed up by Java, Rust and JavaScript" (~37:45)
- [CLNT] Previously hidden tooling such as the JSM report utilities is now surfaced through Orbit; even Synadia staff did not know some existed. "some like in JSM report that almost nobody externally uses and it was hidden very deeply" (~39:49)
- [CLNT][ANTI] The service API being placed in the clients is regretted because its API was frozen immediately; if built today it would live in Orbit. "we were actually not very happy that the service API was in the clients because we very quickly felt that we couldn't break the API" (~40:51)
- [CLNT] Rule for where new features go: server features go straight into the clients (server API is public and stable since 2.x); non-parity items and abstractions go to Orbit; server features with uncertain client API shape incubate in Orbit and move back when mature. "most features will come directly to the clients ... every new abstraction ... will land in Orbit" (~42:54)
- [CLNT] The clients' feature set is frozen at core NATS, JetStream, KV and Object Store; the long-term goal is to make clients lighter, closer to a low-level wire-protocol binding, without breaking anything. "we froze the clients with the feature set at core NATS, JetStream, KV, Object Store" (~43:57)
- [CONS][CLNT] For 2.11 priority groups, pinning and overflow are supported in the clients as basic primitives, while the full consumer-group abstraction built on pinning is implemented and iterated in Orbit. "the pinning and overflow will be supported in the clients ... the actual whole consumer group abstraction implementation will be in Orbit" (~45:59)
- [CLNT] The best way to discover Orbit extensions is the per-language repo, where each extension has its own README with version, docs and examples. "each extension is a separate readme page ... with all the details, all the docs and all the examples" (~48:01)

## EP03S3: NATS 2.11 Release
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t7m3BgLGHfU
- speaker: Tomasz Pietrek (host), Maurice van Veen, Neil Twigg (Synadia server maintainers) | date: 2025 (recorded March 2025, just before the 2.11 release) | duration: 47:07
- version context: 2.11 release candidates (RC2/RC3); comparisons to 2.10.26

### Claims
- [OPS][TOPO] Distributed message tracing exists because in large topologies (leaf nodes, clusters, superclusters, account import/export, subject mappings) "where did my message go" previously required subscribing at many points. "you kind of needed to subscribe in different places in your system and check if messages are there and in which form" (~05:06)
- [OPS] A traced message reports every hop: leaf node, route, gateway, subject mapping, account boundary, and JetStream ingest. "you will know which through which leaf node, which route connection, which gateway, mapping, account boundaries, JetStream ingest, all of it" (~05:06)
- [OPS][PATTERN] Tracing is opt-in per message via a trace-destination header (an inbox); each hop sends a trace message back to that inbox, and the CLI wraps this as `nats trace <subject>`. "you provide an inbox and every step of the message ... will send back a trace message to the inbox that you specified" (~06:07)
- [OPS] Tracing is aimed at developers as much as operators, especially where the team writing apps and the team running NATS are separate groups. "probably more useful to developers than it would be to system operators" (~09:09)
- [OPS][STRM] A trace can be configured so the message is neither persisted into a stream nor delivered to the final client, giving a dry-run of the path. "you can literally ask the system stop just short of finally delivering the message" (~08:09)
- [STRM] Per-message TTL is set with the `Nats-TTL` header plus a duration on publish and controls how long that individual message survives regardless of, or in combination with, stream limits. "activated using a header when you publish the message, which is just Nats-TTL and then a duration" (~11:11)
- [KV][STRM] Per-message TTL is planned to clean up KV delete tombstones, which accumulate in buckets with high delete rates; watchers still get the delete notification but the markers no longer live forever. "if you have a very high incidence of deletes you can end up with an awful lot of history in your KV bucket which is just delete tombstones" (~12:13)
- [STRM][KV] 2.11 includes a first pass at subject delete markers when a subject disappears from a stream via max age, to support the KV use case, with more iteration planned. "in 2.11 we'll have an initial pass of that that just happens with max age" (~14:18)
- [STRM][SIZE] Per-message TTL is implemented with a timed hash wheel so very large numbers of expiries can be tracked with little memory. "it actually uses an exotic data structure called a timed hash wheel ... track an awful lot of key expiries without actually using too much memory" (~15:21)
- [SUBJ][SIZE] The server's subject interest handling uses an in-house adaptive radix tree (with node-size tweaks learned from real customer subject hierarchies) and modified Patricia trees for the interest graph. "the adaptive radix tree implementation actually has a couple of slight tweaks that differ from the paper" (~16:23)
- [OPS] Server testing includes thousands of unit tests, in-house chaos tooling (high latency, dead links, power pulls), continuous comparative benchmarking per commit, and deterministic simulation with Antithesis. "we've been working quite a lot with a company called Antithesis ... deterministic testing ... you can rewind time" (~20:27)
- [OPS][MIG] Most 2.11 stability fixes (including Antithesis findings) were backported into the 2.10 series from about 2.10.23 onward, so upgrading from a late 2.10.x to 2.11 is a small delta. "pretty much since 2.10.23 we've kind of already been backporting lots of fixes that were kind of scheduled for 2.11" (~21:28)
- [OPS][MIG] The reliability difference between 2.10.0 and 2.10.26/2.11 is described as huge, mainly in clustering and Raft; the maintainers say evaluating the latest version is always worth it. "the improvements that we've made to the clustering logic, to the Raft application, it's massive" (~22:29)
- [CONS] Consumer priority groups began as a request for Kafka-like consumer groups; the team deliberately designed a NATS-native solution rather than copying. "instead of just copying ideas, solutions, just try to solve the problem" (~23:29)
- [CONS] In 2.11 a consumer may have only one priority group, but the config takes an array so clients are ready for multiple groups later without a type change. "for now it's only one group per consumer ... we wanted clients to be ready to be able to pass an array or slice" (~23:29)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Overflow lets a client set a threshold (pending messages or pending acks) above which it starts receiving; e.g. three same-region clients serve normally and clients in another availability zone only pull when the primaries are too busy, minimizing cross-region cost without losing availability. "they will start getting messages only if the primary ones will get too busy" (~25:33)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Pinning makes one client of many on a consumer receive all messages; the server uses TTLs to detect it stopped pulling and fails over to another client, replacing hand-rolled orchestration of a single active worker. "you can say that client A will get all the messages and the server has mechanisms and TTLs to find out that this client is no longer getting messages and the other one will take over" (~26:34)
- [CONS][CLNT] At 2.11 launch overflow is in all clients; pinning ships in Go first while the Orbit consumer-group abstraction built on pinning is validated. "overflow will be available in all the clients when 2.11 launches, the pinning will be available in Go first" (~27:36)
- [CONS][MYTH] Maintainers insist new abstractions fit JetStream's native concepts rather than bolting on leaky models copied from other tools. "we're not just bolting something in that feels like either a leaky or a not very watertight model" (~28:38)
- [KV][SIZE][ANTI] KV was introduced (KubeCon Valencia) as a small experiment for IoT caches; users now load millions of keys, so 2.11 is the first release adding default soft limits and safe defaults to features. "now we are at I don't know millions of keys ... this is the first release where we started adding default limit soft cuts" (~30:40)
- [STRM][CONS] Multi-message (batch) get is "a consumer without a consumer": one request returning many responses, with filters, start sequence/time, up-to sequence/time, and multiple subject filters, which plain direct get could not do. "you can specify multiple subject filters as well which I think wasn't possible before with the old direct gets" (~33:45)
- [STRM][SIZE] Batch get responses are capped (the speaker recalls 64 messages, and a byte limit) after which you paginate with another request. "maximum amount of messages or maximum amount of bytes that can be sent back before you need to paginate in some way, 64 messages I think" (~33:45)
- [STRM][CONS][ANTI] Consumers are server-side state; many small operations via consumers eat server resources, whereas batch get creates no server state and is fire-and-forget. "the biggest difference is that batch get does not create state on the server, it just gives you what you asked for and it's done" (~34:46)
- [KV][OBJ] Batch get is intended to improve future KV fetching and possibly Object Store, which would rather rip through a stream without creating a consumer. "object store is a great example, you really don't need the consumer" (~35:47)
- [OPS] Limits on new features are set deliberately low because raising a limit later is far easier than lowering one. "they're quite low, so if you'll see need for making them higher that's much easier than the other way around" (~36:48)
- [CONS][OPS] Consumer pause is a consumer config option with a deadline timestamp; delivery resumes at that time, a past timestamp or absent option means unpaused, and it is meant as a maintenance/migration tool. "you specify a deadline, at 2:00 p.m. on the 12th of March start delivering messages again" (~37:48)
- [CONS][CLNT] Paused consumers keep sending idle heartbeats, so client applications see no errors, only an absence of messages until resume. "the consumers still continue to receive idle heartbeats so the applications won't get errors" (~38:49)
- [OPS] Pedantic mode (implemented in the JSM library, used by NACK and Terraform) makes the server accept or reject exactly the values sent with no defaulting, which desired-state tooling needs. "there is no dynamic, no defaulting or failing, no defaulting to some limits" (~41:55)
- [OPS] 2.11 adds a configuration state digest: the running config is hashed and can be queried or generated from the command line to check whether a modified file has been loaded. "the running configuration gets hashed and you can ask the server at any time, tell me what the hash of the configuration file that you're running" (~42:56)
- [OPS][MIG] New 2.11 features are opt-in and not enabled by default; the upgrade from 2.10.26 is expected to be straightforward, and the diff between 2.10.0 and 2.10.26 is larger than between 2.10.26 and 2.11. "you'll mostly get new features which will not even be enabled by default and you have to opt in" (~44:58)
- [OPS] The year-and-a-half 2.11 cycle is not something the maintainers want to repeat. "this year and a half long cycle is not something we're keen to repeat" (~43:57)

## NATS tools and benchmarking with JNM! NATS Community Office Hours (Reupload)
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwQCPP8TGUQ
- speaker: Nate (host, Synadia community office hours), Jean-Noël Moyne (JNM, Synadia) | date: unknown (after Current conference in Austin, before 2.11 release → late 2024) | duration: 71:45
- version context: 2.10 era, 2.11 upcoming; new rewritten `nats bench` in a recent NATS CLI release

### Claims
- [SIZE][OPS] The whole NATS server with JetStream ships as a single ~12 MB binary; Kafka-experienced conference attendees did not believe it until shown. "everything in a single 12 MB binary ... They don't believe it actually at first" (~02:03)
- [MYTH][STRM][CONS] NATS positions itself against Kafka on "proper queuing, proper request reply, proper multi-tenancy, no partitions unless you want them". "proper queuing, proper request reply, proper multi-tenancy ... no partitions unless you want them" (~02:03)
- [TOPO][USECASE] A NATS server can run on a Raspberry Pi or inside a vehicle; production examples cited are vehicles of a car brand, trains, taxi cabs in Europe, and oil drilling stations, all partially connected over cellular. "there's a vehicle of a certain manufacturer that literally actually a NATS server running in the vehicle" (~05:06)
- [TOPO][STRM][PATTERN] JetStream-enabled leaf nodes at the edge give store-and-forward: publishes are stored locally and guaranteed to be mirrored or sourced to the hub when connectivity returns, within milliseconds if the link is up. "it still is stored locally by the stream at the edge and reliably forwarded" (~06:08)
- [MYTH][TOPO] Equivalent edge/mirroring behavior in Kafka or Pulsar requires extra JVM components (Kafka Streams, MirrorMaker, brokers plus bookkeepers plus zookeepers), which the speaker calls infrastructure sprawl. "JVMs as far as the eye can see" (~07:10)
- [CONS][MYTH] Kafka is not "proper queuing" because committing an offset implicitly acknowledges every earlier sequence; JetStream acknowledges each message individually. "when you acknowledge a message or commit a message ... you're committing that sequence number and automatically committing all the other sequence numbers before that" (~10:14)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Guaranteed delivery is not enough for a queue; you need guaranteed processing, e.g. a message whose database insert fails because the database is down for 10 minutes should be redelivered later, not block the partition. "it's not just the guaranteed delivery, you also want to do guaranteed processing" (~09:11)
- [CONS] JetStream supports negative acknowledgement with a backoff delay (retry in 10 minutes, 20 minutes, an hour) and automatic redelivery; Kafka has neither. "you can say I negatively acknowledge this message and you can specify a backoff time" (~11:15)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Terminate (term) is for messages that are themselves bad; unlike nak, it stops redelivery so a poison message does not loop forever. "the message itself is bad ... you can terminate the message" (~11:15)
- [MYTH] A Kafka KIP for queuing describes essentially the per-message ack, nak and redelivery features JetStream already has. "if you look at the features that they have described in a KIP ... it's basically all of the features I just talked about" (~12:17)
- [CORE][PATTERN][MYTH] Kafka-style request/reply is CQRS (submit to one topic, poll another later); NATS offers interactive request/reply with geo-affinity where you learn within a timeout that nobody can process the request and can decide whether to resubmit. "I send a request, if there's no one able to process at this point I want to know about this in whatever timeout is" (~13:18)
- [PATTERN][ANTI] With CQRS-style requests, re-publishing after 30 seconds without an answer risks duplicating the work. "if you don't get an answer within 30 seconds and you publish another request, you're going to possibly duplicate the work" (~14:18)
- [SUBJ][STRM][MYTH] Subject-based addressing lets a consumer filter messages from a stream; Kafka is one topic, one stream, with no server-side filtering. "Kafka is one topic one stream and when you read messages from a stream in Kafka there's no filtering" (~14:18)
- [OPS][MYTH] Kafka exposes many timing knobs with hard-to-find correct values; NATS has few, and the speaker's rule is "with 100 knob positions, 99 are wrong". "if there's 100 positions, possibly there's 99 wrong ones" (~17:23)
- [OPS][SEC] The server has very few Go module dependencies, which keeps the binary small and reduces exposure to dependency security advisories; the CLI is intentionally larger and that is fine. "the more dependencies you have the more chances that some point there'll be a security advisory on one of those dependencies" (~19:24)
- [TOPO][CLNT] The NATS server is also a built-in MQTT server for edge devices, and switching a client from TCP to WebSocket (or secure WebSocket) is only a change of the connection URL scheme. "the NATS server is also an MQTT server built in ... changing two or three characters in a connection URL" (~21:26)
- [OPS] `nats top` is now built into the CLI; it needs a system-account context and a server name and refreshes every second, acting as a real-time speedometer complementing Prometheus/Grafana history. "you need to have a speedometer, right? You need to know how hard am I working right now" (~27:33)
- [OPS] `nats cheat <subcommand>` prints commonly used example commands for any subcommand. "you can do nats cheat on any of these subcommands and it will give you examples" (~28:35)
- [OPS] `nats stream edit -i` opens the full stream config as YAML with schema and descriptions in an editor; `nats stream info --json | jq .config` extracts only the config for automation, diffing, and `nats stream edit --config file`. "you pipe it to jq .config, that's just the config part" (~30:38)
- [OPS] `nats sub --translate 'jq ...'` pipes each received payload through an external command; `--subjects-only`, timestamps and delta-time flags give tcpdump-style views of traffic. "pass the message to jq, could be jq, could be you can translate to anything you want" (~32:39)
- [OPS] The rewritten `nats bench` uses `nats bench pub|sub <subject>` and `nats bench js ...` subcommands, defaults to 100,000 messages of 128 bytes, and uses the simplified JetStream API instead of push/pull flags. "it's basically been completely rewritten, especially to be much easier to use" (~36:45)
- [SIZE][OPS][MYTH] Synadia publishes no official throughput numbers because distributed-system results depend on network, traffic, disk and cloud variability; they ship a tool to run in your own environment instead. "three kinds of lies in the software business: big lies, small lies, and benchmarks" (~38:47)
- [OPS][ANTI] Cloud burstable instances and general-purpose EBS (gp2/gp3) show good numbers for short tests but throttle after roughly 20 minutes of sustained JetStream writes; io1/io2 volumes cost more but are not throttled. "you'll get like maybe 20 minutes worth of good traffic and all of a sudden it'll throttle you way down" (~40:52)
- [SIZE][CORE] On a ~3-year-old M1 Ultra Mac Studio over loopback, a single publisher with no subscribers reached about 5 million 128-byte msgs/s (~600 MB/s); at 1 MB messages it did about 3,700-4,000 msgs/s but 3.6-3.8 GB/s. "it's 5 million messages a second, they're 128 bytes ... 3.8 gigabytes per second" (~42:54)
- [SIZE][MYTH] Loopback numbers show what the software can do with near-infinite bandwidth; real deployments are lower purely because of the network, so a faster network gives faster numbers on the same machines. "buy a faster network, you'll get faster numbers with the same machines" (~44:55)
- [OPS][PATTERN] `nats bench` doubles as a load generator via a sleep between publishes (e.g. 200 µs), and multiple bench instances can be combined for steady load plus bursts. "you can also use it to generate load, generate traffic ... you can set the duration here" (~45:56)
- [CORE][SIZE] A publish-only bench with no subscribers is artificially high because the server drops messages with no interest; with four core subscribers each message is copied four times and it is still very fast. "no one is subscribing ... the server says there's no interest for the message and subject, they're dropping there" (~46:59)
- [OPS][ANTI] Benchmarks shorter than a few seconds are unreliable; make runs longer to get a proper number. "if the benchmark takes tenths of a second or less ... you may want to make it a little bit longer" (~48:01)
- [OPS][ANTI] Do not benchmark on laptops: thermal throttling kicks in after about 30 seconds at full clock; if you must, run 20-30 s tests then wait 20-30 s to cool. "on a laptop you got about 30 seconds and then at full speed ... your clock speed is going to be throttled down" (~49:02)
- [STRM][OPS][PATTERN] Benchmark JetStream publish and consume separately before combining them, because together they compete for CPU and you cannot tell which limits the other. "when you do the both together you don't know which one is limiting the other" (~52:04)
- [OPS] `nats bench js pub` expects the stream to exist unless `--create` is given; the default stream is file storage with one replica, and it publishes asynchronously in batches of 500. "it does async publishes in batches of 500 messages" (~53:04)
- [OPS][TOPO][ANTI] In a cluster, bench publisher and subscriber connect to random servers; landing on the same server gives better numbers than being on different servers (extra route hop), so run several times or pin to one server for consistency. "if you happen to have your pub and your sub connecting to the same server you're going to get better numbers" (~54:06)
- [CONS][OPS] A server-side max ack pending limit (100 in the demo config) blocked bench's default consumer creation (it wants 500); the workaround was to pre-create the consumer and pass its name. "I probably set up the limit for 100 for max ack pending, by default it wants to do 500" (~57:10)
- [CONS] `nats bench js` can consume three ways with the simplified API: `consume` (callback, library manages pulls), `fetch` (explicit batches, default 500), and an ordered consumer. "you can test three different ways you can consume messages in JetStream with the JS simplified API" (~55:08)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Consumer decision tree: multiple apps sharing a stream or needing resumable position → durable; otherwise ephemeral, and among ephemerals the ordered consumer should be the default. "Ordered consumer should be your default go-to" (~59:19)
- [CONS][MYTH] Ordered consumers need no application acks yet guarantee in-order, gap-free delivery; the client library tracks sequences, detects gaps, and recreates the ephemeral consumer after reconnects. "if it sees a gap of any kind it knows that something must have happened ... it will not deliver the messages until it recovers the messages missing" (~63:24)
- [CONS][MYTH] Acks in JetStream are for guaranteed consumption (exactly-once processing), not guaranteed delivery; "no acks" does not mean unreliable. "acknowledgements in NATS are really not for guaranteed delivery, but guaranteed consumption" (~61:22)
- [CONS][SIZE] On the same local setup, consuming with explicit acks ran up to about 200,000 msgs/s while an ordered consumer reached about 650,000 msgs/s from a file-backed stream. "up to 200,000 per second with explicit acks ... with an ordered consumer we're in 650,000 per second" (~62:24)
- [CONS] The performance gap is mostly the cost of acknowledging every message at the application level; max-ack-pending flow control still applies to acking consumers. "this difference between 200 and 600 is mostly due to the fact that you don't have to acknowledge at the application every time" (~64:24)
- [OPS][SIZE] A community member hit Windows desktop kernel networking throttling before NATS itself throttled, at roughly 5-6 million core msgs/s. "he throttled the Windows kernel before NATS actually hit that throttling point" (~68:28)
- [OPS] `nats bench js pub --purge` clears the stream first; otherwise repeated benches keep appending. "you can also pass a purge if you want to purge the stream first before you publish" (~69:29)
- [STRM][SIZE] With a subscriber attached, JetStream publish throughput dropped from about 139k to about 84k msgs/s in the demo, with the consumer side being the limiting factor. "with no one listening you got 139 ... with someone listening, 84" (~70:30)

## Benchmark Core NATS & NATS JetStream using the NATS CLI tool
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HwwvFeUHAyo
- speaker: Jean-Noël Moyne (Synadia, solutions engineering) | date: unknown (mid-2021 MacBook Pro used; old `nats bench --pub/--sub/--pull` flag syntax → 2021-2022) | duration: 27:16
- version context: 2.6-2.8 era (old nats bench flag syntax, push/pull consumer flags, pre-simplified JetStream API)

### Claims
- [OPS][PATTERN] Run benchmarks on your own target environment (machines, network, pods) rather than trusting published numbers; the CLI is the tool for that. "run benchmarks on your own target environments to see what kind of actual realistic performance you will get" (~00:00)
- [OPS] `nats top` connects via the monitoring port (`-m 8222`) and shows per-connection stats plus server CPU, memory, slow consumers, messages and bytes in/out per second. "you can also monitor the CPU utilization of the NATS server process, memory utilization, number of slow consumers" (~02:02)
- [OPS] `nats bench` produces two kinds of numbers: latency and throughput; latency is measured with request/reply mode and a single synchronous thread. "you can use nats bench to produce two kinds of numbers, one is latency, the other one is throughput" (~02:02)
- [CORE][SIZE] Single-threaded synchronous request/reply on a 2021 Intel MacBook Pro over loopback did about 7,500 round trips per second, i.e. ~133 µs average process-to-process round trip through NATS. "7,500 about ... that's a 133 about microseconds an average of a round trip" (~04:04)
- [OPS][ANTI] Sub-second benchmark runs show noticeable variation; use runs of 30 seconds to a minute or more (increase the message count above the 100,000 default) for sustained numbers. "you would want to do benchmarks that run for more than a fraction of a second, you know 30 seconds a minute or more" (~05:06)
- [CORE][SIZE] Core pub/sub with one publisher and one subscriber (each on its own connection) reached about 3.9-4.2 million 128-byte msgs/s, roughly 500 MB/s, on the laptop. "we got 3.9 million and we got 4.2 and now we get 4 million" (~07:07)
- [CORE][SIZE] With one publisher and 10 subscribers (fan-out), the aggregate was about 5.3 million msgs/s: the publisher at ~500k msgs/s and each subscriber at ~480k msgs/s. "the publisher probably shot about 500,000 per second and the subscribers are for 480 thousands" (~08:09)
- [SIZE][OPS] With 128-byte messages the bottleneck is CPU (per-message overhead), not bandwidth; raise the message size to measure bandwidth-bound throughput. "you're going to be CPU bound rather than bandwidth bound as your limit" (~09:09)
- [CORE][SIZE] Two publishers, four subscribers with larger messages showed the server receiving ~26k msgs/s and sending ~103k msgs/s, about 2 GB/s aggregate on the laptop. "it's receiving 25,000 messages per second, around 26,000, and sending out 103 or so ... two gigabytes per second" (~10:11)
- [OPS][ANTI] Laptops throttle CPU frequency as temperature rises during benchmarks; let them cool between runs and do multiple runs, dropping outliers and averaging. "do more than one benchmark, more than one run ... that allows you to eliminate the outliers" (~11:12)
- [STRM][CORE] A core publish returns no server acknowledgement; a JetStream publish returns an ack that the message was received and persisted, so use JetStream publish to get the full benefit of a stream. "a JetStream publish operation lets you get an acknowledgement that the message was properly received and persisted" (~13:15)
- [STRM][SIZE] Synchronous JetStream publishing is bounded by round-trip time like any request/reply; raise throughput with many synchronous clients or with batching (async publish with a batch size). "the way to increase throughput in those situations is to either have a lot of clients ... or start using batching" (~14:16)
- [STRM][SIZE] Publish batch size 10 gives a dramatic improvement, 100 another large one, 1000 only a little more: diminishing returns set in around a batch of 100. "you start getting to where you have a diminishing return of increasing the batch size" (~14:16)
- [STRM][SIZE] Two publishers with the default batch of 100 reached nearly the same rate as one publisher with batches of 1000. "we get pretty close to the maximum that we saw with batches of a thousand, except in this case we have two guys just using batches of 100" (~15:17)
- [STRM][CORE] Core NATS subscribers can observe messages being published into a stream at the same time, with high fan-out still possible. "these are core NATS subscribers onto the JetStream publisher" (~15:17)
- [CONS] Consumers are views onto a stream with cursor-like state; acknowledging consumers require the app to ack, nak, or ask for more time per message, and with a work-queue stream an acked message is removed. "you can look at consumers as views onto the stream" (~16:18)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Ephemeral consumers suit one app instance getting its own copy of the data at its own pace, disappearing when the app quits; durable consumers are shared by many instances and distribute messages between them like a queue. "a durable consumer essentially acts as a queue for distribution purposes" (~18:19)
- [CONS][SIZE] Ten ephemeral ordered push consumers each reading 700,000 messages from a memory stream on the laptop totalled roughly 1.2-3 million msgs/s delivered (7 million messages in total). "1.2 whatever three million messages ... this is distributing seven million messages total" (~20:21)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Pull consumers let you specify a batch, which matters because downstream processing (e.g. writing to a database) also needs batching to keep up with the message rate. "if you end up writing one by one to for example a database without batching things then you would never be able to keep up" (~21:22)
- [CONS][SIZE] A single pull consumer with batch 1 and per-message ack uses little CPU and is slow; batch 100 gives a huge improvement, and adding more pullers scales further (from ~210k msgs/s on the laptop). "going from 210 to, if I had more than just a single laptop ... would obviously be able to scale a lot further" (~23:26)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Pull consumers are the horizontal-scaling primitive: add more instances for throughput, or use bigger batches on fewer, faster machines. "pull consumers ... allow you to scale out horizontally" (~22:23)
- [OPS] The bench defaults to a memory stream with replication 1; `--replicas` and `--storage file` change that, and the auto-created `benchstream` is deliberately not deleted so later consumer benches have data. "you don't want it to delete the stream at the end because that would delete all the data" (~24:26)
- [OPS][ANTI] Changing storage type between runs requires deleting the existing bench stream first (`nats stream rm benchstream -f`), otherwise the old config is reused. "simply remember to remove the stream, that's the simplest thing" (~25:26)
- [STRM][SIZE] File storage publishes slower than memory, but reading back from disk is still fast: a push consumer delivered 4 × 400,000 messages in about 4 seconds (~400k msgs/s) on the laptop. "retrieving from disk is still quite fast ... about 400,000 per second" (~26:27)
- [CONS] Pull consumers with acks are a bit slower than push/ordered consumers because of acknowledgements but give a higher quality of service. "it's a little bit slower because of the acknowledgements but you get much higher quality of service" (~26:27)
