## Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS: Ordered, Scalable Stream Processing
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2Z0J0iSp9dk
- speaker: unknown (Synadia channel narrator) | date: unknown (post-2.11; uses pinned client priority groups and the CG tool) | duration: 31:20
- version context: 2.11+ era (pull-consumer priority groups / pinned client policy, Orbit-style consumer-groups library, CG tool)

### Claims
- [CONS][PATTERN] Ordinary NATS load balancing is non-deterministic, so two messages on the same subject can land on different workers and lose per-key order. "ordinary load balancing in NATS is non-deterministic. Two messages on the same subject can land on two different workers" (~01:00)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Partitioned consumer groups route every message sharing a partition key to the same worker while different keys run in parallel; it is the Kafka consumer group model built from two JetStream pieces. "If that sounds like Kafka consumer groups, that is the same model built in NATS from two JetStream pieces" (~01:00)
- [SUBJ][STRM] The partition function is a subject transform that hashes the chosen subject tokens into a partition number from 0 to X-1, deterministically and roughly balanced. "It hashes the subject tokens you choose and turns them into a partition number from zero up to X minus one" (~02:00)
- [STRM][SUBJ] The transform is applied at stream ingress and appends a partition token to each subject, so messages are physically separated by key inside the stream. "You apply the transform at the stream's ingress and it appends a partition token to each subject" (~02:00)
- [CONS] Pull consumer priority groups are pull-only and require explicit acknowledgement. "They are pull only and need explicit acknowledgement" (~02:00)
- [CONS] With the pinned client policy the server picks one client to receive all of a group's messages; others stand by, and if the pinned client goes quiet past its timeout the server re-pins to a standby. "If that client goes quiet past its timeout, the server simply re-pins to a standby" (~02:00)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Pinning gives a single active worker with hot standby and no separate leader election system. "a single active worker with a hot standby and no separate leader election system to run" (~03:02)
- [CONS][ANTI] Pinning is affinity plus failover, not a distributed lock; a client may briefly still think it is pinned after the server moved on, and buffered messages cannot be pulled back. "Pinning is affinity and failover. It is not a distributed lock" (~03:02)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Handlers should be idempotent because a rare double delivery during failover is possible. "That is why your handlers should be idempotent" (~03:02)
- [CONS][ANTI] Client-side per-key threading breaks under redelivery: a failed earlier message can be redelivered after a later one for the same key was already processed. "if buy fails and gets redelivered later, it comes back after pay was already processed and the order breaks again" (~06:04)
- [CONS] max_ack_pending=1 forces one unacknowledged message in flight so the server guarantees order with no application cooperation; even a redelivery arrives before the next message. "Even a redelivery of buy always arrives before you could ever see pay" (~07:05)
- [CONS][ANTI] max_ack_pending=1 serializes unrelated keys behind each other and makes the single worker a single point of failure; a second worker becomes load balancing, not standby. "With max ack pending equal to one, only one worker can be active at a time, so there's no safe way to add a hot standby" (~08:05)
- [CONS] A pinned member can be unpinned administratively (step down) so another instance becomes the active worker. "You can also unpin one at will, whenever you want. This is an admin command" (~08:05)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Vocabulary: the stream holds data, a group is a kind of work over the stream, a group's work is split into partitions, and each partition is owned by a member (a consumer plus its worker and standbys); one stream can feed many groups. "a single stream can feed many groups, each reading it independently" (~09:07)
- [STRM][CONS] Elastic groups use a work-queue stream that sources from the main stream, with a filter for the partitioning; static groups put consumers directly on the stream. "Elastic uses a work queue stream, which sources from the main stream" (~10:07)
- [SUBJ] You can partition on one wildcard token, several wildcard tokens, or the whole subject. "you can partition on just one wildcard, more than one wildcard, or the whole subject" (~11:08)
- [CONS] In partitioned groups max_ack_pending=1 is the safeguard that enforces serial processing if a worker would otherwise pull several messages at once. "Max ack pending equals one is the safeguard that enforces this in case a worker would otherwise pull several at once" (~11:08)
- [CONS][ANTI] With more partitions than members, a hot partition sharing a member with a quiet one starves the quiet key. "if a hot partition lands on the same member as a quiet one, that quiet key starves waiting in line behind the flood" (~12:10)
- [CONS][PATTERN] The fix for a known hot key is custom partition-to-member mapping (dedicate a member to the hot partition), not more partitions. "the fix isn't really adding more partitions. It's custom mapping" (~12:10)
- [CONS][ANTI] Static group membership is fixed at creation; changing the mapping means deleting and recreating the group, so custom mapping suits a known hot key, not a moving one. "static membership is fixed at creation. To change the mapping, you delete and recreate the group" (~13:11)
- [CONS] Elastic groups work on any stream without a pre-baked partition token and allow adding or dropping members at any time up to a maximum set at creation. "you can add or drop members at any time up to a maximum set at creation" (~13:11)
- [CONS][STRM] The elastic library owns a hidden work-queue stream and its consumers, so it can reshuffle partition filters live without teardown. "Because the library owns that stream and its consumers, it can reshuffle the partition filters live with no teardown" (~13:11)
- [CONS] Dropping the last member of an elastic group does not delete the group; messages pile up until a member is added back. "dropping the last member doesn't delete the group. Messages simply pile up until you add a member back" (~14:14)
- [SIZE][CONS] Size the elastic work-queue buffer (cap by bytes or message count) to more than a few seconds of processing: when the cap is hit, sourcing is suspended for up to a few seconds before it resumes, and a too-small buffer starves workers. "keep it above a few seconds worth of processing" (~14:14)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Key-to-worker affinity also yields a high local cache hit rate for slow external lookups; that use does not need max_ack_pending=1, so a worker can keep several messages in flight. "this doesn't need max act pending equals one. You only need key to worker affinity, not serial processing" (~15:16)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Static groups have the lowest latency and fewest resources; elastic costs a duplicate copy of your messages in the hidden work queue. "at the cost of a duplicate copy of your messages" (~16:17)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Rule of thumb: static when membership is known and stable; elastic when membership changes, when you can't transform the stream, or when several groups share one stream. "reach for static when membership is known and stable, reach for elastic when membership changes" (~16:17)
- [CONS] In both static and elastic groups the partition count is fixed at creation; only elastic lets membership change live. "In both, the partition count is fixed at creation, only elastic lets you change the membership live" (~16:17)
- [CLNT][OPS] In the CG tool the filter must be passed with the filter flag; passed as a plain argument it is read as a member name. "If you pass the arrow as a plain argument, it gets read as a member name instead, so don't do that" (~17:19)
- [KV][CONS] Consumer-group configuration (max members, filters, members) is stored in a KV bucket, which is what allows live changes. "this is all configuration just stored in NATS KV store ... you can change it live" (~25:30)
- [CONS] In elastic groups adding a member to the config and starting a consumer instance are separate steps; a consume for a member not in the roster just sits idle. "If we consume for a member that isn't in the roster, it just sits idle" (~23:28)
- [CONS] While an elastic partition has no owner, its messages buffer in the group's work-queue stream and later drain in order to whoever takes it over. "While a partition has no owner, its messages buffer in the group's work queue stream and then later drain in order" (~26:30)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Partitioning is useful even without strict ordering (max_ack_pending=1), e.g. for local caching. "If you don't require this ordering, you can still use this partitioning. There's other reasons such as optimizing local caching" (~30:34)

## NATS JetStream Pull Consumer Priority Groups: Overflow, Pinned & Prioritized
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3KBFdUXYpyY
- speaker: unknown (Synadia channel narrator) | date: unknown (post-2.12, since the prioritized policy is described as shipped) | duration: 25:33
- version context: 2.11 (overflow, pinned client) and 2.12 (prioritized policy) explicitly named

### Claims
- [CONS] Without priority groups, multiple clients pulling from one consumer get plain round-robin and the server has no notion of which client should get the work. "It's plain round robin, and the server has no idea which client should actually get the work" (~01:00)
- [CONS] Pull consumer priority groups arrived in NATS server 2.11: multiple clients pull from one consumer under a configurable policy, expressed purely as consumer configuration. "Starting in NATS server 2.11, pull consumer priority groups ... it's all just consumer configuration" (~01:00)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Priority groups replace leader election, lock services, and coordination code for "send all work to one client, fail over instantly" and "drain locally first, spill to another region" patterns. "There's no leader election, no lock service, and no coordination code for you to write and maintain" (~01:00)
- [CONS] Three policies exist: overflow (latency/cost-aware routing), pinned client (single active worker with fast failover), prioritized (tiered worker pools). "overflow for latency and cost-aware routing, pinned client for one active worker with fast failover and prioritize for tiered worker pools" (~02:00)
- [CONS] Overflow serves a pull only once pending messages cross that pull's min_pending or unacknowledged messages cross its min_ack_pending (either/or of whichever the pull sets); pulls without a threshold drain normally. "A pull is served only when pending messages cross min pending or unacknowledged messages cross min ack pending" (~02:00)
- [CONS][TOPO][PATTERN] Overflow suits regional routing: local clients handle the common case and cross-region traffic is paid for only when locals genuinely fall behind. "you only pay for cross-region traffic when there's genuinely too much work for the locals to keep up" (~02:00)
- [CONS] Under pinned client policy the server stamps messages with a pin ID header (Nats-Pin-Id); the client echoes it on every later pull, and a fresh ID is issued each time the pin moves. "stamps its messages with a pin ID header. The client echoes that ID back on every later pull" (~03:01)
- [CONS][OPS] The server re-pins to a standby when the pinned client stays quiet past the configured timeout or an admin unpins it; `nats consumer unpin` forces a handoff, useful before a deploy. "An operator can also force that handoff out of band with NATS consumer unpin, which is handy for rotating the active client before a deploy" (~03:01)
- [CONS][OPS] The server publishes an advisory on every pin change (pinned and unpinned events), usable as an audit trail of who holds the work. "the server publishes an advisory on every pin change, so you can watch handoffs as they happen" (~03:01)
- [CONS] The prioritized policy arrived in NATS server 2.12: pulls are served by a priority number 0–9, lower served first; a secondary pool picks up immediately when the primary isn't pulling. "The third policy, prioritized, arrived in NATS server 2.12 ... priority number from zero to nine, with lower numbers served first" (~03:01)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Overflow vs prioritized trade-off: overflow's threshold keeps assignments stable but lets backlog build; prioritized hands over with zero delay and no threshold, at the cost of flip-flopping between clients or regions. "Prioritized hands work over with zero delay and no threshold at all. And the trade-off is some flip-flopping" (~04:02)
- [CONS][TOPO][PATTERN] Tiers can be stacked with prioritized: US East priority 0, US West priority 1, EU West priority 2 only sees traffic when both US regions are quiet. "Put EU West at priority two, so it only ever sees traffic when both US regions are quiet" (~05:02)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Pinned client fits jobs that must not run in parallel (billing run, stateful migration): HA without duplicate processors or a separate lock service. "You get high availability without running duplicate processors and without standing up a separate lock service" (~05:02)
- [CONS] Priority groups are pull-only and require explicit ack; configuring them on a push consumer or with any other ack policy is an error. "Configuring them on a push consumer or with any other act policy is an error" (~06:04)
- [CONS][ANTI] A message can briefly be processed by two clients during failover overlap, so handlers must be idempotent; pinning is affinity and failover, not a distributed lock, and buffered messages cannot be revoked. "pinning is affinity and failover, not a distributed lock ... messages already in its buffer can't be revoked" (~06:04)
- [CONS][SIZE] Keep the priority timeout comfortably above pull expiry, because the pin resets only when the pinned client issues a new pull within the window; default timeout is 2 minutes, which pairs with pulls expiring in a minute or less. "The default timeout is 2 minutes, which pairs nicely with polls that expire in a minute or less" (~06:04)
- [CONS][CLNT] A stale or wrong pin ID is rejected with a 423 mismatch; the client clears its ID and repulls with none to rejoin the standby pool. "the server rejects that poll with a 423 mismatch. The client just clears its ID and repolls with none" (~07:04)
- [CONS][CLNT] A pull that doesn't claim the pin is not rejected; it gets a 408 and waits its turn behind the pinned client. "A client that doesn't claim the pin isn't rejected, it just waits its turn behind the pin client" (~09:06)
- [CONS] Under overflow, a pull with min_pending below threshold is held and returns nothing (a 408) even if messages sit in the stream. "Below the threshold, the poll is held and returns nothing, just a 408, even if messages are sitting in the stream" (~11:09)
- [CONS] min_ack_pending lets a worker help only once N messages are stuck in flight (delivered but unacked) on the main client. "worker can also be told only help once end messages are stuck in flight, delivered but not yet act" (~14:11)
- [CONS] With prioritized, when a message arrives and several workers are waiting, the server picks the lowest priority number; the higher-numbered worker only gets work when the lower one isn't waiting. "the priority nine worker only gets work when the priority zero worker isn't waiting" (~16:13)
- [CONS][OPS] Priority groups are configured through consumer flags or a JSON config (priority_policy plus priority group name); the CLI shows the policy and group in consumer info. "Our priority policy is overflow and our priority group will be called jobs" (~12:10)

## Distributed Counters in NATS — Global Totals Without Locks
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1Vx8CbrO89Y
- speaker: unknown (Synadia channel narrator) | date: unknown (post-2.12 release) | duration: 16:18
- version context: NATS 2.12 (distributed counters) explicitly named

### Claims
- [STRM][PATTERN] NATS 2.12 adds a distributed counter to JetStream: enable a stream flag, publish signed deltas as headers, and every replica converges to the same total without consensus or locks, even with out-of-order arrival. "every replica converges to the same total without consensus, without locks, even with messages arriving out of order" (~01:01)
- [STRM] A stream that only accepts signed deltas is automatically a CRDT because addition is commutative; NATS builds the PN-counter idea into JetStream as a first-class primitive. "a stream that only accepts signed deltas is automatically a CRDT. Order doesn't matter. Retries don't matter" (~01:01)
- [STRM] Set allow_message_counter to true and every subject in the stream becomes a counter; every message must carry a Nats-Incr header with a signed integer. "every subject in the stream is a counter, and every message has to carry a NATS increment header with a signed integer" (~02:01)
- [STRM] On an increment the server reads the current total from the last message on that subject, applies the delta, stores a new message with the updated value, and returns the post-increment total in the publish ack. "returns the post-increment total in the publish acknowledgement. No extra read" (~02:01)
- [STRM][CLNT] Counter values are big integers stored as JSON strings so they can exceed 2^63 and JavaScript won't lose precision. "Values are big integers, not 64-bit ints ... They're stored as JSON strings for exactly this reason" (~02:01)
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Multi-region aggregation: regional counters publish to their own subjects, a continental stream sources them with subject transforms, and a global stream sources the continental ones. "A continental stream sources both with subject transforms, and a global stream sources the continental ones" (~03:03)
- [STRM] When a sourced counter message arrives, the server computes the delta from the last seen source value and rewrites the header to that change only, so there is no double counting even with replays or lost messages. "the server calculates the delta from the last seen source value, and rewrites the header to reflect only that change. No double counting" (~03:03)
- [STRM][ANTI] Caveats: once allow_message_counter is on it cannot be turned off; counter streams cannot be mirrors (use sources); limits retention is required; no discard new, no per-message TTLs, no Nats-Rollup header. "Once you turn allow message counter on, you can't turn it off. Counter streams can't be mirrors. Use sources instead" (~03:03)
- [STRM][ANTI][PATTERN] Resetting a replicated counter means publishing a matching negative delta; purge alone will not propagate across sources. "resetting a replicated counter means publishing a matching negative delta. Purge alone won't propagate across sources" (~04:03)
- [CLNT] The typed Go client is the orbit.go counters module (NewCounterFromStream, then Add/Load/Get, using big integers); other clients can publish the header directly and parse the JSON body. "Other language clients can interact with counter streams today by publishing the header directly and parsing the JSON body" (~04:03)
- [STRM] Each subject in a counter stream is its own counter; subjects do not share state. "each subject in a counter stream is its own counter. They don't share state" (~06:05)
- [STRM] A publish to a counter stream with incorrect headers returns an error. "when you use the incorrect headers for this counter stream ... you'll see we get an error" (~06:05)
- [TOPO][USECASE] The demo runs seven nodes in a three-level hierarchy joined by leaf-node connections, with Europe both a leaf of global and a hub for Spain/France/England; counters written on a disconnected node converge to the correct total when it reconnects. "Everything converged and we have the right amount right when Europe came back up online" (~14:17)
- [STRM][OPS] Stream info on a sourcing counter stream tracks per-source values, so the global total can be broken down by origin. "global tracks where it came from under sources" (~12:14)
- [USECASE] Target uses named: view counts that survive partitions, edge rate limiters without a central lock, billing meters across regions, leaderboards under load. "edge rate limiters that don't need a central lock, billing meters that work across regions" (~03:03)

## Delayed Message Scheduling in NATS — One-Time, Cron, and Subject Sampling
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6dkzZonDI9M
- speaker: unknown (Synadia channel narrator) | date: unknown (post-2.14, since 2.14 recurring schedules are described as shipped) | duration: 14:03
- version context: NATS 2.12 (one-time schedules) and 2.14 (cron/recurring schedules, subject sampling) explicitly named

### Claims
- [STRM][ANTI] Before 2.12 there was no native way to hold a message for later; NAK-with-delay on a consumer was a workaround that did not scale. "You could use NACK with delay on a consumer, but that was a workaround and it didn't scale" (~01:01)
- [STRM] Starting in 2.12 you publish with a Nats-Schedule header ("at" plus an RFC 3339 timestamp for one-time delivery) and a Nats-Schedule-Target header naming the subject that receives the message. "you set it to at followed by an RFC 3339 timestamp. You also set a NATS schedule target header" (~01:01)
- [STRM][SUBJ] Each schedule lives on its own unique subject; the most recent message on that subject is the active schedule, so publishing again updates it, and independent delays need distinct subjects (e.g. append a UUID). "Each schedule lives on its own unique subject. The most recent message on that subject is the active schedule" (~02:01)
- [STRM] In 2.14 the scheduler gained recurring schedules: cron expressions, fixed intervals like every 5 minutes, and aliases like @hourly and @daily; NATS cron uses a six-field format with a seconds field. "NATS uses a six-field format that adds a seconds field for finer precision" (~02:01)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Subject sampling (2.14) republishes the latest message from a source subject on a schedule, e.g. the latest reading every 5 minutes from a sensor emitting hundreds per second. "you can capture just the latest reading every 5 minutes, reducing noise for downstream analytics without touching the sensor code" (~03:03)
- [STRM][ANTI] The stream must opt in with allow_message_schedules; once enabled it cannot be disabled, and it cannot be enabled on source or mirror streams. "Once you enable it, you cannot disable it on that stream. It also cannot be enabled on source or mirror streams" (~03:03)
- [STRM] A schedule in the past fires immediately, and after a server restart all past-due schedules execute right away. "Any past due schedules execute right away" (~03:03)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Set Nats-Schedule-TTL so generated messages expire and consumers can discard stale deliveries, e.g. after a restart replays past-due schedules; this requires allow_message_ttl on the stream. "You can set a NATS schedule TTL to give generated messages an expiration, so consumers can detect and discard stale deliveries" (~03:03)
- [STRM][ANTI] Cron schedules with a time zone are exposed to DST transitions (skipped hour on spring forward, double fire on fall back); use UTC. "Sticking with UTC avoids this entirely" (~03:03)
- [STRM] The scheduler can only deliver within its own stream, so schedule subjects and target subjects must be in the same stream; scheduling headers are rejected on streams without the flag. "they must be in the same stream because the scheduler can only deliver within its own stream" (~05:05)
- [STRM] A scheduled publish parks the message on its schedule subject; at fire time the server produces a new message on the target subject with the same body and custom headers propagated verbatim, plus Nats-Scheduler (pointing to the schedule subject) and Nats-Schedule-Next (purge for one-time). "your custom headers are propagated verbatim. But, the server also stamps on its own headers" (~06:06)
- [STRM] After a one-time delivery the original schedule message is purged from its holding subject. "Once that happens, the original schedule message is purged from its holding subject" (~06:06)
- [STRM] For recurring schedules Nats-Schedule-Next carries the next fire timestamp, and republishing to the schedule subject changes the recurrence. "we can publish to it again if we want to update the recurrence rate of each message" (~08:08)
- [STRM] Sampling uses a Nats-Schedule-Source header telling the server which subject to read the latest message from. "A schedule with NATS schedule source tells the server to grab the latest reading from that subject every 5 seconds" (~12:13)

## NATS Per-Message TTL — Fine-Grained Expiration for JetStream Messages
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wwwPfuhDnos
- speaker: unknown (Synadia channel narrator) | date: unknown (post-2.11) | duration: 07:19
- version context: NATS 2.11 (per-message TTL) explicitly named

### Claims
- [STRM] By default a stream has one expiration rule, max_age, applied to every message equally. "a Jetstream stream gives you one expiration rule, max age, and it applies to every message equally" (~00:00)
- [STRM] Per-message TTL was added in NATS 2.11: set a TTL on individual messages with the Nats-TTL header after enabling allow_message_ttl on the stream. "Set expiration per message with the NATS TTL header. Enable it in your stream config by setting allow_message_ttl to true" (~01:00)
- [STRM] Each message's TTL countdown runs independently, and max_age still applies as an upper bound that a message TTL cannot exceed. "Max age still applies as an upper bound. A message's TTL can't exceed it" (~01:00)
- [STRM] A Nats-TTL of "never" makes a message outlive the stream's max_age and be retained forever. "we're going to send a message in with a NATS TTL of never, so it never expires. It will outlive the max age" (~02:02)
- [KV] KV buckets get per-key TTL with automatic delete markers; when a key expires, NATS places a delete marker (tombstone) so watchers know the data is gone. "it places a delete marker, or a tombstone, to signal to watchers and subscribers that the data is gone" (~05:06)
- [KV] The bucket's limit_marker_ttl controls how long that delete marker persists before the key is fully purged; it is required to enable per-key TTL on a bucket. "Notice the field limit marker TTL. This enables us to do per-key TTL on this bucket" (~05:06)
- [USECASE][PATTERN] Named uses: session state that auto-expires without cleanup jobs, distributed cache entries with natural TTLs, per-key KV TTLs. "You can auto expire sessions without cleanup jobs" (~01:00)

## Message Tracing | NATS 2.11
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pkvlPq3nWUM
- speaker: unknown (Synadia channel narrator) | date: unknown (2.11 series) | duration: 12:14
- version context: NATS 2.11 (message tracing) per title

### Claims
- [OPS] Message tracing is built into the server; the `nats trace` CLI command sends a message to a subject and reports the complete path it took, with no code changes or external tools. "No external tool or code changes, just run a command and see exactly where your messages go" (~00:00)
- [OPS] A trace message carries three headers: Nats-Trace-Dest (subject receiving trace events), Nats-Trace-Only (dry-run: traced but not delivered or stored), and Accept-Encoding (gzip or snappy compression of trace events). "NATS trace only. This enables dry run mode. Your initial message is traced throughout the system, but not actually delivered or stored" (~02:01)
- [OPS] Every server the message passes through emits its own trace event to a temporary inbox that aggregates them; the CLI builds the final output from these. "each node or server sends its own trace message reporting its current progress" (~01:00)
- [OPS] Each trace event has four main fields: server (name, cluster), request (headers), hops (outgoing hop count), and events. "The server field ... The request field ... The hops field ... And the events field" (~03:02)
- [OPS] Event types: IN ingress, EG egress, JS JetStream access, SE/SI stream export/import when crossing an account boundary, SM subject mapping when a mapping rule transformed the subject. "SE and SI for stream export and import when the message crossed an account boundary, and SM for subject mapping" (~04:05)
- [OPS][TOPO] Event kinds identify the connection type: client, router (same cluster), gateway (other cluster), leaf node, JetStream, plus internal system and account kinds. "you can see your usual client, router, or gateway. And you also have leaf node and JetStream. And system and account are internal" (~04:05)
- [OPS][TOPO] A single leaf node reports itself as its own cluster in the server field. "since this is a single leaf node, it's its own cluster" (~05:06)
- [OPS] A Nats-Trace-Hop header builds a routing tree: multiple egress events from one server get hop ids 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, and further branching nests (1.3.1, 1.3.2). "Since there's multiple branches, we increment the number" (~07:06)
- [OPS][STRM] A server that only stores the message into a stream shows a JS egress event and no hops field. "our only egress event is type JS for JetStream. Notice that there is no hop field because there are no hops from this server" (~08:06)
- [OPS][SEC] Tracing stops at account boundaries by default; the receiver must opt in with allow_trace on the import/export: the importer for a stream import, the exporter for a service import. "The rule being the receiver always opts in. If it's a stream import, the importer sets it. If it's a service import, the exporter sets it" (~09:08)
- [OPS] `nats trace` without the trace flag prints a minimal summary; with it, the full per-server trace messages. "With the trace flag, it's going to give us the entire trace message that we broke down server by server" (~10:08)

## NATS JetStream Expected Sequence Headers — Optimistic Concurrency Control Explained
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jypgwaoY0kI
- speaker: unknown (Synadia channel narrator) | date: unknown (mentions atomic batch publishing, so 2.12 era) | duration: 11:14
- version context: 2.12 era (references atomic batch publishing; per-pattern header)

### Claims
- [STRM][PATTERN] Expected sequence headers give optimistic concurrency control: multiple processes work in parallel without locks and conflicting writes are detected and rejected rather than prevented. "It'll detect and reject conflicting rights instead of just outright preventing them" (~00:00)
- [STRM] Two writers that both read sequence 4 and publish with expected last sequence 4: one succeeds (stream at 5), the other is rejected and retries with expected 5. "only one succeeds setting the sequence to five and the other is rejected because by the time it arrives the stream is already at five" (~00:00)
- [STRM][MYTH] There is only one sequence counter, the stream sequence; all three expected-sequence header variants validate against it and just filter what they compare with. "there's only one sequence counter the stream sequence ... these headers just filter what they check against" (~01:01)
- [STRM] Three variants: global (Nats-Expected-Last-Sequence), per subject (Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence), and per pattern (Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence combined with Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence-Subject). "per pattern ... uses the NATS expected last subject sequence header in combination with the NATS expected last subject sequence subject header" (~01:01)
- [STRM] Global expected-last-sequence suits a single writer needing strict ordering across all subjects, such as a global event log. "If you're the only writer and need strict ordering across everything, this is what you want" (~02:03)
- [STRM] A rejected publish returns a "wrong last sequence" error that includes the actual last sequence. "it says wrong last sequence and gives us the last sequence number" (~04:05)
- [STRM][MYTH] Per-subject does not give each subject its own 0,1,2 counter: the expected value is the stream sequence of that subject's last message, and a never-used subject expects 0. "the common misconception is that each subject has its own counter starting at 0 1 2 3 but the expected value is the stream sequence of that subject's last message" (~07:09)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Track the sequence returned in each pub ack and use it as the expected value for the next publish. "You track the return sequence and use it for the next publish" (~07:09)
- [STRM][ANTI] Per-subject tracks each distinct subject separately, so order.1.created and order.1.shipped cannot share tracking; publishing to a new subject with expected 1 fails because its last sequence is 0. "events.order.1 shipped is a different subject with no prior messages. Its last sequence is zero, not one" (~07:09)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Per-pattern lets you supply a wildcard pattern (e.g. events.order.1.>) so related subjects for one entity share sequence tracking while other entities stay independent; use it for event sourcing where entity events span multiple subjects. "order.1.created and order.1.shipped can share the same sequence tracking while order two anything stays independent" (~08:10)
- [STRM][CLNT] In Go the options are WithExpectLastSequence, WithExpectLastSequencePerSubject, and the per-subject-pattern variant. "You would use jetstream with expect last sequence" (~04:05)
- [STRM] Expected sequence headers are also used by atomic batch publishing. "it's also used by atomic batch publishing" (~02:03)

## Consumer Pausing | NATS 2.11
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vE7Y5Sh2eAI
- speaker: unknown (Synadia channel narrator) | date: unknown (2.11 series) | duration: 07:26
- version context: NATS 2.11 (consumer pause) explicitly named

### Claims
- [CONS] Consumer pause temporarily halts delivery to a consumer until a deadline; messages keep arriving in the stream and are delivered when the pause expires or is lifted early. "Messages continue arriving to the stream. They just aren't delivered until the pause expires or is manually lifted" (~00:01)
- [CONS][OPS] Pausing is a normal consumer config update that sets a pause deadline; it works the same for push and pull consumers. "It's just a normal config update. Nothing special ... This works the same for both push and pull consumers" (~01:02)
- [CONS][CLNT] A paused consumer's application sees no errors or disconnects and keeps receiving heartbeats. "No errors, no disconnects. It keeps getting heartbeats like everything's fine" (~01:02)
- [CONS] An in-flight batch is not pulled back: if 100 messages were pulled, the pause takes effect before the next batch. "NATS won't yank those away from you. It waits until the batch is done, then pauses before the next one" (~02:03)
- [CONS][OPS] Consumer info shows the pause deadline and remaining time; resuming early is a separate command and a consumer can be created already paused, using a duration or an absolute timestamp. "You can initialize a pause upon creation. You can also use a timestamp for an absolute time" (~05:08)
- [USECASE][PATTERN] Named uses: deployments and migrations, emergency maintenance, debugging production issues, rate limiting downstream services. "Deployments and migrations, emergency maintenance, debugging production issues, or rate limiting downstream services" (~01:02)

## Atomic Batch Publishing | NATS 2.12
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MvfiskARAq8
- speaker: unknown (Synadia channel narrator) | date: unknown (2.12 release; mentions 2.12.1 behavior) | duration: 08:47
- version context: NATS 2.12 (atomic batch publishing), with a 2.12.1 validation change mentioned

### Claims
- [STRM] Atomic batch publishing is a stream configuration option that publishes N messages into a stream with all-or-nothing guarantees. "Either every message commits together or none of them do" (~00:00)
- [STRM][ANTI] Without atomic batching each publish is independent, so a connection drop after the third of five related messages leaves a partial write. "your connection drops after the third? Well, you have a partial right. Your data is inconsistent" (~01:01)
- [STRM] Batch messages are staged invisibly on the server (consumers see nothing) until the last message carries Nats-Batch-Commit, then all appear at once. "messages are staged invisibly on the server. Consumers don't see anything" (~01:01)
- [STRM] Three headers drive batching: Nats-Batch-Id (unique id), Nats-Batch-Sequence (incrementing per message), Nats-Batch-Commit (commit signal on the last message). "First is the NATS batch ID ... Second is the NATS batch sequence ... And third is NATS batch commit" (~01:01)
- [STRM][SIZE] A batch is rejected if the batch id exceeds 64 characters, if sequence numbers have gaps, or if the stream uses async persist mode; as of 2.12.1 duplicate messages in a batch also fail validation. "A batch ID over 64 characters, gaps in your sequence numbers, or running on a stream with async persist mode" (~02:03)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Nats-Expected-Last-Sequence (or the per-subject variant) on the first message of a batch gives optimistic locking: the batch fails if the stream moved while it was built, and you retry with fresh data. "This header is only allowed on the first message of a batch" (~02:03)
- [STRM][SIZE] Limits: up to 1,000 messages per batch, 50 batches in flight per stream, 1,000 batches per server, and a batch is abandoned after 10 seconds of inactivity; all are configurable in server config. "you can have up to a thousand messages per batch. Each stream can have 50 batches in flight at once. Each server can have a thousand batches total" (~02:03)
- [STRM] Batches must go into a single stream; they cannot cross streams. "batches must go into a single stream. They can't cross streams" (~03:04)
- [STRM] The stream must be created with allow batch (allow_atomic_publish in the Go config) to accept batches. "including the allow batch flag to enable atomic batching" (~03:04)
- [STRM][PATTERN] A batch can span multiple subjects in one stream, so messages fanned out to warehouse, payment, and notification consumers commit together. "Different messages going to different consumers but all committed together" (~06:05)
- [CLNT] Orbit's JetStream extension package manages batch ids, sequence numbers, and commit for you (add messages, call commit). "You just add messages and call commit. The library handles batch IDs, sequence numbers, everything" (~07:06)
- [USECASE] Named uses: event sourcing where one command produces multiple events, and batch telemetry tying related messages together. "event sourcing where you rebuild state from a sequence of events and also batch telemetry" (~03:04)

## NATS 2.11: What's New?
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p0R1DWO1Fuc
- speaker: Neil Twigg (lead server developer, Synadia), with a RethinkConn host for Q&A | date: 2025 (RethinkConn 2025 session) | duration: 09:35
- version context: NATS 2.11 release

### Claims
- [OPS] 2.11 focused on three areas: visibility into what the server is doing, enabling new patterns, and correctness/resilience against failures. "improving visibility about what the NAT server is doing, enabling new patterns for users and developers, and improving correctness" (~00:05)
- [OPS] Five headline 2.11 features: distributed message tracing, per-message TTLs, consumer pause, pull consumer priority groups, and stream multi-get. "distributed message tracing, per message TTLs, consumer pause, pull consumer priority groups, and stream multig" (~00:05)
- [OPS][TOPO] Tracing answers where a message goes across routes, gateways, leaf nodes, account import/export boundaries, and subject transforms; `nats trace subject` prints an IP-traceroute-like story. "you'll basically get a print out like doing an IP trace route" (~01:07)
- [OPS] Tracing can run as a dry run without the remote applications ever seeing the message. "you can also do that as well without the remote applications ever being aware that it took place" (~02:07)
- [STRM] Per-message TTLs are the first limit that applies to individual messages rather than the whole stream; the TTL is optional and can differ per message. "the first time that we've been able to introduce a limit that applies only to individual messages rather than to the entire stream" (~02:07)
- [KV][OPS] KV delete markers build up with heavy deletes and make the underlying stream big and expensive; Synadia plans to give delete markers TTLs so watchers still see deletes but markers don't stay forever, reducing manual compaction. "We will be changing those delete markers to use TTLs so that even if you have KV watchers looking for deletes, you'll still be able to get those notifications" (~03:11)
- [CONS] In 2.10 there is no way to control behavior when multiple clients pull from one consumer; 2.11 priority groups allow pinning clients and overflow based on pending messages or pending acks, with more elaborate policies planned. "at the moment you'll be able to pin clients and overflow based on these two controls" (~04:13)
- [CONS] Consumer pause is set as a pause deadline in the consumer config via a normal update, is identical for push and pull, resumes automatically at the deadline, and heartbeats continue so client SDKs surface no errors. "the consumer heartbeats continue to be sent to the client. So you won't get unexpected errors being surfaced from your client SDKs" (~05:15)
- [STRM] Stream multi-get is for applications reading streams directly without consumers: multiple subject filters, bounds such as up-to sequence or time, returning a batch in sequence order; it is the first of several planned batch operations. "you can provide multiple subject filters. You can provide additional bounds such as only up to a certain sequence number or time" (~06:15)
- [KV] Because KV is an abstraction over streams, per-message TTL enables per-key TTL in KV buckets, coming to clients soon. "the fact that you can apply a TTL to an individual message means that we can also do the same for message entries in a KV bucket" (~08:18)
- [OPS][STRM] A trace into JetStream reports the message reaching JetStream at the server that is the stream leader at that time. "it would probably report whichever the server was that was the leader for that stream at that time" (~08:18)
- [STRM] Max pending per subject was not planned as of this talk. "Any plans to implement max pending per subject. Not aware of that at the moment" (~09:18)

## NATS: Orbit – Extending NATS Clients with Richer Capabilities
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a4DO0zN1yhI
- speaker: Tomasz Pietrek (manager, open source engineering, Synadia), with a RethinkConn host for Q&A | date: 2025 (RethinkConn 2025 session; 2.11 just released) | duration: 18:25
- version context: 2.11 era (mentions "direct batch, the new feature of 2.11")

### Claims
- [CLNT] Every client PR faces a trade-off: added utilities grow client complexity, and language-specific abstractions break parity; parity across tier-1 clients is a core goal so users can rely on every feature in every language. "we really strive that all tier one clients, the most used ones have parity" (~00:06)
- [CLNT][ANTI] Opinionated defaults (e.g. timeouts) in the core clients are regretted over time because NATS use cases are too varied (cars on bad networks vs cloud) for one sensible default. "every opinion that we try to land in the client, it's just matter of time, we will regret it" (~02:08)
- [CLNT] Clients cannot break stable 1.0 APIs even for experimental additions like the service API or KV API, so design mistakes had to be kept. "even if we marked it as experimental like service API, key value API we have to keep the API even we found problems with them" (~04:13)
- [CLNT] Users care about the number of client dependencies; abstractions like KV and object store often needed new ones. "our users really care about number of dependencies in the clients" (~04:13)
- [CLNT] Orbit is a set of separately versioned libraries on top of the clients, available in Go, Rust, Java, JavaScript, and Python, with others coming. "for now it's available in Go, Rust, Java, JavaScript and and Python and others are coming soon" (~05:14)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Request-many (one request, many replies) landed in Orbit rather than the clients because the termination strategies are opinions. "there are quite a few strategies you can terminate the responses and those felt like opinions" (~06:16)
- [CLNT] Other Orbit contents: language-specific publishers, a system client for NATS contexts, retriers in some languages, and direct batch (a 2.11 feature) incubated in Orbit before merging back to clients. "all of the languages will have direct batch the new feature of 211" (~07:18)
- [CLNT] The split: core clients focus on performance, stability, parity, being lightweight and unopinionated; Orbit holds high-level abstractions, new APIs, and opinions. "stable and performant versus new and abstractions plus opinions" (~09:19)
- [CLNT] Planned for Orbit: KV codecs, more core NATS and JetStream utilities, object store iterations, and incubating non-server APIs that may merge back to clients once stable; Orbit libraries need not have full parity. "we allow to be not not have full parity in orbit and also to have some discrepancies across orbit libraries" (~10:21)
- [CLNT] The biggest upcoming Orbit capability named is a schema registry. "the big one that will land hopefully soon is schema registry" (~12:24)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] JetStream retry strategies could not go into clients because banking and vehicle use cases differ too much; they land in Orbit as quality-of-life additions. "retrying is quite often in JetStream is tricky and very opinionated ... impossible to have one solution" (~13:26)
- [CLNT] Orbit is not exclusive to the client: you use the client and load Orbit extensions (in Rust as an extension crate); only larger abstractions like schema registry or KV codecs might not need the client loaded directly. "it's not exclusive definitely it's extending" (~15:29)
- [CLNT][OPS] Client unit tests cover features and error cases but not network problems; Synadia runs private nightly chaos tests plus Antithesis deterministic simulation to reproduce one-in-a-million bugs. "we have the antithesis tooling ... deterministically reproduce very one in a million bugs" (~16:30)

## Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Two-Node Engine with David & Byron
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWhUJvGnwLY
- speaker: David Gee and Byron Ruth (Synadia) | date: 2024 (RethinkConn 2024) | duration: 12:36
- version context: 2.10 era (RethinkConn 2024)

### Claims
- [TOPO][MYTH] The Synadia two-node engine is not a general-purpose two-node NATS system; it is a standalone leadership election service for a two-node setup whose state lives in a NATS KV bucket. "this is not a general purpose two node NATS system" (~00:02)
- [TOPO] It runs a finite state machine with internal and external probes on each node; each node independently derives leader, follower, impaired, or leader-RX (constrained leadership) status. "both systems in independent time space will decide what status it should be" (~01:03)
- [USECASE][PATTERN] Use case: making two identical simple services (e.g. two web servers) highly available with a floating IP and no load balancer, in constrained or remote systems. "without requiring a low balancer" (~02:04)
- [KV][PATTERN] External integration works through a "transitioning" KV key: the FSM sets it during a transition, your code (any NATS client) does its work, then updates the key so the engine finishes the transition. "once your code has completed you then update this NATS KV value this transitioning key value and the engine will basically carry on" (~03:04)
- [OPS][PATTERN] Without a preemption flag the engine latches into the failed-over state, so restoring the configured leader is a deliberate step, avoiding disruptive preemptive restoration in mission-critical stacks. "we might not want the disruption of a preemptive restoration" (~06:07)
- [TOPO][USECASE] The engine is written in Go and can be embedded; it was embedded in Kine (the k3s datastore layer that replaces etcd) so two k3s nodes replicate a KV bucket and fail over, given a virtual IP in front. "the two node engine is actually embedded within the Kine layer that is the data store component of k3s" (~08:11)
- [TOPO] A two-node system has different constraints than three-node RAFT high availability. "with the two node system you have different constraints than you do with a three node with RAFT" (~10:13)

## The Future of NATS: Roadmap & Vision
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CifAoRYefVM
- speaker: Byron Ruth (Synadia; closing keynote) | date: 2025 (RethinkConn 2025, right after the 2.11 release) | duration: 31:43
- version context: 2.11 just released; 2.12 planning

### Claims
- [TOPO] Synadia frames three personas: developers want primitives (messaging, request-reply, data storage), architects decide where services and data are located (multi-cloud, geographies, edge), operators want fewer systems to run. "architecture from this perspective is just saying well where do we need these services and data to actually be located" (~06:16)
- [TOPO] NATS deployment shapes named: simple clusters, stretch clusters, superclusters across geos and clouds, and leaf nodes for hub-and-spoke, with leaf-node expansion planned for 2025. "You have simple clusters, stretch clusters as a thing, superclusters that can go multigeo and across clouds ... and leaf nodes" (~07:17)
- [SEC][TOPO] Multi-tenancy is built in: messages in one account never bleed across account boundaries, so you don't deploy many NATS systems for isolation; cross-account sharing is opt-in. "you can send and receive messages over subjects in that account that will never bleed over any other account boundary" (~07:17)
- [OPS] Because all data flows through NATS, the server can expose visibility that otherwise needs separate monitoring stacks; 2.10 and 2.11 invested heavily in this. "because NATS is like every all the data is flowing through NATS we can expose everything through it" (~09:19)
- [OPS] Client and tooling releases for 2.11 features roll out in the week after the server release, with docs following in days. "client releases, tooling releases, we're going to be rolling those out over the next week or so" (~11:21)
- [CLNT] Orbit functionality may be ported into core clients once solidified, or remain as stabilized Orbit packages. "once they sort of get solidified we can basically port and move that functionality into the core clients if it makes sense" (~11:21)
- [USECASE][OPS] Control plane stream/KV viewers let QA engineers validate data without knowing NATS. "they don't know anything about NATS they don't need to care about NATS ... they just need to go in and actually validate that the data looks correct" (~13:25)
- [TOPO][USECASE] "Edge" here means the user-defined edge (factory, car, a house), not CDNs or cloud edge; NATS and Nex run wherever the user defines their edge. "We're talking about the user the customer the user-defined edge wherever you want to run it" (~15:27)
- [OPS] Synadia aims to stay 6 to 18 months ahead of customer demand on performance and scale; performance and scale remain a constant focus. "we always have to try to stay like six to 12 to 18 months ahead of the curve with demand, scale" (~20:34)
- [CLNT][STRM] 2.12 focus: higher-order client-side patterns, some requiring native server capabilities, because clients are good at primitives and need to move up the stack. "some of these require native NATS server capabilities so that we can build client side higher order patterns" (~21:36)
- [OPS] Release cadence lesson: 2.10 and 2.11 took a long time; the team is scoping releases down so slipped features move to the next release about six months later. "if something doesn't land in this release, then it can just get kicked over in the next release and it's going to be another six months" (~22:37)
- [OPS] A new docs site was announced as coming soon; the 2.12 candidate list is the GitHub issues under the 2.12 label, explicitly not all of which will ship. "We are not going to be doing all of those things. Just to be very clear, we are scoping that down" (~22:37)
- [OPS] Roadmap observability: see the system tier (clusters, superclusters, leaf nodes) and the application tier (clients, micro services, workloads, connectors), drill down, alert; Prometheus is the default supported monitoring system. "Prometheus for example since that's our default monitoring system that we support" (~26:40)
- [CLNT][MYTH] NATS has always been payload-agnostic; schema registry and codecs are a first step up the stack into data governance. "NATS doesn't care about the payload ... schema registry is sort of a first pass to that" (~26:40)
- [OPS] Fleet management roadmap covers both platform components (servers, control plane, Nex nodes, connectors) and customers' own device fleets: deploy, lifecycle, monitor, redeploy, health-check. "how do you deploy and life cycle that component? How do you monitor that component?" (~29:43)
- [OPS] A local-first NATS workbench UI with configurable panes and sharing is planned. "it's being built and driven by a very local first perspective" (~30:46)
