## We need to talk about Microservices... (And how NATS.io can simplify things)
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AiUazlrtgyU
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz (Synadia) | date: unknown (2024 era; says tracing is "coming very soon in nats-server 2.11", available in nightlies) | duration: 34:17
- version context: 2.10 era, previewing 2.11 message tracing via nightly builds

### Claims
- [PATTERN][CORE] The core design shift for microservices on NATS is location transparency: stop asking "who do I talk to" (IP, DNS) and ask "what do I want to talk about" (a subject). "shifting from this who do I talk to to what do I want to talk about really is a fundamental shift" (~03:04)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Services are addressed by subjects such as math.add, payments.create, search.add_index; the only location a client needs is the NATS server it connects to. "you just need to know the NATS server that you connect to and then you just want to know what you want to talk about" (~04:04)
- [PATTERN][SEC] An API gateway's two jobs (aggregating many service endpoints behind one endpoint, and a single auth layer) are things the NATS server already does by brokering subjects between clients. "NATS actually just naturally does this ... NATS is the broker between those subjects" (~05:04)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Load balancing between service instances is built in via queue groups, with no reverse proxy or separate service-discovery process needed. "NATS has load balancing just built in out of the box with a feature called queue groups" (~06:04)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Queue groups work across clusters and superclusters: a request is first served by a responder in the local cluster and only goes outside if none exists, which gives geo load balancing plus automatic regional failover. "it's going to first try to see if there is anything that can respond ... in its local cluster and if not it's going to search outside" (~06:04)
- [PATTERN][CLNT] The NATS server has no concept of a registered service; service discovery is pure convention built on request/reply to $SRV.PING, where every subscribed instance self-reports. "the NATS server actually doesn't have a concept of services ... we just use convention" (~08:08)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] The `micro` service library exists in many client libraries and lets you declare a service with name, version, endpoints and arbitrary metadata (e.g. description, request/response schema). "we have a little library called micro and it's in many of our client libraries already" (~09:11)
- [PATTERN][USECASE] Self-reported schemas in service metadata could replace a schema registry if adopted as an organizational convention. "maybe you don't need a schema registry if all of the microservices are self-reporting their own schemas by convention" (~10:12)
- [OPS][CLNT] `nats micro list` / `nats micro info <svc>` / `nats micro stats <svc>` discover instances, endpoints, metadata and per-instance request/error counts; `--json` makes the output automatable. "if I actually run this again with a json flag you can see all this is just pure json" (~12:14)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] The `micro info` response is itself load balanced: whichever instance answers reports its own ID. "this is the ID of the actual instance that decided to respond ... it's actually load balancing the info response" (~12:14)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Requests to an endpoint served by three micro instances are split fairly evenly between them without any extra configuration. "they've been split fairly evenly between the three nodes" (~13:16)
- [PATTERN][OPS] Canary deployments are done with weighted subject mappings (server config, or per-account under JWT auth) so callers keep using the same subject. "you might want to route a certain percentage of traffic ... to a V1 versus a V2 and still not have to update any of the clients" (~15:20)
- [SUBJ][OPS] Example: map math.> to math.v2.> with a 50% weight; half of math.add requests then land on the v2 responder. "we could simply map it to math.v2.> and we'll just map 50% of the traffic there" (~16:20)
- [SUBJ][TOPO] Subject mappings can also be scoped per cluster. "you can do things like set mappings for certain clusters" (~17:22)
- [PATTERN][USECASE] A "log tap" pattern: services publish structured logs to core NATS (not JetStream) on subjects that carry instance, level, region; any subscriber can filter them in real time. "because it's subject based addressing you can key off of the instance of the service or the log level" (~18:23)
- [ANTI][PATTERN] The speaker does not suggest NATS replace a log store outright; treat the log tap as a debugging "break the glass" switch and keep the default level at error so you don't flood the server. "I've set the log level ... to actually just show me errors that way I'm just not slamming the NATS server with all of my logs" (~19:24)
- [STRM][PATTERN] The same log subjects can be captured into a stream on demand (nats stream add with subjects math.log.>) for later analysis. "I can even put this into a JetStream if I wanted to" (~20:26)
- [PATTERN][OPS] Monitoring uses scatter-gather: one stats request fans out to every instance and each responds with its own counters, which can feed a Prometheus-style scrape without an index of URLs. "you can get this very very easily without having to have some sort of index of all of the URLs" (~22:27)
- [OPS][CORE] Message tracing (nats-server 2.11) is enabled by a header on the message; the server emits ingress/egress events, server identity, whether the message went through JetStream or crossed an account boundary, to a chosen subject. "whether or not it went through JetStream whether or not it went over an account boundary and then also its egress" (~22:27)
- [OPS] Tracing demo used a Nats-Trace-Dest header pointing at a subject the operator subscribes to; the payload includes server name, server ID, version and an events list. "we have an ingress event and we have an egress event of who sent it and then who received it" (~24:29)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Authorization in NATS is subject based: JWT claims list which subjects a user may publish or subscribe to, with wildcards, so service-to-service permissions are as fine grained as subjects. "all of the permissions are also driven by subjects" (~26:30)
- [SEC][SIZE] Decentralized JWT/NKey auth scales because creating a user does not require updating servers; the credential is signed up the trust chain and verified by the server. "we don't have to update servers every time we want to create a user" (~26:30)
- [SEC][PATTERN] One credential authenticates a service to every other service and to the data stores, giving a single unified security model. "one credential to access all of those things" (~26:30)
- [KV][PATTERN] Dynamic configuration: services read config from a KV bucket and watch for changes, so log level or other settings change live without restarting pods. "these apps that don't need to be restarted ... they could live update" (~27:32)
- [KV][USECASE] Demo: `nats kv put config math.log_level 0` flipped the running service from error-only to info logging immediately. "we immediately received another log line that says that our log level was set to info" (~28:34)
- [STRM][KV][OBJ] For distributed data, JetStream streams, KV (Redis replacement) and Object Store (S3/MinIO replacement) share the same security model and are replicated globally from day zero. "on day zero ready to replicate and scale out globally" (~29:35)
- [ANTI] The speaker explicitly does not argue against relational databases; the JetStream stores are proposed only where distributed scale-out is the need. "SQL databases and relational databases have their own use cases ... I'm not going to fight anybody on that" (~29:35)
- [USECASE][OPS] Nex (NATS execution engine, early days) uses NATS as the control plane to place binaries or serverless JS on nodes running Firecracker microVMs, needing only a NATS server and a Nex node. "you need to run a NATS server and you need to run a Nex node and you're pretty much there" (~32:40)

## JetStream KV: A fascinating alternative to Redis...
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XLJ5_5MsgGQ
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz (Synadia) | date: unknown (2024 era; per-key TTL, counters, batch get and TTL watch notifications described as "coming in NATS 2.11") | duration: 35:13
- version context: 2.10 era, previewing 2.11 KV features (per-key TTL, value semantics, LRU, TTL watch notifications)

### Claims
- [KV][STRM] A KV bucket is a stream under the hood with a thin layer of client-side sugar; everything learned about streams (replication, mirrors, sources, accounts, ACLs) applies to KV. "a key value store is no different than a stream in terms of all of the internals" (~02:01)
- [KV][SUBJ] Keys are subjects; every key carries a value plus a configurable per-bucket history of previous values. "we actually have full history of these values ... you could set on a per bucket basis how much history you want" (~02:01)
- [KV] Revisions are globally ordered at the bucket level (not per key) and are the basis for optimistic concurrency control. "these are kind of globally ordered on a bucket level" (~03:01)
- [KV][PATTERN] Watching keys replaces polling and restarts for configuration: "many many companies" use KV as a configuration-management layer with apps watching for changes. "instead of your applications having to poll ... you can just have them watch for changes" (~04:02)
- [KV] Optimistic concurrency control keeps concurrent writers from stomping on each other's read-modify-write of a value. "make sure that clients aren't stomping on each other when you have multiple concurrent writers" (~05:03)
- [KV] TTL/expiry currently exists at bucket level only; per-key TTLs are a future server feature. "we have that on a bucket level ... in a future update to the server we're going to be supporting per key TTLs" (~05:03)
- [KV][STRM][TOPO] Because a KV is a stream you get replication, mirror, source, mux/demux, multi-tenancy via accounts, and subject-based ACLs on buckets. "being able to mirror source mux and demux ... you get all the multi-tenancy with accounts" (~06:04)
- [KV][MYTH] The speaker positions JetStream KV as comparable to Redis, not 10x faster; single-node Redis wins on latency for few writers, JetStream KV has a higher ceiling for concurrent requests and throughput. "Redis is going to win out on the latency side especially for a small number of writers and JetStream's KV is going to have a larger ceiling in terms of handling concurrent requests" (~08:06)
- [KV][MYTH] Replication and clustering differ so much that comparing them to Redis is "apples and oranges"; the advantage claimed is at supercluster / multi-region scale, not single-cluster speed. "you might see some advantages when it comes to global scale moving out to a super cluster" (~07:05)
- [KV] The KV-specific concepts layered on streams are history, TTL and a compression flag. "the three kind of concepts ... that's new to KVs is the idea of history of TTLs and compression" (~09:06)
- [KV][ANTI] The KV does not have all of Redis's operations; the value slot is currently opaque ("dumb") with no value-based semantics. "the NATS key value store right now is kind of dumb when it comes to the types of values" (~09:06)
- [KV] Put sets a key and returns a revision number; Get returns the latest value with subject, headers and metadata, or a specific historical revision on request. "you can request a specific revision as well" (~10:06)
- [KV][PATTERN] Create fails if the key already exists and, combined with TTL, is the primitive for leader election, distributed locks and leases. "the create command ... will fail if that key already exists ... we can use this in combination with TTLs to do very cool things like leadership elections" (~11:08)
- [KV] Update requires the caller's last-known revision; a stale revision is rejected and the client must re-get and retry. "the KV store is going to reject that because it knows it's had a later revision" (~12:09)
- [KV] Delete is a soft delete: it writes a delete marker as the newest revision, keeps prior history, and is visible to watchers. "a delete actually does not delete the data itself but instead puts a delete marker as the latest revision" (~13:09)
- [KV] Purge writes the delete marker (so watchers still fire) and removes all earlier revisions of that key; delete can also take an expected revision for OCC. "it's going to delete all of the revisions before it in that particular key space" (~13:09)
- [KV][CONS] Watch is implemented as a lightweight consumer, so it supports subject filtering, choosing headers-only/latest/history/delete notifications, and a starting revision. "this is going to create a lightweight consumer to be able to get all of the notifications for that particular watch" (~14:10)
- [KV][SIZE] Users store tens to hundreds of millions of keys in a single KV bucket, which is why filtered watches matter. "we have people that put millions and millions ... tens of millions hundreds of millions of keys inside of a key value store" (~15:12)
- [KV] A watcher first delivers all current values, then an empty marker meaning "caught up", then live update/delete/create notifications. "it's going to send a message that's essentially blank to signify that it sent you all the most recent values" (~16:12)
- [KV][TOPO] R1/R3/R5 replication lives within a single cluster; with R3 you can lose one node and still accept writes, lose two and still serve reads. "you can take one node down and still accept writes you can take two nodes down and still accept reads" (~17:13)
- [KV][TOPO] Cross-region or leaf-node replication of a KV uses mirrors and sources, not the replica count. "if you want to go outside of a data center or ... into another region this is where mirroring and sourcing come into play" (~17:13)
- [KV][TOPO][PATTERN] A KV mirror is an automatic read replica: NATS serves reads from the closest mirror and forwards writes to the origin leader with no application change. "NATS is smart enough to serve up requests from the closest mirror ... all of the writes are going to go through the leader" (~18:14)
- [KV][PATTERN] Sourcing with subject filters "demuxes" a large central KV into smaller regional or per-business-unit buckets near the consuming apps. "I can source all of this data and just filter on the stuff that I care about" (~19:16)
- [KV][PATTERN] The inverse, "muxing", sources many edge KVs (e.g. on Raspberry Pis) into one central cloud KV; subject remapping while sourcing lets each edge key space be rewritten into the aggregate. "you can now do remapping as soon as you're sourcing into these streams" (~21:17)
- [KV] Upcoming (next server release): value-based semantics (counters, lists, sets, maps), per-key TTL, LRU-style cache eviction, and watch notifications for TTL expiries and other system deletes. "currently we don't get any sort of watch notification for it but we will be getting watch notifications for any sort of system delete events TTLs" (~23:21)
- [KV][PATTERN] Batch get across related keys (user.id, user.name, user.email) fetches a "row" of fields in one request, approaching Redis/DynamoDB semantics. "you can actually use a batch get to get all of those fields in one request" (~23:21)
- [KV][TOPO][SIZE] Demo latency: a get every second against a bucket in Azure Europe West from Southern California took about 200 ms; moving the bucket to AWS us-west-2 dropped it to about 40 ms. "we're getting about 200 milliseconds of latency" (~25:25)
- [KV][OPS] Changing a bucket's cluster placement moves it in flight; clients keep accessing it while it is mirrored and relocated. "it's actually going to move the bucket mid-flight everything's going to stay the same" (~25:25)
- [KV][TOPO] Keeping the bucket in Europe and adding a mirror in us-west-2 brought reads back to about 40 ms while writes still went through Europe. "we drop our reads to back to those 40 milliseconds ... all the writes are still going through Europe" (~27:27)
- [KV][PATTERN] Leader election recipe: bucket with a ~3 s TTL; non-leaders loop every second calling Create on key "leader"; the leader renews with Update using its last revision, and an Update error means leadership was lost. "we want the key value store to be able to tell us hey you're working on outdated information and you are no longer the leader" (~30:30)
- [KV][OPS] On Synadia Cloud a bucket must set max bytes. "we're using Synadia cloud and we absolutely need to have max bytes set" (~28:28)
- [KV] TTL expiry is what frees the lock when a leader dies; until TTL watch notifications ship, failover speed is bounded by the TTL. "we are leaning on TTLs a little bit so until we get that new feature around TTL notifications we won't be able to speed this up a ton" (~33:31)

## The ONE feature that makes NATS more powerful than Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ & Redis
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=334XuMma1fk
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz (Synadia) | date: unknown (2024 era; mentions multiple filter subjects as "new in a recent version", batch direct get as "future versions") | duration: 40:23
- version context: 2.10 era (multi-filter consumers exist; batch direct get still future). Note: the "one feature" is consumer design, not subjects.

### Claims
- [CONS][MYTH] The feature claimed to set JetStream apart from Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ and Redis is the flexibility of consumer configuration, which the speaker says removes upfront design cost. "that feature is how NATS designs its consumers" (~00:00)
- [CONS][STRM] Consumers are "windows into the data of the stream": server-side filtering on the whole subject plus control over delivery, redelivery and start position. "they're really windows into the data of the stream" (~01:00)
- [SUBJ][STRM] JetStream indexes on subject tokens (e.g. orders.<location>.<orderID>.<status>), which is the source of consumer filtering flexibility. "JetStream does index on these topics ... this is kind of the crux of where a lot of the flexibility in JetStream consumers comes from" (~02:01)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Three consumer archetypes: event-sourcing (durable, explicit ack, max-ack-pending 1, all subjects), reporting (ephemeral, start-time, filter), lookup (ephemeral, filter by ID, last-per-subject). "we probably want ... durable we want our acks to be explicit and our max ack pending to one" (~03:03)
- [CONS][MYTH][ANTI] Alternatives give a firehose and expect client-side filtering, which at high scale is slow and inefficient; JetStream filters before sending over the wire. "the alternatives kind of just give you a firehose of messages and expect you to filter them out on the client side" (~04:04)
- [CONS] Synadia has moved to "do almost everything" with pull consumers; push is not deprecated but pull is easier to reason about. "we've recently kind of moved to more of a do almost everything in a pull-based consumer" (~05:05)
- [CONS][ANTI] Push consumers send as fast as the server can, making flow control hard for slow consumers even with the built-in flow control and heartbeats; they suit monitoring / most-real-time cases. "it still gets a bit challenging to reason about flow control" (~06:06)
- [CONS] Pull consumers are recommended: better performance and scalability, easier horizontal scaling, better flow control, and the default under the hood in newer client SDKs. "they're easier to horizontally scale they give you a bit better flow control and in the newer versions ... pull consumers are kind of the default" (~07:07)
- [CONS] Durable consumers track delivered/acked/redelivery state and usually must be deleted explicitly; since nats-server 2.9 durables can also set inactive threshold. "in 2.9 you can actually set inactive threshold which was reserved for ephemeral for a long time but now can apply to durable" (~08:09)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Ephemeral consumers are cleaned up by the server after an inactivity threshold and are very fast to create, which makes ad hoc queries, reporting and browser sessions scalable. "consumers are very very fast to spin up ... ephemeral consumers are actually possible to do in a very scalable way" (~09:11)
- [CONS][MYTH] In Kafka, Kafka Streams filtering happens client-side so the broker ships every message; that disincentivizes wide topics and forces upfront topic design, which does not apply to JetStream. "the Kafka broker itself is going to send every single message over the wire" (~10:12)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Recommendation: consolidate related data into one stream (e.g. one orders stream with the whole lifecycle) rather than a topic per event type, and rely on filter subjects. "we usually recommend people try to consolidate a lot of things to one stream" (~10:12)
- [CONS][OPS] Consumers are replicated with their own RAFT groups; an R3 consumer keeps operating with a node down and in rare cases with two down. Ephemeral consumers are in-memory R1. "consumers are also replicated and have their own raft groups" (~11:13)
- [CONS] Durable/ephemeral, R1/R3, memory/file consumers can all coexist against one stream. "all of those things can coexist against a single stream" (~12:15)
- [CONS] Ack policies: explicit (default, per message), all (acks everything since the last ack, good for batch ingestion), none (fastest, no delivery guarantees). "you can set an ack policy to none and that will be your fastest option because you don't have to have round trip times" (~13:15)
- [CONS] Acks are asynchronous and non-blocking unless bounded by max ack pending; explicit is "generally better" for most cases. "these acknowledgements are all asynchronous they're not going to be blocking necessarily unless you have kind of a max ack pending" (~13:15)
- [CONS][SIZE] Max ack pending caps outstanding unacked deliveries; the default is 100. "by default this is actually set to 100" (~15:18)
- [CONS][PATTERN][ANTI] Max ack pending 1 gives strict in-order processing but is very slow; try to avoid it unless a downstream state machine truly needs strict ordering. "I would actually recommend trying to see if you can get away without having a max ack pending of one" (~25:26)
- [PATTERN][MYTH] Rule of thumb: if you are just inserting events into a database with indexed timestamps, you do not need strict ordering; only decision-making state machines do. "a lot of people think that they need ordering but often ... they're just putting them in a database" (~25:26)
- [CONS] Ack wait is a per-delivery timer; when it expires the server assumes the client failed and redelivers. "when these timers expire the server has decided that whatever client they sent that message to is not going to continue processing" (~16:19)
- [CONS] Deliver policies: all (default, from the start), new (only future messages; good for monitoring), last (just the latest message), by start sequence, by start time (ad hoc "last 7 days" reporting), last per subject. "last by subject ... is kind of one of the core things that drives our key value store" (~18:22)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Last-per-subject suits change-data-capture style reads where only the latest state per subject matters. "give me all the last updated events from all of the orders" (~19:23)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Replay policy "original" reproduces the original inter-message timing, useful for replaying sessions or debugging spikes; "instant" delivers as fast as flow control allows. "play back the messages in the same timings that they were originally done in" (~20:24)
- [CONS][OPS][PATTERN] Debugging in production: create an ephemeral debug consumer with any configuration without touching or reconfiguring the stream. "the stream is the stream and the consumers are all the consumers" (~21:24)
- [CONS] Other options: max deliver and backoff (redelivery), headers-only (saves bytes for counting/aggregation), sampling (monitoring), consumer metadata, inactive threshold. "you can save some bytes over the wire by saying just give me the headers" (~21:24)
- [CONS][SIZE] Demo: processing ~31,620 messages one at a time with max ack pending 1 against Synadia Cloud was slow; with the default it finished the whole batch quickly while still acking each message individually. "we've processed the entire batch of 31,000 messages we are all caught up" (~30:31)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Preserving full ordering while scaling out requires partitioning, called out as a separate topic. "maintain complete ordering here and scale these out via partitioning" (~29:30)
- [CONS][CLNT] Reconnecting quickly re-binds to the same ephemeral consumer because the server keeps ephemerals around briefly for network jitter; add randomness to the name or use create-consumer (which errors on conflict) to force a fresh one. "we keep ephemeral consumers around just for a little bit because we know that there's network jitter" (~31:32)
- [CONS][SIZE] Reporting consumer: ephemeral, headers only, max request batch 1000, ack none, deliver by start time (7 days ago), filter subject orders.us.*.shipped. "max request batch we're going to bump this up to a thousand" (~32:34)
- [CONS] Multiple filter subjects on one consumer are supported in a recent server version (e.g. US shipped plus Canada shipped). "you could actually pass multiple filter subjects this is new in a recent version of NATS server" (~33:34)
- [CONS][MYTH] A filtered consumer is not as fast as a SQL aggregation query, but it answers ad hoc questions without copying data to another store and stays live for new matches. "is this going to be as fast as a SQL query if you're doing aggregation ... no it won't be" (~35:37)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Lookup: ephemeral consumer filtered on orders.*.<orderID>.* with deliver-last gives the current status; last-per-subject gives the full status lifecycle in order. "we could actually use deliver last as well if we just wanted the last status update for this particular order" (~37:39)
- [STRM][CONS] For single-message lookups the direct get API is more efficient than a consumer, and a batch direct get is coming in future server versions to do these lookups in one call without a consumer. "we're actually introducing a batch version of the direct get API call" (~38:40)

## Give your Go app superpowers with an Embedded NATS Server
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cdTrl8UfcBo
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz (Synadia) | date: unknown (2024 era; uses the nats.go InProcessServer option and JetStream domains, demos against Synadia Cloud) | duration: 27:24
- version context: 2.10 era (nats-server/v2 imported as a Go module; JetStream domain + leaf node to Synadia Cloud)

### Claims
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Go applications can import nats-server/v2 and run the server in process; benefits are no separate NATS distribution and the option to bypass the network stack entirely. "we can actually bypass the network interface altogether and directly talk to NATS in process" (~00:00)
- [PATTERN][USECASE] Target use cases: modular monoliths, offline-first desktop apps, applications-as-infrastructure that auto-mesh or leaf-node to each other, and environments with no network such as Wasm in the browser. "what if you're building something like a modular monolith or a offline first desktop application" (~02:03)
- [CLNT] Embedding alone still connects over the loopback interface, so you still pay network-stack latency; the in-process connection option removes that. "even though you're embedding NATS server you're still connecting over the localhost loopback interface" (~03:04)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] With in-process connections you keep multi-tenancy, JetStream, KV and Object Store while "literally just pushing bytes around inside of the application". "we're not going through the network layer we're literally just pushing bytes around inside of the application" (~04:05)
- [PATTERN] A single NATS protocol becomes the unified RPC layer whether the peer is in process, on the same box, or across the world; this keeps separation of concerns in a monolith and eases later extraction into microservices. "you have this single protocol that you use to be able to communicate with things" (~06:06)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] An embedded server can leaf-node to a remote/cloud NATS server so JetStream data written locally syncs to the cloud, with control over whether the network is used. "we might want to sync that over to the cloud on a remote NATS server ... we can actually do that with leaf nodes" (~05:06)
- [USECASE] The speaker runs a NATS server inside the browser under Wasm using a shimmed network layer and talks to it with a NATS client. "you can actually run a NATS server in the browser and you could talk to it with a NATS client" (~06:06)
- [CLNT][OPS] Startup is asynchronous: after calling Start in a goroutine you must block on ReadyForConnections with a timeout (5 s in the demo) before connecting a client. "we actually need to wait for it to be ready for connections" (~09:10)
- [CLNT][OPS] server.Options is the programmatic equivalent of the config file; the client URL can be taken from the server's ClientURL method; WaitForShutdown handles termination signals for the server lifecycle. "you can kind of think about this as like your config file" (~08:08)
- [CLNT][OPS] Server logging is off by default when embedded; call ConfigureLogger to enable it. "we can actually have configurable logging for this NATS server but trust me silence is golden" (~13:14)
- [SEC][CLNT] Setting the DontListen option makes the embedded server open no network port at all, so the app is fully closed; a normal client connect then fails and only in-process connections work. "you can actually create this really closed application and use the NATS server without actually exposing any sort of network interface" (~16:15)
- [CLNT] The client-side option is nats.InProcessServer(server); it accepts an InProcessConnProvider interface, so any custom transport can be substituted for TCP. "it actually takes an interface called the InProcess Connection Provider" (~17:17)
- [SIZE][CLNT] Benchmark of a full synchronous request/reply: in-process was about 4x faster than loopback on camera and about 5x when not recording, with loopback measured at roughly 16,000 ns per round trip. "I was getting like a 5x improvement over loopback when you're using in-process" (~19:19)
- [STRM][TOPO] To enable JetStream in an embedded server that also leaf-nodes to a cloud account, set a server name, JetStream true, and a JetStream domain so the local assets are addressable distinctly from the cloud's. "we need a JetStream domain to be able to identify all of these stream assets" (~20:20)
- [TOPO] The leaf node remote is configured as a LeafNode Remotes entry with the parsed URL of the cloud leaf endpoint (nats-leaf://connect.ngs.global for Synadia Cloud). "we want to connect to nats leaf connect.ngs.global" (~21:21)
- [TOPO][OPS] Once the leaf connects, the cloud side shows the embedded server's subscriptions, including the whole JetStream API under the embedded domain ($JS.embedded.API...), which is how the cloud can administer the local JetStream. "the whole JetStream API has been subscribed to under the embedded domain" (~22:23)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] A request from the cloud account reaches the in-process responder through the leaf node and the reply is forwarded back, so in-process connections remain fully reachable across the topology. "even though you're using in-process connections you could still reach in and all the NATS stuff kind of works" (~23:24)
- [STRM][OPS] Use `nats --js-domain embedded stream list/add` from the cloud context to manage streams that live inside the embedded server. "I can say js domain embedded and then it's going to list out the streams for this embedded context" (~23:24)
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Publishes into the cloud account on the embedded stream's subjects are captured by the embedded stream because the subscription crossed the leaf connection. "this is again sending it to Synadia Cloud but this is actually being picked up by the embedded NATS server" (~24:26)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Backing up the local stream to the cloud is a mirror created in the cloud with "import from a different JetStream domain" set to the embedded domain; this is the offline-first sync pattern. "we just created essentially an offline first application ... NATS kind of forwards all that data once we get connected again" (~25:29)

## Stream processing: the easy way (with NATS and Benthos)
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EA2Pco3EvpU
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz (Synadia) | date: unknown (2024 era; Benthos pre-Redpanda-Connect naming, nats_kv processors) | duration: 37:17
- version context: 2.10 era (JetStream + KV via Benthos nats_jetstream / nats_kv components)

### Claims
- [PATTERN][USECASE] Positioning: NATS plus Benthos is offered as a third option between a bespoke program and a heavyweight stateful stream processor such as Flink or Spark. "either you go and write a bespoke program ... or you opt into a heavyweight stream processing tool a stateful stream processor" (~00:00)
- [PATTERN] Benthos is a stateless source→pipeline→sink processor; because it holds no state it scales horizontally and relies on sources/sinks for state, which JetStream provides. "benthos really doesn't need to store any state about what it's doing it can remain completely stateless" (~02:04)
- [PATTERN][KV][STRM] JetStream streams or KV can sit on the source side, the sink side, or as intermediate state between pipeline stages. "you can have JetStream whether it's a stream or a KV end up on either the source or the sink side ... and then things like NATS KV store some intermediate state" (~04:05)
- [PATTERN][OPS] With NATS as communication and persistence layer, you run as many stateless Benthos processes as needed without a Flink cluster to babysit. "you're not babysitting like a Flink cluster ... you're really just using this configuration based data processing pipeline" (~05:06)
- [OPS] Learning curve: about a day to get comfortable with Benthos components. "it takes about a day or so to really get it" (~06:06)
- [PATTERN][SUBJ] Bridging (e.g. Kinesis→JetStream) lets you pull a field out of the payload and use it as the JetStream subject to get subject indexing. "pull something out of its payload and use that as a subject inside of JetStream so you get all that really nice fun indexing" (~07:07)
- [OPS][MIG] Kinesis keeps no consumer cursor, so the bridge needs an external DynamoDB table for offsets; the JetStream side needs a stream whose subjects match the publish subject. "Kinesis doesn't really store the cursor or the offset for a particular consumer we need someplace to store that" (~10:09)
- [SIZE][PATTERN] The Kinesis→JetStream bridge was about 11 lines of YAML and moved 123,000 rating events into the stream. "we have 123,000 events coming into the ratings" (~12:12)
- [PATTERN] Benthos's transactional model covers source and sink being offline so messages are not dropped, without Benthos storing state. "if either one of these things are offline benthos has a really great transactional model to make sure ... messages aren't dropped" (~13:13)
- [PATTERN][KV] Enrichment pipeline: S3 CSV input → HTTP lookup (OMDb) in a branch processor → write to a NATS KV keyed by media ID, so a rate-limited API is called once per record instead of on every read. "I don't want to have to look up that poster every time especially since I have an API key that has a rate limit" (~17:17)
- [OPS] Parallelism is set with pipeline threads (12 in the demo) so HTTP enrichment calls run concurrently. "since we're making HTTP calls we want to kind of run some of this stuff concurrently so I'm just going to say threads 12" (~18:19)
- [KV][OPS] The nats_kv output takes URLs, bucket and an interpolated key expression; the bucket must already exist (nats kv add media). "let's go ahead and do a nats kv add media" (~22:24)
- [KV][SIZE] The enrichment run pushed about 6,000 movies through parallel HTTP calls into the KV, observable live with nats kv watch. "it's going through about 6,000 movies and it's parallelizing a lot of the HTTP calls" (~22:24)
- [PATTERN][MYTH] Lightweight analytics does not always need a stateful stream processor; the speaker scopes this to lightweight pipelines, not terabyte-scale stateful jobs. "you don't always need to have a big stateful stream processor in order to do a lot of work" (~23:26)
- [KV][PATTERN] The analytics pipeline reads the ratings stream, looks up media in KV and customers in SQLite (results stored as message metadata, not payload), and updates a media_ratings KV with count and rolling average. "we want to update a new key value store called media ratings" (~25:27)
- [KV][PATTERN] Scaling to many Benthos instances without KV write contention has two options: partition on the source side, or use optimistic concurrency control so concurrent writers to the same key serialize instead of overwriting. "one is to partition on the source side ... the other one is to use optimistic concurrency control" (~25:27)
- [KV][PATTERN] The custom nats_kv_update template does get → mutate → write back with OCC so writers on the same media ID "do a single file line" and apply sequentially. "we're using our optimistic concurrency control to make sure that clients who are processing the same rating ... are not stomping on each other" (~29:33)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Error handling is delegated to NATS: on any processor error the output NAKs the JetStream message so redelivery/retries come from the consumer rather than from Benthos logic. "if anything's errored then make sure you nack on the NATS side so we can do any sort of retries" (~30:35)
- [SIZE] The full analytics use case was about 50 lines of YAML. "this is still only 50 lines of code for ... not a trivial analytics use case" (~30:35)
- [STRM][PATTERN][OPS] Backup/tiered-storage pattern: JetStream input → batch 1,000 (max ack pending set to 10,000) → tar + gzip → S3 with a timestamped path; sending message-by-message to S3 is called out as inefficient. "you don't want to just send a message by message over to S3 that's going to be really inefficient" (~33:40)
- [STRM][OPS] Restore is the inverse: S3 input with a gzip-decompress + untar scanner turns archives back into messages; the backup config was about 19 lines. "in 19 lines of yaml I have a backup strategy" (~34:41)
- [STRM][OPS] JetStream has its own backup mechanism; the S3 archive is presented as an alternative for messages that will expire or have TTLs on the JetStream side. "JetStream does have a backup mechanism but there's also other ways that you can do backups" (~32:38)

## NATS Connect Live! | NATS Surveyor
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9u-hciRTRkM
- speaker: R.I. Pienaar (Surveyor overview), Colin Sullivan (demo), Derek Collison (closing remarks) — identified from context, ASR is poor | date: 2020 (NATS Connect Live) | duration: 20:21
- version context: NATS 2.0 era (requires NATS 2.0 system account; JetStream dashboards described as future work) — pre-JetStream GA

### Claims
- [OPS][STALE?] The previous monitoring model was a Prometheus exporter sidecar next to every server scraping the HTTP monitoring endpoint; Surveyor replaces the per-server sidecars with one process that talks over NATS. "previously you had a Prometheus exporter ... deploy next to every server you run the sidecar" (~00:00)
- [OPS][SIZE] Surveyor can run anywhere (laptop, Docker, Kubernetes) and view 50–100 servers as long as it has credentials and access to the NATS port. "you could run this thing on your laptop and see how 50 or 100 NATS servers behave" (~01:01)
- [OPS][SEC] Surveyor requires NATS 2.0 and system-account credentials because server internals and names are published over the network and must not be visible to ordinary users. "it requires you to have access to the system credentials" (~01:01)
- [OPS] Surveyor works by publishing a ping on a system subject; every server responds with a JSON blob of connections, memory, version and similar stats, which become Prometheus metrics. "we send a ping to the network everyone who owns that server should receive the ping will respond with a big old json blob" (~04:07)
- [OPS][SEC][ANTI] Enterprise pain motivating Surveyor: opening Prometheus scrape ports across data centers and securing exporter connections is slow and complex; the speaker never got a Prometheus port opened in a three-year enterprise stint. "my very first task was open a port for Prometheus and I left three years later having never achieved that goal" (~03:06)
- [OPS] With Surveyor there are no extra ports, protocols or security paths: if you have NATS you can monitor NATS. "once you have NATS deployed there's no additional ports there's no additional security there's no other protocols" (~05:09)
- [OPS] Dashboards drill down per server, per cluster, routes and gateways; the Prometheus data can also be scraped into your own Prometheus (e.g. a globe of connections per region). "you can in fact scrape this Prometheus into your other Prometheus" (~06:09)
- [OPS][ANTI] Trade-off: Surveyor uses the system it monitors as transport, so a split brain or outage blinds it; it is not the be-all of monitoring and additional node-level monitoring is still needed. "we are using the thing that we're monitoring as a transport for monitoring ... so you also need some additional monitoring" (~07:11)
- [OPS] Surveyor must currently be told how many servers exist so it knows how long to wait for ping responses. "right now you have to tell it how many servers there are so it knows ... how long to wait" (~09:14)
- [OPS][STALE?] Planned: JetStream dashboards for message acknowledgment latency, redelivery counts and max-delivery (dead-letter style) events, plus graphs from server events (connect/disconnect/auth errors) to catch reconnect spirals. "if you suddenly see one of your services going into a reconnect spiral ... you'll be able to see an alert" (~08:12)
- [OPS][SIZE] Demo: a simulated 3-region supercluster of 9 servers (3 per cluster) on one Mac, showing 18 route connections and 18 gateway connections, with no sidecars. "three clusters nine servers 18 route connections ... and then 18 gateway connections" (~11:16)
- [OPS] Gateway detail views show per-link traffic between clusters (e.g. region3a→region1 at ~1.18 Mbit/s during a benchmark). "region 3a to region 1 is getting 1.18 megabits a second" (~13:24)
- [SEC][OPS] Service latency tracking is enabled per exported service in the account (via nsc), can be added after the service exists, and was set to 100% sampling in the demo; it works across account import/export boundaries with zero client instrumentation. "there was zero instrumentation in the client and I simply enabled this in the account" (~17:32)
- [OPS] Latency observations arrive as histograms (10th/50th/100th percentiles) split into requester-side, responder-side and NATS-system time. "how much latency is in the NATS system versus from requester and versus from responder" (~17:32)
- [OPS][PATTERN] Derek Collison: service latency in a global supercluster is four-dimensional (responder processing time, responder-to-server distance, requester-to-server distance, server-to-server distance), and Surveyor reports all four in real time; single-number latency is "too limiting". "service latency is not a single dimension it's actually four dimensions" (~19:34)
- [SEC][OPS] Every server has a locked-down system account that can answer "how are you doing" requests targeted at one or many servers, which is the observability pattern Surveyor builds on. "all of our servers by default have a system account which is locked down and secure but can respond to requests" (~18:32)
