## Transcending microservices with NATS | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5A2l27p9d5s
- speaker: Byron Ruth (Synadia, Director of Developer Relations) with Jeremy Saenz (host) | date: 2022 (RethinkConn '22) | duration: 30:42
- version context: 2.8/2.9 era (RethinkConn 2022; auth callout described as "something we're working on")

### Claims
- [PATTERN][ANTI] Microservices are not a free lunch; adopt them only for a real need such as multiple geographies, data sovereignty, multi-cloud, acquisitions, or extending to the edge. "we certainly don't want to advocate for people to move to microservices for the heck of it" (~02:02)
- [TOPO][USECASE] Kubernetes works well in a high-throughput, low-latency data center, but NATS targets running clients or whole servers on small edge devices beyond that. "what if you have to be able to run clients or whole servers on small devices at the edge" (~03:04)
- [SEC][ANTI] A perimeter-based security model (everything inside a VPC, cloud-specific IAM) breaks down once systems span clouds and the edge; NATS' cloud-agnostic security model is meant to replace it. "having this notion of a perimeter-based security model really breaks down it doesn't work anymore" (~08:10)
- [SEC][TOPO] NATS' security model is provider-agnostic; integrating with cloud-local services still requires obeying that cloud's IAM. "you have to obey their IAM permissions but as the connective mesh substrate ... you can't be locked into this perimeter mindset" (~10:12)
- [ANTI][PATTERN] Leaky service addressability and point-to-point service interactions create a "Death Star" web of services that needs load balancers and service discovery layered in; pub/sub with end-to-end communication removes those layers. "you have to add all these layers in between like load balancers and service discovery" (~11:13)
- [PATTERN][CORE] Goals of the NATS design: decentralized zero trust, provider agnosticism, location transparency, many-to-many communication, and one uniform connective layer. "I want to send a message I want to receive that message no matter where you are in the world" (~12:13)
- [PATTERN][MYTH] The many separate stacks (RPC, message queue, durable job queue, append-only log, KV) all reduce to sending, receiving, or asking a question; one substrate can replace them. "we're either sending or receiving data or we're asking it a question" (~13:15)
- [PATTERN][CORE] A "request many"/broadcast roll call every 5 seconds fans out one request to 60+ browser clients worldwide, each replying, and the replies are aggregated. "this is actually using a request many broadcast ... every five seconds" (~16:16)
- [PATTERN][MYTH] HTTP cannot do fan-in/fan-out roll calls (one request, many responders); NATS pub/sub patterns apply to microservices, not just queues and jobs. "you can't just ping a URL and have a roll call come back via HTTP" (~17:17)
- [TOPO][SIZE] NGS is a globally deployed supercluster across multiple clouds and regions; each regional cluster has a minimum of three servers, and clusters are networked together transparently. "at a minimum three per region and then you have multiple clusters across regions or across clouds" (~18:17)
- [CLNT][TOPO] Browser apps connect directly to the NATS server over its native WebSocket support using the nats.ws library; the same messaging semantics flow over WebSocket without an intermediary. "you don't have to throw anything in between your application and the NATS server" (~20:20)
- [SIZE][TOPO] A request from the demo client through NGS to a single service instance in Los Angeles (on Fly.io, connected to an AWS us-west node) had a 139 ms round trip. "the round trip time ... all the way to US West and then back is 139 milliseconds" (~22:21)
- [PATTERN][CLNT] Native HTTP/REST from the browser can be bridged to NATS with simple shims; treat HTTP as a ports-and-adapters layer on the perimeter, with NATS connecting everything behind it. "there's very very simple shims that can be deployed to do a nice translation directly from native HTTP requests into a NATS message" (~25:28)
- [MYTH][CLNT] Concern that adopting a non-HTTP/non-gRPC protocol will cause problems is unfounded; NATS' role is connecting the components within the system, with UIs layered on the edge. "people get a little nervous ... the answer is no" (~25:28)
- [SEC][ANTI] The demo used a single shared bearer JWT embedded in the web app; one bad actor can ruin it for everyone, so this is demo-only, not best practice. "one bad actor could ruin the whole bunch" (~27:30)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Best practice for web clients: a backend exchanges the app's identity token (e.g. OIDC/Google) for a freshly minted NATS user JWT with a short expiration, reissued as needed. "issuing JWTs on the fly as bearer tokens with very short windows for expiration" (~28:30)
- [SEC] Synadia was building server-side support so the identity exchange could happen in a single connection (the precursor of auth callout). "we're working on ... inside of the NATS server ... that you can maybe do that in a single connection" (~29:32)
- [SEC][OPS] Rate limiting per WebSocket user is done via limits on the minted user JWT, e.g. message-count limits, like any NATS user. "when you're minting user JWTs you can set limits on all of those just like you can with any other NATS user" (~29:32)
- [SEC] Accounts in NGS are fully isolated from one another; a user with a permission set belongs to one account, which is the multi-tenancy boundary. "that account is completely isolated from all other accounts that's the whole nice multi-tenancy feature" (~27:30)

## Seamless evolution across geos and clouds | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uq8Axe_GoC8
- speaker: Byron Ruth (Synadia) with Jeremy Saenz (host) | date: 2022 (RethinkConn '22) | duration: 28:51
- version context: 2.8/2.9 era (RethinkConn 2022; NGS described as ~72 servers across 4 clouds)

### Claims
- [PATTERN][TOPO] Scale and latency are usually treated as non-functional requirements, but in practice they are functional: the system has to work and respond in time; topology becomes a design lever once the technology lets you place services anywhere. "if you actually care about latency or scale it actually becomes arguably a functional requirement" (~00:00)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] With freedom of topology you can place services for data sovereignty or co-locate them with clients for ultra-low latency (e.g. factory floors), and topology directly affects network latency. "topology also impacts your network latency overall if you can place services in the right location" (~03:02)
- [CORE][TOPO] Location transparency: a request sent from anywhere is routed by subject to a responder wherever it is connected, replacing DNS/anycast, load balancers, and routing rules. "with DNS you'd have to use anycast and all kinds of really complicated technologies to make this work" (~04:03)
- [TOPO][CORE] NATS routes a request to a responder in the requester's own cluster when one exists, and otherwise to the next closest cluster geographically. "we'll find the next closest cluster geographically to respond to" (~05:05)
- [TOPO] A leaf node is still just a NATS server; it enables a hub-and-spoke model, can run anywhere, can itself be clustered, and links into the bigger cluster via a leaf node connection. "It's still just a NATS server ... it allows you to essentially create this hub and spoke model" (~06:06)
- [TOPO][SEC] A leaf node acts like a separate NATS system that extends yours with fine-grained control over what crosses the connection, which suits the edge, partner organizations, and anything outside the security perimeter. "fine-grain control over what transfers over that leaf node" (~07:07)
- [TOPO][STRM][KV] Leaf-node bridging applies not only to core pub/sub but to data streaming, mirroring streams, and key-value stores. "we're talking data streaming, mirroring streams and key-value stores" (~08:07)
- [OPS][PATTERN] Deploying a NATS-connected app is minimal configuration: a container plus replica count on any hosting provider, and it connects and communicates. "How do you deploy a NATS app via Kubernetes? And it's like a three-line YAML file" (~10:11)
- [PATTERN][CORE] Adding a second service instance in another region gave load balancing and intelligent routing for free; clients nearer the East Coast got much lower RTTs because requests stopped hopping to Los Angeles. "load balancing happens for free. And intelligent routing happens for free" (~11:12)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Service instances share a queue group; by default NATS randomly selects one member to service a request. "NATS is going to randomly select, by default ... an instance to service that request" (~12:22)
- [TOPO][CORE] Queue-group routing is cluster-local first: if any responder in the group is in the cluster the request entered, NATS responds from there instead of routing across gateway connections to other regions. "if there are any responders available in that same cluster ... it's going to immediately respond with one of those members" (~13:22)
- [TOPO][SIZE] Co-locating a full cluster with the application in the same data center gives the lowest RTTs; the geo-aware routing works across clouds as well as regions. "you would even be able to get lower RTTs by having a cluster and an application that's co-located in the same data center" (~14:23)
- [TOPO][SEC][USECASE] Data-sovereignty restrictions on in-flight data are handled by shaping the interest graph so only subscribers on a specific cluster care about that data, using superclusters or leaf nodes. "we really only want things that care about this particular data to exist on this cluster" (~16:24)
- [STRM][OPS][USECASE] For data-at-rest sovereignty (e.g. "stored only in Germany"), JetStream placement uses server tags that can encode geography; many customers do this. "configure NATS JetStream ... to place assets based off of server tags which you could base off of geography" (~17:26)
- [CORE][PATTERN] NATS is deliberately payload-agnostic (strings, base64, JSON, BSON, protobuf); schema validation will not be a core feature but an opt-in add-on, and can be built today with subject mapping and conventions routing traffic through a validating service. "Is it going to be in core NATS and a core feature? Probably not" (~18:27)
- [TOPO] A leaf node can establish multiple leaf connections into a single cluster or into multiple clusters, enabling hub-and-spoke or a leaf node acting as a bridge between two systems with transformation in between. "you can have a leaf node that creates multiple connections into multiple clusters" (~19:28)
- [TOPO][SEC] Leaf node connections bind to an account on the cluster side, so you can select all or part of that account's traffic to cross the leaf connection. "leaf nodes bind to an account on the cluster side ... I want all the traffic from this particular account or some of the traffic" (~20:30)
- [CORE][OPS] Head-of-line blocking is not a concern for a leaf node with multiple high-traffic clients; the server is designed to avoid it at the network and messaging layers. "you're not going to experience hardly any head-of-line blocking in reality" (~20:30)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Clients and services were flipped from NGS nodes to a local leaf node without changing the application; 24 leaf nodes on Fly.io extended NGS and services reconnected to their local leaf node. "24 leaf nodes all extending the NGS cluster deployed all over the place" (~24:34)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] With a regular account and no admin access you can extend a SaaS supercluster with your own leaf nodes; or leaf-node a single-region self-hosted system into NGS so edge traffic uses NGS's global footprint. "you can leaf node your system into NGS and have ... everything at the edge talking to NGS" (~25:37)
- [SIZE][TOPO] NGS at the time ran roughly 72 servers across four clouds. "like 72 servers, like four different clouds" (~25:37)
- [TOPO][SEC] A leaf node is its own territory with its own permission boundary, data locality, and ownership of local services and data; it can run on phones, cars, or factory devices with full server capabilities co-located on the device. "the leaf node as its own little territory that has its own permission boundaries" (~26:37)

## Where are we now and where to next? | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VxIvWzdtRk4
- speaker: Colin Sullivan (Synadia, head of product) | date: 2022 (RethinkConn '22) | duration: 20:05
- version context: 2.9 era (KV GA, tag-based placement, replica scaling listed as shipped; auth callout, leaf compression, "new JetStream API" as roadmap for 2023)

### Claims
- [TOPO][CORE] NATS is a single binary with no external dependencies that needs only TCP, so it runs on a Raspberry Pi, VMs, bare metal, on-prem, or cloud, and ties any combination together. "we just basically need TCP so given those two primitives we can tie together cloud, on-premise, edge" (~01:01)
- [USECASE][TOPO] Real deployments include leaf nodes in restaurants, stores, and coffee shops over 5G, tying clouds together, factory floors, and in space. "we are even in space, we're on factory floors" (~02:03)
- [PATTERN][USECASE] Most customers adopt NATS to attack one of four macro problems: speed of innovation, time to market, total cost of ownership, and vendor lock-in. "speed of innovation, time to market, total cost of ownership and vendor lock-in" (~02:03)
- [PATTERN][OPS] One deployment gives streams, KV, and object store from edge to cloud; an app written on a laptop moves to cloud or edge by changing one URL. "I have to change one URL and the same thing can run in the cloud, on the edge, wherever" (~03:04)
- [OPS][MIG] Moving a NATS system between clouds or from on-prem to cloud is mostly changing host names and some configuration; applications only change where they connect. "basically changing host names, some configuration as well, but the applications wouldn't have to change a bit" (~04:06)
- [OPS][PATTERN] Scaling services is not a configuration issue: launching more instances into a queue group scales up, and APIs exist to scale down without losing data. "scalability isn't a configuration issue ... it's just launching more instances" (~05:08)
- [SIZE][PATTERN] Most users do not need 20 million messages per second, but that headroom means smaller machines that do not need re-provisioning for years. "a lot of users may not necessarily need 20 million messages a second ... I can do a lot more with less" (~05:08)
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] Operators use accounts as guard rails: a fixed number of connections, subscriptions, and HA JetStream assets per account prevents the noisy-neighbor problem and lets teams work in their own sandbox. "set up an account with a specified number of connections, subscriptions, number of high availability assets ... that development team won't exceed that" (~06:08)
- [SEC] Security evolved from username/password to JWTs with ed25519 signing, so the NATS system never reads or accesses a private key; x509 TLS certificates can also map to identities. "the NATS system never ever has to read or access a private key" (~07:10)
- [PATTERN] Layer model: communications is the grid where data can go, security is the switches deciding where it is allowed, and persistence (streams, KV, object store) sits on top. "communications is like a power grid ... security are your switches" (~08:10)
- [STRM][TOPO] Data needs mobility: move a stream, replicate it closer to the application, aggregate streams or KV stores, or mirror a subset. "we need to be able to move a stream, we need to be able to replicate a stream" (~08:10)
- [STRM][OPS] Shipped: tag-based stream placement (server tags, useful for GDPR/geo), stream migration, and replica scaling from R1 to R3 and back at any time. "I can take an R1 stream turn it into an R3 back down to an R1 as I need to" (~09:11)
- [SUBJ][STRM] Subject hash partitioning (by Jean-Noël) splits a subject into several subjects for ordered processing spread across consumers, plus streaming publish as a scalability play. "take a subject, partition it into several other subjects for ordered processing" (~09:11)
- [KV][SIZE] Roadmap target for KV is one billion keys; KV mirrors give a single source of truth with near-local key access. "we want to get to that billion key capability" (~10:13)
- [CONS][SIZE][ANTI] JetStream was designed assuming a few thousand durable consumers, but users want 30–40 thousand, so large consumer sets need optimization work. "we've seen users want 30, 40 thousands so we're going to be doing some work optimizing for large consumer sets" (~10:13)
- [CLNT][STRM] A new simplified JetStream API is coming because JetStream's internal complexity leaked into the original API; it is beta/experimental in some clients and will long-term replace the old one. "unfortunately some of that was reflected in the API" (~11:14)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Experimental service API: write a service in a few lines and get health endpoints, statistics, and eventually command and control. "that service would have health endpoints ... I could poll it for statistics" (~11:14)
- [SEC] Roadmap: auth callouts where NATS hands a credential/token to an external process that mints NATS credentials, plus message-flow callouts for schema validation, PII scrubbing, and data enrichment. "call out to a different process and that process would mint credentials that make sense for NATS" (~12:15)
- [TOPO][OPS] Roadmap: multi-connection gateways between superclusters to better use long-haul links for performance and resilience, and a hub-and-spoke backbone from which superclusters extend. "imagine multi-connection gateways between these servers to better utilize these long-haul connections" (~12:15)
- [TOPO][OPS] Roadmap: leaf node compression so data leaving over constrained links (e.g. laptop Wi-Fi to NGS) is compressed automatically, and leaf node encryption so the intermediate system cannot see payloads. "as data leaves my security context it's encrypted, the general NATS system cannot see that payload" (~13:15)
- [CONS][SIZE] Roadmap: extremely lightweight stream consumers for IoT at the scale of millions, and interest-graph partitioning to individually address a billion endpoints. "we're talking about millions of consumers ... I want to individually address a billion endpoints" (~14:16)
- [KV][TOPO] Roadmap "attraction": a KV store weighted to follow a moving application (e.g. a truck driving from the Midwest to the West Coast) by automatic mirror/migration so latency stays similar. "that KV store is automatically mirrored migrated to the West Coast" (~15:17)
- [PATTERN][MYTH] Service mesh was built to solve point-to-point, location-based addressing; NATS lacks that flaw, so discovery (a no-op once connected), load balancing, traffic management, and canary testing come built in without Kubernetes. "service mesh ... was built to solve a fundamental design flaw which was point-to-point location-based addressing" (~17:20)
- [USECASE][TOPO] With NATS as the k3s state backend (replacing etcd via Kine), leaf-noding every remote k3s deployment gives central observability and command-and-control, effectively fleet management. "if I choose to leaf node into every single one of my remote k3s deployments I have observability and command and control from a central place" (~17:20)

## Versioning and canary deployments with subject mapping | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EahUbcLTYIo
- speaker: Byron Ruth (Synadia) with Jeremy Saenz (host) | date: 2022 (RethinkConn '22) | duration: 12:36
- version context: 2.9 era (RethinkConn 2022)

### Claims
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Subject mapping converts a published subject into a different subject before delivery; this replaces API gateways or load balancers for versioning and canaries. "takes the input subject name and converts it to a different subject name that is then routed to a subscriber" (~01:02)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Version subjects internally (e.g. greeter.v1) but expose an unversioned public subject and map it, so version numbers stay out of the public API. "maybe you don't want to necessarily expose the version number as part of your public subject names" (~02:03)
- [SUBJ] Mappings support wildcards with token capture, e.g. mapping rethinkconn.* to rethinkconn.greeter.$1. "rethinkconn.star and then map it to rethinkconn.greeter dot dollar sign one" (~03:04)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Weighted mappings do traffic shaping for canaries: route 90% to stable v1 and 10% to v2, then raise the weight until v2 takes all traffic. "90 of the time route it to the stable V1 version ... only 10 of the traffic actually goes to V2" (~03:04)
- [SUBJ][SEC] Mappings can be defined in server configuration or at the account level with nsc; tenants can manage their own canaries. "you can define this as server configuration or you can define this at the account level as well using the NSC tool" (~04:04)
- [SEC][SUBJ][PATTERN] Use permissions to keep versioned subjects internal: services may subscribe to v1/v2/v3 subjects while clients may publish only to the unversioned public subject. "restricts the clients to be able to publish only to that non-versioned subject" (~05:06)
- [SUBJ][TOPO][PATTERN] Subject mapping on a leaf node connection lets a site publish to a plain local subject (inventory) that is remapped to a namespaced hub subject (inventory.storeID), so the site needs less knowledge about itself. "inventory dot store ID to just be mapped to inventory and so the locality has to know less information about itself" (~06:08)
- [SUBJ][OPS] Weights across destinations for one mapping must add up to 100; a total under 100 intentionally drops the remainder to emulate data loss and test failure handling. "if you don't add all of your weights up to 100 you can emulate data loss" (~11:15)
- [SUBJ][OPS] With nsc you define from-subject, to-subject, and a weight (e.g. 50%), push to the server, and the mapping just works. "you can define through NSC ... get it pushed up to your server and the subject mapping just works" (~12:16)

## Extending stateful services to the edge | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vr9TSoK4ExI
- speaker: Byron Ruth (Synadia) with Jeremy Saenz (host) | date: 2022 (RethinkConn '22) | duration: 16:58
- version context: 2.9 era (RethinkConn 2022; JetStream domains and mirrors on leaf nodes)

### Claims
- [PATTERN][ANTI] Stateful services usually push state to a pristine central database, which adds another network hop and a system you must protect as the source of truth. "you have the service deployed, it has to talk to typically a database which is another network hop" (~01:04)
- [PATTERN][TOPO] Edge compute (workers, edge functions) still suffers central-store latency; the next problem is moving data close to compute at the edge, and large localized clusters holding data are not a great answer. "I still have the same latency problems in a lot of ways" (~03:05)
- [STRM][TOPO] A stream mirror is the construct for data locality: an origin stream lives in the cloud hub and a local device mirrors it, keeping access even when disconnected; the same applies to KV. "the mirror construct is exactly what we need to support data locality" (~07:10)
- [STRM][TOPO] Each leaf node can have its own JetStream domain, a separate namespace; a mirror is created there by referencing the hub's domain (NGS) as the mirror source. "every leaf node can have its own JetStream domain ... you create a mirror from that specifying the NGS domain" (~08:11)
- [KV][PATTERN][TOPO] To get Redis-like tight RTTs from a JetStream KV, run leaf nodes near the application with local read replicas; you gain lower RTT and continued reads when the leaf node is disconnected from the hub. "when that leaf node gets disconnected from the hub it can still function and it can still read from its config" (~09:14)
- [STRM] A direct mirror received all 100 origin messages almost instantly after creation. "the mirror already has almost instantaneously all of the 100 messages" (~10:14)
- [STRM][PATTERN] A mirror can have a completely different configuration from its origin: the origin was file-based, R3, limits retention, while the leaf mirror was R1, memory storage, work-queue retention. "when I created my mirror I said I only want one replica ... memory and I want it to be a work queue retention" (~11:17)
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Reverse direction: small edge boxes (e.g. Raspberry Pis) use tight retention and store-and-forward via sourcing/mirroring into a hub stream with near-unlimited retention. "retention policy is pretty tight and we do a store and forward over to the hub in the cloud" (~11:17)
- [CONS][PATTERN] Many clients fetching from one shared consumer bound to the local mirror compete for messages; unacknowledged messages get redelivered (delivery count rises) once the end is reached. "it's starting to now redeliver unless you're acknowledging the messages" (~13:20)
- [STRM][CONS] Consuming from the leaf mirror left the NGS origin stream untouched, because no consumer is bound to the origin; the work-queue mirror removes messages as they are acknowledged. "the NGS stream hasn't been touched because we don't actually have a consumer bound to that" (~14:21)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Mirrors act as digital twins (same messages elsewhere); sourcing muxes many leaf streams into one central "mega stream" for processing pipelines, or demuxes a central stream out to leaf nodes/accounts filtered by subject or wildcard. "we can also demux data ... you get a replica of this data but only a portion of it" (~15:22)

## Effective debugging using the NATS CLI | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pf8jSMMuPr4
- speaker: Todd Beets (Synadia, director of product) | date: 2022 (RethinkConn '22) | duration: 09:55
- version context: 2.9 era (RethinkConn 2022; `nats traffic` described as newly added to the CLI)

### Claims
- [OPS][CLNT] The NATS CLI has no special powers; it is just a NATS application, so everything it does can be done programmatically. "the NATS CLI doesn't have special powers, it is just a NATS application" (~00:00)
- [OPS] "Big three" first commands for diagnosing an environment: `nats server list`, `nats server report jetstream`, and `nats traffic`. "the big three commands that we initially run" (~01:00)
- [OPS] `nats server list` works for a single server, cluster, or supercluster with or without JetStream; it scatter-gathers an info ping to all servers from the system account and shows clusters, routes, gateways, versions, host memory/CPU, and slow consumers. "we're really doing that info ping in scatter gather" (~02:02)
- [OPS][ANTI] `nats server list` is an unopinionated snapshot of what can be seen now; it does not flag right or wrong, so the operator must know what to look for, e.g. a missing node or changed route/gateway counts after a network outage. "it's not going to flash any warnings at you ... you need to bring your own knowledge" (~03:04)
- [OPS][STRM] With JetStream enabled you get the JetStream meta service, which runs across all nodes with no single point of failure and tracks JetStream-enabled servers. "this magic service called the JetStream meta service ... runs on all of your nodes so there's not a single point of failure" (~05:06)
- [OPS][STRM] `nats server report jetstream` adds the RAFT meta-group block showing whether the meta leader has connectivity to every expected node, health, and lag; it is a more opinionated view that marks a lost server as not current/offline. "it's a little bit more of an opinionated view" (~06:08)
- [OPS][STRM] When a JetStream server is lost the meta leader moves to another node almost instantaneously. "it automatically and almost instantaneously moved from vbox6 ... to vbox7" (~06:08)
- [OPS][STRM] `nats traffic` listens to everything in the cluster and shows rolling statistics; in a stable system with no asset changes the RAFT proposals/votes columns show no votes. "a happy stable system ... generally you won't see votes here" (~07:08)
- [OPS][STRM] If two of three availability zones go down, an R3 stream is effectively disabled and `nats traffic` shows continuous voting as the remaining node looks for peers, a quick sign that assets are impaired. "two out of three availability zones go down ... a stream asset ... is essentially disabled" (~07:08)
- [OPS][SUBJ] Anything the HTTP monitor exposes is reachable via CLI server requests, e.g. asking across a supercluster who is subscribed to a subject, or listing one user's subscription interest to find a case mismatch like "Fufu" vs "fufu". "the capital letters is always a killer, it's the off by one character" (~09:10)

## Using JetStream KV for dynamic microservice configuration | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fIg9Qhkm8zQ
- speaker: Byron Ruth (Synadia) with Jeremy Saenz (host) | date: 2022 (RethinkConn '22) | duration: 06:46
- version context: 2.9 era (RethinkConn 2022)

### Claims
- [KV][PATTERN] A KV bucket held live configuration (server URL, subject mapping target, feature flags) that all 55 web apps and every leaf node watched; one put fanned out a watch event to all of them. "with one little push to a KV they all received this watched event that this value has been changed" (~02:03)
- [KV][PATTERN] Leaf nodes and clients reacted to the watched key by dynamically unsubscribing and resubscribing to the newly specified server. "those are dynamically unsubscribing and then resubscribing to the server that I specify" (~02:03)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Browsers acted as queue-group members of a V3 service; requesters got responses from members in their own cluster (e.g. GCP vs AWS), demonstrating closest-responder routing. "it really does do that location transparency and intelligent routing" (~05:10)
- [KV][PATTERN][ANTI] Prefer KV-backed dynamic configuration with locked-down permissions over environment variables, files, or Kubernetes config management; it allows hot reload without restarting services. "you can hot reload their configuration ... without having to restart them" (~06:11)

## Rethinking connectivity from cloud to edge | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z0620i9RA7s
- speaker: Derek Collison (creator of NATS, Synadia CEO), introduced by Jeremy Saenz | date: 2022 (first RethinkConn) | duration: 11:59
- version context: 2.9 era (RethinkConn 2022 keynote; no version numbers stated)

### Claims
- [PATTERN][CORE] Distributed systems have only two interactions: asking and answering questions (microservices/SOA) and making and processing statements (event and data streaming, telemetry). "they can ask and answer questions ... and they can make and process statements" (~04:07)
- [PATTERN] Event and data streaming exists mainly to let systems answer microservice questions better, with more data to personalize responses. "event and data streaming are generally used to allow systems to better answer these questions" (~04:07)
- [SIZE][TOPO] Latency is both processing time and distance from the request; an instantaneous response on the other side of the world still feels slow, so placement matters. "latency is both processing time and distance from the request" (~05:08)
- [TOPO] The demand is now multi-geo, multi-cloud, and intelligently edge-aware systems, and operating them at scale with observability and security is hard today. "we not only want now multi-geo but we're being asked to do multi-cloud and ... edge aware systems" (~06:09)
- [TOPO][USECASE] Derek predicts edge will dwarf cloud by several orders of magnitude within about a decade, but edge is still early and siloed like early cloud. "I really do believe edge is going to dwarf cloud by several orders of magnitude" (~07:09)
- [PATTERN][ANTI] Stateless edge functions (Lambda, edge functions, Wasm) are fine, but once an edge function needs state that lives across the globe the experience is still poor; this is the unsolved problem. "once that edge function really needs data it needs state, it becomes kind of a different story" (~08:10)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Kubernetes made multi-cloud approachable for compute; a similar technology is needed to treat all infrastructure the same across edge providers, clouds, geos, and your own edge (stores, factories, cars, satellites, ships, medical devices). "the ability to treat all infrastructure the same, any edge provider, any cloud provider across any geos" (~09:12)
- [USECASE] NATS is claimed to be running in production today across all of those scenarios, including IoT, cars, trains, satellites, ships, medical facilities, AI systems, web apps, and online gaming. "NATS is already powering every one of these scenarios today as we speak in production" (~10:12)

## Lightweight relational databases at the edge | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x8NUDCZgHBU
- speaker: Byron Ruth (Synadia) with Jeremy Saenz (host) | date: 2022 (RethinkConn '22) | duration: 11:27
- version context: 2.9 era (RethinkConn 2022 proof of concept "nsql")

### Claims
- [STRM][PATTERN] Streams and KV are built into the server, but different data models are needed to query data; the proof of concept projects a raw stream into a relational table for edge workloads. "how can we take a raw stream and actually represent that as a table in a relational database" (~01:01)
- [PATTERN][TOPO] For edge friendliness the PoC uses embedded SQLite on disk, with DuckDB planned for OLAP-style queries; drivers can be extended to other databases. "let's use existing databases that work well there so this is actually using SQLite embedded" (~03:02)
- [STRM][CONS][PATTERN] Creating a table creates a consumer on the same-named stream and subscribes; default columns are the sequence, subject, timestamp, headers (as JSON), and the raw data blob, because nothing more can be inferred from an opaque payload. "create a table, create a consumer and then subscribe" (~04:02)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Declaring the payload encoding as JSON lets you map explicit JSON fields (id, name, preferences) to real columns and choose a key column as primary key. "you can actually define explicit columns to augment the table" (~06:05)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Without a declared key the table is append-only, so retries produce duplicate rows keyed by sequence; with a key it behaves like a KSQL-style table where a new message for the same key updates the row in place. "we didn't append a new customer record, we actually updated the record in place" (~09:08)
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Intended architecture: mirror streams down to edge devices and run the projection process locally, joining across tables in a real database; the process resumes populating after disconnect and reconnect. "the nsql process can get disconnected from the server and then you reconnect and then it just keeps resuming" (~11:11)

## Using NATS JetStream as a Kine backend for k3s | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CetW4eGkyS0
- speaker: Caleb Lloyd (Synadia, NGS/Helix) | date: 2022 (RethinkConn '22) | duration: 12:30
- version context: 2.9 era (Kine JetStream driver landed in k3s May 2022)

### Claims
- [KV][USECASE] Kubernetes talks to etcd; k3s added Kine, an etcd shim, and community member Matt Devaney contributed a Kine driver backed by JetStream KV because the KV API is similar to etcd's; it landed in k3s in May 2022. "the KV implementation in JetStream has a similar API to etcd" (~01:03)
- [KV][OPS] k3s is pointed at NATS via a datastore endpoint URL with the nats:// scheme, a KV bucket name, and any NATS-supported authentication (the demo used username/password). "this driver does support any kind of authentication that NATS supports" (~03:07)
- [KV][SIZE] A freshly created single-node k3s cluster wrote about 528 KB of etcd state into its KV bucket. "it's already got 528 kilobytes of data in it" (~04:10)
- [KV][TOPO][PATTERN] Multiple edge k3s clusters (NYC, LA, Chicago) each used their own KV bucket on one shared NATS server at the distribution center. "run three clusters but back them all to the same NATS server" (~06:11)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Extending to the cloud was done by reconfiguring the distribution-center server as a leaf node into NGS; store inventory then appeared in a cloud web app without VPN access. "reconfigure my NATS server here and have it point to NGS as a leaf node" (~07:13)
- [KV][STRM][OPS] All k3s KV buckets were mirrored up to NGS; after destroying the local server, backups taken from the cloud were restored in seconds and the clusters came back with their state after ~20 s of startup. "it takes probably about 20 seconds of course these k3s clusters have to start up" (~10:19)
- [KV][OPS][ANTI] When restoring mirrored buckets as primary buckets, edit the backup to remove the mirror configuration first, or you recreate them as mirrors. "I have to go into these backups and just remove this mirror" (~09:17)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] The pattern generalizes to multiple distribution centers, NATS at the store level, store-to-store communication, and feeding data down from the top rather than only up from the edge. "you can feed in data from the top as opposed to pushing it all up through the bottom" (~11:19)

## Service monitoring with Helix and Surveyor | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1yw0dHXIw
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz (Synadia) | date: 2022 (RethinkConn '22) | duration: 20:22
- version context: 2.9 era (RethinkConn 2022; Helix pre-release, "import my own export" noted as available in recent server versions)

### Claims
- [OPS][CORE] NATS is observable by default: "matrix mode" or wiretap mode is subscribing to everything in an account to see all messages and replies flowing. "we call this like matrix mode or wiretap mode where you're able to sub to everything in this particular account" (~00:01)
- [OPS][SEC] Latency tracking is a little-known server feature tied to service imports/exports: the server emits a JSON latency event per request/reply for an exported service. "with your services when you work with imports and exports you can get all this latency tracking information JSON blob" (~01:02)
- [OPS] Surveyor is the open-source component that collects cluster metrics and service latency observations for Prometheus scraping; setting up Prometheus, Grafana, Surveyor, and the imports/exports is a lot of kit. "that's a lot of kit to set up" (~01:02)
- [SEC][ANTI] Decentralized auth with nsc is deliberately unopinionated about where JWTs are stored, which causes ergonomic friction; nsc is a utility for a decentralized design, not a management UX. "because it's decentralized there's some like ergonomic issues that naturally come up with it" (~02:02)
- [OPS] Helix scrapes account metrics roughly every 10 seconds; the demo showed ~4.9 messages/s for a service with ~100 ms simulated latency. "we scrape about every 10 seconds or so" (~09:10)
- [OPS][SIZE] Service latency tracking supports a sample rate; lower it for heavily hammered, horizontally scaled services so you approximate metrics without overloading the time-series database or network. "you can actually set a sample rate to lower so you can kind of approximate metrics" (~10:11)
- [OPS] Latency events carry a status: 200 for success, 400 when a publish arrives with no reply subject, 408 for timeouts, so errors are recorded automatically. "200 means everything went well ... no reply header ... that's going to result in a 400 ... timeouts ... 408s" (~11:12)
- [OPS][SEC] The latency event identifies the requester (client type, version, name, account, JWT) and the responder, plus which server/cluster each is connected to. "who the requester was, what kind of client they came from, what version ... what account and what JWT" (~12:13)
- [OPS][SIZE] Latency is broken down like the `time` command into service time, system (NATS) time, and total, so you can tell whether slowness is the client's network hops, the server, or the service. "you get all of that stuff broken down into ... service, system and total" (~13:14)
- [OPS] Metrics are stored as a Prometheus histogram, so p50 and p99 per service are available and a Grafana dashboard can be layered on top. "you can also see hey what's my P99 here" (~13:14)
- [SEC][OPS] Latency tracking is configured in the account JWT: the export declares the service subject, "track service latency" with a sample rate (100 = every request), and the subject to which the server emits the events. "we want to track service latency on this service for a sample rate of 100 and we want to send it to this subject" (~15:17)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Recent server versions let an account import its own export, so latency tracking also covers requests made inside the same account. "I can import my own export ... so I can also get latency tracking for things that are happening inside my account" (~16:19)
- [OPS] Sending plain publishes (no reply) to the tracked service produced an error rate of 557/s as status 400 events, and measured latency dropped because those requests never got answered. "our error rate went up to 557 per second because we were sending a bunch of publishes with no replies" (~16:19)
- [OPS][PATTERN] This gives client-to-server-to-responder-and-back RTT plus client location metadata, which is hard to get from HTTP or a load balancer. "this kind of gives you information that you can't even get very easily with HTTP itself or with a load balancer" (~17:19)

## Short break and Q&A! | RethinkConn '22
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jO0mnoTohJI
- speaker: Derek Collison (Synadia CEO, NATS creator) and Jeremy Saenz (host) | date: 2022 (RethinkConn '22) | duration: 34:18
- version context: 2.9 era (RethinkConn 2022; "46 plus clients", KV compare-and-set, sources, JetStream file/memory only)

### Claims
- [PATTERN] Derek predicts that within 2–5 years all software will be designed this way: globally observable, managed via KV-driven configuration, regardless of cloud, edge provider, or own infrastructure. "as we approach 2 to 5 years out, all software will be designed like this" (~01:00)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Subject naming rule of thumb: organize by the groups and hierarchies you want to filter on; subscribers can wildcard in and need not know the full subject, but publishers must know exactly what they publish to. "your subscribers don't really have to know the full subject ... but your publishers do" (~04:04)
- [SUBJ][SEC] When importing an exported service, the importer chooses the local subject it appears on, e.g. import "Jeremy's cool service" as foo. "if Jeremy exports something and I import it into my world, my account, I dictate where that shows up" (~05:05)
- [SUBJ][SEC][PATTERN] Across import/export mappings the system can inject the caller's true account (as trusted by the system, not as claimed) into the subject delivered to the service; the NGS usage service works this way so every tenant calls the same subject but the service receives NGS.usage.<account>. "map in his true account as understood by the system and deliver that to Jeremy as part of the subject" (~06:06)
- [SEC] Account, not user, can currently be auto-inserted into the import subject space. "You can have the system automatically put the account, not the user right now, but the account into that subject space" (~09:09)
- [SEC][CLNT] Every request across an import carries a system-vouched client info header; by default it shares little (location, account), but the importer can opt in to share everything: app version, language, IP, account, user ID. "there's a consumer info header on every request that the system is actually validating and vouching for" (~07:07)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Zero trust framing: even with permission to use a service, the importer decides whether to share the bare minimum or full identity; JetStream itself is built on these same primitives. "by default it's just the bare minimum, but you can opt in" (~10:10)
- [STRM][MYTH] Replicas vs mirrors: an R3 stream is one system; a publish is not acknowledged until a quorum of replicas agrees and commits to stable storage (file) or memory. Mirrors and sources are kept in sync asynchronously and self-heal. "you're not going to get an acknowledgement back until a quorum of those servers that are hosting that asset agree" (~12:12)
- [STRM][SIZE][PATTERN] A memory-only close cluster can ingest 200–400k messages/s and be mirrored out worldwide, trading a small loss on catastrophic failure for very high ingest. "cluster memory only 2 3 400,000 ingest per second, and then they're mirrored out" (~13:15)
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Future vision: because NATS is inherently observable, the system could autonomously spin up services and data mirrors where requests originate (e.g. Japan) based on threshold modeling, instead of doing it manually. "we could make this totally autonomous" (~15:18)
- [KV][CLNT] There is no official web UI for KV, but building one over the WebSocket API is an afternoon project; Derek built a Deno Deploy front end using plain fetch/POST to a TypeScript service that writes to streams and KV in about 20 minutes. "that exercise really took me about 20 minutes" (~16:20)
- [PATTERN][CLNT] The "last mile" interface is a target pattern: a web app using only normal HTTP (fetch, GET/POST, event sourcing) while a thin service leverages NATS behind it. "what does a world look like where the web app just has normal HTTP stuff" (~17:22)
- [STRM][MYTH] Mirrors are strictly read-only, bit-for-bit replicas including sequence and timestamps; a publish or KV put against a mirror fails when the origin is unavailable. "mirrors are read-only. If the origin server is not around and you try to do a publish or a KV put, that will fail" (~18:23)
- [STRM][PATTERN] For active-active or east/west failover use sources, not mirrors: sources can pull from many streams, have their own subjects, and accept direct writes, e.g. orders.east and orders.west each sourcing the other. "you're going to not use mirrors, you're going to use sources" (~18:23)
- [STRM][SUBJ][PATTERN] Combine sources with subject mapping so a client publishing to "orders" is mapped to orders.west locally; on failover to east the mapping there routes "orders" to orders.east. "orders goes to order.east" (~19:23)
- [STRM][TOPO] Mirrors and sources work across leaf node boundaries in both directions and can be daisy-chained: origin, a single leaf mirror, then five local replicas on a 6-million-square-foot factory floor for low-latency reads. "You can even daisy chain them" (~20:24)
- [TOPO][SEC] A leaf node is a special connection that binds to an account or credential to lock down what traffic crosses it; unlike clustering it is a separate NATS system with its own security domain. "a leaf node is a separate NATS system. So it has its own security domain" (~21:24)
- [TOPO][MYTH] The server binary is identical for leaf, cluster, and supercluster roles; only the relationships (client, gateway, cluster, leaf node connection types) differ. "The binary is exactly the same" (~21:24)
- [CLNT][OPS] Servers and the 46+ clients self-heal; clients learn about other cluster members via gossip even if DNS only lists one, augmenting rather than replacing DNS, so topology changes need no maintenance window. "clients and servers are gossiping all of the time about topology changes" (~22:26)
- [KV][SIZE] KV handles millions of keys without problem; Derek regularly runs hundreds of millions of keys on a home dev box, and customers ask for billions to tens of billions, which needs enough hardware and memory. "I myself regularly on my home development box run hundreds of millions of keys" (~24:29)
- [KV][MYTH][ANTI] JetStream KV has no value-based constructs (push, pop, Redis data-type semantics); it is a payload per key, like memcached, so tightly Redis-typed workloads will not map. "the NATS key value store does not have any kind of like value-based constructs in it" (~23:28)
- [KV][PATTERN] KV's advantages over Redis are intricate replication (mirrors/sources) and fine-grained authentication/authorization over who accesses what. "trying to configure Redis to do that is tough" (~24:29)
- [KV][SUBJ][PATTERN] Subject mapping can transparently shard a KV across e.g. 10 buckets, each independently replicated, while clients simply get and put keys unaware of topology. "through that subject mapping construct, to transparently shard" (~25:31)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] Clients should stay simple and be agnostic to topology changes (servers, asset placement, number of mirrors/sources), which is why adding mirrors required no client restart. "the client should be very simple, and they should be agnostic to any of the topology changes" (~25:31)
- [KV][PATTERN] KV supports compare-and-set, unlike memcached; community members use KV for distributed locks and counting semaphores at global scale. "uses KVs as distributed locks and gaining counting semaphores at a global scale" (~26:33)
- [SUBJ][SEC] Subject mappings can be created dynamically by writing them into an account JWT and pushing it; the server updates automatically. "write it to an account JWT and push it to the server and it automatically gets updated" (~27:35)
- [TOPO][SIZE][USECASE] A supercluster can handle 10 million IoT devices with cloud-to-device subject routing; such topologies are being actively built with customers and can extend further with leaf nodes. "Can a supercluster handle ... 10 million devices ... The short answer is yes" (~27:35)
- [TOPO][USECASE] NATS natively accepts MQTT connections; smart-infrastructure customers pull limited sensor data from factory floors into clusters that extend transparently from multi-cloud services. "NATS can natively accept MQTT connections" (~28:37)
- [CLNT][TOPO] Mobile/web clients can connect directly (no load balancers, firewalls, or VPNs): the WebSocket client finds the nearest server, and back-end services are auto load balanced; proxying through a back end is optional for gating logic. "We don't have any load balancers, we don't have firewalls or VPNs" (~28:37)
- [SIZE][CONS][ANTI] Core NATS servers handle millions of connections, but making millions of devices each a JetStream consumer raises real state and persistence questions. "if you're saying we want to have millions and millions of devices, and we all want them all to be consumers of a JetStream ... there's some real things to figure out" (~29:38)
- [STRM][PATTERN] For tens or hundreds of millions of observers of persistent state, the "hybrid structure" is a stream or KV configured to republish events over core NATS, with enough info in each republished event to detect a lost message. "it can be told to republish events. And the republish events have enough information to understand if an endpoint is lost" (~30:39)
- [SEC][PATTERN] A NATS-only chat app can have a back end that only mints user JWTs, adding stateless claims such as OIDC info; retries and exponential back-off constructs let job services run on NATS alone. "I have no back end except NATS" (~31:40)
- [STRM][MIG] There are no plans for pluggable JetStream persistence beyond file and memory (NATS Streaming had database backends); instead the direction is applying JetStream to external data stores decomposed into a globally ordered sequence of events. "for JetStream right now I think we're still going to stick with file and memory" (~32:41)
