## Derek Collison RethinkConn 2025 Keynote and Closing Remarks
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TcDpJuOcBqI
- speaker: Derek Collison (closing Q&A with Byron Ruth) | date: 2025 (RethinkConn 2025) | duration: 19:22
- version context: 2.11 era (RethinkConn 2025; mentions workloads/Nex, connectors, republish + direct get)

### Claims
- [PATTERN][TOPO] Synadia's stack is layered connectivity first, then data, then workloads, which is the reverse of stacks that start with workloads and bolt on networking and security. "we started with intelligent connectivity, then move to data and then workloads. This is the exact opposite of most approaches" (~00:50)
- [CORE] The connectivity layer rests on a few concepts: location-independent end-to-end communication plus push and pull patterns. "Location independent, end to end communications, and pull and push patterns." (~01:00)
- [STRM][KV][OBJ] The data layer sits on connectivity and provides synchronous and asynchronous replication plus materialized views (KV, object store). "For data, we built on the connectivity layer, providing synchronous and asynchronous replication and materialized views." (~01:05)
- [SIZE][USECASE] Synadia Cloud, a multi-tenant SaaS on NATS, handles over 100 billion messages per day. "our multi-tenant SaaS does over 100 billion messages per day" (~01:40)
- [TOPO][USECASE] EU financial customers with a single-region but multi-cloud requirement use NATS to span Azure, GCP and AWS inside one region. "single region but multiple cloud requirements... able to provide access to both Azure, GCP and AWS in single regions" (~02:00)
- [TOPO][MYTH] Global microservices on NATS across regions, clouds and edge need no DNS tricks, load balancers, API gateways or service meshes. "no DNS tricks are needed, no load balancers or GSLBs, no API gateways, no service meshes are required" (~02:20)
- [TOPO][SEC] Leaf nodes give a logical and secure separation between organizations, companies and partners, which is the basis for fleet management. "leaf nodes are a superpower within the NATS ecosystem; they provide a logical and secure separation between organizations, companies, partners" (~02:35)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Fleet data flows use "source muxing" (aggregating every fleet member's data into cloud streams/KV) and "demuxing" (pulling individual members' data back out on the cloud side). "source muxing and demuxing... we can collect data from all of the fleet items and collect them within the cloud" (~03:00)
- [KV][CONS][SIZE] Traditional consumers are heavyweight and can clog a system, so massive KV observer populations (100,000 to 1 million watchers) are achieved with republish and direct gets with global sequencing instead. "key values with over 100,000 or 1 million observers... traditional consumers are very heavyweight and can clog systems down... republish and direct gets with global sequencing" (~03:30)
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Edge AI data-collection pattern: apps store data locally and NATS mirrors it to the cloud, self-healing after outages, so the app never handles transport. "data is stored locally and then the NATS system takes over and mirrors that into the cloud. It self-heals itself" (~04:20)
- [PATTERN][USECASE] Customers use east-west signaling between edge locations to check whether an anomaly seen in one site is appearing in others. "start to use east west signaling for things like anomalies" (~04:35)
- [PATTERN][SIZE] Push-vs-pull sizing argument: if inference runs at 1M requests/s and pulls context, the RAG layer must also serve 1M request-replies/s; pushing data changes to all inference endpoints avoids that. "whenever this data changes, just let all of the inference endpoints know so that they don't even have to ask" (~05:30)
- [USECASE] Manufacturing deployments combine low-level MQTT device data with higher-level information flows on the same NATS system. "combining information flows with low-level device information from MQTT devices" (~06:50)
- [SIZE][USECASE] Fleet-management targets range from tens to hundreds of thousands to millions of managed items. "from tens to hundreds of thousands to millions of managed items within a fleet" (~07:30)
- [OPS][SUBJ] NATS started payload-agnostic; a schema registry is being designed with both advisory and enforcement modes, in a NATS-native way. "NATS was started as a payload agnostic system... there's obviously advisory type and there's enforcement type of schema implementations" (~10:50)
- [TOPO][OPS] Workloads (Nex) and connectors are federation-free and need no perimeter security model, which suits edge targets like Raspberry Pis and air-gapped sites where Kubernetes-style federation feels heavy. "these technologies in ecosystem are federation free. They don't require a perimeter-based security models" (~12:00)
- [TOPO] Leaf nodes were introduced specifically so any deployment can be extended arbitrarily; Nex and connectors build on that and inherit the NATS security model and topology flexibility. "one of the core visions that when Leaf Nodes was even introduced... being able to extend arbitrarily" (~14:40)
- [OPS] Connector runtimes are pluggable; Wombat (a pre-acquisition fork of Benthos) is one runtime and higher-performance runtimes can be added by users. "the runtimes are pluggable and so yes Wombat, which is a pre-fork of Benthos before the acquisition, is definitely there" (~16:40)
- [USECASE] NATS is over 12 years old and powers critical infrastructure at the world's largest company. "NATS is, I think, over 12 years old now" (~17:40)

## Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia CEO Derek Collison Keynote
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n9XpZTBwQcc
- speaker: Derek Collison | date: 2024 (RethinkConn 2024) | duration: 06:42
- version context: 2.10 era (2024 roadmap: counters, per-message TTL, lists/sets not yet shipped)

### Claims
- [PATTERN] Modern distributed systems are fundamentally about reducing latency to access services and data. "modern distributed systems are a case study in reducing latency to access of services and data" (~00:50)
- [CORE][MYTH] NATS challenges two assumptions, location dependence and one-to-one communication; other technologies only appear location independent and need much extra tooling to fake it. "Technologies today can make this look like they are not location dependent or that all communications are truly one to one, but they are under the covers" (~02:00)
- [TOPO] Responders can come and go and be load balanced with geo awareness with no DNS tricks or global load balancers. "properly load balanced with geo awareness and no additional moving parts, no DNS tricks, no load balancers" (~02:30)
- [STRM][KV][OBJ] JetStream provides synchronous and asynchronous replication, and KV and object store are materialized views layered on streams. "JetStream technology is all about access, reducing latency and flow... synchronous and asynchronous replication" (~03:10)
- [KV][TOPO][PATTERN] A common customer deployment: a KV synchronously replicated in one region (possibly across all three major clouds in that region) with asynchronous digital twins transparently served on get; twins can come and go and the system adapts. "a key value store that is synchronously replicated in a single region but could be across all three major cloud providers... that also has asynchronous digital twins that are transparently accessed" (~03:40)
- [KV][SIZE] Roadmap target: massive KV stores serving tens or hundreds of thousands to millions of edge locations. "massive key value stores with tens and hundreds of thousands to millions of edge locations" (~04:20)
- [KV] 2024 roadmap includes value semantics: distributed counters, LRU via per-message TTLs, lists and sets. "distributed counters, LRU with per message TTLs, lists, sets and more" (~04:50)
- [PATTERN] The microservices abstraction is seeing explosive growth because most systems are dominated by service interactions. "explosive growth in our microservices abstractions" (~05:00)

## Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia Roadmap with Byron Ruth
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aBfA90xY_tQ
- speaker: Byron Ruth | date: 2024 (RethinkConn 2024) | duration: 12:48
- version context: 2.10 shipping, 2.11 planned (roadmap talk; items described as future)

### Claims
- [KV] Planned KV value types are counters, lists, sets and maps with native operations, chosen because those are the four Redis structures people actually use. "being able to actually model counters, lists, sets and maps and having native operations" (~00:40)
- [KV][STRM] As of 2.10 a stream or KV bucket has a single TTL that applies to every entry; per-message TTL is a planned addition. "today within a stream or a KV bucket you can only set a single TTL value... that applies to the entire bucket" (~01:20)
- [KV][PATTERN] Per-message TTL lets you re-up a TTL to emulate an LRU cache or lease without writing a new value revision, saving bandwidth and latency. "re-up a TTL to actually emulate an LRU cache... without the need to actually put a new version of the value" (~01:50)
- [KV] Planned multi-key direct get gives a consistent snapshot read across multiple keys at one sequence number. "a consistent read across multiple keys... at that sequence number... a snapshot bulk batch read of keys" (~02:30)
- [OPS][CLNT] Headers already propagate on delivery so app-level OpenTelemetry spans were always possible; native tracing adds server-injected metadata using OTel-compatible header semantics. "because headers are propagated... you could at the application level express your spans... now this is going to actually support some additional metadata that gets incorporated via the servers" (~03:20)
- [SUBJ][MYTH][ANTI] Server-side filtering is subject-level only (per-token wildcards); filtering on headers or message body is not supported by the server and will not be; a message-processing callout to an external service is the planned way. "if you wanted to filter based on headers or the message body... that's not supported in the server and it won't be" (~04:30)
- [STRM] Planned multi-message atomic publish differs from today's async publish (which only overlaps ack waits); it is an atomic write at the storage level, motivated by event-sourcing command handlers that emit several events. "packaging up a set of messages and supporting it at the storage level as an atomic write" (~05:30)
- [CONS][SIZE] Consumers are heavy because of their Raft traffic; lighter consumers akin to client subscriptions are planned so you could have on the order of millions. "consumers today have a little bit of heaviness... all of the Raft traffic... akin to a standard client subscription... in the order of millions of them" (~06:30)
- [CLNT] An HTTP connectivity layer (KV, object store, basic pub/sub and watcher semantics over HTTP) is planned for Synadia Cloud and platform. "support basically KV, Object Store, basic pub sub and sort of watcher semantics over HTTP" (~08:30)
- [SUBJ] A NATS schema registry can't be Kafka's one-to-one topic-to-schema mapping because subject-based addressing gives more flexibility. "subject based addressing within NATS versus existing solutions like Kafka that is more kind of one to one between a topic and a schema" (~10:50)
- [CLNT] Orbit is a planned set of open-source Synadia libraries layering opinionated capabilities on top of the standard clients. "a new set of client libraries that are going to layer on top and be used in conjunction with the standard client libraries" (~11:20)
- [TOPO] Synadia Cloud runs on NGS, a multi-cloud, multi-geo NATS deployment; planned workload placement follows where client traffic originates. "NGS... a multi-cloud and multi-geo deployment of NATS" (~12:00)

## Synadia RethinkConn 2024: After event Q&A with Derek on Zoom
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Csx6HEH30wI
- speaker: Derek Collison, Byron Ruth, Jeremy Saenz, David Gee (Synadia), Maurice van Veen and audience members | date: 2024 (RethinkConn 2024) | duration: 40:27
- version context: 2.10.x shipping (mentions 2.10.1/2.10.2/2.10.3 point releases), 2.11 in planning (per-message TTL, KV semantics, file store v3)

### Claims
- [OPS] The imperative Nex engine (pick a workload, run it on this engine) will always be open source; a declarative Synadia scheduler that attracts services to where requests originate, with KV digital twins following the service and scaling to zero, is a planned commercial service. "the imperative version... will always be open source... KV digital twins are also moving around and following it around" (~07:30)
- [SEC][OPS] A Nex engine operator requires workloads to prove a root of trust via xkeys, the same trust-chain idea as operator mode and Synadia Cloud; a workload's interactions with the outside world are NATS-initiated and the operator controls what it may talk to. "they have to prove to me that I know the root of trust... your interactions with the outside world are all NATS initiated" (~12:00)
- [OPS][OBJ] Nex isolates workloads with Firecracker; a suspended workload with state could be moved around as an object-store object because JetStream is good at moving data. "we've got firecracker so it does the isolation there... a workload inside of an engine is just an object store that's moving around" (~13:00)
- [OPS] First Nex workload types are static binaries, JavaScript, Python (for AI/ML) and containers (which bloat the VM); wasm was judged too limiting to lead with. "it can't be wasm because it just it's too limiting right now... static binaries, JS... python... container based" (~14:50)
- [OPS] Point releases (2.10.1, 2.10.2, 2.10.3) are driven by customers pushing the system in unexpected ways, not by lack of testing. "you'll see 2.10 come out and then 2.10.1 and then 2.10.2 and 2.10.3 and it's not for our lack of testing" (~17:40)
- [STRM][OPS][SIZE] A customer log-replication stream with only ~1M messages but 640M interior deletes made an R1-to-R3 scale-up and async mirror crawl; a fix shipped within days took completion from 14 hours to about a minute and async replication from 20-some minutes to 15 seconds. "it only had about a million or so but it had 640 million interior deletes... first time I got it to complete was 14 hours... now it's about a minute" (~18:30)
- [STRM][SIZE] A file store redesign (file store v3) is planned to handle petabytes and billions of interior deletes. "a redo of the file store to get into the petabytes... billions of interior deletes" (~19:40)
- [KV][STRM] Per-message TTL is the first 2.11 item because it serves LRU use cases and lets KV tombstones auto-remove after a shorter period than the bucket's limits. "per message TTLs... it also allows the KV tombstones to auto remove themselves after a shorter period of time" (~20:00)
- [OPS] The server main branch builds nightly, and formal release candidates are planned so users can try features like KV semantics and per-message TTL before release. "on main we build nightly every night... formalizing some of the release candidates" (~21:00)
- [STRM][PATTERN] For delayed/embargoed delivery, Derek's earlier TIBCO trading designs used per-endpoint RTT so embargoed messages arrived simultaneously for fairness; NATS already tracks every link's RTT, so an embargo-style TTL is feasible. "NATS systems already track every single link RTT all the time" (~22:30)
- [KV][PATTERN] The KV LRU will refresh a key's TTL on every get, but only when enabled on the bucket, never by default. "every time you do a get refresh the TTL on that message individually... it's not going to be by default" (~24:00)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] A planned processing callout works like subject mapping plus auth callout: an account marks subjects for callout and a microservice may transform, deny or pass each message, enabling schema validation, PII enforcement and ETL. "just like the auth call out there can be a microservice... they're allowed to transform it, deny it, or just let it pass through" (~25:40)
- [OPS][SIZE] Callout services are expected to be placed next to the server, even over loopback, so the added latency should be near negligible and run at wire speed. "potentially even over a 127.1 loopback... the impact on measurable latency will almost be negligible" (~26:20)
- [OPS] The schema registry is expected to land as a reasonably priced Synadia service, with possible OSS reference implementations later. "right now I think it's going to land as a Synadia service" (~27:40)
- [OPS] The NATS server alone represents over $40 million of investment. "NATS just the server itself probably has over $40 million of investment in it" (~28:40)
- [OPS] Everything in NATS is monitorable but not easily discoverable; the tools are Surveyor, the NATS CLI (which Surveyor uses), the legacy HTTP endpoints, and, as Synadia does internally, system-account requests. "everything in the NATS system is monitorable but it's also not easily discoverable" (~30:00)
- [SIZE][TOPO][USECASE] Synadia Cloud's global supercluster was near 20 billion messages per day in early 2024 and was expected to double within two months. "we're getting close to 20 billion messages a day" (~31:30)
- [OPS] Account watch and server watch commands were added to the NATS CLI overnight on request. "the NATS CLI should have something like account watch or server watch... when I woke up he's like yep here it is" (~31:00)
- [OPS][ANTI] A recurring adoption problem is that people skip the basics and start with advanced topics. "folks seem to start on chapter 20 instead of chapter 1" (~35:00)
- [TOPO][OPS] Advanced topologies are considered a four-hour workshop topic on their own. "Advanced topologies is like that's a 4-hour workshop in and of itself" (~34:00)

## Introducing Synadia Insights: Catch the NATS Failures Nothing Else Reports
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=51b6i3usZmo
- speaker: unknown (Synadia presenter) | date: unknown (recent; Insights launch video) | duration: 22:19
- version context: 2.11+ era (recent product; uses `nats stream report`, prometheus-nats-exporter jsz flag)

### Claims
- [STRM][CONS][ANTI] A stream with a message-count limit discards the oldest messages while consumer positions have no limit, so a stopped consumer whose position falls below the stream's first sequence silently loses every message in between, with no error, log line or alert. "The logbook has a limit. The bookmarks do not." (~03:00)
- [CONS] Consumer state lives on the server, not in the application, which is what lets an app resume after restart and also what lets the gap accumulate while it is down. "the bookmark stays behind. It lives on the server, not in the app" (~05:20)
- [STRM][OPS] This data loss is independent of replication; it happens identically on a single server and on a three-node cluster. "Nothing in this failure depends on replication, and it happens exactly the same way on three nodes" (~03:40)
- [OPS][MYTH] In `nats stream report`, "Lost" counts messages the disk failed to keep (corruption, hardware failure); messages removed to honor a retention limit are discarded, not lost, so Lost stays zero. "To NATS, lost means messages on the disk failed to keep... Messages deleted on purpose to honor a limit aren't lost." (~07:10)
- [OPS][CONS][MYTH] A consumer's unprocessed/pending count shows only what it will still receive (at most the stream's current contents), not what it will never receive. "2,000 is what analytics is about to receive. It says nothing at all about the 10,000 it never will" (~08:00)
- [OPS][PATTERN] The detection rule is to compare each consumer's delivered stream sequence with the stream's first sequence; the moment the stream floor crosses the consumer position, everything between has been deleted. "Red is the log book's floor... Orange is analytics bookmark... Eventually, red crosses orange and that crossing is the moment" (~12:00)
- [OPS] The Prometheus NATS exporter doesn't expose stream first-sequence and consumer sequence unless started with the jsz=all flag, and no shipped Grafana dashboard compares the two. "The exporter doesn't publish these two by default. There's a flag, JSZ equals all, and without it, none of this exists" (~12:40)
- [OPS] Prometheus keeps history so the failure can be inspected after the fact, unlike the CLI where the evidence disappears once the consumer catches up. "Prometheus kept every sample, and you can watch the whole thing happen after the fact" (~14:00)
- [OPS][PATTERN] Insights is one binary that scrapes cluster state over the system account each minute with 13 requests, the first a broadcast that discovers every server, and publishes replies to a JetStream stream so the indexer can catch up after a restart. "It asks over NATS on the system account. 13 requests. The first is a broadcast that discovers every server" (~15:00)
- [OPS] Insights commits epoch snapshots transactionally and runs 142 SQL checks inside the same transaction, so a finding is never visible before its data. "142 SQL checks read the pass and write their findings" (~16:00)
- [OPS][USECASE] Real customer tickets included a KV mirror whose replication silently stalled for weeks, found only when a release updated bucket policy, and a mirror stream that stopped advancing with no signal until lag was large. "A KV mirror replication that had been silently stalled, and it lasted for weeks" (~20:40)
- [OPS][CONS] Insights raises a consumer health event when delivery falls below the stream's first sequence. "we delivered below the stream first sequence" (~19:30)

## Event-Driven Systems Need a Security Gateway — Meet Synadia Protect for NATS
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KF20ruhNhgo
- speaker: Bruno Beloy (as transcribed; Synadia) | date: unknown (recent product launch) | duration: 41:19
- version context: 2.11+ era (recent; mentions Synadia schema registry as shipped, leaf node port 7422)

### Claims
- [SEC][MYTH] Traditional brokers (JMS, Solace, MQ, AMQP) secure the connection with TLS/mTLS and apply ACLs to addresses, but offer no content-based policies, unlike REST API gateways. "there are zero content based policies to be applicable at this level" (~02:00)
- [SEC][PATTERN] An event gateway applies API-gateway-style policies to subjects, and covers both request-reply and pub/sub, with operational policies such as throttling plus content policies. "secure subjects or channels of communication and apply policies to those channels much like you did with APIs in a restful gateway" (~03:20)
- [SEC] An event gateway is a plain proxy rather than a router plus proxy, so it is lighter than a REST gateway. "the event gateway is just a simple proxy... much lighter than its counterpart in the RESTful domain" (~04:10)
- [SEC][TOPO] The gateway can be placed between websocket clients and the enterprise, inside the enterprise between clients, or between edge leaf nodes and the cloud hub. "security gateways applied between the edge domain, sensors, devices and whatnot and the cloud or hub domain" (~04:50)
- [SEC] Synadia's security layers are NATS auth (centralized or decentralized, ACLs, per-domain token creation and revocation), schema validation of payload structure, and Protect for payload content. "you have really three layers... infrastructure validation, structural validation of the payload itself, and... content validation" (~05:40)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Enforcement order for a message: TLS on the connection, publish/subscribe permissions on the subject, schema validation of the payload, then content validation. "first of all, you secure the channel, you apply certificates... Then... permissions... schema validation... content" (~06:20)
- [SEC][USECASE] Content-policy use cases include rejecting orders with negative prices, payment and fraud checks, exfiltration prevention for government, healthcare and finance, compliance, per-subject rate limits that close the connection, and prompt-injection detection in agent-to-agent messages. "am I allowed to send X amount of messages per second on a particular subject? And if not, shut down the connection" (~09:00)
- [SEC][TOPO] Deployment roles: a firewall in front of the core cluster for incoming leaf nodes and clients, internal domain traffic control, and protection of AI agent-to-agent traffic. "I want to ensure that whatever traffic comes in there, I block it or protect it before it hits the core cluster" (~10:40)
- [SEC][OPS][PATTERN] A fleet of gateways split by domain is kept in sync by a config server that gateways reach over NATS, never point-to-point, and rule bundles are stored in a JetStream stream. "The gateway itself talk through NATS to the actual config server. So there's no direct point-to-point connection" (~12:50)
- [SEC][TOPO] The gateway is configured with a backend URL for the NATS server it fronts; for leaf nodes, the leaf points at the gateway's leaf port and the gateway connects to the hub's 7422 leaf port. "the leaf nodes point to the gateway and the gateway points to the actual leaf node connection in the hub" (~13:50)
- [SEC] Native rules are a fixed list toggled on or off with regular expressions (conf format); custom rules (YAML, an expression language) cover content, connections and CIDR ranges. "custom rules... apply to both content and connections and whatnot. You can apply CIDR rules as well" (~15:40)
- [SEC][OPS] Rule lifecycle is create a signed zip bundle, install it, activate it, later deactivate and uninstall; all of it is scriptable from the CLI for DevOps. "create the rules bundle... generate a zip file... install... activate" (~16:40)
- [SEC][OPS] Every gateway action is auditable: an audit log, a policy execution log of each triggered rule, forwarding to SIEMs like ArcSight or Splunk, and custom tracing for forensics. "you can actually forward those logs you create to a particular SIEM" (~17:50)
- [SEC] The gateway runs either allow-all-and-deny-by-rule or deny-all-and-allow-by-rule, and rules can apply client-to-server, server-to-client, or both directions. "It can operate and allow everything, but block only through rules or block everything and allow the rules to allow traffic through" (~22:30)
- [SEC] The gateway only sees traffic routed through it; in the demo the sys user is blocked via the gateway port but connects fine directly to the server. "if I connect without the gateway, I should be allowed to and it's going to work" (~28:40)
- [SEC][USECASE] Edge devices can be tampered with to inject commands into payloads headed for the cloud; a leaf-to-hub gateway rule blocks such payloads before they reach the backend. "you can actually do a lot of tampering with devices out on the edge... insert maybe commands in there that could simply trigger actions in the back end" (~38:00)
- [SEC] Around 20 out-of-the-box policies exist, including CIDR allow/deny lists, payload allow/deny, and time-window rules. "right now we have, I don't know, 20 or so policies that are out-of-the-box" (~39:50)
- [SEC][OPS] The UI can only add native rules; custom rules must be authored separately and imported. "The UI currently supports only adding native rules" (~19:20)

## Rethinking Connectivity - Hyper-Connectivity & The Intelligent Edge
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SVN2Rfd2WDA
- speaker: Jeremy Saenz (Synadia) | date: 2022 (IoT Grand Slam 2022; survey site "grandslam22") | duration: 29:31
- version context: 2.9 era (2022; JetStream, KV, object store, leaf nodes, superclusters)

### Claims
- [CORE][MYTH] Today's limitations: DNS, hostnames and IPs as the addressing basis, poll-based HTTP everywhere, VPC-perimeter security that edge breaks, location-dependent monolithic backends, and layers built on one-to-one HTTP. "we're still kind of using IP addresses to get machines to talk to each other and maybe that's not scaling" (~04:40)
- [SUBJ][TOPO] Location-independent subject addressing lets a service be truly nomadic, moving from an on-prem or cloud data center to an edge site and still working. "truly nomadic in a sense where you can move it from some data center... over into an edge site and have it just work" (~07:50)
- [CORE][SIZE][ANTI] Poll-based semantics don't scale when millions of devices hit a central place, so push had to be a native pattern. "poll based semantics does not scale when you have millions of devices all trying to hit some centralized place" (~08:50)
- [SEC] The security model is meant to replace the wall around the VPC with modern cryptography and zero-trust constructs for a multi-tenant, decentralized model. "not just based off of building a big wall around your virtual private cloud" (~09:10)
- [OPS][SIZE] The server is small, written in Go, and runs on Raspberry Pi-class devices, unlike most persistence-capable messaging systems. "you can put this on a very low compute device like Raspberry Pi like devices" (~11:00)
- [CLNT] Over 40 client libraries exist. "we support over 40 different client libraries in different languages" (~11:20)
- [CORE][SIZE] Core NATS scales to millions of messages per second on one instance; a nats bench on a Mac Studio showed 6.3 million messages per second. "6.3 million messages per second" (~14:50)
- [SEC][TOPO] Accounts make NATS securely multi-tenant so it can be a public utility inside an organization, solving the "Coke and Pepsi" problem logically; leaf nodes are the way to get physical isolation. "if you do want physical isolation... leaf nodes... another really good way to achieve physical isolation" (~13:20)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Queue groups load-balance globally and NATS finds the closest responder; if latency trombones to the cloud, move the service into the edge site. "you could just pick up that service and you could put it in your Edge site and get much quicker latencies" (~14:10)
- [CORE][PATTERN] A roll-call request where every connected client answers demonstrates scatter-gather that HTTP can't do. "you can't do this with HTTP but you can do this with NATS" (~16:20)
- [STRM][PATTERN] JetStream aims to solve about 80% of distributed persistence problems with one configurable streams-and-consumers model: queues, append-only logs, replays, roll-ups and compaction. "we want to try to solve like 80 percent of the distributed computing problems... streams and consumers" (~19:00)
- [STRM][CONS] Qualities of service: at-most-once with core NATS fire-and-forget, at-least-once and exactly-once with JetStream. "at least once exactly once and so at most once with just core NATS fire and forget" (~20:00)
- [STRM][TOPO][PATTERN] Sourcing lets edge servers' local streams store-and-forward into one larger cloud stream (mux), or one cloud stream filter down into leaf-local streams with only relevant data (demux). "you can have one big stream in the cloud that then filters down into a stream inside of... an edge location that is data that's only relevant to them" (~20:40)
- [KV] KV is a data structure built on globally ordered streams and was designed to be globally replicatable. "creating a globally replicatable key value store and that's exactly what we did" (~21:00)
- [CORE][SIZE] NATS servers have been observed saturating 70 gigabit NICs. "we've seen NATS servers flood 70 gigabit NICs in terms of throughput" (~21:50)
- [TOPO][OPS] Clusters are fully meshed; clients learn peers through gossip and fail over automatically; stream replicas survive a server loss with a new leader elected. "clients automatically know about the server's peers through our gossip protocol and can switch over" (~23:00)
- [TOPO] Clusters need not be three nodes; five and seven node clusters are used, all fully meshed. "you can do five nodes seven node clusters and they're all fully meshed together" (~23:40)
- [TOPO][USECASE] Superclusters span geos, data centers and clouds; customers run a cluster per cloud so a cloud or multi-AZ outage doesn't take NATS down. "they want to have clusters in each kind of cloud so if a particular Cloud outage happens... they can still make sure NATS is up" (~24:00)
- [TOPO] A supercluster assumes one NATS system under one security and operational model; leaf nodes deliberately break that assumption. "the super cluster kind of assumes it's all one big NATS system... Leaf nodes kind of defy those rules" (~24:40)
- [TOPO][OPS] With a supercluster plus leaf nodes NATS still routes to a distant responder; the higher latency is the signal to redeploy the service closer, in a nearer cluster or the edge site. "latencies might be higher even though NATS figures it out and that's some insight... deploy this service closer" (~25:10)
- [TOPO] A leaf node extends a NATS system of any size, supports separate operational and security domains, and keeps operating without a hub connection. "it can operate normally without a connection to the hub" (~26:00)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Leaf node uses: hub-and-spoke extension, bridging partner or OEM NATS systems, store-and-forward where a leaf-local stream is sourced or muxed by the hub, and command-and-control for fleets. "you'll have a stream inside of a leaf node... configure the hub to say... I want to replicate that stream maybe inside of a bigger stream" (~26:40)
- [USECASE] Observed deployments: factories to cloud, retail sites with a large local service footprint, planes, trains, automobiles, satellites, and partner or multi-prem bridging. "retail sites are super interesting because their service footprint locally can actually be quite big" (~27:30)

## A New Way of Thinking | NATS 2.0 and Connectivity
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0dtATLMy-M
- speaker: Derek Collison (CNCF webinar) | date: 2019 (NATS 2.0 released June 10 2019; JetStream still in design) | duration: 51:02
- version context: NATS 2.0 (2019); JetStream pre-release, NATS Streaming current. Era-specific items tagged [STALE?]

### Claims
- [CORE] NATS has stayed wire-compatible: applications written almost ten years earlier run unchanged on NATS 2.0. "applications that were written almost ten years ago... can still run on a modern NATS 2.0 system today" (~08:30)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Services scale by running more or fewer endpoints, with no load balancers, sidecars or proxies. "to scale them up you just run more of them there's no load balancers there's no sidecars there's no proxies" (~08:10)
- [CORE][OPS] Core philosophy: the server protects itself at all costs rather than any single user, avoiding the "query of death" where one client's request degrades everyone; this is what a shared utility (not a silo) requires. "it protects itself at all costs it doesn't protect you the user at all costs" (~09:10)
- [OPS][SIZE][STALE?] A full server runs on a Raspberry Pi; clients existed for over 32 languages in 2019. "you can run a full-blown server on a Raspberry Pi... clients for over 32 and counting different programming languages" (~09:50)
- [SUBJ][CORE] NATS routes by subject not IP, is message-based not byte-stream, and natively does end-to-end communication with queue delivery. "it's subject based routing not IP... it's message based not packet or byte streams" (~10:40)
- [SEC][TOPO] Accounts were created by concentrating multi-tenancy at the subject router: a user authorizes into an account, a messaging sandbox, so Coke and Pepsi share infrastructure and never see each other's messages; sharing is a mutual export/import agreement. "accounts were born they're isolated meaning Coke and Pepsi can exist on the exact same infrastructure" (~15:40)
- [SUBJ][SEC][PATTERN] An importer chooses where an imported subject appears in its own namespace, which removes the brittle multi-week subject-topology design sessions of older messaging systems and leads to short two-token subjects like kv.get. "when you import something you get to pick where it shows up" (~16:50)
- [SEC][OPS] Account owners add, revoke and re-permission users themselves without helpdesk requests to a central operator. "all of that is managed by the account owners" (~18:00)
- [OPS][PATTERN] Because everything is pub/sub underneath, any exported service is observable from day one without adding a sidecar, proxy or framework. "in order to do that you already had it when you started you're not now deploying with a sidecar or a proxy" (~19:40)
- [OPS] Most changes to a NATS system require zero client configuration or API changes and no recompile. "the majority of changes to a modern NATS system are zero client configuration or API changes" (~20:20)
- [TOPO][OPS] Servers coordinate through a system account, sending messages like any application instead of adding protocol, even across a global supercluster; that account has the same auth and permissions as any other. "an individual server inside of a NATS system can have its own account... we just send messages" (~20:50)
- [TOPO][OPS] Clients learn the topology without DNS or configuration; clusters grow and shrink dynamically and clients are told without application code. "a client knows about the topology even if it wasn't in a DNS name or configured in the application" (~22:50)
- [TOPO][SIZE][ANTI] Most distributed systems work well with low RTT and high bandwidth but degrade on long RTTs; at large scale the coordination chatter alone can bring a system down even with little data flowing, which the supercluster gateway design (optimistic sends with interest-graph pruning) was built to avoid. "a lot of times just the chatter that's going back and forth on one of these systems actually brings the system down" (~24:40)
- [CORE][TOPO] Queue subscribers on a supercluster are geo-aware: the closest subgroup is chosen and if unavailable traffic fails over to the next closest cluster by RTT, with no change to decade-old applications. "understands the closest one and the closest subgroups and picks those automatically" (~25:20)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Leaf nodes exist because groups resist being forced onto a shared utility; they let a team keep its own servers (sub-microsecond local latency sometimes) while bridging transparently into the shared supercluster. "leaf nodes is our answer to that it allows you to have your cake and eat it too" (~26:20)
- [TOPO][SEC] Leaf nodes extend superclusters hub-and-spoke and bridge separate security domains, so an IoT deployment with its own security can attach to a supercluster of backend services. "you are allowed to bridge separate security domains" (~26:50)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Derek runs an unsecured local server bound only to 127.0.0.1 as a leaf into Synadia's supercluster for instant local tooling. "no security except for the fact that it's only running on 127.0.0.1" (~28:10)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] If requests from Asia are hitting west-coast responders, deploying responders in Asia makes the system route there automatically with no load balancers or cloud configuration. "you just deploy these service responders in Asia the system automatically will route request from Asia directly to those" (~29:30)
- [SEC] Security covers TLS including bidirectional certs, SPIFFE identities, username/password, and permissions on subjects and payload size, making least privilege easy. "they can only send up to 256 bytes only on this subject" (~30:30)
- [SEC] Operator mode is a chain: an operator vouches for accounts, accounts vouch for users; a server boots knowing only its trusted operators and derives everything else. "there's an operator and then an operator will vouch for accounts and accounts vouch for users" (~31:00)
- [SEC] A NATS 2.0 system never holds or receives private keys or passwords; it challenges the client with a nonce that must be signed by the credential's private key, unexpired, and signed by a valid account. "the NATS 2.0 systems never have any private keys or passwords whatsoever" (~31:20)
- [SEC][TOPO] The model is federated by design: multiple operators can run servers (e.g. Google, Amazon, Azure) and a user presents the same credentials to any of them. "it could have servers that are being operated by Google and by Amazon and by Azure yet as a user they all look the same" (~32:20)
- [SEC] The PKI uses Ed25519 keys, chosen as branch-prediction-attack resistant after Spectre and Meltdown, and JWTs are public. "we use encoded ed25519s which at the time we were making these decisions were the most branch resistant" (~32:50)
- [SEC][OPS][SIZE] Account limits (max connections, max leaf connections, bandwidth, exports/imports) are enforced globally and instantly: an 11th connection against a limit of 10 is denied anywhere in the world, and a revoked user is disconnected within about 10 ms globally. "if Colin revoked me as a user my application would instantaneously be disconnected... within 10 milliseconds globally" (~33:40)
- [SIZE][STALE?] NATS and NATS Streaming had about 85 million combined Docker downloads in 2019. "about eighty-five million combined downloads between NATS and NATS streaming on docker" (~35:00)
- [OPS][STALE?] Transparent bidirectional bridges for Kafka and MQ Series existed in 2019. "we already have transparent bi-directional bridges for Kafka and MQ series" (~35:50)
- [OPS][PATTERN] Built-in service observability: export a service, sample e.g. 50% of requests to a subject in your account, and get service time, responder RTT, requester RTT and internal NATS latency per sample, across a supercluster. "here's how long the service itself took here's the responder RTT the request RTT and the internal NATS latency" (~36:20)
- [SEC] Synadia's definition of zero trust: everything is encrypted before the system sees it and the system doesn't have the keys. "before our system ever sees anything everything's already encrypted and we don't have the keys" (~37:40)
- [OPS][STALE?] 2019 roadmap: native MQTT (3.1.1 and MQTT-SN), WebSocket support, and signed WebAssembly modules on subject ingress for filtering and GDPR-style processing. "we're going to introduce native MQTT support... we're also going to introduce WebSocket support" (~37:00)
- [STRM][STALE?] A stated tenet of NATS Streaming and the planned JetStream: once an order is defined it is the same order for every subscriber (global ordering per message set). "once an order is defined it's the exact same order for every subscriber in the system" (~41:00)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Gap detection without a streaming layer: each message carries the sender's unique ID and a +1 sequence; the receiver stores last sequence per sender and reacts on a gap, which is how NATS servers coordinate internally. "every time I send a message I send a unique identifier and a sequence number that's always plus one" (~42:00)
- [SUBJ][MYTH] Core NATS is deliberately payload-agnostic, like a phone that carries any language; schema and encoding helpers belong in clients and the ecosystem, not the core. "the core NATS will remain payload agnostic" (~44:20)
- [PATTERN][MIG] Moving an existing request/response API onto NATS is often a ten-minute exercise; the real gain is lockdown without code, scaling without load balancers, global requesters and built-in observability. "a lot of times it can be as easy as a 10 minute exercise" (~45:00)
- [MIG][ANTI] When not to use NATS: don't rip and replace working HTTP, gRPC, Kafka or MQ investments; use NATS for new greenfield work. "don't replace what you have... use NATS to do new greenfield type of implementations" (~47:20)
- [STRM][STALE?] JetStream as designed in 2019: successor to NATS Streaming, built into the server, horizontally scalable, with work-queue (SQS-like unordered task queue) semantics; explicitly not "STAN v2" but native to the NATS API with wildcards. "we're not trying to design JetStream as STAN v2" (~48:00)
