## Customer Story - PowerFlex Solves Intermittent Connectivity at the Edge w/ NATS - RethinkConn 2025
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vwTDumFKbXo
- speaker: Robbie Hughes (engineering manager, PowerFlex), interviewed by Andrew (Synadia) | date: 2025 (RethinkConn 2025) | duration: 18:31
- version context: 2.11 era (speaker looks forward to message tracing, a 2.11 feature)

### Claims
- [USECASE][TOPO] PowerFlex runs one edge Kubernetes cluster per customer site; edge-to-cloud traffic migrated organically onto NATS after one engineer introduced it. "every customer of ours has their own edge Kubernetes cluster... all the traffic just kind of gradually started going towards NATS" (~02:02)
- [ANTI][CORE][STRM] They used core NATS fire-and-forget for transactional data in parking garages with bad internet, then moved that traffic to JetStream. "We were using fire and forget for things that shouldn't be fire and forgot about" (~03:04)
- [MYTH][CORE] Message loss with core NATS was real but much rarer than newcomers reading the docs expect. "you start thinking oh no NATS will drop messages, wasn't really that common but it definitely happened" (~03:04)
- [PATTERN][STRM][TOPO] Streams are split into named "domains" (e.g. orders); every edge site has the same set of streams and they source into the cloud. "every single edge site has these same streams and they're sourcing from one another" (~04:05)
- [PATTERN][STRM][SIZE] Instead of sourcing each edge stream individually to the cloud, they bucket all edge streams into a single upload stream and source that once, which was more efficient (designed with Synadia). "we bucketed all the edge sourcing streams into one upload stream and then uploaded all of those with one sourcing to the cloud" (~05:05)
- [STRM][TOPO][USECASE] The key JetStream feature for them is guaranteed delivery when the internet drops; store-and-forward via stream sourcing over leaf nodes. "the guarantees of sends even when the internet connection goes out... that's become extremely useful time and time again" (~06:06)
- [TOPO][SIZE] Each site's leaf node is a 3-server cluster; the cloud hub is a larger cluster; every server carries a unique server name. "each leaf node is a three node cluster of servers... our cloud cluster is obviously way bigger" (~08:10)
- [TOPO][SIZE] Scale: about 500 leaf-node sites, each a 3-server cluster, connecting to one hub of about 13 servers. "we have about 500 leaf nodes... each leaf node is a three server cluster... one hub I think it's 13 servers" (~15:20)
- [SIZE][USECASE] Per leaf node they send a few GB per day, equating to a few million messages: small messages. "on average a few gigs per leaf node a day. It equates to like a few million" (~16:20)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Auth is decentralized JWT/NKeys: one account spans hub and leaf nodes; each customer gets a unique NKey user issued by one signing key, with permissions scoped via wildcards. "each customer through signing keys gets a unique NKey for authentication but managed with one signing key and permissions and wildcards" (~16:20)
- [OPS][ANTI] The main operational friction is that JetStream requires stream setup per site, so commissioning each new customer means creating new streams. "every time we get a new customer and we have to commission a new site, we have to add new streams. That's maybe the biggest hiccup" (~10:14)
- [PATTERN][OPS] They maintain a spec repo (CloudEvents + AsyncAPI) with CI that generates typed event payload and publisher libraries for Python, TypeScript, and Rust. "it takes the spec and it generates event payloads and even publishers into libraries" (~17:20)
- [OPS] Subscribing to server events / internal $JS.API and $SYS subjects is a key debugging tool for admins. "listening to server events is wildly useful" (~12:18)
- [CLNT][USECASE] They plan to have NATS act as an MQTT broker for a customer who wants MQTT access; many users don't know NATS can do this. "people often don't even know that NATS is an MQTT broker" (~14:19)
- [OPS] The speaker found the JetStream docs confusing and recommends the YouTube tutorials instead. "the documentation really confused me and I found YouTube tutorials that were way better" (~12:18)

## Customer Story - MachineMetrics on Industrial IoT & Predictive Analytics w/ NATS at RethinkConn 2025
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5NIeSw9PslM
- speaker: Johan Ralf (engineering manager, data platform, MachineMetrics) and Tyler Shoppee (staff engineer, MachineMetrics); host Andrew Connelly (Synadia) | date: 2025 (RethinkConn 2025) | duration: 38:30
- version context: 2.11 era (RethinkConn 2025; Synadia Control Plane REST API mentioned)

### Claims
- [USECASE][SIZE] MachineMetrics connects thousands of machines at hundreds of customer sites via thousands of deployed edge devices. "we're connecting to thousands of machines at hundreds of customer sites and factory floors" (~00:01)
- [USECASE][CLNT] NATS was chosen for the edge because of small binary size and low resource use, as a Kinesis-like pub/sub that fits on an edge device. "because of the size of the binary and not that much resource that it uses was very attractive" (~02:01)
- [PATTERN][SUBJ] The winning design idea was decoupling where data is produced from where it is consumed, so compute can move freely. "allows us to basically decouple where data is consumed and where we have our compute" (~02:01)
- [TOPO][USECASE] The leaf-node hub-and-spoke model was the initial fit: every edge device communicates back into the cloud through a leaf node. "that works really nicely with the leaf node model that NATS provides. So that hub and spoke type of architecture" (~06:05)
- [PATTERN][CONS] JetStream work queues with shared consumers let one piece of service code scale up and down without changes. "the consumer model just makes it so easy to scale services up and down really with just one piece of code" (~07:07)
- [MIG][ANTI] They chose not to rip and replace Kinesis wholesale (too large a project for a small team); new development defaults to NATS/JetStream/KV. "let's just replace Kinesis with NATS for all our data ingestion is a massive project" (~09:12)
- [MIG][PATTERN] Their migration bridge copies the tail of the Kinesis stream into NATS, so consumers move to NATS first and producers can later publish directly on the leaf node. "we take the end of that Kinesis stream and copy it into NATS... it gives us this nice way to gradually switch over" (~11:13)
- [CORE][PATTERN] They pick NATS over Redis for internal brokering when they need stronger pub/sub or exactly-once guarantees. "it might make sense to use NATS over something like Redis just to get better pub sub guarantees" (~09:12)
- [PATTERN][SUBJ][ANTI] Biggest lesson: subject and payload shape matter enormously and must be designed deliberately, so they built internal libraries that hide connection setup and subject construction from developers. "the shape of the data whether that be subjects or payloads is very very important and you need to be very intentful" (~11:13)
- [SIZE][USECASE] Normal ingest is about 1 Hz per metric, but tool-break prediction needs about 1 kHz, which factory bandwidth can't ship to the cloud, so that processing runs on the edge device and only alerts go up. "for tool monitoring you need about a kilohertz of data and that is usually not given the bandwidth that factory floors have" (~13:17)
- [PATTERN][TOPO] Goal of edge compute is location freedom: a service shouldn't have to be designed up front for edge or cloud, only constrained by resources. "we don't have to think first and foremost about where it's going to end up on the edge or in the cloud" (~14:17)
- [STRM][TOPO] They don't yet run JetStream on edge devices; today SQLite buffers data during outages, which forces a serialization/technology break, and JetStream on the edge would remove it. "with JetStream on the edge device it's the same technology, you just write it to NATS and it's going to be persisted until it's reconnected" (~16:19)
- [OPS] Core NATS operational overhead is minimal compared with Kafka, which they say needs far more people to operate; JetStream adds some complexity depending on setup. "the operational overhead is so minimal for vanilla NATS" (~18:23)
- [SEC][PATTERN] They issue short-lived NATS credentials through their own APIs so clients and edge devices get location-specific credentials that refresh. "we issue short-term NATS credentials through our APIs so that clients as well as edge devices can have location-specific credentials" (~21:27)
- [PATTERN][KV] Front ends can read KV and NATS data directly, skipping the traditional React → Node API → DB path. "we can skip that middleman and have access to so much data" (~22:28)
- [CLNT][USECASE] Some power-user customers consume their data directly over MQTT from NATS; most of IoT is MQTT so getting a broker for free matters. "we have a handful of customers that consume MQTT data directly from NATS" (~23:30)
- [OBJ][PATTERN] Planned use of Object Store to distribute small WASM compute modules to edge devices instead of pulling large OCI images. "a piece of code that could live in a NATS object store and that can be distributed everywhere automatically... we're talking kilobytes, not 100 megabytes" (~24:31)
- [SUBJ][MYTH] The distinctive NATS property is that data addressing (subjects) is decoupled from the access point (server URLs), unlike REST where the URI is both identifier and server. "NATS... really decouples the addressing of data from the access point of data" (~25:33)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Decentralized auth gives one account per customer plus mapping back into an account they own; scoped signing keys issue users and revocation is an administrative change that propagates. "an account per customer, but then be able to map things back into an account that we own" (~27:36)
- [SEC][ANTI] Decentralized auth is worth learning thoroughly before use; it is the tricky part and they are reworking their auth model with Synadia. "it's certainly a topic to spend some time making sure that you understand thoroughly" (~27:36)
- [PATTERN][OPS] Payload schemas: developer libraries encapsulate the domain model, generate subjects, and use CloudEvents as the envelope, with message ID used for deduplication. "we use cloud events as the envelope format... deduplicating data on that through message ID" (~31:43)
- [CLNT][PATTERN] The domain-model library is written in Rust and compiled to TypeScript with wasm-bindgen, giving code completion for complex subject hierarchies. "we translate that Rust into TypeScript using wasm-bindgen" (~32:43)
- [SEC][OPS] Credentials for edge nodes are set up with the nsc CLI; account seeds then issue short-term user credentials via their API; currently a single account with backend code isolating companies, moving to account-per-company. "most of what we do we set up using NSC CLI. And then we use those account seeds to issue short-term user credentials" (~33:44)
- [OPS][PATTERN] They plan to automate account/user provisioning via the Synadia Control Plane REST API and react to change-data-capture events flowing over NATS. "now that you can do that through the REST APIs in the Synadia control plane, it is considerably easier" (~35:45)
- [MIG][USECASE] Before NATS, edge devices spoke WebSocket into Kinesis; NATS won on the "data is ubiquitous" philosophy versus A-to-B streaming. "You're not thinking in streaming from A to B. you just say okay I'm producing data somewhere and I'm consuming data somewhere else" (~36:46)
- [TOPO][USECASE] Recommendation for IoT: the leaf node concept is a very good fit. "the leaf node concept is just a very good fit for IoT use cases" (~37:47)

## NATS at the Edge with F1 Arcade
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KY_1AkUKcJM
- speaker: Jamie Allen (lead engineer, F1 Arcade) | date: 2025 (speaker references 2025 openings and "end of last year" decision) | duration: 09:26
- version context: 2.10/2.11 era (2025 talk; mirror streams, leaf nodes)

### Claims
- [USECASE][SIZE] Each venue runs roughly 50 to 120 racing simulators, each with two PCs, all constantly connected to an on-site central server. "each venue consists of probably between 50 to 120 simulators" (~02:03)
- [MIG][ANTI] The previous stack was MQTT plus Redis with a hand-rolled queuing system; Redis went down under load testing at the largest venue despite being adequately provisioned, and messaging lacked observability. "Redis despite being adequately provisioned would go down when running our load testing suite" (~04:05)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Each venue runs NATS as a leaf node talking to local services; they wrote a custom NestJS transport to get type-safe subjects. "one of our venues with NATS as a leaf node... we actually have a custom NestJS transport which we've used to give us type safety in our subjects" (~05:07)
- [STRM][USECASE] JetStream at-least-once delivery fixed missed race-result syncs that the old stack suffered. "sometimes the race data had gone missing due to missed messages and a race would finish, but the results might not sync" (~06:08)
- [STRM][PATTERN][OPS] Mirror streams are used to add observability and replication without touching the core messaging path. "the ability to replicate and observe JetStreams using things like mirror streams allows us to add on observability without impacting that core messaging" (~05:07)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Plan: connect all venue leaf nodes to a centralized cluster hosted with Synadia. "plans to connect our venues which are essentially leaf nodes to a centralized cluster with Synadia" (~06:08)
- [MIG][ANTI] Migration required replacing WebSockets, HTTP calls, and MQTT with NATS; settling subject names and learning streams/consumers/acks is a real learning curve. "nailing down subject names... is something you're just going to have to work through" (~07:11)
- [SIZE][OPS][TOPO] Each venue leaf node is 3 replica servers; streams are currently split across them but will be replicated on each for full failover; minimum spec cited as 2–4 CPUs and 8 GB RAM per server. "the minimum requirements something like two to four CPUs and 8 gig of RAM for each one" (~08:12)
- [STRM][TOPO] Outcome: dropped messages can be replayed and a venue losing connectivity loses no data. "if a message drops, we can replay it. If a venue loses connection, we don't lose data" (~08:12)

## Customer Lightning Talk - ACI Worldwide at RethinkConn 2025
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ETQwFbHCUfY
- speaker: Adrian Florian (senior architect, ACI Worldwide) | date: 2025 (RethinkConn 2025) | duration: 07:55
- version context: 2.10 in production; 2.11 features (per-message TTL) anticipated

### Claims
- [USECASE][SIZE] Base24-EPS card-payment switch runs about 2,000 TPS with a hard maximum of 200 ms per transaction including messaging, database, and HSM access. "currently sits around 2,000 TPS... a maximum of 200 ms latency per transaction that includes messaging subsystem, database access, and hardware security devices" (~00:07)
- [USECASE][CLNT] The application is a C++ modular monolith using mostly asynchronous service invocations; NATS is being adopted after 2022 POCs as the internal messaging system. "It's based generally on asynchronous service invocations, and we have a few synchronous use cases" (~01:07)
- [PATTERN][SUBJ][STRM] Application symbolic destinations are mapped onto NATS subjects, streams, and consumers; internal command messages use subject filtering; a predefined subject hierarchy is used. "All usage is based on Base24-EPS symbolic destination that's mapped to NATS constructs like subjects, streams, and consumers" (~02:08)
- [KV][USECASE] The KV store holds application context for the payment switch. "We also use the KV store to maintain application context" (~02:08)
- [PATTERN][STRM][OPS] Their congestion control ("network overload management") reads stream characteristics such as pending count and max messages to drive selective message rejection. "leveraging some stream characteristics like num-pending and max messages. From here, we derived a configurable application selective message rejection algorithm" (~02:08)
- [OPS][CLNT] Observed low latency on pub/sub and request/reply, easy install and operation, a good C API, and easy clustering; targeting Kubernetes deployments first. "We like the very good C API. NATS fits in our distributed horizontally scalable model, being so easy to deploy clusters" (~03:09)
- [KV][MYTH] A distributed KV built into the messaging system is hard to get from other messaging systems and was a decisive plus for card payments. "the KV... it's one of the main items that is not so easy to achieve with other messaging systems" (~05:12)
- [STRM][KV] Most anticipated 2.11 features: per-message TTL and selective delete markers, mainly for KV cleanup. "probably the features related to TTL of messages and... selective delete tags" (~06:14)

## Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Franco Sabini from Fineco Bank on NATS
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dsIcmoGXGQQ
- speaker: Franco Sabini (trading online backend manager, Fineco Bank); host David Gee (Synadia) | date: 2024 (RethinkConn 2024) | duration: 14:07
- version context: 2.10 era (RethinkConn 2024); adoption began when JetStream was in its first versions (~2020-2021)

### Claims
- [USECASE][CORE] NATS carries order flow between front end and back end of an online broker (pre-trade checks, routing to exchanges) and between back-end programs; market data is starting to use KV. "all these messages are now exchanged from the front end via NATS and also within the back end itself" (~01:02)
- [TOPO][USECASE] Deployment is two on-premises clusters in Milan, one for back end and one for front end, across two premises; cloud is not near-term. "we have two clusters on premises one for the back end one for the front end" (~02:05)
- [MIG][ANTI] The trigger to leave TIBCO Rendezvous was a sysadmin mandate against multicast protocols, which also don't work well on-prem-to-cloud. "a very strong request from our system administrators not to use multicast protocols anywhere in our environment" (~03:06)
- [MIG][SUBJ] Rendezvous to NATS was easy because subjects, fire-and-forget, and request/reply map almost one to one (same lineage of designers). "the protocol is very similar the concepts behind are very similar" (~05:08)
- [MIG][STRM][STALE?] They were advised to wait for JetStream GA rather than adopt STAN (NATS Streaming) for a months-away rollout; JetStream needed more adaptation work than the fire-and-forget part. "it was better to wait for JetStream to be general available and that's what we did" (~05:08)
- [CLNT][USECASE] Stack is C++ back end and Java front end; NATS adoption led them to start shipping Go programs to production. "with NATS we started looking at Golang and we now have a few programs written in Golang in production" (~07:09)
- [KV][PATTERN] KV changed their design habits most: previous caching products each had drawbacks, now KV is the default answer for new projects. "the key values changed a lot... every time we have a new project we always think oh yeah that could be a key value" (~08:11)
- [SIZE][USECASE] Peak traffic is around 10,000 messages per second; reliability matters more than performance for them. "we are around 10,000 messages per second... it's our peak we are more concerned by reliability than performance" (~11:15)
- [STRM][KV][OPS] Everything is replicated R3 because they have no performance pressure. "we have everything replicated in three... just because we don't have any performance issue" (~12:16)
- [OPS] Developers also run operations and are on call 24/7; no major NATS incident to date; Synadia support contract was the answer to "what if something happens in production" after 20 years on one product. "till today there hasn't been any major issue with NATS" (~10:14)
- [OPS][MYTH] Compared with Kafka and Solace, NATS needs no knob-tuning to work out of the box. "you don't need to pull levers, change flags... when it works it works" (~13:17)

## Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Jaxon Repp from HarperDB on NATS and distributed databases
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UjVhw59u5NU
- speaker: Jaxon Repp (field CTO, HarperDB); host David Gee (Synadia) | date: 2024 (RethinkConn 2024) | duration: 15:39
- version context: JetStream adopted pre-GA (~2020-2021); HarperDB 4.0-4.3 era

### Claims
- [USECASE][PATTERN] HarperDB uses NATS pub/sub between database nodes at the table level to replicate writes so any node can accept writes. "we use NATS in between each node to pub sub at a table level what data moves and where" (~02:05)
- [MIG][ANTI] Raw WebSockets and then SocketCluster gave no delivery guarantee and created network storms at scale; a database must guarantee delivery, so they moved to JetStream while it was still in beta. "if there's one thing that a database is responsible for is guaranteeing delivery of data" (~03:07)
- [STRM][PATTERN] JetStream replaced hand-written queueing, connectivity checks, and retry logic for disconnected replication; it became a black box that just delivers. "all of that is taken care of by NATS so it became less our code and more a black box" (~04:08)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Every HarperDB node is both a hub and runs leaf nodes, so a severed network (e.g. shop-floor firewall) leaves each side fully functional; on reconnect it converges as one system. "every node is a hub and runs leafs as well... if the network is severed to completely maintain all the functionality" (~05:11)
- [SIZE][STRM][ANTI] Throughput was never a problem for fire-and-forget, but enabling fully acknowledged, exactly-once writes is where they hit throughput limits and back pressure. "as soon as we enable guaranteed delivery... that's when we push up against things" (~06:12)
- [PATTERN][OPS] They are using NATS for inter-node status chatter to route writes away from an overwhelmed node to another that can persist and relay later. "I'm going to route it over to another node that I know has that data" (~07:13)
- [PATTERN][STRM] Table-level replication choice lets a node be a fast local single-instance database while selectively replicating subsets (e.g. threshold events) globally. "the ability at a table level to replicate data or not allows us to... rely on very very fast local transactions" (~09:16)
- [PATTERN][ANTI] Lesson: lean into JetStream's built-in features instead of keeping a parallel bookkeeping list of what was sent; trust was built through testing over time. "the first iteration was okay but we send it there but we still hold on to the list" (~13:19)
- [PATTERN] NATS as a pluggable module was the first step toward HarperDB's fully componentized architecture (REST, MQTT, WebSocket endpoints as modules). "NATS was that first step in our evolution toward a truly componentized architecture" (~12:18)

## Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Nathan Mellis from Modzy on NATS as a foundational building block
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gekULQXXCe0
- speaker: Nathan Mellis (director of engineering, Modzy); host David Gee (Synadia) | date: 2024 (RethinkConn 2024) | duration: 16:32
- version context: 2.10 era (RethinkConn 2024; superclusters, leaf nodes, WebSocket)

### Claims
- [USECASE][PATTERN][CONS] All model inference is asynchronous: inputs go into a NATS queue, Modzy spins up the model, drains the queue, then shuts the model down, so expensive GPU models only run when there is work. "it will spin up that model it will drain the queue and then shut the model down" (~02:04)
- [MIG][ANTI] Their previous queue took many resources, was hard to configure, and could only be used one way; NATS replaced it over several months. "it took up a lot of resources it was hard to configure and you could only use it pretty much one way" (~05:07)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] The theme of their NATS adoption is topologies: clusters for HA, superclusters for multi-cloud/hybrid across geographies, leaf nodes at the edge. "the ability to do super clusters enables you to do multicloud or hybrid" (~07:09)
- [TOPO][SUBJ][PATTERN] A leaf node exposes a portion of the subject/JetStream space to an otherwise independent edge, enabling push-based self-updating configuration to ~10,000 devices without polling. "those changes can get automatically pushed down to 10,000 devices which can then all reconfigure themselves" (~08:10)
- [SEC][TOPO][CLNT] Edge devices connect over a single WebSocket connection on port 443, so no extra firewall ports are needed. "we're actually doing it all over the websocket connection so the edge devices only ever have to talk on port 443" (~08:10)
- [OPS][TOPO] Connection balancing is left to NATS and Kubernetes, not an L4 load balancer. "we let NATS slash Kubernetes take care of it" (~09:12)
- [PATTERN][CORE][TOPO] Request/reply over a supercluster beats HTTP/gRPC for hybrid cloud: a request unanswered locally percolates out to the supercluster, avoiding per-region service deployments and a service mesh. "if the cluster that you're in knows how to answer it it will answer it if it doesn't that'll get percolated out to your super cluster" (~11:16)
- [CLNT] They are polyglot (Java, Go, Python, Rust, JS/TS) and value that each NATS client is written idiomatically for its language. "they have been written in a way that is appropriate for the paradigms of that language" (~13:18)

## Simple Solutions for Complex Problems - How Workiva uses NATS as a Microservices and RPC transport
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G9XNApxA0UI
- speaker: unknown (self-introduces only by role: tech lead, messaging team, Workiva; name not stated in transcript) | date: unknown (~2016-2017; mentions "we saw STAN introduced today", pre-2.0 era) | duration: 27:45
- version context: [STALE?] NATS 1.x / gnatsd era, before JetStream and accounts; STAN (NATS Streaming) had just been introduced

### Claims
- [MYTH][PATTERN][STALE?] Delivery guarantees have many definitions (handed to transport, enqueued, processing started, finished), each with different costs; guaranteed ordered exactly-once is expensive and, by some definitions, impossible. "guaranteed ordered exactly once delivery they're really expensive to provide and depending on your definition they might be impossible" (~04:09)
- [PATTERN] Design around replayability, idempotence, and commutativity so you stop needing guaranteed, exactly-once, ordered delivery from the transport. "if we can think about idempotence... we don't care about exactly once delivery and if we can think about commutativity... we don't care about ordered delivery" (~05:09)
- [PATTERN][MYTH] Delivery is not processing; business-level guarantees must be built in the business layer because infrastructure can't provide them. "if you need business level guarantees you really have to build those into the business layer because the infrastructure can't provide that" (~06:10)
- [MYTH] TCP guaranteeing packet delivery doesn't give application-level guarantees; the end-to-end argument applies. "your application doesn't care about packets and bytes it cares about messages" (~07:10)
- [PATTERN][STALE?] Stronger guarantees can be layered on top (STAN was cited as a layer on NATS) but cannot be removed from below, so pushing guarantees into the base makes everyone pay. "we can always build stronger guarantees on top... we can't remove those from below" (~07:10)
- [CORE][OPS] NATS protects availability by disconnecting slow consumers and lazy listeners that miss pings rather than degrading everyone. "if you have a slow subscriber slow consumer it will just disconnect that consumer nobody else is impacted" (~11:15)
- [CLNT][CORE] Clients are cluster-aware, fail over automatically on partition, have built-in reconnect, and buffer published messages during disconnect then flush on reconnect. "the client will buffer messages for you so if you become partitioned your publishing they get buffered up reconnect flushes" (~12:17)
- [OPS][MYTH] NATS needs no external coordination service (ZooKeeper/etcd) and has minimal configuration, which is key to operational simplicity. "you don't have to deal with configuring like zookeeper etcd these other external dependencies" (~13:17)
- [CORE][OPS] The text-based protocol makes debugging, sniffing, and writing your own client easy, unlike AMQP or binary protocols. "if you've ever tried to implement like an AMQP client or a binary protocol... it can be an absolute nightmare" (~14:18)
- [SIZE][CORE][STALE?] Benchmarks show tight tail latency versus RabbitMQ and Redis pub/sub, predictable up to six nines, and roughly 8 million messages/second depending on measurement. "can do roughly eight million messages a second depending on how you measure it" (~15:18)
- [CORE] Part of the performance comes from automatic pruning of the interest graph. "it auto prunes the interest graph so that's part of it" (~15:18)
- [PATTERN][USECASE] Workiva uses NATS as a service bus: pub/sub, RPC, async messaging; all web traffic passes a gateway that proxies to NATS; queue groups give load balancing between service instances. "the fact that NATS has queue groups queuing built in gives us a really simple way to do balancing" (~16:19)
- [ANTI][PATTERN] Raw pub/sub with hand-agreed encodings decouples services but couples teams; they generate cross-language pub/sub APIs from an IDL (Frugal, a Thrift extension) so developers think in services, not topics. "pub/sub is meant to decouple services but when it's done in that way it kind of couples the teams" (~18:19)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] Subjects are derived from IDL: prefix (with variables such as user) + scope name + operation name, so developers never hand-build subjects. "the topic name is comprised of the prefix plus the scope name plus the operation name" (~20:23)
- [PATTERN][CORE] RPC over NATS: service instances form a queue group, a client publishes to it, one instance answers with an inbox, and the client sends requests on that inbox; no service discovery or sockets, so connections are cheap to set up and tear down, with heartbeats for health. "there's no service discovery involved there's no sockets that we're creating it's literally just a matter of publishing" (~21:28)
- [TOPO][PATTERN][STALE?] Deployment: each VM ("drone") runs a local NATS daemon clustered with the others; services talk to localhost and cluster membership JSON is pulled from S3 at startup to set up routes. "each drone also has a NATS daemon running on it and those daemons are clustered together" (~22:28)
- [SEC][TOPO] Running NATS on localhost means only inter-server (route) traffic needs encryption, and same-host messages never hit the network. "we only have to worry about encryption between the NATS peers" (~23:29)
- [TOPO][ANTI][SIZE] A NATS daemon on every VM doesn't scale to hundreds of nodes; they'd move to a floating cluster or NATS on a subset of machines, which the service abstraction makes painless. "we don't really want to be running a NATS cluster of like hundreds of nodes" (~24:30)
- [CLNT] Cross-language first-party clients (Go, Java, Python) were a selection criterion, versus JVM-centric messaging systems. "a lot of messaging systems tend to be very JVM focused" (~25:32)

## NATS Connect Live! | Pub Sub on the Power Grid
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YB-zPHxrJ6k
- speaker: Wayne (Duke Energy engineer, 23 years at Duke; surname not stated in transcript); Derek Collison closes | date: 2020 (NATS Connect Live, pandemic-era remarks; "DistribuTECH 2019 / this year") | duration: 31:06
- version context: [STALE?] NATS 2.0/2.1 era (mentions "version 2 releases" security features; pre-JetStream GA)

### Claims
- [USECASE][PATTERN][STALE?] Duke Energy's Open Field Message Bus (OpenFMB), ratified by the North American Energy Standards Board, uses NATS pub/sub so grid devices publish their state instead of being polled by central SCADA. "having the devices tell us what the current state is and also that they're listening for control messages" (~08:12)
- [PATTERN][TOPO][STALE?] Compute is pushed to nodes at the grid edge so control loops (solar dips → battery compensates) run locally while data still flows back to the central office. "we want to distribute compute resources out at the edge of the electric grid" (~07:12)
- [SIZE][USECASE][STALE?] A proof of concept ~6 years earlier coordinated a 1 MW solar farm and 500 kW battery with ~250 ms control communication. "1 megawatt solar farm 500 kW battery... communicate in like 250 milliseconds" (~10:15)
- [PATTERN][USECASE][STALE?] Back-office enterprise systems become clients of the field message bus rather than holding direct connections to end devices. "instead of having the direct connection all the way to the end devices they wind up becoming clients of the field message buses" (~09:13)
- [TOPO][STALE?] The microgrid lab currently publishes everything into a single NATS server, with a planned move to a NATS broker on every edge node (leaf-node style). "they're all publishing into right now a single NATS server but we are getting ready to push that out to every one of these nodes" (~16:29)
- [OPS][CLNT][STALE?] Applications are distributed across nodes with Kubernetes/Rancher and written in C++, Go, and increasingly Rust for small, secure binaries. "looking at those tightly compiled languages that produce those small secure applications" (~18:31)
- [TOPO][PATTERN][STALE?] Feeder-level bus and microgrid bus must be bridged carefully because a customer-owned microgrid exposes only capabilities, not internal components; the feeder sends rules (e.g. absorb 100 kW in an hour). "we're gonna have to build that bridge connectivity between both of those NATS buses and we've got to be careful" (~21:35)
- [PATTERN][USECASE][STALE?] Cell gateways (Sierra Wireless) with idle compute run Docker and an OpenFMB app that polls the meter locally at 1 Hz and publishes over NATS; end-to-end dashboard latency was about 1.5 s, dominated by polling and Grafana refresh. "about a second and a half later you would see the graph change and part of that is the polling rate" (~25:41)
- [SIZE][USECASE][STALE?] Microgrid telemetry (switches, meters, solar, generators) is published at roughly once per second per device onto the bus. "publishing data like once a second from inside the micro grid" (~27:45)
- [SEC][STALE?] They plan to adopt NATS 2.x security features going forward. "all the things that you guys have added in the version 2 releases from a security standpoint... we're definitely planning on taking advantage" (~30:48)

## Partner Talk - NATS on Akamai Cloud - RethinkConn 2025
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gaa48R4ihOU
- speaker: Brian Appley (principal cloud architect, Akamai Technologies) | date: 2025 (RethinkConn 2025) | duration: 15:41
- version context: 2.10/2.11 era (RethinkConn 2025)

### Claims
- [TOPO][SIZE][USECASE] A global stretched NATS cluster runs across ~40 Akamai compute regions on shared 2-core/4 GB VMs, showing the binary needs little horsepower. "these are what we call 4 gig Linodes which are shared instances... I think there's two cores and four gigs" (~05:07)
- [PATTERN][CLNT] NATS was used as a GraphQL resolver for both queries and subscriptions via a sidecar/protocol adapter alongside the server. "we were using NATS as a GraphQL resolver for both queries as well as subscriptions" (~05:07)
- [OPS] Server-to-server route latency in milliseconds is reported natively by the server (HTTP monitoring), though the speaker had to write a lightweight exporter because the default Prometheus exporter lacked it. "it is available in the NATS HTTP interface but I don't think it was available in Prometheus" (~08:12)
- [SIZE][TOPO] Measured worst-case intra-cluster latency in the global stretch cluster: US West to Mumbai ~285 ms; São Paulo to Mumbai ~350 ms; most non-India regions under 100–200 ms; North America under 70 ms; US to Europe ~150 ms; LA to San Francisco 7 ms. "it's going to take US West about 285 milliseconds to reach Mumbai" (~09:13)
- [TOPO][SIZE][PATTERN] Speaker frames these route latencies as the worst-case bound for data consistency in a stretched cluster (e.g. writing into LA becomes consistent globally in under a third of a second). "you can achieve consistency on your data if you're writing into Los Angeles... in a little bit under one-third of a second" (~09:13)
- [OPS] Route latency shows very little jitter over time, which they use to demonstrate reliability. "there's hardly any latency at all or jitter at all on that region to region latency" (~12:18)
- [OPS][CLNT] Per-client latency reporting is native, so client latency can be graphed and alerted on in Grafana/Prometheus. "you get that client reporting all the way down to the individual client" (~11:16)
- [PATTERN][USECASE] A fan-out job over NATS makes every cluster node run an MTR traceroute to customer IPs and return per-hop latency, used to pick regions for a P95 latency target. "each node in the cluster will run an MTR basically a traceroute to those IP addresses and then using NATS as well they'll return what the latency was" (~14:21)
- [OPS] The whole ~40-node cluster is scripted with Terraform/Ansible and a Kubernetes deployment YAML, recreated in a couple of minutes. "I can recreate this entire cluster with just a couple of clicks and have this up and running in a couple of minutes" (~07:11)

## Go Beyond Kubernetes Native Events with NATS
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sQN5ZTcVm2Q
- speaker: Gianluca Mardente (principal engineer, Cisco; creator of Sveltos); host from Synadia | date: 2025 (RethinkConn 2025 community lightning talk) | duration: 16:44
- version context: 2.10/2.11 era (2025)

### Claims
- [USECASE][PATTERN] Sveltos, a Kubernetes fleet manager, uses NATS so its event framework can react to events from outside the cluster (user login, onboarding), not only Kubernetes resources. "I needed something to be able to watch for those events happening outside of the cluster" (~02:08)
- [ANTI][OPS] Kafka was rejected as too heavy and operationally noisy to deploy on 100 clusters; NATS via the Helm chart was deployed to all staging clusters in ~5 minutes. "I could have used Kafka but it's very heavy. It consumes a lot of resources. It's not really that straightforward to set it up" (~03:08)
- [SIZE][OPS] Resource footprint matters multiplicatively in fleets: a server deployed per cluster multiplies cost by cluster count. "if it consumes a lot in one cluster and then you have to deploy in 10 clusters now your costs are going up by 10" (~06:14)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] NATS can be per-cluster (one per tenant) or one central server that receives all events and lets Sveltos distribute them. "user can have NATS deployed in a single cluster and all the events are pushed to that NATS server and from there distributed everywhere" (~05:13)
- [CLNT] Prototype integration (agent subscribing to subjects, custom publisher client) took under half a day using the Go docs. "it took me less than half a day to have a prototype which was working" (~04:12)
- [CORE][STRM][PATTERN] Users choose core NATS for prototyping and switch to JetStream in production when events must not be lost. "if they don't want to lose an event they want to make sure that the events is delivered then they have to go with JetStream" (~10:20)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Requested pattern: NATS in each managed cluster forwards events to a NATS server in the management cluster, which forwards on to external clients. "they are all forwarded to the management cluster and from the management cluster there is another NATS server which forwards" (~11:23)
- [PATTERN] Schema handling is delegated to users: Sveltos expects CloudEvents envelopes over NATS and leaves payload contents to the publisher. "the content for Sveltos is a cloud event and it's up to the user what they want to put in the cloud event" (~13:25)
- [OPS] Advice: build a prototype from the docs quickly rather than designing the perfect solution first. "Do not spend too much time trying to have the perfect solution. Just go with the prototype" (~08:16)

## Connectors – Seamlessly Integrate NATS with Other Systems
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iYmhVN0RqQc
- speaker: Daan (Synadia; connectors lead, surname not stated in transcript) | date: 2025 (RethinkConn 2025) | duration: 19:19
- version context: 2.11 era (Synadia Connect / workloads, 2025)

### Claims
- [PATTERN][USECASE] Before connectors, integrating NATS with databases or legacy systems meant writing your own bridge application. "Basically, you would be on your own and write a little application to communicate and to send the messages over" (~00:00)
- [PATTERN][TOPO] The connectors framework is built on top of workloads (Nex), so a connector can run in the cloud, on-prem, or at the edge. "we build the connectors framework on top of workloads. And this allowed us to basically run your connector anywhere" (~01:02)
- [PATTERN][ANTI] A connector has exactly one responsibility, getting data into or out of NATS, with only per-message transformations; it deliberately is not a full data pipeline. "A connector should have one responsibility. It's getting data into NATS or getting data out of NATS" (~01:02)
- [PATTERN][SUBJ] Pipelines are composed by chaining: inlet → NATS → workload transforms → NATS → ... → outlet; messages hop between components over NATS subjects. "this goes on and on and on until at some point you want to write that information back to an existing system" (~02:03)
- [PATTERN][CLNT] Runtimes are language-agnostic executors that run connectors as workloads; any language works if it conforms to the connector specification, and all are managed by the same tooling. "a runtime... can be written in any language as long as it is conformed to the connector specification" (~03:05)
- [PATTERN] Inlet = external source into NATS (demo: MongoDB change stream scoped to a database and collection, published to a subject); outlet = NATS to external system (demo: MongoDB insert). "The kind of connector that we want to create is called an inlet" (~06:09)
- [PATTERN][CORE] An outlet that reads from a subject should use a queue group so multiple connector instances don't process the same message. "I will also add a queue just to make sure that if we have multiple instances of our connector... you won't get multiple instances that will be processing the same message" (~11:15)
- [PATTERN] Two transformer types: a mapping script, or a service transformer that calls out to a NATS service and uses its response. "a service transformer which allows us to call out to a different service on NATS" (~09:14)
- [PATTERN] Filtering is done in a mapping by emitting a tombstone (drop) for messages that don't match (demo: temperature > 35 °C). "If it isn't, we will drop a tombstone, which is as much as saying we're not interested in this message anymore" (~13:19)
- [CLNT] The reference runtime uses Bloblang from a Benthos fork called Wombat; the mapping language is dictated by the runtime, and Rust or Java runtimes can be built by anyone. "it's running on top of Wombat... You're perfectly free to build whatever runtime you see fit in whatever language" (~17:26)

## Workloads - Distributed cloud-to-edge compute with NATS Execution Engine
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4F_03Pim1j0
- speaker: Jordan Rash (Synadia, NATS Execution Engine / Nex) | date: 2025 (RethinkConn 2025) | duration: 29:36
- version context: 2.11 era (Orbit, micro framework, Synadia Cloud; Nex re-architecture 2025)

### Claims
- [PATTERN][TOPO] Because NATS built the connectivity layer first and the data layer on top, Nex inherited security, replication, KV, and Object Store for free instead of re-implementing networking, firewalls, and security. "Nex inherited security. Nex inherited replication of data. It inherited KV. It inherited object store" (~03:12)
- [PATTERN][CLNT] Nex was re-architected to decouple the control plane (nex core) from agents ("nexlets"), which are built entirely on the NATS micro services framework, so agents can be written in any client language that supports micro. "they've been built completely on top of the NATS micro construct... we can build nexlets to extend Nex on any NATS client that supports micro" (~04:14)
- [ANTI][OPS] Packing everything into one binary bloated builds, made build tags confusing, and slowed debugging; that drove the rearchitecture toward "nothing but NATS" using Orbit and micro. "we had packed everything into a single binary, and it was starting to get really bloated" (~04:14)
- [MYTH][TOPO] "The edge" has no single definition (mainframe, cloud, ESP32 on a farm); workloads must be movable to whatever the user's edge is. "The edge is not concrete, but one of the key values of Nex was these workloads need to be able to move to whatever edge" (~06:16)
- [SEC][PATTERN] When agents or workloads start, nodes mint credentials in real time scoped to the subjects those workloads need; a workload in account A can't talk into account B unless intended. "the nodes are actually minting credentials real time that are scoped to the subjects that those things need to talk to" (~08:19)
- [PATTERN][TOPO] Three nexlet deployment types: embedded (Go, compiled into a single binary), local (child process, any language, suits Rust-native Firecracker/microVM tooling), and remote (compiled agent shipped anywhere and kept alive by systemd, extending Nex to the far edge). "we've created a way that you can compile a nexlet, make it aware that it will be connecting remotely, you ship it to wherever you want" (~10:19)
- [PATTERN] Workload kinds: services (restart if they die), jobs, and functions (kept warm, invoked by a trigger message on a subject, run, then shut down). "as soon as it gets a valid request, it spins up your workload, runs it and shuts it down" (~11:19)
- [PATTERN] Nexlets declare their own start-workload request schema at registration; the node validates incoming requests against it before forwarding. "upon registering with the node upstream you say this is what my start workload request looks like... anytime a workload request comes in, we actually validate it" (~12:22)
- [OBJ][PATTERN] The demo agent's start request is a NATS Object Store reference; the agent pulls the binary from the object store, saves it locally, and runs it. "The agent's then going to go pull the binary, save it locally, and then start it" (~15:24)
- [PATTERN][TOPO] Synadia managed workloads run a Nex cluster ("nexus") in every NGS region; placement uses tags exactly like JetStream placement, so re-tagging moves a workload between clouds with near-zero downtime. "placement feels the same as JetStream... If you want a workload from AWS to Azure, you just tag it and it moves it for you" (~17:28)
- [OPS][ANTI] Live demo hit the account's connection limit when many viewers connected, locking the presenter out. "There's so many of y'all on this. You took up all my connections" (~20:35)
- [KV][PATTERN] The multi-cloud demo app shares state through a KV store so workloads can be stopped and started elsewhere without losing state. "The state of this app pulls from a KV store... so it's all sharing state centralized" (~22:39)
- [CORE][STRM] Nex uses core NATS (publish, request/reply) under the hood, and additionally emits events into a stream for future event sourcing. "Nex is pretty much core NATS under the hood... it is emitting events that we are saving to a stream" (~23:43)
- [KV][OPS] Nex is stateless by default (killing a node loses its workloads); the official binaries ship a KV-backed state so a restarted node re-reads and auto-starts its workloads, which is how the cloud nodes recover. "the official binaries will come with a KV-backed state... If you kill the node and turn it back on... it'll auto start them all" (~23:43)
- [OPS][ANTI] Firecracker was the original sandbox but doesn't run on Windows, is hard on macOS, and in cloud only GCP allows nested virtualization without expensive bare-metal instances, so it was dropped from the happy path. "the only cloud it ran in without problem was GCP because it was the only one that allowed nested virtualization" (~26:45)
- [PATTERN][CLNT] JavaScript functions in Synadia Cloud run as Deno isolates (the earlier v8go binding looked unmaintained), with KV and pub/sub exposed as global functions. "we landed on Deno isolates in our cloud offering" (~27:47)
- [OPS] A nexus exposes health, metrics, and error codes via the micro framework, visible with `nats micro ls`. "if you do a NATS micro ls you can actually view all the free stuff we give you there" (~28:49)
