## Migrating from NATS Streaming to JetStream
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yKI9YmLx_8A
- speaker: unnamed Synadia presenter (states he curates the weekly NATS newsletter and authors NATS by Example; not named in transcript) | date: 2023 (inferred: "we're at the 2.9 series", 2.10 is "next minor release", Streaming deprecation window "ends June of this year") | duration: 66:09
- version context: NATS Server 2.9 (2.10 upcoming); NATS Streaming (STAN) deprecated April 2021

### Claims
- [MIG][STALE?] NATS Streaming was released in 2016, gained clustering with Raft in 2018, and was deprecated one month after JetStream shipped in server 2.2 (March 2021). "In April, so a month later after JetStream was released, NATS Streaming was marked as deprecated." (~06:43)
- [MIG][OPS] The two-year Streaming deprecation window ends June 2023; after that no security or bug fixes land. "No more security fixes and bug fixes are going to be landing after June." (~07:45)
- [MIG][CORE] JetStream is a subsystem inside the NATS server, whereas NATS Streaming was a separate server acting as a NATS client. "JetStream is an actual subsystem within the NATS server proper... whereas NATS Streaming is an external server." (~06:43)
- [MIG][SUBJ][STALE?] NATS Streaming did not support wildcards in channels or subscriptions, forcing one subscription per channel and shaping channel naming. "NATS Streaming doesn't support that... subscriptions do not support wildcards." (~09:47)
- [MIG][STALE?] Streaming channels and core NATS subjects were two separate namespaces with no interop, no headers, and mandatory client IDs. "No interop between this concept of channels... and actual core NATS subjects." (~09:47)
- [MIG][STALE?][ANTI] Streaming's reconnection behavior needed large documented caveats and was a known pain point. "There's like these big caveats and these big explanations about how to properly do reconnection." (~10:49)
- [CORE][CLNT] MQTT 3.1.1 support is native in the server and uses JetStream transparently; you only need JetStream enabled and the MQTT listener configured. "Under the hood, MQTT is using actually JetStream transparently." (~11:51)
- [MIG][STRM] A Streaming channel maps to a stream, but a stream binds any number of subjects including wildcards. "You can create a stream called just named events, but you can define any number of subjects, including wildcards." (~14:55)
- [STRM][OPS] Most stream options (subjects, limits, retention age) can be changed at runtime. "You can dynamically change most of the options at runtime." (~15:56)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Max messages per subject gives per-subject retention within one stream. "On a per subject basis, you can say for any given subject, I only want three messages, five messages." (~16:57)
- [STRM][SIZE] Stream deduplication by message ID uses a default 2-minute window and holds IDs in memory, so size the window against expected message volume. "By default, it gives you a 2-minute window... it does keep these message IDs in memory." (~16:57)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Optimistic concurrency via expected stream or per-subject sequence lets concurrent publishers be serialized. "You can actually specify the expected sequence number of the stream at publish time." (~17:58)
- [STRM][PATTERN] Republish rebroadcasts every stream write to a core NATS subject for lightweight fan-out. "The stream internally on the NATS server is actually rebroadcasting that message out to a core NATS subject." (~17:58)
- [MIG][CONS] A Streaming subscription is analogous to a JetStream push consumer; JetStream adds pull consumers which Streaming lacked. "A NATS Streaming subscription is analogous to a push consumer." (~22:05)
- [CONS] A consumer is a view of state over a stream, tracking delivered and acknowledged messages server-side. "Your mental model of a consumer can be this is a view of state over a stream." (~22:05)
- [CONS][CLNT] The legacy js.Subscribe convenience API implicitly creates an ephemeral consumer unless a durable name is given. "This subscribe is sort of implicitly creating a consumer under the hood." (~24:06)
- [CONS] Pull consumers fetch a batch; if fewer messages are available the fetch returns what exists without waiting. "If there happens to be 10 messages available to be fetched, it'll fetch all 10. If there isn't, it's not going to wait." (~25:07)
- [CONS][SUBJ] Consumer subject filtering happens on the server, saving bandwidth and client CPU; 2.10 will add multiple filter subjects per consumer. "It happens on the server... you're saving on bandwidth." (~34:20)
- [CONS] Ack options are ack, nak, nak with delay, in-progress (resets the ack-wait timer), and term (no redelivery); default ack wait is 30 seconds. "The default ack wait time is 30 seconds if I recall properly." (~28:11)
- [KV][OBJ] KV is built directly on streams, not a new persistence layer; object store (still experimental) chunks blobs larger than the default 1 MB max message size into ordered messages. "It's literally built on the same persistence foundation of a stream." (~29:14)
- [STRM][ANTI][SUBJ] A stream bound to `*` or `>` captures every publish in the account; always scope streams under a single-token prefix. "That would be a problem. So, in practice, what you typically do is create a stream that has a single token prefix." (~31:18)
- [STRM][TOPO] File-store persistence survives restarts; clustered streams use Raft, an R3 stream tolerates one node down and R5 is the upper end. "If two nodes go offline, then you're stuck because that's what the Raft protocol allows. You can go up to five nodes." (~33:19)
- [STRM][OPS] R3 in-memory streams can survive a careful rolling restart because replica state moves between servers. "You can have in-memory streams that are R3 that still can technically tolerate a good rolling restart... if you're careful." (~33:19)
- [OPS] Production JetStream config sets store directory, max memory, max file storage, and optional encryption at rest with the key passed via environment variable. "You can pass in your encryption key as an environment variable is typically what is recommended." (~36:22)
- [MIG][OPS] Migrating removes a component: drop the Streaming servers and let clients talk to a JetStream-enabled cluster; embedded-mode Streaming deployments must move to a vanilla NATS cluster with routes. "In my opinion, it's actually simpler because we're removing a component." (~37:25)
- [SEC] Username/password configs still run inside an implicit global account; explicit accounts give full subject-level isolation between tenants on one deployment. "Those two client applications by default will never see any messages even if they're publishing and subscribing to the exact same subjects." (~40:28)
- [SEC][STRM] Each account can carry its own JetStream limits, useful when mapping accounts to customers; exports/imports enable cross-account sharing, typically for operational hub use. "Every account can have its own JetStream configuration in the sense that you can enforce certain limits at the account level." (~41:30)
- [SEC][STRM] Locked-down publishers still need subscribe permission on their inbox because stream publish acks come back via request-reply. "The stream is actually going to be sending back an acknowledgement to an inbox." (~44:35)
- [OPS][CLNT] The NATS CLI has full stream/consumer management plus a JetStream benchmark mode for measuring replicated write throughput and latency on real VMs and disks. "It also has this benchmarking capability that supports JetStream." (~46:38)
- [MIG][PATTERN] Data migration algorithm: create a stream per channel, republish channel messages, map old channel sequence to new stream sequence (optionally stored in a header), then create consumers with an explicit start sequence from the mapping. "You need to map the sequence number from the message in a channel to the new sequence number that gets created in the stream." (~48:39)
- [MIG][STRM] Unlike Streaming's implicit channel creation, a stream must exist before publishing to JetStream, because core subjects and stream subjects coexist. "Do you have to declare a stream before publishing to JetStream? Yes, you do." (~54:47)
- [PATTERN][USECASE] No KSQL on the roadmap; the demonstrated alternative materializes streams into SQLite tables at a leaf node so edge apps query a native database. "Deploy a leaf node or a small little relational database at an edge location... able to source data from streams, materialize it locally." (~56:48)
- [OPS][STRM] Native backup/restore in the CLI snapshots all streams and consumer state per account, but is point-in-time; mirrors give a near-current async copy in another cluster. "A mirror allows you to basically create a bit for bit copy of a stream... replicate it asynchronously over to another cluster." (~60:54)
- [STRM][TOPO] Consumer replica count inherits from the stream; a three-node cluster with one server per availability zone in one region tolerates a lost node or corrupted disk. "The consumer replicas actually inherit from the stream." (~59:51)
- [TOPO][USECASE] NGS is a globally deployed cluster across the three major clouds in about 13 regions, extendable with leaf nodes. "Across all three cloud major cloud providers across I think it's 13 regions." (~62:56)

## NATS KubeCon Tutorial on Twitch
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vk8HOMMXmXc
- speaker: Jaime Piña and Waldemar (Wally) Quevedo (Synadia, NATS maintainers) | date: 2020 (KubeCon 2020 "from zero to hero" session; NATS "10 years old since last week", 2.2 "coming soon") | duration: 52:47
- version context: NATS Server 2.1 → 2.2 pre-release (headers, WebSocket on master, MQTT branch); JetStream "in the pipeline"

### Claims
- [CORE][STALE?] NATS is a 10-year-old CNCF project that started in Ruby for Cloud Foundry; its wire protocol has barely changed, the main addition being headers in 2.2 via new HPUB/HMSG commands. "The only main change into the protocol is... support for headers... HPUB and the H messages." (~03:05)
- [CORE][OPS] The server has no external dependencies; one URL gives you pub/sub, request-reply, and load balancing without extra services. "It is a lightweight, no dependencies, a very small Docker image." (~04:07)
- [SUBJ][PATTERN] NATS 2.x vocabulary frames usage as streams (sequence of data broadcast to consumers) and services (request-reply), both built on subjects with `*` single-token and `>` tail wildcards. "We talk more about NATS in terms of streams and services." (~05:07)
- [SEC][SUBJ] Accounts are namespaces for subjects; users of one account only see another account's data if that account exports a stream or service and the consumer imports it. "You can think of them as namespaces for your subjects." (~08:15)
- [SEC][OPS] The server warns on plaintext passwords in config and suggests bcrypt or NKeys; NKeys are a challenge-based public/private key scheme. "It will suggest to use either bcrypt for the password or you can use also NKeys." (~12:21)
- [SEC] Authentication options include user/password, tokens, bcrypt, NKeys, TLS certificate DN mapped to a user identity (e.g. SPIFFE IDs), decentralized JWTs, and custom auth when embedding the server in Go. "If you embed the NATS server you can also have your own custom authentication if you implement the auth interface." (~15:30)
- [SEC][CORE] Request-reply across accounts works by remapping the requester's unique inbox to a hidden `_R_` subject on the service side; all transparent to clients. "When it traverses into another account it becomes a special subject called underscore R." (~17:31)
- [TOPO] With 2.x, gateway connections join clusters into a supercluster; servers route by interest, so a subscriber in Berlin receives a publish from San Diego. "You can have a multi region and then have a gateway connection... between many of these clusters." (~19:33)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] For queue groups across a supercluster, the server prefers a local queue subscriber and otherwise forwards to another cluster chosen by RTT, giving lowest-latency load balancing. "It is going to be able to determine, based on the RTT, which is the appropriate load balancer node." (~19:33)
- [TOPO][SEC] Leaf nodes act like a proxy that is itself NATS; an edge device that can't afford expensive auth connects to a sidecar leaf node which holds the secure TLS link to the supercluster. "You can connect them to your own attached... sidecar leaf node and then this other leaf node will have the secure TLS connection." (~20:35)
- [TOPO][USECASE] IBM modelled satellites as leaf nodes connected to a ground supercluster so satellites could talk to each other through it. "Multiple satellites on the edge be able to... communicate... all through the same supercluster." (~21:36)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] The "NATS adaptive edge architecture": a central cloud supercluster with edge clusters attached by a single leaf-node connection, so edge sites keep communicating locally while consuming cloud-only services. "A centralized supercluster... and you can connect your edge devices or your local superclusters on the edge with a single leaf node connection." (~22:38)
- [MIG][MYTH] NATS v2 is backward compatible and a drop-in replacement for v1; users saw an automatic performance boost, and subject cardinality with millions of subscriptions is handled. "You could actually, if you're on v1, use v2 as a drop-in replacement." (~23:40)
- [OPS][ANTI] Never enable debug and trace logging in production; throughput drops by at least half. "The performance drops at least half when you have this logging." (~26:42)
- [CLNT] WebSocket needs only a `websocket` block with a port (9222 in the demo) and TLS; browser clients then use the same NATS API as TCP clients with no translation layer. "You can have your servers in the cloud use TCP but... web apps or mobile app... can use WebSockets." (~31:51)
- [CLNT][CORE] All clients move raw bytes; encoding (JSON, protobuf) is the application's concern, e.g. a StringCodec in the JS client. "NATS all it cares about is moving bytes. It doesn't care about whether it's protobuf or JSON." (~28:48)
- [CLNT] Clients reconnect automatically after a server restart; the JS client also receives an async close event when the server revokes its user. "It disconnected but it reconnected automatically... all that is taken care of in the client libraries." (~27:44)
- [SEC][PATTERN] The chat demo splits an admin account (credential provisioning) from a user account so subject namespaces don't cross-talk. "We have separated these subject namespaces so that you can have as less as possible cross-talking." (~35:58)
- [SEC][PATTERN] Dynamic credential provisioning: connect with near-permissionless default creds, request upgraded creds from a provisioner service, then close and reconnect with the new JWT. "We request upgraded credentials based on a username we give and the API will either grant us the new credentials or... an error." (~46:16)
- [SEC] A provisioner can revoke a user by public key by signing an updated account JWT and pushing it to the servers over the account management subject, disconnecting that user immediately. "We're revoking the public key... signing the JWT and then sending that back once again to the NATS server." (~40:06)
- [SEC][SUBJ] Per-user permissions in the demo restrict a user to publish on online/posts/DMs and to subscribe only to DMs addressed to its own public key plus its inbox. "You're only able to receive messages under your own public key and able to reply into the inbox." (~44:13)
- [OPS] In restricted environments you can debug a NATS server with plain telnet since the protocol is text-based. "You can just straight up use telnet." (~43:12)
- [CLNT][STALE?] MQTT support existed as a server branch and was on the roadmap at the time; WebSocket was on master pending the 2.2 release. "In the roadmap there's also a support for MQTT incoming. There's an MQTT branch in the server." (~31:51)

## The Zen of High Performance Messaging with NATS by Waldemar Quevedo Salinas
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e_mfyHpVYOk
- speaker: Waldemar Quevedo (Apcera; NATS Ruby/Python client maintainer) | date: 2017 (Strange Loop era; references Tyler Treat's benchmarks and "Papers We Love" the same week) | duration: 39:31
- version context: pre-2.0 gnatsd era (NATS Streaming named as the separate persistence project; no accounts/JetStream)

### Claims
- [CORE][STALE?] NATS began in 2010 in Ruby for Cloud Foundry, was rewritten in Go in 2012, and ships as a ~7 MB single binary with no deployment dependencies. "It is only seven megabytes in size... it's a single binary." (~02:06)
- [CORE][SIZE][STALE?] The nats-bench micro-benchmark shows around 10 million messages per second with 1-byte payloads over 100 million messages; the speaker calls this a micro-benchmark and defers to Tyler Treat's comparisons for trade-offs. "You can get a throughput of around 10 million messages per second with a single byte." (~02:06)
- [CORE] NATS deliberately does nothing but pure publish/subscribe; persistence and exactly-once are pushed out of the core to keep it operationally simple. "It does nothing but pure publish/subscribe... it doesn't have built-in persistence of messages." (~04:10)
- [CORE] The design question NATS answers is the fastest, simplest, most reliable way to read/write a socket for 1:1 and 1:N, hence one always-established TCP connection with a plaintext protocol. "Choosing TCP/IP and having an always established TCP connection with the server." (~05:10)
- [CORE] Core delivery is fire-and-forget, at-most-once: a message with no interested subscriber is dropped. "If someone is not plugged into the system and interested in a subject then that message will be just dropped on the floor." (~05:10)
- [CORE] The protocol is a handful of commands: PUB, SUB, UNSUB, MSG, PING/PONG, INFO from the server, CONNECT from the client, plus errors; INFO includes the max payload size. "The first thing we get is this INFO... and also what is the maximum payload size." (~06:14)
- [CORE][OPS] If client or server don't exchange PING/PONG within the interval (default two minutes) the server drops the connection; PING also gives a round-trip latency measure. "By default this is an interval of every two minutes, the server will chop the connection off." (~07:15)
- [CORE] The payload is opaque bytes to the server; the byte count on the control line must be followed exactly or the client is disconnected for a protocol violation. "The payload is opaque to the server... for the server it's just bytes." (~08:15)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Request-reply is built from pure pub/sub using an ephemeral random inbox subscription with an UNSUB limit of one message; the first reply wins. "It does so by having this ephemeral subscription, inboxes." (~09:17)
- [CLNT] Because inboxes rely on random strings, clients depend on the quality of the runtime's pseudo-random number generator. "They are sensitive to the reliability of the available pseudo random number generation that you have in your runtime." (~09:17)
- [CLNT] The Go client is the canonical implementation other clients reference; an nginx module lets nginx learn proxy routes over NATS without config reloads. "By having nginx hooked into NATS it will almost instantly know where to send the traffic." (~12:19)
- [CLNT][CORE] Client publishes are buffered and coalesced, so after a publish loop there is no guarantee bytes were sent; flush by appending a PING and waiting for the PONG. "We append an extra ping at the end of the buffer and we make a future so that we're expecting a pong back." (~13:21)
- [ANTI][OPS] Benchmarking with a tight publish loop plus a subscription in the same client makes that client a slow consumer: the server grows its pending buffer, then disconnects it to protect itself. "The NATS server is protecting itself." (~15:25)
- [CORE][SEC] The `_INBOX.*` wildcard subscription sees every request in a server; subjects starting with `_SYS` are reserved and publishes there are rejected. "We can subscribe to all of the requests... by using underscore INBOX dot asterisk." (~16:27)
- [CORE][SUBJ] `*` matches one token, `>` matches everything after the dot; a subscription to just `>` shows all traffic on the server. "This one will match everything after the dot." (~17:31)
- [PATTERN][CORE] NATS replaces the point-to-point "death star" of microservice connections with one always-on connection per service, avoiding separate discovery and load balancing when sub-millisecond latency matters. "It becomes this whole death star microservices kind of thing." (~19:36)
- [ANTI][CORE] NATS is not meant for a new connection per request; keep one persistent connection as a dial tone. "NATS is not a system where you have to create a new connection for each one of the requests." (~20:37)
- [TOPO][CLNT] A full-mesh cluster removes the single point of failure; clients reconnect to another server, and newer clients learn cluster topology dynamically as servers join. "The original server will notify all of the clients where is the new member from the cluster." (~22:39)
- [CLNT] On server loss, clients by default reconnect randomly to one of the other known cluster members. "By default they will randomly try to reconnect to one of the other immediately available nodes." (~23:44)
- [PATTERN] Periodic heartbeats on `service.<name>.heartbeats` plus a wildcard subscription give simple liveness and discovery. "You can leverage these heartbeats to create some sort of discovery as well." (~24:45)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Queue groups distribute messages randomly, not round-robin, among members. "One of these messages will be balanced randomly among the different service nodes... it's not round-robin." (~25:48)
- [CORE][PATTERN] NATS "does not assume the audience": several queue groups and plain subscribers on the same subject each get a copy independently. "You can have multiple distribution queues from the same subjects." (~26:51)
- [CORE][PATTERN] By definition the first reply to a request is the lowest-latency responder. "The first message that you get back from a request in NATS is the one with the lowest latency." (~26:51)
- [CLNT][ANTI] A request timeout is ambiguous: no responder, dropped request, slow responder, or responder crash mid-processing, so callers must handle errors deliberately. "We need to be more careful when how to do error handling in these cases." (~28:53)
- [PATTERN] To confirm availability, first request "anyone there?", have the service reply with its own inbox, then talk to that inbox directly. "This other service could reply back with its own inbox and then we use that inbox... to communicate directly." (~29:55)
- [CORE][MYTH] Choosing reliability over guaranteed delivery does not constrain application guarantees; per the end-to-end argument, guarantees belong in the application layer, and "we can always build stronger guarantees on top but never remove them from below." "We can always build stronger guarantees on top but we can always remove them from below." (~31:57)
- [PATTERN] Designing for replay, safe retries, and tolerance of reordering yields more resilient systems than relying on exactly-once or ordered delivery from the transport. "If we can design our system so that you can safely retry the requests that can be better than having exactly-once delivery." (~31:57)
- [STALE?][STRM] NATS Streaming was the separate project layered on NATS for replay and at-least-once concerns; the two concerns were intentionally split into two projects. "Those concerns were separated with two different projects." (~37:35)

## SCaLE 13x Derek Collison  NATS A new nervous system for distributed cloud platforms
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t_USxxOGzcw
- speaker: Derek Collison (Apcera CEO; NATS creator) | date: 2015 (SCaLE 13x; "first GopherCon launched last year") | duration: 55:25
- version context: pre-1.0 gnatsd era (no TLS yet, no clustering auto-config, no persistence)

### Claims
- [CORE][STALE?] Derek's background: ~12 years at TIBCO building Rendezvous and EMS, ~6 years at Google, architect of Cloud Foundry; NATS was written in a weekend to power Cloud Foundry. "It was written in a weekend so the first version just had a Ruby server and a Ruby client." (~25:31)
- [CORE][PATTERN] HTTP is loved as an interface but is point-to-point; NATS targets 1:N, 1-of-N, cascading request-reply, and subject-based routing instead of IP+port routing. "HTTP... only goes so far right it's usually point-to-point." (~04:06)
- [CORE][MYTH] Multicast effectively failed operationally and is disallowed on cloud platforms; for fan-out of roughly 30 or fewer receivers, sending the message N times from one point is faster. "For certain types of N, probably depending on your message size, 30 or so or less, it actually is faster to send it 30 times." (~07:12)
- [PATTERN][CORE] The "ask everyone, take the first best answer" pattern (as Google search does across shards) was built into NATS from day one; on JMS/RabbitMQ style systems the requester's CPU spikes linearly with responder count. "You can see massive spikes all day long... linearly proportional to how many responders are out there." (~09:14)
- [PATTERN] Design principle "don't assume the audience": later observers (logging, metrics) must be able to see any message, which publish-based queuing prevents. "Don't assume who's going to actually be watching it or looking at it." (~12:16)
- [CORE][MYTH] NATS queuing is a subscribe operation ("distributed queuing"), not a publish operation that physically enqueues; only one member of a queue group receives a given message while plain subscribers still get it. "Subscribe is what I call distributed queuing." (~13:17)
- [CORE] Request-reply creates an ephemeral unique subject, subscribes, and sends it as the reply-to; wildcard observers see both request and response, unlike many systems. "A lot of systems you see the requests, you can't see the response." (~14:19)
- [CORE][MYTH] Exactly-once done correctly requires transactional semantics down to disk hardware; Derek considers it "a problem that doesn't really need a solution" compared to idempotent designs. "Exactly once is a problem that doesn't really need a solution." (~15:21)
- [ANTI][CORE] Expecting the messaging system to guarantee delivery once handed a message is often an anti-pattern; store-and-forward has a place for batch work, but the app must handle failure. "A lot of times it's almost an anti-pattern to expect that once I give it to the messaging system it's going to take care of everything." (~17:21)
- [CORE][OPS] NATS is designed to protect itself at all costs and stay available, unlike enterprise brokers that take everyone offline while servicing one client's pathological request. "My version of the world is I protect myself at all costs and I always have to be available." (~19:24)
- [CORE] Underneath, NATS is a pub/sub engine with a high-performance subject router; queuing and request-reply are built on it, and multiple queue groups plus plain subscribers can coexist on one subject. "Underneath the covers it is a pub sub engine with an extremely high performance routing mechanism." (~19:24)
- [PATTERN][USECASE] Cloud Foundry and Apcera's scheduler use scatter/first-reply: every node decides if it can run a job and delays its reply proportionally to memory pressure or co-location, so the first reply is the best placement. "They actually determine how long they're going to wait before they respond based on things like memory pressure." (~21:26)
- [CORE] NATS is not an enterprise messaging system: no persistence, transactions, enhanced delivery models, or store-and-forward; it is trivial to build those on top. "It's really not a queuing product per se, it's not a store and forward mechanism." (~21:26)
- [TOPO] Clustering is full-mesh one-hop (every server links to every other), not a DAG; routes only need one side to initiate and become bidirectional once established. "NATS is a full mesh one hop clustering mechanism." (~23:30)
- [CLNT][TOPO] Clients are cluster-aware without DNS or load balancers: given a server pool they pick randomly and reconnect to another on failure, typically in 10–15 ms once the socket drop is seen. "The reconnect speed is usually about ten fifteen milliseconds or so." (~35:54)
- [TOPO][CORE] Distributed queuing works across the cluster: queue group members can attach to any server, unlike early EMS where you had to attach to the queue's home server. "You can attach to any server you want... and it just works." (~24:30)
- [CORE][MYTH] The protocol is text-based by choice; Derek and Redis' author agree computers are fast enough that text framing does not matter for performance. "Computers are so fast I don't think text-based matters anymore and that's actually the truth." (~24:30)
- [SIZE][STALE?] Historical throughput: Ruby server ~150k msgs/s (vs RabbitMQ ~9–10k), first Go port ~500k, 2015 Go server 5–6 M msgs/s on a MacBook Air, with 8 M believed reachable. "The current performance of it is about five to six million messages a second on this MacBook Air." (~25:31)
- [SIZE][STALE?] Server-side benchmark: ~186 ns per operation with empty payload (~5 M/s) versus ~48,000 ns per op at 4 KB payload, which Derek called the worst case with a known fix pending. "It takes about 186 nanoseconds per operation... 4k payload that's the worst." (~28:34)
- [OPS] A bare protocol error (e.g. pressing Enter) gets a client disconnected immediately: the server protects itself. "I hit enter which was a protocol error so it immediately chopped me off." (~30:39)
- [CORE] Subscription IDs are per-connection closures: `SUB foo 1` then `SUB foo bar 3` joins queue group bar; publishing delivers one copy to the plain sub and one to a single member of the group. "You see that we got two messages... one was for one, one was for two." (~31:50)
- [OPS] Monitoring is HTTP JSON modelled on Google's /varz: varz reports max connections, ping interval, memory, cores, connections, routes, in/out messages; connz gives per-connection detail. "Every single server has that varz endpoint on it that you can pull all of the statistics in real time." (~33:53)
- [CLNT][USECASE][STALE?] Apcera embedded a C++ NATS client directly in nginx's event loop to update routing tables on the fly at ~400–500k signed and encrypted updates per second. "Update nginx routing tables on the fly... about four to five hundred thousand times a second." (~34:54)
- [OPS][CORE] The ping interval exists because cloud hosts vanish without the socket closing; either side can initiate pings so dead peers are detected. "In cloud platforms a lot of times that happens... the machine just goes away but nobody that's connected to the socket thinks they did." (~35:54)
- [CORE][PATTERN] Auto-pruning of the interest graph: `UNSUB <sid> <max>` sets a circuit breaker propagated across the cluster, so a requester of 10,000 responders receives maybe 6–7 replies instead of discarding all 10,000 client-side. "Your client library might see six, seven, maybe... most messaging platforms you have to throw away all 10,000 on the client." (~36:55)
- [CORE] The interest graph flows toward subscribers and data flows the reverse way; the server tracks delivered counts so an UNSUB-after-N takes effect exactly. "The interest graph flows towards me, data flows in the reverse way." (~39:01)
- [PATTERN] NATS suits control planes built on idempotent state transitions and compensating transactions rather than transactional messaging. "Idempotent means I can keep sending it as many times as I want and the state transitions always consistent on the other side." (~41:02)
- [SEC][STALE?] In 2015 the Go server had no TLS yet (the Ruby server's TLS was "kind of broken"); Apcera signed and encrypted every message at the application layer instead. TLS was on the futures list. "For that reason it doesn't do TLS yet but part of the futures." (~48:19)
- [ANTI][PATTERN] Avoid "positive chatter" on a control plane: non-helping responders should stay silent rather than replying "I can't help", because such traffic grows with N. "If you can't help me I don't want you to say a word." (~53:25)
- [SIZE][SEC] Max payload is configurable but should not be set very large, since large payloads enable memory-based denial of service against the server; the demo server allowed up to 10 MB. "If it's big you can do a denial of service based on a memory footprint of a server." (~54:25)
- [CORE] Once the byte count on PUB is read, the server is in binary mode for exactly that many bytes and never inspects the payload. "Once it hits that it's in binary mode... I don't look inside of the payload whatsoever." (~51:23)
- [OPS][STALE?] Roadmap items in 2015: C/C++ and Lua clients, monitoring dashboards, and an auto-configuration service to join a full mesh by API token because manual mesh setup is tedious. "If you're actually trying to set up a full mesh one hop it's tedious." (~42:06)

## Native MQTT Support in NATS Server
- url: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hiYmh9n8Yv8
- speaker: Ivan Kozlovic (Synadia) | date: unknown (MQTT native support era, ~2021; server 2.2+) | duration: 08:31
- version context: NATS Server 2.2+ (native MQTT, JetStream required)

### Claims
- [CLNT][OPS] Enabling MQTT needs only a server name, JetStream enabled (MQTT persists state in JetStream), and an `mqtt` port block; the server then accepts both MQTT and native clients. "Enable JetStream which is needed by MQTT in order to persist some state, then we open the MQTT port." (~02:06)
- [CLNT][OPS] On MQTT client connect the server creates JetStream assets for that client automatically. "It did accept an MQTT client and created JetStream assets for that client." (~03:07)
- [SUBJ][CLNT] MQTT topics map to NATS subjects by replacing slashes with dots; a NATS `>` subscription receives MQTT messages and NATS publishes are converted back to MQTT for MQTT subscribers. "Simply replacing slashes by dots... the exchange goes both ways." (~04:08)
- [MIG][USECASE] Existing MQTT applications only need to be repointed at the NATS MQTT port; nothing else changes, so IoT investments are preserved. "The application did not have to do anything, just point to the NATS server's MQTT port." (~05:09)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] A local NATS server with MQTT can leaf-node into NGS; `connect.ngs.global` attaches to the geographically closest cluster. "The connect.ngs.global URL will connect it to the closest cluster in NGS." (~06:10)
- [TOPO][PATTERN] Queue groups across a supercluster prefer the member local to where data enters; when that member stops, messages fail over to the member connected in Japan. "As soon as we do that then the new messages are automatically routed to the other member." (~07:11)

### The 15 most valuable design statements (with source video ids)

1. **Start with core NATS; adopt JetStream only when you find yourself reinventing consensus or replicated persistence.** Skipping core NATS "because we need persistence" is called a mistake; a persistence layer stores everything, core lets you be selective. (mGzqEnIs7sk)
2. **Replication sizing: R1 is the default, use R3/R5 (odd numbers, max 5); with R3 one node down still serves writes, two down still serves reads, three down is disaster recovery.** Every R3 stream adds Raft load, so size streams to hardware I/O, not administrative units, and a single stream cannot exceed its disk's throughput. (ChSVWDW-874, _CN1OO7yN0I, Ds71axJRFm0, jDBwS-FuRG8)
3. **Clusters (routes) assume low RTT and good bandwidth, i.e. one region; do not stretch a cluster across coasts or continents. Use superclusters (gateways) for that, and three clusters is the recommended shape for redundancy.** Gateways use optimistic sends with interest-graph pruning so coordination chatter does not grow with scale. (01VPY86f78w, 6O_sNSJ2p70, N0dtATLMy-M)
4. **Stream defaults are unlimited; always set limits (max bytes, max age, max msgs per subject). Synadia Cloud requires max bytes on every stream.** Scope every stream under a single-token subject prefix; a stream on `>` captures every publish in the account. (s6THUHpvtY4, ChSVWDW-874, yKI9YmLx_8A)
5. **Consumers are heavyweight server-side state carrying Raft traffic. JetStream was designed for a few thousand durable consumers; do not design for 100k or 1M consumers, one per entity. Pick a wildcard granularity the client can process in order, and use direct/batch get (no server state) for read paths.** (jDBwS-FuRG8, VxIvWzdtRk4, t7m3BgLGHfU, n9XpZTBwQcc)
6. **Latency is measured in microseconds for core and JetStream (100–200 µs over a network, tens of µs on loopback for direct get) versus milliseconds for Kafka; synchronous JetStream publish is RTT-bound, and batching gives diminishing returns past ~100.** (C4BnJ5QLeTY, HwwvFeUHAyo)
7. **Benchmark in your own environment: Synadia publishes no official numbers. Loopback numbers only show software headroom (M1 Ultra: ~5M 128-byte msgs/s single publisher; ~4M with one subscriber). Cloud burstable instances and gp2/gp3 volumes throttle after ~20 minutes of sustained JetStream writes; laptops throttle after ~30 s; runs under a few seconds are unreliable.** (HwQCPP8TGUQ, HwwvFeUHAyo, mGzqEnIs7sk)
8. **Keep max payload to a few megabytes at most; very large payloads hurt server responsiveness and enable memory-based denial of service. That is why Object Store chunks.** (kbJTuk2qr4U, t_USxxOGzcw)
9. **Auth: users in the server config are simplest but do not scale; decentralized JWT/NKey auth is the recommended construct for clusters and superclusters. Bake permissions into scoped signing keys, not user JWTs, so you never re-mint credentials. Auth callout connects external identity providers and should run next to the server (loopback) so latency stays negligible.** (5pQVjN0ym5w, KmGtnFxHnVA, VvGxrT-jv64, Csx6HEH30wI)
10. **Edge topology: leaf nodes amortize TLS and key exchange once per site, so requests through a local leaf are faster than direct hub requests. Do not let thousands of sites pull from one giant hub stream; build filtered local read replicas, and aggregate many edge streams into one upload stream before sourcing to the cloud.** (01VPY86f78w, WH55czo1BNk, vwTDumFKbXo)
11. **Retention gotchas: in a work-queue stream a message that exhausts max deliveries stays until acked or deleted; mirrors of interest-based origins are unsupported and mirrors of work queues are not resilient over leaf links; filter subject and subject transform cannot be combined on a mirror; promotion does not verify the mirror is caught up.** (7Jp3tyCGMZs, rGT6DlQkyEY)
12. **Silent-loss failure mode: a stream with a message-count limit discards the oldest messages while consumer positions have no limit, so a stopped consumer whose position falls below the first sequence loses everything in between with no error or log line.** (51b6i3usZmo)
13. **Client design: one connection per process (pooling loses ordering and is deliberately not provided); no built-in generic request retries because stacked retries can take a system down; every opinionated client default is eventually regretted because NATS use cases are too varied.** (mGzqEnIs7sk, o4rmeqfE5HE, CifAoRYefVM)
14. **Ordered processing: max_ack_pending=1 serialises unrelated keys and makes the worker a single point of failure; client-side per-key threading breaks under redelivery. Partitioned consumer groups fix this, but pinning is affinity plus failover, not a distributed lock, so handlers must be idempotent.** (2Z0J0iSp9dk, 3KBFdUXYpyY, 334XuMma1fk)
15. **Server-side filtering is subject-level only (per-token wildcards); filtering on headers or body is not supported and will not be, a message-processing callout is the planned route. Before 2.10 a single TCP route per server pair caused cross-account head-of-line blocking; 2.10 added per-account route pooling.** (Csx6HEH30wI, 9J4pRzHSc2k, Ds71axJRFm0)

Notable additional operational rules: never run debug/trace logging in production (throughput drops by at least half) (Vk8HOMMXmXc); features like message counters, schedules and per-message TTL cannot be disabled once enabled on a stream, and cron schedules should use UTC to avoid DST double-fires (1Vx8CbrO89Y, 6dkzZonDI9M); atomic batch limits are 1,000 messages per batch, 50 in-flight batches per stream, 1,000 per server, abandoned after 10 s idle (MvfiskARAq8); the dedup window defaults to 2 minutes and holds IDs in memory (ChSVWDW-874, yKI9YmLx_8A).

# Part 2: Topic index


## SUBJ: Subjects, wildcards, naming (400 claims)


**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject-Based Messaging**

- NATS is "an `interest-based` messaging system, where the listener has to `subscribe` to a subset of `subjects`."
- Other systems call subjects topics/channels/streams; in NATS "stream" means a JetStream message store.
- Location transparency: subscriptions "are automatically propagated within the server cloud", messages routed to all interested subscribers regardless of location, and "Messages with no subscribers to their subject are automatically discarded".
- Publishers "will always send a message to a fully specified subject, without the wildcard"; only subscribers use wildcards.
- "There is no hard limit to subject size, but it is recommended to keep the maximum number of tokens in your subjects to a reasonable value. E.g. a maximum of 16 tokens and the subject length to less than 256 characters."
- "NATS can manage 10s of millions of subjects efficiently"; subjects are ephemeral and disappear when no longer subscribed.
- Subscriptions are cached in server memory: "when increasing your subscribed subject count to more than one million you will need more than 1GB of server memory and it will grow linearly from there."
- Subject filtering happens in many places: per-user allow/deny, account import/export, automatic transformations, stream ingest, sourcing/mirroring, leaf node connections. "A well-designed subject hierarchy will make the job a lot easier".
- "you should refrain from over-complicating your subject design at the start of the project."
- Guidelines: first token(s) establish a general namespace (e.g. `factory1.tools.group42.unit17`); final token(s) are identifiers (e.g. `service.deploy.server-acme.app123`).
- "A subject _should_ be used for more than one message." "Subscriptions _should_ be stable (exist for receiving more than one message)."
- "Use wildcard subscriptions over subscribing to individual subjects whenever feasible."
- "Name business or physical entities. Refrain from encoding too much data into the subject." "Encode (business) intent into the subject, not technical details." Pragmatic: `orders.online.store123.order171711`; not useful: a 11-token subject encoding server, payment, tier, carrier, verb.
- Headers can carry extra metadata; "There are subscription modes, which deliver headers only, allowing for efficient scanning of metadata".
- `*` matches exactly one token and cannot match a substring inside a token (`time.New*.east` is invalid). `>` matches one or more tokens and only at the end. `*` may appear several times and be mixed with `>` (`*.*.east.>`).
- Wire tap: subscribe to `>` to receive all messages, "subject to security settings", for monitoring.
- Recommended characters for all user-created names (subjects, streams, durables, buckets, keys): alphanumeric, `-`, `_`; UTF-8 is supported "at your own risk". "NATS will enforce these constraints in most cases, but we recommend not relying on this."
- Allowed: any Unicode except null, space, `.`, `*`, `>`. Names are case sensitive. Delimit words with PascalCase or `-`/`_`.
- Names starting with `$` are reserved for system use (`$SYS`, `$JS`, `$KV`); many system subjects also use `_` (`_INBOX`, `KV_ABC`, `OBJ_XYZ`).
- By default subject names are not verified on publish; programmatically generated illegal subjects (e.g. containing wildcards) "may be ignored". Enable `pedantic` mode in the client to verify.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Sequence Numbers (concept)**

- Sequence ids can be a subject token (`updates.1`, `updates.2`, subscribe `updates.*`) when the payload cannot carry it.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Queue Groups**

- Queue group names follow subject naming rules, are case sensitive, no whitespace; "Consider structuring queue groups hierarchically using a period" because queue permissions can wildcard-match them.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Streams**

- Stream names must be unique per account and cannot contain whitespace, `.`, `*`, `>`, path separators, or non-printable characters.
- SubjectTransform rewrites the subject before storing.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Consumers**

- FilterSubject (single) or FilterSubjects (2.10, multiple, e.g. `[factory-events.A.*, factory-events.B.*]`); they cannot be combined.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Key/Value store (concept)**

- Valid key characters: `a-z A-Z 0-9 _ - . = /`; dot-separated keys allow wildcard watching of key hierarchies.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject Mapping and Transforms**

- Transforms can be defined at config root ($G account), per account, on imports, and in JetStream (stream ingress, republish, source/mirror where they also filter).
- Uses: translating namespaces between accounts or cluster/leaf semantics; suppressing subjects; backward compatibility after renaming hierarchies; merging subjects; disambiguation/isolation on super-clusters or leaf nodes; testing reroutes; partitioning; filtering sourced/mirrored data; weighted chaos/sampling.
- Transforms apply as soon as a message enters the scope, before routing or interest; "The message will appear as if published from the transformed subject under all circumstances."
- "Transforms are not applied recursively in the same scope" (prevents loops; only the first matching rule applies), but they apply "in sequence as they pass through different scopes" (publish -> leaf -> stream ingest -> republish).
- Hub/leaf disambiguation example: hub maps `orders.* -> orders.central.{{wildcard(1)}}`; leaf maps `orders.central.* -> orders.local.{{wildcard(1)}}`; leaf stream stores under `orders.{{wildcard(1)}}` and republishes to `orders.trace.*`.
- With config-file accounts, reload the config to apply transform changes; with operator JWT, transforms and imports/exports live in the account JWT and apply when pushed.
- A full wildcard `>` may be used once in source and must appear exactly once in destination.
- Token reordering with `{{wildcard(n)}}` (2.8.0+); `$1`/`$2` syntax is deprecated.
- Tokens can be dropped by not using all wildcards, "with the exception of mappings defined as part of import/export between accounts in which case all the wildcard tokens must be used". "Import/export mapping must be mapped bidirectionally unambiguous."
- Functions: `split(idx, sep)`, `splitfromleft/right(idx, offset)`, `slicefromleft/right(idx, n)`, `random(n)` (0..n-1), `partition(buckets, tokens...)`.
- `partition(n, pos...)` is deterministic hash-based; "may not be fair for a small number of subjects"; distribution "tends towards 'perfectly balanced'" as keys grow; multiple positions form a composite key. `partition(n)` alone hashes the full subject.
- Queue groups and durable consumers "are partition-less and non-deterministic": no guarantee two sequential messages on one subject reach the same subscriber, so ordering can be lost.
- Weighted mappings for canary: `myservice.requests -> v1 98%, v2 2%`; traffic shaping to a failure-simulating service (e.g. 20%); artificial loss by mapping <100% (`foo.loss.>` at 50% drops half).
- Cluster-scoped mappings (`cluster: "west"` in destination) let an app publish to `foo` and get `foo.west` etc. without knowing its cluster.
- In mirror/source/republish, transforms are filters (non-matching ignored); the stream-level `subject_transform` only rewrites matches and leaves others untouched.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream on Leaf Nodes (domains)**

- Delivery prefix convention to avoid overlaps across multiple imports: `<static type>.<exporting account>.<exporting domain>.<importing account>.<importing domain>.<importing stream name>`.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Naming Streams, Consumers, and Accounts**

- Stream, consumer (durable) and account names appear in both the JetStream subject namespace and the filesystem, so they must follow subject rules and be file-system friendly.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — MQTT**

- Topic mapping: `/` -> `.`; leading `/` -> `/.`; trailing `/` -> `./`; `.` -> `//` (2.10+; rejected before); space not supported (connection closed on publish, SUBACK failure on subscribe). `#` -> `>` (server creates two subscriptions `foo.>` and `foo`); `+` -> `*`. `*` and `>` inside topics become NATS wildcards if they form a whole token.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — FAQ**

- You cannot list subjects: "Do not think of it as a 'directory' that is aggregated over time. The interest graph is dynamic"; it can be derived at an instant by polling `/connz` and `/routez`.
- "As of nats-server v0.8.0, there is no hard limit on the maximum number of subjects."
- "a subject does not exist in a NATS cluster until a client subscribes to it, and the subject goes away after the last subscribing client unsubscribes".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Receiving: async, sync, drain, queues, unsubscribe, wildcards, structure**

- With wildcard subscriptions "it is a common technique to use the subject provided with the incoming message to determine what to do with the message."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Key Value Store (developer guide) / Object Store (developer guide)**

- Keys follow subject format (dot-separated tokens, subject-valid characters) so wildcards can watch key hierarchies.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS API Reference (JetStream wire API)**

- `$JS.FC` is not domain-prefixed, so "identically named streams in different domains cannot be reliably sourced/mirrored into the same account. Please create unique stream names".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject Mapping and Traffic Shaping (server config)**

- Subject mapping is "useful for canary deployments, A/B testing, chaos testing, and migrating to a new subject namespace." Mappings are applied at the account level; with JWT security they are edited via `nsc add mapping` and take effect on `nsc push`; with static config they take effect on reload.
- Canary rollout: v1 100% -> v1 98% / v2 2% -> v2 100%, each step via config reload "with zero downtime"; remember queue subscribers/load balancing when launching v2.
- Mappings can be scoped to a cluster (`cluster: us-west-1`).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-6: Naming Rules**

- Subjects are case-sensitive, non-empty, tokenised by `.`; `*` matches one token; `>` "is only valid as the last token and matches all tokens past that point."
- Character encoding: "Subject names should be ascii characters for maximum interoperability ... No guarantees of non-ASCII support are provided."
- Grammar: `term = (printable ascii 33-126 except dot, asterisk or gt)+`; `message-subject = term (dot term | asterisk)* (dot gt)?`; `reply-to = term (dot term)*` (no wildcards in reply subjects); `queue-name = term`.
- JetStream prefixes: `js-internal-prefix = dollar (prefix dot)+`; `js-user-prefix = (prefix dot)+` where prefix excludes dot, asterisk, gt, dollar.
- `kv-key-name = limited-term (dot limited-term)*` with `limited-term = (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, dash, underscore, fwd-slash, equals)+`; `kv-bucket-name = restricted-term = (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, dash, underscore)+`. "Keys starting with `_kv` are limited to internal use."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-19: API prefixes for materialized JetStream views**

- Implication: JetStream must "NOT start the first token after the API prefix with `$`"; "JetStream will never expose any functionality under `$JS.API.$KV.>`."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-20: JetStream based Object Stores**

- Templates: stream `OBJ_<bucket>`; chunk subject `$O.<bucket>.C.<object-nuid>`; meta subject `$O.<bucket>.M.<name-encoded>` (name base64-encoded); bucket name is `restricted-term` (A-Z a-z 0-9 dash underscore).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-26: NATS Authorization Callouts**

- Server sends a signed authorization request JWT to `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH` on `$G` (or the configured account in config mode; in operator mode the connected account). "This subject is automatically protected in the system for all users on the authorization callout account."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-30: Subject Transform**

- Transforms are used in: core account subject mapping, stream definitions, stream sourcing, RePublish, cross-account service/stream imports, shadow subscriptions across leafs.
- Core account mappings support multiple weighted destinations per source (weights sum to 100%); "as of 2.10" mappings can be `cluster`-scoped and "take precedence" when published from that cluster; a non-scoped 100% set is the catch-all for other clusters or non-clustered servers.
- Rules: literal source tokens are not usable by mapping functions; `*` tokens are referenced by cardinal position `$x` / `{{wildcard(x)}}`; `>` maps to the `>` position in the destination.
- "For transforms that are defined in inter-account imports (streams and services) the destinations _MUST_ make use of _ALL_ of the wildcard-tokens"; from 2.10 all other uses may drop wildcard tokens. In imports "the _ONLY_ allowed mapping function is `{{Wildcard(x)}}`."
- Mapping functions (2.9.0): `Wildcard(x)`, `Partition(x,a,b,c,...)` ("a partition number between `0` and `x-1` assigned from a deterministic hashing" of the named wildcard tokens), `Split(x,y)`, `SplitFromLeft(x,y)`, `SplitFromRight(x,y)`, `SliceFromLeft(x,y)`, `SliceFromRight(x,y)`. Names valid in CamelCase or lowercase.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-32: Service API**

- Service `name` "can only have `A-Z, a-z, 0-9, dash, underscore`"; `version` must be validated as SemVer with the official regex; `metadata` "Must be immutable once set."
- Discovery verbs `PING`, `STATS`, `INFO` under `$SRV` (prefix must be overridable like `$JS`): `$SRV.<VERB>`, `$SRV.<VERB>.<name>`, `$SRV.<VERB>.<name>.<id>`; services respond to all three levels.
- "Handler subject does not contain the `$SRV` prefix. This prefix is reserved for internal handlers."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-36: Subject Mapping Transforms in Streams**

- Rationale: core-level mapping needs server config or the account key; stream-level transforms "makes it very easy for the application developers or the NATS administrators to define and manage those mappings."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-8: JetStream based Key-Value Stores**

- Bucket = stream `KV_<Bucket>` with subjects `$KV.<Bucket>.>`; history = `max_msgs_per_subject`.

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — Hot reload restrictions and misc server internals (server/reload.go, server/sublist.go, server/monitor.go)**

- Sublist front-end match cache max 1024 entries, swept down to 256; fast plist created at 256+ subscribers on a subject. `slCacheMax = 1024`, `slCacheSweep = 256`, `plistMin = 256` (server/sublist.go:48-56)

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — JetStream Anti-Patterns: Avoid these pitfalls to scale more efficiently**

- Alternatives to many disjoint filters: split into separate consumers each with fewer filters, or "re-evaluate your subject name hierarchy so you can better leverage wildcard filters."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — How to Design NATS Subject Hierarchies (Patterns, Pitfalls & Best Practices)**

- Subject design is the most expensive decision to reverse: "Publishers and subscribers both encode your subject schema into their code; changing it later means coordinating every service."
- Subjects are case-sensitive, dot-separated tokens; "Orders.Created" and "orders.created" are different subjects. Tokens should be lowercase alphanumeric with hyphens, not underscores.
- `*` matches exactly one token; `>` matches one or more and must be last. Wildcards are valid in subscriptions and server-side mappings, never in publishes.
- Practical guidance: at or below 16 tokens and 256 characters per subject.
- The subscription matcher uses a stack-allocated array sized for 32 tokens; "beyond that, matching spills to the heap and pays a small per-message allocation cost." Exceeding is a soft cliff, not a rejection.
- Three patterns: namespace-first `{namespace}.{entity}.{action}` (service-oriented, team-owned domains); identifier-first `{identifier}.{namespace}.{action}` (per-tenant, per-entity audit); multi-dimensional `{env}.{region}.{service}.{entity}.{action}` (only with genuine routing dependencies).
- "If two patterns look equally good, default to namespace-first." A tenant token can be prepended later; identifier-first "cannot easily un-prepend one."
- Multi-dimensional patterns are "powerful but expensive"; don't adopt speculatively.
- Reserved prefixes: `$SYS.`, `$JS.`, `$JSC.`, `$KV.`, `$OBJ.`, `$NRG.`, `_INBOX.`. Never publish to `$`/`_` prefixes; subscribing to `$SYS.>` for monitoring is fine.
- Never put high-cardinality per-message data (correlation IDs, request IDs) in subjects; it burns the subject cache. "The right place for a correlation ID is a message header."
- Don't reuse `Nats-Msg-Id` as a correlation header; JetStream reserves it for dedup.
- Entity IDs as tokens are fine: `customer-123` is "bounded by your customer count."
- One stream per top-level namespace is the common default; splitting at namespace boundaries avoids coupling retention and storage budgets.
- "your subject hierarchy is your authorization model"; there is no separate ACL layer. Namespace-first gives team-aligned permissions; identifier-first gives tenant-aligned permissions.
- Hard multi-tenant isolation = "identifier-first subjects combined with separate NATS Accounts."
- Anti-patterns: flat subjects (no wildcards, no clean permissions, no filters); payload data in subjects; inconsistent casing/separators; no evolution plan. "Schemas change. If you haven't decided how, you've decided to break things."
- Routing-affecting version changes go in the subject (`orders.v1.customer.created`) so v1 and v2 subscribers run side by side; payload-only schema changes can use headers. Counter-position (header-only versioning) avoids subject churn but loses routing clarity.
- Server-side subject mappings allow parallel publisher/subscriber migration; "they're the one place wildcards appear on the publish side."
- Schema evolution order: stream filters, then consumer filters, then permissions; skipping any "turns migrations into incidents."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS JetStream: Ordered, Scalable Processing**

- Partitioning uses the `{{partition(N, token...)}}` mapping function: "an FNV-1a 32-bit hash modulo the partition count", prepended as a leading token; same key always lands in the same partition.
- `{{partition(...)}}` "cannot cross accounts"; only `{{wildcard(x)}}` is allowed in inter-account import transforms.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Mirror, Merge, or Consume: How to Choose Your Edge-to-Core Streaming Pattern**

- Subject transforms in the source configuration normalize edge naming into a global taxonomy; "the normalization lives in topology."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Stop Building Firehoses: Flow Control Isn't a Performance Optimization — It's an Architectural Decision**

- "Publish everything, let consumers filter" bakes routing into application code: "Each consumer receives the full stream and discards most of it"; the system is "Decoupled on the surface but is actually tightly coupled at the routing layer."
- "Filtering is declarative. It lives in the subscription, not in the application." Example hierarchy `sensors.<plant>.<line>.<machine>.<metric>`.
- Subject mapping puts translation "in the topology. No additional service. No additional failure mode." Translation microservices add deployment, monitoring, scaling overhead.
- Weighted subject mapping enables canaries: "route 90% of events to the stable consumer version and 10% to the new one" without external load balancers.

- Command targeting uses the same hierarchy as telemetry, e.g. `cmd.<site>.<device-class>.<device-id>.stream.pause`.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — From Solace to NATS: One Platform for Messaging, Streaming, and the Edge**

- Solace `orders/state/city/store` maps to `orders.state.city.store`; wildcards `*` and `>` are the same; "Replacing `/` with `.` covers most cases." Prefix wildcards like `red*`, reserved namespaces (`$`, `#P2P`), and literal `.` in topic levels need explicit handling.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Migrating from TIBCO to NATS: A Modernization Guide for Financial Services**

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Coordinating Teams of AI Agents in Real Time on NATS and JetStream**

- Three addressing modes map to NATS primitives: multicast = subject fan-out on `cotal.<space>.chat.>`; unicast = per-agent durable consumers on `inst.>`; anycast = work-queue streams on `svc.>` for exactly-once handoff across roles.
- Sender identity is the last subject token (`cotal.<space>.inst.<target>.<sender>`) enforced against the agent's JWT so "one agent cannot impersonate another"; account-as-space, user-as-agent; deny-by-default ACLs; inboxes are pre-created bind-only durables.

- Use core NATS subject mapping with `{{partition(N,token)}}` to have the server insert the partition number; partition count and which tokens hash are then administrative decisions, not client code — jnmoyne.
