**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Simple Leafnode**

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Private Inbox**

- A requesting user needs subscribe permission on its inbox subjects (`_INBOX.>` by default) or it cannot receive replies. "The `_INBOX.>` subscription permission is required in order to receive replies from a requester."
- Inbox subjects are randomly generated, so by default there is no fixed set of subjects to grant per user; the client-side option is to choose an explicit inbox prefix other than `_INBOX`. "Sinces inboxes are randomly generated by the server, by default we can't pin down the specific set of subjects to provide permission to. However, as a client, there is the option of defining an explicit *inbox prefix* other than `_INBOX`."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Services Framework (category)**

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Services Intro**

- The services framework "automatically places all subscriptions in a queue group and provides functionality for building subject hierarchies and their handlers."
- The framework enables automatic service discovery and status reporting without extra effort; `nats micro` queries and reports all framework services.
- A service definition is name (no whitespace), version, and description; "Even with no running endpoints, this service is discoverable via the micro protocol." Default background handlers for discovery, PING, and stats start at creation.
- Each service instance gets a unique ID; multiple copies with the same name are treated as instances of one service, and because endpoint subscriptions are queue-subscribed "requests will only be sent to one endpoint instance at a time."
- Each endpoint is a subscription; requests to service endpoints are ordinary NATS requests, "nothing special about this request."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Messaging (category)**

- Core messaging comprises pub-sub, request-reply, and queue groups.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Core Publish-Subscribe**

- Publish-subscribe "is the fundamental pattern that all other NATS patterns and higher-level APIs build upon."
- Core delivery is at-most-once; "For MQTT users, this is referred to as Quality of Service (QoS) 0."
- A published message is not delivered when the subscriber has no active connection (temporarily offline) or when a network interruption drops the message.
- Publishing with no subscriber succeeds but nothing is delivered; a subscription created after a publish does not receive that earlier message.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Request-Reply**

- A request is either a command ("an intention for service to carry out some work that results in a state change") or a query ("a request for information").
- "Unlike request-reply constrained protocols like HTTP, NATS is not limited to a strict point-to-point interaction"; request-reply is built on publish-subscribe.
- By default any one subscriber can be the responder; the client can also indicate to NATS that multiple replies should be allowed.
- If no subscribers are available to handle the request, the standard "no responders" error is returned.
- Request-reply "is just an optimized pair of publish-subscribe operations"; a request handler is a subscription that responds, called a service.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JSON for Message Payloads**

- A NATS message is the subject, an application-defined payload, optional headers, and for requests a reply-to subject. "The payload is a sequence of bytes, so it is up to the application to define how to serialize and deserialize the payload."
- JSON is a ubiquitous, simple interchange format supported in virtually all languages.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Protobuf for Message Payloads**

- Message types can be defined in the Protocol Buffers IDL, code-generated per language, and used as request/reply payloads over NATS.

- Plain core NATS drops a message the moment no service is listening; a stream saves it instead. "Plain core NATS drops any of these messages the moment no service is listening. A stream saves them instead."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Filtering what you consume**

- A consumer differs from a core queue group: a queue group splits one subject's live traffic across workers; each JetStream consumer gets its own full (filtered) view of the stored stream.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling a consumer**

- A queue group splits live messages with no storage; an offline subscriber misses them for good. Workers sharing a consumer split stored messages, so an offline worker just leaves its share for the others. "Only the stream-backed split survives a worker dropping out or a restart."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject mapping and transforms**

- Republish re-emits every stored message onto a second subject in real time so core subscribers can watch a stream without a consumer; a low-cost way to feed a dashboard or monitor.
- Republish is not a consumer: it's plain core NATS, fire-and-forget, no storage, no acks, no replay; a subscriber that's down misses what was republished. "use a consumer when a reader has to catch up on what it missed."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next**

- Checklist: Stay on plain pub-sub when the next message supersedes the last; reach for a stream only when a missed message has consequences.
- Checklist: Use a consumer when a reader has to catch up on what it missed; republish is fire-and-forget core NATS with no storage or replay.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Core NATS Deep Dive**

- Core NATS is publish-subscribe with no broker queue, no storage, and no acknowledgment; the message goes only to whoever is listening at publish time. "There's no broker queue, no storage, and no acknowledgment."
- Core NATS is at-most-once: a message reaches every interested subscriber connected at the moment of publish, at most once; offline, restarting, or not-yet-subscribed subscribers never see it. "core NATS is at-most-once"
- At-most-once is the right fit when each message is superseded by the next: a live price, a current temperature, a cache invalidation.
- When messages must wait for a subscriber, survive a restart, or be replayed, add a stream (JetStream) on top of core NATS.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subjects & wildcards**

- A wildcard subscriber is just another interested subscriber; delivery is still at-most-once, and a wildcard subscriber that joins now sees only what's published from now on.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publish-subscribe**

- Publish is fire-and-forget: the call returns immediately, doesn't wait for a subscriber, and doesn't tell you how many subscribers received the message.
- Each subscriber gets an independent copy; subscribing isn't taking from a queue.
- Unsubscribe removes interest as soon as the server processes it, with nothing to clean up server-side; auto-unsubscribe ends a subscription after N messages server-side.
- The interest graph is an in-memory structure; fan-out happens entirely on the server, and the publisher holds no list of subscribers.
- A publish with no interest is a silent no-op: no error, no stored backlog, and the publisher can't tell "delivered to three" from "delivered to nobody".
- Core NATS doesn't retry a missed message, doesn't detect or suppress duplicates, and doesn't guarantee two subscribers see messages in the same order under load; each is a JetStream property.
- At-most-once suits telemetry you sample, cache invalidations, and live dashboard feeds; it is not enough for an order that must be packed exactly once.
- Default max payload is 1 MB (`max_payload`, 1048576 bytes), announced to every client on connect. "By default the server caps it at **1 MB**"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Request-reply**

- Request-reply is pub/sub used twice: the client subscribes to a fresh unique subject, publishes the request with that reply subject attached, and the responder publishes its answer there.
- Clients generate inboxes under the reserved `_INBOX.` prefix with a random unique tail; each request uses a fresh inbox so in-flight requests never get each other's replies.
- The CLI's `nats reply` joins the default queue group `NATS-RPLY-22`.
- Replies are at-most-once; every request carries a timeout (CLI default five seconds), sized to cover the responder's work plus the network round-trip.
- When a request goes to a subject with zero subscribers, the server sends back a no-responders signal immediately, a reply with a `503` status (`NATS/1.0 503` header), surfaced as a distinct error rather than a timeout.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue groups**

- A queue group is a set of subscribers on the same subject sharing a name; the server treats it as one logical subscriber and delivers each message to exactly one member.
- Nothing is configured on the server for queue groups; the application picks the name and the server learns of the group when its first member subscribes.
- On a single server, member selection is uniform-random per message, not round-robin; the same member can be chosen twice in a row and a short burst can look lopsided.
- Queue-group membership is dynamic (join by subscribe, leave by unsubscribe or disconnect), which makes it a good fit for an autoscaler with no broker reconfiguration.
- Core NATS is at-most-once: if the picked member dies after delivery, the message is gone and the server won't retry with another member; work that must survive a worker crash belongs in a JetStream work queue.
- Queue members and plain subscribers coexist on the same subject: plain subscribers always get every message while the group gets one shared copy.
- Group membership is evaluated after subject matching; the same group name across different subjects does not share load. A queue group on a wildcard load-balances across everything the wildcard matches.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scatter-gather**

- Scatter-gather fans one request to every responder and gathers the replies; nothing in the inbox mechanism limits the number of responders.
- Scatter-gather works only when responders are not in a queue group; every responder must subscribe plainly.
- The CLI's `nats reply` defaults to queue group `NATS-RPLY-22`, so multiple instances form one group and only one answers; a queue group of one member behaves like a plain subscriber.
- With `--replies 0`, the CLI holds for the full timeout window even if all replies arrive early; with no subscribers at all it returns immediately with no responders.
- Scatter-gather is at-most-once: a dropped reply is simply absent from the set, and arrival order carries no meaning.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Message headers**

- Headers are key/value metadata riding beside the payload in an HTTP-like `NATS/1.0` block; a key can appear on multiple lines to carry several values.
- Header keys are case-sensitive and NATS keeps their case exactly; `Content-Type` and `content-type` are two different keys, unlike many HTTP libraries.
- Keep the `Nats-` prefix out of your own header keys; NATS reserves it for system headers.
- The server signals status in-band with a code on the header version line (`NATS/1.0 503`) and no payload; that's how no-responders reaches the client.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connection lifecycle**

- Messages other publishers send while you're disconnected are gone; no client-side buffer can change that.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Debugging delivery**

- A published message that never arrived has one of three causes: no subscriber at publish time, a subscription on a different subject (typo/extra token), or the subscriber's connection had dropped so its interest was gone.
- If `test=` and `nats trace` both show a matching subscriber but the message still didn't arrive, the subscriber was absent at the instant of publish: at-most-once, never retried.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Core NATS)**

- The four core ideas are subject, interest, reply subject, and queue group; scatter-gather is a reply subject with the first-answer-wins step removed, not a fifth idea.
- Core NATS does not store messages; at-most-once is a deliberate choice that keeps a publisher from blocking on slow or offline subscribers.
- Checklist: Pass a timeout on every request, sized to the responder's work plus the round-trip.
- Checklist: Branch on no responders separately from a timeout.
- Checklist: Gather explicitly when more than one service may answer; don't assume exactly one reply.
- Checklist: Keep the reply path fast, or spread responders across a queue group.
- Checklist: Give every queue-group member the byte-for-byte identical queue group name.
- Checklist: Don't expect ordering or an even split from a queue group; keep strictly-ordered work on a single subscriber.
- Checklist: Make a queue member's work safe to repeat, since core NATS does not send a message again after a hand-off.
- Checklist: Gather replies in a loop instead of taking the first reply.
- Checklist: Bound the scatter-gather wait with a deadline so a missing responder costs only the timeout.
- Checklist: Treat the gathered set as unordered; compare every reply on its merits, never by arrival order.
- Checklist: Treat header keys as case-sensitive; read them back with the exact case you set.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Super-clusters**

- Geo-affinity: NATS prefers a local queue subscriber first; a message published in a region goes to a worker in that region even though a remote worker is subscribed, so it never crosses the gateway.
- The gateway carries a queue-group message only when the local side can't serve; if all local workers are down the message crosses to a remote cluster with an interested worker. When more than one remote cluster has a worker, NATS picks one and sends across that single gateway, so it still reaches exactly one worker.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Topologies)**

- Checklist: Place a queue subscriber for each workload in every region that produces it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Authorization**

- A denied request looks silent: the publish is denied, no responder sees it, and the requester just times out. Every JetStream API call is a request, so a locked-down user running `nats stream info` fails with `context deadline exceeded` rather than a permission error.
- `allow_responses` lets a service reply to requests without a broad publish allow; the server tracks each reply subject and permits exactly that one reply.
- Queue-group permissions: a subscribe entry `"orders.created billing-workers"` permits subscribing to that subject only as a member of that queue group; a plain subscribe stays denied.
- Pitfall: A subscribe deny silently breaks request-reply. `subscribe: { deny: [">"] }` blocks the inbox subscription; adding `allow: ["_INBOX.>"]` next to it doesn't help because deny beats allow. Replace the deny with the allow. "Adding `allow: ["_INBOX.>"]` next to the deny doesn't help — deny beats allow"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Accounts and multitenancy**

- A request across an account boundary returns `No responders are available` immediately, not a permissions error; when a request that "should" work reports no responders, check which account each side is in.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Cross-account**

- Pitfall: Service and stream are not interchangeable. A service import with no responder running in the exporting account returns `No responders are available` immediately (exit 0, no timeout).
- `No responders` on a service import means the import matched the export but nothing answered; a request with no import at all gets the same immediate answer because it never leaves the local account.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Security)**

- Checklist: Allow `_INBOX.>` on the subscribe side for any user that makes requests.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Drain & Shutdown**

- Draining a single subscription unsubscribes, lets the handler finish that subscription's buffered messages, and leaves the connection and other subscriptions open; the canonical use is rotating one queue-group member out while the group keeps consuming.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Slow Consumers**

- When one subscriber genuinely can't keep up, the real answer is usually more subscribers sharing the load via a queue group, not a bigger buffer; pending limits protect each member. "the real answer is usually not a bigger buffer but more subscribers sharing the load"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Request-Reply Resilience**

- The `_INBOX` prefix is configurable (`inboxPrefix`, `CustomInboxPrefix`); when a user's subscribe permissions don't cover `_INBOX.>`, grant subscribe on a dedicated prefix and have the client set it.
- A request has three outcomes: a reply within the deadline; a timeout (the responder may be up but slow — no answer arrived in time); or no responders (the server knows no subscription is listening and sends an immediate 503 with no body, returning at once).
- No responder means the service isn't running, isn't registered, or its account can't see the subject. "Rather than a slow answer, this means there is no one to answer."
- No-responders is the most useful failure NATS gives you because it's fast and certain; without it a request to an unlistened subject would block for the full timeout. "the no-responders signal is the most useful failure NATS gives you, because it's fast and certain"
- The no-responders signal needs a server new enough to send the 503 and a client that advertised support in the connect handshake; both have been the default for years.
- Retry differently per failure: a timeout means someone is there, so a short bounded fast retry; no responders means nothing is listening, so exponential backoff to give the responder time to register. "Use a short, bounded retry for a timeout and an exponential backoff for no responders."
- The retry loop must be bounded: cap the attempts (five is a reasonable default) and add jitter so a fleet of requesters doesn't retry in lockstep. "five is a reasonable default"
- A retried request is a duplicate; make it idempotent by keying every request by a business ID (e.g. `order_id`) and having the responder remember recently seen IDs and return the cached reply. It's a discipline on both ends, not a new message.
- A request in flight when the connection drops is lost outright; NATS doesn't persist it. The inbox re-subscribes on reconnect, so an idempotent retry after the link returns is safe.
- Pitfall: Treating a timeout and no-responders as the same failure wastes a fast-retry opportunity on a slow responder and floods an unlistened subject. Branch on the error.
- Pitfall: A timeout shorter than the responder's real latency makes every busy moment look like a failure. Measure the responder's latency and set the timeout to two or three times its p99. "set the timeout to two or three times its p99"
- Pitfall: An unbounded retry loop pins a CPU and never reports the problem. Cap attempts, add jitter, and stop with a clear signal (log and let the caller decide).
- Pitfall: A non-idempotent retry that double-acts (e.g. reserves stock twice when only the reply was lost). Key every request by `order_id` and de-dupe on the responder.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where Next (Resilient Clients)**

- Checklist: Measure the responder's p99 and set the request timeout to two or three times it.
- Checklist: Handle no-responders and a timeout separately; absent responder warrants backoff, slow one warrants fast retry.
- Checklist: Key retries by `order_id` and de-dupe on the responder so a re-sent request is a no-op.
- Checklist: Cap the retry count and add jitter.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Services**

- The Services framework (`micro` in Go/Python, `service`/`services` in JS/Java/Rust/C#) formalizes a request-reply responder into a named, versioned handler the server can discover, that reports stats, and that load-balances across copies. No new infrastructure: a service is still request-reply underneath.
- A service stores nothing; it answers a request and retains no record of it (at-most-once request-reply). Work that must survive a restart or be retried belongs to JetStream. "A service stores nothing; it answers a request and retains no record of it."
- The Services framework needs nothing special enabled on the server; a plain `nats-server` is enough.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first service**

- A service is created with `Name` (shared by every copy), `Version` (SemVer), and `Description`; the framework generates a unique per-instance service ID (a NUID). The name identifies the kind of service; the ID identifies one instance.
- A service needs an endpoint (a named handler bound to a subject) to answer anything.
- An endpoint joins the default queue group `"q"` automatically, so running more copies gives load balancing for free.
- Creating a service subscribes it to discovery subjects under `$SRV` the moment it starts.
- The handler contract is `Data()` to read and `Respond()` to answer; the framework handles subscribing, the queue group, reading the reply subject, and publishing the answer.
- Pitfall: Validate the request body; never let bad input crash the handler. The framework doesn't validate payloads; on parse failure respond with a service error (`Nats-Service-Error` + `Nats-Service-Error-Code` headers, code always safe to parse as a number, `400` for bad input) so the caller sees "bad request" rather than a hang. "Don't assume the payload is well-formed."
- Pitfall: A service `Name` and `Version` are validated at creation. `Name` allows letters, digits, hyphens, underscores (no dots or spaces); `Version` must be valid SemVer; an invalid value fails `AddService` outright.
- Service `Metadata` is immutable once set; to change it you stop the service and start a new one.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Endpoints and groups**

- A service can hold multiple endpoints; an endpoint's subject defaults to its name, and you set it explicitly only when the wire subject and endpoint name differ (the common case once subjects carry structure).
- A group is a subject prefix: an endpoint added to group `orders.inventory` answers on `{group}.{endpoint}`. There's no separate routing layer; the wire looks identical whether the endpoint was added directly or through a group. Groups nest (`{outer}.{inner}.{endpoint}`).
- The queue group is set at three levels, each overriding the one above: service default, group override, endpoint override; if none set, the endpoint falls back to `"q"`.
- Most services never need a queue-group override; the default `"q"` already load-balances all instances of a service. Reach for an override only when a subset of endpoints should load-balance separately. "Most services never need this."
- Pitfall: Disabling the queue group turns an endpoint into broadcast — every instance receives every request and the caller gets one reply per instance. Never disable it on an endpoint that responds; do not disable it to "make sure a request is handled". "never disable it on an endpoint that responds"
- Pitfall: Endpoints are immutable once added: no remove, rename, or subject change on a running service; metadata is fixed at creation. Decide endpoint names and subjects deliberately before going live, the way you pick a stream name. To change shape, stop and start a replacement.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Discovery**

- Every service answers three discovery verbs under `$SRV`: PING (presence: name, instance id, version; use to find services and measure RTT), INFO (adds description and endpoint list with subject and queue group), STATS (per-endpoint counters).
- A service doesn't publish to `$SRV`; it subscribes there and replies to requests.
- Each verb answers at three address levels: `$SRV.INFO` (every service in the account), `$SRV.INFO.<Name>` (every instance of that name), `$SRV.INFO.<Name>.<id>` (one instance).
- Discovery is broadcast, not load-balanced: the discovery verbs are not in a queue group, so a `$SRV.INFO.<Name>` request reaches every instance and every one replies. A caller waits a short deadline and collects however many responses arrive. "Discovery is broadcast, not load-balanced"
- When you know an instance id, address the third level to get exactly one reply with no deadline loop.
- Pitfall: Discovery is broadcast: a single reply is not the whole answer. A plain request returns the first response and silently hides the rest, so five instances appear as one. Wait a deadline and collect every reply, as the CLI does.
- Pitfall: `$SRV` is a reserved subject prefix; do not publish to it yourself. Publishing under `$SRV` collides with the framework's machinery and corrupts what callers discover. Keep your subjects under your own prefixes.
- Who may see `$SRV` across account boundaries is a security/account question.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Observability**

- Every endpoint carries a counter set the framework updates on each request under the service lock: `num_requests`, `num_errors`, `last_error`, `processing_time` (total handler time, ns), `average_processing_time` (ns). No metrics code needed.
- Stats are per endpoint, not per service; that's the level for reasoning about load — which handler is busy and which is slow.
- A service error is a reply carrying `Nats-Service-Error` (description) and `Nats-Service-Error-Code` (short code string like `"400"`); `req.Error(code, description, data)` attaches both headers, sends the response, and bumps `num_errors` and `last_error` in one step.
- A service error is a delivered reply, not a transport failure; it differs from no-responders, where nothing is listening at all.
- Return a service error for bad input, an unavailable downstream dependency, or a business rule rejecting the request; a handler that responds normally instead leaves `num_errors` at zero and hides the problem.
- Pitfall: A service error arrives as headers, not as a failed call. A caller that only checks "did I get a reply" reads every service error as success. Check `Nats-Service-Error-Code` on every response; do not treat a returned message as proof the request succeeded.
- Pitfall: Stats are per instance, and `Reset()` zeroes them. `$SRV.STATS.<Name>` returns one `stats_response` per instance; sum across IDs yourself (the server keeps no aggregate), and don't assume counters only ever grow — `Reset()` zeroes them and resets `started`.
- A custom `StatsHandler` can attach your own `data` blob per endpoint, and the server can emit service-latency advisories measuring round-trip time from outside the service.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling**

- Horizontal scaling means running more instances with the same `Name`, `Version`, and endpoint; you don't register instances or configure a load balancer. The default queue group `"q"` is the entire scaling story. "That queue group is the entire scaling story."
- The split across instances isn't a round-robin you control; the server delivers each request to whichever queue-group member is ready, with no coordinator.
- Disabling the queue group (`WithEndpointQueueGroupDisabled`) is broadcast, not scaling: useful for fan-out work, wrong for load balancing. Keep it on when you want to scale.
- `Stop()` drains each endpoint subscription: it removes queue-group interest immediately (so the server stops routing new requests there), then unsubscribes the `$SRV` verbs; accepted requests keep processing in the background.
- `Stop()` returns before background processing finishes; don't exit the process the moment it returns — drain the connection or wait on the `DoneHandler` until in-flight work completes. "don't exit the process the moment it returns"
- Because the endpoint leaves the queue group as part of the stop, there's no window where a request lands on a queue group whose only member vanished; roll a new version by starting fresh instances then stopping old ones one at a time.
- Durable state (a count that must not reset, a queue of work that outlives the process) doesn't belong in the instance; put it behind JetStream.
- Pitfall: Instances don't share memory — protect external state. Each instance keeps its own counter/cache/"remaining stock" and they drift. Keep handlers stateless; push shared state into a database or a JetStream stream/KV bucket. "Keep handlers stateless"
- Pitfall: A blocking handler stops its instance from serving other requests; handlers run synchronously on the service's connection. The queue group masks it by routing to peers, but if every instance blocks the whole service stalls. Keep handlers fast, move long work off the request path, add instances.
- Instances are disposable; make stopping one safe with a graceful stop that drains in-flight work and hands new requests to survivors.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Services)**

- Four pieces: the service (named, versioned, auto-ID, discovery subscribed, stats tracked), endpoints and groups (`{prefix}.{endpoint}`), the `$SRV` discovery verbs, and the default queue group `"q"` that scales it with no coordinator and no config.
- A service is at-most-once request-reply; when an instance stops, its in-flight work is gone. State that must survive a restart belongs in a stream, not the service.
- Checklist: Unmarshal `req.Data()` inside the handler and respond with a service error on bad input.
- Checklist: Pick a `Name` matching the allowed character set and a valid SemVer `Version`; an invalid value fails service creation outright.
- Checklist: Override an endpoint's queue group only when you mean to change who load-balances with whom; the change is silent and easy to get wrong.
- Checklist: Disabling the queue group turns an endpoint into broadcast (every instance answers) instead of load balancing.
- Checklist: Treat endpoints and metadata as immutable once added; name and shape them deliberately the first time.
- Checklist: Collect discovery responses with a deadline-or-count loop; a single request returns only one instance.
- Checklist: Treat `$SRV` as a reserved subject prefix; never publish to it yourself.
- Checklist: Check `Nats-Service-Error-Code` on every reply; an unchecked failed call looks like success.
- Checklist: Aggregate stats across instance IDs yourself; counters are per-instance and `Reset()` zeroes them.
- Checklist: Protect any external state instances share (a database or a stream); the framework holds no shared memory across instances.
- Checklist: Keep handlers non-blocking, or run more instances; a blocking handler stalls every other request on that instance.

- Nothing on the NATS side is MQTT-aware; any NATS subscriber, JetStream stream, or service consumes device traffic as normal messages.
- An MQTT subscription is a real NATS subscription on the converted subject, so it propagates across a cluster like any other; publishers on other servers reach the device without knowing about MQTT.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first WebSocket connection**

- The WebSocket listener is another door into the same server; there's no bridging step and no separate subject space, so a `nats://` publisher and a `ws://` subscriber share subjects.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Learn**

- Core NATS is the foundation every other chapter builds on; if you're new to NATS start there, and go straight to JetStream if you're here for persistence.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — What is NATS?**

- NATS is an open source messaging system; applications connect to a server and exchange messages by subject without knowing each other's network addresses.
- NATS optimizes for a small single binary, low latency at high message rates, and secure defaults; it runs from one server on a laptop up to clusters spanning regions.
- Core components: the NATS server (broker that routes messages), publishers, subscribers, and subjects (named channels).
- Location transparency: applications don't need to know where other services are; NATS handles service discovery, load balancing, and fault tolerance.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subjects**

- NATS is a subject-based messaging system: publishers and subscribers communicate through named channels, giving a location-transparent, interest-based pattern that routes across distributed servers.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publish-Subscribe**

- A publisher sends a message to a subject and every subscriber listening on that subject gets a copy; this is the foundation everything else builds on.
- Publishers don't know about subscribers and subscribers don't know about publishers; services can be added, removed, or restarted without coordinating.
- Publishers don't wait for acknowledgments (fire-and-forget); if no subscribers exist, the message is simply discarded.
- Pub/sub is ideal when multiple services need to react to the same event: event broadcasting, data distribution, fan-out notifications, audit logging.
- Fan-out is one publisher to multiple subscribers (event notification); fan-in is multiple publishers to one subscriber (aggregation).
- Core NATS is at-most-once delivery without persistence; for guaranteed delivery use JetStream.
- Only subscribers connected when the message is published receive it; messages aren't stored for later.
- Every subscriber gets a copy; subscribing doesn't consume or remove messages.
- NATS has a default max message size of 1MB (configurable). "For large data, consider using object stores or passing references."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Request-Reply**

- Request-reply brings synchronous, RPC-style interaction on top of pub/sub: the client creates a unique reply subject (inbox), subscribes to it, publishes the request with the reply subject, and the service publishes the response to it.
- Timeouts are crucial in request-reply to prevent indefinite waiting; all clients support configurable timeouts.
- With multiple responders and no queue group, all services receive the request and all can respond (scatter-gather), useful for gathering data from multiple sources, aggregating results, or querying replicas for consensus.
- With queue groups, only one service receives the request and responds, giving automatic load distribution, horizontal scalability, and built-in failover.
- By default `request()` returns the first response and drops the rest; to gather every response, subscribe to a reply inbox directly and read until a timeout.
- When no subscribers exist for the request subject, the server returns a "no responders" error immediately.
- Headers are supported in request-reply for metadata exchange.
- Timeout strategy: too short may miss valid responses, too long blocks unnecessarily; add buffer for network round-trip; implement retry logic for transient failures.
- Error handling: always handle timeouts, check for no responders, validate responses before processing.
- Service design: idempotent operations (requests might be retried), lightweight processing (long operations should be async), health checks, graceful shutdown (drain pending requests).
- Performance: reuse connections for multiple requests; modern clients reuse inbox subjects; batch related requests when possible.
- Choose request-reply for synchronous communication, service discovery via no-responders detection, load balancing with queue groups, and RPC-style APIs. Use pub/sub for fire-and-forget, multiple consumers, event streaming, and decoupled systems.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue Groups**

- When subscribers share a queue name, NATS delivers each message to only one randomly chosen member of that group.
- A lone subscriber in a queue group receives all messages; with multiple members NATS randomly selects one per message; distribution adjusts automatically as members join and leave.
- The queue name is application-defined, not server-configured.
- Selection is random per message and does not account for how busy a member is.
- A member stops receiving only when its subscription or connection goes away, including when the server disconnects it as a slow consumer.
- Common uses: background job processing, API request handling across service instances, event processing pipelines, batch operations.
- When a worker leaves, NATS stops routing to it within milliseconds.
- Queue groups enable horizontally scalable services without a service mesh or API gateway; service code needs no knowledge of other instances, leader election, or coordination.
- Queue groups coexist with regular subscribers on the same subject. "Use queue groups for operational work that needs to happen exactly once, and regular subscribers for observational tasks (audit logging, monitoring, analytics)."
- In super-clusters queue groups exhibit geo-affinity: messages go to workers in the same cluster/region as the publisher, with automatic failover to other regions if no local workers are available, with no configuration.
- Queue group naming follows subject-like conventions: service-based (`api.auth.workers`), environment-based (`prod.order-processors`), version-based (`service.v1.workers`).
- Core queue groups never redeliver: a message sent to a worker that crashes mid-processing is lost. For redelivery and durability, use JetStream worker pools.
- Duplicates come only from publisher retries, so make processing idempotent if the publisher may resend.
- Worker design: drain messages before stopping, handle failed messages, monitor worker health.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream**

- Core NATS delivers only to subscribers connected at publication (at most once, never replayed); JetStream adds a persistence layer giving at-least-once delivery, with messages surviving restarts and replayable.

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Replace Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis and more w/NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity Ep 10**

- Core NATS is a pub/sub model where the cluster brokers communication between two live clients; this covers pub/sub, request/reply, fan-in and fan-out. "a NATS cluster is really brokering communication between two live clients" (~01:03)
- In core NATS, if a subscriber is offline when a message is published, the server drops it or delivers only to online subscribers; the offline one never gets it. "there's no subscribers so I'm just going to drop the message" (~02:03)
- This behaviour is called temporal coupling: both parties must be online for the logic to work. "they are coupled in the sense that they both need to be online for them to work" (~02:03)
- Core NATS is recommended for RPC and microservices; stream processing and distributing large datasets for one-at-a-time processing need temporal decoupling, which is JetStream. "fantastic for RPCs and for microservices ... stream processing ... that's when we start getting into temporal decoupling" (~02:03)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared: Part 1 | Rethink Connectivity**

- Kafka is "semi-real time but not real real time" by its own admission and was not designed as a messaging system, although people use it for pub/sub and queues. "it really is not initially meant or designed to be a messaging system" (~03:03)
- NATS was designed as a low-latency, high-throughput, high-fan-out messaging system with subject-based addressing, proper interactive request/reply and proper message queues. "low latency high throughput high fan out messaging system implementing publish subscribe with subject-based addressing" (~05:05)
- Core NATS and even JetStream latencies are measured in microseconds: one-way or two-way in the 100–200 µs range over a network, under 100 µs one-way on a fast network. "over this network you're talking 1 to 200 microsecond ranges ... with fast network below 100 microseconds" (~34:41)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Comparing and contrasting NATS and Kafka | RethinkConn '22**

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | JetStream**

- JetStream brings at-least-once delivery only to specific subjects; core publish to no listeners is gone, at-least-once means the server holds it for later consumers. "brings at least once delivery model only to specific subjects" (~01:03)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers**

- A NATS stream provides a total ordering on ingest; consumers always observe the same order regardless of how many publishers there are. "a stream in NATS provides a total ordering on ingest ... from a consumption side it's always going to observe the same order" (~11:14)
- A stream is an internal server-side subscriber on the configured subjects whose job is to persist messages to disk or memory; it decouples time as core NATS decouples space. "the job of the stream is literally an internal subscriber in the server ... my job is literally to persist this on your behalf" (~34:46)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.10 Webinar**

- Native MQTT support requires JetStream because MQTT QoS relies on it, but no streams need to be defined by hand; the server translates between MQTT topics and NATS subjects. "it does require JetStream because of the quality of service mechanisms ... but beyond that you don't have to define any streams" (~08:11)
- Before 2.10 MQTT supported QoS 0 (at most once, like fire-and-forget) and QoS 1 (at least once); 2.10 adds QoS 2 (exactly once) and from 2.10.3 the server runs an external MQTT compliance test suite. "with 2.10 QoS 2 has been implemented ... as of 2.10.3 we actually introduced a proper external MQTT compliance test suite" (~09:12)
- NATS has four connection types: client, route (server-to-server within a cluster), gateway (cluster-to-cluster forming a supercluster), and leaf node. "you have a client connection ... route connections ... gateway connections ... leaf node connections" (~17:21)
- Traffic between servers in a cluster is always a single hop before landing on a subscriber. "it's always a single hop before it actually lands to a subscriber" (~18:21)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- The auth callout service is just a NATS subscriber on a predefined subject that responds; there is no new protocol. "it's literally just another NATS subscriber right and then it just responds so it's not like a new protocol" (~53:55)
- MQTT QoS 2 was added because applications such as Home Assistant rely on it, making MQTT an entry point for moving workloads onto NATS. "one of the big projects that comes to mind is Home Assistant that uses MQTT integration relies on QoS 2" (~56:58)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03: Escaping the HTTP Mindset with NATS.io**

- Using NATS as the communication mechanism between modules from the start gives location transparency: modules can live in one monolith or be split and distributed without changing how they talk. "those modules all connect to NATS... you don't have to know physically where they're located" (~09:14)
- HTTP cannot broadcast or publish to unknown receivers, which is why teams add a broker or SQS; NATS natively supports request-reply, request-reply-many (scatter/gather), fire-and-forget pub/sub, and persistent streams. "you can do request reply, request reply many... you can publish fire and forget... and then you also have persistent streams" (~28:36)

"whoever is connected at that time will receive that message, maybe it's a time sensitive event" (~28:36)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02: Monolith to Modular Monolith with NATS.io**

- Load balancing is a native server primitive in NATS: subscribers forming a queue group get messages distributed at random across members with no extra software or external dependency. "the NATS server will distribute those messages across at random to those various members in that group without any additional software" (~07:06)
- Define a subscription as a queue group from day one even if it has a single member; adding instances later scales out transparently because new members just join the group. "you might only have one member of that group right now... from day one you can design this knowing that this is a potential point of distribution" (~11:13)
- Because queue-group routing in a multi-region NATS system is RTT-aware, the closest responder answers without extra logic; one data fabric can stretch across EMEA and US regions instead of per-region load balancer pairs. "it also does RTT so round trip time responses... you could have the closest NATS service respond without any further logic" (~10:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP04: A Service Mesh Pattern for NATS.io**

- Request/reply works transparently through mapping: the requester attaches a unique reply subject, whichever versioned responder receives the message replies to it, and the requester waits with a configurable timeout on that temporary subscription. "it actually supplies a reply subject that is unique... the responder is basically just waiting for a set timeout" (~25:35)
- Capacity example: 100 concurrent users, 20 per responder, 80/20 split, plus headroom gives 5 V1 and 2 V2 responders, all in queue groups, with no L4 load balancer. "we would basically have five... for the eighty percent case and two for the V2 case" (~28:37)
- A queue group is identified by queue name plus subject; the server randomly distributes each request to one member of the group. "the queue name with the subject... makes that unique identifier for that particular group" (~30:40)
- Request/reply across regions: several queue groups in different regions can subscribe to the same subject; the request is broadcast, each group picks one member, and the fastest reply wins. "whoever is the fastest responder on that subject that's the one that's actually going to come back" (~33:41)
- NATS sends requests to the closest responders relative to the ingress point on a region-by-region basis, giving geographic distribution for free. "it's going to transparently send it to the closest responders wherever that ingress point is" (~33:41)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Micro-services with auto discovery, observability and load balancing. | Rethink Connectivity Ep 9**

- Discovery is a one-to-many request: one request on the control subject gets a reply from every running instance, so no stateful service registry exists; the query reaches the services themselves. "these services aren't necessarily registering themselves with some stateful service discovery engine" (~16:17)
- Ten requests to two instances were split five and five, showing queue-group load balancing between service instances with no configuration. "they got load balanced between the two, five and five" (~17:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS as a ServiceMesh**

- Load balancing in NATS is queue subscriptions (register the client with a queue name, effectively round-robin); locality-aware balancing comes from gateways, superclusters, and leaf nodes where closer subscribers get the message. "register your client with the queue name, that's how you load balance" (~17:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP01S3: Going back to basics with core NATS!**

- Understanding core NATS is the foundation; JetStream, KV, Object Store and the service API are all layered on it, so learn core first. "if you understand core NATS you will be fine with JetStream, Object, Key Value and whatever other abstractions we built on top of it" (~03:20)
- People skip core NATS and go straight to JetStream "because we need persistence"; the speakers consider this a mistake. "sometimes people don't know where to start or they even skip core NATS entirely and go straight to JetStream" (~03:20)
- Everything in NATS is pub/sub: request/reply is pub/sub with a reply inbox, JetStream is request/reply, KV is JetStream. "request reply is pub sub with reply subject, JetStream is request reply which is pub sub, key value is JetStream which is again pub sub" (~22:40)
- Host reports an early bench on an M1 Mac at roughly 48 gigabits per second for the simplest single-server pub/sub setup (unverified anecdote). "I think I was getting ridiculous numbers like 48 gigabits per second or something crazy" (~07:23)
- A single client can push on the order of 10 million messages per second if you try very hard, somewhat less on the subscriber side; persistent layers cannot match this. "you can get like 10 million messages per second if you try very hard on single client, a little bit less on subscriber side" (~20:37)
- Engineers reflexively demand maximum guarantees ("at most once? no, I need guarantees") but core NATS without persistence already gives useful guarantees, e.g. no-responders in request/reply. "core NATS even without any persistence can give you quite some guarantees" (~10:26)
- Request/reply solves a whole class of timeout ambiguity: if the network is functional, NATS tells you immediately that nobody is listening instead of a timeout of unknown meaning. "you very quickly get an answer that nobody is there, maybe the service is down" (~11:27)
- A persistence layer (JetStream) is heavyweight and "stores everything"; with core NATS you can be selective about what gets stored. "every persistence layer is pretty heavy, it just stores everything if you use JetStream, while here you can be way more selective" (~11:27)
- For publisher-side reliability in core NATS, assume anything can fail and require an acknowledgement/response; use request/reply plus timeouts and retries where you need to know the message arrived. "you always need to retry and hopefully be prepared for the worst cases" (~14:31)
- Some publishers (e.g. a temperature sensor broadcasting every half second) legitimately do not care whether anyone is listening; that is a valid core-NATS design. "if I'm a temperature sensor ... do I care that anybody's listening" (~16:32)
- Periodic signalling (an aggregate or heartbeat every 10 seconds) is a lightweight core-NATS way to know a system is alive without JetStream. "you might want a response back every 10 seconds to say here's an aggregate or here's the last thing that we received" (~16:32)
- JetStream, including its Raft layer, is built purely on core NATS publish/subscribe and request/reply with heartbeats; its reliability patterns can be borrowed selectively. "JetStream is actually built on top of core NATS, it's just using publish subscribe request reply and that's all it is, even the Raft layer" (~17:33)
- Pull consumers already use heartbeats; a core-NATS app can adopt just the heartbeat idea ("once in 10 seconds let me know you're alive") without the rest of the guarantees. "in your specific use case you might not need all of those guarantees ... just one in 10 seconds just let me know" (~18:34)
- JetStream is described as core NATS with the server subscribing to your messages to store them. "JetStream is just core NATS with server subscribing to your messages to store them" (~21:38)
- Presence-style features (which page each user is viewing, Google-Docs-like) were built in a few hours with plain pub/sub request/reply: open page, request everyone on the page, they respond. "I opened the page and I request everyone that on the page and they respond" (~51:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02S3: Orbit - The NATS Client Extensions**

- The server keeps core, JetStream, KV and Object Store in one process on purpose: splitting into services would add operational complexity and inter-service latency that would make current performance unreachable. "it would be impossible to reach the current performance limits of NATS JetStream and KV and Object Store if it was not all in one package" (~17:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS tools and benchmarking with JNM! NATS Community Office Hours (Reupload)**

- Kafka-style request/reply is CQRS (submit to one topic, poll another later); NATS offers interactive request/reply with geo-affinity where you learn within a timeout that nobody can process the request and can decide whether to resubmit. "I send a request, if there's no one able to process at this point I want to know about this in whatever timeout is" (~13:18)
- On a ~3-year-old M1 Ultra Mac Studio over loopback, a single publisher with no subscribers reached about 5 million 128-byte msgs/s (~600 MB/s); at 1 MB messages it did about 3,700-4,000 msgs/s but 3.6-3.8 GB/s. "it's 5 million messages a second, they're 128 bytes ... 3.8 gigabytes per second" (~42:54)
- A publish-only bench with no subscribers is artificially high because the server drops messages with no interest; with four core subscribers each message is copied four times and it is still very fast. "no one is subscribing ... the server says there's no interest for the message and subject, they're dropping there" (~46:59)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Benchmark Core NATS & NATS JetStream using the NATS CLI tool**

- Single-threaded synchronous request/reply on a 2021 Intel MacBook Pro over loopback did about 7,500 round trips per second, i.e. ~133 µs average process-to-process round trip through NATS. "7,500 about ... that's a 133 about microseconds an average of a round trip" (~04:04)
- Core pub/sub with one publisher and one subscriber (each on its own connection) reached about 3.9-4.2 million 128-byte msgs/s, roughly 500 MB/s, on the laptop. "we got 3.9 million and we got 4.2 and now we get 4 million" (~07:07)
- With one publisher and 10 subscribers (fan-out), the aggregate was about 5.3 million msgs/s: the publisher at ~500k msgs/s and each subscriber at ~480k msgs/s. "the publisher probably shot about 500,000 per second and the subscribers are for 480 thousands" (~08:09)
- Two publishers, four subscribers with larger messages showed the server receiving ~26k msgs/s and sending ~103k msgs/s, about 2 GB/s aggregate on the laptop. "it's receiving 25,000 messages per second, around 26,000, and sending out 103 or so ... two gigabytes per second" (~10:11)
- A core publish returns no server acknowledgement; a JetStream publish returns an ack that the message was received and persisted, so use JetStream publish to get the full benefit of a stream. "a JetStream publish operation lets you get an acknowledgement that the message was properly received and persisted" (~13:15)
- Core NATS subscribers can observe messages being published into a stream at the same time, with high fan-out still possible. "these are core NATS subscribers onto the JetStream publisher" (~15:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — We need to talk about Microservices... (And how NATS.io can simplify things)**

- The core design shift for microservices on NATS is location transparency: stop asking "who do I talk to" (IP, DNS) and ask "what do I want to talk about" (a subject). "shifting from this who do I talk to to what do I want to talk about really is a fundamental shift" (~03:04)
- Load balancing between service instances is built in via queue groups, with no reverse proxy or separate service-discovery process needed. "NATS has load balancing just built in out of the box with a feature called queue groups" (~06:04)
- Requests to an endpoint served by three micro instances are split fairly evenly between them without any extra configuration. "they've been split fairly evenly between the three nodes" (~13:16)
- Message tracing (nats-server 2.11) is enabled by a header on the message; the server emits ingress/egress events, server identity, whether the message went through JetStream or crossed an account boundary, to a chosen subject. "whether or not it went through JetStream whether or not it went over an account boundary and then also its egress" (~22:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Transcending microservices with NATS | RethinkConn '22**

- Goals of the NATS design: decentralized zero trust, provider agnosticism, location transparency, many-to-many communication, and one uniform connective layer. "I want to send a message I want to receive that message no matter where you are in the world" (~12:13)
- A "request many"/broadcast roll call every 5 seconds fans out one request to 60+ browser clients worldwide, each replying, and the replies are aggregated. "this is actually using a request many broadcast ... every five seconds" (~16:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Seamless evolution across geos and clouds | RethinkConn '22**

- Location transparency: a request sent from anywhere is routed by subject to a responder wherever it is connected, replacing DNS/anycast, load balancers, and routing rules. "with DNS you'd have to use anycast and all kinds of really complicated technologies to make this work" (~04:03)
- NATS routes a request to a responder in the requester's own cluster when one exists, and otherwise to the next closest cluster geographically. "we'll find the next closest cluster geographically to respond to" (~05:05)
- Adding a second service instance in another region gave load balancing and intelligent routing for free; clients nearer the East Coast got much lower RTTs because requests stopped hopping to Los Angeles. "load balancing happens for free. And intelligent routing happens for free" (~11:12)
- Service instances share a queue group; by default NATS randomly selects one member to service a request. "NATS is going to randomly select, by default ... an instance to service that request" (~12:22)
- Queue-group routing is cluster-local first: if any responder in the group is in the cluster the request entered, NATS responds from there instead of routing across gateway connections to other regions. "if there are any responders available in that same cluster ... it's going to immediately respond with one of those members" (~13:22)
- NATS is deliberately payload-agnostic (strings, base64, JSON, BSON, protobuf); schema validation will not be a core feature but an opt-in add-on, and can be built today with subject mapping and conventions routing traffic through a validating service. "Is it going to be in core NATS and a core feature? Probably not" (~18:27)
- Head-of-line blocking is not a concern for a leaf node with multiple high-traffic clients; the server is designed to avoid it at the network and messaging layers. "you're not going to experience hardly any head-of-line blocking in reality" (~20:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Where are we now and where to next? | RethinkConn '22**

- NATS is a single binary with no external dependencies that needs only TCP, so it runs on a Raspberry Pi, VMs, bare metal, on-prem, or cloud, and ties any combination together. "we just basically need TCP so given those two primitives we can tie together cloud, on-premise, edge" (~01:01)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Using JetStream KV for dynamic microservice configuration | RethinkConn '22**

- Browsers acted as queue-group members of a V3 service; requesters got responses from members in their own cluster (e.g. GCP vs AWS), demonstrating closest-responder routing. "it really does do that location transparency and intelligent routing" (~05:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking connectivity from cloud to edge | RethinkConn '22**

- Distributed systems have only two interactions: asking and answering questions (microservices/SOA) and making and processing statements (event and data streaming, telemetry). "they can ask and answer questions ... and they can make and process statements" (~04:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Service monitoring with Helix and Surveyor | RethinkConn '22**

- NATS is observable by default: "matrix mode" or wiretap mode is subscribing to everything in an account to see all messages and replies flowing. "we call this like matrix mode or wiretap mode where you're able to sub to everything in this particular account" (~00:01)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Derek Collison RethinkConn 2025 Keynote and Closing Remarks**

- The connectivity layer rests on a few concepts: location-independent end-to-end communication plus push and pull patterns. "Location independent, end to end communications, and pull and push patterns." (~01:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia CEO Derek Collison Keynote**

- NATS challenges two assumptions, location dependence and one-to-one communication; other technologies only appear location independent and need much extra tooling to fake it. "Technologies today can make this look like they are not location dependent or that all communications are truly one to one, but they are under the covers" (~02:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking Connectivity - Hyper-Connectivity & The Intelligent Edge**

- Today's limitations: DNS, hostnames and IPs as the addressing basis, poll-based HTTP everywhere, VPC-perimeter security that edge breaks, location-dependent monolithic backends, and layers built on one-to-one HTTP. "we're still kind of using IP addresses to get machines to talk to each other and maybe that's not scaling" (~04:40)
- Poll-based semantics don't scale when millions of devices hit a central place, so push had to be a native pattern. "poll based semantics does not scale when you have millions of devices all trying to hit some centralized place" (~08:50)
- Core NATS scales to millions of messages per second on one instance; a nats bench on a Mac Studio showed 6.3 million messages per second. "6.3 million messages per second" (~14:50)
- Queue groups load-balance globally and NATS finds the closest responder; if latency trombones to the cloud, move the service into the edge site. "you could just pick up that service and you could put it in your Edge site and get much quicker latencies" (~14:10)
- A roll-call request where every connected client answers demonstrates scatter-gather that HTTP can't do. "you can't do this with HTTP but you can do this with NATS" (~16:20)
- NATS servers have been observed saturating 70 gigabit NICs. "we've seen NATS servers flood 70 gigabit NICs in terms of throughput" (~21:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — A New Way of Thinking | NATS 2.0 and Connectivity**

- NATS has stayed wire-compatible: applications written almost ten years earlier run unchanged on NATS 2.0. "applications that were written almost ten years ago... can still run on a modern NATS 2.0 system today" (~08:30)
- Services scale by running more or fewer endpoints, with no load balancers, sidecars or proxies. "to scale them up you just run more of them there's no load balancers there's no sidecars there's no proxies" (~08:10)
- Core philosophy: the server protects itself at all costs rather than any single user, avoiding the "query of death" where one client's request degrades everyone; this is what a shared utility (not a silo) requires. "it protects itself at all costs it doesn't protect you the user at all costs" (~09:10)
- NATS routes by subject not IP, is message-based not byte-stream, and natively does end-to-end communication with queue delivery. "it's subject based routing not IP... it's message based not packet or byte streams" (~10:40)
- Queue subscribers on a supercluster are geo-aware: the closest subgroup is chosen and if unavailable traffic fails over to the next closest cluster by RTT, with no change to decade-old applications. "understands the closest one and the closest subgroups and picks those automatically" (~25:20)
- Gap detection without a streaming layer: each message carries the sender's unique ID and a +1 sequence; the receiver stores last sequence per sender and reacts on a gap, which is how NATS servers coordinate internally. "every time I send a message I send a unique identifier and a sequence number that's always plus one" (~42:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - PowerFlex Solves Intermittent Connectivity at the Edge w/ NATS - RethinkConn 2025**

- They used core NATS fire-and-forget for transactional data in parking garages with bad internet, then moved that traffic to JetStream. "We were using fire and forget for things that shouldn't be fire and forgot about" (~03:04)
- Message loss with core NATS was real but much rarer than newcomers reading the docs expect. "you start thinking oh no NATS will drop messages, wasn't really that common but it definitely happened" (~03:04)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - MachineMetrics on Industrial IoT & Predictive Analytics w/ NATS at RethinkConn 2025**

- They pick NATS over Redis for internal brokering when they need stronger pub/sub or exactly-once guarantees. "it might make sense to use NATS over something like Redis just to get better pub sub guarantees" (~09:12)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Franco Sabini from Fineco Bank on NATS**

- NATS carries order flow between front end and back end of an online broker (pre-trade checks, routing to exchanges) and between back-end programs; market data is starting to use KV. "all these messages are now exchanged from the front end via NATS and also within the back end itself" (~01:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Nathan Mellis from Modzy on NATS as a foundational building block**

- Request/reply over a supercluster beats HTTP/gRPC for hybrid cloud: a request unanswered locally percolates out to the supercluster, avoiding per-region service deployments and a service mesh. "if the cluster that you're in knows how to answer it it will answer it if it doesn't that'll get percolated out to your super cluster" (~11:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Simple Solutions for Complex Problems - How Workiva uses NATS as a Microservices and RPC transport**

- NATS protects availability by disconnecting slow consumers and lazy listeners that miss pings rather than degrading everyone. "if you have a slow subscriber slow consumer it will just disconnect that consumer nobody else is impacted" (~11:15)
- Clients are cluster-aware, fail over automatically on partition, have built-in reconnect, and buffer published messages during disconnect then flush on reconnect. "the client will buffer messages for you so if you become partitioned your publishing they get buffered up reconnect flushes" (~12:17)
- The text-based protocol makes debugging, sniffing, and writing your own client easy, unlike AMQP or binary protocols. "if you've ever tried to implement like an AMQP client or a binary protocol... it can be an absolute nightmare" (~14:18)
- Benchmarks show tight tail latency versus RabbitMQ and Redis pub/sub, predictable up to six nines, and roughly 8 million messages/second depending on measurement. "can do roughly eight million messages a second depending on how you measure it" (~15:18)
- Part of the performance comes from automatic pruning of the interest graph. "it auto prunes the interest graph so that's part of it" (~15:18)
- RPC over NATS: service instances form a queue group, a client publishes to it, one instance answers with an inbox, and the client sends requests on that inbox; no service discovery or sockets, so connections are cheap to set up and tear down, with heartbeats for health. "there's no service discovery involved there's no sockets that we're creating it's literally just a matter of publishing" (~21:28)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Go Beyond Kubernetes Native Events with NATS**

- Users choose core NATS for prototyping and switch to JetStream in production when events must not be lost. "if they don't want to lose an event they want to make sure that the events is delivered then they have to go with JetStream" (~10:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Connectors – Seamlessly Integrate NATS with Other Systems**

- An outlet that reads from a subject should use a queue group so multiple connector instances don't process the same message. "I will also add a queue just to make sure that if we have multiple instances of our connector... you won't get multiple instances that will be processing the same message" (~11:15)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Workloads - Distributed cloud-to-edge compute with NATS Execution Engine**

- Nex uses core NATS (publish, request/reply) under the hood, and additionally emits events into a stream for future event sourcing. "Nex is pretty much core NATS under the hood... it is emitting events that we are saving to a stream" (~23:43)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Migrating from NATS Streaming to JetStream**

- JetStream is a subsystem inside the NATS server, whereas NATS Streaming was a separate server acting as a NATS client. "JetStream is an actual subsystem within the NATS server proper... whereas NATS Streaming is an external server." (~06:43)
- MQTT 3.1.1 support is native in the server and uses JetStream transparently; you only need JetStream enabled and the MQTT listener configured. "Under the hood, MQTT is using actually JetStream transparently." (~11:51)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS KubeCon Tutorial on Twitch**

- NATS is a 10-year-old CNCF project that started in Ruby for Cloud Foundry; its wire protocol has barely changed, the main addition being headers in 2.2 via new HPUB/HMSG commands. "The only main change into the protocol is... support for headers... HPUB and the H messages." (~03:05)
- The server has no external dependencies; one URL gives you pub/sub, request-reply, and load balancing without extra services. "It is a lightweight, no dependencies, a very small Docker image." (~04:07)
- Request-reply across accounts works by remapping the requester's unique inbox to a hidden `_R_` subject on the service side; all transparent to clients. "When it traverses into another account it becomes a special subject called underscore R." (~17:31)
- All clients move raw bytes; encoding (JSON, protobuf) is the application's concern, e.g. a StringCodec in the JS client. "NATS all it cares about is moving bytes. It doesn't care about whether it's protobuf or JSON." (~28:48)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Zen of High Performance Messaging with NATS by Waldemar Quevedo Salinas**

- NATS began in 2010 in Ruby for Cloud Foundry, was rewritten in Go in 2012, and ships as a ~7 MB single binary with no deployment dependencies. "It is only seven megabytes in size... it's a single binary." (~02:06)
- The nats-bench micro-benchmark shows around 10 million messages per second with 1-byte payloads over 100 million messages; the speaker calls this a micro-benchmark and defers to Tyler Treat's comparisons for trade-offs. "You can get a throughput of around 10 million messages per second with a single byte." (~02:06)
- NATS deliberately does nothing but pure publish/subscribe; persistence and exactly-once are pushed out of the core to keep it operationally simple. "It does nothing but pure publish/subscribe... it doesn't have built-in persistence of messages." (~04:10)
- The design question NATS answers is the fastest, simplest, most reliable way to read/write a socket for 1:1 and 1:N, hence one always-established TCP connection with a plaintext protocol. "Choosing TCP/IP and having an always established TCP connection with the server." (~05:10)
- Core delivery is fire-and-forget, at-most-once: a message with no interested subscriber is dropped. "If someone is not plugged into the system and interested in a subject then that message will be just dropped on the floor." (~05:10)
- The protocol is a handful of commands: PUB, SUB, UNSUB, MSG, PING/PONG, INFO from the server, CONNECT from the client, plus errors; INFO includes the max payload size. "The first thing we get is this INFO... and also what is the maximum payload size." (~06:14)
- If client or server don't exchange PING/PONG within the interval (default two minutes) the server drops the connection; PING also gives a round-trip latency measure. "By default this is an interval of every two minutes, the server will chop the connection off." (~07:15)
- The payload is opaque bytes to the server; the byte count on the control line must be followed exactly or the client is disconnected for a protocol violation. "The payload is opaque to the server... for the server it's just bytes." (~08:15)
- Request-reply is built from pure pub/sub using an ephemeral random inbox subscription with an UNSUB limit of one message; the first reply wins. "It does so by having this ephemeral subscription, inboxes." (~09:17)
- Client publishes are buffered and coalesced, so after a publish loop there is no guarantee bytes were sent; flush by appending a PING and waiting for the PONG. "We append an extra ping at the end of the buffer and we make a future so that we're expecting a pong back." (~13:21)
- The `_INBOX.*` wildcard subscription sees every request in a server; subjects starting with `_SYS` are reserved and publishes there are rejected. "We can subscribe to all of the requests... by using underscore INBOX dot asterisk." (~16:27)
- `*` matches one token, `>` matches everything after the dot; a subscription to just `>` shows all traffic on the server. "This one will match everything after the dot." (~17:31)
- NATS replaces the point-to-point "death star" of microservice connections with one always-on connection per service, avoiding separate discovery and load balancing when sub-millisecond latency matters. "It becomes this whole death star microservices kind of thing." (~19:36)
- NATS is not meant for a new connection per request; keep one persistent connection as a dial tone. "NATS is not a system where you have to create a new connection for each one of the requests." (~20:37)
- Queue groups distribute messages randomly, not round-robin, among members. "One of these messages will be balanced randomly among the different service nodes... it's not round-robin." (~25:48)
- NATS "does not assume the audience": several queue groups and plain subscribers on the same subject each get a copy independently. "You can have multiple distribution queues from the same subjects." (~26:51)
- By definition the first reply to a request is the lowest-latency responder. "The first message that you get back from a request in NATS is the one with the lowest latency." (~26:51)
- Choosing reliability over guaranteed delivery does not constrain application guarantees; per the end-to-end argument, guarantees belong in the application layer, and "we can always build stronger guarantees on top but never remove them from below." "We can always build stronger guarantees on top but we can always remove them from below." (~31:57)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — SCaLE 13x Derek Collison  NATS A new nervous system for distributed cloud platforms**

- Derek's background: ~12 years at TIBCO building Rendezvous and EMS, ~6 years at Google, architect of Cloud Foundry; NATS was written in a weekend to power Cloud Foundry. "It was written in a weekend so the first version just had a Ruby server and a Ruby client." (~25:31)
- HTTP is loved as an interface but is point-to-point; NATS targets 1:N, 1-of-N, cascading request-reply, and subject-based routing instead of IP+port routing. "HTTP... only goes so far right it's usually point-to-point." (~04:06)
- Multicast effectively failed operationally and is disallowed on cloud platforms; for fan-out of roughly 30 or fewer receivers, sending the message N times from one point is faster. "For certain types of N, probably depending on your message size, 30 or so or less, it actually is faster to send it 30 times." (~07:12)
- The "ask everyone, take the first best answer" pattern (as Google search does across shards) was built into NATS from day one; on JMS/RabbitMQ style systems the requester's CPU spikes linearly with responder count. "You can see massive spikes all day long... linearly proportional to how many responders are out there." (~09:14)
- NATS queuing is a subscribe operation ("distributed queuing"), not a publish operation that physically enqueues; only one member of a queue group receives a given message while plain subscribers still get it. "Subscribe is what I call distributed queuing." (~13:17)
- Request-reply creates an ephemeral unique subject, subscribes, and sends it as the reply-to; wildcard observers see both request and response, unlike many systems. "A lot of systems you see the requests, you can't see the response." (~14:19)
- Exactly-once done correctly requires transactional semantics down to disk hardware; Derek considers it "a problem that doesn't really need a solution" compared to idempotent designs. "Exactly once is a problem that doesn't really need a solution." (~15:21)
- Expecting the messaging system to guarantee delivery once handed a message is often an anti-pattern; store-and-forward has a place for batch work, but the app must handle failure. "A lot of times it's almost an anti-pattern to expect that once I give it to the messaging system it's going to take care of everything." (~17:21)
- NATS is designed to protect itself at all costs and stay available, unlike enterprise brokers that take everyone offline while servicing one client's pathological request. "My version of the world is I protect myself at all costs and I always have to be available." (~19:24)
