- When stream MaxBytes is set, block size = MaxBytes/4 + 1 ("25% overhead"), clamped to [32000 B, 8 MiB]; otherwise falls to 4 MiB in the middle range. `FileStoreMinBlkSize = 32 * 1000`, `FileStoreMaxBlkSize = maxBlockSize` (8 MiB) (server/filestore.go:378-381, 809-828)
- Background fsync interval default 2 minutes (`sync_interval`); write cache buffer expiry 10s; idle FDs closed after 30s; per-block subject index expires after 2 min idle; flush coalescing waits at most 8ms. `defaultSyncInterval = 2 * time.Minute`, `defaultCacheBufferExpiration = 10 * time.Second`, `closeFDsIdle = 30 * time.Second`, `defaultFssExpiration = 2 * time.Minute`, `maxFlushWait = 8 * time.Millisecond` (server/filestore.go:329-340)
- Compaction minimum threshold 2 MiB. `compactMinimum = 2 * 1024 * 1024` (server/filestore.go:376-377)
- Per-message on-disk overhead: 22-byte record header + 8-byte checksum (+ subject length + 4). `msgHdrSize = 22`, `checksumSize = 8`, `fileStoreMsgSizeEstimate = emptyRecordLen + slen + 4 + maxPayload` (server/filestore.go:1111-1114, 9722-9724)
- Store directory and file permissions 0700/0600 (server/filestore.go:163-166)
- On-disk layout: `streams/<name>/msgs/<n>.blk`, `<n>.idx`, `<n>.key`; stream meta `meta.inf`/`meta.sum`/`meta.key`; full-state snapshot `index.db`; TTL wheel `thw.db`; scheduling `sched.db`; consumer state `o.dat` (server/filestore.go:292-355)
- Encryption ciphers: ChaCha20-Poly1305 (default), AES-GCM, or none; compression: none or S2 (server/filestore.go:89-130)
- Store limit errors surfaced to publishers under discard-new: "maximum messages exceeded", "maximum bytes exceeded", "maximum messages per subject exceeded", "message too large" (server/store.go:49-58)
- Raft WAL replay on startup pauses apply when more than 32 MiB is queued. `const maxQsz = 32 * 1024 * 1024` (server/raft.go:575)
- Replicated stream messages are S2-compressed over the wire when payload > 8 KiB and the peer supports it. `compressThreshold = 8192` (server/jetstream_cluster.go:11416)
- Lost-quorum advisories throttled to one per 10s per stream. `lostQuorumAdvInterval = 10 * time.Second` (server/jetstream_cluster.go:5440)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — Client connection handling: slow consumers, stalls, buffers (server/client.go, server/opts.go)**

- JetStream option defaults: max_memory_store -1 (dynamic), max_file_store -1 (dynamic), sync_interval 2m, request_queue_limit 10000, info queue limit = request queue limit, concurrent IOs 4096. `defaultConcurrentIOs = 4096` (server/dios.go:21; server/opts.go:6171-6189)
- Server-wide `jetstream.limits` fields: max_request_batch, max_ack_pending, max_ha_assets ("maximum of Streams and Consumers that may have more than 1 replica"), max_duplicate_window, max_batch_inflight_per_stream, max_batch_inflight_total, max_batch_size, max_batch_timeout (server/opts.go:375-384)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — jsm.go JSON schema field documentation and defaults (schema_source/jetstream/api/v1)**

- Stream name pattern `^[^.*>]*$`; description maxLength 4096 (`stream_configuration.name`, `.description`)
- Stream defaults per schema: retention=limits, max_consumers=-1, max_msgs=-1, max_msgs_per_subject=-1, max_bytes=-1, max_age=0 (unlimited), max_msg_size=-1, storage=file, compression=none, num_replicas=1 (min 0, max 5), no_ack=false, discard=old, duplicate_window=0 ("0 for default"), persist_mode="" (`stream_configuration.*`)
- "subjects ... Must be empty when a mirror is configured. May be empty when sources are configured." (`stream_configuration.subjects`)
- "sealed: Sealed streams do not allow messages to be deleted via limits or API, sealed streams can not be unsealed via configuration update. Can only be set on already created streams via the Update API" (`stream_configuration.sealed`)
- deny_delete / deny_purge: "Cannot be changed once set to true" (`stream_configuration.deny_delete`, `.deny_purge`)
- discard_new_per_subject: "Essentially turning discard new from maximum number of subjects into maximum number of messages in a subject." (`stream_configuration.discard_new_per_subject`)
- max_msgs_per_subject: "For wildcard streams ensure that for every unique subject this many messages are kept - a per subject retention limit" (`stream_configuration.max_msgs_per_subject`)
- placement: "Placement requirements for a Stream or asset leader": cluster, tags ("Tags required on servers hosting this stream or leader"), preferred ("A preferred server name to move the leader to"); "random placement when unset" (`placement`, `stream_configuration.placement`)
- republish: "Rules for republishing messages from a stream with subject mapping onto new subjects for partitioning and more" (`republish`)
- consumer_limits: "Maximum value for inactive_threshold/max_ack_pending for consumers of this stream. Acts as a default when consumers do not set this value." (`stream_consumer_limits`)
- external source: api = "The subject prefix that imports the other account/domain $JS.API.CONSUMER.> subjects"; deliver = "The delivery subject to use for the push consumer" (`external_stream_source`)
- stream_source_info.active: "-1 when there has been no activity"; lag: "How many messages behind the mirror operation is" (`stream_source_info`)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — natscli cheat sheets and help-text guidance (cli/cheats/*.md, cli/*_command.go)**

- Cheat sheet stream ops: `nats stream purge ORDERS --seq 1000` "deletes up to, but not including, 1000"; `--keep 100`; `--subject one.subject`; `nats stream seal ORDERS` "Marks a stream as read only"; `nats stream cluster ORDERS down` "Force a cluster leader election"; `stream cluster peer-remove ORDERS nats1.example.net` "Evict the stream from a node"; `nats stream copy ORDERS ARCHIVE` "does not copy data" (cli/cheats/stream.md:19-50)
- Peer-remove refuses when it would remove the only peer: "removing the only peer on a stream will result in data loss, use --force to force" (cli/stream_command.go:1092-1094)
- `nats stream add` defaults: `--allow-direct` default true ("Allows fast, direct, access to stream data via the direct get API"); `--max-consumers` default -1; `--max-msgs`/`--max-msgs-per-subject` default 0; `--discard-per-subject` "Sets the 'new' discard policy and applies it to every subject in the stream"; `--retention` accepts limits, interest, workq/work (cli/stream_command.go:201-248)
- Interactive help: retention "Messages are retained either based on limits like size and age (Limits), as long as there are Consumers (Interest) or until any worker processed them (Work Queue)"; discard "the New policy will prevent further messages from being added while Old will delete old messages"; dupe window "Duplicate messages are identified by the Msg-Id headers and tracked within a window of this size" (cli/stream_command.go:2707, 2717, 2798)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — JetStream account limits, reservations and naming (server/jetstream.go, server/server.go)**

- Account reservation for a stream = max_bytes x replicas when the account has NO tiers (`tier == ""` and replicas > 1); with tiered limits (R1/R3 tiers) the reservation is a single replica's bytes against that tier. `accountReservation`: "if tier == _EMPTY_ && replicas > 1 { return replicas * bytes }" (server/jetstream.go:2500-2508)
- Per-server footprint is one replica's bytes; a stream create/update fails with "insufficient memory/storage resources available" when account reserved + new reservation exceeds account MaxMemory/MaxStore, or when server reserved + one replica exceeds server max_memory_store/max_file_store (server/jetstream.go:2512-2545)
- Stream max_consumers may not exceed the account's max_consumers; "stream limit is checked separately on stream create only!" (server/jetstream.go:2481-2498)
- Asset (stream/consumer) names may not contain whitespace, '.', '*', '>', '\\', '/'. `isValidAssetName` (server/jetstream.go:2811-2816); general names (domains, etc.) forbid whitespace, '.', '*', '>' (`isValidName` server/jetstream.go:2804-2809)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — JetStream API levels, advisories, and API backpressure (server/jetstream_versioning.go, server/jetstream_api.go)**

- Stream feature -> required API level: per-message TTL (2.11) = 1; counters, atomic batch publish, message scheduling, async persist mode (2.12) = 2; fast batch publishing (2.14) = 4 (server/jetstream_versioning.go:60-88)

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — JetStream Anti-Patterns: Avoid these pitfalls to scale more efficiently**

- Republish combines core NATS and JetStream: "ideal for use cases where subscribers can handle messages in real time and do not require strict delivery guarantees"; gives filtering without consumer state.
- Direct Get API is "even faster and more lightweight than consumers, making it ideal for getting specific messages from streams"; suited for mobile/IoT fetching latest data per subject. Batch Get (2.11) returns multiple messages across multiple subject filters.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — How to Design NATS Subject Hierarchies (Patterns, Pitfalls & Best Practices)**

- One stream per top-level namespace is the common default; splitting at namespace boundaries avoids coupling retention and storage budgets.
- JetStream subject-detail listings cap at 100,000 subject entries per request; high-cardinality schemas make them "unusable."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Mirror, Merge, or Consume: How to Choose Your Edge-to-Core Streaming Pattern**

- Consume, mirror, and merge (source) "represent three different relationships between producers and consumers, with different tradeoffs"; teams "default to whichever pattern is easiest" and then "spend months working around its limitations."
- Consume: a core consumer reads an edge stream directly and selectively; puts "the selection logic where it belongs: at the consumer, at the point of ingest." Dependency: "A consumer pulling directly from an edge stream depends on the edge node being reachable."
- Mirror "creates an exact 1:1 replica of an edge stream in the core. Sequence numbers are preserved"; catches up automatically after reconnect; "clients cannot write to a mirror directly. It is read-only by design."
- Mirror for compliance/audit, backup/DR, distributing read load, consumers needing the complete unaltered sequence. "Consume applies logic and filters. Mirror preserves everything."
- Mirror is a full-copy operation: storage "scale[s] with edge volume rather than with actual consumption."
- Merge (sourcing) aggregates multiple edge streams into one core stream; "A sourced stream does not preserve origin sequence numbers — messages from different sources are interleaved"; per-source ordering is preserved, global ordering is not.
- Subject transforms in the source configuration normalize edge naming into a global taxonomy; "the normalization lives in topology."
- Most common failure: "defaulting to mirror when consume would be more appropriate, because mirror feels safer." Result: a firehose where "downstream consumers ... end up doing in application code the filtering that should have happened at the ingest boundary."
- Inverse failure: consume when merge is needed, turning a unified query into "a distributed coordination problem that the application has to solve."
- "In a mature edge-to-core architecture, all three patterns often appear simultaneously on different data paths."
- "JetStream implements mirrors and sources natively — without external connector processes, without separate mirror-maker jobs"; pattern selection "is a configuration decision, not a development project."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — The Hidden Cost of Active-Passive Clustering (And What to Do Instead)**

- Clustering and Raft are different layers: clustering handles client connectivity; Raft handles replicated state. JetStream's default is "full-mesh: all nodes active" with "Raft for replication"; per-stream leaders are elected automatically; writes are acknowledged only after quorum commit.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Why "Just Retry" Will Kill Your Edge System**

- Store-and-forward: collect locally, forward when connected, keep collecting while disconnected, catch up at a controlled rate. "Catch up" must mean "resume forwarding at a rate the core can absorb", which needs flow control and pull consumers.
- Local durability: "Events get written locally before anything else happens." Survives process crash, network drop, upstream throttling.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — You Don't Need Two Platforms: The Case for Hybrid Eventing**

- Pub/sub is stateless: "if a subscriber is offline when the message arrives, it misses it." Streaming is stateful: replay from time, sequence, or last position; new consumers catch up from the beginning.
- JetStream feature list quoted: "durable streams, configurable retention, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery, consumer replay, and pull-based consumption for backpressure management"; same binary, no separate process, cluster, or client library.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS and Kafka Compared**

- JetStream offers at-least-once and exactly-once options; individual ack, double ack, nak with backoff.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS vs RabbitMQ: How to Choose the Right Messaging System**

- Rule: use "Core NATS when losing an occasional message is acceptable" and "JetStream when messages need to be stored, replayed, or acknowledged."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — MQTT vs. NATS for Fleet Management: Hub-and-Spoke vs. Distributed Mesh**

- Offline commands: "If a device loses connectivity when a command is sent, the command sits in a stream. When the device reconnects" it's delivered; no per-device sender state.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Multi-Region Consistency: Have Your Cake and Eat it Too!**

- Clustered JetStream is immediately consistent within a cluster via RAFT: "When a client application receives the publication acknowledgement it is assured that the message has been safely replicated to (and persisted by) the majority of the servers."
- Replicas are a subset: in a 9-server cluster only 3 servers participate in an R3 stream. Placement tags control AZ placement. Replication degree can be changed at any time without interruption.
- Mirroring preserves sequence numbers; sourcing does not. Both are reliable store-and-forward that catches up after disconnect.
- Read mirrors give "eventual coherency" not true eventual consistency: writes serialize at the origin; mirrors don't help write scaling or availability if the origin region fails.
- Stretch clusters need at least 3 regions; "Stretched streams will be immediately consistent between regions, at the expense of much higher latency of synchronous operations." R5 across 5 regions survives two region failures. At least 2 of 3 nodes must be reachable for RAFT votes.
- Virtual streams (2.10): per region a 'write' stream on region-prefixed subjects plus a 'read' stream sourcing all write streams and stripping the region token via transform (`foo.*.>` to `foo.>`); cluster-scoped mappings route local publishes transparently. "all read streams eventually contain all published messages, though not necessarily in same order."
- Virtual stream limits: no work-queue or interest retention (limits only); not for KV if the same key is modified from different regions; consumers are per-region (no global durable); message deletes are not propagated; no compare-and-set because read/write sequences differ.
- Global ordering can be kept with a stretch-cluster 'ordering' stream sourced from write streams and mirrored locally: lower write latency than direct stretched writes, but no compare-and-set.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Understanding JetStream Memory Usage Patterns**

- JetStream memory comes from: dedup IDs kept for the window "(default: 2 minutes)"; file-store caching of recently accessed messages; metadata and subject tracking for streams/consumers/subjects; extra overhead on meta-leader nodes.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Why NATS**

- Spatial decoupling via pub/sub, request/reply, request/reply-many; temporal decoupling via JetStream where clients consume at their own rate.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Per-Message TTL: Unlocking Ephemeral State Patterns in NATS**

- Before 2.11 all messages in a stream shared `MaxAge`. Per-message TTL needs `allow_msg_ttl: true` on the stream and a `Nats-TTL` header at publish. "Messages without a `Nats-TTL` header fall back to the stream's `MaxAge`." `Nats-TTL: never` ignores `MaxAge`.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Mirror Streams in NATS JetStream: One-Way Replication Made Simple**

- Mirrors are "one-way, asynchronous replication"; "Your origin stream doesn't need any special setup—it won't even see a consumer created." One origin per mirror; mirrors are read-only; consumers on mirrors have full capabilities.
- Mirror config: name (required), start sequence, start time, filter subject, subject transforms, domain. Filter subject and subject transforms cannot be combined. Domain supports hub/leaf JetStream domains.
- "Delete a message from the origin, the mirror still has it. Delete from the mirror, the origin is unaffected." Deletes never replicate in either direction, which makes mirrors independent backups.
- Work-queue retention has only partial mirror support and is "not resilient over intermittent connections"; interest retention with mirrors is unsupported and undefined.
- On origin unavailability the mirror retries "about 10–20 seconds" before reconnecting.
- Uses: geographic distribution ("One origin can feed multiple mirrors"), cross-account/domain replication, load distribution via `mirror_direct` so clients read from mirrors instead of the origin.
- Mirror promotion (2.12): unbind subjects from the old primary (use `$devnull` placeholder), remove mirror config, bind subjects to the promoted mirror. "the server won't verify if the mirror is fully caught up, so any unreplicated messages will be lost." Publishes fail briefly during the switch; clients need retries.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — JetStream Expected Sequence Headers: Optimistic Concurrency Without Locks**

- Expected-sequence headers detect conflicts rather than prevent them: "Only one succeeds, advancing the stream to sequence 5. The other is rejected because by the time it arrives, the stream has already moved to 5."
- There is one sequence counter per stream; per-subject expected values "are still stream sequence numbers, not independent counters starting from zero."
- Headers: `NATS-Expected-Last-Sequence` (global, single-writer strict ordering), `NATS-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` (per subject, concurrent writers on different subjects), plus `NATS-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence-Subject` for per-pattern grouping (e.g. `order.1.*` shares tracking while `order.2.*` is independent), suited to event sourcing.
- Applications must handle retries; capture sequences from PubAcks for the next attempt. Atomic batches use `NATS-Expected-Last-Sequence` on the first message to detect stream changes during batch construction.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Atomic Batch Publishing in NATS 2.12: All-or-Nothing Message Guarantees**

- Atomic batches stage messages invisibly and commit all-or-nothing; consumers never see partial batches. Headers: `NATS-Batch-ID` (max 64 chars), `NATS-Batch-Sequence` (incrementing), `NATS-Batch-Commit`.
- Use cases quoted: "Consistent multi-consumer fan-out", "Idempotent full-state replacement", "Snapshot + delta bootstrapping", multi-event commits ("Consumers should see all three or none"). Event sourcing is the primary use case.
- Batches rejected if: ID > 64 chars; sequence gaps; stream uses async persist mode; duplicate messages present (as of 2.12.1). Batches cannot cross streams.
- `NATS-Expected-Last-Sequence` is "only allowed on the first message of a batch"; `NATS-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` gives subject-scoped checks.
- Defaults (configurable): 1,000 messages per batch; 50 batches in flight per stream; 1,000 batches per server; 10 seconds inactivity before abandonment.
- Streams need `--allow-batch`. Orbit's `BatchPublisher` manages IDs and sequence numbers.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Jepsen: NATS 2.12.1**

- Bug in 2.10.20-2.10.22: "a stream could be unexpectedly deleted after process kills"; fixed in 2.10.23.
- JetStream verifies message checksums on each load by design; known limitation: nodes may not auto-recover corrupted data from peers when corruption hits the beginning or middle of a stream; filestore struggles with corrupted blocks/metadata from bitflips or truncation.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Distributed Counters in NATS JetStream: A CRDT-Based Approach to Global Counting**

- Counter streams are CRDTs: "multiple servers can update their own copies independently and still arrive at the same result when they merge." Enable with `AllowMsgCounter: true` plus `AllowDirect: true` (to batch-read).
- Increment via `Nats-Incr` header matching `^[+-]\d+$`; server uses `big.Int` for "arbitrary precision by default"; values serialize as JSON strings so "JavaScript clients, capped at 53-bit safe integers" don't lose precision; PubAck `val` returns the post-increment value.
- Sources rewrite deltas: "the server does not replay the sourced message's `Nats-Incr` verbatim"; `Nats-Counter-Sources` tracks per-source last values as `{stream name}#{original subject}` and entries are "never removed, even if you later drop a source."
- Incompatible with counters: mirrors ("would replay raw deltas and double-count"), `DiscardNew`, Interest/WorkQueue retention, per-message TTL, `Nats-Rollup`, `Nats-Expected-*` headers. `AllowMsgCounter` "cannot be turned off." Subject purge does not replicate across sourced counters; reset by publishing a negative delta then purging.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Delayed Message Scheduling in NATS JetStream**

- The `NakWithDelay` retry workaround "does not scale well when you have thousands of pending scheduled messages" because it ties up consumer state.
- `Nats-Schedule` header formats: `@at <timestamp>`, six-field cron (seconds first), `@every <interval>`, aliases `@hourly`/`@daily`/`@weekly`. `Nats-Schedule-Target` "must differ from the schedule subject." `Nats-Schedule-Source` (2.14) samples the latest message from another subject. `Nats-Schedule-TTL` needs `AllowMsgTTL`. `Nats-Schedule-Time-Zone` (2.14) applies to cron only; default UTC.
- Each schedule is one subject; the latest message on the subject is the active schedule; publishing replaces it. Delivered messages carry `Nats-Scheduler` and `Nats-Schedule-Next` (or `"purge"`). `@at` schedules purge after delivery.
- `AllowMsgSchedules: true` "cannot be reverted" and cannot be enabled on source or mirror streams. Put `schedules.>` and delivery subjects in the same stream.
- "Past-dated schedules fire immediately"; after a restart all past-due schedules fire at once; "Use `Nats-Schedule-TTL` so consumers can detect and discard stale deliveries." DST can skip or duplicate cron jobs; stay on UTC.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Monitoring NATS: From HTTP Scrapes to System Events**

- JetStream advisories under `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.*` (lifecycle, leader elections, delivery failures), API audit at `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.API`, metrics under `$JS.EVENT.METRIC.*` (e.g. ack latency).

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Server 2.14 Release**

- Fast batch publish persists messages continuously as they arrive with inline per-message consistency checks, "effectively unbounded batch sizes" unlike atomic batch, multiple acks in flight for pipelined batches, and gap detection.
- Fast batch "can almost double throughput compared to async publish depending on settings" and allows hundreds of concurrent publishers into one stream with flow control.
- "Atomic batch rejects the entire batch if any message fails a check (including deduplication), fast batch behaves like traditional async publish." Modes `gap:fail` (hard fail) and `gap:ok` (report gaps without failing).
- Recurring schedules (`@every 5s`, cron) move periodic work server-side; can combine with TTL to stop scheduling. Scheduled subject sampling reads the latest value on a source subject each fire, falling back to the schedule payload; primary use is server-side downsampling.
- Before 2.14 mirrors/sources used internal ephemeral consumers; now WorkQueue and Interest retention sources use durable consumers, "visible in consumer listings, carries metadata showing the source domain, account, and stream", holding state across disconnects. Users can pre-create the consumer used for sourcing/mirroring.
- Streams with sources no longer need a 100ms minimum dedup window when dedup is disabled; dedup can be disabled entirely for mirrors/sourced streams; sourced streams now dedup to avoid stalling when sourcing overlapping streams.
- EOB (end of batch) lets a batch commit without persisting the final message, for atomic and fast batch.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Server 2.12 Release**

- Atomic batch publish: "atomically write a batch of messages into a stream" with staging and per-message checks; "there can be no partially committed batches"; combinable with scheduling and counters. ADR-50.
- Delayed Message Scheduling (ADR-51): single delayed messages only in 2.12, no repeats.
- Distributed Counters (ADR-49) use `big.Int`; limit is what "is allowed to be stored in the payload of a single message"; support mirroring/sourcing via CRDT composition.
- Mirror promotion: remove mirror config to make it primary; delete the previous primary first.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Server 2.11 Release**

- Single Message TTL: "set a TTL for individual messages"; delete markers on MaxAge expiry; improves KV expired-key notifications.
- Message Get existed since 2.8; Multi Message Get batches retrieval, "vastly more efficient approach to processing streams without the overhead" of dedicated consumers.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Server 2.10 Release**

- New filestore reduces lock contention; "P99 stream publish times reduced and stabilized considerably"; large/encrypted streams "will now typically take less than a second to recover" at startup (no linear scan of blocks).

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Server 2.9 Release**

- Catch-up replication traffic is compressed; `max_outstanding_catchup` "limits the total bytes that are in-flight during stream catch-up."
- `AllowDirect` serves gets from any replica (auto-on for KV, opt-in for streams); `MirrorDirect` lets mirrors serve gets. Direct get headers: `Nats-Stream`, `Nats-Sequence`, `Nats-Time-Stamp`, `Nats-Subject`.
- Republish graduated from experimental; supports "millions of concurrent subscriptions"; `HeadersOnly` republish enables lazy fetch via direct get; `Nats-Last-Sequence` header for gap detection.
- Consumer `Replicas`, `MemoryStorage`, `FilterSubject` editable after creation; stream `Placement` editable to move streams transparently.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Building a Wallet Event Backbone with NATS JetStream: Lessons from BroSettlement's Staging Tests**

- Delivery is "at-least-once, not magical exactly-once"; duplicates are a "normal recovery condition"; consumers dedup by globally unique eventId (plus chain tx identity for blockchain data); handlers idempotent via unique constraints; client requests carry Idempotency-Key.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Delegate with trust**

- One subject per order plus publish expectation `lastSubjectSequence: 0` enforces "there will be only one subject per order payment" (first-writer-wins single withdrawal).
- Dedup window is per-stream in nanoseconds; example `duplicate_window: 5_000_000_000` (5s); duplicates in the window are rejected.
- Query the order subject "like a database" to rebuild aggregate state from prior events; `lastSubjectSequence: 2` forces the message into exactly 3rd position or fails.
- Sequence numbering is stream-wide; per-subject ordering requires tracking the last subject sequence (from subscription metadata, fetching the last event, or in-memory).
- For high-frequency events (10ms intervals = 360,000 events/hour) publish snapshot/aggregate events (e.g. hourly average) to a separate subject to avoid reading the full history.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Infinite message deduplication in JetStream**

- Exactly-once needs two parts: publish-side dedup and ack-based consumption. Time-window dedup (Nats-Msg-Id) "cannot guarantee restart timeframes"; Kafka's connection-scoped producer idempotence "guarantees only single-session idempotence" and can't cover a client crash before ack.
- `DiscardNewPerSubject` + max-msgs-per-subject 1 + discard `new` yields infinite BYOID dedup: a duplicate subject fails with "maximum messages per subject exceeded". Without it, per-subject limits with discard `new` behave as `old` (last-value cache).
- JetStream "enforces exactly n maximum messages per subject; Kafka log compaction ensures at least one." Distributed WAL systems lack a `new` discard policy because they're designed to always accept or block.
- "compare-and-append" via `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` gives SQL-update-like semantics.
- Per-subject limits need indexing; more subjects means more server memory. Subject filter needs at least one `*` or `>` where the unique ID token sits. Default "Duplicate Window: 2m0s".

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — How Form3 built a multi-cloud low-latency payments service with NATS.io + JetStream**

- JetStream used for payment status streams needing at-least-once; "data-at-rest encryption by default."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — The Matrix Dendrite Project move from Kafka to NATS**

- Heavy use of "interest-based retention policies to ensure that work is cleaned up when it is complete" with manual acks; worker pools fed from streams; removed per-component persistent storage.

- JetStream adopted (fall 2023) first for durable work queues; KV ("think: Redis"), Object Store ("think: S3"); home-brew chunked propagation of large graph structures "very similar to how the object store works."

- Exactly-once via "message de-duplication, delivery tracking and acknowledgement mechanisms" for the Trigger Server ("execute once – no more, no less"), yet idempotent operations remain "a best practice."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Building Event-Driven Banking as a Service (BaaS) with NATS**

- Core: "fire-and-forget ultra-low-latency delivery"; JetStream: "at-least-once or exactly-once semantics"; single supercluster spans "data center, AWS, or branch edge."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Q&A - Financial Services Event Architectures**

- Core = eventing (fire-and-forget routing); JetStream = streaming (order, replay, retention, historical query) on one platform.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Scaling Global AI Inference with NATS JetStream**

- Streams buffer requests when no workers are active, giving scale-to-zero without losing requests. Superclusters, leaf nodes, and mirrors provide global routing and locality.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Event-Driven Systems with NATS and Jetstream**

- Core NATS is fire-and-forget, "comparable to Redis Pub/Sub"; JetStream "is closer to Kafka in persistence model."
- Example stream: `Limits` retention, file storage, max_bytes 100MB, max_age 7 days (nanoseconds), num_replicas 1.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — How to Build NATS Consumers**

- Example stream: file storage, `MaxAge: 7 * 24 * time.Hour`, `Replicas: 3`.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS JetStream: Streams, Consumers, and Durable Messaging**

- JetStream adds "at-least-once delivery (exactly-once is opt-in)"; a consumer is "a stateful view of a stream — it tracks which messages were delivered and acknowledged."
- Retention: `limits` (default), `workqueue` (delete on ack), `interest`; storage file (default) or memory; replicas 1-5; discard old (default) or new. "Prefer JetStream publish APIs over plain Core NATS publish — the server returns an acknowledgment."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Bridging the Edge: Using NATS Leaf Nodes to Build Hybrid and Multi-Cloud Systems**

- JetStream domains (`hub` vs `branch-1`, API `$JS.hub.API.>`) separate instances; store-and-forward = persist locally, mirror/source into hub streams when connectivity returns.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Deploying a scalable NATS cluster part 1: core architecture and considerations**

- Meta group leader handles API and placement; each stream and each consumer is its own RAFT group; leadership churn hurts performance. [DUBIOUS] "NATS core servers form their own RAFT group for cluster synchronization" (core routing is not RAFT-based).

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Cluster Architectures: Multiregional Clusters - Connecting the Globe**

- Streams/consumers are placed within one cluster and replicate only over routes, not gateways; the meta group spans the whole supercluster and quorum loss blocks new resources; cross-region is eventual via mirrors (read-only) and sources (writable); regional loss can lose data within the replication window.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS vs. Kafka: Comparison for the Unified Namespace (UNS)**

- JetStream "last-value caching, where only the most recent value per subject is retained"; NATS "both push and pull subscriptions, whereas Kafka relies solely on pull"; Kafka "manages acknowledgments at the consumer group level" vs JetStream per-message acks, custom redelivery, timeouts.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Replace Redis with NATS: Atomic Counters and Microsecond Key-Value**

- Counters (ADR-49): `Nats-Incr` header `+N`/`-N`, big-integer precision, server serializes updates per subject (no client read-modify-write, no retries under contention); "sourcing-compatible" across streams/accounts/regions.
- Counter streams need `AllowMsgCounter: true`, `AllowDirect: true`, Limits retention set at creation only; cannot be mirrors; incompatible with per-message TTL; every subject becomes a counter.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — From Solace to NATS: One Platform for Messaging, Streaming, and the Edge**

- Solace guaranteed delivery maps to "explicit JetStream stream and consumer designs"; "A consumer can be a pub/sub subscriber today and a durable, replayable stream consumer tomorrow without changing brokers"; Solace shops typically add Kafka for log semantics.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Orbit.go: A Guide to NATS Client-Side Abstractions for Go**

- jetstreamext atomic batch publish: all-or-nothing, fewer round-trips; [ANTI] avoid when "message deduplication is required" as it is "not compatible with batch publishing." Batch get: N messages from a sequence or last per subject set; "often simpler and more efficient than using a consumer for ad-hoc retrieval"; not for real-time, work-queue, interest, or very large datasets.
- counters module needs `AllowMsgCounter: true` and `AllowDirect: true`; works across sources and mirrors [note: contradicts later counter post which says mirrors are incompatible]; source tracking shows "exactly which service instances contributed."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — SOX compliance with NATS**

- Streams are "tamper-proof, with the exception of erasing a message for GDPR purposes (this action can be locked down and audited)"; every message gets a server timestamp "set at the time the message was first stored"; encryption at rest; JetStream CRUD advisories carry user identity; replay streams for audit reports; read-only permissions for auditors.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Building a Job Queue With NATS.io and Go**

- Work-queue retention "keeps the messages until it is delivered to one consumer that explicitly acknowledges receipt, and then it's cleared"; discard `new` drops incoming when limits hit; dedup window 2 minutes with MsgId.
- Example stream: `--max-bytes=256MB`, `--max-msg-size=1MIB`, unlimited age/msgs, `--replicas=1`, `--allow-direct`, `--deny-delete`.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — What's New in NATS 2.2**

- JetStream: "at-least-once delivery and exactly once within a window"; replay by time or sequence; NATS 2.0 security aware; encryption at rest from 2.2.3; GDPR message cleansing; ingestion and consumption bifurcated via streams and consumers; horizontally scalable "at runtime by simply adding more servers with zero downtime"; mix JetStream-enabled and plain servers; per-stream compressed snapshot backup/restore; Terraform provider and GitHub Actions.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Use cases for persistent logs with NATS Streaming**

- STAN: at-least-once, subscriber offsets, replay; default in-memory store; default retention 1 million messages or ~100 MB per channel.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Nothin' but NATS - Building Natster**

- Event sourcing: state from an "ordered sequence of immutable events"; each state-producing service has its own consumer so speeds and failures are independent; replay to rebuild.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Simplifying Microservices Architecture for the Edge and AI Era**

- JetStream "guaranteed store-and-forward" during connectivity loss; distribute updated AI models to the edge.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Rethinking the System of Record**

- Event logs are "optimized for writing, but when it comes to reading, we must go through the entire log"; ad hoc queries need materialized views.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — How to Stream NATS Messages to ClickHouse in Real Time**

- JetStream durable pull consumers resume from the last ack across ClickHouse downtime; "--replicas 3" needed for availability during rolling upgrades; replay by creating a consumer with `--deliver all`.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — GitHub discussion: NATS Jetstreams creation and management (#4457)**

- Streams cannot be declared in server config: "NATS is a multi tenant system and we support decentralised authorization where no credentials for the accounts are stored on the server." Manage via client APIs, CLI, Terraform, GitHub Actions, or a setup container at boot.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Over-Replicated Inactive Streams: What They Mean and How to Fix Them (Synadia Insights check)**

- Idle R3 streams still cost storage on three nodes, Raft heartbeats, and meta-cluster entries "that slow cluster-wide operations"; causes: decommissioned services, staging copies of prod templates, seasonal workloads, blanket R3 policies.
- Find with `nats stream report` or `nats stream list --json | jq` on `num_replicas >= 3`; fix with `nats stream edit <stream> --replicas 1` (non-destructive, reversible, dissolves the Raft group).
- "Ephemeral, test, and archival streams should default to R1"; keep replication for streams receiving "a few messages per day" where loss is unacceptable; 50+ idle R3 streams "meaningfully reduces capacity."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Weekly #32**

- Default R1 on any JetStream-enabled server; R1 memory loses data on restart; R1 file is unavailable until recovery; "At least three replicas (R3) are required" for fault tolerance; R3 tolerates one down, R5 two; max five replicas.
- Even replica counts (R2, R4) are "generally not useful from an availability standpoint"; R2 adds a storage copy but cannot progress if the leader fails.
- Tags place replicas across AZs; mirrors are lightweight eventually consistent async replication that can use different configs (memory, R1); sourcing aggregates streams so one consumer replaces many; DR ladder: regional mirrors (most real-time), consumer-to-object-storage batches, offline backups.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS JetStream Deduplication for LinuxForHealth Blockchain Smart Contract Messaging**

- Every blockchain node runs the same smart contract and publishes the same event; `Nats-Msg-Id` set to the transaction ID lets "JetStream deduplicate the messages so that only one message from all the smart contract copies running on all the blockchain nodes is delivered." Dupe window 30 seconds.
- Stream: limits retention, `--max-age=1y`, unlimited msgs/bytes, file storage; consumer with filter subject, `--target` republish-style delivery subject, deliver last, `--ack none`.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — How Intelecy optimizes factory processes with NATS, NGS and JetStream**

- Originally BoltDB cache; JetStream "persistence and durability layer" "made Synadia Cloud far more useful"; handles large messages, mixed streaming and batch, multi-tenant segmentation.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — How to Configure NATS Cluster with Leaf Nodes for Edge Connectivity**

- Example JetStream limits at the edge "max_mem: 512M, max_file: 5G" vs hub "max_mem: 2G, max_file: 20G"; alert when `/leafz` RTT > 0.5s for 10 minutes.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS JetStream Explained: Streams, Consumers, and Durable Messaging (NATS Explorer)**

- Retention: limits (default, "keep everything up to configured bounds, then drop oldest"), interest (kept "while at least one consumer is behind"), work queue ("each message delivered to exactly one consumer and removed once acknowledged").

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS JetStream as a Durable Job Queue in .NET**

- Work-queue retention makes the stream a queue; one shared durable pull consumer gives competing consumers; adding a worker is "starting another process with zero configuration."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Grokking NATS Consumers: Intro and push-based**

- Limits streams are consumer-stateless; work-queue and interest retention are consumer-influenced. "Streams cannot have overlapping subject spaces."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Weekly #13**

- Interest retention: with zero consumers messages are discarded immediately; with one consumer messages are retained even without an active subscription; with several, "the message is not removed until all consumers consume the message (ack or term)"; consumers must exist before messages to see them.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Inquiry on Limits for Streams and Consumers in a NATS JetStream Cluster**

- Synadia's global clusters cap each server at 2k HA (replicated) assets; some customers run higher and are fine — derekcollison. "In our global clusters we limit servers, at the moment, to 2k HA Assets."
- Prefer muxed (multiplexed) streams with consumers filtering what they need, or R1 mirrors that filter, over many streams — derekcollison. "We suggest folks use muxed streams and have consumers filter out what they need, or R1 mirrors that do the same."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Maximum known-good value for `MaxMsgs` in a JetStream stream**

- There is no hard limit on stream size; many users run unlimited streams; the practical limit is disk or memory, since the server keeps per-subject indexing in memory — jnmoyne. "practically you will eventually run out of some kind of resource, be it disk space or memory space on the servers (as they maintain some per subject indexing)."
- When a stream outgrows a server, shard onto multiple streams by time (stream per year or decade) and add servers — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Does Stream Per Subject have any performance benefits over multiple subjects within same stream**

- Many consumers on a single stream is the simple, good starting pattern; a stream per subject is rarely a good idea — Jarema. "It's rarely a good idea to have stream per subject."
- Each replicated stream (R3+) carries overhead for its own RAFT group — Jarema.
- Split into separate streams only when subjects need different retention policies — Jarema. "I would stick to one stream, unless you need different retention policies for some subjects"

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Why JetStream doesn't achieve linear scalability through partitioning?**

- A Kafka partition, not a Kafka topic, is the equivalent of a NATS stream — derekcollison. "A partition in Kafka is equivalent to a stream in NATS."
- An R1 stream is served by exactly one server; R3 by three; R5 by five. Placement tags select which servers participate — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Sharding Jetstream**

- A single R3 stream can run ~250k msgs/sec with proper hardware and setup; question whether sharding is needed at all — derekcollison. "A single stream, even an R3 can run ~250k msgs/sec with proper hardware and setup."
- The stream leader receives the message directly from the app, replicates to followers, and replies to the app once a quorum has acknowledged — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Can JetStream support multiple partitions distributed to multiple machines, like Kafka?**

- Partitions/shards are not needed for HA or disaster resilience; that is what replicas (R3) are for. Sharding is only for performance scaling — Jarema. "You don't need partitions (or shards) to improve HA... Those are needed for performance scalability."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Subject Indexing and Ordering Internals**

- Streams keep meta state indexed by sequence and by subject; walking a filtered subject set is efficient in the modern server — derekcollison.
- Memory for a stream's subject-addressing layer grows with the number of unique subjects; work to reduce this was planned for 2.10 — derekcollison. "the subject addressing layer to a stream takes more memory the more unique subjects that you have." [STALE?] (2.10/2.11 later improved this)
- JetStream consumption is globally ordered; core NATS only guarantees ordering per publishing connection — derekcollison. "For NATS core the only ordering guarantee is per publishing connection."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Using Nats Jetstream as an event store**

- Event sourcing: a stream `orders` with subjects `orders.*` where each subject is an aggregate; concurrent appends across subjects have no contention, per-subject linearizability via `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence`, and total order across the stream for consumption — bruth.
- Subjects are indexed within a stream, so the optimistic-concurrency header check adds no overhead; a filtered replay does a linear scan only over blocks between the subject's earliest and latest messages — bruth.
- Kafka topic vs NATS stream is the wrong comparison; a Kafka partition is the comparable unit of total ordering and replication — bruth. "a single *partition* is comparable to NATS stream since it is the unit of total ordering and replication."
- Write and read throughput and latency of one NATS stream beat one Kafka partition "in nearly every way" (unpublished Synadia benchmark) — bruth [maintainer claim, benchmark not shown].
- Tiered/cold storage was not built in as of 2023; a separate archiving consumer is the workaround — bruth. [STALE?] (still no built-in tiering as of 2026 per later threads)
- Storage is a custom append-only log with per-message get/delete and subject indexing, both memory and file backed — bruth.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Need Some General Info Regarding Client Design & partitioning**

- Only when inbound throughput exceeds what one stream can write do you use account-level (Core NATS) subject transforms to insert a partition number and create one stream per partition — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Ordering guarantees per entity**

- To scale out: subject-mapping partition on the server, N streams (one per partition), one consumer per stream; publishers keep publishing to the unpartitioned subject — bruth.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Use thousands of leaf nodes at the edge**

- A central stream sourcing from 1000+ edge domains needs every edge listed in `sources` manually; no auto-discovery of leaf JetStream sources exists (as of 2025-12), acknowledged as a management gap — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Super-cluster, geolocation and temporary broken gateway link**

- A stream lives in exactly one cluster; mirror/source to other clusters if needed — ripienaar, jnmoyne. "Streams are located in one and only one cluster"

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Cluster can't tolerate more than one service failure**

- Belief: any stream on a cluster is HA. Correction: an R1 stream hosted on the stopped server is unavailable; make it R3 — kozlovic.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Source stream from multiple leaf nodes**

- Stream sources can be added or removed at any time by editing the stream config (`nats stream info --json | jq .config`, edit, `nats stream edit --config`) — jnmoyne.
- No hard-coded limit on the number of sources per stream — jnmoyne.
- Scale many sources with intermediary streams (each sourcing half the leaves) feeding a final central stream — jnmoyne.
- Do not create a 1:1 stream on the cloud side for every fleet member — derekcollison. "We do not recommend cloud side has a 1:1 stream for every fleet member."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Leaf node with standalone (non-cluster) Primary NATS server**

- Cross-domain sourcing uses `external.api: $JS.<domain>.API`; catch-up after a leaf disconnect is expected behavior — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Distributing messages across leaf nodes**

- For once-only delivery to either leaf: a WorkQueue stream on the hub with an explicit-ack consumer that clients on the leaves pull from, instead of per-leaf source streams — roded [UNVERIFIED, self-answer; consistent with docs warning about sourcing WorkQueue streams].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — locks/leases with KV similar to SETNX**

- Distributed lock via a stream with `DiscardNewPerSubject`, max 1 message per subject, and a max age: publish succeeds = lock acquired; delete the message = release; publish fails = lock held — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — JetStream file-store ~65x slower than memory-store on KV mirror (83% of seq space is deleted)**

- A KV bucket with many overwrites leaves a sparse sequence space (here 83% interior deletes), which hurts file-store scans — cyqsign (measured), acknowledged by MauriceVanVeen who is "working on an improvement in the filestore for a situation like this where the number of deletes are greater than the number of unique subjects."
- A message block never starts with deleted messages; interior deletes are tracked in the block's delete map and tail deletes are compacted away; the linear scan covers only that range — MauriceVanVeen.
- Purging many subjects needs a proper subject hierarchy: `js.PurgeStream` with filter `event.foo.>` purges without storing a marker message; do not publish a rollup message just to delete — MauriceVanVeen.
- There is no atomic swap between distinct subjects; rollup atomically replaces only the same subject. Redesign the subject hierarchy so rollup on one subject works — MauriceVanVeen.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — KV storage operations timeout [v2.10.20]**

- A stream with 17M interior deletes (2.2M live of 23M sequences) was the suspected cause of stalls; frequent purge streams and old clients aggravate it — wallyqs (inferred from thread).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — AckWait does not publish to dead letter queue with zero clients**

- Instead of many work-queue streams, run one large muxed stream and have consumers pull only the subjects they need, keyed by event type — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Message Scheduler vs NAK-with-delay for scheduled notifications at scale**

- Use the 2.12 message scheduler over NakWithDelay; Nak is not meant for scheduling and only worked as a workaround before 2.12 — MauriceVanVeen.
- The scheduler is built on per-message TTL machinery and should support a very large number of schedules; test for your use case — MauriceVanVeen.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — ack-wait and dupe-window behavior when used together**

- AckWait (consumer redelivery timer) and DupeWindow (stream publish dedup by Nats-Msg-Id) are unrelated settings — MauriceVanVeen.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Sharing many distributed account streams with a server-side account**

- Publishing to a stream requires a response, so a service export from the central account fits; a stream export from each new account would force a central import per account — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Memory usage when replaying messages with filter subject on a large stream**

- Filtered replays where matches sit at the end of a large stream caused multi-GiB memory spikes on 2.10.5-2.10.9; fixed via PR 4969 and 2.10.11 — derekcollison.
- Per-block subject index (fss) lingers up to the sync interval (default 2 min) if the block is idle; block data cache expires faster — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Why increasing of "Unprocessed Messages" leads to increasing nats memory usage?**

- Interior deletes (acked messages behind an unacked head in a WorkQueue) are tracked in a bitmask; at 175-196 million interior deletes this measurably costs memory — MauriceVanVeen. "We keep track of interior deletes by sequence number in a bit mask data structure. So efficient but at those numbers will have an impact"
- "Deleted Messages" in stream info counts interior deletes only; FirstSeq not advancing means one consumer holds the oldest message — MauriceVanVeen.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Mirror leaf node stream on the main server**

- Mirroring streams across a leaf node is "very common" — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Leaf-node JetStream retention policy for hub-sourced streams**

- The consumer between a source/mirror and its origin is ephemeral, so Interest retention on the origin (leaf) stream gives inconsistent results and can lose messages published while the link is down — derekcollison.
- Some users run WorkQueue on the leaf origin stream, but there were reports of messages not cleaned up after long outages — derekcollison. [STALE?] (2.11 work planned)
- Recommended: Limits retention on the leaf stream with max age set to the longest expected network outage, plus a max bytes limit so the leaf does not run away with disk or memory — derekcollison. "The age limit should be your maximum outage window allowance."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How to distribute load from one stream to all JetStream cluster nodes?**

- A consumer is bound to a single node and writes to a stream go through one node; WorkQueue and Interest add further constraints, so this is the hardest combination to scale horizontally — ripienaar. "Consumers are bound to a single node and writes into a stream also"
- Spread with server-side subject mapping so producers stay unaware of partitions, or one Limits stream that sources into N WorkQueue streams; consumers enumerate the streams programmatically — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Which NATS JetStream Setup is Better? (WorkQueue plus mirror vs one Limits stream)**

- A larger stream does not slow delivery to consumers; one Limits stream with two consumers is simpler and more efficient than WorkQueue plus mirror — jnmoyne. "It's not because a stream is larger that delivery of messages to consumers takes longer"
- The main cost of a large stream is memory for per-subject indexing when there are many distinct subjects — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — NATS Jetstreams creation and management (streams in server config?)**

- Streams are API-first by design: NATS is multi-tenant with decentralized auth where account definitions may not live in the server config, and users of a centrally run system cannot touch config files — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — InterestPolicy variation (per-user subjects, millions of subjects)**

- A stream with millions of per-user subjects was accepted as a workable design — derekcollison (implicit).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Time-sensitive messages (expiry and deferred delivery)**

- Per-message TTL and deferred delivery were "being considered" in 2022; per-message TTL shipped in 2.11 and message scheduling in 2.12 — derekcollison. [STALE?]
- Re-injecting a message with the same Nats-Msg-Id inside the dedup window makes it vanish; requires a new ID plus an Original-Id header — andreib1 [UNVERIFIED, user report].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — JetStream and NATS server Data Store**

- JetStream has its own store implementation with no dependency on an external database; storage is file or memory — ripienaar, derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Backup data in nats-server with jetstream enabled where storage is memory**

- Memory streams survive restarts only when R3 with rolling restarts and healthz checks; for backup create a file-backed mirror and back that up — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Is Tiered Storage currently planned?**

- Tiered storage is planned with no schedule (2023); still absent as of 2025 with users running custom offload jobs to cloud storage — derekcollison, thread.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — how to recover from DiscardNew policy?**

- Stream state is separate from consumer state; acks do not delete messages under Limits retention. Interest retention removes a message once all interested consumers ack it — derekcollison.
- Producer back pressure that recovers as consumers catch up: Interest retention plus DiscardNew — derekcollison (implicit "That is probably what you want").

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How do I inspect the contents of a workqueue stream?**

- Viewing a WorkQueue stream requires `allow_direct` on the stream and a CLI that uses direct gets instead of consumers (top of main in late 2024; error 10099 otherwise) — ripienaar, derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Mirror Stream sync is ~2.9x slower when a Consumer cold-scans the mirror during catch-up**

- Mirror catch-up of a sparse (75% holes) 4M-sequence stream: 14.2 s alone vs 41.0 s with a concurrent cold-scan consumer — cyqsign [UNVERIFIED, reproducible package attached].
- Hypothesis: a single store-wide RWMutex is shared by the mirror write path and consumer reads, and holes double writer lock acquisitions — gitsult4n [UNVERIFIED, code-reading, non-maintainer].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Is there performance issues possible with a high cardinality subjects for a stream?**

- Many subjects (well beyond a million) are not a performance problem; the cost is RAM for the radix-tree subject index, roughly 100 MB for about 1 million small subjects — jnmoyne. "for something around 1 million subjects it would be in the order of 100 megs of RAM (with small subjects)."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Is jetstream message count capped at 1 billion for a single stream?**

- No 1-billion cap: a Limits stream ran past 1.17 billion messages (36 GiB) on 2.11.7 — wallyqs.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — kvBuckets are unexpectedly slow (list and compact at 100k keys)**

- When the KV abstraction does not fit, use the underlying stream directly: purge by subject, stream-info subject listing (fast, paged, up to 100k subjects), batched gets in 2.11 — ripienaar.
- Thousands or more subjects with one message each is exactly how KV works — ripienaar.
- No responders from a stream publish means the stream is unhealthy; a stream captures messages without any subscriber — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Are there tradeoffs with `AllowDirect: true`?**

- AllowDirect can be enabled by editing any stream; the maintainer gave no stated tradeoff — derekcollison (first answer retracted as about direct consumers).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How does compression work?**

- Compression is per block in the filestore; all limits (MaxBytes, account limits, and the server's max_file_store check) apply to raw message bytes, not bytes on disk — derekcollison, ripienaar. "Compression works per block under filestore but we do report raw usage and that is what is used for limits."
- Belief: compression lets you store more within the server's storage limit. Correction: it saves physical disk for operators only; set `max_file_store` and stream limits in raw terms — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How to find number of subscriptions on jetstream**

- Core publishing into a stream subject works but returns no ack and gives no back pressure; use JetStream publish — Jarema.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Understanding jetstream warnings ("high message lag")**

- "high message lag" means publishers send faster than the system can store into the stream, typically from core publishes into a stream or many async JetStream publishers — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Some questions about NATS (Limits vs Interest, pagination, fetch expiry)**

- Interest retention removes a message when all interested (filter-matching) consumers ack; with no interested consumers the publisher still gets a PubAck but the message is dropped and the sequence skipped — neilalexander.
- Paginate a stream with the message get API combining sequence and batch size — neilalexander.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — NATS Task Scheduler**

- Native message scheduling arrived in 2.12 (see 7628); before that choria-io/asyncjobs (Go) was the community option — thread. [STALE?]

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Event Synchronization with NATS (nats.go)**

- Kafka partitions one topic by an app-provided key; NATS splits a subject space into partitions and creates one stream per partition, with the key being part of the subject — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Can I use JetStream KV as cache? (nats.go)**

- File vs memory KV: if the block is cached, file get is ~50 us like memory; an uncached block costs a couple of milliseconds — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Ephemeral Consumer Cleanup Rate? (nats.go)**

- Streams are optimized for the tail, not random access; compact per-entity history into one key with rollups (as KV does) — ripienaar.
- JetStream publish returns an ack via request/response without any consumer; for loop-back results use one long-lived wildcard consumer or Republish plus a core subscription — Jarema.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Sourcing streams between hub and leaf instances, both directions (nats.go)**

- If the sourcing stream also lists the same subjects as the origin, and core traffic flows across the leaf link, both streams capture the message directly and the source adds it again, duplicating — jnmoyne. Fix: sourcing stream has no `subjects`, only `sources` with a filter — cbrake (verified).
- After a leaf reconnect, sourced messages published during the outage arrived in about 6 s — cbrake [UNVERIFIED, observed].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How to create queue group consumer with new jetstream api (nats.go)**

- A WorkQueue stream may have many durable consumers as long as their subject filters do not overlap — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Queued pull consumers with WorkQueue retention (nats.go)**

- WorkQueue binds a stream to single-consumer semantics per subject; bind many pull subscribers to that consumer for scale. For multiple mutually exclusive consumers on the same subjects use Interest retention — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Aggregate KV? (nats.go)**

- Mirroring and sourcing propagate only new messages, never deletes — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Cluster size scalability question (issue)**

- Segmented streams remain "on the fuzzy roadmap"; 2.11's new filestore targets petabyte scale; TB streams are fine with reasonable subject cardinality and interior deletes — derekcollison (2024-01).
- One KV or stream per customer is "ultimately not a good design pattern"; 33,931 streams took over 10 minutes to restart on 48 CPUs because restore was serial; prefer few buckets with millions of hierarchical keys and per-user permissions on `$JS.API` subjects — jnmoyne, williamstein (measured).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Jetstream: transactional batch publish messages (issue)**

- Async publish (track PubAcks asynchronously, bounded outstanding) is the throughput path; async publishes preserve order — derekcollison.
- Full transactional semantics "would need quite a bit of work" (2021); users were pointed at async publish and saga-style decomposition — derekcollison. [STALE?] (atomic batch publish exists in 2.12+)

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — JetStream pre-allocates memory reservations based on max_bytes (issue)**

- Stream `max_bytes` is reserved against the server's JetStream store limits at creation; over-committing reservations is intentionally unsupported — neilalexander.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Invalidate deduplication window after ack (issue)**

- Dedup exists to protect publish retries when the ack was lost; acked messages must still be deduped; Msg-Id must be unique per event (UUID), not per entity — ripienaar. "This feature exist to ensure that ... the server got the message but the ack got lost - does not result in a duplicate message."
- Exactly-once-ish job intake: an audit (Limits) stream with the "infinite deduplication window" technique (per-subject DiscardNew, max 1 per subject) feeding a WorkQueue stream by source — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Ability to reset consumer start sequence (issue)**

- On Interest retention, deleting and recreating a consumer signals no interest and can lose messages; a native reset would be safer — neilalexander.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — WorkQueue messages not deleted on non-leader nodes when used as mirror source (issue)**

- Removing from one stream never affects a source or mirror; sourcing from a WorkQueue is by design not a supported use — derekcollison, jnmoyne. "Work queue stream exist in order to provide exactly once consumption ... not really to be sourced from."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Consumer and Stream Name Validation (ADR issue)**

- Stream, durable, consumer and account names are "filename-safe" (printable except `.`, `*`, `>`, `/`, `\`, max 255 chars); KV and Object bucket names are restricted to A-Z a-z 0-9 dash underscore (ADR-6) — scottf.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Support S3 API for JetStream / S3 next level**

- Synadia is considering "virtual blocks" to offload filestore blocks to S3 when not needed locally; timeframe "2.12 though" — derekcollison. [STALE?] (not shipped by 2.14 per later threads)

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How can I schedule message?**

- Message scheduling (ADR-51) stores the schedule message in the same stream (`--allow-schedules`); the target message is published to `Nats-Schedule-Target` after the delay, so consumers see both — MauriceVanVeen.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Can you provide a js.PublishBatch function?**

- Sync JetStream publish is RTT bound (~1000/s at 1 ms RTT); batch publishing was planned "in a future version" (arrived as atomic batch publish in 2.12) — ripienaar. [STALE?]

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Removing records from KV that exceed the limit (LRU-style)**

- `MaxMsgsPerSubject` (KV history) caps versions per key; `MaxMsgs` with DiscardOld caps total messages in the bucket's stream; both can be set together — jnmoyne.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Supercluster with JetStream**

- In a JetStream-enabled supercluster, one server across the entire supercluster is elected leader of the meta/API layer and handles JetStream API requests for placing streams and consumers. "one server across the entire supercluster is elected to handle JetStream API requests specifically for the placement of streams and consumers."
- The meta layer is a Raft group, so electing its leader needs a quorum; in practice the supercluster needs an odd number of servers in total. "Since this is a Raft group as well, electing a leader requires a quorum across servers. What this means in practice is that there needs to be an odd number of servers across the supercluster."
- JetStream superclusters should have at least three clusters, or use the arbiter pattern to reach an odd server count. "Supercluster deployments with JetStream-enabled servers should include at least three clusters or use the arbiter pattern."
- For production, run three nodes per cluster so that R3 streams can be created. "for a production deployment it is recommended to have three nodes per cluster to support R3 streams."
- JetStream requires a `cluster` block with `routes` defined even for a single-node cluster. "A requirement of JetStream is to have a cluster block with routes defined, even for single node clusters."
- Stream replicas never cross gateway connections; with one node per cluster only R1 streams can be created. "In this test setup, only R1 streams can be created since streams replicas do not cross gateway connections."
- An odd number of servers across the supercluster is required to reach consensus for the meta group leader. "across a supercluster, an odd number of servers must exist to support reaching consensus for the meta group leader."
- Each JetStream server in the supercluster needs its own `jetstream.store_dir` and a `server_name`; the gateway block lists all three clusters including its own.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Supercluster Arbiter**

- The arbiter is a lighter-weight way to satisfy the odd-number-of-servers requirement of a JetStream supercluster than deploying a third full cluster. "a lighter-weight alternative for satisfying the requirement of an odd number of servers (across clusters)"
- An arbiter is a single-node cluster with JetStream disabled that has gateway connections to each of the JetStream-hosting clusters. "a single node cluster that is not JetStream-enabled can be deployed which connects to both clusters that are hosting the JetStream-enabled servers."
- The arbiter config sets `jetstream: { enabled: false }` and its `gateway.gateways` list gives every route-able URL of each remote cluster (all three nodes of east and all three of west).
- Observed output: the arbiter shows `JS no`, `Routes 0`, `GWs 2`, and it does NOT appear in the RAFT Meta Group table (only the six JetStream-enabled servers are meta-group peers), while it does appear in the JetStream Summary with zeros.
- Place JetStream nodes across availability zones with `server_tags: [az:N]` and set `jetstream.unique_tag: "az:"` so replicas of a stream are spread over distinct zones. "JetStream enabled with the unique tag as well as basic accounts."
- Two clusters with three nodes each plus the arbiter gives 7 servers total (6 JetStream-enabled), an odd count for meta-group quorum.
- A client connected to one cluster (east) can request that a stream be placed in another cluster by passing `--cluster=west` on stream creation; placement is a JetStream API concern, not a connection concern. "Connect to east (port 4222), but request that a stream be added to the west."
- Observed output (unexplained in narrative): in the recorded run the cross-cluster `stream add --cluster=west --replicas=3` failed with `nats: error: could not create Stream: raft: corrupt peer state (10049)`; the meta table at that moment showed `east-az3` with `Current false`, `Active 2.35s`, `Lag 3`, i.e. one peer not yet caught up shortly after startup. The narrative does not comment on this, so treat it as an observed timing artifact, not documented behaviour.
- The application account must have `jetstream: true` (here `APP`) for its users to create streams; the `$SYS` account is separate and used only for `server list`/`server report`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Regional and Cross Region Streams (Supercluster)**

- Use a supercluster of three regional clusters plus one dedicated cross-region cluster when you need streams that survive a regional failure by spreading replicas across three regions. "The use case is for streams that are resilient to regional failures by having replicas spread out across three different regions."
- Cross-region replication costs latency; accept the trade-off only for streams that are critical for availability and can tolerate somewhat higher latency. "This of course comes at a cost of latency, but this trade-off may be appropriate for streams that are critical for availability, but can tolerate slightly higher latencies."
- `jetstream.unique_tag` forces all replicas of a given stream or consumer onto nodes whose value for that tag prefix differs; regional clusters use `unique_tag: "az:"` so replicas land in different availability zones. "the `unique_tag` option which enforces all replicas for a given stream or consumer to be placed on nodes with different availability zones (AZ)."
- The cross-region cluster (`xr`) sets `unique_tag: "rg:"` so each replica lands in a different region; which AZ each of its nodes lives in does not matter as long as the region is unique. "The cross-region cluster defines a unique_tag on the cluster. Any AZ can be chosen as long as the region is unique."
- Nodes in the cross-region cluster carry both tags (`server_tags: [rg:1, az:1]`), one node per region chosen from an arbitrary AZ.
- A three-node cross-region cluster has one node per region; if more AZs per region are wanted, a six- or nine-node cross-region cluster may be desirable. "If may be desirable to have a six or nine node cross-region cluster if more AZs per region are desired."
- Placement is chosen at stream creation: `--cluster=xr` places a stream on the cross-region cluster; `--cluster=rg2` places a regional stream in region 2. The stream is created from a client connected to rg1, so placement is independent of where the client is connected.
- Observed output: EVENTS (cluster xr, R3) got replicas `rg1-az1-x, rg2-az2-x, rg3-az3-x` (one per region); ORDERS (cluster rg2, R3) got replicas `rg2-az1, rg2-az2, rg2-az3` (one per AZ within the region).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Regional and Cross Region Streams (Cluster)**

- An alternative to the supercluster layout is a single nine-node cluster stretched across three regions with three AZs each; regional and cross-region placement is then done with tags rather than clusters. "Rather than a supercluster, this relies on a nine node cluster spread out across three regions and three availability zones each."
- NATS placement tags cannot express logical OR or exclusive OR, so valid replica combinations must be precomputed and encoded as tags on the servers. "NATS does not currently support declaring tags with logical OR (or exclusive OR), so valid combinations can be precomputed as tags and then used when creating streams."
- Encode each valid cross-region combination as an `xr:` tag whose digit positions are regions and digit values are AZs; `xr:231` means one replica in region 1 AZ 2, one in region 2 AZ 3, one in region 3 AZ 1. "a tag `xr:231` can be read as a cross-region stream where one replica is placed in region 1 in AZ 2, another in region 2 in AZ 3, and the third replica in region 3 in AZ 1."
- The `xr:` scheme still satisfies `unique_tag: "az:"`, because each precomputed combination uses a different AZ in each region. "the `xr:` tag encodes the cluster/AZ combination while still adhering to the `unique_tag` requirement."
- Each server carries the plain `rg:` and `az:` tags in addition to its `xr:` tags so that regional streams can be placed with `--tag=rg:N`; `unique_tag: "az:"` then spreads the three replicas over the region's three AZs. "the standard `rg:` (region) and `az:` (AZ) tags are set to support _regional_ streams."
- Each of the nine servers carries exactly two `xr:` tags (e.g. `rg1-az1` has `xr:123, xr:132`), so that every `xr:` combination matches exactly three servers, one per region.
- Observed output: `--tag=xr:123` placed EVENTS on `rg1-az1, rg2-az2, rg3-az3`; `--tag=rg:2` placed ORDERS on `rg2-az1, rg2-az2, rg2-az3`. The stream info reports these as `Placement Tags` rather than `Placement Cluster`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Replace cluster nodes**

- Removing a peer is done with `nats server raft peer-remove --force <name>` using a system-account user; lame duck is signalled with `nats-server --signal ldm=<pidfile>`.
- Node configs set `pid_file` (used for signalling lame duck / stop) and per-node `jetstream.store_dir`, `max_memory_store` and `max_file_store` (1 GiB each in the demo).
- The demo uses one R3 file stream (unlimited) and one R3 memory stream capped at 100k messages so that both storage types are exercised by the migration; both are watched via `nats stream report` and `nats consumer report` during migration.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — NATS Streaming to JetStream Migration**

- The stan2js tool migrates NATS Streaming channels to JetStream streams and STAN subscriptions to JetStream consumers; it is a one-time exercise run once per set of channels. "This is a one time exercise and stan2js only needs to be run once for each set of STAN channels that require migration to JetStream streams."
- The stan2js config declares which channels and subscriptions to migrate plus a subset of stream/consumer options; the options are not exhaustive because many stream and consumer options can be changed after the migration. "These options are not exhaustive since many options on streams and consumers can be changed after the migration."
- Per channel the config can set the target stream name and options such as `replicas`, `max_consumers`, `max_bytes`, `max_age`; per client subscription it can set the consumer name, whether to convert to pull (`pull: true`), and a queue name.
- Observed output: STAN channel sequence numbers are re-based in JetStream (foo `501 -> 1`, `1000 -> 500`); the migrated streams contain only the messages the channel still held under its STAN `max_msgs` limit (500 for foo, 700 for bar, 1000 for baz).
- Observed output: each migrated message carries headers `Nats-Streaming-Channel`, `Nats-Streaming-Sequence` and `Nats-Streaming-Timestamp` preserving the original STAN channel, sequence and publish time.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Programmatic NKeys and JWTs**
