- The only requirement to enable JetStream for an account is setting its disk and memory storage limits to non-zero; -1 means unlimited. "The only requirement to "enable" JetStream is setting the disk and memory limits to anything other than zero. -1 indicates "unlimited"."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Change Data Capture via Debezium**

- Change data capture on a database streams granular change events to other parts of the system as data changes; Debezium handles the database-specific capture and Debezium Server can sink directly into a NATS stream. "stream granular change events to other parts of the system as data changes."
- For Postgres, Debezium registers itself as a logical-replication target, converts the raw change to a standard event model, and publishes to a NATS stream named `DebeziumStream` by default. "it publishes to the configured NATS stream, by default, called `DebeziumStream`."
- Sink configuration uses `debezium.sink.type=nats-jetstream`, `create-stream=true` (Debezium creates the stream itself) and `subjects=postgres.*.*` to match the prefix/schema/table subject shape.
- Observed output: `nats stream subjects DebeziumStream` lists one subject per schema/table pair (`postgres.public.profile` 5 events, `postgres.public.books` 1 event), and each event payload carries `before`, `after`, `source` (db, schema, table, txId, lsn) and `op` (`c`, `u`, `d`).
- Observed output: update events had `before: null` and delete events had `before` with only the id and null columns (the narrative does not comment on this; it is what the default Postgres setup produced).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream (category)**

- JetStream is "An integrated subsystem providing distributed persistence."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Limits-based Stream**

- A stream binds a set of subjects; messages published to those subjects are persisted. "The mental model for a stream is that it binds a set of subjects for which messages published to those subjects will be persisted."
- A stream is implemented as an implicit server-side service: the published message is the request and the reply comes once the message has been persisted. JetStream publish is therefore "a convenience for sending a `nc.Request` and waiting for the acknowledgement."
- Limits-based retention is the default retention policy, and limits still apply to streams with other retention policies. "This policy is the default, however, limits still apply to streams with other retention policies."
- The stream limit choices are: maximum number of messages, maximum total size in bytes, maximum age of a message.
- There is a separate per-subject maximum-messages limit ("a specialized maximum messages limit that can be applied at the subject level").
- By default no limits are set, "which would require manually managing the ever-growing stream." Turn limits on and let the server truncate if any of them fit.
- Stream configuration can be changed dynamically on demand; JetStream supports "dynamically changing the stream configuration on-demand."
- Stream names are commonly uppercased to visually differentiate them from subjects, but this is not required.
- A stream binds one or more subjects which "almost always include wildcards."
- No two streams can have overlapping subjects, "otherwise the primary messages would be persisted twice."
- JetStream offers file and in-memory storage; file storage is the default and is required for data to survive crashes and restarts. "For durability of the stream data, file storage must be chosen to survive crashes and restarts."
- By default a stream has one replica and uses file storage (deno narrative). "By default, a stream will have one replica and use file storage."
- Async publish batches messages to the server and receives acknowledgements asynchronously; a batch is awaited via PublishAsyncComplete.
- Setting MaxMsgs to 10 on a 12-message stream truncates the two oldest messages; first sequence and first timestamp then reflect the third message.
- Limits combine: "Limits can be combined and whichever one is reached, it will be applied to truncate the stream."
- Max age truncation is not instantaneous on config update; messages remain visible until the age elapses ("we still see all the messages.. until a second passes").
- Max age is expressed in nanoseconds in the JS client (deno narrative): "the age is in nanoseconds, so 1000 milliseconds (1 second) converted to nanos."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Interest-based Stream**

- Interest retention "retains messages for as long as there are consumers which have interest in a particular message."
- With no consumers, published messages are immediately deleted from an interest stream. "By definition, they are immediately deleted from the stream since there are no consumers."
- An interest stream is a middle ground between core NATS at-most-once QoS (all subscribers must be connected to receive) and a pure limits-based stream.
- A message stays in an interest stream until, for each consumer whose filter overlaps it, a subscription bound to that consumer "successfully acks the message, terminates it, or the max redelivery has been reached."
- Interest retention is additive to stream limits; with `max-msgs` = 1 and discard-old, each new message deletes the prior one "regardless if any of the consumer subscriptions were available to process the message."
- If you need a stream that behaves as a queue, use a work-queue stream instead of an interest stream.
- Stream info on an empty interest stream after 3 publishes shows 0 messages, `last_seq` 3, and `first_seq` one greater than `last_seq`; first_seq "behaves as a sentinel value indicating the stream is empty."
- Interest is established by the existence of a consumer, not by active consumption. "it is not required to be actively consuming messages to show interest, but it is the presence of a consumer which the stream cares about."
- Each consumer is a separate view over the stream; if one consumer acked but another did not, the message is retained.
- A late consumer cannot retroactively show interest; messages deleted before it was created are gone. "this reinforces that a late consumer cannot retroactively show interest."
- Interest respects the consumer's FilterSubject: a consumer filtered to `events.mouse_clicked` is not interested in `events.input_focused`, so that message's retention depends only on consumers whose filter overlaps.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Work-queue Stream**

- Work-queue retention is for "queuing up messages that are intended to be processed once and only once."
- Work-queue retention decouples queuing from consumption: it "supports queuing up messages from publishers independent of consummption."
- Consumers on a work-queue stream must have non-overlapping (disjoint) filter subjects, unlike limits- and interest-based streams which support overlapping consumers. "if multiple consumers are bound to a work-queue stream, they must have disjoint filter subjects."
- Work-queue retention is additive to limits: with `max-msgs` = 1 and discard-old, every new message deletes the prior one regardless of whether any subscription processed it.
- Messages in a work-queue stream are removed once acked; after fetching and acking all queued messages, stream info shows no messages.
- A work-queue stream allows "at most one consumer with interest on a subject at any given time"; creating a second unfiltered consumer fails until the first is deleted.
- To run multiple consumers on a work-queue stream, give each a subject filter scoping it to a disjoint subset (example: `events.us.>` and `events.eu.>` per geo).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Multi-Stream Consumption (legacy)**

- To fan in messages across multiple streams, create a push consumer per stream with the same `DeliverSubject` and optionally the same `DeliverGroup`; each consumer then delivers to the clients subscribed to that subject and/or queue group.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Migration to new JetStream API**

- "deleting a stream will also delete all consumers on that stream."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject-Mapped Partitions**

- "A stream provides total order over the set of messages it stores." With replicas, each stream has a dedicated Raft group that replicates every published message to a majority of the replica servers.
- On a successful publish every replica has the same order of messages, and consumers always receive messages in stored order.
- A single serialized stream is highly performant; to scale out publishing or consumption, create N streams each representing a partition. "The trade-off introduced here is the ability to support concurrent publishes to N streams, while giving up total order across streams."
- Deterministic distribution of messages to a partition stream uses subject mapping with `partition(N, token)` (deterministic subject token partitioning); `events.*` mapped to `events.{{wildcard(1)}}.{{partition(5,1)}}` maps `events.1` to `events.1.4`, a partition number in 0..4.
- Each partition stream binds `events.*.<i>`; published messages are transparently routed and written to the partition stream, and `nats stream report` shows them spread across all streams.
- Synchronous publish (one ack per message) gives quite low throughput; async batch of 100 raises it; 5 concurrent publishers raise it a bit more. "throughput and latency will highly depend on the quality of the network, and the resources available on the servers."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — List Subjects for a Specific Stream**

- Stream state includes a map of subjects to message counts, "but the server only collects and returns that information if WithSubjectFilter is set with a non-empty subject filter." Use `>` to get all subjects.
- The subject map lists actual published subjects, not the wildcard templates the stream was configured with. "Wildcard subjects show the actual subject, not the template."
- A subject only appears in state once it has messages (deno: "there are no subjects in the state unless there are messages in the subject").
- The subject filter narrows the map to matching entries (e.g. `greater.>` or `greater.A.>`).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Key-Value (category)**

- Key-Value is "A layer on top of JetStream for utilizing a stream as a key-value store."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Key-Value Intro**

- KV "is an abstraction over a stream which models message subjects as keys. It uses a standard set of stream configuration to be optimized for KV workloads."
- A KV bucket is "light abstraction over a standard stream. This is by design since it enables some powerful features." Internally a stream is created with the `KV_` prefix by convention.
- Because a bucket is a normal stream, a consumer can be created on it and each Put arrives as a stream message.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Object-Store (category)**

- Object-Store is "A layer on top of JetStream for utilizing a stream as an object store."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Object-Store Intro**

- Object store is "an abstraction over a stream which models message subjects as keys similar to KV, but with payloads that span multiple chunks," for larger assets "typically loaded and read as readable/writable streams."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream Deep Dive**

- JetStream is the part of NATS that stores messages; stored messages can be read again later and replayed as many times as needed. "Once a message is stored, you can read it again later, and replay it as many times as you need."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first stream**

- Plain core NATS drops a message the moment no service is listening; a stream saves it instead. "Plain core NATS drops any of these messages the moment no service is listening. A stream saves them instead."
- A stream is a server-side store that keeps every message on the subjects you choose, readable minutes or a month later.
- Stream names are case-sensitive and cannot contain dots, `*`, `>`, spaces, or slashes. "They can't contain dots, `*`, `>`, spaces, or slashes, so a subject like `orders.created` won't work as a name."
- A stream bound to a wildcard such as `orders.>` captures any current or future subject under that prefix with no stream change. "So would `orders.refunded` next month, with no change to the stream."
- Default stream config: Replicas 1, Storage File, Retention Limits, Discard Policy Old, Duplicate Window 2m0s, all Maximum limits (Messages, Per Subject, Bytes, Age, Message Size, Consumers) unlimited.
- The CLI turns Direct Get on by default when creating a stream; client libraries leave it off unless you set it. "The CLI turns direct get on by default, so that line shows here; client libraries leave it off unless you set it."
- A new stream is empty and the first message published gets sequence 1.
- Replicas 1 means the stream lives on one server and goes down with it; fine on a laptop, risky in production. "If that server goes down, the stream goes down with it."
- Storage File writes messages to disk; memory storage is faster but lost on restart. "The other option is memory, which is faster but lost on restart."
- Retention Limits keeps messages until a size, age, or count limit is hit; Interest and WorkQueue delete messages once a consumer has read them.
- Discard Policy Old deletes the oldest messages to make room when a limit is hit; Discard New turns away new messages when the stream is full.
- On a real cluster you'd always set at least one of Maximum Messages / Bytes / Age / Message Size. "On a real cluster you'd always set at least one of these."
- Duplicate Window default is 2 minutes: for that long after a message is stored, the server turns away a second message carrying the same `Nats-Msg-Id` header.
- Only one stream can keep a given subject; creating a second stream whose subjects overlap is rejected with error 10065 "subjects overlap with an existing stream".
- The overlap check covers any overlap, not just an identical filter: with `orders.>` taken, `orders.*` or even the single subject `orders.created` is rejected the same way.
- The single-stream-per-subject rule exists so JetStream always knows which stream a message on a subject goes into.
- To keep overlapping subjects in more than one stream, use mirrors (copy of one other stream) and sources (pull from several streams into one).
- Unlimited defaults grow forever: with `--defaults` the stream keeps every message until the disk fills, and a full disk takes the server down. "a production stream needs at least one limit so old orders age out before the disk does."
- A stream name is permanent; there is no rename, and the server rejects any update that changes the name with `stream configuration name must match original`. "The only way to 'rename' `ORDERS` is to delete it and create a new stream, which loses every order already stored."
- If you outgrow a stream name, add a new stream on new subjects and let the old one age out rather than delete-and-recreate.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publishing**

- Publishing into a stream works like a normal NATS publish except the server sends back a `PubAck` confirmation that it stored the message.
- Stream sequence numbers start at 1, only increase, and are never reused. "Sequence numbers start at `1` and only increase. The server gives each new message the next number and never reuses one."
- You publish to a subject, not to a stream; the server finds the stream that captures the subject. "Your code doesn't need to know which stream is bound to which subject."
- A `PubAck` has three regularly-used fields: stream, sequence, duplicate; it may also carry situational fields such as `domain` for multi-tenant or leaf-node setups.
- Saving the PubAck sequence next to your business record lets you replay the stream from that point later.
- The `PubAck` is your only proof that the message was stored. "The rule: the `PubAck` is your only proof that the message was stored."
- A publish to a subject no stream captures fails immediately with "no responders" and nothing was stored; a network timeout means no confirmation, not no write. "the server may have stored the message and the ack got lost on the way back."
- A `PubAck` confirms storage, not delivery; storage and delivery are separate and can be minutes, hours, or days apart. "It does not confirm that any consumer has received it."
- Tag retryable publishes with a `Nats-Msg-Id` header; the server refuses to store the same ID twice within the stream's duplicate-tracking window and returns `duplicate: true` with the original sequence.
- Give every publish you might retry a stable `Nats-Msg-Id` the producer can recompute, such as an order ID, a request ID, or a hash of the payload.
- The duplicate-tracking window is a stream setting (`Duplicate Window`), not a header.
- Atomic batch publish (all-or-nothing group store) requires server 2.12+; fast-ingest batch publish (flow-controlled, no atomicity) requires server 2.14+.
- Expected-stream and expected-sequence headers fail a publish unless the stream is in a specific state, for optimistic concurrency.
- Ignoring the `PubAck`: code that discards it can't tell a stored message from a lost one; plain `nats pub` prints `Published N bytes` whether or not a stream captured the subject. "That line doesn't prove the message was stored."
- Retrying without a `Nats-Msg-Id` can store the message twice; the duplicate window is two minutes by default, so a retry arriving after that also stores a second copy. "Don't retry a bare publish."
- Treating "published" as "delivered": a `PubAck` means the stream stored the message, not that a consumer processed it. "Keep business outcomes separate from the publish."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reading back the stream**

- Three pieces move a message through JetStream: a producer (publishes, reads PubAck, retries), a stream (stores in order, assigns stream sequence), and a consumer (server-side cursor a client connects to).
- A stream can feed many consumers at once, each reading at its own pace and each with its own position.
- Stream messages are durable records with fixed sequences; reading does not remove or move them. "Reading message 1 leaves message 1 where it was, available to the next reader."
- A new consumer created a month later starts at the same sequence 1 as one created today.
- Stream sequence is the message's fixed position in the log, assigned at publish and never changed; consumer sequence is the consumer's own delivery counter.
- Reading a stream doesn't remove its data; unlike taking an item off a queue, the messages stay in place for the next reader.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Filtering what you consume**

- The filter lives on the consumer; nothing about the stream changes. "The stream still captures all of `orders.>`; nothing about the stream changes."
- Expecting a filter to delete from the stream: a filter narrows one consumer's view and never removes messages. "Don't use a filter to prune a stream."
- Filter overlap between consumers is fine on limits and interest streams; on work-queue retention, consumers' filters must not overlap each other.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Delivery and acknowledgment**

- At-least-once relies on both the durable stream and the consumer's ack loop.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Ack responses and redelivery**

- After a term the message is gone from this consumer but not from the stream under Limits retention; on WorkQueue or Interest a term removes it just as an ack would.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling a consumer**

- Sharing is a property of the consumer, not the stream; workers share a position, not the messages, and an ack advances the position without removing the message under Limits retention.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Pausing a consumer**

- While a consumer is paused the stream keeps accepting messages; pause stops delivery, not storage.
- Pausing does not stop publishers: new messages count toward the stream's limits, and a long pause on a tight `MaxMsgs`/`MaxBytes` stream can drop the oldest messages before the consumer reads them. "Size the stream for the longest pause you expect, or keep pauses short."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Shaping the stream**

- Without a limit, a stream grows until it fills the disk and takes the server down with it.
- Under Limits retention, three independent caps are all active at once: MaxAge (age), MaxBytes (disk), MaxMsgs (count); whichever is reached first triggers a discard. "You don't have to set all three."
- MaxAge fits when only recent events matter; MaxBytes protects the server itself; MaxMsgs fits when message count is what you reason about.
- `nats stream edit` changes limits in place; messages already stored stay where they are (editing limits doesn't discard messages already within them).
- Maximum Message Size is a cap on a single message, not the whole stream.
- Discard Old (default): when a limit is hit the server discards the oldest messages; the publish always succeeds.
- Discard New: when a size or count limit (`MaxMsgs`, `MaxBytes`, or a per-subject cap) is hit the server rejects the publish with an error and nothing stored is dropped.
- MaxAge is not a Discard-policy choice; it expires stored messages on its own timer under either policy. "the first limit to hit applies."
- Use Discard Old for a rolling window of recent events; use Discard New when discarding an old message would lose data you're required to keep and you'd rather slow the publisher. Discard New is the less common choice because the publisher must handle rejected publishes.
- A limit discards a message for everyone; a consumer's position or filter doesn't protect a message from the stream's limits. "If a consumer is too slow and a message ages out before that consumer reads it, the message is gone."
- `MaxMsgsPerSubject` limits messages per subject rather than across the whole stream (e.g. last hundred per subject).
- Discard Old discards the oldest message silently with no warning to the publisher; switch to Discard New to reject the publish (`maximum bytes exceeded` / `maximum messages exceeded`) instead. Discard New still leaves MaxAge in force, so remove or raise the age limit too if you must keep history.
- A seven-day MaxAge does not guarantee seven days of history: a traffic spike can hit MaxBytes first and discard messages only hours old. "Set MaxBytes for your busiest traffic, not your average, if the age window matters to you."
- Whole-stream limits don't balance across subjects: a high-volume subject counts toward the same ceiling, so Discard Old can discard a shipped order to make room for a created one. Add `MaxMsgsPerSubject` when each subject needs its own limit.
- Under Discard New a per-subject limit still rolls by default (discards the subject's oldest); rejecting requires `DiscardNewPerSubject` (`discard_new_per_subject`) on top of Discard New, which fails the publish with `maximum messages per subject exceeded`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Retention policies**

- Limits decide when a message leaves because the stream ran out of room; the retention policy decides whether a message leaves because a consumer finished with it. "A message capped only by age or size stays until its limit hits, read or unread, acked or not."
- A stream has exactly one retention policy: Limits (default), Interest, or WorkQueue.
- Limits: messages stay until MaxMsgs, MaxBytes, or MaxAge is reached; consumers reading and acking has no effect on what the stream keeps.
- Interest: a message is removed once every consumer whose filter covers it has acked it; if no consumer is interested in a subject, a message on that subject is removed right away.
- WorkQueue: a message is kept only until one consumer acks it; the first ack removes it for everyone, so each message is delivered once and then removed.
- Limits still apply under all three policies; on Interest or WorkQueue streams the limits are the backstop when consumers fall behind. "retention doesn't replace limits, it adds a second way a message can leave."
- Audit log or event history → Limits (replay from any point, late consumers, re-reads). "Limits is the only policy that allows that"
- Fan-out where every consumer must process each message → Interest (fan-out delivery without an ever-growing log).
- Job queue where each message is work for one worker → WorkQueue (task removed on ack so no one does it twice).
- Keep the record log (Limits) and the work queue (WorkQueue) as separate streams; a worker publishes the completion event back to the log as it finishes.
- On a WorkQueue stream scale by adding workers to one consumer, not by adding consumers.
- Set retention at creation and leave it there; the server allows exactly one live change, swapping Limits and Interest in either direction; anything involving WorkQueue is locked.
- Even the allowed Limits→Interest swap applies to stored messages immediately: the server removes any message every consumer has acked and any message on a subject no consumer is interested in, including history you meant to keep.
- Treat the retention policy as fixed at creation; to change it, create a new stream with the right policy rather than editing the running one.
- Interest can fill the disk: a stalled consumer holds up cleanup for every message it owes an ack on, so the stream grows until its limits. "Interest retention still needs limits set, and it makes watching consumer health more important."
- WorkQueue allows more than one consumer only if their filters partition the subjects; each then handles only its slice. For several consumers that each see every message, use Interest or Limits.
- Retention to or from WorkQueue is locked after creation; the edit is rejected with `stream configuration update can not change retention policy to/from workqueue`. "Create a new stream with the policy you want and move the data."
- WorkQueue rejects consumers that overlap: a second unfiltered consumer fails with `multiple non-filtered consumers not allowed on workqueue stream`; overlapping filters fail with `filtered consumer not unique on workqueue stream`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Altering stream state**

- Delete-message and purge change what the stream holds without touching its config or consumers, and both leave sequence numbers alone.
- `nats stream rmm` securely removes a message: the server overwrites the stored bytes so the old contents can't be read back; right for a message that held data it shouldn't have (e.g. a card number).
- From a client library, `DeleteMsg(seq)` marks the message erased but leaves bytes until later overwritten (cheap); `SecureDeleteMsg(seq)` overwrites right away (slower). The server sees only a `no_erase` flag.
- Purge removes every message but keeps the stream: same config, same consumers, same name. `nats stream rm` deletes the whole stream, config and consumers included.
- Purge can be narrowed by `--subject`, `--seq` (drop everything older than a sequence), or `--keep` (retain a number of newest); `--seq` and `--keep` can't be combined, but either can pair with `--subject`.
- Sequence numbers never backfill: deleting sequence 2 leaves a hole, the server doesn't renumber 3, and never reuses 2. "sequence numbers only ever climb."
- After a full purge the next message gets the number after the last one the stream ever held, because purge sets the stream's first sequence to one past its last.
- Consumers skip deleted sequences; a consumer never blocks waiting for a deleted message, and a missing sequence is not redelivered.
- A stored sequence is a stable address: a saved pointer either still points at the same message or at nothing, never at a different message.
- Use delete and purge for one-off removals; use limits and TTL for the steady state.
- `purge` empties the stream; `rm` destroys it including config and every consumer. "don't type `rm` for that, and read the confirmation prompt before answering it."
- A deleted sequence is gone, not renumbered: code that assumes messages run 1..N with no holes breaks. "don't work out 'the next message' as `count + 1`, and don't read a message count as the highest sequence."
- A purge can't be undone: on a stream that matters set `DenyPurge` so a stray call can't wipe it, and keep a mirror if the data is worth recovering.
- Setting `DenyPurge` is permanent: the server refuses any later update that turns it off; the only way to purge again is delete and recreate the stream.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Surviving node loss**

- R=1 means the stream exists on exactly one server with no fault tolerance: lose that server and you lose every message and every consumer's position.
- R=3 is the production floor: three copies across three servers tolerate one server failure with no data loss and no manual recovery. "This is R=3, and it's the production floor."
- Replicas agree on message order by majority vote (Raft); the group keeps working as long as more than half its members are reachable.
- R=5 tolerates two simultaneous failures and is the maximum a stream supports. "Most production streams run R=3; R=5 is for state you can't afford to re-derive."
- Every write goes through the stream leader, which assigns the sequence, stores the message, and returns the `PubAck` only once a majority of replicas have it. "That's what makes the `PubAck` on an R=3 stream a real durability promise"
- Each consumer has its own leader that can sit on any of the stream's replicas, so delivery spreads across replica servers; a Direct Get can be answered by any replica, leader or not.
- On leader loss the remaining replicas elect a new leader automatically; writes pause for the election window, then resume. No acked message is lost because every acked message was already on a majority.
- A publish in flight when the leader crashed, not yet on a majority, is lost and never acked; the client must treat a missing `PubAck` as failed and resend. "The durability promise covers acked messages, not ones that were still on their way"
- If no majority remains (two of three gone), no leader can be elected and writes are blocked until enough replicas return. "The stream would rather stop than accept writes it couldn't safely copy to a majority."
- File storage is the default and the durable one; Memory storage keeps messages in RAM only and loses its copy on restart. "It's not suitable for an order log."
- Storage type is a property of the whole stream, not individual replicas; an R=3 stream is all file or all memory.
- R=3 memory storage survives a single server crash through replicas but loses everything if the whole group restarts at once.
- File storage doesn't sync every write to disk right away; a write can sit unsynced after its `PubAck` long enough that an OS crash could lose it.
- On a limits-retention stream a consumer may have fewer replicas than its stream (never more); on interest and work-queue streams the consumer replica count must match the stream's.
- Replicas are a durability control, not a throughput control; adding replicas is not how you scale throughput.
- R=3 is roughly three times the storage and write traffic of R=1; every write still goes through one leader, so a higher count lowers peak write throughput.
- To scale a consumer add workers; to scale writes past one leader split subjects across streams; to spread streams across servers use clustering.
- A single server rejects `--replicas=3` because there aren't three servers to hold the copies.
- Trusting R=1 in production: no recovery after disk loss because there was no second copy. "Before you trust a stream with real orders, check its replica count rather than assuming it."
- Setting an even replica count: R=2 still has a single point of failure (one of two can't form a majority, writes block); R=4 tolerates only one loss like R=3 while paying for a fourth copy. "Use odd counts: R=3 for the production floor, R=5 for state you can't re-derive."
- Reading failover from a single-server demo proves nothing about fault tolerance; prove failover on a real cluster.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Advanced publishing**

- One-at-a-time publish with a `PubAck` wait per message is the right default; most services never need anything else. "That's the right default, and most services never need anything else."
- Async publish fires each publish without waiting and collects acks later; the contract is unchanged (one `PubAck` per message, at-least-once storage), so you still check every ack.
- The async order trap: a failed publish is re-sent after later messages were stored, so the retry takes a higher sequence and lands after messages you sent next.
- If the ack was lost but the message stored, a stable `Nats-Msg-Id` makes the server drop the repeat; if order matters, set `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` so an out-of-order retry fails fast instead of silently landing in the wrong place.
- An async publish you never check is a lost write. "Firing publishes without reading the acks gives up the only guarantee a JetStream publish offers."
- Async publish is a client-library feature with no stream setting; Go, Java, .NET, Rust have a dedicated call returning a future; nats.js gathers un-awaited promises; nats.py has no first-class async publish (approximate with `asyncio.gather` plus your own concurrency limit); CLI async path is only `nats bench`.
- Atomic batch stores a group all-or-nothing; use it when several messages only make sense together (e.g. line items of one order).
- Atomic batch requires the stream to opt in with `AllowAtomicPublish`; the client uses `Nats-Batch-Id`, increasing `Nats-Batch-Sequence`, and `Nats-Batch-Commit` on the last message; the server stages and writes on commit; the committing `PubAck` carries `batch` and `count`.
- Atomic batch defaults: capped at 1,000 messages per batch and at most 50 batches in flight per stream; both are operator-configurable server limits, not fixed protocol caps.
- A sequence gap or over-limit atomic batch is rejected with an error `PubAck`; a batch that goes ten seconds without a message is dropped with no error reply, only a `stream_batch_abandoned` advisory. "Treat the final `PubAck` as the only proof the batch committed."
- Atomic batch client support: CLI and nats.js in the core client; Go, Java, Rust, .NET via Synadia Orbit; nats.py via raw `Nats-Batch-*` headers.
- Fast-ingest batch publish is built to replace async publish: the client opens one channel and the server runs flow control, acking in batches and telling each publisher how fast it may go.
- Fast-ingest trades away atomicity; a batch can run unbounded; per-batch gap handling: `gap: fail` abandons on the first gap (ordered data like object chunks), `gap: ok` reports and continues (e.g. metrics).
- Fast-ingest requires stream opt-in `AllowBatchPublish`; client support: CLI benchmark only, Go/Rust/nats.js via Synadia Orbit, Python/Java/.NET only the stream flag so far.
- Mode choice: one-at-a-time by default; async when one-at-a-time is too slow at volume; atomic batch when a group must land together; fast-ingest for maximum sustained throughput tolerating (or failing on) gaps.
- An async publish you never check is a lost write; collect and check every ack, and add `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` if order matters.
- An atomic batch can be abandoned: a gap or over-size (1,000 default) batch errors; ten seconds idle drops it silently with only an advisory. "don't assume a half-sent batch landed."
- `AllowAtomicPublish` and async persistence don't mix: a stream with `PersistMode: async` rejects atomic publishing because atomicity depends on the synchronous write path; fast-ingest batches are fine on such a stream.
- Fast-ingest `gap: ok` loses data on purpose; use it only when a hole is acceptable, otherwise `gap: fail` or an atomic batch.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mirrors and sources**

- A mirror is a read-only stream that continuously copies every message from exactly one upstream stream; behavior is specified in ADR-59.
- A mirror's copy is exact: same sequence number, same timestamp, same subject as upstream.
- A mirror listens on no subjects of its own, so it can't be published to directly; a publish lands in whatever stream owns the subject.
- A mirror keeps its own retention, independent of the upstream's limits (e.g. upstream seven days, mirror forever).
- A mirror's configuration is fixed at creation: you can't re-point it or add a filter later; delete and recreate, which is cheap because the new mirror catches up from the upstream.
- A source-fed stream pulls from one or many upstreams and merges them; messages from one upstream keep their order, but across upstreams there's no ordering guarantee and the aggregate assigns fresh sequence numbers.
- A sourced stream may also listen on its own subjects and accept direct publishes alongside sourced messages.
- Sources can change after creation: add, drop, or adjust a filter by updating the stream config.
- Use a mirror for a second copy of one stream: a read replica near a remote region, a stream that survives loss of the upstream's cluster, or a long-retention archive of a short-retention stream.
- Use sources to combine many streams: merging per-region or per-tenant streams for reporting, or a derived view from several streams.
- Mirror/source info: `Lag` is how many messages behind (0 = caught up; climbing and staying high means it can't keep pace); `Last Seen` is time since last message or heartbeat (small, steady is healthy).
- A mirror catches up on its own with no consumer and no client code; each source replicates independently with its own Lag and Last Seen.
- A mirror or source can filter subjects, rewrite subjects with a subject transform, or reach a stream in another account or JetStream domain via the `external` field.
- Treating a mirror as writable: a publish routes to the origin stream; forcing with `Nats-Expected-Stream: <mirror>` is rejected with `expected stream does not match` (error 10060). "publish to the upstream `ORDERS` and let the mirror copy the message on its own."
- Treating mirror contents as real-time: a mirror is eventually consistent and `Lag` climbs during write bursts. "Don't assume a message in `ORDERS` is already in `ORDERS-ARCHIVE` the instant it lands."
- Combining `filter_subject` and `subject_transforms` on one source or mirror entry is rejected; a transform filters and renames in one step, so pick one.
- Cross-domain config fails silently: the consumer API and flow-control subjects must be service exports, the delivery subject a stream export; a wrong type doesn't error, the mirror just never catches up.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reading messages directly**

- A stream-get (by sequence or last-for-subject) is a lighter read than a consumer for a point read: no consumer to create, no position to track.
- "Get the last message on this subject" is the read a key-value lookup is built on; a KV bucket is a stream keyed by subject.
- `nats stream get` asks the stream's leader, the one server with the latest write, so a get right after a publish always sees it.
- Direct Get answers the same reads from any server holding a copy of the stream, not only the leader; use it for reads you run often or from far away.
- Direct Get is the stream's `allow_direct` setting; `nats stream info` shows `Direct Get: true` when on and no line when off. The CLI enables it for new streams.
- When a mirror sets `mirror_direct`, the mirror's servers also answer Direct Get requests for the origin, so a reader can be served by a nearby mirror.
- Direct Get is not read-after-write coherent: a replica or mirror can trail the leader, so a just-published message may not appear on a direct read for a beat. "When you must see your own most recent write, read the leader with `nats stream get`."
- Direct Get suits latest-value lookups that tolerate a little staleness (a cache, a dashboard) in exchange for spreading load.
- A batched Direct Get streams matching messages over one request; each carries a `Nats-Num-Pending` header that reaches 0 on the last message. A batch is bounded by a count or byte budget (`batch`, `max_bytes`, `multi_last`).
- nats.js sends batched Direct Get natively; Go, Rust, Java, and C# reach it through Synadia Orbit helper libraries.
- Direct Get for point reads (one by sequence, latest on a subject, bounded batch snapshot: nothing acked, no position, any replica answers); a consumer to work through the log (in order, durable position, ack, follow new messages).
- A direct read never moves a consumer's position and never removes a message.
- Direct Get off makes the read hang: with `allow_direct` unset no server answers and the request times out with nothing returned.
- A direct read can be stale; don't use it for read-after-write checks such as confirming a publish landed. "keep Direct Get for high-volume or far-away reads that tolerate a little lag."
- A direct batch isn't a subscription: it returns matching stored messages and stops; use a consumer to follow the stream as it grows.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject mapping and transforms**

- Subject mapping rewrites a subject in three places: a stream subject transform on the way in, republish on the way out, and per-source/mirror transforms while copying; all use the same transform language.
- A stream subject transform rewrites the stored subject for matching messages; non-matching messages keep their original subject. "A transform rewrites subjects; it never drops a message."
- A common transform use is deterministic partitioning: hash a token into a fixed set of buckets so consumers filtered to one bucket always read the same share.
- A transform affects only messages stored from the moment it's set; it doesn't touch messages already in the stream.
- Republish re-emits every stored message onto a second subject in real time so core subscribers can watch a stream without a consumer; a low-cost way to feed a dashboard or monitor.
- Republished messages carry `Nats-Stream`, `Nats-Subject`, `Nats-Sequence`, `Nats-Time-Stamp`, and `Nats-Last-Sequence` (previous sequence on the same subject, or 0), plus any publisher headers; `--republish-headers` sends headers only with a `Nats-Msg-Size` header.
- A republish destination that overlaps the stream's own subjects is rejected as a cycle (error 10052); use a separate subject space, and watch for loops spanning two streams in one account, which the server can't always catch.
- Editing a transform doesn't rewrite what's already stored; to re-namespace existing data, copy it into a new stream that sources from the old one with the transform applied.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Per-message TTL**

- `MaxAge` applies one deadline to every message in the stream; a per-message TTL attaches a lifespan to one message so the server deletes it after a stated time even when `MaxAge` would keep it longer.
- TTL is set with the `Nats-TTL` publish header (duration like `1h`, `5s`, `30m`), counted from when the message was stored.
- Per-message TTL is off by default; the stream must opt in with `AllowMsgTTL`, and a stream rejects a `Nats-TTL` header until then.
- Turning `AllowMsgTTL` on cannot be reversed; the server refuses to turn it back off.
- Per-message TTL needs server 2.11 or newer; on older servers the setting doesn't exist and the edit has no effect.
- A message lives until the first deadline that arrives: the earlier of per-message TTL and stream `MaxAge` applies. "A per-message TTL only ever makes a message expire sooner than `MaxAge` would, never later, with one exception"
- `Nats-TTL: never` makes a message permanent: it never expires, not even at the stream's `MaxAge`, until something deletes it on purpose (e.g. a schema definition or baseline snapshot).
- A TTL is a deadline on the stored copy and says nothing about delivery; if no consumer reads and acks before the deadline the message expires unread.
- `SubjectDeleteMarkerTTL` can leave a delete marker in place of an expired message, but only when the expired message was the last one on its subject; on an active subject with newer messages no marker is placed.
- Size the TTL shorter than the time in which the message still matters but long enough for a healthy consumer to keep up.
- The TTL must be at least one second; a sub-second or zero `Nats-TTL` is rejected with invalid-TTL error (`err_code` 10165) and nothing is stored.
- A valid `Nats-TTL` on a stream that hasn't opted in is rejected with TTL-disabled error (`err_code` 10166); no message stored. The server never quietly drops the header.
- A TTL header on a stream that never opted in fails the publish; it does not store the message without a TTL instead. "Don't publish a TTL message and walk away on a stream you haven't confirmed opted in."
- A short TTL deletes the message whether or not a consumer read it; a consumer holding a message doesn't pause its TTL. "Do size the TTL to outlast the lag of your slowest healthy consumer."
- Turning `AllowMsgTTL` on can't be undone; the stream keeps the feature for life. "Don't flip it on to test something and expect to undo it."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Stream and consumer policies**

- There are nine policies (five stream, four consumer); each has a safe default, and five of the nine are fixed the moment the stream or consumer exists.
- Retention: `limits` keeps until a cap removes; `interest` and `workqueue` remove once consumers have acked.
- Discard: `old` deletes the oldest messages to make room; `new` refuses the publish.
- Storage: `file` survives restart; `memory` is faster and gone on restart; the choice applies to the whole stream, replicas included.
- Compression `s2` (default `none`) makes a file-storage stream compress message blocks on disk, spending CPU for disk; JSON compresses well, images don't. Editing later is allowed but takes effect only after the stream's store restarts (server restart or leader change), and blocks already on disk stay as they are.
- Persist mode: default flushes to storage before the `PubAck`; `async` acks first and flushes in the background, buying ingest rate for a window in which a crash can lose acked messages. "it fits data that arrives in volume and tolerates a lost tail, such as metrics — not an order log."
- `async` persist mode is only accepted on a file-storage stream with a single replica, and an `async` stream refuses atomic batch publishing.
- Live-stream changeability: Retention `limits`↔`interest` allowed (re-applies to stored messages), to/from `workqueue` refused; Discard can change; Storage fixed at creation; Compression can change (effective after restart); Persist mode fixed at creation.
- Changing a fixed policy means recreating the object: storage edit fails with `stream configuration update can not change storage type`; deliver policy update fails with `deliver policy can not be updated`. Recreating a consumer loses the saved position.
- Two features answer to "last per subject"; check which feature a flag or value belongs to before copying it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next**

- Core model: a stream is a server-side log; a consumer is a position marker tracked separately from every other consumer; an ack is how a reader says a message is handled, and until then the server resends it after a timeout. "A stored message has not yet been processed."
- A key-value bucket is a stream underneath: keys become subjects, history becomes sequence numbers, a watch is a consumer; retention and limits apply directly.
- An object store splits an object across many messages in a stream and reassembles it on read.
- Checklist: Stay on plain pub-sub when the next message supersedes the last; reach for a stream only when a missed message has consequences.
- Checklist: Set at least one limit (`MaxAge`, `MaxBytes`, or `MaxMsgs`) so an unbounded stream never fills the disk.
- Checklist: Pick the stream name deliberately the first time; there's no rename, only delete-and-recreate.
- Checklist: Choose the retention policy before messages flow; switching to or from WorkQueue on a live stream is rejected.
- Checklist: Read the `PubAck` back; a plain `nats pub` line isn't proof the message was stored.
- Checklist: Give every retryable publish a stable `Nats-Msg-Id` so a retry doesn't double-store.
- Checklist: Wait for delivery and ack before acting on a business outcome; a `PubAck` means stored, not processed.
- Checklist: Decide retention through stream limits, not filters; a filter narrows a view, it never deletes messages.
- Checklist: Size the stream for the longest pause you expect; publishes keep landing and count against the limits while a consumer sleeps.
- Checklist: Switch to Discard New when you need backpressure; Discard Old drops the oldest message silently.
- Checklist: Size `MaxBytes` for your peak, not your average, when the age window matters; either limit can fire first.
- Checklist: Add `MaxMsgsPerSubject` when each subject deserves its own retention; whole-stream limits let one noisy subject starve a quiet one.
- Checklist: Create a new stream to move to or from WorkQueue; the server locks that change on a live stream.
- Checklist: Give each WorkQueue consumer a disjoint filter, or share one consumer as a pool; overlapping consumers are rejected.
- Checklist: Watch disk on an Interest stream with a stopped consumer; interest means messages wait for every registered consumer's ack.
- Checklist: Treat a live switch from Limits to Interest as destructive; it re-applies to stored messages and can drop already-acked history.
- Checklist: Confirm `Allows Per-Message TTL` is on before relying on `Nats-TTL`; a header on an opted-out stream fails the publish.
- Checklist: Size a TTL to outlast the slowest healthy consumer's lag; the clock deletes the stored copy whether or not it was read.
- Checklist: Set `SubjectDeleteMarkerTTL` only when consumers must learn a value expired, and keep it at or below your shortest TTL.
- Checklist: Use `nats stream purge` to clear messages and `nats stream rm` to delete the stream; don't swap the two.
- Checklist: Treat a sequence as a stable address that may hold no message; never assume messages run `1..N` without gaps.
- Checklist: Set `DenyPurge` on a stream that matters, and keep a mirror; a purge can't be undone.
- Checklist: Confirm the replica count before trusting a stream with real orders; R=1 has no copy to recover from.
- Checklist: Use odd replica counts: R=3 for the production floor, R=5 for state you can't re-derive.
- Checklist: Prove failover on a real cluster; a green single-node run can't show leader election or a node loss.
- Checklist: Collect and check every `PubAck` on an async publish; add `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` when order matters so a retry fails fast.
- Checklist: Treat the final `PubAck` as the only proof an atomic batch committed; a sequence gap, an oversized batch, or a ten-second idle drops the whole batch.
- Checklist: Keep atomic publishing off a stream set to `PersistMode: async`; the server rejects it, though fast-ingest batches are fine there.
- Checklist: Choose `gap: ok` only when a lost message is acceptable; use `gap: fail` or an atomic batch for anything you can't lose.
- Checklist: Publish to the upstream stream, not the mirror; a mirror captures no subjects, and forcing it by name errors with `expected stream does not match`.
- Checklist: Read the `Lag` field before assuming a mirror is current; a mirror is eventually consistent, not synchronous.
- Checklist: Pick `filter_subject` or `subject_transforms` on one entry, never both; the server rejects a config that sets both.
- Checklist: Verify each export type for cross-domain sourcing; a wrong type lets the mirror silently never catch up.
- Checklist: Confirm `Direct Get: true`, or set `--allow-direct`, before a direct read; without it the request just times out.
- Checklist: Keep direct reads off read-after-write checks; they can answer from a trailing replica, so read with `nats stream get` against the leader there.
- Checklist: Use a consumer, not a direct batch, when you need to follow the stream; a batch reads the backlog once and stops.
- Checklist: Point a republish destination at a separate subject space, not one under the stream's own subjects; an overlap is rejected as a cycle (`10052`).
- Checklist: Re-namespace existing data by sourcing it into a new stream with the transform; editing a transform leaves already-stored messages untouched.
- Checklist: Settle the fixed policies (storage, persist mode, deliver, ack, and replay) before creating anything durable; `stream edit` and `consumer edit` can't change them.
- Checklist: Plan the data move when a fixed policy must change; recreating a stream needs a mirror or a re-publish, and a recreated consumer starts fresh.
- Checklist: Check whether "last per subject" means the deliver policy or the Direct Get flag before copying a command.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Core NATS Deep Dive**

- When messages must wait for a subscriber, survive a restart, or be replayed, add a stream (JetStream) on top of core NATS.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject mapping**

- Account-level (server-config) mapping runs on plain core subjects before any stream is involved; a stream's subject transform or republish is a different, stream-configured mechanism.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Raft and leaders**

- Plain core traffic needs no agreement; stored data does: the servers holding a replicated stream's copies must agree on which messages exist and in what order.
- Every replicated stream and every replicated consumer gets its own RAFT group; the stream leader is the server that accepts writes to the stream.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Replication and R=3**

- A stream's replica count is the number of copies; each copy lives on a different server and the servers holding them form one RAFT group. Every write goes through the leader; followers never take writes directly.
- Three is the minimum replica count for production, and a stream supports at most R=5. "Three is the minimum for production, and a stream supports at most `R=5`."
- Raising R=1 to R=3 is done in place with `nats stream edit --replicas=3`; application code doesn't change.
- The leader appends a write locally, sends an append entry to each follower, and counts acks; the write is committed once a quorum (majority) holds it. For R=3 that's two of three, so one follower ack suffices.
- Commit is the point at which durability is reached: a committed entry survives the loss of any single server. The leader returns `PubAck` only after commit.
- The third peer isn't on the critical path; the group makes progress as long as a majority is reachable.
- Apply copies a committed entry from the log into the stream store; the leader's commit index rides on the next append entry or heartbeat. Every peer applies the same entries in the same order, so copies converge; a follower can lag but never reorders or skips.
- Reads from the leader are read-after-write; reads from a follower can lag (correct but slightly behind). For read-after-write, read from the leader.
- JetStream doesn't `fsync` every write; it batches disk syncs on `sync_interval`, which defaults to 2 minutes. Until the next sync an applied write can sit in the OS write cache. "`sync_interval`, which defaults to 2 minutes."
- A `PubAck` only confirms quorum; quorum commit protects against losing a server, not against losing a server's disk. Two peers can hold a write in memory and still lose it if hardware fails before either syncs.
- `sync_interval: always` closes the window entirely (every write syncs before `PubAck`) at the cost of the slowest writes; combined with peers spread across availability zones it gives the strongest durability available.
- The 2-minute default balances risk against performance for a typical production deployment spread across multiple availability zones; log divergence needs several independent faults landing in a specific order.
- Mitigation after a crash: wait until `nats stream info` shows the remaining peers fully caught up before restarting the crashed server, or remove the crashed peer and let it rejoin wiped and resync over the network.
- `sync_interval: always` costs performance cluster-wide, even for streams that don't need it; weigh before turning it on everywhere.
- Run most clusters on the default `sync_interval` and add a separate cluster tagged (e.g. `server_tags: ["sync:always"]`) with `sync_interval: always`; place only the streams needing strongest durability there via placement tags.
- R=1 has no copy: no second peer, no quorum; if that server's disk is lost the data is lost with no failover. Only R>=3 survives a node loss; don't run real orders at R=1. "`R=1` has no copy."
- A follower read can be stale; don't assume any peer is current just because the write was acked. "A follower may lag, so a follower read can be stale."
- A `PubAck` proves quorum, not full replication; if you need every copy current (before taking a server down), verify each replica shows `current` in `nats stream info` first. "A `PubAck` proves quorum, not full replication."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Placement**

- Without placement the meta leader puts replicas on any servers in the cluster with capacity; with placement it must honor the constraint or refuse to create the stream.
- Placement has two levers: a cluster name (every replica must live there; a no-op in a single cluster, useful to pin a stream to one region) and server tags.
- Tag matching is an intersection: a server qualifies only if it carries every tag in the list, never either-or.
- Tag matching folds case (`disk:ssd` equals `disk:SSD`) but spelling is exact; an unmatched tag fails with `no suitable peers for placement, tags not matched [...] (10005)`.
- Asking for three replicas when only two servers carry the required tags fails the same way; placement doesn't relax the constraint to fit the replica count.
- Placement cannot name a leader: a `preferred` server in placement is rejected with `preferred server not permitted in placement`, and no client library exposes such a field.
- Tags are an intersection; a missing tag fails the placement rather than falling back to any server. Read tags back from servers first, then place against exactly what they advertise. "Tags are an intersection; a missing tag fails the placement."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling and peer management**

- You grow a stream's group by raising its replica count; the meta leader assigns the extra replica to a server qualifying under the stream's placement. The new server must already be a cluster member.
- A new peer catches up by streaming the entries it's missing from the leader; lag is a count of entries behind.
- Adding a peer changes the quorum right away: an R=4 group commits once three peers hold a write, not two. A new empty peer can't win an election until the leader's first entries reach it.
- Don't lean on a new peer as a data-bearing replica until `stream info` shows it `current`.
- `peer-remove` doesn't shrink the stream: it evicts the replica from the named server and the meta leader re-places it elsewhere, keeping the replica count. If the evicted peer held leadership, the group elects a new leader first.
- If placement leaves nowhere to re-place the replica, an R>1 stream still loses the peer and returns `peer remap failed`, leaving the group a replica short; only a single-replica stream is spared.
- `peer-remove` moves a replica between servers; `nats stream edit --replicas` sets how many replicas there are.
- Don't stack membership changes before the replacement catches up; a second change can drop the peers holding the data below the majority and the group stops committing. Make one change, wait for a named leader and a caught-up replacement, then the next. "Don't stack membership changes before the replacement catches up."
- If `stream info` shows `no leader` after a change, stop: you've lost quorum and the fix is to restore a peer, not make another change.
- A freshly added peer isn't safe until its lag is zero; it can't win an election or serve a read while catching up, and killing another server mid-catchup can stall the group. "A freshly added peer isn't safe until its lag is zero."
- Removing the only peer needs `--force` (`removing the only peer on a stream will result in data loss`), and even forced the server answers `peer remap failed`; change the count with `nats stream edit --replicas` instead. "Removing the only peer needs `--force`, and forcing it doesn't move the data."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Clustering)**

- Checklist: Run real orders at R>=3, never R=1; a single copy is gone with its server's disk.
- Checklist: Read from the leader when you need read-after-write; a follower can lag, so a Direct Get from one returns data that's correct but not the newest.
- Checklist: Read a `PubAck` as quorum held, not full replication; before deliberately taking a server down, verify each replica shows `current`.
- Checklist: Read a server's tags back before placing against them; tags are an intersection and a missing one fails rather than falling back.
- Checklist: Spell tags exactly; matching folds case but a misspelling matches nothing.
- Checklist: Placement can't name a leader; to move leadership to a specific server use `step-down --preferred` (NATS Server 2.11+) and treat it as a request the election can overrule.
- Checklist: Make one membership change at a time; stacking a second before the replacement is `current` can drop the data-holding peers below a majority and the stream stops committing.
- Checklist: Wait for a freshly added peer to show `current` with zero lag before trusting it; don't kill another server mid-catchup.
- Checklist: Change the replica count with `nats stream edit --replicas`, not by removing the last peer.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topologies Deep Dive**

- Every shape does two separate jobs: core messaging (routes, gateways, leaf connections carry messages to matching interest) and JetStream (stores and replicates across the servers the topology provides).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Single server**

- On one server JetStream gives durability against a crash (messages survive a process restart) but never against loss of the server itself; lose that disk and you lose the stream.
- A single server can't hold a replicated stream: asking for three replicas answers `replicas > 1 not supported in non-clustered mode`; redundancy is a cluster's job, don't treat the error as a config typo to override. "Reaching for redundancy too late."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream in a cluster**

- A JetStream cluster elects one meta leader that owns every decision about where streams and consumers live; every JetStream-enabled server belongs to the meta group. You don't choose which server wins.
- The meta leader decides where a stream lives but doesn't handle writes to it; writes go through the stream's own replication.
- A write is never stored on a single copy that a majority hasn't confirmed.
- R1 is the default replica factor unless you ask for more; R3 is the production floor, and a three-server cluster is exactly enough to hold it. "Three copies is `R3`, the production floor"
- Replication stays inside one cluster; the cluster is the unit a stream is replicated across. Each stream gets its own Raft group separate from the meta group.
- The stream leader takes every write first, sends it to the replicas, and the write is acknowledged only once a majority hold it; `current` means a replica has recently checked in and holds the same data.
- The stream leader is chosen independently of the meta leader; you configure neither.
- Consumers replicate too: each consumer gets its own Raft group and leader, chosen independently of the stream's, so a consumer can lead on one server while its stream leads on another.
- An R1 stream on a cluster still has no HA; the cluster around it changes nothing. Audit replica counts (`nats stream find --replicas=1`) and raise the streams that matter to R3; `nats server check stream --peer-expect=3` exits non-zero when under-replicated. "An R1 stream on a cluster still has no HA."
- All three replicas in one failure domain defeat R3: three copies survive one loss only if the servers can fail independently; spread across one rack or one availability zone a single power or network event takes all three. "All three replicas in one failure domain defeat R3."
- Joining clusters into a super-cluster doesn't stretch one stream across them; the stream's replicas stay inside its cluster.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Super-clusters**

- A gateway carries interest across regions, not stream copies.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leaf nodes**

- If a leaf runs its own JetStream, it needs a JetStream domain; without distinct domains a leaf's JetStream and its hub's JetStream collide.
- A leaf enabling JetStream while sharing the hub's system account extends the hub's JetStream rather than running its own, so a stream created on the leaf may land on the hub; give the leaf its own JetStream domain for a distinct local store. "Expecting JetStream to span the leaf without a domain."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Topologies)**

- Checklist: Add redundancy before an outage, not after; one server can't hold a replicated stream, so R1 survives a restart but never the loss of the box.
- Checklist: Audit replica counts and raise the streams that matter to R3; a cluster alone is not HA.
- Checklist: Spread R3 replicas across independent failure domains, not one rack or zone.
- Checklist: Give a leaf its own JetStream `domain` when it needs a distinct local store.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Sizing & resources**

- At R3 each node stores the full stream once (one copy per node). The Helm chart defaults `max_file_store` to the PVC size.
- On an un-tiered account an R3 stream counts as `replicas × bytes` against `MaxStore`: a 10 GiB R3 stream spends 30 GiB. Forget the multiplier and the third replica fails to place. "a 10 GiB ORDERS stream at R3 spends 30 GiB of the account's `MaxStore`"
- On a tiered account replication is baked into the tier: the reported bytes are usable bytes, so a 10 GiB tier holds a 10 GiB R3 stream.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Config management**

- Don't SIGHUP a node while JetStream is moving replicas or handing off Raft leadership; wait for the cluster to settle. "A reload during a rebalance can interrupt a leadership transfer."
- Lowering a store limit on reload changes the ceiling, not the contents: existing messages stay but new writes fail until an admin trims the stream under the limit. Raise limits freely; lower them only after checking current storage. "Lowering a store limit on reload does not evict data already stored."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Deployment)**

- Checklist: Confirm the CRD-created stream is R3 with `nats stream info` before trusting the declarative path.
- Checklist: Fit a SIGHUP inside the graceful window; a reload during a rebalance can interrupt leadership transfer.
- Checklist: Trim oversized streams by hand after lowering `max_file`; a reload changes the ceiling, not the contents.
- Checklist: Read replicas and leader with `nats stream info` before and after the upgrade to confirm the stream stayed R3.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Accounts and multitenancy**

- On a server running JetStream, declaring an `accounts` block makes JetStream opt-in per account (`jetstream: enabled`); an account without it gets `JetStream not enabled for account (10039)` on every JetStream call.
- Each account gets its own JetStream store; a stream created in `$G` before accounts existed doesn't follow a user into its new account.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Encryption & TLS**

- Encryption at rest is a server-wide `jetstream {}` setting that encrypts stream data and metadata on disk with an AEAD cipher; it's global, not per account, and independent of TLS.
- Pitfall: A wrong at-rest key hides streams; it doesn't destroy them. `Error decrypting our stream metafile: unable to recover keys` means the wrong key; restart with the right one and the stream returns.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Security)**

- Whether a stream survives losing its server is replication, not security: security decides who may access a stream; replication decides whether it's still there.
- Checklist: Keep the JetStream encryption key out of the config file (`key: $JS_KEY`), and carry `prev_key` for one rotation restart only.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling**

- Durable state (a count that must not reset, a queue of work that outlives the process) doesn't belong in the instance; put it behind JetStream.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Services)**

- A service is at-most-once request-reply; when an instance stops, its in-flight work is gone. State that must survive a restart belongs in a stream, not the service.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Monitoring endpoints**

- `/jsz` reports JetStream state on a node: stream and consumer counts, the meta leader, and per-stream/per-consumer numbers; `last_seq` there is raw material for lag.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream health**

- Stream state (separate from configuration) is what's actually in the stream now: `messages`, `bytes`, first/last sequence, `num_subjects`, active consumers. `last_seq` only ever climbs.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Advisories & events**

- An advisory is a transient JSON message JetStream publishes once, the moment something noteworthy happens to a stream or consumer, on a well-known subject under `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.>`; stream and consumer names are baked into the subject so wildcards can narrow to exactly the events you care about.
- The fix for transient advisories is to point a stream at the advisory subjects; a stream is always subscribed and stores what it captures. "point a stream at the advisory subjects"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Monitoring)**

- Checklist: Persist advisories to a stream subscribed to `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.>`; advisories are transient.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Key-Value Store**

- A KV bucket is not a separate database; it is a JetStream stream named `KV_<bucket>` whose subjects are `$KV.<bucket>.>`. "a key is the last token of that subject, and a value is a message on it"
- A `put` appends a message, a `get` reads the last message for a subject, and a `watch` opens a consumer.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first bucket**

- A bucket is a JetStream stream the key-value API creates and configures for you; the bucket `INVENTORY` becomes the stream `KV_INVENTORY`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TTL and limits**

- A bucket-wide TTL (`--ttl`) is the stream's `MaxAge` limit applied to every value; a per-key TTL expires one value and is built on JetStream per-message TTL.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Under the hood**

- Backing stream config for a bucket: `Maximum Per Subject` is the history depth; `Discard Policy: New`; `Direct Get: true`; `Allows Rollups: true`; `Allows Msg Delete: false` (`deny_delete`).
- Discard policy `New` is why limits reject: once the bucket hits a limit it rejects the newest write rather than dropping older messages.
- `deny_delete` makes the stream refuse the JetStream message-delete API so raw stream ops can't remove entries behind the KV API.
- A get uses direct get: the server returns the last message on a subject straight from storage via `$JS.API.DIRECT.GET.<stream>.<subject>`, with no consumer, no position, and no ack.
- Do not operate the backing stream directly: don't hand-edit `KV_INVENTORY` config and don't publish to `$KV.INVENTORY.>` with raw `nats pub`, because raw publishes lack the CAS, `KV-Operation`, and `Nats-Rollup` headers.
- `deny_delete` does not stop a raw publish to the bucket's subjects.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Key-Value)**

- Mapping: a bucket is a stream, a key is a subject token, a put is a message, a revision is a sequence, a watch is an ephemeral ordered consumer; every bucket limit is a stream limit.
- A bucket can be sourced from or mirrored into another bucket via a subject transform from `$KV.SRC.>` to `$KV.DST.>` (e.g. regional `EU_INVENTORY` sourcing `INVENTORY`).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Object Store**

- An object is a stored file too large or too binary to ride on a plain message; a bucket is the named store, and both live inside a single JetStream stream named `OBJ_<bucket>`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Under the hood (Object Store)**

- The backing stream `OBJ_<bucket>` captures two subject spaces: `$O.<bucket>.C.>` for chunk messages and `$O.<bucket>.M.>` for metadata messages.
- Every metadata publish carries `Nats-Rollup: sub`, which purges every earlier message on the same subject; this keeps exactly one current `ObjectInfo` per name and makes the store rollup-latest, not multi-revision.
- Backing stream config: `AllowRollup` true, discard policy `new` (reject writes when full rather than dropping old chunks), `AllowDirect` true, `max_age: 0`, `max_bytes: -1`, `storage: file`, `num_replicas: 1`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Backup & Recovery Deep Dive**

- A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a stream (messages, config, optionally consumer state) written off-site; it answers "how much data can I afford to lose" (recovery point).
- A mirror is a live, read-only copy of a stream at a second site kept current by replication; it answers "how long can recovery take" (recovery time).
- R3 replication is high availability, not a backup; a bad write (accidental delete, corrupt message) is applied to every replica. "R3 keeps the stream *available*; only a snapshot lets you go *back* to before the mistake."
- Memory streams can't be snapshotted, so file storage is required for any stream you want to back up.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Stream backup and restore**

- Replication doesn't protect from a mistake (accidental purge, bad migration, logic bug); recovering from those needs a copy the cluster can't touch.
- A snapshot is a complete copy of a stream at one instant: every message, the stream config, and optionally consumer state; the server streams it in chunks to a directory.
- A snapshot directory holds `backup.json` (config and state: subjects, retention, limits, sequence range) and `stream.tar.s2` (messages packed in a tarball compressed with S2).
- Restore recreates the stream from a snapshot: same messages, same sequence numbers, same configuration, plus consumers if the snapshot included them.
- The stream name cannot change on restore; the server rejects a restore under a different name. "A snapshot of `ORDERS` restores as `ORDERS`, never as `ORDERS_COPY`."
- Restore expects the stream not to already exist; it recreates, it doesn't merge into a live stream. "confirm the broken stream is gone (or remove it), then restore"
- Memory streams cannot be snapshotted; the backup fails with `memory streams do not support snapshots`. Set `Storage: File` on any stream you want to back up.
- The stream name cannot change on restore; the server rejects with `stream name may not be changed during restore`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mirrors as a DR tool**

- R3 replication protects against losing one node; it does nothing when you lose the whole cluster. A mirror lives at a separate site reachable over a gateway or leaf-node link.
- A DR mirror accepts no direct writes; the copy flows one way, upstream to mirror, never back.
- A mirror's configuration is fixed once the stream exists; you can't re-point a running mirror or change what it copies. Changing it means delete and recreate, after which messages re-replicate.
- Replication is asynchronous: the upstream acks the publisher before the mirror has the message; the gap is lag, the count of messages the mirror trails behind.
- Mirror info fields: `Stream Name` (upstream), `Lag` (messages upstream has that the mirror doesn't), `Last Seen` (time since the mirror last heard from upstream; in monitoring JSON the field is `active`).
- A mirror is not a backup. "A mirror follows the upstream's live writes, so a corrupt write lands in the mirror too — and a mirror keeps no earlier state to rewind to."
- A mirror gives availability (short RTO because the data is already there) but no recovery point; its own retention limits can age messages out on their own schedule.
- Deleting the upstream does not delete the mirror: it keeps every message already copied, stops receiving, and records the fault in the `Error` field of its Mirror Information.
- Purging a range on the upstream leaves the mirror's already-stored messages in place; the mirror detects the sequence gap and skips missing messages.
