- Don't reach for R3 as DR: a corrupt write replicates across all three R3 replicas just as it lands in a mirror.
- A mirror is not a backup; don't run a mirror instead of snapshots. "Pair them: the mirror for site failure, the snapshot for bad data."
- A mirror's config is effectively locked after creation; settle upstream, site, and subjects upfront.
- Avoid a Work Queue upstream under a mirror: the mirror's hidden internal consumer is a direct consumer that bypasses the work queue's subject-overlap check, so a worker and the mirror can both receive the same message. Use a `Limits` upstream instead.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Disaster recovery**

- A snapshot is the only copy that predates a mistake; a mirror survives an upstream delete only as a copy frozen at the break.
- Promotion step 1: verify lag is zero. If the site is unreachable, lag stalls at the last successful copy; that stalled number is your real recovery point. "Waiting for a lag that will never move to zero only extends the outage."
- A mirror is read-only by design and rejects direct publishes; promotion removes the mirror relationship (`--no-mirror`), which doesn't touch the data.
- Promotion must clear the lost stream's assignment first (`stream rm --force`) or the subject bind fails with `subjects overlap with an existing stream (10065)`; losing the site doesn't remove the dead stream from JetStream metadata.
- A mirror has no subjects of its own; a promoted primary needs the subjects bound to it so publishers can reach it.
- For an accidental delete, restore straight from the snapshot; don't recreate an empty stream first because restore creates it and an existing stream makes it fail.
- Never promote a mirror before lag reaches zero, or with a stalled lag you've consciously accepted; tail messages in flight are lost and new writes land on top of the gap.
- R3 replication will not save you from a mistake; an accidental delete or bad publish replicates to all three copies at once.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Backup & Recovery)**

- Checklist: use file storage for any stream you must snapshot; a memory stream cannot be backed up.
- Checklist: restore to the original stream name; mirror or source afterward if you need a copy under a new name.
- Checklist: pair every mirror with snapshots; a mirror is not a backup.
- Checklist: plan the mirror topology upfront; config is effectively locked after creation.
- Checklist: read the `Lag` field before trusting a mirror; replication is eventually consistent, not synchronous.
- Checklist: avoid Work Queue retention on a mirrored upstream; use Limits.
- Checklist: verify lag has reached 0 before promoting a mirror.
- Checklist: reach for a snapshot, not R3, against an accidental delete or logical error.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connect MQTT devices to NATS**

- Where a broker's persistence stops at a last-value cache per topic, device traffic on NATS lands in JetStream streams with retention limits, replay, and consumers written later.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first MQTT client**

- MQTT needs state that outlives a connection (session subscriptions, unacked QoS 1/2 messages, retained messages); the server keeps all of it in JetStream streams, so JetStream must be reachable.
- Capture device traffic in a normal stream (e.g. `DEVICES` on `sensors.>,fleet.>`) so a QoS 0 reading, gone once delivered, and a QoS 1 reading, which only reaches subscribers that exist at the time, are still readable by a consumer written later.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — QoS, sessions, and retained messages**

- If traffic starts on the NATS side and delivery matters, keep the durability on the NATS side in a stream rather than expecting MQTT redelivery.
- Sessions are stored in JetStream, so they outlive both the connection and a server restart; a reconnecting device with the same client ID finds subscriptions still in place and unacked QoS 1/2 messages pending.
- Retained messages are stored regardless of QoS; a retained QoS 0 message is still persisted, which is part of why the account needs JetStream even for a fleet that never uses QoS 1.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth and clustering (MQTT)**

- A QoS 1 or 2 subscription is backed by a JetStream durable delivered over an internal subject under `$MQTT.sub.`.
- MQTT state streams are replicated automatically once JetStream is clustered; the replica count is derived from the number of addresses in the server's own `routes` list, clamped between 1 and 3, not from how many servers the cluster has.
- A server listing two routes brings its MQTT streams up at `R=2`, not `R=3`; list all peers in `routes` or set `stream_replicas: 3` explicitly. Asking for more replicas than the cluster can satisfy makes the streams fail to create, surfacing as MQTT clients unable to connect.
- `js_domain` selects the JetStream domain MQTT stores its state in; set it to the leaf's local domain so sessions and retained messages stay on the leaf and local devices keep working when the hub link is down. The domain is part of the session's storage identity, keeping sessions in different domains from colliding.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (MQTT)**

- Sessions, retained messages, and in-flight QoS 1/2 deliveries are all stored in streams the server manages; that's why the account needs JetStream and why sessions survive reconnect and restart.
- Checklist: don't rely on a QoS 1 subscription to make NATS-originated traffic durable; put that data in a stream.
- Checklist: use JetStream where you need history; only the last retained value per topic is kept.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue Groups**

- Core queue groups never redeliver: a message sent to a worker that crashes mid-processing is lost. For redelivery and durability, use JetStream worker pools.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream**

- Core NATS delivers only to subscribers connected at publication (at most once, never replayed); JetStream adds a persistence layer giving at-least-once delivery, with messages surviving restarts and replayable.
- JetStream extends decoupling to time: publisher and subscriber no longer need to be online at the same moment.
- Three pieces: a stream (server-side store bound to one or more subjects), a consumer (server-side stateful view tracking client progress), and a client (application that receives and acknowledges messages).
- A stream is bound to one or more subject patterns; a matching publish is appended and assigned a sequence number. Streams are configurable for storage (memory or disk), retention (limits or consumer acks), replication, and more.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Security**

- JetStream streams can be encrypted on disk using AES or ChaCha20-Poly1305, protecting persisted data against attackers with filesystem or physical access.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topologies**

- JetStream streams can be mirrored or sourced across a leaf link for local copies of data.

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to build a NATS Supercluster | Rethink Connectivity Episode 5**

- Replicated JetStream assets (R3, even R5) survive node loss; the replica count is a trade-off against the performance characteristics you want. "you can make an R3 or even an R5 and it's just going to be dependent on your performance characteristics that you want for your system" (~03:50)
- The system account should not have JetStream enabled; create a separate account for a business use case and set `jetstream: enabled` on that account. "we don't want to enable JetStream here, in fact we want to create an account that can utilize JetStream for maybe a particular business case" (~04:20)
- Enabling JetStream on a cluster only requires the `jetstream` directive (no config needed) on each server plus a JetStream-enabled account. "you edit the config to enable JetStream and then you work with a JetStream enabled account" (~07:40)
- A KV bucket created without replicas lives on one node (the leader) and all access is served from that node; recreate with `--replicas 3` to place a replica on each node. "any time I talk to this cluster about this kv store it's actually going to be polling from north america 2... if I wanted redundancy here I would use what are called replicas" (~07:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extend your NATS Cluster with Leaf Nodes | Rethink Connectivity Episode 7**

- JetStream domains identify which JetStream (hub or leaf) a command such as stream/consumer creation targets. "JetStream domains which is a way to identify... where you want to operate that actual command" (~08:00)
- With one giant cloud stream and many (e.g. 2000) stores, having every store fetch messages from the cloud hammers the hub; instead build filtered local read replicas. "everybody's going to be hammering the cloud with requests for orders and you might not want that" (~19:30)
- From a leaf node, viewing or getting from a hub stream requires specifying the hub's JetStream domain (e.g. `--js-domain NGS`); without it the leaf's own (empty) domain is used. "there are no streams in our leaf node right now there's only a stream on NGS... that's where we need to specify a JS domain" (~20:20)
- A leaf-local stream that sources the hub stream with a subject filter (e.g. `orders.store1.*`) yields a real read replica with sequences, not just a cache, and local gets become much faster. "it's not just a cache, it's a real read replica of a stream" (~22:00)
- A sourced stream need not follow the source's storage rules: it can be memory instead of file, with its own replication and its own start position. "I don't have to follow the rules of the source stream... if this original order stream is file based I could say I just want this thing in memory" (~23:00)
- Layer decentralized auth on top so a leaf node's credentials only permit sourcing specific subjects from the hub stream, giving partners scoped access to a global data store. "you can only source from this subject on this stream... a global data store that can only be accessed in certain ways" (~24:40)
- If the leaf goes down while messages are added at the hub, the sourced stream catches up automatically and in order when the leaf returns. "I can take down this leaf node and add messages to it and then pull a leaf node back up and NATS is automatically going to be syncing all that data in order" (~25:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Building an Interactive Whiteboard with NATS Websockets | Rethink Connectivity Episode 3**

- Persistence is added by creating a stream on `whiteboard.*` and switching the subscription to a JetStream ordered consumer; each page load creates a fresh ephemeral consumer and replays the whole stream. "every time this thing refreshes it creates a new consumer and pulls in all the data via the stream" (~14:00)
- The stream is created with `--allow-rollup` and `--no-deny-purge` so a "clear" message published with the `Nats-Rollup: sub` header replaces all prior messages on that subject, keeping replay cheap for new consumers. "when I send this message clear all of the messages before them so next time a consumer connects it's not getting all of those messages" (~15:30)
- Rollup can be per subject or for the entire stream. "you could roll up the subject or you could roll up the entire stream" (~16:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS Leafnodes**

- JetStream enabled on a leaf's global account becomes JetStream for the bound hub account across NGS worldwide; leaf nodes with JetStream can extend a core cluster's storage (e.g. add a petabyte for one account) without touching the core. "you can utilize these leaf nodes that are running JetStream just to be extensions to your storage" (~24:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Replace Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis and more w/NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity Ep 10**

- JetStream is a subsystem bundled into the NATS server that can be turned on or off, and it is built on top of core NATS using the same protocol. "it's not like it uses a different protocol or anything like that it's all still NATS under the hood" (~03:05)
- A JetStream publish is a request to the subject; the server responds with a publish acknowledgement (pub ack) that means the message has been saved. "we call a pub ack or a publish acknowledgement ... telling the publisher that the NATS server has saved that message" (~04:07)
- A stream ingests every message whose subject matches its configured patterns (e.g. hello.*) and orders them globally. "it's going to order each of these globally which is actually a very important topic" (~05:07)
- Streams can optionally be replicated across cluster nodes; with R1 the stream lives on one node and if that node goes down you cannot read or write to it. "you can't write to it you can't read to it or anything like that" (~05:07)
- JetStream replication is built on an implementation of the Raft consensus protocol. "JetStream is built on top of an implementation of the Raft protocol" (~05:07)
- With R3, JetStream picks three available nodes; losing one node still allows reads and writes, losing two still allows reads, losing all three is disaster-recovery territory. "if a second node goes down you can actually still read from that stream" (~06:08)
- Streams are indexed on a per-subject level, which lets you reach a particular message by subject without scanning; this indexing underpins the KV and Object Store implementations. "streams are indexed on a subject level ... this is actually what under the hood drives a lot of our KV and Object Store" (~08:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to configure NATS JetStream streams | Rethink Connectivity Ep 11**

- A stream is a single primitive that can be configured to express many distributed-systems patterns: distributed queue, key-value store, object store, append-only log. "you can have multiple different kind of patterns supported ... replace a whole swath of different tools" (~01:02)
- Name, description, subjects and storage are the baseline options every stream uses; the name is the identifier used to look up the stream and create consumers. "these are kind of your primary bread and butter" (~04:05)
- Description is not used by any JetStream machinery; it is a human-readable label that shows in `nats stream list`. "description isn't really used in any kind of infrastructure portion" (~05:06)
- A stream can have multiple subjects, including wildcards like orders.*, which it "slurps up" from core NATS and persists to disk. "you can have multiple subjects that the stream is essentially slurping up from core NATS" (~05:06)
- Memory storage is ephemeral: if the server goes offline those messages are lost; it is niche and suited to caches or hosts without fast disk writes. "if that server goes offline those messages are going to be lost" (~06:07)
- Limits drive stream behaviour: max messages, max bytes (required on Synadia Cloud), max age (per-message TTL for retention like 30 or 365 days), max messages per subject, max message size, max consumers. "limits drives a lot of behavior inside of the stream" (~07:08)
- Max messages per subject set to 1 keeps only the last message per subject; the KV store's history setting is driven by this option. "this is actually in use inside of our key value store where you can set a history" (~08:09)
- Keep the default retention policy (limits) in most cases; the other policies build on it. "for the most part you can keep it at the default which is limit" (~09:10)
- With limits retention and discard old, when a limit is hit the oldest messages are deleted so the stream stays within limits. "it's going to start deleting the older messages to make sure that the stream stays within those limits" (~10:10)
- Interest retention is a superset of limits: it still enforces limits but also deletes a message once every interested consumer has acknowledged it. "it will delete messages once they have been consumed by every consumer that's interested in it" (~11:11)
- Interest retention suits multiple consumers each picking messages for different reasons where persistence after processing does not matter. "you have kind of multiple consumers that are using ... but you also want to keep this acting very much like a queue" (~11:11)
- Work-queue retention behaves like interest retention but restricts the stream to one consumer; that one consumer can still be shared by many clients for load balancing. "just because I have one consumer it means I can't load balance between them ... that's actually not true" (~12:13)
- A work-queue stream behaves like RabbitMQ or any durable queue: message goes in, gets processed, gets deleted. "works very similar to like a RabbitMQ or any other kind of durable queue system" (~12:13)
- Discard policy chooses between dropping old messages and rejecting new publishes when a limit is hit; discard new rejects publishes until the condition changes; default is discard old. "start rejecting API calls or publishes to that stream until the limit is lifted" (~13:15)
- Choose discard new when you absolutely must not lose data and would rather fail publishes at the limit. "you would rather start rejecting API calls in order to not lose data" (~13:15)
- Deduplication uses the Nats-Msg-Id header with a sliding window that defaults to two minutes and is configurable. "by default this duplicate window is going to be two minutes" (~14:15)
- Republish is for cases needing millions of consumers, where consumer machinery costs hardware; the stream republishes a core NATS notification when a message is persisted. "once you get into the use case where you might need like millions of consumers ... might not be worth the added cost" (~15:15)
- Republish can be configured headers-only to minimise bytes on the wire; suited to monitoring and logging that is not mission critical. "you could also make this very performant over the wire where it's just sending the bare minimum" (~16:17)
- Data must live somewhere; Raft-based immediate consistency constrains where replication can happen. "we have to abide by the laws of physics" (~17:17)
- Use replication factors of 3, 5 or 7; with R3, one node offline still handles writes and two nodes offline still handles reads; default is R1. "you're going to want to use multiples of like three five seven" (~18:19)
- Replication-factor replicas are immediately consistent but must stay inside one cluster; they cannot span clusters. "I can't go outside the cluster with this version of replication" (~19:21)
- Placement selects the cluster and server tags; tag servers when building a supercluster (e.g. region, cloud, SSD) so stream creators can express affinity. "we recommend when you're building the NATS supercluster that you tag things appropriately" (~19:21)
- Mirrors and sources are the way to replicate outside a cluster. "if you want to go outside of your cluster for replication then you need to start looking to mirrors or sources" (~20:22)
- A mirror is a one-to-one twin of a stream in another cluster; reads are served from the mirror while writes are forwarded to the origin stream to keep global consistency. "all reads will be served from this mirror but all writes will actually be forwarded to the source" (~21:22)
- Sources aggregate and filter many streams into one, and the sourcing stream may also ingest its own subjects; a good use is aggregating leaf-node edge streams into one cloud stream. "aggregate them all into one mega stream in the cloud" (~22:23)
- A sourced stream is a brand new stream with its own sequence numbers, not a one-to-one mapping. "sequence IDs are going to be unique and different ... specifically unique to this stream" (~22:23)
- Compression is only available for file-based stores, not memory stores. "it's only limited to the file based stores of streams" (~23:24)
- Allow rollup lets a specially-headed message replace everything before it on the whole stream or one subject, useful for derived or computable state. "it will persist that message that just came through and it will delete everything before it" (~24:25)
- Deny delete and deny purge flags control whether individual message deletes (e.g. GDPR) or subject/stream purges are allowed. "deleting messages is being able to pick out a particular message and delete it great for like GDPR purposes" (~24:25)
- Consumer limits on a stream set default limits for consumers created on it. "configure default consumer limits for consumers that are created on this stream" (~24:25)
- Stream subject transforms rewrite a message's subject before it is stored; useful when aggregating via sources into a mega stream. "transform the message's subject before it gets saved to disk" (~25:26)
- Almost all stream options, including placement, can be changed at runtime; the server moves a replicated stream live while consumers and publishers keep working. "we actually take the stream we replicate it we move it in flight while consumers are consuming from it" (~26:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Build Priority Background Jobs & Dead Letter Queues with NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity ep 12**

- A worker/job queue is one of the most common queuing patterns (RabbitMQ, Sidekiq, Celery); JetStream can be shaped into this durable-queue form. "Jet Stream can kind of be molded and shaped into all kinds of different expressions of distributed systems" (~00:00)
- JetStream has no built-in priority semantics; priorities are expressed through subject-based addressing (e.g. jobs.high.*, jobs.low.*) with separate worker pools sized differently. "NATS JetStream doesn't have priority semantics built in ... you can have priority semantics by using our subject based addressing" (~02:03)
- Correction to the previous episode: a work-queue stream can have multiple consumers as long as their filter subjects do not overlap. "you can actually have multiple consumers in a work queue stream as long as the subjects that they're interested in don't overlap" (~04:05)
- In a work-queue stream, processed messages are deleted, so the stream size represents in-progress work. "you can look at the size of the queue as kind of your in progress work" (~04:05)
- Dead-letter queues are deliberately not a first-class JetStream feature; they are a specific pattern expressible through configuration without code. "we wanted to be able to express it but not necessarily bake it into JetStream as a core thing" (~05:05)
- In a work-queue stream, a message that exhausted max deliveries stays in the stream until manually acknowledged or deleted, so failures stack up the queue size. "it will stay there in the stream until you either manually acknowledge it or manually delete it" (~05:05)
- JetStream advisories report which messages hit max failed deliveries; you can capture these into a stream to build your own dead-letter queue. "we have some JetStream advisories that you could listen to and actually insert into a queue" (~06:06)
- For a work queue, use discard policy "new" so a backed-up queue rejects new jobs rather than deleting old ones. "if my queue gets backed up I don't want to start deleting old messages ... I want to start actually rejecting" (~08:08)
- Put a message-count cap on queues (example 20,000) for monitoring and SLA purposes. "these queues have some sort of limit on them ... you might want to set kind of a cap on this" (~08:08)
- Set a max age (example 7 days) on the work-queue stream so dead messages that exhausted retries eventually expire rather than backing up forever. "I'm okay having a sort of lifetime to my dead messages" (~09:10)
- Creating two consumers with overlapping filter subjects on a work-queue stream errors; newer servers allow multiple filter subjects per consumer. "I'm actually going to get an error because I'm going to try to create two consumers that overlap" (~18:26)
- The max-deliveries advisory subject is $JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<stream>.<consumer>; wildcard the consumer so new priorities do not require DLQ changes. "I want to add a medium priority and I don't want to have to change the dead letter queue semantics" (~26:34)
- The advisory includes stream, consumer and stream sequence; use `nats stream get <stream> <seq>` to fetch the original failed message, which stays in the stream until its max age. "we also get the stream sequence which is really important here" (~28:36)
- Stream metadata (new feature) can label a stream, e.g. dead-letter-queue=true, so tooling can discover DLQ streams. "I could look through all my streams and I could find the ones that are dead letter queues" (~30:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared: Part 1 | Rethink Connectivity**

- Kafka was designed as a streaming/distributed-log processing platform; NATS was first a messaging system and JetStream was a persistence layer added on top. "NATS historically came as being first and foremost a messaging system and then later on a persistence layer was added" (~02:02)
- Subject-based addressing lets you address individual messages or ranges in a stream directly, e.g. get orders.eu.12345 or query orders.us.*. "you can address individual messages or series of messages directly in the stream" (~10:09)
- Kafka can only address messages by offset (partition number plus sequence); the publish key is used solely to hash onto partitions and cannot be queried. "the key ... is purely used for one thing and one thing only which is distribution over the partitions" (~12:13)
- JetStream maintains indexes on subject names inside streams, so getting the first or last message for nasdaq.microsoft is a single fast operation, not a scan; filtering happens server-side and only matching messages are transmitted. "internally JetStream maintains indexes on those subject names that are contained into the streams" (~16:16)
- Kafka stores data in a write-ahead log where you can only append at the head and compact the tail; individual messages cannot be deleted. "there's no ability to delete individual messages in a Kafka stream" (~22:25)
- JetStream behaves like a NoSQL-style data store, including deleting individual messages. "it has a functionality that you expect of a form of database ... that includes the ability to delete individual messages" (~23:25)
- Kafka always wants to accept writes; the only limit is stream size or time; JetStream lets you choose what happens at a limit, including per-subject limits Kafka cannot express. "you can also have limits on a per subject basis ... you can't do that with Kafka" (~24:25)
- Kafka's compaction keeps "at least" one message per key; a JetStream per-subject limit of 1 is exactly one. "it's a limit of exactly one right not an at least" (~25:26)
- Discard-new plus max-messages-per-subject gives database-like constraints usable for distributed locking or gating: a second publish to a subject at its limit fails in the ack. "using a stream for distributed locking logic gating things like that" (~26:26)
- KV and Object Store are possible only because streams combine subject-based addressing with enforced limits (e.g. keep last 5 per subject). "this is only possible because both you have subject-based addressing in streams and you have this ability to have constraints" (~27:27)
- JetStream supports CRUD-style concurrency control: insert only if no message exists on the subject, and compare-and-set updates by expecting the last sequence on the subject. "I'm expecting the current last message on that subject to be sequence number 37 ... if it has been changed then that operation fails" (~29:29)
- Rollup is an atomic controlled update that replaces all prior messages on a subject with one summarising message. "replace them with just one message ... that's one atomic operation in JetStream" (~32:35)
- Core NATS and even JetStream latencies are measured in microseconds: one-way or two-way in the 100–200 µs range over a network, under 100 µs one-way on a fast network. "over this network you're talking 1 to 200 microsecond ranges ... with fast network below 100 microseconds" (~34:41)
- JetStream can also batch via asynchronous publishes for much higher write throughput; batching trades away real-time latency, and NATS leaves that trade-off to the engineer. "you can use asynchronous operations to get much higher write throughputs by doing batching" (~33:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared Pt 2: Consumers | Rethink Connectivity**

- Direct get of the last or first message for an exact subject is how KV works; it is a get, not a query, and over loopback runs in the tens of microseconds. "the order of magnitude is tens of microseconds when going over loopback" (~15:17)
- A stream has exactly one order for all messages and every consumer, ephemeral or durable, delivers in that order; the tricky part is preserving order under errors. "there's just one order of all the messages into your stream" (~20:23)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Move over Kafka! Let's try NATS JetStream**

- JetStream is a persistence layer on top of core NATS: same pub/sub APIs, with opt-in persistence for certain messages so they can be delivered later. "you get to use all of the same NATS pub sub APIs but you get to opt in to have certain messages persisted" (~00:01)
- Retention policies: limits (default), interest and work queue; the latter two still obey limits but add rules. The speaker's description of work queue as "discard after all consumers acknowledged" and interest as "throw away messages no consumer is interested in" is the reverse of the definitions given in later episodes. "the work queue policy will discard the message after all of the consumers have acknowledged it whereas the interest policy will actually throw away any messages that no consumers are interested in" (~03:04)
- Publishers can keep using plain core NATS publish with no JetStream knowledge; the server decides whether a message needs persisting. "publishers can continue to use NATS core they actually don't have to have any knowledge of JetStream" (~04:04)
- KV buckets are streams underneath: you configure history depth and, because it is a stream, placement in the cluster. "because this is just a stream underneath you also get to choose where in the cluster you want to put your store" (~09:07)
- Stream sourcing builds a stream from one or more other streams, with its own ownership, location and retention rules, including per-source start sequence and subject filters (e.g. orders.eu plus returns.eu into archive-eu). "a stream that gets its data from one or more other streams with all of its own rules around ownership location and retention" (~11:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Comparing and contrasting NATS and Kafka | RethinkConn '22**

- Kafka is a distributed append-only commit log; NATS with JetStream is a distributed messaging platform with added persistent storage. "Kafka is a distributed append-only commit log ... NATS and JetStream which is a distributed messaging platform with added persistent storage" (~01:00)
- Kafka only compacts logs; JetStream is an immediately consistent messaging store where individual messages can be deleted, which changes which use cases are feasible. "JetStream which is actually an immediately consistent messaging store ... you can delete individual messages" (~02:03)
- Stream subjects do not need to be created ahead of time; streams capture by wildcard. "the subjects do not need to be created ahead of time" (~04:06)
- JetStream consumer filters are pushed to the server, which uses indexing rather than a full scan and sends only matching records; filters support `*` and `>` and can combine with a start time. "it doesn't normally do a full table scan over the stream ... it uses indexing" (~08:10)
- Core NATS is at-most-once; JetStream and Kafka default to at-least-once, redelivering to subscribers that were absent at publish time. "core NATS is at most once ... JetStream and Kafka give you by default at least once" (~12:17)
- Exactly-once has two parts; the publishing half is deduplication, needed when a pub ack is lost or the client crashes between publish and ack and republishes. "you end up having that message twice in the stream" (~14:19)
- JetStream has a built-in deduplication window over a configurable time that works across client sessions; Kafka's built-in dedup is per session, so a crash-and-resend still duplicates unless you use Kafka Streams. "the built-in deduplication feature of Kafka is only per session" (~15:22)
- JetStream streams are read-write: usable as queues, safe deletion of individual messages, encryption, limits and discard policies richer than Kafka's. "JetStream streams are actually read write which means you can use them as queues" (~16:23)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | JetStream**

- JetStream is the next generation of NATS streaming technology, replacing the separate NATS Streaming server binary with one server binary. "we've made it into a single server binary so anyone who has NATS will have JetStream" (~01:03)
- JetStream brings at-least-once delivery only to specific subjects; core publish to no listeners is gone, at-least-once means the server holds it for later consumers. "brings at least once delivery model only to specific subjects" (~01:03)
- JetStream plugs into NATS routing, security and multi-tenancy: one compute set can serve completely isolated data stores per account, sharing data only when required. "completely isolated data stores streaming services from completely isolated subject namespaces on top of NATS" (~03:07)
- JetStream administration is an API over the NATS wire: publish JSON to well-known subjects, so no custom client is required. "you just publish a JSON message on to a well-known subject and that's how you access the API" (~04:09)
- Streams listen on wildcard subjects, a key difference from NATS Streaming; order.received, order.processed and order.completed can all land in one stream. "we support wildcards ... this is a key difference from NATS streaming server to JetStream" (~07:13)
- A dead-letter-queue equivalent: configure max delivery attempts (e.g. 10) and JetStream publishes an event with the message content when exceeded. "configure messages only let me try ten times ... then we will publish an event saying that message's bad" (~16:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Getting Started with NATS JetStream: Streams, Storage, and Data Lifecycle**

- A stream is dedicated data storage for a named set of subjects; with clustering you add replication so one server or disk failure leaves a copy. "if one of these NATS servers goes down, one of these discs get corrupted, you have a backup copy for high availability" (~02:03)
- A stream retains data even with no consumers, so a consumer created later still receives it (at-least-once). "Even if you don't have any consumers, the stream will retain that data for you" (~03:04)
- Memory storage works but is not durable; use file storage for disk durability. "If you used the storage memory mechanism ... it would store data in memory. I don't want that" (~08:08)
- Default limits are unlimited, meaning data piles up with no cleanup; set limits so NATS cleans up automatically. "my maximums are all set to be unlimited, which means I'm just going to keep on piling data on without any data cleanup. That's not great" (~09:09)
- Lowering max bytes (46 KB to 1 KB) or max messages on a live stream immediately truncates to the newest messages that fit. "I have eight messages left. It all has to sit under this 1 kilobyte limit" (~11:11)
- When setting max age, the duplicate window must be set lower than the max age. "I also have to decrease the duplicate window to less than the max age, a configuration setting you just have to be aware of" (~12:11)
- Setting max age below the age of existing messages deletes them on apply. "they're gone. Why are they gone? Because they were older than 20 seconds" (~13:12)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream for Key-Value Store Tech Preview**

- Max-messages-per-subject limits keep N historical values per subject (e.g. 100 per device) instead of a global total, so busy writers do not push out idle ones. "keep a hundred historical values per device rather than keep a thousand messages in total" (~00:00)
- Storing every key as a subject and values as messages, with per-subject limits, is what makes a KV store on JetStream possible. "if you store every key as a subject and the value as values in the stream you have a kv store" (~01:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Mirror Streams Explained — One-Way Replication Made Simple**

- A mirror is a replica that automatically and asynchronously syncs from exactly one origin stream; the relationship is strictly one-to-one. "each mirror can only replicate from a single origin stream. It's a strict one-to-one relationship" (~00:00)
- Mirrors are read-only for publishing, but you can delete messages on demand and consumers have full capabilities. "mirrors are read only. Your clients can't directly publish to them ... you can still delete messages on demand" (~00:00)
- Mirrors preserve origin sequence numbers and timestamps: sequence 42 at the origin is 42 in the mirror. "if a message was sequence number 42 in the origin, it'll be 42 in the mirror also" (~01:00)
- Mirror configuration lives entirely on the receiving side; the origin needs no setup and does not even see a consumer created. "It won't even see a consumer created for the replication" (~01:00)
- Mirror options: name (required), start sequence, start time, filter subject, subject transforms, and domain for hub-and-leaf topologies. "domain specifies which JetStream domain the origin stream lives in. Useful for hub and leaf topologies" (~01:00)
- Filter subject and subject transform cannot be combined on a mirror. "you can't use filter subject and subject transform together. You got to pick one" (~02:00)
- Use mirrors for geographic distribution, fan-out from one origin to many mirrors serving millions of clients, and cross-account or cross-domain replication. "One origin stream can feed multiple mirrors, perfect for fan-out topologies that serve millions of client connections" (~02:00)
- With the mirror direct attribute, clients read directly from mirror replicas instead of being routed to the origin, spreading read load. "With mirror direct clients can read directly from the mirror replicas instead of being routed back to the origin" (~02:00)
- Changes never flow backward: deleting from a mirror leaves the origin untouched, and origin deletes are not replicated to the mirror. "deletes in the origin stream are not replicated" (~03:02)
- Mirroring a work-queue origin is only partially supported and not resilient over intermittent links like leaf nodes; interest-based origins are unsupported with undefined behaviour. "if you're using interest-based retention, don't try it. Mirror streams don't officially support that" (~03:02)
- Mirrors tolerate a temporarily unreachable origin and retry after roughly 10 to 20 seconds. "the mirror waits about 10 to 20 seconds before retrying" (~03:02)
- Publishing to a mirror fails with an "expected stream does not match" error. "it says expected stream does not match because mirrors only pull from the origin" (~05:06)
- Because deletes are independent on each side, mirrors can serve as independent backups. "Deletes on one side don't affect the other. This makes mirrors useful as independent backups" (~06:06)
- Mirror promotion (2.12): unbind subjects from the old primary (e.g. set subjects to a dev-null placeholder), remove the mirror config and bind the subjects to it, then clean up the old stream. "first unbind subjects from the old primary so you don't have two streams competing for the same subjects" (~07:07)
- The server does not verify the mirror is caught up before promotion, so unreplicated messages are lost. "the server won't verify if the mirror is fully caught up, so any unreplicated messages will be lost" (~07:07)
- Mirrors are the tool for one-way replication across regions and unreliable networks without full synchronisation; they work best with standard (limits) retention. "they work best with standard retention policies" (~09:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers**

- Put the discriminating data (e.g. dwelling ID, room) in the subject, not buried in the payload or header, because consumer filtering works only on subjects. "definitely expose that bit of data in the subject so you can discriminate ... the degree of subscription filtering on the consumer side is all based on the subject" (~06:30)
- Co-locating a stream near the data source (per region/neighbourhood) reduces collection latency and improves availability compared with publishing across the country. "whatever the granularity ... to make a stream accessible to that's going to obviously reduce latency of collection ... provide availability" (~10:11)
- A NATS stream provides a total ordering on ingest; consumers always observe the same order regardless of how many publishers there are. "a stream in NATS provides a total ordering on ingest ... from a consumption side it's always going to observe the same order" (~11:14)
- Choose one stream vs many based on access patterns: how much ordering you need across entities, how co-located streams should be, and ingest rate. "the choice of one stream versus many streams really kind of comes down to how collocated do you want those streams to be and also frankly the rate of ingest" (~12:16)
- A single stream cannot exceed the throughput of the disk it writes to, so ingest rate alone may force you to split into multiple streams. "you can't obviously exceed past the throughput of your disk ... it might be necessary from a purely physical technical perspective that you actually have to break up the ingestion" (~13:17)
- Even with N streams, consumers still address data by subject filter, so you can drill down to a dwelling or zip code across a region-partitioned layout. "you can have n number of streams and you can still say I define a consumer I'm still interested in these particular subjects" (~13:17)
- Publishers only care about the subject, not the physical stream; subject mapping and stream sourcing let you route to the right underlying stream and change the stream topology over time. "on the publisher side all you care about is what subject you're publishing to not concretely the stream behind the scenes" (~16:23)
- The stream ingest timestamp is storage time when the server received the message, not the time the data was collected at the source; carry a source timestamp in the message if you need it. "it gives you a time stamp but that's really storage time when the server gets it not necessarily the time that the data was actually collected" (~18:24)
- Consumers must know which physical stream they bind to; this is the asymmetry with the publisher side. "you do have to know which physical stream you're consuming from" (~19:26)
- Stream sourcing multiplexes many origin streams into one aggregate stream asynchronously, like a materialized view; origin streams stay lightweight and highly available while the sourcing stream can have different retention. "I'm going to multiplex all of the data from all of these source streams ... and I'm going to funnel it all into one stream" (~22:32)
- A sourcing stream that aggregates tens, hundreds or thousands of origin streams needs correspondingly large disk. "if you're sourcing data from tens hundreds thousands of streams ... you're probably going to need a fairly beefy amount of disk space" (~23:32)
- 2.10 added multiple, possibly disjoint, subject filters on a single consumer. "with 2.10 we added the ability to define multiple filters now which is really nice that can be disjoint" (~24:34)
- Split workflows with two consumers on the same stream: one for real-time analytics and one archiving to external object storage; the aggregate can be short-retention while origins retain. "I have two consumers one for the real-time analytics and one for persisting out to stable object storage" (~25:35)
- Avoid the design where everything must synchronously deluge into one single stream; prefer origin streams plus async sourcing. "rather than saying I have this one single stream that everything basically has to deluge into synchronously" (~25:35)
- Every R3 stream adds load; a per-dwelling stream model multiplies replication cost, so size streams to hardware I/O limits rather than administrative units. "once you say let's have an R3 ... immediately the load on the system increases with each and every stream" (~27:36)
- Start with the simplest setup, a single stream, if throughput, reachability and latency allow; only add streams when requirements force it. "if we can get by with a single stream that can handle everything that's the simplest thing to operate" (~28:37)
- Unlike topic/partition systems where the partition is the unit of total order and replication, a NATS stream is itself totally ordered in storage and messages are addressable by subject. "NATS is different in that we have a single stream which is totally ordered on ingest ... versus other systems that are more like topic and partition based" (~29:40)
- Partition-based systems cannot filter by a subject hierarchy or tell you which partition holds a given key; NATS can address by known subject. "I can't address it by a subject that's known" (~30:42)
- A single stream can hold heterogeneous message types, discriminated by subject. "you can have heterogeneous types of data in a single stream and you can discriminate them again based on subject" (~31:42)
- A stream capturing foo.> stores foo.1, foo.10, foo.42 in one ordered log; subjects sort data within the stream, they do not route it elsewhere unless configured. "it's not going to break the ordering either so the subject names really give us a means of sorting data" (~33:46)
- A stream is an internal server-side subscriber on the configured subjects whose job is to persist messages to disk or memory; it decouples time as core NATS decouples space. "the job of the stream is literally an internal subscriber in the server ... my job is literally to persist this on your behalf" (~34:46)
- In a replicated stream the leader receives the message, stores it, sends it to replicas, and the ack chain completes; consumption is fully decoupled from that. "the leader's job is to say I'm subscribed to this subject ... stores it to disk ... sends it off to its other replicas they store it you get your ack chain" (~35:49)
- 2.10 logical partitioning: on ingest the stream deterministically appends a partition-number token derived from the subject; consumers filter with wildcards plus a concrete partition ID to get total order within a bucket. "it's deterministic so given the same input subject it's going to derive the same partition ID" (~66:30)
- 2.10 partitions are logical tokens in the subject, not physical partitions like other systems. "this is not a physical partition like we talked about with the other systems this is a logical partition ID" (~66:30)
- CLI backup/restore is out of band and never incremental or real time; the general recommendation is a mirror stream, possibly in another region, plus backups. "you're never going to with this mechanism it's never going to be incremental in real time ... you could very simply have a mirror stream" (~74:43)
- A mirror can live on slower disks with compression and long retention as an archive while the origin is pruned or compacted. "your mirror stream that is literally for archival ... on slower disks you could apply compression to that stream" (~75:43)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.10 Webinar**

- 2.10 adds opt-in per-stream compression using S2 (a Snappy variant), trading storage for CPU. "this is using S2 compression which is a variation on top of Snappy compression ... you're trading off storage and CPU" (~01:00)
- Compression is editable on an existing stream; the server compresses existing message blocks in real time after the edit. "this field is editable you define compression to S2 and then it will effectively rip through all the message blocks in real time" (~02:01)
- Compression does not degrade ingest throughput because the active block being appended to is left uncompressed; a block is compressed asynchronously only once it is full. "the active block that is actually being written to appended to is basically not compressed and only once the message block is done and filled up then it actually gets asynchronously compressed" (~03:03)
- Storage-level encryption and compression compose correctly because data is compressed before it is encrypted. "the data actually gets compressed prior to being encrypted so you actually get that benefit of compression" (~04:03)
- The 2.10 stream storage format is not backward compatible with 2.9 except that 2.9.22 and later patch releases understand it; downgrading is not recommended. "we did release 2.9.22 and then any patch release after that ... are aware of this new format" (~04:03)
- The new storage format cut restart/recovery of a 2.1 TB, 300-million-message stream from roughly 15 minutes on 2.9 to 1.1 seconds on 2.10, because 2.9 scanned and checksummed every block. "2.1 terabytes in size with 300 million messages ... roughly 15 minutes to actually restart the stream ... with 2.10 it takes 1.1 seconds" (~05:05)
- Fast stream recovery matters for rolling upgrades, Kubernetes restarts, and placing replicas on new nodes, and the 15-minute figure was for one stream; many streams multiply the wait. "this is just for one stream mind you so for people who have a lot of streams this time can add up" (~06:05)
- Native MQTT support requires JetStream because MQTT QoS relies on it, but no streams need to be defined by hand; the server translates between MQTT topics and NATS subjects. "it does require JetStream because of the quality of service mechanisms ... but beyond that you don't have to define any streams" (~08:11)
- Stream replicas must be placed within a single cluster; they cannot be spread across a supercluster. "when you define a stream the replicas have to be placed within the same cluster you can't spread replicas across a super cluster" (~22:23)
- Max stream replicas remain five in 2.10; in a stretch cluster those replicas can sit in different regions. "the max stream replicas continue to be five yep but now you can place those replicas in servers that go across completely different regions" (~26:30)
- All filter subjects of a consumer must belong to the same stream; to consume across streams, create a stream that sources from multiple origins and consume from that. "the pattern would be to create a stream that is actually sourcing from multiple origin streams and then create a consumer on that stream" (~29:34)
- Stream-level subject transforms (implemented by Jean-Noël Moyne) generalize server-config subject mapping and remove the pre-2.10 limitation that KV mirrors could not be created within the same account and cluster. "there was a limitation that you couldn't do that previously unless you were spanning a JetStream domain or cross accounts" (~31:36)
- A stream subject transform can append a deterministic partition token computed from a wildcard token, e.g. events.* -> events.{{wildcard(1)}}.{{partition(5,1)}}; ordered pull consumers then bind to events.*.0 through events.*.4. "give me five partitions and compute that relative to the first wild card" (~32:37)
- Partition mapping stays stable unless you edit the partition count; changing it moves subjects between buckets, though strategies exist to handle that. "unless you're messing around with the partition count and editing those things" (~34:41)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- Users put and delete hundreds of millions of KV keys, producing streams with data at the head and tail and a huge deleted gap in the middle; this "interior deletes" state dominated Raft snapshots. "the state snapshot for the messages we're retaining and deleting ends up being really big because it's tracking more information about things that we no longer want to keep" (~26:29)
- Marshalling large delete-state snapshots for replication consumed increasing CPU and backed up the server, so 2.10 reworked the file store; most 2.10 performance gains come from that work. "more and more CPU time was going into this process and the server is backing up behind that work" (~27:30)
- Unlike append-only logs with only tail compaction, a NATS stream supports explicit deletion of an arbitrary interior message; that is how KV tombstoning works. "you can actually explicitly delete an arbitrary interior message within a stream ... this is how frankly the KV abstraction actually works" (~28:31)
- KV buckets and object stores are streams, so file-store improvements benefit all of them. "KV buckets are streams object stores are streams so everything benefits from this" (~29:33)
- 2.10 stores deleted-message state as AVL trees for sparse deletes and run-length encoding for large deleted ranges, and the server picks whichever structure fits the pattern. "we've tried to use AVL trees for what is effectively quite a sparse set of deletions and then we also use run length encoding for ... large blocks" (~29:33)
- In a supercluster each JetStream Raft group is bounded to one cluster, so persistence performance does not suffer from inter-region latency while global connectivity remains. "each JetStream group is only bounded to this specific cluster in a super cluster so ... persistence with JetStream does not suffer because you have more regions" (~43:43)
- Choose a stretch cluster when regulation requires data replicated consistently across regions and you accept higher-latency persistence; mirroring/sourcing across a supercluster gives similar reach but with secondary, eventually available copies. "you can achieve something similar with super clusters but then you need to include some mirroring and sourcing ... the guarantees around when the data will be available its consistency is a little different" (~44:45)
- Server tags let you dictate where stream replicas land, including anti-affinity across regions or providers, or you can let NATS place them. "you can actually tag the servers and say where the data lands ... or you can just say to NATS just do how you think" (~45:45)
- Enabling JetStream encryption destroys file-system block-level compressibility, so 2.10 compresses in the file store before encryption. "if you enable encryption in JetStream today pretty much all of your compressibility on the disk ... goes completely out of the window" (~55:58)
- Subject mapping existed since 2.9 at server level and was heavily used for cross-account imports/exports; 2.10 moves it to stream, source and mirror level. "you can have subject mapping on stream level sources and mirrors level" (~64:06)
- Stream-level transforms let you change subjects for API changes without breaking clients, and aggregate identical subjects from many factories or leaf nodes without compromising your subject architecture. "it allows you to even handle switching subjects for API changes without any breaking changes" (~62:02)
- Transforms on sources/mirrors solve subject-namespace collisions when bridging systems by rewriting subjects on the fly. "subject namespace collisions ... you can now just rewrite these on the fly so that you don't have to worry about whether you're polluting one namespace with another" (~65:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP07: Going off piste; KV patterns with NATS.io (pt1)**

- Byron's first NATS use was pub/sub fan-out to notify many things instead of HTTP hacks, then NATS Streaming for ETL pipelines: extract, transform, publish to a stream, fan out to consumers that load other systems. "taking data out transforming it throwing it into a stream and then I was able to fan out effectively consume from that stream and plop it in other systems" (~04:09)
- NATS Streaming had only a handful of stream knobs, mostly limits like max messages; JetStream, KV and Object Store have many more options that can overwhelm newcomers, and each exists for a reason. "NATS Streaming had a handful of knobs ... fairly limited it was mostly around limits" (~04:09)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02: Monolith to Modular Monolith with NATS.io**

- Polling a database for updates can be inverted into streaming state transitions or KV watchers, which is more responsive and optimized for that use. "if you invert that and you can just stream it out and you can model your state transitions in that way, that can be very powerful" (~26:36)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP05: Exploring Powerful Client-side Features and Abstractions in NATS.io**

- KV is a client-side abstraction over a stream; the server does not know a stream is a KV bucket. The `max messages per subject` stream option was added specifically because KV history needed it. "that max message per subject stream configuration option was created purely because it was needed for key value" (~37:48)
- Setting max messages per subject to 1 yields a stream that keeps only the latest message per subject, which spawned new non-KV use cases. "thanks to that you can have infinite application of messages if you set it to one" (~37:48)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP01S3: Going back to basics with core NATS!**

- JetStream, including its Raft layer, is built purely on core NATS publish/subscribe and request/reply with heartbeats; its reliability patterns can be borrowed selectively. "JetStream is actually built on top of core NATS, it's just using publish subscribe request reply and that's all it is, even the Raft layer" (~17:33)
- JetStream is described as core NATS with the server subscribing to your messages to store them. "JetStream is just core NATS with server subscribing to your messages to store them" (~21:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02S3: Orbit - The NATS Client Extensions**

- Batch (direct) get is a 2.12 feature that will be implemented in Orbit rather than the client, not because the server side is unstable but because the client API shape could not be agreed within a few weeks. "batch get which will be the 2.12 feature ... we decided to get it into Orbit instead of the client" (~32:37)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03S3: NATS 2.11 Release**

- A trace can be configured so the message is neither persisted into a stream nor delivered to the final client, giving a dry-run of the path. "you can literally ask the system stop just short of finally delivering the message" (~08:09)
- Per-message TTL is set with the `Nats-TTL` header plus a duration on publish and controls how long that individual message survives regardless of, or in combination with, stream limits. "activated using a header when you publish the message, which is just Nats-TTL and then a duration" (~11:11)
- Per-message TTL is planned to clean up KV delete tombstones, which accumulate in buckets with high delete rates; watchers still get the delete notification but the markers no longer live forever. "if you have a very high incidence of deletes you can end up with an awful lot of history in your KV bucket which is just delete tombstones" (~12:13)
- 2.11 includes a first pass at subject delete markers when a subject disappears from a stream via max age, to support the KV use case, with more iteration planned. "in 2.11 we'll have an initial pass of that that just happens with max age" (~14:18)
- Per-message TTL is implemented with a timed hash wheel so very large numbers of expiries can be tracked with little memory. "it actually uses an exotic data structure called a timed hash wheel ... track an awful lot of key expiries without actually using too much memory" (~15:21)
- Multi-message (batch) get is "a consumer without a consumer": one request returning many responses, with filters, start sequence/time, up-to sequence/time, and multiple subject filters, which plain direct get could not do. "you can specify multiple subject filters as well which I think wasn't possible before with the old direct gets" (~33:45)
- Batch get responses are capped (the speaker recalls 64 messages, and a byte limit) after which you paginate with another request. "maximum amount of messages or maximum amount of bytes that can be sent back before you need to paginate in some way, 64 messages I think" (~33:45)
- Consumers are server-side state; many small operations via consumers eat server resources, whereas batch get creates no server state and is fire-and-forget. "the biggest difference is that batch get does not create state on the server, it just gives you what you asked for and it's done" (~34:46)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS tools and benchmarking with JNM! NATS Community Office Hours (Reupload)**

- NATS positions itself against Kafka on "proper queuing, proper request reply, proper multi-tenancy, no partitions unless you want them". "proper queuing, proper request reply, proper multi-tenancy ... no partitions unless you want them" (~02:03)
- JetStream-enabled leaf nodes at the edge give store-and-forward: publishes are stored locally and guaranteed to be mirrored or sourced to the hub when connectivity returns, within milliseconds if the link is up. "it still is stored locally by the stream at the edge and reliably forwarded" (~06:08)
- Subject-based addressing lets a consumer filter messages from a stream; Kafka is one topic, one stream, with no server-side filtering. "Kafka is one topic one stream and when you read messages from a stream in Kafka there's no filtering" (~14:18)
- Benchmark JetStream publish and consume separately before combining them, because together they compete for CPU and you cannot tell which limits the other. "when you do the both together you don't know which one is limiting the other" (~52:04)
- With a subscriber attached, JetStream publish throughput dropped from about 139k to about 84k msgs/s in the demo, with the consumer side being the limiting factor. "with no one listening you got 139 ... with someone listening, 84" (~70:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Benchmark Core NATS & NATS JetStream using the NATS CLI tool**

- A core publish returns no server acknowledgement; a JetStream publish returns an ack that the message was received and persisted, so use JetStream publish to get the full benefit of a stream. "a JetStream publish operation lets you get an acknowledgement that the message was properly received and persisted" (~13:15)
- Synchronous JetStream publishing is bounded by round-trip time like any request/reply; raise throughput with many synchronous clients or with batching (async publish with a batch size). "the way to increase throughput in those situations is to either have a lot of clients ... or start using batching" (~14:16)
- Publish batch size 10 gives a dramatic improvement, 100 another large one, 1000 only a little more: diminishing returns set in around a batch of 100. "you start getting to where you have a diminishing return of increasing the batch size" (~14:16)
- Two publishers with the default batch of 100 reached nearly the same rate as one publisher with batches of 1000. "we get pretty close to the maximum that we saw with batches of a thousand, except in this case we have two guys just using batches of 100" (~15:17)
- Core NATS subscribers can observe messages being published into a stream at the same time, with high fan-out still possible. "these are core NATS subscribers onto the JetStream publisher" (~15:17)
- File storage publishes slower than memory, but reading back from disk is still fast: a push consumer delivered 4 × 400,000 messages in about 4 seconds (~400k msgs/s) on the laptop. "retrieving from disk is still quite fast ... about 400,000 per second" (~26:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS: Ordered, Scalable Stream Processing**

- The partition function is a subject transform that hashes the chosen subject tokens into a partition number from 0 to X-1, deterministically and roughly balanced. "It hashes the subject tokens you choose and turns them into a partition number from zero up to X minus one" (~02:00)
- The transform is applied at stream ingress and appends a partition token to each subject, so messages are physically separated by key inside the stream. "You apply the transform at the stream's ingress and it appends a partition token to each subject" (~02:00)
- Elastic groups use a work-queue stream that sources from the main stream, with a filter for the partitioning; static groups put consumers directly on the stream. "Elastic uses a work queue stream, which sources from the main stream" (~10:07)
- The elastic library owns a hidden work-queue stream and its consumers, so it can reshuffle partition filters live without teardown. "Because the library owns that stream and its consumers, it can reshuffle the partition filters live with no teardown" (~13:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Distributed Counters in NATS — Global Totals Without Locks**

- NATS 2.12 adds a distributed counter to JetStream: enable a stream flag, publish signed deltas as headers, and every replica converges to the same total without consensus or locks, even with out-of-order arrival. "every replica converges to the same total without consensus, without locks, even with messages arriving out of order" (~01:01)
- A stream that only accepts signed deltas is automatically a CRDT because addition is commutative; NATS builds the PN-counter idea into JetStream as a first-class primitive. "a stream that only accepts signed deltas is automatically a CRDT. Order doesn't matter. Retries don't matter" (~01:01)
- Set allow_message_counter to true and every subject in the stream becomes a counter; every message must carry a Nats-Incr header with a signed integer. "every subject in the stream is a counter, and every message has to carry a NATS increment header with a signed integer" (~02:01)
- On an increment the server reads the current total from the last message on that subject, applies the delta, stores a new message with the updated value, and returns the post-increment total in the publish ack. "returns the post-increment total in the publish acknowledgement. No extra read" (~02:01)
- Counter values are big integers stored as JSON strings so they can exceed 2^63 and JavaScript won't lose precision. "Values are big integers, not 64-bit ints ... They're stored as JSON strings for exactly this reason" (~02:01)
- Multi-region aggregation: regional counters publish to their own subjects, a continental stream sources them with subject transforms, and a global stream sources the continental ones. "A continental stream sources both with subject transforms, and a global stream sources the continental ones" (~03:03)
- When a sourced counter message arrives, the server computes the delta from the last seen source value and rewrites the header to that change only, so there is no double counting even with replays or lost messages. "the server calculates the delta from the last seen source value, and rewrites the header to reflect only that change. No double counting" (~03:03)
- Caveats: once allow_message_counter is on it cannot be turned off; counter streams cannot be mirrors (use sources); limits retention is required; no discard new, no per-message TTLs, no Nats-Rollup header. "Once you turn allow message counter on, you can't turn it off. Counter streams can't be mirrors. Use sources instead" (~03:03)
- Resetting a replicated counter means publishing a matching negative delta; purge alone will not propagate across sources. "resetting a replicated counter means publishing a matching negative delta. Purge alone won't propagate across sources" (~04:03)
- Each subject in a counter stream is its own counter; subjects do not share state. "each subject in a counter stream is its own counter. They don't share state" (~06:05)
- A publish to a counter stream with incorrect headers returns an error. "when you use the incorrect headers for this counter stream ... you'll see we get an error" (~06:05)
- Stream info on a sourcing counter stream tracks per-source values, so the global total can be broken down by origin. "global tracks where it came from under sources" (~12:14)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Delayed Message Scheduling in NATS — One-Time, Cron, and Subject Sampling**

- Before 2.12 there was no native way to hold a message for later; NAK-with-delay on a consumer was a workaround that did not scale. "You could use NACK with delay on a consumer, but that was a workaround and it didn't scale" (~01:01)
- Starting in 2.12 you publish with a Nats-Schedule header ("at" plus an RFC 3339 timestamp for one-time delivery) and a Nats-Schedule-Target header naming the subject that receives the message. "you set it to at followed by an RFC 3339 timestamp. You also set a NATS schedule target header" (~01:01)
- Each schedule lives on its own unique subject; the most recent message on that subject is the active schedule, so publishing again updates it, and independent delays need distinct subjects (e.g. append a UUID). "Each schedule lives on its own unique subject. The most recent message on that subject is the active schedule" (~02:01)
- In 2.14 the scheduler gained recurring schedules: cron expressions, fixed intervals like every 5 minutes, and aliases like @hourly and @daily; NATS cron uses a six-field format with a seconds field. "NATS uses a six-field format that adds a seconds field for finer precision" (~02:01)
- Subject sampling (2.14) republishes the latest message from a source subject on a schedule, e.g. the latest reading every 5 minutes from a sensor emitting hundreds per second. "you can capture just the latest reading every 5 minutes, reducing noise for downstream analytics without touching the sensor code" (~03:03)
- The stream must opt in with allow_message_schedules; once enabled it cannot be disabled, and it cannot be enabled on source or mirror streams. "Once you enable it, you cannot disable it on that stream. It also cannot be enabled on source or mirror streams" (~03:03)
- A schedule in the past fires immediately, and after a server restart all past-due schedules execute right away. "Any past due schedules execute right away" (~03:03)
- Set Nats-Schedule-TTL so generated messages expire and consumers can discard stale deliveries, e.g. after a restart replays past-due schedules; this requires allow_message_ttl on the stream. "You can set a NATS schedule TTL to give generated messages an expiration, so consumers can detect and discard stale deliveries" (~03:03)
- Cron schedules with a time zone are exposed to DST transitions (skipped hour on spring forward, double fire on fall back); use UTC. "Sticking with UTC avoids this entirely" (~03:03)
- The scheduler can only deliver within its own stream, so schedule subjects and target subjects must be in the same stream; scheduling headers are rejected on streams without the flag. "they must be in the same stream because the scheduler can only deliver within its own stream" (~05:05)
- A scheduled publish parks the message on its schedule subject; at fire time the server produces a new message on the target subject with the same body and custom headers propagated verbatim, plus Nats-Scheduler (pointing to the schedule subject) and Nats-Schedule-Next (purge for one-time). "your custom headers are propagated verbatim. But, the server also stamps on its own headers" (~06:06)
- After a one-time delivery the original schedule message is purged from its holding subject. "Once that happens, the original schedule message is purged from its holding subject" (~06:06)
- For recurring schedules Nats-Schedule-Next carries the next fire timestamp, and republishing to the schedule subject changes the recurrence. "we can publish to it again if we want to update the recurrence rate of each message" (~08:08)
- Sampling uses a Nats-Schedule-Source header telling the server which subject to read the latest message from. "A schedule with NATS schedule source tells the server to grab the latest reading from that subject every 5 seconds" (~12:13)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Per-Message TTL — Fine-Grained Expiration for JetStream Messages**

- By default a stream has one expiration rule, max_age, applied to every message equally. "a Jetstream stream gives you one expiration rule, max age, and it applies to every message equally" (~00:00)
- Per-message TTL was added in NATS 2.11: set a TTL on individual messages with the Nats-TTL header after enabling allow_message_ttl on the stream. "Set expiration per message with the NATS TTL header. Enable it in your stream config by setting allow_message_ttl to true" (~01:00)
- Each message's TTL countdown runs independently, and max_age still applies as an upper bound that a message TTL cannot exceed. "Max age still applies as an upper bound. A message's TTL can't exceed it" (~01:00)
- A Nats-TTL of "never" makes a message outlive the stream's max_age and be retained forever. "we're going to send a message in with a NATS TTL of never, so it never expires. It will outlive the max age" (~02:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Message Tracing | NATS 2.11**

- A server that only stores the message into a stream shows a JS egress event and no hops field. "our only egress event is type JS for JetStream. Notice that there is no hop field because there are no hops from this server" (~08:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Expected Sequence Headers — Optimistic Concurrency Control Explained**

- Expected sequence headers give optimistic concurrency control: multiple processes work in parallel without locks and conflicting writes are detected and rejected rather than prevented. "It'll detect and reject conflicting rights instead of just outright preventing them" (~00:00)
- Two writers that both read sequence 4 and publish with expected last sequence 4: one succeeds (stream at 5), the other is rejected and retries with expected 5. "only one succeeds setting the sequence to five and the other is rejected because by the time it arrives the stream is already at five" (~00:00)
- There is only one sequence counter, the stream sequence; all three expected-sequence header variants validate against it and just filter what they compare with. "there's only one sequence counter the stream sequence ... these headers just filter what they check against" (~01:01)
- Three variants: global (Nats-Expected-Last-Sequence), per subject (Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence), and per pattern (Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence combined with Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence-Subject). "per pattern ... uses the NATS expected last subject sequence header in combination with the NATS expected last subject sequence subject header" (~01:01)
- Global expected-last-sequence suits a single writer needing strict ordering across all subjects, such as a global event log. "If you're the only writer and need strict ordering across everything, this is what you want" (~02:03)
- A rejected publish returns a "wrong last sequence" error that includes the actual last sequence. "it says wrong last sequence and gives us the last sequence number" (~04:05)
- Per-subject does not give each subject its own 0,1,2 counter: the expected value is the stream sequence of that subject's last message, and a never-used subject expects 0. "the common misconception is that each subject has its own counter starting at 0 1 2 3 but the expected value is the stream sequence of that subject's last message" (~07:09)
- Track the sequence returned in each pub ack and use it as the expected value for the next publish. "You track the return sequence and use it for the next publish" (~07:09)
- Per-subject tracks each distinct subject separately, so order.1.created and order.1.shipped cannot share tracking; publishing to a new subject with expected 1 fails because its last sequence is 0. "events.order.1 shipped is a different subject with no prior messages. Its last sequence is zero, not one" (~07:09)
- Per-pattern lets you supply a wildcard pattern (e.g. events.order.1.>) so related subjects for one entity share sequence tracking while other entities stay independent; use it for event sourcing where entity events span multiple subjects. "order.1.created and order.1.shipped can share the same sequence tracking while order two anything stays independent" (~08:10)
- In Go the options are WithExpectLastSequence, WithExpectLastSequencePerSubject, and the per-subject-pattern variant. "You would use jetstream with expect last sequence" (~04:05)
- Expected sequence headers are also used by atomic batch publishing. "it's also used by atomic batch publishing" (~02:03)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Atomic Batch Publishing | NATS 2.12**

- Atomic batch publishing is a stream configuration option that publishes N messages into a stream with all-or-nothing guarantees. "Either every message commits together or none of them do" (~00:00)
- Without atomic batching each publish is independent, so a connection drop after the third of five related messages leaves a partial write. "your connection drops after the third? Well, you have a partial right. Your data is inconsistent" (~01:01)
- Batch messages are staged invisibly on the server (consumers see nothing) until the last message carries Nats-Batch-Commit, then all appear at once. "messages are staged invisibly on the server. Consumers don't see anything" (~01:01)
- Three headers drive batching: Nats-Batch-Id (unique id), Nats-Batch-Sequence (incrementing per message), Nats-Batch-Commit (commit signal on the last message). "First is the NATS batch ID ... Second is the NATS batch sequence ... And third is NATS batch commit" (~01:01)
- A batch is rejected if the batch id exceeds 64 characters, if sequence numbers have gaps, or if the stream uses async persist mode; as of 2.12.1 duplicate messages in a batch also fail validation. "A batch ID over 64 characters, gaps in your sequence numbers, or running on a stream with async persist mode" (~02:03)
- Nats-Expected-Last-Sequence (or the per-subject variant) on the first message of a batch gives optimistic locking: the batch fails if the stream moved while it was built, and you retry with fresh data. "This header is only allowed on the first message of a batch" (~02:03)
