- Limits: up to 1,000 messages per batch, 50 batches in flight per stream, 1,000 batches per server, and a batch is abandoned after 10 seconds of inactivity; all are configurable in server config. "you can have up to a thousand messages per batch. Each stream can have 50 batches in flight at once. Each server can have a thousand batches total" (~02:03)
- Batches must go into a single stream; they cannot cross streams. "batches must go into a single stream. They can't cross streams" (~03:04)
- The stream must be created with allow batch (allow_atomic_publish in the Go config) to accept batches. "including the allow batch flag to enable atomic batching" (~03:04)
- A batch can span multiple subjects in one stream, so messages fanned out to warehouse, payment, and notification consumers commit together. "Different messages going to different consumers but all committed together" (~06:05)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.11: What's New?**

- Per-message TTLs are the first limit that applies to individual messages rather than the whole stream; the TTL is optional and can differ per message. "the first time that we've been able to introduce a limit that applies only to individual messages rather than to the entire stream" (~02:07)
- Stream multi-get is for applications reading streams directly without consumers: multiple subject filters, bounds such as up-to sequence or time, returning a batch in sequence order; it is the first of several planned batch operations. "you can provide multiple subject filters. You can provide additional bounds such as only up to a certain sequence number or time" (~06:15)
- A trace into JetStream reports the message reaching JetStream at the server that is the stream leader at that time. "it would probably report whichever the server was that was the leader for that stream at that time" (~08:18)
- Max pending per subject was not planned as of this talk. "Any plans to implement max pending per subject. Not aware of that at the moment" (~09:18)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Future of NATS: Roadmap & Vision**

- 2.12 focus: higher-order client-side patterns, some requiring native server capabilities, because clients are good at primitives and need to move up the stack. "some of these require native NATS server capabilities so that we can build client side higher order patterns" (~21:36)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — We need to talk about Microservices... (And how NATS.io can simplify things)**

- The same log subjects can be captured into a stream on demand (nats stream add with subjects math.log.>) for later analysis. "I can even put this into a JetStream if I wanted to" (~20:26)
- For distributed data, JetStream streams, KV (Redis replacement) and Object Store (S3/MinIO replacement) share the same security model and are replicated globally from day zero. "on day zero ready to replicate and scale out globally" (~29:35)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — JetStream KV: A fascinating alternative to Redis...**

- A KV bucket is a stream under the hood with a thin layer of client-side sugar; everything learned about streams (replication, mirrors, sources, accounts, ACLs) applies to KV. "a key value store is no different than a stream in terms of all of the internals" (~02:01)
- Because a KV is a stream you get replication, mirror, source, mux/demux, multi-tenancy via accounts, and subject-based ACLs on buckets. "being able to mirror source mux and demux ... you get all the multi-tenancy with accounts" (~06:04)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The ONE feature that makes NATS more powerful than Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ & Redis**

- Consumers are "windows into the data of the stream": server-side filtering on the whole subject plus control over delivery, redelivery and start position. "they're really windows into the data of the stream" (~01:00)
- JetStream indexes on subject tokens (e.g. orders.<location>.<orderID>.<status>), which is the source of consumer filtering flexibility. "JetStream does index on these topics ... this is kind of the crux of where a lot of the flexibility in JetStream consumers comes from" (~02:01)
- Recommendation: consolidate related data into one stream (e.g. one orders stream with the whole lifecycle) rather than a topic per event type, and rely on filter subjects. "we usually recommend people try to consolidate a lot of things to one stream" (~10:12)
- For single-message lookups the direct get API is more efficient than a consumer, and a batch direct get is coming in future server versions to do these lookups in one call without a consumer. "we're actually introducing a batch version of the direct get API call" (~38:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Give your Go app superpowers with an Embedded NATS Server**

- To enable JetStream in an embedded server that also leaf-nodes to a cloud account, set a server name, JetStream true, and a JetStream domain so the local assets are addressable distinctly from the cloud's. "we need a JetStream domain to be able to identify all of these stream assets" (~20:20)
- Use `nats --js-domain embedded stream list/add` from the cloud context to manage streams that live inside the embedded server. "I can say js domain embedded and then it's going to list out the streams for this embedded context" (~23:24)
- Publishes into the cloud account on the embedded stream's subjects are captured by the embedded stream because the subscription crossed the leaf connection. "this is again sending it to Synadia Cloud but this is actually being picked up by the embedded NATS server" (~24:26)
- Backing up the local stream to the cloud is a mirror created in the cloud with "import from a different JetStream domain" set to the embedded domain; this is the offline-first sync pattern. "we just created essentially an offline first application ... NATS kind of forwards all that data once we get connected again" (~25:29)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Stream processing: the easy way (with NATS and Benthos)**

- JetStream streams or KV can sit on the source side, the sink side, or as intermediate state between pipeline stages. "you can have JetStream whether it's a stream or a KV end up on either the source or the sink side ... and then things like NATS KV store some intermediate state" (~04:05)
- Backup/tiered-storage pattern: JetStream input → batch 1,000 (max ack pending set to 10,000) → tar + gzip → S3 with a timestamped path; sending message-by-message to S3 is called out as inefficient. "you don't want to just send a message by message over to S3 that's going to be really inefficient" (~33:40)
- Restore is the inverse: S3 input with a gzip-decompress + untar scanner turns archives back into messages; the backup config was about 19 lines. "in 19 lines of yaml I have a backup strategy" (~34:41)
- JetStream has its own backup mechanism; the S3 archive is presented as an alternative for messages that will expire or have TTLs on the JetStream side. "JetStream does have a backup mechanism but there's also other ways that you can do backups" (~32:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Seamless evolution across geos and clouds | RethinkConn '22**

- Leaf-node bridging applies not only to core pub/sub but to data streaming, mirroring streams, and key-value stores. "we're talking data streaming, mirroring streams and key-value stores" (~08:07)
- For data-at-rest sovereignty (e.g. "stored only in Germany"), JetStream placement uses server tags that can encode geography; many customers do this. "configure NATS JetStream ... to place assets based off of server tags which you could base off of geography" (~17:26)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Where are we now and where to next? | RethinkConn '22**

- Data needs mobility: move a stream, replicate it closer to the application, aggregate streams or KV stores, or mirror a subset. "we need to be able to move a stream, we need to be able to replicate a stream" (~08:10)
- Shipped: tag-based stream placement (server tags, useful for GDPR/geo), stream migration, and replica scaling from R1 to R3 and back at any time. "I can take an R1 stream turn it into an R3 back down to an R1 as I need to" (~09:11)
- Subject hash partitioning (by Jean-Noël) splits a subject into several subjects for ordered processing spread across consumers, plus streaming publish as a scalability play. "take a subject, partition it into several other subjects for ordered processing" (~09:11)
- A new simplified JetStream API is coming because JetStream's internal complexity leaked into the original API; it is beta/experimental in some clients and will long-term replace the old one. "unfortunately some of that was reflected in the API" (~11:14)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extending stateful services to the edge | RethinkConn '22**

- A stream mirror is the construct for data locality: an origin stream lives in the cloud hub and a local device mirrors it, keeping access even when disconnected; the same applies to KV. "the mirror construct is exactly what we need to support data locality" (~07:10)
- Each leaf node can have its own JetStream domain, a separate namespace; a mirror is created there by referencing the hub's domain (NGS) as the mirror source. "every leaf node can have its own JetStream domain ... you create a mirror from that specifying the NGS domain" (~08:11)
- A direct mirror received all 100 origin messages almost instantly after creation. "the mirror already has almost instantaneously all of the 100 messages" (~10:14)
- A mirror can have a completely different configuration from its origin: the origin was file-based, R3, limits retention, while the leaf mirror was R1, memory storage, work-queue retention. "when I created my mirror I said I only want one replica ... memory and I want it to be a work queue retention" (~11:17)
- Reverse direction: small edge boxes (e.g. Raspberry Pis) use tight retention and store-and-forward via sourcing/mirroring into a hub stream with near-unlimited retention. "retention policy is pretty tight and we do a store and forward over to the hub in the cloud" (~11:17)
- Consuming from the leaf mirror left the NGS origin stream untouched, because no consumer is bound to the origin; the work-queue mirror removes messages as they are acknowledged. "the NGS stream hasn't been touched because we don't actually have a consumer bound to that" (~14:21)
- Mirrors act as digital twins (same messages elsewhere); sourcing muxes many leaf streams into one central "mega stream" for processing pipelines, or demuxes a central stream out to leaf nodes/accounts filtered by subject or wildcard. "we can also demux data ... you get a replica of this data but only a portion of it" (~15:22)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Effective debugging using the NATS CLI | RethinkConn '22**

- With JetStream enabled you get the JetStream meta service, which runs across all nodes with no single point of failure and tracks JetStream-enabled servers. "this magic service called the JetStream meta service ... runs on all of your nodes so there's not a single point of failure" (~05:06)
- `nats server report jetstream` adds the RAFT meta-group block showing whether the meta leader has connectivity to every expected node, health, and lag; it is a more opinionated view that marks a lost server as not current/offline. "it's a little bit more of an opinionated view" (~06:08)
- When a JetStream server is lost the meta leader moves to another node almost instantaneously. "it automatically and almost instantaneously moved from vbox6 ... to vbox7" (~06:08)
- `nats traffic` listens to everything in the cluster and shows rolling statistics; in a stable system with no asset changes the RAFT proposals/votes columns show no votes. "a happy stable system ... generally you won't see votes here" (~07:08)
- If two of three availability zones go down, an R3 stream is effectively disabled and `nats traffic` shows continuous voting as the remaining node looks for peers, a quick sign that assets are impaired. "two out of three availability zones go down ... a stream asset ... is essentially disabled" (~07:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Lightweight relational databases at the edge | RethinkConn '22**

- Streams and KV are built into the server, but different data models are needed to query data; the proof of concept projects a raw stream into a relational table for edge workloads. "how can we take a raw stream and actually represent that as a table in a relational database" (~01:01)
- Creating a table creates a consumer on the same-named stream and subscribes; default columns are the sequence, subject, timestamp, headers (as JSON), and the raw data blob, because nothing more can be inferred from an opaque payload. "create a table, create a consumer and then subscribe" (~04:02)
- Declaring the payload encoding as JSON lets you map explicit JSON fields (id, name, preferences) to real columns and choose a key column as primary key. "you can actually define explicit columns to augment the table" (~06:05)
- Without a declared key the table is append-only, so retries produce duplicate rows keyed by sequence; with a key it behaves like a KSQL-style table where a new message for the same key updates the row in place. "we didn't append a new customer record, we actually updated the record in place" (~09:08)
- Intended architecture: mirror streams down to edge devices and run the projection process locally, joining across tables in a real database; the process resumes populating after disconnect and reconnect. "the nsql process can get disconnected from the server and then you reconnect and then it just keeps resuming" (~11:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Using NATS JetStream as a Kine backend for k3s | RethinkConn '22**

- All k3s KV buckets were mirrored up to NGS; after destroying the local server, backups taken from the cloud were restored in seconds and the clusters came back with their state after ~20 s of startup. "it takes probably about 20 seconds of course these k3s clusters have to start up" (~10:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Short break and Q&A! | RethinkConn '22**

- Replicas vs mirrors: an R3 stream is one system; a publish is not acknowledged until a quorum of replicas agrees and commits to stable storage (file) or memory. Mirrors and sources are kept in sync asynchronously and self-heal. "you're not going to get an acknowledgement back until a quorum of those servers that are hosting that asset agree" (~12:12)
- A memory-only close cluster can ingest 200–400k messages/s and be mirrored out worldwide, trading a small loss on catastrophic failure for very high ingest. "cluster memory only 2 3 400,000 ingest per second, and then they're mirrored out" (~13:15)
- Future vision: because NATS is inherently observable, the system could autonomously spin up services and data mirrors where requests originate (e.g. Japan) based on threshold modeling, instead of doing it manually. "we could make this totally autonomous" (~15:18)
- Mirrors are strictly read-only, bit-for-bit replicas including sequence and timestamps; a publish or KV put against a mirror fails when the origin is unavailable. "mirrors are read-only. If the origin server is not around and you try to do a publish or a KV put, that will fail" (~18:23)
- For active-active or east/west failover use sources, not mirrors: sources can pull from many streams, have their own subjects, and accept direct writes, e.g. orders.east and orders.west each sourcing the other. "you're going to not use mirrors, you're going to use sources" (~18:23)
- Combine sources with subject mapping so a client publishing to "orders" is mapped to orders.west locally; on failover to east the mapping there routes "orders" to orders.east. "orders goes to order.east" (~19:23)
- Mirrors and sources work across leaf node boundaries in both directions and can be daisy-chained: origin, a single leaf mirror, then five local replicas on a 6-million-square-foot factory floor for low-latency reads. "You can even daisy chain them" (~20:24)
- For tens or hundreds of millions of observers of persistent state, the "hybrid structure" is a stream or KV configured to republish events over core NATS, with enough info in each republished event to detect a lost message. "it can be told to republish events. And the republish events have enough information to understand if an endpoint is lost" (~30:39)
- There are no plans for pluggable JetStream persistence beyond file and memory (NATS Streaming had database backends); instead the direction is applying JetStream to external data stores decomposed into a globally ordered sequence of events. "for JetStream right now I think we're still going to stick with file and memory" (~32:41)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Derek Collison RethinkConn 2025 Keynote and Closing Remarks**

- The data layer sits on connectivity and provides synchronous and asynchronous replication plus materialized views (KV, object store). "For data, we built on the connectivity layer, providing synchronous and asynchronous replication and materialized views." (~01:05)
- Fleet data flows use "source muxing" (aggregating every fleet member's data into cloud streams/KV) and "demuxing" (pulling individual members' data back out on the cloud side). "source muxing and demuxing... we can collect data from all of the fleet items and collect them within the cloud" (~03:00)
- Edge AI data-collection pattern: apps store data locally and NATS mirrors it to the cloud, self-healing after outages, so the app never handles transport. "data is stored locally and then the NATS system takes over and mirrors that into the cloud. It self-heals itself" (~04:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia CEO Derek Collison Keynote**

- JetStream provides synchronous and asynchronous replication, and KV and object store are materialized views layered on streams. "JetStream technology is all about access, reducing latency and flow... synchronous and asynchronous replication" (~03:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia Roadmap with Byron Ruth**

- As of 2.10 a stream or KV bucket has a single TTL that applies to every entry; per-message TTL is a planned addition. "today within a stream or a KV bucket you can only set a single TTL value... that applies to the entire bucket" (~01:20)
- Planned multi-message atomic publish differs from today's async publish (which only overlaps ack waits); it is an atomic write at the storage level, motivated by event-sourcing command handlers that emit several events. "packaging up a set of messages and supporting it at the storage level as an atomic write" (~05:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: After event Q&A with Derek on Zoom**

- A customer log-replication stream with only ~1M messages but 640M interior deletes made an R1-to-R3 scale-up and async mirror crawl; a fix shipped within days took completion from 14 hours to about a minute and async replication from 20-some minutes to 15 seconds. "it only had about a million or so but it had 640 million interior deletes... first time I got it to complete was 14 hours... now it's about a minute" (~18:30)
- A file store redesign (file store v3) is planned to handle petabytes and billions of interior deletes. "a redo of the file store to get into the petabytes... billions of interior deletes" (~19:40)
- Per-message TTL is the first 2.11 item because it serves LRU use cases and lets KV tombstones auto-remove after a shorter period than the bucket's limits. "per message TTLs... it also allows the KV tombstones to auto remove themselves after a shorter period of time" (~20:00)
- For delayed/embargoed delivery, Derek's earlier TIBCO trading designs used per-endpoint RTT so embargoed messages arrived simultaneously for fairness; NATS already tracks every link's RTT, so an embargo-style TTL is feasible. "NATS systems already track every single link RTT all the time" (~22:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Introducing Synadia Insights: Catch the NATS Failures Nothing Else Reports**

- A stream with a message-count limit discards the oldest messages while consumer positions have no limit, so a stopped consumer whose position falls below the stream's first sequence silently loses every message in between, with no error, log line or alert. "The logbook has a limit. The bookmarks do not." (~03:00)
- This data loss is independent of replication; it happens identically on a single server and on a three-node cluster. "Nothing in this failure depends on replication, and it happens exactly the same way on three nodes" (~03:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking Connectivity - Hyper-Connectivity & The Intelligent Edge**

- JetStream aims to solve about 80% of distributed persistence problems with one configurable streams-and-consumers model: queues, append-only logs, replays, roll-ups and compaction. "we want to try to solve like 80 percent of the distributed computing problems... streams and consumers" (~19:00)
- Qualities of service: at-most-once with core NATS fire-and-forget, at-least-once and exactly-once with JetStream. "at least once exactly once and so at most once with just core NATS fire and forget" (~20:00)
- Sourcing lets edge servers' local streams store-and-forward into one larger cloud stream (mux), or one cloud stream filter down into leaf-local streams with only relevant data (demux). "you can have one big stream in the cloud that then filters down into a stream inside of... an edge location that is data that's only relevant to them" (~20:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — A New Way of Thinking | NATS 2.0 and Connectivity**

- A stated tenet of NATS Streaming and the planned JetStream: once an order is defined it is the same order for every subscriber (global ordering per message set). "once an order is defined it's the exact same order for every subscriber in the system" (~41:00)
- JetStream as designed in 2019: successor to NATS Streaming, built into the server, horizontally scalable, with work-queue (SQS-like unordered task queue) semantics; explicitly not "STAN v2" but native to the NATS API with wildcards. "we're not trying to design JetStream as STAN v2" (~48:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - PowerFlex Solves Intermittent Connectivity at the Edge w/ NATS - RethinkConn 2025**

- They used core NATS fire-and-forget for transactional data in parking garages with bad internet, then moved that traffic to JetStream. "We were using fire and forget for things that shouldn't be fire and forgot about" (~03:04)
- Streams are split into named "domains" (e.g. orders); every edge site has the same set of streams and they source into the cloud. "every single edge site has these same streams and they're sourcing from one another" (~04:05)
- Instead of sourcing each edge stream individually to the cloud, they bucket all edge streams into a single upload stream and source that once, which was more efficient (designed with Synadia). "we bucketed all the edge sourcing streams into one upload stream and then uploaded all of those with one sourcing to the cloud" (~05:05)
- The key JetStream feature for them is guaranteed delivery when the internet drops; store-and-forward via stream sourcing over leaf nodes. "the guarantees of sends even when the internet connection goes out... that's become extremely useful time and time again" (~06:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - MachineMetrics on Industrial IoT & Predictive Analytics w/ NATS at RethinkConn 2025**

- They don't yet run JetStream on edge devices; today SQLite buffers data during outages, which forces a serialization/technology break, and JetStream on the edge would remove it. "with JetStream on the edge device it's the same technology, you just write it to NATS and it's going to be persisted until it's reconnected" (~16:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS at the Edge with F1 Arcade**

- JetStream at-least-once delivery fixed missed race-result syncs that the old stack suffered. "sometimes the race data had gone missing due to missed messages and a race would finish, but the results might not sync" (~06:08)
- Mirror streams are used to add observability and replication without touching the core messaging path. "the ability to replicate and observe JetStreams using things like mirror streams allows us to add on observability without impacting that core messaging" (~05:07)
- Outcome: dropped messages can be replayed and a venue losing connectivity loses no data. "if a message drops, we can replay it. If a venue loses connection, we don't lose data" (~08:12)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Lightning Talk - ACI Worldwide at RethinkConn 2025**

- Application symbolic destinations are mapped onto NATS subjects, streams, and consumers; internal command messages use subject filtering; a predefined subject hierarchy is used. "All usage is based on Base24-EPS symbolic destination that's mapped to NATS constructs like subjects, streams, and consumers" (~02:08)
- Their congestion control ("network overload management") reads stream characteristics such as pending count and max messages to drive selective message rejection. "leveraging some stream characteristics like num-pending and max messages. From here, we derived a configurable application selective message rejection algorithm" (~02:08)
- Most anticipated 2.11 features: per-message TTL and selective delete markers, mainly for KV cleanup. "probably the features related to TTL of messages and... selective delete tags" (~06:14)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Franco Sabini from Fineco Bank on NATS**

- They were advised to wait for JetStream GA rather than adopt STAN (NATS Streaming) for a months-away rollout; JetStream needed more adaptation work than the fire-and-forget part. "it was better to wait for JetStream to be general available and that's what we did" (~05:08)
- Everything is replicated R3 because they have no performance pressure. "we have everything replicated in three... just because we don't have any performance issue" (~12:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Jaxon Repp from HarperDB on NATS and distributed databases**

- JetStream replaced hand-written queueing, connectivity checks, and retry logic for disconnected replication; it became a black box that just delivers. "all of that is taken care of by NATS so it became less our code and more a black box" (~04:08)
- Throughput was never a problem for fire-and-forget, but enabling fully acknowledged, exactly-once writes is where they hit throughput limits and back pressure. "as soon as we enable guaranteed delivery... that's when we push up against things" (~06:12)
- Table-level replication choice lets a node be a fast local single-instance database while selectively replicating subsets (e.g. threshold events) globally. "the ability at a table level to replicate data or not allows us to... rely on very very fast local transactions" (~09:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Go Beyond Kubernetes Native Events with NATS**

- Users choose core NATS for prototyping and switch to JetStream in production when events must not be lost. "if they don't want to lose an event they want to make sure that the events is delivered then they have to go with JetStream" (~10:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Workloads - Distributed cloud-to-edge compute with NATS Execution Engine**

- Nex uses core NATS (publish, request/reply) under the hood, and additionally emits events into a stream for future event sourcing. "Nex is pretty much core NATS under the hood... it is emitting events that we are saving to a stream" (~23:43)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Migrating from NATS Streaming to JetStream**

- A Streaming channel maps to a stream, but a stream binds any number of subjects including wildcards. "You can create a stream called just named events, but you can define any number of subjects, including wildcards." (~14:55)
- Most stream options (subjects, limits, retention age) can be changed at runtime. "You can dynamically change most of the options at runtime." (~15:56)
- Max messages per subject gives per-subject retention within one stream. "On a per subject basis, you can say for any given subject, I only want three messages, five messages." (~16:57)
- Stream deduplication by message ID uses a default 2-minute window and holds IDs in memory, so size the window against expected message volume. "By default, it gives you a 2-minute window... it does keep these message IDs in memory." (~16:57)
- Optimistic concurrency via expected stream or per-subject sequence lets concurrent publishers be serialized. "You can actually specify the expected sequence number of the stream at publish time." (~17:58)
- Republish rebroadcasts every stream write to a core NATS subject for lightweight fan-out. "The stream internally on the NATS server is actually rebroadcasting that message out to a core NATS subject." (~17:58)
- A stream bound to `*` or `>` captures every publish in the account; always scope streams under a single-token prefix. "That would be a problem. So, in practice, what you typically do is create a stream that has a single token prefix." (~31:18)
- File-store persistence survives restarts; clustered streams use Raft, an R3 stream tolerates one node down and R5 is the upper end. "If two nodes go offline, then you're stuck because that's what the Raft protocol allows. You can go up to five nodes." (~33:19)
- R3 in-memory streams can survive a careful rolling restart because replica state moves between servers. "You can have in-memory streams that are R3 that still can technically tolerate a good rolling restart... if you're careful." (~33:19)
- Each account can carry its own JetStream limits, useful when mapping accounts to customers; exports/imports enable cross-account sharing, typically for operational hub use. "Every account can have its own JetStream configuration in the sense that you can enforce certain limits at the account level." (~41:30)
- Locked-down publishers still need subscribe permission on their inbox because stream publish acks come back via request-reply. "The stream is actually going to be sending back an acknowledgement to an inbox." (~44:35)
- Unlike Streaming's implicit channel creation, a stream must exist before publishing to JetStream, because core subjects and stream subjects coexist. "Do you have to declare a stream before publishing to JetStream? Yes, you do." (~54:47)
- Native backup/restore in the CLI snapshots all streams and consumer state per account, but is point-in-time; mirrors give a near-current async copy in another cluster. "A mirror allows you to basically create a bit for bit copy of a stream... replicate it asynchronously over to another cluster." (~60:54)
- Consumer replica count inherits from the stream; a three-node cluster with one server per availability zone in one region tolerates a lost node or corrupted disk. "The consumer replicas actually inherit from the stream." (~59:51)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Zen of High Performance Messaging with NATS by Waldemar Quevedo Salinas**

- NATS Streaming was the separate project layered on NATS for replay and at-least-once concerns; the two concerns were intentionally split into two projects. "Those concerns were separated with two different projects." (~37:35)

## CONS: Consumers: types, ack, redelivery, filters (1018 claims)


**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Queue Groups**

- "Stream as a queue": use `WorkQueuePolicy` retention with pull consumers for horizontal scaling, "or using an explicit ack push consumer with a queue group of subscribers" [STALE? push-consumer guidance].

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream (concept overview)**

- Replay options: all messages with replay policy `instant` or `original` ("at the rate they were published ... useful for example for staging production traffic"); last message; last per subject; from sequence; from start time.
- Exactly-once = publisher attaches a unique message ID header tracked by the server "for a configurable rolling period of time" plus a double-acknowledgment on the consumer side.
- Consumers are "views" on a stream.
- "fast un-acknowledged push (ordered) consumers" are "meant to be used to 'replay' rather than 'consume'".
- Pull consumers are demand-driven, batch, require explicit ack, and "are meant to be shared between applications (just like queue groups)" for horizontal scaling "without having ... to worry about having to define partitions or worry about fault-tolerance."
- Pull consumers still get real-time updates: pass a reasonable timeout to Fetch and call it in a loop.
- Ack kinds: ack-all up to a sequence; explicit per-message ack with an ack-wait timeout before redelivery to another process; negative ack; in-progress ack to extend time.
- "most processing is not idem-potent and requires higher qualities of service ... you will want to use acknowledged consumers."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Streams**

- WorkQueuePolicy: FIFO, each message consumed once, enforced by "only allowing one consumer to be created per subject" (filters must not overlap); message deleted once acked.
- InterestPolicy with zero consumers deletes messages immediately: "consumers need to be bound to the stream ahead of messages being published"; deleted once acked by all consumers filtering on the subject.
- In WorkQueue streams, messages that hit the consumer's `MaxDeliver` "will remain in the stream and must be manually deleted via the JetStream API."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Consumers**

- A consumer is "a stateful view of a stream" that tracks delivery and acknowledgments and provides at-least-once delivery.
- Unacked or nacked messages are redelivered automatically; after the configured number of delivery attempts "an advisory notification is emitted."
- Choice guidance: pull consumer for application-controlled processing and easy horizontal scaling; "ordered push consumer" for simple sequential replay; regular push consumer for load balancing or individual acks. [STALE? push guidance]
- "We recommend pull consumers for new projects. In particular when scalability, detailed flow control or error handling are a concern."
- Ordered consumers: always ephemeral, no acks (recreated on gap), automatic flow control, single-threaded dispatch, no load balancing; for data inspection/analysis.
- A consumer is durable only when `Durable` is set. "Setting `InactiveThreshold` does not make a consumer durable." Setting `Name` without `Durable` creates a named consumer that the server still treats as ephemeral.
- InactiveThreshold applies to both durable and ephemeral consumers since 2.9 (before 2.9 ephemeral only).
- Ephemeral consumers have no persisted state or fault tolerance (server memory only) and are cleaned up after inactivity with no bound subscriptions.
- By default consumers "have the same replication factor as the stream they consume" and remain during inactivity unless InactiveThreshold is set.
- MaxAckPending default is 1000; -1 means unlimited (no flow control); applies across all bound subscriptions; delivery is suspended at the limit.
- MaxDeliver default is -1 (redeliver until acked); messages at max delivery count "will stay in the stream."
- Backoff (2.7.1): list of delays on ack timeout, length must be <= MaxDeliver; not applied to nak (nak = immediate redelivery unless nakWithDelay); "When BackOff is set, it overrides AckWait entirely. The first value in the BackOff determines the AckWait value." Example: `MaxDeliver=5 backoff=[5s, 30s, 300s, 3600s, 84000s]` redelivers 5 times over one day.
- AckWait is only effective when BackOff is not configured.
- ReplayPolicy: ReplayInstant (default) as fast as possible honoring ack policy and MaxAckPending; ReplayOriginal simulates original timing.
- Replicas (2.8.3): 0 inherits from stream. MemoryStorage (2.8.3): keeps consumer state in memory "reduces I/O from acknowledgments, useful for ephemeral consumers."
- SampleFrequency: percentage of acks sampled for observability (`30` or `30%`).
- Not editable: Durable, AckPolicy, DeliverPolicy, OptStartSeq/Time, ReplayPolicy, MemoryStorage, MaxWaiting, DeliverSubject.
- AckPolicy: AckExplicit default "Recommended for most reliability and functionality"; AckNone assumes ack on delivery; AckAll acks all prior (and for pull consumers "all pending messages for all subscribers"); AckFlowControl (2.14) for sourcing/mirroring with a durable consumer.
- Out-of-window acks may still count: "if a first process fails to acknowledge within the window and the message has been redelivered to another consumer, the acknowledgment from the first consumer will be considered."
- DeliverPolicy options: DeliverAll (default), DeliverLast, DeliverLastPerSubject, DeliverNew, DeliverByStartSequence (+OptStartSeq), DeliverByStartTime (+OptStartTime).
- "For push consumers, MaxAckPending is the only form of flow control. For pull consumers, client-driven message delivery creates implicit one-to-one flow control".
- "For high throughput, set MaxAckPending to a high value. For applications with high latency due to external services, use a lower value and adjust AckWait to avoid re-deliveries."
- FilterSubject (single) or FilterSubjects (2.10, multiple, e.g. `[factory-events.A.*, factory-events.B.*]`); they cannot be combined.
- Granular permissions: single filter uses `$JS.API.CONSUMER.CREATE.{stream}.{consumer}.{filter}`; multiple filters use `$JS.API.CONSUMER.DURABLE.CREATE.{stream}.{consumer}` without the filter token, so "Use a different strategy for granular permissions."
- Pull options: MaxWaiting (max waiting pull requests), MaxRequestExpires (2.7.0), MaxRequestBatch (2.7.0), MaxRequestMaxBytes (2.8.3); batch constrained by whichever limit hits first.
- Push options: DeliverSubject decides push vs pull; DeliverGroup is a queue group; FlowControl is per-subscription sliding-window working with MaxAckPending; IdleHeartbeat sends status 100 with no reply; RateLimit in bits per second.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Example configuration (ORDERS)**

- ORDERS pipeline: one stream for `ORDERS.*`; pull consumers NEW (`ORDERS.received`) and DISPATCH (`ORDERS.processed`) with explicit ack scale horizontally as work queues; each stage publishes the next message back into the same stream; a MONITOR push consumer with ack none gets all messages.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream walkthrough**

- Consumer defaults shown: Ack Wait 30.00s, Max Ack Pending 1,000, Max Waiting Pulls 512.
- A durable pull consumer "can be shared between as many consuming processes as you want"; two `nats consumer next` instances split the messages.
- To replay again, create a new consumer or delete and recreate it. Deleting a stream deletes all its consumers.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject Mapping and Transforms**

- Queue groups and durable consumers "are partition-less and non-deterministic": no guarantee two sequential messages on one subject reach the same subscriber, so ordering can be lost.
- Strict ordering otherwise requires "one at a time" per consumer/queue-group via max acks pending, "which in turn hurts scalability".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream on Leaf Nodes (domains)**

- 2021 CLI output shows a pull consumer default Max Ack Pending of 20,000 (contradicts 1,000 in newer walkthrough output, nats-concepts/jetstream/js_walkthrough.md).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Streams / Consumers (JetStream admin CLI walkthrough)**

- Pull consumers let you "easily scale your services up by adding more workers and the messages will get spread across the workers based on their availability."
- Pull vs push is decided by the presence of a delivery target. Example NEW/DISPATCH: explicit ack, ack wait 30s, max deliver 20, sample 100.
- "Stream vs Consumer sequence numbers ... are not directly related": stream sequence points to the message; consumer sequence is an ever-increasing counter of deliveries (10 redeliveries of one message -> consumer seq 10 or 11).
- Pull is a `Request()` to `$JS.API.CONSUMER.MSG.NEXT.<stream>.<consumer>`; ack by responding with an empty payload.
- Push consumer messages preserve the original subject (e.g. `ORDERS.processed`) so wildcard-stream consumers can distinguish them.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — FAQ**

- Consumer choice: shared pull consumer to horizontally scale or process high-throughput streams ("batching is in practice key to achieving high throughput"); ordered push consumer when each instance needs its own on-demand replay; durable push consumer with a queue group for "scalable low latency real time processing".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Anatomy of a NATS Client Application**

- Consumers are like database views: subject filter, ack policy (explicit acks "are required for some types of streams and consumer"), deliver policy, replay policy; "You can have as many consumers as you need per stream."
- "Applications typically use ephemeral ordered push consumers to get they own copy of the messages" [STALE? push]; "Applications typically use durable pull consumers to distribute and scale horizontally the processing".
- Ephemeral consumers are cleaned up when the creating instance shuts down and used only by it; durables are "always on" and shared or reused across restarts.
- Ack semantics: `ack()` success; `term()` "when the request is invalid" (never redeliver); `nack()` "when the request is valid but you are unable to process it" and if temporary "you should also close your subscription temporarily until you are able to process again"; `inProgress()` to extend.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Developing with JetStream**

- "Push consumers (specifically ordered push consumers) are the best way for an application to receive its own complete copy"; "Pull consumers are the best way to scale horizontally ... and allow for the processing of messages in batches."
- Ack kinds: Ack, Nak (retried), InProgress (extends by another AckWait), Term (stop redelivery without success).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Model Deep Dive**

- WorkQueuePolicy: "you can not have any overlapping consumers defined on the Stream - each subject captured by the stream can only have one consumer at a time".
- Ack modes: AckExplicit ("the only supported option for pull-based Consumers"), AckAll ("good for processing batches and to reduce ack overhead"), AckNone, AckFlowControl (2.14).
- Consumer sequence increments on every delivery attempt; ack floor stays at the last acked; Pending and Redelivered counts show unacked/redelivered messages.
- Ack protocol bodies: `+ACK`/nil, `-NAK`, `+WPI` (progress, extends by AckWait), `+NXT` (pull only; `+NXT 10`, `+NXT {"no_wait": true}`), `+TERM`. All except `+NXT` support double ack via a reply subject.
- Exactly-once consumption: `AckSync()` sets a reply subject on the ack and waits; on success "you can be sure that the message will never be re-delivered by the consumer (due to a loss of your acknowledgement)."
- DeliverPolicy "is only the starting point. Once started it will always give you what you have not seen or acknowledged."
- Ephemeral consumer "exists as long as any subscription is active on its delivery subject" and is removed "after a short grace period to handle restarts" [STALE? push-only description].
- "You can only set ReplayPolicy on push-based Consumers" (contradicts nats-concepts/jetstream/consumers.md which lists ReplayPolicy as a general option).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Consumers (developer guide)**

- Durable consumers persist delivery progress server-side, can be shared for load balancing, and "can be made highly available through replicas"; ephemeral consumers are deleted when no client instances remain.
- Durables "are typically created and deleted administratively rather than by the application code, which only needs to specify the durable consumer's well-known name".
- Ephemeral consumers are for a single instance's own replay; `Drain()` on the subscription deletes the underlying ephemeral consumer.
- Push consumers: server-controlled flow, load balancing via core queue groups. Pull consumers: explicit batch requests, "giving the client full control over dispatching, flow control, pending (unacknowledged) messages and load balancing."
- "We recommend using pull consumers for new projects. In particular when scalability, detailed flow control or error handling are a design focus."
- "Pull consumers create less CPU load on the NATS servers and therefore scale better"; the difference shows "if you have sustained high message rates."
- Ordered consumers: ephemeral, single-threaded in-sequence dispatch, client checks sequence to prevent gaps, recovers from server failure but not client failure.
- AckWait timer starts on delivery, is deleted on Ack or Term, reset on inProgress; on expiry the message is redelivered and "there is no guarantee that the re-delivery would be to any particular client instance."
- Redelivery timing: `AckWait` or `BackOff` (overrides AckWait); `NakWithDelay()` for delayed nak, else immediate.
- "Dead Letter Queue" functionality: use `MaxDeliver`; advisories `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<STREAM>.<CONSUMER>` and `...MSG_TERMINATED...` carry `stream_seq`; fetch the message by sequence if needed. "If a message reaches its maximum level of delivery attempts, it will still stay in the stream until it is manually deleted or manually acknowledged."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS API Reference (JetStream wire API)**

- Ack reply subject format: `$JS.ACK.<stream>.<consumer>.<delivered count>.<stream sequence>.<consumer sequence>.<timestamp>.<pending messages>`.
- Flow control messages (`NATS/1.0 100 FlowControl Request`) "must be replied to, otherwise the consumer may stall"; Synadia clients handle it (`msg.Respond(nil)`).
- Plain pull requests accumulate on the server while the client is connected: "if you ask for 1 message 100 times and 1000 messages arrive you'll get sent 100 messages not 1." Use `{"expires": ns, "batch": n}` ("Set the expire time to now + your poll frequency") or `{"batch": n, "no_wait": true}` (404 status when empty, 409 when MaxAckPending reached).
- Batch pulls "combine well with the AckAll Ack policy."
- `$JS.API.CONSUMER.RESET` resets a consumer to a sequence/timestamp or original start; "The effective reset floor will never be earlier than the one set when the consumer was created." `CONSUMER.PAUSE` pauses until a timestamp.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — nats bench (benchmarking guide)**

- Example replay: ordered ephemeral consumer 1.2M msgs/s (128 B); durable fetch with 2 clients 1.13M msgs/s aggregate; sync direct get ~33k/s at ~30 microseconds; KV put ~30k/s, KV get 16 clients ~103k/s aggregate.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-6: Naming Rules**

- `stream-name`, `durable-name`, `consumer-name`, `account-name` are `filename-safe`: printable except dot, asterisk, gt, fwd-slash, backslash, "maximum 255 characters"; on Windows also excludes `< : " | ?`. "The server will reject names (return an API error) when it cannot build a valid path."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-9: JetStream Consumer Idle Heartbeats**

- Consumer config `idle_heartbeat` (nanoseconds) makes the server send a heartbeat "only after the specified interval has elapsed and no new messages have been delivered"; delivering a message resets the interval.
- Heartbeat is a regular message with status `100` and description `Idle Heartbeat`, headers `Nats-Last-Consumer` (last consumer seq delivered; 0 = none) and `Nats-Last-Stream` (newest stream seq).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-13: Pull Subscribe internals**

- A pull consumer "does not have a `delivery subject`, that is the server _does not know_ where to send the messages"; clients request via `$JS.API.CONSUMER.MSG.NEXT.<stream>.<consumer>` with an inbox reply.
- "all pull subscribers have to be durable" (as of this 2021 ADR; ADR-37 later relaxes this).
- Pull request body fields: `batch` (min 1, "There is not a limit on the batch size at the level of the library"), `no_wait` (bool, default false), `expires` (ns from now; <= 0 means no expiry). "No wait takes precedence over expires if both are supplied."
- Empty payload = batch of 1. Delivered messages arrive with the subject rewritten to the stored subject (not the inbox); reply subject is the `$JS.ACK...` subject.
- "At most, a consumer can only have 512 inflight pull requests, though this can be changed when creating the consumer with the `max_waiting` option." `num_waiting` in consumer info counts inflight pulls.
- Example consumer defaults shown: `ack_wait` 30s, `max_deliver` -1, `max_waiting` 512, `max_ack_pending` 20000.
- `no_wait` gives "a guaranteed instant response" which is either a message or a status; most commonly `404 No Messages`. `503` if JS unavailable; `408 Request Timeout` when too many inflight pull requests.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-17: Ordered Consumer**

- Ordered consumer is "an ordered push subscription ... that automatically checks and recovers when a gap occurs in the consumer sequence."
- Cannot be a pull consumer, durable, bind/direct, or use queue/deliver groups.
- Forced config: ack_policy none, max_deliver 1, flow_control true, mem_storage true, num_replicas 1; defaults `idle_heartbeat` 5s, `ack_wait` "something large like 22 hours."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-15: JetStream Subscribe Workflow [STALE?]**

- `ConsumerInfo.push_bound` (server v2.3.5+) "indicates that the server has already registered an interest on the push consumer's deliver subject."
- JSAck reply subject "will always start with `$JS.ACK`"; v1 = 9 tokens `$JS.ACK.<stream>.<consumer>.<num delivered>.<stream seq>.<consumer seq>.<timestamp>.<num pending>`; v2 = 11+ tokens inserting `<domain>.<account hash>` after `$JS.ACK.`; no domain is encoded as `_` ("the server will make sure that users can't pick this as a domain name").
- Ack types: terminal `+ACK`, `-NAK`, `+TERM`; progress `+WPI`. "Once a terminal Ack Type has been published for a message, the client should ignore all other user requests to send any type of ack." With ack policy `none`, ignore all acks.
- Flow control (push only): reply to the FC message's reply-to with an empty message; "The format of the Flow Control subject should not to be inspected." Server "requires that when flow control is turned on, an idle heartbeat is set." Missed FC shows as `Nats-Consumer-Stalled` header on heartbeats; respond once, "The server will ignore duplicates."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-33: Metadata for Stream and Consumer**

- Both stream and consumer config gain a `metadata` map of string→string; previously "The only solution was using `Description` field, which is a not ergonomic workaround."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-34: JetStream Consumers Multiple Filters**

- Consumer config gains `filter_subjects []string`; motivation: feature requests and "That could also reduce the number of Consumers in general."
- "Subjects can't overlap each other and have to fit the interest of the Stream. In case of overlapping subjects, error (10136) will be returned."
- Only one of `filter_subject` / `filter_subjects` may be passed (error 10134); at the time, only the old consumer create API (without filter in subject) could be used (error 10135).
- Server keeps "a buffer of first message for each subject filtered and will deliver them in order", refilled per subject after delivery.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-42: Pull Consumer Priority Groups**

- Consumer config gains `PriorityGroups: [...]` and `PriorityPolicy`; the policy activates the feature; "PriorityGroups require at least one entry."
- "In the initial implementation we should limit `PriorityGroups` to one per consumer only and error should one be made with multiple groups." Group names must match ADR-6 `limited-term` "and may not exceed 16 characters."
- "This is only supported on Pull Consumers, configuring this on a Push consumer must raise an error."
- "we cannot support updating a consumer from one with groups to one without and vice versa ... We also cannot switch between different policies." Only `PriorityTimeout` is updatable today.
- `overflow` policy: pulls are served only when `num_pending >= min_pending` OR `num_ack_pending >= min_ack_pending`; otherwise they idle like empty pulls (still get heartbeats). Use case: `us-west-1` takes overflow when `us-east-1` backlog is high. Requires `AckPolicy: explicit` (pedantic mode errors otherwise).
- Pull fields: `group` (mandatory; unknown group = error), `min_pending`, `min_ack_pending`, `failover` (seconds; min 5, max 3600; nearest failover value wins; nearer pulls reset timers). "As of NATS Server 2.14 the `failover` option is not implemented; the server silently ignores the field."
- `pinned_client` policy: one client receives all messages; standbys keep pulls waiting; server re-pins on `PriorityTimeout` expiry or admin unpin. Default example `PriorityTimeout: 2*time.Minute`; requires explicit ack.
- "We should not describe this in terms of exclusivity as there is no such guarantee, there will be times when one client thinks it is pinned while processing messages when it isn't anymore because the server switched."
- Pinned flow: server sets `Nats-Pin-Id: xyz` header on delivered messages; the client must send that `id` on all later pulls; pulls with a wrong `id` get a `423` status (`Nats-Wrong-Pin-Id` / `Nats-Pin-Id mismatch`) and the client "will clear its stored ID and issue subsequent pull requests with no ID set so it remains in the candidate pool."
- Pulls that omit `id` while another client is pinned "is **not** rejected" and stay queued as standby candidates.
- Re-pin procedure: stop delivery for the group, "wait for all in-flight messages to be completed, continue to serve heartbeats", pick new client, store nuid, deliver with ID, emit advisory, `423` to stale-ID pulls.
- "The `PriorityTimeout` is recommended to be sufficiently above the `Expires` value of the pull request"; with 2-minute timeout "a recommended maximum value of `Expires` could be 1 minute"; a new pull acts as a liveness heartbeat for the pin.
- Unpin API: `$JS.API.CONSUMER.UNPIN.<STREAM>.<CONSUMER>` with payload `{"group": "groupName"}`. Consumer state adds `priority_groups: [{group, pinned_client_id, pinned_ts}]`.
- `prioritized` policy: pulls carry `priority` 0–9 (default 0); "Lower priorities will always be served first"; round-robin within a priority. Trade-off vs overflow: "zero delay and with less configuration, it could however result in some flip-flop in work moving between regions quite frequently."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-44: Versioning for JetStream Assets**

- Server-set metadata keys: `_nats.ver` (hosting server version), `_nats.level` (hosting API level), `_nats.req.level` (required level to start the asset); e.g. consumer `PauseUntil` set → required level 1. Also created-version/level keys on create.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-8: JetStream based Key-Value Stores**

- History and Watch use ephemeral Ordered Consumers; History = `deliver_all` filtered by key; Watch starts with `last_per_subject`; latest value has pending 0.
- `Keys` uses a headers-only consumer with deliver last per subject; delete bucket = delete stream.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-60: JetStream reliable stream sourcing/mirroring on WQ/Interest streams (updates ADR-59)**

- Fix: when the upstream is WQ or Interest the server "upgrade[s]" to a durable consumer, replicated if the upstream is replicated, reused for the life of the source config, best-effort deleted on removal.
- Naming/metadata: mirror consumers `JS_MIRROR_<suffix>` with `_nats.mirror.stream`, `_nats.mirror.acc`, `_nats.mirror.domain`; source consumers `JS_SRC_<suffix>` with `_nats.src.*`.
- New `AckPolicy=AckFlowControl`: "will function like `AckAll`" but flow-control replies (with `Nats-Last-Stream` and `Nats-Last-Consumer` headers) act as acks; requires `FlowControl` and `Heartbeat`; idle heartbeat also advances the ack floor; `MaxAckPending` bounds in-flight and triggers an automatic FC message.
- With `AckFlowControl` "the consumer cannot have an `AckWait` or `BackOff` setting ... or an error will be returned"; "`MaxDeliver` must be set to `-1`."
- New API `$JS.API.CONSUMER.RESET.<STREAM>.<CONSUMER>`: resets delivery sequence to 1 and redelivers pending; empty payload keeps the ack floor stream seq; `{"seq":N}` sets ack floor to N-1 so next delivered `msg.seq >= N`; only for `DeliverPolicy` all / by_start_sequence / by_start_time, and cannot go before `opt_start_seq`/`opt_start_time`; response looks like a consumer create response plus `ResetSeq`.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-62: JetStream desired state reconciliation**

- Scale up stream: consumers without explicit replicas scale too; "Interest/WorkQueue consumers are also scaled up to match the stream's replica count." Scale down: "Prefers keeping the stream leader and online and caught up peers"; R1 consumers on a doomed peer are moved first.

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — JetStream consumer defaults (server/consumer.go, server/jetstream_api.go)**

- Default AckWait for explicit/all ack consumers. `JsAckWaitDefault = 30 * time.Second` (server/consumer.go:572); applied when `config.AckWait == 0 && (AckExplicit || AckAll)` (server/consumer.go:649-650)
- Default inactive threshold before an ephemeral consumer is deleted. `JsDeleteWaitTimeDefault = 5 * time.Second` (server/consumer.go:575). Comment: "Ephemerals will always have inactive thresholds." The effective timer adds 100ms + up to 900ms random jitter; pull consumers with an explicit threshold also get that jitter (server/consumer.go:1464-1481)
- Flow control default max outstanding pending bytes. `JsFlowControlMaxPending = 32 * 1024 * 1024` = 32 MiB (server/consumer.go:577)
- Default MaxAckPending for non-AckNone consumers when unset. `JsDefaultMaxAckPending = 1000`; lowered to server `jetstream.limits.max_ack_pending` or account `max_ack_pending` if those are smaller (server/consumer.go:579, 672-680)
- Default pinned-client TTL (grace before re-pin). `JsDefaultPinnedTTL = 2 * time.Minute` (server/consumer.go:582, 691-692)
- Default MaxWaiting (pull request wait queue) for pull consumers. `JSWaitQueueDefaultMax = 512` (server/jetstream_api.go:756; applied server/consumer.go:645-646)
- MaxDeliver default is -1 meaning unlimited; 0 is normalized to -1 (server/consumer.go:588-594)
- BackOff overrides AckWait: first backoff value becomes AckWait ("If BackOff was specified that will override the AckWait and the MaxDeliver") (server/consumer.go:653-658)
- Stream `consumer_limits` (max_ack_pending, inactive_threshold) become the consumer default when the consumer leaves them at 0 (server/consumer.go:659-671)
- AckFlowControl policy auto-sets FlowControl=true and Heartbeat=1s (sourceHealthHB) unless pedantic (server/consumer.go:696-699; `sourceHealthHB = 1 * time.Second` server/stream.go:3120)
- Priority group names: regex `^[a-zA-Z0-9/_=-]{1,16}$` (server/consumer.go:49)
- Ephemeral deletion retry schedule in clustered mode: start 30s, max 5min. `defaultConsumerNotActiveStartInterval = 30 * time.Second`, `defaultConsumerNotActiveMaxInterval = 5 * time.Minute` (server/consumer.go:2145-2148)
- Pull-consumer inactivity: server waits for the last pending message's AckWait (or backoff) to expire plus the inactive threshold before deleting; "Acknowledging a message will reset this back down to just the inactive threshold." (server/consumer.go:2200-2235)
- NAK with delay (`-NAK {"delay":...}` or `-NAK 5s`): redelivery timestamp is set to now - AckWait + delay; bad delay value is logged and treated as plain NAK (server/consumer.go:3193-3230)
- Redelivery timer uses the largest BackOff value as the initial next-fire interval, and per-message deadline = BackOff[deliveryCount] capped at last element ("Prevent consumer backoff from going backwards") (server/consumer.go:6003-6050)
- Max-deliveries check moved from getNextMsg to checkPending because pull consumers "would require a new pull request to be present to process and redelivered could be reported incorrectly" (server/consumer.go:6053-6058)
- Ack reply subject token counts: v1 = 9 tokens, v2 = 11 tokens. `expectedNumReplyTokensV1 = 9`, `expectedNumReplyTokensV2 = 11` (server/consumer.go:6129-6132)
- Ack protocol bytes: `+ACK` (nil payload also means ack), `+OK` deprecated ack, `-NAK`, `+WPI` progress, `+NXT` ack+next, `+TERM` terminate (server/consumer.go:380-393)
- Deliver policies: all, last, new, by_start_sequence, by_start_time, last_per_subject (server/consumer.go:296-325). Ack policies: none, all, explicit, flow_control (server/consumer.go:333-355). Replay: instant, original (server/consumer.go:360-366). Priority policies: none, overflow, pinned_client, prioritized (server/consumer.go:224-240)
- Pull request headers: `Nats-Pending-Messages`, `Nats-Pending-Bytes`, `Nats-Pin-Id` (server/consumer.go:43-45); batch-completed status `NATS/1.0 409 Batch Completed` (server/consumer.go:53)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — JetStream consumer validation rules (server/consumer.go checkConsumerCfg / addConsumerWithAssignment / checkNewConsumerConfig)**

- Consumer name/durable name can not contain '.', '*', '>', '\\', '/' (server/consumer.go:713-718)
- Consumer replicas may not exceed the parent stream's replicas (server/consumer.go:721-722)
- On Interest or WorkQueue retention streams, consumer replicas MUST equal stream replicas. Comment: "This is REQUIRED for now." (server/consumer.go:728-736)
- AckFlowControl requires: push (DeliverSubject), FlowControl=true, Heartbeat exactly 1s ("flow control ack policy heartbeat needs to be 1s"), MaxAckPending > 0, no AckWait/BackOff, no MaxDeliver (server/consumer.go:754-778)
- len(BackOff) must be <= MaxDeliver when MaxDeliver != -1 (server/consumer.go:782-783; also on update 2521-2522)
- Description max 4 KiB. `JSMaxDescriptionLen = 4 * 1024` (server/jetstream_api.go:381; consumer.go:786)
- Push consumer: deliver subject must be literal (no wildcards), must be valid, must not form a delivery cycle back into the stream, MaxWaiting must be 0, MaxAckPending>0 requires ack policy != none, heartbeat if set must be >= 100ms (server/consumer.go:791-809)
- Pull consumer: AckNone not allowed on WorkQueue stream; RateLimit not allowed; Heartbeat not allowed; FlowControl not allowed; MaxRequestExpires if set must be >= 1ms; MaxRequestBatch may not exceed server `jetstream.limits.max_request_batch` (server/consumer.go:811-835)
- MaxAckPending may not exceed server limit, account limit, or stream consumer_limits.max_ack_pending; InactiveThreshold may not exceed stream consumer_limits.inactive_threshold (server/consumer.go:837-848)
- Direct consumers must be push and ephemeral (server/consumer.go:851-858)
- FilterSubject and FilterSubjects can not both be set (server/consumer.go:863-865); empty string in FilterSubjects rejected (server/consumer.go:872-876)
- Multiple filter subjects may not overlap (subset match in either direction) (server/consumer.go:881-888)
- DeliverPolicy/start conflicts: all/last/new/last_per_subject reject OptStartSeq or OptStartTime; by_start_sequence requires OptStartSeq and rejects OptStartTime; by_start_time requires OptStartTime and rejects OptStartSeq; last_per_subject requires a filter subject (server/consumer.go:899-946)
- FlowControl without Heartbeat rejected (server/consumer.go:956-957)
- If both Durable and Name set they must match (server/consumer.go:960-964)
- Metadata total (sum of key+value lengths) max 128 KiB. `JSMaxMetadataLen = 128 * 1024` (server/jetstream_api.go:385; consumer.go:966-972)
- Priority policy: not allowed on push consumers; requires at least one PriorityGroups entry; group names must match `^[a-zA-Z0-9/_=-]{1,16}$`. Conversely PriorityGroups or PinnedTTL with policy none are rejected (server/consumer.go:974-998)
- Consumer creation rejected when the stream placement has a `preferred` server: "preferred server not permitted in placement" (server/consumer.go:1000-1003)
- Create with action=create on an existing consumer with a different config fails with "consumer already exists" (server/consumer.go:1088-1096)
- Max consumers per stream enforced from stream `max_consumers` or the account limit, whichever is more restrictive ("if account limits is more restrictive than stream config we prefer the account limits") (server/consumer.go:1121-1136)
- WorkQueue streams: consumers must be AckExplicit (or AckFlowControl); must be DeliverAll; a second consumer must have a filter and its filter must not overlap with any existing consumer's filters (partition must be unique). Pre-2.9.7 servers missed some overlap orderings ("foo.*.bar" then "foo.>"); on recovery such a consumer is only warned about and "should be administratively deleted" (server/consumer.go:1140-1176)
- Durable name max 255 chars. `JSMaxNameLen = 255` "Picked 255 as it seems to be a widely used file name limit" (server/jetstream_api.go:388-389; consumer.go:1216-1219)
- Immutable on consumer update: deliver policy, storage type (memory), start sequence, start time, ack policy, replay policy, heartbeat, flow control, max waiting; can not switch pull<->push; changing deliver subject to one with existing interest fails (server/consumer.go:2467-2525)
- Updatable on consumer update: DeliverSubject (push->push), MaxAckPending, AckWait, RateLimit, SampleFrequency, MaxDeliver, InactiveThreshold, PauseUntil, FilterSubject(s); "Allowed but considered no-op, [Description, SampleFrequency, MaxWaiting, HeadersOnly]" (server/consumer.go:2557-2650)
- Changing filters on an Interest-retention stream triggers cleanup of messages that lost interest (server/consumer.go:2660-2670)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — jsm.go JSON schema field documentation and defaults (schema_source/jetstream/api/v1)**

- Consumer defaults per schema: deliver_policy=all, ack_policy=none, ack_wait=30000000000 ns (30s, min 1), max_deliver=-1, replay_policy=instant, max_ack_pending=1000, max_waiting=512, max_batch=0, max_expires=0, max_bytes=0, inactive_threshold=0, priority_timeout=0, num_replicas min 0 max 5 (`consumer_configuration.*`)
- max_ack_pending: "once this limit is reached message delivery will be suspended" (`consumer_configuration.max_ack_pending`)
- max_waiting: "The number of pulls that can be outstanding on a pull consumer, pulls received after this is reached are ignored" (`consumer_configuration.max_waiting`)
- idle_heartbeat: "If the Consumer is idle for more than this many nano seconds a empty message with Status header 100 will be sent"; flow_control: "consumers must reply to these messages to control the rate of message delivery" (`consumer_configuration.idle_heartbeat`, `.flow_control`)
- direct / sourcing: "not for general use by clients, internal use only" (`consumer_configuration.direct`, `.sourcing`)
- headers_only: "Additionally adds Nats-Msg-Size header to indicate the size of the removed payload" (`consumer_configuration.headers_only`)
- backoff: "List of durations in Go format that represents a retry time scale for NaK'd messages" (`consumer_configuration.backoff`)
- mem_storage: "Force the consumer state to be kept in memory rather than inherit the setting from the stream" (`consumer_configuration.mem_storage`)
- pause_until: "supplying a time in the future will act as a deadline for when the consumer will be paused till" (`consumer_configuration.pause_until`)
- priority_policy enum: none, overflow, pinned_client, prioritized (`priority_policy`)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — JetStream API levels, advisories, and API backpressure (server/jetstream_versioning.go, server/jetstream_api.go)**

- Consumer feature -> required API level: pause_until and priority groups/policy/pinned TTL (2.11) = 1; AckFlowControl ack policy (2.14) = 4 (server/jetstream_versioning.go:155-170)

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — JetStream Anti-Patterns: Avoid these pitfalls to scale more efficiently**

- Consumer info is a monitoring/debugging call, not for operational decision-making. "intended to provide insights for monitoring or debugging"
- Consumer info requests go to the meta-leader and involve expensive state calculation; repeated calls "become very expensive across ten of thousands of clients."
- Consumer create is idempotent: if a consumer with matching config exists the call succeeds without change; if configs differ it updates, unless a non-editable field (e.g., start sequence) is changed. Use create instead of info to check existence.
- Get pending counts from message metadata rather than consumer info.
- "Beyond 100,000 consumers, the potential for issues increases significantly." Consumers cost state management and cluster replication (Raft traffic, meta-leader load).
- "Too many consumers" often reflects "overstated persistence and delivery guarantee requirements."
- Multiple disjoint subject filters per consumer arrived in 2.10, but "More than a few hundred disjoint subject filters will likely lead to slowness and instability." Cost: more subject indexing/matching and scanning more message blocks.
- Alternatives to many disjoint filters: split into separate consumers each with fewer filters, or "re-evaluate your subject name hierarchy so you can better leverage wildcard filters."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS JetStream: Ordered, Scalable Processing**

- Most workloads need ordering only among related keys (customer/account/device), not across the whole stream. Standard consumers load-balance and break per-key order.
- `max_ack_pending = 1` restores strict order but serializes the whole stream: no throughput, single point of failure.
- Design mirrors Kafka consumer groups: "Split the stream into buckets by key, assign each bucket to exactly one worker, and you get ordering within a bucket while running many buckets in parallel."
- Partitioning uses the `{{partition(N, token...)}}` mapping function: "an FNV-1a 32-bit hash modulo the partition count", prepended as a leading token; same key always lands in the same partition.
- With `pinned_client`, delivered messages carry `Nats-Pin-Id`; the client must echo it on every pull; a mismatch is rejected with status 423. After `PinnedTTL` silence or unpin, the server re-pins a standby: failover "with no external leader-election."
- Effective parallelism = `min(partitions, members)`. Partition count is fixed at creation and immutable; members are cheap to add/remove up to that ceiling. A 5th member on 4 partitions idles as standby.
- A member drains all its partitions serially through one consumer; "piling more partitions onto a member is parked ownership, not added throughput."
- Static flavor: consumers directly on a partition-stamped stream, durable `<group>-<member>`, frozen membership; lower latency, fewer server resources, any ack policy.
- Elastic flavor: sources the origin stream into a hidden work-queue stream `<stream>-<group>` with partitioning applied during copy; live membership changes via KV config watched by members; requires explicit ack.
- Neither flavor changes partition count live; both require delete and recreate. Elastic = "elastic members over a fixed number of partitions."
- Pinning is affinity plus failover, not a distributed lock; windows exist where a client believes it is pinned after the server re-pinned, and buffered messages cannot be revoked. Handlers must be idempotent.
- Size partitions for peak future parallelism; raising later requires deleting the group and re-hashing every key.
- Cap the elastic work-queue buffer above one second of throughput; hitting `max_buffered_msgs`/`max_buffered_bytes` pauses sourcing for at least a second, causing periodic stalls.
- For a hot key at 10x volume, hand-assign partitions so that key gets its own member.
- Use cases: ordered per-key processing at scale; single-active-worker with hot standby replacing leader-election machinery.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Pull Consumer Priority Groups in NATS JetStream: Overflow, Pinned, and Prioritized Routing**

- "Pull consumer priority groups, introduced in NATS Server 2.11, add a routing layer directly to the consumer." Server-side policy replaces round-robin; "no leader election, no external lock, and no coordination code."
- Pull-only; requires explicit ack policy (shipped validation does not currently reject other ack policies); rejected on push consumers. Exactly one priority group per consumer today; group names capped at 16 characters from a restricted alphabet.
- Overflow policy serves a pull only when backlog crosses a threshold: "num_pending ... is at least min_pending, or num_ack_pending ... is at least min_pending." Designed for latency/cost-aware regional routing: local workers drain first; remote workers wake past the threshold.
- Pinned client: one designated client gets all messages; others stand by. `PinnedTTL` defaults to 2 minutes (wire 0 = default). Advisories `consumer_group_pinned` and `consumer_group_unpinned` (reason admin or timeout) are published on every change.
- Operators can force a hand-off with `nats consumer unpin <stream> <consumer> <group>` for clean deployment rotation.
- Prioritized (2.12+) serves pulls by priority 0-9 (lower first); secondary pool picks up immediately when primary is not pulling. Trade-off: "some flip-flopping, where work bounces between clients more readily because there is no deliberate threshold."
- Pinning is "not a hard guarantee"; an old client may believe it's pinned after the server moved on. Handler "must be idempotent."
- Fetch(N) is not an atomic reservation; the server may spread N messages across concurrent pulls.
- Keep priority_timeout comfortably above pull expires; the 2-minute default pairs with pulls expiring in one minute or less. A 423 `Nats-Pin-Id` mismatch means clear the id and re-pull without one.
- Use cases: active/standby exclusive processing; regional routing; tiered worker pools stacked by priority for zero-delay escalation.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Stop Building Firehoses: Flow Control Isn't a Performance Optimization — It's an Architectural Decision**

- "At the edge, 'consumers that can't keep up' is a routine condition, not a failure mode." Push delivery replays backlogs as spikes after reconnect.
- Pull consumption: "Catch-up happens at a rate the consumer declares — not at whatever rate the producer decides." At the edge, consumers should control ingestion rate.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS and Kafka Compared**

- JetStream offers at-least-once and exactly-once options; individual ack, double ack, nak with backoff.
- Kafka order is guaranteed only within a partition; "Maintaining global order can be difficult across multiple partitions." In JetStream strict in-order delivery is "affected only by acknowledgment settings"; parallelism without partition planning.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Consumer Pausing in NATS 2.11: Hit Pause Without Losing Messages**

- Pausing halts delivery until a deadline for push and pull consumers alike; messages keep accumulating in the stream; clients see "No errors, no disconnects" and heartbeats continue.
- In-flight batches are not revoked; the server waits for them to complete. Deadlines can be extended/shortened by re-issuing; consumers can be created paused (`--pause=1h`, `--pause-until=<ISO8601>`).
- Uses: deployments/migrations, emergency maintenance, freezing flow for debugging, giving overwhelmed downstreams time to recover; removes the need for custom backpressure logic.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Server 2.12 Release**

- Prioritized pull policy (ADR-42) prefers local clients but lets remote clients pull immediately when no local client is pulling; Overflow (2.11) "may delay remote client message delivery if local clients are inactive."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Server 2.11 Release**

- Consumer pinning (on priority groups) with standby clients for HA; Overflow spills to remote clients based on pending acks or messages; Consumer Pause until a deadline.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Server 2.9 Release**

- Pull consumer distribution became round-robin across subscriptions; `InactiveThreshold` (default five seconds) now also applies to durable consumers.
- Consumer `Replicas`, `MemoryStorage`, `FilterSubject` editable after creation; stream `Placement` editable to move streams transparently.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Building a Wallet Event Backbone with NATS JetStream: Lessons from BroSettlement's Staging Tests**

- Durable consumers with queue-based processing for horizontal scale; retries with backoff; no assumption of "single global order across unrelated subjects."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS at System Initiative**

- Synadia guidance: "you might not want to create and destroy thousands of durable JetStream consumers in short bursts."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS: The Secret Weapon Behind Vitrifi's Workflow Automation Platform**

- Pull consumers for large-volume state updates ("allows for lots of control"); push for pause/cancel needing "immediate action."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Scaling Global AI Inference with NATS JetStream**

- GPU workers use "pull-based JetStream consumers with explicit acknowledgements"; workers pull only when they have capacity, making GPU capacity "a first-class control signal"; crash mid-inference means no ack and redelivery to another GPU; no custom retry or DLQ plumbing.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Event-Driven Systems with NATS and Jetstream**

- Same durable name across instances = competing consumers "analogous to Kafka consumer groups"; separate durables on one stream = fan-out with independent positions; server-side subject filters plus app-level content routing can combine.
