- Ack after processing gives at-least-once: "Messages may be delivered multiple times (if your service crashes mid-processing), but they won't be lost." `nak()` triggers redelivery.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — How to Build NATS Consumers**

- "Streams store messages persistently, while consumers track delivery state for subscriber groups. A single stream can have multiple consumers, each maintaining independent delivery positions."
- Push for real-time low-latency; pull "when backpressure control or batch processing is needed." [DUBIOUS] Push-first framing contradicts current official guidance favoring pull.
- Deliver policies: All (full history), New (post-creation only), Last, ByStartSequence, ByStartTime. Explicit ack required in production; `NakWithDelay` (5s example) "useful for rate limiting or waiting for external services"; `Term` stops redelivery.
- Examples: AckWait 30s push / 60s pull ("Longer wait for batch processing"); MaxDeliver 5 push / 3 pull; MaxAckPending 1000; fetch batch 100 with 5s timeout; `DeliverGroup: "order-workers"` for push queue groups.
- DLQ pattern: stream with 30-day MaxAge, subject `dlq.<original subject>`, publish when MaxDeliver reached then Term.
- Set AckWait "based on your actual processing time, plus a safety margin": if p95 is 5 seconds "set AckWait to 15-30 seconds"; MaxAckPending trades throughput for memory; graceful shutdown drains in-flight with a timeout.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS JetStream: Streams, Consumers, and Durable Messaging**

- JetStream adds "at-least-once delivery (exactly-once is opt-in)"; a consumer is "a stateful view of a stream — it tracks which messages were delivered and acknowledged."
- Durable pull consumers are "the recommended default for new projects: explicit ack, flow control, scalable batch fetching." Push: "`MaxAckPending` is the only flow-control mechanism."
- "`MaxDeliver` is not a dead-letter queue — after max attempts, NATS stops redelivering but the message remains in the stream." Plan explicit poison-message handling.
- `BackOff` "Overrides `AckWait` when configured"; raise AckWait "for slow external APIs (e.g. OpenSearch bulk)"; "One consumer per downstream concern keeps projectors independent."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Deploying a scalable NATS cluster part 1: core architecture and considerations**

- No native DLQ; implement via advisory streams capturing max-delivery advisories.
- Batch 100-1000 for throughput; max-ack-pending 1000-10,000; [DUBIOUS] "Prefer AckAll acknowledgment strategy for bulk processing."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — How NATS Cuts Costs for Distributed AI**

- Priority groups (2.11) let "requests piling up in the work queue stream for one region to be automatically and transparently consumed by workers in other regions"; reduces the need to "size for the peaks" per region.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Orbit.go: A Guide to NATS Client-Side Abstractions for Go**

- pcgroups "brings Kafka-style consumer groups to NATS, leveraging the server's consumer priority policies"; static vs elastic membership; avoid when needing "strict global ordering across all messages on stream" or for "relatively low-throughput streams."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Building a Job Queue With NATS.io and Go**

- Consumer: `MaxDeliver: 2`, `BackOff: 5s`, `AckExplicitPolicy`, `FilterSubject`; ack only after success.
- DLQ via advisory subject `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<STREAM>.<CONSUMER>`, captured into a DLQ stream; advisory payload `stream_seq` used with `GetMsg` to retrieve the original.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Use cases for persistent logs with NATS Streaming**

- `MaxInflight(1)` for full ordering; exactly-once needs client-side dedup persisting `lastProcessed` externally; durable queue subs need a centralized atomic KV for exactly-once across subscribers; close the subscription on the first non-retryable error to avoid out-of-order redelivery interleaving.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Client-side Partitioned Consumer Groups for JetStream**

- "NATS JetStream does not require Stream partitioning to parallelize consumption, unlike Kafka"; standard consumption is elastic and on-demand; strict order needs max-ack-pending 1 which serializes the whole stream.
- Pinned consumers give fault tolerance: only one instance of a member delivers at a time. Partition = consistent hash of subject token(s); users see member names and max members, partition numbers are "basically invisible."
- Elastic groups are a materialized view (work-queue stream sourced from the origin, partition token inserted during sourcing); lag observable via work-queue size; size caps cause a ~1 second sourcing pause when hit. Static: lower latency, fewer resources, any ack mode (explicit needed for strict order); elastic: explicit ack, live membership changes. Multiple elastic groups can exist per stream. `cg` CLI tool provided.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS JetStream Explained: Streams, Consumers, and Durable Messaging (NATS Explorer)**

- Ack none / explicit (redeliver after `ack_wait`) / all ("acking message N also acks everything before it"); `max_deliver` bounds redelivery [DUBIOUS: says exceeded messages are "moved to a dead-letter subject or dropped"; JetStream has no automatic DLQ].

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS JetStream as a Durable Job Queue in .NET**

- Work-queue retention makes the stream a queue; one shared durable pull consumer gives competing consumers; adding a worker is "starting another process with zero configuration."
- Consumer `AckWait = 60s`, `MaxDeliver = 4`; poison jobs drop after bounded redelivery with a `MAX_DELIVERIES` advisory. Results stream: limits retention, `MaxAge = 5 minutes`, file storage; persist long-lived results to Postgres instead.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Grokking NATS Consumers: Push-based queue groups**

- Core queue groups give HA ("Members can cleanly disconnect and reconnect or new members can join without interrupting") but "concurrent message processing gives up message order" and in-flight messages "may be dropped" on abrupt disconnect; slow consumers are disconnected.
- JetStream push queue groups: `DeliverGroup` in ConsumerConfig; ack wait default 30s; `MaxDeliver -1` = unlimited; default max ack pending 65536; `MaxAckPending(1)` means "only one message will ever be in-flight at a given time across the queue group" (ordered + HA).
- Redelivery can happen even when processing succeeded but the ack was lost; publisher dedup is windowed so consumers still need idempotency.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Grokking NATS Consumers: Intro and push-based**

- Consumers are "stateful views" with their own sequence numbers; push consumers deliver "without waiting to be asked"; ephemeral consumers are auto-named and deleted on unsubscribe; durables need `nats.Durable()`.
- Defaults: `DeliverPolicy all`; `AckPolicy explicit` requires Ack/Nak; `AckWait` 30s; `MaxDeliver -1` retries forever; `MaxAckPending 65536` (1 forces serial); `ReplayPolicy instant` vs `original`.
- `AckFloor` is the highest contiguous acked sequence (gaps block it); `NumRedelivered` can rise and fall; `NumWaiting` is pull-only; `PushBound` shows a live deliver subscription; delivery happens on the deliver subject, not the filter subject.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Inquiry on Limits for Streams and Consumers in a NATS JetStream Cluster**

- Consumers that inherit R3 from the parent stream are heavy (state machine with consensus) and expected to be limited in number; lighter consumer variants scale further — derekcollison.
- Over 100k consumers is possible "with custom solutions"; reach out to Synadia — derekcollison.
- For ~100k browser-ish subscribers: use R1 (possibly memory) consumers that clients recreate on demand, plus a single R3 muxed KV storing each consumer's last sequence; recreate with OptStartSeq from the KV — derekcollison. "have a single muxed KV that stores the sequences for the 100k ... consumers that is an R3 and highly available."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Jetstream Max Consumers per Stream**

- 50M traditional consumers per stream is not supported; consumers can be heavyweight state machines with consensus (NRG) — derekcollison. "you can not use a traditional consumer here"
- Massive fan-out to millions of endpoints should use stream re-publish plus client-side gap logic with a muxed KV holding per-endpoint sequence offsets — derekcollison. "look into stream re-publish and gap logic with a mux'd KV for sequence offsets"

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Maximum number of consumers**

- Shard streams so no stream has more than ~20K consumers — wallyqs. "it would be better if you shard the streams so that you do not have more than 20K consumers or so per stream."
- Main branch has optimizations toward millions of consumers by raising `meta_compact_size` — wallyqs.
- With very many consumers use R1 memory-based consumers to reduce I/O; or run many clusters capped at ~200K consumers each — wallyqs. "create many clusters and cap the number of consumers per cluster to 200K or so."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Number of consumers**

- 100-1,000 (under 10k) filtered consumers on an R1 WorkQueue stream is fine — derekcollison. "That should be fine.."
- Per-tenant consumers isolate a slow tenant from the others; that isolation is a valid reason for per-tenant consumers — niondir (asker's rationale, implicitly accepted by derekcollison).
- Maintainer's first diagnostic questions for consumer-count designs: retention policy, replica count, total expected count — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Maximum known-good value for `MaxMsgs` in a JetStream stream**

- For fast ordered replay of many messages use ordered consumers — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Does Stream Per Subject have any performance benefits over multiple subjects within same stream**

- Consumers scale across a stream's replicas: each replicated consumer's leader can sit on a different stream replica, balancing load — Jarema.
- One slow/down filtered consumer does not block other filtered consumers on the same stream — YashasAnand (tested, [UNVERIFIED] but consistent with maintainer answer).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Jetstreams publisher performance decreases rapidly with large number of parallel consumers (50x drop at 100 consumers)**

- Publisher throughput with 1000 parallel JS consumers was measured at ~83 msg/s vs ~19k msg/s with 1 consumer (10KB payload, single stream); horizontal scaling to 3-5 servers did not help; CPU stayed under 25% — mranish592 [UNVERIFIED, benchmark data].
- The many-consumers-per-stream throughput collapse "should have improved quite significantly since the more recent 2.11 versions" — neilalexander.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Need Some General Info Regarding Client Design & partitioning**

- Distributing messages across instances of one consuming app needs no partitioning: all instances share one durable consumer — jnmoyne.
- Strict ordering of consumption requires `max acks pending` = 1, which cuts throughput to one message at a time — jnmoyne.
- Strict ordering plus parallelism: put a partition number in the subject (stream config subject transform) and create one durable consumer per partition with max acks pending 1 — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Consuming partitioned stream**

- Partitioned consumption needs only one stream: the stream's subject transform inserts the partition number as the first token, then one consumer per partition via subject filter; one consumer per app instance may hold several partitions — jnmoyne.
- Orbit.go `pcgroups` (released 2025-05) implements static and elastic partitioned consumer groups; it depends on 2.11 pinned consumers for member failover — jnmoyne.
- Static groups: membership list plus max members (= partition count); the library assigns partitions to members and creates a consumer with the matching filter list; a single goroutine consumes all assigned partitions — jnmoyne.
- Elastic groups: an intermediary WorkQueue stream sources from the original stream and adds the partition token; member consumers' filter lists adjust as membership changes — jnmoyne.
- Pinned consumer: several instances of the same member can run, only one is pinned and receives messages until it steps down, crashes or is suspended — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Are Client-side Partitioned Consumer Groups equivalent to Pulsar Key-Shared subscriptions?**

- Only two consumer modes deliver strictly in order: ordered consumers (ephemeral, no ack/nak, single client, offset must be persisted by you e.g. in KV) and explicit-ack consumers with max acks pending 1 (one message at a time regardless of client count) — jnmoyne.
- Orbit partitioned consumer groups give Kafka/Pulsar consumer-group semantics: per-key strict order with individual ack/nak and redelivery, parallel via consistent hashing, elastic membership up to a pre-configured maximum — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Ordering guarantees per entity**

- One stream plus one consumer with one subscription already gives ordered processing per entity (barring redeliveries) — bruth.
- Before partitioning, benchmark a single stream/consumer baseline; 100 goroutines cap out at CPU cores and add context-switch cost — bruth.
- Nak counts as an outstanding ack, so MaxAckPending=1 still preserves order under Nak — ripienaar. "You can control ordering by forcing only max 1 outstanding ack. A Nak is considered outstanding"
- WorkQueue retention with MaxAckPending=1 is still a work queue; partitioning scales it out — ripienaar.
- For high speed plus order use an ordered consumer: lightweight, 1:1 — derekcollison.
- Automatic partition rebalancing (Kafka/Pulsar style) was not available out of the box in 2023 — arnarg (later addressed by Orbit pcgroups in 2025).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Produce from anywhere, consume from the same availability zone**

- Reads from a consumer always go through the consumer leader; in a multi-AZ cluster the leader can move on election, so the app must find the leader and connect there — derekcollison. "Reading from consumers is always done from the leader"
- Asker runs ~100,000 partition-mapped consumers; maintainer response was a Synadia consult, not a public recipe — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — locks/leases with KV similar to SETNX**

- `InProgress` (`+WPI`) extends ack wait; the client library call never fails, but `nc.Request(msg.Reply, "+WPI")` returns an error when the server is gone, so it can double as a liveness check on the lock — ripienaar (verified by aep).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — JetStream file-store ~65x slower than memory-store on KV mirror (83% of seq space is deleted)**

- Do not pass a `FilterSubject` that matches everything on a mirror: a mirror has no ingest subjects so the server cannot recognize the filter as "all", the 4x messages-vs-subjects heuristic uses the huge first/last range, and every message lookup does an expensive per-subject-state read. Removing the filter gave 150k+ msg/s — MauriceVanVeen. "best is to just not pass a filter subject if you don't intend on filtering"

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Automatic Message Payload Preservation in DLQ Stream**

- Including payloads in DLQ advisories was rejected on user feedback: payloads can be sensitive and advisories often leave NATS; a per-consumer opt-in might be acceptable — ripienaar.
- Belief: a WorkQueue message is removed when it hits max_deliver. Correction: it stays in the stream (removed only on ack or TTL) and can be fetched by the advisory's sequence with payload; verified on 2.12.4 R1, with a suspected loss on R3 — jgriegershs [UNVERIFIED, non-maintainer].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — AckWait does not publish to dead letter queue with zero clients**

- NATS has no automated DLQ by design because consumer semantics are kept separate from stream semantics — derekcollison. "We do not have automated DLQs ... since we truly separate consumers from stream semantics."
- DLQ pattern: Term the message and run a service that captures the advisory and moves the message to a chosen stream — derekcollison.
- Redelivery/MaxDeliver processing for pull consumers happens when clients fetch; with zero fetchers a message sits in AckPending after AckWait (issue 1716, by design) — gongy (asker, confirmed behaviour).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — ack-wait and dupe-window behavior when used together**

- AckWait (consumer redelivery timer) and DupeWindow (stream publish dedup by Nats-Msg-Id) are unrelated settings — MauriceVanVeen.
- To process at most once set MaxDeliver=1 or always Ack/Term; defaults are DupeWindow 2 min and AckWait 30 s — MauriceVanVeen.
- Fetching a batch of 100 with long per-message processing caused AckWait expiry and redelivery; fetching one at a time fixed it — s4iko (asker, verified fix).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Message prioritization to certain consumers**

- For deterministic routing of related requests to the same worker, use partitioned consumer groups (Orbit pcgroups) keyed on a subject token — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Max Ack Pending per Subject?**

- MaxAckPending cannot be set per subject; strict per-subject order needs a consumer per subject, because MaxAckPending above 1 can cause out-of-order redeliveries on missed acks — Jarema.
- Hash the entity ID into buckets and create one consumer per bucket — praveenperera (asker workaround, later endorsed as the pcgroups model by jnmoyne).
- If strict per-device order is not needed: MaxAckPending greater than the worker-thread count, one fetch loop handing off to a thread pool, so slow messages do not block fast ones — jnmoyne.
- Two-level partitioning: hash device ID modulo thread count inside the app, and pcgroups across app instances — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — JetStream. "Queue group" feature with pull subscribers**

- One durable pull consumer, any number of app instances bound to it; messages are distributed automatically; drain subscriptions when scaling down — derekcollison.
- Two clients on the same durable cannot receive the same message unless it is a redelivery; check the delivery count in the message metadata — jnmoyne.
- If `backoff` is set, the first backoff value overrides AckWait (server behaviour); a backoff of [1s, 60s] with AckWait 30s gives 1 s before redelivery — EvilaMany (asker, cites consumer.go) [UNVERIFIED but source-cited].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Why increasing of "Unprocessed Messages" leads to increasing nats memory usage?**

- Set `MaxBytes` on fetches (e.g. 8-16 MiB, never below max message size or `max_payload`); a client behind with MaxAckPending 56,000 makes the server allocate many buffers at once that are slow to release — wallyqs.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Is $JS.ACK purposefully domain-unaware? Potential interference with leaf nodes**

- In the domain design, `$JS.ACK` and message gets (direct and original) are not domain-aware; a fix is planned — derekcollison. "ACK and MSG gets (both direct and original) are not domain aware. We plan to fix for sure."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How to distribute load from one stream to all JetStream cluster nodes?**

- A consumer is bound to a single node and writes to a stream go through one node; WorkQueue and Interest add further constraints, so this is the hardest combination to scale horizontally — ripienaar. "Consumers are bound to a single node and writes into a stream also"
- Consumer leaders need not sit on the stream leader's server; move a leader with a step-down to rebalance — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — has NO quorum, stalled on jetstream consumers**

- Ephemeral consumers default to R1 unless the stream uses WorkQueue or Interest retention; consumer replica count and store can be set explicitly — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — InterestPolicy variation (per-user subjects, millions of subjects)**

- Per-device durable consumers that are only active while the device is online keep persistent state and prevent deletion under Interest retention — derekcollison. "You will have persistent consumer state for each device, but those consumers are only active when the device is online and connected. Will work fine for you."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How do I inspect the contents of a workqueue stream?**

- Redelivery counts and next-delivery time live in the consumer and are visible only in delivered message metadata, not by inspecting the stream — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How to find number of subscriptions on jetstream**

- Consumers are named and unique; creating "6 consumers" with the same name yields one consumer with 6 bound clients, round-robin for pull; 6 distinct consumers each get every message — Jarema.
- Whether many filtered consumers beat one shared consumer depends on subject cardinality and replication; benchmark with `nats bench` — Jarema.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Jetstream durable queue-group subscription based MaxAckPending**

- Scale-out work queues belong on pull consumers, which scale by design with batch size and MaxBatch; long-poll (2.7+) lets push be built on pull — derekcollison. [STALE?] pre-2.10 API shown.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Some questions about NATS (Limits vs Interest, pagination, fetch expiry)**

- Push and pull consumers deliver identical metadata (stream, consumer, sequences, pending) via the ack reply subject — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Event Synchronization with NATS (nats.go)**

- To scale strictly ordered consumption: one stream on `foo.bar.*` with one durable consumer per partition (`foo.bar.0`, `foo.bar.1`...). Only when a single stream's write throughput is exceeded create one stream per partition — jnmoyne.
- Elasticity without repartitioning: treat the partition count as the maximum number of consumers you will ever need and redistribute partitions over the present members when membership changes — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — OrderedConsumer Usage (nats.go)**

- Ordered consumer is a client-side construct: ephemeral no-ack consumer with client-side sequence tracking and recreation on gaps; meant for fast one-off passes — Jarema.
- For long-lived ordered processing, a durable consumer with MaxAckPending=1 is all you need — Jarema.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Ephemeral Consumer Cleanup Rate? (nats.go)**

- Creating and discarding consumers at API-call rate "will not really work well"; use message get APIs (batched direct get, ADR-31 batches) instead — ripienaar.
- If a consumer is needed to read history, make it R1 memory-backed, or use an ordered consumer (R1, flow controlled); or walk with NextFor by start sequence — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Multiple instances of the same durable pull consumer (nats.go)**

- JetStream is partition-less: any number of app instances bind to the same durable and messages are distributed automatically, add or remove at any time, regardless of cluster size — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How to create queue group consumer with new jetstream api (nats.go)**

- The new JetStream API is built on pull consumers; a pull consumer load-balances across all subscriptions bound to it, so queue groups are unnecessary — Jarema.
- Push and pull are two APIs over the same server construct differing in back pressure (flow control vs message requests); pull handles back pressure much better; new features (overflow, priority groups, pinning) are pull-only — Jarema.
- The only missing old-API feature is "push consumer without a queue group", which is almost never needed; performance is equivalent or better — jnmoyne.
- Fan-out with persistence: one consumer per receiving application; work-queue semantics: one durable with many workers — Jarema, jnmoyne.
- A WorkQueue stream may have many durable consumers as long as their subject filters do not overlap — jnmoyne.
- `BackOff` overrides `AckWait`: the first backoff value becomes the effective ack wait — eau-u4f (verified), jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Queued pull consumers with WorkQueue retention (nats.go)**

- WorkQueue binds a stream to single-consumer semantics per subject; bind many pull subscribers to that consumer for scale. For multiple mutually exclusive consumers on the same subjects use Interest retention — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Why are push consumers not implemented? (nats.go)**

- Push would not help: MaxAckPending applies to both; use `FetchNoWait`/fetch with high message limit and a 10 s expiry, or `Consume` for sustained flow — Jarema.
- Set MaxAckPending greater than fetch batch size times number of fetching clients, or some fetches get partial batches — jnmoyne.
- Ordered consumers get messages fast with reliable ordered delivery without explicit acks — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — load balancing in a queue group (nats.go)**

- Core queue groups are random; JetStream pull consumers round-robin across fetches — derekcollison, Jarema.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Auto deletion of inactive durable consumers (nats.go)**

- Consumer state is small; idle durables cost little. Inactivity can be detected from the consumer's delivered `Last` time — bruth.
- `InactiveThreshold` applies to durable consumers too (later servers); for pull it means no pull requests in the window, for push no binding — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Need help in understanding MaxAckPending behaviour (nats.go)**

- NAK resets AckWait; the message stays delivered-but-unacked and counts toward MaxAckPending for the whole delay — kozlovic.
- Many long NAKs indicate a design problem; move such messages to a different stream rather than inflating MaxAckPending — kozlovic.
- Prefer pull consumers with a very high MaxAckPending and let `Fetch(n)` per client provide flow control (10 clients x Fetch(100) = 1000 in flight) — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How to resume fetching messages after restart (nats.go)**

- A durable pull consumer resumes after the last acked message; PullSubscribe looks up the stream by subject (subjects cannot overlap across streams); BindStream skips that round trip — piotrpio.
- Unacked messages with MaxAckPending 10 and AckWait 1 h block delivery of the next messages after restart — zerlok (root cause of a similar report) [UNVERIFIED, plausible].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Message Group / Sequential Convoy pattern (issue)**

- Pulling a message gives a lock on it for AckWait — ripienaar.
- JetStream has no consumer groups or rebalancing; a JetStream "consumer" is like a Kafka partition and a JetStream "subscriber" is like a Kafka consumer; container orchestration provides worker elasticity — jnmoyne. "a 'consumer' in JetStream is like a 'partition' in Kafka and a 'subscriber' in JetStream is like a 'consumer' in Kafka."
- Multiple workers on one MaxAckPending=1 partition consumer give HA with strict order: only one message in flight, but a worker can die or roll without losing the partition — bruth, jnmoyne.
- MaxAckPending and MaxWaiting are independent: MaxWaiting=1 limits outstanding pull requests, MaxAckPending limits in-flight messages; MaxAckPending=1 returns only one message per pull — jnmoyne.
- Elastic consumer groups shipped in Orbit.go in 2025-05 (static and elastic flavors), requiring 2.11 pinned consumers — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Cannot use Subscribe when ephemeral consumers reach ~30,000 (issue)**

- Creating and abandoning tens of thousands of consumers continuously prompted an architecture-review recommendation rather than a tuning fix — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — NATS server panics when creating many consumers (issue)**

- 16k R3 consumers are "alot of HA assets": each is a complete Raft group; heartbeats alone would be ~16k msgs/sec plus memory — derekcollison. "Heartbeats alone would be ~16k msgs/sec not to mention the memory footprint."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Include payload in term advisories (issue)**

- Parked because of data-leakage feedback; blanket publishing of payloads "wouldn't help or work for many" — ripienaar.
- DLQ is per consumer, not per stream, because streams deliver the same message to many consumers; consumers can be ephemeral or single-use, so DLQ design is application-specific — ripienaar. "you need a DLQ per consumer not per stream."
- Consume the advisories in real time, fetch the message by sequence for reprocessing; WorkQueue streams keep messages that were not successfully processed; set MaxAge to your operational window — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Ability to reset consumer start sequence (issue)**

- Start options are used once at creation; resetting means blowing away consumer state, so delete and recreate with the same name — ripienaar.
- On Interest retention, deleting and recreating a consumer signals no interest and can lose messages; a native reset would be safer — neilalexander.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — MQTT support should be horizontally scalable (issue)**

- Horizontal scalability is limited by the number of Raft groups (one per stream or consumer); many consumers make Raft traffic exceed data traffic — kozlovic. "the more consumers you have, the more basic RAFT traffic will increase, potentially more than actual data flow."
- `mqtt { stream_replicas: 5, consumer_replicas: 1 }` lets consumers be R1 under an R5 stream; consumer leaders spread across servers — kozlovic.
- Consumers cannot span multiple streams — kozlovic.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Messages stop being delivered from a WorkQueue stream (issue)**

- A consumer sequence advancing on a single message means it is being redelivered without ack; check client acking — Jarema.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Message Ack Behavior (ADR issue)**

- Decision (ADR-15): repeat acks are a client no-op after a terminal ack (ACK/TERM/NAK) to save traffic; auto-ack happens after the callback returns, WPI inside the callback is allowed — kozlovic, aricart.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Pull request MaxBytes and status handling (ADR issues 112 and 116)**

- Pull responses use HTTP-like status codes and cannot abandon them; a message larger than the pull's max_bytes returns "409 Message Size Exceeds MaxBytes" (changed from 408) and stalls the pull — derekcollison, aricart.
- Pull requests stay publish-based rather than request/reply because request/reply breaks cross-account imports/exports — wallyqs, derekcollison.
- "409 Exceeded MaxWaiting" is transient (retry later); other 409s (consumer deleted, push based, limits exceeded) are terminal — aricart, derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Consumer and Stream Name Validation (ADR issue)**

- A space in a consumer name broke consumer creation with a cryptic error after a client upgrade — Jarema.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Doesn't NakWithDelay reduce the MaxAckPending counter?**

- Any delivered message awaiting retry counts as pending because MaxAckPending is also used to manage ordering; the only option is to raise MaxAckPending — ripienaar.
- Maintainers disagreed whether delayed NAKs should count; noted NAK already violates observed ordering — derekcollison (open design point).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Clarification for Ack Sequence**

- Stream sequence is the stable message index; consumer sequence increments by one per delivery, so a redelivery has the same stream sequence, a new consumer sequence and NumDelivered=2 — derekcollison.
- "Redelivered" counts in consumer info are server-lifetime counters; consumer state persists across restarts but the counter resets — derekcollison.
- With a filter subject the two sequences never move in lock step; treat them as unrelated — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How to troubleshoot messages not picked up by consumer (stuck WorkQueue message)**

- If MaxDeliver is hit the ack floor moves past the message and an advisory is sent — derekcollison.
- A consumer reporting sequences ahead of the stream is stalled; that happens when the stream's first/last sequence reset (store_dir wiped, e.g. `/tmp`); `sync: always` in the jetstream block can help durability on abrupt kills — neilalexander.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — What is the exact meaning of "Unprocessed Messages" in consumer info?**

- Unprocessed = messages the consumer has never attempted to deliver — ripienaar.
- `MaxWaiting` caps outstanding pull requests; each `Consume()` client keeps 1-2 pulls pending, so MaxWaiting of 10 throttles 10 clients; the default 512 is there for a reason — Jarema.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — NATS Streaming to JetStream Migration**

- The stan2js tool migrates NATS Streaming channels to JetStream streams and STAN subscriptions to JetStream consumers; it is a one-time exercise run once per set of channels. "This is a one time exercise and stan2js only needs to be run once for each set of STAN channels that require migration to JetStream streams."
- Observed output: a STAN durable subscription can be converted to a JetStream pull consumer (`CONVERTED TO PULL? true`), otherwise it becomes a push consumer; a STAN queue subscription becomes a queue (deliver-group) push consumer.
- Observed output: subscription progress is preserved by mapping the STAN next sequence to the corresponding JetStream sequence (e.g. sub-foo `601 -> 101`, sub-bar `701 -> 401`); migrated consumers report Ack Policy Explicit and Ack Wait 30.00s.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Interest-based Stream**

- A message stays in an interest stream until, for each consumer whose filter overlaps it, a subscription bound to that consumer "successfully acks the message, terminates it, or the max redelivery has been reached."
- Interest is established by the existence of a consumer, not by active consumption. "it is not required to be actively consuming messages to show interest, but it is the presence of a consumer which the stream cares about."
- Each consumer is a separate view over the stream; if one consumer acked but another did not, the message is retained.
- A late consumer cannot retroactively show interest; messages deleted before it was created are gone. "this reinforces that a late consumer cannot retroactively show interest."
- Interest respects the consumer's FilterSubject: a consumer filtered to `events.mouse_clicked` is not interested in `events.input_focused`, so that message's retention depends only on consumers whose filter overlaps.
- Term (terminate) counts the same as ack for releasing interest. "Fetch and term (also works) and ack from the first consumers that do have interest."
- DoubleAck/AckSync is used "to ensure the stream state has been synced up for this subsequent retrieval" before reading stream info.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Work-queue Stream**

- Consumers on a work-queue stream must have non-overlapping (disjoint) filter subjects, unlike limits- and interest-based streams which support overlapping consumers. "if multiple consumers are bound to a work-queue stream, they must have disjoint filter subjects."
- A work-queue stream allows "at most one consumer with interest on a subject at any given time"; creating a second unfiltered consumer fails until the first is deleted.
- To run multiple consumers on a work-queue stream, give each a subject filter scoping it to a disjoint subset (example: `events.us.>` and `events.eu.>` per geo).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Pull Consumers**

- A pull consumer lets the application fetch messages on demand, so "the application [can] control the flow of the messages coming in so it can process and ack them in an appropriate amount of time."
- A durable consumer has its state tracked on the server, "most importantly, the last acknowledged message from the client."
- Ephemeral consumers are "useful as one-off needs and are a bit cheaper in terms of resources and management"; they do not persist after the primary subscriber unsubscribes and the server auto-deletes them after a period of time.
- Without a durable name a consumer is removed after InactiveThreshold, which defaults to 5 seconds, when not actively consuming. "consumer will be removed after InactiveThreshold (defaults to 5 seconds) is reached when not actively consuming messages."
- Consumer `Name` is optional; if not provided it is auto-generated.
- Multiple subscriptions can bind to the same pull consumer without additional configuration; each subscriber fetches batches and processes them concurrently.
- Messages within one batch are ordered relative to each other, but each subscriber handles its batch independently, so cross-subscriber order is not guaranteed. For deterministic partitioning "for scalable order processing" the text points to deterministic subject token partitioning (subject mapping).
- The fetch batch size is the maximum number of messages that may be returned, not a guaranteed count.
- Fetch's Messages() channel closes only when the requested number of messages has been received or the operation times out; FetchNoWait returns whatever is available up to the batch size without waiting.
- A fetch at the end of the stream blocks until the max wait, "which is 5 seconds by default, but this can be set explicitly as an option."
- Durable consumers are never removed automatically regardless of InactiveThreshold; they must be deleted explicitly with DeleteConsumer.
- Ack after processing "so they are not redelivered."
- (deno narrative) The new consumer API is pull-based; an ordered consumer is an ephemeral consumer "that guarantees that messages are delivered in order" and is managed under the covers given only the stream name.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Pull Consumer - Applying Limits**

- Server-enforced pull consumer limits include: max non-acked in-flight messages, max in-flight pull requests (across subscribers), max pull batch size per request, max timeout on a pull request, and max total bytes of a pulled batch.
- Batch size and timeout can be set and changed per fetch request and can differ across subscribers.
- Consumer configuration can be changed on demand, with one exception: `MaxWaiting` "cannot be updated on a consumer as of now. This must be set up front when the consumer is created."
- MaxAckPending limits un-acked in-flight messages across all subscriptions bound to the consumer; with MaxAckPending=1 a fetch for 3 returns 1 and the next fetch times out with nothing until that message is acked. "This essentially forces serial processing messages for a pull consumer."
- MaxRequestBatch caps the batch size of any one fetch; requesting more than the limit is an error. "This can be used to keep the fetches to a reasonable size."
- MaxWaiting limits the number of fetch requests waiting in parallel; "This prevents building up too many requests that the server will have to distribute to for a given consumer." Extra concurrent fetches beyond the limit error.
- MaxRequestExpires caps the per-fetch max wait "to prevent requests waiting too long for messages"; a fetch with a longer timeout returns immediately with an error, while one equal or less works.
- MaxRequestMaxBytes caps the total bytes of a pulled batch; a FetchBytes over the limit errors.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Push Consumers (legacy)**

- With a push consumer the server proactively pushes messages to the active subscription "up to the consumer's max ack pending limit," rather than the client fetching sized batches.
- Happy path: the subscription keeps up and acks before ack wait elapses.
- Push consumers "can get unwieldy and confusing" when the subscriber cannot keep up, processing errors occur, or the subscription is interrupted: redeliveries interleave with newly pushed messages.
- Ephemeral push consumers are "a lightweight and useful way to do one-off consumption of a subset of messages in a stream."
- For durable use cases, "it is recommended to access pull consumers first which provides more control and implicit support for scaling out consumption."
- The maximum number of messages a push subscription buffers is set by `MaxAckPending`; "The default is 1,000."
- Push subscription messages are pre-buffered asynchronously, so the client-side pending count "may or may not be" the number published.
- By default the underlying consumer requires explicit acks, "otherwise messages will get redelivered."
- Unsubscribing an ephemeral push subscription deletes the consumer; even if omitted, the server eventually cleans up the ephemeral when it determines the subscription is no longer active.
- Helper-created durables (SubscribeSync with nats.Durable) are deleted when `Unsubscribe` or `Drain` is called: "these helpers should only be used if neither of those methods are called."
- "A more explicit and safer way to create durables is using `js.AddConsumer`"; push consumers require a `DeliverSubject`.
- Subscriptions bound to a consumer "cannot independently define their own subject to filter on"; the filter lives on the consumer.
- On unsubscribe (or client crash), pending buffered messages are effectively dropped client-side; the server waits `AckWait` before redelivering, and "will only re-deliver if there is an active subscription."
- Consumer info tracks the last stream sequence a delivery was attempted for and a separate consumer sequence per delivery attempt; "These should not be treated as correlated since the consumer sequence for a given message will increment on each delivery attempt."
- "num ack pending" counts delivered messages awaiting ack; "num redelivered" is zero while each message has been delivered only once.
- A new subscription bound before AckWait expires gets a timeout because messages are still pending; after AckWait the message is redelivered with delivery attempt 2.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue Push Consumers (legacy)**

- A queue push consumer is analogous to a core NATS queue group but for streams; a standard push consumer "only supports a single bound subscription at any time," while a queue push consumer supports multiple bound subscriptions.
- Messages are "distributed randomly among active subscribers which can freely come and go."
- As of NATS server v2.8.4, ephemeral queue push consumers are not supported; the server does not track them and auto-cleans up when no subscriptions are bound. If you create a durable and your program crashes before deleting it, check for it on startup.
- Internally the `DeliverGroup` corresponds to a core NATS queue group name; a plain core NATS queue subscription on the DeliverSubject + DeliverGroup can join the group.
- `DeliverSubject` is randomly generated by default but can be set explicitly in the consumer config.
- With a group of subscriptions each receives a different subset; messages can be processed out of order, there is no correlation between message order and subscription creation order, and "it is possible that not all subscriptions will necessarily get a message."
- Helper-created queue push consumers are deleted when any subscription unsubscribes or drains.
- With AddConsumer, both a durable name and a deliver group must be defined: the durable name is used for all consumer types while the deliver group is exclusive to queue push consumers; using the same name for both is a convention.
- Core NATS subscriptions are JetStream-unaware, so `msg.Ack` must be called explicitly; a `js.QueueSubscribe` handler auto-acks by default unless `nats.ManualAck` is supplied.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Multi-Stream Consumption (legacy)**

- To fan in messages across multiple streams, create a push consumer per stream with the same `DeliverSubject` and optionally the same `DeliverGroup`; each consumer then delivers to the clients subscribed to that subject and/or queue group.
- Sharing one deliver subject across streams is "a straightforward way to do this in a single account. It is recommended a user is created with specific permissions to subscribe to this subject."
- A plain core NATS queue subscription on the shared deliver subject receives messages from both streams and can ack them; each stream's consumer state updates independently.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Migration to new JetStream API**

- The new JetStream API "removes the complexity of `Subscribe()` in favor of more explicit separation of creating consumers and consuming messages."
- The new API "focuses on using Pull Consumers as the primary means of consuming messages from a stream."
- The legacy API supported pull consumers only in limited capacity: "it was not possible to retrieve messages from a stream in a continuous fashion."
- With `Consume`, `Fetch` and `Next`, users choose how to consume depending on use case.
- In the legacy API the only way to continuously receive messages is push consumers; `Subscribe()` "leads to complications because it implicitly creates and manages underlying consumers."
- Unsubscribing a legacy `Subscribe()` subscription deletes the underlying consumer it created; `AddConsumer` "is the only way to create a consumer in the legacy API which will not be deleted when the subscription is unsubscribed."
- Legacy `Subscribe()` performs stream lookup by subject by default; `BindStream` skips that lookup.
- Legacy push subscriptions hide complexity and need many options; "when using push consumers, there is no simple way to rate limit the message delivery, which leads to slow consumer errors."
- Legacy pull consumers "are greatly limited in functionality since it is only possible to pull a specific number of messages, without any optimization or coordination between pulls," making them inefficient versus push.
- The new API "does not auto-create consumers"; consumers must be created or retrieved explicitly, giving control over the consumer lifecycle and removing the hidden logic of `Subscribe()`.
- Pull consumers do not need a `DeliverSubject`.
- Stopping `Consume()`/`Messages()` in the new API does not delete the consumer, unlike legacy `Unsubscribe()`; the server deletes it when `InactiveThreshold` is reached.
- An ephemeral short-lived consumer is made by setting a low `InactiveThreshold` and no name; `InactiveThreshold` "can be omitted for durable consumers."
- `FilterSubject` on a consumer "is equivalent to providing a subject to `Subscribe` in the legacy API."
- `Messages()` still pre-fetches messages but returns them on `Next` instead of a handler.
- `Next` works like `Fetch(1)`.
- "deleting a stream will also delete all consumers on that stream."
- (deno narrative) Legacy `subscribe()` created the consumer if it did not exist and updated it if options differed; the new API only supports pull consumers, so an existing push consumer "will have to [be] recreate[d] as a pull consumer."
- (deno) "Durable consumers are not deleted, will consume resources forever if not managed."
- (deno) With legacy push on streams with huge message counts, missing options caused "slow consumers, or ... a consumer that cannot be horizontally scaled."
- (deno) The different consumption methods exist "to help you align the buffering requirements of your application with what the client is doing"; consume defaults "are safe," but "you can ask for as many messages as you will be able to process within your ack window."
- (deno) Delete a consumer preemptively "only if you know you are not going to need that consumer to resume processing."
- (deno) Services typically process one message at a time; "instead of optimizing a client to pull many messages for processing, you can horizontally scale the number of process that work on just one message."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Consumer - Fetch Messages**

- "Although you can make consumers on the fly, typically consumers will be created ahead of time."
- A FetchConsumer has no stop; "the fetch stops by itself." The new fetch "does not block before returning the entire batch," and returns null once there are no more messages to consume.
- A consumer with `filterSubject` `events.1` on a stream with 4 messages reports 2 pending; the filter determines what the consumer sees.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Confirmed Message Ack**

- A confirmed ack "means that the client waits for an ack from the server to ensure that the ack was received and processed."
- Client naming: "ack ack" (JavaScript), "double ack" (Rust, C# .NET V2), "ack sync" (Go, Python, Java, C).
- "Any stream can work with confirmed acks."
- A standard ack does not wait for server confirmation; "If server is experiencing high load, or the connection is severed before the ack is received, the ack can be lost, leading to a redelivery."
- An error from a plain Ack "only means that the client failed to send the ack message. There will be no error if the client published the ack, but the server did not receive (or process) it."
- A confirmed ack "allows us to react to the ack being lost by sending it again, potentially avoiding redelivery"; its error can mean the ack failed to send or the server failed to confirm.
- Consumer info shows NumPending decrease on receive and NumAckPending go to 1 until the ack; after ack, NumAckPending returns to 0.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream Deep Dive**

- JetStream is the part of NATS that stores messages; stored messages can be read again later and replayed as many times as needed. "Once a message is stored, you can read it again later, and replay it as many times as you need."
- Delivery is tracked per reader; a message counts as handled only once it is acknowledged. "Delivery is tracked per reader: a message counts as handled once it's acknowledged."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publishing**

- A `PubAck` confirms storage, not delivery; storage and delivery are separate and can be minutes, hours, or days apart. "It does not confirm that any consumer has received it."
- A message is considered handled only after the client acknowledges it, after processing.
- Treating "published" as "delivered": a `PubAck` means the stream stored the message, not that a consumer processed it. "Keep business outcomes separate from the publish."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reading back the stream**

- Three pieces move a message through JetStream: a producer (publishes, reads PubAck, retries), a stream (stores in order, assigns stream sequence), and a consumer (server-side cursor a client connects to).
- A consumer sequence is bumped on every delivery, redeliveries included, so it counts deliveries, not distinct messages. "so it counts deliveries, not distinct messages."
- A stream can feed many consumers at once, each reading at its own pace and each with its own position.
- A consumer is an object on the server, not part of the application; stored messages and read position stay server-side so a client can disconnect and reconnect without losing its place. "The stored messages and the read position both stay on the server"
- Deliver All starts the consumer at sequence 1 and reads the whole log.
- Pull is the default for new consumers; an older push model exists. "Pull is the default for new consumers; an older push model exists"
- Ack explicit is the default for a pull consumer; the consumer's position advances only as acks arrive.
- Default consumer limits: Outstanding Acks maximum 1,000 (MaxAckPending); Waiting Pulls maximum 512.
- `Unprocessed Messages` is how many stored messages the consumer hasn't delivered yet.
- Messages are delivered oldest first, each with its stream sequence; the `pending` count is how many stored messages are still waiting.
- Stream sequence is the message's fixed position in the log, assigned at publish and never changed; consumer sequence is the consumer's own delivery counter.
- Stream and consumer sequences drift apart when a consumer starts partway through, filters to a subset, or has a message redelivered.
- Every delivered message carries metadata (stream/consumer sequence, pending, delivery count); read state off the message in handlers rather than calling `nats consumer info` per message. "fine for a one-off check, too costly to call for every message."
- A durable consumer's position is durable on disk and tied to the consumer name; a disconnect or server restart doesn't change it.
- Create a durable consumer when a reader comes back; for a throwaway look at a stream, an ephemeral consumer suffices.
- An ephemeral consumer keeps no position you can return to; it is removed once it goes idle, and a reconnect then starts over from the beginning. "an ephemeral one is removed once it goes idle, and a reconnect then starts over from the beginning."
- Re-running a caught-up reader waits: with nothing new to deliver, the read command waits for the next message instead of returning.
- Replaying a huge stream from the beginning: Deliver All on a stream holding millions of messages takes time and moves a lot of data. "Read the whole history only when you want it."
- Delivery policy alternatives to All: most recent (`--deliver last`), a time window back (`--deliver 1h`), or a known sequence (`--deliver 1000`).
- Delivery policy sets where a consumer starts; replay policy sets the pace. Default replay `instant` hands messages over as fast as the client reads; `original` spaces deliveries to match the original timestamp gaps.
- Reusing a durable name with a different config returns "consumer already exists"; the server won't silently reconfigure a consumer a reader is using. Edit the consumer or pick a new name.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Filtering what you consume**

- A filter is a subject pattern attached to a consumer; the consumer receives only matching messages and the rest of the stream is skipped. The `*` and `>` wildcards behave as in a core subscription.
- The filter lives on the consumer; nothing about the stream changes. "The stream still captures all of `orders.>`; nothing about the stream changes."
- A consumer with no `Filter Subject` line receives every subject in the stream.
- Default consumer config shown: Pull Mode true, Deliver Policy All, Ack Policy Explicit, Ack Wait 30.00s, Replay Policy Instant, Max Ack Pending 1,000, Max Waiting Pulls 512.
- Each consumer keeps its own cursor, stored alongside its config and ack state, separate from the stream's messages; advancing one consumer's cursor does not move another's.
- A consumer is an independent view over the stored messages with its own filter, cursor, and ack state; the stream holds the one shared copy.
- A filter is a cheap way to send the same messages to more than one reader: it copies no data, doesn't slow other consumers, and one consumer can start, stop, or fall behind without affecting others.
- A consumer differs from a core queue group: a queue group splits one subject's live traffic across workers; each JetStream consumer gets its own full (filtered) view of the stored stream.
- A consumer can filter on several subjects at once (multiple filter subjects).
- A filter that matches nothing is accepted silently: a typo like `orders.shiped` creates a valid consumer that never receives anything, with no error and no warning. "Don't assume an empty pull means the stream is empty"
- Expecting a filter to delete from the stream: a filter narrows one consumer's view and never removes messages. "Don't use a filter to prune a stream."
- Filter overlap between consumers is fine on limits and interest streams; on work-queue retention, consumers' filters must not overlap each other.
- Overlapping filters inside one consumer fail: if one filter subject covers another (e.g. `orders.>` next to `orders.shipped`), create fails with `consumer subject filters cannot overlap`; partial overlap where neither covers the other is accepted.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Delivery and acknowledgment**

- The ack/redeliver loop gives JetStream at-least-once delivery: a message stays available and is redelivered until a reader confirms it. "so it's handled at least once even when things fail."
- At-least-once relies on both the durable stream and the consumer's ack loop.
- Delivery lifecycle: delivered/in flight (ack floor not past it), acked (floor advances), redelivered (no ack within Ack Wait, so the server delivers again to the same or another reader on the same consumer).
- The gap between what's been delivered and what's been acked is the set of in-flight messages.
- The delivery count (`tries`) rides along on each delivered message.
- A plain ack is fire-and-forget; if the ack is lost in transit the server never advances the floor, Ack Wait elapses, and the message is redelivered.
- A double ack waits for the server to confirm the ack; use it when reprocessing would be harmful and the handler can't be made idempotent (e.g. a payment capture). "It costs a round-trip per message, so it's a deliberate choice, not the default."
- Double ack is a client-library call with no CLI flag (DoubleAck in Go, ackAck in JS, ack_sync in Python, ackSync in Java, AckAsync with double-ack option in .NET, double_ack in Rust).
- Ack Wait default is 30 seconds; an unacked message is redelivered after it with an incremented delivery count.
- MaxAckPending (default 1,000) caps how many messages a consumer delivers before they're acked.
- A redelivery doesn't slot back into stream order: while one message waits for redelivery the consumer keeps handing out later ones, so the repeat can arrive after higher-sequence messages.
- For strict in-order processing set MaxAckPending to 1: the consumer delivers one message at a time and a redelivery always comes back before anything new. "That ordering guarantee costs throughput ... so use it only when order actually matters."
- Forgetting to ack looks identical to a crashed reader: the message is redelivered after Ack Wait, and with the default unlimited delivery limit that repeats forever. "Always ack on the success path."
- Acking the same message twice does nothing useful; some clients (Go, Python) reject it locally with "message was already acknowledged", others ignore or resend it, and the server ignores the duplicate. "Ack each delivery exactly once, in one place in your handler."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Ack responses and redelivery**

- With `AckPolicy=explicit` every delivered message must be answered; a message is not done until the client says so.
- A message stays in flight from delivery until the consumer answers; the server keeps a copy on the pending list and starts a timer.
- AckWait is the redelivery timer and defaults to 30 seconds.
- A client answers a delivered message in exactly one of four ways: ack (done, never redelivered), nak (failed, redeliver), term (never deliver again to anyone), in-progress (reset AckWait, not final).
- ack, nak, and term are final and close out a delivery; in-progress only extends the timer.
- A plain nak redelivers immediately, which is rarely what you want for a temporary failure. "A plain nak redelivers immediately. That's rarely what you want."
- Nak with a delay for temporary failures (dependent service down, locked row, rate limit); the server holds the message for the delay and then puts it back. This is a client-library call; the CLI `--nak` only does immediate redelivery.
- A nak returns the message to the consumer, not to the worker that nak'd it; with several workers the redelivery can land on a different worker.
- Each nak raises an advisory on `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MSG_NAKED.<stream>.<consumer>`.
- A consumer backoff only shapes redeliveries that fire when the AckWait timer runs out; it doesn't slow a nak. "it only shapes redeliveries that fire when the AckWait timer runs out — it doesn't slow a nak."
- Use term for poison messages (broken payload, a check that will never pass); the message leaves the pending list and is never delivered again no matter how many attempts remain.
- After a term the message is gone from this consumer but not from the stream under Limits retention; on WorkQueue or Interest a term removes it just as an ack would.
- Term runs through the same path as an ack: pending entry clears and the ack floor moves past the message.
- A term publishes a terminated advisory on `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MSG_TERMINATED.<stream>.<consumer>` carrying stream/consumer sequence, delivery count, and an optional reason.
- Use term only when the code can tell no future attempt will succeed; when in doubt, nak with a delay and let the delivery limit decide. "Use term only when the code can tell that no future attempt will succeed."
- AckWait: shorten it for fast work, lengthen it for slow work.
- MaxDeliver caps delivery attempts per message; default is -1 meaning no limit, so a message can be redelivered forever.
- AckWait handles the case where no answer arrives; MaxDeliver caps the case where a worker keeps nak'ing the same message.
- With `--max-deliver=5`, a message that fails five times stops being delivered; without a term path it's dropped after the fifth attempt.
- A backoff is a list of delays, one per attempt (e.g. 1s before the second delivery, 5s before the third, 30s before the fourth); if the list is shorter than MaxDeliver the server reuses the last entry.
- Setting a backoff replaces AckWait: the first entry becomes the ack deadline for the first delivery. "Pick a `--backoff-min` at least as long as normal processing takes, or a slow job trips redelivery while it's still running."
- AckPolicy `explicit` is the right default for work that must not be lost.
- AckPolicy `none` requires no answer: a message is done the moment it's delivered, so no pending list, no Ack Wait, no redelivery.
- AckPolicy `all` lets one ack retire every earlier message; it only fits a consumer that processes strictly in order (MaxAckPending 1), otherwise acking message 10 also retires a failed message 7 waiting for redelivery. "silent data loss."
- AckPolicy `flow_control` is for the push consumers the server creates for durable mirrors and sources; acks ride flow-control responses and behave like `all`.
- A plain nak retries with no delay, tying up one worker on one message. "Don't send a bare nak for a temporary failure." A consumer backoff won't help; it spaces AckWait timeouts, not naks.
- A poison message with no term path uses every attempt until MaxDeliver gives up, holding up the messages behind it.
- MaxDeliver drops a message with no dead-letter: the message stays in the stream but leaves the consumer's pending list silently. "JetStream has no built-in dead-letter queue." Catch it via the `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<stream>.<consumer>` advisory.
- AckWait shorter than real processing time causes double work: the server redelivers a message still being handled, so two workers run the same order. Raise AckWait or send in-progress during long jobs.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Pull consumers in depth**

- Two pull patterns exist in every client library: fetch (batch of up to N, returns when full or on timeout) and consume (continuous flow, library keeps pull requests open, runs until stopped).
- Use fetch when your code wants control over each round (a cron job draining a queue, a request handler); use consume for a long-running worker. "Most services use consume."
- A fetch timeout is a ceiling: the call always returns within it, with whatever messages it has.
- The CLI has no single batch fetch; `nats consumer next --count N` issues N single-message pulls in a row.
- A long-running worker shouldn't loop on fetch by hand; consume keeps pull requests open so a new message is delivered as soon as it's stored.
- Two pull request fields bound a pull: `batch` (max messages returned) and `expires` (how long the server holds the pull open).
- A bigger batch means fewer round trips and higher throughput; a smaller batch means lower per-message latency and less work lost if the worker dies mid-batch.
- Client libraries set defaults for batch and expires, so a plain consume loop behaves well without tuning.
- An empty fetch is normal: after `expires` the server replies `408 Request Timeout` (a no-wait fetch with no messages gets `404 No Messages`), and clients report an empty batch (CLI exits non-zero). "A worker that treats an empty fetch as a failure fails on a quiet stream."
- A raw fetch with `expires` zero never times out; the server holds it until the batch fills. Client libraries default to about 30 seconds.
- MaxAckPending set too low limits throughput: a limit of 10 against a batch of 100 delivers ten then stops until acks arrive. "Keep it at or above your batch size. The default is 1000; lower it only when you know the in-flight count you want."
- A batch set too large uses more memory than expected because `batch` counts messages, not bytes; most clients offer a `max_bytes` option to bound a pull by size, and whichever limit is hit first ends the pull.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling a consumer**

- Point several processes at the same pull consumer to share load; the server hands each stored message to exactly one worker, serving pull requests in arrival order.
- A worker only takes a turn while it has a pull request open; distribution follows demand, so a faster worker pulls more often.
- The consumer tracks a single position regardless of worker count; the position belongs to the consumer, not each worker.
- Sharing is a property of the consumer, not the stream; workers share a position, not the messages, and an ack advances the position without removing the message under Limits retention.
- A queue group splits live messages with no storage; an offline subscriber misses them for good. Workers sharing a consumer split stored messages, so an offline worker just leaves its share for the others. "Only the stream-backed split survives a worker dropping out or a restart."
- When a worker dies before acking, the server hands the message to another worker after AckWait (30 seconds by default).
- If a dead worker had already completed the side effect before crashing, the work runs twice on redelivery.
- MaxAckPending (default 1000) is the ceiling on delivered-but-unacked messages across the whole consumer, shared by all workers: five workers get 1000 between them, not 1000 each. "The cap is shared across the whole consumer, not per worker"
- MaxAckPending too low leaves workers idle; too high leaves a big in-progress backlog that all redelivers at once if many workers die together.
- A redelivered order can arrive at a second worker and run twice; key side effects by a business ID such as `order_id`. A redelivery shows in the message's delivery count.
- The pool shares work by demand, so you don't choose which worker gets a message; for that control use priority groups.
- A low MaxAckPending starves a large set of workers: set to 3, ten workers leave seven idle. "Set the cap to at least your worker count, with room to spare."
- A crashed worker holds its message until AckWait (30s default) because the server can't tell a crash from slow work. "Set `AckWait` to your normal processing time: too short redelivers while a healthy worker is still working, too long leaves real failures stuck."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Ordered consumers**

- An ordered consumer is for a fast, in-order, one-pass read of a stream that cleans up after itself: no name to pick, no ack to send, no consumer to delete.
- The ordered consumer is a client-library construct; there is no CLI form.
- The library creates a consumer with a short inactivity threshold, tracks the stream sequence of each delivery, and on a missing sequence or lost heartbeats throws the consumer away and creates a fresh one at the next expected sequence (named `prefix_1`, `prefix_2`, ...). "the recovery is invisible."
- Without acks a plain no-ack consumer that missed a message would skip it with a gap; the ordered consumer spots the gap and rebuilds from the missing sequence, so order holds with no acks.
- An ordered consumer is an ordinary server consumer configured as: AckPolicy none, memory storage, one replica, inactivity threshold of five minutes, start at the requested point.
- After a recovery the library pins the replacement consumer to the next sequence it expected.
- Ordered consumers give up per-message acks (not for exactly-once work), sharing (each reader creates its own), and parallelism (single-threaded, in order).
- A Key-Value watch and an Object Store read are both ordered consumers under the cover.
- Using an ordered consumer for work that must be processed once: it can't mark individual messages handled. "use a named consumer with explicit ack and let redelivery cover failures."
- Expecting to share progress across processes: two processes reading with ordered consumers both read the whole stream; they don't split it.
- Counting on the position to survive: memory storage, one replica, and a short inactivity threshold make the cursor disposable; after a crash a long-running job starts over.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Priority groups**

- Priority groups (ADR-42) let a pull consumer steer which client gets messages: overflow, pinned_client, or prioritized policy.
- A consumer uses exactly one priority group today; naming more than one is accepted but only the first takes effect.
- Overflow and pinned_client need the consumer to acknowledge messages (`--ack explicit`) because the server keeps per-client counts only when the consumer acks; prioritized needs no acks.
- Once a consumer has a priority policy, every pull must name its group; a pull without one is rejected with `Bad Request - Priority Group missing`, and the group on the pull and consumer must match.
- Overflow policy: near workers pull with no threshold; far workers pull with `min_pending` so the server answers only when at least that many messages are waiting. "You want `us-west` to stay idle unless `us-east` falls behind."
- Overflow thresholds go on the pull request, not on the consumer; `min_ack_pending` is a related threshold counted against unacknowledged messages, and meeting either triggers delivery.
- `nats consumer next` issues a plain pull with no flag for overflow thresholds or priority; those pulls must come from a client library.
- pinned_client policy: the server pins one waiting pull as the active client and every other pull waits as standby; if the pinned client stops pulling past the pin timeout, the server pins a standby. Use it for strictly ordered pipelines with one active and one standby.
- The pin timeout (`--pinned-ttl`) must sit comfortably above the pull's `expires`; the server's default pin timeout is two minutes, so keep `expires` under a minute. "The server's default timeout is two minutes; keep `expires` under a minute and the whole cycle fits."
- Pinning is agreed via the `Nats-Pin-Id` header on the first delivered message; the client sends it back on every later pull. A stale ID gets a `423` status; the client clears its ID and rejoins the standby pool.
- The pinned-client loop (store `Nats-Pin-Id`, send it back, handle `423`) runs in Go, Java, JavaScript/TypeScript, and .NET; Rust and Python let you set config fields but don't run the client-side pinning loop.
- prioritized policy: each pull carries a `priority` from 0 to 9; the server serves the lowest number present first, and pulls at the same priority share round-robin.
- Overflow waits for a backlog to cross a threshold before a standby gets anything (avoids churn, far regions wait); prioritized shifts work the moment a higher-priority puller goes quiet, at the cost of some flip-flop.
- The server lets you switch a live consumer's priority policy (via a full `--config`), though `nats consumer edit` has no flag for it.
- One group per consumer: passing two groups is accepted but only the first is used. "To split work by region or tier now, run separate consumers on the same stream, each with its own group."
- The pin does not give one client sole ownership: the server can switch the pinned client while it still believes it holds the pin. "If the same message must never be processed twice, use explicit acks and handlers that are safe to run more than once, not the pin alone."
- A quiet pinned client keeps the pin until the timeout, parking every other client; keep each pull's `expires` comfortably under the pin timeout so the client renews in time.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Pausing a consumer**

- A paused consumer stops receiving messages until a deadline and keeps all progress: cursor, acked state, and redelivery counts don't change; delivery resumes from the stopped position.
- Pausing differs from deleting and recreating a consumer, which throws away how far it read and which messages it acked.
- Pause is until a fixed moment; when it arrives the consumer resumes on its own with no second command.
- Clients can create a consumer already paused by setting `PauseUntil` in the consumer config.
- While a consumer is paused the stream keeps accepting messages; pause stops delivery, not storage.
- Pause for a maintenance window (downstream planned offline) or backpressure (downstream overloaded). "nothing is lost and nothing is handled twice."
- Pause runs on the consumer's leader; if the leader changes while paused, the new leader takes over the deadline and resumes on time.
- Pausing consumers needs NATS Server 2.11 or later; an older server rejects the command.
- A deadline in the past does nothing: the server leaves the consumer running. Pause with a duration like `1h` instead.
- Pausing does not stop publishers: new messages count toward the stream's limits, and a long pause on a tight `MaxMsgs`/`MaxBytes` stream can drop the oldest messages before the consumer reads them. "Size the stream for the longest pause you expect, or keep pauses short."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Shaping the stream**

- A limit discards a message for everyone; a consumer's position or filter doesn't protect a message from the stream's limits. "If a consumer is too slow and a message ages out before that consumer reads it, the message is gone."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Retention policies**

- Interest: a message is removed once every consumer whose filter covers it has acked it; if no consumer is interested in a subject, a message on that subject is removed right away.
- WorkQueue: a message is kept only until one consumer acks it; the first ack removes it for everyone, so each message is delivered once and then removed.
- On a WorkQueue stream scale by adding workers to one consumer, not by adding consumers.
- Interest can fill the disk: a stalled consumer holds up cleanup for every message it owes an ack on, so the stream grows until its limits. "Interest retention still needs limits set, and it makes watching consumer health more important."
- WorkQueue allows more than one consumer only if their filters partition the subjects; each then handles only its slice. For several consumers that each see every message, use Interest or Limits.
- WorkQueue rejects consumers that overlap: a second unfiltered consumer fails with `multiple non-filtered consumers not allowed on workqueue stream`; overlapping filters fail with `filtered consumer not unique on workqueue stream`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Altering stream state**

- Consumers skip deleted sequences; a consumer never blocks waiting for a deleted message, and a missing sequence is not redelivered.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Surviving node loss**

- Each consumer has its own leader that can sit on any of the stream's replicas, so delivery spreads across replica servers; a Direct Get can be answered by any replica, leader or not.
- Consumer state (read position, pending acks) replicates on an R=3 stream; by default a durable consumer takes its stream's replica count.
- On a limits-retention stream a consumer may have fewer replicas than its stream (never more); on interest and work-queue streams the consumer replica count must match the stream's.
- Consumer replicas don't scale delivery: one consumer leader does all the work, followers only stand by.
- To scale a consumer add workers; to scale writes past one leader split subjects across streams; to spread streams across servers use clustering.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reading messages directly**

- A direct read never moves a consumer's position and never removes a message.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject mapping and transforms**

- A transform that drops a token a consumer filters on collapses distinct subjects into one, so a consumer can no longer filter by type. "Keep every token a downstream filter needs in the destination."
- A partition count is fixed once consumers depend on it: changing `partition(3, …)` to `partition(4, …)` can hash the same key to a different bucket and silently change a consumer's coverage. "Pick the bucket count up front"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Per-message TTL**

- A TTL is a deadline on the stored copy and says nothing about delivery; if no consumer reads and acks before the deadline the message expires unread.
- A short TTL deletes the message whether or not a consumer read it; a consumer holding a message doesn't pause its TTL. "Do size the TTL to outlast the lag of your slowest healthy consumer."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Stream and consumer policies**

- There are nine policies (five stream, four consumer); each has a safe default, and five of the nine are fixed the moment the stream or consumer exists.
