- Deliver policy values: `all` (default, first message), `last` (newest then live), `new` (only messages after creation), `by_start_sequence`, `by_start_time`, `last_per_subject` (newest per matched subject, what KV watches are built on).
- Deliver policy `last_per_subject` and the Direct Get `--last-per-subject` flag are different features sharing a name: one is a consumer start position, the other a one-shot read.
- Ack policy values: `explicit`, `none`, `all`, `flow_control`.
- Replay policy: `instant` (default, as fast as the reader takes them) or `original` (spaces deliveries to match original timestamp gaps).
- Priority policy default `none` applies no steering; `overflow`, `pinned_client`, `prioritized` steer.
- Live-consumer changeability: Deliver policy, Ack policy, and Replay policy fixed at creation; Priority policy can change via `--config`.
- Changing a fixed policy means recreating the object: storage edit fails with `stream configuration update can not change storage type`; deliver policy update fails with `deliver policy can not be updated`. Recreating a consumer loses the saved position.
- Expecting `new` to skip the backlog on every restart: a deliver policy applies once at creation; a durable created with `new` keeps a saved position and resumes from it, backlog included. "Don't use it hoping each reconnect jumps to live traffic."
- Two features answer to "last per subject"; check which feature a flag or value belongs to before copying it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next**

- Core model: a stream is a server-side log; a consumer is a position marker tracked separately from every other consumer; an ack is how a reader says a message is handled, and until then the server resends it after a timeout. "A stored message has not yet been processed."
- Checklist: Wait for delivery and ack before acting on a business outcome; a `PubAck` means stored, not processed.
- Checklist: Reach for `--all` only when you want the whole history; sample the tail with `--last`, `--since`, or `--start-sequence`.
- Checklist: Use a named, durable consumer for any read you must resume after a disconnect; an ephemeral one restarts from sequence 1.
- Checklist: Edit a durable consumer to change it; recreating with a new config is rejected as already-exists.
- Checklist: Confirm `--all` versus `--new` matches the question (backlog or live traffic) before you run the command.
- Checklist: Pair `--all` with `--terminate-at-end` for a one-shot replay; on its own it drains the backlog then blocks waiting for more.
- Checklist: Set Ack Wait longer than your slowest handler, with headroom, to avoid a redelivery storm.
- Checklist: Ack on every success path, and term a genuinely unprocessable message so it stops coming back.
- Checklist: Ack each delivery exactly once, in one place in your handler; a second ack is a no-op the server ignores.
- Checklist: Confirm the filter matches a subject the stream stores before assuming an empty pull means an empty stream.
- Checklist: Decide retention through stream limits, not filters; a filter narrows a view, it never deletes messages.
- Checklist: Keep multiple filter subjects on one consumer disjoint; the server rejects overlap inside a single consumer.
- Checklist: Nak a transient failure with a delay, or set a backoff, instead of a bare nak that loops at network speed.
- Checklist: Term a poison message the moment the code knows no attempt will succeed, rather than burning the delivery budget.
- Checklist: Subscribe to the max-deliveries advisory so a dropped message doesn't vanish unnoticed; JetStream has no dead-letter queue.
- Checklist: Raise AckWait or send in-progress for long jobs so a slow handler doesn't trigger double work.
- Checklist: Treat an empty fetch as "nothing right now" and loop; never as an error that crashes the worker.
- Checklist: Always set an `expires` on a fetch so a quiet stream returns control instead of stalling.
- Checklist: Keep `MaxAckPending` at or above your batch size so it doesn't throttle throughput.
- Checklist: Pair `batch` with `max_bytes` so a single pull is bounded by size as well as count.
- Checklist: Key every side effect by `order_id` so a redelivered message is a no-op, not a double shipment.
- Checklist: Size `MaxAckPending` to at least your worker count, with headroom; the cap is shared across the whole pool.
- Checklist: Tune `AckWait` to real processing time so a crashed worker's message recovers without redelivering honest work.
- Checklist: Reach for an ordered consumer only for a read you can restart from the top; for work that must land once, use a named consumer with explicit ack.
- Checklist: Split work across processes with a named consumer and a worker pool; two ordered consumers each read the whole stream instead of sharing it.
- Checklist: Don't build a resumable job on an ordered consumer; its cursor is disposable by design and starts over after a crash.
- Checklist: Run one priority group per consumer; passing more than one silently uses only the first.
- Checklist: Drive failover with `min_pending` or `min_ack_pending`; the ADR-42 `failover` timer isn't shipped yet.
- Checklist: Lean on explicit acks and idempotent handlers, not the pin, to keep work from doubling up; the pin is not a lock.
- Checklist: Keep each pull's `expires` comfortably under `--pinned-ttl` so a pinned client renews in time.
- Checklist: Pause with a duration like `1h` so the deadline can never land in the past and no-op.
- Checklist: Size the stream for the longest pause you expect; publishes keep landing and count against the limits while a consumer sleeps.
- Checklist: Give each WorkQueue consumer a disjoint filter, or share one consumer as a pool; overlapping consumers are rejected.
- Checklist: Size a TTL to outlast the slowest healthy consumer's lag; the clock deletes the stored copy whether or not it was read.
- Checklist: Use a consumer, not a direct batch, when you need to follow the stream; a batch reads the backlog once and stops.
- Checklist: Keep every token a downstream consumer filters on in the transform's destination; dropping a `{{wildcard}}` collapses messages under one subject.
- Checklist: Pick the partition count up front; raising it later re-hashes keys, so a consumer's filter quietly starts covering a different set.
- Checklist: Settle the fixed policies (storage, persist mode, deliver, ack, and replay) before creating anything durable; `stream edit` and `consumer edit` can't change them.
- Checklist: Plan the data move when a fixed policy must change; recreating a stream needs a mirror or a re-publish, and a recreated consumer starts fresh.
- Checklist: Treat `--deliver new` as a one-time start position, not a per-restart skip; a durable resumes from its saved position on reconnect.
- Checklist: Check whether "last per subject" means the deliver policy or the Direct Get flag before copying a command.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Raft and leaders**

- Every replicated stream and every replicated consumer gets its own RAFT group; the stream leader is the server that accepts writes to the stream.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream in a cluster**

- Consumers replicate too: each consumer gets its own Raft group and leader, chosen independently of the stream's, so a consumer can lead on one server while its stream leads on another.
- By default a consumer takes its stream's replica count; an R1 consumer on an R3 stream is its own single point of failure, since its position lives on one server and losing it loses the reader's place even though the stream survives.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reconnection**

- The reconnect buffer does not restore a JetStream consumer's place in the stream; acknowledgment position is the JetStream layer's bookkeeping, not the connection's.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Drain & Shutdown**

- Pitfall: Assuming a core drain acks your JetStream messages. Drain winds down the connection; it does not acknowledge a consumer's messages. Ack explicitly before the connection closes or JetStream redelivers to the next client. "It does not acknowledge a JetStream consumer's messages for you."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where Next (Resilient Clients)**

- Checklist: Ack JetStream in-flight messages before a core drain; a connection drain does not handle a consumer's ack position.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream health**

- Consumer state fields: `delivered.stream_seq` (last order handed to a worker), `ack_floor.stream_seq` (sequence below which everything is acked), `num_ack_pending` (in-flight: delivered but not acked), `num_redelivered` (currently tracked as delivered more than once — not a lifetime tally; it drops when the message is finally acked), `num_waiting` (waiting pulls).
- Lag is a computed number: `lag = stream.last_seq − consumer.delivered.stream_seq`; a pull consumer reports the same value directly as `num_pending` (Unprocessed Messages). "lag = stream.last_seq − consumer.delivered.stream_seq"
- Three numbers describe a consumer's full state: lag (`num_pending`), in-flight (`num_ack_pending`), redelivered (`num_redelivered`).
- A healthy consumer keeps lag near zero and `num_redelivered` near zero. Lag climbing while `last_seq` climbs means orders arrive faster than they're processed; `num_redelivered` staying high or growing means workers keep taking orders and failing to ack. "A healthy consumer keeps lag near zero and `num_redelivered` near zero."
- A redelivery happens when a worker takes a message and never acks it, or naks it, so the server hands it to another worker.
- Pitfall: Crashed workers show up as rising lag with nobody fetching. `num_pending` climbs whether or not any client fetches, so it's ambiguous alone; the signature of crashed workers is lag rising while `num_waiting` is `0` and `delivered.stream_seq` stops advancing. Read all three together.
- Pitfall: In-flight is not lag. `num_ack_pending` counts messages a worker holds; `num_pending` counts messages no worker has taken. Rising in-flight means a stuck handler; rising lag means not enough handlers. "rising in-flight means a stuck handler, rising lag means not enough handlers"
- Pitfall: A filtered consumer's lag counts only its subjects. Empty pending on a filtered consumer doesn't mean the stream is empty; compare it against the stream's per-subject counts, not `last_seq`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Advisories & events**

- When a message exhausts its delivery attempts, the server publishes `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<stream>.<consumer>` with body `{type: io.nats.jetstream.advisory.v1.max_deliver, stream, consumer, stream_seq, deliveries}`. The message stays in the stream under its retention policy; only delivery to that consumer stops.
- The `max_deliver` advisory is the only built-in signal that a message stopped being delivered. There's no dead-letter queue, and the advisory is published once; if no one is subscribed when it fires, you never learn it happened. "There's no dead-letter queue, and the advisory is published once."
- Pitfall: A `max_deliver` advisory is the only built-in signal a message was dropped. Subscribe to `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.>` or capture it in a stream; otherwise poison messages disappear silently.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Prometheus & dashboards**

- JetStream collector series: `num_pending` becomes `nats_consumer_num_pending`, redeliveries `nats_consumer_num_redelivered`, in-flight `nats_consumer_num_ack_pending`, stream message count `nats_stream_total_messages`; labeled by `account`, `stream_name`, `consumer_name`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Monitoring)**

- Checklist: Read crashed workers as rising `num_pending` with `num_waiting` at `0` and `delivered.stream_seq` stalled; watch those three fields together.
- Checklist: Read in-flight (`num_ack_pending`) and lag (`num_pending`) as two separate numbers; confusing them hides a stuck handler.
- Checklist: A filtered consumer's `num_pending` counts only matching subjects; empty pending does not mean an empty stream.
- Checklist: Treat the `max_deliver` advisory as the only built-in signal a message was dropped; JetStream has no dead-letter queue, so subscribe or lose poison messages silently.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Watching**

- A watch delivers the current value of every matching key as an initial snapshot, then streams every later change. "One call gives you both halves: the state of the bucket now, and the changes from now on."
- Underneath, a watch is an ephemeral ordered consumer on the backing stream, replaying the last value per key then following new writes; opening the watch creates it and closing removes it.
- A watch filter applies to both snapshot and live halves, so a filtered watch is a smaller, cheaper view rather than every change filtered client-side.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TTL and limits**

- When a per-key TTL fires, the server leaves a marker with reason `MaxAge` rather than silently dropping the value; watchers receive it as a purge (CLI prints `PURGE`).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Watching and listing**

- A watch streams metadata updates in the order the bucket recorded them, then delivers a single nil sentinel when it has caught up; the CLI consumes the sentinel, client code must recognize it and keep reading.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Stream backup and restore**

- By default a snapshot records each durable consumer's config and delivery position, so restored consumers resume where they left off; `--no-consumers` drops that. "keep the default when you back up a production stream"
- `--no-consumers` silently drops consumer state; the restore rebuilds the stream with no consumers and nothing warns you.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mirrors as a DR tool**

- Avoid a Work Queue upstream under a mirror: the mirror's hidden internal consumer is a direct consumer that bypasses the work queue's subject-overlap check, so a worker and the mirror can both receive the same message. Use a `Limits` upstream instead.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Disaster recovery**

- Consumer lost its position: restore a `--consumers` snapshot; only the snapshot captured the saved delivery position.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Backup & Recovery)**

- Checklist: keep consumer state in the snapshot; `--no-consumers` silently drops durable consumer config and delivery position.
- Checklist: avoid Work Queue retention on a mirrored upstream; use Limits.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream**

- Three pieces: a stream (server-side store bound to one or more subjects), a consumer (server-side stateful view tracking client progress), and a client (application that receives and acknowledges messages).
- A consumer can be shared by multiple clients to divide the work; each acknowledgment advances the consumer's position.
- Multiple consumers can read the same stream independently, each with its own position, maintained by the server.
- If a message isn't acknowledged in time, the server redelivers it, which is what gives at-least-once delivery.
- A consumer can start from the beginning of the stream, the latest message, a specific sequence number, or a specific time.

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Building an Interactive Whiteboard with NATS Websockets | Rethink Connectivity Episode 3**

- An ordered consumer is an ephemeral consumer that guarantees ordered delivery and, on detecting a gap, restarts by creating a new consumer. "as soon as we find that there's gaps we kind of restart and create a new consumer" (~12:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Replace Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis and more w/NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity Ep 10**

- The JetStream consumer API is built on core NATS request/reply on `$JS` subjects, so it can technically be used by hand, though the subjects are long and fiddly. "JetStream is actually built on top of core NATS request reply" (~07:10)
- Consumers are described as windows into a stream; a consumer may take all data or a filtered subset by subject. "consumers are like windows into a stream" (~07:10)
- Unlike Kafka, where you'd have to deliver the whole stream, NATS filters at the consumer level by subject. "instead of having to whip through an entire stream ... NATS can actually filter on a consumer level" (~08:10)
- Consumers are stored on the server and replicated across nodes, so clients can stay stateless. "consumers are also stored on the server and replicated ... so your clients can stay stateless" (~09:10)
- A consumer must acknowledge messages; it can also signal it has not processed one or that it is in a bad state and wants no more messages for now. "I've not processed it or I'm in a really bad state don't send more messages to me right now" (~09:10)
- Consumers live server-side; many clients can consume from one consumer and are naturally load balanced, unlike Kafka where partitioning and consumer groups are needed. "I could have a lot of clients consuming from one consumer and they're naturally load balanced" (~20:28)
- Consumers are ephemeral by default: after the client dies there is a timeout, then the server cleans the consumer up; setting a durable name keeps it around. "they are ephemeral by default ... eventually clean up that consumer" (~21:30)
- A restarted durable consumer resumes exactly where it left off. "it's going to pick up right where it left off" (~24:33)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to configure NATS JetStream streams | Rethink Connectivity Ep 11**

- Interest retention is a superset of limits: it still enforces limits but also deletes a message once every interested consumer has acknowledged it. "it will delete messages once they have been consumed by every consumer that's interested in it" (~11:11)
- Work-queue retention behaves like interest retention but restricts the stream to one consumer; that one consumer can still be shared by many clients for load balancing. "just because I have one consumer it means I can't load balance between them ... that's actually not true" (~12:13)
- Consumer limits on a stream set default limits for consumers created on it. "configure default consumer limits for consumers that are created on this stream" (~24:25)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Build Priority Background Jobs & Dead Letter Queues with NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity ep 12**

- Correction to the previous episode: a work-queue stream can have multiple consumers as long as their filter subjects do not overlap. "you can actually have multiple consumers in a work queue stream as long as the subjects that they're interested in don't overlap" (~04:05)
- JetStream retries failed or unacknowledged deliveries automatically; the number of attempts and the backoff schedule are configurable. "that's a configurable setting to set how many times we want to retry as well as what the back off policy looks like" (~04:05)
- In a work-queue stream, a message that exhausted max deliveries stays in the stream until manually acknowledged or deleted, so failures stack up the queue size. "it will stay there in the stream until you either manually acknowledge it or manually delete it" (~05:05)
- Name the connection and the consumer after the worker role and instance so monitoring and logging can identify each worker. "use these to create the name for our JetStream consumer as well as kind of just a worker name to use for both logging and for monitoring" (~11:14)
- Max deliver (example 4) plus a backoff list (example 5s, 10s, 15s) controls redelivery; each backoff entry is how long to wait for an ack before redelivering. "this is how long it's waiting for an acknowledgement so if the job doesn't get back to you in 5 seconds then it's going to attempt to redeliver" (~17:25)
- Exponential-backoff retry logic like a webhook system is pure JetStream consumer configuration, not code. "you could do all of this straight inside of JetStream without really having to write much code" (~18:26)
- Creating two consumers with overlapping filter subjects on a work-queue stream errors; newer servers allow multiple filter subjects per consumer. "I'm actually going to get an error because I'm going to try to create two consumers that overlap" (~18:26)
- Every consumed JetStream message carries metadata including the stream sequence and consumer sequence. "every single message in JetStream as you're consuming it has metadata about the message" (~19:27)
- Nak retries immediately; nak-with-delay schedules redelivery later; simply not acking lets the ack wait expire so the server detects hung or dead workers and retries. "what if one of these workers cannot respond and it needs to shut down or it's hanging ... I want JetStream to pick up on that fact" (~24:32)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared: Part 1 | Rethink Connectivity**

- Terminology mapping: a Kafka consumer group is what JetStream calls a consumer; Kafka's consumers are JetStream's client applications. "Kafka's concept of consumer groups is what in JetStream we call just consumers" (~17:17)
- A JetStream consumer is like a database view on a stream: it can filter and can be shared by many client applications. "you can look at a consumer ... as essentially like a view on a stream" (~18:19)
- JetStream consumers hold state on the server (position, pending acks); Kafka consumer groups leave offset persistence to client applications, so NATS clients are purely stateless. "there's nothing for the client application to persist ever" (~19:21)
- Kafka is designed for one client application at a time per topic partition; distributing a topic across clients requires partitioning, whereas JetStream needs no partitions by default. "if you want to distribute messages in a topic amongst a set of client applications ... you must use partitioning" (~20:22)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared Pt 2: Consumers | Rethink Connectivity**

- Kafka consumer group = JetStream consumer; JetStream consumers can be shared by any number of client applications without partitions. "consumers in JetStream can be shared by any number of client applications at any given time without having to have partitioning" (~02:02)
- In Kafka only one consuming application at a time can read a topic partition, because of how (the lack of) acknowledgments work. "you can only have one consuming application at a time per partition of a topic" (~03:03)
- JetStream distributes messages among client applications attached to a consumer evenly and according to demand, so you can scale clients up and down freely. "the consumer will automatically evenly and according to demand distribute the messages between those consuming applications" (~04:06)
- Kafka client applications must persist their own offset; JetStream client applications persist no state. "the consuming applications in JetStream do not need to persist any state at all" (~07:10)
- Kafka replay options are start, end, or a specific offset; JetStream adds last-per-subject, first-per-subject, by-time (e.g. last 2 hours), and rate-limited original-timing replay. "play back everything for the last two hours 10 minutes whatever it is" (~09:11)
- Original-rate replay (metered at the ingest rate) is useful for debugging real-time applications. "only replay it at the same rate that it was initially put into the stream" (~10:13)
- A consumer subject filter (explicit or wildcard) acts like a non-materialized SQL view: no copy of messages, only a little iteration state. "it's not materialized ... the stream doesn't create another copy of the messages" (~11:14)
- For edge devices on flaky 5G, deliver-last-per-subject avoids replaying five stale "beep" commands after reconnect; the consumer policy encodes business intent. "it probably doesn't want to beep five times ... give me the last message per this particular subject" (~13:16)
- Durable consumers are long-lived and typically created administratively; use them to distribute messages across clients, or for a single transient application that must resume where it left off without client state. "it picks up automatically from that consumer where it was" (~18:21)
- An ephemeral consumer is auto-deleted after a configurable inactivity period; it suits an application wanting its own copy of the messages and willing to re-read from the start on restart. "if there's no client application connected to it for a certain amount of time ... it automatically gets cleared up" (~18:21)
- Analogy: a durable is a view on a table; an ephemeral is a query whose result set you iterate again on restart. "ephemeral it's just simply a query over which you iterate the result set" (~19:22)
- A browser whiteboard used ephemeral consumers per JavaScript client (start at beginning, then live updates), cleaned up when the browser closes; a web service or data pipeline should use a durable. "somebody closes their browser and we want that to be cleaned up" (~20:23)
- A stream has exactly one order for all messages and every consumer, ephemeral or durable, delivers in that order; the tricky part is preserving order under errors. "there's just one order of all the messages into your stream" (~20:23)
- JetStream consumers are flow controlled with two forms: one-to-many via max ack pending across all clients on a consumer, and one-to-one via pull batch sizes. "the maximum number of acknowledgments pending at any given time that you can control" (~23:25)
- Push consumers send ahead using pub/sub underneath; pull consumers send only on fetch demand (next message or batch of N). "pull the messages are only sent on demand when the application says fetch me the next message" (~23:25)
- Kafka is pull-only with one-to-one flow control and has no one-to-many flow control. "in the case of Kafka it's only pull so you only have one to one flow control" (~24:27)
- You can create as many consumers as you want on a stream; each iterates its own view of all messages, and a deletion in the stream is reflected in every consumer. "each consumer will iterate through its own set of all the messages in the stream" (~26:29)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Move over Kafka! Let's try NATS JetStream**

- `nats sub --stream` reads from a stream with start options: all, new, last, last-per-subject (with a subject), or from a specific sequence number. "if i wanted to read a last message from a certain subject i can just say last per subject" (~05:05)
- CLI subscriptions so far were ephemeral consumers, created on the fly and cleaned up on disconnect; a durable consumer remembers what has been consumed across runs. "when the client disconnects they get cleaned up" (~06:05)
- Consumer state (cursor, last consumed) is stored server-side, so clients need no cursor handling. "the clients don't have to have any sort of special handling of cursors" (~06:05)
- Push consumers receive messages as fast as the server can send; pull consumers fetch one at a time or in batches. "the server pushes messages to this consumer as fast as it possibly can" (~07:06)
- Pull consumers require the explicit ack policy; replay policy can be instant or original (same spacing as first published). "since we're using a pull consumer we actually have to choose the explicit policy" (~07:06)
- Pull fetches with timeouts let you scale down workers when the queue drains. "it allows you to essentially scale down workers as they time out and there's no messages left in the queue" (~08:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Comparing and contrasting NATS and Kafka | RethinkConn '22**

- JetStream consumer filters are pushed to the server, which uses indexing rather than a full scan and sends only matching records; filters support `*` and `>` and can combine with a start time. "it doesn't normally do a full table scan over the stream ... it uses indexing" (~08:10)
- JetStream consumers (Kafka consumer groups) are partition-less, stateful, and their state is persisted and replicated along with the stream. "they also are stateful and the state can be persisted and replicated along with the stream of the data" (~10:13)
- JetStream has push and pull delivery with one-to-one and one-to-many flow control; Kafka has pull only with one-to-one flow control. "Kafka only has the one to one flow control using pull" (~11:14)
- JetStream cursor positioning: start, new, sequence, last, last-per-subject, or a time in the past; Kafka can only seek start, end or offset. "there's no ability to say give me the last hour or give me the last message on this subject" (~11:14)
- JetStream acknowledgments are per individual message with ack, term (do not redeliver), nak (reprocess later) and in-progress (extend the deadline), plus nak backoff timing and DLQ-style functionality. "term a message saying don't try to redeliver it, nak saying I cannot process this message reprocess it later, or in progress" (~13:18)
- Kafka consumer groups only support cumulative offset acks; there is no individual acknowledgment and redelivery means the application seeks manually. "there's no concept of acknowledging individual messages" (~13:18)
- JetStream provides double acknowledgments for reliable consumption. "JetStream gives you double acknowledgements" (~16:23)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | JetStream**

- JetStream supports push (messages as soon as available) and pull (good for horizontal scale-out of workers), plus a work-queue style where a message is removed once all interested parties have consumed it. "pull base model which is really good for scaling out horizontally" (~03:07)
- A stream is a log; multiple services consume it with each having a unique view (position, ack state, push or pull, acks or not); a consumer describes how a set of related services consumes. "each have a unique view over that data that can be in different places within the data" (~07:13)
- Pull consumers let 20–40 worker services each ask for the next message when ready, replacing round-robin or least-weighted routing; a worker can ack, refuse work, or ask for more time. "you can scale up horizontally by having 20 or 30 or 40 of these worker services" (~09:15)
- For observability the key metrics are how many times a message had to be redelivered and how long processing took; JetStream emits advisory events (e.g. "took ten milliseconds, tried four times") usable for dashboards and alerting without extra logic in services. "how many times has this message had to be redelivered ... and how long did it take for that message to be processed" (~11:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Getting Started with NATS JetStream: Streams, Storage, and Data Lifecycle**

- A stream retains data even with no consumers, so a consumer created later still receives it (at-least-once). "Even if you don't have any consumers, the stream will retain that data for you" (~03:04)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Why NATS Consumers Just Work (And How to Use Them in 15 Minutes)**

- A consumer is how you get data out of a stream; it can pull a filtered subset or everything from the beginning, and multiple consumers can share a stream to build fan-out, fan-in and saga patterns. "you can follow all the standard event-driven patterns like fan out, fan in, saga" (~01:01)
- Consumers are filters on a specific stream and must be bound to one at creation. "consumers are filters on a specific stream. So when you set up a consumer, it has to be tied to a stream" (~03:05)
- A client must be authorized to subscribe on subjects matching the consumer's filter (a broader wildcard is fine); otherwise the subscription is rejected. "Without this block, any service that tries to subscribe to this consumer will get rejected because it hasn't been authorized" (~04:07)
- Pull fetches need a timeout so the process can leave the fetch, re-evaluate and run other work; the speaker uses 5 seconds, not 500 ms or 1 s. "You have to pass in a timeout ... 5 seconds is good" (~08:11)
- Three pods pulling on one durable consumer were load balanced automatically and roughly evenly, with variance explained by node speed or distance from the data. "that's automatic load balancing built in because each pod is pulling whenever it's ready" (~10:13)
- A durable consumer is stateful: after draining it reports zero unprocessed and will only deliver the next new messages. "My answers consumer is now aware that it has no unprocessed messages. So, it's stateful" (~12:14)
- An ephemeral consumer does not track progress: it is created with a generated name, disappears when done, and re-running re-delivers everything (92 rows became 184). "I'm creating a new consumer that isn't tracking state ... 92 throwaway answers twice" (~15:18)
- Ephemeral consumers suit one-off fire-hose reads of a stream or subject. "useful if you ever want to just pull fire hose of all the data that's stored in a stream" (~15:18)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers**

- Consumers must know which physical stream they bind to; this is the asymmetry with the publisher side. "you do have to know which physical stream you're consuming from" (~19:26)
- 2.10 added multiple, possibly disjoint, subject filters on a single consumer. "with 2.10 we added the ability to define multiple filters now which is really nice that can be disjoint" (~24:34)
- You do not subscribe to a stream; you consume from it via a consumer, which is a server-side construct you attach to from the client. "you don't subscribe to the stream you consume from the stream this is where we see this a lot" (~39:53)
- A consumer tracks delivered, in-flight and acknowledged messages; on ack it advances its offset. "it has all this internal state to keep track of which messages have I delivered which messages are in flight" (~41:55)
- Consumers give at-least-once delivery by default and redeliver unacked messages after the ack wait timer as long as client interest exists. "I have this at least once guarantee of delivery by default with a consumer and so it's just going to redeliver until the client says otherwise" (~42:57)
- Consumer state is replicated; by default a consumer inherits the replication factor of its stream and is co-located on the same servers. "if it's an R3 stream you create a consumer if you don't change the replication factor it's actually going to inherit the replication factor of the stream" (~43:58)
- Use an R1 consumer for short-lived, one-off, process-lifetime consumption to avoid replication overhead; use replicated durables for resumable long-running work. "you can opt for saying I only want a single replica consumer ... if it's not going to be a long lived durable consumer" (~43:58)
- An ordered consumer is a bundle of defaults: R1, no acks, client-side reset/retry on gaps, minimal server state, more work on the client. "ordered consumer ... an R1 no acknowledgement it handles if there are dropped messages it actually retries and resets itself internally" (~47:03)
- In-progress acks extend the ack wait window (30s mentioned as the window) to stop redelivery while still working on a message; nack and no-ack modes also exist. "within a 30 second time window send it in progress to stop redelivery attempts" (~50:08)
- The new JetStream client API removes the push/pull distinction; internally everything is pull-based. "there's actually no distinction anymore of a push versus pull consumer internally it actually is all pull-based now" (~51:10)
- Push consumers deliver to an inbox subscription as fast as the publish side sends, which can overwhelm applications and forced developers to think about flow control and max ack pending. "that can overwhelm applications ... that whole push-based model even though it sounded nice in theory I think actually confused quite a few people" (~53:11)
- Pull consumers with batching are not slower than push; clients interleave pull requests so latency between batches is minimized and it is on par or faster. "on par if not in some cases faster than a push consumer model" (~54:13)
- Batch fetching amortizes network overhead: one round trip for ten messages beats ten round trips. "you lose the network overhead of fetching one at a time pack a load of stuff together" (~56:14)
- Two application instances bound to the same consumer get different batches (load balancing), not copies of the same data. "they're getting individual batches because now the server is assuming okay you're trying to actually parallelize the work" (~59:16)
- Any number of workers can bind to one consumer for Lambda-style fan-out parallelism. "the consumer will happily basically load balance across and deliver across any number of instances" (~60:19)
- To retain order per entity, create a filtered consumer at the granularity you need (e.g. per dwelling subject). "you apply a subject filter and then that consumer will basically only deliver the relevant data" (~61:20)
- Do not plan on 100k or a million consumers, one per entity; you will never deploy that many client applications, so pick a wildcard granularity your app can handle in order. "nobody's running 100,000 a million containers ... the middle ground can be having a client application that can apply a wild card at the level of granularity" (~63:23)
- Max ack pending of 1 has historically been the recommended way to retain perfect order with a shared consumer. "you can define this max ack pending ... you probably should do this if you want to truly retain perfect order" (~64:26)
- NATS (at 2.10) has no native exclusive consumer with automatic failover between two client instances; it is discussed for the roadmap. "we don't yet have this ability to define an exclusive consumer" (~68:34)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.10 Webinar**

- 2.10 multi-filter consumers take an array of disjoint filter subjects instead of one, avoiding over-subscribing to a common root and dropping the rest client-side. "you don't have to over subscribe to the common root token in your subject hierarchy and then basically drop everything else" (~28:32)
- Because a multi-filter consumer is a single server-side source, relative delivery order across the filtered subjects matches stream order, unlike the old workaround of two unsynchronized consumers. "the relative order for all messages being delivered by that consumer are now in the order that you would expect from the original stream" (~29:34)
- All filter subjects of a consumer must belong to the same stream; to consume across streams, create a stream that sources from multiple origins and consume from that. "the pattern would be to create a stream that is actually sourcing from multiple origin streams and then create a consumer on that stream" (~29:34)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- Before 2.10 users needing several non-wildcard subsets (e.g. factories 1-5 of 10) had to create many consumers, which costs the server and forces the client to re-order across consumers. "people needed to create many consumers to get this one specific stream of data which is not only not perfect from optimization point of view for the server ... you have to handle the order" (~60:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP05: Exploring Powerful Client-side Features and Abstractions in NATS.io**

- The "simplification" API deliberately requires more explicit calls (create stream, create consumer, then consume) so the server-side resources and their behaviour are visible to the developer. "you explicitly have to do those things... oh I have to create some stream, oh I have to create some consumer" (~07:09)
- Ephemeral vs durable was reduced to a simpler concept: a consumer is ephemeral when it is cleaned up after an inactivity threshold; otherwise you delete it explicitly. "it's ephemeral based on some inactivity thresholds... or you say don't clean it up server for me" (~13:16)
- Auto-ack in the old subscribe-style API looked simpler but raised cognitive load because users could not tell whether messages were acked, and behaviour differed between clients. "even if the code looks simpler the cognitive load was bigger" (~14:18)
- Push and pull consumers' capabilities overlapped more with each server release until "when should I use pull vs push" had no single answer; simplification leans on pull consumers. "with every single server release it was harder to answer in one way" (~15:18)
- Old fetch-loop pull consumption left gaps in network utilization between one fetch finishing and the next; the new consume method interleaves fetches under the hood so delivery never pauses. "the client will under the hood optimize the fetches, meaning it will interleave the fetches so there is never a pause" (~17:22)
- Pull consumers now match or beat push performance (use-case dependent) with better client resource utilization because the client controls flow, so client buffers can be much smaller at the same throughput. "the buffer on the client side can be much smaller while having the same throughput" (~16:19)
- For IoT or CPU/memory-constrained devices, pull with a low pending limit avoids being flooded by a push consumer until flow control kicks in. "you can just lower how many things can be pending... without this compromise of now the server can flood me with messages" (~17:22)
- A consumer cannot be rewound; it is a pointer/view into the stream with its own sequence, so to go back you delete it and create a new consumer starting at the desired stream sequence (consumers are lightweight). "you cannot go back with this specific consumer but as consumers being pretty lightweight it's really pretty easy to just remove this consumer" (~20:25)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02S3: Orbit - The NATS Client Extensions**

- For 2.11 priority groups, pinning and overflow are supported in the clients as basic primitives, while the full consumer-group abstraction built on pinning is implemented and iterated in Orbit. "the pinning and overflow will be supported in the clients ... the actual whole consumer group abstraction implementation will be in Orbit" (~45:59)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03S3: NATS 2.11 Release**

- Consumer priority groups began as a request for Kafka-like consumer groups; the team deliberately designed a NATS-native solution rather than copying. "instead of just copying ideas, solutions, just try to solve the problem" (~23:29)
- In 2.11 a consumer may have only one priority group, but the config takes an array so clients are ready for multiple groups later without a type change. "for now it's only one group per consumer ... we wanted clients to be ready to be able to pass an array or slice" (~23:29)
- Overflow lets a client set a threshold (pending messages or pending acks) above which it starts receiving; e.g. three same-region clients serve normally and clients in another availability zone only pull when the primaries are too busy, minimizing cross-region cost without losing availability. "they will start getting messages only if the primary ones will get too busy" (~25:33)
- Pinning makes one client of many on a consumer receive all messages; the server uses TTLs to detect it stopped pulling and fails over to another client, replacing hand-rolled orchestration of a single active worker. "you can say that client A will get all the messages and the server has mechanisms and TTLs to find out that this client is no longer getting messages and the other one will take over" (~26:34)
- At 2.11 launch overflow is in all clients; pinning ships in Go first while the Orbit consumer-group abstraction built on pinning is validated. "overflow will be available in all the clients when 2.11 launches, the pinning will be available in Go first" (~27:36)
- Maintainers insist new abstractions fit JetStream's native concepts rather than bolting on leaky models copied from other tools. "we're not just bolting something in that feels like either a leaky or a not very watertight model" (~28:38)
- Multi-message (batch) get is "a consumer without a consumer": one request returning many responses, with filters, start sequence/time, up-to sequence/time, and multiple subject filters, which plain direct get could not do. "you can specify multiple subject filters as well which I think wasn't possible before with the old direct gets" (~33:45)
- Consumers are server-side state; many small operations via consumers eat server resources, whereas batch get creates no server state and is fire-and-forget. "the biggest difference is that batch get does not create state on the server, it just gives you what you asked for and it's done" (~34:46)
- Consumer pause is a consumer config option with a deadline timestamp; delivery resumes at that time, a past timestamp or absent option means unpaused, and it is meant as a maintenance/migration tool. "you specify a deadline, at 2:00 p.m. on the 12th of March start delivering messages again" (~37:48)
- Paused consumers keep sending idle heartbeats, so client applications see no errors, only an absence of messages until resume. "the consumers still continue to receive idle heartbeats so the applications won't get errors" (~38:49)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS tools and benchmarking with JNM! NATS Community Office Hours (Reupload)**

- NATS positions itself against Kafka on "proper queuing, proper request reply, proper multi-tenancy, no partitions unless you want them". "proper queuing, proper request reply, proper multi-tenancy ... no partitions unless you want them" (~02:03)
- Kafka is not "proper queuing" because committing an offset implicitly acknowledges every earlier sequence; JetStream acknowledges each message individually. "when you acknowledge a message or commit a message ... you're committing that sequence number and automatically committing all the other sequence numbers before that" (~10:14)
- Guaranteed delivery is not enough for a queue; you need guaranteed processing, e.g. a message whose database insert fails because the database is down for 10 minutes should be redelivered later, not block the partition. "it's not just the guaranteed delivery, you also want to do guaranteed processing" (~09:11)
- JetStream supports negative acknowledgement with a backoff delay (retry in 10 minutes, 20 minutes, an hour) and automatic redelivery; Kafka has neither. "you can say I negatively acknowledge this message and you can specify a backoff time" (~11:15)
- Terminate (term) is for messages that are themselves bad; unlike nak, it stops redelivery so a poison message does not loop forever. "the message itself is bad ... you can terminate the message" (~11:15)
- A server-side max ack pending limit (100 in the demo config) blocked bench's default consumer creation (it wants 500); the workaround was to pre-create the consumer and pass its name. "I probably set up the limit for 100 for max ack pending, by default it wants to do 500" (~57:10)
- `nats bench js` can consume three ways with the simplified API: `consume` (callback, library manages pulls), `fetch` (explicit batches, default 500), and an ordered consumer. "you can test three different ways you can consume messages in JetStream with the JS simplified API" (~55:08)
- Consumer decision tree: multiple apps sharing a stream or needing resumable position → durable; otherwise ephemeral, and among ephemerals the ordered consumer should be the default. "Ordered consumer should be your default go-to" (~59:19)
- Ordered consumers need no application acks yet guarantee in-order, gap-free delivery; the client library tracks sequences, detects gaps, and recreates the ephemeral consumer after reconnects. "if it sees a gap of any kind it knows that something must have happened ... it will not deliver the messages until it recovers the messages missing" (~63:24)
- Acks in JetStream are for guaranteed consumption (exactly-once processing), not guaranteed delivery; "no acks" does not mean unreliable. "acknowledgements in NATS are really not for guaranteed delivery, but guaranteed consumption" (~61:22)
- On the same local setup, consuming with explicit acks ran up to about 200,000 msgs/s while an ordered consumer reached about 650,000 msgs/s from a file-backed stream. "up to 200,000 per second with explicit acks ... with an ordered consumer we're in 650,000 per second" (~62:24)
- The performance gap is mostly the cost of acknowledging every message at the application level; max-ack-pending flow control still applies to acking consumers. "this difference between 200 and 600 is mostly due to the fact that you don't have to acknowledge at the application every time" (~64:24)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Benchmark Core NATS & NATS JetStream using the NATS CLI tool**

- Consumers are views onto a stream with cursor-like state; acknowledging consumers require the app to ack, nak, or ask for more time per message, and with a work-queue stream an acked message is removed. "you can look at consumers as views onto the stream" (~16:18)
- Ephemeral consumers suit one app instance getting its own copy of the data at its own pace, disappearing when the app quits; durable consumers are shared by many instances and distribute messages between them like a queue. "a durable consumer essentially acts as a queue for distribution purposes" (~18:19)
- Ten ephemeral ordered push consumers each reading 700,000 messages from a memory stream on the laptop totalled roughly 1.2-3 million msgs/s delivered (7 million messages in total). "1.2 whatever three million messages ... this is distributing seven million messages total" (~20:21)
- Pull consumers let you specify a batch, which matters because downstream processing (e.g. writing to a database) also needs batching to keep up with the message rate. "if you end up writing one by one to for example a database without batching things then you would never be able to keep up" (~21:22)
- A single pull consumer with batch 1 and per-message ack uses little CPU and is slow; batch 100 gives a huge improvement, and adding more pullers scales further (from ~210k msgs/s on the laptop). "going from 210 to, if I had more than just a single laptop ... would obviously be able to scale a lot further" (~23:26)
- Pull consumers are the horizontal-scaling primitive: add more instances for throughput, or use bigger batches on fewer, faster machines. "pull consumers ... allow you to scale out horizontally" (~22:23)
- Pull consumers with acks are a bit slower than push/ordered consumers because of acknowledgements but give a higher quality of service. "it's a little bit slower because of the acknowledgements but you get much higher quality of service" (~26:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS: Ordered, Scalable Stream Processing**

- Ordinary NATS load balancing is non-deterministic, so two messages on the same subject can land on different workers and lose per-key order. "ordinary load balancing in NATS is non-deterministic. Two messages on the same subject can land on two different workers" (~01:00)
- Partitioned consumer groups route every message sharing a partition key to the same worker while different keys run in parallel; it is the Kafka consumer group model built from two JetStream pieces. "If that sounds like Kafka consumer groups, that is the same model built in NATS from two JetStream pieces" (~01:00)
- Pull consumer priority groups are pull-only and require explicit acknowledgement. "They are pull only and need explicit acknowledgement" (~02:00)
- With the pinned client policy the server picks one client to receive all of a group's messages; others stand by, and if the pinned client goes quiet past its timeout the server re-pins to a standby. "If that client goes quiet past its timeout, the server simply re-pins to a standby" (~02:00)
- Pinning gives a single active worker with hot standby and no separate leader election system. "a single active worker with a hot standby and no separate leader election system to run" (~03:02)
- Pinning is affinity plus failover, not a distributed lock; a client may briefly still think it is pinned after the server moved on, and buffered messages cannot be pulled back. "Pinning is affinity and failover. It is not a distributed lock" (~03:02)
- Handlers should be idempotent because a rare double delivery during failover is possible. "That is why your handlers should be idempotent" (~03:02)
- Client-side per-key threading breaks under redelivery: a failed earlier message can be redelivered after a later one for the same key was already processed. "if buy fails and gets redelivered later, it comes back after pay was already processed and the order breaks again" (~06:04)
- max_ack_pending=1 forces one unacknowledged message in flight so the server guarantees order with no application cooperation; even a redelivery arrives before the next message. "Even a redelivery of buy always arrives before you could ever see pay" (~07:05)
- max_ack_pending=1 serializes unrelated keys behind each other and makes the single worker a single point of failure; a second worker becomes load balancing, not standby. "With max ack pending equal to one, only one worker can be active at a time, so there's no safe way to add a hot standby" (~08:05)
- A pinned member can be unpinned administratively (step down) so another instance becomes the active worker. "You can also unpin one at will, whenever you want. This is an admin command" (~08:05)
- Vocabulary: the stream holds data, a group is a kind of work over the stream, a group's work is split into partitions, and each partition is owned by a member (a consumer plus its worker and standbys); one stream can feed many groups. "a single stream can feed many groups, each reading it independently" (~09:07)
- Elastic groups use a work-queue stream that sources from the main stream, with a filter for the partitioning; static groups put consumers directly on the stream. "Elastic uses a work queue stream, which sources from the main stream" (~10:07)
- In partitioned groups max_ack_pending=1 is the safeguard that enforces serial processing if a worker would otherwise pull several messages at once. "Max ack pending equals one is the safeguard that enforces this in case a worker would otherwise pull several at once" (~11:08)
- With more partitions than members, a hot partition sharing a member with a quiet one starves the quiet key. "if a hot partition lands on the same member as a quiet one, that quiet key starves waiting in line behind the flood" (~12:10)
- The fix for a known hot key is custom partition-to-member mapping (dedicate a member to the hot partition), not more partitions. "the fix isn't really adding more partitions. It's custom mapping" (~12:10)
- Static group membership is fixed at creation; changing the mapping means deleting and recreating the group, so custom mapping suits a known hot key, not a moving one. "static membership is fixed at creation. To change the mapping, you delete and recreate the group" (~13:11)
- Elastic groups work on any stream without a pre-baked partition token and allow adding or dropping members at any time up to a maximum set at creation. "you can add or drop members at any time up to a maximum set at creation" (~13:11)
- The elastic library owns a hidden work-queue stream and its consumers, so it can reshuffle partition filters live without teardown. "Because the library owns that stream and its consumers, it can reshuffle the partition filters live with no teardown" (~13:11)
- Dropping the last member of an elastic group does not delete the group; messages pile up until a member is added back. "dropping the last member doesn't delete the group. Messages simply pile up until you add a member back" (~14:14)
- Size the elastic work-queue buffer (cap by bytes or message count) to more than a few seconds of processing: when the cap is hit, sourcing is suspended for up to a few seconds before it resumes, and a too-small buffer starves workers. "keep it above a few seconds worth of processing" (~14:14)
- Key-to-worker affinity also yields a high local cache hit rate for slow external lookups; that use does not need max_ack_pending=1, so a worker can keep several messages in flight. "this doesn't need max act pending equals one. You only need key to worker affinity, not serial processing" (~15:16)
- Static groups have the lowest latency and fewest resources; elastic costs a duplicate copy of your messages in the hidden work queue. "at the cost of a duplicate copy of your messages" (~16:17)
- Rule of thumb: static when membership is known and stable; elastic when membership changes, when you can't transform the stream, or when several groups share one stream. "reach for static when membership is known and stable, reach for elastic when membership changes" (~16:17)
- In both static and elastic groups the partition count is fixed at creation; only elastic lets membership change live. "In both, the partition count is fixed at creation, only elastic lets you change the membership live" (~16:17)
- Consumer-group configuration (max members, filters, members) is stored in a KV bucket, which is what allows live changes. "this is all configuration just stored in NATS KV store ... you can change it live" (~25:30)
- In elastic groups adding a member to the config and starting a consumer instance are separate steps; a consume for a member not in the roster just sits idle. "If we consume for a member that isn't in the roster, it just sits idle" (~23:28)
- While an elastic partition has no owner, its messages buffer in the group's work-queue stream and later drain in order to whoever takes it over. "While a partition has no owner, its messages buffer in the group's work queue stream and then later drain in order" (~26:30)
- Partitioning is useful even without strict ordering (max_ack_pending=1), e.g. for local caching. "If you don't require this ordering, you can still use this partitioning. There's other reasons such as optimizing local caching" (~30:34)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Pull Consumer Priority Groups: Overflow, Pinned & Prioritized**

- Without priority groups, multiple clients pulling from one consumer get plain round-robin and the server has no notion of which client should get the work. "It's plain round robin, and the server has no idea which client should actually get the work" (~01:00)
- Pull consumer priority groups arrived in NATS server 2.11: multiple clients pull from one consumer under a configurable policy, expressed purely as consumer configuration. "Starting in NATS server 2.11, pull consumer priority groups ... it's all just consumer configuration" (~01:00)
- Priority groups replace leader election, lock services, and coordination code for "send all work to one client, fail over instantly" and "drain locally first, spill to another region" patterns. "There's no leader election, no lock service, and no coordination code for you to write and maintain" (~01:00)
- Three policies exist: overflow (latency/cost-aware routing), pinned client (single active worker with fast failover), prioritized (tiered worker pools). "overflow for latency and cost-aware routing, pinned client for one active worker with fast failover and prioritize for tiered worker pools" (~02:00)
- Overflow serves a pull only once pending messages cross that pull's min_pending or unacknowledged messages cross its min_ack_pending (either/or of whichever the pull sets); pulls without a threshold drain normally. "A pull is served only when pending messages cross min pending or unacknowledged messages cross min ack pending" (~02:00)
- Overflow suits regional routing: local clients handle the common case and cross-region traffic is paid for only when locals genuinely fall behind. "you only pay for cross-region traffic when there's genuinely too much work for the locals to keep up" (~02:00)
- Under pinned client policy the server stamps messages with a pin ID header (Nats-Pin-Id); the client echoes it on every later pull, and a fresh ID is issued each time the pin moves. "stamps its messages with a pin ID header. The client echoes that ID back on every later pull" (~03:01)
- The server re-pins to a standby when the pinned client stays quiet past the configured timeout or an admin unpins it; `nats consumer unpin` forces a handoff, useful before a deploy. "An operator can also force that handoff out of band with NATS consumer unpin, which is handy for rotating the active client before a deploy" (~03:01)
- The server publishes an advisory on every pin change (pinned and unpinned events), usable as an audit trail of who holds the work. "the server publishes an advisory on every pin change, so you can watch handoffs as they happen" (~03:01)
- The prioritized policy arrived in NATS server 2.12: pulls are served by a priority number 0–9, lower served first; a secondary pool picks up immediately when the primary isn't pulling. "The third policy, prioritized, arrived in NATS server 2.12 ... priority number from zero to nine, with lower numbers served first" (~03:01)
- Overflow vs prioritized trade-off: overflow's threshold keeps assignments stable but lets backlog build; prioritized hands over with zero delay and no threshold, at the cost of flip-flopping between clients or regions. "Prioritized hands work over with zero delay and no threshold at all. And the trade-off is some flip-flopping" (~04:02)
- Tiers can be stacked with prioritized: US East priority 0, US West priority 1, EU West priority 2 only sees traffic when both US regions are quiet. "Put EU West at priority two, so it only ever sees traffic when both US regions are quiet" (~05:02)
- Pinned client fits jobs that must not run in parallel (billing run, stateful migration): HA without duplicate processors or a separate lock service. "You get high availability without running duplicate processors and without standing up a separate lock service" (~05:02)
- Priority groups are pull-only and require explicit ack; configuring them on a push consumer or with any other ack policy is an error. "Configuring them on a push consumer or with any other act policy is an error" (~06:04)
- A message can briefly be processed by two clients during failover overlap, so handlers must be idempotent; pinning is affinity and failover, not a distributed lock, and buffered messages cannot be revoked. "pinning is affinity and failover, not a distributed lock ... messages already in its buffer can't be revoked" (~06:04)
- Keep the priority timeout comfortably above pull expiry, because the pin resets only when the pinned client issues a new pull within the window; default timeout is 2 minutes, which pairs with pulls expiring in a minute or less. "The default timeout is 2 minutes, which pairs nicely with polls that expire in a minute or less" (~06:04)
- A stale or wrong pin ID is rejected with a 423 mismatch; the client clears its ID and repulls with none to rejoin the standby pool. "the server rejects that poll with a 423 mismatch. The client just clears its ID and repolls with none" (~07:04)
- A pull that doesn't claim the pin is not rejected; it gets a 408 and waits its turn behind the pinned client. "A client that doesn't claim the pin isn't rejected, it just waits its turn behind the pin client" (~09:06)
- Under overflow, a pull with min_pending below threshold is held and returns nothing (a 408) even if messages sit in the stream. "Below the threshold, the poll is held and returns nothing, just a 408, even if messages are sitting in the stream" (~11:09)
- min_ack_pending lets a worker help only once N messages are stuck in flight (delivered but unacked) on the main client. "worker can also be told only help once end messages are stuck in flight, delivered but not yet act" (~14:11)
- With prioritized, when a message arrives and several workers are waiting, the server picks the lowest priority number; the higher-numbered worker only gets work when the lower one isn't waiting. "the priority nine worker only gets work when the priority zero worker isn't waiting" (~16:13)
- Priority groups are configured through consumer flags or a JSON config (priority_policy plus priority group name); the CLI shows the policy and group in consumer info. "Our priority policy is overflow and our priority group will be called jobs" (~12:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Consumer Pausing | NATS 2.11**

- Consumer pause temporarily halts delivery to a consumer until a deadline; messages keep arriving in the stream and are delivered when the pause expires or is lifted early. "Messages continue arriving to the stream. They just aren't delivered until the pause expires or is manually lifted" (~00:01)
- Pausing is a normal consumer config update that sets a pause deadline; it works the same for push and pull consumers. "It's just a normal config update. Nothing special ... This works the same for both push and pull consumers" (~01:02)
- A paused consumer's application sees no errors or disconnects and keeps receiving heartbeats. "No errors, no disconnects. It keeps getting heartbeats like everything's fine" (~01:02)
- An in-flight batch is not pulled back: if 100 messages were pulled, the pause takes effect before the next batch. "NATS won't yank those away from you. It waits until the batch is done, then pauses before the next one" (~02:03)
- Consumer info shows the pause deadline and remaining time; resuming early is a separate command and a consumer can be created already paused, using a duration or an absolute timestamp. "You can initialize a pause upon creation. You can also use a timestamp for an absolute time" (~05:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.11: What's New?**

- In 2.10 there is no way to control behavior when multiple clients pull from one consumer; 2.11 priority groups allow pinning clients and overflow based on pending messages or pending acks, with more elaborate policies planned. "at the moment you'll be able to pin clients and overflow based on these two controls" (~04:13)
- Consumer pause is set as a pause deadline in the consumer config via a normal update, is identical for push and pull, resumes automatically at the deadline, and heartbeats continue so client SDKs surface no errors. "the consumer heartbeats continue to be sent to the client. So you won't get unexpected errors being surfaced from your client SDKs" (~05:15)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — JetStream KV: A fascinating alternative to Redis...**

- Watch is implemented as a lightweight consumer, so it supports subject filtering, choosing headers-only/latest/history/delete notifications, and a starting revision. "this is going to create a lightweight consumer to be able to get all of the notifications for that particular watch" (~14:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The ONE feature that makes NATS more powerful than Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ & Redis**

- The feature claimed to set JetStream apart from Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ and Redis is the flexibility of consumer configuration, which the speaker says removes upfront design cost. "that feature is how NATS designs its consumers" (~00:00)
- Consumers are "windows into the data of the stream": server-side filtering on the whole subject plus control over delivery, redelivery and start position. "they're really windows into the data of the stream" (~01:00)
- Three consumer archetypes: event-sourcing (durable, explicit ack, max-ack-pending 1, all subjects), reporting (ephemeral, start-time, filter), lookup (ephemeral, filter by ID, last-per-subject). "we probably want ... durable we want our acks to be explicit and our max ack pending to one" (~03:03)
- Alternatives give a firehose and expect client-side filtering, which at high scale is slow and inefficient; JetStream filters before sending over the wire. "the alternatives kind of just give you a firehose of messages and expect you to filter them out on the client side" (~04:04)
- Synadia has moved to "do almost everything" with pull consumers; push is not deprecated but pull is easier to reason about. "we've recently kind of moved to more of a do almost everything in a pull-based consumer" (~05:05)
- Push consumers send as fast as the server can, making flow control hard for slow consumers even with the built-in flow control and heartbeats; they suit monitoring / most-real-time cases. "it still gets a bit challenging to reason about flow control" (~06:06)
- Pull consumers are recommended: better performance and scalability, easier horizontal scaling, better flow control, and the default under the hood in newer client SDKs. "they're easier to horizontally scale they give you a bit better flow control and in the newer versions ... pull consumers are kind of the default" (~07:07)
- Durable consumers track delivered/acked/redelivery state and usually must be deleted explicitly; since nats-server 2.9 durables can also set inactive threshold. "in 2.9 you can actually set inactive threshold which was reserved for ephemeral for a long time but now can apply to durable" (~08:09)
- Ephemeral consumers are cleaned up by the server after an inactivity threshold and are very fast to create, which makes ad hoc queries, reporting and browser sessions scalable. "consumers are very very fast to spin up ... ephemeral consumers are actually possible to do in a very scalable way" (~09:11)
- In Kafka, Kafka Streams filtering happens client-side so the broker ships every message; that disincentivizes wide topics and forces upfront topic design, which does not apply to JetStream. "the Kafka broker itself is going to send every single message over the wire" (~10:12)
- Consumers are replicated with their own RAFT groups; an R3 consumer keeps operating with a node down and in rare cases with two down. Ephemeral consumers are in-memory R1. "consumers are also replicated and have their own raft groups" (~11:13)
- Durable/ephemeral, R1/R3, memory/file consumers can all coexist against one stream. "all of those things can coexist against a single stream" (~12:15)
- Ack policies: explicit (default, per message), all (acks everything since the last ack, good for batch ingestion), none (fastest, no delivery guarantees). "you can set an ack policy to none and that will be your fastest option because you don't have to have round trip times" (~13:15)
- Acks are asynchronous and non-blocking unless bounded by max ack pending; explicit is "generally better" for most cases. "these acknowledgements are all asynchronous they're not going to be blocking necessarily unless you have kind of a max ack pending" (~13:15)
- Max ack pending caps outstanding unacked deliveries; the default is 100. "by default this is actually set to 100" (~15:18)
- Max ack pending 1 gives strict in-order processing but is very slow; try to avoid it unless a downstream state machine truly needs strict ordering. "I would actually recommend trying to see if you can get away without having a max ack pending of one" (~25:26)
- Ack wait is a per-delivery timer; when it expires the server assumes the client failed and redelivers. "when these timers expire the server has decided that whatever client they sent that message to is not going to continue processing" (~16:19)
- Deliver policies: all (default, from the start), new (only future messages; good for monitoring), last (just the latest message), by start sequence, by start time (ad hoc "last 7 days" reporting), last per subject. "last by subject ... is kind of one of the core things that drives our key value store" (~18:22)
- Last-per-subject suits change-data-capture style reads where only the latest state per subject matters. "give me all the last updated events from all of the orders" (~19:23)
- Replay policy "original" reproduces the original inter-message timing, useful for replaying sessions or debugging spikes; "instant" delivers as fast as flow control allows. "play back the messages in the same timings that they were originally done in" (~20:24)
- Debugging in production: create an ephemeral debug consumer with any configuration without touching or reconfiguring the stream. "the stream is the stream and the consumers are all the consumers" (~21:24)
- Other options: max deliver and backoff (redelivery), headers-only (saves bytes for counting/aggregation), sampling (monitoring), consumer metadata, inactive threshold. "you can save some bytes over the wire by saying just give me the headers" (~21:24)
- Demo: processing ~31,620 messages one at a time with max ack pending 1 against Synadia Cloud was slow; with the default it finished the whole batch quickly while still acking each message individually. "we've processed the entire batch of 31,000 messages we are all caught up" (~30:31)
- Preserving full ordering while scaling out requires partitioning, called out as a separate topic. "maintain complete ordering here and scale these out via partitioning" (~29:30)
- Reconnecting quickly re-binds to the same ephemeral consumer because the server keeps ephemerals around briefly for network jitter; add randomness to the name or use create-consumer (which errors on conflict) to force a fresh one. "we keep ephemeral consumers around just for a little bit because we know that there's network jitter" (~31:32)
- Reporting consumer: ephemeral, headers only, max request batch 1000, ack none, deliver by start time (7 days ago), filter subject orders.us.*.shipped. "max request batch we're going to bump this up to a thousand" (~32:34)
- Multiple filter subjects on one consumer are supported in a recent server version (e.g. US shipped plus Canada shipped). "you could actually pass multiple filter subjects this is new in a recent version of NATS server" (~33:34)
- A filtered consumer is not as fast as a SQL aggregation query, but it answers ad hoc questions without copying data to another store and stays live for new matches. "is this going to be as fast as a SQL query if you're doing aggregation ... no it won't be" (~35:37)
- Lookup: ephemeral consumer filtered on orders.*.<orderID>.* with deliver-last gives the current status; last-per-subject gives the full status lifecycle in order. "we could actually use deliver last as well if we just wanted the last status update for this particular order" (~37:39)
- For single-message lookups the direct get API is more efficient than a consumer, and a batch direct get is coming in future server versions to do these lookups in one call without a consumer. "we're actually introducing a batch version of the direct get API call" (~38:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Stream processing: the easy way (with NATS and Benthos)**

- Error handling is delegated to NATS: on any processor error the output NAKs the JetStream message so redelivery/retries come from the consumer rather than from Benthos logic. "if anything's errored then make sure you nack on the NATS side so we can do any sort of retries" (~30:35)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Where are we now and where to next? | RethinkConn '22**

- JetStream was designed assuming a few thousand durable consumers, but users want 30–40 thousand, so large consumer sets need optimization work. "we've seen users want 30, 40 thousands so we're going to be doing some work optimizing for large consumer sets" (~10:13)
- Roadmap: extremely lightweight stream consumers for IoT at the scale of millions, and interest-graph partitioning to individually address a billion endpoints. "we're talking about millions of consumers ... I want to individually address a billion endpoints" (~14:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extending stateful services to the edge | RethinkConn '22**

- Many clients fetching from one shared consumer bound to the local mirror compete for messages; unacknowledged messages get redelivered (delivery count rises) once the end is reached. "it's starting to now redeliver unless you're acknowledging the messages" (~13:20)
- Consuming from the leaf mirror left the NGS origin stream untouched, because no consumer is bound to the origin; the work-queue mirror removes messages as they are acknowledged. "the NGS stream hasn't been touched because we don't actually have a consumer bound to that" (~14:21)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Lightweight relational databases at the edge | RethinkConn '22**

- Creating a table creates a consumer on the same-named stream and subscribes; default columns are the sequence, subject, timestamp, headers (as JSON), and the raw data blob, because nothing more can be inferred from an opaque payload. "create a table, create a consumer and then subscribe" (~04:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Short break and Q&A! | RethinkConn '22**

- Core NATS servers handle millions of connections, but making millions of devices each a JetStream consumer raises real state and persistence questions. "if you're saying we want to have millions and millions of devices, and we all want them all to be consumers of a JetStream ... there's some real things to figure out" (~29:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Derek Collison RethinkConn 2025 Keynote and Closing Remarks**

- Traditional consumers are heavyweight and can clog a system, so massive KV observer populations (100,000 to 1 million watchers) are achieved with republish and direct gets with global sequencing instead. "key values with over 100,000 or 1 million observers... traditional consumers are very heavyweight and can clog systems down... republish and direct gets with global sequencing" (~03:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia Roadmap with Byron Ruth**

- Consumers are heavy because of their Raft traffic; lighter consumers akin to client subscriptions are planned so you could have on the order of millions. "consumers today have a little bit of heaviness... all of the Raft traffic... akin to a standard client subscription... in the order of millions of them" (~06:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Introducing Synadia Insights: Catch the NATS Failures Nothing Else Reports**

- A stream with a message-count limit discards the oldest messages while consumer positions have no limit, so a stopped consumer whose position falls below the stream's first sequence silently loses every message in between, with no error, log line or alert. "The logbook has a limit. The bookmarks do not." (~03:00)
