- Consumer state lives on the server, not in the application, which is what lets an app resume after restart and also what lets the gap accumulate while it is down. "the bookmark stays behind. It lives on the server, not in the app" (~05:20)
- A consumer's unprocessed/pending count shows only what it will still receive (at most the stream's current contents), not what it will never receive. "2,000 is what analytics is about to receive. It says nothing at all about the 10,000 it never will" (~08:00)
- Insights raises a consumer health event when delivery falls below the stream's first sequence. "we delivered below the stream first sequence" (~19:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking Connectivity - Hyper-Connectivity & The Intelligent Edge**

- Qualities of service: at-most-once with core NATS fire-and-forget, at-least-once and exactly-once with JetStream. "at least once exactly once and so at most once with just core NATS fire and forget" (~20:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - MachineMetrics on Industrial IoT & Predictive Analytics w/ NATS at RethinkConn 2025**

- JetStream work queues with shared consumers let one piece of service code scale up and down without changes. "the consumer model just makes it so easy to scale services up and down really with just one piece of code" (~07:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Nathan Mellis from Modzy on NATS as a foundational building block**

- All model inference is asynchronous: inputs go into a NATS queue, Modzy spins up the model, drains the queue, then shuts the model down, so expensive GPU models only run when there is work. "it will spin up that model it will drain the queue and then shut the model down" (~02:04)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Migrating from NATS Streaming to JetStream**

- A Streaming subscription is analogous to a JetStream push consumer; JetStream adds pull consumers which Streaming lacked. "A NATS Streaming subscription is analogous to a push consumer." (~22:05)
- A consumer is a view of state over a stream, tracking delivered and acknowledged messages server-side. "Your mental model of a consumer can be this is a view of state over a stream." (~22:05)
- The legacy js.Subscribe convenience API implicitly creates an ephemeral consumer unless a durable name is given. "This subscribe is sort of implicitly creating a consumer under the hood." (~24:06)
- Pull consumers fetch a batch; if fewer messages are available the fetch returns what exists without waiting. "If there happens to be 10 messages available to be fetched, it'll fetch all 10. If there isn't, it's not going to wait." (~25:07)
- Consumer subject filtering happens on the server, saving bandwidth and client CPU; 2.10 will add multiple filter subjects per consumer. "It happens on the server... you're saving on bandwidth." (~34:20)
- Ack options are ack, nak, nak with delay, in-progress (resets the ack-wait timer), and term (no redelivery); default ack wait is 30 seconds. "The default ack wait time is 30 seconds if I recall properly." (~28:11)

## KV: Key-Value (398 claims)


**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream (concept overview)**

- KV and Object Store are built on JetStream and "inherit the core capabilities of JetStream, replication, security, routing limits, and mirroring"; Object Store uses chunked transfers.
- KV supports watch on bucket or key, optional history, atomic create/update enabling pessimistic locks (create and hold a key) and optimistic locks (CAS).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Headers**

- `KV-Operation: DEL|PURGE`; purge must be combined with `Nats-Rollup`; since 2.14 PURGE can carry `Nats-TTL` to auto-delete the marker and avoid `nats kv compact`.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Key/Value store (concept)**

- Buckets are "immediately (as opposed to eventually) consistent, persistent associative arrays"; materialized as streams named `KV_...`; "everything you can do with a bucket you can do with a Stream" and using the stream directly gives more control.
- Monotonic writes/reads guaranteed; "We don't guarantee read your writes at this time, as reads through direct get requests may be served by followers or mirrors." Send gets to the underlying stream leader for stronger consistency.
- Atomic ops: create (compare-to-null-and-set) and update (CAS) for locking and concurrency control.
- Bucket limits: max bucket size, max single value size, TTL. History default is 1 (only latest value/operation stored).
- watch / watch all / history make the KV a message stream.
- Valid key characters: `a-z A-Z 0-9 _ - . = /`; dot-separated keys allow wildcard watching of key hierarchies.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — KV walkthrough / Object Store walkthrough**

- Default bucket: History Kept 1, unlimited bucket size/value size/age, backing stream `KV_<name>`, file storage.
- Semaphore/exclusive lock: `create` a key (first come first served; concurrent creates error "wrong last sequence ... key exists"); make it resilient with a bucket TTL and keep-alive via `update` with revision.
- Optimistic locking: `update` with a revision; a second update with a stale revision fails "wrong last sequence".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Key Value Store (developer guide) / Object Store (developer guide)**

- Keys follow subject format (dot-separated tokens, subject-valid characters) so wildcards can watch key hierarchies.
- "Buckets are typically created, purged or deleted administratively".
- History default 1; "The maximum history size is 64, if you need more your use case will be better implemented using the Stream functionality directly (where you can set the max number of messages per subject to any value you want)".

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-6: Naming Rules**

- `kv-key-name = limited-term (dot limited-term)*` with `limited-term = (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, dash, underscore, fwd-slash, equals)+`; `kv-bucket-name = restricted-term = (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, dash, underscore)+`. "Keys starting with `_kv` are limited to internal use."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-19: API prefixes for materialized JetStream views**

- KV and Object Store must reuse the same API prefix: `$KV` and `$OBJ` are the default first tokens; with prefix `JS.from-acc1` a put goes to `JS.from-acc1.$KV.bin.key`, translated back to `$KV.bin.key`. Domain form: `$JS.<domain>.API.$KV.bin.key`.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-31: JetStream Direct Get**

- `multi_last` + `up_to_seq`/`up_to_time` gives "consistent point in time reads" ("temporal querying"), e.g. reading a KV record as it was at seq 3.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-36: Subject Mapping Transforms in Streams**

- KV bucket sourcing: bucket B sourcing A adds transform `{"src": "$KV.A.>", "dest": "$KV.B.>"}` on the source.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-43: JetStream Per-Message TTL**

- Limit markers: when age-based removal (stream MaxAge or per-message TTL) removes the last message on a subject, the server places a marker with `Nats-Marker-Reason: MaxAge` and `Nats-TTL` = `SubjectDeleteMarkerTTL` (e.g. `1m0s`). "This behavior is off by default unless opted in on the `SubjectDeleteMarkerTTL`."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-48: TTL Support for Key-Value Buckets (updates ADR-8)**

- Goals built on per-message TTL: notify watchers of MaxAge-deleted keys, "Improve Purge so that old subjects can be permanently removed, removing the need for costly compacts", and "Creating keys with a custom lifetime." KV calls these Limit Markers.
- Bucket option "Limit Markers" sets `allow_msg_ttl: true` and `subject_delete_marker_ttl` = supplied duration; "must larger than or equal to 1 second"; requires API level >= 1 (check `$JS.API.INFO`).
- Can be enabled on existing buckets "but should not support disabling it."
- `Status.LimitMarkerTTL()` returns the configured duration, "0 meaning markers are not supported."
- `Create()` and `Purge()` accept a TTL (adds `Nats-TTL` header).
- "do not accept a TTL for other API ... a TTL on `Put()` might mean older revisions could come back from the dead once the TTL expires."
- `Nats-Marker-Reason` mapping for readers/watchers: `MaxAge` → treat as PURGE, `Purge` → PURGE, `Remove` → DEL.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-50: JetStream Batch Publishing**

- Atomic use case: a KV user record spanning 5 keys (address) "Performing updates on these related keys is not safe today as writes might fail after a first update resulting in an address line in one city but a post code in another."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-54: KV Codecs (updates ADR-8)**

- Client-side codec layer wraps a KV bucket with independent `KeyCodec` (string↔string) and `ValueCodec` (bytes↔bytes) for "character escaping, path notation conversion, encryption, and custom transformations." (ADR: proposed; Orbit.)
- Motivating cases: keys with characters invalid in subjects (spaces, dots), filesystem-path keys, end-to-end encryption, app-specific encodings.
- Codecs must be transparent across Put/Get/Watch/Keys/History/Delete/Purge; a `FilterableKeyCodec.EncodeFilter` preserves wildcards for watch/list; codecs may be chained (encode in order, decode in reverse).
- Built-ins: NoOp, Base64 (url-safe; "Acme Inc.contact" → "QWNtZSBJbmMuY29udGFjdA=="), Path (`/`→`.`; leading slash encoded as `_root_`, trailing slashes trimmed).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-57: KV Subject Transforms (updates ADR-8)**

- KV mirror: clients "Prefix the mirror stream name with `KV_` if not already prefixed" and "Enable `MirrorDirect` on the underlying stream configuration" so mirrored buckets "Support direct reads via the Direct GET API" and "Automatically participate in RTT-based replica selection."
- KV sources without explicit transforms: clients prefix `KV_` and auto-add `{"src": "$KV.<source>.>", "dest": "$KV.<bucket>.>"}` (with key filter folded into src, e.g. `$KV.ORDERS.NEW.>` → `$KV.NEW_ORDERS.>`).
- Explicit `SubjectTransforms` are preserved exactly and skip auto-generation, enabling a non-KV stream as a KV source (`events.processed.>` → `$KV.EVENT_CACHE.>`) or custom key mapping (`$KV.INVENTORY.warehouse.*.product.>` → `$KV.PRODUCTS.>`, so `warehouse.nyc.product.item123` becomes `item123`). In that case "Do not modify the source stream name prefix."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-58: Key-Value Store Roadmap and future considerations (updates ADR-8)**

- Read-only KV handle (`RoKV`: Get, History, Watch, Keys, Close, Status) must be supportable "against a read replica and cannot support `Put()`." (ADR: proposed)
- "A bucket, being backed by a Stream, lives in one Cluster only. To make buckets available elsewhere we have to use JetStream Sources and Mirrors."
- KV Mirror (Replica): "Copy of exactly 1 other bucket. Used primarily for scaling out the `Get()` operations"; always read-only; may filter keys; "Replicas are automatically picked using a RTT-nearest algorithm"; replicas can be added/removed at runtime "without any re-configuration of already running KV clients"; "Writes and Watchers are transparently sent to the origin bucket"; can span accounts and domains.
- KV Aggregate (Source): combines one or many buckets into a new bucket "to provide a full local copy of other buckets that support watchers and gets locally in edge scenarios"; accessed by its own name; read-only or read-write; may hold key subsets; hosts watchers; "Writes are not transparently sent to the origin Bucket ... they either fail (default) or succeed and modify the Aggregate (opt-in)"; sources can be added later.
- "The existing domain based mirrors that are supported in KeyValueConfig will be deprecated but supported for the foreseeable future."
- Read-only aggregate stream config: `subjects: []`, `deny_delete: true`, `deny_purge: true`, sources with transform `$KV.ORDERS.NEW.>` → `$KV.NEW_ORDERS.>`; "When writable, configure as normal just add the sources."
- Mirrors "are not called `Bucket` and may not have the `KV_` string name prefix as they are not buckets ... we have done this in the leafnode mode and decided it's not a good pattern." Requires `mirror_direct: true` and origin `allow_direct`; "We should also set the options to deny deletes and purges."
- `nats s info KV_ORDERS` shows `Alternates:` RTT-sorted; direct get reply header `Nats-Stream: MIRROR_ORDERS_NYC` confirms which replica served.
- Future list: merged buckets, replica auto-discovery, read cache, ranged ops, limits-deleted marker op, zero-trust codecs, "Formalise leader election against keys", set management for service discovery, "Distributed locks against a key", pluggable storage backends. (ADR: proposed/not implemented)

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-8: JetStream based Key-Value Stores**

- "The API is now stable and considered version 1.0"; "All tier-1 clients support KV."
- `Entry` exposes Bucket, Key, Value, Created, Revision (stream sequence), Delta ("distance from the latest value", 0 = latest), Operation (PUT/DEL/PURGE). `Status` exposes Values, History, TTL, LimitMarkerTTL, IsCompressed, BackingStore (`JetStream`), Bytes, Metadata.
- KV interface: `Put`, `Create` ("only succeeds when the key does not exist if last historic event is a delete or purge"), `Update(key, value, lastRevision)`, `Delete` (preserves history), `Purge` (removes history, leaves the purge entry), `Get`, `GetRevision`, `History`, `Watch` ("the same Entry might be delivered more than once"), `Keys` (with filters), `Status`, `Info`.
- Manager: `KeyValue` (bind), `CreateKeyValue`, `UpdateKeyValue`, `CreateOrUpdateKeyValue`, `DeleteKeyValue`, `KeyValueBucketNames`, `KeyValueBuckets`.
- Consistency: "We do not provide read-after-write consistency. Reads are performed directly to any replica, including out of date ones. If those replicas do not catch up multiple reads of the same key can give different values between reads." "Historically we had read-after-write consistency, this has been deprecated."
- Bucket = stream `KV_<Bucket>` with subjects `$KV.<Bucket>.>`; history = `max_msgs_per_subject`.
- History: "The maximum allowed size is 64. The minimum allowed size is 1. When creating a stream, 1 should be used when the user does not supply a value."
- TTL via `max_age`; if set: "if `max_age` is greater than 2 minutes, `duplicate_window` must be set to 2 minutes"; "if `max_age` is less than or equal to 2 minutes, `duplicate_window` must be set the same as `max_age`"; if no TTL "The server will set it to 2 minutes if not supplied." (Note: server applies this logic itself if `duplicate_window` is omitted.)
- Fixed stream settings: `discard: new`, `rollup_hdrs: true`, `deny_delete: true`, `allow_direct: true` ("can be modified out-of-band only if desired, but not through KV bucket update"); `max_msg_size` caps value size; `max_bytes` caps bucket; "Maximum number of keys cannot currently be limited"; placement, republish, metadata allowed; compression → `s2`; storage file; R value varies.
- Limit markers need `allow_msg_ttl: true` and `subject_delete_marker_ttl` > 1 s; require API level 1 (2.11+) "clients should assert this using the `$JS.API.INFO` call or similar means (not connected server version)."
- Writes are JetStream requests to `$KV.<bucket>.<key>`; CAS via `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence`; value `0` = "only be accepted if it's the first message on a subject. This is purge aware."
- `Create()` on a deleted key: on `0`-failure, load current value; if it is a delete, retry with expected sequence = the delete's sequence.
- TTL accepted only on `Create()` (not `Put`) because Put "might have the effect of surfacing history once the latest value is removed."
- Deleted data carries `KV-Operation: DEL` or `PURGE`; basic Get turns a delete into `key not found`; watchers/history return the Entry with the operation set. `Nats-Marker-Reason` mapping: MaxAge→PURGE, Purge→PURGE, Remove→DEL.
- Gets use Direct Get `$JS.API.DIRECT.GET.<STREAM>.<SUBJECT>`; non-direct `last_by_subj` is legacy: "we do not support disabling direct get on any buckets."
- History and Watch use ephemeral Ordered Consumers; History = `deliver_all` filtered by key; Watch starts with `last_per_subject`; latest value has pending 0.
- Delete = message with nil body and `KV-Operation: DEL`; Purge = `KV-Operation: PURGE` + `Nats-Rollup: sub` (server deletes prior messages on that key); purge TTL adds `Nats-TTL`.
- `Keys` uses a headers-only consumer with deliver last per subject; delete bucket = delete stream.
- Watchers must emit an End Of Initial Data signal "the first time any message has a `Pending==0`" and "must also be sent if no data is present." Options: `IncludeHistory`, `IgnoreDeletes`, `MetaOnly`, `UpdatesOnly` (EOID sent immediately). Default sends all `last_per_subject` values including delete/purge ops.

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — natscli cheat sheets and help-text guidance (cli/cheats/*.md, cli/*_command.go)**

- KV/Object backup and restore go through the underlying stream: `nats stream backup <stream name> backups/CONFIG` / `nats stream restore` (cli/cheats/kv.md:21-26, cli/cheats/object.md:34-39); `nats kv add CONFIG --replicas 3` "to create a replicated KV bucket" (kv.md:1-2)
- KV bucket flags: `--history` "How many historic values to keep per key" default 1, validated to range 1..64; `--replicas` default 1; `--ttl`, `--max-value-size`, `--max-bucket-size`, `--compress`, `--republish-source/-destination`, `--mirror`, `--source`; per-key `--ttl` on create and purge marker TTL (cli/kv_command.go:105-179)

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — The Edge Talks Back: Building Bidirectional Control Into Your Architecture**

- "The KV store is built on JetStream — which means it's persistent, replicated, and designed to survive connectivity gaps." Watchers propagate config immediately; disconnected nodes catch up on reconnect; KV history gives an audit trail per device; eliminates separate OTA/polling infrastructure.
- Fleet firmware upgrades: KV for artifacts, subjects for status, request-reply for confirmation; rollback targets specific failed devices.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Multi-Region Consistency: Have Your Cake and Eat it Too!**

- KV direct gets go to local cluster replicas; needs cluster-scoped API subject mappings for transparency.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Rethinking Microservices: Using NATS to Dramatically Simplify Your Microservices**

- KV and object stores "are abstractions over streams"; the example uses KV for candidates and Object Store for vote counts.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Per-Message TTL: Unlocking Ephemeral State Patterns in NATS**

- KV buckets expose per-key TTL (Go: `KeyTTL()`); expiry creates a short-lived delete marker for watchers whose lifetime is `LimitMarkerTTL`; watchers get real-time expiry notifications.
- Patterns: session + token stores in one bucket with different TTLs; "A lock can expire automatically if the holder dies"; job claims with 20-second `KeyTTL` renewed on heartbeat; IoT presence with 15-second refreshed keys so device-offline events fire without polling.
- "Per-message TTL makes NATS a natural fit for ephemeral state and cache patterns"; positioned as a Redis alternative for some cache/ephemeral uses. Expired data remains replayable until the server deletes it.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Server 2.11 Release**

- Single Message TTL: "set a TTL for individual messages"; delete markers on MaxAge expiry; improves KV expired-key notifications.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Server 2.9 Release**

- `AllowDirect` serves gets from any replica (auto-on for KV, opt-in for streams); `MirrorDirect` lets mirrors serve gets. Direct get headers: `Nats-Stream`, `Nats-Sequence`, `Nats-Time-Stamp`, `Nats-Subject`.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Why FinecoBank chose NATS.io & Synadia for its NextGen stock trade processing layer**

- KV used to offload account balances from the database, cache stock master data, replace market-data HTML files (filename as key) with frontend notification on key creation, and (planned) centralize per-user market-data entitlements.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS at System Initiative**

- JetStream adopted (fall 2023) first for durable work queues; KV ("think: Redis"), Object Store ("think: S3"); home-brew chunked propagation of large graph structures "very similar to how the object store works."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS: The Secret Weapon Behind Vitrifi's Workflow Automation Platform**

- KV with "bucket-based organisation with hierarchical keys", "strong consistency guarantees within clusters" and "eventual consistency across distributed deployments", revision history, key expiration.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Building Event-Driven Banking as a Service (BaaS) with NATS**

- KV/Object stores "complement, rather than fully replace, transactional databases."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS JetStream: Streams, Consumers, and Durable Messaging**

- KV buckets "implemented as streams named `KV_<bucket>`" and inherit stream limits/replication/storage.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Building Distributed State Stores with NATS JetStream: KV and Object Storage Patterns**

- KV operations "typically land in the 1-5ms range for local deployments, while Redis serves requests in microseconds" (contradicts Synadia's 40µs in-cache figure).
- "TTL is applied at the bucket level to all entries" (per-key TTL exists since 2.11); advice to "create multiple buckets rather than fighting the single-TTL constraint."
- Revision is bucket-scoped: "Each new write to any key increments the bucket's global sequence." CAS: update succeeds "only if the current revision matches"; "revision 0 means key must not exist."
- Watcher case: 50 instances in three regions, "12ms average latency" vs "45-180ms with Redis polling at one-second intervals"; local evaluation "100,000+ flag evaluations per second per instance"; eliminated "50,000 unnecessary Redis queries per second."
- Use KV for "feature flags, service discovery metadata, or circuit breaker state"; Object Store for workflow artifacts and pipeline uploads; avoid for "high-frequency trading data, session storage with millions of writes per second, or multi-terabyte datasets." Keep S3 for multi-TB files, CDN delivery, compliance certifications.
- Don't embed volatile data in key names (`cache.response.{hash}.expires-{timestamp}`); use dots for hierarchy; watch with `*`/`>`.
- Examples: sessions ttl 1h history 1; feature flags ttl 0 history 64; locks ttl 30s history 1 replicas 3. `replicas: 3` "survives two simultaneous node failures" [DUBIOUS: R3 tolerates one failure for writes].

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Replace Redis with NATS: Atomic Counters and Microsecond Key-Value**

- "in-cache get is around 40 microseconds plus the network round trip" on low-end cloud hardware; "within roughly 5–10 microseconds of Redis on the same hardware, and faster than Redis for writes" in those tests; on-disk reads "around 1 to 1.5 milliseconds depending on the disk, with NVMe at the lower end." Figures are "representative test results, not a guarantee."
- Counters (ADR-49): `Nats-Incr` header `+N`/`-N`, big-integer precision, server serializes updates per subject (no client read-modify-write, no retries under contention); "sourcing-compatible" across streams/accounts/regions.
- CAS is optimistic and best when "writers rarely collide"; counters when "many writers hit the same key." Uses: "rate limiters, quotas, view/like/vote tallies, and inventory decrements."
- "The working set must fit in memory" for microsecond figures; "NATS is optimized for streaming, not random access"; high-churn random updates are slow because "overwriting a KV key deletes the previous message in the backing stream."

- kvcodec encodes keys with special characters (dots, spaces) and encrypts/compresses values transparently.

So can nats"); "I don't really think a cache is what our KV is going to be the best at." derekcollison disagrees: "no reason it can not be very fast IMO"; "We can be on par with Redis when there is a real network"; enable direct get; cache a KV subset in-app via watchers.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Jetstream KV/ObjectStore as a database?**

- JetStream covers "no SQL" needs: KV, Object store, subject-addressed streams, compare-and-set instead of transactions. Full SQL, schemas, joins, transactions and isolation are the domain of real databases — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — locks/leases with KV similar to SETNX**

- Distributed lock via a stream with `DiscardNewPerSubject`, max 1 message per subject, and a max age: publish succeeds = lock acquired; delete the message = release; publish fails = lock held — jnmoyne.
- With the KV API: `Create()` to obtain the lock, `Update()` (CAS on revision) to keep it, bucket TTL to expire stale locks — ripienaar.
- The KV lease pattern does not guarantee exclusivity but is on par with widely used Kubernetes lease options — ripienaar. "it does not guarantee exclusivity but its on par with options in K8s etc"

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — JetStream file-store ~65x slower than memory-store on KV mirror (83% of seq space is deleted)**

- A KV bucket with many overwrites leaves a sparse sequence space (here 83% interior deletes), which hurts file-store scans — cyqsign (measured), acknowledged by MauriceVanVeen who is "working on an improvement in the filestore for a situation like this where the number of deletes are greater than the number of unique subjects."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Automatic Chunking**

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Message prioritization to certain consumers**

- For data locality, use KV or Object store with real-time mirrors on every node, with expiry or replacement on new entries — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — kvBuckets are unexpectedly slow (list and compact at 100k keys)**

- KV is optimized for Get, Put, Update, Create, Delete; listing keys is a slow client-side operation and should be rare — ripienaar. "listing keys is not fast and probably something that in typical use cases should not be done that often."
- KV delete writes a delete marker per key for audit and watch semantics and cannot be turned off; purge of a subject hierarchy is the fast bulk delete — ripienaar.
- Design keys hierarchically so whole subtrees can be purged with wildcards (`$KV.BUCKET.prefix.>`) — ripienaar.
- When the KV abstraction does not fit, use the underlying stream directly: purge by subject, stream-info subject listing (fast, paged, up to 100k subjects), batched gets in 2.11 — ripienaar.
- Thousands or more subjects with one message each is exactly how KV works — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Key Value with TTL (bucket MaxAge vs per-key TTL)**

- Bucket MaxAge takes precedence over a longer per-key TTL; set MaxAge longer than any per-key TTL — MauriceVanVeen.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Remove deleted/purged data from bucket not possible?**

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Recording Connection & Disconnection events (100k clients)**

- Presence via KV: clients put a key with TTL; TTL expiry reported to watchers landed on main for 2.11 — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Can I use JetStream KV as cache? (nats.go)**

- Loopback benchmark: NATS KV sync get ~24,000 ops/s (about 41.7 us) vs Redis ~18 us on an M1 Ultra; over a real LAN the network RTT dominates and the difference becomes insignificant — jnmoyne.
- KV "can be on par with Redis when there is a real network"; enable direct get; use KV watchers to keep a local subset hot — derekcollison (disagreeing with ripienaar's "not optimised as a very fast cache").
- Sync KV get/put throughput is RTT bound (~16k/s single client); parallel clients or async batches scale it (10 clients ~43-54k/s, 25 clients ~55-66k/s); batched direct gets reach hundreds of thousands/s and are served by all replicas — jnmoyne.
- File vs memory KV: if the block is cached, file get is ~50 us like memory; an uncached block costs a couple of milliseconds — jnmoyne.
- NATS is a few percent faster than Redis on writes and a few percent slower on cached reads in the maintainer's testing — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Ephemeral Consumer Cleanup Rate? (nats.go)**

- Streams are optimized for the tail, not random access; compact per-entity history into one key with rollups (as KV does) — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Aggregate KV? (nats.go)**

- Aggregating KV buckets requires a subject transform per source (`$KV.A.>` to `$KV.C.>`) because the bucket name is part of the key subject — jnmoyne.
- When the source is itself a mirror, the transform source must use the ORIGIN bucket's subject prefix (`$KV.kv1.>`), not the mirror bucket's name; the CLI's automatic transform used the mirror name and yielded nothing — uli42 (verified fix).
- Mirroring and sourcing propagate only new messages, never deletes — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Jetstream kv store - Prefix search / Wildcard search (nats.go)**

- A wildcard watch over 3M keys took ~400 ms for 10 matches on 2.9.16 because the per-block subject state was a map; a sublist/patricia tree was planned for 2.10 — HeavyHorst (measured), derekcollison. [STALE?]
