**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Cluster size scalability question (issue)**

- One KV or stream per customer is "ultimately not a good design pattern"; 33,931 streams took over 10 minutes to restart on 48 CPUs because restore was serial; prefer few buckets with millions of hierarchical keys and per-user permissions on `$JS.API` subjects — jnmoyne, williamstein (measured).
- Keys can be multi-token, so many users fit in one KV under `uuid.>` with permissions — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Headers on KV entries (ADR issue)**

- KV does not support headers; KV is deliberately a small abstraction over streams that removes features; when needs do not fit, use streams — ripienaar. "KV is inherently about limitations ... Adding to it removes from its purpose."
- Structs are planned to be stored as one key per field (`123.name`, `123.age`); without transactions or batch writes, partial failures are the crux — ripienaar.
- Real customers have multi-thousand-key structs; batch reads are point-in-time atomic even when paged — ripienaar.
- KV buckets can be mirrored or sourced with subject transforms; master-master replication is not supported in general — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — KeyValue atomic delete and purge (ADR issue)**

- KV delete/purge can be made atomic by sending `KV-Operation: DEL` with `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence: <revision>`; clients were asked to expose it everywhere — davidmcote (verified), ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — KeyValue Revision is bucket wide? (per-key history)**

- Revision is a bucket-wide stream sequence; per-key revision "will be very hard in our current storage model"; history is optimized for gets, not history walks — ripienaar.
- A bucket's history can be raised after creation by editing the underlying stream — ripienaar.
- Pull a key's history with a lightweight R1 memory consumer filtered by subject and optionally start time — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Removing records from KV that exceed the limit (LRU-style)**

- `MaxMsgsPerSubject` (KV history) caps versions per key; `MaxMsgs` with DiscardOld caps total messages in the bucket's stream; both can be set together — jnmoyne.
- KV delete markers are messages too and may be the ones evicted by MaxMsgs; use the stream directly or `stream.purge` on the KV stream if that matters — jnmoyne.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Key-Value (category)**

- Key-Value is "A layer on top of JetStream for utilizing a stream as a key-value store."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Key-Value Intro**

- KV "is an abstraction over a stream which models message subjects as keys. It uses a standard set of stream configuration to be optimized for KV workloads."
- Unlike most KV stores, a revision number of each entry is tracked.
- Revisions enable optimistic concurrency control: with multiple concurrent writers, `Update` with an expected revision prevents non-deterministic "last writer wins"; the value is updated only if the revision matches on the server.
- A KV bucket is "light abstraction over a standard stream. This is by design since it enables some powerful features." Internally a stream is created with the `KV_` prefix by convention.
- KV subjects are: a reserved first token, the bucket name as second token, then the key as the suffix. "The bucket name is inherently a namespace for all keys and thus there is no concern for conflict across buckets," unlike a stream binding public subjects.
- Because a bucket is a normal stream, a consumer can be created on it and each Put arrives as a stream message.
- A Delete produces a new message and a new revision; delete messages carry a `KV-Operation: DEL` header to distinguish deletion from a nil value.
- Use a `KeyWatcher` rather than subscribing to the stream directly; it yields `KeyValueEntry` values "which exposes more KV-specific information than the raw stream message ... (so this API is recommended)." Watch supports wildcards on keys.
- A watcher first delivers existing values (deno: "the watcher by default shows the last value for all the keys"), then a nil entry marking that it has "caught up with the current updates before tracking the new ones."
- The revision of a new key is not 1: revisions are the underlying stream sequence, "always monotonically increasing, but numbers will be shared across keys (like subjects) rather than sequence numbers relative to each key."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Ordered consumers**

- A Key-Value watch and an Object Store read are both ordered consumers under the cover.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reading messages directly**

- "Get the last message on this subject" is the read a key-value lookup is built on; a KV bucket is a stream keyed by subject.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Stream and consumer policies**

- Deliver policy `last_per_subject` and the Direct Get `--last-per-subject` flag are different features sharing a name: one is a consumer start position, the other a one-shot read.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next**

- A key-value bucket is a stream underneath: keys become subjects, history becomes sequence numbers, a watch is a consumer; retention and limits apply directly.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Key-Value Store**

- A KV bucket is not a separate database; it is a JetStream stream named `KV_<bucket>` whose subjects are `$KV.<bucket>.>`. "a key is the last token of that subject, and a value is a message on it"
- A `put` appends a message, a `get` reads the last message for a subject, and a `watch` opens a consumer.
- The key-value store requires JetStream to be enabled on the server. "The key-value store is built on JetStream, so JetStream must be on."
- Compare-and-swap is the mechanism for safe concurrent decrements so "two concurrent sales never lose a write".
- A watch delivers the current value of every key as a snapshot, then live updates as values change.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first bucket**

- A bucket is a JetStream stream the key-value API creates and configures for you; the bucket `INVENTORY` becomes the stream `KV_INVENTORY`.
- Bucket names are case-sensitive identifiers.
- History is how many prior values the bucket keeps per key; the default is 1 (only the current value). "One means the bucket holds only the current value of a key and forgets the rest. That's the default"
- History depth can go as high as 64 and no higher. "The depth can go as high as 64, but no higher"
- A put is an unconditional write that stores the value whether or not the key already exists.
- The revision counter is bucket-wide, not per key. "a number the bucket assigns from a single counter it keeps across every key, not a per-key count"
- A get returns an entry (value, revision, write time), not a bare value.
- The entry timestamp records when the value was written, not when it was read.
- A get returns an entry rather than a value, and a missing key is signaled distinctly from an empty one; don't treat a missing key as "the count is zero". "an empty value is a value, and a missing key is the absence of one"
- Client behaviour on a missing key differs: the CLI, Go, Python, and C# fail with a key-not-found error; JavaScript, Rust, and Java return null/None.
- Bucket and key names are validated. A bucket name may contain only letters, digits, dash, and underscore, and can't be empty.
- A key may contain only letters, digits, and `-`, `/`, `_`, `=`, and `.`, with no leading or trailing dot and no two dots in a row. "`a..b` is rejected even though `a.b` is fine"
- A colon is not allowed in a key (`ord:8w2k` is rejected client-side before sending); use an underscore or dash instead.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Watching**

- A watch delivers the current value of every matching key as an initial snapshot, then streams every later change. "One call gives you both halves: the state of the bucket now, and the changes from now on."
- Underneath, a watch is an ephemeral ordered consumer on the backing stream, replaying the last value per key then following new writes; opening the watch creates it and closing removes it.
- After the last snapshot entry and before the first live change, the watch delivers one end-of-initial-data signal: a single nil entry with no key and no value.
- The end-of-initial-data signal differs per client: Go and Python deliver a nil/None entry in-stream; JavaScript sets an `isUpdate` flag; Java calls `endOfData()`; C# takes an `OnNoData` option; Rust has no marker and you choose snapshot-plus-live or live-only at open time.
- Use the end-of-initial-data signal to hold a "loading" state until the snapshot is complete, or to mark a cache as warm before switching to incremental updates.
- A watch key filter is matched like a subject: keys are dot-separated tokens, `*` matches exactly one whole token, `>` matches one or more tokens at the end.
- `widget-*` is not a wildcard; `*` is only special as a whole token, so a hyphenated prefix filter matches nothing. "To split keys with a wildcard you'd design them with dots, such as `widget.blue` and `widget.red`, so that `widget.*` matches both."
- A watch filter applies to both snapshot and live halves, so a filtered watch is a smaller, cheaper view rather than every change filtered client-side.
- Watch options: `IncludeHistory` replays full history per key, `IgnoreDeletes` skips deleted keys, `UpdatesOnly` drops the snapshot, `MetaOnly` sends metadata without values.
- `IncludeHistory` and `UpdatesOnly` conflict and a client rejects the pair.
- Don't stop reading at the boundary signal; a loop that treats the nil entry as end-of-stream quits before every live change. "when an entry is nil, skip it and keep looping. Do not break."
- A watch is live state, not a point read; don't open a watch, read the first entry, and close it to fake a get. "you pay for a consumer and a snapshot to get one value get would have handed you directly"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — History and revisions**

- A revision always increases when you write a key, but not by one each time, because writes to other keys advance the shared counter in between.
- History depth caps at 64; values written before a history-depth raise are already gone because depth 1 dropped each prior write.
- Optimistic concurrency via compare-and-swap uses no locks: read the revision, write on the condition the revision hasn't changed, retry on rejection.
- `create` writes a key only if it doesn't exist (CAS against revision 0); `update` writes only if the key is at the revision you name.
- Use the read-modify-write with update whenever the new value depends on the old one (decrement, increment, status transition).
- History holds the prior revisions of a single key up to the depth; it's not an audit log of the whole bucket and doesn't grow without bound. "once a key has more revisions than the depth allows, the oldest one is removed"
- A rejected update is dropped rather than queued, and you must retry; a fire-and-forget update silently loses the write on conflict. "Don't assume an update succeeded; check the result, and on a revision mismatch, re-get the key and try again"
- Do not use put for a read-modify-write; put is unconditional and overwrites a concurrent writer's value. "Use put to set a key to a given value, and update to change it from the value it currently holds."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TTL and limits**

- Per-key TTL suits values that should clean themselves up: a flash-sale price, a short-lived session token, a time-boxed lock flag.
- Per-key TTL is set at create time, and only at create time; the countdown starts the moment the value lands. "a TTL belongs to the value you're writing now, not to a value that might be put over it later"
- Per-key TTLs require the bucket feature "limit markers" enabled; a bucket needs limit markers on before any key can carry a TTL.
- Per-key TTL needs nats-server 2.11 or newer, the release that added limit markers; on an older server enabling markers is rejected and the timed create fails.
- Three bucket limits matter most: max bucket size (total bytes across all keys and kept revisions), max value size (largest single value), and history depth.
- History depth caps at 64 and doubles as a per-key cap: the most messages any single key may hold.
- Key-value values are meant to be small; large values belong in the Object Store.
- A bucket-wide TTL (`--ttl`) is the stream's `MaxAge` limit applied to every value; a per-key TTL expires one value and is built on JetStream per-message TTL.
- When a per-key TTL fires, the server leaves a marker with reason `MaxAge` rather than silently dropping the value; watchers receive it as a purge (CLI prints `PURGE`).
- A per-key TTL is set at create, and only at create; neither put nor update takes a TTL, and rewriting the key appends a value with no TTL so the key stops expiring. "Use delete-then-create to change a TTL, not put or update."
- Limits reject, they do not make room for an oversized value; a put over max value size or that would exceed max bucket size returns an error and leaves existing values in place.
- Size the bucket for the working set you need to hold, not the average, and cap max value size above the largest value you legitimately store.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Under the hood**

- Backing stream config for a bucket: `Maximum Per Subject` is the history depth; `Discard Policy: New`; `Direct Get: true`; `Allows Rollups: true`; `Allows Msg Delete: false` (`deny_delete`).
- Discard policy `New` is why limits reject: once the bucket hits a limit it rejects the newest write rather than dropping older messages.
- `deny_delete` makes the stream refuse the JetStream message-delete API so raw stream ops can't remove entries behind the KV API.
- A get uses direct get: the server returns the last message on a subject straight from storage via `$JS.API.DIRECT.GET.<stream>.<subject>`, with no consumer, no position, and no ack.
- The last message's sequence is the revision and its store time is the entry timestamp.
- A delete leaves a non-destructive marker with a `KV-Operation: DEL` header; prior revisions up to history depth stay readable through history.
- A purge writes a marker with `KV-Operation: PURGE` and `Nats-Rollup: sub` headers; the rollup drops every earlier message on the subject, collapsing history to one marker.
- Reach for purge when you must actually remove old values (for size, or because they were sensitive), not just hide them.
- Delete does not remove history; only purge does. "If you delete `widget-blue` to scrub a wrong count and assume the bad value is unrecoverable, it's sitting one `nats kv history` away."
- Do not operate the backing stream directly: don't hand-edit `KV_INVENTORY` config and don't publish to `$KV.INVENTORY.>` with raw `nats pub`, because raw publishes lack the CAS, `KV-Operation`, and `Nats-Rollup` headers.
- `deny_delete` does not stop a raw publish to the bucket's subjects.
- A key has to be a legal subject token because it becomes the last token of `$KV.INVENTORY.<key>`; a colon or double dot is rejected.
- A bucket's `Replicas` field is the number of servers holding a copy; replication and placement belong to the Clustering chapter.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Key-Value)**

- Mapping: a bucket is a stream, a key is a subject token, a put is a message, a revision is a sequence, a watch is an ephemeral ordered consumer; every bucket limit is a stream limit.
- Key-value values are small and capped; the object store is for large values reassembled from multiple messages on read (a file, a build artifact, anything multi-megabyte).
- A bucket can be sourced from or mirrored into another bucket via a subject transform from `$KV.SRC.>` to `$KV.DST.>` (e.g. regional `EU_INVENTORY` sourcing `INVENTORY`).
- Checklist: check that an entry exists before reading its value; key-not-found is not an empty value.
- Checklist: keep bucket names to alphanumerics, dashes, and underscores.
- Checklist: keep keys to alphanumerics and `-/_=.` with no leading or trailing dot; a `:` or leading dot is rejected.
- Checklist: consume the end-of-initial-data nil entry; stopping at the snapshot boundary misses every live update.
- Checklist: treat a watch as live state, not a query; use get or history for a point read.
- Checklist: wrap every update in a re-get-and-retry loop; a stale-revision update is rejected, not queued.
- Checklist: use update (CAS), not put, for any read-modify-write like a decrement.
- Checklist: set a per-key TTL at create time only; delete then create to change a key's TTL.
- Checklist: size the bucket for the working set, not the average; at its byte limit the bucket rejects the next put instead of dropping old values.
- Checklist: reach for purge, not delete, when you must drop prior revisions.
- Checklist: use the key-value API, never raw `nats pub` to `$KV.INVENTORY.>` or hand edits to `KV_INVENTORY` config.
- Checklist: keep keys to legal subject tokens; `:` or two dots in a row is rejected.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Object Store**

- Key-Value keeps small structured values with full revision history per key; Object Store keeps large chunked files and only the latest metadata per object. "Use key-value when you want many small values that you read, overwrite, and audit; use the object store when you want whole files that you put and fetch."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Metadata and links**

- Metadata describes only the current object; each re-put replaces it. For a full revision history per name use the Key-Value store.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Watching and listing**

- An object watch delivers only `ObjectInfo` metadata, never chunk bytes; the KV watch delivers values directly because values are small. "the rule for objects is that watch tells you what changed and get returns the bytes"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Under the hood (Object Store)**

- A re-put after a delete is a new object identity, not a restored history. "Don't reach for the object store when you need the *previous* version after an overwrite; that history lives in the Key-Value Store."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Object Store)**

- Key-value is the sibling store for "small structured values and a full revision history per key"; go there when you need versioning of a value, and for the per-key watch the object store doesn't have.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Learn**

- Key-Value Store: buckets, watches, history and revisions, TTLs, and how KV sits on top of a stream.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream**

- Higher-level abstractions on streams and consumers: Key Value Store (replication and durability built in) and Object Store (objects larger than a single message, split into chunks, with per-object metadata).

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to build a NATS Supercluster | Rethink Connectivity Episode 5**

- A KV bucket created without replicas lives on one node (the leader) and all access is served from that node; recreate with `--replicas 3` to place a replica on each node. "any time I talk to this cluster about this kv store it's actually going to be polling from north america 2... if I wanted redundancy here I would use what are called replicas" (~07:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Connect ANY Auth System to NATS.io with Auth Callout**

- The auth service also upserts the user's profile (name, email, photo) into a KV bucket on each login; clients watching that bucket update instantly, giving zero-touch onboarding. "all the chat applications were watching that key value store so they also updated their profile info before I even jumped into chat" (~28:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Replace Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis and more w/NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity Ep 10**

- Streams are indexed on a per-subject level, which lets you reach a particular message by subject without scanning; this indexing underpins the KV and Object Store implementations. "streams are indexed on a subject level ... this is actually what under the hood drives a lot of our KV and Object Store" (~08:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to configure NATS JetStream streams | Rethink Connectivity Ep 11**

- Max messages per subject set to 1 keeps only the last message per subject; the KV store's history setting is driven by this option. "this is actually in use inside of our key value store where you can set a history" (~08:09)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared: Part 1 | Rethink Connectivity**

- Kafka's compaction keeps "at least" one message per key; a JetStream per-subject limit of 1 is exactly one. "it's a limit of exactly one right not an at least" (~25:26)
- KV and Object Store are possible only because streams combine subject-based addressing with enforced limits (e.g. keep last 5 per subject). "this is only possible because both you have subject-based addressing in streams and you have this ability to have constraints" (~27:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared Pt 2: Consumers | Rethink Connectivity**

- Direct get of the last or first message for an exact subject is how KV works; it is a get, not a query, and over loopback runs in the tens of microseconds. "the order of magnitude is tens of microseconds when going over loopback" (~15:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Move over Kafka! Let's try NATS JetStream**

- KV buckets are streams underneath: you configure history depth and, because it is a stream, placement in the cluster. "because this is just a stream underneath you also get to choose where in the cluster you want to put your store" (~09:07)
- KV watch notifies on key updates, a powerful primitive for distributed systems. "being able to know when certain values get updated" (~10:08)
- KV and object store streams are hidden from normal stream commands; use the `-a` flag to list them. "you can fix this by using the a flag to list all the streams" (~10:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream for Key-Value Store Tech Preview**

- Storing every key as a subject and values as messages, with per-subject limits, is what makes a KV store on JetStream possible. "if you store every key as a subject and the value as values in the stream you have a kv store" (~01:02)
- A bucket is created with replicas (e.g. 3), placement (e.g. London cluster), a history depth (e.g. 5 values per key), and optional TTL that expires keys regardless of access. "we want to keep five historical values for every key so if you make a mistake you can just go back" (~01:02)
- KV supports watchers on the whole bucket or a single key, and per-key history shows how a value changed over time. "we support watchers so i can say watch cfg so we'll watch the entire bucket for all writes" (~03:06)
- Deleting a key writes a delete marker into history rather than removing data; a get then reports unknown key while history remains for recovery. "we're actually writing a delete operation into the history rather than deleting the data" (~04:07)
- KV workloads are read-heavy; APIs were added to make reads in that scenario very fast. "kv tend to be very read heavy operations so you will write few times but very often read" (~05:08)
- The backing stream can be replicated to other clusters in a supercluster as read replicas; read-only workers read locally and never talk to the origin, while writes go to the origin with a small replication delay. "if they know they're only ever going to read they never have to communicate to london" (~06:09)
- The Go client offers an in-memory bucket cache: it starts a watcher, loads the whole bucket, marks ready, serves reads from memory, and writes invalidate the key until the watcher refreshes it. "before you need it even your cache will already be up to date" (~07:10)
- Encoders and decoders allow encrypting keys and values for end-to-end zero-trust storage. "you can encrypt your keys and your values to have completely end-to-end zero trust storage" (~07:10)
- KV design is documented in an ADR (architecture design record); at the time the API and model might still change. "we'll be tweaking the api a little bit we'll be maybe changing the model a little bit" (~08:12)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers**

- Emulate exclusive consumption today with a KV-based lease/lock: multiple instances, one acquires the lock with a TTL and is the active participant. "I have a KV bucket ... leasing ... only one basically acquires a lock ... you can have a TTL" (~72:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.10 Webinar**

- Stream-level subject transforms (implemented by Jean-Noël Moyne) generalize server-config subject mapping and remove the pre-2.10 limitation that KV mirrors could not be created within the same account and cluster. "there was a limitation that you couldn't do that previously unless you were spanning a JetStream domain or cross accounts" (~31:36)
- An OAuth-to-NATS bridge can store the IdP user claims in a KV bucket keyed by session ID; the client presents the session ID as its token and the callout service looks it up to mint the user JWT. "the key value bucket is the link between setting a token through my auth callout callback flow and then your auth callout service being able to observe this token" (~51:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- Users put and delete hundreds of millions of KV keys, producing streams with data at the head and tail and a huge deleted gap in the middle; this "interior deletes" state dominated Raft snapshots. "the state snapshot for the messages we're retaining and deleting ends up being really big because it's tracking more information about things that we no longer want to keep" (~26:29)
- Unlike append-only logs with only tail compaction, a NATS stream supports explicit deletion of an arbitrary interior message; that is how KV tombstoning works. "you can actually explicitly delete an arbitrary interior message within a stream ... this is how frankly the KV abstraction actually works" (~28:31)
- KV buckets and object stores are streams, so file-store improvements benefit all of them. "KV buckets are streams object stores are streams so everything benefits from this" (~29:33)
- KV was released as a convenience API and a year later a user ran a 10 TB KV store spanning the globe; it worked but needed to work better. "how about 10 terabytes key value store span across the whole globe will it work too yeah the thing is it worked it's just we needed it to work better" (~30:33)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP07: Going off piste; KV patterns with NATS.io (pt1)**

- Byron's first NATS use was pub/sub fan-out to notify many things instead of HTTP hacks, then NATS Streaming for ETL pipelines: extract, transform, publish to a stream, fan out to consumers that load other systems. "taking data out transforming it throwing it into a stream and then I was able to fan out effectively consume from that stream and plop it in other systems" (~04:09)
- KV and Object Store are client-side abstractions layered on a stream, with a deliberately smaller set of knobs. "KV and Object Store are client abstractions that lay on top of the stream and these abstractions are very convenient to use because the amount of knobs that they have are smaller" (~11:20)
- KV supports optimistic concurrency control via a revision (sequence) number, with create and update operations distinct from put. "KV buckets support optimistic concurrency control you can have a sequence number" (~11:20)
- Because a KV bucket is a stream, watchers let you subscribe to puts, updates and deletes as a change stream over time. "it's inherently a stream under the hood so ... you can watch changes over time" (~12:23)
- The server can reject one of two concurrent writes to the same key, which gives you a distributed mutex across processes without slapping a local mutex on. "the server has the ability to basically prevent both concurrent writes to happen at the same time" (~12:23)
- A lease adds a time element: set a TTL on the lock key so competitors retry until it expires and someone else acquires it; the TTL bounds how long any holder can own the resource. "you can set a TTL on keys ... this key will eventually expire after a certain number of seconds" (~15:29)
- Simplest distributed lock: every worker races to create the key with its node ID as the value, then reads back to see who won; losers stand down. "there's a race all of the machines try and write the key and the one that writes it ... they all go and do a read and go oh I'm not the one that won" (~17:32)
- A KV lock is advisory: nothing locks the data out, so correctness depends on workers honouring the lock in code; NATS is not a magic firewall. "it's down to the developer to adhere to the lock nothing's going to actually lock the data out ... NATS isn't some kind of magic firewall" (~18:34)
- The lock holder can use the revision of its last write to update the key, extend the TTL or record progress for a long-lived job. "the one that won now has a revision of the last write so we can go back and even update it maybe increment the TTL" (~18:34)
- A "witness" process watches the lock key and heartbeats; when the worker's heartbeat disappears it deletes the key and signals a job restart. "as soon as the heartbeat disappears ... they go back and actually delete the key and then maybe issue another signal saying restart job" (~19:36)
- A semaphore generalizes the mutex: a pool of N resources that workers acquire and release, depleting and refilling over time. "more generalized from a mutex is a semaphore where you can have maybe a pool of resources that everyone is trying to compete for" (~20:37)
- Batch data pipelines need a shared, distributed record of the last processed offset; store it as a KV key so a pool of workers can grab a job and its offset instead of using a local file or SAN. "you could maintain a key the last offset ... you just have a pool of workers just grab a job grab the last offset" (~28:46)
- A lock key need not be boolean: store a state-machine value (acquired, in progress, next state) so a witness can detect a stalled transition, reset it and let another worker retry. "it doesn't have to be a binary true false mutex you can have a state machine almost in a way" (~29:49)
- Storing job state in KV rather than a database gives you real-time watching of state changes and an external witness that can intervene. "you don't have that benefit of really watching the state changes over time" (~31:50)
- Keys are subjects with a token hierarchy, so you can model a DAG of job states as a key hierarchy and watch a subtree; the watch history doubles as a write-ahead log for free. "because keys are under the hood just subjects and you have a token hierarchy you can model a DAG as a hierarchy naturally and then you can watch a sub tree" (~33:53)
- Distribute policy (e.g. firewall rules) by having each host run a local agent that watches a KV bucket and realises its own desired state, instead of a central orchestration pool. "there's a local agent running you watch the KV store and then it programmed its own IP tables stuff" (~34:55)
- Kine (the k3s etcd-replacement layer) gained a community-contributed NATS KV backend, so k3s can run with NATS instead of etcd or SQLite; the original was single-node, and HA three-node k3s over NATS was later built. "somebody contributed NATS as an alternate backend within the Kine abstraction layer" (~40:00)
- Three k3s servers continuously try to acquire a lease on a KV key for leader election; that is the same mechanism they use with etcd. "these three k3s servers that at a minimum all trying to acquire a lease on the KV bucket" (~42:02)
- Application-level leader election, quorum and leasing can be built on NATS KV even though the bucket has its own Raft leader underneath. "I need a leader election I need quorum I need leasing and unleasing you can use NATS KV to do that" (~44:05)
- KV is more than a cache; locks, leases, semaphores, job state, policy distribution and leader election are all valid uses. "people go well great I can use it as a cache but there's so many other areas that you can apply this thing to" (~44:05)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02: Monolith to Modular Monolith with NATS.io**

- Inventory example: the game watches a KV bucket key for the player, the transaction service updates that key, and the game gets the change notification without polling the database. "watching the KV inventory from the game with the C++ client... no database dips required" (~24:33)
- Polling a database for updates can be inverted into streaming state transitions or KV watchers, which is more responsive and optimized for that use. "if you invert that and you can just stream it out and you can model your state transitions in that way, that can be very powerful" (~26:36)
- KV buckets can be placed in memory or on disk depending on need; a hot player inventory can be loaded from disk once at login into a memory bucket for speed. "you could put some things in memory, some things on disk" (~26:36)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP04: A Service Mesh Pattern for NATS.io**

- A KV bucket can act as a scheduler substitute: keys hold a minimum service count and workers on VMware, Hyper-V, or Kubernetes claim keys semaphore-style. "we could be using a KV bucket on NATS to say minimum number of services five and you could have some keys that can be claimed" (~30:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP05: Exploring Powerful Client-side Features and Abstractions in NATS.io**

- KV is a client-side abstraction over a stream; the server does not know a stream is a KV bucket. The `max messages per subject` stream option was added specifically because KV history needed it. "that max message per subject stream configuration option was created purely because it was needed for key value" (~37:48)
- KV was pitched (KubeCon Valencia, ~2.8) as "for simple use cases", but within 18 months it was in use as a Kubernetes persistence layer replacing etcd and for large key counts. "key value being able to be used as a Kubernetes persistence layer instead of etcd" (~39:51)
- KV was motivated by leaf-node and factory-floor topologies where you want as little extra infrastructure as possible; JetStream users get a KV for free. "factory floor where you want to have as little infrastructure and tools installed as possible" (~39:51)
- Transactional multi-key updates in KV were requested; the team says it is a wide change across the ecosystem and especially the server, not a workaround, and not coming soon. "don't expect it to be very soon but that's something you would love to have but it has to be done right" (~49:58)
- Object Store adds no new server API; it is a specific stream and consumer configuration on top of JetStream, and watch is just a consumer with a particular configuration. "consumers just can be treated as a watcher with different configurations" (~55:03)
- Because KV and Object Store are streams, they inherit mirroring and replication: read-only mirrors can be pushed to edge locations and data flows per mirror definitions with no extra dependencies. "you can create mirrors, read-only mirrors and push it down to edge locations" (~57:07)
- KV data does not have to be local to be accessible: if the NATS system is JetStream-enabled, a client in another region can still read the bucket where the data is not present. "you can still access the key value store from a different location where the data isn't" (~64:17)
- The underlying KV/Object stream can be used directly with normal stream operations if the abstraction's API is not enough; recurring workarounds become API candidates. "if this workaround looks like a pattern in the whole community then it will be considered as part of the API" (~59:09)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03S3: NATS 2.11 Release**

- Per-message TTL is planned to clean up KV delete tombstones, which accumulate in buckets with high delete rates; watchers still get the delete notification but the markers no longer live forever. "if you have a very high incidence of deletes you can end up with an awful lot of history in your KV bucket which is just delete tombstones" (~12:13)
- 2.11 includes a first pass at subject delete markers when a subject disappears from a stream via max age, to support the KV use case, with more iteration planned. "in 2.11 we'll have an initial pass of that that just happens with max age" (~14:18)
- KV was introduced (KubeCon Valencia) as a small experiment for IoT caches; users now load millions of keys, so 2.11 is the first release adding default soft limits and safe defaults to features. "now we are at I don't know millions of keys ... this is the first release where we started adding default limit soft cuts" (~30:40)
- Batch get is intended to improve future KV fetching and possibly Object Store, which would rather rip through a stream without creating a consumer. "object store is a great example, you really don't need the consumer" (~35:47)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS: Ordered, Scalable Stream Processing**

- Consumer-group configuration (max members, filters, members) is stored in a KV bucket, which is what allows live changes. "this is all configuration just stored in NATS KV store ... you can change it live" (~25:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Per-Message TTL — Fine-Grained Expiration for JetStream Messages**

- KV buckets get per-key TTL with automatic delete markers; when a key expires, NATS places a delete marker (tombstone) so watchers know the data is gone. "it places a delete marker, or a tombstone, to signal to watchers and subscribers that the data is gone" (~05:06)
- The bucket's limit_marker_ttl controls how long that delete marker persists before the key is fully purged; it is required to enable per-key TTL on a bucket. "Notice the field limit marker TTL. This enables us to do per-key TTL on this bucket" (~05:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.11: What's New?**

- KV delete markers build up with heavy deletes and make the underlying stream big and expensive; Synadia plans to give delete markers TTLs so watchers still see deletes but markers don't stay forever, reducing manual compaction. "We will be changing those delete markers to use TTLs so that even if you have KV watchers looking for deletes, you'll still be able to get those notifications" (~03:11)
- Because KV is an abstraction over streams, per-message TTL enables per-key TTL in KV buckets, coming to clients soon. "the fact that you can apply a TTL to an individual message means that we can also do the same for message entries in a KV bucket" (~08:18)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Two-Node Engine with David & Byron**

- External integration works through a "transitioning" KV key: the FSM sets it during a transition, your code (any NATS client) does its work, then updates the key so the engine finishes the transition. "once your code has completed you then update this NATS KV value this transitioning key value and the engine will basically carry on" (~03:04)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — We need to talk about Microservices... (And how NATS.io can simplify things)**

- Dynamic configuration: services read config from a KV bucket and watch for changes, so log level or other settings change live without restarting pods. "these apps that don't need to be restarted ... they could live update" (~27:32)
- Demo: `nats kv put config math.log_level 0` flipped the running service from error-only to info logging immediately. "we immediately received another log line that says that our log level was set to info" (~28:34)
- For distributed data, JetStream streams, KV (Redis replacement) and Object Store (S3/MinIO replacement) share the same security model and are replicated globally from day zero. "on day zero ready to replicate and scale out globally" (~29:35)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — JetStream KV: A fascinating alternative to Redis...**

- A KV bucket is a stream under the hood with a thin layer of client-side sugar; everything learned about streams (replication, mirrors, sources, accounts, ACLs) applies to KV. "a key value store is no different than a stream in terms of all of the internals" (~02:01)
- Keys are subjects; every key carries a value plus a configurable per-bucket history of previous values. "we actually have full history of these values ... you could set on a per bucket basis how much history you want" (~02:01)
- Revisions are globally ordered at the bucket level (not per key) and are the basis for optimistic concurrency control. "these are kind of globally ordered on a bucket level" (~03:01)
- Watching keys replaces polling and restarts for configuration: "many many companies" use KV as a configuration-management layer with apps watching for changes. "instead of your applications having to poll ... you can just have them watch for changes" (~04:02)
- Optimistic concurrency control keeps concurrent writers from stomping on each other's read-modify-write of a value. "make sure that clients aren't stomping on each other when you have multiple concurrent writers" (~05:03)
- TTL/expiry currently exists at bucket level only; per-key TTLs are a future server feature. "we have that on a bucket level ... in a future update to the server we're going to be supporting per key TTLs" (~05:03)
- Because a KV is a stream you get replication, mirror, source, mux/demux, multi-tenancy via accounts, and subject-based ACLs on buckets. "being able to mirror source mux and demux ... you get all the multi-tenancy with accounts" (~06:04)
- The speaker positions JetStream KV as comparable to Redis, not 10x faster; single-node Redis wins on latency for few writers, JetStream KV has a higher ceiling for concurrent requests and throughput. "Redis is going to win out on the latency side especially for a small number of writers and JetStream's KV is going to have a larger ceiling in terms of handling concurrent requests" (~08:06)
- Replication and clustering differ so much that comparing them to Redis is "apples and oranges"; the advantage claimed is at supercluster / multi-region scale, not single-cluster speed. "you might see some advantages when it comes to global scale moving out to a super cluster" (~07:05)
- The KV-specific concepts layered on streams are history, TTL and a compression flag. "the three kind of concepts ... that's new to KVs is the idea of history of TTLs and compression" (~09:06)
- The KV does not have all of Redis's operations; the value slot is currently opaque ("dumb") with no value-based semantics. "the NATS key value store right now is kind of dumb when it comes to the types of values" (~09:06)
- Put sets a key and returns a revision number; Get returns the latest value with subject, headers and metadata, or a specific historical revision on request. "you can request a specific revision as well" (~10:06)
- Create fails if the key already exists and, combined with TTL, is the primitive for leader election, distributed locks and leases. "the create command ... will fail if that key already exists ... we can use this in combination with TTLs to do very cool things like leadership elections" (~11:08)
- Update requires the caller's last-known revision; a stale revision is rejected and the client must re-get and retry. "the KV store is going to reject that because it knows it's had a later revision" (~12:09)
- Delete is a soft delete: it writes a delete marker as the newest revision, keeps prior history, and is visible to watchers. "a delete actually does not delete the data itself but instead puts a delete marker as the latest revision" (~13:09)
- Purge writes the delete marker (so watchers still fire) and removes all earlier revisions of that key; delete can also take an expected revision for OCC. "it's going to delete all of the revisions before it in that particular key space" (~13:09)
- Watch is implemented as a lightweight consumer, so it supports subject filtering, choosing headers-only/latest/history/delete notifications, and a starting revision. "this is going to create a lightweight consumer to be able to get all of the notifications for that particular watch" (~14:10)
- Users store tens to hundreds of millions of keys in a single KV bucket, which is why filtered watches matter. "we have people that put millions and millions ... tens of millions hundreds of millions of keys inside of a key value store" (~15:12)
- A watcher first delivers all current values, then an empty marker meaning "caught up", then live update/delete/create notifications. "it's going to send a message that's essentially blank to signify that it sent you all the most recent values" (~16:12)
- R1/R3/R5 replication lives within a single cluster; with R3 you can lose one node and still accept writes, lose two and still serve reads. "you can take one node down and still accept writes you can take two nodes down and still accept reads" (~17:13)
- Cross-region or leaf-node replication of a KV uses mirrors and sources, not the replica count. "if you want to go outside of a data center or ... into another region this is where mirroring and sourcing come into play" (~17:13)
- A KV mirror is an automatic read replica: NATS serves reads from the closest mirror and forwards writes to the origin leader with no application change. "NATS is smart enough to serve up requests from the closest mirror ... all of the writes are going to go through the leader" (~18:14)
- Sourcing with subject filters "demuxes" a large central KV into smaller regional or per-business-unit buckets near the consuming apps. "I can source all of this data and just filter on the stuff that I care about" (~19:16)
- The inverse, "muxing", sources many edge KVs (e.g. on Raspberry Pis) into one central cloud KV; subject remapping while sourcing lets each edge key space be rewritten into the aggregate. "you can now do remapping as soon as you're sourcing into these streams" (~21:17)
- Upcoming (next server release): value-based semantics (counters, lists, sets, maps), per-key TTL, LRU-style cache eviction, and watch notifications for TTL expiries and other system deletes. "currently we don't get any sort of watch notification for it but we will be getting watch notifications for any sort of system delete events TTLs" (~23:21)
- Batch get across related keys (user.id, user.name, user.email) fetches a "row" of fields in one request, approaching Redis/DynamoDB semantics. "you can actually use a batch get to get all of those fields in one request" (~23:21)
- Demo latency: a get every second against a bucket in Azure Europe West from Southern California took about 200 ms; moving the bucket to AWS us-west-2 dropped it to about 40 ms. "we're getting about 200 milliseconds of latency" (~25:25)
- Changing a bucket's cluster placement moves it in flight; clients keep accessing it while it is mirrored and relocated. "it's actually going to move the bucket mid-flight everything's going to stay the same" (~25:25)
- Keeping the bucket in Europe and adding a mirror in us-west-2 brought reads back to about 40 ms while writes still went through Europe. "we drop our reads to back to those 40 milliseconds ... all the writes are still going through Europe" (~27:27)
- Leader election recipe: bucket with a ~3 s TTL; non-leaders loop every second calling Create on key "leader"; the leader renews with Update using its last revision, and an Update error means leadership was lost. "we want the key value store to be able to tell us hey you're working on outdated information and you are no longer the leader" (~30:30)
- On Synadia Cloud a bucket must set max bytes. "we're using Synadia cloud and we absolutely need to have max bytes set" (~28:28)
- TTL expiry is what frees the lock when a leader dies; until TTL watch notifications ship, failover speed is bounded by the TTL. "we are leaning on TTLs a little bit so until we get that new feature around TTL notifications we won't be able to speed this up a ton" (~33:31)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Stream processing: the easy way (with NATS and Benthos)**

- JetStream streams or KV can sit on the source side, the sink side, or as intermediate state between pipeline stages. "you can have JetStream whether it's a stream or a KV end up on either the source or the sink side ... and then things like NATS KV store some intermediate state" (~04:05)
- Enrichment pipeline: S3 CSV input → HTTP lookup (OMDb) in a branch processor → write to a NATS KV keyed by media ID, so a rate-limited API is called once per record instead of on every read. "I don't want to have to look up that poster every time especially since I have an API key that has a rate limit" (~17:17)
- The nats_kv output takes URLs, bucket and an interpolated key expression; the bucket must already exist (nats kv add media). "let's go ahead and do a nats kv add media" (~22:24)
- The enrichment run pushed about 6,000 movies through parallel HTTP calls into the KV, observable live with nats kv watch. "it's going through about 6,000 movies and it's parallelizing a lot of the HTTP calls" (~22:24)
- The analytics pipeline reads the ratings stream, looks up media in KV and customers in SQLite (results stored as message metadata, not payload), and updates a media_ratings KV with count and rolling average. "we want to update a new key value store called media ratings" (~25:27)
- Scaling to many Benthos instances without KV write contention has two options: partition on the source side, or use optimistic concurrency control so concurrent writers to the same key serialize instead of overwriting. "one is to partition on the source side ... the other one is to use optimistic concurrency control" (~25:27)
- The custom nats_kv_update template does get → mutate → write back with OCC so writers on the same media ID "do a single file line" and apply sequentially. "we're using our optimistic concurrency control to make sure that clients who are processing the same rating ... are not stomping on each other" (~29:33)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Seamless evolution across geos and clouds | RethinkConn '22**

- Leaf-node bridging applies not only to core pub/sub but to data streaming, mirroring streams, and key-value stores. "we're talking data streaming, mirroring streams and key-value stores" (~08:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Where are we now and where to next? | RethinkConn '22**

- Roadmap target for KV is one billion keys; KV mirrors give a single source of truth with near-local key access. "we want to get to that billion key capability" (~10:13)
- Roadmap "attraction": a KV store weighted to follow a moving application (e.g. a truck driving from the Midwest to the West Coast) by automatic mirror/migration so latency stays similar. "that KV store is automatically mirrored migrated to the West Coast" (~15:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extending stateful services to the edge | RethinkConn '22**

- To get Redis-like tight RTTs from a JetStream KV, run leaf nodes near the application with local read replicas; you gain lower RTT and continued reads when the leaf node is disconnected from the hub. "when that leaf node gets disconnected from the hub it can still function and it can still read from its config" (~09:14)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Using JetStream KV for dynamic microservice configuration | RethinkConn '22**

- A KV bucket held live configuration (server URL, subject mapping target, feature flags) that all 55 web apps and every leaf node watched; one put fanned out a watch event to all of them. "with one little push to a KV they all received this watched event that this value has been changed" (~02:03)
- Leaf nodes and clients reacted to the watched key by dynamically unsubscribing and resubscribing to the newly specified server. "those are dynamically unsubscribing and then resubscribing to the server that I specify" (~02:03)
- Prefer KV-backed dynamic configuration with locked-down permissions over environment variables, files, or Kubernetes config management; it allows hot reload without restarting services. "you can hot reload their configuration ... without having to restart them" (~06:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Using NATS JetStream as a Kine backend for k3s | RethinkConn '22**

- Kubernetes talks to etcd; k3s added Kine, an etcd shim, and community member Matt Devaney contributed a Kine driver backed by JetStream KV because the KV API is similar to etcd's; it landed in k3s in May 2022. "the KV implementation in JetStream has a similar API to etcd" (~01:03)
- k3s is pointed at NATS via a datastore endpoint URL with the nats:// scheme, a KV bucket name, and any NATS-supported authentication (the demo used username/password). "this driver does support any kind of authentication that NATS supports" (~03:07)
- A freshly created single-node k3s cluster wrote about 528 KB of etcd state into its KV bucket. "it's already got 528 kilobytes of data in it" (~04:10)
- Multiple edge k3s clusters (NYC, LA, Chicago) each used their own KV bucket on one shared NATS server at the distribution center. "run three clusters but back them all to the same NATS server" (~06:11)
- All k3s KV buckets were mirrored up to NGS; after destroying the local server, backups taken from the cloud were restored in seconds and the clusters came back with their state after ~20 s of startup. "it takes probably about 20 seconds of course these k3s clusters have to start up" (~10:19)
- When restoring mirrored buckets as primary buckets, edit the backup to remove the mirror configuration first, or you recreate them as mirrors. "I have to go into these backups and just remove this mirror" (~09:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Short break and Q&A! | RethinkConn '22**

- There is no official web UI for KV, but building one over the WebSocket API is an afternoon project; Derek built a Deno Deploy front end using plain fetch/POST to a TypeScript service that writes to streams and KV in about 20 minutes. "that exercise really took me about 20 minutes" (~16:20)
- KV handles millions of keys without problem; Derek regularly runs hundreds of millions of keys on a home dev box, and customers ask for billions to tens of billions, which needs enough hardware and memory. "I myself regularly on my home development box run hundreds of millions of keys" (~24:29)
- JetStream KV has no value-based constructs (push, pop, Redis data-type semantics); it is a payload per key, like memcached, so tightly Redis-typed workloads will not map. "the NATS key value store does not have any kind of like value-based constructs in it" (~23:28)
- KV's advantages over Redis are intricate replication (mirrors/sources) and fine-grained authentication/authorization over who accesses what. "trying to configure Redis to do that is tough" (~24:29)
- Subject mapping can transparently shard a KV across e.g. 10 buckets, each independently replicated, while clients simply get and put keys unaware of topology. "through that subject mapping construct, to transparently shard" (~25:31)
- KV supports compare-and-set, unlike memcached; community members use KV for distributed locks and counting semaphores at global scale. "uses KVs as distributed locks and gaining counting semaphores at a global scale" (~26:33)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Derek Collison RethinkConn 2025 Keynote and Closing Remarks**

- The data layer sits on connectivity and provides synchronous and asynchronous replication plus materialized views (KV, object store). "For data, we built on the connectivity layer, providing synchronous and asynchronous replication and materialized views." (~01:05)
- Traditional consumers are heavyweight and can clog a system, so massive KV observer populations (100,000 to 1 million watchers) are achieved with republish and direct gets with global sequencing instead. "key values with over 100,000 or 1 million observers... traditional consumers are very heavyweight and can clog systems down... republish and direct gets with global sequencing" (~03:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia CEO Derek Collison Keynote**

- JetStream provides synchronous and asynchronous replication, and KV and object store are materialized views layered on streams. "JetStream technology is all about access, reducing latency and flow... synchronous and asynchronous replication" (~03:10)
- A common customer deployment: a KV synchronously replicated in one region (possibly across all three major clouds in that region) with asynchronous digital twins transparently served on get; twins can come and go and the system adapts. "a key value store that is synchronously replicated in a single region but could be across all three major cloud providers... that also has asynchronous digital twins that are transparently accessed" (~03:40)
- Roadmap target: massive KV stores serving tens or hundreds of thousands to millions of edge locations. "massive key value stores with tens and hundreds of thousands to millions of edge locations" (~04:20)
- 2024 roadmap includes value semantics: distributed counters, LRU via per-message TTLs, lists and sets. "distributed counters, LRU with per message TTLs, lists, sets and more" (~04:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia Roadmap with Byron Ruth**

- Planned KV value types are counters, lists, sets and maps with native operations, chosen because those are the four Redis structures people actually use. "being able to actually model counters, lists, sets and maps and having native operations" (~00:40)
- As of 2.10 a stream or KV bucket has a single TTL that applies to every entry; per-message TTL is a planned addition. "today within a stream or a KV bucket you can only set a single TTL value... that applies to the entire bucket" (~01:20)
- Per-message TTL lets you re-up a TTL to emulate an LRU cache or lease without writing a new value revision, saving bandwidth and latency. "re-up a TTL to actually emulate an LRU cache... without the need to actually put a new version of the value" (~01:50)
- Planned multi-key direct get gives a consistent snapshot read across multiple keys at one sequence number. "a consistent read across multiple keys... at that sequence number... a snapshot bulk batch read of keys" (~02:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: After event Q&A with Derek on Zoom**

- Per-message TTL is the first 2.11 item because it serves LRU use cases and lets KV tombstones auto-remove after a shorter period than the bucket's limits. "per message TTLs... it also allows the KV tombstones to auto remove themselves after a shorter period of time" (~20:00)
- The KV LRU will refresh a key's TTL on every get, but only when enabled on the bucket, never by default. "every time you do a get refresh the TTL on that message individually... it's not going to be by default" (~24:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking Connectivity - Hyper-Connectivity & The Intelligent Edge**

- KV is a data structure built on globally ordered streams and was designed to be globally replicatable. "creating a globally replicatable key value store and that's exactly what we did" (~21:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - MachineMetrics on Industrial IoT & Predictive Analytics w/ NATS at RethinkConn 2025**

- Front ends can read KV and NATS data directly, skipping the traditional React → Node API → DB path. "we can skip that middleman and have access to so much data" (~22:28)

## OBJ: Object Store (149 claims)


**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream (concept overview)**

- KV and Object Store are built on JetStream and "inherit the core capabilities of JetStream, replication, security, routing limits, and mirroring"; Object Store uses chunked transfers.
- Object Store stores arbitrarily large objects by chunking, versus values "limited to 1Mb by default".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Object Store (concept)**

- Buckets correspond to streams; files stored and transmitted in chunks so "files of arbitrary size" transfer safely.
- "Object store is not a distributed storage system. All files in a bucket will need to fit on the target file system."
- Operations: add bucket, put, get, del, watch (notifies on put and del).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — KV walkthrough / Object Store walkthrough**

- Object bucket backs onto stream `OBJ_<name>`; a 1.5 GiB file was stored in 12,656 chunks; sealed buckets "can not be unsealed or modified".
- After deleting an object the bucket still reports size (16 MiB in the example), i.e. metadata/chunks are not immediately reclaimed to zero.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Anatomy of a NATS Client Application**

- "Object Store ... NOTICE: Technology Preview".

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-19: API prefixes for materialized JetStream views**

- KV and Object Store must reuse the same API prefix: `$KV` and `$OBJ` are the default first tokens; with prefix `JS.from-acc1` a put goes to `JS.from-acc1.$KV.bin.key`, translated back to `$KV.bin.key`. Domain form: `$JS.<domain>.API.$KV.bin.key`.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-20: JetStream based Object Stores**

- Object store = one stream per bucket; objects stored as chunk messages; object info stored as JSON on a meta subject that "is always rolled up (per subject)."
- Default chunk size: "128k (128 * 1024)"; "Clients may tune this as appropriate." Can be overridden per object via `max_chunk_size`.
- Templates: stream `OBJ_<bucket>`; chunk subject `$O.<bucket>.C.<object-nuid>`; meta subject `$O.<bucket>.M.<name-encoded>` (name base64-encoded); bucket name is `restricted-term` (A-Z a-z 0-9 dash underscore).
- Backing stream config: `rollup_hdrs: true`, `allow_direct: true`, `discard: "new"`, `max_age` = TTL, `max_bytes`, storage, replicas, placement; compression bool maps to stream `compression: "s2"`.
- Digest: "Currently `SHA-256` is the only supported digest", formatted `SHA-256=<base64>`.
- "Modified time is never stored"; clients set `mtime` from the message timestamp on read, current UTC on put.
- ObjectInfo fields: name, description, headers, metadata, options{link, max_chunk_size}, bucket, nuid, size, chunks, digest, deleted.
- Semantics: "Deleted objects should be treated the same as objects that don't exist" for Get; `UpdateMeta` may change only name, description, headers; renaming onto an existing object is an error; Delete of a non-existent object is an error, of an already-deleted object may no-op.
- `Seal()` makes the bucket immutable ("no further modifications will be allowed"); status exposes `Sealed()`, `Size()`, `IsCompressed()`, `BackingStore()` (only `JetStream`).
- Links: "It is an error to link to a deleted object. It is an error to link to a link."; a link may overwrite another link or a deleted object but not a live regular object. "Links are currently under discussion whether they are necessary."
- Future (ADR: proposed/not implemented): event notifications, locking, tiered archiving, indexing, versioning, content-type, per-chunk encoding, single-chunk read.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Object-Store (category)**

- Object-Store is "A layer on top of JetStream for utilizing a stream as an object store."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Object-Store Intro**

- Object store is "an abstraction over a stream which models message subjects as keys similar to KV, but with payloads that span multiple chunks," for larger assets "typically loaded and read as readable/writable streams."
- The server's default max payload is "about 1MiB"; a 10MiB object works because the client "automatically splits data into multiple chunks and stores it" as multiple stream messages and reassembles on read.
- Entries consist of metadata (name, description) plus payload, so information about the object is stored separately from the raw data; metadata can be updated directly.
- Because assets may be large, the object store "normally presents a 'Stream' based API" (readable streams) rather than whole-blob calls.
- When reading via a readable stream, an error can occur mid-read, so "when you think you are done reading, you must check if there was an error" and discard staged data on error.
- Destroying an object store means "the data is gone forever."
- (java narrative) Chunk size defaults to 128K and is configurable (32K shown); "Setting chunk size is important to consider ... if you know you are on a connection with limited bandwidth or your server has been configured to only accept smaller messages."
- (java narrative) Object store watch "currently uses a push consumer under the covers," so large objects may generate flow-control warnings; "These are just warnings."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Ordered consumers**

- A Key-Value watch and an Object Store read are both ordered consumers under the cover.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next**

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publish-subscribe**

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TTL and limits**

- Key-value values are meant to be small; large values belong in the Object Store.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Key-Value)**

- Key-value values are small and capped; the object store is for large values reassembled from multiple messages on read (a file, a build artifact, anything multi-megabyte).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Object Store**

- An object is a stored file too large or too binary to ride on a plain message; a bucket is the named store, and both live inside a single JetStream stream named `OBJ_<bucket>`.
- On put the store splits bytes into chunks, writes each chunk as a message, then writes one metadata message; on get it reads the metadata, replays chunks in order, and verifies them.
- Key-Value keeps small structured values with full revision history per key; Object Store keeps large chunked files and only the latest metadata per object. "Use key-value when you want many small values that you read, overwrite, and audit; use the object store when you want whole files that you put and fetch."
- The object store is built on JetStream, so JetStream must be enabled.
- Some operations, like creating a link, are client-library only (not in the `nats` CLI).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first object**

- Bucket name follows the same rule as a stream name: letters, digits, underscores, and dashes only.
- Put computes a running SHA-256 digest over the exact bytes and writes a final metadata record holding name, size, chunk count, and digest.
- Get recomputes the SHA-256 over the reassembled bytes and returns them only if the digest matches; otherwise it returns an error. "what you get is byte-for-byte what you put, or you get an error. The store does not return a quietly truncated file."
- Put writes the pieces then the metadata; get reads the metadata then the pieces then verifies.
- A digest mismatch means do not use the bytes; `ErrDigestMismatch` means retry the get, and a repeated mismatch means the object is damaged and should be put again.
- An interrupted put leaves no gettable object at all because the metadata record is written last; a get reports not-found, not a corrupt file.
- Getting a missing object is an error, not empty bytes; treat "not found" as a real branch. "don't ship the order on the assumption that an absent invoice is an empty one"
- Don't assume a put "worked" without a get confirming it round-trips.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Chunking**

- The default chunk size is 128 KB. "The default chunk size is **128 KB**."
- At the 128 KB default, a 3 MB file lands in roughly 24 chunks.
- Chunks are an implementation detail; you never ask for them or see them separately after the fact.
- The digest is computed over the whole object, so a single missing or reordered chunk changes it and the get refuses to return.
- The metadata message is written last, so an interrupted put never produces a gettable object; a surviving client also purges the partial chunks it already wrote.
- A hard crash mid-put runs no cleanup; already-written chunks stay in the stream as orphans, invisible to get but holding storage until the bucket's limits or age reclaim them.
- Each put gets a fresh NUID separate from the object name, so a re-put's chunks never overlap the previous put's; a re-put replaces the object cleanly rather than merging bytes.
- Chunk size is configurable per put; the 128 KB default is "a reasonable middle for most files, and most of the time you leave it alone."
- A chunk size at the extremes causes problems: too small wastes storage on per-message framing overhead and slows puts/gets; too large exceeds the server's `max_payload` (1 MB by default) or a smaller stream max message size and the put fails outright.
- Don't tune chunk size to chase a benchmark; if you must raise it, keep each chunk under `max_payload`. "the 128 KB default fits almost every file and stays well under the default payload limit"
- Always check the get result before you use the bytes; re-put from the source on failure rather than shipping a partial file.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Metadata and links**

- The `ObjectInfo` record has store-computed fields (size, chunk count, SHA-256 digest, modification time, deleted flag) and three user-set fields: description, headers (HTTP-style), and a free-form metadata map.
- Metadata is held in the one trailing metadata message, so it adds no extra storage cost and no extra read cost.
- Reading metadata (`info`) doesn't fetch the bytes; use it as a low-cost index over the bucket and read bytes only when needed.
- Metadata describes only the current object; each re-put replaces it. For a full revision history per name use the Key-Value store.
- A link is an object whose target is another object; get on the link returns the target's bytes; a link stores no chunks, only the target's bucket and name.
- Links are useful when two names should resolve to the same bytes, or a stable name serves as an entry point for a changing set of files.
- A bucket link has an empty target name and records only a reference to another bucket; get on it returns an error (`ErrCantGetBucket` in Go).
- Two link rules the store enforces: a link can't point at a deleted object, and a link can't point at another link.
- A link is a snapshot rather than a live reference; deleting the target leaves the link dangling (`ErrObjectNotFound`), and renaming the target breaks it too. "Do verify the target exists with `info` before you depend on the link, and re-create the link after you delete or rename its target."
- `UpdateMeta` changes name, description, headers, and metadata, not chunk size or link; a new chunk size or link target is silently discarded. "To change the chunk size, delete the object and put it again. To change a link target, delete the link and add a new one."
- Renaming onto an existing, non-deleted name fails with `ErrObjectAlreadyExists`; renaming onto a deleted name reclaims it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Watching and listing**

- A list returns every non-deleted object as a one-time snapshot of metadata; it reads metadata, never chunks, so listing is cheap regardless of object size.
- A list skips soft-deleted objects; the deletion leaves a lingering metadata record that list filters out.
- Listing an empty bucket returns an empty result ("no objects found"), not a failure.
- A watch streams metadata updates in the order the bucket recorded them, then delivers a single nil sentinel when it has caught up; the CLI consumes the sentinel, client code must recognize it and keep reading.
- An object watch delivers only `ObjectInfo` metadata, never chunk bytes; the KV watch delivers values directly because values are small. "the rule for objects is that watch tells you what changed and get returns the bytes"
- The two-step pattern: watch to learn what changed, then get the bytes you actually want.
- Watch delivers metadata, not the bytes; a service that tries to read a large payload off the watch finds only metadata and breaks.
- An empty bucket is an empty result, not an error; don't conflate "no objects" with "the bucket is missing".

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Under the hood (Object Store)**

- The backing stream `OBJ_<bucket>` captures two subject spaces: `$O.<bucket>.C.>` for chunk messages and `$O.<bucket>.M.>` for metadata messages.
- The chunk subject ends in a per-put NUID (`$O.INVOICES.C.<object-nuid>`) so a re-put never collides with old chunks; the metadata subject ends in the base64url-encoded object name (`$O.INVOICES.M.<base64url(name)>`) so any name, spaces and slashes included, is a safe subject.
- The digest is stored as `SHA-256=<base64url(hash)>`.
- Every metadata publish carries `Nats-Rollup: sub`, which purges every earlier message on the same subject; this keeps exactly one current `ObjectInfo` per name and makes the store rollup-latest, not multi-revision.
- Backing stream config: `AllowRollup` true, discard policy `new` (reject writes when full rather than dropping old chunks), `AllowDirect` true, `max_age: 0`, `max_bytes: -1`, `storage: file`, `num_replicas: 1`.
- A soft delete writes one more metadata message with `Deleted=true`, `Size` and `Chunks` zero, and a cleared digest, carrying the rollup header; the chunk messages are then purged.
- After a soft delete the name still has one metadata message (the marker), which is what lets `watch` report an object disappeared.
- Securing `$O.<bucket>.C.>` / `$O.<bucket>.M.>` or exporting a bucket to another account is an account/permission concern.
- A soft delete does not reclaim disk the instant you call it; the purge frees bytes as the stream cleans up. "Don't delete a large object and immediately assert the disk is smaller."
- The soft-delete tombstone is hidden by default; reading it requires the client show-deleted option (`GetObjectInfoShowDeleted` / `ListObjectsShowDeleted` in Go), which the `nats` CLI doesn't expose.
- A re-put after a delete is a new object identity, not a restored history. "Don't reach for the object store when you need the *previous* version after an overwrite; that history lives in the Key-Value Store."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Object Store)**

- Three core ideas: a bucket is an API over one stream `OBJ_<bucket>`; a chunk is one slice written as a message with a whole-object SHA-256 digest; a rollup keeps only the latest metadata per name.
- Key-value is the sibling store for "small structured values and a full revision history per key"; go there when you need versioning of a value, and for the per-key watch the object store doesn't have.
- `replicas` on the backing stream (e.g. `R=3`) is what lets a bucket survive node loss.
- Checklist: check the result and error of every get before using the bytes.
- Checklist: retry a failed get or put with backoff; a put isn't done until you confirm it.
- Checklist: treat `ErrObjectNotFound` as a normal outcome on a missing or deleted name, not a crash.
- Checklist: leave chunk size at its default unless you have a reason; too small floods the stream, too large can exceed the stream's max message size.
- Checklist: check the get result; an unchecked async put failure can leave an object that fails its digest check.
- Checklist: re-put from the source on a failed get rather than shipping a partial file.
- Checklist: verify a link's target still exists before relying on get-via-link.
- Checklist: re-create a link after deleting or renaming its target; a get on a bucket link returns `ErrCantGetBucket`.
- Checklist: delete and re-put to change chunk size, delete and re-add to change a link target; `UpdateMeta` silently keeps the old ones.
- Checklist: don't rename onto a name already in use (`ErrObjectAlreadyExists`).
- Checklist: use watch to learn what changed, then a separate get for bytes.
- Checklist: never try to read a large payload off the watch channel.
- Checklist: treat an empty bucket as an empty result; list returns `ErrNoObjectsFound`.
- Checklist: expect a soft delete to mark deleted and purge chunks but not reclaim disk until the purge completes; size the backing stream accordingly.
- Checklist: treat a re-put after a delete as a new object identity, not a restored history.
