**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP05: Exploring Powerful Client-side Features and Abstractions in NATS.io**

- Object Store stayed "experimental" until a cross-language compatibility test tool asserted put/get/update across Go, Rust, JavaScript, .NET, and Java, because a later fix would require migrating existing buckets. "we created... a tool that tests and asserts the results across all the languages" (~41:52)
- Max payload can be raised but that hurts server performance and responsiveness; going beyond a few megabytes per message is not advised, which is why Object Store chunks. "it's not advised to go beyond some few megabytes of the max payload size of each message" (~50:59)
- Object Store exists because chunking large blobs correctly is tedious and error-prone and every user was re-implementing it; it is an opinion on how to store a large blob, not a full storage framework. "anybody who dealt with chunking some bytes know how easy it is to mess this up" (~50:59)
- Object Store adds no new server API; it is a specific stream and consumer configuration on top of JetStream, and watch is just a consumer with a particular configuration. "consumers just can be treated as a watcher with different configurations" (~55:03)
- Because KV and Object Store are streams, they inherit mirroring and replication: read-only mirrors can be pushed to edge locations and data flows per mirror definitions with no extra dependencies. "you can create mirrors, read-only mirrors and push it down to edge locations" (~57:07)
- Object Store API was kept deliberately tiny rather than S3-compatible from day one, because it is easier to liberalize an API later than to shrink it. "it's much easier to become liberal over time and expand it" (~57:07)

## TOPO: Topology: clusters, gateways, leaf nodes, placement, domains (957 claims)


**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — What is NATS**

- The NATS service infrastructure scales from a single nats-server on an end device to a global super-cluster; "the `nats-server` process is less than 20 MB in size!"

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Compare NATS**

- "Core NATS supports full mesh clustering with self-healing features"; "JetStream supports horizontal scalability with built-in mirroring." [STALE?] mentions NATS Streaming FT/full clustering.
- NATS server is "a small static binary" deployable from cloud instances to Raspberry Pi; single servers, leaf nodes, clusters, superclusters "can be combined in any fashion"; "Clients are unaware of topology and can connect to any NATS server".
- RabbitMQ clusters "require low-latency networks where network partitions are rare"; server needs the Erlang VM.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject-Based Messaging**

- Location transparency: subscriptions "are automatically propagated within the server cloud", messages routed to all interested subscribers regardless of location, and "Messages with no subscribers to their subject are automatically discarded".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS Service Infrastructure**

- Infrastructure ranges from one local process to "an 'Internet of NATS' of Leaf Nodes, and Leaf Node clusters all interconnected in a secure way over a global shared NATS super-cluster."
- Go applications may embed the NATS server, but then need server configuration.
- Evolution path: single local server -> single server or cluster per VPC/region/on-prem -> connect them as leaf nodes to a backbone cluster/super-cluster, or directly via gateways -> clusters in multiple locations/providers joined into a global super-cluster plus "a scheme to intelligently direct your client applications to the right 'closest' NATS server cluster."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS Adaptive Deployment Architectures**

- Single server: simplest deployment; nats-server is "highly optimized, very lightweight and extremely efficient".
- Cluster: "If you need a fault-tolerant NATS service or if you need to scale your service capacity"; clients hold a list of server URLs.
- Super-cluster: "disaster recovery and ... global deployments" by connecting clusters "via gateway connections (which are interest pruned)".
- Leaf nodes proxy/route between local clients and the infrastructure; locality can be physical, an edge device, a dev machine, a VPC, an app's process group, different accounts, or a business unit. Leaf nodes can connect over WebSocket.
- "Leaf nodes appear to the cluster as a single account connection."
- "Leaf nodes can provide continuous NATS service for their clients, even while being temporarily disconnected from the cluster(s)."
- JetStream on leaf nodes: local streams mirrored to global streams upstream; "mirroring is store and forward and therefore can recover from connectivity outages".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Queue Groups**

- Queue geo-affinity in a super-cluster: "a service request message will only be routed to another cluster (i.e. another region) if there are no listeners on the cluster available to handle the request locally."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream (concept overview)**

- With a cluster of JetStream-enabled servers "you can enable data replication and thus guard against failures".
- Mirrors between JetStream domains offer disaster recovery; a stream can source from one or more streams.
- Hybrid durability: add a dedicated cluster with `server_tags: ["sync:always"]` and `jetstream { sync_interval: always }`, then `nats stream add --replicas 3 --tag sync:always` for only the streams that need it.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Streams**

- Placement: "A given stream, including all replicas (not mirrors), are bound to a single cluster." Default: created in the cluster the client is connected to "assuming it has sufficient storage available."
- Explicit placement is useful "to co-locate with the most active clients (publishers or consumers) or may be required for data sovereignty reasons."
- Placement by cluster requires every server to set `cluster { name }`; super-cluster clusters must have distinct names.
- Tags (`server_tags`, e.g. `cloud:aws`, `region:us-east1`, `az:a`) plus `jetstream.unique_tag: "az"` force replicas onto servers with different tag values (one replica per AZ). Cluster and tags can be combined.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Source and Mirror Streams**

- Source/mirror "are designed to be robust and will recover from a loss of connection. They are suitable for geographic distribution over high latency and unreliable connections." Even a leaf node connecting "every few days" still syncs.
- Leaf nodes and domains supported via the API prefix.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Source and Mirror configuration example**

- Cross-domain source/mirror uses `external.api: "$JS.domainA.API"` with empty `deliver`.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject Mapping and Transforms**

- Hub/leaf disambiguation example: hub maps `orders.* -> orders.central.{{wildcard(1)}}`; leaf maps `orders.central.* -> orders.local.{{wildcard(1)}}`; leaf stream stores under `orders.{{wildcard(1)}}` and republishes to `orders.trace.*`.
- Cluster-scoped mappings (`cluster: "west"` in destination) let an app publish to `foo` and get `foo.west` etc. without knowing its cluster.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Clustering**

- Clustering is for "high volume messaging systems and resiliency and high availability"; servers gossip and connect to all known servers "thus dynamically forming a full mesh"; a cluster "can grow, shrink and self heal".
- "NATS clustered servers have a forwarding limit of one hop": a server forwards client-received messages only to adjacent routed servers; "Messages received from a route will only be distributed to local clients."
- The full mesh requires that servers can connect to each other and clients can connect to each server in the cluster.
- Seed servers have no special configuration; they are the discovery starting point for servers (routes) and clients (connect URLs); "the ability for other server and clients to successfully connect depends on seed server running." Multiple seeds should route to each other.
- `-routes` requires `-cluster`; a routing server advertises its own cluster URL to all others, creating the mesh.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Clustering Configuration**

- Cluster `name` is "recommended for NATS +v2.2".
- Cluster `tls`: "`verify` is always enabled and `cert_file` is used for client and server."
- `advertise`/`cluster_advertise` is useful behind NAT; with TLS it controls the hostname clients use when discovering routes, "otherwise TLS hostname verification may fail with an IP SANs error."
- `no_advertise: true` stops gossiping server URLs to clients (also disables client_advertise); useful when reachable "via different load balancers and interfaces from different networks. Automatically advertising an internal IP address could result in reconnect delays due to failed attempts."
- Route `authorization` with a single username/password applies to discovered routes only; explicit routes need credentials in the URL. "either use the same credentials throughout the system or list every route explicitly on every server." `users` and `token` are not supported and prevent startup; `permissions` is ignored.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — TLS Authentication in clusters**

- Cluster TLS verifies certificates in both directions; cluster identity certs can be separate from client-facing certs.
- "TLS Mutual Authentication is the only way of securing routes."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — v2 Routes**

- Before 2.10.0 two servers shared a single route connection for all accounts, "which could lead to slow down and increased memory usage"; 2.10.0+ creates 3 route connections by default (`pool_size`).
- Each pooled connection handles a fixed subset of accounts; "It is required that each server in the cluster have the same pool size value" or clustering fails ("Mismatch route pool size").
- When one pool connection breaks, traffic for its accounts stops until reconnect (not rerouted through other connections).
- `pool_size: -1` disables pooling (pre-2.10 behavior, single route); then no `accounts` list may be defined.
- Account pinning (`cluster { accounts: [...] }`) gives an account a dedicated route: "improves performance and reduces latency" and saves bytes because the account name isn't in the route protocol. The system account gets a dedicated route by default.
- Route compression (2.10.0) uses S2; default off (mode `accept` doesn't initiate). Modes: off, accept, s2_fast, s2_better, s2_best, s2_auto. Modes need not match between peers.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Clustering**

- "Clustering in JetStream is required for a highly available and scalable system." It uses a NATS-optimized RAFT that combines the data plane for replication with consensus messages.
- Each participating server needs a unique `server_name` (only within the same domain).
- "A quorum is 1/2 cluster size + 1": cluster of 3 needs at least 2 JetStream servers up to store new messages; cluster of 5 needs 3.
- RAFT groups: Meta Group (all servers; owns the API and server placement), Stream Group (one per stream; leader handles ACKs; "if there is no leader the stream will not accept messages"), Consumer Group (one per consumer, lives on the stream group's machines).
- "Generally, we recommend 3 or 5 JetStream enabled servers in a NATS cluster." With 5, place 2+2+1 across three zones so "you can lose any one 'zone' at any time and continue operating."
- Mixing JetStream and non-JetStream servers in one cluster "is possible and even recommended in some cases": storage-optimized machines for JetStream, compute-optimized for core NATS, "reducing operational expense".
- Unlike core clustering, each JetStream node "must specify a server name and cluster name".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Super-cluster with Gateways**

- Gateways join clusters into a full mesh of clusters (superclusters); "Clustering is used for adjacent servers; gateways are for joining clusters together." Cluster and gateway protocols use different ports.
- Unlike clusters, gateways have names (their cluster), form a mesh between clusters not between nodes, use uni-directional connections, and "don't gossip gateway nodes to clients".
- Gateways exist to "reduce the number of connections required between servers" and "optimize the interest graph propagation".
- "all servers of this cluster need to have a gateway configuration with the same name" and "every gateway node needs to be able to connect to any other gateway node and vice versa. Everything else is considered a misconfiguration."
- "It is recommended to have all seed server of a cluster listed in the gateways section"; discovery depends on those servers running.
- Each node makes one outbound connection to a single node in every remote cluster; with 3 gateway nodes locally there are 3 outbound connections per remote cluster. Cluster connections are N(N-1)/2; for 3 clusters of 5 nodes: full mesh 105 vs gateway 30; of 30 nodes: 4005 vs 180.
- Gateways work with single servers too but "start to be useful when participating cluster consist of more than one server".
- Interest propagation: interest-only mode (A sends only subjects B has expressed interest in) and queue subscriptions (propagated once per account and subject).
- Queue semantics across a super-cluster: "a server will always try to serve local queue subscribers first and only failover when a local queue subscriber is not found. The server will pick the cluster with the lowest RTT."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Gateway Configuration**

- Self-gateway entries are ignored, so one gateway config can be shared across all servers.
- `reject_unknown_cluster: true` rejects connections from clusters not listed in `gateways`, disabling gossip of new clusters (but not growth of configured ones).
- Gateway `tls`: "`verify` is always enabled". Authorization: single user/password for discovered gateways only; explicit gateways need creds in URL; `users`/`token` unsupported; `permissions` ignored.
- With `urls` list per remote gateway, a server picks one randomly and establishes "a single outbound gateway connection to one of the members from another cluster."
- Behind a load balancer set `advertise` to the LB hostname/port; "Otherwise, they will advertise their own private IP and port, and can generate failures and downtime if any reconnection is required."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Leaf Nodes**

- A leaf node "extends an existing NATS system of any size, optionally bridging both operator and security domains"; it authenticates local clients with local policy and routes to one or more remote systems.
- "Leaf nodes are useful in IoT and edge scenarios and when the local server traffic should be low RTT and local unless routed to the super cluster." Queue semantics are honored "by serving local queue consumers first."
- Traffic between leaf and cluster takes the restrictions of the user used for the leaf connection: subjects the user may publish are exported to the cluster; subjects it may subscribe to are imported into the leaf.
- "leaf nodes do not need to be reachable themselves and can be used to explicitly configure any acyclic graph topologies."
- Configure a leaf with all seed servers; each seed must accept leaf connections; each URL in a remote must point to the same cluster; a leaf may have multiple remotes to different clusters.
- "If one node in a cluster is configured as leaf node, all nodes need to. Likewise, if one server in a cluster accepts leaf node connections, all servers need to."
- Leaf nodes bridge servers you control with third-party managed servers (e.g. NGS) "to inexpensively connect geographically distributed servers or small clusters."
- TLS-first handshake (2.10.0): normally the server sends INFO in clear text first; `handshake_first` avoids any clear-text traffic when websocket isn't desired.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — LeafNode Configuration**

- Leaf `compression` defaults to `s2_auto` (unlike routes which default to accept).
- Remote `account` selects which local account is bound to the remote; `deny_imports`/`deny_exports` block subject propagation per direction.
- Remote `urls` are shuffled by default (`no_randomize` to connect in sequence).
- `hub: true` reverses roles so the hub initiates the connection to the leaf.
- WebSocket leaf remotes (2.2.0): all URLs in a list must be `ws`; mixing `ws` and `nats` prevents startup. TLS is decided by presence of a tls config, not by `wss://`.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream on Leaf Nodes (domains)**

- Leaf nodes can "provide a local NATS network even when the connection to a hub or the cloud is down"; JetStream supports this via "independent JetStream islands" (domains).
- `domain` in the jetstream block disambiguates which JetStream answers `$JS.API.>`; the API is also exposed as `$JS.<domain>.API.>`.
- "Every server in a cluster and super cluster needs to have the same domain name"; domains can change only across a leaf node connection; domain names must be unique.
- Connecting system accounts across a leaf link gives: monitoring of all servers, account resolver across the network, and "extended JetStream cluster". "You probably don't want to connect your cloud and edge device system accounts" except when only firewalls prevent a super-cluster.
- When `domain` is set, JetStream traffic on the system account and `$JS.API.>` traffic are suppressed across the leaf link, so clients use the local JetStream; other domains are reached via `$JS.<domain>.API`.
- Each domain is an independent namespace: the same stream name may exist in different domains within one account.
- Regular message flow is not restricted by domains: if streams in two domains (same account) subscribe to the same subject, both store the message while the leaf link is up. Avoid with different subjects, different accounts, or isolated accounts.
- Known issue: with more than one JetStream-enabled leaf in a different cluster, the connected cluster also needs JetStream enabled and a domain set. Known issue: extending a central JetStream (leaf without domain) requires the central JetStream to be clustered.
- "If you want to connect a leaf to the hub and get commands, even when the leaf node connection is offline, mirroring a stream located in the hub is the way to go."
- "if you want to aggregate streams located in any number of leaf nodes use source ... it is recommended to aggregate them in the hub for processing via source."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Configuring JetStream (resource management)**

- "JetStream environments in leaf nodes should be isolated in their own JetStream domain".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Configuration (server config reference)**

- `client_advertise` is useful behind a load balancer or when TLS server auth needs the correct DNS name; fully disable with `no_advertise: true`.
- `domain` (2.2.3): "Isolates the JetStream cluster to the local cluster. Recommended use with leaf nodes."
- `extension_hint` (2.2.3) `no_extend`/`will_extend` only matters when the system account is shared between leaf and hub: a standalone leaf extending the hub domain needs `will_extend`; a leaf cluster with a different domain should set `no_extend` or "JetStream will NOT become ready on first startup until the hub can be connected." Only matters at initial start.
- `unique_tag` (2.8.0) "MUST be the same across all nodes in a cluster AND supercluster"; with `az` tags an R3 stream lands in all three AZs.
- `cluster_traffic` (2.11.0): `system` (default; all replication/RAFT traffic in the system account, as in all prior versions) or `owner` (traffic in the stream's own account).
- `server_name` defaults to server id; "within a domain, all server names need to be unique." `server_tags` recommended in `key:value` notation; `server_metadata` (2.12.0).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Enabling TLS**

- `verify_cert_and_check_known_urls` (cluster/gateway only) matches cert SAN DNS entries against configured route/gateway URLs; "dynamic cluster growth may require config changes in other clusters where this flag is true"; wildcard SANs keep growth flexible.
- Cluster advertises IPs by default, which "may result in a failed TLS hostname verification with an IP SANs error"; set `advertise`/`cluster_advertise` to verifiable names.
- Key usage: server needs "TLS WWW server authentication"; clients need "TLS WWW client authentication" when verify is on. "Cluster connections always have verify enabled ... Certificates containing both values are a must." Gateways always verify but may use a separate outgoing cert.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Mixed Authentication/Authorization Setup**

- "Even though they have different authorization mechanisms, these two servers are able to route account messages because they share the same NKEY."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Running a NATS service (introduction)**

- Server binary is "less than 20 MB"; runs from Raspberry Pi to large servers, bare metal, VMs, containers.
- Leaf nodes extend NATS and JetStream to "a VPC, a VLAN, a remote office, a single machine at home or even an edge location with partial connectivity."
- Gateways "filter unneeded traffic and allow for disaster recovery and queued distributed processing with geo-location affinity."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Environmental considerations**

- Load balancers are possible "but you don't need to": NATS balances across seed URLs (clients randomize DNS A records) and reconnects automatically. "If you have a cluster with 3 seed nodes you often get more network throughput than going through a load balancer".
- "Client connections and routes are permanent. Therefore a load balancer will not distribute messages from one client connections between servers"; a common failure is "redundant, but disconnected (non-clustered) servers to which the clients will randomly connect." Advertising must be off or point at the LB address.
- Load balancers can cause idle-detection, packet-inspection protocol, and ephemeral-port problems at scale; routes or gateways through LBs "could results in JetStream lost quorum periods and create undue re-synchronization and protocol overhead traffic."
- Sensible LB use: a single entry point for clustered servers, or auto-connecting to the geographically closest cluster node.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS Server Clients**

- Go apps can embed a NATS server.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS on Kubernetes**

- "The recommended way to deploy NATS on Kubernetes is using Helm with the official NATS Helm Chart"; default values deploy a single-server StatefulSet plus a nats-box Deployment.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS and Docker / JetStream in Docker / NGS leaf nodes in Docker / Swarm**

- A leaf node connecting to NGS logs `JetStream using domains: local "", remote "ngs"`.
- In Swarm, one seed service and other services routing to it form the cluster via autodiscovery; clients are automatically updated about new servers.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — FAQ**

- With clusters, superclusters and leaf nodes "one can build a NATS deployment supporting many millions of connections."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS API Reference (JetStream wire API)**

- JetStream is a set of services over core NATS; with a domain the API prefix is `$JS.{domain}.API`.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — In Depth JWT Guide**

- "leaf nodes do not multiplex between accounts. Every account that you wish to connect across a leaf node connection needs to be explicitly listed." The system account is not connected automatically even when both sides share it; add it as a separate `remote` with heavily restricted credentials, also when only needed for the NATS resolver or centralized monitoring.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject Mapping and Traffic Shaping (server config)**

- Mappings can be scoped to a cluster (`cluster: us-west-1`).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-5: Lame Duck Notification**

- In lame duck mode a server "removes itself from being advertised in the cluster, and slowly starts evicting connected clients as per `lame_duck_duration`."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-13: Pull Subscribe internals**

- Pull(1) optimization uses a wildcard inbox subscription and no-wait first; "works better with topologies where JetStream is running as a leafnode on the edge." "Each pull subscriber must have its own pull request/response handler."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-19: API prefixes for materialized JetStream views**

- "Each JetStream only listens to default API subjects with the prefix `$JS.API`"; API prefixes let a client pick a JetStream in another account or domain.
- Isolation mechanisms: cross-account requires an import with an altered prefix ("an import without a prefix set will result in an error as JetStream is imported as well and we error on import overlaps"); "On leaf node connections, the nats server adds in denies for `$JS.API.>`."
- Crossing an account import strips the prefix back to `$JS.API`; crossing a leaf node between domains uses "an automatically inserted mapping" to do the same.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-15: JetStream Subscribe Workflow [STALE?]**

- Why domain/account tokens are near the front: "to simplify the export/import subject, ie `$JS.ACK.<domain>.<account>.>`."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-30: Subject Transform**

- Core account mappings support multiple weighted destinations per source (weights sum to 100%); "as of 2.10" mappings can be `cluster`-scoped and "take precedence" when published from that cluster; a non-scoped 100% set is the catch-all for other clusters or non-clustered servers.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-31: JetStream Direct Get**

- Mirrors with `mirror_direct: true` join the upstream's Direct Get queue group `_sys_` on `$JS.API.DIRECT.GET.<SRC>` and `.<SRC>.>`; mirrors "can be strategically placed for client latency-reduction" and "may be available to clients when the upstream is offline."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-37: JetStream Simplification**

- `info()` and `delete()` are optional because "a consumer that is exported across an account" may not have those APIs available.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-40: NATS Connection**

- INFO may carry additional cluster URLs; clients store them for reconnect; "A client should have an option to turn off using advertised URLs. By default, those URLs are used."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-41: NATS Message Path Tracing**

- Motivation: with super clusters, leafnodes, accounts and JetStream "knowing the path that messages take through the system is hard to predict" and "it's hard to know where messages can be lost, denied or delayed."
- "By default a trace will end at an account boundary when crossing an Import or Export. This is a security measure"; opt in with `allow_trace: true` on the service export (exporter side) or on the stream import (importer side).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-43: JetStream Per-Message TTL**

- "Sources and Mirrors will always accept and store messages with `Nats-TTL` header present, even if the `AllowMsgTTL` setting is disabled"; with it disabled "the messages are just stored" (enables audit-trail replication of tombstones).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-44: Versioning for JetStream Assets**

- Version skew problem: the connected server may be an old leafnode without JetStream; the meta-leader "would not forward the API fields it is unaware of"; asset hosts "would silently drop fields." "Our current approach is to check the connected-server version and project that it's representitive of the cluster as a whole but this is a known incorrect approach especially for Leafnodes."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-49: JetStream Distributed Counter CRDT**

- Received via Source (feature off) or Mirror: "the message is stored verbatim."
- Source-aware tracking: `Nats-Counter-Sources` header (keyed by source stream name + pre-transform subject) holds last seen `val` per source; on a sourced message the server rewrites `Nats-Incr` to the delta vs last seen value, so recounts stay correct "even if some messages from the source were lost"; adding a source with existing value 10 yields first `Nats-Incr: 10`. Source keys "is not ever removed."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-50: JetStream Batch Publishing**

- "Mirrors can't enable these settings, and will ignore the various headers"; sourcing streams may enable them but "sources will ignore the batching headers when sourced."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-55: Trusted Protocol Aware Proxies**

- A NATS-protocol-aware proxy connects on behalf of clients/leafnodes and must securely pass source IP, TLS properties, etc.; trust is established by listing proxy public nkeys in `proxies { trusted = [ {key: ...} ] }`.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-58: Key-Value Store Roadmap and future considerations (updates ADR-8)**

- "A bucket, being backed by a Stream, lives in one Cluster only. To make buckets available elsewhere we have to use JetStream Sources and Mirrors."
- KV Mirror (Replica): "Copy of exactly 1 other bucket. Used primarily for scaling out the `Get()` operations"; always read-only; may filter keys; "Replicas are automatically picked using a RTT-nearest algorithm"; replicas can be added/removed at runtime "without any re-configuration of already running KV clients"; "Writes and Watchers are transparently sent to the origin bucket"; can span accounts and domains.
- KV Aggregate (Source): combines one or many buckets into a new bucket "to provide a full local copy of other buckets that support watchers and gets locally in edge scenarios"; accessed by its own name; read-only or read-write; may hold key subsets; hosts watchers; "Writes are not transparently sent to the origin Bucket ... they either fail (default) or succeed and modify the Aggregate (opt-in)"; sources can be added later.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-59: JetStream Stream Sourcing and Mirroring**

- Mirroring = "an exact, read-only copy of a single upstream stream ... primarily used for read scaling, disaster recovery, and geographic distribution." Sourcing = aggregate one or more upstreams "suitable for data aggregation, fan-in patterns, and building derived data views." Both work in one account, across accounts, and across domains.
- `mirror_direct` on the mirror lets it serve `$JS.API.DIRECT.GET.<UPSTREAM>`; "particularly useful for KV store mirrors where reads should land on the closest replica"; joins only after catching up "within a small lag window"; captured at create, not auto-refreshed; "we recommend that operators always set `mirror_direct` explicitly."
- Cross-account sourcing needs three exports/imports: `$JS.API.CONSUMER.>` (service), `deliver.mirror.>` (stream), `$JS.FC.>` (service). "Getting the type wrong (e.g., using a stream import for the API subject) will cause silent failures."
- "Cycle detection **does not** apply across external streams in different domains. It is the operator's responsibility to ensure that cross-domain configurations do not create replication cycles." Within an account the server prevents cycles when subjects overlap.
- "In a cluster, only the stream leader manages the replication consumers. If leadership changes, the new leader takes over replication from the last known position."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-61: Unsafe meta group quorum rescue for disaster recovery**

- Meta group quorum "is computed from the configured peer set, not from the set of currently live peers. A peer that is shut down and intended to not come back, without being explicitly peer-removed still counts toward the quorum requirement."
- Disaster trap: grow 3→5 for a migration, turn off the 2 extras without peer-removing, then lose one original: "only 2 peers remain reachable, the metagroup loses quorum ... With no quorum there is no leader to process a peer-remove either."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-62: JetStream desired state reconciliation**

- Raft membership "can't just be swapped for a new one in a single step: adding or removing several peers at once can produce two quorums that never overlap, which risks electing two independent leaders over the same data." Every change is "a sequence of safe, single-peer adds/removes."
- Pre-2.15 flaw: the Raft layer "automatically adds peers that it hears from ... During a scale-down, move, or peer-remove it means a peer that was meant to be evicted can silently reappear." Progress was inferred from peer-list shape ("more peers than configured replicas" meant "a move is in progress").
- New model: `raftGroup.Desired` (peers, cluster, `move`, `scale_down`, `removed`, `origin`) fenced by assignment `id` and leader `term`; "The meta layer is in control of the desired state in the assignment, but the group leader is in control of the assignment's peer set."
- `origin` "captured once and never overwritten" so any pending change can be cancelled back; "A stream keeps running at its origin configuration (placement, retention) until desired state is reached." Legacy moves (peers > replicas) are converted to desired state on upgrade.
- Stream leader loop: request desired state → snapshot if growing ("when scaling up from R1 to R3, the snapshot is what makes sure that the new peers require catchup") → drop peers no longer in cluster → add desired peers (assignment first, then Raft log) → select scale-down victims → remove one old peer at a time (Raft log first, then assignment; check quorum and consumer dependence) → finalize. Consumers "may only add a peer if it's already in the stream's peer set."

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — Core protocol and connection defaults (server/const.go)**

- Route solicitation: initial 1s, backing off to max 30s; reconnect delay 1s; dial timeout 1s. `DEFAULT_ROUTE_CONNECT = 1 * time.Second`, `DEFAULT_ROUTE_CONNECT_MAX = 30 * time.Second`, `DEFAULT_ROUTE_RECONNECT = 1 * time.Second`, `DEFAULT_ROUTE_DIAL = 1 * time.Second` (server/const.go:147-156)
- Route connection pool size default (connections per route peer). `DEFAULT_ROUTE_POOL_SIZE = 3` (server/const.go:159)
- Leafnode reconnect interval 1s; leafnode INFO wait 1s; default leafnode port 7422. `DEFAULT_LEAF_NODE_RECONNECT = time.Second` (server/const.go:162), `DEFAULT_LEAFNODE_INFO_WAIT = 1 * time.Second` (server/const.go:203), `DEFAULT_LEAFNODE_PORT = 7422` (server/const.go:206)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — RAFT (NRG) timing, quorum and backpressure (server/raft.go)**

- Election timeout is random in [4s, 9s]. `minElectionTimeoutDefault = 4 * time.Second`, `maxElectionTimeoutDefault = 9 * time.Second` (server/raft.go:298-299)
- Campaign timeout random in [100ms, 800ms]. `minCampaignTimeoutDefault = 100 * time.Millisecond`, `maxCampaignTimeoutDefault = 8 * minCampaignTimeoutDefault` (server/raft.go:300-301)
- Leader heartbeat interval 1s. `hbIntervalDefault = 1 * time.Second` (server/raft.go:302)
- Lost quorum is declared after 10s without quorum heartbeats and checked every 10s; lost-quorum advisory/signal every 20s. `lostQuorumIntervalDefault = hbIntervalDefault * 10`, `lostQuorumCheckIntervalDefault = hbIntervalDefault * 10`, `lostQuorumSignalIntervalDefault = 20 * time.Second` (server/raft.go:303-305)
- Observer-mode election timer 48h (an observer effectively never campaigns). `observerModeIntervalDefault = 48 * time.Hour` (server/raft.go:306)
- Peer remove timeout and unsafe quorum rescue timeout both 5 minutes. `peerRemoveTimeoutDefault = 5 * time.Minute`, `rescueQuorumTimeoutDefault = 5 * time.Minute` (server/raft.go:307-308)
- Quorum = clusterSize/2 + 1. `qn := n.csz/2 + 1` (server/raft.go:1236); logged at start as "Started (cluster size %d, quorum %d)" (server/raft.go:622)
- Leader steps down when overrun: more than 100,000 uncommitted OR more than 100,000 committed-but-unapplied entries. `pauseQuorumThreshold = 100_000` (server/raft.go:4966); comment "Stepping down means the system gets to 'breathe' for a bit, until a new leader can be elected." (server/raft.go:995-1011)
- Pending append-entry cache: warn at 10,000 (every 5,000), stop caching at 20,000. `paeDropThreshold = 20_000`, `paeWarnThreshold = 10_000`, `paeWarnModulo = 5_000` (server/raft.go:4967-4969, 5016-5028)
- Servers in lame duck mode start their Raft nodes as observers so they never become leader: "This will stop us from taking on the leader role when we're about to shutdown anyway." (server/raft.go:625-630)
- Scale-up peers with an empty log are forced into observer mode until they receive data from the leader: "We need to protect against losing state due to the new peers starting with an empty log. Therefore, these empty servers can't try to become leader until they at least have _some_ state." (server/raft.go:338-341, 640-648)
- `Recovering` flag: "If a server recovers with an empty log, we know to protect against data loss." (server/raft.go:333-336)
- EvictPeers (meta-authorized unilateral peer removal for a leaderless group) is refused for unmanaged groups, groups that still have a leader ("we can remove peers through the log, which is ordered and therefore always preferred"), or when the peers left behind could still reach quorum without us ("otherwise they could commit entries we'd never see and we would diverge") (server/raft.go:1098-1135)
- RescueQuorum (unsafe, disaster-recovery): quorum can only be lowered, only when no leader is known, only on a voting non-observer member, and NEVER on a server with an empty log ("a lowered quorum could let it be elected off empty votes while the lost peers hold the only copies of the data... If all servers are empty, this requires a cluster bootstrap"); the rescue auto-expires after `rescueQuorumTimeout` (5 min) (server/raft.go:1248-1300)
- Raft subjects: `$NRG.>` (all), `$NRG.V.%s` vote, `$NRG.AE.%s` append entry, `$NRG.P.%s` proposal, `$NRG.RP.%s` remove peer, `$NRG.R.%s` reply, `$NRG.CR.%s` catchup reply (server/raft.go:2494-2502)
- Snapshot files are `snapshots/snap.<term>.<index>` (server/raft.go:1833-1836)
- Raft states: FOLLOWER, LEADER, CANDIDATE, CLOSED (server/raft.go:137-142)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — JetStream cluster placement and catch-up (server/jetstream_cluster.go)**

- Meta group name `_meta_`, store dir `_js_`, meta filestore block size 1 MiB. `defaultMetaGroupName = "_meta_"`, `defaultStoreDirName = "_js_"`, `defaultMetaFSBlkSize = 1024 * 1024` (server/jetstream_cluster.go:689-693)
- Server tag `!jetstream` excludes a server from stream placement. `jsExcludePlacement = "!jetstream"` (server/jetstream_cluster.go:693, used 9481-9486)
- Placement tags: a tag prefixed with `!` is an exclusion; all non-excluded tags are mandatory (every listed tag must be present on the peer) (server/jetstream_cluster.go:9338-9346, 9488-9508)
- Placement only selects peers from the target cluster and skips peers never heard from ("offline") (server/jetstream_cluster.go:9448-9462)
- Placement rejects a peer when the stream's MaxBytes exceeds the peer's available storage for that storage type (available = MaxStore/MaxMemory minus max(reserved, used)) (server/jetstream_cluster.go:9510-9538)
- Placement rejects a peer whose HA asset count exceeds `jetstream.limits.max_ha_assets` (strictly >, because `_meta_` counts as one) (server/jetstream_cluster.go:9539-9544)
- `jetstream.unique_tag` prefix: each selected peer must carry a distinct tag with that prefix (for example az:); a peer lacking the prefix is rejected ("default requires the unique prefix to be present"); uniqueness is disabled when the stream's placement tags themselves include the unique prefix (server/jetstream_cluster.go:9362-9388, 9546-9558)
- Placement fails when fewer than r peers are eligible OR fewer than quorum (r/2+1) of them are online. `quorum := r/2 + 1` (server/jetstream_cluster.go:9566-9578). Error string: "no suitable peers for placement" plus reasons: peer offline, exclude tag set, insufficient storage, server tag not unique, miscellaneous issue, jetstream not enabled in cluster, tags not matched [...], tags excluded [...] (server/jetstream_cluster.go:9233-9282)
- Peer ranking: online before offline; then most available storage first, ties broken by fewest streams assigned; for replicas > 1 a stable re-sort by HA asset count "as that is more important to balance" (server/jetstream_cluster.go:9579-9600)
- Stream catch-up inactivity: start timeout 5s, activity timeout 30s. `defaultStreamCatchupStartInterval = 5 * time.Second`, `defaultStreamCatchupActivityInterval = 30 * time.Second` (server/jetstream_cluster.go:11893-11896); errors include "catchup stalled", "catchup failed, too many retries", "corrupt stream snapshot detected" (11882-11890)
- Stream migration check intervals 50ms fast / 500ms fallback (server/jetstream_cluster.go:5446-5449)
- Consumer assignments in cluster: "Durable immediately jumps to the desired peers." on peer-set change (server/jetstream_cluster.go:9213-9214)
- System subjects for assignment results: `$SYS.JSC.STREAM.ASSIGNMENT.RESULT`, `$SYS.JSC.CONSUMER.ASSIGNMENT.RESULT` (+ RECONCILE) (server/jetstream_cluster.go:8710-8715); cluster info subjects `$JSC.SI.%s.%s`, `$JSC.CI.%s.%s.%s` (13016-13021)
- JetStream domain mapping: `$JS.<domain>.API.>` maps to `$JS.API.>`; comment calls $KV/$OBJ independent subject spaces "very unfortunate!!!" (server/jetstream_api.go:352-378)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — Routes, gateways, leaf nodes (server/route.go, server/gateway.go, server/leafnode.go)**

- Route ping interval capped at 30s (below client default 2 min) because S2-auto compression uses RTT from ping/pong. `defaultRouteMaxPingInterval = 30 * time.Second` (server/route.go:132-141)
- Route pooling: an account is hashed (FNV-32a) to a fixed pool index in [0..poolSize-1], "constant and same on all servers (given the same poolSize value)"; poolSize <= 1 always maps to 0 (server/route.go:530-540); since v2.11.0 remotes may have a different pool size (server/route.go:630-636)
- Routes are Implicit ("we learned from speaking to other routes") or Explicit ("explicitly configured"); gossip modes default/disabled/override (server/route.go:39-44, 104-108)
- Insecure TLS on routes/gateways/leafnodes logs: "TLS certificate chain and hostname of solicited ... will not be verified. DO NOT USE IN PRODUCTION!" (server/route.go:127-128, server/gateway.go:71, server/leafnode.go:46)
- Gateway timers: solicit delay 1s, connect delay 1s backing off to 30s max, reconnect 1s, recent-sub expiration 2s, ping at most every 15s regardless of traffic. `defaultSolicitGatewaysDelay = time.Second`, `defaultGatewayConnectDelay = time.Second`, `defaultGatewayConnectMaxDelay = 30 * time.Second`, `defaultGatewayReconnectDelay = time.Second`, `defaultGatewayRecentSubExpiration = 2 * time.Second`, `gwMaxPingInterval = 15 * time.Second` (server/gateway.go:35-58)
- Gateway switches an account from optimistic to interest-only after 1000 remote unsubs/no-interest notices. `defaultGatewayMaxRUnsubBeforeSwitch = 1000` (server/gateway.go:41)
- Gateway interest modes: Optimistic ("a cluster will send to a gateway unless it is been told that there is no interest (this is for plain subscribers only)"), Transitioning, InterestOnly ("a cluster sends all it subscriptions interest to the gateway, which in return does not send a message unless it knows that there is explicit interest") (server/gateway.go:96-110)
- Since 2.9.0 optimistic mode is being phased out: all accounts are switched to interest-only on gateway connect; JetStream-enabled accounts always switch (server/gateway.go:1219-1245)
- Outbound gateway connections are ordered by lowest RTT (server/gateway.go:1751-1775)
- Gateway reply prefix is `_GR_.<6-char cluster hash>.<6-char server hash>.` (old prefix `$GR.`) (server/gateway.go:43-54)
- Leaf node reconnect delays: 30s after a loop is detected, 30s after a permission violation, 30s when leaf and hub share the same cluster name. `leafNodeReconnectDelayAfterLoopDetected = 30 * time.Second`, `leafNodeReconnectAfterPermViolation = 30 * time.Second`, `leafNodeReconnectDelayAfterClusterNameSame = 30 * time.Second` (server/leafnode.go:48-56)
- Leaf loop detection: each account subscribes to a `$LDS.<nuid>` subject; seeing your own LDS subject come back over a leaf means a loop; error text "Loop detected for leafnode account=%q. Delaying attempt to reconnect for %v" and the connection is closed as a protocol violation (server/leafnode.go:58-59, 2497, 2963-2969, 3061-3073)
- Same cluster name on both ends of a leaf connection is rejected (ErrLeafNodeHasSameClusterName) with 30s reconnect delay (server/leafnode.go:3503-3509)
- On the hub (accept) side, the spoke's permissions are reversed: "the perms that it will use on the soliciting leafnode's behalf are correct for them, but inside the hub need to be reversed since data is flowing in the opposite direction" (server/leafnode.go:2310-2318)
- JetStream over leaf nodes: `$JS.API.>`, `$KV.>`, `$OBJ.>` are denied on the leaf account unless the system account is shared, domains match, and extension is not disabled. "If domain names mismatch always deny." With different domains the log says "JetStream using domains: local %q, remote %q"; cross-domain access uses the `$JS.<domain>.API.>` mapping instead (server/leafnode.go:2034-2124)
- Extending JetStream via leaf node is mutually exclusive with a `default_js_domain` mapping to the empty domain: "As soon as one mapping to "" is found, disable the ability to extend JS via a leaf node." (server/leafnode.go:2040-2048)
- When the system account leaf connects with the same domain, the leaf server's meta controller is put in observer mode and reset ("pin leadership to server remotes connect to"; "The parent's view is now authoritative") (server/leafnode.go:2089-2104)
- Guard against duplicate domain names: outgoing `$JS.<domain>.API.>` is denied on the leaf link when not extending, "This guards against a hub and a spoke having the same domain name. But not two spokes having the same one" (server/leafnode.go:2125-2134)
- Leaf hub/spoke: "If the other side has declared itself a hub, so we will take on the spoke role." (server/leafnode.go:2298-2301)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — Client connection handling: slow consumers, stalls, buffers (server/client.go, server/opts.go)**

- Cluster compression default is `accept` ("compression is not initiated, but if the remote selects compression, this server will use the same"); leafnode compression default is `s2_auto` (server/opts.go:6062-6070, 6085-6108)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — Accounts, imports/exports, system events (server/accounts.go, server/errors.go, server/events.go, server/auth.go)**

- Naming: "server name cannot contain spaces", "cluster name cannot contain spaces", "gateway name cannot contain spaces", "duplicate server name", "cluster name conflicts between cluster and gateway definitions" (server/errors.go:173-214)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — jsm.go JSON schema field documentation and defaults (schema_source/jetstream/api/v1)**

- cluster_info: system_account "Indicates if the traffic_account is the system account. When true, replication traffic goes over the system account."; traffic_account "The account where the replication traffic goes over." (`cluster_info`)

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Mirror, Merge, or Consume: How to Choose Your Edge-to-Core Streaming Pattern**

- Consume, mirror, and merge (source) "represent three different relationships between producers and consumers, with different tradeoffs"; teams "default to whichever pattern is easiest" and then "spend months working around its limitations."
- Consume: a core consumer reads an edge stream directly and selectively; puts "the selection logic where it belongs: at the consumer, at the point of ingest." Dependency: "A consumer pulling directly from an edge stream depends on the edge node being reachable."
- Mirror "creates an exact 1:1 replica of an edge stream in the core. Sequence numbers are preserved"; catches up automatically after reconnect; "clients cannot write to a mirror directly. It is read-only by design."
- Merge (sourcing) aggregates multiple edge streams into one core stream; "A sourced stream does not preserve origin sequence numbers — messages from different sources are interleaved"; per-source ordering is preserved, global ordering is not.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — The Hidden Cost of Active-Passive Clustering (And What to Do Instead)**

- Active-passive clustering means "paying for N nodes but only using one of them for productive work"; it forces vertical scaling and needs a load balancer tier that is itself a single point of failure.
- Active-passive failover has a latency spike between failure detection and promotion; at the edge "downstream consumers have their own backlogs and time-sensitive operations."
- Full-mesh: "Every node in the cluster is active. Every node handles traffic"; "no load balancer tier required for basic operation"; "Adding a node to a full-mesh cluster adds proportional throughput capacity."
- "cost of handling twice the traffic is approximately twice the nodes"; on node failure "capacity decreases proportionally, but the cluster remains operational and observable."
- Clustering and Raft are different layers: clustering handles client connectivity; Raft handles replicated state. JetStream's default is "full-mesh: all nodes active" with "Raft for replication"; per-stream leaders are elected automatically; writes are acknowledged only after quorum commit.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Stop Building Firehoses: Flow Control Isn't a Performance Optimization — It's an Architectural Decision**

- "At the edge, 'consumers that can't keep up' is a routine condition, not a failure mode." Push delivery replays backlogs as spikes after reconnect.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Why "Just Retry" Will Kill Your Edge System**

- Retry assumes "the service was temporarily unavailable"; at the edge the failure mode is "the network doesn't exist right now and won't for… unknown hours." Retrying "burns CPU. It piles up in-memory state."
- Disconnection "is a first-class operating condition. It's not an exception."
- Treat edge and core as "separate operational realms connected by controlled paths, not assumed ones."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — The Edge Talks Back: Building Bidirectional Control Into Your Architecture**

- "An architecture that can only receive from the edge is an architecture that can observe problems but not respond to them."
- "The same fabric that carries telemetry from edge to core carries commands from core to edge"; leaf nodes carry both without separate protocols.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — You Don't Need Two Platforms: The Case for Hybrid Eventing**

- Edge needs both: real-time commands need pub/sub; telemetry surviving disconnects needs streaming.
- Same binary on edge leaf nodes, core hub clusters, and cloud with identical operational model.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS and Kafka Compared**

- NATS full-mesh cluster; "one-hop message routing" so messages don't loop; super-clusters connect clusters.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS vs RabbitMQ: How to Choose the Right Messaging System**

- NATS topology is "opaque to clients"; RabbitMQ clustering needs "external peer discovery infrastructure, such as DNS, Consul, etcd."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — MQTT vs. NATS for Fleet Management: Hub-and-Spoke vs. Distributed Mesh**

- "MQTT is built around a central broker. NATS is built as a distributed mesh." "Every MQTT message from a field device travels to a central broker before routing anywhere else — the network trombone effect."
- "Any edge device can run its own local NATS server as a leaf node"; "When connectivity drops, local operations continue. Messages destined for the cloud queue up and sync automatically."
- "NATS servers discover each other through gossip protocols and form clusters automatically"; on failure "clients reconnect to another cluster member without message loss (with JetStream persistence)."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Multi-Region Consistency: Have Your Cake and Eat it Too!**

- Clustered JetStream is immediately consistent within a cluster via RAFT: "When a client application receives the publication acknowledgement it is assured that the message has been safely replicated to (and persisted by) the majority of the servers."
- Super-clusters connect regional clusters via gateways; "A client application can be connected to any server in any cluster and still transparently be able to publish and consume from the streams." Streams can be moved between clusters without interruption.
- Stretch clusters need at least 3 regions; "Stretched streams will be immediately consistent between regions, at the expense of much higher latency of synchronous operations." R5 across 5 regions survives two region failures. At least 2 of 3 nodes must be reachable for RAFT votes.
- If one region fails publishes continue; if two or three fail, no new consumer/stream creation but publishes and gets still work.
- Leaf nodes are recommended for edge without guaranteed connectivity (vehicles, mobile).
- KV direct gets go to local cluster replicas; needs cluster-scoped API subject mappings for transparency.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS for Retail: Manage Thousands of Nodes at the Edge by Reducing East-West Traffic**

- North-south = "communication between different layers or network boundaries" (clients<->servers, leaf nodes<->servers); east-west = within a layer (servers in a cluster, clusters in a super-cluster, leaf servers in the same cluster).
- Leaf nodes "generally do not communicate directly with one another unless there's legitimate interest," but with JetStream subscription propagation creates overhead "particularly noticeable during startup": "when the Nth leaf node starts, it receives N-1 leaf subscriptions."
- Give all leaf nodes the same cluster name to prevent "interest graph propagation between individual leaf nodes"; "will be formalized in the 2.11 release."
- Hub-and-spoke: stores talk to the hub; JetStream source/mirror syncs store data; leaf nodes buffer locally while disconnected and sync on reconnect. Suits "point of sale applications, automated manufacturing, IoT devices, autonomous vehicles."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Why NATS**

- NATS 2.0 (2019): multi-tenancy, decentralized auth, superclusters, leaf nodes. NATS 2.2 (2021): JetStream (at-least-once delivery, exactly-once processing), WebSocket, MQTT 3.1.1.
- Leaf nodes, async replication, and small footprint are "natural extensions" of async-first design, not bolted-on edge features.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS and Decentralized Security: A Modern Approach to Scalable Authentication**

- "Authentication and authorization aren't dictated by your topology. They're overlays on top of your topology."
- "Authentication works the same for leaf nodes and regular nodes"; cross-account service imports "must be authorized at the hub/root as well"; leaf tenants can run their own auth callout per account.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Jepsen: NATS 2.12.1**

- Multiple peer-removal fixes landed in 2.12.3; Synadia contributed membership-change safety fixes to Jepsen's library.
- Multi-AZ clusters resist simultaneous power/storage failures and reconcile lost minority nodes over the network; single nodes can replicate via leaf-node sourcing/mirroring.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Distributed Counters in NATS JetStream: A CRDT-Based Approach to Global Counting**

Leaf nodes bridge clouds; JetStream deployed in a physical Faster Payments data center thanks to its "limited footprint."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Real-time analytics from Edge to multiple factories with NATS and i-flow**

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Scaling Global AI Inference with NATS JetStream**

- NVIDIA Cloud Functions runs on a Synadia-managed supercluster; JetStream is "the durable, low-latency work queue that decouples bursty HTTP/gRPC traffic from GPU capacity across multiple regions."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Bridging the Edge: Using NATS Leaf Nodes to Build Hybrid and Multi-Cloud Systems**

- Leaf nodes "accept client connections locally, dial out to a remote NATS system, forward only allowed/necessary traffic, and keep working locally if upstream connection fails"; "dial-out only ... great for NAT and strict firewalls"; hub sees one account-owned connection per leaf.
- Queue groups prefer local: "the leaf will route that request to a local member if any exist, and only go upstream if none available." Interest-pruned: hub delivers only over leaf connections "whose remote side expressed interest."
- Only subjects the leaf user may publish are exported; only subjects it may subscribe to are imported. Sidecar pattern: leaf next to the app, apps connect to localhost without credentials, leaf holds the real credentials.
- Rule: "clusters for same region/LAN with low latency; gateways for peer regions/clouds; leaf nodes for crossing network ownership/security boundaries." Stretched clusters "get chatty and fragile." Keep leaf graphs acyclic: "trees and forests, not arbitrary meshes."
- JetStream domains (`hub` vs `branch-1`, API `$JS.hub.API.>`) separate instances; store-and-forward = persist locally, mirror/source into hub streams when connectivity returns.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Deploying a scalable NATS cluster part 1: core architecture and considerations**

- Quorum "(Cluster Size / 2) + 1"; "deploy Jetstream cluster with 3 or 5 servers. The maximum replication factor per stream is 5"; odd sizes avoid split-brain; R3 balances cost/fault tolerance; R5 tolerates two failures.
- Meta group leader handles API and placement; each stream and each consumer is its own RAFT group; leadership churn hurts performance. [DUBIOUS] "NATS core servers form their own RAFT group for cluster synchronization" (core routing is not RAFT-based).

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Cluster Architectures: Multiregional Clusters - Connecting the Globe**

- Gateways form a full mesh between clusters, on a dedicated port; connections are unidirectional though discovery makes them appear bidirectional; client connection info is not gossiped across gateways.
- Three 3-node clusters: 36 full-mesh routed connections vs 18 gateway connections.
- Gateways use interest-only mode and queue-subscription optimization; "messages are delivered to a single subscriber in a queue group across the Supercluster, prioritizing local queue subscribers."
- Streams/consumers are placed within one cluster and replicate only over routes, not gateways; the meta group spans the whole supercluster and quorum loss blocks new resources; cross-region is eventual via mirrors (read-only) and sources (writable); regional loss can lose data within the replication window.
- All gateways in a cluster must share the cluster name. Leaf nodes are account-scoped point-to-point connections, not part of the routing mesh, presenting "a discrete NATS context distinct from that of the remote"; JetStream domain is "an independent namespace within JetStream that disambiguates requests between NATS deployments"; hub and leaf should use different domains.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Connecting distributed SCADA with NATS.io (part one)**

- SCADA levels 0-4; a data fabric should sit "between Level 1 and Level 2" so PLCs aren't exposed to enterprise networks; the fabric must "transform point-to-point IP communications to named conversations."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Connecting distributed SCADA with NATS.io (part two)**

- "Level 1.5" zero-trust substrate with two components: Data Fabric Client (initiates connections to PLCs and NATS, easing firewalls) and Data Fabric Node (local NATS leaf node with local streams sourced from published subjects, surviving WAN loss).
- "NATS leaf nodes initiate a connection to a server (just like NATS client code)"; "NATS servers when clustered initiate full mesh unicast connections to each other"; "Islands of NATS clusters connect to each other through gateways, in which one gateway connection per cluster is made"; unicast IPv4/IPv6, no multicast/IGMP.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — 14 factors of adaptive edge (part one)**

- Legacy brokers give "high-latency and inconsistent delivery of key data to or between edge clients"; apps are forced to "trombone" data to cloud data centers.
- Adaptive Edge is "a flexible deployment topology overlaid atop of legacy architectures"; supports one-to-many, many-to-many, "sharding of the connection fabric into local clusters" that keep working "even with eventual and discontinued connectivity."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — The Edge Isn't a Place — It's an Operating Reality**

- Edge is "a different operating dimension entirely"; geographic framing optimizes for distance instead of disconnection. Four constraints: connectivity (intermittent by nature), security (physical exposure), distribution (data rates the core can't absorb naively; "a routing/filtering problem, not a throughput problem"), observability (end-to-end).
- "Two separate operating environments with an explicit, managed boundary"; HTTP synchronous request-reply fails at the edge; async event-driven plus store-and-forward with controlled-rate forwarding.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — You can't forklift apps from Cloud to Edge**

- Edge has fewer resources, intermittent networks, different security, broader attack surface; "Moving apps from cloud to edge requires a new approach." Data "tromboning" adds latency.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Introducing the Synadia Adaptive Edge Architecture**

- Leaf nodes let a server "connect to a cluster and act more like a client than a server" and run autonomously when disconnected; superclusters use gateways with a "spline based architecture" for interest propagation; a single stretched cluster "generates excessive chatter."
- Accounts are "containers for messaging"; "data will never traverse an account boundary" by default; sharing via import/export of streams and services (public or private); accounts "may only exist on a subset of servers to create data silos"; leaf nodes "bridge security domains"; "the NATS system never stores or accesses a private NATS key"; "Security is truly bifurcated from connectivity."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Exploring NATS as a backend for k3s**

- Embedded NATS in k3s (`--datastore-endpoint=nats://`, default 0.0.0.0:4222); `noEmbed` for remote; `serverConfig` for leaf-node config; embedded leaf keeps local state if the hub is unreachable.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Nothin' but NATS - Building Natster**

- Global service via unprivileged exports: "No firewall ports, ingress controllers, or load balancers required."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Why NATS.io JetStream is so well suited to AI at the edge**

- Leaf nodes "can safely store and forward messages", "something unique to NATS that you will not find in other 'streaming' platforms", and can be daisy-chained.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Simplifying Microservices Architecture for the Edge and AI Era**

- JetStream "guaranteed store-and-forward" during connectivity loss; distribute updated AI models to the edge.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Weekly #32**

- Tags place replicas across AZs; mirrors are lightweight eventually consistent async replication that can use different configs (memory, R1); sourcing aggregates streams so one consumer replaces many; DR ladder: regional mirrors (most real-time), consumer-to-object-storage batches, offline backups.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Exposing Dynamic Resources in Diagrid Catalyst with NATS**

- Regional leaf nodes receive events and connect to a hub cluster; native KV avoids materializing events into another store.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — What are NATS Leaf Nodes? (Synadia glossary)**

- Leaf nodes dial out on port 7422, need no inbound rules, work behind NAT/firewalls/cellular; keep local messaging and buffer during outages; multiple leaf nodes can form a local edge cluster each with its own leaf connection; mirrors/sources replicate persisted data on reconnect.
- "Queue semantics are honored across leaf connections, serving local consumers first"; request-reply routes to the shortest path and falls back to remote regions transparently.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — What is a Multi-Cluster NATS Deployment? A supercluster (Synadia glossary)**

- Superclusters: independent clusters in "a shared message space"; add/remove clusters without disruption; failure in one cluster does not impact others; streams "can replicate across clusters"; account permissions apply across clusters.
- Says "Leaf Nodes or direct links connect clusters" and leaf nodes act "as bridges for message routing" between clusters; superclusters are formed with gateways, not leaf nodes.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — How to Configure NATS Cluster with Leaf Nodes for Edge Connectivity**

- Ports: 4222 client, 6222 routes, 7422 leaf, 8222 monitoring; leaf `remotes` with `url`; `reconnect: 5s` recommended; TLS with `verify: true`; multi-tier (leaf to regional hub to global hub).
- `deny_imports`/`deny_exports` trim routed traffic; hub-to-edge commands as `commands.{edgeID}.{action}`.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Does Stream Per Subject have any performance benefits over multiple subjects within same stream**

- Consumers scale across a stream's replicas: each replicated consumer's leader can sit on a different stream replica, balancing load — Jarema.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Jetstreams publisher performance decreases rapidly with large number of parallel consumers (50x drop at 100 consumers)**

- A super-cluster with consumers on a separate cluster from publishers helped up to ~1000 consumers but not beyond — mranish592 [UNVERIFIED].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Why JetStream doesn't achieve linear scalability through partitioning?**

- An R1 stream is served by exactly one server; R3 by three; R5 by five. Placement tags select which servers participate — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — NATS JetStream Sharding (placement tags on Kubernetes)**

- Belief: NATS picks the fastest-responding servers for a new stream, so streams cluster on a few nodes. Correction: peer selection at stream creation is load balanced using the current distribution of JS assets — jnmoyne. "the selection of the peers at stream creation time is load balanced (it looks at the current distribution of JS assets when making the selection)."
- Load-balanced placement only works when the number of tag-matching servers exceeds the stream's replication degree — jnmoyne.
- On the official Helm chart, server tags can be generated with an initContainer that reads node labels via kubectl into `server-tags/tags.conf` and `$include`s it — jnmoyne (full values example in thread).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Using Nats Jetstream as an event store**

- Theoretical upper bounds of one cluster: Raft heartbeat traffic per replicated asset (hundreds of thousands of assets could saturate network and CPU), and full-mesh gossip between servers limits cluster size; no large users had hit these in practice — bruth. "A theoretical upper may be on the order of 100s of thousands of assets could likely saturate the network and CPU"

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Use thousands of leaf nodes at the edge**

- Leaf nodes do not gossip to other leaf nodes unless there is legitimate interest — ripienaar.
- Each new leaf node received `LS+` subscriptions from the N-1 other leaf nodes (including per-domain `$JS.<domain>.API.>` subs), which is normal but can be a problem at thousands of leaves — pgentile2 (observed), confirmed "that's normal and I agree can be an issue" — ripienaar.
- To stop interest-graph propagation between leaf nodes that never need east-west traffic, give all leaf nodes the same cluster name; to be formalized in 2.11 — derekcollison. "The trick ... is to have them use the same cluster name. This prevents the hub/cloud side from having to deal with interest graph propagation between each leafnode."
- Putting each store in its own account did NOT by itself suppress `LS+` between leaf nodes; the shared cluster name did — pgentile2 (verified by asker).
- One account per store is "probably a good idea in general" for isolation — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Multi-Region Without Sacrificing Availability**

- With imbalanced cluster sizes or bad inter-region connectivity, run one cluster (the largest) and connect the other regions as leaf nodes each with its own JetStream domain — jnmoyne. "you are better off using one cluster (using your largest one) and the others connecting as Leaf Nodes, each one with their own JS domain name."
- Sourcing and consuming across regions works the same, but JS API calls must specify the target domain; default is the domain of the server the client is connected to — jnmoyne.
- Through a leaf node, core NATS publish/subscribe is transparent (subject to leaf permissions); publishing to a subject captured by a stream in another region stores it there — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Nats SuperCluster with Gateways Adding Jetstream**

- Raft groups: one meta group spanning the whole super-cluster (all nodes; placement, resource availability) plus per-stream and per-consumer groups that live in one cluster only — ripienaar. "the bulk of the replication lives in your datacenter and needs kind of LAN latencies."
- A "stretch" cluster (a normal cluster over long-latency links) works up to roughly 100-150 ms and is "a very advanced use case example and to be used as a last resort" — ripienaar. "max around 100 to 150m"
- When the DC holding a stream is unreachable, mirrors/sources in other clusters are read-only; circular replication keeps read and write during outages — ripienaar.
- Circular replication: per-cluster subject mapping rewrites `stream.in.>` to `stream.in.A.>`, streams `STREAM_A/B/C` each capture their own token and source the others; apps publish the same subject everywhere; subscribers need awareness — ripienaar.
- All 9 nodes of a 3x3 super-cluster belong to the meta group; you can lose 3 nodes before things break — ripienaar.
- While the meta group has no quorum: publishing to existing streams and consuming from existing consumers works; creating streams/consumers and operations like moving streams do not — ripienaar.
- Reference for circular replicated streams: Synadia blog "multi-cluster-consistency-models" — MauriceVanVeen.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Is non-clustered JetStream possible with Gateways?**

- No super-cluster needed: single regional nodes connect as leaf nodes with JetStream enabled and hold read-replica streams sourcing from the hub cluster — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Super-cluster, geolocation and temporary broken gateway link**

- A stream lives in exactly one cluster; mirror/source to other clusters if needed — ripienaar, jnmoyne. "Streams are located in one and only one cluster"
- For JetStream in a super-cluster you need 3 clusters to keep the meta layer up during a cluster outage — ripienaar. "For JetStream you need 3 clusters to keep things up during an outage."
- `nats: no response from stream` when publishing from a cluster cut off from the cluster hosting the stream is expected — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Duplicate messages on a leafnode cluster connected to a supercluster**

- A leaf node bridges NATS systems; a super-cluster is a single system, so a leaf cluster must connect once to the super-cluster, not to each member cluster — derekcollison. "the LN connections from cluster 3 in Asia should only connect once to the supercluster, not to each cluster 1 & 2."
- For super-clusters use CNAME DNS per cluster and geo-aware global DNS for the whole system, as Synadia Cloud does — derekcollison.
- Loops can also be created through account imports/exports; ordinary misconfiguration loops are caught when leaf connections are established — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Produce from anywhere, consume from the same availability zone**

- Reads from a consumer always go through the consumer leader; in a multi-AZ cluster the leader can move on election, so the app must find the leader and connect there — derekcollison. "Reading from consumers is always done from the leader"
- If the consumer's cluster is known in advance, give consuming apps a DNS name resolving only to that cluster's servers; otherwise read cluster info to locate it — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Zone-aware consumer reads for JetStream (similar to Kafka's KIP-392)**

- With R3 across AZs one payload can cross AZ boundaries up to three times: Raft replication, consumer leader delivery, core routing to subscribers — bobo [UNVERIFIED, plausible mechanism, not disputed].
- AllowDirect already lets any replica serve Direct Get, trading read-after-write consistency for read distribution — bobo [UNVERIFIED but matches docs].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — NATS Witness Node**

- No witness concept: each replicated asset holds its own election and only the nodes the asset is placed on vote — neilalexander. "only nodes that an asset is placed on participate in an election."
- Servers can join the meta-layer election without hosting assets via placement tags restricting streams/consumers to a subset, but this does not improve stream/consumer availability — neilalexander.
- The `!jetstream` server tag keeps a server in the meta group while preventing stream placement on it — ramonberrutti [UNVERIFIED, non-maintainer].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Cluster can't tolerate more than one service failure**

- A 3-server cluster survives exactly one failure; quorum rules as in any Raft system — kozlovic.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — 2 Node High Availability cluster for nats stream**

- A 2-node JetStream cluster gives durability but blocks all streams when either server is down until both return — derekcollison. "if any of the servers has an issue the system and all streams will be blocked until both servers are back"
- The supported 2-server replication path is a leaf-node connection between them plus source/mirror stream config, which backfills gaps after interruptions — neilalexander.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Active-active, eventually consistent replication for JetStream?**

- Per-region streams `ORDERS_LON/SFO/NYC` on `orders.<region>.>` plus a central `ORDERS` that sources all, or cross-sourcing between regions for eventually consistent full views — ripienaar.
- Two streams A and B on `ORDERS.A.>` and `ORDERS.B.>` can source each other as long as subject spaces do not overlap; a node-local subject mapping `ORDERS.>` to `ORDERS.A.>` lets apps publish the plain subject and land in the local stream, replicated asynchronously — derekcollison.
- KV mirrors and sources were coming in the next major release (2023); Object store replication was not supported — ripienaar. [STALE?] (KV mirror/source now supported)
- To replicate between otherwise unconnected servers, leaf-node them together so native replication works; else an external watcher-based replicator for KV is easy — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Source stream from multiple leaf nodes**

- Edge fleets: the hub side uses muxed streams holding up to N fleet nodes, grouped into "cells" with fixed capacity deployed as the fleet grows — derekcollison. "the hub/cloud side has muxed streams that hold up to N fleet nodes. Each architecture here is usually referred to as a 'cell'"

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Leaf node with standalone (non-cluster) Primary NATS server**

- By default the two sides of a leaf connection are different JetStream domains; domain names must differ unless the system account is shared — derekcollison. "Unless you also share the system account, the domain names need to be different."
- Share the system account across a leaf link only when truly extending one system, not when connecting two systems — derekcollison. "we only suggest to share the system account if you are truly extended a system through a leafnode vs connecting two systems via a leafnode."
- Cross-domain sourcing uses `external.api: $JS.<domain>.API`; catch-up after a leaf disconnect is expected behavior — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — ObjectStore to share audio/video files between microservices**

- With many mirrors ("digital twins") of an Object store, ask StreamInfo/ObjectInfo on the origin: it lists alternates in RTT order from the requesting app; bind to the closest for low-latency reads — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Mirror leaf node stream on the main server**

- To extend one NATS system (one JS domain) across a leaf, connect the system accounts across the leaf link; for separate JS domains, do not — derekcollison. "If you are trying to extend a NATS system, and hence a JS domain, yes you should connect the system accounts across the leafnode. If you want separate JS domains, do not."
- Mirroring streams across a leaf node is "very common" — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Cross-domain JetStream sourcing, how do I set that up?**
