- `service import not authorized` on `$JS.<domain>.API.>` means the JS API subjects were not exported/imported between the accounts on each side — tbalbers (error), mg1986jp [UNVERIFIED, non-maintainer explanation].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Is $JS.ACK purposefully domain-unaware? Potential interference with leaf nodes**

- In the domain design, `$JS.ACK` and message gets (direct and original) are not domain-aware; a fix is planned — derekcollison. "ACK and MSG gets (both direct and original) are not domain aware. We plan to fix for sure."
- Identically named streams and consumers in different leaf domains sharing a hub can cross-talk on ACK subjects; workaround is deny rules on `$JS.ACK` across the leaf link — cbecker (asker workaround, confirmed problem by derekcollison).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Leaf-node JetStream retention policy for hub-sourced streams**

- The consumer between a source/mirror and its origin is ephemeral, so Interest retention on the origin (leaf) stream gives inconsistent results and can lose messages published while the link is down — derekcollison.
- Recommended: Limits retention on the leaf stream with max age set to the longest expected network outage, plus a max bytes limit so the leaf does not run away with disk or memory — derekcollison. "The age limit should be your maximum outage window allowance."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Leaf-node -> cluster connection pooling plans and simulation**

- Each leaf server has a single connection per account; separate traffic classes by using different local accounts on the leaf, each with its own remote connection — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How to distribute load from one stream to all JetStream cluster nodes?**

- A consumer is bound to a single node and writes to a stream go through one node; WorkQueue and Interest add further constraints, so this is the hardest combination to scale horizontally — ripienaar. "Consumers are bound to a single node and writes into a stream also"
- Consumer leaders need not sit on the stream leader's server; move a leader with a step-down to rebalance — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — has NO quorum, stalled on jetstream consumers**

- An R3 stream that loses two of its three peers cannot progress; surviving two down needs R5, "generally not recommended since cloud providers do things in 3s" — derekcollison.
- Use placement tags so an R3 stream's peers land in different AZs, so one AZ loss removes one peer — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Hot scaling core NATS (no JetStream) for bursty traffic**

- Adding cluster nodes needs no restarts; a new node pointed at a few seeds joins the full mesh; keep a stable core and scale out against it — ripienaar.
- A separate burst cluster via gateways is not better than adding nodes; the real problem is rebalancing existing connections — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Symptom: Unexpected `nats: timeout`**

- On Kubernetes the routes list must contain every StatefulSet pod DNS name; a single service name will not work; the official Helm chart does this — wallyqs.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — NATS supercluster server/cluster discovery from client**

- Server auto-discovery and INFO updates are cluster-scoped; clients never learn other clusters' URLs — derekcollison.
- Cross-cluster failover today: two DNS names (primary, DR), client set not to shuffle resolved addresses so it exhausts the primary before falling to DR; no automatic switch-back yet — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Sourcing streams between hub and leaf instances, both directions (nats.go)**

- If the sourcing stream also lists the same subjects as the origin, and core traffic flows across the leaf link, both streams capture the message directly and the source adds it again, duplicating — jnmoyne. Fix: sourcing stream has no `subjects`, only `sources` with a filter — cbrake (verified).
- After a leaf reconnect, sourced messages published during the outage arrived in about 6 s — cbrake [UNVERIFIED, observed].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Cluster size scalability question (issue)**

- Clusters can be any size; if they get too big, use a super-cluster of many clusters, as NGS does — derekcollison. "if they get too big we might recommend a super cluster (many clusters). This is how we setup NGS ourselves."
- R5 makes little sense where cloud providers have only 3 AZs — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — JetStream HA when part of a 2-cluster super-cluster goes down (issue)**

- HA needs an odd number of nodes and an odd number of clusters; with two clusters any split leaves no majority. "3 clusters minimum." — ripienaar.
- For cross-cluster gateways on Kubernetes use node ports with static names, external DNS, or an L4 load balancer with static IPs per pod — ripienaar, wallyqs.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Headers on KV entries (ADR issue)**

- KV buckets can be mirrored or sourced with subject transforms; master-master replication is not supported in general — ripienaar.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Subscribe to LEAFNODE.CONNECT and LEAFNODE.DISCONNECT events**

- From the system account subscribe to `$SYS.ACCOUNT.*.CONNECT` for all connection types (third token is the account) or `$SYS.ACCOUNT.*.LEAFNODE.>` for leaf nodes only; verified against Synadia Cloud — derekcollison.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topologies (category)**

- NATS supports three deployment topology building blocks: clusters, superclusters, and leaf nodes. "various deployment topologies NATS supports including clusters, superclusters, and leaf nodes"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Simple Leafnode**

- The most minimal leafnode setup is a main server with only a `leafnodes.port` and a leaf server with only `leafnodes.remotes` pointing at the main server's leafnode port; no other configuration is required. "Create the most basic server config which enables leaf node connections."
- The leaf node's `leafnodes.remotes` list names the main server(s) the leaf will dial; the leaf initiates the connection, using the `nats-leaf://` URL scheme. "This needs to define the leaf node _remotes_ which is the main server it will be connecting to."
- A request published by a client connected to the leaf node is transparently routed to a responder connected to the main server; the client needs no knowledge of where the service lives. "As expected, this will get routed to the service connected to the main server."
- When the same request subject has responders on both the leaf and the main server, NATS delivers requests from leaf-connected clients to the closest responder (the one on the leaf). "NATS is smart enough to route messages to _closest_ service relative to where the client request comes from."
- Observed output: with a responder on both sides, three consecutive requests from the leaf-connected client were all answered by "hello from leaf"; the leaf-local responder wins over the remote one.
- If the leaf-local responder is removed, requests from the leaf fall back automatically to the responder connected to the main server. "If we remove the leaf-base service, it will fallback to the main service."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leafnode with JWT Auth**

- The main server enables JWT auth by including the nsc-generated NATS resolver config (`nsc generate config --nats-resolver --sys-account SYS`) alongside its `leafnodes.port`. "generates the bit of configuration to be used by the server to setup the embedded JWT resolver."
- With the full NATS resolver, an account JWT must be pushed to the main server (`nsc push -a APP`) before users of that account (and the leaf's remote credentials) are trusted. "We need to put up the `APP` account JWT we created previously to the main server so that the user credentials file ... is trusted."
- In a JWT setup, the leaf node authenticates to the hub by placing a user `.creds` file in `leafnodes.remotes[].credentials`; the leaf server itself can then have no client authentication configured. "no credentials file is specified since the leaf server does not have authentication setup. Instead the `leafnodes.remotes` section of the config defines the main server and provides the credentials so that the leaf node is authenticated for forwarding messaging."
- The leaf's remote credentials bind the leaf connection into the `APP` account on the hub, so unauthenticated clients on the leaf transparently reach a service connected to the hub under APP. "This request will be transparently fullfilled by the service connected to the main server."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Supercluster**

- A supercluster is a set of clusters joined by gateway connections; the gateway bridges communication by propagating the subject-interest graph across clusters. "A gateway connection bridges communication, specifically by propagating the subject-interest graph across clusters."
- A client on cluster A can use a service hosted by a client on cluster B; messages flow across clusters transparently and the client has no knowledge of physical location. "messages will transparently flow across clusters without the client needing to have any knowledge of physical location."
- If JetStream is in play, do not follow the plain supercluster example; use the dedicated Supercluster with JetStream layout (it has extra requirements). "if you are using JetStream, please refer to the dedicated Supercluster with JetStream example."
- Every server in a supercluster includes a shared `$SYS` account definition; the example factors it into a `sys.conf` included by all configs. "Define the system account to be included by all configurations."
- If the `cluster` block is omitted, the gateway name is used as the cluster name by default. "By default, the gateway name will be used as the cluster name even if the cluster block is not specified."
- A real multi-node cluster in a supercluster must still define its `cluster` block with routes; the single-node-per-cluster layout in the example is a simplification. "if this were a real cluster with routes defined, this would need to be defined as well."
- Each server's `gateway.gateways` list enumerates every cluster in the supercluster, including its own gateway name and URL. (Both east.conf and west.conf list both `east` and `west` entries.)
- Observed output: with two single-node clusters, each server shows `Routes 0`, `GWs 1`, and each cluster shows 1 outgoing and 1 incoming gateway.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Supercluster with JetStream**

- In a JetStream-enabled supercluster, one server across the entire supercluster is elected leader of the meta/API layer and handles JetStream API requests for placing streams and consumers. "one server across the entire supercluster is elected to handle JetStream API requests specifically for the placement of streams and consumers."
- The meta layer is a Raft group, so electing its leader needs a quorum; in practice the supercluster needs an odd number of servers in total. "Since this is a Raft group as well, electing a leader requires a quorum across servers. What this means in practice is that there needs to be an odd number of servers across the supercluster."
- JetStream superclusters should have at least three clusters, or use the arbiter pattern to reach an odd server count. "Supercluster deployments with JetStream-enabled servers should include at least three clusters or use the arbiter pattern."
- For production, run three nodes per cluster so that R3 streams can be created. "for a production deployment it is recommended to have three nodes per cluster to support R3 streams."
- JetStream requires a `cluster` block with `routes` defined even for a single-node cluster. "A requirement of JetStream is to have a cluster block with routes defined, even for single node clusters."
- Stream replicas never cross gateway connections; with one node per cluster only R1 streams can be created. "In this test setup, only R1 streams can be created since streams replicas do not cross gateway connections."
- An odd number of servers across the supercluster is required to reach consensus for the meta group leader. "across a supercluster, an odd number of servers must exist to support reaching consensus for the meta group leader."
- Each JetStream server in the supercluster needs its own `jetstream.store_dir` and a `server_name`; the gateway block lists all three clusters including its own.
- Observed output: a request from a client on west was served by a responder on east across the gateway with sub-millisecond rtt in the local test.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Supercluster Arbiter**

- The arbiter is a lighter-weight way to satisfy the odd-number-of-servers requirement of a JetStream supercluster than deploying a third full cluster. "a lighter-weight alternative for satisfying the requirement of an odd number of servers (across clusters)"
- An arbiter is a single-node cluster with JetStream disabled that has gateway connections to each of the JetStream-hosting clusters. "a single node cluster that is not JetStream-enabled can be deployed which connects to both clusters that are hosting the JetStream-enabled servers."
- The arbiter config sets `jetstream: { enabled: false }` and its `gateway.gateways` list gives every route-able URL of each remote cluster (all three nodes of east and all three of west).
- Observed output: the arbiter shows `JS no`, `Routes 0`, `GWs 2`, and it does NOT appear in the RAFT Meta Group table (only the six JetStream-enabled servers are meta-group peers), while it does appear in the JetStream Summary with zeros.
- Place JetStream nodes across availability zones with `server_tags: [az:N]` and set `jetstream.unique_tag: "az:"` so replicas of a stream are spread over distinct zones. "JetStream enabled with the unique tag as well as basic accounts."
- Two clusters with three nodes each plus the arbiter gives 7 servers total (6 JetStream-enabled), an odd count for meta-group quorum.
- A client connected to one cluster (east) can request that a stream be placed in another cluster by passing `--cluster=west` on stream creation; placement is a JetStream API concern, not a connection concern. "Connect to east (port 4222), but request that a stream be added to the west."
- Observed output (unexplained in narrative): in the recorded run the cross-cluster `stream add --cluster=west --replicas=3` failed with `nats: error: could not create Stream: raft: corrupt peer state (10049)`; the meta table at that moment showed `east-az3` with `Current false`, `Active 2.35s`, `Lag 3`, i.e. one peer not yet caught up shortly after startup. The narrative does not comment on this, so treat it as an observed timing artifact, not documented behaviour.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Regional and Cross Region Streams (Supercluster)**

- Use a supercluster of three regional clusters plus one dedicated cross-region cluster when you need streams that survive a regional failure by spreading replicas across three regions. "The use case is for streams that are resilient to regional failures by having replicas spread out across three different regions."
- Cross-region replication costs latency; accept the trade-off only for streams that are critical for availability and can tolerate somewhat higher latency. "This of course comes at a cost of latency, but this trade-off may be appropriate for streams that are critical for availability, but can tolerate slightly higher latencies."
- `jetstream.unique_tag` forces all replicas of a given stream or consumer onto nodes whose value for that tag prefix differs; regional clusters use `unique_tag: "az:"` so replicas land in different availability zones. "the `unique_tag` option which enforces all replicas for a given stream or consumer to be placed on nodes with different availability zones (AZ)."
- The cross-region cluster (`xr`) sets `unique_tag: "rg:"` so each replica lands in a different region; which AZ each of its nodes lives in does not matter as long as the region is unique. "The cross-region cluster defines a unique_tag on the cluster. Any AZ can be chosen as long as the region is unique."
- Nodes in the cross-region cluster carry both tags (`server_tags: [rg:1, az:1]`), one node per region chosen from an arbitrary AZ.
- A three-node cross-region cluster has one node per region; if more AZs per region are wanted, a six- or nine-node cross-region cluster may be desirable. "If may be desirable to have a six or nine node cross-region cluster if more AZs per region are desired."
- The full gateway list (all four clusters, all nodes) is factored into one `gateway-routes.conf` included by every server's `gateway` block; each server still declares its own `gateway.name` and `port`.
- Every server needs a unique `server_name`, its own `jetstream.store_dir`, `server_tags`, a `cluster` block with the routes of its own cluster, and a `gateway` block naming its cluster.
- Placement is chosen at stream creation: `--cluster=xr` places a stream on the cross-region cluster; `--cluster=rg2` places a regional stream in region 2. The stream is created from a client connected to rg1, so placement is independent of where the client is connected.
- Observed output: EVENTS (cluster xr, R3) got replicas `rg1-az1-x, rg2-az2-x, rg3-az3-x` (one per region); ORDERS (cluster rg2, R3) got replicas `rg2-az1, rg2-az2, rg2-az3` (one per AZ within the region).
- Observed output: `nats server info` on a supercluster member shows a `Super Cluster` section listing all gateway-connected cluster names (rg1, rg2, rg3, xr); each server shows `GWs 3` (one gateway to each other cluster) and `Routes 8`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Regional and Cross Region Streams (Cluster)**

- An alternative to the supercluster layout is a single nine-node cluster stretched across three regions with three AZs each; regional and cross-region placement is then done with tags rather than clusters. "Rather than a supercluster, this relies on a nine node cluster spread out across three regions and three availability zones each."
- NATS placement tags cannot express logical OR or exclusive OR, so valid replica combinations must be precomputed and encoded as tags on the servers. "NATS does not currently support declaring tags with logical OR (or exclusive OR), so valid combinations can be precomputed as tags and then used when creating streams."
- Encode each valid cross-region combination as an `xr:` tag whose digit positions are regions and digit values are AZs; `xr:231` means one replica in region 1 AZ 2, one in region 2 AZ 3, one in region 3 AZ 1. "a tag `xr:231` can be read as a cross-region stream where one replica is placed in region 1 in AZ 2, another in region 2 in AZ 3, and the third replica in region 3 in AZ 1."
- The `xr:` scheme still satisfies `unique_tag: "az:"`, because each precomputed combination uses a different AZ in each region. "the `xr:` tag encodes the cluster/AZ combination while still adhering to the `unique_tag` requirement."
- Each server carries the plain `rg:` and `az:` tags in addition to its `xr:` tags so that regional streams can be placed with `--tag=rg:N`; `unique_tag: "az:"` then spreads the three replicas over the region's three AZs. "the standard `rg:` (region) and `az:` (AZ) tags are set to support _regional_ streams."
- Each of the nine servers carries exactly two `xr:` tags (e.g. `rg1-az1` has `xr:123, xr:132`), so that every `xr:` combination matches exactly three servers, one per region.
- Observed output: `--tag=xr:123` placed EVENTS on `rg1-az1, rg2-az2, rg3-az3`; `--tag=rg:2` placed ORDERS on `rg2-az1, rg2-az2, rg2-az3`. The stream info reports these as `Placement Tags` rather than `Placement Cluster`.
- Observed output: in a nine-node full-mesh cluster each server shows `Routes 32` and `GWs 0`; the seed routes list only three nodes and the rest discover each other.
- Only the three seed servers' route URLs are listed in the shared `cluster.conf`; every node includes the same routes and cluster name.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Replace cluster nodes**

- The new nodes n3 and n4 are configured with only a single seed route (n3 -> n2's route port, n4 -> n3's route port), showing that a joining node needs only one reachable existing peer to join the cluster.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject-Mapped Partitions**

- "A stream provides total order over the set of messages it stores." With replicas, each stream has a dedicated Raft group that replicates every published message to a majority of the replica servers.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first stream**

- Replicas 1 means the stream lives on one server and goes down with it; fine on a laptop, risky in production. "If that server goes down, the stream goes down with it."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Priority groups**

- Overflow policy: near workers pull with no threshold; far workers pull with `min_pending` so the server answers only when at least that many messages are waiting. "You want `us-west` to stay idle unless `us-east` falls behind."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Pausing a consumer**

- Pause runs on the consumer's leader; if the leader changes while paused, the new leader takes over the deadline and resumes on time.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Surviving node loss**

- R=1 means the stream exists on exactly one server with no fault tolerance: lose that server and you lose every message and every consumer's position.
- R=3 is the production floor: three copies across three servers tolerate one server failure with no data loss and no manual recovery. "This is R=3, and it's the production floor."
- Replicas agree on message order by majority vote (Raft); the group keeps working as long as more than half its members are reachable.
- R=5 tolerates two simultaneous failures and is the maximum a stream supports. "Most production streams run R=3; R=5 is for state you can't afford to re-derive."
- Every write goes through the stream leader, which assigns the sequence, stores the message, and returns the `PubAck` only once a majority of replicas have it. "That's what makes the `PubAck` on an R=3 stream a real durability promise"
- Each consumer has its own leader that can sit on any of the stream's replicas, so delivery spreads across replica servers; a Direct Get can be answered by any replica, leader or not.
- On leader loss the remaining replicas elect a new leader automatically; writes pause for the election window, then resume. No acked message is lost because every acked message was already on a majority.
- If no majority remains (two of three gone), no leader can be elected and writes are blocked until enough replicas return. "The stream would rather stop than accept writes it couldn't safely copy to a majority."
- R=3 memory storage survives a single server crash through replicas but loses everything if the whole group restarts at once.
- Consumer state (read position, pending acks) replicates on an R=3 stream; by default a durable consumer takes its stream's replica count.
- Replicas are a durability control, not a throughput control; adding replicas is not how you scale throughput.
- Consumer replicas don't scale delivery: one consumer leader does all the work, followers only stand by.
- A single server rejects `--replicas=3` because there aren't three servers to hold the copies.
- Trusting R=1 in production: no recovery after disk loss because there was no second copy. "Before you trust a stream with real orders, check its replica count rather than assuming it."
- Setting an even replica count: R=2 still has a single point of failure (one of two can't form a majority, writes block); R=4 tolerates only one loss like R=3 while paying for a fourth copy. "Use odd counts: R=3 for the production floor, R=5 for state you can't re-derive."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mirrors and sources**

- A mirror is a read-only stream that continuously copies every message from exactly one upstream stream; behavior is specified in ADR-59.
- Use a mirror for a second copy of one stream: a read replica near a remote region, a stream that survives loss of the upstream's cluster, or a long-retention archive of a short-retention stream.
- Cross-domain config fails silently: the consumer API and flow-control subjects must be service exports, the delivery subject a stream export; a wrong type doesn't error, the mirror just never catches up.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reading messages directly**

- `nats stream get` asks the stream's leader, the one server with the latest write, so a get right after a publish always sees it.
- Direct Get answers the same reads from any server holding a copy of the stream, not only the leader; use it for reads you run often or from far away.
- When a mirror sets `mirror_direct`, the mirror's servers also answer Direct Get requests for the origin, so a reader can be served by a nearby mirror.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next**

- Checklist: Confirm the replica count before trusting a stream with real orders; R=1 has no copy to recover from.
- Checklist: Use odd replica counts: R=3 for the production floor, R=5 for state you can't re-derive.
- Checklist: Prove failover on a real cluster; a green single-node run can't show leader election or a node loss.
- Checklist: Verify each export type for cross-domain sourcing; a wrong type lets the mirror silently never catch up.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue groups**

- When a queue group has members in several clusters, the server prefers a member in the publisher's own cluster before reaching across regions (geo-affinity).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject mapping**

- A destination can carry a `cluster` field so the mapping applies only to messages published through a server in that cluster, with fallback to the unscoped mapping.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connecting**

- `ws://`/`wss://` carries the protocol over WebSocket, the transport a browser has to use and the one that gets through a network allowing only outbound 443.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connection lifecycle**

- Lame-duck mode matters most across a cluster, where the client has another server to move to.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Clustering & Replication Deep Dive**

- A cluster's five moving parts: routes form the mesh, RAFT groups agree, a quorum commits each write, placement decides where replicas live, and peer management grows or shrinks the set safely.
- A single server isn't enough to see the replication mechanism: RAFT needs a majority, so it only appears once three servers are talking. "RAFT needs a majority, so the mechanism only appears once three servers are talking."
- Replication within one cluster is the clustering mechanism; replication across clusters (gateways, geo-affinity, super-cluster traffic) is a separate super-cluster concern.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Forming a cluster**

- A route is a server-to-server connection on a separate route port (6222), never the client port (4222); the two never share a port. "half of cluster-formation bugs are a route pointed at the client port."
- A route is bidirectional once open: subscription interest flows one way, matching messages the other; in a fully connected cluster each server is exactly one hop from all the rest.
- Explicit routes are configured seeds in the `routes` list; implicit routes are opened by the server on its own from gossip (INFO redistribution), completing the mesh.
- Each server only needs one seed address; gossip discovers the rest. Adding a fourth server means giving it one route to a seed.
- Every server that should join must set the exact same `cluster.name`; a mismatched name is rejected with `Rejecting connection, cluster name ... does not match ...` and the odd server forms a separate cluster.
- The `Routes` count in `nats server list` counts route connections, not peers: each link to a peer is a pool of connections (three by default) plus a dedicated system-account route. "each link to a peer is a small pool of connections (three by default) plus a dedicated system-account route"
- The mesh is confirmed when every row of `nats server list` shows the same cluster name and the same non-zero route count.
- A mismatched `cluster.name` forms two clusters that look like one until a message fails to cross; confirm all rows show the same name before trusting the cluster. "A mismatched `cluster.name` forms two clusters."
- Pointing `routes` at the client port (4222) never forms the mesh; always point at a peer's route port. "Pointing `routes` at the client port (4222) never forms the mesh."
- One seed is enough for gossip, but list two or three seed routes so formation survives any one seed being down at boot; don't rely on a single seed in production. "One seed is enough, but list two or three anyway."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Raft and leaders**

- Plain core traffic needs no agreement; stored data does: the servers holding a replicated stream's copies must agree on which messages exist and in what order.
- A RAFT group is a fixed set of peers keeping one shared log; the leader is the only peer that accepts new entries and copies each to followers.
- The meta group is one cluster-wide RAFT group whose peers are all servers; its log holds assignments (which streams exist, replica counts, which servers hold them) and its leader, the meta leader, decides where new streams and consumers are placed.
- Every replicated stream and every replicated consumer gets its own RAFT group; the stream leader is the server that accepts writes to the stream.
- The meta leader and a stream leader are independent; they may be the same or different servers and a change to one doesn't move the other.
- The leader sends a heartbeat to followers by default about once a second; followers stay followers as long as it arrives. "by default about once a second"
- A term counts elections and only goes up; every entry and vote is stamped with it, so a leader from an older term is obsolete the moment a newer term exists.
- A peer votes for at most one candidate per term, granting the vote only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date as its own; this is what stops two leaders from emerging.
- A candidate becomes leader on a quorum of votes, a majority `(N+1)/2`; for three peers that's two.
- A three-peer group keeps a leader as long as two peers are up; lose two and the survivor can't reach a majority and the group goes leaderless. This is the consensus math behind odd server counts: an even count buys no extra majority. "an even count buys no extra majority."
- The meta leader and a stream leader are different groups; losing one doesn't lose the other. Check `nats server report jetstream` for meta, `nats stream info` for the stream. "The meta leader and a stream leader are different groups."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Replication and R=3**

- A stream's replica count is the number of copies; each copy lives on a different server and the servers holding them form one RAFT group. Every write goes through the leader; followers never take writes directly.
- The leader appends a write locally, sends an append entry to each follower, and counts acks; the write is committed once a quorum (majority) holds it. For R=3 that's two of three, so one follower ack suffices.
- Commit is the point at which durability is reached: a committed entry survives the loss of any single server. The leader returns `PubAck` only after commit.
- The third peer isn't on the critical path; the group makes progress as long as a majority is reachable.
- Apply copies a committed entry from the log into the stream store; the leader's commit index rides on the next append entry or heartbeat. Every peer applies the same entries in the same order, so copies converge; a follower can lag but never reorders or skips.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Placement**

- Without placement the meta leader puts replicas on any servers in the cluster with capacity; with placement it must honor the constraint or refuse to create the stream.
- Placement has two levers: a cluster name (every replica must live there; a no-op in a single cluster, useful to pin a stream to one region) and server tags.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling and peer management**

- A new peer catches up by streaming the entries it's missing from the leader; lag is a count of entries behind.
- Adding a peer changes the quorum right away: an R=4 group commits once three peers hold a write, not two. A new empty peer can't win an election until the leader's first entries reach it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Clustering)**

- The five core ideas of clustering are routes, RAFT, quorum, placement, and peers; terms, elections, append entries, apply, preferred leader, and migration are refinements.
- Quorum is what lets a group make progress while a minority is down, and lose nothing when it returns.
- Checklist: Give every server the same `cluster.name`; a mismatch silently forms two clusters that look like one until a message fails to cross.
- Checklist: Point `routes` at the route port (6222), not the client port (4222).
- Checklist: List two or three seed routes so the cluster still forms if one seed server is down at boot.
- Checklist: Treat a brief "no leader" window during failover as normal; the election timer is 4–9s, so let the client retry instead of failing the write.
- Checklist: Track the meta leader and a stream leader as different RAFT groups; losing one is not losing the other.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topologies Deep Dive**

- NATS scales by composing servers; growing a deployment means building bigger topologies (single server, cluster, super-cluster, leaf nodes) out of smaller ones.
- The application never changes across shapes: the same server binary and the same client code run on every topology, so you change the deployment rather than the code.
- The growth path: single server for a developer laptop; a cluster (three servers joined by routes) to survive a server outage; a super-cluster joined by gateways when traffic arrives from a second region; a leaf node when a site needs NATS on-site with only outbound network access.
- Every shape does two separate jobs: core messaging (routes, gateways, leaf connections carry messages to matching interest) and JetStream (stores and replicates across the servers the topology provides).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Single server**

- One server is the right tool for development (a laptop or a CI run), for NATS on the device itself (edge hardware or embedded in-process), and for a small single-instance service.
- A device server often later dials out to a central system as a leaf node, but on its own it's still a single server.
- Clustering NATS behind a single-instance service raises the broker's uptime but not the feature's, because the service still fails first; lifting availability means a second copy of the service too. "one server is the correct amount of infrastructure rather than a compromise."
- A single server is a single point of failure: if the process dies every client loses its connection at once and routing stops until it returns; not fine for production where a reboot during a deploy drops every order in flight.
- On one server JetStream gives durability against a crash (messages survive a process restart) but never against loss of the server itself; lose that disk and you lose the stream.
- A single server scales vertically (bigger CPU, more RAM, faster disk), sometimes the right fix, but every machine has a ceiling; past it the way forward is more servers.
- A single server can't hold a replicated stream: asking for three replicas answers `replicas > 1 not supported in non-clustered mode`; redundancy is a cluster's job, don't treat the error as a config typo to override. "Reaching for redundancy too late."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first cluster**

- A cluster is a set of servers that act as one logical NATS system; a client on any server can reach a subscriber on any other server.
- Clients connect on the client port (4222 default); servers connect to each other on a separate cluster port (6222 in the configs).
- Every server holds a route to every other, so each is one hop from all the rest; there's no central coordinator. A message received over a route is delivered to that server's own clients and forwarded no further, because one hop is always enough.
- With three servers the full mesh is three routes.
- A mismatched cluster name (a typo like `eats`) gets that server's route refused (`cluster name "eats" does not match "east"`) and it ends up a cluster of its own.
- Each server needs only one route entry; servers discover the rest from their peers and dial them (gossip). Hand-writing the full mesh is valid (extras dropped as `Duplicate Route`) but every new server then means editing every config; the trade-off is that a single-seed setup depends on the seed being up first.
- On connect a server sends an INFO message including the other servers' client URLs, so a client knows all cluster members even if configured with one; this discovery is what enables failover to a server the client never named.
- Loss of one server is a reconnect, not an outage.
- `no_advertise: true` stops a server advertising its peers, so a client only knows the URLs given by hand; leave it off (the default) and failover spans the whole cluster.
- Misspelling a cluster name raises no error; the odd server forms its own cluster. Catch it with the rejection line in the log or a cross-server publish test. "Misspell a cluster name."
- The cluster port accepts routes, which are trusted links carrying every account's traffic plus the system account; left reachable with no authorization, anyone with the cluster name can join as a server and read or inject messages across accounts. Bind it to a private interface, firewall it, and in production require route credentials or TLS. "Expose the cluster port to the world."
- Plan for an odd server count once you replicate: two servers lose their majority as soon as one is down, and four tolerate only one loss, the same as three, so the extra server adds cost without failure tolerance. For a pure routing cluster any count is fine. "Plan for an even server count."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream in a cluster**

- A JetStream cluster elects one meta leader that owns every decision about where streams and consumers live; every JetStream-enabled server belongs to the meta group. You don't choose which server wins.
- The meta leader decides where a stream lives but doesn't handle writes to it; writes go through the stream's own replication.
- The meta group decides by majority vote, so a JetStream cluster wants an odd number of servers. Three servers form a majority of two; lose one and streams keep serving; lose a second and no write can reach a majority, so the stream stops accepting messages until a server returns.
- Production clusters run an odd count, typically three or five; a stream keeps at most five copies, so more servers add capacity, not more copies of one stream. "typically three or five — a stream keeps at most five copies"
- Replication stays inside one cluster; the cluster is the unit a stream is replicated across. Each stream gets its own Raft group separate from the meta group.
- The stream leader is chosen independently of the meta leader; you configure neither.
- An even server count gives no extra protection: four tolerate the same single loss as three at the cost of an extra server; run an odd number, never four or six. "An even server count gives you no extra protection."
- All three replicas in one failure domain defeat R3: three copies survive one loss only if the servers can fail independently; spread across one rack or one availability zone a single power or network event takes all three. "All three replicas in one failure domain defeat R3."
- Joining clusters into a super-cluster doesn't stretch one stream across them; the stream's replicas stay inside its cluster.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Super-clusters**

- A super-cluster joins independent clusters into one logical system without combining them into a single mesh; it is the shape for a second region. "A full mesh assumes the members are close together."
- Stretching one cluster across regions works but every server holds a route to every other and route traffic flows freely across the slow, expensive link.
- A route ties two servers and assumes they're close; a gateway ties two clusters and assumes they're far apart. Each server opens just one gateway connection to each other cluster, never one to every remote server.
- A gateway forwards a message to another cluster only when that cluster has a subscriber for it (interest-based forwarding); no interest on the far side means no traffic across the gateway. "no interest on the far side means no traffic across the gateway."
- The gateway `name` identifies the cluster, not the server, and must match the `cluster {}` name exactly; otherwise the server refuses to start with `cluster name conflicts between cluster and gateway definitions`. A server's own entry in `gateways` is ignored automatically.
- List all remote gateway URLs so the connection has somewhere to land if one remote server is down; on separate hosts every server in a cluster can use the identical gateway block, port included.
- Gateways gossip like routes: point a server at a few remote gateways and it discovers the rest, including clusters it was never told about. URLs are a seed for discovery and a fallback, not a list you must keep complete.
- The `gateway {}` block is additive; each cluster keeps its `cluster {}` block and client port.
- Geo-affinity: NATS prefers a local queue subscriber first; a message published in a region goes to a worker in that region even though a remote worker is subscribed, so it never crosses the gateway.
- The gateway carries a queue-group message only when the local side can't serve; if all local workers are down the message crosses to a remote cluster with an interested worker. When more than one remote cluster has a worker, NATS picks one and sends across that single gateway, so it still reaches exactly one worker.
- Don't grow a cluster across regions with routes; join two independent clusters with a `gateway {}` block so only interested traffic crosses. "Reaching for routes to span regions."
- A typo in a `gateways` entry name never connects and logs `Failing connection to gateway "wset", remote gateway name is "west"` on every retry, but the super-cluster still forms through the other side's reverse connection and gossip, so a working cross-region publish doesn't prove the config is right. "Mismatched gateway names."
- Geo-affinity only keeps traffic home when a local queue subscriber exists; centralize all workers in one region and every other region's messages cross the gateway as steady-state load. Place a queue subscriber for each workload in every region that produces that work. "Chatty cross-region traffic without local workers."
- A gateway carries interest across regions, not stream copies.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leaf nodes**

- A gateway joins two clusters that can both accept connections from each other; a site behind a firewall that can only reach out needs a leaf node instead. "A gateway won't help here."
- A leaf node is a server that opens an outbound connection to a remote NATS system (the hub) and bridges subject interest across it; the hub never dials the leaf, so no inbound firewall rule or public address is needed on the leaf side.
- To local clients the leaf is a regular NATS server; a machine needs no leaf-specific configuration.
- The leaf carries only subjects that have interest on the other side, the same interest propagation clusters use internally, extended across one outbound hop.
- The default leaf node port is 7422, a fourth kind of listener separate from the client port (4222), route port (6222), and gateway port (7222). "one port per kind of connection."
- A leaf can dial any hub server; listing several hub URLs in the remote gives it somewhere to reconnect if one is down.
- A leaf has no `cluster {}` or `gateway {}` block; it's a standalone server reaching the rest through one outbound link.
- `remotes` is a list: a leaf can dial several different NATS systems and bridge them all; a leaf can also run its own `leafnodes { listen }` and become a hub for leaves further out, so leaf links compose into trees.
- In production a remote carries `credentials` (a `.creds` file proving the leaf's identity) and `account` (which local account the bridged interest joins); point both ends at the same account and the leaf and cloud share one isolated subject space.
- Local clients stay hidden behind the leaf: the hub sees one leaf link no matter how many machines connect to the leaf. "Add a thousand more machines and the hub still sees one leaf link."
- Address-space isolation (only subjects the account imports and exports cross the link) is an account decision, not something the leaf link gives for free; in the default account there is no subject boundary.
- If a leaf runs its own JetStream, it needs a JetStream domain; without distinct domains a leaf's JetStream and its hub's JetStream collide.
- A leaf dials out: put the `remotes` block on the egress-only side and `leafnodes { listen }` on the side that accepts connections; reversing them means nothing connects. "Treating the leaf like an inbound connection."
- A leaf enabling JetStream while sharing the hub's system account extends the hub's JetStream rather than running its own, so a stream created on the leaf may land on the hub; give the leaf its own JetStream domain for a distinct local store. "Expecting JetStream to span the leaf without a domain."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Putting it together**

- Shapes are layers you combine, not options you choose between; each layer is added when the current one runs out of room and the layer below keeps working unchanged.
- Wiring stays local to each layer: routes wire servers inside a cluster, gateways wire clusters, leaf remotes wire a leaf to a hub; no config block has to know the whole picture.
- One server can take part in several layers at once (`cluster`, `gateway`, and `leafnodes` blocks in one config file).
- Stacking shapes gives one address space by default: routes carry an account's full interest across a cluster and a gateway forwards any subject the far side wants; neither partitions anything. Only a leaf bound to its own account draws a boundary. "stacking shapes adds reach, not boundaries."
- Layer selection: one server until a single point of failure is unacceptable or one server can't carry the load, then a cluster; one cluster until you need a second region or a failure domain a single mesh can't give, then a gateway; a super-cluster reaches every region but not every site, so attach a leaf when a factory, ship, or laptop needs NATS locally with only outbound access.
- Each step is reversible: the layer below never changed, so removing the layer above leaves a working deployment.
- The topology is an operations concern, not an application one; you can start on a laptop and grow to multi-region edge without rewriting business logic.
- Each layer adds operational cost; a super-cluster stood up "to be safe" is two regions to keep healthy before you have a second region's traffic. Add the next layer only when the current one runs out of room; adding early gives no benefit. "Building the whole stack before a limit forces it."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Topologies)**

- A single server is for development and small workloads; in production it's a single point of failure. A cluster is the shape you run in production. A super-cluster is how a deployment spans regions. A leaf node is how NATS reaches the edge.
- A leaf opens a connection across a trust boundary, often the public internet, so authenticating it and scoping what it can publish and subscribe is not optional in production.
- Checklist: Move production workloads off a single server before a reboot can drop orders in flight.
- Checklist: Plan for horizontal growth, not a bigger box; vertical scaling has a ceiling.
- Checklist: Add redundancy before an outage, not after; one server can't hold a replicated stream, so R1 survives a restart but never the loss of the box.
- Checklist: Set the same `name` on all servers, then confirm they joined as one cluster.
- Checklist: Bind the cluster port to a private interface and firewall it off the open internet.
- Checklist: Run an odd server count once you replicate a stream.
- Checklist: Run an odd count (three or five), never an even count; a stream replicates across at most five servers.
- Checklist: Spread R3 replicas across independent failure domains, not one rack or zone.
- Checklist: Join regions with a `gateway {}` block, never a `cluster {}` stretched across them.
- Checklist: Match the local gateway `name` to the `cluster {}` name (the server won't start otherwise), and each `gateways` entry to the remote cluster's exact name; a remote typo fails silently, so confirm a publish crosses regions.
- Checklist: Place a queue subscriber for each workload in every region that produces it.
- Checklist: Put `remotes` on the egress-only side and `leafnodes { listen }` on the hub.
- Checklist: Give a leaf its own JetStream `domain` when it needs a distinct local store.
- Checklist: Reach for accounts (with a leaf where the boundary follows a network edge) when you need an isolation wall, not another route or gateway.
- Checklist: Add each layer only when the current one runs out of room.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Hardening**

- There are three independent TLS blocks: top-level `tls {}` for clients, `cluster { tls {} }` for routes, `gateway { tls {} }` for supercluster links; turning on client TLS leaves routes plaintext until the cluster block is configured too. "These blocks are independent."
- Cluster and gateway routes force mutual verification whether or not `verify` is set, because each end acts as both client and server; a node can't join just by knowing the route address, it must present a certificate chaining to `ca_file`.
- Denying cluster port 6222 globally without allowing it between nodes means route handshakes never complete and each node comes up as an orphan; allow 6222 explicitly from the cluster subnet, then deny elsewhere. "A firewall blocking cluster port 6222 leaves nodes unable to form quorum."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Deployment)**

- Checklist: Open cluster port 6222 between nodes; a firewall that blocks it leaves nodes unable to form quorum.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Decentralized authentication**

- The server supports multiple operators; they are equivalent and the account namespace is flat across all operators.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Encryption & TLS**

- TLS is per connection type: the top-level `tls {}` block secures only client connections; monitoring, websocket, mqtt, leafnode, cluster, and gateway each have their own nested `tls {}` sub-block. "Turning on TLS for clients leaves cluster routes plaintext until you configure the cluster block too."
- The server you connect to is the TLS endpoint and sees plaintext; routed copies of the traffic happen outside your TLS connection and depend on whatever TLS exists on those onward links.
- Pitfall: Cluster and gateway certificates need both `serverAuth` and `clientAuth` key usages. Route/gateway TLS is always mutual and each node presents its one cert as both server and client; a `serverAuth`-only cert fails the route handshake — the most common cluster-TLS failure. "the most common cluster-TLS failure"
- The route key-usage rejection is logged on the peer, not the misconfigured node (`TLS route handshake error: ... certificate specifies an incompatible key usage`); the cluster can still come up through the one working direction, leaving a mesh that works but logs the error on every reconnect.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Security)**

- A cluster, a leaf node, and a gateway are each a connection type carrying its own TLS and authentication.
- A leaf node authenticates to the hub with the same accounts and credentials; the credentials attach in the hub's `leafnodes {}` block.
- Checklist: Configure TLS on cluster, leafnode, and gateway blocks too, not just clients.
- Checklist: Give each cluster node's certificate both `serverAuth` and `clientAuth` extended key usage; the same cert acts as server and client on routes.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connecting**

- The `INFO` message carries `connect_urls` listing cluster members' client addresses, and the server sends a fresh `INFO` whenever the list changes (gossip); the client merges each list into its pool as discovered servers.
- With `no_advertise` set in cluster configuration, `INFO` carries no `connect_urls` and the pool stays exactly what you configured.
- Pitfall: A one-URL configuration that depends on discovery fails where discovery is off (`no_advertise`) or where advertised addresses aren't reachable. Configure every server you want the client to rely on, and treat discovered servers as additions.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Drain & Shutdown**

- A server entering graceful shutdown signals lame duck via an `ldm` flag in `INFO`; a client watching for it can stop publishing and reconnect to another server before the link is cut. The departing server's `connect_urls` omits its own address so a reconnecting client won't pick it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where Next (Resilient Clients)**

- Checklist: Configure every server the client must rely on and treat discovered servers as additions; a one-URL setup that leans on gossip loses failover where `no_advertise` is set or addresses aren't reachable.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Monitoring endpoints**

- Since 2.10 routes are pooled: each peer contributes several route entries (a pool of three plus a dedicated system-account route), so a default three-node cluster shows eight entries on one node, four per peer.
- Route health is presence, not raw count: group `/routez` by `remote_name` and confirm each peer is still there; a vanished peer or a climbing `rtt` is the first sign a node dropped off the mesh.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Advisories & events**

- A flapping leader showing up as repeated leader-elected advisories is worth watching; the advisory reports the fact, not the election mechanics.
- Pitfall: A leader-elected advisory reports a flap, not its cause. Treat it as a symptom; don't diagnose the election from the advisory body alone.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Prometheus & dashboards**

- nats-surveyor connects to the system account, polls every server for its `Statz`, and exposes combined metrics on one `/metrics` endpoint; it needs a system-account credential and is an alternative to running the exporter against one node at a time.
- Pitfall: A node-local health check passes even with no quorum. `/healthz?js-enabled-only=true` returns `200` even when the cluster has lost the quorum that keeps a stream writable, because it never looks past the local server. Don't wire it as your only JetStream alert; add `/healthz?js-meta-only=true`, which turns `503` when the cluster loses quorum. "Do not wire a node-local check as your only JetStream alert."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Monitoring)**

- Checklist: Read a leader-elected advisory as a flap report only.
- Checklist: Use `/healthz?js-meta-only=true` to check cluster quorum; `?js-enabled-only=true` returns 200 even with no quorum.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Under the hood**

- A bucket's `Replicas` field is the number of servers holding a copy; replication and placement belong to the Clustering chapter.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Object Store)**

- `replicas` on the backing stream (e.g. `R=3`) is what lets a bucket survive node loss.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Backup & Recovery Deep Dive**

- A mirror is a live, read-only copy of a stream at a second site kept current by replication; it answers "how long can recovery take" (recovery time).
- A DR mirror needs a second site: a separate cluster reachable over a gateway or leaf-node link.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mirrors as a DR tool**

- R3 replication protects against losing one node; it does nothing when you lose the whole cluster. A mirror lives at a separate site reachable over a gateway or leaf-node link.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Disaster recovery**

- Whole cluster gone: promote the mirror. "promotion is minutes, a restore is hours."
- Promotion edits go through the JetStream metadata group, which must keep quorum after the site is lost; if the failed site held the meta majority, no edit succeeds until the cluster recovers.
- A DR mirror is normally placed in its own JetStream domain (a leaf node) or an independent cluster, rather than sharing one meta group that spans both sites.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connect MQTT devices to NATS**

- `nats-server` speaks MQTT natively on its own listener; there's no bridge process and no second broker to run.
- A standalone MQTT broker scales by making one node bigger; `nats-server` scales by adding servers (clusters, superclusters, leaf nodes), which carry MQTT traffic like everything else.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first MQTT client**

- An MQTT subscription is a real NATS subscription on the converted subject, so it propagates across a cluster like any other; publishers on other servers reach the device without knowing about MQTT.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — QoS, sessions, and retained messages**

- Client-ID eviction across a cluster is less immediate because it travels between servers; the server sometimes refuses the new connection instead of closing the old one.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth and clustering (MQTT)**

- Once a server has a `cluster` or `gateway` block, MQTT requires `server_name` and startup fails otherwise: `mqtt requires server name to be explicitly set`. Server names must be unique across the cluster or super-cluster.
- MQTT state streams are replicated automatically once JetStream is clustered; the replica count is derived from the number of addresses in the server's own `routes` list, clamped between 1 and 3, not from how many servers the cluster has.
- A server listing two routes brings its MQTT streams up at `R=2`, not `R=3`; list all peers in `routes` or set `stream_replicas: 3` explicitly. Asking for more replicas than the cluster can satisfy makes the streams fail to create, surfacing as MQTT clients unable to connect.
- A leaf node close to devices can serve MQTT without running JetStream itself; the standalone JetStream check doesn't apply once the server has a `leafnodes` configuration.
- `js_domain` selects the JetStream domain MQTT stores its state in; set it to the leaf's local domain so sessions and retained messages stay on the leaf and local devices keep working when the hub link is down. The domain is part of the session's storage identity, keeping sessions in different domains from colliding.
- Retained messages are best-effort in a cluster: propagation isn't instant, so a subscriber on a different server microseconds later may see nothing. "When an application depends on reading a retained value immediately, have it connect to the server that produced it."
- Client-ID collision detection is slower in a cluster; both connections can be briefly alive at once.
- Adding a cluster block without `server_name` makes the server refuse to start; set `server_name` on every server from the beginning.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (MQTT)**

- Leaf nodes suit devices well: a leaf on a factory floor or in a vehicle gives local MQTT clients a nearby server that needs only outbound connectivity to the hub, so they keep working when the cloud link is down.
- Checklist: set `server_name` on every server; MQTT requires it as soon as a cluster or gateway block exists.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connect over WebSocket**

- The other case is infrastructure that only speaks HTTP: a cloud HTTP load balancer or CDN routes HTTP only, so exposing NATS behind one means exposing the WebSocket listener; the same applies to a leaf node reaching a hub behind that edge.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TLS and proxies**

- `advertise` is what the server tells clients about itself; without it a server behind NAT or a proxy hands out the address it sees locally, which clients can't reach.
- If NATS is published under a path prefix, the prefix must appear in the client URL; for leaf nodes the server appends `/leafnode`, so a `location /nats` rule must also match `/nats/leafnode`.
- Forgetting `advertise` behind NAT: connections succeed and then fail on a later reconnect to an unreachable advertised URL.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leaf nodes over WebSocket**

- A leaf node can dial its hub over WebSocket instead of the leafnode port; account, subject interest, and link-down behaviour are unchanged, only the transport differs.
- The reason is usually on the hub side: the leafnode port isn't published through an HTTPS ingress but the WebSocket listener is.
- Leaf nodes and browser clients share the WebSocket listener; the upgrade path tells them apart (`/leafnode` for a leaf, `/` for a client). The server appends `/leafnode` itself; you never write it.
- The hub needs both blocks: `leafnodes { port: ... }` is the switch that makes the server accept leaf nodes at all, and `websocket {}` is the door they arrive through. Without a `leafnodes` block (or with an empty one) the WebSocket listener accepts the connection and then closes it.
- The leafnode port (7422) is a real listener open to whatever can reach it even when no WebSocket leaf uses it; restrict it to the peers that need it.
- On the branch side the only change from a leafnode-port remote is the URL: `wss://` scheme and port 443.
- Either the `wss://` scheme or a `tls {}` block on the remote turns TLS on; you don't need both. `ws://` alone against a TLS hub fails; `ws://` with `tls {}` connects; `wss://` alone connects if the hub certificate is publicly trusted.
- Every URL in a single remote must use the same kind of scheme; mixing `wss://` and `nats://` stops the server at startup (`cannot have a mix of websocket and non-websocket urls`). You can't list the ingress and a direct leafnode port as alternatives.
- A leafnode URL without a port gets `:7422` appended whatever its scheme, so `wss://nats.acme.example` quietly dials the leafnode port and fails; write the port explicitly on every remote URL.
- `ws_compression` (alias `websocket_compression`) asks the hub to negotiate compression on the link with the same CPU-versus-bytes trade as for clients; measure rather than assume.
- `ws_no_masking` (alias `websocket_no_masking`) asks the hub to accept unmasked frames; masking exists to stop browsers poisoning intermediary caches, a concern that doesn't apply to server-to-server links. Both are requests the hub may decline, and the link works either way.
- The connection type for a leaf arriving over WebSocket is `LEAFNODE_WS`, not `LEAFNODE`; granting `LEAFNODE` refuses the branch.
- Mixing schemes in one `urls` list refuses to start.
- Pointing the remote at the leafnode port: 7422 speaks the leafnode protocol directly and will not complete a WebSocket handshake.
- Reaching a hub that isn't running a WebSocket listener: a hub with only a leafnode port has nothing for a `wss://` remote to connect to.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (WebSocket)**

- Reaching for WebSocket is often nothing to do with browsers: where an HTTP ingress or load balancer is the only path into the network, the WebSocket listener is what gets published, and a leaf node uses it exactly as a client does.
- Checklist: set `advertise` behind NAT or a proxy.
- Checklist: keep every URL in a remote on the same kind of scheme.
- Checklist: point the remote at the hub's WebSocket listener, not the leafnode port.
- Checklist: keep a `leafnodes { port: ... }` block on the hub even when every leaf arrives over WebSocket, and firewall that port like any other.
- Checklist: give the hub a `websocket {}` listener as well.
- Checklist: write an explicit port on every leafnode remote URL; without one the server appends `:7422`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Learn**

- Clustering & Replication covers the mechanism under a cluster: routes and gossip, RAFT and leaders, `R=3` quorum, placement, and peer management.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — What is NATS?**

- Clustering, JetStream, leaf nodes, MQTT, and WebSocket are all configuration on the same single `nats-server` process.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subjects**

- Subscriptions automatically propagate across the cluster; messages route to all interested subscribers regardless of location with no routing configuration.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue Groups**

- In super-clusters queue groups exhibit geo-affinity: messages go to workers in the same cluster/region as the publisher, with automatic failover to other regions if no local workers are available, with no configuration.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Security**

- Each connection type can have TLS configured independently: client-server, server-server routes, leaf nodes, and gateways; with certificate pinning, CA pools, custom cipher suites, and mTLS.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topologies**

- NATS scales by composing servers; the same binary and client APIs work across every shape, so you change the deployment topology, not your application.
- Use a single server for local development and demos, embedded use inside another application, small services where one node is enough, and quick experiments.
- A cluster is a group of servers connected by routes in a full mesh; clients connect to any server, messages flow across routes, and clients reconnect to another server if one goes down.
- Reach for a cluster for high availability, more throughput than one server, production deployments, rolling upgrades without downtime, and JetStream replication.
- A super-cluster connects multiple clusters with gateways; each cluster operates independently (usually its own region or cloud), and gateways carry only traffic that has interest on the other side.
- Super-clusters fit multi-region or multi-cloud deployments and global services with regional locality; queue groups prefer local workers automatically (geo-affinity).
- A leaf node initiates an outbound connection to a remote NATS system and bridges subject interest; because the connection is from the leaf side, it can run anywhere with outbound access. Clients on the leaf see a regular NATS server.
- JetStream streams can be mirrored or sourced across a leaf link for local copies of data.
- Leaf nodes suit edge and IoT deployments, on-prem services bridging to a cloud cluster, hub-and-spoke architectures, and multi-tenant isolation where each tenant runs its own leaf.
- The hub sees one leaf connection rather than the individual clients, which the leaf authenticates on its own; the leaf still bridges subject interest into the account it binds to, so the subject namespace is shared unless you bind each leaf to its own account.
- Real deployments combine all shapes: clusters across regions via gateways, each fanning out to leaf nodes at edge sites, with the same client code everywhere.

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Achieve MASSIVE Scale with NATS Clustering | Rethink Connectivity Episode 4**

- Clustering is the answer when you need more scalability or redundancy than a single server gives; a super cluster is a "cluster of clusters" that can live in different regions and clouds. "clusters of clusters called super clusters... these clusters can live in different locations and regions and clouds" (~01:40)
- A cluster is configured with a `cluster` block containing a cluster name, a dedicated cluster port (6222 by convention, any free port works) and a `routes` list acting as seed servers. "we give this cluster a connection port which is 6222... routes, this is kind of like your list of seed servers" (~08:40)
- Routes use a gossip protocol: a server only needs to reach one seed server; it then learns about all its neighbours and the full mesh forms automatically. "once one of these servers connects to the seed server it will gossip about all of its neighbors and everything will get connected... automatically" (~09:30)
- When a cluster server is killed, its client connections automatically fail over to the remaining servers and traffic continues. "I can kill one of these servers... and it will automatically move those connections over to either na1 or na3 and everything still works" (~12:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to build a NATS Supercluster | Rethink Connectivity Episode 5**

- A cluster behaves as one logical system: a client connected to any node talks transparently to clients on other nodes, while the nodes give redundancy. "it operates as one singular system like it's one server that you connect to but in fact we have the redundancy of multiple nodes" (~00:40)
- Nodes of a single cluster are assumed to live in the same data center or availability zone; a super cluster spans geographies and even different public clouds (e.g. GCP, AWS, Azure mixed). "nodes in a single cluster are kind of assumed that they live in the same data center or the same availability zone... a super cluster spans not only different geographies but different public clouds" (~01:10)
- Routes gossip so one seed route suffices to form a mesh, but in practice you should list two or three seed servers (and likewise for gateways) so that losing the single seed does not strand new nodes. "in practice you're probably going to want to maybe double or triple up for these connections... so if na1 goes down you're not out of luck" (~02:40)
- Use one config file per cluster: most content is shared, but cluster name, cluster seed routes and gateway name differ. "split this into multiple configurations one for each cluster... most of the stuff will be the same but some of it will have to change" (~08:30)
- A `gateway` block mirrors the `cluster` block: a name (matching the cluster), a port (7222 by convention) and a `gateways` list of the other clusters' name plus URL; gateways also gossip so a single seed per remote cluster works. "instead of route we're actually going to call this gateways... these also gossip between each other so we can also just have single seeds" (~10:10)
- The gateway block must be present in every cluster's config, each naming its own cluster, so connections are mutual. "we'll need this gateway also inside of our NA cluster" (~11:00)
- Three clusters is the recommended shape for the redundancy you need; a 3x3 super cluster shows 6 outgoing and 6 incoming gateway connections per cluster (18 total), meaning a full gateway mesh. "in order to achieve the amount of redundancy that we need it would be good to have three clusters... six outgoing gateway six incoming gateways there's a total of 18" (~13:00)
- Clients connect to the geographically nearest cluster and still reach clients on other clusters transparently. "you can have clients connect to different clusters based on where they are geographically and they can start talking with clients that are connected to other clusters" (~14:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to set up Decentralized Authentication/Authorization in NATS | Rethink Connectivity Episode 6**

- The operator model is a hierarchy operator → accounts → users; a "NATS system" (single node, leaf node, cluster or super cluster) treats itself as one system with one operator. "a NATS system can be a single NATS node, it can be a leaf node, but it can also be a cluster or a super cluster... one operator operating it" (~02:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extend your NATS Cluster with Leaf Nodes | Rethink Connectivity Episode 7**

- A leaf node is a second, separate NATS system (single server, cluster or super cluster) that connects into another NATS system, with its own auth model, its own JetStream assets and its own local interest. "a leaf node is a second NATS system that gets to connect into another NATS system" (~00:50)
- Hub-and-spoke: cloud cluster as hub, each store/factory/site as a leaf node running local services, which gives better performance and isolation than having every site connect straight to the cloud. "instead of everything connecting to the cloud we actually get better performance and better isolation by separating these two things out" (~03:00)
- Run sites you don't fully control (partner sites, factories, retail) as their own NATS systems because they may need a different security model than the hub. "they might have some different use cases for what they need out of a security model so it's better to operate these things as separate NATS systems" (~02:20)
- Three things leaf nodes are good for: extending a hub in hub-and-spoke, bridging two NATS systems that must stay separate but exchange some data, and edge connectivity over unreliable links such as 5G. "extending a hub in a hub and spoke topology... bridging two NATS systems... connectivity at the edge" (~03:30)
- Good leaf-node candidates: location-based communication (factories, retail stores, planes/trains/automobiles) that operates independently and syncs with the cloud, plus inter-organization sharing (partners, OEMs, multi-prem deployments). "planes trains automobiles things that move around these are all really good candidates" (~04:40)
- Leaf node links carry explicit interest propagation: no traffic crosses the link unless it is authorized and there is actual interest on the other side, which cuts chattiness. "there's not going to be any traffic that goes over this leaf node connection unless one it's authorized and two there's actual interest" (~05:50)
- Hub and leaf have separate operational models: the hub can use decentralized auth while the leaf runs with no auth behind a firewall; what crosses the link is bounded by the hub-side user the leaf connects with. "the authorization of what kind of goes over the wire is bound to this user from the operational model of the hub" (~06:40)
- Leaf nodes are daisy-chainable into a constellation without strange performance issues, because they behave like cluster/super-cluster links but with explicit rather than optimistic interest propagation. "these leaf nodes are naturally daisy chainable... only with explicit interest propagation instead of any optimistic" (~07:00)
- Leaf node connections are self-healing: they fail over to gossiped hub servers, keep retrying while disconnected, keep operating locally in the meantime, and resync when the link returns. "I could turn off my internet... the leaf node will still operate as is because it's a separate NATS system... when it comes back up it'll sync back up" (~07:40)
- JetStream domains identify which JetStream (hub or leaf) a command such as stream/consumer creation targets. "JetStream domains which is a way to identify... where you want to operate that actual command" (~08:00)
- A leaf node into NGS needs only a `leafnodes { remotes [...] }` block with the hub URL and credentials, plus `jetstream` enabled; the JetStream domain may be left default or named explicitly. "I only need two things here, I need the url... and then we'll also grab these credentials" (~13:00)
- Running a responder locally on the leaf lets requests be served locally with sub-millisecond latency and never leave for the hub; kill it and requests transparently fall back to the hub responder. "it didn't actually ever hit the NGS cloud because it can see that there's somebody who's able to respond... if I kill this service... it's just going to go back to Oregon" (~17:40)
- If the leaf goes down while messages are added at the hub, the sourced stream catches up automatically and in order when the leaf returns. "I can take down this leaf node and add messages to it and then pull a leaf node back up and NATS is automatically going to be syncing all that data in order" (~25:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Dynamic Permissions with Scoped Signing Keys | Rethink Connectivity Episode 8**

- NGS, Synadia's global super cluster, ran about 72 NATS servers across geos and clouds at the time. "we have about 72 different NATS servers at play in various geos and clouds" (~01:03)
