- Scoped signing keys work across leaf nodes and edge devices as well as the core cluster. "especially in the case of either leaf nodes or edge devices... this all works across all of it" (~16:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Superclusters in Kubernetes: Cross-Cloud Geo-Affinity for High Availability and Low Latency**

- A three-server JetStream-enabled cluster in EKS was deployed with the maintainers' Helm chart and a values file; the options map straight onto standard NATS config documentation. "all I had to do was create this values.yaml file... they all point back to the NATS documentation" (~01:20)
- With a super cluster spanning AWS us-east-1 (EKS) and Azure (AKS), requests from the east were served by an adder service running only in the west when the east instance was removed, giving cross-cloud failover with no noticeable delay to the caller. "the NATS cluster in US East 1 is talking to a NATS cluster in Azure running on the other side of the country and that has an adder service deployed" (~08:00)
- Cross-cloud gateway connectivity was done by exposing each cluster's gateway port through a Kubernetes LoadBalancer Service mapped to a cloud NLB / Azure LB; each gateway block advertises its own LB hostname on 7222 and lists the other cluster's LB address on 7222. "this Kubernetes service, I deployed it as a load balancer type... it's advertising the NLB hostname on port 7222" (~10:00)
- Once a local responder reappears, super cluster geo-affinity routes all local requests to the local instance rather than the remote cluster, reducing latency (all 10 subsequent requests hit the east instance). "NATS clusters have geo affinity to make sure your traffic is handled as closely to the requester as possible" (~13:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Mutually Trusted NGS Credentials**

- Running your own JWT-auth servers alongside NGS normally forces dual management: two sets of accounts and two sets of credentials. "dual management of accounts, you have one set of accounts in NGS and you have a corresponding set of accounts in your local environment" (~00:30)
- With a leaf node config that connects each local account to its NGS counterpart, the import resolution moves from subscribe time to server startup, and the same creds subscribe locally and publish via NGS. "what used to be done with the connect during subscribe now is done during server startup because the server connects to NGS" (~09:13)
- A NATS resolver in full mode holds all account JWTs and answers lookups; with at least one full-mode server, other servers (e.g. leaf nodes) can run in cache mode, downloading only locally used account JWTs and caching them for offline use for the resolver TTL. "as long as you have at least one server running with a NATS resolver in full mode you can start others in cache mode" (~12:00)
- A cache-mode server keeps serving cached accounts while the full-mode server is offline. "we can still access it despite the NATS server with the full resolver being offline" (~14:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | Bearer Tokens in NATS**

- Synadia's guidance to a project needing a non-standard auth model: run your own servers as leaf nodes with your model and let the core catch up, because leaf nodes allow mixing operator and security models. "with leaf nodes you can run your own servers for endpoints using the bearer tokens, don't wait on us, run ahead" (~17:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS Leafnodes**

- Leaf nodes were born to amortize the cost of NATS 2.0 security setup (TLS to dynamic DNS, nonce challenge, JWT exchange) for short-lived utilities; they then became "the missing topology link". "leaf nodes were kind of born out of hey I want to try to solve this one specific problem of amortization of the security and TLS constructs" (~01:20)
- Routes (clusters) assume good signal-to-noise, low RTT and decent bandwidth, i.e. a single region or availability zone; stretching a cluster coast-to-coast or across continents does not work well, and NATS was originally the same as Kubernetes or Kafka in this respect. "they don't like to be stretched from east coast to west coast or to Asia Pacific to Europe, and to be frank NATS was the same way with its initial clustering algorithms" (~02:50)
- Gateways (NATS 2.0) are the second topology and are extremely tolerant of long RTT, low bandwidth and spotty connections; leaf nodes add a hub-and-spoke third topology where the hub can be a server, cluster or super cluster and spokes can be daisy chained. "gateways which are extremely tolerant of very long RTT, low bandwidth, spotty connections" (~03:20)
- Leaf nodes bridge operator and security domains: a shared utility (inside a company or NGS) can be extended by servers that people own, operate and secure differently, e.g. WebSocket and MQTT each have their own security model. "they allow us to bridge operator and security domains, and this one is very subtle and nuanced but it's extremely important" (~04:00)
- Architecture endorsed: a central server/cluster/super cluster with many leaf-node spokes that absorb inbound web/mobile client connections. "a very legitimate architecture of a single server cluster or super cluster that then has lots of hub and spokes to actually take on all of the inbound clients" (~06:00)
- Almost every large proof of concept at the time used leaf nodes. "most of the large POCs we've been doing today, we're using them in almost every single one" (~06:20)
- Run leaf spokes as a small cluster rather than a singleton; each server solicits its own connection to the hub and self-heals independently, so there is no leader election or single point of failure. "every single one of those NATS servers has configured it exactly the same way to solicit a connection to the NATS super cluster... there is no single point of failure" (~08:00)
- Clients on a leaf node need not be aware of hub accounts: a leaf can use the global account with its own security domain while the hub side binds the connection to account A/B/C, and any client bound to the same hub account anywhere in the super cluster can talk transparently. "they can actually not even expose accounts at all... but once it's inside of here it's bound to let's say account A, B or C" (~09:10)
- A leaf node into NGS requires no auth, TLS or user/password locally if you trust the machine; the hub side still sees strong NATS 2.0 security, and NGS never holds your private keys. "everything that's coming and going looks like Derek's account and everything over here is just, there's no authentication authorization TLS, it's just open port" (~15:10)
- Requests via a local leaf node returned noticeably faster than direct requests to NGS because TLS and key-exchange costs are amortized once on the leaf connection. "it seemed very fast, right, because we've amortized all of the cost of TLS and all of the complexities around the key exchange" (~16:00)
- Purely local traffic between clients on the leaf never leaves for the hub. "if I started talking amongst myself just on my local computer here no traffic would ever move to NGS whatsoever" (~16:20)
- A leaf server can be multi-account locally: a remote can bind local account A to a hub account, while local account B (with no remote) stays isolated and requests to hub services from B simply time out. "if it's on account B it does not... it'll stall and just time out because there's no rule to propagate that information to NGS through that leaf node" (~17:20)
- Multiple leaf remotes can run from one server, each binding a different local account to a different hub account. "I'm actually going to create multiple leaf node connections bound to the different local accounts" (~18:40)
- Leaf nodes are the only NATS topology that is interest-only in both directions: unlike clients, whose publishes always go to the connected server, a leaf link sends nothing either way without explicit interest. "leaf nodes are the only network topology that NATS has that is interest only both ways" (~19:20)
- Leaf connections self-heal like everything else: if the hub server disappears the leaf re-solicits and rehooks automatically. "if all of a sudden the server that I was connected to inside of NGS went away the system would automatically try to reseal itself, re-solicit the connection" (~23:20)
- JetStream enabled on a leaf's global account becomes JetStream for the bound hub account across NGS worldwide; leaf nodes with JetStream can extend a core cluster's storage (e.g. add a petabyte for one account) without touching the core. "you can utilize these leaf nodes that are running JetStream just to be extensions to your storage" (~24:30)
- Client applications are unaffected by topology: connecting to a route server, leaf node or super cluster server works exactly the same. "it doesn't matter if it's connecting to a route server or a leaf node server, a super cluster server, it all works exactly the same" (~28:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Andrew Gracey on Two Node K3S**

- Synadia built a two-node leadership election engine (taking Raft out of the equation, borrowing telecom floating-IP/first-hop-redundancy ideas) and bound it to k3s so k3s can run on two nodes backed by NATS. "we've taken raft out of the equation to allow us to have two nodes and then we've bound that to k3s" (~01:50)
- NATS already underpins k3s for multi-node (3/5/7 node) systems; the two-node k3s option was targeted for later in 2024 and was not yet available. "we can actually underpin k3s now with NATS for multi node systems... at some point we're going to have a two node k3s system" (~02:10)
- Moving the edge control loop to the cloud fails on latency and bandwidth (5G, satellite, DSL downstream links) and on cloud outages; companies that moved control loops to the cloud are moving them back. "imagine trying to run Kubernetes over DSL right, it's not going to happen, there's just not enough bandwidth" (~06:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Replace Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis and more w/NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity Ep 10**

- Streams can optionally be replicated across cluster nodes; with R1 the stream lives on one node and if that node goes down you cannot read or write to it. "you can't write to it you can't read to it or anything like that" (~05:07)
- JetStream replication is built on an implementation of the Raft consensus protocol. "JetStream is built on top of an implementation of the Raft protocol" (~05:07)
- With R3, JetStream picks three available nodes; losing one node still allows reads and writes, losing two still allows reads, losing all three is disaster-recovery territory. "if a second node goes down you can actually still read from that stream" (~06:08)
- Consumers are stored on the server and replicated across nodes, so clients can stay stateless. "consumers are also stored on the server and replicated ... so your clients can stay stateless" (~09:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to configure NATS JetStream streams | Rethink Connectivity Ep 11**

- Data must live somewhere; Raft-based immediate consistency constrains where replication can happen. "we have to abide by the laws of physics" (~17:17)
- Use replication factors of 3, 5 or 7; with R3, one node offline still handles writes and two nodes offline still handles reads; default is R1. "you're going to want to use multiples of like three five seven" (~18:19)
- Replication-factor replicas are immediately consistent but must stay inside one cluster; they cannot span clusters. "I can't go outside the cluster with this version of replication" (~19:21)
- Placement selects the cluster and server tags; tag servers when building a supercluster (e.g. region, cloud, SSD) so stream creators can express affinity. "we recommend when you're building the NATS supercluster that you tag things appropriately" (~19:21)
- Mirrors and sources are the way to replicate outside a cluster. "if you want to go outside of your cluster for replication then you need to start looking to mirrors or sources" (~20:22)
- A mirror is a one-to-one twin of a stream in another cluster; reads are served from the mirror while writes are forwarded to the origin stream to keep global consistency. "all reads will be served from this mirror but all writes will actually be forwarded to the source" (~21:22)
- Sources aggregate and filter many streams into one, and the sourcing stream may also ingest its own subjects; a good use is aggregating leaf-node edge streams into one cloud stream. "aggregate them all into one mega stream in the cloud" (~22:23)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Move over Kafka! Let's try NATS JetStream**

- NATS runs a hybrid model: in a cluster some servers can be core-only and some JetStream-enabled, mixed to match required scale, and stream placement is chosen deliberately. "you can run some of them as NATS core servers or you can run some of them as JetStream servers" (~01:03)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | JetStream**

- JetStream plugs into NATS routing, security and multi-tenancy: one compute set can serve completely isolated data stores per account, sharing data only when required. "completely isolated data stores streaming services from completely isolated subject namespaces on top of NATS" (~03:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream for Key-Value Store Tech Preview**

- The backing stream can be replicated to other clusters in a supercluster as read replicas; read-only workers read locally and never talk to the origin, while writes go to the origin with a small replication delay. "if they know they're only ever going to read they never have to communicate to london" (~06:09)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Mirror Streams Explained — One-Way Replication Made Simple**

- A mirror is a replica that automatically and asynchronously syncs from exactly one origin stream; the relationship is strictly one-to-one. "each mirror can only replicate from a single origin stream. It's a strict one-to-one relationship" (~00:00)
- Use mirrors for geographic distribution, fan-out from one origin to many mirrors serving millions of clients, and cross-account or cross-domain replication. "One origin stream can feed multiple mirrors, perfect for fan-out topologies that serve millions of client connections" (~02:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers**

- Co-locating a stream near the data source (per region/neighbourhood) reduces collection latency and improves availability compared with publishing across the country. "whatever the granularity ... to make a stream accessible to that's going to obviously reduce latency of collection ... provide availability" (~10:11)
- In a replicated stream the leader receives the message, stores it, sends it to replicas, and the ack chain completes; consumption is fully decoupled from that. "the leader's job is to say I'm subscribed to this subject ... stores it to disk ... sends it off to its other replicas they store it you get your ack chain" (~35:49)
- Consumer state is replicated; by default a consumer inherits the replication factor of its stream and is co-located on the same servers. "if it's an R3 stream you create a consumer if you don't change the replication factor it's actually going to inherit the replication factor of the stream" (~43:58)
- For latency-sensitive alerting, co-locate the workload with the origin stream (even on a Raspberry Pi at the edge) rather than on the async sourced/mirrored copy, because sourcing and mirroring are asynchronous with retries and partitions. "collocate your application workload to where the origin stream is ... sourcing things mirroring things that's all asynchronous" (~79:48)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.10 Webinar**

- 2.10 adds opt-in TLS-first for leaf nodes: `handshake_first: true` must be set on both hub and remote or the connection is rejected; rollout to other connection types follows later. "you can say handshake first true and then on the remote ... you would also define handshake first true and those have to be in agreement" (~13:18)
- NATS has four connection types: client, route (server-to-server within a cluster), gateway (cluster-to-cluster forming a supercluster), and leaf node. "you have a client connection ... route connections ... gateway connections ... leaf node connections" (~17:21)
- Traffic between servers in a cluster is always a single hop before landing on a subscriber. "it's always a single hop before it actually lands to a subscriber" (~18:21)
- Before 2.10 any two servers shared one TCP route connection, so a very active account could cause head-of-line blocking for other accounts sharing it. "any two pairs of servers only had a single TCP connection between them ... there can be some unintentional unfairness or head of line blocking" (~19:22)
- 2.10 "v2 routes" use multiple TCP connections per server pair out of the box: the system account is pinned to a dedicated connection and other accounts are spread over a pool of three. "you're going to get a pinned account for the system account ... and then there's going to be a pool size of three TCP connections" (~20:22)
- You can list specific accounts in the route config to pin each to its own dedicated TCP connection; throughput goes up "basically for free" but you should test in your environment. "there's going to be an additional TCP connection that actually gets pinned for that explicit account ... the throughput goes up significantly" (~21:22)
- Stream replicas must be placed within a single cluster; they cannot be spread across a supercluster. "when you define a stream the replicas have to be placed within the same cluster you can't spread replicas across a super cluster" (~22:23)
- The recommended scope of a cluster is a region (AZ-level fault tolerance); a supercluster spans regions. A "stretch cluster" spreads one cluster (e.g. 9 or 13 nodes) across regions to get multi-region stream replicas. "the scope of a cluster is typically regional a super cluster can span multiple regions ... we've been calling it the pattern as a stretch cluster" (~23:25)
- Route (and leaf node) compression is off by default; with `s2_auto` the server picks a compression level from measured round-trip time using RTT thresholds, and it adapts rather than pinning heavy compression after one bad RTT sample. "based on the round trip time between any two servers it's going to choose a level of compression that is appropriate" (~25:29)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- Even a three-node cluster can have asymmetric latency (A-B fast, A-C slow), and consensus must cope with that. "traffic between nodes A and B is significantly quicker than traffic that goes from A to C" (~14:14)
- NATS is deployed in heterogeneous environments (leaf nodes in cars, factories, oil rigs), unlike databases that assume sub-millisecond cloud links; this makes debugging dropped messages much harder. "we have leaf nodes running in cars ... on random edge devices in factories on oil rigs" (~15:16)
- Leaf nodes were not designed for IoT use cases, but that became their main purpose. "the leaf nodes being used for those IoT use cases in the first place because they were not designed for it and now it is their main purpose" (~17:18)
- Raft consensus traffic is itself carried over NATS between cluster nodes; with a single TCP route per server pair, application traffic and consensus traffic could block each other, and one account could effectively deny service to another. "what we don't want to happen is that application traffic gets stuck behind consensus traffic ... you don't want one to be able to cause a denial of service effectively to another" (~34:36)
- V2 routes give multiple connections per server pair; the server assigns accounts to routes automatically or an administrator can reserve a dedicated route for a latency-sensitive account. "the administrator can make that decision explicitly and say look this specific account is one that we care very deeply about having low latency for" (~35:38)
- Route head-of-line blocking is worse over the public internet or between cloud regions because of TCP congestion control; with V2 routes consensus stays up to date faster and application traffic moves faster, with no config required. "consensus stays up to date more quickly that application traffic makes around the cluster faster ... it works out of the box" (~36:38)
- Route and leaf compression uses fast algorithms with low CPU cost to gain network headroom; it is automatic on route and leaf connections in 2.10 and on by default for leaf nodes because they are assumed to be over longer, less reliable links. "it's by default for leaf nodes because it's the assumption that you're going to be over a longer distance" (~39:41)
- A stretch cluster is the regular clustering mechanism pushed across zones, regions or data centers (e.g. one nine-node cluster instead of three three-node clusters joined as a supercluster). "the alternative is that you just have a nine node cluster and it's the fact that it scales out of a specific location is what we refer to as the stretch clustering" (~42:42)
- In a supercluster each JetStream Raft group is bounded to one cluster, so persistence performance does not suffer from inter-region latency while global connectivity remains. "each JetStream group is only bounded to this specific cluster in a super cluster so ... persistence with JetStream does not suffer because you have more regions" (~43:43)
- Choose a stretch cluster when regulation requires data replicated consistently across regions and you accept higher-latency persistence; mirroring/sourcing across a supercluster gives similar reach but with secondary, eventually available copies. "you can achieve something similar with super clusters but then you need to include some mirroring and sourcing ... the guarantees around when the data will be available its consistency is a little different" (~44:45)
- Server tags let you dictate where stream replicas land, including anti-affinity across regions or providers, or you can let NATS place them. "you can actually tag the servers and say where the data lands ... or you can just say to NATS just do how you think" (~45:45)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02: Monolith to Modular Monolith with NATS.io**

- Because queue-group routing in a multi-region NATS system is RTT-aware, the closest responder answers without extra logic; one data fabric can stretch across EMEA and US regions instead of per-region load balancer pairs. "it also does RTT so round trip time responses... you could have the closest NATS service respond without any further logic" (~10:10)
- Embedding NATS in each modular-monolith instance and connecting instances effectively builds a cluster gradually. "connecting that instance to another modular monolith, you build a cluster out effectively in slow-mo" (~18:21)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP04: A Service Mesh Pattern for NATS.io**

- Service meshes fall apart in heterogeneous estates (Kubernetes plus VMware, Hyper-V, bare Linux, mainframes, telco packet-centric environments) because they are Kubernetes-centric. "is it Kubernetes centric at that point and is everything else a satellite" (~18:21)
- Request/reply across regions: several queue groups in different regions can subscribe to the same subject; the request is broadcast, each group picks one member, and the fastest reply wins. "whoever is the fastest responder on that subject that's the one that's actually going to come back" (~33:41)
- NATS sends requests to the closest responders relative to the ingress point on a region-by-region basis, giving geographic distribution for free. "it's going to transparently send it to the closest responders wherever that ingress point is" (~33:41)
- Anycast HTTP gateways in multiple regions all bridging to one NATS system yields one globally deployed service set where the nearest responder answers. "one set of services running globally and the nearest one responds to that gateway" (~36:45)
- If a region is down, routing fails over transparently; traffic stays local when it can and is routed remotely only when the responder exists elsewhere. "everything that can be local will be local and everything that needs to get routed... it will do that" (~38:47)
- Multi-region service mesh and multi-cluster Kubernetes are non-trivial and not out-of-the-box, in contrast to NATS's transparent cross-region routing. "how do you do a multi-cluster setup, it's non-trivial as far as I know" (~37:46)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP05: Exploring Powerful Client-side Features and Abstractions in NATS.io**

- Because KV and Object Store are streams, they inherit mirroring and replication: read-only mirrors can be pushed to edge locations and data flows per mirror definitions with no extra dependencies. "you can create mirrors, read-only mirrors and push it down to edge locations" (~57:07)
- KV data does not have to be local to be accessible: if the NATS system is JetStream-enabled, a client in another region can still read the bucket where the data is not present. "you can still access the key value store from a different location where the data isn't" (~64:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS as a ServiceMesh**

- Mesh-like functionality via NATS is not tied to Kubernetes; the speaker ran the same setup with Docker Compose, Kubernetes, and plain servers. "you can create a service mesh without Kubernetes as the basis" (~22:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP01S3: Going back to basics with core NATS!**

- Some customers with unusual cloud network setups do get an improvement from multiple connections; creating two client instances works fine for that. "some customers who have very specific network setups over the cloud providers ... for them it actually makes an improvement to have more connections" (~41:03)
- NATS has three "planes" (API: core/JetStream; security; topology); starting with all of them at once (JetStream over clustered leaf nodes with auth callout) piles on complexity, so start with a single server, one connection, and add features as they solve problems. "start with probably simple single server ... run an app with one connection ... make it use more features from there on" (~45:08)
- The scale path is incremental: core → JetStream, single server → cluster → leaf nodes/edge, unsecured → multi-tenancy with accounts. "you can scale it really easily from core NATS to JetStream, from single server to cluster, from cluster to leaf nodes" (~46:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03S3: NATS 2.11 Release**

- Distributed message tracing exists because in large topologies (leaf nodes, clusters, superclusters, account import/export, subject mappings) "where did my message go" previously required subscribing at many points. "you kind of needed to subscribe in different places in your system and check if messages are there and in which form" (~05:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS tools and benchmarking with JNM! NATS Community Office Hours (Reupload)**

- A NATS server can run on a Raspberry Pi or inside a vehicle; production examples cited are vehicles of a car brand, trains, taxi cabs in Europe, and oil drilling stations, all partially connected over cellular. "there's a vehicle of a certain manufacturer that literally actually a NATS server running in the vehicle" (~05:06)
- JetStream-enabled leaf nodes at the edge give store-and-forward: publishes are stored locally and guaranteed to be mirrored or sourced to the hub when connectivity returns, within milliseconds if the link is up. "it still is stored locally by the stream at the edge and reliably forwarded" (~06:08)
- Equivalent edge/mirroring behavior in Kafka or Pulsar requires extra JVM components (Kafka Streams, MirrorMaker, brokers plus bookkeepers plus zookeepers), which the speaker calls infrastructure sprawl. "JVMs as far as the eye can see" (~07:10)
- The NATS server is also a built-in MQTT server for edge devices, and switching a client from TCP to WebSocket (or secure WebSocket) is only a change of the connection URL scheme. "the NATS server is also an MQTT server built in ... changing two or three characters in a connection URL" (~21:26)
- In a cluster, bench publisher and subscriber connect to random servers; landing on the same server gives better numbers than being on different servers (extra route hop), so run several times or pin to one server for consistency. "if you happen to have your pub and your sub connecting to the same server you're going to get better numbers" (~54:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Pull Consumer Priority Groups: Overflow, Pinned & Prioritized**

- Overflow suits regional routing: local clients handle the common case and cross-region traffic is paid for only when locals genuinely fall behind. "you only pay for cross-region traffic when there's genuinely too much work for the locals to keep up" (~02:00)
- Tiers can be stacked with prioritized: US East priority 0, US West priority 1, EU West priority 2 only sees traffic when both US regions are quiet. "Put EU West at priority two, so it only ever sees traffic when both US regions are quiet" (~05:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Distributed Counters in NATS — Global Totals Without Locks**

- Multi-region aggregation: regional counters publish to their own subjects, a continental stream sources them with subject transforms, and a global stream sources the continental ones. "A continental stream sources both with subject transforms, and a global stream sources the continental ones" (~03:03)
- The demo runs seven nodes in a three-level hierarchy joined by leaf-node connections, with Europe both a leaf of global and a hub for Spain/France/England; counters written on a disconnected node converge to the correct total when it reconnects. "Everything converged and we have the right amount right when Europe came back up online" (~14:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Message Tracing | NATS 2.11**

- Event kinds identify the connection type: client, router (same cluster), gateway (other cluster), leaf node, JetStream, plus internal system and account kinds. "you can see your usual client, router, or gateway. And you also have leaf node and JetStream. And system and account are internal" (~04:05)
- A single leaf node reports itself as its own cluster in the server field. "since this is a single leaf node, it's its own cluster" (~05:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.11: What's New?**

- Tracing answers where a message goes across routes, gateways, leaf nodes, account import/export boundaries, and subject transforms; `nats trace subject` prints an IP-traceroute-like story. "you'll basically get a print out like doing an IP trace route" (~01:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Two-Node Engine with David & Byron**

- The Synadia two-node engine is not a general-purpose two-node NATS system; it is a standalone leadership election service for a two-node setup whose state lives in a NATS KV bucket. "this is not a general purpose two node NATS system" (~00:02)
- It runs a finite state machine with internal and external probes on each node; each node independently derives leader, follower, impaired, or leader-RX (constrained leadership) status. "both systems in independent time space will decide what status it should be" (~01:03)
- The engine is written in Go and can be embedded; it was embedded in Kine (the k3s datastore layer that replaces etcd) so two k3s nodes replicate a KV bucket and fail over, given a virtual IP in front. "the two node engine is actually embedded within the Kine layer that is the data store component of k3s" (~08:11)
- A two-node system has different constraints than three-node RAFT high availability. "with the two node system you have different constraints than you do with a three node with RAFT" (~10:13)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Future of NATS: Roadmap & Vision**

- Synadia frames three personas: developers want primitives (messaging, request-reply, data storage), architects decide where services and data are located (multi-cloud, geographies, edge), operators want fewer systems to run. "architecture from this perspective is just saying well where do we need these services and data to actually be located" (~06:16)
- NATS deployment shapes named: simple clusters, stretch clusters, superclusters across geos and clouds, and leaf nodes for hub-and-spoke, with leaf-node expansion planned for 2025. "You have simple clusters, stretch clusters as a thing, superclusters that can go multigeo and across clouds ... and leaf nodes" (~07:17)
- Multi-tenancy is built in: messages in one account never bleed across account boundaries, so you don't deploy many NATS systems for isolation; cross-account sharing is opt-in. "you can send and receive messages over subjects in that account that will never bleed over any other account boundary" (~07:17)
- "Edge" here means the user-defined edge (factory, car, a house), not CDNs or cloud edge; NATS and Nex run wherever the user defines their edge. "We're talking about the user the customer the user-defined edge wherever you want to run it" (~15:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — We need to talk about Microservices... (And how NATS.io can simplify things)**

- Queue groups work across clusters and superclusters: a request is first served by a responder in the local cluster and only goes outside if none exists, which gives geo load balancing plus automatic regional failover. "it's going to first try to see if there is anything that can respond ... in its local cluster and if not it's going to search outside" (~06:04)
- Subject mappings can also be scoped per cluster. "you can do things like set mappings for certain clusters" (~17:22)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — JetStream KV: A fascinating alternative to Redis...**

- Because a KV is a stream you get replication, mirror, source, mux/demux, multi-tenancy via accounts, and subject-based ACLs on buckets. "being able to mirror source mux and demux ... you get all the multi-tenancy with accounts" (~06:04)
- R1/R3/R5 replication lives within a single cluster; with R3 you can lose one node and still accept writes, lose two and still serve reads. "you can take one node down and still accept writes you can take two nodes down and still accept reads" (~17:13)
- Cross-region or leaf-node replication of a KV uses mirrors and sources, not the replica count. "if you want to go outside of a data center or ... into another region this is where mirroring and sourcing come into play" (~17:13)
- A KV mirror is an automatic read replica: NATS serves reads from the closest mirror and forwards writes to the origin leader with no application change. "NATS is smart enough to serve up requests from the closest mirror ... all of the writes are going to go through the leader" (~18:14)
- Demo latency: a get every second against a bucket in Azure Europe West from Southern California took about 200 ms; moving the bucket to AWS us-west-2 dropped it to about 40 ms. "we're getting about 200 milliseconds of latency" (~25:25)
- Keeping the bucket in Europe and adding a mirror in us-west-2 brought reads back to about 40 ms while writes still went through Europe. "we drop our reads to back to those 40 milliseconds ... all the writes are still going through Europe" (~27:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Give your Go app superpowers with an Embedded NATS Server**

- An embedded server can leaf-node to a remote/cloud NATS server so JetStream data written locally syncs to the cloud, with control over whether the network is used. "we might want to sync that over to the cloud on a remote NATS server ... we can actually do that with leaf nodes" (~05:06)
- To enable JetStream in an embedded server that also leaf-nodes to a cloud account, set a server name, JetStream true, and a JetStream domain so the local assets are addressable distinctly from the cloud's. "we need a JetStream domain to be able to identify all of these stream assets" (~20:20)
- The leaf node remote is configured as a LeafNode Remotes entry with the parsed URL of the cloud leaf endpoint (nats-leaf://connect.ngs.global for Synadia Cloud). "we want to connect to nats leaf connect.ngs.global" (~21:21)
- Once the leaf connects, the cloud side shows the embedded server's subscriptions, including the whole JetStream API under the embedded domain ($JS.embedded.API...), which is how the cloud can administer the local JetStream. "the whole JetStream API has been subscribed to under the embedded domain" (~22:23)
- A request from the cloud account reaches the in-process responder through the leaf node and the reply is forwarded back, so in-process connections remain fully reachable across the topology. "even though you're using in-process connections you could still reach in and all the NATS stuff kind of works" (~23:24)
- Publishes into the cloud account on the embedded stream's subjects are captured by the embedded stream because the subscription crossed the leaf connection. "this is again sending it to Synadia Cloud but this is actually being picked up by the embedded NATS server" (~24:26)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Transcending microservices with NATS | RethinkConn '22**

- Kubernetes works well in a high-throughput, low-latency data center, but NATS targets running clients or whole servers on small edge devices beyond that. "what if you have to be able to run clients or whole servers on small devices at the edge" (~03:04)
- NATS' security model is provider-agnostic; integrating with cloud-local services still requires obeying that cloud's IAM. "you have to obey their IAM permissions but as the connective mesh substrate ... you can't be locked into this perimeter mindset" (~10:12)
- NGS is a globally deployed supercluster across multiple clouds and regions; each regional cluster has a minimum of three servers, and clusters are networked together transparently. "at a minimum three per region and then you have multiple clusters across regions or across clouds" (~18:17)
- Browser apps connect directly to the NATS server over its native WebSocket support using the nats.ws library; the same messaging semantics flow over WebSocket without an intermediary. "you don't have to throw anything in between your application and the NATS server" (~20:20)
- A request from the demo client through NGS to a single service instance in Los Angeles (on Fly.io, connected to an AWS us-west node) had a 139 ms round trip. "the round trip time ... all the way to US West and then back is 139 milliseconds" (~22:21)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Seamless evolution across geos and clouds | RethinkConn '22**

- Scale and latency are usually treated as non-functional requirements, but in practice they are functional: the system has to work and respond in time; topology becomes a design lever once the technology lets you place services anywhere. "if you actually care about latency or scale it actually becomes arguably a functional requirement" (~00:00)
- With freedom of topology you can place services for data sovereignty or co-locate them with clients for ultra-low latency (e.g. factory floors), and topology directly affects network latency. "topology also impacts your network latency overall if you can place services in the right location" (~03:02)
- Location transparency: a request sent from anywhere is routed by subject to a responder wherever it is connected, replacing DNS/anycast, load balancers, and routing rules. "with DNS you'd have to use anycast and all kinds of really complicated technologies to make this work" (~04:03)
- NATS routes a request to a responder in the requester's own cluster when one exists, and otherwise to the next closest cluster geographically. "we'll find the next closest cluster geographically to respond to" (~05:05)
- A leaf node is still just a NATS server; it enables a hub-and-spoke model, can run anywhere, can itself be clustered, and links into the bigger cluster via a leaf node connection. "It's still just a NATS server ... it allows you to essentially create this hub and spoke model" (~06:06)
- A leaf node acts like a separate NATS system that extends yours with fine-grained control over what crosses the connection, which suits the edge, partner organizations, and anything outside the security perimeter. "fine-grain control over what transfers over that leaf node" (~07:07)
- Leaf-node bridging applies not only to core pub/sub but to data streaming, mirroring streams, and key-value stores. "we're talking data streaming, mirroring streams and key-value stores" (~08:07)
- Queue-group routing is cluster-local first: if any responder in the group is in the cluster the request entered, NATS responds from there instead of routing across gateway connections to other regions. "if there are any responders available in that same cluster ... it's going to immediately respond with one of those members" (~13:22)
- Co-locating a full cluster with the application in the same data center gives the lowest RTTs; the geo-aware routing works across clouds as well as regions. "you would even be able to get lower RTTs by having a cluster and an application that's co-located in the same data center" (~14:23)
- Data-sovereignty restrictions on in-flight data are handled by shaping the interest graph so only subscribers on a specific cluster care about that data, using superclusters or leaf nodes. "we really only want things that care about this particular data to exist on this cluster" (~16:24)
- A leaf node can establish multiple leaf connections into a single cluster or into multiple clusters, enabling hub-and-spoke or a leaf node acting as a bridge between two systems with transformation in between. "you can have a leaf node that creates multiple connections into multiple clusters" (~19:28)
- Leaf node connections bind to an account on the cluster side, so you can select all or part of that account's traffic to cross the leaf connection. "leaf nodes bind to an account on the cluster side ... I want all the traffic from this particular account or some of the traffic" (~20:30)
- Clients and services were flipped from NGS nodes to a local leaf node without changing the application; 24 leaf nodes on Fly.io extended NGS and services reconnected to their local leaf node. "24 leaf nodes all extending the NGS cluster deployed all over the place" (~24:34)
- With a regular account and no admin access you can extend a SaaS supercluster with your own leaf nodes; or leaf-node a single-region self-hosted system into NGS so edge traffic uses NGS's global footprint. "you can leaf node your system into NGS and have ... everything at the edge talking to NGS" (~25:37)
- NGS at the time ran roughly 72 servers across four clouds. "like 72 servers, like four different clouds" (~25:37)
- A leaf node is its own territory with its own permission boundary, data locality, and ownership of local services and data; it can run on phones, cars, or factory devices with full server capabilities co-located on the device. "the leaf node as its own little territory that has its own permission boundaries" (~26:37)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Where are we now and where to next? | RethinkConn '22**

- NATS is a single binary with no external dependencies that needs only TCP, so it runs on a Raspberry Pi, VMs, bare metal, on-prem, or cloud, and ties any combination together. "we just basically need TCP so given those two primitives we can tie together cloud, on-premise, edge" (~01:01)
- Real deployments include leaf nodes in restaurants, stores, and coffee shops over 5G, tying clouds together, factory floors, and in space. "we are even in space, we're on factory floors" (~02:03)
- Data needs mobility: move a stream, replicate it closer to the application, aggregate streams or KV stores, or mirror a subset. "we need to be able to move a stream, we need to be able to replicate a stream" (~08:10)
- Roadmap: multi-connection gateways between superclusters to better use long-haul links for performance and resilience, and a hub-and-spoke backbone from which superclusters extend. "imagine multi-connection gateways between these servers to better utilize these long-haul connections" (~12:15)
- Roadmap: leaf node compression so data leaving over constrained links (e.g. laptop Wi-Fi to NGS) is compressed automatically, and leaf node encryption so the intermediate system cannot see payloads. "as data leaves my security context it's encrypted, the general NATS system cannot see that payload" (~13:15)
- Roadmap "attraction": a KV store weighted to follow a moving application (e.g. a truck driving from the Midwest to the West Coast) by automatic mirror/migration so latency stays similar. "that KV store is automatically mirrored migrated to the West Coast" (~15:17)
- With NATS as the k3s state backend (replacing etcd via Kine), leaf-noding every remote k3s deployment gives central observability and command-and-control, effectively fleet management. "if I choose to leaf node into every single one of my remote k3s deployments I have observability and command and control from a central place" (~17:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Versioning and canary deployments with subject mapping | RethinkConn '22**

- Subject mapping on a leaf node connection lets a site publish to a plain local subject (inventory) that is remapped to a namespaced hub subject (inventory.storeID), so the site needs less knowledge about itself. "inventory dot store ID to just be mapped to inventory and so the locality has to know less information about itself" (~06:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extending stateful services to the edge | RethinkConn '22**

- Edge compute (workers, edge functions) still suffers central-store latency; the next problem is moving data close to compute at the edge, and large localized clusters holding data are not a great answer. "I still have the same latency problems in a lot of ways" (~03:05)
- A stream mirror is the construct for data locality: an origin stream lives in the cloud hub and a local device mirrors it, keeping access even when disconnected; the same applies to KV. "the mirror construct is exactly what we need to support data locality" (~07:10)
- Each leaf node can have its own JetStream domain, a separate namespace; a mirror is created there by referencing the hub's domain (NGS) as the mirror source. "every leaf node can have its own JetStream domain ... you create a mirror from that specifying the NGS domain" (~08:11)
- To get Redis-like tight RTTs from a JetStream KV, run leaf nodes near the application with local read replicas; you gain lower RTT and continued reads when the leaf node is disconnected from the hub. "when that leaf node gets disconnected from the hub it can still function and it can still read from its config" (~09:14)
- Reverse direction: small edge boxes (e.g. Raspberry Pis) use tight retention and store-and-forward via sourcing/mirroring into a hub stream with near-unlimited retention. "retention policy is pretty tight and we do a store and forward over to the hub in the cloud" (~11:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking connectivity from cloud to edge | RethinkConn '22**

- Latency is both processing time and distance from the request; an instantaneous response on the other side of the world still feels slow, so placement matters. "latency is both processing time and distance from the request" (~05:08)
- The demand is now multi-geo, multi-cloud, and intelligently edge-aware systems, and operating them at scale with observability and security is hard today. "we not only want now multi-geo but we're being asked to do multi-cloud and ... edge aware systems" (~06:09)
- Derek predicts edge will dwarf cloud by several orders of magnitude within about a decade, but edge is still early and siloed like early cloud. "I really do believe edge is going to dwarf cloud by several orders of magnitude" (~07:09)
- Kubernetes made multi-cloud approachable for compute; a similar technology is needed to treat all infrastructure the same across edge providers, clouds, geos, and your own edge (stores, factories, cars, satellites, ships, medical devices). "the ability to treat all infrastructure the same, any edge provider, any cloud provider across any geos" (~09:12)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Lightweight relational databases at the edge | RethinkConn '22**

- For edge friendliness the PoC uses embedded SQLite on disk, with DuckDB planned for OLAP-style queries; drivers can be extended to other databases. "let's use existing databases that work well there so this is actually using SQLite embedded" (~03:02)
- Intended architecture: mirror streams down to edge devices and run the projection process locally, joining across tables in a real database; the process resumes populating after disconnect and reconnect. "the nsql process can get disconnected from the server and then you reconnect and then it just keeps resuming" (~11:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Using NATS JetStream as a Kine backend for k3s | RethinkConn '22**

- Multiple edge k3s clusters (NYC, LA, Chicago) each used their own KV bucket on one shared NATS server at the distribution center. "run three clusters but back them all to the same NATS server" (~06:11)
- Extending to the cloud was done by reconfiguring the distribution-center server as a leaf node into NGS; store inventory then appeared in a cloud web app without VPN access. "reconfigure my NATS server here and have it point to NGS as a leaf node" (~07:13)
- The pattern generalizes to multiple distribution centers, NATS at the store level, store-to-store communication, and feeding data down from the top rather than only up from the edge. "you can feed in data from the top as opposed to pushing it all up through the bottom" (~11:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Short break and Q&A! | RethinkConn '22**

- Future vision: because NATS is inherently observable, the system could autonomously spin up services and data mirrors where requests originate (e.g. Japan) based on threshold modeling, instead of doing it manually. "we could make this totally autonomous" (~15:18)
- Mirrors and sources work across leaf node boundaries in both directions and can be daisy-chained: origin, a single leaf mirror, then five local replicas on a 6-million-square-foot factory floor for low-latency reads. "You can even daisy chain them" (~20:24)
- A leaf node is a special connection that binds to an account or credential to lock down what traffic crosses it; unlike clustering it is a separate NATS system with its own security domain. "a leaf node is a separate NATS system. So it has its own security domain" (~21:24)
- The server binary is identical for leaf, cluster, and supercluster roles; only the relationships (client, gateway, cluster, leaf node connection types) differ. "The binary is exactly the same" (~21:24)
- A supercluster can handle 10 million IoT devices with cloud-to-device subject routing; such topologies are being actively built with customers and can extend further with leaf nodes. "Can a supercluster handle ... 10 million devices ... The short answer is yes" (~27:35)
- NATS natively accepts MQTT connections; smart-infrastructure customers pull limited sensor data from factory floors into clusters that extend transparently from multi-cloud services. "NATS can natively accept MQTT connections" (~28:37)
- Mobile/web clients can connect directly (no load balancers, firewalls, or VPNs): the WebSocket client finds the nearest server, and back-end services are auto load balanced; proxying through a back end is optional for gating logic. "We don't have any load balancers, we don't have firewalls or VPNs" (~28:37)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Derek Collison RethinkConn 2025 Keynote and Closing Remarks**

- Synadia's stack is layered connectivity first, then data, then workloads, which is the reverse of stacks that start with workloads and bolt on networking and security. "we started with intelligent connectivity, then move to data and then workloads. This is the exact opposite of most approaches" (~00:50)
- EU financial customers with a single-region but multi-cloud requirement use NATS to span Azure, GCP and AWS inside one region. "single region but multiple cloud requirements... able to provide access to both Azure, GCP and AWS in single regions" (~02:00)
- Global microservices on NATS across regions, clouds and edge need no DNS tricks, load balancers, API gateways or service meshes. "no DNS tricks are needed, no load balancers or GSLBs, no API gateways, no service meshes are required" (~02:20)
- Leaf nodes give a logical and secure separation between organizations, companies and partners, which is the basis for fleet management. "leaf nodes are a superpower within the NATS ecosystem; they provide a logical and secure separation between organizations, companies, partners" (~02:35)
- Edge AI data-collection pattern: apps store data locally and NATS mirrors it to the cloud, self-healing after outages, so the app never handles transport. "data is stored locally and then the NATS system takes over and mirrors that into the cloud. It self-heals itself" (~04:20)
- Workloads (Nex) and connectors are federation-free and need no perimeter security model, which suits edge targets like Raspberry Pis and air-gapped sites where Kubernetes-style federation feels heavy. "these technologies in ecosystem are federation free. They don't require a perimeter-based security models" (~12:00)
- Leaf nodes were introduced specifically so any deployment can be extended arbitrarily; Nex and connectors build on that and inherit the NATS security model and topology flexibility. "one of the core visions that when Leaf Nodes was even introduced... being able to extend arbitrarily" (~14:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia CEO Derek Collison Keynote**

- Responders can come and go and be load balanced with geo awareness with no DNS tricks or global load balancers. "properly load balanced with geo awareness and no additional moving parts, no DNS tricks, no load balancers" (~02:30)
- A common customer deployment: a KV synchronously replicated in one region (possibly across all three major clouds in that region) with asynchronous digital twins transparently served on get; twins can come and go and the system adapts. "a key value store that is synchronously replicated in a single region but could be across all three major cloud providers... that also has asynchronous digital twins that are transparently accessed" (~03:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia Roadmap with Byron Ruth**

- Synadia Cloud runs on NGS, a multi-cloud, multi-geo NATS deployment; planned workload placement follows where client traffic originates. "NGS... a multi-cloud and multi-geo deployment of NATS" (~12:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: After event Q&A with Derek on Zoom**

- Synadia Cloud's global supercluster was near 20 billion messages per day in early 2024 and was expected to double within two months. "we're getting close to 20 billion messages a day" (~31:30)
- Advanced topologies are considered a four-hour workshop topic on their own. "Advanced topologies is like that's a 4-hour workshop in and of itself" (~34:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Event-Driven Systems Need a Security Gateway — Meet Synadia Protect for NATS**

- The gateway can be placed between websocket clients and the enterprise, inside the enterprise between clients, or between edge leaf nodes and the cloud hub. "security gateways applied between the edge domain, sensors, devices and whatnot and the cloud or hub domain" (~04:50)
- Deployment roles: a firewall in front of the core cluster for incoming leaf nodes and clients, internal domain traffic control, and protection of AI agent-to-agent traffic. "I want to ensure that whatever traffic comes in there, I block it or protect it before it hits the core cluster" (~10:40)
- The gateway is configured with a backend URL for the NATS server it fronts; for leaf nodes, the leaf points at the gateway's leaf port and the gateway connects to the hub's 7422 leaf port. "the leaf nodes point to the gateway and the gateway points to the actual leaf node connection in the hub" (~13:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking Connectivity - Hyper-Connectivity & The Intelligent Edge**

- Location-independent subject addressing lets a service be truly nomadic, moving from an on-prem or cloud data center to an edge site and still working. "truly nomadic in a sense where you can move it from some data center... over into an edge site and have it just work" (~07:50)
- Accounts make NATS securely multi-tenant so it can be a public utility inside an organization, solving the "Coke and Pepsi" problem logically; leaf nodes are the way to get physical isolation. "if you do want physical isolation... leaf nodes... another really good way to achieve physical isolation" (~13:20)
- Sourcing lets edge servers' local streams store-and-forward into one larger cloud stream (mux), or one cloud stream filter down into leaf-local streams with only relevant data (demux). "you can have one big stream in the cloud that then filters down into a stream inside of... an edge location that is data that's only relevant to them" (~20:40)
- Clusters are fully meshed; clients learn peers through gossip and fail over automatically; stream replicas survive a server loss with a new leader elected. "clients automatically know about the server's peers through our gossip protocol and can switch over" (~23:00)
- Clusters need not be three nodes; five and seven node clusters are used, all fully meshed. "you can do five nodes seven node clusters and they're all fully meshed together" (~23:40)
- Superclusters span geos, data centers and clouds; customers run a cluster per cloud so a cloud or multi-AZ outage doesn't take NATS down. "they want to have clusters in each kind of cloud so if a particular Cloud outage happens... they can still make sure NATS is up" (~24:00)
- A supercluster assumes one NATS system under one security and operational model; leaf nodes deliberately break that assumption. "the super cluster kind of assumes it's all one big NATS system... Leaf nodes kind of defy those rules" (~24:40)
- With a supercluster plus leaf nodes NATS still routes to a distant responder; the higher latency is the signal to redeploy the service closer, in a nearer cluster or the edge site. "latencies might be higher even though NATS figures it out and that's some insight... deploy this service closer" (~25:10)
- A leaf node extends a NATS system of any size, supports separate operational and security domains, and keeps operating without a hub connection. "it can operate normally without a connection to the hub" (~26:00)
- Leaf node uses: hub-and-spoke extension, bridging partner or OEM NATS systems, store-and-forward where a leaf-local stream is sourced or muxed by the hub, and command-and-control for fleets. "you'll have a stream inside of a leaf node... configure the hub to say... I want to replicate that stream maybe inside of a bigger stream" (~26:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — A New Way of Thinking | NATS 2.0 and Connectivity**

- Accounts were created by concentrating multi-tenancy at the subject router: a user authorizes into an account, a messaging sandbox, so Coke and Pepsi share infrastructure and never see each other's messages; sharing is a mutual export/import agreement. "accounts were born they're isolated meaning Coke and Pepsi can exist on the exact same infrastructure" (~15:40)
- Servers coordinate through a system account, sending messages like any application instead of adding protocol, even across a global supercluster; that account has the same auth and permissions as any other. "an individual server inside of a NATS system can have its own account... we just send messages" (~20:50)
- Clients learn the topology without DNS or configuration; clusters grow and shrink dynamically and clients are told without application code. "a client knows about the topology even if it wasn't in a DNS name or configured in the application" (~22:50)
- Most distributed systems work well with low RTT and high bandwidth but degrade on long RTTs; at large scale the coordination chatter alone can bring a system down even with little data flowing, which the supercluster gateway design (optimistic sends with interest-graph pruning) was built to avoid. "a lot of times just the chatter that's going back and forth on one of these systems actually brings the system down" (~24:40)
- Queue subscribers on a supercluster are geo-aware: the closest subgroup is chosen and if unavailable traffic fails over to the next closest cluster by RTT, with no change to decade-old applications. "understands the closest one and the closest subgroups and picks those automatically" (~25:20)
- Leaf nodes exist because groups resist being forced onto a shared utility; they let a team keep its own servers (sub-microsecond local latency sometimes) while bridging transparently into the shared supercluster. "leaf nodes is our answer to that it allows you to have your cake and eat it too" (~26:20)
- Leaf nodes extend superclusters hub-and-spoke and bridge separate security domains, so an IoT deployment with its own security can attach to a supercluster of backend services. "you are allowed to bridge separate security domains" (~26:50)
- Derek runs an unsecured local server bound only to 127.0.0.1 as a leaf into Synadia's supercluster for instant local tooling. "no security except for the fact that it's only running on 127.0.0.1" (~28:10)
- If requests from Asia are hitting west-coast responders, deploying responders in Asia makes the system route there automatically with no load balancers or cloud configuration. "you just deploy these service responders in Asia the system automatically will route request from Asia directly to those" (~29:30)
- The model is federated by design: multiple operators can run servers (e.g. Google, Amazon, Azure) and a user presents the same credentials to any of them. "it could have servers that are being operated by Google and by Amazon and by Azure yet as a user they all look the same" (~32:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - PowerFlex Solves Intermittent Connectivity at the Edge w/ NATS - RethinkConn 2025**

- PowerFlex runs one edge Kubernetes cluster per customer site; edge-to-cloud traffic migrated organically onto NATS after one engineer introduced it. "every customer of ours has their own edge Kubernetes cluster... all the traffic just kind of gradually started going towards NATS" (~02:02)
- Streams are split into named "domains" (e.g. orders); every edge site has the same set of streams and they source into the cloud. "every single edge site has these same streams and they're sourcing from one another" (~04:05)
- The key JetStream feature for them is guaranteed delivery when the internet drops; store-and-forward via stream sourcing over leaf nodes. "the guarantees of sends even when the internet connection goes out... that's become extremely useful time and time again" (~06:06)
- Each site's leaf node is a 3-server cluster; the cloud hub is a larger cluster; every server carries a unique server name. "each leaf node is a three node cluster of servers... our cloud cluster is obviously way bigger" (~08:10)
- Scale: about 500 leaf-node sites, each a 3-server cluster, connecting to one hub of about 13 servers. "we have about 500 leaf nodes... each leaf node is a three server cluster... one hub I think it's 13 servers" (~15:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - MachineMetrics on Industrial IoT & Predictive Analytics w/ NATS at RethinkConn 2025**

- The leaf-node hub-and-spoke model was the initial fit: every edge device communicates back into the cloud through a leaf node. "that works really nicely with the leaf node model that NATS provides. So that hub and spoke type of architecture" (~06:05)
- Goal of edge compute is location freedom: a service shouldn't have to be designed up front for edge or cloud, only constrained by resources. "we don't have to think first and foremost about where it's going to end up on the edge or in the cloud" (~14:17)
- They don't yet run JetStream on edge devices; today SQLite buffers data during outages, which forces a serialization/technology break, and JetStream on the edge would remove it. "with JetStream on the edge device it's the same technology, you just write it to NATS and it's going to be persisted until it's reconnected" (~16:19)
- Recommendation for IoT: the leaf node concept is a very good fit. "the leaf node concept is just a very good fit for IoT use cases" (~37:47)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS at the Edge with F1 Arcade**

- Each venue runs NATS as a leaf node talking to local services; they wrote a custom NestJS transport to get type-safe subjects. "one of our venues with NATS as a leaf node... we actually have a custom NestJS transport which we've used to give us type safety in our subjects" (~05:07)
- Plan: connect all venue leaf nodes to a centralized cluster hosted with Synadia. "plans to connect our venues which are essentially leaf nodes to a centralized cluster with Synadia" (~06:08)
- Each venue leaf node is 3 replica servers; streams are currently split across them but will be replicated on each for full failover; minimum spec cited as 2–4 CPUs and 8 GB RAM per server. "the minimum requirements something like two to four CPUs and 8 gig of RAM for each one" (~08:12)
- Outcome: dropped messages can be replayed and a venue losing connectivity loses no data. "if a message drops, we can replay it. If a venue loses connection, we don't lose data" (~08:12)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Franco Sabini from Fineco Bank on NATS**

- Deployment is two on-premises clusters in Milan, one for back end and one for front end, across two premises; cloud is not near-term. "we have two clusters on premises one for the back end one for the front end" (~02:05)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Jaxon Repp from HarperDB on NATS and distributed databases**

- Every HarperDB node is both a hub and runs leaf nodes, so a severed network (e.g. shop-floor firewall) leaves each side fully functional; on reconnect it converges as one system. "every node is a hub and runs leafs as well... if the network is severed to completely maintain all the functionality" (~05:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Nathan Mellis from Modzy on NATS as a foundational building block**

- The theme of their NATS adoption is topologies: clusters for HA, superclusters for multi-cloud/hybrid across geographies, leaf nodes at the edge. "the ability to do super clusters enables you to do multicloud or hybrid" (~07:09)
- A leaf node exposes a portion of the subject/JetStream space to an otherwise independent edge, enabling push-based self-updating configuration to ~10,000 devices without polling. "those changes can get automatically pushed down to 10,000 devices which can then all reconfigure themselves" (~08:10)
- Edge devices connect over a single WebSocket connection on port 443, so no extra firewall ports are needed. "we're actually doing it all over the websocket connection so the edge devices only ever have to talk on port 443" (~08:10)
- Connection balancing is left to NATS and Kubernetes, not an L4 load balancer. "we let NATS slash Kubernetes take care of it" (~09:12)
- Request/reply over a supercluster beats HTTP/gRPC for hybrid cloud: a request unanswered locally percolates out to the supercluster, avoiding per-region service deployments and a service mesh. "if the cluster that you're in knows how to answer it it will answer it if it doesn't that'll get percolated out to your super cluster" (~11:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Simple Solutions for Complex Problems - How Workiva uses NATS as a Microservices and RPC transport**

- Deployment: each VM ("drone") runs a local NATS daemon clustered with the others; services talk to localhost and cluster membership JSON is pulled from S3 at startup to set up routes. "each drone also has a NATS daemon running on it and those daemons are clustered together" (~22:28)
- Running NATS on localhost means only inter-server (route) traffic needs encryption, and same-host messages never hit the network. "we only have to worry about encryption between the NATS peers" (~23:29)
- A NATS daemon on every VM doesn't scale to hundreds of nodes; they'd move to a floating cluster or NATS on a subset of machines, which the service abstraction makes painless. "we don't really want to be running a NATS cluster of like hundreds of nodes" (~24:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | Pub Sub on the Power Grid**

- Compute is pushed to nodes at the grid edge so control loops (solar dips → battery compensates) run locally while data still flows back to the central office. "we want to distribute compute resources out at the edge of the electric grid" (~07:12)
- The microgrid lab currently publishes everything into a single NATS server, with a planned move to a NATS broker on every edge node (leaf-node style). "they're all publishing into right now a single NATS server but we are getting ready to push that out to every one of these nodes" (~16:29)
- Feeder-level bus and microgrid bus must be bridged carefully because a customer-owned microgrid exposes only capabilities, not internal components; the feeder sends rules (e.g. absorb 100 kW in an hour). "we're gonna have to build that bridge connectivity between both of those NATS buses and we've got to be careful" (~21:35)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Partner Talk - NATS on Akamai Cloud - RethinkConn 2025**

- A global stretched NATS cluster runs across ~40 Akamai compute regions on shared 2-core/4 GB VMs, showing the binary needs little horsepower. "these are what we call 4 gig Linodes which are shared instances... I think there's two cores and four gigs" (~05:07)
- Measured worst-case intra-cluster latency in the global stretch cluster: US West to Mumbai ~285 ms; São Paulo to Mumbai ~350 ms; most non-India regions under 100–200 ms; North America under 70 ms; US to Europe ~150 ms; LA to San Francisco 7 ms. "it's going to take US West about 285 milliseconds to reach Mumbai" (~09:13)
- Speaker frames these route latencies as the worst-case bound for data consistency in a stretched cluster (e.g. writing into LA becomes consistent globally in under a third of a second). "you can achieve consistency on your data if you're writing into Los Angeles... in a little bit under one-third of a second" (~09:13)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Go Beyond Kubernetes Native Events with NATS**

- NATS can be per-cluster (one per tenant) or one central server that receives all events and lets Sveltos distribute them. "user can have NATS deployed in a single cluster and all the events are pushed to that NATS server and from there distributed everywhere" (~05:13)
- Requested pattern: NATS in each managed cluster forwards events to a NATS server in the management cluster, which forwards on to external clients. "they are all forwarded to the management cluster and from the management cluster there is another NATS server which forwards" (~11:23)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Connectors – Seamlessly Integrate NATS with Other Systems**

- The connectors framework is built on top of workloads (Nex), so a connector can run in the cloud, on-prem, or at the edge. "we build the connectors framework on top of workloads. And this allowed us to basically run your connector anywhere" (~01:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Workloads - Distributed cloud-to-edge compute with NATS Execution Engine**

- Because NATS built the connectivity layer first and the data layer on top, Nex inherited security, replication, KV, and Object Store for free instead of re-implementing networking, firewalls, and security. "Nex inherited security. Nex inherited replication of data. It inherited KV. It inherited object store" (~03:12)
- "The edge" has no single definition (mainframe, cloud, ESP32 on a farm); workloads must be movable to whatever the user's edge is. "The edge is not concrete, but one of the key values of Nex was these workloads need to be able to move to whatever edge" (~06:16)
- Three nexlet deployment types: embedded (Go, compiled into a single binary), local (child process, any language, suits Rust-native Firecracker/microVM tooling), and remote (compiled agent shipped anywhere and kept alive by systemd, extending Nex to the far edge). "we've created a way that you can compile a nexlet, make it aware that it will be connecting remotely, you ship it to wherever you want" (~10:19)
- Synadia managed workloads run a Nex cluster ("nexus") in every NGS region; placement uses tags exactly like JetStream placement, so re-tagging moves a workload between clouds with near-zero downtime. "placement feels the same as JetStream... If you want a workload from AWS to Azure, you just tag it and it moves it for you" (~17:28)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Migrating from NATS Streaming to JetStream**

- File-store persistence survives restarts; clustered streams use Raft, an R3 stream tolerates one node down and R5 is the upper end. "If two nodes go offline, then you're stuck because that's what the Raft protocol allows. You can go up to five nodes." (~33:19)
- Consumer replica count inherits from the stream; a three-node cluster with one server per availability zone in one region tolerates a lost node or corrupted disk. "The consumer replicas actually inherit from the stream." (~59:51)
- NGS is a globally deployed cluster across the three major clouds in about 13 regions, extendable with leaf nodes. "Across all three cloud major cloud providers across I think it's 13 regions." (~62:56)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS KubeCon Tutorial on Twitch**

- With 2.x, gateway connections join clusters into a supercluster; servers route by interest, so a subscriber in Berlin receives a publish from San Diego. "You can have a multi region and then have a gateway connection... between many of these clusters." (~19:33)
- For queue groups across a supercluster, the server prefers a local queue subscriber and otherwise forwards to another cluster chosen by RTT, giving lowest-latency load balancing. "It is going to be able to determine, based on the RTT, which is the appropriate load balancer node." (~19:33)
- Leaf nodes act like a proxy that is itself NATS; an edge device that can't afford expensive auth connects to a sidecar leaf node which holds the secure TLS link to the supercluster. "You can connect them to your own attached... sidecar leaf node and then this other leaf node will have the secure TLS connection." (~20:35)
- IBM modelled satellites as leaf nodes connected to a ground supercluster so satellites could talk to each other through it. "Multiple satellites on the edge be able to... communicate... all through the same supercluster." (~21:36)
- The "NATS adaptive edge architecture": a central cloud supercluster with edge clusters attached by a single leaf-node connection, so edge sites keep communicating locally while consuming cloud-only services. "A centralized supercluster... and you can connect your edge devices or your local superclusters on the edge with a single leaf node connection." (~22:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Zen of High Performance Messaging with NATS by Waldemar Quevedo Salinas**

- A full-mesh cluster removes the single point of failure; clients reconnect to another server, and newer clients learn cluster topology dynamically as servers join. "The original server will notify all of the clients where is the new member from the cluster." (~22:39)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — SCaLE 13x Derek Collison  NATS A new nervous system for distributed cloud platforms**

- Clustering is full-mesh one-hop (every server links to every other), not a DAG; routes only need one side to initiate and become bidirectional once established. "NATS is a full mesh one hop clustering mechanism." (~23:30)
- Clients are cluster-aware without DNS or load balancers: given a server pool they pick randomly and reconnect to another on failure, typically in 10–15 ms once the socket drop is seen. "The reconnect speed is usually about ten fifteen milliseconds or so." (~35:54)
- Distributed queuing works across the cluster: queue group members can attach to any server, unlike early EMS where you had to attach to the queue's home server. "You can attach to any server you want... and it just works." (~24:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Native MQTT Support in NATS Server**

- A local NATS server with MQTT can leaf-node into NGS; `connect.ngs.global` attaches to the geographically closest cluster. "The connect.ngs.global URL will connect it to the closest cluster in NGS." (~06:10)
- Queue groups across a supercluster prefer the member local to where data enters; when that member stops, messages fail over to the member connected in Japan. "As soon as we do that then the new messages are automatically routed to the other member." (~07:11)

## SEC: Security: accounts, auth, permissions, TLS (1041 claims)


**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — What is NATS**

- A client needs only a NATS URL (IP/port + connection kind: plain TCP, TLS, or WebSocket) and, if needed, authentication (username/password, decentralized JWT, token, TLS certificates, NKey with challenge).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Compare NATS**

- "NATS supports true multi-tenancy and decentralized security through accounts and defining shared streams and services." Kafka: "Multi-tenancy is not supported." Pulsar tenants: no built-in cross-tenant data sharing. Rabbit vhosts: no data sharing.
