- NATS AuthZ: account limits (connections, message size, imports/exports count), user-level pub/sub permissions, connection restrictions, CIDR restrictions, time-of-day restrictions.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject-Based Messaging**

- Subject filtering happens in many places: per-user allow/deny, account import/export, automatic transformations, stream ingest, sourcing/mirroring, leaf node connections. "A well-designed subject hierarchy will make the job a lot easier".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Security (concept)**

- Authentication options: token, username/password, TLS certificate, NKEY with challenge, decentralized JWT, and auth callout to integrate an existing auth system.
- Accounts provide multi-tenancy: "each account has its own independent 'subject namespace'" with controlled import/export of streams and services between accounts.
- JWT administration is decentralized: account private key holders mint user JWTs themselves "without the need for any configuration change on the NATS servers"; the server never stores user private keys and only validates the signature chain of trust.
- JetStream provides encryption at rest.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS Adaptive Deployment Architectures**

- "Leaf nodes appear to the cluster as a single account connection."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Consumers**

- Granular permissions: single filter uses `$JS.API.CONSUMER.CREATE.{stream}.{consumer}.{filter}`; multiple filters use `$JS.API.CONSUMER.DURABLE.CREATE.{stream}.{consumer}` without the filter token, so "Use a different strategy for granular permissions."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Source and Mirror Streams**

- Another use case: connecting streams cross-account.
- 2.14 "bring your own" sourcing consumer (`Consumer.Name`, `Consumer.DeliverSubject`) must use `AckFlowControl`; useful for monitoring or "when you're not in control of 'the other side' ... from a security point of view."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject Mapping and Transforms**

- With config-file accounts, reload the config to apply transform changes; with operator JWT, transforms and imports/exports live in the account JWT and apply when pushed.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Clustering Configuration**

- Cluster `tls`: "`verify` is always enabled and `cert_file` is used for client and server."
- Route `authorization` with a single username/password applies to discovered routes only; explicit routes need credentials in the URL. "either use the same credentials throughout the system or list every route explicitly on every server." `users` and `token` are not supported and prevent startup; `permissions` is ignored.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — TLS Authentication in clusters**

- Cluster TLS verifies certificates in both directions; cluster identity certs can be separate from client-facing certs.
- "TLS Mutual Authentication is the only way of securing routes."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Clustering**

- A system account (`$SYS`) user/password should be configured (example uses a bcrypted password).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Administration (cluster)**

- Meta group management (step-down, peer-remove, `nats server report jetstream`) requires a SYSTEM user; system users see the meta group but not individual streams/consumers.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Troubleshooting**

- "Make sure that ... at least one system user is configured" under `$SYS`.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Gateway Configuration**

- `reject_unknown_cluster: true` rejects connections from clusters not listed in `gateways`, disabling gossip of new clusters (but not growth of configured ones).
- Gateway `tls`: "`verify` is always enabled". Authorization: single user/password for discovered gateways only; explicit gateways need creds in URL; `users`/`token` unsupported; `permissions` ignored.
- Certificate rotation: clusters rarely rotate at the same time; "Make sure that the ca_file contains both old and new root or intermediate CAs." Using only the CA from an issuance bundle "is ill-advised"; keep a separate verification bundle so "when DC-B rolls before DC-A, it will not be cut off from your supercluster." Reload config to apply.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Leaf Nodes**

- A leaf node "extends an existing NATS system of any size, optionally bridging both operator and security domains"; it authenticates local clients with local policy and routes to one or more remote systems.
- Traffic between leaf and cluster takes the restrictions of the user used for the leaf connection: subjects the user may publish are exported to the cluster; subjects it may subscribe to are imported into the leaf.
- Restrict leaf import/export by limiting what the leaf connection user can publish/subscribe.
- TLS-first handshake (2.10.0): normally the server sends INFO in clear text first; `handshake_first` avoids any clear-text traffic when websocket isn't desired.
- NGS free account example limits: 10 connections, leaf nodes not allowed, 1.0 GB data, 2 exports, 7 imports, 1.0 kB max payload, 10 subscriptions.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — LeafNode Configuration**

- `handshake_first: true` must be set on both accepting side and remote; a mismatch fails the connection in either direction.
- Leaf connections can authenticate against any user account on the hub; the dedicated authorization block is optional. Singleton mode binds all leaf connections to one account (which must exist); multi-users mode binds per user; an `account`-only block binds credential-less connections.
- Remote `account` selects which local account is bound to the remote; `deny_imports`/`deny_exports` block subject propagation per direction.
- `verify_and_map` maps certificate values to a user for auth; `cipher_suites` must match the Go version used to build the server.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream on Leaf Nodes (domains)**

- Connecting system accounts across a leaf link gives: monitoring of all servers, account resolver across the network, and "extended JetStream cluster". "You probably don't want to connect your cloud and edge device system accounts" except when only firewalls prevent a super-cluster.
- Cross-account JetStream import renames `$JS.hub.API` to e.g. `JS.acc@hub.API`; "the general recommendation is to export the domain specific API `$JS.<domain>.API` as this allows you to pin the export to a particular domain."
- "Known issue: Currently, across accounts, push consumer are not supported."
- Minimum cross-account exports for source/mirror: `$JS.<domain>.API.CONSUMER.CREATE.*` (service, response_type stream), a delivery stream `deliver.<acc>.<domain>.>`, and `$JS.FC.<stream>.<consumer>.>`; for client pull consumers add `$JS.<domain>.API.CONSUMER.MSG.NEXT.<stream>.<consumer>` and `$JS.ACK.<stream>.<consumer>.>`.
- Delivery prefix convention to avoid overlaps across multiple imports: `<static type>.<exporting account>.<exporting domain>.<importing account>.<importing domain>.<importing stream name>`.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Configuring JetStream (resource management)**

- JetStream is compatible with NATS 2.0 multi-tenancy: "fully isolated JetStream environments for different accounts."
- Without accounts enabled, "all users in the server would have access to JetStream." Per-account limits: `max_mem`, `max_file`, `max_streams`, `max_consumers` (example 512M / 1G / 10 / 100).
- Configuring JetStream for an account without global enablement warns; "the account designated as System cannot have JetStream enabled."
- In operator mode account JetStream limits live in the account JWT (`nsc edit account --js-mem-storage 1G --js-disk-storage 512M --js-streams 10 --js-consumer 100`).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Configuration (server config reference)**

- Encryption at rest: `cipher` `chacha`/`chachapoly` or `aes` (2.3.0); key of at least 32 bytes recommended; `prev_encryption_key` (2.10.0) for rotation. TPM-based encryption (2.11.0) with `keys_file`, `encryption_password`, `pcr` default 22.
- Account JetStream settings: `max_memory`/`max_file` (sums must be under the server limit), `max_streams`, `max_consumers` ("per stream(!)"), `max_ack_pending` (2.8.0), `max_bytes_required` (2.7.0, default false), `store_max_stream_bytes`/`memory_max_stream_bytes` (2.8.0).
- A default server has no auth; default account is `$G`; once any user is configured, `$G` and no-auth access are disabled unless `no_auth_user` is set.
- Accounts: "Each account forms its own subject and stream namespace, with no data shared unless explicit import and export is configured."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Enabling Monitoring**

- "`nats-server` does not have authentication/authorization for the monitoring endpoint. When you plan to open your nats-server to the internet make sure to not expose the monitoring port as well." Monitoring binds `0.0.0.0` by default; bind to localhost or firewall it.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — System Events (system account)**

- System events (connect/disconnect, auth errors, shutdown, stats) require configuring `system_account` and using a system-account user; accounts keep app subscriptions like `>` from receiving system events.
- "The default global account `$G` does not publish advisories."
- `$SYS.ACCOUNT.<id>.CLAIMS.UPDATE` is how account servers push updated JWT claims to servers.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — System Events & Decentralized JWT Tutorial**

- Uses `nats-account-server` (URL resolver `resolver: URL(...)`) to vend JWTs; `system_account` holds the account public key.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Multi Tenancy using Accounts**

- Accounts are "securely isolated communication contexts that allow multi-tenancy"; "data silos are created by design, not software limitations", with controlled exchange between them.
- With traditional authorization "all clients can publish and subscribe to anything unless explicitly configured otherwise"; accounts make the subject space non-global so "clients can use short subjects without explicit authorization rules."
- "think of one account as a messaging container for one application ... more accounts with few (even one) clients is a better design topology than a large account with many users with complex authorization configuration."
- Exports: streams (messages you publish; importers can consume but not request) and services (requests fulfilled by your account). Export `accounts` list makes it private; unspecified = public. `response_type` `single` or `stream`.
- The term "stream" in import/export "does not refer to ... a JetStream stream"; it predates JetStream and means a stream of Core NATS messages.
- Imports need a matching export; "Accounts cannot do self-imports." `prefix` remaps stream imports (wildcards allowed, so only a prefix can be applied); `to` remaps service imports ("Currently, a service import can not make use of wildcards").
- "Typically an account will export a wildcard service but then coordinate with a client account on specific subjects where requests will be answered."
- `no_auth_user` maps unauthenticated clients to a user; "will not work with nkeys or bcrypted passwords"; the auth timeout still applies to the no-credentials handshake and slow links may hit "Authentication Timeout".
- Cross-account JetStream: "in most use cases people want a setup where a stream in one account is mirrored or sourced in another account ... as this is a more 'locked-down' way to share messages", rather than letting apps use a stream in another account directly. References synadia-labs/cross-account-jetstream-sourcing (static security, "probably the best one to start with") and jetstream-leaf-nodes-demo (operator mode).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Authorization**

- Per-user `publish`/`subscribe` permissions; `subscribe` entries may carry a queue name (`<subject> <queue>`) with wildcards; `default_permissions` applies to users without explicit permissions.
- Permission map `allow`/`deny`; "In case of overlap deny has priority."
- "It is important to not break request-reply patterns": add `_INBOX.>` rules, or use `allow_responses`. Unauthorized pub/sub fails, is logged, and errors back to the client.
- `allow_responses: true` = `{max: 1}` with no time limit; a map allows `max` and `expires`. It "implicitly denies publish to other subjects" except explicit publish allows.
- With `allow_responses` "the reply subject is not constrained to the publish allow or deny list"; for explicit control "do not use allow_responses and instead define allow/deny lists under the publish permission map."
- Any client allowed to subscribe to `_INBOX.>` "can receive all responses published"; sensitive installs should narrow the inbox prefix or use accounts for isolation.
- Queue permissions: allow `"foo queue"` restricts subscribing to foo only inside that queue; `deny: ["> *.prod"]` blocks prod queue groups; `"foo *.dev"` limits queue names by wildcard.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Authentication (intro), timeout, tokens, username/password, NKeys, TLS auth**

- Auth is multi-level: accounts with users; JWT mode adds an operator. Each account is an independent subject namespace; users share it but can be restricted.
- Auth methods: token, plain or bcrypted username/password, TLS certificate, NKEY challenge, decentralized JWT; all but JWT are configured in `authorization`.
- Auth `timeout` default is 1 second more than `tls_timeout`; invalid values default to 1s; numeric seconds only (fractional ok). "long timeouts can be an opportunity for abuse"; must exceed the TLS timeout since it includes the TLS upgrade.
- Tokens can be bcrypted (`nats server passwd`) so clear-text isn't in the config; clients still send the clear token. Token auth also works for clusters.
- Bcrypted passwords supported; reload with `nats-server --signal reload` without disconnecting clients.
- NKeys (Ed25519): server never stores private keys; random challenge per connection makes it "immune to playback attacks". "NKey is an excellent replacement for token authentication". Seeds start with `S`, user public keys with `U`.
- TLS `verify` checks the client cert against `ca_file` (system trust store if absent) and requires extended key usage "TLS Web Client Authentication". `verify` and `verify_and_map` do not apply to the monitoring port.
- `verify_and_map` searches SAN emails first, then DNS names, then the certificate subject (RFC 2253 DN, attribute order matters); "This mechanism will pick the user it finds first. There is no configuration to restrict this."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Enabling TLS**

- TLS defaults: `min_version "1.2"`, handshake `timeout` 2 seconds; `ca_file` absent = system trust store; `insecure` skips verification for outgoing connections only and is "NOT Recommended".
- `verify_cert_and_check_known_urls` (cluster/gateway only) matches cert SAN DNS entries against configured route/gateway URLs; "dynamic cluster growth may require config changes in other clusters where this flag is true"; wildcard SANs keep growth flexible.
- `pinned_certs` restricts accepted certs to listed SHA256 public-key fingerprints.
- Root `tls` also applies to the monitoring port when `https_port` is set; cluster/gateway/leaf blocks can have their own.
- Certificate rotation: "Make sure that the ca_file contains both old and new root or intermediate CAs"; reload config to apply file changes.
- TLS-first handshake (2.10.4) `handshake_first: true|auto|<duration>`; `auto` falls back to INFO after 50 milliseconds; only `true` guarantees no plaintext, and requires upgraded client libraries. TLS-first clients are marked in Connz.
- TLS `timeout`: increase if clients disconnect during handshake, but "an extended timeout exposes your server to attacks where a client doesn't upgrade to TLS and thus consumes resources."
- `connection_rate_limit` (2.7.0) caps new TLS client connections per second server-wide (example 1000); excess get "Connection throttling is active. Please try again later."; default 0 disables; not applied to cluster/gateway/leaf/websocket/MQTT listeners. Rationale: "TLS handshakes are expensive, and a burst of reconnecting clients can keep the server busy".
- Trust both active and standby intermediates in `ca_file` "to be prepared for such a day" when the CA switches.
- Self-signed certs: "DO NOT USE these certificates in production!!!" Use a public CA if outsiders connect, in-house CA for internal apps, environment CA (e.g. Kubernetes) for a single environment.
- Cluster advertises IPs by default, which "may result in a failed TLS hostname verification with an IP SANs error"; set `advertise`/`cluster_advertise` to verifiable names.
- The connecting IP/DNS must match a SAN or the handshake fails.
- Key usage: server needs "TLS WWW server authentication"; clients need "TLS WWW client authentication" when verify is on. "Cluster connections always have verify enabled ... Certificates containing both values are a must." Gateways always verify but may use a separate outgoing cert.
- Behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy configure `tls {}` plus `allow_non_tls: true`; minimum client versions: nats.go v1.31.0, nats.js 2024.1.2, nats.java 2.18.0, nats.rs 0.33, nats.net.v2 2.0.0, nats.net v1 1.1.5.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — OCSP Stapling**

- OCSP stapling is honored by default (`auto` mode) for Must-Staple certs; modes `auto`, `must` (shutdown on revoked), `always` (all certs, shutdown on revoked), `never`. `url` overrides the responder in the cert.
- Staples are cached on disk in `store_dir` (shared with JetStream if enabled) so restarts don't refetch.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Decentralized JWT Authentication/Authorization**

- JWT auth moves user/account config out of server files into signed tokens: "Users are not directly tracked by the server, but rather verified as and belonging to an Account", enabling user management "without requiring server configuration updates."
- Isolation and import/export of accounts remain; JWT adds expiration and revocation.
- NATS JWTs must be Ed25519-signed; Issuer and Subject are public NKEYs; roles Operator -> Account -> User form a chain of trust; servers trust specific operators.
- Authentication: user presents account-issued JWT, signs a server nonce, server fetches account JWT, checks issuer chain to a trusted operator.
- "NATS JWTs are only used as configuration", not as sessions or proof of authentication; identity proof is the nonce signature.
- Fully decentralized: operator admins issue account JWTs to prod/dev teams who issue their own users; "Neither entity has to be aware of the other's private Nkey."
- JWT and NKEY/account-config auth can be mixed.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Account lookup using Resolver / Memory Resolver**

- Three resolvers: NATS-based ("the preferred option and should be your default selection"), `MEMORY` (static accounts in config), `URL` (build your own account service; standalone nats-account-server "is now legacy").
- NATS-based resolver stores JWTs in a local, not shared, directory ("you can't have more than one nats-servers using the same directory"); all servers in the cluster/super-cluster must use it; sync is eventually consistent via the system account.
- `full` resolver: `allow_delete` (default false; deletes rename to `.delete`), `interval "2m"` state comparison with one random peer, `limit 1000` JWTs. "Not every server in a cluster needs to be set to full. You need enough to still serve your workload adequately, while some servers are offline."
- `cache` resolver: LRU subset, `limit 1000`, `ttl "2m"`; "does NOT accept account push messages from nsc and therefore is not suitable for stand-alone operation without a full resolver present."
- Integration subjects: `$SYS.REQ.CLAIMS.UPDATE` to push a JWT; subscribe `$SYS.REQ.ACCOUNT.*.CLAIMS.LOOKUP` to implement an account server.
- Migration from REST account server: `nsc pull`, reconfigure to nats resolver, `nsc edit operator --account-jwt-server-url nats://...`, `nsc push -A`.
- "The MEMORY resolver is recommended when the server has a small number of accounts that don't change very often"; supports config reload of preloads; `nsc generate config --mem-resolver` generates it.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Mixed Authentication/Authorization Setup**

- To mix static NKEY config and operator JWT auth: first prepare the trusted-operator setup, reuse the same account public NKEYs in the static config, and bridge the two servers via cluster routes during transition.
- "Even though they have different authorization mechanisms, these two servers are able to route account messages because they share the same NKEY."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Auth Callout**

- Auth callout delegates client authentication/authorization to an application-defined NATS service, for external IAM (LDAP, SAML, OAuth, a database, or a file).
- Order: implement the service, plan migration, then configure; "enabling the configuration before deploying a service could cause issues for existing systems."
- In centralized mode "existing users defined in the config file will be ignored"; the auth service must authenticate all users including system account users and the implicit no-auth user, so port users first.
- Config: `authorization { auth_callout { issuer, auth_users, account (default $G), xkey } }`.
- "For new setups, it is recommended to use explicit accounts": an `AUTH` account for callout users, `APP` accounts for applications instead of `$G`, and `SYS` as system account.
- `xkey` (x25519) encryption of payloads "is recommended as a security best practice, but not required"; the server generates a one-time XKey per connection which "prevents replay attacks".
- "Decentralized Auth: Coming soon!"
- Response claims carry a user JWT used "for the duration of the client connection"; `issuer_account` indicates a signing key was used.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Managing NATS Security**

- "you should use a 'signing key' to create the account JWTs (as singing keys can be revoked/rotated easily)".
- Delete accounts via `$SYS.REQ.CLAIMS.DELETE` with `allow_delete: true` in the resolver.
- "The system is just like any other account, the only difference is that it is listed as system account in the operator's JWT (and the server config)."
- JWTs can be created programmatically with Go nkeys/jwt libraries and Java NKey/JwtUtils.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Profiling NATS**

- The `prof_port` endpoint has no auth, binds `0.0.0.0` by default, must not be exposed to the internet; it does not support config reload.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Administration (CLI intro), Account Information**

- "JetStream is multi-tenant so you will need to check that your account is enabled for JetStream and is not limited" (`nats account info` shows memory/storage/streams/consumers limits).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Encryption at Rest**

- "although encryption at rest by the NATS server is fully supported, we recommend using file system encryption where available" because it is throughput-optimized, adds no server burden, and removes secret management from NATS.
- Ciphers: `chachapoly` (ChaCha20-Poly1305) and `aes` (AES-GCM); encrypts message blocks (headers+payloads) and stream/consumer metadata files.
- Provide the key via an environment variable (e.g. `$JS_KEY`) "so it will not be persisted in a file."
- Enabling on existing data encrypts only new blocks; back up and restore to re-encrypt old blocks. Restarting with a different or no key fails decryption ("message authentication failed") and breaks JetStream but core NATS still works. Cipher can change if the key stays the same.
- Performance cost observed from "as little as 1% decrease to more than 30%" on a MacBook Pro test; encrypted files may be larger.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Monitoring (endpoints reference)**

- Monitoring has no auth and binds `0.0.0.0` by default; don't expose it to the internet.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Environmental considerations**

- "if you want to use TLS for authentication you do not want the load balancer to be the TLS termination point."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Running**

- With no flags the server listens on 4222 with security disabled. The Docker image's default config enables monitoring on 8222 and routes on 6222; it warns "Cluster name was dynamically generated, consider setting one".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — WebSocket Configuration**

- WebSocket "TLS configuration is required by default"; `no_tls: true` only for test environments.
- `same_origin` (default false) and `allowed_origins` only apply when the request carries an Origin header (browsers).
- `jwt_cookie`: an HTTP server can set a NATS Bearer user JWT in a secure cookie after its own authentication, so browser clients authenticate without embedding credentials.
- WebSocket-level `no_auth_user` overrides the main one for websocket clients; "not compatible with running the server in operator mode."
- `allowed_connection_types` (aliases `connection_types`, `clients`) restricts a user to `STANDARD`, `WEBSOCKET`, `LEAFNODE`, `MQTT`; absence allows all.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — MQTT**

- Permissions for MQTT users are written as NATS subjects (conversion happens before authz); QoS 1 subscriptions need subscribe permission on `$MQTT.sub.>`.
- MQTT requires a unique `server_name`. In operator mode MQTT clients cannot sign the nonce, so pass a Bearer user JWT (`nsc edit user --bearer`) as the MQTT password with any non-empty username.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — FAQ**

- TLS negotiation CPU during a thundering herd "is usually the constraint limiting the number of connections a single server should support"; mitigate with TLS-accelerated cipher suites (AES on x86) and reconnect jitter/delay ranges.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Connecting to a Cluster / timeouts / misc / name / noecho / ping-pong / security**

- A credentials file bundles the user JWT and NKey seed and "should be protected because it contains a private key."
- NKey challenge-response "protects the private key from the server, which never has access to it!"
- A TLS-mode server requires TLS from all clients; a TLS-configured client fails against a non-TLS server. Using just a `tls://` URL "is very likely to fail" unless the language's TLS defaults find the CA.
- Tokens "are only as safe as they are secret ... It is highly recommended to use one of the other NATS authentication mechanisms."
- Bcrypted passwords in server config; client still sends plain text; `nats://user:password@server:port` URL form.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS API Reference (JetStream wire API)**

- Subject patterns are designed so ACLs can "limit users to a specific Stream or Consumer and to specific verbs"; response permissions ensure only the receiver of a message can Ack it.
- Classic source/mirror uses 5 subjects: `$JS.API.CONSUMER.CREATE.<stream>[.<consumer>.<filter>]` (outbound), `$JS.FC.<stream>.>` (outbound), `$JSC.R.<uid>` (inbound reply), `$JS.S.<uid>`/`$JS.M.<uid>`/custom deliver (inbound). "all 5 subjects may need to be considered" for permissions/imports.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — nats CLI / nats-top / nk**

- Use `nats context` to store server URLs and credentials; passwords can come from `NATS_PASSWORD` or a prompt so they don't appear in `ps`/history.
- NKeys: server verifies identity "without ever storing secrets on the server"; seeds (`S...`) are secrets, public keys (`U...`) are shareable.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — nsc (basics, streams, services, signing keys, revocation, managed operators), NATS tools overview**

- Hierarchy: Operators run servers and issue account JWTs and set account limits (connections, data); Accounts issue user JWTs and define exports/imports; Users encode limits and authorization over the account's subject space.
- nsc directories: `~/.nsc` home, `~/.nkeys` (private keys and creds; "should be treated as secrets"), stores in `$NSC_HOME/nats` ("can stored under revision control. The JWTs themselves do not contain any secrets").
- Stream exports forward messages published on the exported subject to importers; stream imports can be prefixed with `--local-subject`; "Self-imports are not valid".
- With the built-in NATS resolver you must `nsc push` local account changes for them to take effect.
- Private exports (`--private`) require an activation token (a JWT signed by the exporting account) per importing account; the token can also "subset the exported stream's subject" and be hosted at a stable URL so updates propagate.
- Service import: local subject may differ; the request is forwarded on the remote subject.
- "if someone gets a hold of an account or operator nkey they can do everything you can do as you."
- Signing keys are "the first and most important line of defense": a JWT is valid if signed by the issuer's subject or one of its signing keys, so the operator/account identity key can be guarded more closely. On compromise: remove the signing key, reissue the entity, and reissue every JWT it signed ("effectively a large hammer"); mitigate by having many signing keys and rotating them.
- "On a production environment private keys should be saved to a file and always referenced from the secured file." nsc doesn't track private signing keys; you must manage them.
- Scoped signing keys attach a permission set to a signing key; users signed with it "must not have any permissions assigned"; updating the key's permissions "will immediately update permissions for users signed with that key."
- Template functions (2.9.0) `{{name()}}`, `{{subject()}}`, `{{account-name()}}`, `{{account-subject()}}`, `{{tag(key)}}` give per-user subjects (e.g. `pam.>`) from one scoped key.
- Revocations live in the account JWT; users are revoked by public key and time, activations per account and time: JWTs issued before T are invalid, later ones valid, so you can "revoke a user and renew their access at the same time." Deleting a revocation is permanent and should only happen if the tokens expired. Pushing a revocation immediately terminates matching connections.
- Managed operators (e.g. NGS) hold the operator key; they may add limits or imports to your account JWT ("the operator gets the final call on all Account edits"); `nsc push`/`pull` keep local and server JWTs in sync.
- "most should use the NATS account resolver built-in to 'nats-server'"; nats-account-server is "legacy, replaced by the built-in NATS resolver" but usable as a reference implementation; nsc "is the preferred tools to create security configuration unless you are using Synadia Control Plane."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — In Depth JWT Guide**

- Motivation: "Accounts do NOT correspond to infrastructure, they correspond to teams or applications." "Infrastructure and its topology have nothing to do with Accounts and where an Account's User connects from." Users of one account can connect anywhere in the same authentication domain.
- Operator = "operator of a set of NATS servers in the same authentication domain (entire topology, crossing gateways and leaf nodes)".
- JWT names "are only used by tooling, nats-server does not read this value"; names may collide, so keep them unique in nsc. "JWT content can be viewed as public, although it's content may reveal which subjects/limits/permissions exist."
- Clients present only the User JWT; the server fetches the Account JWT itself and verifies the three-level chain. Changing the operator JWT needs a restart or reload.
- Resolver choice: mem-resolver for "Very few or very static accounts"; url-resolver for "Very large volume of accounts" (needs a web server, nats-account-server legacy); nats-resolver = same over NATS, "No separate binary", "Easier clustering", needs an exclusive directory per server ("it can be on a shared Network File System, but the directories themselves can not be shared"). "Between nats-resolver and url-resolver, the nats-resolver is the clear recommendation." "JWT nats-resolver is recommended to use in production".
- Deployment models: centralized (admins hold all keys); decentralized (admins hold operator keys and enforce limits by signing accounts; teams hold account keys and issue users); self-service (teams also hold an operator signing key; "there should be at least one organizational mechanism to prevent unchecked usage"); mixed. "pick the simplest deployment model that enables what you need ... NOT the most complicated one".
- "Our official suggestion is to scope accounts by application/service"; accounts "can be arbitrarily scoped, from Application to Team".
- User JWTs depend only on the issuing Account NKEY, not on a particular Account JWT version; a newer Account JWT causes existing connections to be re-evaluated.
- NKEY backups "should therefore best be offline and access to them should be severely restricted"; identity NKEYs "should be archived and then removed" from the nsc store once signing keys exist, so a breach doesn't force "a flag-day change-over of identities."
- JWT store directory contains no private keys and may go in git, but restoring an old version may undo revocations and restore expired JWTs; keep NKEYs in tandem.
- "We always recommend using signing keys for an operator" and likewise for accounts; nsc never updates the operator installed on servers automatically.
- After `nsc push`, if fewer servers respond than exist "it is best practice to resolve this issue and retry"; if only one server holds a new account and dies, "the pushed account is not available to the network at large" so "make sure that initially, more servers respond than what you are comfortable with losing".
- Exchange only public NKEYs when generating users for another entity (`nsc generate nkey -u` without `--store`, then `nsc add user -k <pub>`).
- Automated sign-up services: use NKEY+JWT libraries; "Dynamically provision user and integrate that process with your existing infrastructure, say LDAP, is the most common use case"; signing keys "highly recommended". "it becomes YOUR RESPONSIBILITY to properly authenticate incoming requests"; "For sign up service issued JWTs, ALWAYS set the SHORTEST POSSIBLE EXPIRATION".
- Sign-up requestor credentials: "Do not use this JWT/NKEY for anything else but contacting the sign up service"; allow publish only to the well-known subject; back up the account signing NKEY so requestors need not be replaced.
- System account: "It is NOT recommended to use this account to facilitate communication between your own applications. Its sole purpose is to facilitate communication with and between nats-server."
- "leaf nodes do not multiplex between accounts. Every account that you wish to connect across a leaf node connection needs to be explicitly listed." The system account is not connected automatically even when both sides share it; add it as a separate `remote` with heavily restricted credentials, also when only needed for the NATS resolver or centralized monitoring.
- `nsc generate diagram component` produces a plantuml diagram of account import/export relationships.
- Key importance: operator keys > account keys; identity keys > signing keys. For huge deployments (IoT) where regenerating identities is infeasible, back up identity keys offline and use exchangeable signing keys; "prepare and try this out beforehand and not wait until disaster strikes."
- Identity NKEY is the only key that can add/remove signing keys, so create signing keys before taking the identity key offline; delete user keys/creds from nsc after distribution.
- "for user NKEYs and JWT, generating and distributing new ones to affected applications is the best option" when compromised.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Legacy: NATS Streaming (STAN) and nats-account-server**

- nats-account-server: "If you are creating a new NATS deployment we highly recommend using the internal NATS Resolver"; it remains "a good reference to build upon for custom account resolution" and also speaks the NATS resolver protocol.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-3: NATS Service Latency Distributed Tracing Interoperability**

- Service latency tracking is configured per exported service via `latency: { sampling: 50%, subject: ... }` on an account export; today sampling is a static percentage.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-12: JetStream Encryption At Rest**

- Server-side encryption at rest is "an alternative to an encrypted filesystem or block storage that would be provided by a cloud provider."
- Key hierarchy: EK (external key from config/env), KEK derived `KEK := PRF(EK, IV, Context)` (never stored), AEK (asset key, encrypted by KEK, stored alongside the asset).
- Assets = account info, stream and consumer metadata and data; "each block will have a different asset key."
- Cipher: AEAD ChaCha20-Poly1305.
- No key rolling in the initial release: "a backup and restore will be equivalent to changing all of the encryption keys." KMS access and client-supplied EK are future ideas (ADR: proposed/not implemented).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-14: JWT library free jwt user generation**

- With scoped signing keys "limits and permissions are **attached to the signing key instead of the user**", so a user-JWT issuer needs no jwt data model.
- "The use of scoped signing keys is highly encouraged as a compromised key can only be used to issue certain user, NOT user with arbitrary permissions."
- Proposed `IssueUserJWT(signingKey, accountId, publicUserKey, name, expiration, tags)`; expiration is "optional but recommended"; "If not set, JWT will not expire." Target languages first: go, java, csharp.
- JWT header is static `{"typ":"JWT","alg":"ed25519-nkey"}`; body has `iss` (signing key public), `sub` (user public key), `nats.issuer_account` (account id), `nats.type: user`, `nats.version: 2`.
- `jti` is base32 sha256 of the body computed with `jti:""`; encoding is base64url without padding; signature over `header.body`.
- "The `user nkey` can be generated by the signer or a requestor can provide it so the signer is unaware of the private nkey portion."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-19: API prefixes for materialized JetStream views**

- Isolation mechanisms: cross-account requires an import with an altered prefix ("an import without a prefix set will result in an error as JetStream is imported as well and we error on import overlaps"); "On leaf node connections, the nats server adds in denies for `$JS.API.>`."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-21: NATS Configuration Contexts**

- `nsc` key takes URLs like `nsc://operator/account/user`; the context runs `nsc generate profile <url>` to fill `creds` and `url`; explicit `url`/`creds` override nsc output.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-26: NATS Authorization Callouts**

- Auth callout lets "an external NATS service ... generate NATS authorization and credentials by authenticating connection requests"; works in both server-config mode and operator mode.
- Server sends a signed authorization request JWT to `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH` on `$G` (or the configured account in config mode; in operator mode the connected account). "This subject is automatically protected in the system for all users on the authorization callout account."
- Request includes `client_info`, `client_opts` (incl. user/pass/token/nkey/JWT as sent), optional `client_tls` (cipher, version, PEM certs, verified chains), `server_id`, and `user_nkey` (server-generated) that "must be the subject of the response" ("This assists against replay attacks").
- Response is a user JWT signed by the configured `issuer` account key (config mode) or by the account bound to the client (operator mode); `aud` must be the issuing server's public key.
- "A good pattern to follow is that the authorization service runs isolated in its own account, since the system can bind a user to any authorized account."
- Config: `auth_callout { issuer: <account public nkey>, auth_users: [ ... ], xkey: <optional> }`; users listed in `auth_users` bypass the callout (so the callout service itself can connect); any other configured user still triggers the callout.
- Account switching: the response "can override the account that the request was processed in"; in operator mode the auth account claim lists allowed target accounts and "The response user JWT must be signed by the private key of one of these other accounts."
- Encryption uses xkeys (x25519, NaCl Seal/Open); when `xkey` is set the request is encrypted and the server's public xkey appears in `ServerID` and plaintext header `Nats-Server-Xkey`; response may be encrypted for the server. Operator mode: xkey lives in the account's `ExternalAuthorization` claim.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-30: Subject Transform**

- "For transforms that are defined in inter-account imports (streams and services) the destinations _MUST_ make use of _ALL_ of the wildcard-tokens"; from 2.10 all other uses may drop wildcard tokens. In imports "the _ONLY_ allowed mapping function is `{{Wildcard(x)}}`."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-31: JetStream Direct Get**

- Subject-Appended form `$JS.API.DIRECT.GET.<stream>.<subject>` is a `last_by_subj` shortcut so "subject-based interest restrictions ... such that only specific subjects in stream may be read" can be applied via permissions/imports. Payload with this form is a `408` error.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-38: OCSP Peer Verification**

- OCSP Peer verifies an external peer's cert chain against the CA's OCSP responder during TLS handshake, "after trust-chain verification is successful"; applies to CLIENT (NATS, MQTT, WebSocket) and LEAF connections only; "does not overlap or supersede the OCSP Stapling feature" (which covers ROUTE/GATEWAY).
- Adding OCSP responder dependency "necessarily adds a single point of failure (SPOF) from the NATS Server point of view and will in any case slow overall connection time"; mitigated by a local response cache.
- `ocsp_peer` in a `tls` map: short form bool (default false) or long form with `verify` (false), `ca_timeout` (2s), `allowed_clockskew` (30s), `warn_only` (false), `unknown_is_good` (false), `allow_when_ca_unreachable` (false), `cache_ttl_when_next_update_unset` (3600s).
- mTLS `verify: true` is required for inbound NATS/MQTT/WebSocket/leaf-hub OCSP peer; outbound leaf (spoke) verifies the TLS server and does not require mTLS.
- `ocsp_cache`: default `true`/`local` when any listener has ocsp_peer; long form `type` (local|none), `local_store` (default `_rc_`, "Setting a fully qualified directory path for `local_store` is recommended"), `preserve_revoked` (false), `save_interval` (300s, min 1s).
- Verification passes if: self-signed cert, or a chain with zero OCSP-eligible links, or a chain whose eligible links all return Good. Eligibility = issuing CA declares an http/https OCSP URI in the AIA extension; trust anchors are not evaluated.
- Responder non-response or non-200 → "consider the certificate not OCSP valid" (no advisory emitted); `allow_when_ca_unreachable` treats non-response as Good unless a cached Revoked entry exists ("even if expired").
- Rejection handshake errors: `client not OCSP valid` / `server not OCSP valid`; advisories `io.nats.server.advisory.v1.ocsp_peer_reject` on `$SYS.SERVER.<server>.OCSP.PEER.CONN.REJECT` and `ocsp_peer_link_invalid` on `$SYS.SERVER.<server>.OCSP.PEER.LINK.INVALID`.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-39: Certificate Store**

- TLS map gains `cert_store`, `cert_match_by` (default `Subject`), `cert_match` so the server's TLS identity can come from a credential store instead of files; "Edge computing scenarios involving large 'fleets' of managed servers may especially require credential store integration."
- `cert_store` replaces `cert_file`/`key_file`; configuring both errors at startup: `'cert_file' and 'cert_store' may not both be configured`; `key_file` is ignored if `cert_store` is set.
- Providers: `WindowsCurrentUser`, `WindowsLocalMachine` (Microsoft KSP "MY" store); provider name case-insensitive; unknown provider errors `cert store type not implemented`.
- Server tries to build a trust chain from the Windows store and includes non-self-signed intermediates in the presented chain; if none found, presents the leaf only.
- `cert_match_by` is `Subject` or `Issuer`, matched against individual RDN values (e.g. `example.com` matches, `CN = example.com` does not); recommended: look up by the unique Subject CN "to avoid TLS negotiation failure caused by return of the wrong certificate."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-40: NATS Connection**

- Explicit TLS: upgrade after INFO if `tls_required` or client demands TLS. TLS First (implicit) requires server `tls { handshake_first }` and client `tls_first`; "available since NATS Server 2.10.4".
- `handshake_first` values: `false` (default), `true` (enforced; "Clients that do not use this flow will fail to connect"), a duration (hybrid wait), `auto` ("By default it waits 50ms for TLS upgrade before sending the INFO").
- `-ERR Permissions Violation` matches `/(Publish|Subscription) to (\S+)/` and optionally `/using queue "(\S+)"/`; for subscriptions "errors are _terminal_ for the subscription, as the server cancels the clients interest"; notify the first matching subscription (server sends one error per offense).
- `Authorization Violation` → server disconnect; `User Authentication Expired` and `Account Authentication Expired` → disconnect, then reconnect is rejected with `Authorization Violation` until refreshed.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-41: NATS Message Path Tracing**

- "By default a trace will end at an account boundary when crossing an Import or Export. This is a security measure"; opt in with `allow_trace: true` on the service export (exporter side) or on the stream import (importer side).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-55: Trusted Protocol Aware Proxies**

- A NATS-protocol-aware proxy connects on behalf of clients/leafnodes and must securely pass source IP, TLS properties, etc.; trust is established by listing proxy public nkeys in `proxies { trusted = [ {key: ...} ] }`.
- `proxies` block supports config reload; "should a trusted proxy be removed we will disconnect all connections that came from that proxy"; exposed in `VARZ`.
- `proxy_required: true` per user (config), on `leafnodes.authorization`, and a `ProxyRequired` boolean in JWTs.
- With any proxies configured the server "always include a `nonce` in the `INFO` line" and always reports `api_lvl`; the proxy injects `proxy_sig` (signature over the nonce plus all client CONNECT fields) into `CONNECT`.
- Server rejects a present-but-invalid `proxy_sig`; auth callout may set `ProxyRequired` so "Auth Callout does not need to know which proxies are trusted"; the proxy is recorded in `CONNZ`/`LEAFZ`; rejected clients "get the same nondescript error message as today" while logs, CONNZ reason and `client_disconnect` advisory carry the real reason.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-59: JetStream Stream Sourcing and Mirroring**

- Cross-account sourcing needs three exports/imports: `$JS.API.CONSUMER.>` (service), `deliver.mirror.>` (stream), `$JS.FC.>` (service). "Getting the type wrong (e.g., using a stream import for the API subject) will cause silent failures."

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — Core protocol and connection defaults (server/const.go)**

- TLS handshake wait time. `TLS_TIMEOUT = 2 * time.Second` (server/const.go:108); leafnode TLS timeout same `DEFAULT_LEAF_TLS_TIMEOUT = 2 * time.Second` (server/const.go:165)
- TLS-handshake-first fallback delay before server sends INFO first. `DEFAULT_TLS_HANDSHAKE_FIRST_FALLBACK_DELAY = 50 * time.Millisecond` (server/const.go:114)
- Authorization wait time. `AUTH_TIMEOUT = 2 * time.Second` (server/const.go:117)
- `allow_responses` permission defaults: 1 response, 2 minute expiry. `DEFAULT_ALLOW_RESPONSE_MAX_MSGS = 1`, `DEFAULT_ALLOW_RESPONSE_EXPIRATION = 2 * time.Minute` (server/const.go:228-232)
- Service export response threshold (time server expects a service response to be delivered; drives cleanup of reverse mappings). `DEFAULT_SERVICE_EXPORT_RESPONSE_THRESHOLD = 2 * time.Minute` (server/const.go:237)
- Service latency sampling default 100%. `DEFAULT_SERVICE_LATENCY_SAMPLING = 100` (server/const.go:241)
- Default account names. `DEFAULT_SYSTEM_ACCOUNT = "$SYS"`, `DEFAULT_GLOBAL_ACCOUNT = "$G"` (server/const.go:244-247)
- Account resolver fetch timeout. `DEFAULT_ACCOUNT_FETCH_TIMEOUT = 1900 * time.Millisecond` (server/const.go:250)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — JetStream cluster placement and catch-up (server/jetstream_cluster.go)**

- Client-facing deny list for JetStream-disabled accounts: `$JS.API.>`, `$KV.>`, `$OBJ.>`; internal deny adds `$JSC.>` and `$NRG.>` (server/jetstream_api.go:349-350)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — Routes, gateways, leaf nodes (server/route.go, server/gateway.go, server/leafnode.go)**

- Insecure TLS on routes/gateways/leafnodes logs: "TLS certificate chain and hostname of solicited ... will not be verified. DO NOT USE IN PRODUCTION!" (server/route.go:127-128, server/gateway.go:71, server/leafnode.go:46)
- On the hub (accept) side, the spoke's permissions are reversed: "the perms that it will use on the soliciting leafnode's behalf are correct for them, but inside the hub need to be reversed since data is flowing in the opposite direction" (server/leafnode.go:2310-2318)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — Accounts, imports/exports, system events (server/accounts.go, server/errors.go, server/events.go, server/auth.go)**

- "Account are subject namespace definitions. By default no messages are shared between accounts. You can share via Exports and Imports of Streams and Services." (server/accounts.go:50-51)
- Service response types: Singleton (default), Streamed, Chunked (server/accounts.go:199-209)
- Service import cycle detection: an import is rejected if the destination account's own imports collide back to the source ("import forms a cycle"); search depth capped at 1024 accounts ("search cycle depth exhausted"). `MaxAccountCycleSearchDepth = 1024` (server/accounts.go:1588-1625; server/errors.go:150-153)
- Import authorization: "service import not authorized" / "stream import not authorized" when the exporter has not granted the importing account (server/accounts.go:1583-1586; server/errors.go:138-147)
- Stream import prefix can not contain wildcard tokens; duplicate stream imports rejected: "stream import prefix can not contain wildcard tokens", "stream import already exists" (server/errors.go:140-144)
- Service latency sampling must be 1-100: "bad sampling percentage, should be 1-100" (server/errors.go:118)
- Account limits struct: max payload, max subs, max connections, max leafnodes, disallow bearer (server/accounts.go:127-133)
- Permission templates ({{...}} in user permissions) expand to at most 4096 subjects. `maxPermTemplateSubjectExpansions = 4096` (server/auth.go:475)
- Service reply subjects use prefix `_R_.` (server/accounts.go:2362-2370)

- Decentralized auth flow from cheat: `nats auth operator add`, `nats server generate server.conf`, `nats auth account add`, `nats auth user add admin SYSTEM`, `nats auth account push MyAccount --server ... --creds sys_admin.cred`; "All configuration changes are stored locally until `nats auth account push`ed" (cli/cheats/auth.md:1-31)

NATS: "The private key never leaves the device"; "Identity is proven through cryptographic challenge-response, not credential transmission"; revocation reaches "the entire cluster — including leaf nodes — within seconds."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Why NATS**

- NATS 2.0 (2019): multi-tenancy, decentralized auth, superclusters, leaf nodes. NATS 2.2 (2021): JetStream (at-least-once delivery, exactly-once processing), WebSocket, MQTT 3.1.1.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS and Decentralized Security: A Modern Approach to Scalable Authentication**

- Centralized auth "reaching their limits" at "millions per second" of auth requests; "The bottleneck isn't just technical; it's architectural." Regional security domains distribute the load.
- "Authentication and authorization aren't dictated by your topology. They're overlays on top of your topology."
- Operator model suits "high connection churn environments"; hierarchical signing scales; config-based auth is "Better suited for less dynamic environments or deployments with lower volumes of authentication traffic"; hybrid (operator keys managed via config) is possible.
- "Accounts define natural security boundaries." Exports/imports: streams (read-only subjects for other accounts) and services (request/reply across accounts).
- Auth callout delegates to "IBM DC, LDAP, OAuth, OIDC" and allows gradual migration.
- Resolvers: memory (dev), file, URL. File-based auth needs files updated on every node and "each node must be restarted"; operator-based "updating an account on one node will automatically synchronize the changes with the other two."
- Resolver-based JWT auth and config-based auth "are different authentication models" and typically cannot be mixed within one; a cluster can support multiple operators; JWT verification needs only the public signing key; accounts can add signing keys for delegation or rotation.
- "Authentication works the same for leaf nodes and regular nodes"; cross-account service imports "must be authorized at the hub/root as well"; leaf tenants can run their own auth callout per account.
- "you can't mix Auth Callout and JWT auth within the same Account", but one server can host accounts with different mechanisms (static, callout, resolver). Rotation disconnects clients; reconnect triggers a new callout.
- Publisher identity is "not part of NATS's core design, as publishers and subscribers are decoupled"; workaround: put a source_id in the payload.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Message Tracing in NATS 2.11: Debug Your Entire System with One Command**

- Tracing stops at account boundaries by default; cross-account needs `allow_trace: true`: "For stream imports, the importer sets it. For service imports, the exporter sets it."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Your Perimeter Is Already Gone — Edge Security Isn't a Checkbox**

- "The edge doesn't have a perimeter. It has exposure." Edge is "adversarial by nature, not by exception"; encryption "addresses only part of the edge security problem."
- Default/hardcoded and shared, unrotated credentials; compromised devices injecting plausible bad data for months; lateral movement via over-scoped credentials; supply-chain (BadBox 2.0 on "more than 10 million devices").
- Realm-based security: "Each edge device gets credentials that authorize only what that device legitimately needs to publish and subscribe to, nothing more"; "A compromised edge node can't suddenly start publishing to a core command channel; the topology simply doesn't permit it."
- Decentralized, cryptographically scoped credentials remove a single credential-store target; constraints must be "built into the topology" not layered on. The question is "what can this device actually reach, and what happens if it's compromised?"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leafnode with JWT Auth**

- When bootstrapping an operator with nsc, generate an operator signing key; the text calls this a best practice. "Create the operator, generate a signing key (which is a best practice), and initialize the default SYS account and sys user."
- Edit the operator to require signing keys so that accounts must also be signed with signing keys rather than identity keys. "A follow-up edit of the operator enforces signing keys are used for accounts as well."
- Setting `account-jwt-server-url` on the operator is only a convenience so `nsc push` does not need the server URL each time. "Setting the server URL is a convenience so that it does not need to be specified with call `nsc push`."
- Keep application traffic in a dedicated account (here `APP`) and reserve the `SYS` account for operational purposes. "The `SYS` account should be used for operational purposes."
- Give the application account its own signing key (`nsc edit account APP --sk generate`) and create users under it, following the operator/account/user hierarchy.
- The main server enables JWT auth by including the nsc-generated NATS resolver config (`nsc generate config --nats-resolver --sys-account SYS`) alongside its `leafnodes.port`. "generates the bit of configuration to be used by the server to setup the embedded JWT resolver."
- With the full NATS resolver, an account JWT must be pushed to the main server (`nsc push -a APP`) before users of that account (and the leaf's remote credentials) are trusted. "We need to put up the `APP` account JWT we created previously to the main server so that the user credentials file ... is trusted."
- In a JWT setup, the leaf node authenticates to the hub by placing a user `.creds` file in `leafnodes.remotes[].credentials`; the leaf server itself can then have no client authentication configured. "no credentials file is specified since the leaf server does not have authentication setup. Instead the `leafnodes.remotes` section of the config defines the main server and provides the credentials so that the leaf node is authenticated for forwarding messaging."
- The leaf's remote credentials bind the leaf connection into the `APP` account on the hub, so unauthenticated clients on the leaf transparently reach a service connected to the hub under APP. "This request will be transparently fullfilled by the service connected to the main server."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Authentication and Authorization (category)**

- The auth category orders its examples as: programmatic nkeys/JWTs, system account, private inbox, centralized auth callout, decentralized auth callout.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Configuring the System Account**

- The system account is a designated account for operations and monitoring of the server, cluster, or supercluster. "NATS has the notion of a *system account* which is a designated account for operations and monitoring of the server, cluster, or supercluster."
- A server always has an implicit system account, but by default it has no users, so no client can run administrative commands until one is defined. "Although there is an implicit system account created on the server, there are no _users_ associated with it, by default."
- Observed output: with no system user defined, `nats server info` fails with `no results received, ensure the account used has system privileges and appropriate permissions`.
- The default system account is named `$SYS`; the minimal config to activate it is an `accounts` block defining `$SYS` with at least one user. "To activate we need to define a user associated with this account."
- Adding or changing the `accounts` block can be applied with `nats-server --signal reload`, no restart required. "Simply reload the server with the `--signal` option."
- You may use a differently named system account by defining any account and pointing `system_account:` at it; this is required for decentralized JWT auth. "There is another option to change the default system account name which is required when using the decentralized JWT auth method."
- For decentralized JWT auth the system-account setup differs from the config-file method (nsc creates SYS and the resolver config handles it). "For the decentralized JWT authentication method, configuring the system account is a slightly different process"
- Save the sys credentials as a `nats context` so the password is not typed on the command line every time.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Private Inbox**

- All replies using the built-in request-reply pattern share the subject pattern `_INBOX.>`. "Replies to a request using the built-in request-reply pattern all share the same subject pattern `_INBOX.>`."
- For multi-user applications needing isolation of messages inside one account, have each client connect with an explicit inbox prefix and combine it with explicit permissions so users cannot snoop on each other's service replies. "an explicit **inbox prefix** can be used when a client connects to the server. This combined with explicit permissions prevents users from _snooping_ on service replies."
- A requesting user needs subscribe permission on its inbox subjects (`_INBOX.>` by default) or it cannot receive replies. "The `_INBOX.>` subscription permission is required in order to receive replies from a requester."
- A service user can be limited to `sub.allow: [services.greet]` plus `allow_responses: true`, so it can only reply to requests it received rather than publish freely.
- Declaring an explicit `sub.allow` list is an implicit deny of everything else: joe cannot subscribe to `pam.>` and vice versa. "A nice side effect of this is that now, joe and pam can't subscribe to each other's subjects (since an explicit allow has been declared)"
- Observed output: with `sub.allow: [_INBOX.>]`, pam subscribing to `_INBOX.>` receives the reply to joe's request. The text says this is expected: accounts are the isolation boundary; per-user granular permissions become necessary at scale. "This is actually expected and generally fine since _accounts_ are expected to be the isolation boundary, at a certain level of scale, creating users with granular permissions becomes increasingly necessary."
- Inbox subjects are randomly generated, so by default there is no fixed set of subjects to grant per user; the client-side option is to choose an explicit inbox prefix other than `_INBOX`. "Sinces inboxes are randomly generated by the server, by default we can't pin down the specific set of subjects to provide permission to. However, as a client, there is the option of defining an explicit *inbox prefix* other than `_INBOX`."
- Observed output: connecting with `--inbox-prefix _INBOX_joe` while the user is only allowed `_INBOX.>` fails with `Permissions Violation for Subscription to "_INBOX_joe.<random>"`; the custom prefix must be in the user's subscribe allow list.
- Per-user private inbox pattern: set each user's `sub.allow` to only `_INBOX_<user>.>` and have that user's client connect with the matching inbox prefix; then a user can subscribe neither to `_INBOX.>` nor to another user's prefix. "Now pam cannot subscribe to the general `_INBOX` nor joe's specific one since it does not have an explicit allow."
- Permission changes in the config file are applied with `nats-server --signal reload=<pid>`; observed output shows subsequent subscribe attempts to `_INBOX.>` and `_INBOX_joe.>` by pam rejected with Permissions Violation while requests with the correct prefix succeed.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Private Inbox using JWT**

- With nsc the service user is given `--allow-sub services.greet --allow-pub-response`; observed nsc output confirms `--allow-pub-response` sets `max responses to 1` (one reply per request).
- A JWT user with only publish allows and no explicit subscribe allow can still subscribe to `>`, so joe could subscribe to `pam.>`; add an explicit `--allow-sub` to close this. "Since we didn't set an explicit allow for subscriptions, these users can still subscribe to `>` which means joe could subscribe to `pam.>` and vice versa."
- JWT version of the private-inbox fix: `nsc edit user --deny-sub '_INBOX.>' --allow-sub '_INBOX_<user>.>'`, i.e. explicitly deny the shared default prefix and allow only the user's own prefix. "we can deny the default one and allow for the custom one."
- Every `nsc edit user` regenerates that user's `.creds` file; in the recorded run no server reload was needed for the new user permissions to take effect on the next connection (observed).
- Creating an account with nsc is a two-step process: `nsc add account` then `nsc edit account --sk generate` to add a signing key. "It is currently a two-step process to create the account, followed by generating the signing key."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth Callout - Centralized**

- Auth callout was introduced in nats-server v2.10.0 as an extension point for integrating alternative identity and access management (IAM) backends. "Auth callout is a new feature in NATS v2.10.0 providing an extension point for integrating with alternative identity and access management (IAM) backends."
- Centralized (config-file) auth callout is configured under `authorization.auth_callout` with `issuer` (public account nkey that signs responses), `users` (the users in the auth account allowed to answer callouts), `account` (the account the callout service connects with), and optional `xkey` (public curve key enabling encryption).
- The issuer nkey and xkey are normally generated with `nsc generate nkey --account` and `nsc generate nkey --curve`, or programmatically with an nkeys library; the example hardcodes them only for demonstration.
- Use a dedicated `AUTH` account whose only user is the callout service; application users get bound into separate accounts (`APP`, `SYS`) by the service's response.
- Implement the callout responder as a NATS micro service with endpoint `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH` so several instances can share load, expose stats, and give high availability. "This allows for running multiple instances to distribute the load, observe stats, and provide high availability."
- When `xkey` is configured the server includes a `Nats-Server-Xkey` header and encrypts the request; the service must decrypt with its curve keypair and seal the response to the server's xkey. A service without a curve key should respond with an error ("xkey not supported").
- The authorization response is an AuthorizationResponseClaims for the requesting user nkey, with `Audience` set to the server ID, containing either an error string or the issued user JWT, signed by the issuer keypair.
- In non-operator (config) mode the issued user JWT sets `Audience` to the target account name and is signed with the issuer key. "Audience contains the account in non-operator mode." / "Sign it with the issuer key since this is non-operator mode."
- The callout service can attach per-user permissions (pub/sub allow lists, `resp.max`) in the user JWT; the server enforces them. Observed output: bob publishing to `test` gets `Permissions Violation for Publish to "test"` while `bob.test` succeeds.
- Observed output: an unknown user is rejected at connect with `Authorization Violation`; a callout-authorized user bound to the `SYS` account can run `nats server list`.
- The Java variant of this example runs auth callout without the `xkey`, showing encryption is optional. "Encryption is not enabled in this example."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth Callout - Decentralized**

- In an existing JWT environment the operator/resolver bootstrapping step can be skipped; only the AUTH account and service need adding. "if this is an existing environment, this bootstrapping can be skipped."
- Decentralized auth callout is enabled on an account with `nsc edit authcallout --account AUTH --curve <xkey> --auth-user <user pubkey> --allowed-account <...>`, then pushed to the server.
- `--allowed-account` lists which accounts the callout service may bind authorized users to; `*` means any account, otherwise list account public nkeys. "The `--allowed-account` option is used to define which accounts this account is allowed to bind authorized users to. In this case, `*` indicates that any account can be bound."
- Enabling auth callout does not break existing JWT users: observed output shows app1/app2 creds still publish after the AUTH account is pushed. "Confirm existing creds still work even with auth callout enabled."
- The decentralized callout service needs three kinds of keys: creds for its own auth user, the AUTH account signing key to sign responses, and the signing key of every application account it is allowed to create users in. "we need the signing keys for the application accounts that the auth callout service is *allowed* to create and bind users to."
- In operator mode the issued user JWT is signed with the target account's signing key and `IssuerAccount` is set to that account's public key (in non-operator mode the service instead sets `Audience` to the account name).
- Clients must present a "sentinel" credential of the AUTH account (a user with `--deny-pubsub ">"`) together with their real username/password; the server uses the sentinel creds to delegate to the correct callout service. "The final requirement for clients to be able to connect is having a set of credentials of the AUTH acount which will be used to by the server to delegate to the correct auth callout service."
- The client connects with both `nats.UserCredentials(sentinel.creds)` and `nats.UserInfo(user, pass)`; the sentinel proves which account's callout to use and the user/pass are forwarded to the service.
- Observed output: the service logs one "responding to authorization request" per connect and alice (bound to APP1) and bob (bound to APP2) both connect through the same AUTH account.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Programmatic NKeys and JWTs**

- nsc is the primary and recommended way to create and manage accounts and users; programmatic creation is for on-demand, application-level account/user workflows, and shelling out to nsc is another option. "The primary (and recommended) way to create and manage accounts and users is using the nsc command-line tool."
- Not all client languages have standalone NKeys or JWT libraries. "not all languages currently implement standalone NKeys or JWT libraries."
- The operator must exist ahead of time to configure the resolver in the server config; signing keys are technically optional but a best practice. "Signing keys are technically optional, but a best practice."
- Public keys are prefixed O (operator), A (account), U (user); seeds (private keys) are prefixed S.
- The only requirement to enable JetStream for an account is setting its disk and memory storage limits to non-zero; -1 means unlimited. "The only requirement to "enable" JetStream is setting the disk and memory limits to anything other than zero. -1 indicates "unlimited"."
- In an account JWT the `sub` field is the account public key and `iss` is the operator public key; in a user JWT `iss` is the account key.
- A dynamically created account is activated by pushing its JWT to the server via a request to `$SYS.REQ.CLAIMS.UPDATE` from a connection authenticated as a SYS-account user.
- nsc stores and organizes every nkey and JWT for you; if you create accounts or users dynamically you must store and manage the keypairs and JWTs yourself. "If you opt to create accounts or users dynamically, keep in mind you need to store and manage the keypairs and JWTs yourself."
- A creds file is the user JWT decorated with the user seed; the seed can sign and prove identity and must be treated as a secret (observed creds file banner).
- Observed default account claim limits: subs -1, data -1, payload -1, imports -1, exports -1, wildcards true, conn -1, leaf -1; user claims default subs -1 and payload -1, with `Limits.Data` settable (1 GiB in the example).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mutual TLS**

- An embedded server enforces mTLS by building its TLS config with `server.GenTLSConfig` from a server cert, key and CA file with `Verify: true`, so clients must present a certificate signed by that CA.
- The example sets the TLS handshake `Timeout` to 2 (seconds) in the embedded server's TLS options.
- A client connecting to an mTLS server uses a `tls://` URL, supplies the CA via `RootCAs`, and its own certificate and key via `ClientCert`.
- Development certs for mTLS can be produced with mkcert: a server cert for `localhost`, a client cert with `mkcert -client`, and the mkcert root CA used as the CA file for both sides. "This example relies on the mkcert tool ... to generate the necessary server and client certs."

- Sharing one deliver subject across streams is "a straightforward way to do this in a single account. It is recommended a user is created with specific permissions to subscribe to this subject."
