**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Security**

- NATS security rests on three independent pillars: authentication, authorization, and encryption.
- NATS is multi-tenant by design: each user belongs to an account, a self-contained tenant with its own isolated subject space, users, and permissions; unrelated tenants can use the same subject names without collision.
- Cross-account communication is possible but requires explicit configuration.
- NATS doesn't require authentication by default, so production deployments should always configure one of: config-based auth, decentralized auth (operator mode), or auth callouts.
- Config-based authentication defines accounts, users, and credentials in the server config; credential types include username/password, token, NKeys, and TLS client certificates; simplest for development and smaller deployments.
- Operator mode is a hierarchical trust chain: an operator signs accounts, each account signs its own users; credentials are JWTs signed with NKey (Ed25519) keypairs; the server needs only the operator's public key, with no server-side user list.
- Operator mode scales to multi-tenant or large deployments because accounts issue and revoke their own users independently; you choose a resolver model for the server to locate account information.
- Auth callouts delegate the authentication decision to an application-defined NATS service returning a signed JWT; useful for external identity providers (OIDC, LDAP) or custom logic.
- Authorization is a subject-based permissions model: which subjects a user can publish to, subscribe to, or both, with the same wildcards as subjects; permissions are per user, in config or embedded in the user's JWT.
- The presence of an allow list closes off everything else; deny takes precedence over allow.
- Each connection type can have TLS configured independently: client-server, server-server routes, leaf nodes, and gateways; with certificate pinning, CA pools, custom cipher suites, and mTLS.
- mTLS proves the client holds a certificate signed by a trusted CA; `verify_and_map` maps the certificate's SAN or DN to a configured user, tying encryption into authentication.
- JetStream streams can be encrypted on disk using AES or ChaCha20-Poly1305, protecting persisted data against attackers with filesystem or physical access.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topologies**

- The hub sees one leaf connection rather than the individual clients, which the leaf authenticates on its own; the leaf still bridges subject interest into the account it binds to, so the subject namespace is shared unless you bind each leaf to its own account.

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Achieve MASSIVE Scale with NATS Clustering | Rethink Connectivity Episode 4**

- To observe cluster state you need a user in the built-in `$SYS` system account, which has extended admin privileges and exposes server metrics via system events. "a special account called dollar sign sys and this account already has extended admin privileges so you can get all of the metrics" (~03:06)
- Username/password in the config file is the simplest but least secure auth flow because the credentials sit in plain text. "this one isn't the most secure because the username and password is in plain text on your config file" (~03:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to build a NATS Supercluster | Rethink Connectivity Episode 5**

- The system account should not have JetStream enabled; create a separate account for a business use case and set `jetstream: enabled` on that account. "we don't want to enable JetStream here, in fact we want to create an account that can utilize JetStream for maybe a particular business case" (~04:20)
- Defining accounts and users inline in the server config is not ideal; decentralized JWT auth is the recommended construct for secure clusters and super clusters. "we're defining all of our accounts and all of our users inside of our server config and this might not be ideal" (~04:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to set up Decentralized Authentication/Authorization in NATS | Rethink Connectivity Episode 6**

- NATS deliberately splits authentication ("I am who I say I am") from authorization ("what I'm allowed to do") because combining them causes problems. "we've split those two things apart, some systems put them together and it causes all sorts of problems" (~01:10)
- Authentication uses NKeys: an ed25519 public/private key pair where the public key is the identity and the private key proves it by signing nonces; keys can be used hierarchically. "n keys which is just basically an ed25519 based public private key pair" (~01:40)
- Authorization is expressed in a JWT that carries limits on messages, connections and allowed publish/subscribe subjects. "here are my limits on the amount of messages I could send or the amount of connections I can have or what kind of subjects I can publish to or subscribe to" (~02:10)
- The operator model is a hierarchy operator → accounts → users; a "NATS system" (single node, leaf node, cluster or super cluster) treats itself as one system with one operator. "a NATS system can be a single NATS node, it can be a leaf node, but it can also be a cluster or a super cluster... one operator operating it" (~02:40)
- The operator is the entity running the system at the infrastructure level, e.g. a platform team or the company running NATS as a utility across an organization. "you're operating a NATS cluster across an entire organization as a utility and so your company name Acme Corp would be your operator" (~03:10)
- Accounts are completely segregated messaging namespaces; by default messages never cross accounts unless explicitly shared via imports and exports. "by default you can't really cross accounts via messaging unless you explicitly describe it in imports and exports" (~03:40)
- Accounts give multi-tenancy: Synadia's global network runs multiple companies on one NATS system, separated only by accounts. "we have a global network that we have multiple companies using one NATS system and they're all separated via accounts" (~04:07)
- Users are the end identities used by programs (microservices, producers, consumers); fine-grained pub/sub permissions and limits are defined at the user level. "these are the programs that are using them and this is really where you can get into some fine-grained permissions" (~04:30)
- Each level (operator, account, user) has both an NKey pair and a JWT; JWTs are minted and signed with the parent's key so a user JWT is verifiable up the trust chain to the operator. "I can verify that it's signed by an account that I know and that that account was actually signed by my operator" (~05:09)
- The server stores only the operator JWT and account JWTs; it stores no user JWTs and no private keys. "all that we really store are the account and the operator JWTs... we don't store any user JWTs... and then we store no private keys" (~05:40)
- Because user JWTs are not stored server-side, users can be minted without updating the system, and creation of accounts/users happens entirely out of band of NATS (only account JWTs must be pushed). "you could actually mint user JWTs without having to update it in the system... the creation process actually happens outside of NATS" (~06:09)
- Connect flow: server INFO carries a nonce; the client signs it with the user private key, sends the signature plus its JWT in CONNECT; the server validates the signature against the public key in the JWT, checks expiry/revocation, checks the signing account is known and was signed by the operator. "is the JWT expired or has it been revoked, was the JWT signed by an account that I know about, and was this account... did I sign it" (~08:13)
- nsc is the recommended way to start managing operators/accounts/users, but it is not required; the design is intentionally open so organizations can build their own issuance flow without sharing private keys. "you don't necessarily have to use nsc but this is the best way to get started... it's a very open design and that's on purpose" (~09:40)
- Always generate signing keys and never use root keys operationally: signing keys can be rotated if compromised, root keys cannot be recovered from compromise. "root keys are great for printing out putting in a safe... if your root key gets compromised you're kind of out of luck" (~10:40)
- Edit the operator to require signing keys on all accounts (strict signing key usage) and set the account JWT server URL so nsc knows where to push account JWTs. "we want to require all of our accounts to have signing keys as well... set up an account JWT server URL" (~12:16)
- The memory resolver holds account JWTs in memory and suits small systems; the NATS resolver is needed when you want to push accounts dynamically to servers. "a memory resolver... that's great for smaller systems but if we want things more dynamic where we can actually push accounts to servers we'll want to use a NATS resolver" (~15:20)
- `nsc generate config --nats-resolver --sys-account SYS` produces a server config containing the operator JWT, system account, resolver settings and a preloaded system account JWT; `nsc push -A` pushes accounts to the running server. "here's my operator's JWT, here's also the account that I want to use for system accounts, and we want to use a NATS resolver" (~16:00)
- A creds file is just the user JWT plus the NKey seed (private key), everything a client needs to connect; treat it as sensitive. "all a creds file is is it's a combination of the JWT and the private key" (~19:22)
- A request from a user in another account to a service gets "no responders" because accounts are isolated; sharing requires an export from the serving account and an import in the consuming account. "it's going to say no responders are available because these two users actually exist in completely different accounts" (~21:40)
- Exports are typed as either a service (request/response) or a stream (access to data); the import can alias the subject locally so the importer chooses its own naming. "there's either a service or a stream, a service is kind of a request response... a stream is access to data" (~22:50)
- Adding the first `allow-pub` clamps the user down so it can publish only to the listed subjects; deny lists are an alternative when it is easier to exclude a few subjects. "once I put in my very first allow pub we really clamp down all of the permissions" (~26:00)
- A user that must do request/reply needs subscribe permission on its inbox (`_INBOX.>`) in addition to publish permission on the service subject. "allow it to subscribe to its inbox which happens to be inbox dot wildcard, this allows us to have request response" (~25:50)
- Publishing to a subject outside the user's permissions yields a "permissions violation for publish" authorization error. "we get an authorization error which is great, permissions violation for publish" (~27:29)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extend your NATS Cluster with Leaf Nodes | Rethink Connectivity Episode 7**

- Run sites you don't fully control (partner sites, factories, retail) as their own NATS systems because they may need a different security model than the hub. "they might have some different use cases for what they need out of a security model so it's better to operate these things as separate NATS systems" (~02:20)
- Hub and leaf have separate operational models: the hub can use decentralized auth while the leaf runs with no auth behind a firewall; what crosses the link is bounded by the hub-side user the leaf connects with. "the authorization of what kind of goes over the wire is bound to this user from the operational model of the hub" (~06:40)
- Layer decentralized auth on top so a leaf node's credentials only permit sourcing specific subjects from the hub stream, giving partners scoped access to a global data store. "you can only source from this subject on this stream... a global data store that can only be accessed in certain ways" (~24:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Dynamic Permissions with Scoped Signing Keys | Rethink Connectivity Episode 8**

- Signing keys are basic hygiene: if the account root key is compromised you are stuck, whereas a compromised signing key can be revoked and replaced and users reissued. "if that signing key gets compromised your whole system's not compromised... you can revoke that key, issue another one and reissue all of your users" (~02:40)
- A scoped signing key is a signing key given a role and a permission template; every user signed with it inherits those permissions, which acts as role-based authorization inside an account. "you give it a role and then you can give it a template and every time a user is signed with that signing key they get those permissions out of the box" (~04:40)
- Permission templates can interpolate the user's name, user tags, account name/tags or public keys, e.g. `chat.post.{{tag(org)}}.{{name}}`, so one template yields per-user subject permissions. "we can use templates to insert dynamic content in here based on user's tags or the user's name, the account tags or name, or even the actual public keys" (~06:11)
- Scoped keys suit fleets of edge devices where re-minting and redistributing user JWTs is impractical; permissions are updated centrally instead. "you have a lot of devices at the edge and it's not very convenient to update permissions to them and re-mint user JWTs" (~07:00)
- Include `allow-pub-response` on the scoped key so users can reply to requests later. "just for good hygiene in case we want to put in request reply at some point we should probably say allow pub response" (~08:00)
- A user created with `-K <scoped key>` and tags has no explicit pub/sub permissions in its JWT JSON; all permissions are inferred from the issuer key at connect time. "if I look at the JSON output here it doesn't actually have any pub or sub permissions assigned to it, all of this is inferred from the key that signed it" (~09:40)
- Because permissions live on the signing key, updating the key changes permissions for already-issued users without reconnecting or reissuing credentials. "they don't have to reload, they don't have to reconnect, they don't have to get new user JWTs" (~10:00)
- Subject permissions are strict per token: a user permitted `chat.post.synadia.jeremy` cannot subscribe to `chat.post.*.*` or publish under another user's name. "if Liz tries to post into the Jeremy subject... she's going to get a permission denied" (~11:50)
- Minting users with permissions baked into the JWT means adding a new feature later requires re-minting and redistributing JWTs, which may be infeasible; scoped signing keys avoid this. "we would have no way of expanding the subjects they're allowed to use unless we re-minted the JWT... that might not be feasible" (~12:50)
- A DM subject design `chat.dm.{org}.{receiver}.{sender}` with allow-pub on `chat.dm.{org}.*.{name}` and allow-sub on `chat.dm.{org}.{name}.*` lets users send to anyone but only read DMs addressed to them. "they can listen in on any DMs directed to them... but they can only publish on things that they should be able to send" (~14:19)
- Scoped signing keys work across leaf nodes and edge devices as well as the core cluster. "especially in the case of either leaf nodes or edge devices... this all works across all of it" (~16:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Connect ANY Auth System to NATS.io with Auth Callout**

- On connect the server authenticates the client, assigns a connection ID (CID), binds it to an account (the `$G` global account if not multi-tenant) and attaches permissions and limits. "it creates a connection ID or a CID for that client, it then binds that client to a particular account... if you're not using multi-tenancy it's just going to be the dollar sign G account" (~02:30)
- Users defined in the server config are the easiest option but do not scale; decentralized JWT auth scales far, needs no config updates and keeps secrets out of config files, but is more complex and cumbersome. "put your users defined inside of a NATS server config which is the easiest approach but isn't super scalable" (~03:00)
- Auth callout is a third option: on CONNECT the server delegates authentication to a request/reply service you write and run instead of using its own knowledge. "the server instead of with its knowledge trying to authenticate the user, it's actually going to delegate that to an auth service that you create and maintain" (~03:50)
- The callout request carries client info, a server-generated NKey that is the user's temporary identity for the life of the connection, the server ID (anti-spoofing), and the full connect options including any mTLS certificate, token, JWT or username/password. "it's going to pass an NKey that it generates, this is going to be the user's temporary identity while it maintains connection to the server" (~04:20)
- The auth service returns a signed user JWT, reusing the decentralized-auth toolset, but without minting and distributing JWTs to clients or restarting them when permissions change. "it's using all the same tool set except that you don't have to mint that JWT and hand it to another client" (~05:10)
- Auth callout payloads can optionally be end-to-end encrypted between server and auth service using an XKey (curve key), so privileged operators cannot snoop the exchange. "the auth callout mechanism is end-to-end encrypted, or you actually have the option to do that... with an encryption key called an X key" (~05:40)
- Any external system (Active Directory, OAuth, OIDC, your own database) can be plugged in; the auth service is a normal NATS connection, so it can also use KV/object store as its user database with no separate backend. "you might not even need to have your own database, you could have a database powered by KV that has all of your user permissions in it" (~06:30)
- Auth callout can run in mixed mode alongside config-defined users or decentralized JWT auth. "you can support mix mode auth... some users defined in the config plus auth callout or you want to do the decentralized auth plus auth callout" (~07:05)
- A chat app using a single all-powerful shared NATS user lets anyone impersonate anyone; that is the anti-pattern the callout replaces. "I have a single NATS user that just has permissions to do anything that they want which obviously isn't great" (~09:00)
- Pattern: client does Google OIDC first, passes the Google-signed JWT unchanged as the NATS token; the auth service verifies Google's signature and mints NATS user claims from the Google claims. "it's not a NATS JWT... it's exactly what Google handed back to us, we're just going to give that to the NATS server when we connect" (~10:00)
- Server config: an `authorization { auth_callout { ... } }` block with `issuer` (public account NKey generated via `nsc generate nkey --account`, so the server can verify signed responses), `auth_users` (users that bypass callout, including the auth service itself), and the `account` in which callout users live. "we want to pass an issuer and this issuer is going to be the public key of the NKey that we just generated" (~12:40)
- The auth service's own user should use NKeys or decentralized JWTs rather than a plaintext username/password in config. "I recommend that you use something like NKeys or even the decentralized JWT auth for a lot of these users" (~13:20)
- Inject the auth service's NKey seed via environment or secrets in production, never hard-coded. "you likely want to inject this in via the environment or via secrets in some way shape or form when you're actually deploying" (~15:20)
- In the handler, create user claims with subject = the request's user NKey, set the audience to the target account name, and return the claims; the server signs and binds them. "the subject is actually going to be coming from our request... request.user_nkey" and "we do that by configuring the claim audience" (~19:20)
- Returning an error from the handler surfaces to the client as an authorization error. "if there was an error here we want to make sure we return it and that will result in an authorization error" (~20:20)
- Permissions minted per user: read JetStream API info, chat-messages stream info, create/operate consumers on it, read the workspace KV, but publish only to `chat.<channel>.<own user id>`, which makes authorship verifiable. "they can only post on behalf of their own user ID... we kind of use this as a mechanism to verify who has posted what" (~24:00)
- The auth service subscribes to the fixed subject `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH`; the example uses the micro framework with that as the endpoint subject. "the NATS server is going to send an $SYS request user auth, this is the subject that NATS is going to be using the callout for" (~26:29)
- The auth service also upserts the user's profile (name, email, photo) into a KV bucket on each login; clients watching that bucket update instantly, giving zero-touch onboarding. "all the chat applications were watching that key value store so they also updated their profile info before I even jumped into chat" (~28:40)
- A client holding only a Google JWT gets an authentication error on `nats stream list` but can subscribe to the stream and publish only under its own user id; impersonation attempts fail with a permissions violation. "if I want to just throw some gobbledygook in here or try to impersonate somebody it's going to result in a permissions violation" (~30:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Superclusters in Kubernetes: Cross-Cloud Geo-Affinity for High Availability and Low Latency**

- Gateway connections were authenticated with username/password for the demo; production should use something stronger like JWT. "in a production environment you might want something more like JWT" (~11:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Mutually Trusted NGS Credentials**

- Running your own JWT-auth servers alongside NGS normally forces dual management: two sets of accounts and two sets of credentials. "dual management of accounts, you have one set of accounts in NGS and you have a corresponding set of accounts in your local environment" (~00:30)
- One credential set can work in NGS and self-hosted servers if you accept that the account configuration is identical in both environments. "you are okay with your account configuration in either environment be identical, then this video is for you" (~01:10)
- JWT identity chain: each JWT references a public NKey; the operator JWT is self-signed by the operator NKey, which also signs account JWTs; the account NKey signs user JWTs; the user NKey proves possession via challenge/response. "the operator JWT in a sense is self-signed, it also signs the account JWT, the account NKey signs and therefore authorizes the user JWT" (~02:30)
- Permissions come both explicitly from the user JWT and implicitly from the account that signed it; the server verifies by downloading the account JWT via the resolver, checking its operator signature, then checking the user JWT was signed by an NKey referenced in the account JWT. "it verifies the user JWT was signed by an NKey referenced in the account JWT" (~03:20)
- To trust NGS credentials on your own server: configure the server with the NGS operator, set up an account resolver (memory or NATS), and create a dedicated system account for your own servers. "we configure our NATS server with the NGS operator and we configure an account resolver" (~03:50)
- With a leaf node config that connects each local account to its NGS counterpart, the import resolution moves from subscribe time to server startup, and the same creds subscribe locally and publish via NGS. "what used to be done with the connect during subscribe now is done during server startup because the server connects to NGS" (~09:13)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | Bearer Tokens in NATS**

- Provide used NATS as a fault-tolerant backplane for a blockchain-oriented orchestration platform and wanted decentralized, private messaging with no central authority. "our requirements are obviously no central authority, we wanted to allow organizations to be self sovereign" (~02:50)
- Their model: organizations sign bearer JWTs to delegate authorization; a verified token creates an ephemeral in-memory user for the duration of the connection, with no operator/account/user configuration on the server. "if the token is verified an ephemeral user is created in memory for the duration of the connection" (~03:20)
- They needed RS256 and ed25519 signing/verification and did not want to depend on nsc for key material, to keep infra complexity low. "we wanted to support RS256 and ed25519 signing and verification and we didn't want to depend on NSC" (~03:40)
- JWT fields that matter to the server: `exp` (server sets a timeout and drops the connection when it expires), `alg`, and `kid` to pick the verification key when multiple keys sign. "the server actually will set a timeout given this header and... when the expiration occurs then the connection will be dropped" (~04:40)
- The NATS permissions claim in a token lists allowed publish subjects, allowed subscribe subjects and an allow-responses flag (false by default); on valid signature these permissions are applied in memory. "a list of publish subjects, subscribe subjects that are allowed for the connection, allow responses you can set it to true or false" (~05:30)
- One JWT can carry both application permissions and the NATS permissions claim, so a single token serves the app and NATS. "if you generate and sign a JWT that has other application permissions... it's very nicely in line with a single token" (~06:20)
- Their fork honored the plain auth token as a fallback when no JWT was present, because NATS Streaming still connected with a token. "if no JWT is provided but an auth token is provided then that will still be honored" (~07:20)
- Verification keys were supplied through an environment variable; a WebSocket server was embedded in the fork ahead of official websocket support. "currently it's just done with an environment variable" (~08:10)
- Synadia's guidance to a project needing a non-standard auth model: run your own servers as leaf nodes with your model and let the core catch up, because leaf nodes allow mixing operator and security models. "with leaf nodes you can run your own servers for endpoints using the bearer tokens, don't wait on us, run ahead" (~17:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS Leafnodes**

- Leaf nodes bridge operator and security domains: a shared utility (inside a company or NGS) can be extended by servers that people own, operate and secure differently, e.g. WebSocket and MQTT each have their own security model. "they allow us to bridge operator and security domains, and this one is very subtle and nuanced but it's extremely important" (~04:00)
- Clients on a leaf node need not be aware of hub accounts: a leaf can use the global account with its own security domain while the hub side binds the connection to account A/B/C, and any client bound to the same hub account anywhere in the super cluster can talk transparently. "they can actually not even expose accounts at all... but once it's inside of here it's bound to let's say account A, B or C" (~09:10)
- A leaf node into NGS requires no auth, TLS or user/password locally if you trust the machine; the hub side still sees strong NATS 2.0 security, and NGS never holds your private keys. "everything that's coming and going looks like Derek's account and everything over here is just, there's no authentication authorization TLS, it's just open port" (~15:10)
- A leaf server can be multi-account locally: a remote can bind local account A to a hub account, while local account B (with no remote) stays isolated and requests to hub services from B simply time out. "if it's on account B it does not... it'll stall and just time out because there's no rule to propagate that information to NGS through that leaf node" (~17:20)
- Multiple leaf remotes can run from one server, each binding a different local account to a different hub account. "I'm actually going to create multiple leaf node connections bound to the different local accounts" (~18:40)
- NATS permissions cover what you can send/receive, where you may connect from and at what times, giving building blocks (not packaged solutions) for data-residency needs like GDPR. "we also have the notion of where are you allowed to connect from, what times can you connect from" (~26:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to configure NATS JetStream streams | Rethink Connectivity Ep 11**

- Deny delete and deny purge flags control whether individual message deletes (e.g. GDPR) or subject/stream purges are allowed. "deleting messages is being able to pick out a particular message and delete it great for like GDPR purposes" (~24:25)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | JetStream**

- JetStream plugs into NATS routing, security and multi-tenancy: one compute set can serve completely isolated data stores per account, sharing data only when required. "completely isolated data stores streaming services from completely isolated subject namespaces on top of NATS" (~03:07)
- JetStream publishes a full ordered log of API interactions (who created streams, changed config, tried to consume), and all APIs fit into normal NATS authorization so you can restrict who may create or only view. "we have a full ordered log of all the API interactions" (~15:25)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Getting Started with NATS JetStream: Streams, Storage, and Data Lifecycle**

- JetStream must be enabled at the server level and separately at the account level; without both it is not usable by that account. "you also have to activate it at the account level" (~04:04)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Why NATS Consumers Just Work (And How to Use Them in 15 Minutes)**

- A client must be authorized to subscribe on subjects matching the consumer's filter (a broader wildcard is fine); otherwise the subscription is rejected. "Without this block, any service that tries to subscribe to this consumer will get rejected because it hasn't been authorized" (~04:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream for Key-Value Store Tech Preview**

- Encoders and decoders allow encrypting keys and values for end-to-end zero-trust storage. "you can encrypt your keys and your values to have completely end-to-end zero trust storage" (~07:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers**

- A sensor should be authorized to publish only to its own dwelling-ID-prefixed subject pattern, which doubles as a sort key over the data. "it should only in theory be authorized to publish to say a guid dot something or a pattern" (~20:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.10 Webinar**

- Storage-level encryption and compression compose correctly because data is compressed before it is encrypted. "the data actually gets compressed prior to being encrypted so you actually get that benefit of compression" (~04:03)
- By default the initial CONNECT/INFO exchange happens in clear text before the TLS handshake, even with TLS configured; it carries minimal client metadata. "that first initial message is basically in clear text and it has minimal metadata ... and then the TLS connection handshake actually occurs after that" (~12:16)
- 2.10 adds opt-in TLS-first for leaf nodes: `handshake_first: true` must be set on both hub and remote or the connection is rejected; rollout to other connection types follows later. "you can say handshake first true and then on the remote ... you would also define handshake first true and those have to be in agreement" (~13:18)
- Auth callout exists so identity and permissions can be managed in an external IdP (SAML, Active Directory, OAuth) while NATS still enforces per-connection permissions and limits. "where you manage those permissions where you manage how those users are defined don't necessarily need to be in NATS itself" (~15:19)
- Auth callout is an extension point: the server delegates connection credentials and metadata to your service, which validates identity and returns a user JWT with permissions and limits; the server verifies it and accepts or rejects. "generate a user JWT which has permissions and limits ... that service returns that user JWT to NATS ... it does a couple extra checks" (~16:20)
- Centralized auth callout config has only four options: issuer NKey, the auth account's users allowed to run the callout service, the auth account, and an optional XKey. "these are literally the only four config options that you can define for auth callout in this centralized mode" (~39:50)
- The optional XKey encrypts the authorization request to the callout service, which decrypts it and re-encrypts the response with a one-time server key to prevent replay attacks. "it's able to re-encrypt it back with a public key that the server gives and that's a one-time key to prevent replay attacks" (~40:51)
- An OAuth-to-NATS bridge can store the IdP user claims in a KV bucket keyed by session ID; the client presents the session ID as its token and the callout service looks it up to mint the user JWT. "the key value bucket is the link between setting a token through my auth callout callback flow and then your auth callout service being able to observe this token" (~51:00)
- Put NATS permissions and target account in IdP app metadata claims so users are managed in one place and the callout service maps them to a NATS user JWT. "you can define permissions anything that is relevant for your NATS user ... and you can manage it in one place" (~45:57)
- The server respects an expiry on the callout-issued user JWT; today it disconnects the client at expiry and the client must reconnect, and retaining connection state across credential renewal was future work. "once the JWT has expired the user JWT it will effectively today disconnect the client and the client would just have to reconnect" (~53:04)
- Decentralized auth callout needs a few extra config options and a "sentinel" credential; both modes are walked through end to end on NATS by Example. "you need to work with a sentinel credential and there's a reason for that" (~56:08)
- Auth callout is deliberately an extension point and is harder to set up than most NATS features. "it's not going to be as trivial to set up as some of the other NATS features" (~56:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- Auth callout is the first built-in server extension point; it lets the server ask an external service whether a connecting client is allowed and what it may access, replacing large static configs. "the call out is basically a way of a NATS server reaching out to an external service to say hey I've got this client connecting should it be allowed what should it be allowed access to" (~51:52)
- The callout service can consult LDAP, OIDC, a file or SQLite and can generate permissions dynamically per session, e.g. by time of day. "maybe at this time of day for this particular user ... they have this degree of permission at this time" (~52:52)
- The auth callout service is just a NATS subscriber on a predefined subject that responds; there is no new protocol. "it's literally just another NATS subscriber right and then it just responds so it's not like a new protocol" (~53:55)
- Enabling JetStream encryption destroys file-system block-level compressibility, so 2.10 compresses in the file store before encryption. "if you enable encryption in JetStream today pretty much all of your compressibility on the disk ... goes completely out of the window" (~55:58)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP04: A Service Mesh Pattern for NATS.io**

- Under decentralized auth, subject mappings are per account, so each tenant (account = the application; user = the connection) can have its own mappings, pushed live via JWT update. "you can define subject mapping on an account by account basis which is our multi-tenancy mechanism" (~23:32)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS as a ServiceMesh**

- NATS 2.0 security (JWT operator/account/user model, decentralized, TLS with your own certs) replaces mesh-managed mTLS, but you have to manage certificate lifecycle yourself. "the caveat being for NATS... you have to manage it, you have to make sure that you maintain the certificate" (~09:09)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP01S3: Going back to basics with core NATS!**

- NATS has three "planes" (API: core/JetStream; security; topology); starting with all of them at once (JetStream over clustered leaf nodes with auth callout) piles on complexity, so start with a single server, one connection, and add features as they solve problems. "start with probably simple single server ... run an app with one connection ... make it use more features from there on" (~45:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS tools and benchmarking with JNM! NATS Community Office Hours (Reupload)**

- The server has very few Go module dependencies, which keeps the binary small and reduces exposure to dependency security advisories; the CLI is intentionally larger and that is fine. "the more dependencies you have the more chances that some point there'll be a security advisory on one of those dependencies" (~19:24)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Message Tracing | NATS 2.11**

- Tracing stops at account boundaries by default; the receiver must opt in with allow_trace on the import/export: the importer for a stream import, the exporter for a service import. "The rule being the receiver always opts in. If it's a stream import, the importer sets it. If it's a service import, the exporter sets it" (~09:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Future of NATS: Roadmap & Vision**

- Multi-tenancy is built in: messages in one account never bleed across account boundaries, so you don't deploy many NATS systems for isolation; cross-account sharing is opt-in. "you can send and receive messages over subjects in that account that will never bleed over any other account boundary" (~07:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — We need to talk about Microservices... (And how NATS.io can simplify things)**

- An API gateway's two jobs (aggregating many service endpoints behind one endpoint, and a single auth layer) are things the NATS server already does by brokering subjects between clients. "NATS actually just naturally does this ... NATS is the broker between those subjects" (~05:04)
- Authorization in NATS is subject based: JWT claims list which subjects a user may publish or subscribe to, with wildcards, so service-to-service permissions are as fine grained as subjects. "all of the permissions are also driven by subjects" (~26:30)
- Decentralized JWT/NKey auth scales because creating a user does not require updating servers; the credential is signed up the trust chain and verified by the server. "we don't have to update servers every time we want to create a user" (~26:30)
- One credential authenticates a service to every other service and to the data stores, giving a single unified security model. "one credential to access all of those things" (~26:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Give your Go app superpowers with an Embedded NATS Server**

- Setting the DontListen option makes the embedded server open no network port at all, so the app is fully closed; a normal client connect then fails and only in-process connections work. "you can actually create this really closed application and use the NATS server without actually exposing any sort of network interface" (~16:15)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS Surveyor**

- Surveyor requires NATS 2.0 and system-account credentials because server internals and names are published over the network and must not be visible to ordinary users. "it requires you to have access to the system credentials" (~01:01)
- Enterprise pain motivating Surveyor: opening Prometheus scrape ports across data centers and securing exporter connections is slow and complex; the speaker never got a Prometheus port opened in a three-year enterprise stint. "my very first task was open a port for Prometheus and I left three years later having never achieved that goal" (~03:06)
- Service latency tracking is enabled per exported service in the account (via nsc), can be added after the service exists, and was set to 100% sampling in the demo; it works across account import/export boundaries with zero client instrumentation. "there was zero instrumentation in the client and I simply enabled this in the account" (~17:32)
- Every server has a locked-down system account that can answer "how are you doing" requests targeted at one or many servers, which is the observability pattern Surveyor builds on. "all of our servers by default have a system account which is locked down and secure but can respond to requests" (~18:32)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Transcending microservices with NATS | RethinkConn '22**

- A perimeter-based security model (everything inside a VPC, cloud-specific IAM) breaks down once systems span clouds and the edge; NATS' cloud-agnostic security model is meant to replace it. "having this notion of a perimeter-based security model really breaks down it doesn't work anymore" (~08:10)
- NATS' security model is provider-agnostic; integrating with cloud-local services still requires obeying that cloud's IAM. "you have to obey their IAM permissions but as the connective mesh substrate ... you can't be locked into this perimeter mindset" (~10:12)
- The demo used a single shared bearer JWT embedded in the web app; one bad actor can ruin it for everyone, so this is demo-only, not best practice. "one bad actor could ruin the whole bunch" (~27:30)
- Best practice for web clients: a backend exchanges the app's identity token (e.g. OIDC/Google) for a freshly minted NATS user JWT with a short expiration, reissued as needed. "issuing JWTs on the fly as bearer tokens with very short windows for expiration" (~28:30)
- Synadia was building server-side support so the identity exchange could happen in a single connection (the precursor of auth callout). "we're working on ... inside of the NATS server ... that you can maybe do that in a single connection" (~29:32)
- Rate limiting per WebSocket user is done via limits on the minted user JWT, e.g. message-count limits, like any NATS user. "when you're minting user JWTs you can set limits on all of those just like you can with any other NATS user" (~29:32)
- Accounts in NGS are fully isolated from one another; a user with a permission set belongs to one account, which is the multi-tenancy boundary. "that account is completely isolated from all other accounts that's the whole nice multi-tenancy feature" (~27:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Seamless evolution across geos and clouds | RethinkConn '22**

- A leaf node acts like a separate NATS system that extends yours with fine-grained control over what crosses the connection, which suits the edge, partner organizations, and anything outside the security perimeter. "fine-grain control over what transfers over that leaf node" (~07:07)
- Data-sovereignty restrictions on in-flight data are handled by shaping the interest graph so only subscribers on a specific cluster care about that data, using superclusters or leaf nodes. "we really only want things that care about this particular data to exist on this cluster" (~16:24)
- Leaf node connections bind to an account on the cluster side, so you can select all or part of that account's traffic to cross the leaf connection. "leaf nodes bind to an account on the cluster side ... I want all the traffic from this particular account or some of the traffic" (~20:30)
- A leaf node is its own territory with its own permission boundary, data locality, and ownership of local services and data; it can run on phones, cars, or factory devices with full server capabilities co-located on the device. "the leaf node as its own little territory that has its own permission boundaries" (~26:37)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Where are we now and where to next? | RethinkConn '22**

- Operators use accounts as guard rails: a fixed number of connections, subscriptions, and HA JetStream assets per account prevents the noisy-neighbor problem and lets teams work in their own sandbox. "set up an account with a specified number of connections, subscriptions, number of high availability assets ... that development team won't exceed that" (~06:08)
- Security evolved from username/password to JWTs with ed25519 signing, so the NATS system never reads or accesses a private key; x509 TLS certificates can also map to identities. "the NATS system never ever has to read or access a private key" (~07:10)
- Roadmap: auth callouts where NATS hands a credential/token to an external process that mints NATS credentials, plus message-flow callouts for schema validation, PII scrubbing, and data enrichment. "call out to a different process and that process would mint credentials that make sense for NATS" (~12:15)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Versioning and canary deployments with subject mapping | RethinkConn '22**

- Mappings can be defined in server configuration or at the account level with nsc; tenants can manage their own canaries. "you can define this as server configuration or you can define this at the account level as well using the NSC tool" (~04:04)
- Use permissions to keep versioned subjects internal: services may subscribe to v1/v2/v3 subjects while clients may publish only to the unversioned public subject. "restricts the clients to be able to publish only to that non-versioned subject" (~05:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Service monitoring with Helix and Surveyor | RethinkConn '22**

- Latency tracking is a little-known server feature tied to service imports/exports: the server emits a JSON latency event per request/reply for an exported service. "with your services when you work with imports and exports you can get all this latency tracking information JSON blob" (~01:02)
- Decentralized auth with nsc is deliberately unopinionated about where JWTs are stored, which causes ergonomic friction; nsc is a utility for a decentralized design, not a management UX. "because it's decentralized there's some like ergonomic issues that naturally come up with it" (~02:02)
- The latency event identifies the requester (client type, version, name, account, JWT) and the responder, plus which server/cluster each is connected to. "who the requester was, what kind of client they came from, what version ... what account and what JWT" (~12:13)
- Latency tracking is configured in the account JWT: the export declares the service subject, "track service latency" with a sample rate (100 = every request), and the subject to which the server emits the events. "we want to track service latency on this service for a sample rate of 100 and we want to send it to this subject" (~15:17)
- Recent server versions let an account import its own export, so latency tracking also covers requests made inside the same account. "I can import my own export ... so I can also get latency tracking for things that are happening inside my account" (~16:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Short break and Q&A! | RethinkConn '22**

- When importing an exported service, the importer chooses the local subject it appears on, e.g. import "Jeremy's cool service" as foo. "if Jeremy exports something and I import it into my world, my account, I dictate where that shows up" (~05:05)
- Across import/export mappings the system can inject the caller's true account (as trusted by the system, not as claimed) into the subject delivered to the service; the NGS usage service works this way so every tenant calls the same subject but the service receives NGS.usage.<account>. "map in his true account as understood by the system and deliver that to Jeremy as part of the subject" (~06:06)
- Account, not user, can currently be auto-inserted into the import subject space. "You can have the system automatically put the account, not the user right now, but the account into that subject space" (~09:09)
- Every request across an import carries a system-vouched client info header; by default it shares little (location, account), but the importer can opt in to share everything: app version, language, IP, account, user ID. "there's a consumer info header on every request that the system is actually validating and vouching for" (~07:07)
- Zero trust framing: even with permission to use a service, the importer decides whether to share the bare minimum or full identity; JetStream itself is built on these same primitives. "by default it's just the bare minimum, but you can opt in" (~10:10)
- A leaf node is a special connection that binds to an account or credential to lock down what traffic crosses it; unlike clustering it is a separate NATS system with its own security domain. "a leaf node is a separate NATS system. So it has its own security domain" (~21:24)
- Subject mappings can be created dynamically by writing them into an account JWT and pushing it; the server updates automatically. "write it to an account JWT and push it to the server and it automatically gets updated" (~27:35)
- A NATS-only chat app can have a back end that only mints user JWTs, adding stateless claims such as OIDC info; retries and exponential back-off constructs let job services run on NATS alone. "I have no back end except NATS" (~31:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Derek Collison RethinkConn 2025 Keynote and Closing Remarks**

- Leaf nodes give a logical and secure separation between organizations, companies and partners, which is the basis for fleet management. "leaf nodes are a superpower within the NATS ecosystem; they provide a logical and secure separation between organizations, companies, partners" (~02:35)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: After event Q&A with Derek on Zoom**

- A Nex engine operator requires workloads to prove a root of trust via xkeys, the same trust-chain idea as operator mode and Synadia Cloud; a workload's interactions with the outside world are NATS-initiated and the operator controls what it may talk to. "they have to prove to me that I know the root of trust... your interactions with the outside world are all NATS initiated" (~12:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Event-Driven Systems Need a Security Gateway — Meet Synadia Protect for NATS**

- Traditional brokers (JMS, Solace, MQ, AMQP) secure the connection with TLS/mTLS and apply ACLs to addresses, but offer no content-based policies, unlike REST API gateways. "there are zero content based policies to be applicable at this level" (~02:00)
- An event gateway applies API-gateway-style policies to subjects, and covers both request-reply and pub/sub, with operational policies such as throttling plus content policies. "secure subjects or channels of communication and apply policies to those channels much like you did with APIs in a restful gateway" (~03:20)
- An event gateway is a plain proxy rather than a router plus proxy, so it is lighter than a REST gateway. "the event gateway is just a simple proxy... much lighter than its counterpart in the RESTful domain" (~04:10)
- The gateway can be placed between websocket clients and the enterprise, inside the enterprise between clients, or between edge leaf nodes and the cloud hub. "security gateways applied between the edge domain, sensors, devices and whatnot and the cloud or hub domain" (~04:50)
- Synadia's security layers are NATS auth (centralized or decentralized, ACLs, per-domain token creation and revocation), schema validation of payload structure, and Protect for payload content. "you have really three layers... infrastructure validation, structural validation of the payload itself, and... content validation" (~05:40)
- Enforcement order for a message: TLS on the connection, publish/subscribe permissions on the subject, schema validation of the payload, then content validation. "first of all, you secure the channel, you apply certificates... Then... permissions... schema validation... content" (~06:20)
- Content-policy use cases include rejecting orders with negative prices, payment and fraud checks, exfiltration prevention for government, healthcare and finance, compliance, per-subject rate limits that close the connection, and prompt-injection detection in agent-to-agent messages. "am I allowed to send X amount of messages per second on a particular subject? And if not, shut down the connection" (~09:00)
- Deployment roles: a firewall in front of the core cluster for incoming leaf nodes and clients, internal domain traffic control, and protection of AI agent-to-agent traffic. "I want to ensure that whatever traffic comes in there, I block it or protect it before it hits the core cluster" (~10:40)
- A fleet of gateways split by domain is kept in sync by a config server that gateways reach over NATS, never point-to-point, and rule bundles are stored in a JetStream stream. "The gateway itself talk through NATS to the actual config server. So there's no direct point-to-point connection" (~12:50)
- The gateway is configured with a backend URL for the NATS server it fronts; for leaf nodes, the leaf points at the gateway's leaf port and the gateway connects to the hub's 7422 leaf port. "the leaf nodes point to the gateway and the gateway points to the actual leaf node connection in the hub" (~13:50)
- Native rules are a fixed list toggled on or off with regular expressions (conf format); custom rules (YAML, an expression language) cover content, connections and CIDR ranges. "custom rules... apply to both content and connections and whatnot. You can apply CIDR rules as well" (~15:40)
- Rule lifecycle is create a signed zip bundle, install it, activate it, later deactivate and uninstall; all of it is scriptable from the CLI for DevOps. "create the rules bundle... generate a zip file... install... activate" (~16:40)
- Every gateway action is auditable: an audit log, a policy execution log of each triggered rule, forwarding to SIEMs like ArcSight or Splunk, and custom tracing for forensics. "you can actually forward those logs you create to a particular SIEM" (~17:50)
- The gateway runs either allow-all-and-deny-by-rule or deny-all-and-allow-by-rule, and rules can apply client-to-server, server-to-client, or both directions. "It can operate and allow everything, but block only through rules or block everything and allow the rules to allow traffic through" (~22:30)
- The gateway only sees traffic routed through it; in the demo the sys user is blocked via the gateway port but connects fine directly to the server. "if I connect without the gateway, I should be allowed to and it's going to work" (~28:40)
- Edge devices can be tampered with to inject commands into payloads headed for the cloud; a leaf-to-hub gateway rule blocks such payloads before they reach the backend. "you can actually do a lot of tampering with devices out on the edge... insert maybe commands in there that could simply trigger actions in the back end" (~38:00)
- Around 20 out-of-the-box policies exist, including CIDR allow/deny lists, payload allow/deny, and time-window rules. "right now we have, I don't know, 20 or so policies that are out-of-the-box" (~39:50)
- The UI can only add native rules; custom rules must be authored separately and imported. "The UI currently supports only adding native rules" (~19:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking Connectivity - Hyper-Connectivity & The Intelligent Edge**

- The security model is meant to replace the wall around the VPC with modern cryptography and zero-trust constructs for a multi-tenant, decentralized model. "not just based off of building a big wall around your virtual private cloud" (~09:10)
- Accounts make NATS securely multi-tenant so it can be a public utility inside an organization, solving the "Coke and Pepsi" problem logically; leaf nodes are the way to get physical isolation. "if you do want physical isolation... leaf nodes... another really good way to achieve physical isolation" (~13:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — A New Way of Thinking | NATS 2.0 and Connectivity**

- Accounts were created by concentrating multi-tenancy at the subject router: a user authorizes into an account, a messaging sandbox, so Coke and Pepsi share infrastructure and never see each other's messages; sharing is a mutual export/import agreement. "accounts were born they're isolated meaning Coke and Pepsi can exist on the exact same infrastructure" (~15:40)
- An importer chooses where an imported subject appears in its own namespace, which removes the brittle multi-week subject-topology design sessions of older messaging systems and leads to short two-token subjects like kv.get. "when you import something you get to pick where it shows up" (~16:50)
- Account owners add, revoke and re-permission users themselves without helpdesk requests to a central operator. "all of that is managed by the account owners" (~18:00)
- Leaf nodes extend superclusters hub-and-spoke and bridge separate security domains, so an IoT deployment with its own security can attach to a supercluster of backend services. "you are allowed to bridge separate security domains" (~26:50)
- Security covers TLS including bidirectional certs, SPIFFE identities, username/password, and permissions on subjects and payload size, making least privilege easy. "they can only send up to 256 bytes only on this subject" (~30:30)
- Operator mode is a chain: an operator vouches for accounts, accounts vouch for users; a server boots knowing only its trusted operators and derives everything else. "there's an operator and then an operator will vouch for accounts and accounts vouch for users" (~31:00)
- A NATS 2.0 system never holds or receives private keys or passwords; it challenges the client with a nonce that must be signed by the credential's private key, unexpired, and signed by a valid account. "the NATS 2.0 systems never have any private keys or passwords whatsoever" (~31:20)
- The model is federated by design: multiple operators can run servers (e.g. Google, Amazon, Azure) and a user presents the same credentials to any of them. "it could have servers that are being operated by Google and by Amazon and by Azure yet as a user they all look the same" (~32:20)
- The PKI uses Ed25519 keys, chosen as branch-prediction-attack resistant after Spectre and Meltdown, and JWTs are public. "we use encoded ed25519s which at the time we were making these decisions were the most branch resistant" (~32:50)
- Account limits (max connections, max leaf connections, bandwidth, exports/imports) are enforced globally and instantly: an 11th connection against a limit of 10 is denied anywhere in the world, and a revoked user is disconnected within about 10 ms globally. "if Colin revoked me as a user my application would instantaneously be disconnected... within 10 milliseconds globally" (~33:40)
- Synadia's definition of zero trust: everything is encrypted before the system sees it and the system doesn't have the keys. "before our system ever sees anything everything's already encrypted and we don't have the keys" (~37:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - PowerFlex Solves Intermittent Connectivity at the Edge w/ NATS - RethinkConn 2025**

- Auth is decentralized JWT/NKeys: one account spans hub and leaf nodes; each customer gets a unique NKey user issued by one signing key, with permissions scoped via wildcards. "each customer through signing keys gets a unique NKey for authentication but managed with one signing key and permissions and wildcards" (~16:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - MachineMetrics on Industrial IoT & Predictive Analytics w/ NATS at RethinkConn 2025**

- They issue short-lived NATS credentials through their own APIs so clients and edge devices get location-specific credentials that refresh. "we issue short-term NATS credentials through our APIs so that clients as well as edge devices can have location-specific credentials" (~21:27)
- Decentralized auth gives one account per customer plus mapping back into an account they own; scoped signing keys issue users and revocation is an administrative change that propagates. "an account per customer, but then be able to map things back into an account that we own" (~27:36)
- Decentralized auth is worth learning thoroughly before use; it is the tricky part and they are reworking their auth model with Synadia. "it's certainly a topic to spend some time making sure that you understand thoroughly" (~27:36)
- Credentials for edge nodes are set up with the nsc CLI; account seeds then issue short-term user credentials via their API; currently a single account with backend code isolating companies, moving to account-per-company. "most of what we do we set up using NSC CLI. And then we use those account seeds to issue short-term user credentials" (~33:44)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Nathan Mellis from Modzy on NATS as a foundational building block**

- Edge devices connect over a single WebSocket connection on port 443, so no extra firewall ports are needed. "we're actually doing it all over the websocket connection so the edge devices only ever have to talk on port 443" (~08:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Simple Solutions for Complex Problems - How Workiva uses NATS as a Microservices and RPC transport**

- Running NATS on localhost means only inter-server (route) traffic needs encryption, and same-host messages never hit the network. "we only have to worry about encryption between the NATS peers" (~23:29)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | Pub Sub on the Power Grid**

- They plan to adopt NATS 2.x security features going forward. "all the things that you guys have added in the version 2 releases from a security standpoint... we're definitely planning on taking advantage" (~30:48)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Workloads - Distributed cloud-to-edge compute with NATS Execution Engine**

- When agents or workloads start, nodes mint credentials in real time scoped to the subjects those workloads need; a workload in account A can't talk into account B unless intended. "the nodes are actually minting credentials real time that are scoped to the subjects that those things need to talk to" (~08:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Migrating from NATS Streaming to JetStream**

- Username/password configs still run inside an implicit global account; explicit accounts give full subject-level isolation between tenants on one deployment. "Those two client applications by default will never see any messages even if they're publishing and subscribing to the exact same subjects." (~40:28)
- Each account can carry its own JetStream limits, useful when mapping accounts to customers; exports/imports enable cross-account sharing, typically for operational hub use. "Every account can have its own JetStream configuration in the sense that you can enforce certain limits at the account level." (~41:30)
- Locked-down publishers still need subscribe permission on their inbox because stream publish acks come back via request-reply. "The stream is actually going to be sending back an acknowledgement to an inbox." (~44:35)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS KubeCon Tutorial on Twitch**

- Accounts are namespaces for subjects; users of one account only see another account's data if that account exports a stream or service and the consumer imports it. "You can think of them as namespaces for your subjects." (~08:15)
- The server warns on plaintext passwords in config and suggests bcrypt or NKeys; NKeys are a challenge-based public/private key scheme. "It will suggest to use either bcrypt for the password or you can use also NKeys." (~12:21)
- Authentication options include user/password, tokens, bcrypt, NKeys, TLS certificate DN mapped to a user identity (e.g. SPIFFE IDs), decentralized JWTs, and custom auth when embedding the server in Go. "If you embed the NATS server you can also have your own custom authentication if you implement the auth interface." (~15:30)
- Request-reply across accounts works by remapping the requester's unique inbox to a hidden `_R_` subject on the service side; all transparent to clients. "When it traverses into another account it becomes a special subject called underscore R." (~17:31)
- Leaf nodes act like a proxy that is itself NATS; an edge device that can't afford expensive auth connects to a sidecar leaf node which holds the secure TLS link to the supercluster. "You can connect them to your own attached... sidecar leaf node and then this other leaf node will have the secure TLS connection." (~20:35)
- The chat demo splits an admin account (credential provisioning) from a user account so subject namespaces don't cross-talk. "We have separated these subject namespaces so that you can have as less as possible cross-talking." (~35:58)
- Dynamic credential provisioning: connect with near-permissionless default creds, request upgraded creds from a provisioner service, then close and reconnect with the new JWT. "We request upgraded credentials based on a username we give and the API will either grant us the new credentials or... an error." (~46:16)
- A provisioner can revoke a user by public key by signing an updated account JWT and pushing it to the servers over the account management subject, disconnecting that user immediately. "We're revoking the public key... signing the JWT and then sending that back once again to the NATS server." (~40:06)
- Per-user permissions in the demo restrict a user to publish on online/posts/DMs and to subscribe only to DMs addressed to its own public key plus its inbox. "You're only able to receive messages under your own public key and able to reply into the inbox." (~44:13)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Zen of High Performance Messaging with NATS by Waldemar Quevedo Salinas**

- The `_INBOX.*` wildcard subscription sees every request in a server; subjects starting with `_SYS` are reserved and publishes there are rejected. "We can subscribe to all of the requests... by using underscore INBOX dot asterisk." (~16:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — SCaLE 13x Derek Collison  NATS A new nervous system for distributed cloud platforms**

- In 2015 the Go server had no TLS yet (the Ruby server's TLS was "kind of broken"); Apcera signed and encrypted every message at the application layer instead. TLS was on the futures list. "For that reason it doesn't do TLS yet but part of the futures." (~48:19)
- Max payload is configurable but should not be set very large, since large payloads enable memory-based denial of service against the server; the demo server allowed up to 10 MB. "If it's big you can do a denial of service based on a memory footprint of a server." (~54:25)

## CLNT: Client library behaviour (822 claims)


**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — What is NATS**

- A client needs only a NATS URL (IP/port + connection kind: plain TCP, TLS, or WebSocket) and, if needed, authentication (username/password, decentralized JWT, token, TLS certificates, NKey with challenge).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject-Based Messaging**

- By default subject names are not verified on publish; programmatically generated illegal subjects (e.g. containing wildcards) "may be ignored". Enable `pedantic` mode in the client to verify.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS connectivity**

- Direct connectivity kinds: plain NATS, TLS NATS, WebSocket, MQTT.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Acknowledgements (concept)**

- With at-most-once semantics, request-reply "should use timeouts"; "It is always a good idea to place a timeout on a request and have code that deals with timeouts."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS Service Infrastructure**

- Regardless of topology, clients need only NATS URLs and credentials.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Queue Groups**

- Scale-down is "terminating the application with a signal that drains the in flight requests".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Request-Reply**

- "NATS applications 'drain before exiting'" so they can scale down without dropping requests.
- No-responders requires header-capable server and client; the requester immediately gets an empty reply with `503` status; clients surface it as an error (Go: `nats.ErrNoResponders`).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream (concept overview)**

- Flow control is decoupled, per client-server link, not end-to-end; publishers aren't limited to the slowest consumer. JetStream publish can be sync or async ("batched").

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Clustering**

- Clients connecting to any server discover the others; on interruption they try all known servers.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream on Leaf Nodes (domains)**

- With limited API access, clients set the API prefix (`nats.APIPrefix("JS.acc@hub.API")`) and bind explicitly (`nats.Bind(stream, durable)`) to avoid stream/durable inference calls.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Configuration (server config reference)**

- Defaults: `host 0.0.0.0`, `port 4222`; no TLS by default; gateway/leafnodes/mqtt/websocket/cluster inactive by default.
- `ping_interval` default `2m`, `ping_max` 2; "it is recommended to keep this value bigger than what clients use". `write_deadline` default `10s`: exceeding it closes the connection (slow consumer).
- `no_fast_producer_stall` default false: server stalls the fast producer when a consumer is slow; `true` drops the message for that consumer instead.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Enabling TLS**

- Behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy configure `tls {}` plus `allow_non_tls: true`; minimum client versions: nats.go v1.31.0, nats.js 2024.1.2, nats.java 2.18.0, nats.rs 0.33, nats.net.v2 2.0.0, nats.net v1 1.1.5.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Lame Duck Mode**

- The server notifies clients on LDM; some clients invoke an optional callback so apps can prepare for the short outage before reconnecting elsewhere.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Slow Consumers**

- "NATS favors the approach of protecting the system as a whole over accommodating a particular consumer to ensure message delivery." Slow consumers are cut off; clients not answering pings are disconnected and need reconnect logic.
- Client-detected slow consumer: app notified via async error callback and messages dropped; "It is better to catch a slow consumer locally in the client rather than to allow the server to detect this condition."
- Default subscriber pending limits: `65536` messages and `65536*1024` bytes; on reaching them the client drops messages and continues ("aligned with NATS at most once delivery"); the app must detect and recover. A local error doesn't mean the server flagged the subscription.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Environmental considerations**

- Load balancers are possible "but you don't need to": NATS balances across seed URLs (clients randomize DNS A records) and reconnects automatically. "If you have a cluster with 3 seed nodes you often get more network throughput than going through a load balancer".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS Server Clients**

- NATS URLs: `nats://host:port`, `tls://host:port`; multiple comma-separated URLs for a cluster.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Installing (hardware requirements)**

- TLS CPU: "After a network partition, every disconnected client will attempt to connect to a NATS server in the cluster simultaneously, so CPU on those servers will momentarily spike." Mitigate with reconnect jitter, longer TLS timeouts, and larger clusters.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — WebSocket Configuration**

- WebSocket "TLS configuration is required by default"; `no_tls: true` only for test environments.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — FAQ**

- Verbose mode acks every protocol command with +OK/-ERR and "is ON by default for new connections; most client implementations disable verbose mode by default"; pedantic adds subject checking.
- Graceful async subscriber shutdown: call `sub.Unsubscribe()` so outstanding handlers finish; one goroutine per subscription (Go).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — How to Develop with the NATS Client API**

- Synadia-supported clients: Go, Java, .NET, Rust, JavaScript, Python, C; also Ruby, Elixir, Zig, Swift listed; many community clients (Kotlin, Dart, Tcl, Crystal, PHP, Pascal).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Anatomy of a NATS Client Application**

- With NATS the developer never worries about who sends/receives, where services are or how many instances, "How many partitions or servers there are in the cluster", fault tolerance, or topology.
- Apps can open many independent connections (e.g. as two users) but "typically most applications only make a single NATS connection."
- "It is recommended that the application use connection event listeners" to log connects/reconnects/disconnects.
- "The recommended way to disconnect is to use Drain()"; use `close()` only when immediate close is needed.
- Flush after publishing if latency-sensitive; flush uses PING/PONG and those pings don't count toward max outgoing pings.
- "A client will receive a message for each matching subscription" so overlapping subscriptions (`foo` and `>`) deliver the same message multiple times.
- Core subscribers "must be able to keep up with the flow of messages ... or it will otherwise become a slow consumer".
- JetStream contexts are lightweight: "while it is safe to share a JS context between threads, for best performance do not be afraid to have a context per thread."
- Core publish to a stream subject is stored but unacknowledged; "you will get higher quality of service by publishing using the JetStream Context's publish call" because it is acknowledged after storage; hence sync and async variants.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Connecting**

- URL schemes: `tls://` TLS-only; `nats://` TLS if the server requires it else plain; `ws://` WebSocket.
- "When connecting to a cluster it is best to provide the complete set of 'seed' URLs for the cluster."
- "Your application should expose a way to be configured at run time with the NATS URL(s)" and credentials file/token/NKey.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Receiving Messages / Sending Messages**

- "The client API (asynchronous) subscribe call can return before the subscription is actually fully established at the nats-server. Call Flush() on the connection right after you call subscribe if you need to synchronize".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Automatic Reconnections**

- All nats-io clients auto-reconnect and re-establish all subscriptions; they use URLs from connect plus URLs gossiped by the servers; "This feature allows NATS applications and the NATS system itself to self-heal".
- Callbacks: ClosedCB, DisconnectedErrCB (DisconnectedCB deprecated), ReconnectedCB, DiscoveredServersCB, AsyncErrorCB (e.g. slow consumer).
- Go defaults: `Timeout` 2s dial; `PingInterval` 2 minutes; `MaxPingsOut` 2 (then ErrStaleConnection); `AllowReconnect` true; `MaxReconnect` 60 (negative = forever); `ReconnectWait` 2s; `ReconnectJitter` 100ms (no TLS); `ReconnectJitterTLS` 1s; `ReconnectBufSize` 8 MiB ("Once this has been exhausted publish operations will return an error"); `RetryOnFailedConnect` false.
- `CustomReconnectDelayCB`: "It is strongly recommended that this value contains some jitter to prevent all connections to attempt reconnecting at the same time."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Monitoring the Connection**

- Libraries expose connection status (CONNECTED/CLOSED/reconnecting) and in/out stats.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Connecting to a Cluster / timeouts / misc / name / noecho / ping-pong / security**

- Connect URLs "are usually checked in random order as to not have every client connect to the same server"; first success wins; randomization can be disabled.
- "your code should include a list of reasonable front line or seed servers"; you don't need every member, the server gossips the rest; "the mesh created by a cluster can grow and change organically while the clients are running."
- Connect timeout applies to each cluster member URL individually (example 10 seconds).
- Clients can read the server's `max_payload` after connect to chunk or limit data.
- Pedantic mode is off by default; publishing to a subject containing a wildcard is not checked unless pedantic is on.
- `max_control_line` limits combined subject + queue group length; "It is not recommended to set this to a value that is higher than the one of other clients or the nats-server."
- Verbose mode "is only used for debugging the client library or the nats-server themselves. By default the server sets it to on, but every client turns it off."
- A connection name "is highly recommended as a friendly connection name will help in monitoring, error reporting, debugging, and testing."
- Echo is on by default (a connection's own subscribers get its publishes). NoEcho "can be useful in BUS patterns where all applications subscribe and publish to the same subject." It is per connection, and toggling it "can result in a major change to your applications communications protocol".
- Ping interval x max pings outstanding sets how fast a stale connection is detected, including partitions the OS doesn't notice; default interval "is typically on the order of minutes"; example: interval 20s and 5 max pings closes after 100s. The server doesn't initiate PING/PONG while traffic flows.
- A credentials file bundles the user JWT and NKey seed and "should be protected because it contains a private key."
- NKey challenge-response "protects the private key from the server, which never has access to it!"
