- A TLS-mode server requires TLS from all clients; a TLS-configured client fails against a non-TLS server. Using just a `tls://` URL "is very likely to fail" unless the language's TLS defaults find the CA.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Receiving: async, sync, drain, queues, unsubscribe, wildcards, structure**

- "For a given subscription, messages are dispatched serially, one message at a time." Concurrent processing requires the app to move messages to its own queue/worker pool.
- Async subscriptions cost library resources (threads); sync subscriptions suit single-expected-message cases.
- Drain vs close: close/unsubscribe are immediate and halt pending messages; drain "will process any inflight and cached/pending messages before closing." Connection drain: drain all subs, stop publishing, flush, close. Subscription drain: unsubscribe, process cached/inflight, clean up.
- "Drain provides clients that use queue subscriptions with a way to bring down applications without losing any messages": bring up a new queue member, drain the old, shut down. "Without drain, there is the possibility of lost messages due to delivery timing."
- "the timeout for drain should generally be higher than the timeout for a simple message request-reply".
- The server never processes payloads; structured data (JSON etc.) is encoded by the app or library helpers.
- Auto-unsubscribe after N counts total messages ever sent to that subscription, not new ones; "If the subscriber has already received one or more messages, the unsubscribe will be immediate." Libraries resend the updated total on reconnect.
- Unsubscribe requires a server round trip, so an async subscription may still receive a message during the window.
- With wildcard subscriptions "it is a common technique to use the subject provided with the incoming message to determine what to do with the message."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Sending: caches/flush, reply-to, request-reply, structured data**

- Libraries buffer outgoing data for throughput while keeping low latency at low rates; use flush when a message must have "hit the wire"; flush is implemented with PING/PONG.
- Newer libraries use one wildcard inbox subscription with unique child subjects per request instead of a new subscription per request.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Reconnect: buffer, disable, events, max, random, wait**

- "The Core NATS client libraries try as much as possible to be fire and forget, and you should use JetStream functionalities to get higher qualities of service" when connection interruptions drop messages.
- The reconnect buffer caches publishes while disconnected and sends them on reconnect; when full, publishes error. "while the message appears to be sent to the application it is possible that it is never sent because the connection is never remade." Use acks or JetStream publish to ensure delivery.
- Max reconnect attempts are counted per server (including discovered ones); a server exceeding the count in a row is removed from the list, reset on success or rediscovery; running out of servers closes the connection with an error.
- Thundering herd: "all of the clients try to reconnect immediately, thus creating a denial of service attack"; libraries randomize server order so "no one server bears the brunt"; randomization can be disabled.
- Reconnect wait avoids thrashing the same server "especially when using TLS" and eases thundering herd when no other servers are available.
- Reconnect event listeners are "especially important for applications sending a lot of messages."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Events: connection events, slow consumers (client side)**

- Listen for closed/disconnected/reconnected events, discovered servers, and errors; reconnecting may involve multiple disconnects while searching for a server.
- "NATS depends on the applications to consider and respond to changing message rates. The server will do a bit of impedance matching, but if a client is too slow the server will eventually cut them off".
- Library-side pending buffers absorb bursts (e.g. app handles 10 msg/s, receives 20); the server sees a healthy connection; on overflow the library raises SlowConsumer and discards messages.
- Pending limits (count and bytes, e.g. 1,000 messages or 5mb) help with bursty publishers, not continuous mismatch; "Disabling these limits can be dangerous in production" and setting them to 0 "is also a dangerous proposition in production."
- Some libraries (Java) notify once per time the subscriber falls behind, not per dropped message; a dropped-message count may be available.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Advanced Connect and Custom Dialer in Go**

- Go `CustomDialer` lets the app use `context` deadlines/cancellation for connect and retry loops without modifying the client; ends with `Drain()` to flush pending messages.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Developing with JetStream**

- JetStream publish acks mean the publisher "can safely discard any state it has for that publication"; sync and async both imply flow control; exactly-once needs a unique publication ID header.
- Newer clients have "a more ergonomic API to work with Consumers" than the original Subscribe/QueueSubscribe/PullSubscribe calls.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream contexts / Managing streams and consumers / Publishing to streams**

- Some clients (Java) separate a JetStream Management context from the JetStream context; Go uses one for both; the context sets the JetStream operation timeout.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — WebSocket (overview) / Windows Service / Server flags**

- WebSocket support (2.2) works alongside TCP; "NATS Supports only WebSocket data frames in Binary, not Text format"; a frame is not guaranteed to hold a full protocol message, so client parsers must handle partial protocols.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-1: JetStream JSON API Design**

- JetStream API is built on NATS request-reply; every API has a unique subject under `$JS.API.` with tokens naming the item, "to assist in generating ACLs giving people access to either subsets of API or even down to a single Stream or Consumer."
- Server accepts nil payload, empty string, or `{}` as an empty request body.
- Responses carry a `type` field like `io.nats.jetstream.api.v1.stream_info_response`; requests generally do not include a type ("it's inferred from which subject is accessed").
- Paged APIs (e.g. `$JS.API.STREAM.NAMES`) return `total`, `offset`, `limit`; default page limit shown is 1024; pass `{"offset": N}` to page.
- Error responses have `error.code` (HTTP-style), `error.err_code` (unique NATS code, e.g. 10059 stream not found vs 10014 consumer not found), and `error.description` which "is variable and can change it's content between server versions." Absence of `error` indicates success.
- JSON Schema Draft 7 documents describe all JSON requests/responses; schemas live in the jsm.go repo `schemas/` directory; `nats schema list|show|validate` inspects them.
- Sequence fields are unsigned 64-bit ("JetStream can store up to the limit of an unsigned 64bit integer messages"); this "exceeds what is possible with JSON, languages might need to have custom JSON parsers."
- Some fields are platform-dynamic (e.g. `max_deliver`): "in practise you have to assume they are 64bit integer."
- `max_msg_size` is a signed 32-bit integer, min -1 (unlimited), max 2147483647.
- Durations are sent to the server as nanoseconds; timestamps are RFC 3339 strings with sub-second precision, ideally UTC, but server accepts and may return zoned times.
- Text-based `-ERR <reason>` API errors "are very uncommon now in the API and will likely be entirely removed in time."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-2: NATS Typed Messages**

- All outward-facing JSON (monitoring, JetStream API, advisories) is described by JSON Schema Draft 7; "Specifically this is not for server to server communication protocols."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-4: NATS Message Headers**

- NATS headers are HTTP-like (rfc7230/rfc822 field syntax): `name: value`, no space before the colon, keys may repeat, values may have surrounding whitespace.
- Server advertises header support via `headers` boolean in `INFO`; a client that wants to send headers must set `"headers": true` in `CONNECT`.
- Client header API operations (`GET`, `VALUES`, `SET`, `DELETE`, `APPEND`) "are _case-sensitive_"; `SET` = case-sensitive `DELETE` then `APPEND`; case-insensitive variants "are only suggested, and not required."
- Multiple values for one key "should be serialized one per line", not comma-joined: comma lists "introduces additional parsing requirements and ambiguity."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-5: Lame Duck Notification**

- Server signals lame duck by an `INFO` update with `ldm: true`; "the client should initiate an orderly self-disconnect or close."
- `ldm` is only present on servers that implement the notification.
- Consequence: "Currently clients have no automatic support to _disconnect_ while keeping current state."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-6: Naming Rules**

- Go client only checks stream/consumer names are non-empty and lack `.`; NATS CLI additionally rejects `. * > / \`.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-7: NATS Server Error Codes**

- Do not parse error description strings: "If users are parsing our error strings it means our error text form part of the Public API, we can never improve errors."
- `code` and `err_code` are the Public API; `description` is "specifically out of scope for SemVer protection."
- Example codes: 10059 stream not found (404), 10014 consumer not found, 10040 peer not a member (400), 10039 "JetStream not enabled for account" (503).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-9: JetStream Consumer Idle Heartbeats**

- Heartbeat is a regular message with status `100` and description `Idle Heartbeat`, headers `Nats-Last-Consumer` (last consumer seq delivered; 0 = none) and `Nats-Last-Stream` (newest stream seq).
- Purpose: "an aid to clients to detect when they have been disconnected" when "the server might have simply gone away and recovered elsewhere."
- Clients may count missed heartbeats and "re-create a subscription to resume messages."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-11: Hostname resolution**

- When a server URL is a hostname resolving to >1 IP, the client "should be randomized, unless the existing `NoRandomize` option is enabled", then try IPs in order and stop at first success.
- Rationale: "Some users have DNS where the order almost never change ... would cause all clients to connect to the same server."
- "This should be considered as a CHANGE for client libraries, since we are changing the default behavior."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-13: Pull Subscribe internals**

- `no_wait` gives "a guaranteed instant response" which is either a message or a status; most commonly `404 No Messages`. `503` if JS unavailable; `408 Request Timeout` when too many inflight pull requests.
- Client pattern: first a `no_wait` request, then on 404 a long pull with `expires` set "100ms before the client side timeout" (e.g. 5s → 4990000000 ns).
- Clients should auto-unsubscribe at `batch+1` (to account for the leading status message) and unsubscribe when leaving early, "otherwise this risks the server sending messages to an inbox from a connected client that is no longer expecting messages."
- Status messages "is not returned to the user as a processable message and instead handle is as the error condition."
- Pull(1) optimization uses a wildcard inbox subscription and no-wait first; "works better with topologies where JetStream is running as a leafnode on the edge." "Each pull subscriber must have its own pull request/response handler."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-14: JWT library free jwt user generation**

- Proposed `IssueUserJWT(signingKey, accountId, publicUserKey, name, expiration, tags)`; expiration is "optional but recommended"; "If not set, JWT will not expire." Target languages first: go, java, csharp.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-17: Ordered Consumer**

- Ordered consumer is "an ordered push subscription ... that automatically checks and recovers when a gap occurs in the consumer sequence."
- "The subscription must track the last good stream and consumer sequences. When a gap is observed, the subscription closes its current subscription, releases its consumer and creates a new one starting at the proper stream sequence."
- "If hearbeats are missed, consumer might be gone (deleted, lost after reconnect, node restart, etc.), and it should be recreated from last known stream sequence."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-18: URL support for all client options [STALE?]**

- Client authors decided NOT to encode connect options in URLs: URLs "could expose sensitive information in logs", parity across clients "would be forever churn", and URL-vs-option precedence is ambiguous.
- Superseded by nothing specific; ADR-40 (NATS Connection) is the spec for connect options.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-19: API prefixes for materialized JetStream views**

- "Each JetStream only listens to default API subjects with the prefix `$JS.API`"; API prefixes let a client pick a JetStream in another account or domain.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-15: JetStream Subscribe Workflow [STALE?]**

- "If a queue name is provided, configuring heartbeat or flow control is a mistake, since the server would send those message to random members."
- "For pull subscriptions ack policy of "none" or "all" is an error."
- Stream lookup by subject uses `<JS prefix>.STREAM.NAMES` with `{"subject": "..."}`; error unless exactly one stream matches.
- Common queue-subscribe mistake: two `js.QueueSubscribe("foo","bar")` calls each create their own ephemeral consumer, so "both members were receiving the same message." Go's fix: use the queue name as the durable name when no durable/bind given.
- Errors to raise: non-queue sub on a consumer with `DeliverGroup`; queue name mismatch with `DeliverGroup`; pull sub on a consumer with `DeliverSubject`; "only a deliver subject can be changed for an existing JS consumer."
- The NATS subscription must be created before the consumer create "because for durable subscriptions, this is the only way for the server to detect if the durable is already in use."
- Clients "must ensure that your client can support the 9 token version (v1) and versions with 11 or more tokens (v2), as new tokens may be added to the end."
- Ack types: terminal `+ACK`, `-NAK`, `+TERM`; progress `+WPI`. "Once a terminal Ack Type has been published for a message, the client should ignore all other user requests to send any type of ack." With ack policy `none`, ignore all acks.
- Automatic Status Management (ASM) is the default: heartbeats, flow control, pull 404/408, gap awareness handled by the library.
- Heartbeat alarm: "The time allowed before an alarm is raised should be 3 times the idle heartbeat interval."
- Gap detection compares consumer sequences from JSAck / `Nats-Last-Consumer`; "Gap checking should be disabled on queue / deliver group subscriptions."
- Flow control (push only): reply to the FC message's reply-to with an empty message; "The format of the Flow Control subject should not to be inspected." Server "requires that when flow control is turned on, an idle heartbeat is set." Missed FC shows as `Nats-Consumer-Stalled` header on heartbeats; respond once, "The server will ignore duplicates."
- Status handling: pull 404/408 never surfaced; 409 ("trying to pull from a push consumer, exceeding max ack pending") and 503 raised as errors; unknown statuses raised as errors.
- Auto-deleting a library-created consumer on Unsubscribe/Drain breaks queue groups: the first member creates it and deleting it "will cause member2 to stop receiving messages."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-21: NATS Configuration Contexts**

- A context is a named JSON config used by the `nats` CLI (`--context`) holding credentials, servers, domains, API prefixes; "This reflects a current implementation in use widely via the CLI as such it's a stable release. Only non breaking additions will be considered."
- Context keys: `url` (default `nats://localhost:4222`, comma-separated), `token`, `user`, `password`, `creds`, `nkey`, `cert`, `key`, `ca`, `nsc`, `jetstream_domain`, `jetstream_api_prefix`, `jetstream_event_prefix`, `inbox_prefix`, `user_jwt`, `tls_first`, `windows_cert_store`, `windows_cert_match_by`, `windows_cert_match`, `windows_ca_certs_match`. All optional, none `omitempty`.
- Go sample API: `Connect(name, opts...)` or `Load(name, overrides...)`; empty name = selected context; no selected context and empty name is an error.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-22: JetStream Publish Retries on No Responders**

- In clustered JetStream "there can be occasional blips in leadership which can result in a number of `no responders available` errors during the election."
- A JetStream publish is a `Request`; if JS is not ready "the server will send to the requestor a 503 status message right away."
- Go default retry: "waits for `250ms` and will retry 2 times sending the message (so that in total it would have attempted to send the message 3 times)." Options `RetryWait`, `RetryAttempts`; `RetryAttempts(-1)` retries until the context/AckWait deadline.
- After exhausting attempts the error is a timeout or `nats: no response from stream` if the last attempt was still no-responders.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-31: JetStream Direct Get**

- If `allow_direct` is false "there will be no responder at the Direct Get API ... Clients that make requests will receive no reply message and will time out."
- Multi pagination: pass EOB's `Nats-UpTo-Sequence` back as `up_to_seq` (stable snapshot) and `Nats-Last-Sequence + 1` as `seq` (inclusive lower bound); ends when `Nats-Num-Pending` is 0.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-32: Service API**

- Goal: "reduce development to having a complexity similar to that of writing a NATS subscription" plus metadata "for standardization of discovery and observability."
- Discovery verbs `PING`, `STATS`, `INFO` under `$SRV` (prefix must be overridable like `$JS`): `$SRV.<VERB>`, `$SRV.<VERB>.<name>`, `$SRV.<VERB>.<name>.<id>`; services respond to all three levels.
- Response types: `io.nats.micro.v1.info_response`, `io.nats.micro.v1.ping_response`, `io.nats.micro.v1.stats_response`; common fields `type,name,id,version,metadata`.
- Error convention: responses must include headers `Nats-Service-Error` and `Nats-Service-Error-Code` (numeric); "clients making request from the service _must_ check if the response is an error by looking for these headers."
- Handlers behave like normal subscription handlers: "no assumption is made on whether returning from the callback signals that the request is completed."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-34: JetStream Consumers Multiple Filters**

- Clients must check returned consumer info to confirm filters "to ensure compatibility with old servers that are not aware of `filter_subjects`."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-37: JetStream Simplification**

- Problem with legacy API: clients "create and update a consumer definition on the fly as `subscribe()` ... is invoked. This leads to some unexpected behaviors as different clients ... attempt to consume from the same consumer." Also forced Push vs Pull choice.
- New API components: JetStreamContext (stream mgmt + direct consumer mgmt), Stream (consumer mgmt, purge, info, getMsg, deleteMsg), Consumer (`consume()`, `fetch()`, `next()`, `info()`, optional `delete()`).
- Consumer creation: `createConsumer`, `updateConsumer`, `createOrUpdateConsumer`.
- "pull requests issued by clients should have client-side timeouts in addition to server-side timeout (`expiry`). Client-side timeout value should always be larger than expiry."
- Fetch: ends when the request expires or the requested count/bytes are delivered; at least one of `max_messages` / `max_bytes` is required; "For requests with `expires > 30s`, heartbeats should be enabled by default."
- Next: "The pull request to fetch the message should only be sent once `Next` is invoked."
- Consume: keeps a refillable buffer; "`max_messages` and `max_bytes` are exclusive"; if `max_bytes` set, "set `batch_size` in requests to a large number (e.g., 1 000 000)" because "`batch_size == 0`" makes the server send only one message.
- Consume defaults: `max_messages` "probably between 100 and 1000"; `expires` default 30s, minimum 1s; `idle_heartbeat` = 1/2 of expires, min 500ms, max 30s; `threshold_messages` 50% of max_messages; `threshold_bytes` 50% of max_bytes. Must work when `max_messages` is 1.
- Consume uses "a single subscription to handle responses for all pull requests"; tracks aggregate pending messages/bytes; new pull when threshold reached; each pull sized "so that the pull request will fill the buffer."
- Pending counters are corrected from termination statuses carrying `Nats-Pending-Messages` / `Nats-Pending-Bytes` headers: 408 Request Timeout, 409 Message Size Exceeds MaxBytes, 408 Interest Expired, 423 Nats-Wrong-Pin-Id.
- Message size for byte accounting = `len(subject) + len(ackReply) + len(hdr) + len(msg)` (server's formula, transport subject excluded).
- Status classes: Errors = 400 Bad Request, 409 Consumer Deleted, 409 Consumer is push based. Warnings = 409 Exceeded MaxRequestBatch / MaxRequestExpires / MaxRequestMaxBytes / MaxWaiting. Not telegraphed = 404 No Messages, 408 Request Timeout, 409 Message Size Exceeds MaxBytes, 408 Interest Expired, 423 Nats-Wrong-Pin-Id.
- `next()`/`fetch()` conclude when the pull terminates; `consume()` recovers by re-pulling "unless the status is `409 Consumer Deleted` or `409 Consumer is push based`."
- "`Consume()` should always use idle heartbeats"; warning if timer reaches "2 * request's idle_heartbeat"; timer reset on any message; "Heartbeat errors are not terminal."
- Reconnect behaviour (rev 2): on disconnect pause heartbeat timer and stop publishing pulls; on reconnect reset timer and publish a new pull. "Clients should never terminate the `Consume()` call on disconnect and reconnect events and should not check if consumer is still available after a reconnect."
- `info()` and `delete()` are optional because "a consumer that is exported across an account" may not have those APIs available.
- "The legacy functionality will be deprecated."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-40: NATS Connection**

- Connect flow: TCP → server `INFO` → client `CONNECT` → PING/PONG. With `protocol >= 1` in CONNECT "Server can send subsequent `INFO` on a ongoing connection" and clients must update server lists.
- Explicit TLS: upgrade after INFO if `tls_required` or client demands TLS. TLS First (implicit) requires server `tls { handshake_first }` and client `tls_first`; "available since NATS Server 2.10.4".
- INFO may carry additional cluster URLs; clients store them for reconnect; "A client should have an option to turn off using advertised URLs. By default, those URLs are used."
- On-demand `reconnect()` for auth refresh / rebalancing: drops the connection and performs standard reconnect with full resubscribe.
- Custom server pool (rev 4): option to use only a provided pool; "By default, advertised servers are merged with the provided pool"; new pool follows the same randomisation/max-reconnect rules. Reconnect-to-specific-server callback may pick only from the pool and may return a delay.
- Disconnect detection: "Missing two consecutive PONGs from the Server" (configurable) or network errors.
- Reconnect rules: immediate first attempt; then "Exponential backoff with jitter" ("to avoid thundering herd problems"); random order over advertised servers unless randomisation disabled; success resets timers; resubscribe everything.
- Disconnect buffer aggregates publishes during outage; when full "publish attempts should return error."
- Defaults: ping interval 2 minutes; max pings out 2; retry on failed initial connect false; max reconnects "3 / none" ("can also be a footgun and surprise for users who do not expect that the client can give up entirely"); connection timeout 5s; tls required false; ignore advertised servers false; retain servers order false.
- `-ERR Permissions Violation` matches `/(Publish|Subscription) to (\S+)/` and optionally `/using queue "(\S+)"/`; for subscriptions "errors are _terminal_ for the subscription, as the server cancels the clients interest"; notify the first matching subscription (server sends one error per offense).
- `Authorization Violation` → server disconnect; `User Authentication Expired` and `Account Authentication Expired` → disconnect, then reconnect is rejected with `Authorization Violation` until refreshed.
- `Maximum Payload Violation` → disconnect; "clients should test payload sizes and fail publishes that exceed the server configuration." `maximum subscriptions exceeded` "is not terminal to the connection."
- `maximum connections exceeded` and `Connection throttling is active...` (from tls `connection_rate_limit`) → reconnect loop; `invalid client protocol`, `Unknown Protocol Operation` → disconnect; `no responders requires headers support` should not occur since "Current clients hardcode `headers: true`" and "`headers` connect option shouldn't be exposed by the clients."
- `maximum account active connections exceeded` is not notified; the client just sees a refused connection.
- Client statistics (persist across reconnects): bytes in/out (socket level), messages in (`MSG`/`HMSG`), messages out (`PUB`/`HPUB`), connects/reconnects; new parity fields should use new names (e.g. Go `TotalBytesIn`).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-42: Pull Consumer Priority Groups**

- Pinned flow: server sets `Nats-Pin-Id: xyz` header on delivered messages; the client must send that `id` on all later pulls; pulls with a wrong `id` get a `423` status (`Nats-Wrong-Pin-Id` / `Nats-Pin-Id mismatch`) and the client "will clear its stored ID and issue subsequent pull requests with no ID set so it remains in the candidate pool."
- Clients must expose `group`, `min_pending`, `min_ack_pending`, `priority` on fetch/consume, track and clear `Nats-Pin-Id`, and implement `unpin`. Callbacks for becoming pinned / losing pin are suggested.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-44: Versioning for JetStream Assets**

- Clients may send `Nats-Required-Api-Level` header on any `$JS.API.>` request; server errors `api level not supported` if lower. "A single server does not represent a cluster-wide supported API level" (future: cluster-agreed level).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-47: Request Many**

- Request Many lets a client receive multiple replies to one request, supporting "patterns like scatter-gather and sentinel."
- "The client doesn't assume success or failure - only that it might receive messages"; "Request Many is not a recoverable operation, but it could be wrapped in a retry pattern."
- Config: total timeout (always used; defaults to connection request timeout; first wait always uses total); stall timer (optional; "Less than 1 or greater than or equal to the total timeout behaves the same as if not supplied"); max messages; sentinel predicate ("standard sentinel ... a message with a null/nil or empty payload").
- A status such as 503 or an error in place of a user message "is terminal" and should be conveyed at end of data.
- Blocking callbacks: user processing time must not count against timeouts.
- Strategies: "Timeout or Wait" (default, total only); "Stall" ("lessor of 1/10th of the total wait time ... or the default connection timeout"); "Max Responses".
- "it should always unsubscribe upon completion of the request handling instead of leaving it up to the server to time it out"; max-responses may `UNSUB <count>` immediately but "you still must check the count manually"; mux inbox variant cannot use that optimisation.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-48: TTL Support for Key-Value Buckets (updates ADR-8)**

- `Create()` and `Purge()` accept a TTL (adds `Nats-TTL` header).
- `Nats-Marker-Reason` mapping for readers/watchers: `MaxAge` → treat as PURGE, `Purge` → PURGE, `Remove` → DEL.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-49: JetStream Distributed Counter CRDT**

- Client lands in Orbit as a dedicated Counter module (not KV) because counter management "would not belong in KV"; requires `AllowMsgCounter` and `AllowDirect` (batch direct get for `GetMultiple`); API `Add`, `AddInt`, `Get`, `GetMultiple` with wildcard subjects; `Entry{Subject, Value *big.Int, Sources, Incr}`.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-50: JetStream Batch Publishing**

- Atomic protocol: first message is a *request* with `Nats-Batch-Id:<uuid>` and `Nats-Batch-Sequence:1` (server replies error or zero-byte); subsequent messages increment the sequence (optional reply gets zero-byte ack); final message has `Nats-Batch-Commit:1` (stored) or `Nats-Batch-Commit:eob` (2.14; not stored, `BatchSize` excludes it) and receives the pub ack.
- Fast-ingest control channel: reply subject `<prefix>.<uuid>.<initial flow>.<gap ok|fail>.<batch seq>.<operation>.$FI`; operations 0 start, 1 append, 2 commit+store, 3 commit EOB, 4 ping; "this must be an old style inbox" subscribed to `<prefix>.uuid.>` so unsubscribing short-circuits acks on error.
- "The client MUST wait for the first reply" before blasting messages; server dictates actual flow: starts low (e.g. client asks 100, server starts at 1), "usually doubles" to ramp up, "usually halves" to slow down, never exceeds the client's initial flow ("the server must treat the initial flow parameters as the upper bound").
- `BatchFlowAck {"type":"ack","seq":N,"msgs":M}`: with `gap: fail` "messages up to and including Sequence were persisted"; with `gap: ok` "_some_ of the messages ... were persisted." Acks are cumulative: a later ack implies earlier ones were received ("critical to avoid unrecoverable stalls").

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-54: KV Codecs (updates ADR-8)**

- Client-side codec layer wraps a KV bucket with independent `KeyCodec` (string↔string) and `ValueCodec` (bytes↔bytes) for "character escaping, path notation conversion, encryption, and custom transformations." (ADR: proposed; Orbit.)
- Codecs must be transparent across Put/Get/Watch/Keys/History/Delete/Purge; a `FilterableKeyCodec.EncodeFilter` preserves wildcards for watch/list; codecs may be chained (encode in order, decode in reverse).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-57: KV Subject Transforms (updates ADR-8)**

- KV mirror: clients "Prefix the mirror stream name with `KV_` if not already prefixed" and "Enable `MirrorDirect` on the underlying stream configuration" so mirrored buckets "Support direct reads via the Direct GET API" and "Automatically participate in RTT-based replica selection."
- KV sources without explicit transforms: clients prefix `KV_` and auto-add `{"src": "$KV.<source>.>", "dest": "$KV.<bucket>.>"}` (with key filter folded into src, e.g. `$KV.ORDERS.NEW.>` → `$KV.NEW_ORDERS.>`).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-58: Key-Value Store Roadmap and future considerations (updates ADR-8)**

- Read-only KV handle (`RoKV`: Get, History, Watch, Keys, Close, Status) must be supportable "against a read replica and cannot support `Put()`." (ADR: proposed)

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-8: JetStream based Key-Value Stores**

- `Entry` exposes Bucket, Key, Value, Created, Revision (stream sequence), Delta ("distance from the latest value", 0 = latest), Operation (PUT/DEL/PURGE). `Status` exposes Values, History, TTL, LimitMarkerTTL, IsCompressed, BackingStore (`JetStream`), Bytes, Metadata.
- KV interface: `Put`, `Create` ("only succeeds when the key does not exist if last historic event is a delete or purge"), `Update(key, value, lastRevision)`, `Delete` (preserves history), `Purge` (removes history, leaves the purge entry), `Get`, `GetRevision`, `History`, `Watch` ("the same Entry might be delivered more than once"), `Keys` (with filters), `Status`, `Info`.
- Manager: `KeyValue` (bind), `CreateKeyValue`, `UpdateKeyValue`, `CreateOrUpdateKeyValue`, `DeleteKeyValue`, `KeyValueBucketNames`, `KeyValueBuckets`.
- `Create()` on a deleted key: on `0`-failure, load current value; if it is a delete, retry with expected sequence = the delete's sequence.
- Watchers must emit an End Of Initial Data signal "the first time any message has a `Pending==0`" and "must also be sent if no data is present." Options: `IncludeHistory`, `IgnoreDeletes`, `MetaOnly`, `UpdatesOnly` (EOID sent immediately). Default sends all `last_per_subject` values including delete/purge ops.
- API design prior art: 20+ Consul/etcd libraries reviewed; `Get()` returns an `Entry` (not raw bytes); `Create`/`Update` as helpers over Put options.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-60: JetStream reliable stream sourcing/mirroring on WQ/Interest streams (updates ADR-59)**

- "clients should not fail when the consumer delivery sequence is not monotonic, except when needed for the 'ordered consumer' implementations"; a reset on an ordered consumer is treated as a gap and the consumer recreated.

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — Core protocol and connection defaults (server/const.go)**

- Default maximum outbound pending bytes per client before slow-consumer disconnect. `MAX_PENDING_SIZE = (64 * 1024 * 1024)` = 64 MiB (server/const.go:101-102)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — Client connection handling: slow consumers, stalls, buffers (server/client.go, server/opts.go)**

- Slow consumer by pending bytes: a CLIENT whose outbound pending exceeds max_pending (default 64 MiB) is closed with "Slow Consumer Detected: MaxPending of %d Exceeded" (server/client.go:2595-2612)
- Stall gate: when a client's outbound pending exceeds 75% of max_pending, fast producers publishing to it are stalled. `c.out.pb > c.out.mp/4*3` (server/client.go:2615-2621). Stall durations: 2ms minimum, 5ms when at/over the limit, at most 10ms total per readLoop pass. `stallClientMinDuration = 2 * time.Millisecond`, `stallClientMaxDuration = 5 * time.Millisecond`, `stallTotalAllowed = 10 * time.Millisecond` (server/client.go:124-127, 3708-3722)
- Slow consumer by write deadline: an i/o timeout on flush (write_deadline, default 10s) marks the connection slow consumer; routes count each event once; a write timeout before CONNECT is handled as slow consumer without incrementing the counter "as that can be misleading" (server/client.go:1944-1985)
- Per-connection read buffer grows from 512 B to 64 KiB and shrinks to 64 B; readLoop reports if a pass takes over 2s. `startBufSize = 512`, `minBufSize = 64`, `maxBufSize = 65536`, `readLoopReport = 2 * time.Second` (server/client.go:110-116)
- Server will not send an RTT PING before the first PONG, capped at 2s. `maxNoRTTPingBeforeFirstPong = 2 * time.Second` (server/client.go:118-122)
- Permission/result caches per client: 512 sublist results, 256 deny-perm, 128 perm entries; reply-permission tracking limit 4096 entries pruned every 1s. `maxResultCacheSize = 512`, `maxDenyPermCacheSize = 256`, `maxPermCacheSize = 128`, `replyPermLimit = 4096`, `replyPruneTime = time.Second` (server/client.go:471-479)
- On close, a minimal flush uses a 100ms write deadline. `lowWriteDeadline = 100 * time.Millisecond` (server/client.go:6002)
- Connection kinds: CLIENT, ROUTER, GATEWAY, SYSTEM, LEAF, JETSTREAM, ACCOUNT; client sub-types NATS, MQTT, WS (server/client.go:46-79)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — MQTT and WebSocket defaults (server/mqtt.go, server/websocket.go)**

- MQTT QoS1/2 redelivery: "As per spec, MQTT server may not redeliver QoS 1 and 2 messages to clients, except after client reconnects. However, NATS Server will redeliver unacknowledged messages after this default interval." `mqttDefaultAckWait = 30 * time.Second` (server/mqtt.go:143-147)
- MQTT default max ack pending per session 1024; cumulative across a session's subscriptions capped at 65535. `mqttDefaultMaxAckPending = 1024`, `mqttMaxAckTotalLimit = 0xFFFF` (server/mqtt.go:149-155)
- MQTT max payload 268435455 bytes (0xFFFFFFF, the protocol max) (server/mqtt.go:96)
- MQTT state lives in JetStream streams: `$MQTT_msgs` (subjects `$MQTT.msgs.`), `$MQTT_rmsgs` retained, `$MQTT_sess` sessions, `$MQTT_out`, PUBREL consumer prefix `$MQTT_PUBREL_` (server/mqtt.go:118-141)
- MQTT timers: session flapping jail 1s, flapper cleanup 5s, session transfer retry 5s, retained cache TTL 2m, retained transfer timeout 10s, JS API timeout 5s (server/mqtt.go:184-199)
- WebSocket: browser-friendly frame size 4096 ("From experiment, webrowsers behave better with limited frame size"); compression skipped under 64 bytes; max WS message = 8 x max_payload capped at 64 MiB. `wsFrameSizeForBrowsers = 4096`, `wsCompressThreshold = 64`, `wsMaxMsgPayloadMultiple = 8`, `wsMaxMsgPayloadLimit = 64 * 1024 * 1024` (server/websocket.go:59-63, 190-196)
- WebSocket permessage-deflate is negotiated with `server_no_context_takeover; client_no_context_takeover`; `Nats-No-Masking: true` header disables client masking (server/websocket.go:86-93)

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Orbit.go: A Guide to NATS Client-Side Abstractions for Go**

- Orbit is "the umbrella project for client-side abstractions which are above the NATS protocol level or need incubation before being incorporated"; modules independently versioned; some may "graduate to main clients."
- natsext RequestMany: iterator over multiple responses with termination by "timeout, maximum number of responses or even a custom predicate"; for scatter-gather/discovery; not for single-responder request-reply.
- jetstreamext atomic batch publish: all-or-nothing, fewer round-trips; [ANTI] avoid when "message deduplication is required" as it is "not compatible with batch publishing." Batch get: N messages from a sequence or last per subject set; "often simpler and more efficient than using a consumer for ad-hoc retrieval"; not for real-time, work-queue, interest, or very large datasets.
- natscontext reuses NATS CLI contexts ("eliminates configuration drift"); natssysclient queries monitoring endpoints per server or cluster-wide (not full coverage yet; skip if using Prometheus/Surveyor).
- pcgroups "brings Kafka-style consumer groups to NATS, leveraging the server's consumer priority policies"; static vs elastic membership; avoid when needing "strict global ordering across all messages on stream" or for "relatively low-throughput streams."
- kvcodec encodes keys with special characters (dots, spaces) and encrypts/compresses values transparently.
- counters module needs `AllowMsgCounter: true` and `AllowDirect: true`; works across sources and mirrors [note: contradicts later counter post which says mirrors are incompatible]; source tracking shows "exactly which service instances contributed."

- Core clients: "stability, performance, and reliability", "as un-opinionated as possible", "minimize dependencies." Orbit: experimental APIs, language-specific extensions, opinionated abstractions, staging ground.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Pull request MaxBytes and status handling (ADR issues 112 and 116)**

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Push Consumers (legacy)**

- Push subscription messages are pre-buffered asynchronously, so the client-side pending count "may or may not be" the number published.
- Unsubscribing an ephemeral push subscription deletes the consumer; even if omitted, the server eventually cleans up the ephemeral when it determines the subscription is no longer active.
- Helper-created durables (SubscribeSync with nats.Durable) are deleted when `Unsubscribe` or `Drain` is called: "these helpers should only be used if neither of those methods are called."
- On unsubscribe (or client crash), pending buffered messages are effectively dropped client-side; the server waits `AckWait` before redelivering, and "will only re-deliver if there is an active subscription."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publishing**

- Publishing into a stream works like a normal NATS publish except the server sends back a `PubAck` confirmation that it stored the message.
- A plain `nats pub` is a core NATS publish and the server returns nothing; use `--jetstream` to get the confirmation.
- You publish to a subject, not to a stream; the server finds the stream that captures the subject. "Your code doesn't need to know which stream is bound to which subject."
- The `PubAck` is your only proof that the message was stored. "The rule: the `PubAck` is your only proof that the message was stored."
- A publish to a subject no stream captures fails immediately with "no responders" and nothing was stored; a network timeout means no confirmation, not no write. "the server may have stored the message and the ack got lost on the way back."
- Handle a failed publish by retrying it or reporting the failure, and make the retry safe with the `Nats-Msg-Id` header.
- Ignoring the `PubAck`: code that discards it can't tell a stored message from a lost one; plain `nats pub` prints `Published N bytes` whether or not a stream captured the subject. "That line doesn't prove the message was stored."

- A consumer is an object on the server, not part of the application; stored messages and read position stay server-side so a client can disconnect and reconnect without losing its place. "The stored messages and the read position both stay on the server"
- Every delivered message carries metadata (stream/consumer sequence, pending, delivery count); read state off the message in handlers rather than calling `nats consumer info` per message. "fine for a one-off check, too costly to call for every message."
- Re-running a caught-up reader waits: with nothing new to deliver, the read command waits for the next message instead of returning.

- Two pull patterns exist in every client library: fetch (batch of up to N, returns when full or on timeout) and consume (continuous flow, library keeps pull requests open, runs until stopped).
- A fetch timeout is a ceiling: the call always returns within it, with whatever messages it has.
- The CLI has no single batch fetch; `nats consumer next --count N` issues N single-message pulls in a row.
- Client libraries set defaults for batch and expires, so a plain consume loop behaves well without tuning.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connecting**

- A connection is a single long-lived TCP connection opened once at application start and kept for the application's lifetime; every publish and subscription is multiplexed onto it. "A single connection handles thousands of subscriptions and a high message rate"
- `ws://`/`wss://` carries the protocol over WebSocket, the transport a browser has to use and the one that gets through a network allowing only outbound 443.
- A production client usually passes several URLs so it can fail over when one server is unreachable.
- The server sends `INFO` first (announcing `max_payload`, 1 MB by default, and header support); the client replies with `CONNECT` declaring name, features, and credentials.
- Echo is on by default; `NoEcho` at connect makes the server skip the originating connection. Name and echo are fixed for the life of the connection.
- PING/PONG defaults match on both sides: a PING every two minutes, and the connection is declared dead after two unanswered PINGs. "a PING every two minutes, and the connection is declared dead after two unanswered PINGs."
- Opening a new connection per message repeats the whole handshake each time; open one connection at service start and reuse it. "Opening a new connection per message."
- A client that publishes and subscribes on one subject receives its own messages with echo on (the default). "A client that publishes and subscribes on one subject receives its own messages."
- A short-lived program that exits immediately after publish can quit before the write buffer reaches the server; flush before exit. "Exiting before buffered publishes are sent."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connection lifecycle**

- The client owns reconnection: it re-dials, replays the handshake, and re-sends every subscription, on by default in every client library.
- The server keeps no per-client memory; a subscription exists only as an interest-graph entry tied to one socket, so a reconnecting client is a brand-new connection to the server.
- Publishes made while disconnected go into a bounded reconnect buffer, 8 MB by default, flushed in order on reconnect; a publish that would overflow it returns an error. "That buffer is bounded (8 MB by default)"
- Messages other publishers send while you're disconnected are gone; no client-side buffer can change that.
- Register the disconnect, reconnect, closed, and async error handlers before publishing or subscribing anything; the closed handler is the one that matters (client gave up or you closed deliberately).
- Wire the async error handler in every real service; without it, errors with no call to attach to (e.g. a subscription rejected by permissions) are invisible.
- Force reconnect (nats.go `Conn.ForceReconnect()`) is how you spread clients onto a newly added server after scaling out, or leave a server you know is about to go down on your schedule.
- Lame-duck mode stops accepting new connections, announces to connected clients, and closes existing connections gradually rather than all at once; a client watching for the notice can reconnect to another pool server before its socket is cut.
- The reconnect buffer lives in client memory and dies with the process; treat it as a short-term hold over a brief outage, not durable storage. "Trusting the reconnect buffer as a delivery guarantee."
- Connection callbacks run on the client's own thread; blocking one with a database write or slow HTTP call stalls other callbacks and in some clients the connection's processing. Keep handlers to a log line or a channel signal. "Doing real work inside a connection callback."
- Infinite reconnect can hide a wrong address or auth refusal as silent healthy-looking retries; log the drop and every failed attempt. "Letting infinite reconnect hide a dead configuration."

- Checklist: Open one connection per process and share it; don't connect per message or per request.
- Checklist: Decide about echo up front; a service that publishes and subscribes on the same subject receives its own messages unless it connects with echo off.
- Checklist: Flush or drain before a short-lived publisher exits, so buffered messages reach the server.
- Checklist: Process messages fast enough (or hand off to a worker) so a slow subscriber isn't cut off.
- Checklist: Wire the disconnect, reconnect, and async error callbacks first, and keep them to a log line or a signal.
- Checklist: Log the drop from the disconnect handler and every failed attempt from the reconnect-error callback.
- Checklist: Treat the reconnect buffer as best-effort client memory, not a delivery guarantee.

- On connect a server sends an INFO message including the other servers' client URLs, so a client knows all cluster members even if configured with one; this discovery is what enables failover to a server the client never named.
- Loss of one server is a reconnect, not an outage.
- `no_advertise: true` stops a server advertising its peers, so a client only knows the URLs given by hand; leave it off (the default) and failover spans the whole cluster.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leaf nodes**

- To local clients the leaf is a regular NATS server; a machine needs no leaf-specific configuration.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Rolling upgrades**

- The `INFO ldm:true` update drops the node from each client's server pool so the next reconnect lands elsewhere; the client takes no other action on the INFO itself.
- A node leaving in lame-duck mode requires no action from a correctly configured client; it keeps its existing connection, no client dials the node again, and on the staggered close the normal reconnect logic dials another node, resubscribes, and resumes.
- A reconnect storm comes from abrupt kills or a duration so short the spread collapses, not from lame-duck mode, which staggers closes precisely to spread reconnects. Roll one node at a time and let it rejoin before starting the next. "A reconnect storm comes from abrupt kills, not from lame-duck."
