- Give clients (and the CLI context) the URLs of all cluster servers; the client randomly picks one and moves on if a server is offline, which spreads connections evenly across the cluster. "NATS will be smart about randomly selecting one of these... if it doesn't detect that a server is online it will move on to another one" (~11:20)
- When a cluster server is killed, its client connections automatically fail over to the remaining servers and traffic continues. "I can kill one of these servers... and it will automatically move those connections over to either na1 or na3 and everything still works" (~12:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to set up Decentralized Authentication/Authorization in NATS | Rethink Connectivity Episode 6**

- Connect flow: server INFO carries a nonce; the client signs it with the user private key, sends the signature plus its JWT in CONNECT; the server validates the signature against the public key in the JWT, checks expiry/revocation, checks the signing account is known and was signed by the operator. "is the JWT expired or has it been revoked, was the JWT signed by an account that I know about, and was this account... did I sign it" (~08:13)
- A creds file is just the user JWT plus the NKey seed (private key), everything a client needs to connect; treat it as sensitive. "all a creds file is is it's a combination of the JWT and the private key" (~19:22)
- A user that must do request/reply needs subscribe permission on its inbox (`_INBOX.>`) in addition to publish permission on the service subject. "allow it to subscribe to its inbox which happens to be inbox dot wildcard, this allows us to have request response" (~25:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extend your NATS Cluster with Leaf Nodes | Rethink Connectivity Episode 7**

- Requests through an already-connected leaf link can return faster than a fresh direct connection to the hub because the direct path pays the TLS handshake each time. "that's actually the TLS delay making that TLS connection... via the leaf node connection we actually get much faster responses" (~16:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Dynamic Permissions with Scoped Signing Keys | Rethink Connectivity Episode 8**

- Include `allow-pub-response` on the scoped key so users can reply to requests later. "just for good hygiene in case we want to put in request reply at some point we should probably say allow pub response" (~08:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Connect ANY Auth System to NATS.io with Auth Callout**

- In the handler, create user claims with subject = the request's user NKey, set the audience to the target account name, and return the claims; the server signs and binds them. "the subject is actually going to be coming from our request... request.user_nkey" and "we do that by configuring the claim audience" (~19:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Superclusters in Kubernetes: Cross-Cloud Geo-Affinity for High Availability and Low Latency**

- A service in the services framework is declared with a name, version/description and endpoints that bind a handler to a full subject such as `math.numbers.add`; the Python `nats micro` module is one of many language implementations. "I'm using the NATS micro module and I'm going to add a service... declare the service name... and then add an endpoint" (~03:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Building an Interactive Whiteboard with NATS Websockets | Rethink Connectivity Episode 3**

- WebSocket support is off by default; enable it with a `websocket` block giving a listen port, and `no_tls: true` only for local dev — the server warns that non-TLS websockets should not be used in production. "websocket isn't turned on by default inside of NATS, you have to turn it on yourself" (~01:50)
- Turning websocket `compression` on is recommended for better performance. "I'll turn compression on just for better performance" (~02:20)
- NATS is payload agnostic, so browser code needs a codec (here JSON) to encode objects to a byte array before publish and decode on receive. "remember that NATS is payload agnostic so we have to use some sort of codec to encode and decode the message" (~05:08)
- Draw locally first for responsiveness, tag each message with a random per-player id, and on receipt ignore your own messages so only other players' strokes are applied. "if the data's id is not equal to this id then we can call draw raw" (~11:00)
- The nats.ws subscription is consumed as an async iterator (`for await (const m of sub)`). "we want to use an async iterator for this subscription" (~10:12)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS Leafnodes**

- Client applications are unaffected by topology: connecting to a route server, leaf node or super cluster server works exactly the same. "it doesn't matter if it's connecting to a route server or a leaf node server, a super cluster server, it all works exactly the same" (~28:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Replace Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis and more w/NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity Ep 10**

- A JetStream publish is a request to the subject; the server responds with a publish acknowledgement (pub ack) that means the message has been saved. "we call a pub ack or a publish acknowledgement ... telling the publisher that the NATS server has saved that message" (~04:07)
- The JetStream consumer API is built on core NATS request/reply on `$JS` subjects, so it can technically be used by hand, though the subjects are long and fiddly. "JetStream is actually built on top of core NATS request reply" (~07:10)
- The new JetStream Go API uses `jetstream.New(nc)` instead of `nc.JetStream()`, `CreateOrUpdateStream` instead of `AddStream`, and accepts `context.Context` for deadlines and cancellation. "a lot of these functions now support the context package ... hugely requested feature" (~14:20)
- Use create-or-update for streams so re-running the program keeps the server config matching the code. "we want to be able to run through it and make sure if we make any updates to the config of the stream that it matches" (~14:20)
- The new API's `consumer.Consume(callback)` replaces the old mix of push/pull, ephemeral/durable options; messages expose data, subject, headers and metadata (metadata new in 2.10). "now it's just so much more simple to consume from" (~22:30)
- Stop the consume context on graceful shutdown (signal handling) to clean up. "it does return a consume context which we will want to stop when we gracefully shut down" (~23:31)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Build Priority Background Jobs & Dead Letter Queues with NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity ep 12**

- Every consumed JetStream message carries metadata including the stream sequence and consumer sequence. "every single message in JetStream as you're consuming it has metadata about the message" (~19:27)
- Nak retries immediately; nak-with-delay schedules redelivery later; simply not acking lets the ack wait expire so the server detects hung or dead workers and retries. "what if one of these workers cannot respond and it needs to shut down or it's hanging ... I want JetStream to pick up on that fact" (~24:32)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared: Part 1 | Rethink Connectivity**

- JetStream consumers hold state on the server (position, pending acks); Kafka consumer groups leave offset persistence to client applications, so NATS clients are purely stateless. "there's nothing for the client application to persist ever" (~19:21)
- JetStream can also batch via asynchronous publishes for much higher write throughput; batching trades away real-time latency, and NATS leaves that trade-off to the engineer. "you can use asynchronous operations to get much higher write throughputs by doing batching" (~33:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared Pt 2: Consumers | Rethink Connectivity**

- Kafka client applications must persist their own offset; JetStream client applications persist no state. "the consuming applications in JetStream do not need to persist any state at all" (~07:10)
- The new simplified JetStream API hides push-versus-pull; you just create consumers and choose how to iterate. "it totally hides those subtleties" (~25:29)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Move over Kafka! Let's try NATS JetStream**

- Publishers can keep using plain core NATS publish with no JetStream knowledge; the server decides whether a message needs persisting. "publishers can continue to use NATS core they actually don't have to have any knowledge of JetStream" (~04:04)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | JetStream**

- Any standard NATS client in any of the 40+ languages can interact with JetStream, unlike Streaming server which needed dedicated clients. "you can use any standard NATS client that you have" (~02:06)
- JetStream administration is an API over the NATS wire: publish JSON to well-known subjects, so no custom client is required. "you just publish a JSON message on to a well-known subject and that's how you access the API" (~04:09)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Why NATS Consumers Just Work (And How to Use Them in 15 Minutes)**

- Pull fetches need a timeout so the process can leave the fetch, re-evaluate and run other work; the speaker uses 5 seconds, not 500 ms or 1 s. "You have to pass in a timeout ... 5 seconds is good" (~08:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream for Key-Value Store Tech Preview**

- The Go client offers an in-memory bucket cache: it starts a watcher, loads the whole bucket, marks ready, serves reads from memory, and writes invalidate the key until the watcher refreshes it. "before you need it even your cache will already be up to date" (~07:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers**

- An ordered consumer is a bundle of defaults: R1, no acks, client-side reset/retry on gaps, minimal server state, more work on the client. "ordered consumer ... an R1 no acknowledgement it handles if there are dropped messages it actually retries and resets itself internally" (~47:03)
- A client that processes too slowly on a fast delivery path becomes a slow consumer and the server disconnects it. "the server is not going to be happy ... you're a slow consumer of this data so I'm going to disconnect you" (~48:05)
- In-progress acks extend the ack wait window (30s mentioned as the window) to stop redelivery while still working on a message; nack and no-ack modes also exist. "within a 30 second time window send it in progress to stop redelivery attempts" (~50:08)
- The new JetStream client API removes the push/pull distinction; internally everything is pull-based. "there's actually no distinction anymore of a push versus pull consumer internally it actually is all pull-based now" (~51:10)
- Pull consumers with batching are not slower than push; clients interleave pull requests so latency between batches is minimized and it is on par or faster. "on par if not in some cases faster than a push consumer model" (~54:13)
- Batch fetching amortizes network overhead: one round trip for ten messages beats ten round trips. "you lose the network overhead of fetching one at a time pack a load of stuff together" (~56:14)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.10 Webinar**

- The NATS CLI `--defaults` flag skips the interactive stream-creation prompts. "there's this really nice new feature ... dash dash defaults so you don't have to fill out all this other stuff" (~02:01)
- By default the initial CONNECT/INFO exchange happens in clear text before the TLS handshake, even with TLS configured; it carries minimal client metadata. "that first initial message is basically in clear text and it has minimal metadata ... and then the TLS connection handshake actually occurs after that" (~12:16)
- The server respects an expiry on the callout-issued user JWT; today it disconnects the client at expiry and the client must reconnect, and retaining connection state across credential renewal was future work. "once the JWT has expired the user JWT it will effectively today disconnect the client and the client would just have to reconnect" (~53:04)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- Chaos tests showed that when servers go down, problems are often on the client side: clients reconnect too aggressively while "trying to be smart". "sometimes it's the clients ... they try to be smart and reconnect but we see they end up doing it quick enough we found also those issues" (~20:24)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP07: Going off piste; KV patterns with NATS.io (pt1)**

- KV and Object Store are client-side abstractions layered on a stream, with a deliberately smaller set of knobs. "KV and Object Store are client abstractions that lay on top of the stream and these abstractions are very convenient to use because the amount of knobs that they have are smaller" (~11:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03: Escaping the HTTP Mindset with NATS.io**

- NATS can be taken all the way to the front end (browser NATS client with its own auth), so HTTP is only needed at the authentication step. "the only time you use REST or HTTP... is maybe at the point of authentication" (~34:44)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02: Monolith to Modular Monolith with NATS.io**

- In Go the NATS server can be embedded directly in the application with no exposed TCP port, or an external server can broker the internal communication as a starting point. "you can even embed the NATS server directly into your application... you don't have to even expose any TCP connection" (~16:19)
- Agreeing on a payload schema (protobuf, JSON schema) over NATS lets teams with different skills (C++ game engine vs. .NET monetization) keep their own language; NATS's client coverage makes polyglot splits natural. "each team gets to use their beloved language" (~22:29)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP04: A Service Mesh Pattern for NATS.io**

- WebSocket support and the JavaScript client already extend NATS to the browser without an HTTP proxy. "we have the WebSocket interfaces... if you're a JavaScript junkie then we also have the JS library" (~49:59)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP05: Exploring Powerful Client-side Features and Abstractions in NATS.io**

- Client design goal: shared orientation points (same verbs and nouns, same structure) across languages, but each client stays idiomatic; identical APIs everywhere is only something NATS engineers think users want. "we don't also want to fall into the trap to make each client the same" (~04:05)
- The original JetStream API mimicked core NATS Subscribe so closely that users jumped into JetStream without learning it and did not realize a consumer is a server-side construct, producing surprises. "people didn't even realize that the consumer's a server-side construct" (~06:07)
- The "simplification" API deliberately requires more explicit calls (create stream, create consumer, then consume) so the server-side resources and their behaviour are visible to the developer. "you explicitly have to do those things... oh I have to create some stream, oh I have to create some consumer" (~07:09)
- The JetStream API rewrite was treated as a once-in-a-long-time opportunity to fix the API, because the team otherwise avoids breaking changes and that makes iteration hard. "that's probably the only opportunity we have in quite a long time to in general improve the JetStream API" (~08:10)
- Historically the Go client was the role model that other clients copied (callbacks everywhere even where iterators are idiomatic); the new approach decides per language how close to stay. "we have this role model Go client and then others are following it and we never discussed how close they should be" (~09:10)
- Ephemeral vs durable was reduced to a simpler concept: a consumer is ephemeral when it is cleaned up after an inactivity threshold; otherwise you delete it explicitly. "it's ephemeral based on some inactivity thresholds... or you say don't clean it up server for me" (~13:16)
- Old fetch-loop pull consumption left gaps in network utilization between one fetch finishing and the next; the new consume method interleaves fetches under the hood so delivery never pauses. "the client will under the hood optimize the fetches, meaning it will interleave the fetches so there is never a pause" (~17:22)
- The services (micro) API is a purely client-side abstraction combining three server capabilities: the interest graph, subject-based routing, and queue groups; no server changes and no JetStream involved. "interest graph with subject based routing and the queue groups, those are the three elements" (~33:45)
- Because the services API is a thin layer, code outside the framework can talk to services written with it and vice versa; using it never cuts you off from low-level NATS. "there's no cutting out of capabilities because of using the service API" (~34:46)
- For client-side abstractions (KV, Object Store, services) the server cannot validate compatibility, so a bucket written from Rust can silently not work from Go unless the clients are cross-tested. "server will not help you here because it's just an abstraction layer" (~40:51)
- Object Store stayed "experimental" until a cross-language compatibility test tool asserted put/get/update across Go, Rust, JavaScript, .NET, and Java, because a later fix would require migrating existing buckets. "we created... a tool that tests and asserts the results across all the languages" (~41:52)
- Client behaviour is specified in public ADR documents in the nats-io org, used as the spec for client maintainers; the team is moving toward test-driven specs where each ADR feature ships with a compatibility test. "use this testing tool to do something like test driven spec" (~44:55)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Micro-services with auto discovery, observability and load balancing. | Rethink Connectivity Ep 9**

- The NATS services API is a set of conventions baked into client libraries (Go `micro` package, JS/TS, Rust, Java) rather than a framework, proxy, or extra tooling. "the NATS service API is a set of conventions that is baked into a lot of our client libraries" (~01:01)
- Service config carries name, version, description, optional API URL (e.g. an OpenAPI spec), a default endpoint or multiple endpoints; an endpoint is a schema coupled with a handler on a subject (wildcards allowed). "an endpoint is really a schema coupled with an actual handler" (~06:05)
- The stats, done, and error handlers are optional extension points; stats come out of the box and custom metrics can be pushed via the stats handler. "we actually bring stats out of the box with this services API" (~07:05)
- Handler errors are returned with a code and description carried as headers (a 400-style code for malformed input); a payload can optionally be attached. "return a 400... I'm okay just having the error be embedded as a header" (~10:11)
- The schema field is an opaque string: JSON Schema, protobuf, or anything encodable (base64 if needed), so tooling can generate clients in any language. "these are all just a string so... you could really use whatever kind of schema that you want" (~18:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP01S3: Going back to basics with core NATS!**

- The clients deliberately do not add generic request retry logic: a built-in retry is an opinion that suits ~90% of use cases but is wrong for the other 10% (e.g. transactional systems needing immediate failure). "for 90% of use cases yeah it should retry but it will then make very bad user experience for those 10%" (~29:46)
- Stacked retries across layers (front end retries, back end retries, next back end retries) can bring a whole system down; a single enforced retry opinion is dangerous. "based on timing it would just bring the whole system down" (~30:50)
- Clients do reconnect automatically and resubscribe to prior subscriptions, and surface disconnect/reconnect events, because the network is usually the weakest link (e.g. clients in vehicles). "our clients do reconnect automatically and resubscribe to the subjects that they were subscribed before the connection was lost" (~28:45)
- Maintainers keep feature parity across clients while staying idiomatic per language; language-specific feature requests create a domino effect on every client. "we try to keep parity across the clients and this feature makes zero sense in like Rust or Go" (~31:51)
- Breaking changes to APIs like Object Store are avoided because honoring semver would force a major release across every client; this is why the API is hard to improve in place. "we are stuck with this API which we couldn't improve because we don't want to break any of our users" (~33:54)
- Strategy shift: core clients focus on reliability and low-level protocol bindings with unopinionated patterns; opinionated/experimental abstractions go to the separately versioned Orbit umbrella project. "switch the focus and the client to focus on reliability, basically low-level NATS protocol binding ... and then to create separately versioned libraries elsewhere" (~32:52)
- Connection pooling is a frequent request from database-minded users; the answer is to start with one connection and keep it unless you have a very specific reason. "you should start with one connection and unless you are something very specific use case you should keep that one connection" (~37:58)
- Considerable effort has gone into removing head-of-line blocking in the clients; a single TCP connection should not slow you down unless the network itself is misbehaving. "we did a really hard effort ... to remove the head of line blocking problems in NATS" (~37:58)
- One connection preserves publish ordering across all publishers in the application, and subscribers see that same ordering. "with one connection you also preserve publish ordering" (~38:59)
- You do not need separate connections per stream, consumer, or publisher; all of them multiplex over one connection. "you don't need a new connection for a consumer then also a new one for a publisher and then you maybe have five streams" (~40:02)
- A reason for a second connection is client-implementation specific, e.g. Java client internal queue sizes when one publisher saturates the queue. "in the Java client there are some triggers to do with queue sizes" (~41:03)
- Some customers with unusual cloud network setups do get an improvement from multiple connections; creating two client instances works fine for that. "some customers who have very specific network setups over the cloud providers ... for them it actually makes an improvement to have more connections" (~41:03)
- Pooling is deliberately not provided because users would default to it out of habit and then be confused by lost ordering. "if we give pooling to the users everybody would start with pooled connections and half of the people will be confused why I lost the order" (~42:05)
- The ~10 million msgs/s a single client can publish goes over one connection; the speaker doubts two connections from the same client would exceed it. "they can go for one connection and I don't think you can get more if you do over two the same client" (~44:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02S3: Orbit - The NATS Client Extensions**

- Tier-one clients (Go, Java, JavaScript, Rust, Python, C, Ruby, .NET) get every new server feature and promise parity; tier-two clients such as Swift are maintained by Synadia but may lag behind. "tier one clients are always in parity, that they have feature coverage ... each of them is idiomatic to their own language" (~04:06)
- Tier-one status is decided mostly by user, customer and community demand; Swift was not considered until interest from edge devices grew quickly. "that's how we mostly decide what's tier one what's not" (~05:08)
- In the past, features were merged into individual clients as users asked; every such feature soon triggered "why is it not in the other language", so now every new tier-one feature must pass a parity check agreed by all maintainers. "every new feature added to tier one client has to go through the parity check" (~09:15)
- Language-agnostic client APIs that look identical across languages end up feeling foreign in every language; NATS prefers idiomatic clients and steers users to per-language examples. "it felt very weird for me as a Gopher, like it didn't feel like Go" (~12:16)
- The ADR and design process was strengthened because parity failures were often about how a feature works, not just whether it exists. "we didn't have always the parity ... not just parity of features but parity in terms of how a given feature works" (~15:18)
- Bundling JetStream, KV and Object Store in one client with a single version makes breaking changes practically impossible under semver, even for APIs marked experimental. "it feels like we never can break anything, we can mark a specific API experimental but how does it matter" (~16:20)
- Orbit is a line in the sand: existing client features stay, and every new client-side abstraction built on streams/consumers (like KV, Object Store and the service API are) lands in Orbit instead of the client. "every new abstraction built on top of ... will land in Orbit, so it's like a line in the sand to not break the clients" (~19:21)
- Server APIs are performance-oriented (one struct for many operations), so clients do not expose them one-to-one; Orbit also serves as an incubator for new server-feature APIs whose client shape is not yet settled. "Orbit ... as an incubator for the new features and new APIs which we are not confident the shape of yet" (~21:23)
- Orbit is one umbrella repository per language containing many independently versioned modules, so each can evolve, be released weekly, be stabilized, or be deprecated without a client breaking change. "each client has their own umbrella repository with many crates, modules ... each having separate versioning" (~22:24)
- Orbit does not promise parity: request-many is expected in every tier-one Orbit library, but Go-specific utilities (context helpers) and Java-specific ones (publisher factory) stay language-local. "we also don't promise parity in Orbit" (~24:29)
- Contributing to Orbit only requires knowing the public client API, not client internals, which lowers the barrier compared with the large client codebases. "the only knowledge necessary being I know how to use the client, not the machinery of the client itself" (~25:29)
- Orbit modules use only public client APIs (dogfooding), which exposed several internals that SDK builders need and that the clients had not exposed. "we learn along the way that we didn't expose some really important bit to be able to write really flexible SDKs on top of it" (~29:35)
- Maintainers are conservative about exposing client internals because each exposed piece becomes something that can break during client evolution; needs are now justified by concrete Orbit usage. "we are always very careful with exposing any internals because it makes evolving the client even harder" (~31:36)
- Batch (direct) get is a 2.12 feature that will be implemented in Orbit rather than the client, not because the server side is unstable but because the client API shape could not be agreed within a few weeks. "batch get which will be the 2.12 feature ... we decided to get it into Orbit instead of the client" (~32:37)
- Orbit never talks the wire protocol directly; it builds on the highest available client abstraction and drops at most one layer down to publish/subscribe. "never wire protocol ... we try to use as high level abstraction from the client in Orbit as possible" (~34:41)
- Typed JetStream request helpers (with typed errors and success responses) are being exposed in Go so users can build their own admin APIs on top. "allow people to build their own additional like admin API ... which is actually now exposed in the Orbit of Go" (~34:41)
- Request-many sends one request and collects multiple responses with pluggable stop strategies: expected message count, stall/jitter timeout since the last message, and others; it is a core-NATS extension built on pub/sub. "one of them being how many messages you expect, the other being the jitter, how long you expect to wait for the next message" (~35:41)
- Orbit coverage in early 2025: Go has the most modules, followed by Java, Rust and JavaScript; .NET, C and Ruby are following; Rust had only request-many at the time. "the most amount of modules are in Go and then it's followed up by Java, Rust and JavaScript" (~37:45)
- Previously hidden tooling such as the JSM report utilities is now surfaced through Orbit; even Synadia staff did not know some existed. "some like in JSM report that almost nobody externally uses and it was hidden very deeply" (~39:49)
- The service API being placed in the clients is regretted because its API was frozen immediately; if built today it would live in Orbit. "we were actually not very happy that the service API was in the clients because we very quickly felt that we couldn't break the API" (~40:51)
- Rule for where new features go: server features go straight into the clients (server API is public and stable since 2.x); non-parity items and abstractions go to Orbit; server features with uncertain client API shape incubate in Orbit and move back when mature. "most features will come directly to the clients ... every new abstraction ... will land in Orbit" (~42:54)
- The clients' feature set is frozen at core NATS, JetStream, KV and Object Store; the long-term goal is to make clients lighter, closer to a low-level wire-protocol binding, without breaking anything. "we froze the clients with the feature set at core NATS, JetStream, KV, Object Store" (~43:57)
- For 2.11 priority groups, pinning and overflow are supported in the clients as basic primitives, while the full consumer-group abstraction built on pinning is implemented and iterated in Orbit. "the pinning and overflow will be supported in the clients ... the actual whole consumer group abstraction implementation will be in Orbit" (~45:59)
- The best way to discover Orbit extensions is the per-language repo, where each extension has its own README with version, docs and examples. "each extension is a separate readme page ... with all the details, all the docs and all the examples" (~48:01)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03S3: NATS 2.11 Release**

- At 2.11 launch overflow is in all clients; pinning ships in Go first while the Orbit consumer-group abstraction built on pinning is validated. "overflow will be available in all the clients when 2.11 launches, the pinning will be available in Go first" (~27:36)
- Paused consumers keep sending idle heartbeats, so client applications see no errors, only an absence of messages until resume. "the consumers still continue to receive idle heartbeats so the applications won't get errors" (~38:49)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS tools and benchmarking with JNM! NATS Community Office Hours (Reupload)**

- The NATS server is also a built-in MQTT server for edge devices, and switching a client from TCP to WebSocket (or secure WebSocket) is only a change of the connection URL scheme. "the NATS server is also an MQTT server built in ... changing two or three characters in a connection URL" (~21:26)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS: Ordered, Scalable Stream Processing**

- In the CG tool the filter must be passed with the filter flag; passed as a plain argument it is read as a member name. "If you pass the arrow as a plain argument, it gets read as a member name instead, so don't do that" (~17:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Pull Consumer Priority Groups: Overflow, Pinned & Prioritized**

- A stale or wrong pin ID is rejected with a 423 mismatch; the client clears its ID and repulls with none to rejoin the standby pool. "the server rejects that poll with a 423 mismatch. The client just clears its ID and repolls with none" (~07:04)
- A pull that doesn't claim the pin is not rejected; it gets a 408 and waits its turn behind the pinned client. "A client that doesn't claim the pin isn't rejected, it just waits its turn behind the pin client" (~09:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Distributed Counters in NATS — Global Totals Without Locks**

- Counter values are big integers stored as JSON strings so they can exceed 2^63 and JavaScript won't lose precision. "Values are big integers, not 64-bit ints ... They're stored as JSON strings for exactly this reason" (~02:01)
- The typed Go client is the orbit.go counters module (NewCounterFromStream, then Add/Load/Get, using big integers); other clients can publish the header directly and parse the JSON body. "Other language clients can interact with counter streams today by publishing the header directly and parsing the JSON body" (~04:03)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Expected Sequence Headers — Optimistic Concurrency Control Explained**

- In Go the options are WithExpectLastSequence, WithExpectLastSequencePerSubject, and the per-subject-pattern variant. "You would use jetstream with expect last sequence" (~04:05)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Consumer Pausing | NATS 2.11**

- A paused consumer's application sees no errors or disconnects and keeps receiving heartbeats. "No errors, no disconnects. It keeps getting heartbeats like everything's fine" (~01:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Atomic Batch Publishing | NATS 2.12**

- Orbit's JetStream extension package manages batch ids, sequence numbers, and commit for you (add messages, call commit). "You just add messages and call commit. The library handles batch IDs, sequence numbers, everything" (~07:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS: Orbit – Extending NATS Clients with Richer Capabilities**

- Every client PR faces a trade-off: added utilities grow client complexity, and language-specific abstractions break parity; parity across tier-1 clients is a core goal so users can rely on every feature in every language. "we really strive that all tier one clients, the most used ones have parity" (~00:06)
- Opinionated defaults (e.g. timeouts) in the core clients are regretted over time because NATS use cases are too varied (cars on bad networks vs cloud) for one sensible default. "every opinion that we try to land in the client, it's just matter of time, we will regret it" (~02:08)
- Clients cannot break stable 1.0 APIs even for experimental additions like the service API or KV API, so design mistakes had to be kept. "even if we marked it as experimental like service API, key value API we have to keep the API even we found problems with them" (~04:13)
- Users care about the number of client dependencies; abstractions like KV and object store often needed new ones. "our users really care about number of dependencies in the clients" (~04:13)
- Orbit is a set of separately versioned libraries on top of the clients, available in Go, Rust, Java, JavaScript, and Python, with others coming. "for now it's available in Go, Rust, Java, JavaScript and and Python and others are coming soon" (~05:14)
- Request-many (one request, many replies) landed in Orbit rather than the clients because the termination strategies are opinions. "there are quite a few strategies you can terminate the responses and those felt like opinions" (~06:16)
- Other Orbit contents: language-specific publishers, a system client for NATS contexts, retriers in some languages, and direct batch (a 2.11 feature) incubated in Orbit before merging back to clients. "all of the languages will have direct batch the new feature of 211" (~07:18)
- The split: core clients focus on performance, stability, parity, being lightweight and unopinionated; Orbit holds high-level abstractions, new APIs, and opinions. "stable and performant versus new and abstractions plus opinions" (~09:19)
- Planned for Orbit: KV codecs, more core NATS and JetStream utilities, object store iterations, and incubating non-server APIs that may merge back to clients once stable; Orbit libraries need not have full parity. "we allow to be not not have full parity in orbit and also to have some discrepancies across orbit libraries" (~10:21)
- The biggest upcoming Orbit capability named is a schema registry. "the big one that will land hopefully soon is schema registry" (~12:24)
- JetStream retry strategies could not go into clients because banking and vehicle use cases differ too much; they land in Orbit as quality-of-life additions. "retrying is quite often in JetStream is tricky and very opinionated ... impossible to have one solution" (~13:26)
- Orbit is not exclusive to the client: you use the client and load Orbit extensions (in Rust as an extension crate); only larger abstractions like schema registry or KV codecs might not need the client loaded directly. "it's not exclusive definitely it's extending" (~15:29)
- Client unit tests cover features and error cases but not network problems; Synadia runs private nightly chaos tests plus Antithesis deterministic simulation to reproduce one-in-a-million bugs. "we have the antithesis tooling ... deterministically reproduce very one in a million bugs" (~16:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Future of NATS: Roadmap & Vision**

- Orbit functionality may be ported into core clients once solidified, or remain as stabilized Orbit packages. "once they sort of get solidified we can basically port and move that functionality into the core clients if it makes sense" (~11:21)
- 2.12 focus: higher-order client-side patterns, some requiring native server capabilities, because clients are good at primitives and need to move up the stack. "some of these require native NATS server capabilities so that we can build client side higher order patterns" (~21:36)
- NATS has always been payload-agnostic; schema registry and codecs are a first step up the stack into data governance. "NATS doesn't care about the payload ... schema registry is sort of a first pass to that" (~26:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — We need to talk about Microservices... (And how NATS.io can simplify things)**

- The NATS server has no concept of a registered service; service discovery is pure convention built on request/reply to $SRV.PING, where every subscribed instance self-reports. "the NATS server actually doesn't have a concept of services ... we just use convention" (~08:08)
- The `micro` service library exists in many client libraries and lets you declare a service with name, version, endpoints and arbitrary metadata (e.g. description, request/response schema). "we have a little library called micro and it's in many of our client libraries already" (~09:11)
- `nats micro list` / `nats micro info <svc>` / `nats micro stats <svc>` discover instances, endpoints, metadata and per-instance request/error counts; `--json` makes the output automatable. "if I actually run this again with a json flag you can see all this is just pure json" (~12:14)
- The `micro info` response is itself load balanced: whichever instance answers reports its own ID. "this is the ID of the actual instance that decided to respond ... it's actually load balancing the info response" (~12:14)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The ONE feature that makes NATS more powerful than Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ & Redis**

- Reconnecting quickly re-binds to the same ephemeral consumer because the server keeps ephemerals around briefly for network jitter; add randomness to the name or use create-consumer (which errors on conflict) to force a fresh one. "we keep ephemeral consumers around just for a little bit because we know that there's network jitter" (~31:32)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Give your Go app superpowers with an Embedded NATS Server**

- Go applications can import nats-server/v2 and run the server in process; benefits are no separate NATS distribution and the option to bypass the network stack entirely. "we can actually bypass the network interface altogether and directly talk to NATS in process" (~00:00)
- Embedding alone still connects over the loopback interface, so you still pay network-stack latency; the in-process connection option removes that. "even though you're embedding NATS server you're still connecting over the localhost loopback interface" (~03:04)
- With in-process connections you keep multi-tenancy, JetStream, KV and Object Store while "literally just pushing bytes around inside of the application". "we're not going through the network layer we're literally just pushing bytes around inside of the application" (~04:05)
- Startup is asynchronous: after calling Start in a goroutine you must block on ReadyForConnections with a timeout (5 s in the demo) before connecting a client. "we actually need to wait for it to be ready for connections" (~09:10)
- server.Options is the programmatic equivalent of the config file; the client URL can be taken from the server's ClientURL method; WaitForShutdown handles termination signals for the server lifecycle. "you can kind of think about this as like your config file" (~08:08)
- Server logging is off by default when embedded; call ConfigureLogger to enable it. "we can actually have configurable logging for this NATS server but trust me silence is golden" (~13:14)
- Setting the DontListen option makes the embedded server open no network port at all, so the app is fully closed; a normal client connect then fails and only in-process connections work. "you can actually create this really closed application and use the NATS server without actually exposing any sort of network interface" (~16:15)
- The client-side option is nats.InProcessServer(server); it accepts an InProcessConnProvider interface, so any custom transport can be substituted for TCP. "it actually takes an interface called the InProcess Connection Provider" (~17:17)
- Benchmark of a full synchronous request/reply: in-process was about 4x faster than loopback on camera and about 5x when not recording, with loopback measured at roughly 16,000 ns per round trip. "I was getting like a 5x improvement over loopback when you're using in-process" (~19:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Transcending microservices with NATS | RethinkConn '22**

- Native HTTP/REST from the browser can be bridged to NATS with simple shims; treat HTTP as a ports-and-adapters layer on the perimeter, with NATS connecting everything behind it. "there's very very simple shims that can be deployed to do a nice translation directly from native HTTP requests into a NATS message" (~25:28)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Short break and Q&A! | RethinkConn '22**

- Every request across an import carries a system-vouched client info header; by default it shares little (location, account), but the importer can opt in to share everything: app version, language, IP, account, user ID. "there's a consumer info header on every request that the system is actually validating and vouching for" (~07:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS KubeCon Tutorial on Twitch**

- WebSocket needs only a `websocket` block with a port (9222 in the demo) and TLS; browser clients then use the same NATS API as TCP clients with no translation layer. "You can have your servers in the cloud use TCP but... web apps or mobile app... can use WebSockets." (~31:51)
- All clients move raw bytes; encoding (JSON, protobuf) is the application's concern, e.g. a StringCodec in the JS client. "NATS all it cares about is moving bytes. It doesn't care about whether it's protobuf or JSON." (~28:48)
- Clients reconnect automatically after a server restart; the JS client also receives an async close event when the server revokes its user. "It disconnected but it reconnected automatically... all that is taken care of in the client libraries." (~27:44)
