**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Zen of High Performance Messaging with NATS by Waldemar Quevedo Salinas**

- Because inboxes rely on random strings, clients depend on the quality of the runtime's pseudo-random number generator. "They are sensitive to the reliability of the available pseudo random number generation that you have in your runtime." (~09:17)
- The Go client is the canonical implementation other clients reference; an nginx module lets nginx learn proxy routes over NATS without config reloads. "By having nginx hooked into NATS it will almost instantly know where to send the traffic." (~12:19)
- Client publishes are buffered and coalesced, so after a publish loop there is no guarantee bytes were sent; flush by appending a PING and waiting for the PONG. "We append an extra ping at the end of the buffer and we make a future so that we're expecting a pong back." (~13:21)
- A full-mesh cluster removes the single point of failure; clients reconnect to another server, and newer clients learn cluster topology dynamically as servers join. "The original server will notify all of the clients where is the new member from the cluster." (~22:39)
- On server loss, clients by default reconnect randomly to one of the other known cluster members. "By default they will randomly try to reconnect to one of the other immediately available nodes." (~23:44)
- A request timeout is ambiguous: no responder, dropped request, slow responder, or responder crash mid-processing, so callers must handle errors deliberately. "We need to be more careful when how to do error handling in these cases." (~28:53)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — SCaLE 13x Derek Collison  NATS A new nervous system for distributed cloud platforms**

- Clients are cluster-aware without DNS or load balancers: given a server pool they pick randomly and reconnect to another on failure, typically in 10–15 ms once the socket drop is seen. "The reconnect speed is usually about ten fifteen milliseconds or so." (~35:54)
- Apcera embedded a C++ NATS client directly in nginx's event loop to update routing tables on the fly at ~400–500k signed and encrypted updates per second. "Update nginx routing tables on the fly... about four to five hundred thousand times a second." (~34:54)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Native MQTT Support in NATS Server**

- Enabling MQTT needs only a server name, JetStream enabled (MQTT persists state in JetStream), and an `mqtt` port block; the server then accepts both MQTT and native clients. "Enable JetStream which is needed by MQTT in order to persist some state, then we open the MQTT port." (~02:06)
- On MQTT client connect the server creates JetStream assets for that client automatically. "It did accept an MQTT client and created JetStream assets for that client." (~03:07)
- MQTT topics map to NATS subjects by replacing slashes with dots; a NATS `>` subscription receives MQTT messages and NATS publishes are converted back to MQTT for MQTT subscribers. "Simply replacing slashes by dots... the exchange goes both ways." (~04:08)

## OPS: Operations: monitoring, upgrades, backup, capacity (1475 claims)


**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Compare NATS**

- NATS monitoring: Prometheus exporter, Grafana dashboards, nats-top, NATS surveyor ("side car deployment or a simple connect-and-view model").
- "NATS separates operations from security. User and Account management in a deployment may be decentralized and managed through a CLI." Server config can be reloaded at runtime.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject-Based Messaging**

- Subscriptions are cached in server memory: "when increasing your subscribed subject count to more than one million you will need more than 1GB of server memory and it will grow linearly from there."
- Wire tap: subscribe to `>` to receive all messages, "subject to security settings", for monitoring.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS Service Infrastructure**

- On Kubernetes, "we recommend you use the Helm charts" (nats-io/k8s).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Request-Reply**

- Observability "is as simple as running another application that can view requests and responses to measure latency".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Queueing / Pub-Sub / Request-Reply walkthroughs, Walkthrough setup**

- Server listens for clients on TCP 4222; `-m 8222` enables HTTP monitoring.
- A public demo server exists at `nats://demo.nats.io`.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream (concept overview)**

- File streams flush writes to the OS synchronously but by default do not fsync immediately; `sync_interval` default is 2 minutes; "The data will be fsync-ed no later than this interval."
- Non-replicated: an OS failure (power loss, not just process kill) may lose acknowledged messages. Replicated: acknowledged after quorum, but simultaneous OS failures before fsync can lose recently acked messages; a data-losing server may rejoin and "form a new majority with nodes that have never received or persisted a given message".
- `sync_interval: always` fsyncs after every message before ack; "combined with replication in different data centers or availability zones, provides the strongest durability guarantees but at the slowest performance." It has a server-wide performance impact.
- Defaults chosen for "a typical production deployment scenario across multiple availability zones"; divergence for an R3 stream across 3 AZs needs a specific 5-step chain of failures.
- Mitigation: don't auto-restart an OS-failed server until a majority has the new writes, or peer-remove it and re-admit as a wiped peer to recover over the network.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Consumers**

- SampleFrequency: percentage of acks sampled for observability (`30` or `30%`).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Headers**

- Tracing (2.11, ADR-41): `traceparent` (W3C, needs `msg_trace` account config) or `Nats-Trace-Dest`; `Nats-Trace-Only: true` skips delivery; `Accept-Encoding` gzip/snappy compresses traces.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Example configuration (ORDERS)**

- Sample 100% of acks on NEW/DISPATCH so redelivery counts and ack delays go to monitoring.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Source and Mirror configuration example**

- "Streams with source and mirror configurations are best managed through a client API"; from CLI use a JSON config (`nats stream add --config`).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream walkthrough**

- Enable JetStream with `nats-server -js`; `nats account info` shows "JetStream is not supported in this account" when disabled.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject Mapping and Transforms**

- With config-file accounts, reload the config to apply transform changes; with operator JWT, transforms and imports/exports live in the account JWT and apply when pushed.
- Test rules with `nats server mapping`; from 2.11 observe with `nats trace`.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Clustering**

- The full mesh requires that servers can connect to each other and clients can connect to each server in the cluster.
- Seed servers have no special configuration; they are the discovery starting point for servers (routes) and clients (connect URLs); "the ability for other server and clients to successfully connect depends on seed server running." Multiple seeds should route to each other.
- Cluster `listen` with no host binds all interfaces (0.0.0.0); port is the minimum required.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Clustering Configuration**

- `advertise`/`cluster_advertise` is useful behind NAT; with TLS it controls the hostname clients use when discovering routes, "otherwise TLS hostname verification may fail with an IP SANs error."
- `no_advertise: true` stops gossiping server URLs to clients (also disables client_advertise); useful when reachable "via different load balancers and interfaces from different networks. Automatically advertising an internal IP address could result in reconnect delays due to failed attempts."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — v2 Routes**

- Each pooled connection handles a fixed subset of accounts; "It is required that each server in the cluster have the same pool size value" or clustering fails ("Mismatch route pool size").
- When one pool connection breaks, traffic for its accounts stops until reconnect (not rerouted through other connections).
- Changing `pool_size` via reload breaks route connections unless done as a rolling reload with the same value; client connections stay up.
- Pinned `accounts` list must match on all servers, but rolling reload works: traffic for a newly pinned account stops until the peer reloads too.
- "it is recommended that all servers part of the same cluster be at the same version number"; a 2.10 server connects to older servers with a single route.
- Toggling compression between `off` and anything else closes and recreates route connections; other mode changes are dynamic.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Clustering**

- Unlike core clustering, each JetStream node "must specify a server name and cluster name".
- A system account (`$SYS`) user/password should be configured (example uses a bcrypted password).
- Choose a store directory "ideally a fast SSD"; "After two servers are running you'll be ready to use JetStream" (3-node example).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Administration (cluster)**

- Stream info reports Cluster name, Leader, replicas with `current`/`outdated` and last-seen time.
- "Leader elections will represent short interruptions to the stream so if you know you will work on a node later it might be worth moving leadership away from it ahead of time" (`nats stream cluster step-down`, consumer and meta variants). Step-down doesn't remove the node or stop it from being re-elected.
- Meta group management (step-down, peer-remove, `nats server report jetstream`) requires a SYSTEM user; system users see the meta group but not individual streams/consumers.
- `nats server report jetstream` shows per-server streams/consumers/messages/bytes/API errors and the RAFT meta group (Leader, Current, Offline, Active, Lag); raw data from `/jsz` or `nats server req jetstream`.
- Normal shutdown including Lame Duck Mode is noticed by the cluster and it keeps functioning; peer-remove is for a node that "will never return".
- After peer-remove "the cluster will notice that the replica count of a stream is not honored anymore and will immediately pick a new node and start replicating data to it" using the stream's placement rules.
- "Peer-removing nodes from the cluster is a destructive operation, and decreases the size of the cluster." The node should be offline; if online, JetStream is disabled on it; it must not restart under the same `server_name` if its disk was wiped.
- Stream-level peer-remove (`nats stream cluster peer-remove`) moves a stream (and its consumers) off a node that stays in the cluster.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Troubleshooting**

- By default only warning and error logs are produced; `-D` debug, `-DV` trace.
- "Make sure that ... at least one system user is configured" under `$SYS`.
- Diagnostic CLI: `nats server ls/ping/info/check`, `nats server report connections|accounts|jetstream`, `nats server request jetstream|subscriptions|variables|connections|routes|gateways|leafnodes|accounts`, `nats server cluster step-down|peer-remove`; `nats traffic` is experimental.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Super-cluster with Gateways**

- "It is recommended to have all seed server of a cluster listed in the gateways section"; discovery depends on those servers running.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Gateway Configuration**

- Certificate rotation: clusters rarely rotate at the same time; "Make sure that the ca_file contains both old and new root or intermediate CAs." Using only the CA from an issuance bundle "is ill-advised"; keep a separate verification bundle so "when DC-B rolls before DC-A, it will not be cut off from your supercluster." Reload config to apply.
- Behind a load balancer set `advertise` to the LB hostname/port; "Otherwise, they will advertise their own private IP and port, and can generate failures and downtime if any reconnection is required."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Leaf Nodes**

- Configure a leaf with all seed servers; each seed must accept leaf connections; each URL in a remote must point to the same cluster; a leaf may have multiple remotes to different clusters.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Configuring JetStream (resource management)**

- Enable with `jetstream: enabled` (or `-js`, `-sd <dir>`).
- Resources are dynamically determined by default, but "It's recommended that you set specific limits": example `max_mem: 1G`, `max_file: 100G`, `domain: acme`.
- Since v2.10.21 "the NATS JetStream API has a limit of 10K inflight requests after which it will start to drop requests"; tunable via `request_queue_limit` (example 1000). "When the request limit is reached, all pending requests are dropped". Log: "JetStream API queue limit reached, dropping N requests"; advisory `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.API.LIMIT_REACHED`; clients must retry.
- `limits { max_ha_assets }` caps the number of R3/R5 streams and consumers per server (example 2000).
- In operator mode account JetStream limits live in the account JWT (`nsc edit account --js-mem-storage 1G --js-disk-storage 512M --js-streams 10 --js-consumer 100`).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Configuration Management (CLI, Terraform, GitHub Actions, Kubernetes)**

- "In many cases managing the configuration in your application code is the best model, many teams though wish to pre-create Streams and Consumers." Tools: `nats --config` JSON files, Terraform provider `terraform-provider-jetstream`, GitHub Actions `jetstream-gh-action`, Kubernetes CRDs (`nack`).
- Extract a stream config with `nats stream info X -j | jq .config` and apply with `nats str add|edit --config`.
- NACK CRDs: `jetstream.nats.io/v1beta1` `Stream` and `Consumer`; `kubectl describe` on Errored state.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Configuration (server config reference)**

- The config file is the standard way to configure; "We strongly recommend using only ASCII for names and values"; "JSON config files should be limited machine generated configuration files."
- Numbers support units: 1K = 1000, 1KB = 1024. String values starting with a digit must be quoted (e.g. `token: "3secret"`).
- Variables are block-scoped, `$`-prefixed, must be used or parsing fails with `unknown field`; undefined references fall back to environment variables; env values starting with a number may fail to resolve.
- `include` uses relative paths from the main config.
- The config is read at startup only; reload via `nats-server --signal reload`; since v2.10.0 via `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.<server-id>.RELOAD` with a system user.
- `client_advertise` is useful behind a load balancer or when TLS server auth needs the correct DNS name; fully disable with `no_advertise: true`.
- "the best place to store JetStream data would be locally on a fast SSD. One should specifically avoid NAS or NFS storage for JetStream."
- "each JetStream enabled server MUST use its own individual storage directory"; "JetStream does not implement standby and fault tolerance through a shared file system"; shared directories: "Access conflicts are not detected. We do not recommend such a setup."
- `sync_interval`: "By default JetStream relies on stream replication in the cluster to guarantee data is available after an OS crash. If you run JetStream without replication or with a replication of just 2 you may want to shorten the fsync/sync interval." `always` "will slow down the throughput to a few hundred msg/s."
- Account `msg_trace { dest, sampling 0-100 }` enables OpenTelemetry-style tracing for `traceparent` messages.
- `disable_sublist_cache: true` "saves resources in situations where different subjects are used all the time."
- `lame_duck_duration` default `2m` ("cannot be set lower than 30 seconds"); `lame_duck_grace_period` default `10s`; started with `nats-server --signal ldm`.
- `no_fast_producer_stall` default false: server stalls the fast producer when a consumer is slow; `true` drops the message for that consumer instead.
- `server_name` defaults to server id; "within a domain, all server names need to be unique." `server_tags` recommended in `key:value` notation; `server_metadata` (2.12.0).
- `system_account` default `$SYS`. `connect_error_reports` default 3600 (approx hourly at 1 attempt/s); `reconnect_error_reports` default 1.
- `trace` excludes the system account; `trace_verbose` includes it.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Enabling Monitoring**

- "`nats-server` does not have authentication/authorization for the monitoring endpoint. When you plan to open your nats-server to the internet make sure to not expose the monitoring port as well." Monitoring binds `0.0.0.0` by default; bind to localhost or firewall it.
- Enable with `-m 8222` or `http_port`/`http: localhost:8222`; endpoints support JSONP and CORS.
- Prometheus NATS Exporter and a sample Grafana dashboard are the recommended external monitoring tools.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Logging**

- `-DV` debug+trace; `-VV`/`-DVV` also trace the system account. Syslog via `udp://` or `syslog://`.
- Built-in rotation since 2.1.4 via `logfile_size_limit`; or logrotate with `postrotate kill -SIGUSR1` to reopen log files.
- A logged `UNSUB` "does not indicate the subscription is gone, only that the message was received"; `DELSUB` marks actual removal.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — System Events (system account)**

- System events (connect/disconnect, auth errors, shutdown, stats) require configuring `system_account` and using a system-account user; accounts keep app subscriptions like `>` from receiving system events.
- Server-initiated events: `$SYS.ACCOUNT.<id>.CONNECT|DISCONNECT|SERVER.CONNS`, `$SYS.SERVER.<id>.CLIENT.AUTH.ERR`, `$SYS.SERVER.<id>.STATSZ`.
- Requests: `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.<id>.<VARZ|CONNZ|ROUTEZ|GATEWAYZ|LEAFZ|SUBSZ|JSZ|ACCOUNTZ|HEALTHZ>`, `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.PING[.<endpoint>]` (multiple responses), `$SYS.REQ.ACCOUNT.<account-id>.<CONNZ|LEAFZ|SUBSZ|JSZ|INFO>`.
- `$SYS.ACCOUNT.<id>.CLAIMS.UPDATE` is how account servers push updated JWT claims to servers.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — System Events & Decentralized JWT Tutorial**

- `$SYS.REQ.USER.INFO` returns account/permissions/expiry for any connected user, not just system users.
- `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.PING.IDZ` discovers servers (id, name); `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.PING` returns stats (mem, cores, cpu, connections, subscriptions, slow_consumers).
- `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.<id>.PROFILEZ` returns base64 pprof profiles (allocs, block, goroutine, heap, mutex, threadcount) when profiling is enabled.
- `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.<id>.RELOAD` hot reloads config; config errors come back in an `error` field.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Enabling TLS**

- Root `tls` also applies to the monitoring port when `https_port` is set; cluster/gateway/leaf blocks can have their own.
- Certificate rotation: "Make sure that the ca_file contains both old and new root or intermediate CAs"; reload config to apply file changes.
- `connection_rate_limit` (2.7.0) caps new TLS client connections per second server-wide (example 1000); excess get "Connection throttling is active. Please try again later."; default 0 disables; not applied to cluster/gateway/leaf/websocket/MQTT listeners. Rationale: "TLS handshakes are expensive, and a burst of reconnecting clients can keep the server busy".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — OCSP Stapling**

- Staples are cached on disk in `store_dir` (shared with JetStream if enabled) so restarts don't refetch.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Account lookup using Resolver / Memory Resolver**

- Three resolvers: NATS-based ("the preferred option and should be your default selection"), `MEMORY` (static accounts in config), `URL` (build your own account service; standalone nats-account-server "is now legacy").
- NATS-based resolver stores JWTs in a local, not shared, directory ("you can't have more than one nats-servers using the same directory"); all servers in the cluster/super-cluster must use it; sync is eventually consistent via the system account.
- Integration subjects: `$SYS.REQ.CLAIMS.UPDATE` to push a JWT; subscribe `$SYS.REQ.ACCOUNT.*.CLAIMS.LOOKUP` to implement an account server.
- Migration from REST account server: `nsc pull`, reconfigure to nats resolver, `nsc edit operator --account-jwt-server-url nats://...`, `nsc push -A`.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Auth Callout**

- Order: implement the service, plan migration, then configure; "enabling the configuration before deploying a service could cause issues for existing systems."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Managing and Monitoring your NATS Server Infrastructure**

- Lifecycle operations: `nats` CLI (cheat, stream/consumer/context), `nsc` for JWTs, signals for reload/log rotation, rolling upgrades, slow consumer understanding, monitoring endpoint + nats-top + system events, lame duck shutdown. Synadia Insights is a commercial high-cardinality monitoring option.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Upgrading a Cluster**

- Rolling upgrade, one node at a time: enter Lame Duck Mode, replace binary/image, restart, "Wait until the `/healthz` endpoint returns `HTTP 200 OK` before moving on to the next cluster node."
- "The support policy for the server is the current release as well as one patch version release prior" (e.g. 2.8.4 -> 2.8.3 downgrade supported); earlier downgrades "may work, but is not recommended." Downgrade path = same rolling procedure.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Lame Duck Mode**

- "In production we recommend that a server is shut down with lame duck mode as a graceful way to slowly evict clients"; it "mitigates the 'thundering herd' situation that will place CPU pressure on servers as TLS enabled clients reconnect."
- LDM: stop accepting new connections, 10 second grace period, then evict clients over `lame_duck_duration` (default 2 minutes).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Slow Consumers**

- Server-detected: server buffers outbound, then designates "slow consumer" and may drop the connection; logged "Slow Consumer Detected"; counted in `varz` `slow_consumers`.
- `write_deadline` can be raised (example `2s`) for bursts, but "Be sure you are not just postponing a slow consumer error." "Increasing buffer sizes is not typically recommended unless you are handling temporary bursts of data. Often, increasing buffer capacity will only postpone slow consumer problems."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Signals**

- `--signal ldm`=SIGUSR2 (graceful, evict gradually), `quit`=SIGINT, `term`=SIGTERM, `stop`=SIGKILL, `reload`=SIGHUP, `reopen`=SIGUSR1 (log rotation); SIGQUIT kills with stack dump.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Managing NATS Security**

- Delete accounts via `$SYS.REQ.CLAIMS.DELETE` with `allow_delete: true` in the resolver.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Profiling NATS**

- Profiling "is an advanced operation for development purposes only"; use the monitoring port for day-to-day stats.
- The `prof_port` endpoint has no auth, binds `0.0.0.0` by default, must not be exposed to the internet; it does not support config reload.
- `nats server request profile allocs|cpu` works only on the system account; CPU profile default 5 seconds; selectors `--name`, `--tags`, `--cluster`.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Administration (CLI intro), Account Information**

- "JetStream is multi-tenant so you will need to check that your account is enabled for JetStream and is not limited" (`nats account info` shows memory/storage/streams/consumers limits).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Data Replication (mirrors/sources admin)**

- `nats stream info` shows per-source Lag and Last Seen; `nats stream report --dot` emits a GraphViz replication map.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Disaster Recovery**

- "For R1 streams, data is persisted on one server node only. If that server node is unrecoverable then recovery from backup is the sole option."
- Automatic recovery conditions: stream is R3 or greater; remaining replicas meet quorum floor(R/2)+1; a free node exists in the stream's cluster; impacted nodes are peer-removed from the meta group.
- Backups (`nats stream backup`) include stream config and state, durable consumer config and state, and all messages with timestamps and headers. `nats account backup` covers all streams in an account.
- "Memory storage streams do not support snapshots. Only file-based storage streams can be backed up."
- During backup the stream's configuration is frozen and "no data will be evicted based on stream retention policies."
- Example backup: 813 MiB uncompressed became 13 MiB compressed in 3368 chunks.
- Administering interactively with the CLI leaves no desired state to recreate from: "This is not the ideal way to administer the server, we recommend Configuration Management".
- `nats account restore` supports `--cluster` and `--tag` placement; it "will fail if a stream with the same name already exists."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Encryption at Rest**

- Provide the key via an environment variable (e.g. `$JS_KEY`) "so it will not be persisted in a file."
- Enabling on existing data encrypts only new blocks; back up and restore to re-encrypt old blocks. Restarting with a different or no key fails decryption ("message authentication failed") and breaks JetStream but core NATS still works. Cipher can change if the key stays the same.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Streams / Consumers (JetStream admin CLI walkthrough)**

- Every `nats` JetStream action can run non-interactively "making it usable as a CLI API"; `-j` gives JSON; config JSON matches `nats str info X -j | jq .config`.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Monitoring JetStream**

- JetStream exposes `/jsz` and advisories under `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.>` (viewable with `nats event --js-advisory`; schemas via `nats schema show`); advisories can themselves be stored in streams.
- Advisory subjects: API audit, STREAM/CONSUMER CREATED, SNAPSHOT_CREATE/COMPLETE, RESTORE_CREATE/COMPLETE, CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES, MSG_NAKED, MSG_TERMINATED, `$JS.EVENT.METRIC.CONSUMER.ACK` (sampled acks), STREAM/CONSUMER LEADER_ELECTED and QUORUM_LOST.
- Dashboards: NATS Surveyor Grafana dashboards; Synadia Insights as commercial option.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Monitoring (endpoints reference)**

- Endpoints: `/varz`, `/connz`, `/routez`, `/gatewayz`, `/leafz`, `/subsz`, `/accountz`, `/accstatz`, `/jsz`, `/healthz`; all also reachable as system services. Conventional port 8222.
- Monitoring has no auth and binds `0.0.0.0` by default; don't expose it to the internet.
- `/connz` pages 1024 connections by default; "The server will default to holding the last 10,000 closed connections."
- Sample `/varz` shows defaults: max_connections 65536, ping_interval 120s, ping_max 2, auth_timeout 1, max_control_line 4096, max_payload 1048576, max_pending 67108864, tls_timeout 0.5 (older default), write_deadline 2s (older default; config page says 10s). Records: contradicts running-a-nats-service/configuration/README.md (`write_deadline` 10s) and tls.md (timeout 2s).
- `/jsz`: "If you're in a clustered environment, it is recommended to retrieve the information from the stream's leader in order to get the most accurate and up-to-date data" (`leader-only=true`); `raft=true` includes RAFT details.
- `/healthz` returns OK when the server accepts connections; `js-enabled-only` errors if JetStream is disabled; `js-server-only` skips account/stream/consumer checks; `js-enabled` is deprecated.
- Prometheus NATS Exporter + Grafana walkthrough are the standard monitoring stack.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Environmental considerations**

- "Think of Core NATS servers as a software equivalent of network switches. Enable JetStream, and they also become a new kind of DB server as well."
- In public clouds "you get what you pay for": non-network-optimized instances may give 10 Gb/s for ~30 minutes then drop (e.g. to 5 Gb/s); choose network-optimized instances for sustained bandwidth. Local SSD gives best latency; network block storage (EBS) can give highest throughput but general-purpose tiers burst then drop IOPS; choose IO-optimized storage for sustained IOPS.
- Container resource limits: nats-server uses resources in proportion to traffic and bursts; set limits accordingly or the orchestrator kills it. It "will try to use all host memory, not the resource limits set for the container, unless you specify GOMEMLIMIT" (available in the official Helm charts).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS Server Clients**

- Install the `nats` CLI "even if you don't intend to run your own servers"; `nats server check connection` gives a Nagios-style health output.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS on Kubernetes**

- "The recommended way to deploy NATS on Kubernetes is using Helm with the official NATS Helm Chart"; default values deploy a single-server StatefulSet plus a nats-box Deployment.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Running**

- With no flags the server listens on 4222 with security disabled. The Docker image's default config enables monitoring on 8222 and routes on 6222; it warns "Cluster name was dynamically generated, consider setting one".
- Exit status: a requested shutdown exits successfully (even via POSIX signal); configure the service manager "to restart the nats-server on non-zero exit status or death by signal" and "probably should not restart the nats-server if it exits successfully."
- JetStream default store is /tmp; "the best place to store JetStream data would be locally on a fast SSD. One should specifically avoid NAS or NFS storage for JetStream."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Installing (hardware requirements)**

- "The NATS server itself has minimal hardware requirements to support small edge devices".
- TLS CPU: "After a network partition, every disconnected client will attempt to connect to a NATS server in the cluster simultaneously, so CPU on those servers will momentarily spike." Mitigate with reconnect jitter, longer TLS timeouts, and larger clusters.
- "We highly recommend testing to see if smaller, cheaper machines suffice for your workload - often they do!" Start small and adjust after load testing; ensure a sufficient NIC.
- "For high throughput use cases, the network interface card (NIC) or the available bandwidth are often the bottleneck".
- Core NATS minimums (containers, GOMEMLIMIT at 90%): 1 core / 32 MiB handles 100 publishers at 1000 msg/s each (100,000 msg/s total) on a single server; 3-node cluster 1 core / 32-64 MiB at 100,000 msg/s total.
- JetStream minimums (file storage, R3 on 3 nodes, pull consumers): 1 core / 32 MiB for 1,000 msg/s; 1 core / 64 MiB for 10,000 msg/s; 3 nodes 1 core / 256 MiB for 100,000 msg/s. "these are minimum configurations".
- "For production deployment of JetStream, we recommend starting with at least 4 CPU cores and 8 GiB of memory".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS and Docker / JetStream in Docker / NGS leaf nodes in Docker / Swarm**

- The Docker image is "under 10 MB"; default ports 4222 (clients), 8222 (monitoring), 6222 (routes); the image protects routes with credentials `ruser:T0pS3cr3t` by default.
- The `nats` image doesn't bundle root certificates; mount `/etc/ssl/cert.pem` to verify TLS (e.g. to NGS).
- Persist JetStream in Docker with a volume and `-sd /data`; otherwise data is ephemeral.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — WebSocket Configuration**

- WebSocket is not enabled by default in Docker; add a `websocket { port, no_tls }` config.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — FAQ**

- Default max connections per server is 65,536; "Most systems can handle several thousand NATS connections per server without any changes" but OS limits (e.g. macOS) and TCP buffer sizes may need tuning.
- TLS negotiation CPU during a thundering herd "is usually the constraint limiting the number of connections a single server should support"; mitigate with TLS-accelerated cipher suites (AES on x86) and reconnect jitter/delay ranges.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Roadmap**

- Roadmap lives at nats.io/about/#roadmap; no design guidance in the page.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Connecting to a Cluster / timeouts / misc / name / noecho / ping-pong / security**

- A connection name "is highly recommended as a friendly connection name will help in monitoring, error reporting, debugging, and testing."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Getting Started / Using Source**

- Default store is /tmp; "the best place to store JetStream data would be locally on a fast SSD. One should specifically avoid NAS or NFS storage for JetStream."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Model Deep Dive**

- Ack sampling (`--sample 80`) publishes redelivery counts and ack latency for monitoring; planned for NATS Surveyor.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS API Reference (JetStream wire API)**

- Admin APIs respond with typed JSON (`type` -> JSON Schema in nats-io/jsm.go/schemas); `nats events` shows an API audit log; `$JS.API.STREAM.MSG.DELETE.*` is "useful for GDPR compliance".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — nats bench (benchmarking guide)**

- Benchmarks can fill streams quickly; purge or delete `benchstream` afterwards to reclaim memory and files. Changing stream attributes between runs requires deleting the stream.
- `--sleep` turns `nats bench` into a steady-rate traffic generator or simulates processing time.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — nats CLI / nats-top / nk**

- Use `nats context` to store server URLs and credentials; passwords can come from `NATS_PASSWORD` or a prompt so they don't appear in `ps`/history.
- nats-top shows per-connection SUBS, PENDING bytes, MSGS_TO/FROM and server-level Slow Consumers in real time.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — nsc (basics, streams, services, signing keys, revocation, managed operators), NATS tools overview**

- nsc directories: `~/.nsc` home, `~/.nkeys` (private keys and creds; "should be treated as secrets"), stores in `$NSC_HOME/nats` ("can stored under revision control. The JWTs themselves do not contain any secrets").
- With the built-in NATS resolver you must `nsc push` local account changes for them to take effect.
- "On a production environment private keys should be saved to a file and always referenced from the secured file." nsc doesn't track private signing keys; you must manage them.
- Managed operators (e.g. NGS) hold the operator key; they may add limits or imports to your account JWT ("the operator gets the final call on all Account edits"); `nsc push`/`pull` keep local and server JWTs in sync.
- "most should use the NATS account resolver built-in to 'nats-server'"; nats-account-server is "legacy, replaced by the built-in NATS resolver" but usable as a reference implementation; nsc "is the preferred tools to create security configuration unless you are using Synadia Control Plane."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — In Depth JWT Guide**

- JWT store directory contains no private keys and may go in git, but restoring an old version may undo revocations and restore expired JWTs; keep NKEYs in tandem.
- After `nsc push`, if fewer servers respond than exist "it is best practice to resolve this issue and retry"; if only one server holds a new account and dies, "the pushed account is not available to the network at large" so "make sure that initially, more servers respond than what you are comfortable with losing".
- System events: "you MUST NOT rely on a particular ordering or due to the possibility of loss, events matching" (a CONNECT may not have a matching DISCONNECT); periodic aggregate messages compensate for misses. Prefer `$SYS.ACCOUNT.<id>.SERVER.CONNS` over the old `$SYS.SERVER.ACCOUNT.<id>.CONNS`.
- `nsc generate diagram component` produces a plantuml diagram of account import/export relationships.
- Identity NKEY is the only key that can add/remove signing keys, so create signing keys before taking the identity key offline; delete user keys/creds from nsc after distribution.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject Mapping and Traffic Shaping (server config)**

- Canary rollout: v1 100% -> v1 98% / v2 2% -> v2 100%, each step via config reload "with zero downtime"; remember queue subscribers/load balancing when launching v2.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — WebSocket (overview) / Windows Service / Server flags**

- Running as a Windows service "is the recommended way of running NATS on Windows"; one service instance per server config; "it is recommended to run a NATS service with an explicit log file".
- Flags: `-a` binds `0.0.0.0` by default; `-p` 4222; `--tls` enables TLS without client verification; `--no_advertise` stops advertising cluster info to clients.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-1: JetStream JSON API Design**

- `nats --trace` logs raw API subjects and bodies; "an invaluable way to observe the interaction model."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-2: NATS Typed Messages**

- `nats events` displays any event; consider adding formatting support whenever a new event is added.
- Consequence: "/varz" and similar data "move into the realm of being controlled and versioned."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-3: NATS Service Latency Distributed Tracing Interoperability**

- Service latency tracking is configured per exported service via `latency: { sampling: 50%, subject: ... }` on an account export; today sampling is a static percentage.
- Proposal: additional sampling value `headers` makes the server "interpret the headers ... to determine if a request should be sampled." (ADR: proposed)
- The `io.nats.server.metric.v1.service_latency` advisory gains a `headers` field containing "only the headers used for the sampling decision."
- Advisory includes `requestor` and `responder` blocks (acc, rtt, start, user, lang, ver, ip, cid, server) plus `service`, `system`, `total` durations and `status`.
- Supported trace header formats intended: Zipkin B3 (`X-B3-TraceId`, single `b3`), Jaeger `uber-trace-id: {trace-id}:{span-id}:{parent-span-id}:{flags}` (bit 0x01 = sampled), W3C Trace Context `traceparent`/`tracestate` (`01` flag = sampled); OpenTelemetry uses Trace Context.
- Author's long-term view: "every server that handles a message should emit a unique trace" but "I don't think we'll be doing that in the hot path of the server." (See ADR-41 for what was later built.)

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-5: Lame Duck Notification**

- In lame duck mode a server "removes itself from being advertised in the cluster, and slowly starts evicting connected clients as per `lame_duck_duration`."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-21: NATS Configuration Contexts**

- Paths follow XDG: `~/.config/nats/context.txt` (selected context name) and `~/.config/nats/context/<name>.json`; `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` honoured.
- `nsc` key takes URLs like `nsc://operator/account/user`; the context runs `nsc generate profile <url>` to fill `creds` and `url`; explicit `url`/`creds` override nsc output.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-31: JetStream Direct Get**

- On mirror create, `mirror_direct` is aligned to the upstream's `allow_direct` when the upstream is visible (pedantic mode rejects disagreement; non-pedantic silently aligns); for External/cross-domain upstreams the user value is kept.
- "The mirror only joins the upstream queue group once it has caught up to within a small lag window of the source"; a fresh mirror "does not yet contribute to read availability."
- `mirror_direct` "is captured on the mirror at create time and is not automatically refreshed when the upstream's `allow_direct` changes later"; operator must update upstream AND re-issue `STREAM.UPDATE` on each mirror. "it's suggested that users always set `mirror_direct` to their desired value."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-35: JetStream Filestore Compression**

- Motivation: "filestore encryption can almost completely prevent host filesystem compression or deduplication from working"; server compresses "before encryption takes place."
- Changing the algorithm later only affects new blocks; "this will not result in existing blocks being proactively compressed or decompressed."
- "a compressed stream may suffer some performance penalties compared to an uncompressed stream."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-38: OCSP Peer Verification**

- Adding OCSP responder dependency "necessarily adds a single point of failure (SPOF) from the NATS Server point of view and will in any case slow overall connection time"; mitigated by a local response cache.
- Rejection handshake errors: `client not OCSP valid` / `server not OCSP valid`; advisories `io.nats.server.advisory.v1.ocsp_peer_reject` on `$SYS.SERVER.<server>.OCSP.PEER.CONN.REJECT` and `ocsp_peer_link_invalid` on `$SYS.SERVER.<server>.OCSP.PEER.LINK.INVALID`.
- Cache eviction is passive (only when the cert is evaluated again); `varz` gains `tls_ocsp_peer_verify` and `ocsp_peer_cache` stats (misses, cached/good/revoked counts).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-39: Certificate Store**

- TLS map gains `cert_store`, `cert_match_by` (default `Subject`), `cert_match` so the server's TLS identity can come from a credential store instead of files; "Edge computing scenarios involving large 'fleets' of managed servers may especially require credential store integration."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-40: NATS Connection**

- Client statistics (persist across reconnects): bytes in/out (socket level), messages in (`MSG`/`HMSG`), messages out (`PUB`/`HPUB`), connects/reconnects; new parity fields should use new names (e.g. Go `TotalBytesIn`).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-41: NATS Message Path Tracing**

- Motivation: with super clusters, leafnodes, accounts and JetStream "knowing the path that messages take through the system is hard to predict" and "it's hard to know where messages can be lost, denied or delayed."
- Trace event types: `in` Ingress, `sm` Subject Mapping, `se` Stream Export, `si` Service Import, `js` JetStream, `eg` Egress; one trace message per server traversed, each holding multiple events.
- Activation is per-message via headers, "there is no flag to enable it on all messages": `Nats-Trace-Dest` (subject for traces), `Nats-Trace-Only` (`1`/`true`/`on`: trace without delivering; also "messages will also not traverse any Route, Gateway or Leafnode that does not support the Tracing feature"), `Accept-Encoding` (`gzip`, `snappy`).
- W3C `traceparent` `sampled` flag can trigger tracing when the account sets `msg_trace { dest, sampling }`; sampling default "100%"; ad-hoc `Nats-Trace-Dest` "has precedence."
- `nats trace <subject>` CLI renders the path; parsing helper in jsm.go `api/server/tracing`.
- Trace messages carry `server` info, `request` (headers, msgsize, `Nats-Trace-Hop`), `hops` (remote destinations this server forwards to), `events`. Hop numbering: origin has none; forwarded copies get `1`, `2`, then `1.1`, `2.1`, forming a DAG.
- `kind` values: 0 CLIENT, 1 ROUTER, 2 GATEWAY, 3 SYSTEM, 4 LEAF, 5 JETSTREAM, 6 ACCOUNT.
- For non-client egresses "the subscription and queue group will be omitted. This is because NATS Servers optimize and send a single message across servers, based on a known interest, and let the remote servers match local subscribers."
- Ingress `error` is filled when ACLs deny a publish (e.g. `Permissions Violation for Publish to "deny.x"`); JetStream event `nointerest: true` means "an `Interest` type Stream did not persist the message because it had no interest."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-42: Pull Consumer Priority Groups**

- Unpin API: `$JS.API.CONSUMER.UNPIN.<STREAM>.<CONSUMER>` with payload `{"group": "groupName"}`. Consumer state adds `priority_groups: [{group, pinned_client_id, pinned_ts}]`.
- Advisories: `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.PINNED` (`io.nats.jetstream.advisory.v1.consumer_group_pinned`) and `...UNPINNED` (`consumer_group_unpinned`, reason `admin` or `timeout`).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-44: Versioning for JetStream Assets**

- Version skew problem: the connected server may be an old leafnode without JetStream; the meta-leader "would not forward the API fields it is unaware of"; asset hosts "would silently drop fields." "Our current approach is to check the connected-server version and project that it's representitive of the cluster as a whole but this is a known incorrect approach especially for Leafnodes."
- "our stance is to insist on homogenous cluster versions in the general case but it's not reasonable to expect this for leafnode servers nor is it possible during upgrading."
- API Support Level: 0 = < 2.11.0, 1 = 2.11.x, 2 = 2.12.x; "we do not require strict SemVer adherence" (may bump mid-release). Advertised in `jsz`, `varz`, `$JS.API.INFO`, and logged at JetStream startup.
- "tools like Terraform and NACK will need to understand to ignore these fields when doing their remediation loops."
- Offline assets: incompatible streams/consumers load in offline mode with a reason map in `stream_list_response` / `consumer_list_response`; also added to the existing `missing` list "This ensure older tools will still understand these streams as inaccessible." Offline streams still reserve their subjects to keep overlap protection.
- Strict JSON: use `DisallowUnknownFields` for API and meta-layer; incompatible API calls error, incompatible assets go offline; "This will prevent assets inadvertently reverting some settings and changing behaviour during downgrades."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-49: JetStream Distributed Counter CRDT**

- Resets: "a purge will not replicate, a roll-up would replicate and destroy the entire counter everywhere so the only real option is to publish a negative value"; preferred reset = negative value then purge up to that message; subject purge only for full deletes.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-51: JetStream Message Scheduler**

- Time zones via `time.LoadLocation()` names (IANA recommended; abbreviations "are ambiguous ... not DST-aware"); fixed offsets like `+02:00` rejected; empty header rejected; "Operators must therefore install and keep tzdata up to date on every server"; DST-boundary schedules "could be skipped" or "executed twice."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-53: Feature flags**

- Problem: breaking behaviour changes (e.g. switching to the ADR-15 v2 `$JS.ACK.<domain>.<account hash>...` format) cannot ship in minor releases because older servers "will not know how to parse the new format", clients/tooling may lag, mixed-version systems need both formats, and "Subject permissions could be using the old format."
- New config block `feature_flags { js_ack_fc_v2: true }` (`map[string]bool`); logged at startup as default / opt-in / opt-out; "The server will not support reloading these flags at runtime"; unknown flags are ignored but logged.
- Flag table: `js_ack_fc_v2` = "Use domain/account-aware JetStream ACK and FC subjects (ADR-15 v2 format)", type Opt-in, introduced 2.14, default flip TBD. In 2.14 the server "uses the V1 ack/fc format by default, but supports parsing the V2 format."
- Convention: opt-in flags for gradual rollout that later become default; opt-out flags should be prefixed e.g. `revert_` "clearly signaling that the server reverts to old/non-default behavior."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-56: JetStream Consistency Models**

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-59: JetStream Stream Sourcing and Mirroring**

- With `mirror_direct: true` the upstream's StreamInfo gets an `alternates` list "sorted by RTT proximity."
- `StreamSourceInfo`: `lag` (messages pending), `active` (ns since last activity), `error` (ApiError). Error codes 10029 "Mirror consumer setup failed", 10045 "Source consumer setup failed"; consumer-create timeout 30 seconds; error clears on reconnect; visible via STREAM.INFO, `/jsz`, `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.PING.JSZ`.
- `/jsz?streams=true&consumers=true&direct-consumers=true` exposes internal replication consumers (`Direct` flag, `AckNone`, flow control, heartbeats; named `mirror-<id>` / `src-<id>` when a single filter exists, else random name).
- Reconnection "uses exponential backoff with jitter"; resumes "from the last successfully stored sequence — no manual intervention is required."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-60: JetStream reliable stream sourcing/mirroring on WQ/Interest streams (updates ADR-59)**

- Naming/metadata: mirror consumers `JS_MIRROR_<suffix>` with `_nats.mirror.stream`, `_nats.mirror.acc`, `_nats.mirror.domain`; source consumers `JS_SRC_<suffix>` with `_nats.src.*`.
- New API `$JS.API.CONSUMER.RESET.<STREAM>.<CONSUMER>`: resets delivery sequence to 1 and redelivers pending; empty payload keeps the ack floor stream seq; `{"seq":N}` sets ack floor to N-1 so next delivered `msg.seq >= N`; only for `DeliverPolicy` all / by_start_sequence / by_start_time, and cannot go before `opt_start_seq`/`opt_start_time`; response looks like a consumer create response plus `ResetSeq`.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-61: Unsafe meta group quorum rescue for disaster recovery**

- Meta group quorum "is computed from the configured peer set, not from the set of currently live peers. A peer that is shut down and intended to not come back, without being explicitly peer-removed still counts toward the quorum requirement."
- Previous remedy: bring every configured peer back "under the same server name, at the same time" and run `$JS.API.SERVER.REMOVE`.
- New operator-only broadcast API `$JS.API.META.RESCUE` on the system account with `{"quorum_needed": N}` (>= 1 and <= current effective quorum); non-system-account requests are silently ignored; "The peer set is not rewritten by this API."
- `JSZ meta_cluster` now populates `replicas` on every server (not only the leader) plus `quorum_needed` and `rescue` (true while active).
- Safety gate: server must be a voting member, must see no meta leader ("a healthy meta layer must not be reconfigured through this API"), and must have a non-empty Raft log ("a lowered quorum could let it be elected on empty votes alone while the lost peers holding the only copies of the data remain unreachable").
- On accept: lowers effective quorum, "starts a 5 minute rescue timeout", logs WARN and emits advisory `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.SERVER.META_RESCUE` (`io.nats.jetstream.advisory.v1.meta_rescue` with `prev_quorum`, `new_quorum`, cluster, domain). During rescue, empty-log peers' votes count only when the candidate has data.
- Quorum recalculation is suppressed during the timeout unless a peer-set change yields a quorum "at or below" the rescued value, which cancels the rescue; on expiry quorum returns to the natural value. A repeat rescue "can only ever lower the value, never raise it" and resets the timeout.
- Rejection error code `10224` (400) "JetStream system rescue not applied: {err}" (leader known, not voting member, empty log, out of bounds, node closed).
- "The API is intentionally unsafe. Lowering the meta quorum weakens the guarantees Raft relies on ... misuse against a not-actually-wedged meta layer can split-brain the meta group"; must be documented "as a last-resort disaster recovery tool." No client library changes.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-62: JetStream desired state reconciliation**

- `STREAM.INFO`/`CONSUMER.INFO` expose `cluster.desired` {name, replicas, origin, status}; `cluster.replicas[].pending` flags a Raft add/remove not yet reflected in the assignment.
- Status types: `meta`, `membership`, `snapshot`, `catchup`, `quorum` ("adding a peer would risk losing quorum"), `blocked` ("waiting for consumer 'X' to migrate"), `unavailable`.
- Meta peer/assignment reconciliation backfills a replacement peer after peer-remove or when a new eligible peer appears ("to heal an under-replicated group"), respecting placement constraints.
- Scale up stream: consumers without explicit replicas scale too; "Interest/WorkQueue consumers are also scaled up to match the stream's replica count." Scale down: "Prefers keeping the stream leader and online and caught up peers"; R1 consumers on a doomed peer are moved first.
- Retention change Limits→Interest on a replicated stream: "the consumers will need to scale up first since their replica count needs to match that of the stream if it's Interest or WorkQueue"; back to Limits allows scaling consumers down.
- Move: `$JS.API.STREAM.UPDATE` or `$JS.API.ACCOUNT.STREAM.MOVE.<account>.<stream>` (system account); adds new peers, catches up, drops old; consumers follow. Evacuate: `$JS.API.STREAM.PEER.EVACUATE.<stream>` / `$JS.API.SERVER.EVACUATE` (evacuating peer can still help catch-up, even for R1).
- Peer remove (`$JS.API.STREAM.PEER.REMOVE.<stream>` / `$JS.API.SERVER.REMOVE`): removes immediately and assigns a replacement if available, else "the group will run under-replicated"; removing the last (R1) peer "moves the stream to a new peer without preserving the data"; "Prefer evacuating a stream peer if it's still able to catch up." Valid no-quorum escape: peer-remove dead nodes then scale config down to match; "Be careful though with peer-removing liberally when peers are planned to come back ... it does not get re-added."
- Cancel via `$JS.API.STREAM.CANCEL_MOVE.<stream>` / `$JS.API.ACCOUNT.STREAM.CANCEL_MOVE.<account>.<stream>`: stream peers "will always return to their original peer set" but consumers may land differently.
- Overlap rules: scale/retention changes may stack; "A move change while another move is in progress is not allowed"; "Scale or retention changes while a move is in progress is not allowed"; consumers can be scaled independently at any time (but may keep moving until stream ops finish).
- "Upgrading directly to 2.15 is **not recommended**"; path is 2.14 → 2.14-compat (adds desired-state encoding only) → 2.15; during mixed versions "any in-flight operation stalls" until all servers are on 2.15. Downgrading below 2.14-compat "is **not recommended**"; let pending changes settle first. Inconsistent state after a direct upgrade/downgrade "may be (partially) repaired by performing a rolling restart of all nodes while on the same version."

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — RAFT (NRG) timing, quorum and backpressure (server/raft.go)**

- EvictPeers (meta-authorized unilateral peer removal for a leaderless group) is refused for unmanaged groups, groups that still have a leader ("we can remove peers through the log, which is ordered and therefore always preferred"), or when the peers left behind could still reach quorum without us ("otherwise they could commit entries we'd never see and we would diverge") (server/raft.go:1098-1135)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — natscli cheat sheets and help-text guidance (cli/cheats/*.md, cli/*_command.go)**

- `nats server check stream` flags cover source/mirror lag and last-seen, min/max sources, peer-expect, peer lag/seen, subjects thresholds; `nats server check meta` requires `--expect`, `--lag-critical`, `--seen-critical` (cli/server_check_command.go:162-213)
- Cheat sheet: `nats server ping --id --graph --user system`, `nats server report jetstream --account WEATHER --sort cluster`, `nats server req jsz --leader`, `nats server raft step-down` "To manage JetStream cluster RAFT membership" (cli/cheats/server.md:1-44)
- Decentralized auth flow from cheat: `nats auth operator add`, `nats server generate server.conf`, `nats auth account add`, `nats auth user add admin SYSTEM`, `nats auth account push MyAccount --server ... --creds sys_admin.cred`; "All configuration changes are stored locally until `nats auth account push`ed" (cli/cheats/auth.md:1-31)

- On recovery the server repairs bad subjects ("Detected bad subject %q while adding stream %q, will attempt to repair"), removes subjects found on a mirrored stream ("Detected subjects on a mirrored stream %q, will remove"), and marks assets it cannot understand as unsupported/offline rather than failing ("Detected unsupported stream '%s > %s': %s") (server/jetstream.go:1478-1560, 1330-1338)

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Understanding JetStream Memory Usage Patterns**

- JetStream memory comes from: dedup IDs kept for the window "(default: 2 minutes)"; file-store caching of recently accessed messages; metadata and subject tracking for streams/consumers/subjects; extra overhead on meta-leader nodes.
- Disable or shrink the dedup window per stream if deduplicating externally (example: 30s "Reduced from default 2 minutes").
- "Use fewer subjects per stream when possible"; "Long-lived consumers are more memory-efficient than short-lived ones"; separate meta leadership from nodes handling high-volume streams.
- Message count and size affect disk, not memory, "unless consumers perform full stream scans or create many short-lived consumers." 300M+ messages across a few streams with single consumers "shouldn't inherently cause high memory usage."
- "Memory usage in JetStream clusters is more influenced by architectural patterns (meta leadership, deduplication settings, consumer lifecycle) than by raw message counts."
- Case: 13GB of a 16GB GOMEMLIMIT on stream/consumer leaders and meta leaders, elevated after all clients stopped, while other nodes sat at 2-3GB. Use Go pprof for definitive allocation data.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Jepsen: NATS 2.12.1**

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Message Tracing in NATS 2.11: Debug Your Entire System with One Command**

- "The `nats trace` command sends a message through your system and shows you exactly where it goes"; "No external tools, no code instrumentation." It creates a temporary inbox to receive trace events from each server.
- Headers added: `Nats-Trace-Dest`, `Nats-Trace-Only`, `Accept-Encoding`. With `Nats-Trace-Only` the "message is traced but never actually delivered or stored in JetStream."
- Event types: `IN`, `EG`, `JS`, `SE` (stream export), `SI` (stream import), `SM` (subject mapping). Connection kinds: 0 client, 1 router, 2 gateway, 3 system, 4 leaf, 5 JetStream, 6 account. `Nats-Trace-Hop` builds the routing tree (1, 1.1, 1.2.1).
- Tracing stops at account boundaries by default; cross-account needs `allow_trace: true`: "For stream imports, the importer sets it. For service imports, the exporter sets it."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Monitoring NATS: From HTTP Scrapes to System Events**

- HTTP endpoints (`/varz`, `/connz`, `/jsz`) are point-in-time snapshots that miss transient events between scrapes; system-account events are delivered as NATS subjects.
- "The system account isolates subjects and permissions, not CPU, memory, or I/O. A severely overloaded server can still impact all traffic."
- `$SYS` must be explicitly enabled (`system_account: SYS` or the account public NKey in operator mode) and users authorized; it uses existing client ports and full NATS auth, while HTTP monitoring needs an extra port and has no built-in auth.
- Subjects: `$SYS.ACCOUNT.<account>.CONNECT`/`DISCONNECT`; auth failures on `$SYS.SERVER.<server>.CLIENT.AUTH.ERR` (structured: client IP, user/account, reason; SIEM-ready); periodic `$SYS.SERVER.<server>.STATSZ` ("periodic snapshots, not strict liveness guarantees"); request/reply `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.<server-id>.<ENDPOINT>` for VARZ/CONNZ/ROUTEZ/LEAFZ/GATEWAYZ/SUBSZ/JSZ/ACCOUNTZ/HEALTHZ; `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.PING` discovers all servers; `$SYS.REQ.SERVER.<id>.RELOAD` (2.10+).
- JetStream advisories under `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.*` (lifecycle, leader elections, delivery failures), API audit at `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.API`, metrics under `$JS.EVENT.METRIC.*` (e.g. ack latency).
- Use HTTP for k8s probes (`/healthz`), Prometheus, `nats-top`, LB checks; use the system account for real-time connection tracking, auth-error alerting, JetStream audit logs, and where HTTP ports can't be exposed. "For liveness checks, continue using `/healthz` via HTTP." Both are "complementary."
- `nats sub '$SYS.>'` is fine for exploration; narrow subscriptions in production to avoid volume. Persist system events in JetStream for audit/replay. Surveyor collects system-account data into Prometheus without per-server HTTP ports or sidecars.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Recovering Quorum After Renaming Servers**

- Rename servers one at a time; remove the stale offline record before the next rename. Changing Helm `serverNamePrefix` during an upgrade renames all servers at once, doubling the recorded peer set and losing quorum. "This setting should only be changed before the first installation."
- Symptoms: warning "JetStream has not established contact with a meta leader"; readiness probe 503; `nats server report jetstream` shows half offline; error "The cluster expects 6 nodes but only 3 responded. JetStream requires at least 4 up nodes."
- On 2.12+ a fresh empty node cannot force itself into the peer set, so scale-up recovery doesn't work; bring nodes back under original names (all originally-named nodes needed simultaneously if disks are empty); reverting the prefix alone doesn't fix a bricked cluster. If original hosts are destroyed, "no in-product recovery exists on 2.12+; restore from backup."
- On 2.10/2.11 add a fourth server (`kubectl scale --replicas=4`) to regain quorum, peer-remove stale entries (`nats server cluster peer-remove -f <peer ID>` or `$JS.API.SERVER.REMOVE`), then scale back down.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS HTTP Monitoring Endpoints: A Complete Guide**

- "no sampling, no asynchronous exporters inside the server, and no continuously running probes"; responses are live state. Monitoring is off by default; enable with `nats-server -m 8222` or `http_port`/`https_port`. No HTTP auth: treat the port as internal-only, bind to localhost/private network, use `https_port` in production, reverse-proxy for external auth.
- Endpoints: `/healthz` (k8s probes), `/varz`, `/connz`, `/routez`, `/leafz`, `/gatewayz`, `/subsz` (can be very large), `/jsz` (`?accounts=1`).
- `/varz`: `mem` growth from slow consumers, JetStream caching, route/leaf buffers, high subscription counts; `cpu` may exceed 100% on multi-core; `slow_consumers` increments when clients can't drain; `in_msgs`/`out_msgs`/bytes need deltas for rates.
- `/connz`: pending bytes growth means a client is falling behind; `msgs_to`/`msgs_from` find hot producers/consumers; `?state=closed` shows exit reasons; `?sort=pending`, `?subs=1`, `?limit=100&offset=0`. `/routez` `pending_size` high means congestion or slow peers. `/jsz` `reserved_mem`/`reserved_store` are logical reservations.
- Prometheus exporter converts JSON; Surveyor gives one Prometheus endpoint per cluster over NATS; `nats-top -s https://localhost:8222`.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — What are strategies for moving a stream to a different set of nodes in the cluster?**

- Keep server names static; replace nodes one at a time on the same name; after a clean shutdown the replacement syncs all streams assigned to it; wait for full sync before touching the next node; always use Lame Duck Mode — ripienaar.
- Removing a peer (`nats cluster peer-remove`) makes the stream pick a new peer at random; with old nodes still present it may pick an old one — ripienaar, derekcollison.
- Alternative: put the departing server in LDM then remove it from the cluster with `nats server raft` to move all its data; for lots of data do it per stream to spread replication load — ripienaar.
- Safe pattern: 3 nodes, add 2 temporary, replace the 3 one by one on the same names, then remove the 2; clients learn topology via gossip — ripienaar.
- Data loss risk: if R3 on 1,2,3 loses 1 and 4 joins, removing 2 before 4 has fully synced every stream in every account can lose data — ripienaar.
- LDM moves leadership away but a new peer is only chosen when the node is removed from the Raft group — ripienaar.
- Backup and restore into a new cluster is the simplest path if downtime is allowed — derekcollison.
- Placement tags (2.10+) let you move existing streams within or between clusters without interruption and transparently to clients — jnmoyne. [STALE?] earlier manual steps superseded.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How nodes work in a cluster (slow consumers on routes, max_payload, reconnects)**

- `write_deadline` applies to client, route, leaf and gateway connections; `max_pending` applies only to clients; `max_control_line` to all — wallyqs.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — k8s: OOM killed when using JetStream WorkQueue on cpu:1 and mem:1GB machines (issue)**

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Regional and Cross Region Streams (Supercluster)**

- Every server needs a unique `server_name`, its own `jetstream.store_dir`, `server_tags`, a `cluster` block with the routes of its own cluster, and a `gateway` block naming its cluster.
- Start servers one at a time with a short delay so the seed routes can come up and become healthy before the next node joins. "sleep a second in between so the seeds can startup and get healthy."
- Observed output: `nats server info` on a supercluster member shows a `Super Cluster` section listing all gateway-connected cluster names (rg1, rg2, rg3, xr); each server shows `GWs 3` (one gateway to each other cluster) and `Routes 8`.
- Observed defaults in `nats server info` output (2.10.1): Max Payload 1.0 MiB, Max Conn 65,536, TLS Timeout 2.00s, Write Deadline 10.00s, JetStream "Always sync writes to disk: false", "Write sync Frequency: 2m0s".

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Regional and Cross Region Streams (Cluster)**

- Only the three seed servers' route URLs are listed in the shared `cluster.conf`; every node includes the same routes and cluster name.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Replace cluster nodes**

- The rotate-nodes procedure exists to replace the underlying hardware of existing cluster nodes with minimal or no downtime. "The original use case was to replace the underlying hardware of existing nodes in a cluster. The goal is to minimize or remove the need for downtime."
- Node replacement algorithm for a 3-node JetStream cluster: add a new node, put the old node in lame duck mode, then remove the old node as a Raft peer, which forces its replicas to be rescheduled onto the new node. "Remove `n0` which forces replicas to be scheduled on `n3`"
- Replace one node at a time, in pairs: n3 replaces n0, n4 replaces n1, then reuse the original names/ports (n0, n1, n2 on new hardware) to replace n2, n3, n4 in turn.
- The reason to cycle back to the original names/ports is so the connection URLs clients already have stay addressable for reconnects; if every replacement had a new hostname or port, every client would need a config change. "This cycle is required so that the original connection URLs used by the clients remain addressable for if/when they need to reconnect. Otherwise if they were all new hostnames or ports, clients would need to update their local configuration."
- Removing a peer is done with `nats server raft peer-remove --force <name>` using a system-account user; lame duck is signalled with `nats-server --signal ldm=<pidfile>`.
- The demo waits only 60 s after lame-ducking and another 60 s after peer removal before the next node; this is described as aggressive and demo-only. In practice the wait depends on how much data must be migrated. "This script choose a fairly aggressive wait time (for demo purpsoes) of only 60 seconds ... In practice, the wait time would be dependent on how much data needs to be migrated."
- Expected client behaviour during rotation: some clients disconnect and reconnect automatically, and consumption may slow down. "Some will disconnect and reconnect automatically. There may be some slow down on consumption"
- Clients in the demo are given the full list of cluster URLs (`-s localhost:4222,localhost:4223,localhost:4224`) so they can fail over to another node when their current server goes lame duck.
- The new nodes n3 and n4 are configured with only a single seed route (n3 -> n2's route port, n4 -> n3's route port), showing that a joining node needs only one reachable existing peer to join the cluster.
- Node configs set `pid_file` (used for signalling lame duck / stop) and per-node `jetstream.store_dir`, `max_memory_store` and `max_file_store` (1 GiB each in the demo).
- The shared config declares `system_account: SYS`, a `USERS` account with `jetstream: enabled`, and `no_auth_user: user` so unauthenticated clients land in the application account while operations use the sys user.
- The demo uses one R3 file stream (unlimited) and one R3 memory stream capped at 100k messages so that both storage types are exercised by the migration; both are watched via `nats stream report` and `nats consumer report` during migration.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — NATS Streaming to JetStream Migration**

- After migration, verify with the NATS CLI: `stream report`, `stream view` to check headers and payloads, and `consumer report` to check consumer state. "Since the NATS CLI supports introspecting JetStream assets, we can use it to verify that the migration was successful."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Configuring the System Account**

- The system account is a designated account for operations and monitoring of the server, cluster, or supercluster. "NATS has the notion of a *system account* which is a designated account for operations and monitoring of the server, cluster, or supercluster."
- A server always has an implicit system account, but by default it has no users, so no client can run administrative commands until one is defined. "Although there is an implicit system account created on the server, there are no _users_ associated with it, by default."
- Observed output: with no system user defined, `nats server info` fails with `no results received, ensure the account used has system privileges and appropriate permissions`.
- The default system account is named `$SYS`; the minimal config to activate it is an `accounts` block defining `$SYS` with at least one user. "To activate we need to define a user associated with this account."
- Adding or changing the `accounts` block can be applied with `nats-server --signal reload`, no restart required. "Simply reload the server with the `--signal` option."
- You may use a differently named system account by defining any account and pointing `system_account:` at it; this is required for decentralized JWT auth. "There is another option to change the default system account name which is required when using the decentralized JWT auth method."
- Save the sys credentials as a `nats context` so the password is not typed on the command line every time.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Private Inbox**

- Permission changes in the config file are applied with `nats-server --signal reload=<pid>`; observed output shows subsequent subscribe attempts to `_INBOX.>` and `_INBOX_joe.>` by pam rejected with Permissions Violation while requests with the correct prefix succeed.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Services Intro**

- The framework enables automatic service discovery and status reporting without extra effort; `nats micro` queries and reports all framework services.
- Per-endpoint statistics (e.g. request counts) are tracked by the framework with no application code.
- (deno) Service APIs live on `$SRV.PING`, `$SRV.INFO`, `$SRV.STATS`; appending the service name narrows scope (`$SRV.PING.minmax`) and appending the ID targets one instance. `info` is a superset of `ping` (adds endpoints); `stats` reports per endpoint.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Core Publish-Subscribe**

- The `nats` CLI uses `NATS_URL` if set; `nats context` manages named connection/auth contexts.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream Deep Dive**

- JetStream must be enabled on the server (`nats-server -js`) before any stream can be created.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first stream**

- A `no responders available for request` error on stream creation means the server was started without `-js`; JetStream isn't running.
- Unlimited defaults grow forever: with `--defaults` the stream keeps every message until the disk fills, and a full disk takes the server down. "a production stream needs at least one limit so old orders age out before the disk does."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reading back the stream**

- Replaying a huge stream from the beginning: Deliver All on a stream holding millions of messages takes time and moves a lot of data. "Read the whole history only when you want it."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Ack responses and redelivery**

- Each nak raises an advisory on `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MSG_NAKED.<stream>.<consumer>`.
- A term publishes a terminated advisory on `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MSG_TERMINATED.<stream>.<consumer>` carrying stream/consumer sequence, delivery count, and an optional reason.
- MaxDeliver drops a message with no dead-letter: the message stays in the stream but leaves the consumer's pending list silently. "JetStream has no built-in dead-letter queue." Catch it via the `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<stream>.<consumer>` advisory.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Shaping the stream**

- Without a limit, a stream grows until it fills the disk and takes the server down with it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Altering stream state**

- `purge` empties the stream; `rm` destroys it including config and every consumer. "don't type `rm` for that, and read the confirmation prompt before answering it."
- A purge can't be undone: on a stream that matters set `DenyPurge` so a stray call can't wipe it, and keep a mirror if the data is worth recovering.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Surviving node loss**

- File storage doesn't sync every write to disk right away; a write can sit unsynced after its `PubAck` long enough that an OS crash could lose it.
- Reading failover from a single-server demo proves nothing about fault tolerance; prove failover on a real cluster.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mirrors and sources**

- Mirror/source info: `Lag` is how many messages behind (0 = caught up; climbing and staying high means it can't keep pace); `Last Seen` is time since last message or heartbeat (small, steady is healthy).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Stream and consumer policies**

- Compression `s2` (default `none`) makes a file-storage stream compress message blocks on disk, spending CPU for disk; JSON compresses well, images don't. Editing later is allowed but takes effect only after the stream's store restarts (server restart or leader change), and blocks already on disk stay as they are.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next**

- Checklist: Set at least one limit (`MaxAge`, `MaxBytes`, or `MaxMsgs`) so an unbounded stream never fills the disk.
- Checklist: Subscribe to the max-deliveries advisory so a dropped message doesn't vanish unnoticed; JetStream has no dead-letter queue.
- Checklist: Watch disk on an Interest stream with a stopped consumer; interest means messages wait for every registered consumer's ack.
- Checklist: Use `nats stream purge` to clear messages and `nats stream rm` to delete the stream; don't swap the two.
- Checklist: Set `DenyPurge` on a stream that matters, and keep a mirror; a purge can't be undone.
- Checklist: Prove failover on a real cluster; a green single-node run can't show leader election or a node loss.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Core NATS Deep Dive**

- Core NATS requires no server flags; the default nats-server build is all you need.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publish-subscribe**

- A subscriber that can't keep up builds a server-side backlog; past a threshold the server logs `Slow Consumer Detected` and closes its connection, other subscribers unaffected. "A slow subscriber gets cut off."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject mapping**

- The `mappings` block is reloadable with `nats-server --signal reload`; open connections stay up.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connecting**

- Set a connection name after the service that owns it; it surfaces in `nats server report connections` and the monitoring endpoint.
- `nats server report connections` answers fully only with system-account credentials; the monitoring endpoint (`nats-server -m 8222`) is the no-credentials alternative.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connection lifecycle**

- Force reconnect (nats.go `Conn.ForceReconnect()`) is how you spread clients onto a newly added server after scaling out, or leave a server you know is about to go down on your schedule.
