- Checklist: re-push each account after an identity restore if the server lost its resolver directory; back up `server.conf` too because its `SYSTEM` preload lets the push in.
- Checklist: tag each identity backup with the operator version or timestamp.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first MQTT client**

- MQTT needs state that outlives a connection (session subscriptions, unacked QoS 1/2 messages, retained messages); the server keeps all of it in JetStream streams, so JetStream must be reachable.
- Configuring `mqtt {}` without JetStream on a standalone server refuses to start: `mqtt requires JetStream to be enabled if running in standalone mode`. A server with a `cluster`, `gateway`, or `leafnode` config can reach JetStream elsewhere, so the check doesn't apply there.
- An `mqtt {}` block with no `listen` or `port` disables MQTT silently, with no error and no log line, so always set one.
- Starting without JetStream fails at startup; the requirement applies per account too: an MQTT user whose account has no JetStream is refused at connect. "Enable JetStream on the server, and on the account your MQTT users bind to."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topics and subjects**

- The server's own MQTT-management traffic runs on `$JS.>` and `$MQTT.>` subjects; device messages are the ones carrying an `Nmqtt-Pub` header.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — QoS, sessions, and retained messages**

- A change to `ack_wait` applies only to subscriptions created after the change; existing subscriptions keep the old value until recreated.
- Lower `max_ack_pending` if you need more subscriptions per session; like `ack_wait`, a change applies only to new subscriptions.
- Retained messages are stored regardless of QoS; a retained QoS 0 message is still persisted, which is part of why the account needs JetStream even for a fleet that never uses QoS 1.
- Testing a will with a clean shutdown discards the will; test with a hard kill or by cutting the network.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth and clustering (MQTT)**

- The `mqtt {}` block takes its own `tls {}` map separate from the client port's; add `ca_file` and `verify: true` for mutual TLS.
- Once a server has a `cluster` or `gateway` block, MQTT requires `server_name` and startup fails otherwise: `mqtt requires server name to be explicitly set`. Server names must be unique across the cluster or super-cluster.
- With `http: 8222`, `/connz?mqtt_client=<id>` filters connections by MQTT client ID; each record carries `mqtt_client`, and `/varz` has an `mqtt` section including the JetStream domain in use.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (MQTT)**

- Checklist: enable JetStream on the server and on the account your MQTT users bind to.
- Checklist: point plain MQTT clients at the MQTT port and MQTT-over-WebSocket clients at the WebSocket listener.
- Checklist: write every permission as a NATS subject with NATS wildcards.
- Checklist: grant both `sensors.>` and `sensors` for a device subscribing to `sensors/#`.
- Checklist: normalize leading and trailing slashes across the fleet, or account for both subject trees.
- Checklist: sanitize anything interpolated into a topic.
- Checklist: don't rely on a QoS 1 subscription to make NATS-originated traffic durable; put that data in a stream.
- Checklist: give every device its own client ID, ideally derived from hardware.
- Checklist: count subscriptions against `max_ack_pending`; at the default of 1024 a session fits 63 subscriptions (31 if they end in `#`) before the 65535 per-session cap.
- Checklist: use JetStream where you need history; only the last retained value per topic is kept.
- Checklist: test wills with a hard kill or a cut network, not a clean shutdown.
- Checklist: put credentials and TLS on the MQTT listener before it leaves a lab.
- Checklist: keep `$MQTT.sub.>` out of permission lists on 2.12.3 and later; on 2.10 and 2.11, allow it explicitly.
- Checklist: set `--bearer` on both the account and the user for operator-mode devices.
- Checklist: set `server_name` on every server; MQTT requires it as soon as a cluster or gateway block exists.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first WebSocket connection**

- The WebSocket listener requires TLS by default; leaving out both a `tls {}` block and `no_tls: true` stops the server at startup: `websocket requires TLS configuration`.
- With `no_tls: true` the server logs `Websocket not configured with TLS. DO NOT USE IN PRODUCTION!`; a WebSocket client sending a bearer token over `ws://` sends it in the clear.
- There is no default WebSocket port; a `websocket {}` block without `port` or `listen` starts the server with no WebSocket listener, no error, and no warning.
- A `websocket {}` block with no port: the server starts and the listener doesn't exist; check the log for `Listening for websocket clients`.
- A FIPS-140 build made with Go 1.25 or earlier refuses the whole WebSocket listener (and `ws://`/`wss://` leafnode remotes) because the handshake computes SHA-1 over `Sec-WebSocket-Key`; build with Go 1.26 or later.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TLS and proxies**

- Two ways to get TLS: a certificate on the NATS WebSocket listener, or terminate TLS at an ingress in front; which depends on whether NATS sits behind the same edge as your web traffic.
- Certificate material is the only part of the `websocket {}` block that reloads; `cert_file`/`key_file` changes apply to new connections while existing ones keep the negotiated certificate.
- Any other `websocket {}` change on reload (`verify_and_map`, `pinned_certs`, `allowed_origins`, timeouts) is rejected, and a rejected field aborts the entire reload, including otherwise-valid changes in the same edit.
- A proxy must pass the `Upgrade` and `Connection` headers through (HTTP/1.1); a proxy that strips them fails silently as a connection that never establishes.
- A NATS connection is idle between messages; a proxy that closes idle connections after 60 seconds will close a working subscription. Set the proxy idle timeout longer than the server's WebSocket ping interval (`ping_interval` in `websocket {}` from 2.12, server-wide ping interval before).
- If NATS is published under a path prefix, the prefix must appear in the client URL; for leaf nodes the server appends `/leafnode`, so a `location /nats` rule must also match `/nats/leafnode`.
- `handshake_timeout` bounds reading the request, the TLS handshake, and writing the response; a value tuned on a laptop can reject real clients behind a slow proxy under load.
- A proxy that drops `Upgrade` and `Connection`: the client reports a connection error, not a protocol error; if `ws://` works directly and fails through the proxy, check this first.
- A proxy idle timeout shorter than the ping interval: connections drop on a timer with no error on either side. "The pattern to look for is disconnects at a suspiciously round interval."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leaf nodes over WebSocket**

- The hub needs both blocks: `leafnodes { port: ... }` is the switch that makes the server accept leaf nodes at all, and `websocket {}` is the door they arrive through. Without a `leafnodes` block (or with an empty one) the WebSocket listener accepts the connection and then closes it.
- A path-routing proxy that doesn't forward `/leafnode`: route `/` or give the remote the proxy's prefix so the path becomes `/nats/leafnode`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (WebSocket)**

- Checklist: set `port` or `listen` in `websocket {}`; there is no default.
- Checklist: confirm `Listening for websocket clients` appears in the log before debugging the client.
- Checklist: point WebSocket clients at the WebSocket port and everything else at the client port.
- Checklist: give every client URL an explicit port; nats.js fills in 443 for a bare host and 80 for `ws://` without one.
- Checklist: a FIPS-140 build must be built with Go 1.26 or later.
- Checklist: set `allowed_origins` to the exact scheme, host, and port, or `same_origin: true` when page and endpoint share one hostname.
- Checklist: treat origin checking as protection against other web pages, not access control; it's skipped when no `Origin` header is present.
- Checklist: keep seeds and credentials files out of front-end code; use a bearer JWT or an `HttpOnly` cookie.
- Checklist: give the browser user subscribe permission on the subjects it displays and no publish rights it doesn't need.
- Checklist: restrict browser credentials with `allowed_connection_types: ["WEBSOCKET"]`.
- Checklist: use `no_tls: true` only behind a TLS-terminating proxy on a trusted network.
- Checklist: make the proxy forward `Upgrade` and `Connection`.
- Checklist: set the proxy's idle timeout longer than the server's WebSocket ping interval.
- Checklist: set `advertise` behind NAT or a proxy.
- Checklist: size `handshake_timeout` against the proxy's latency under load.
- Checklist: configure TLS on the listener or terminate at the proxy; `wss://` in a client URL only says what the client will do.
- Checklist: write `wss://` when the link is encrypted; `ws://` beside a `tls {}` block is encrypted too.
- Checklist: add a `tls {}` block with `ca_file` only when the hub's certificate isn't publicly trusted.
- Checklist: keep every URL in a remote on the same kind of scheme.
- Checklist: point the remote at the hub's WebSocket listener, not the leafnode port.
- Checklist: keep a `leafnodes { port: ... }` block on the hub even when every leaf arrives over WebSocket, and firewall that port like any other.
- Checklist: give the hub a `websocket {}` listener as well.
- Checklist: grant `LEAFNODE_WS`, not `LEAFNODE`, to a leaf that arrives over WebSocket.
- Checklist: write an explicit port on every leafnode remote URL; without one the server appends `:7422`.
- Checklist: if a proxy routes on path, make sure it forwards `/leafnode`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Learn**

- Backup & Recovery: stream snapshots, mirrors for disaster recovery, a recovery runbook, and backing up identity.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — What is NATS?**

- Clustering, JetStream, leaf nodes, MQTT, and WebSocket are all configuration on the same single `nats-server` process.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subjects**

- The `>` wildcard enables wire taps and monitoring of everything under a prefix.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue Groups**

- Scaling: start small, monitor metrics (queue depth with JetStream, processing time), scale based on load, then automate.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — The NATS Ecosystem**

- Clustering, JetStream, leaf nodes, MQTT, and WebSocket are enabled through configuration on the same `nats-server`; there are no separate components to install.
- `nsc` is a standalone CLI for operators, accounts, and users; an alternative to `nats auth`, reads the same on-disk store, and covers operations `nats auth` doesn't yet.
- Kubernetes tooling: official Helm charts (`k8s`) and NACK controllers/CRDs for declarative streams, consumers, and KV/Object stores.
- Observability: `prometheus-nats-exporter` (varz, connz, routez, JetStream stats) and `nats-surveyor` (cluster-wide aggregation), which pair for full-cluster observability.
- `jsm.go` is the canonical source of JetStream API JSON schemas used by tooling and the reference docs.
- Bridges and integrations: Kafka bridge, Spark connector, Flink connector, Vert.x client, Terraform provider for JetStream resources.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Getting Started**

- The default NATS client port is 4222 and the HTTP monitoring port is 8222.
- `nats-server -m 8222` enables monitoring; `nats-server -js` enables JetStream persistence.

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Achieve MASSIVE Scale with NATS Clustering | Rethink Connectivity Episode 4**

- To observe cluster state you need a user in the built-in `$SYS` system account, which has extended admin privileges and exposes server metrics via system events. "a special account called dollar sign sys and this account already has extended admin privileges so you can get all of the metrics" (~03:06)
- The `nats server list` command (run with a $SYS user) shows each server's IP, version, whether JetStream is enabled and its connection count; the episode uses it inside `watch` sorted by name to monitor the cluster. "it will give us a list of the actual server, his ip address, version, whether it's using JetStream, its number of connections" (~05:50)
- Set an explicit short server `name` in the config; otherwise the generated server name is long. "this server name is really long, if we wanted to change it... we could say name equals north america one" (~05:40)
- A cluster is configured with a `cluster` block containing a cluster name, a dedicated cluster port (6222 by convention, any free port works) and a `routes` list acting as seed servers. "we give this cluster a connection port which is 6222... routes, this is kind of like your list of seed servers" (~08:40)
- Give clients (and the CLI context) the URLs of all cluster servers; the client randomly picks one and moves on if a server is offline, which spreads connections evenly across the cluster. "NATS will be smart about randomly selecting one of these... if it doesn't detect that a server is online it will move on to another one" (~11:20)
- `nats bench` with subscribers plus a periodic `nats pub` is a quick way to simulate load and watch connection distribution across a cluster. "nats bench, I'm going to create 10 subscribers to this hello subject so we can actually create some simulation" (~12:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to build a NATS Supercluster | Rethink Connectivity Episode 5**

- Routes gossip so one seed route suffices to form a mesh, but in practice you should list two or three seed servers (and likewise for gateways) so that losing the single seed does not strand new nodes. "in practice you're probably going to want to maybe double or triple up for these connections... so if na1 goes down you're not out of luck" (~02:40)
- Enabling JetStream on a cluster only requires the `jetstream` directive (no config needed) on each server plus a JetStream-enabled account. "you edit the config to enable JetStream and then you work with a JetStream enabled account" (~07:40)
- Use one config file per cluster: most content is shared, but cluster name, cluster seed routes and gateway name differ. "split this into multiple configurations one for each cluster... most of the stuff will be the same but some of it will have to change" (~08:30)
- A `gateway` block mirrors the `cluster` block: a name (matching the cluster), a port (7222 by convention) and a `gateways` list of the other clusters' name plus URL; gateways also gossip so a single seed per remote cluster works. "instead of route we're actually going to call this gateways... these also gossip between each other so we can also just have single seeds" (~10:10)
- Remote-cluster nodes need no client port published when they are only reached through gateways. "it doesn't need to have a port declaration and we're not going to be exporting any ports because we don't need to connect directly to them" (~11:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to set up Decentralized Authentication/Authorization in NATS | Rethink Connectivity Episode 6**

- nsc is the recommended way to start managing operators/accounts/users, but it is not required; the design is intentionally open so organizations can build their own issuance flow without sharing private keys. "you don't necessarily have to use nsc but this is the best way to get started... it's a very open design and that's on purpose" (~09:40)
- Always generate signing keys and never use root keys operationally: signing keys can be rotated if compromised, root keys cannot be recovered from compromise. "root keys are great for printing out putting in a safe... if your root key gets compromised you're kind of out of luck" (~10:40)
- Edit the operator to require signing keys on all accounts (strict signing key usage) and set the account JWT server URL so nsc knows where to push account JWTs. "we want to require all of our accounts to have signing keys as well... set up an account JWT server URL" (~12:16)
- The memory resolver holds account JWTs in memory and suits small systems; the NATS resolver is needed when you want to push accounts dynamically to servers. "a memory resolver... that's great for smaller systems but if we want things more dynamic where we can actually push accounts to servers we'll want to use a NATS resolver" (~15:20)
- `nsc generate config --nats-resolver --sys-account SYS` produces a server config containing the operator JWT, system account, resolver settings and a preloaded system account JWT; `nsc push -A` pushes accounts to the running server. "here's my operator's JWT, here's also the account that I want to use for system accounts, and we want to use a NATS resolver" (~16:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extend your NATS Cluster with Leaf Nodes | Rethink Connectivity Episode 7**

- Leaf node connections are self-healing: they fail over to gossiped hub servers, keep retrying while disconnected, keep operating locally in the meantime, and resync when the link returns. "I could turn off my internet... the leaf node will still operate as is because it's a separate NATS system... when it comes back up it'll sync back up" (~07:40)
- A leaf node into NGS needs only a `leafnodes { remotes [...] }` block with the hub URL and credentials, plus `jetstream` enabled; the JetStream domain may be left default or named explicitly. "I only need two things here, I need the url... and then we'll also grab these credentials" (~13:00)
- Requests through an already-connected leaf link can return faster than a fresh direct connection to the hub because the direct path pays the TLS handshake each time. "that's actually the TLS delay making that TLS connection... via the leaf node connection we actually get much faster responses" (~16:00)
- From a leaf node, viewing or getting from a hub stream requires specifying the hub's JetStream domain (e.g. `--js-domain NGS`); without it the leaf's own (empty) domain is used. "there are no streams in our leaf node right now there's only a stream on NGS... that's where we need to specify a JS domain" (~20:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Connect ANY Auth System to NATS.io with Auth Callout**

- Server config: an `authorization { auth_callout { ... } }` block with `issuer` (public account NKey generated via `nsc generate nkey --account`, so the server can verify signed responses), `auth_users` (users that bypass callout, including the auth service itself), and the `account` in which callout users live. "we want to pass an issuer and this issuer is going to be the public key of the NKey that we just generated" (~12:40)
- The auth service's own user should use NKeys or decentralized JWTs rather than a plaintext username/password in config. "I recommend that you use something like NKeys or even the decentralized JWT auth for a lot of these users" (~13:20)
- Inject the auth service's NKey seed via environment or secrets in production, never hard-coded. "you likely want to inject this in via the environment or via secrets in some way shape or form when you're actually deploying" (~15:20)
- The auth service subscribes to the fixed subject `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH`; the example uses the micro framework with that as the endpoint subject. "the NATS server is going to send an $SYS request user auth, this is the subject that NATS is going to be using the callout for" (~26:29)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Superclusters in Kubernetes: Cross-Cloud Geo-Affinity for High Availability and Low Latency**

- A three-server JetStream-enabled cluster in EKS was deployed with the maintainers' Helm chart and a values file; the options map straight onto standard NATS config documentation. "all I had to do was create this values.yaml file... they all point back to the NATS documentation" (~01:20)
- In Kubernetes, application clients reach the servers through the Kubernetes Service the Helm chart exposes in front of the NATS pods. "they all interact through this service exposed by the Helm chart that fronts my NATS servers" (~01:50)
- `nats micro stats <service>` shows per-instance request counts; requests spread evenly across instances of a service (max 5 of 10 landed on any one instance in the demo). "you can see they pretty evenly distributed, right, no major spikes here" (~06:30)
- Cross-cloud gateway connectivity was done by exposing each cluster's gateway port through a Kubernetes LoadBalancer Service mapped to a cloud NLB / Azure LB; each gateway block advertises its own LB hostname on 7222 and lists the other cluster's LB address on 7222. "this Kubernetes service, I deployed it as a load balancer type... it's advertising the NLB hostname on port 7222" (~10:00)
- Gateway connections were authenticated with username/password for the demo; production should use something stronger like JWT. "in a production environment you might want something more like JWT" (~11:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Building an Interactive Whiteboard with NATS Websockets | Rethink Connectivity Episode 3**

- WebSocket support is off by default; enable it with a `websocket` block giving a listen port, and `no_tls: true` only for local dev — the server warns that non-TLS websockets should not be used in production. "websocket isn't turned on by default inside of NATS, you have to turn it on yourself" (~01:50)
- Turning websocket `compression` on is recommended for better performance. "I'll turn compression on just for better performance" (~02:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Mutually Trusted NGS Credentials**

- To trust NGS credentials on your own server: configure the server with the NGS operator, set up an account resolver (memory or NATS), and create a dedicated system account for your own servers. "we configure our NATS server with the NGS operator and we configure an account resolver" (~03:50)
- Your own servers need their own system account because NGS servers use a different system account; `nats server list` against them with NGS's system creds returns nothing. "the only servers involved so far are NGS servers that are using a different system account, so failed without results as expected" (~05:40)
- Unresolved-import warnings on connect are harmless: NGS accounts import services that do not exist on your servers; the imports can be removed. "these are imports NGS adds for services that do not exist on our end... they're harmless" (~07:50)
- The memory resolver is fine for static accounts; the NATS resolver is more appropriate when accounts change dynamically, and needs an initial `nsc push` (errors until then) plus a push to your own resolver after every change. "NGS the push happens automatically on every change but to make your changes visible you need to push to your resolver as well" (~11:10)
- A NATS resolver in full mode holds all account JWTs and answers lookups; with at least one full-mode server, other servers (e.g. leaf nodes) can run in cache mode, downloading only locally used account JWTs and caching them for offline use for the resolver TTL. "as long as you have at least one server running with a NATS resolver in full mode you can start others in cache mode" (~12:00)
- A cache-mode resolver still needs a leaf node remote for the system account for resolution to work. "I'm only setting one remote, the remote for the system account, that is needed in order to make the NATS resolver work even in cache mode" (~13:00)
- The first connect through a cache-mode resolver for an unseen account may fail due to compounding import-resolution timeouts; the retry succeeds. "this command will fail at first, it does so because of compounding timeouts to resolve the imports" (~13:50)
- A cache-mode server keeps serving cached accounts while the full-mode server is offline. "we can still access it despite the NATS server with the full resolver being offline" (~14:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS Leafnodes**

- Add `-DV` to the server to see the leaf node handshake, credentials exchange and interest propagation in the logs. "you can always add -DV and it'll start showing you lots of stuff, interaction with the leaf node" (~19:00)
- Leaf connections self-heal like everything else: if the hub server disappears the leaf re-solicits and rehooks automatically. "if all of a sudden the server that I was connected to inside of NGS went away the system would automatically try to reseal itself, re-solicit the connection" (~23:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Andrew Gracey on Two Node K3S**

- NATS already underpins k3s for multi-node (3/5/7 node) systems; the two-node k3s option was targeted for later in 2024 and was not yet available. "we can actually underpin k3s now with NATS for multi node systems... at some point we're going to have a two node k3s system" (~02:10)
- Adding a third "witness" node at the edge increases operational complexity and is an extra point of failure, defeating the cost goal; the risk-versus-TCO balance kills the project for many customers. "now you just increase your cost again and increase the complexity of your solution by adding a third different node" (~04:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Replace Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis and more w/NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity Ep 10**

- Synadia Cloud requires max bytes to be set on every stream so a tenant cannot exhaust the service. "it does require that I set max bytes on all of my streams" (~15:21)
- Stop the consume context on graceful shutdown (signal handling) to clean up. "it does return a consume context which we will want to stop when we gracefully shut down" (~23:31)
- Zero "pending" on a consumer means it is fully caught up. "it has zero pending which means it's up to date" (~25:34)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to configure NATS JetStream streams | Rethink Connectivity Ep 11**

- Description is not used by any JetStream machinery; it is a human-readable label that shows in `nats stream list`. "description isn't really used in any kind of infrastructure portion" (~05:06)
- Placement selects the cluster and server tags; tag servers when building a supercluster (e.g. region, cloud, SSD) so stream creators can express affinity. "we recommend when you're building the NATS supercluster that you tag things appropriately" (~19:21)
- Almost all stream options, including placement, can be changed at runtime; the server moves a replicated stream live while consumers and publishers keep working. "we actually take the stream we replicate it we move it in flight while consumers are consuming from it" (~26:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Build Priority Background Jobs & Dead Letter Queues with NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity ep 12**

- In a work-queue stream, processed messages are deleted, so the stream size represents in-progress work. "you can look at the size of the queue as kind of your in progress work" (~04:05)
- JetStream advisories report which messages hit max failed deliveries; you can capture these into a stream to build your own dead-letter queue. "we have some JetStream advisories that you could listen to and actually insert into a queue" (~06:06)
- Put a message-count cap on queues (example 20,000) for monitoring and SLA purposes. "these queues have some sort of limit on them ... you might want to set kind of a cap on this" (~08:08)
- `nats stream subjects <stream>` shows per-subject message counts, useful to see how much of each priority is queued. "I have 5,000 of the clean old upload and low priority queue and 5,000 of the send email" (~10:11)
- Name the connection and the consumer after the worker role and instance so monitoring and logging can identify each worker. "use these to create the name for our JetStream consumer as well as kind of just a worker name to use for both logging and for monitoring" (~11:14)
- The max-deliveries advisory subject is $JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<stream>.<consumer>; wildcard the consumer so new priorities do not require DLQ changes. "I want to add a medium priority and I don't want to have to change the dead letter queue semantics" (~26:34)
- All JetStream advisory events can be listed with the CLI schema command. "you can see all these through the NATS CLI via the schema command" (~26:34)
- The advisory includes stream, consumer and stream sequence; use `nats stream get <stream> <seq>` to fetch the original failed message, which stays in the stream until its max age. "we also get the stream sequence which is really important here" (~28:36)
- Stream metadata (new feature) can label a stream, e.g. dead-letter-queue=true, so tooling can discover DLQ streams. "I could look through all my streams and I could find the ones that are dead letter queues" (~30:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared Pt 2: Consumers | Rethink Connectivity**

- Original-rate replay (metered at the ingest rate) is useful for debugging real-time applications. "only replay it at the same rate that it was initially put into the stream" (~10:13)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Move over Kafka! Let's try NATS JetStream**

- NATS runs a hybrid model: in a cluster some servers can be core-only and some JetStream-enabled, mixed to match required scale, and stream placement is chosen deliberately. "you can run some of them as NATS core servers or you can run some of them as JetStream servers" (~01:03)
- The CLI is only one way to create streams; Terraform and client SDKs can create them too. "you can also create streams through terraform or you can create them directly in the client libraries" (~02:03)
- `nats sub --stream` reads from a stream with start options: all, new, last, last-per-subject (with a subject), or from a specific sequence number. "if i wanted to read a last message from a certain subject i can just say last per subject" (~05:05)
- KV and object store streams are hidden from normal stream commands; use the `-a` flag to list them. "you can fix this by using the a flag to list all the streams" (~10:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Comparing and contrasting NATS and Kafka | RethinkConn '22**

- Matching JetStream's functionality with Kafka means brokers, ZooKeeper, Kafka Streams JVMs, MirrorMaker for cross-cluster replication, Redis for KV, a separate message broker, and Kafka Connect JVMs; NATS covers most of it in one binary, plus Benthos for stream processing apps. "compare the number of JVMs as far as the eye can see ... to a single binary that runs all of these at once" (~18:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | JetStream**

- For observability the key metrics are how many times a message had to be redelivered and how long processing took; JetStream emits advisory events (e.g. "took ten milliseconds, tried four times") usable for dashboards and alerting without extra logic in services. "how many times has this message had to be redelivered ... and how long did it take for that message to be processed" (~11:17)
- The new `nats` CLI consolidated scattered utilities (nats-pub, nats-sub, nats-bench, nats-box) into one tool that also configures JetStream, backed by a Go library for building your own tooling. "I pulled them all into one standard CLI that supports benchmarking ... it is the same utility that you use to configure the entire JetStream system" (~13:20)
- Streams can be created by the microservice on startup, by CI/CD via the CLI's unattended mode, or by the Terraform provider for teams using a remote JetStream. "stand up a JetStream just for the purpose of that single CI run" (~14:21)
- JetStream publishes a full ordered log of API interactions (who created streams, changed config, tried to consume), and all APIs fit into normal NATS authorization so you can restrict who may create or only view. "we have a full ordered log of all the API interactions" (~15:25)
- At the time JetStream was a single-server tech preview not in the release binary; it would ship in 2.2 behind a feature flag, still single-server, with clustering across three servers targeted for around Q3. "by release 2.2 of NATS server you will get JetStream delivered to you ... behind a feature flag" (~17:27)
- Planned: server introspection APIs and event streams so administrators learn about problems (e.g. JetStream unable to write to disk) without log-file access. "we don't want only the people who have access to the log file to be aware of that" (~18:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Getting Started with NATS JetStream: Streams, Storage, and Data Lifecycle**

- JetStream must be enabled at the server level and separately at the account level; without both it is not usable by that account. "you also have to activate it at the account level" (~04:04)
- On Kubernetes, JetStream needs a persistent storage mechanism such as a PVC. "As long as your underlying infrastructure has a storage mechanism that JetStream can use, a PVC in Kubernetes world" (~04:04)
- Streams and consumers can be managed with the CLI, Terraform/OpenTofu provider, GitHub Actions, or the Kubernetes JetStream controller. "You can use Terraform or Open Tofu ... You can use GitHub actions. And you can also use a Kubernetes JetStream controller" (~07:08)
- Default limits are unlimited, meaning data piles up with no cleanup; set limits so NATS cleans up automatically. "my maximums are all set to be unlimited, which means I'm just going to keep on piling data on without any data cleanup. That's not great" (~09:09)
- When setting max age, the duplicate window must be set lower than the max age. "I also have to decrease the duplicate window to less than the max age, a configuration setting you just have to be aware of" (~12:11)
- `nats stream subjects <stream>` breaks down message counts per subject. "92 of the responses that I got were throwaway and 308 were significant" (~15:14)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Why NATS Consumers Just Work (And How to Use Them in 15 Minutes)**

- `nats consumer info` shows where the consumer runs and its unprocessed count, which matches the per-subject count in the stream. "It's got 308 unprocessed messages ... It matches" (~06:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Mirror Streams Explained — One-Way Replication Made Simple**

- Mirror configuration lives entirely on the receiving side; the origin needs no setup and does not even see a consumer created. "It won't even see a consumer created for the replication" (~01:00)
- Mirror promotion (2.12): unbind subjects from the old primary (e.g. set subjects to a dev-null placeholder), remove the mirror config and bind the subjects to it, then clean up the old stream. "first unbind subjects from the old primary so you don't have two streams competing for the same subjects" (~07:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers**

- Every R3 stream adds load; a per-dwelling stream model multiplies replication cost, so size streams to hardware I/O limits rather than administrative units. "once you say let's have an R3 ... immediately the load on the system increases with each and every stream" (~27:36)
- A client that processes too slowly on a fast delivery path becomes a slow consumer and the server disconnects it. "the server is not going to be happy ... you're a slow consumer of this data so I'm going to disconnect you" (~48:05)
- CLI backup/restore is out of band and never incremental or real time; the general recommendation is a mirror stream, possibly in another region, plus backups. "you're never going to with this mechanism it's never going to be incremental in real time ... you could very simply have a mirror stream" (~74:43)
- A mirror can live on slower disks with compression and long retention as an archive while the origin is pruned or compacted. "your mirror stream that is literally for archival ... on slower disks you could apply compression to that stream" (~75:43)
- The defaults are generally fine; beginners get hung up on retention policies and ack modes that they usually do not need to change. "generally the default should be perfectly fine ... retention policies people get hung up on and the ack modes" (~77:46)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.10 Webinar**

- 2.10 adds opt-in per-stream compression using S2 (a Snappy variant), trading storage for CPU. "this is using S2 compression which is a variation on top of Snappy compression ... you're trading off storage and CPU" (~01:00)
- The NATS CLI `--defaults` flag skips the interactive stream-creation prompts. "there's this really nice new feature ... dash dash defaults so you don't have to fill out all this other stuff" (~02:01)
- Compression is editable on an existing stream; the server compresses existing message blocks in real time after the edit. "this field is editable you define compression to S2 and then it will effectively rip through all the message blocks in real time" (~02:01)
- The 2.10 stream storage format is not backward compatible with 2.9 except that 2.9.22 and later patch releases understand it; downgrading is not recommended. "we did release 2.9.22 and then any patch release after that ... are aware of this new format" (~04:03)
- The new storage format cut restart/recovery of a 2.1 TB, 300-million-message stream from roughly 15 minutes on 2.9 to 1.1 seconds on 2.10, because 2.9 scanned and checksummed every block. "2.1 terabytes in size with 300 million messages ... roughly 15 minutes to actually restart the stream ... with 2.10 it takes 1.1 seconds" (~05:05)
- Fast stream recovery matters for rolling upgrades, Kubernetes restarts, and placing replicas on new nodes, and the 15-minute figure was for one stream; many streams multiply the wait. "this is just for one stream mind you so for people who have a lot of streams this time can add up" (~06:05)
- Community contributions added NetBSD (following the OpenBSD build) and a stub IBM z/OS build target in 2.10. "for people wanting to run NATS on NetBSD now you can actually build for that platform and then IBM z/OS ... more of a stub implementation" (~10:14)
- 2.10 "v2 routes" use multiple TCP connections per server pair out of the box: the system account is pinned to a dedicated connection and other accounts are spread over a pool of three. "you're going to get a pinned account for the system account ... and then there's going to be a pool size of three TCP connections" (~20:22)
- You can list specific accounts in the route config to pin each to its own dedicated TCP connection; throughput goes up "basically for free" but you should test in your environment. "there's going to be an additional TCP connection that actually gets pinned for that explicit account ... the throughput goes up significantly" (~21:22)
- Route (and leaf node) compression is off by default; with `s2_auto` the server picks a compression level from measured round-trip time using RTT thresholds, and it adapts rather than pinning heavy compression after one bad RTT sample. "based on the round trip time between any two servers it's going to choose a level of compression that is appropriate" (~25:29)
- Centralized auth callout config has only four options: issuer NKey, the auth account's users allowed to run the callout service, the auth account, and an optional XKey. "these are literally the only four config options that you can define for auth callout in this centralized mode" (~39:50)
- Decentralized auth callout needs a few extra config options and a "sentinel" credential; both modes are walked through end to end on NATS by Example. "you need to work with a sentinel credential and there's a reason for that" (~56:08)
- Auth callout is deliberately an extension point and is harder to set up than most NATS features. "it's not going to be as trivial to set up as some of the other NATS features" (~56:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- 2.10 took over a year after 2.9 (Sept 2022) because effort went into stabilizing 2.9 patch releases for customers and building test infrastructure. "we've spent an awful lot of time focused on quality ... also we had a very big backlog of features going into 2.10" (~02:04)
- Edge conditions that were once rare became common as adoption grew, so Synadia built chaos-test environments to catch them before users do. "edge conditions that we never seen start to be almost common ... we would love to catch those before others do" (~04:06)
- Synadia has a dedicated DevX team running chaos testing and distributed-systems testing beyond the server and client teams. "we also have this sort of DevX team ... they're doing chaos testing and all sorts of crazy distributed systems testing" (~07:09)
- The NATS unit-test suite ran 117 hours of tests in a single day through parallel jobs; "unit" tests spin up whole clusters and dozens of servers. "the NATS test suite ran 117 hours worth of unit tests in a single day" (~10:11)
- Consensus-based systems surface a new class of bugs under high or low latency and jitter, so each scenario must be tested across many variable inputs; perfect conditions do not reveal the most bugs. "if you start working with consensus ... suddenly a whole new set of problems appears that can surface if you have high latency or low latency" (~11:12)
- The hardest part of a distributed bug is correlating which set of inputs reproduces it; once reproducible, fixing is simple. "the hardest part is to actually reproduce the error not to see the error but to then correlate it which set of inputs causes it" (~13:14)
- Even a three-node cluster can have asymmetric latency (A-B fast, A-C slow), and consensus must cope with that. "traffic between nodes A and B is significantly quicker than traffic that goes from A to C" (~14:14)
- NATS is deployed in heterogeneous environments (leaf nodes in cars, factories, oil rigs), unlike databases that assume sub-millisecond cloud links; this makes debugging dropped messages much harder. "we have leaf nodes running in cars ... on random edge devices in factories on oil rigs" (~15:16)
- Daily benchmark runs on every commit have "rescued more than once" by revealing performance regressions; performance is the number-one question users ask. "the number one thing that most customers and most users come to us asking is how do I squeeze the best performance out of this system" (~19:22)
- Chaos tests showed that when servers go down, problems are often on the client side: clients reconnect too aggressively while "trying to be smart". "sometimes it's the clients ... they try to be smart and reconnect but we see they end up doing it quick enough we found also those issues" (~20:24)
- The first support question on an incident is whether anything happened on the network or VMs that day, because those are the usual triggers. "one of the first thing we ask when something breaks is did something happen on your network that day" (~21:25)
- 2.10's three themes are scalability, a new extension point (auth callout), and predictability/stability, with tail-latency and storage work driven by the "millions of interior deletes" problem in KV buckets. "we have increased scalability ... a new point of extensibility ... and then we have predictability" (~22:26)
- Marshalling large delete-state snapshots for replication consumed increasing CPU and backed up the server, so 2.10 reworked the file store; most 2.10 performance gains come from that work. "more and more CPU time was going into this process and the server is backing up behind that work" (~27:30)
- 2.10 stores deleted-message state as AVL trees for sparse deletes and run-length encoding for large deleted ranges, and the server picks whichever structure fits the pattern. "we've tried to use AVL trees for what is effectively quite a sparse set of deletions and then we also use run length encoding for ... large blocks" (~29:33)
- Users adopt NATS as the connectivity layer for their entire infrastructure, so new APIs hit terabyte-scale global use almost immediately. "the new API just blows up almost immediately to the level where our other APIs are used" (~33:36)
- V2 routes give multiple connections per server pair; the server assigns accounts to routes automatically or an administrator can reserve a dedicated route for a latency-sensitive account. "the administrator can make that decision explicitly and say look this specific account is one that we care very deeply about having low latency for" (~35:38)
- Route head-of-line blocking is worse over the public internet or between cloud regions because of TCP congestion control; with V2 routes consensus stays up to date faster and application traffic moves faster, with no config required. "consensus stays up to date more quickly that application traffic makes around the cluster faster ... it works out of the box" (~36:38)
- Route and leaf compression uses fast algorithms with low CPU cost to gain network headroom; it is automatic on route and leaf connections in 2.10 and on by default for leaf nodes because they are assumed to be over longer, less reliable links. "it's by default for leaf nodes because it's the assumption that you're going to be over a longer distance" (~39:41)
- Server tags let you dictate where stream replicas land, including anti-affinity across regions or providers, or you can let NATS place them. "you can actually tag the servers and say where the data lands ... or you can just say to NATS just do how you think" (~45:45)
- Users who learn a system scales to 2 TB then "put one more zero at the end"; supporting that is the ongoing 2.11 focus over new features. "it's so easy to just put one more zero at the end not so easy to support that one more zero" (~68:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02: Monolith to Modular Monolith with NATS.io**

- A load balancer or proxy is another software component to deploy, manage, and learn, separate from the application, and it drags in network, firewall, and TLS-offload concerns. "it's another thing that you would have to manage and deploy and learn... independent of your actual application" (~07:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP04: A Service Mesh Pattern for NATS.io**

- Service meshes inject a sidecar container per pod (Envoy for Istio); it is convenient for the developer but adds compute, cost, and complexity for operators as the fleet scales. "the people that actually are paying the bills to run extra compute... that's where it gets a little interesting" (~09:11)
- Automation and mesh layers make an application's operational behaviour opaque because logic is split between code and layer-specific DSLs and config files. "you begin to lose insight as to how your application runs because the logic and the know-how is split" (~17:20)
- Subject mapping is enforced transparently by the server when it receives the message; it is configured either statically in server config (hot-reloadable without downtime) or in the account JWT claims under decentralized auth. "you can hot reload that without any downtime" (~23:32)
- Autoscaling can be self-organizing: when a gateway times out with no responder it can publish on an infrastructure subject and a listener claims and adds a responder; idle gateways can trigger scale-down. "nothing on Bob's responded, increase the license count maybe and then something listening says... I'm going to make that claim" (~39:48)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP05: Exploring Powerful Client-side Features and Abstractions in NATS.io**

- The 2.10 release was delayed by intensified distributed-systems and chaos testing of RAFT traffic and recovery; every miss led to a new test or tool so it could not slip again. "every single time we missed something we try to add a new tool, a new test" (~23:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Micro-services with auto discovery, observability and load balancing. | Rethink Connectivity Ep 9**

- The CLI `nats micro list` / `nats micro stats` commands discover and inspect services; `--trace` shows the underlying requests on the `$SRV.STATS.<name>` control subjects. "it's sending a request to this what we call a control channel around services, $SRV.STATS.sentiment" (~15:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS as a ServiceMesh**

- Server metrics come from the Prometheus NATS exporter (CPU, memory, messages/bytes in/out, connections, subscriptions) with a Grafana dashboard; the speaker built per-client metrics on top for connection-level visibility. "I can have that kind of information on a per connection level, per client level" (~12:13)
- Tracing is not built into the server; the nats-io "not.go" reference shows carrying an OpenTracing span as a binary prefix on the message payload, stripped by the receiver (worked C# → Go). "you basically shove that on the front of your message data... you chop that piece off" (~15:18)
- Do not use constant sampling for tracing; it locked the speaker's machine up. "make sure... that you don't do constant sampling like I did and lock your machine up" (~16:18)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP01S3: Going back to basics with core NATS!**

- You will hit network limits before NATS limits: the host saturated a 100 Mbit home link while running a bench against a bare-metal cluster in Germany and mistook it for poor NATS performance. "turns out I just saturated 100 megabit link and that's all I'd done" (~48:12)
- Cloud I/O is often burstable: things look fine for hours and then throughput drops with no change in NATS; network/IO is usually the first bottleneck. "in the cloud environment when the I/O is burstable quite often, it looks fine for a few hours and then suddenly drops" (~49:14)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03S3: NATS 2.11 Release**

- Distributed message tracing exists because in large topologies (leaf nodes, clusters, superclusters, account import/export, subject mappings) "where did my message go" previously required subscribing at many points. "you kind of needed to subscribe in different places in your system and check if messages are there and in which form" (~05:06)
- A traced message reports every hop: leaf node, route, gateway, subject mapping, account boundary, and JetStream ingest. "you will know which through which leaf node, which route connection, which gateway, mapping, account boundaries, JetStream ingest, all of it" (~05:06)
- Tracing is opt-in per message via a trace-destination header (an inbox); each hop sends a trace message back to that inbox, and the CLI wraps this as `nats trace <subject>`. "you provide an inbox and every step of the message ... will send back a trace message to the inbox that you specified" (~06:07)
- Tracing is aimed at developers as much as operators, especially where the team writing apps and the team running NATS are separate groups. "probably more useful to developers than it would be to system operators" (~09:09)
- A trace can be configured so the message is neither persisted into a stream nor delivered to the final client, giving a dry-run of the path. "you can literally ask the system stop just short of finally delivering the message" (~08:09)
- Server testing includes thousands of unit tests, in-house chaos tooling (high latency, dead links, power pulls), continuous comparative benchmarking per commit, and deterministic simulation with Antithesis. "we've been working quite a lot with a company called Antithesis ... deterministic testing ... you can rewind time" (~20:27)
- Most 2.11 stability fixes (including Antithesis findings) were backported into the 2.10 series from about 2.10.23 onward, so upgrading from a late 2.10.x to 2.11 is a small delta. "pretty much since 2.10.23 we've kind of already been backporting lots of fixes that were kind of scheduled for 2.11" (~21:28)
- The reliability difference between 2.10.0 and 2.10.26/2.11 is described as huge, mainly in clustering and Raft; the maintainers say evaluating the latest version is always worth it. "the improvements that we've made to the clustering logic, to the Raft application, it's massive" (~22:29)
- Limits on new features are set deliberately low because raising a limit later is far easier than lowering one. "they're quite low, so if you'll see need for making them higher that's much easier than the other way around" (~36:48)
- Consumer pause is a consumer config option with a deadline timestamp; delivery resumes at that time, a past timestamp or absent option means unpaused, and it is meant as a maintenance/migration tool. "you specify a deadline, at 2:00 p.m. on the 12th of March start delivering messages again" (~37:48)
- Pedantic mode (implemented in the JSM library, used by NACK and Terraform) makes the server accept or reject exactly the values sent with no defaulting, which desired-state tooling needs. "there is no dynamic, no defaulting or failing, no defaulting to some limits" (~41:55)
- 2.11 adds a configuration state digest: the running config is hashed and can be queried or generated from the command line to check whether a modified file has been loaded. "the running configuration gets hashed and you can ask the server at any time, tell me what the hash of the configuration file that you're running" (~42:56)
- New 2.11 features are opt-in and not enabled by default; the upgrade from 2.10.26 is expected to be straightforward, and the diff between 2.10.0 and 2.10.26 is larger than between 2.10.26 and 2.11. "you'll mostly get new features which will not even be enabled by default and you have to opt in" (~44:58)
- The year-and-a-half 2.11 cycle is not something the maintainers want to repeat. "this year and a half long cycle is not something we're keen to repeat" (~43:57)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS tools and benchmarking with JNM! NATS Community Office Hours (Reupload)**

- The whole NATS server with JetStream ships as a single ~12 MB binary; Kafka-experienced conference attendees did not believe it until shown. "everything in a single 12 MB binary ... They don't believe it actually at first" (~02:03)
- Kafka exposes many timing knobs with hard-to-find correct values; NATS has few, and the speaker's rule is "with 100 knob positions, 99 are wrong". "if there's 100 positions, possibly there's 99 wrong ones" (~17:23)
- The server has very few Go module dependencies, which keeps the binary small and reduces exposure to dependency security advisories; the CLI is intentionally larger and that is fine. "the more dependencies you have the more chances that some point there'll be a security advisory on one of those dependencies" (~19:24)
- `nats top` is now built into the CLI; it needs a system-account context and a server name and refreshes every second, acting as a real-time speedometer complementing Prometheus/Grafana history. "you need to have a speedometer, right? You need to know how hard am I working right now" (~27:33)
- `nats cheat <subcommand>` prints commonly used example commands for any subcommand. "you can do nats cheat on any of these subcommands and it will give you examples" (~28:35)
- `nats stream edit -i` opens the full stream config as YAML with schema and descriptions in an editor; `nats stream info --json | jq .config` extracts only the config for automation, diffing, and `nats stream edit --config file`. "you pipe it to jq .config, that's just the config part" (~30:38)
- `nats sub --translate 'jq ...'` pipes each received payload through an external command; `--subjects-only`, timestamps and delta-time flags give tcpdump-style views of traffic. "pass the message to jq, could be jq, could be you can translate to anything you want" (~32:39)
- The rewritten `nats bench` uses `nats bench pub|sub <subject>` and `nats bench js ...` subcommands, defaults to 100,000 messages of 128 bytes, and uses the simplified JetStream API instead of push/pull flags. "it's basically been completely rewritten, especially to be much easier to use" (~36:45)
- Synadia publishes no official throughput numbers because distributed-system results depend on network, traffic, disk and cloud variability; they ship a tool to run in your own environment instead. "three kinds of lies in the software business: big lies, small lies, and benchmarks" (~38:47)
- Cloud burstable instances and general-purpose EBS (gp2/gp3) show good numbers for short tests but throttle after roughly 20 minutes of sustained JetStream writes; io1/io2 volumes cost more but are not throttled. "you'll get like maybe 20 minutes worth of good traffic and all of a sudden it'll throttle you way down" (~40:52)
- `nats bench` doubles as a load generator via a sleep between publishes (e.g. 200 µs), and multiple bench instances can be combined for steady load plus bursts. "you can also use it to generate load, generate traffic ... you can set the duration here" (~45:56)
- Benchmarks shorter than a few seconds are unreliable; make runs longer to get a proper number. "if the benchmark takes tenths of a second or less ... you may want to make it a little bit longer" (~48:01)
- Do not benchmark on laptops: thermal throttling kicks in after about 30 seconds at full clock; if you must, run 20-30 s tests then wait 20-30 s to cool. "on a laptop you got about 30 seconds and then at full speed ... your clock speed is going to be throttled down" (~49:02)
- Benchmark JetStream publish and consume separately before combining them, because together they compete for CPU and you cannot tell which limits the other. "when you do the both together you don't know which one is limiting the other" (~52:04)
- `nats bench js pub` expects the stream to exist unless `--create` is given; the default stream is file storage with one replica, and it publishes asynchronously in batches of 500. "it does async publishes in batches of 500 messages" (~53:04)
- In a cluster, bench publisher and subscriber connect to random servers; landing on the same server gives better numbers than being on different servers (extra route hop), so run several times or pin to one server for consistency. "if you happen to have your pub and your sub connecting to the same server you're going to get better numbers" (~54:06)
- A server-side max ack pending limit (100 in the demo config) blocked bench's default consumer creation (it wants 500); the workaround was to pre-create the consumer and pass its name. "I probably set up the limit for 100 for max ack pending, by default it wants to do 500" (~57:10)
- A community member hit Windows desktop kernel networking throttling before NATS itself throttled, at roughly 5-6 million core msgs/s. "he throttled the Windows kernel before NATS actually hit that throttling point" (~68:28)
- `nats bench js pub --purge` clears the stream first; otherwise repeated benches keep appending. "you can also pass a purge if you want to purge the stream first before you publish" (~69:29)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Benchmark Core NATS & NATS JetStream using the NATS CLI tool**

- Run benchmarks on your own target environment (machines, network, pods) rather than trusting published numbers; the CLI is the tool for that. "run benchmarks on your own target environments to see what kind of actual realistic performance you will get" (~00:00)
- `nats top` connects via the monitoring port (`-m 8222`) and shows per-connection stats plus server CPU, memory, slow consumers, messages and bytes in/out per second. "you can also monitor the CPU utilization of the NATS server process, memory utilization, number of slow consumers" (~02:02)
- `nats bench` produces two kinds of numbers: latency and throughput; latency is measured with request/reply mode and a single synchronous thread. "you can use nats bench to produce two kinds of numbers, one is latency, the other one is throughput" (~02:02)
- Sub-second benchmark runs show noticeable variation; use runs of 30 seconds to a minute or more (increase the message count above the 100,000 default) for sustained numbers. "you would want to do benchmarks that run for more than a fraction of a second, you know 30 seconds a minute or more" (~05:06)
- With 128-byte messages the bottleneck is CPU (per-message overhead), not bandwidth; raise the message size to measure bandwidth-bound throughput. "you're going to be CPU bound rather than bandwidth bound as your limit" (~09:09)
- Laptops throttle CPU frequency as temperature rises during benchmarks; let them cool between runs and do multiple runs, dropping outliers and averaging. "do more than one benchmark, more than one run ... that allows you to eliminate the outliers" (~11:12)
- The bench defaults to a memory stream with replication 1; `--replicas` and `--storage file` change that, and the auto-created `benchstream` is deliberately not deleted so later consumer benches have data. "you don't want it to delete the stream at the end because that would delete all the data" (~24:26)
- Changing storage type between runs requires deleting the existing bench stream first (`nats stream rm benchstream -f`), otherwise the old config is reused. "simply remember to remove the stream, that's the simplest thing" (~25:26)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS: Ordered, Scalable Stream Processing**

- In the CG tool the filter must be passed with the filter flag; passed as a plain argument it is read as a member name. "If you pass the arrow as a plain argument, it gets read as a member name instead, so don't do that" (~17:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Pull Consumer Priority Groups: Overflow, Pinned & Prioritized**

- The server re-pins to a standby when the pinned client stays quiet past the configured timeout or an admin unpins it; `nats consumer unpin` forces a handoff, useful before a deploy. "An operator can also force that handoff out of band with NATS consumer unpin, which is handy for rotating the active client before a deploy" (~03:01)
- The server publishes an advisory on every pin change (pinned and unpinned events), usable as an audit trail of who holds the work. "the server publishes an advisory on every pin change, so you can watch handoffs as they happen" (~03:01)
- Priority groups are configured through consumer flags or a JSON config (priority_policy plus priority group name); the CLI shows the policy and group in consumer info. "Our priority policy is overflow and our priority group will be called jobs" (~12:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Distributed Counters in NATS — Global Totals Without Locks**

- Stream info on a sourcing counter stream tracks per-source values, so the global total can be broken down by origin. "global tracks where it came from under sources" (~12:14)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Message Tracing | NATS 2.11**

- Message tracing is built into the server; the `nats trace` CLI command sends a message to a subject and reports the complete path it took, with no code changes or external tools. "No external tool or code changes, just run a command and see exactly where your messages go" (~00:00)
- A trace message carries three headers: Nats-Trace-Dest (subject receiving trace events), Nats-Trace-Only (dry-run: traced but not delivered or stored), and Accept-Encoding (gzip or snappy compression of trace events). "NATS trace only. This enables dry run mode. Your initial message is traced throughout the system, but not actually delivered or stored" (~02:01)
- Every server the message passes through emits its own trace event to a temporary inbox that aggregates them; the CLI builds the final output from these. "each node or server sends its own trace message reporting its current progress" (~01:00)
- Each trace event has four main fields: server (name, cluster), request (headers), hops (outgoing hop count), and events. "The server field ... The request field ... The hops field ... And the events field" (~03:02)
- Event types: IN ingress, EG egress, JS JetStream access, SE/SI stream export/import when crossing an account boundary, SM subject mapping when a mapping rule transformed the subject. "SE and SI for stream export and import when the message crossed an account boundary, and SM for subject mapping" (~04:05)
- Event kinds identify the connection type: client, router (same cluster), gateway (other cluster), leaf node, JetStream, plus internal system and account kinds. "you can see your usual client, router, or gateway. And you also have leaf node and JetStream. And system and account are internal" (~04:05)
- A single leaf node reports itself as its own cluster in the server field. "since this is a single leaf node, it's its own cluster" (~05:06)
- A Nats-Trace-Hop header builds a routing tree: multiple egress events from one server get hop ids 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, and further branching nests (1.3.1, 1.3.2). "Since there's multiple branches, we increment the number" (~07:06)
- A server that only stores the message into a stream shows a JS egress event and no hops field. "our only egress event is type JS for JetStream. Notice that there is no hop field because there are no hops from this server" (~08:06)
- Tracing stops at account boundaries by default; the receiver must opt in with allow_trace on the import/export: the importer for a stream import, the exporter for a service import. "The rule being the receiver always opts in. If it's a stream import, the importer sets it. If it's a service import, the exporter sets it" (~09:08)
- `nats trace` without the trace flag prints a minimal summary; with it, the full per-server trace messages. "With the trace flag, it's going to give us the entire trace message that we broke down server by server" (~10:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Consumer Pausing | NATS 2.11**

- Pausing is a normal consumer config update that sets a pause deadline; it works the same for push and pull consumers. "It's just a normal config update. Nothing special ... This works the same for both push and pull consumers" (~01:02)
- Consumer info shows the pause deadline and remaining time; resuming early is a separate command and a consumer can be created already paused, using a duration or an absolute timestamp. "You can initialize a pause upon creation. You can also use a timestamp for an absolute time" (~05:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.11: What's New?**

- 2.11 focused on three areas: visibility into what the server is doing, enabling new patterns, and correctness/resilience against failures. "improving visibility about what the NAT server is doing, enabling new patterns for users and developers, and improving correctness" (~00:05)
- Five headline 2.11 features: distributed message tracing, per-message TTLs, consumer pause, pull consumer priority groups, and stream multi-get. "distributed message tracing, per message TTLs, consumer pause, pull consumer priority groups, and stream multig" (~00:05)
- Tracing answers where a message goes across routes, gateways, leaf nodes, account import/export boundaries, and subject transforms; `nats trace subject` prints an IP-traceroute-like story. "you'll basically get a print out like doing an IP trace route" (~01:07)
- Tracing can run as a dry run without the remote applications ever seeing the message. "you can also do that as well without the remote applications ever being aware that it took place" (~02:07)
- KV delete markers build up with heavy deletes and make the underlying stream big and expensive; Synadia plans to give delete markers TTLs so watchers still see deletes but markers don't stay forever, reducing manual compaction. "We will be changing those delete markers to use TTLs so that even if you have KV watchers looking for deletes, you'll still be able to get those notifications" (~03:11)
- A trace into JetStream reports the message reaching JetStream at the server that is the stream leader at that time. "it would probably report whichever the server was that was the leader for that stream at that time" (~08:18)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS: Orbit – Extending NATS Clients with Richer Capabilities**

- Client unit tests cover features and error cases but not network problems; Synadia runs private nightly chaos tests plus Antithesis deterministic simulation to reproduce one-in-a-million bugs. "we have the antithesis tooling ... deterministically reproduce very one in a million bugs" (~16:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Two-Node Engine with David & Byron**

- Without a preemption flag the engine latches into the failed-over state, so restoring the configured leader is a deliberate step, avoiding disruptive preemptive restoration in mission-critical stacks. "we might not want the disruption of a preemptive restoration" (~06:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Future of NATS: Roadmap & Vision**

- Because all data flows through NATS, the server can expose visibility that otherwise needs separate monitoring stacks; 2.10 and 2.11 invested heavily in this. "because NATS is like every all the data is flowing through NATS we can expose everything through it" (~09:19)
- Client and tooling releases for 2.11 features roll out in the week after the server release, with docs following in days. "client releases, tooling releases, we're going to be rolling those out over the next week or so" (~11:21)
- Control plane stream/KV viewers let QA engineers validate data without knowing NATS. "they don't know anything about NATS they don't need to care about NATS ... they just need to go in and actually validate that the data looks correct" (~13:25)
- Synadia aims to stay 6 to 18 months ahead of customer demand on performance and scale; performance and scale remain a constant focus. "we always have to try to stay like six to 12 to 18 months ahead of the curve with demand, scale" (~20:34)
- Release cadence lesson: 2.10 and 2.11 took a long time; the team is scoping releases down so slipped features move to the next release about six months later. "if something doesn't land in this release, then it can just get kicked over in the next release and it's going to be another six months" (~22:37)
- A new docs site was announced as coming soon; the 2.12 candidate list is the GitHub issues under the 2.12 label, explicitly not all of which will ship. "We are not going to be doing all of those things. Just to be very clear, we are scoping that down" (~22:37)
- Roadmap observability: see the system tier (clusters, superclusters, leaf nodes) and the application tier (clients, micro services, workloads, connectors), drill down, alert; Prometheus is the default supported monitoring system. "Prometheus for example since that's our default monitoring system that we support" (~26:40)
- Fleet management roadmap covers both platform components (servers, control plane, Nex nodes, connectors) and customers' own device fleets: deploy, lifecycle, monitor, redeploy, health-check. "how do you deploy and life cycle that component? How do you monitor that component?" (~29:43)
- A local-first NATS workbench UI with configurable panes and sharing is planned. "it's being built and driven by a very local first perspective" (~30:46)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — We need to talk about Microservices... (And how NATS.io can simplify things)**

- `nats micro list` / `nats micro info <svc>` / `nats micro stats <svc>` discover instances, endpoints, metadata and per-instance request/error counts; `--json` makes the output automatable. "if I actually run this again with a json flag you can see all this is just pure json" (~12:14)
- Canary deployments are done with weighted subject mappings (server config, or per-account under JWT auth) so callers keep using the same subject. "you might want to route a certain percentage of traffic ... to a V1 versus a V2 and still not have to update any of the clients" (~15:20)
- Example: map math.> to math.v2.> with a 50% weight; half of math.add requests then land on the v2 responder. "we could simply map it to math.v2.> and we'll just map 50% of the traffic there" (~16:20)
- Monitoring uses scatter-gather: one stats request fans out to every instance and each responds with its own counters, which can feed a Prometheus-style scrape without an index of URLs. "you can get this very very easily without having to have some sort of index of all of the URLs" (~22:27)
- Message tracing (nats-server 2.11) is enabled by a header on the message; the server emits ingress/egress events, server identity, whether the message went through JetStream or crossed an account boundary, to a chosen subject. "whether or not it went through JetStream whether or not it went over an account boundary and then also its egress" (~22:27)
- Tracing demo used a Nats-Trace-Dest header pointing at a subject the operator subscribes to; the payload includes server name, server ID, version and an events list. "we have an ingress event and we have an egress event of who sent it and then who received it" (~24:29)
- Nex (NATS execution engine, early days) uses NATS as the control plane to place binaries or serverless JS on nodes running Firecracker microVMs, needing only a NATS server and a Nex node. "you need to run a NATS server and you need to run a Nex node and you're pretty much there" (~32:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — JetStream KV: A fascinating alternative to Redis...**

- Changing a bucket's cluster placement moves it in flight; clients keep accessing it while it is mirrored and relocated. "it's actually going to move the bucket mid-flight everything's going to stay the same" (~25:25)
- On Synadia Cloud a bucket must set max bytes. "we're using Synadia cloud and we absolutely need to have max bytes set" (~28:28)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The ONE feature that makes NATS more powerful than Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ & Redis**

- Consumers are replicated with their own RAFT groups; an R3 consumer keeps operating with a node down and in rare cases with two down. Ephemeral consumers are in-memory R1. "consumers are also replicated and have their own raft groups" (~11:13)
- Debugging in production: create an ephemeral debug consumer with any configuration without touching or reconfiguring the stream. "the stream is the stream and the consumers are all the consumers" (~21:24)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Give your Go app superpowers with an Embedded NATS Server**

- Startup is asynchronous: after calling Start in a goroutine you must block on ReadyForConnections with a timeout (5 s in the demo) before connecting a client. "we actually need to wait for it to be ready for connections" (~09:10)
- server.Options is the programmatic equivalent of the config file; the client URL can be taken from the server's ClientURL method; WaitForShutdown handles termination signals for the server lifecycle. "you can kind of think about this as like your config file" (~08:08)
- Server logging is off by default when embedded; call ConfigureLogger to enable it. "we can actually have configurable logging for this NATS server but trust me silence is golden" (~13:14)
- Once the leaf connects, the cloud side shows the embedded server's subscriptions, including the whole JetStream API under the embedded domain ($JS.embedded.API...), which is how the cloud can administer the local JetStream. "the whole JetStream API has been subscribed to under the embedded domain" (~22:23)
- Use `nats --js-domain embedded stream list/add` from the cloud context to manage streams that live inside the embedded server. "I can say js domain embedded and then it's going to list out the streams for this embedded context" (~23:24)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Stream processing: the easy way (with NATS and Benthos)**

- With NATS as communication and persistence layer, you run as many stateless Benthos processes as needed without a Flink cluster to babysit. "you're not babysitting like a Flink cluster ... you're really just using this configuration based data processing pipeline" (~05:06)
- Learning curve: about a day to get comfortable with Benthos components. "it takes about a day or so to really get it" (~06:06)
- Kinesis keeps no consumer cursor, so the bridge needs an external DynamoDB table for offsets; the JetStream side needs a stream whose subjects match the publish subject. "Kinesis doesn't really store the cursor or the offset for a particular consumer we need someplace to store that" (~10:09)
- Parallelism is set with pipeline threads (12 in the demo) so HTTP enrichment calls run concurrently. "since we're making HTTP calls we want to kind of run some of this stuff concurrently so I'm just going to say threads 12" (~18:19)
- The nats_kv output takes URLs, bucket and an interpolated key expression; the bucket must already exist (nats kv add media). "let's go ahead and do a nats kv add media" (~22:24)
- Backup/tiered-storage pattern: JetStream input → batch 1,000 (max ack pending set to 10,000) → tar + gzip → S3 with a timestamped path; sending message-by-message to S3 is called out as inefficient. "you don't want to just send a message by message over to S3 that's going to be really inefficient" (~33:40)
- Restore is the inverse: S3 input with a gzip-decompress + untar scanner turns archives back into messages; the backup config was about 19 lines. "in 19 lines of yaml I have a backup strategy" (~34:41)
- JetStream has its own backup mechanism; the S3 archive is presented as an alternative for messages that will expire or have TTLs on the JetStream side. "JetStream does have a backup mechanism but there's also other ways that you can do backups" (~32:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS Surveyor**

- The previous monitoring model was a Prometheus exporter sidecar next to every server scraping the HTTP monitoring endpoint; Surveyor replaces the per-server sidecars with one process that talks over NATS. "previously you had a Prometheus exporter ... deploy next to every server you run the sidecar" (~00:00)
