- Surveyor can run anywhere (laptop, Docker, Kubernetes) and view 50–100 servers as long as it has credentials and access to the NATS port. "you could run this thing on your laptop and see how 50 or 100 NATS servers behave" (~01:01)
- Surveyor requires NATS 2.0 and system-account credentials because server internals and names are published over the network and must not be visible to ordinary users. "it requires you to have access to the system credentials" (~01:01)
- Surveyor works by publishing a ping on a system subject; every server responds with a JSON blob of connections, memory, version and similar stats, which become Prometheus metrics. "we send a ping to the network everyone who owns that server should receive the ping will respond with a big old json blob" (~04:07)
- Enterprise pain motivating Surveyor: opening Prometheus scrape ports across data centers and securing exporter connections is slow and complex; the speaker never got a Prometheus port opened in a three-year enterprise stint. "my very first task was open a port for Prometheus and I left three years later having never achieved that goal" (~03:06)
- With Surveyor there are no extra ports, protocols or security paths: if you have NATS you can monitor NATS. "once you have NATS deployed there's no additional ports there's no additional security there's no other protocols" (~05:09)
- Dashboards drill down per server, per cluster, routes and gateways; the Prometheus data can also be scraped into your own Prometheus (e.g. a globe of connections per region). "you can in fact scrape this Prometheus into your other Prometheus" (~06:09)
- Trade-off: Surveyor uses the system it monitors as transport, so a split brain or outage blinds it; it is not the be-all of monitoring and additional node-level monitoring is still needed. "we are using the thing that we're monitoring as a transport for monitoring ... so you also need some additional monitoring" (~07:11)
- Surveyor must currently be told how many servers exist so it knows how long to wait for ping responses. "right now you have to tell it how many servers there are so it knows ... how long to wait" (~09:14)
- Planned: JetStream dashboards for message acknowledgment latency, redelivery counts and max-delivery (dead-letter style) events, plus graphs from server events (connect/disconnect/auth errors) to catch reconnect spirals. "if you suddenly see one of your services going into a reconnect spiral ... you'll be able to see an alert" (~08:12)
- Demo: a simulated 3-region supercluster of 9 servers (3 per cluster) on one Mac, showing 18 route connections and 18 gateway connections, with no sidecars. "three clusters nine servers 18 route connections ... and then 18 gateway connections" (~11:16)
- Gateway detail views show per-link traffic between clusters (e.g. region3a→region1 at ~1.18 Mbit/s during a benchmark). "region 3a to region 1 is getting 1.18 megabits a second" (~13:24)
- Service latency tracking is enabled per exported service in the account (via nsc), can be added after the service exists, and was set to 100% sampling in the demo; it works across account import/export boundaries with zero client instrumentation. "there was zero instrumentation in the client and I simply enabled this in the account" (~17:32)
- Latency observations arrive as histograms (10th/50th/100th percentiles) split into requester-side, responder-side and NATS-system time. "how much latency is in the NATS system versus from requester and versus from responder" (~17:32)
- Derek Collison: service latency in a global supercluster is four-dimensional (responder processing time, responder-to-server distance, requester-to-server distance, server-to-server distance), and Surveyor reports all four in real time; single-number latency is "too limiting". "service latency is not a single dimension it's actually four dimensions" (~19:34)
- Every server has a locked-down system account that can answer "how are you doing" requests targeted at one or many servers, which is the observability pattern Surveyor builds on. "all of our servers by default have a system account which is locked down and secure but can respond to requests" (~18:32)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Transcending microservices with NATS | RethinkConn '22**

- Rate limiting per WebSocket user is done via limits on the minted user JWT, e.g. message-count limits, like any NATS user. "when you're minting user JWTs you can set limits on all of those just like you can with any other NATS user" (~29:32)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Seamless evolution across geos and clouds | RethinkConn '22**

- Deploying a NATS-connected app is minimal configuration: a container plus replica count on any hosting provider, and it connects and communicates. "How do you deploy a NATS app via Kubernetes? And it's like a three-line YAML file" (~10:11)
- For data-at-rest sovereignty (e.g. "stored only in Germany"), JetStream placement uses server tags that can encode geography; many customers do this. "configure NATS JetStream ... to place assets based off of server tags which you could base off of geography" (~17:26)
- Head-of-line blocking is not a concern for a leaf node with multiple high-traffic clients; the server is designed to avoid it at the network and messaging layers. "you're not going to experience hardly any head-of-line blocking in reality" (~20:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Where are we now and where to next? | RethinkConn '22**

- One deployment gives streams, KV, and object store from edge to cloud; an app written on a laptop moves to cloud or edge by changing one URL. "I have to change one URL and the same thing can run in the cloud, on the edge, wherever" (~03:04)
- Moving a NATS system between clouds or from on-prem to cloud is mostly changing host names and some configuration; applications only change where they connect. "basically changing host names, some configuration as well, but the applications wouldn't have to change a bit" (~04:06)
- Scaling services is not a configuration issue: launching more instances into a queue group scales up, and APIs exist to scale down without losing data. "scalability isn't a configuration issue ... it's just launching more instances" (~05:08)
- Operators use accounts as guard rails: a fixed number of connections, subscriptions, and HA JetStream assets per account prevents the noisy-neighbor problem and lets teams work in their own sandbox. "set up an account with a specified number of connections, subscriptions, number of high availability assets ... that development team won't exceed that" (~06:08)
- Shipped: tag-based stream placement (server tags, useful for GDPR/geo), stream migration, and replica scaling from R1 to R3 and back at any time. "I can take an R1 stream turn it into an R3 back down to an R1 as I need to" (~09:11)
- Roadmap: multi-connection gateways between superclusters to better use long-haul links for performance and resilience, and a hub-and-spoke backbone from which superclusters extend. "imagine multi-connection gateways between these servers to better utilize these long-haul connections" (~12:15)
- Roadmap: leaf node compression so data leaving over constrained links (e.g. laptop Wi-Fi to NGS) is compressed automatically, and leaf node encryption so the intermediate system cannot see payloads. "as data leaves my security context it's encrypted, the general NATS system cannot see that payload" (~13:15)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Versioning and canary deployments with subject mapping | RethinkConn '22**

- Weights across destinations for one mapping must add up to 100; a total under 100 intentionally drops the remainder to emulate data loss and test failure handling. "if you don't add all of your weights up to 100 you can emulate data loss" (~11:15)
- With nsc you define from-subject, to-subject, and a weight (e.g. 50%), push to the server, and the mapping just works. "you can define through NSC ... get it pushed up to your server and the subject mapping just works" (~12:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Effective debugging using the NATS CLI | RethinkConn '22**

- The NATS CLI has no special powers; it is just a NATS application, so everything it does can be done programmatically. "the NATS CLI doesn't have special powers, it is just a NATS application" (~00:00)
- "Big three" first commands for diagnosing an environment: `nats server list`, `nats server report jetstream`, and `nats traffic`. "the big three commands that we initially run" (~01:00)
- `nats server list` works for a single server, cluster, or supercluster with or without JetStream; it scatter-gathers an info ping to all servers from the system account and shows clusters, routes, gateways, versions, host memory/CPU, and slow consumers. "we're really doing that info ping in scatter gather" (~02:02)
- `nats server list` is an unopinionated snapshot of what can be seen now; it does not flag right or wrong, so the operator must know what to look for, e.g. a missing node or changed route/gateway counts after a network outage. "it's not going to flash any warnings at you ... you need to bring your own knowledge" (~03:04)
- With JetStream enabled you get the JetStream meta service, which runs across all nodes with no single point of failure and tracks JetStream-enabled servers. "this magic service called the JetStream meta service ... runs on all of your nodes so there's not a single point of failure" (~05:06)
- `nats server report jetstream` adds the RAFT meta-group block showing whether the meta leader has connectivity to every expected node, health, and lag; it is a more opinionated view that marks a lost server as not current/offline. "it's a little bit more of an opinionated view" (~06:08)
- When a JetStream server is lost the meta leader moves to another node almost instantaneously. "it automatically and almost instantaneously moved from vbox6 ... to vbox7" (~06:08)
- `nats traffic` listens to everything in the cluster and shows rolling statistics; in a stable system with no asset changes the RAFT proposals/votes columns show no votes. "a happy stable system ... generally you won't see votes here" (~07:08)
- If two of three availability zones go down, an R3 stream is effectively disabled and `nats traffic` shows continuous voting as the remaining node looks for peers, a quick sign that assets are impaired. "two out of three availability zones go down ... a stream asset ... is essentially disabled" (~07:08)
- Anything the HTTP monitor exposes is reachable via CLI server requests, e.g. asking across a supercluster who is subscribed to a subject, or listing one user's subscription interest to find a case mismatch like "Fufu" vs "fufu". "the capital letters is always a killer, it's the off by one character" (~09:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Using NATS JetStream as a Kine backend for k3s | RethinkConn '22**

- k3s is pointed at NATS via a datastore endpoint URL with the nats:// scheme, a KV bucket name, and any NATS-supported authentication (the demo used username/password). "this driver does support any kind of authentication that NATS supports" (~03:07)
- All k3s KV buckets were mirrored up to NGS; after destroying the local server, backups taken from the cloud were restored in seconds and the clusters came back with their state after ~20 s of startup. "it takes probably about 20 seconds of course these k3s clusters have to start up" (~10:19)
- When restoring mirrored buckets as primary buckets, edit the backup to remove the mirror configuration first, or you recreate them as mirrors. "I have to go into these backups and just remove this mirror" (~09:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Service monitoring with Helix and Surveyor | RethinkConn '22**

- NATS is observable by default: "matrix mode" or wiretap mode is subscribing to everything in an account to see all messages and replies flowing. "we call this like matrix mode or wiretap mode where you're able to sub to everything in this particular account" (~00:01)
- Latency tracking is a little-known server feature tied to service imports/exports: the server emits a JSON latency event per request/reply for an exported service. "with your services when you work with imports and exports you can get all this latency tracking information JSON blob" (~01:02)
- Surveyor is the open-source component that collects cluster metrics and service latency observations for Prometheus scraping; setting up Prometheus, Grafana, Surveyor, and the imports/exports is a lot of kit. "that's a lot of kit to set up" (~01:02)
- Helix scrapes account metrics roughly every 10 seconds; the demo showed ~4.9 messages/s for a service with ~100 ms simulated latency. "we scrape about every 10 seconds or so" (~09:10)
- Service latency tracking supports a sample rate; lower it for heavily hammered, horizontally scaled services so you approximate metrics without overloading the time-series database or network. "you can actually set a sample rate to lower so you can kind of approximate metrics" (~10:11)
- Latency events carry a status: 200 for success, 400 when a publish arrives with no reply subject, 408 for timeouts, so errors are recorded automatically. "200 means everything went well ... no reply header ... that's going to result in a 400 ... timeouts ... 408s" (~11:12)
- The latency event identifies the requester (client type, version, name, account, JWT) and the responder, plus which server/cluster each is connected to. "who the requester was, what kind of client they came from, what version ... what account and what JWT" (~12:13)
- Latency is broken down like the `time` command into service time, system (NATS) time, and total, so you can tell whether slowness is the client's network hops, the server, or the service. "you get all of that stuff broken down into ... service, system and total" (~13:14)
- Metrics are stored as a Prometheus histogram, so p50 and p99 per service are available and a Grafana dashboard can be layered on top. "you can also see hey what's my P99 here" (~13:14)
- Latency tracking is configured in the account JWT: the export declares the service subject, "track service latency" with a sample rate (100 = every request), and the subject to which the server emits the events. "we want to track service latency on this service for a sample rate of 100 and we want to send it to this subject" (~15:17)
- Sending plain publishes (no reply) to the tracked service produced an error rate of 557/s as status 400 events, and measured latency dropped because those requests never got answered. "our error rate went up to 557 per second because we were sending a bunch of publishes with no replies" (~16:19)
- This gives client-to-server-to-responder-and-back RTT plus client location metadata, which is hard to get from HTTP or a load balancer. "this kind of gives you information that you can't even get very easily with HTTP itself or with a load balancer" (~17:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Short break and Q&A! | RethinkConn '22**

- Servers and the 46+ clients self-heal; clients learn about other cluster members via gossip even if DNS only lists one, augmenting rather than replacing DNS, so topology changes need no maintenance window. "clients and servers are gossiping all of the time about topology changes" (~22:26)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Derek Collison RethinkConn 2025 Keynote and Closing Remarks**

- NATS started payload-agnostic; a schema registry is being designed with both advisory and enforcement modes, in a NATS-native way. "NATS was started as a payload agnostic system... there's obviously advisory type and there's enforcement type of schema implementations" (~10:50)
- Workloads (Nex) and connectors are federation-free and need no perimeter security model, which suits edge targets like Raspberry Pis and air-gapped sites where Kubernetes-style federation feels heavy. "these technologies in ecosystem are federation free. They don't require a perimeter-based security models" (~12:00)
- Connector runtimes are pluggable; Wombat (a pre-acquisition fork of Benthos) is one runtime and higher-performance runtimes can be added by users. "the runtimes are pluggable and so yes Wombat, which is a pre-fork of Benthos before the acquisition, is definitely there" (~16:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia Roadmap with Byron Ruth**

- Headers already propagate on delivery so app-level OpenTelemetry spans were always possible; native tracing adds server-injected metadata using OTel-compatible header semantics. "because headers are propagated... you could at the application level express your spans... now this is going to actually support some additional metadata that gets incorporated via the servers" (~03:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: After event Q&A with Derek on Zoom**

- The imperative Nex engine (pick a workload, run it on this engine) will always be open source; a declarative Synadia scheduler that attracts services to where requests originate, with KV digital twins following the service and scaling to zero, is a planned commercial service. "the imperative version... will always be open source... KV digital twins are also moving around and following it around" (~07:30)
- A Nex engine operator requires workloads to prove a root of trust via xkeys, the same trust-chain idea as operator mode and Synadia Cloud; a workload's interactions with the outside world are NATS-initiated and the operator controls what it may talk to. "they have to prove to me that I know the root of trust... your interactions with the outside world are all NATS initiated" (~12:00)
- Nex isolates workloads with Firecracker; a suspended workload with state could be moved around as an object-store object because JetStream is good at moving data. "we've got firecracker so it does the isolation there... a workload inside of an engine is just an object store that's moving around" (~13:00)
- First Nex workload types are static binaries, JavaScript, Python (for AI/ML) and containers (which bloat the VM); wasm was judged too limiting to lead with. "it can't be wasm because it just it's too limiting right now... static binaries, JS... python... container based" (~14:50)
- Point releases (2.10.1, 2.10.2, 2.10.3) are driven by customers pushing the system in unexpected ways, not by lack of testing. "you'll see 2.10 come out and then 2.10.1 and then 2.10.2 and 2.10.3 and it's not for our lack of testing" (~17:40)
- A customer log-replication stream with only ~1M messages but 640M interior deletes made an R1-to-R3 scale-up and async mirror crawl; a fix shipped within days took completion from 14 hours to about a minute and async replication from 20-some minutes to 15 seconds. "it only had about a million or so but it had 640 million interior deletes... first time I got it to complete was 14 hours... now it's about a minute" (~18:30)
- The server main branch builds nightly, and formal release candidates are planned so users can try features like KV semantics and per-message TTL before release. "on main we build nightly every night... formalizing some of the release candidates" (~21:00)
- Callout services are expected to be placed next to the server, even over loopback, so the added latency should be near negligible and run at wire speed. "potentially even over a 127.1 loopback... the impact on measurable latency will almost be negligible" (~26:20)
- The schema registry is expected to land as a reasonably priced Synadia service, with possible OSS reference implementations later. "right now I think it's going to land as a Synadia service" (~27:40)
- The NATS server alone represents over $40 million of investment. "NATS just the server itself probably has over $40 million of investment in it" (~28:40)
- Everything in NATS is monitorable but not easily discoverable; the tools are Surveyor, the NATS CLI (which Surveyor uses), the legacy HTTP endpoints, and, as Synadia does internally, system-account requests. "everything in the NATS system is monitorable but it's also not easily discoverable" (~30:00)
- Account watch and server watch commands were added to the NATS CLI overnight on request. "the NATS CLI should have something like account watch or server watch... when I woke up he's like yep here it is" (~31:00)
- A recurring adoption problem is that people skip the basics and start with advanced topics. "folks seem to start on chapter 20 instead of chapter 1" (~35:00)
- Advanced topologies are considered a four-hour workshop topic on their own. "Advanced topologies is like that's a 4-hour workshop in and of itself" (~34:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Introducing Synadia Insights: Catch the NATS Failures Nothing Else Reports**

- This data loss is independent of replication; it happens identically on a single server and on a three-node cluster. "Nothing in this failure depends on replication, and it happens exactly the same way on three nodes" (~03:40)
- In `nats stream report`, "Lost" counts messages the disk failed to keep (corruption, hardware failure); messages removed to honor a retention limit are discarded, not lost, so Lost stays zero. "To NATS, lost means messages on the disk failed to keep... Messages deleted on purpose to honor a limit aren't lost." (~07:10)
- A consumer's unprocessed/pending count shows only what it will still receive (at most the stream's current contents), not what it will never receive. "2,000 is what analytics is about to receive. It says nothing at all about the 10,000 it never will" (~08:00)
- The detection rule is to compare each consumer's delivered stream sequence with the stream's first sequence; the moment the stream floor crosses the consumer position, everything between has been deleted. "Red is the log book's floor... Orange is analytics bookmark... Eventually, red crosses orange and that crossing is the moment" (~12:00)
- The Prometheus NATS exporter doesn't expose stream first-sequence and consumer sequence unless started with the jsz=all flag, and no shipped Grafana dashboard compares the two. "The exporter doesn't publish these two by default. There's a flag, JSZ equals all, and without it, none of this exists" (~12:40)
- Prometheus keeps history so the failure can be inspected after the fact, unlike the CLI where the evidence disappears once the consumer catches up. "Prometheus kept every sample, and you can watch the whole thing happen after the fact" (~14:00)
- Insights is one binary that scrapes cluster state over the system account each minute with 13 requests, the first a broadcast that discovers every server, and publishes replies to a JetStream stream so the indexer can catch up after a restart. "It asks over NATS on the system account. 13 requests. The first is a broadcast that discovers every server" (~15:00)
- Insights commits epoch snapshots transactionally and runs 142 SQL checks inside the same transaction, so a finding is never visible before its data. "142 SQL checks read the pass and write their findings" (~16:00)
- Real customer tickets included a KV mirror whose replication silently stalled for weeks, found only when a release updated bucket policy, and a mirror stream that stopped advancing with no signal until lag was large. "A KV mirror replication that had been silently stalled, and it lasted for weeks" (~20:40)
- Insights raises a consumer health event when delivery falls below the stream's first sequence. "we delivered below the stream first sequence" (~19:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Event-Driven Systems Need a Security Gateway — Meet Synadia Protect for NATS**

- A fleet of gateways split by domain is kept in sync by a config server that gateways reach over NATS, never point-to-point, and rule bundles are stored in a JetStream stream. "The gateway itself talk through NATS to the actual config server. So there's no direct point-to-point connection" (~12:50)
- Rule lifecycle is create a signed zip bundle, install it, activate it, later deactivate and uninstall; all of it is scriptable from the CLI for DevOps. "create the rules bundle... generate a zip file... install... activate" (~16:40)
- Every gateway action is auditable: an audit log, a policy execution log of each triggered rule, forwarding to SIEMs like ArcSight or Splunk, and custom tracing for forensics. "you can actually forward those logs you create to a particular SIEM" (~17:50)
- The UI can only add native rules; custom rules must be authored separately and imported. "The UI currently supports only adding native rules" (~19:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking Connectivity - Hyper-Connectivity & The Intelligent Edge**

- The server is small, written in Go, and runs on Raspberry Pi-class devices, unlike most persistence-capable messaging systems. "you can put this on a very low compute device like Raspberry Pi like devices" (~11:00)
- Clusters are fully meshed; clients learn peers through gossip and fail over automatically; stream replicas survive a server loss with a new leader elected. "clients automatically know about the server's peers through our gossip protocol and can switch over" (~23:00)
- With a supercluster plus leaf nodes NATS still routes to a distant responder; the higher latency is the signal to redeploy the service closer, in a nearer cluster or the edge site. "latencies might be higher even though NATS figures it out and that's some insight... deploy this service closer" (~25:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — A New Way of Thinking | NATS 2.0 and Connectivity**

- Core philosophy: the server protects itself at all costs rather than any single user, avoiding the "query of death" where one client's request degrades everyone; this is what a shared utility (not a silo) requires. "it protects itself at all costs it doesn't protect you the user at all costs" (~09:10)
- A full server runs on a Raspberry Pi; clients existed for over 32 languages in 2019. "you can run a full-blown server on a Raspberry Pi... clients for over 32 and counting different programming languages" (~09:50)
- Account owners add, revoke and re-permission users themselves without helpdesk requests to a central operator. "all of that is managed by the account owners" (~18:00)
- Because everything is pub/sub underneath, any exported service is observable from day one without adding a sidecar, proxy or framework. "in order to do that you already had it when you started you're not now deploying with a sidecar or a proxy" (~19:40)
- Most changes to a NATS system require zero client configuration or API changes and no recompile. "the majority of changes to a modern NATS system are zero client configuration or API changes" (~20:20)
- Servers coordinate through a system account, sending messages like any application instead of adding protocol, even across a global supercluster; that account has the same auth and permissions as any other. "an individual server inside of a NATS system can have its own account... we just send messages" (~20:50)
- Clients learn the topology without DNS or configuration; clusters grow and shrink dynamically and clients are told without application code. "a client knows about the topology even if it wasn't in a DNS name or configured in the application" (~22:50)
- Account limits (max connections, max leaf connections, bandwidth, exports/imports) are enforced globally and instantly: an 11th connection against a limit of 10 is denied anywhere in the world, and a revoked user is disconnected within about 10 ms globally. "if Colin revoked me as a user my application would instantaneously be disconnected... within 10 milliseconds globally" (~33:40)
- Transparent bidirectional bridges for Kafka and MQ Series existed in 2019. "we already have transparent bi-directional bridges for Kafka and MQ series" (~35:50)
- Built-in service observability: export a service, sample e.g. 50% of requests to a subject in your account, and get service time, responder RTT, requester RTT and internal NATS latency per sample, across a supercluster. "here's how long the service itself took here's the responder RTT the request RTT and the internal NATS latency" (~36:20)
- 2019 roadmap: native MQTT (3.1.1 and MQTT-SN), WebSocket support, and signed WebAssembly modules on subject ingress for filtering and GDPR-style processing. "we're going to introduce native MQTT support... we're also going to introduce WebSocket support" (~37:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - PowerFlex Solves Intermittent Connectivity at the Edge w/ NATS - RethinkConn 2025**

- The main operational friction is that JetStream requires stream setup per site, so commissioning each new customer means creating new streams. "every time we get a new customer and we have to commission a new site, we have to add new streams. That's maybe the biggest hiccup" (~10:14)
- They maintain a spec repo (CloudEvents + AsyncAPI) with CI that generates typed event payload and publisher libraries for Python, TypeScript, and Rust. "it takes the spec and it generates event payloads and even publishers into libraries" (~17:20)
- Subscribing to server events / internal $JS.API and $SYS subjects is a key debugging tool for admins. "listening to server events is wildly useful" (~12:18)
- The speaker found the JetStream docs confusing and recommends the YouTube tutorials instead. "the documentation really confused me and I found YouTube tutorials that were way better" (~12:18)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - MachineMetrics on Industrial IoT & Predictive Analytics w/ NATS at RethinkConn 2025**

- Core NATS operational overhead is minimal compared with Kafka, which they say needs far more people to operate; JetStream adds some complexity depending on setup. "the operational overhead is so minimal for vanilla NATS" (~18:23)
- Payload schemas: developer libraries encapsulate the domain model, generate subjects, and use CloudEvents as the envelope, with message ID used for deduplication. "we use cloud events as the envelope format... deduplicating data on that through message ID" (~31:43)
- Credentials for edge nodes are set up with the nsc CLI; account seeds then issue short-term user credentials via their API; currently a single account with backend code isolating companies, moving to account-per-company. "most of what we do we set up using NSC CLI. And then we use those account seeds to issue short-term user credentials" (~33:44)
- They plan to automate account/user provisioning via the Synadia Control Plane REST API and react to change-data-capture events flowing over NATS. "now that you can do that through the REST APIs in the Synadia control plane, it is considerably easier" (~35:45)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS at the Edge with F1 Arcade**

- Mirror streams are used to add observability and replication without touching the core messaging path. "the ability to replicate and observe JetStreams using things like mirror streams allows us to add on observability without impacting that core messaging" (~05:07)
- Each venue leaf node is 3 replica servers; streams are currently split across them but will be replicated on each for full failover; minimum spec cited as 2–4 CPUs and 8 GB RAM per server. "the minimum requirements something like two to four CPUs and 8 gig of RAM for each one" (~08:12)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Lightning Talk - ACI Worldwide at RethinkConn 2025**

- Their congestion control ("network overload management") reads stream characteristics such as pending count and max messages to drive selective message rejection. "leveraging some stream characteristics like num-pending and max messages. From here, we derived a configurable application selective message rejection algorithm" (~02:08)
- Observed low latency on pub/sub and request/reply, easy install and operation, a good C API, and easy clustering; targeting Kubernetes deployments first. "We like the very good C API. NATS fits in our distributed horizontally scalable model, being so easy to deploy clusters" (~03:09)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Franco Sabini from Fineco Bank on NATS**

- Everything is replicated R3 because they have no performance pressure. "we have everything replicated in three... just because we don't have any performance issue" (~12:16)
- Developers also run operations and are on call 24/7; no major NATS incident to date; Synadia support contract was the answer to "what if something happens in production" after 20 years on one product. "till today there hasn't been any major issue with NATS" (~10:14)
- Compared with Kafka and Solace, NATS needs no knob-tuning to work out of the box. "you don't need to pull levers, change flags... when it works it works" (~13:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Jaxon Repp from HarperDB on NATS and distributed databases**

- They are using NATS for inter-node status chatter to route writes away from an overwhelmed node to another that can persist and relay later. "I'm going to route it over to another node that I know has that data" (~07:13)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Nathan Mellis from Modzy on NATS as a foundational building block**

- Connection balancing is left to NATS and Kubernetes, not an L4 load balancer. "we let NATS slash Kubernetes take care of it" (~09:12)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Simple Solutions for Complex Problems - How Workiva uses NATS as a Microservices and RPC transport**

- NATS protects availability by disconnecting slow consumers and lazy listeners that miss pings rather than degrading everyone. "if you have a slow subscriber slow consumer it will just disconnect that consumer nobody else is impacted" (~11:15)
- NATS needs no external coordination service (ZooKeeper/etcd) and has minimal configuration, which is key to operational simplicity. "you don't have to deal with configuring like zookeeper etcd these other external dependencies" (~13:17)
- The text-based protocol makes debugging, sniffing, and writing your own client easy, unlike AMQP or binary protocols. "if you've ever tried to implement like an AMQP client or a binary protocol... it can be an absolute nightmare" (~14:18)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | Pub Sub on the Power Grid**

- Applications are distributed across nodes with Kubernetes/Rancher and written in C++, Go, and increasingly Rust for small, secure binaries. "looking at those tightly compiled languages that produce those small secure applications" (~18:31)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Partner Talk - NATS on Akamai Cloud - RethinkConn 2025**

- Server-to-server route latency in milliseconds is reported natively by the server (HTTP monitoring), though the speaker had to write a lightweight exporter because the default Prometheus exporter lacked it. "it is available in the NATS HTTP interface but I don't think it was available in Prometheus" (~08:12)
- Route latency shows very little jitter over time, which they use to demonstrate reliability. "there's hardly any latency at all or jitter at all on that region to region latency" (~12:18)
- Per-client latency reporting is native, so client latency can be graphed and alerted on in Grafana/Prometheus. "you get that client reporting all the way down to the individual client" (~11:16)
- The whole ~40-node cluster is scripted with Terraform/Ansible and a Kubernetes deployment YAML, recreated in a couple of minutes. "I can recreate this entire cluster with just a couple of clicks and have this up and running in a couple of minutes" (~07:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Go Beyond Kubernetes Native Events with NATS**

- Kafka was rejected as too heavy and operationally noisy to deploy on 100 clusters; NATS via the Helm chart was deployed to all staging clusters in ~5 minutes. "I could have used Kafka but it's very heavy. It consumes a lot of resources. It's not really that straightforward to set it up" (~03:08)
- Resource footprint matters multiplicatively in fleets: a server deployed per cluster multiplies cost by cluster count. "if it consumes a lot in one cluster and then you have to deploy in 10 clusters now your costs are going up by 10" (~06:14)
- Advice: build a prototype from the docs quickly rather than designing the perfect solution first. "Do not spend too much time trying to have the perfect solution. Just go with the prototype" (~08:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Workloads - Distributed cloud-to-edge compute with NATS Execution Engine**

- Packing everything into one binary bloated builds, made build tags confusing, and slowed debugging; that drove the rearchitecture toward "nothing but NATS" using Orbit and micro. "we had packed everything into a single binary, and it was starting to get really bloated" (~04:14)
- Live demo hit the account's connection limit when many viewers connected, locking the presenter out. "There's so many of y'all on this. You took up all my connections" (~20:35)
- Nex is stateless by default (killing a node loses its workloads); the official binaries ship a KV-backed state so a restarted node re-reads and auto-starts its workloads, which is how the cloud nodes recover. "the official binaries will come with a KV-backed state... If you kill the node and turn it back on... it'll auto start them all" (~23:43)
- Firecracker was the original sandbox but doesn't run on Windows, is hard on macOS, and in cloud only GCP allows nested virtualization without expensive bare-metal instances, so it was dropped from the happy path. "the only cloud it ran in without problem was GCP because it was the only one that allowed nested virtualization" (~26:45)
- A nexus exposes health, metrics, and error codes via the micro framework, visible with `nats micro ls`. "if you do a NATS micro ls you can actually view all the free stuff we give you there" (~28:49)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Migrating from NATS Streaming to JetStream**

- The two-year Streaming deprecation window ends June 2023; after that no security or bug fixes land. "No more security fixes and bug fixes are going to be landing after June." (~07:45)
- Most stream options (subjects, limits, retention age) can be changed at runtime. "You can dynamically change most of the options at runtime." (~15:56)
- R3 in-memory streams can survive a careful rolling restart because replica state moves between servers. "You can have in-memory streams that are R3 that still can technically tolerate a good rolling restart... if you're careful." (~33:19)
- Production JetStream config sets store directory, max memory, max file storage, and optional encryption at rest with the key passed via environment variable. "You can pass in your encryption key as an environment variable is typically what is recommended." (~36:22)
- Migrating removes a component: drop the Streaming servers and let clients talk to a JetStream-enabled cluster; embedded-mode Streaming deployments must move to a vanilla NATS cluster with routes. "In my opinion, it's actually simpler because we're removing a component." (~37:25)
- The NATS CLI has full stream/consumer management plus a JetStream benchmark mode for measuring replicated write throughput and latency on real VMs and disks. "It also has this benchmarking capability that supports JetStream." (~46:38)
- Native backup/restore in the CLI snapshots all streams and consumer state per account, but is point-in-time; mirrors give a near-current async copy in another cluster. "A mirror allows you to basically create a bit for bit copy of a stream... replicate it asynchronously over to another cluster." (~60:54)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS KubeCon Tutorial on Twitch**

- The server has no external dependencies; one URL gives you pub/sub, request-reply, and load balancing without extra services. "It is a lightweight, no dependencies, a very small Docker image." (~04:07)
- The server warns on plaintext passwords in config and suggests bcrypt or NKeys; NKeys are a challenge-based public/private key scheme. "It will suggest to use either bcrypt for the password or you can use also NKeys." (~12:21)
- Never enable debug and trace logging in production; throughput drops by at least half. "The performance drops at least half when you have this logging." (~26:42)
- In restricted environments you can debug a NATS server with plain telnet since the protocol is text-based. "You can just straight up use telnet." (~43:12)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Zen of High Performance Messaging with NATS by Waldemar Quevedo Salinas**

- If client or server don't exchange PING/PONG within the interval (default two minutes) the server drops the connection; PING also gives a round-trip latency measure. "By default this is an interval of every two minutes, the server will chop the connection off." (~07:15)
- Benchmarking with a tight publish loop plus a subscription in the same client makes that client a slow consumer: the server grows its pending buffer, then disconnects it to protect itself. "The NATS server is protecting itself." (~15:25)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — SCaLE 13x Derek Collison  NATS A new nervous system for distributed cloud platforms**

- NATS is designed to protect itself at all costs and stay available, unlike enterprise brokers that take everyone offline while servicing one client's pathological request. "My version of the world is I protect myself at all costs and I always have to be available." (~19:24)
- A bare protocol error (e.g. pressing Enter) gets a client disconnected immediately: the server protects itself. "I hit enter which was a protocol error so it immediately chopped me off." (~30:39)
- Monitoring is HTTP JSON modelled on Google's /varz: varz reports max connections, ping interval, memory, cores, connections, routes, in/out messages; connz gives per-connection detail. "Every single server has that varz endpoint on it that you can pull all of the statistics in real time." (~33:53)
- The ping interval exists because cloud hosts vanish without the socket closing; either side can initiate pings so dead peers are detected. "In cloud platforms a lot of times that happens... the machine just goes away but nobody that's connected to the socket thinks they did." (~35:54)
- Roadmap items in 2015: C/C++ and Lua clients, monitoring dashboards, and an auto-configuration service to join a full mesh by API token because manual mesh setup is tedious. "If you're actually trying to set up a full mesh one hop it's tedious." (~42:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Native MQTT Support in NATS Server**

- Enabling MQTT needs only a server name, JetStream enabled (MQTT persists state in JetStream), and an `mqtt` port block; the server then accepts both MQTT and native clients. "Enable JetStream which is needed by MQTT in order to persist some state, then we open the MQTT port." (~02:06)
- On MQTT client connect the server creates JetStream assets for that client automatically. "It did accept an MQTT client and created JetStream assets for that client." (~03:07)

## MIG: Comparisons / migration from other systems (245 claims)


**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Compare NATS**

- Comparison covers NATS, Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, Apache Pulsar, gRPC; "by no means an exhaustive list".
- "Core NATS: 48 known client types, 11 supported by maintainers, 18 contributed by the community. NATS Streaming: 7 client types supported by maintainers".
- NATS offers streams and services via built-in pub/sub, request-reply, and load-balanced queue subscribers, with "Dynamic request permissioning and request subject obfuscation". Kafka/Pulsar/Rabbit: "Application code must correlate requests with replies over multiple topics" for request-reply.
- Delivery guarantees: NATS "At most once, at least once, and exactly once is available in JetStream"; Kafka and Pulsar same three; Rabbit at most once and at least once; gRPC at most once.
- "NATS supports true multi-tenancy and decentralized security through accounts and defining shared streams and services." Kafka: "Multi-tenancy is not supported." Pulsar tenants: no built-in cross-tenant data sharing. Rabbit vhosts: no data sharing.
- NATS AuthZ: account limits (connections, message size, imports/exports count), user-level pub/sub permissions, connection restrictions, CIDR restrictions, time-of-day restrictions.
- NATS persistence: memory and file; "Messages can be replayed by time, count, or sequence number, and durable subscriptions are supported." Rabbit: queue semantics, "no message replay is available".
- "Core NATS supports full mesh clustering with self-healing features"; "JetStream supports horizontal scalability with built-in mirroring." [STALE?] mentions NATS Streaming FT/full clustering.
- NATS server is "a small static binary" deployable from cloud instances to Raspberry Pi; single servers, leaf nodes, clusters, superclusters "can be combined in any fashion"; "Clients are unaware of topology and can connect to any NATS server".
- Kafka: "Clients are tied to partitions defined within clusters"; servers need a JVM, "eight cores, 64 GB to128 GB of RAM, two or more 8-TB SAS/SSD disks, and a 10-Gig NIC" (cites Cloudera sizing).
- Pulsar "requires a JVM and requires at least 6 Linux machines or VMs. 3 running ZooKeeper. 3 running a Pulsar broker and a BookKeeper bookie."
- RabbitMQ clusters "require low-latency networks where network partitions are rare"; server needs the Erlang VM.
- NATS monitoring: Prometheus exporter, Grafana dashboards, nats-top, NATS surveyor ("side car deployment or a simple connect-and-view model").
- "NATS separates operations from security. User and Account management in a deployment may be decentralized and managed through a CLI." Server config can be reloaded at runtime.
- NATS integrations listed: WebSockets, Kafka bridge, IBM MQ Bridge, Redis Connector, Spark, Flink, Elastic, Prometheus, Telegraf, Fluent Bit/Fluentd, OpenFAAS, HTTP, MQTT.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS connectivity**

- Bridges: Kafka Bridge (nats-kafka), JMS bridge (also covers MQ and RabbitMQ since both offer JMS).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream (concept overview)**

- Stated motivation: existing streaming tech has "complexity, fragility, and a lack of scalability"; "no current streaming technology is truly multi-tenant, horizontally scalable, or supports multiple deployment models."
- "NATS does not intend to compete with the feature set of such tools" (in-memory DBs, deployment tools); goal is a reasonably complete data storage/replication set for microservices, edge, server management.
- "JetStream completely replaces the STAN legacy NATS streaming layer."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — MQTT**

- NATS follows MQTT v3.1.1 and supports QoS 0, 1 and 2.
- MQTT support "is intended to be an enabling technology allowing users to leverage existing investments in their IoT deployments"; "In greenfield IoT deployments, when possible, we prefer NATS extended out to endpoints and devices" for security and observability; NATS is "nearly as lightweight in terms of protocol bandwidth" as MQTT.
- Use NATS as a drop-in MQTT server to connect existing MQTT endpoints to a remote NATS cluster/supercluster.
- "For an MQTT client to connect to the NATS server, the user's account must be JetStream enabled" because sessions and retained messages (even QoS 0) are persisted.
- Topic mapping: `/` -> `.`; leading `/` -> `/.`; trailing `/` -> `./`; `.` -> `//` (2.10+; rejected before); space not supported (connection closed on publish, SUBACK failure on subscribe). `#` -> `>` (server creates two subscriptions `foo.>` and `foo`); `+` -> `*`. `*` and `>` inside topics become NATS wildcards if they form a whole token.
- Permissions for MQTT users are written as NATS subjects (conversion happens before authz); QoS 1 subscriptions need subscribe permission on `$MQTT.sub.>`.
- QoS 1/2 redelivery after `ack_wait` (default 30 seconds); `max_ack_pending` valid 0..65535, session total cannot exceed 65535, `#` subscriptions count double; changes apply only to new subscriptions.
- All sessions are persisted even with "clean session". Duplicate client IDs: the server accepts the new session and delays closing the old to reduce flapping; across servers "Users should avoid this situation".
- Clustered retained messages are best-effort: "applications that rely on the presence of a retained message should connect on the server that produced them." Replication factor is set automatically from cluster size.
- Limitations: NATS-published messages reach MQTT subscribers as QoS 0 only.
- MQTT requires a unique `server_name`. In operator mode MQTT clients cannot sign the nonce, so pass a Bearer user JWT (`nsc edit user --bearer`) as the MQTT password with any non-empty username.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — FAQ**

- "As of NATS Server 2.2, NATS JetStream is the recommended option for persistence ... NATS Streaming a.k.a. 'STAN' is now deprecated."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Legacy: NATS Streaming (STAN) and nats-account-server**

- "The NATS Streaming Server is being deprecated. Critical bug fixes and security fixes will be applied until June of 2023." Persistence users should use JetStream.
- STAN is a client of a NATS server, not a server; NATS clients and STAN clients cannot exchange messages on the same subject (STAN payloads are protobuf with acks). Clients must close connections explicitly or the server keeps them until heartbeats fail.
- STAN clustering is not horizontally scalable (single leader); "The cluster size should probably be limited to 3 to 5 nodes"; odd number, minimum three "to avoid split-brain".

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-42: Pull Consumer Priority Groups**

- "we cannot support updating a consumer from one with groups to one without and vice versa ... We also cannot switch between different policies." Only `PriorityTimeout` is updatable today.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-48: TTL Support for Key-Value Buckets (updates ADR-8)**

- Can be enabled on existing buckets "but should not support disabling it."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-53: Feature flags**

- Problem: breaking behaviour changes (e.g. switching to the ADR-15 v2 `$JS.ACK.<domain>.<account hash>...` format) cannot ship in minor releases because older servers "will not know how to parse the new format", clients/tooling may lag, mixed-version systems need both formats, and "Subject permissions could be using the old format."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-59: JetStream Stream Sourcing and Mirroring**

- "Mirror configuration **cannot be changed** after creation"; promote a mirror by removing the origin's subjects, then removing the mirror config and adding the subjects to the former mirror.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-62: JetStream desired state reconciliation**

- Retention change Limits→Interest on a replicated stream: "the consumers will need to scale up first since their replica count needs to match that of the stream if it's Interest or WorkQueue"; back to Limits allows scaling consumers down.
- "Upgrading directly to 2.15 is **not recommended**"; path is 2.14 → 2.14-compat (adds desired-state encoding only) → 2.15; during mixed versions "any in-flight operation stalls" until all servers are on 2.15. Downgrading below 2.14-compat "is **not recommended**"; let pending changes settle first. Inconsistent state after a direct upgrade/downgrade "may be (partially) repaired by performing a rolling restart of all nodes while on the same version."

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — JetStream account limits, reservations and naming (server/jetstream.go, server/server.go)**

- On recovery the server repairs bad subjects ("Detected bad subject %q while adding stream %q, will attempt to repair"), removes subjects found on a mirrored stream ("Detected subjects on a mirrored stream %q, will remove"), and marks assets it cannot understand as unsupported/offline rather than failing ("Detected unsupported stream '%s > %s': %s") (server/jetstream.go:1478-1560, 1330-1338)

**Source class: Code and tooling (nats-server, jsm.go, natscli) — JetStream API levels, advisories, and API backpressure (server/jetstream_versioning.go, server/jetstream_api.go)**

- Current JetStream API level is 5. `JSApiLevel int = 5` (server/jetstream_versioning.go:19); printed at startup as "API Level: %d" (server/jetstream.go:500)
- Assets record the API level they need in metadata key `_nats.req.level` (plus `_nats.ver`, `_nats.level`); a server with a lower level marks the asset "unsupported - required API level: %s, current API level: %d" and takes it offline instead of loading it (server/jetstream_versioning.go:21-41, server/jetstream.go:1328-1338)
- Stream feature -> required API level: per-message TTL (2.11) = 1; counters, atomic batch publish, message scheduling, async persist mode (2.12) = 2; fast batch publishing (2.14) = 4 (server/jetstream_versioning.go:60-88)
- Consumer feature -> required API level: pause_until and priority groups/policy/pinned TTL (2.11) = 1; AckFlowControl ack policy (2.14) = 4 (server/jetstream_versioning.go:155-170)
- Clients can send header `Nats-Required-Api-Level` to require a minimum responding-server level; error "JetStream minimum api level required" code=412 err_code=10185 (server/jetstream_api.go:341-342)
- Standalone (non-clustered) JetStream can not extend another domain unless `extension_hint: will_extend` is set: "Standalone server started in clustered mode do not support extending domains" (server/jetstream.go:512-517)

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS JetStream: Ordered, Scalable Processing**

- Design mirrors Kafka consumer groups: "Split the stream into buckets by key, assign each bucket to exactly one worker, and you get ordering within a bucket while running many buckets in parallel."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Mirror, Merge, or Consume: How to Choose Your Edge-to-Core Streaming Pattern**

- "JetStream implements mirrors and sources natively — without external connector processes, without separate mirror-maker jobs"; pattern selection "is a configuration decision, not a development project."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — The Hidden Cost of Active-Passive Clustering (And What to Do Instead)**

- Active-passive clustering means "paying for N nodes but only using one of them for productive work"; it forces vertical scaling and needs a load balancer tier that is itself a single point of failure.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — You Don't Need Two Platforms: The Case for Hybrid Eventing**

- Kafka "requires JVM, substantial memory, careful partition planning, and coordination layer (ZooKeeper or KRaft mode)", incompatible with constrained edge gateways; teams end up bridging core Kafka and edge brokers.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS and Kafka Compared**

- "Core NATS alone is sufficient and optimal for fast request paths in scalable services with reliable but not guaranteed quality of service."
- Kafka is log-based with topics; "The architectural tradeoff for Kafka's durability and scalability is additional complexity often encountered when scaling."
- "Kafka can process millions of records per second at a rate of over 500 MB per second." "Kafka has higher latency than NATS due to its batching and compression of messages." NATS positioned at "millions of messages per second" low-latency.
- Many NATS built-in features "would require additional processes or JVMs in Kafka"; "While Kafka has moved away from requiring Zookeeper, many deployments still rely on it."
- Kafka order is guaranteed only within a partition; "Maintaining global order can be difficult across multiple partitions." In JetStream strict in-order delivery is "affected only by acknowledgment settings"; parallelism without partition planning.
- Kafka is pub/sub-only; "Implementing any messaging pattern outside of unidirectional streaming with Kafka can be complex." Fan-out needs multiple consumer groups; request/reply needs manual correlation across topics. "While Kafka is developing similar queue functionality, this capability remains in the proposal stage."
- NATS fits microservices, IoT, embedded, edge; Kafka fits high-throughput, complex event processing, big data, log aggregation.
- NATS claims more security options: multi-tenancy and distributed authentication.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS vs RabbitMQ: How to Choose the Right Messaging System**

- NATS is "minimal, lightweight, and subject-oriented"; RabbitMQ routes through "exchanges, queues, bindings, routing keys, queue types, channels, and plugins."
- NATS is "a single binary with no language VM"; RabbitMQ "requires a compatible version of Erlang on each target machine."
- RabbitMQ classic queues offer "exclusivity, TTL settings, queue length limits, message priority, consumer priority, dead-letter exchanges, prefetch, and lazy queue behavior"; quorum queues are "durable, replicated FIFO queues."
- NATS topology is "opaque to clients"; RabbitMQ clustering needs "external peer discovery infrastructure, such as DNS, Consul, etcd."
- Choose RabbitMQ "when the broker should encode a significant amount of messaging policy"; choose NATS for "simplicity, low latency, and flexible service communication."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — MQTT vs. NATS for Fleet Management: Hub-and-Spoke vs. Distributed Mesh**

- "MQTT is built around a central broker. NATS is built as a distributed mesh." "Every MQTT message from a field device travels to a central broker before routing anywhere else — the network trombone effect."
- "Deploying a local MQTT broker solves the latency problem but creates a separate instance with its own configuration, ACLs, and monitoring." Federation risks "message loops, duplicates, and inconsistent topic namespaces"; bridges "can lose messages during disruptions or restarts."
- MQTT has "no native concept of a message stream"; "MQTT expects clients to acknowledge receipt, not processing completion"; "QoS 1 can also deliver duplicates after network interruptions."
- MQTT ACLs are centralized per broker; "Revoking credentials in one region requires propagation to every other broker." NATS: "The private key never leaves the device"; "Identity is proven through cryptographic challenge-response, not credential transmission"; revocation reaches "the entire cluster — including leaf nodes — within seconds."
- MQTT 5.0 request/reply: "developers still manage response routing and timeout logic themselves." NATS creates a temporary inbox automatically.
- "The NATS server speaks MQTT natively"; "MQTT semantics — retained messages, sessions, QoS delivery guarantees — are implemented on top of JetStream"; MQTT clients get "clustering, leaf nodes, security, multi-tenancy, and subject mapping."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — From Solace to NATS: One Platform for Messaging, Streaming, and the Edge**

- Solace `orders/state/city/store` maps to `orders.state.city.store`; wildcards `*` and `>` are the same; "Replacing `/` with `.` covers most cases." Prefix wildcards like `red*`, reserved namespaces (`$`, `#P2P`), and literal `.` in topic levels need explicit handling.
- Solace DMR interest propagation maps to NATS subject-interest propagation across clusters/superclusters; "DMR clusters become NATS clusters. Cross-region bridging becomes a supercluster with gateway connections"; "Edge sites that used to be broker clients become leaf nodes."
- Solace "typically pair[s] brokers in active-passive configurations, with a monitoring node to arbitrate failover"; NATS clusters are "full meshes of active nodes. There is no standby broker sitting idle"; "Adding capacity means adding nodes to the mesh."
- Solace guaranteed delivery maps to "explicit JetStream stream and consumer designs"; "A consumer can be a pub/sub subscriber today and a durable, replayable stream consumer tomorrow without changing brokers"; Solace shops typically add Kafka for log semantics.
- Solace "exclusive queues with active/standby consumption and partitioned ordering require separate designs"; "Request-reply in NATS uses ephemeral inboxes."
- "Solace's ACL model is broker-scoped"; NATS accounts are "designed for tenancy that spans a mesh"; Auth Callout for IdP delegation; "Security domains isolate edge tenancy from cloud tenancy."
- "NATS is a runtime platform. It does not ship a bundled event design environment"; plan for Event Portal replacement (AsyncAPI). Coexist via bridging; migrate "project by project rather than as a big-bang cutover."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Migrating from TIBCO to NATS: A Modernization Guide for Financial Services**

- "`TRADES.US.EQUITY.>` in RV is `TRADES.US.EQUITY.>` in NATS. Wildcards work the same way." Inboxes mirror RV `_INBOX` request-reply. JetStream covers RVCM (certified messaging): durable subs, at-least-once, acks, replay.
- RV is UDP multicast; NATS is TCP so it crosses cloud networks, meshes, WANs. A NATS cluster replaces an RVRD mesh with all nodes active.
- "Do not deploy NATS the way you deployed RV daemons. It technically works to run a local NATS server per host and treat it as an `rvd`, but you forfeit most of the operational benefits."
- "Migrating EMS applications to NATS is more involved than migrating RV, and any post that pretends otherwise is not worth reading." No drop-in JMS bridge. Non-durable JMS topics map to Core subjects; durable topic subs need a stream plus durable consumer each; JMS queues map to a stream with a shared durable, often work-queue retention and explicit acks.
- EMS selectors filter SQL-like predicates at the broker; NATS "pushes filtering into the subject itself", free at the routing layer; selector-heavy apps and FT pairs need redesign.
- EMS HA is primary plus hot standby with shared storage, "half the HA hardware idle by design"; a three-replica stream across failure domains tolerates one server failure.
- Inventory every RV subject tree and EMS topic/queue (certified delivery, selectors, FT pairs, fire-and-forget); "Bridge selectively between TIBCO and NATS for flows in transition. Producers and consumers move independently. Nothing forces a synchronized cutover"; retire TIBCO capacity as flows move.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — What are strategies for moving a stream to a different set of nodes in the cluster?**

- Keep server names static; replace nodes one at a time on the same name; after a clean shutdown the replacement syncs all streams assigned to it; wait for full sync before touching the next node; always use Lame Duck Mode — ripienaar.
- Removing a peer (`nats cluster peer-remove`) makes the stream pick a new peer at random; with old nodes still present it may pick an old one — ripienaar, derekcollison.
- Alternative: put the departing server in LDM then remove it from the cluster with `nats server raft` to move all its data; for lots of data do it per stream to spread replication load — ripienaar.
- Safe pattern: 3 nodes, add 2 temporary, replace the 3 one by one on the same names, then remove the 2; clients learn topology via gossip — ripienaar.
- Backup and restore into a new cluster is the simplest path if downtime is allowed — derekcollison.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — NATS Streaming to JetStream Migration**

- The stan2js tool migrates NATS Streaming channels to JetStream streams and STAN subscriptions to JetStream consumers; it is a one-time exercise run once per set of channels. "This is a one time exercise and stan2js only needs to be run once for each set of STAN channels that require migration to JetStream streams."
- The migration config names a NATS CLI context for the STAN side and one for the NATS side; if channels or subscriptions must go to different accounts, use multiple contexts. "if channels and/or subscriptions need to be migrated to different accounts, then multiple contexts can be used."
- The stan2js config declares which channels and subscriptions to migrate plus a subset of stream/consumer options; the options are not exhaustive because many stream and consumer options can be changed after the migration. "These options are not exhaustive since many options on streams and consumers can be changed after the migration."
- Per channel the config can set the target stream name and options such as `replicas`, `max_consumers`, `max_bytes`, `max_age`; per client subscription it can set the consumer name, whether to convert to pull (`pull: true`), and a queue name.
- Observed output: a STAN durable subscription can be converted to a JetStream pull consumer (`CONVERTED TO PULL? true`), otherwise it becomes a push consumer; a STAN queue subscription becomes a queue (deliver-group) push consumer.
- Observed output: STAN channel sequence numbers are re-based in JetStream (foo `501 -> 1`, `1000 -> 500`); the migrated streams contain only the messages the channel still held under its STAN `max_msgs` limit (500 for foo, 700 for bar, 1000 for baz).
- Observed output: each migrated message carries headers `Nats-Streaming-Channel`, `Nats-Streaming-Sequence` and `Nats-Streaming-Timestamp` preserving the original STAN channel, sequence and publish time.
- Observed output: subscription progress is preserved by mapping the STAN next sequence to the corresponding JetStream sequence (e.g. sub-foo `601 -> 101`, sub-bar `701 -> 401`); migrated consumers report Ack Policy Explicit and Ack Wait 30.00s.
- After migration, verify with the NATS CLI: `stream report`, `stream view` to check headers and payloads, and `consumer report` to check consumer state. "Since the NATS CLI supports introspecting JetStream assets, we can use it to verify that the migration was successful."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Migration to new JetStream API**

- The new JetStream API "removes the complexity of `Subscribe()` in favor of more explicit separation of creating consumers and consuming messages."
- The new API "focuses on using Pull Consumers as the primary means of consuming messages from a stream."
- The legacy API supported pull consumers only in limited capacity: "it was not possible to retrieve messages from a stream in a continuous fashion."
- With `Consume`, `Fetch` and `Next`, users choose how to consume depending on use case.
- In the legacy API the only way to continuously receive messages is push consumers; `Subscribe()` "leads to complications because it implicitly creates and manages underlying consumers."
- Unsubscribing a legacy `Subscribe()` subscription deletes the underlying consumer it created; `AddConsumer` "is the only way to create a consumer in the legacy API which will not be deleted when the subscription is unsubscribed."
- Legacy `Subscribe()` performs stream lookup by subject by default; `BindStream` skips that lookup.
- Legacy push subscriptions hide complexity and need many options; "when using push consumers, there is no simple way to rate limit the message delivery, which leads to slow consumer errors."
- Legacy pull consumers "are greatly limited in functionality since it is only possible to pull a specific number of messages, without any optimization or coordination between pulls," making them inefficient versus push.
- Because all legacy `Subscribe*` methods return the same `Subscription` interface, "it is very easy to encounter runtime errors by e.g. calling `NextMsg` on a subscription created with `PullSubscribe` or `Subscribe`."
- The new API "does not auto-create consumers"; consumers must be created or retrieved explicitly, giving control over the consumer lifecycle and removing the hidden logic of `Subscribe()`.
- Pull consumers do not need a `DeliverSubject`.
- Stopping `Consume()`/`Messages()` in the new API does not delete the consumer, unlike legacy `Unsubscribe()`; the server deletes it when `InactiveThreshold` is reached.
- (deno narrative) Legacy `subscribe()` created the consumer if it did not exist and updated it if options differed; the new API only supports pull consumers, so an existing push consumer "will have to [be] recreate[d] as a pull consumer."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Rolling upgrades**

- A careless restart drops every client on that node and can leave the stream a node short of quorum; a new server version means the process must restart, so roll one node at a time.
- Lame-duck mode (specified in ADR-5) is entered with `SIGUSR2` (or `nats-server -sl=ldm=<pidfile>`); the node closes its client listener, transfers any Raft leadership it holds, shuts JetStream assets down cleanly flushing to disk, broadcasts `INFO ldm:true` to routes and clients, then after a grace period closes remaining client connections spread over the lame-duck duration.
- Stepping the meta-leader down forces a metadata election during which stream and consumer operations (create, update, leadership moves) pause: typically about 5 to 10 seconds with default timeouts if killed outright, or roughly a second if it handed leadership off first. "typically about 5 to 10 seconds with default timeouts if the node was killed outright, or roughly a second if it handed leadership off first."
- Upgrade order rule: upgrade the non-leaders first and the meta-leader last, so the one unavoidable metadata election is short and happens once. "upgrade the non-leaders first, and the meta-leader last."
- Find the meta-leader with `nats server report jetstream`; it's a separate Raft group from the stream leader and may sit on a different node.
- Per-node procedure: enter lame-duck and let it drain, restart on the new binary, then wait until the stream reports the node as a `current` replica before moving to the next node; taking the next node down while this one is syncing leaves the stream one healthy replica short.
- Restarting the meta-leader without draining leaves no metadata leader until the election timeout fires (about 5 to 10 seconds) and every stream and consumer operation stalls; draining transfers leadership in roughly a second. Always enter lame-duck first and always do non-leaders first. "Upgrading the meta-leader without draining it stalls stream ops until a new leader is elected."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Deployment)**

- Checklist: Keep server versions aligned as you roll operator-mode upgrades so every node reads the same JWT limit fields; account limits change only when you edit and push the account JWT.
- Checklist: Measure rebalance time before setting `lame_duck_duration`.
- Checklist: Transfer leadership before killing the meta-leader (upgrading it directly stalls stream ops for about 5 to 10 seconds); do non-leaders first.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Authentication basics**

- Centralized auth breaks down when many tenants manage their own users or the user set needs to be dynamic; operator mode is built for that.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth callout**

- `allowed_accounts` (2.11+) limits delegation to listed config-defined accounts so you can move one account at a time; without it, once `auth_callout` is on every connection except `auth_users` goes through it, including config users with correct passwords. Connections matching no config user land in `$G` and always go through the callout.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Encryption & TLS**

- For migration, `handshake_first` accepts `"auto"`/`"auto_fallback"` (fall back to plaintext `INFO` if no TLS bytes arrive within 50 ms) or a duration like `"300ms"` for a custom fallback delay.
- Pitfall: `handshake_first: true` locks out every legacy client. Migrate with a duration value (`handshake_first: "300ms"`) that accepts both kinds of client, and flip to `true` only after the last client has opted in.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Security)**

- Checklist: Migrate to TLS-first with a duration value (`handshake_first: "300ms"`) before setting it to `true`, so legacy clients keep connecting during the rollout.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TTL and limits**

- Per-key TTL needs nats-server 2.11 or newer, the release that added limit markers; on an older server enabling markers is rejected and the timed create fails.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connect MQTT devices to NATS**

- Before 2.10, a `.` in an MQTT topic was rejected; the `//` encoding was added in 2.10.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topics and subjects**

- Converting `.` was added in NATS Server 2.10; before that a `.` in a topic was rejected the way whitespace still is.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth and clustering (MQTT)**

- From server 2.12.3 an MQTT connection is implicitly allowed to subscribe to `$MQTT.sub.` and `$MQTT.deliver.pubrel.` subjects; before 2.12.3 (including 2.10 and 2.11) you must allow `$MQTT.sub.>` in the user's subscribe list or every QoS 1/2 subscription fails with `0x80`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (MQTT)**

- Checklist: keep `$MQTT.sub.>` out of permission lists on 2.12.3 and later; on 2.10 and 2.11, allow it explicitly.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first WebSocket connection**

- A FIPS-140 build made with Go 1.25 or earlier refuses the whole WebSocket listener (and `ws://`/`wss://` leafnode remotes) because the handshake computes SHA-1 over `Sec-WebSocket-Key`; build with Go 1.26 or later.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Browsers and origins**

- Four cookie settings: `jwt_cookie` (user JWT), `user_cookie` (user name), `pass_cookie` (password), `token_cookie` (auth token); the last three arrived in nats-server 2.11.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (WebSocket)**

- Checklist: a FIPS-140 build must be built with Go 1.26 or later.

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | JetStream**

- JetStream is the next generation of NATS streaming technology, replacing the separate NATS Streaming server binary with one server binary. "we've made it into a single server binary so anyone who has NATS will have JetStream" (~01:03)
- NATS 2.0 changed the security and deployment model, forcing a revisit of how streaming worked. "NATS 2.0 has changed basically security model and deployment model of NATS and so we have to revisit how we handle streaming" (~01:03)
- Any standard NATS client in any of the 40+ languages can interact with JetStream, unlike Streaming server which needed dedicated clients. "you can use any standard NATS client that you have" (~02:06)
- Streams listen on wildcard subjects, a key difference from NATS Streaming; order.received, order.processed and order.completed can all land in one stream. "we support wildcards ... this is a key difference from NATS streaming server to JetStream" (~07:13)
- NATS Streaming server would be supported as a production platform, with security fixes, through mid-2023 but with no major new feature development; migration guides and a data migration tool were promised. "we will continue to support it as production platform ... we don't anticipate major new feature development" (~20:35)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.10 Webinar**

- The 2.10 stream storage format is not backward compatible with 2.9 except that 2.9.22 and later patch releases understand it; downgrading is not recommended. "we did release 2.9.22 and then any patch release after that ... are aware of this new format" (~04:03)
- Before 2.10 MQTT supported QoS 0 (at most once, like fire-and-forget) and QoS 1 (at least once); 2.10 adds QoS 2 (exactly once) and from 2.10.3 the server runs an external MQTT compliance test suite. "with 2.10 QoS 2 has been implemented ... as of 2.10.3 we actually introduced a proper external MQTT compliance test suite" (~09:12)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03: Escaping the HTTP Mindset with NATS.io**

- Starting with in-process function calls and later distributing means rewriting all the communication logic; that rewrite is the pain NATS-first design avoids. "now you have to completely rewrite all of your logic, all of your communication mechanisms, so it's very painful" (~10:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02: Monolith to Modular Monolith with NATS.io**

- Starting with in-process method calls and later distributing pushes teams to add RabbitMQ for queues and Kafka for streaming, each a new technology, dependency, and operational burden. "you start bringing in all these things and it's like more technologies to learn more dependencies... more operational overhead" (~19:23)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP01S3: Going back to basics with core NATS!**

- Because subjects decouple producers from storage, an app publishing sensor updates over core NATS can later have those subjects captured by a stream without changing the app. "you can just seamlessly switch to those subjects being captured by JetStream and the app doesn't even need to know" (~24:42)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03S3: NATS 2.11 Release**

- Most 2.11 stability fixes (including Antithesis findings) were backported into the 2.10 series from about 2.10.23 onward, so upgrading from a late 2.10.x to 2.11 is a small delta. "pretty much since 2.10.23 we've kind of already been backporting lots of fixes that were kind of scheduled for 2.11" (~21:28)
- The reliability difference between 2.10.0 and 2.10.26/2.11 is described as huge, mainly in clustering and Raft; the maintainers say evaluating the latest version is always worth it. "the improvements that we've made to the clustering logic, to the Raft application, it's massive" (~22:29)
- New 2.11 features are opt-in and not enabled by default; the upgrade from 2.10.26 is expected to be straightforward, and the diff between 2.10.0 and 2.10.26 is larger than between 2.10.26 and 2.11. "you'll mostly get new features which will not even be enabled by default and you have to opt in" (~44:58)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Stream processing: the easy way (with NATS and Benthos)**
