- Kinesis keeps no consumer cursor, so the bridge needs an external DynamoDB table for offsets; the JetStream side needs a stream whose subjects match the publish subject. "Kinesis doesn't really store the cursor or the offset for a particular consumer we need someplace to store that" (~10:09)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Where are we now and where to next? | RethinkConn '22**

- Moving a NATS system between clouds or from on-prem to cloud is mostly changing host names and some configuration; applications only change where they connect. "basically changing host names, some configuration as well, but the applications wouldn't have to change a bit" (~04:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Short break and Q&A! | RethinkConn '22**

- There are no plans for pluggable JetStream persistence beyond file and memory (NATS Streaming had database backends); instead the direction is applying JetStream to external data stores decomposed into a globally ordered sequence of events. "for JetStream right now I think we're still going to stick with file and memory" (~32:41)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — A New Way of Thinking | NATS 2.0 and Connectivity**

- Moving an existing request/response API onto NATS is often a ten-minute exercise; the real gain is lockdown without code, scaling without load balancers, global requesters and built-in observability. "a lot of times it can be as easy as a 10 minute exercise" (~45:00)
- When not to use NATS: don't rip and replace working HTTP, gRPC, Kafka or MQ investments; use NATS for new greenfield work. "don't replace what you have... use NATS to do new greenfield type of implementations" (~47:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - MachineMetrics on Industrial IoT & Predictive Analytics w/ NATS at RethinkConn 2025**

- They chose not to rip and replace Kinesis wholesale (too large a project for a small team); new development defaults to NATS/JetStream/KV. "let's just replace Kinesis with NATS for all our data ingestion is a massive project" (~09:12)
- Their migration bridge copies the tail of the Kinesis stream into NATS, so consumers move to NATS first and producers can later publish directly on the leaf node. "we take the end of that Kinesis stream and copy it into NATS... it gives us this nice way to gradually switch over" (~11:13)
- Before NATS, edge devices spoke WebSocket into Kinesis; NATS won on the "data is ubiquitous" philosophy versus A-to-B streaming. "You're not thinking in streaming from A to B. you just say okay I'm producing data somewhere and I'm consuming data somewhere else" (~36:46)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS at the Edge with F1 Arcade**

- The previous stack was MQTT plus Redis with a hand-rolled queuing system; Redis went down under load testing at the largest venue despite being adequately provisioned, and messaging lacked observability. "Redis despite being adequately provisioned would go down when running our load testing suite" (~04:05)
- Migration required replacing WebSockets, HTTP calls, and MQTT with NATS; settling subject names and learning streams/consumers/acks is a real learning curve. "nailing down subject names... is something you're just going to have to work through" (~07:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Franco Sabini from Fineco Bank on NATS**

- The trigger to leave TIBCO Rendezvous was a sysadmin mandate against multicast protocols, which also don't work well on-prem-to-cloud. "a very strong request from our system administrators not to use multicast protocols anywhere in our environment" (~03:06)
- Rendezvous to NATS was easy because subjects, fire-and-forget, and request/reply map almost one to one (same lineage of designers). "the protocol is very similar the concepts behind are very similar" (~05:08)
- They were advised to wait for JetStream GA rather than adopt STAN (NATS Streaming) for a months-away rollout; JetStream needed more adaptation work than the fire-and-forget part. "it was better to wait for JetStream to be general available and that's what we did" (~05:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Jaxon Repp from HarperDB on NATS and distributed databases**

- Raw WebSockets and then SocketCluster gave no delivery guarantee and created network storms at scale; a database must guarantee delivery, so they moved to JetStream while it was still in beta. "if there's one thing that a database is responsible for is guaranteeing delivery of data" (~03:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Nathan Mellis from Modzy on NATS as a foundational building block**

- Their previous queue took many resources, was hard to configure, and could only be used one way; NATS replaced it over several months. "it took up a lot of resources it was hard to configure and you could only use it pretty much one way" (~05:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Migrating from NATS Streaming to JetStream**

- NATS Streaming was released in 2016, gained clustering with Raft in 2018, and was deprecated one month after JetStream shipped in server 2.2 (March 2021). "In April, so a month later after JetStream was released, NATS Streaming was marked as deprecated." (~06:43)
- The two-year Streaming deprecation window ends June 2023; after that no security or bug fixes land. "No more security fixes and bug fixes are going to be landing after June." (~07:45)
- JetStream is a subsystem inside the NATS server, whereas NATS Streaming was a separate server acting as a NATS client. "JetStream is an actual subsystem within the NATS server proper... whereas NATS Streaming is an external server." (~06:43)
- NATS Streaming did not support wildcards in channels or subscriptions, forcing one subscription per channel and shaping channel naming. "NATS Streaming doesn't support that... subscriptions do not support wildcards." (~09:47)
- Streaming channels and core NATS subjects were two separate namespaces with no interop, no headers, and mandatory client IDs. "No interop between this concept of channels... and actual core NATS subjects." (~09:47)
- Streaming's reconnection behavior needed large documented caveats and was a known pain point. "There's like these big caveats and these big explanations about how to properly do reconnection." (~10:49)
- A Streaming channel maps to a stream, but a stream binds any number of subjects including wildcards. "You can create a stream called just named events, but you can define any number of subjects, including wildcards." (~14:55)
- A Streaming subscription is analogous to a JetStream push consumer; JetStream adds pull consumers which Streaming lacked. "A NATS Streaming subscription is analogous to a push consumer." (~22:05)
- Migrating removes a component: drop the Streaming servers and let clients talk to a JetStream-enabled cluster; embedded-mode Streaming deployments must move to a vanilla NATS cluster with routes. "In my opinion, it's actually simpler because we're removing a component." (~37:25)
- Data migration algorithm: create a stream per channel, republish channel messages, map old channel sequence to new stream sequence (optionally stored in a header), then create consumers with an explicit start sequence from the mapping. "You need to map the sequence number from the message in a channel to the new sequence number that gets created in the stream." (~48:39)
- Unlike Streaming's implicit channel creation, a stream must exist before publishing to JetStream, because core subjects and stream subjects coexist. "Do you have to declare a stream before publishing to JetStream? Yes, you do." (~54:47)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS KubeCon Tutorial on Twitch**

- NATS v2 is backward compatible and a drop-in replacement for v1; users saw an automatic performance boost, and subject cardinality with millions of subscriptions is handled. "You could actually, if you're on v1, use v2 as a drop-in replacement." (~23:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Native MQTT Support in NATS Server**

- Existing MQTT applications only need to be repointed at the NATS MQTT port; nothing else changes, so IoT investments are preserved. "The application did not have to do anything, just point to the NATS server's MQTT port." (~05:09)

## MYTH: Corrections of wrong beliefs (279 claims)


**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — What is NATS**

- Core NATS is at-most-once: if no subscriber matches or the subscriber is not active when sent, the message is not received. "This is the same level of guarantee that TCP/IP provides."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream (concept overview)**

- Traditional temporal decoupling is imperfect: "durable subscribers need to be created before the messages get published"; "queues are meant for workload distribution and consumption, not to be used as a mechanism for message replay."
- Monotonic writes/reads guaranteed, but "We don't guarantee read your writes at this time, as reads through direct get requests may be served by followers or mirrors." Send gets to the stream leader for more consistent results.
- Base QoS is at-least-once: rare failures make a publisher wrongly believe a publish failed and republish, or lose a consumer ack causing redelivery, leading to "perceived 'message duplication' at the application level".
- Pull consumers still get real-time updates: pass a reasonable timeout to Fetch and call it in a loop.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Consumers**

- A consumer is durable only when `Durable` is set. "Setting `InactiveThreshold` does not make a consumer durable." Setting `Name` without `Durable` creates a named consumer that the server still treats as ephemeral.
- Out-of-window acks may still count: "if a first process fails to acknowledge within the window and the message has been redelivered to another consumer, the acknowledgment from the first consumer will be considered."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Source and Mirror Streams**

- "Deletes in the origin stream are NOT replicated through a source or mirror agreement."
- "Sourcing messages does not retain sequence numbers. But it retain the in stream sequence of messages. Between streams sourced to the same target, the sequence of messages is undefined."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Key/Value store (concept)**

- Monotonic writes/reads guaranteed; "We don't guarantee read your writes at this time, as reads through direct get requests may be served by followers or mirrors." Send gets to the underlying stream leader for stronger consistency.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Object Store (concept)**

- "Object store is not a distributed storage system. All files in a bucket will need to fit on the target file system."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream walkthrough**

- A Core NATS subscriber only receives messages published after it started; replaying history requires a consumer.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Subject Mapping and Transforms**

- Queue groups and durable consumers "are partition-less and non-deterministic": no guarantee two sequential messages on one subject reach the same subscriber, so ordering can be lost.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Clustering**

- "NATS clustered servers have a forwarding limit of one hop": a server forwards client-received messages only to adjacent routed servers; "Messages received from a route will only be distributed to local clients."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Logging**

- A logged `UNSUB` "does not indicate the subscription is gone, only that the message was received"; `DELSUB` marks actual removal.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — System Events (system account)**

- "The default global account `$G` does not publish advisories."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Multi Tenancy using Accounts**

- With traditional authorization "all clients can publish and subscribe to anything unless explicitly configured otherwise"; accounts make the subject space non-global so "clients can use short subjects without explicit authorization rules."
- The term "stream" in import/export "does not refer to ... a JetStream stream"; it predates JetStream and means a stream of Core NATS messages.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Decentralized JWT Authentication/Authorization**

- "NATS JWTs are only used as configuration", not as sessions or proof of authentication; identity proof is the nonce signature.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Slow Consumers**

- "NATS favors the approach of protecting the system as a whole over accommodating a particular consumer to ensure message delivery." Slow consumers are cut off; clients not answering pings are disconnected and need reconnect logic.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Administration (CLI intro), Account Information**

- "JetStream is fully usable by only using core NATS" commands (`nats pub`/`nats sub`).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Data Replication (mirrors/sources admin)**

- With sources "We can therefore not maintain absolute ordering, but data from 1 single source will be in the correct order but mixed in with other streams"; timestamps may appear out of order.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Streams / Consumers (JetStream admin CLI walkthrough)**

- "Stream vs Consumer sequence numbers ... are not directly related": stream sequence points to the message; consumer sequence is an ever-increasing counter of deliveries (10 redeliveries of one message -> consumer seq 10 or 11).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Environmental considerations**

- "Client connections and routes are permanent. Therefore a load balancer will not distribute messages from one client connections between servers"; a common failure is "redundant, but disconnected (non-clustered) servers to which the clients will randomly connect." Advertising must be off or point at the LB address.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — FAQ**

- Multiple subscribers can receive a request; with a queue group only one is picked; "the requestor does not know or control this information"; it only asks for one answer and NATS prunes interest after it.
- "NATS implements non-persistent distributed queuing via subscriber queue groups"; queue groups are "a form of message-distribution load balancing"; distribution is "controlled entirely by nats-server", not a publisher operation; messages "are not persisted to secondary storage."
- You cannot list subjects: "Do not think of it as a 'directory' that is aggregated over time. The interest graph is dynamic"; it can be derived at an instant by polling `/connz` and `/routez`.
- "NATS implements source ordered delivery per publisher ... There are no guarantees of message delivery order amongst multiple publishers."
- Core NATS is at-most-once: "messages are guaranteed to arrive intact, in order from a given publisher, but not across different publishers"; "offers only TCP reliability"; problematic or offline subscribers miss messages. JetStream (2.2+) adds at-least-once and "exactly-once (within a time window)".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Anatomy of a NATS Client Application**

- With NATS the developer never worries about who sends/receives, where services are or how many instances, "How many partitions or servers there are in the cluster", fault tolerance, or topology.
- "A client will receive a message for each matching subscription" so overlapping subscriptions (`foo` and `>`) deliver the same message multiple times.
- At-least-once corner cases: double publication, ack loss, or crash after processing before ack; dedup plus double-ack give exactly-once.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Receiving Messages / Sending Messages**

- "The client API (asynchronous) subscribe call can return before the subscription is actually fully established at the nats-server. Call Flush() on the connection right after you call subscribe if you need to synchronize".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Receiving: async, sync, drain, queues, unsubscribe, wildcards, structure**

- "For a given subscription, messages are dispatched serially, one message at a time." Concurrent processing requires the app to move messages to its own queue/worker pool.
- Auto-unsubscribe after N counts total messages ever sent to that subscription, not new ones; "If the subscriber has already received one or more messages, the unsubscribe will be immediate." Libraries resend the updated total on reconnect.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Reconnect: buffer, disable, events, max, random, wait**

- The reconnect buffer caches publishes while disconnected and sends them on reconnect; when full, publishes error. "while the message appears to be sent to the application it is possible that it is never sent because the connection is never remade." Use acks or JetStream publish to ensure delivery.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Developing with JetStream**

- Core publish to a stream subject is stored, "but that's not really the intent ... look at it more as a convenience that you can use to help ease the migration ... rather the desired end state or ideal design."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Concepts (functionalities)**

- Core NATS message-loss scenarios: disconnections long enough to drop/reset TCP lose buffered messages; slow consumers get their connection reset and buffer purged; "from the client application's point of view it simply looks like the application experienced temporary server disconnection".
- Core NATS "does not implement any kind of end-to-end flow control" because 1-to-N flow control would throttle publishers "to the lowest common denominator of all the current subscribers" and pub/sub is for real-time distribution. You could build it with request-reply but JetStream's decoupled flow control is "much easier (and better)".

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream Model Deep Dive**

- DeliverPolicy "is only the starting point. Once started it will always give you what you have not seen or acknowledged."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — NATS API Reference (JetStream wire API)**

- Plain pull requests accumulate on the server while the client is connected: "if you ask for 1 message 100 times and 1000 messages arrive you'll get sent 100 messages not 1." Use `{"expires": ns, "batch": n}` ("Set the expire time to now + your poll frequency") or `{"batch": n, "no_wait": true}` (404 status when empty, 409 when MaxAckPending reached).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — nats bench (benchmarking guide)**

- "by default JetStream flushes disk writes synchronously, meaning that even if the nats-server process is killed suddenly no messages will be lost as the OS already has them in it's buffer"; only a whole-host crash needs sync-after-every-write (at a latency cost). `--persistasync` on R1 gives memory-like throughput.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — In Depth JWT Guide**

- JWT names "are only used by tooling, nats-server does not read this value"; names may collide, so keep them unique in nsc. "JWT content can be viewed as public, although it's content may reveal which subjects/limits/permissions exist."
- System events: "you MUST NOT rely on a particular ordering or due to the possibility of loss, events matching" (a CONNECT may not have a matching DISCONNECT); periodic aggregate messages compensate for misses. Prefer `$SYS.ACCOUNT.<id>.SERVER.CONNS` over the old `$SYS.SERVER.ACCOUNT.<id>.CONNS`.
- "leaf nodes do not multiplex between accounts. Every account that you wish to connect across a leaf node connection needs to be explicitly listed." The system account is not connected automatically even when both sides share it; add it as a separate `remote` with heavily restricted credentials, also when only needed for the NATS resolver or centralized monitoring.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Legacy: NATS Streaming (STAN) and nats-account-server**

- STAN is a client of a NATS server, not a server; NATS clients and STAN clients cannot exchange messages on the same subject (STAN payloads are protobuf with acks). Clients must close connections explicitly or the server keeps them until heartbeats fail.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-4: NATS Message Headers**

- NATS headers are case preserving, unlike HTTP: "NATS treats application headers as a part of the message _payload_ ... The server will not change the case in message conveyance." Case sensitivity "is the responsibility of the application and client participants."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-15: JetStream Subscribe Workflow [STALE?]**

- Common queue-subscribe mistake: two `js.QueueSubscribe("foo","bar")` calls each create their own ephemeral consumer, so "both members were receiving the same message." Go's fix: use the queue name as the durable name when no durable/bind given.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-31: JetStream Direct Get**

- The classic `$JS.API.STREAM.MSG.GET.<stream>` API "All such reads are routed to the current stream leader ... tracked as administrative and incur tracking overhead."
- Read-after-write: the classic Get API "provides read-after-write coherency by routing requests to a stream's current peer leader"; "_Direct Get_ does not assure read-after-write coherency as responders may be non-leader stream servers ... or MIRROR downstream servers."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-36: Subject Mapping Transforms in Streams**

- Ordering: a single source with multiple non-overlapping filters "the ordering of the messages is guaranteed to be preserved"; multiple sources from the same stream may overlap (duplicating messages) "but the order of the messages between the sources is not guaranteed to be preserved."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-41: NATS Message Path Tracing**

- For non-client egresses "the subscription and queue group will be omitted. This is because NATS Servers optimize and send a single message across servers, based on a known interest, and let the remote servers match local subscribers."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-42: Pull Consumer Priority Groups**

- "We should not describe this in terms of exclusivity as there is no such guarantee, there will be times when one client thinks it is pinned while processing messages when it isn't anymore because the server switched."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-43: JetStream Per-Message TTL**

- `Nats-TTL: never` "will result in a message that will never be expired. This applies to both per-message TTL processing and stream-level age limits: a `never` message is not removed by the stream's `MaxAge` setting."
- "Unless `MaxMsgsPer` equals 1 the server treats `SubjectDeleteMarkerTTL` as the minimum effective `Nats-TTL`. A publish with a `Nats-TTL` below this floor is **not** rejected — instead the server raises the effective TTL to the floor and rewrites the stored `Nats-TTL` header."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-44: Versioning for JetStream Assets**

- Version skew problem: the connected server may be an old leafnode without JetStream; the meta-leader "would not forward the API fields it is unaware of"; asset hosts "would silently drop fields." "Our current approach is to check the connected-server version and project that it's representitive of the cluster as a whole but this is a known incorrect approach especially for Leafnodes."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-51: JetStream Message Scheduler**

- "If a message is made with a schedule in the past it is immediately sent. If a server was down for a month and a scheduled message is recovered ... it will be sent immediately. To avoid this, add a `Nats-TTL` header."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-56: JetStream Consistency Models**

- `PersistMode: async` "will result in asynchronous flushing of data to disk ... at the expense of data loss during severe disruptions in power, server or disk subsystems"; "The Publish Ack will be sent before the data is known to be written to disk."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-58: Key-Value Store Roadmap and future considerations (updates ADR-8)**

- "A bucket, being backed by a Stream, lives in one Cluster only. To make buckets available elsewhere we have to use JetStream Sources and Mirrors."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-8: JetStream based Key-Value Stores**

- Consistency: "We do not provide read-after-write consistency. Reads are performed directly to any replica, including out of date ones. If those replicas do not catch up multiple reads of the same key can give different values between reads." "Historically we had read-after-write consistency, this has been deprecated."
- Gets use Direct Get `$JS.API.DIRECT.GET.<STREAM>.<SUBJECT>`; non-direct `last_by_subj` is legacy: "we do not support disabling direct get on any buckets."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-59: JetStream Stream Sourcing and Mirroring**

- Mirror behaviour: "Messages are delivered in the same order and with the same sequence numbers and timestamps as the upstream stream"; read-only; "cannot have `subjects` configured"; retention/limits independent of upstream; "A stream can mirror at most one stream. Multiple streams can mirror the same stream"; `mirror` and `sources` mutually exclusive.
- Sourcing: "Messages from each individual source maintain their relative ordering. When sourcing from multiple streams, messages are interleaved in arrival order. There is no guaranteed ordering across different sources." A sourced stream "**can** also have its own `subjects`."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-60: JetStream reliable stream sourcing/mirroring on WQ/Interest streams (updates ADR-59)**

- Pre-2.14 sourcing/mirroring uses "an ephemeral ordered push consumer using `AckNone`"; "really reliable if the stream that's being mirrored/sourced is a Limits stream" but on WorkQueue/Interest "any messages that are sent are immediately acknowledged and removed. If this message is not received on the other end, this message will be lost"; on Interest "interest will be lost while there's no active connection ... This also results in messages being lost."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-61: Unsafe meta group quorum rescue for disaster recovery**

- Meta group quorum "is computed from the configured peer set, not from the set of currently live peers. A peer that is shut down and intended to not come back, without being explicitly peer-removed still counts toward the quorum requirement."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-62: JetStream desired state reconciliation**

- Raft membership "can't just be swapped for a new one in a single step: adding or removing several peers at once can produce two quorums that never overlap, which risks electing two independent leaders over the same data." Every change is "a sequence of safe, single-peer adds/removes."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — JetStream Anti-Patterns: Avoid these pitfalls to scale more efficiently**

- "Too many consumers" often reflects "overstated persistence and delivery guarantee requirements."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS JetStream: Ordered, Scalable Processing**

- Pinning is affinity plus failover, not a distributed lock; windows exist where a client believes it is pinned after the server re-pinned, and buffered messages cannot be revoked. Handlers must be idempotent.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Pull Consumer Priority Groups in NATS JetStream: Overflow, Pinned, and Prioritized Routing**

- Pinning is "not a hard guarantee"; an old client may believe it's pinned after the server moved on. Handler "must be idempotent."
- Fetch(N) is not an atomic reservation; the server may spread N messages across concurrent pulls.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS and Kafka Compared**

- Core NATS at-most-once delivers messages from a given publisher intact and in order, but "Core NATS's 'at-most-once' guarantee does not extend across different publishers."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS vs RabbitMQ: How to Choose the Right Messaging System**

- "A clean-room benchmark may not predict production behavior"; test under production-like conditions with `nats bench` and `nats-top`.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Multi-Region Consistency: Have Your Cake and Eat it Too!**

- Read mirrors give "eventual coherency" not true eventual consistency: writes serialize at the origin; mirrors don't help write scaling or availability if the origin region fails.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Understanding JetStream Memory Usage Patterns**

- Message count and size affect disk, not memory, "unless consumers perform full stream scans or create many short-lived consumers." 300M+ messages across a few streams with single consumers "shouldn't inherently cause high memory usage."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Why NATS**

- Evaluate NATS against the combination of tools it replaces, not just brokers; tradeoff stated: "NATS may not be the most optimized for any single narrow use case" but covers 80% via one API and one operational surface.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS and Decentralized Security: A Modern Approach to Scalable Authentication**

- Publisher identity is "not part of NATS's core design, as publishers and subscribers are decoupled"; workaround: put a source_id in the payload.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Mirror Streams in NATS JetStream: One-Way Replication Made Simple**

- "Delete a message from the origin, the mirror still has it. Delete from the mirror, the origin is unaffected." Deletes never replicate in either direction, which makes mirrors independent backups.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — JetStream Expected Sequence Headers: Optimistic Concurrency Without Locks**

- There is one sequence counter per stream; per-subject expected values "are still stream sequence numbers, not independent counters starting from zero."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Jepsen: NATS 2.12.1**

- "We did not observe data loss with simple network partitions, process pauses, or crashes in version 2.12.1." Antithesis partnership credited; future work: detect lost data and recover from peers automatically.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Monitoring NATS: From HTTP Scrapes to System Events**

- "The system account isolates subjects and permissions, not CPU, memory, or I/O. A severely overloaded server can still impact all traffic."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Server 2.14 Release**

- Before 2.14 mirrors/sources used internal ephemeral consumers; now WorkQueue and Interest retention sources use durable consumers, "visible in consumer listings, carries metadata showing the source domain, account, and stream", holding state across disconnects. Users can pre-create the consumer used for sourcing/mirroring.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Building a Wallet Event Backbone with NATS JetStream: Lessons from BroSettlement's Staging Tests**

- Delivery is "at-least-once, not magical exactly-once"; duplicates are a "normal recovery condition"; consumers dedup by globally unique eventId (plus chain tx identity for blockchain data); handlers idempotent via unique constraints; client requests carry Idempotency-Key.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Delegate with trust**

- Sequence numbering is stream-wide; per-subject ordering requires tracking the last subject sequence (from subscription metadata, fetching the last event, or in-memory).

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Infinite message deduplication in JetStream**

- Exactly-once needs two parts: publish-side dedup and ack-based consumption. Time-window dedup (Nats-Msg-Id) "cannot guarantee restart timeframes"; Kafka's connection-scoped producer idempotence "guarantees only single-session idempotence" and can't cover a client crash before ack.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Benchmarking Using NATS CLI Tool**

- Published benchmarks are often distrusted because "results can be skewed to improve performance and therefore become unreliable"; run benchmarks "as close to your production use as possible" with `nats bench` for Core and JetStream. (Post body is mostly a pointer to the video; no numbers.)

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS: The Secret Weapon Behind Vitrifi's Workflow Automation Platform**

- Exactly-once via "message de-duplication, delivery tracking and acknowledgement mechanisms" for the Trigger Server ("execute once – no more, no less"), yet idempotent operations remain "a best practice."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Building Event-Driven Banking as a Service (BaaS) with NATS**

- KV/Object stores "complement, rather than fully replace, transactional databases."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Event-Driven Systems with NATS and Jetstream**

- Ack after processing gives at-least-once: "Messages may be delivered multiple times (if your service crashes mid-processing), but they won't be lost." `nak()` triggers redelivery.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS JetStream: Streams, Consumers, and Durable Messaging**

- "`MaxDeliver` is not a dead-letter queue — after max attempts, NATS stops redelivering but the message remains in the stream." Plan explicit poison-message handling.
- Default `sync_interval` "2 minutes — ack does not always mean immediately on disk in all failure modes." Don't treat ack as "job done on disk"; understand replication and sync_interval for RPO.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Replace Redis with NATS: Atomic Counters and Microsecond Key-Value**

- "The working set must fit in memory" for microsecond figures; "NATS is optimized for streaming, not random access"; high-churn random updates are slow because "overwriting a KV key deletes the previous message in the backing stream."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Connecting distributed SCADA with NATS.io (part one)**

- On MQTT: "It doesn't make much sense to rip out one pub/sub system for another, and that's not where NATS shines"; the value is the whole platform ("one system to operate") where "real-time data streams and disk or memory persisted streams can co-exist."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — SOX compliance with NATS**

- Caveat: events/advisories may not be generated or saved during "hardware failure, unexpected server shutdown, and other error conditions."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — GitHub discussion: NATS Jetstreams creation and management (#4457)**

- Streams cannot be declared in server config: "NATS is a multi tenant system and we support decentralised authorization where no credentials for the accounts are stored on the server." Manage via client APIs, CLI, Terraform, GitHub Actions, or a setup container at boot.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — GitHub discussion: Can I use JetStream KV as cache? (#1507)**

- ripienaar: small-dataset cache tests are misleading because OS block cache makes disk-backed queries look RAM-fast; test with large random-read datasets.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Weekly #32**

- Even replica counts (R2, R4) are "generally not useful from an availability standpoint"; R2 adds a storage copy but cannot progress if the leader fails.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Client-side Partitioned Consumer Groups for JetStream**

- "NATS JetStream does not require Stream partitioning to parallelize consumption, unlike Kafka"; standard consumption is elastic and on-demand; strict order needs max-ack-pending 1 which serializes the whole stream.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — How to Configure NATS Cluster with Leaf Nodes for Edge Connectivity**

- Core messages are not persisted across a broken leaf link; buffering requires JetStream streams on the leaf.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS JetStream as a Durable Job Queue in .NET**

- "At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing beats exactly-once delivery promises."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Grokking NATS Consumers: Push-based queue groups**

- Redelivery can happen even when processing succeeded but the ack was lost; publisher dedup is windowed so consumers still need idempotency.

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — Grokking NATS Consumers: Intro and push-based**

- Limits streams are consumer-stateless; work-queue and interest retention are consumer-influenced. "Streams cannot have overlapping subject spaces."

**Source class: Blog posts and articles — NATS Weekly #13**

- Interest retention: with zero consumers messages are discarded immediately; with one consumer messages are retained even without an active subscription; with several, "the message is not removed until all consumers consume the message (ack or term)"; consumers must exist before messages to see them.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Maximum number of consumers**

- Belief: NATS consumers are as cheap as subscriptions, so millions of durable R3 consumers is a natural design. Correction: durable replicated consumers are Raft state machines; shard streams, use R1/memory consumers, or cap per cluster — wallyqs/derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Why JetStream doesn't achieve linear scalability through partitioning?**

- A Kafka partition, not a Kafka topic, is the equivalent of a NATS stream — derekcollison. "A partition in Kafka is equivalent to a stream in NATS."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Can JetStream support multiple partitions distributed to multiple machines, like Kafka?**

- Partitions/shards are not needed for HA or disaster resilience; that is what replicas (R3) are for. Sharding is only for performance scaling — Jarema. "You don't need partitions (or shards) to improve HA... Those are needed for performance scalability."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — NATS JetStream Sharding (placement tags on Kubernetes)**

- Belief: NATS picks the fastest-responding servers for a new stream, so streams cluster on a few nodes. Correction: peer selection at stream creation is load balanced using the current distribution of JS assets — jnmoyne. "the selection of the peers at stream creation time is load balanced (it looks at the current distribution of JS assets when making the selection)."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Subject Indexing and Ordering Internals**

- "Publisher" in docs means the publishing connection, not the application — Zetanova (clarified from derekcollison's wording).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Using Nats Jetstream as an event store**

- Kafka topic vs NATS stream is the wrong comparison; a Kafka partition is the comparable unit of total ordering and replication — bruth. "a single *partition* is comparable to NATS stream since it is the unit of total ordering and replication."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Ordering guarantees per entity**

- Belief: WorkQueue retention breaks ordering when a message is Nak'd. Correction: with MaxAckPending=1 the Nak is outstanding and order holds — ripienaar (correcting Zetanova [UNVERIFIED]).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Multi-Region Without Sacrificing Availability**

- Belief: a gateway super-cluster is the only "one virtual cluster" option for multi-region. Correction: hub cluster plus leaf-node regions gives the same client transparency without the cross-region meta quorum — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Is non-clustered JetStream possible with Gateways?**

- Belief: a leaf node in Asia must route through the US hub before the EU sees an update, so gateways are better. Correction (implicit): leaf plus source replica is the recommended shape for regional read replicas — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Cluster can't tolerate more than one service failure**

- Belief: any stream on a cluster is HA. Correction: an R1 stream hosted on the stopped server is unavailable; make it R3 — kozlovic.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Source stream from multiple leaf nodes**

- Belief: a stream with sources cannot be updated after creation. Correction: sources are editable at any time — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — locks/leases with KV similar to SETNX**

- Belief: exactly-once delivery keeps two workers off the same key. Correction: dedup prevents the same message being replayed, not parallel delivery of different messages for the same key — aep (asker's own discovery, consistent with maintainer replies).

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Automatic Message Payload Preservation in DLQ Stream**

- Belief: a WorkQueue message is removed when it hits max_deliver. Correction: it stays in the stream (removed only on ack or TTL) and can be fetched by the advisory's sequence with payload; verified on 2.12.4 R1, with a suspected loss on R3 — jgriegershs [UNVERIFIED, non-maintainer].

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — ack-wait and dupe-window behavior when used together**

- AckWait (consumer redelivery timer) and DupeWindow (stream publish dedup by Nats-Msg-Id) are unrelated settings — MauriceVanVeen.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — JetStream startup seems slow for ~50M messages**

- `config reload not supported for jetstream max memory and store`: changing JetStream limits needs a restart, not a HUP — server log in thread.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — has NO quorum, stalled on jetstream consumers**

- Belief: a 5-node cluster with R3 streams survives any two node failures. Correction: survival is per stream, depending on which peers hold it — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Which NATS JetStream Setup is Better? (WorkQueue plus mirror vs one Limits stream)**

- A larger stream does not slow delivery to consumers; one Limits stream with two consumers is simpler and more efficient than WorkQueue plus mirror — jnmoyne. "It's not because a stream is larger that delivery of messages to consumers takes longer"

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — how to recover from DiscardNew policy?**

- Stream state is separate from consumer state; acks do not delete messages under Limits retention. Interest retention removes a message once all interested consumers ack it — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Key Value with TTL (bucket MaxAge vs per-key TTL)**

- Bucket MaxAge takes precedence over a longer per-key TTL; set MaxAge longer than any per-key TTL — MauriceVanVeen.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — How does compression work?**

- Belief: compression lets you store more within the server's storage limit. Correction: it saves physical disk for operators only; set `max_file_store` and stream limits in raw terms — derekcollison.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Event Synchronization with NATS (nats.go)**

- Kafka partitions one topic by an app-provided key; NATS splits a subject space into partitions and creates one stream per partition, with the key being part of the subject — jnmoyne.

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Message Group / Sequential Convoy pattern (issue)**

- JetStream has no consumer groups or rebalancing; a JetStream "consumer" is like a Kafka partition and a JetStream "subscriber" is like a Kafka consumer; container orchestration provides worker elasticity — jnmoyne. "a 'consumer' in JetStream is like a 'partition' in Kafka and a 'subscriber' in JetStream is like a 'consumer' in Kafka."

**Source class: GitHub discussions and issues — Subject mapping partition distribution (issue)**

- `partition(N, tokens...)` hashes only the listed wildcard tokens; a constant token maps every message to one partition. Use `{{partition(4,1,2)}}` for a composite key — jnmoyne.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Private Inbox**

- Observed output: with `sub.allow: [_INBOX.>]`, pam subscribing to `_INBOX.>` receives the reply to joe's request. The text says this is expected: accounts are the isolation boundary; per-user granular permissions become necessary at scale. "This is actually expected and generally fine since _accounts_ are expected to be the isolation boundary, at a certain level of scale, creating users with granular permissions becomes increasingly necessary."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Push Consumers (legacy)**

- Consumer info tracks the last stream sequence a delivery was attempted for and a separate consumer sequence per delivery attempt; "These should not be treated as correlated since the consumer sequence for a given message will increment on each delivery attempt."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Confirmed Message Ack**

- An error from a plain Ack "only means that the client failed to send the ack message. There will be no error if the client published the ack, but the server did not receive (or process) it."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Key-Value Intro**

- The revision of a new key is not 1: revisions are the underlying stream sequence, "always monotonically increasing, but numbers will be shared across keys (like subjects) rather than sequence numbers relative to each key."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Request-Reply**

- "Unlike request-reply constrained protocols like HTTP, NATS is not limited to a strict point-to-point interaction"; request-reply is built on publish-subscribe.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first stream**

- Plain core NATS drops a message the moment no service is listening; a stream saves it instead. "Plain core NATS drops any of these messages the moment no service is listening. A stream saves them instead."
- A `no responders available for request` error on stream creation means the server was started without `-js`; JetStream isn't running.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publishing**

- A plain `nats pub` is a core NATS publish and the server returns nothing; use `--jetstream` to get the confirmation.
- A `PubAck` confirms storage, not delivery; storage and delivery are separate and can be minutes, hours, or days apart. "It does not confirm that any consumer has received it."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reading back the stream**

- Stream messages are durable records with fixed sequences; reading does not remove or move them. "Reading message 1 leaves message 1 where it was, available to the next reader."
- Reading a stream doesn't remove its data; unlike taking an item off a queue, the messages stay in place for the next reader.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Filtering what you consume**

- A consumer differs from a core queue group: a queue group splits one subject's live traffic across workers; each JetStream consumer gets its own full (filtered) view of the stored stream.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling a consumer**

- A queue group splits live messages with no storage; an offline subscriber misses them for good. Workers sharing a consumer split stored messages, so an offline worker just leaves its share for the others. "Only the stream-backed split survives a worker dropping out or a restart."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Ordered consumers**

- Without acks a plain no-ack consumer that missed a message would skip it with a gap; the ordered consumer spots the gap and rebuilds from the missing sequence, so order holds with no acks.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Pausing a consumer**

- Pausing differs from deleting and recreating a consumer, which throws away how far it read and which messages it acked.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Surviving node loss**

- Replicas are a durability control, not a throughput control; adding replicas is not how you scale throughput.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject mapping and transforms**

- Stream subject transforms differ from account-level subject mapping, which is server configuration that reroutes core subjects before they reach a stream.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Stream and consumer policies**

- Deliver policy `last_per_subject` and the Direct Get `--last-per-subject` flag are different features sharing a name: one is a consumer start position, the other a one-shot read.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subjects & wildcards**

- Publishing "to a wildcard" produces no error: the `*` is taken as a literal character and the message lands on the literal subject `orders.*.created`, reaching wildcard subscribers but not exact-subject subscribers. "Publishers can't publish \"to a wildcard.\""

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publish-subscribe**

- A publish with no interest is a silent no-op: no error, no stored backlog, and the publisher can't tell "delivered to three" from "delivered to nobody".

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject mapping**

- Weights under 100 keep the rest on the source subject; they don't drop it. "Weights under 100 keep the rest, they don't drop it."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Placement**

- Placement cannot name a leader: a `preferred` server in placement is rejected with `preferred server not permitted in placement`, and no client library exposes such a field.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Authentication basics**

- The server returns the same `Authorization Violation` for a wrong password and an unknown user, so a failed login does not reveal which half was wrong.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Authorization**

- A user with no `permissions` block (no allow, no deny) is unrestricted and can do anything on the server.
- An empty allow list is not a lock-down: `publish: []` parses as no list, so the user can publish anywhere. To block all publishes write `publish: { deny: [">"] }`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Accounts and multitenancy**

- `$SYS.>` subjects aren't blocked for other accounts; a subscription from an ordinary account is accepted and simply never receives anything, because responders exist only inside the system account.
- The lockdown comes from tenant accounts, not the `accounts` block itself: a config whose only account is the system account still admits unauthenticated clients into `$G`.
- Pitfall: A shared subject name doesn't mean shared delivery. Two accounts using `orders.shipped` never exchange a message; connecting tenants is a deliberate export/import act. "Don't reach for a matching name to connect tenants."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Cross-account**

- A stream export has nothing to do with JetStream streams; it only means a one-way flow across the account boundary. "a stream export has nothing to do with JetStream streams"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Decentralized authentication**

- A user JWT isn't the config "token": the token is a password-style secret compared against config, while a JWT is a signed document anyone can inspect but only the right account key can produce.
- A stolen user JWT alone is useless: without the seed it can't sign the nonce (fails check 1). That's why the creds file has two sections.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Encryption & TLS**

- `openssl s_client` fails with `wrong version number` against a default NATS TLS port because the first bytes are the plaintext `INFO` line; that error doesn't mean TLS is broken. Use `gnutls-cli --starttls` or turn on `handshake_first`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Security)**

- Whether a stream survives losing its server is replication, not security: security decides who may access a stream; replication decides whether it's still there.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reconnection**

- Flush is not a delivery guarantee: buffered publishes are still plain core publishes with at-most-once semantics; the buffer doesn't turn a publish into a durable acknowledged write. "Flush is not a delivery guarantee."
- The reconnect buffer does not restore a JetStream consumer's place in the stream; acknowledgment position is the JetStream layer's bookkeeping, not the connection's.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Drain & Shutdown**

- Flush confirms receipt by the server only: it doesn't say any subscriber saw the message, and it isn't a storage acknowledgment (that's a JetStream publish ack).
- Pitfall: Assuming a core drain acks your JetStream messages. Drain winds down the connection; it does not acknowledge a consumer's messages. Ack explicitly before the connection closes or JetStream redelivers to the next client. "It does not acknowledge a JetStream consumer's messages for you."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Slow Consumers**

- Two different "slow consumers": a local slow consumer drops individual messages and keeps the connection (fix with pending limits + callback); a server-side slow consumer is the server closing the whole connection because the client reads its socket too slowly to meet the server's per-client write deadline (looks like a disconnect with a read error; fix by reading faster or spreading load). The server's view is the `slow_consumers` counter on `/varz`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Services**

- A service stores nothing; it answers a request and retains no record of it (at-most-once request-reply). Work that must survive a restart or be retried belongs to JetStream. "A service stores nothing; it answers a request and retains no record of it."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Observability**

- A service error is a delivered reply, not a transport failure; it differs from no-responders, where nothing is listening at all.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream health**

- Pitfall: In-flight is not lag. `num_ack_pending` counts messages a worker holds; `num_pending` counts messages no worker has taken. Rising in-flight means a stuck handler; rising lag means not enough handlers. "rising in-flight means a stuck handler, rising lag means not enough handlers"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Advisories & events**

- The `max_deliver` advisory is the only built-in signal that a message stopped being delivered. There's no dead-letter queue, and the advisory is published once; if no one is subscribed when it fires, you never learn it happened. "There's no dead-letter queue, and the advisory is published once."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first bucket**

- The revision counter is bucket-wide, not per key. "a number the bucket assigns from a single counter it keeps across every key, not a per-key count"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Watching**

- `widget-*` is not a wildcard; `*` is only special as a whole token, so a hyphenated prefix filter matches nothing. "To split keys with a wildcard you'd design them with dots, such as `widget.blue` and `widget.red`, so that `widget.*` matches both."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Backup & Recovery Deep Dive**

- A mirror won't save you from bad data: a corrupt write replicates to the mirror and a mirror keeps no earlier state to rewind to.
- R3 replication is high availability, not a backup; a bad write (accidental delete, corrupt message) is applied to every replica. "R3 keeps the stream *available*; only a snapshot lets you go *back* to before the mistake."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mirrors as a DR tool**

- A mirror is not a backup. "A mirror follows the upstream's live writes, so a corrupt write lands in the mirror too — and a mirror keeps no earlier state to rewind to."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Disaster recovery**

- R3 is on neither recovery row: "replicating a bad write three times doesn't undo it."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Backup & Recovery)**

- R3 is availability, not a backup. "Three replicas keep a stream alive through a node loss, but a bad write replicates to all three just as a good one does."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — QoS, sessions, and retained messages**

- QoS is an MQTT-side contract; NATS has no equivalent, so the guarantees hold end to end only when both ends are MQTT.
- Assuming a retained message is a message queue: only the last retained value per topic is kept. "Use JetStream when you need the history."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Browsers and origins**

- The origin check is skipped when there's no `Origin` header; the CLI connects regardless because it sends none. "That is not a bug, and it isn't something you can configure away."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TLS and proxies**

- `no_tls` and the client's URL scheme are separate questions; the client uses `wss://` because the proxy presents a certificate, while the listener's TLS is decided by its own config.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leaf nodes over WebSocket**

- The URL scheme doesn't tell you whether a link is encrypted: `ws://` with a `tls {}` block beside it is a TLS connection. "If you want that to be obvious to whoever reads the config next, write `wss://` and let the scheme say so."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue Groups**

- Selection is random per message and does not account for how busy a member is.

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Replace Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis and more w/NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity Ep 10**

- Unlike Kafka, where you'd have to deliver the whole stream, NATS filters at the consumer level by subject. "instead of having to whip through an entire stream ... NATS can actually filter on a consumer level" (~08:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Build Priority Background Jobs & Dead Letter Queues with NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity ep 12**

- Correction to the previous episode: a work-queue stream can have multiple consumers as long as their filter subjects do not overlap. "you can actually have multiple consumers in a work queue stream as long as the subjects that they're interested in don't overlap" (~04:05)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared: Part 1 | Rethink Connectivity**

- Kafka was designed as a streaming/distributed-log processing platform; NATS was first a messaging system and JetStream was a persistence layer added on top. "NATS historically came as being first and foremost a messaging system and then later on a persistence layer was added" (~02:02)
- Kafka is "semi-real time but not real real time" by its own admission and was not designed as a messaging system, although people use it for pub/sub and queues. "it really is not initially meant or designed to be a messaging system" (~03:03)
- Kafka has no subject-based addressing; a topic is a plain string, regex topic matching requires the client to keep re-fetching the topic list, and a stream is one topic. "the topic is just a string" (~07:07)
- Kafka can only address messages by offset (partition number plus sequence); the publish key is used solely to hash onto partitions and cannot be queried. "the key ... is purely used for one thing and one thing only which is distribution over the partitions" (~12:13)
- For market data with ~100,000 instruments you would not create 100,000 Kafka topics; you use one topic per exchange with the instrument as key, and then filtering for one instrument means the broker sends everything to a client that discards most of it. "you're transferring all the data over the network to somewhere else where you are discarding most of it" (~15:16)
- Terminology mapping: a Kafka consumer group is what JetStream calls a consumer; Kafka's consumers are JetStream's client applications. "Kafka's concept of consumer groups is what in JetStream we call just consumers" (~17:17)
- Kafka is designed for one client application at a time per topic partition; distributing a topic across clients requires partitioning, whereas JetStream needs no partitions by default. "if you want to distribute messages in a topic amongst a set of client applications ... you must use partitioning" (~20:22)
- Kafka stores data in a write-ahead log where you can only append at the head and compact the tail; individual messages cannot be deleted. "there's no ability to delete individual messages in a Kafka stream" (~22:25)
- Kafka always wants to accept writes; the only limit is stream size or time; JetStream lets you choose what happens at a limit, including per-subject limits Kafka cannot express. "you can also have limits on a per subject basis ... you can't do that with Kafka" (~24:25)
- Kafka has only upsert semantics with no concurrency control for two publishers on the same key. "you don't have the concept of being able to have concurrency access control in Kafka" (~30:31)
- Kafka's throughput comes from batching and a deliberately simple write path aimed at throughput, not latency; Kafka latencies are measured in milliseconds. "latencies in Kafka typically measures in milliseconds" (~34:41)
- The speakers admit Kafka scales beautifully horizontally for accepting writes thanks to hard partitions, at the cost of having to deal with partitions. "Kafka scales beautifully horizontally because of partitions ... which is another issue" (~36:44)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared Pt 2: Consumers | Rethink Connectivity**

- Kafka consumer group = JetStream consumer; JetStream consumers can be shared by any number of client applications without partitions. "consumers in JetStream can be shared by any number of client applications at any given time without having to have partitioning" (~02:02)
- In Kafka only one consuming application at a time can read a topic partition, because of how (the lack of) acknowledgments work. "you can only have one consuming application at a time per partition of a topic" (~03:03)
- Changing Kafka partition counts does not rebalance data, so teams over-partition up front (e.g. 100 partitions as a high-water mark for max consumers). "you cannot have more than just one single client application per topic partition ... so you over partition" (~05:07)
- Kafka gives no filtering: you pick a start position and get a fire hose the application must sift. "there's no filtering right it's all or nothing" (~14:16)
- Kafka is pull-only with one-to-one flow control and has no one-to-many flow control. "in the case of Kafka it's only pull so you only have one to one flow control" (~24:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Comparing and contrasting NATS and Kafka | RethinkConn '22**

- Kafka is a distributed append-only commit log; NATS with JetStream is a distributed messaging platform with added persistent storage. "Kafka is a distributed append-only commit log ... NATS and JetStream which is a distributed messaging platform with added persistent storage" (~01:00)
- Subject-based addressing is not the same as topics; Kafka doing pub/sub on topics does not equal subject-based addressing. "people think because Kafka says we do pub sub with topics that they do proper pub sub with subject-based addressing that's not the case" (~03:04)
- Kafka topics usually need predefinition; auto-created topics default to one partition and topic creation can trigger re-partitioning across servers. "the default number of partition is one and that's not very useful in Kafka for many cases" (~05:06)
- Filtering in Kafka requires a Kafka Streams process that reads everything and writes filtered sub-streams, storing messages more than once. "so you end up storing the message actually more than once" (~07:07)
- JetStream consumers (Kafka consumer groups) are partition-less, stateful, and their state is persisted and replicated along with the stream. "they also are stateful and the state can be persisted and replicated along with the stream of the data" (~10:13)
- JetStream has push and pull delivery with one-to-one and one-to-many flow control; Kafka has pull only with one-to-one flow control. "Kafka only has the one to one flow control using pull" (~11:14)
- Kafka consumer groups only support cumulative offset acks; there is no individual acknowledgment and redelivery means the application seeks manually. "there's no concept of acknowledging individual messages" (~13:18)
- JetStream has a built-in deduplication window over a configurable time that works across client sessions; Kafka's built-in dedup is per session, so a crash-and-resend still duplicates unless you use Kafka Streams. "the built-in deduplication feature of Kafka is only per session" (~15:22)
- Matching JetStream's functionality with Kafka means brokers, ZooKeeper, Kafka Streams JVMs, MirrorMaker for cross-cluster replication, Redis for KV, a separate message broker, and Kafka Connect JVMs; NATS covers most of it in one binary, plus Benthos for stream processing apps. "compare the number of JVMs as far as the eye can see ... to a single binary that runs all of these at once" (~18:27)
- The speaker explicitly does not claim NATS replaces all Kafka; the pitch is fewer moving parts for many use cases. "we're not saying replace all your Kafka with NATS right we're just saying consider NATS" (~19:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers**

- Unlike topic/partition systems where the partition is the unit of total order and replication, a NATS stream is itself totally ordered in storage and messages are addressable by subject. "NATS is different in that we have a single stream which is totally ordered on ingest ... versus other systems that are more like topic and partition based" (~29:40)
- You do not subscribe to a stream; you consume from it via a consumer, which is a server-side construct you attach to from the client. "you don't subscribe to the stream you consume from the stream this is where we see this a lot" (~39:53)
- Pull consumers with batching are not slower than push; clients interleave pull requests so latency between batches is minimized and it is on par or faster. "on par if not in some cases faster than a push consumer model" (~54:13)
- 2.10 partitions are logical tokens in the subject, not physical partitions like other systems. "this is not a physical partition like we talked about with the other systems this is a logical partition ID" (~66:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- Unlike append-only logs with only tail compaction, a NATS stream supports explicit deletion of an arbitrary interior message; that is how KV tombstoning works. "you can actually explicitly delete an arbitrary interior message within a stream ... this is how frankly the KV abstraction actually works" (~28:31)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP07: Going off piste; KV patterns with NATS.io (pt1)**

- NATS Streaming had only a handful of stream knobs, mostly limits like max messages; JetStream, KV and Object Store have many more options that can overwhelm newcomers, and each exists for a reason. "NATS Streaming had a handful of knobs ... fairly limited it was mostly around limits" (~04:09)
- KV is more than a cache; locks, leases, semaphores, job state, policy distribution and leader election are all valid uses. "people go well great I can use it as a cache but there's so many other areas that you can apply this thing to" (~44:05)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03: Escaping the HTTP Mindset with NATS.io**

- Programs embrace async primitives internally, then fall back to synchronous HTTP between components; NATS lets you break that synchronous point-to-point mindset. "we think about HTTP and service calls between components and then we're right back into synchrony land" (~19:27)
- Choreography decouples function invocation but not data: changing an event schema still breaks downstream subscribers, so data contracts must still be coordinated. "it still couples on the data side going back to schema and data, you can't get around that" (~27:34)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP04: A Service Mesh Pattern for NATS.io**

- Networking "service function chaining" (steering packets sequentially through IDS, proxy, WAF via VLANs) is not what an application-level service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) does; the host retracts the conflation from the prior episode. "I completely conflated all of that with service meshes" (~04:05)
- Multi-region service mesh and multi-cluster Kubernetes are non-trivial and not out-of-the-box, in contrast to NATS's transparent cross-region routing. "how do you do a multi-cluster setup, it's non-trivial as far as I know" (~37:46)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP05: Exploring Powerful Client-side Features and Abstractions in NATS.io**

- Service discovery via the services API is not a static registry: an instance is discoverable while connected and disappears immediately when offline, with no de-registration or timeout. "it's not a static register either... the second it goes offline then... it's not there" (~31:43)
- KV data does not have to be local to be accessible: if the NATS system is JetStream-enabled, a client in another region can still read the bucket where the data is not present. "you can still access the key value store from a different location where the data isn't" (~64:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS as a ServiceMesh**

- Mesh-like functionality via NATS is not tied to Kubernetes; the speaker ran the same setup with Docker Compose, Kubernetes, and plain servers. "you can create a service mesh without Kubernetes as the basis" (~22:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP01S3: Going back to basics with core NATS!**

- Engineers reflexively demand maximum guarantees ("at most once? no, I need guarantees") but core NATS without persistence already gives useful guarantees, e.g. no-responders in request/reply. "core NATS even without any persistence can give you quite some guarantees" (~10:26)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03S3: NATS 2.11 Release**

- Maintainers insist new abstractions fit JetStream's native concepts rather than bolting on leaky models copied from other tools. "we're not just bolting something in that feels like either a leaky or a not very watertight model" (~28:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS tools and benchmarking with JNM! NATS Community Office Hours (Reupload)**

- NATS positions itself against Kafka on "proper queuing, proper request reply, proper multi-tenancy, no partitions unless you want them". "proper queuing, proper request reply, proper multi-tenancy ... no partitions unless you want them" (~02:03)
- Equivalent edge/mirroring behavior in Kafka or Pulsar requires extra JVM components (Kafka Streams, MirrorMaker, brokers plus bookkeepers plus zookeepers), which the speaker calls infrastructure sprawl. "JVMs as far as the eye can see" (~07:10)
- Kafka is not "proper queuing" because committing an offset implicitly acknowledges every earlier sequence; JetStream acknowledges each message individually. "when you acknowledge a message or commit a message ... you're committing that sequence number and automatically committing all the other sequence numbers before that" (~10:14)
- A Kafka KIP for queuing describes essentially the per-message ack, nak and redelivery features JetStream already has. "if you look at the features that they have described in a KIP ... it's basically all of the features I just talked about" (~12:17)
- Kafka-style request/reply is CQRS (submit to one topic, poll another later); NATS offers interactive request/reply with geo-affinity where you learn within a timeout that nobody can process the request and can decide whether to resubmit. "I send a request, if there's no one able to process at this point I want to know about this in whatever timeout is" (~13:18)
- Subject-based addressing lets a consumer filter messages from a stream; Kafka is one topic, one stream, with no server-side filtering. "Kafka is one topic one stream and when you read messages from a stream in Kafka there's no filtering" (~14:18)
- Kafka exposes many timing knobs with hard-to-find correct values; NATS has few, and the speaker's rule is "with 100 knob positions, 99 are wrong". "if there's 100 positions, possibly there's 99 wrong ones" (~17:23)
- Synadia publishes no official throughput numbers because distributed-system results depend on network, traffic, disk and cloud variability; they ship a tool to run in your own environment instead. "three kinds of lies in the software business: big lies, small lies, and benchmarks" (~38:47)
- Loopback numbers show what the software can do with near-infinite bandwidth; real deployments are lower purely because of the network, so a faster network gives faster numbers on the same machines. "buy a faster network, you'll get faster numbers with the same machines" (~44:55)
- Ordered consumers need no application acks yet guarantee in-order, gap-free delivery; the client library tracks sequences, detects gaps, and recreates the ephemeral consumer after reconnects. "if it sees a gap of any kind it knows that something must have happened ... it will not deliver the messages until it recovers the messages missing" (~63:24)
- Acks in JetStream are for guaranteed consumption (exactly-once processing), not guaranteed delivery; "no acks" does not mean unreliable. "acknowledgements in NATS are really not for guaranteed delivery, but guaranteed consumption" (~61:22)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Expected Sequence Headers — Optimistic Concurrency Control Explained**

- There is only one sequence counter, the stream sequence; all three expected-sequence header variants validate against it and just filter what they compare with. "there's only one sequence counter the stream sequence ... these headers just filter what they check against" (~01:01)
- Per-subject does not give each subject its own 0,1,2 counter: the expected value is the stream sequence of that subject's last message, and a never-used subject expects 0. "the common misconception is that each subject has its own counter starting at 0 1 2 3 but the expected value is the stream sequence of that subject's last message" (~07:09)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Two-Node Engine with David & Byron**

- The Synadia two-node engine is not a general-purpose two-node NATS system; it is a standalone leadership election service for a two-node setup whose state lives in a NATS KV bucket. "this is not a general purpose two node NATS system" (~00:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Future of NATS: Roadmap & Vision**

- NATS has always been payload-agnostic; schema registry and codecs are a first step up the stack into data governance. "NATS doesn't care about the payload ... schema registry is sort of a first pass to that" (~26:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — JetStream KV: A fascinating alternative to Redis...**

- The speaker positions JetStream KV as comparable to Redis, not 10x faster; single-node Redis wins on latency for few writers, JetStream KV has a higher ceiling for concurrent requests and throughput. "Redis is going to win out on the latency side especially for a small number of writers and JetStream's KV is going to have a larger ceiling in terms of handling concurrent requests" (~08:06)
- Replication and clustering differ so much that comparing them to Redis is "apples and oranges"; the advantage claimed is at supercluster / multi-region scale, not single-cluster speed. "you might see some advantages when it comes to global scale moving out to a super cluster" (~07:05)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The ONE feature that makes NATS more powerful than Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ & Redis**

- The feature claimed to set JetStream apart from Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ and Redis is the flexibility of consumer configuration, which the speaker says removes upfront design cost. "that feature is how NATS designs its consumers" (~00:00)
- Alternatives give a firehose and expect client-side filtering, which at high scale is slow and inefficient; JetStream filters before sending over the wire. "the alternatives kind of just give you a firehose of messages and expect you to filter them out on the client side" (~04:04)
- In Kafka, Kafka Streams filtering happens client-side so the broker ships every message; that disincentivizes wide topics and forces upfront topic design, which does not apply to JetStream. "the Kafka broker itself is going to send every single message over the wire" (~10:12)
