**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mutual TLS**

- The example sets the TLS handshake `Timeout` to 2 (seconds) in the embedded server's TLS options.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Limits-based Stream**

- Limits-based retention is the default retention policy, and limits still apply to streams with other retention policies. "This policy is the default, however, limits still apply to streams with other retention policies."
- The stream limit choices are: maximum number of messages, maximum total size in bytes, maximum age of a message.
- There is a separate per-subject maximum-messages limit ("a specialized maximum messages limit that can be applied at the subject level").
- By default no limits are set, "which would require manually managing the ever-growing stream." Turn limits on and let the server truncate if any of them fit.
- JetStream offers file and in-memory storage; file storage is the default and is required for data to survive crashes and restarts. "For durability of the stream data, file storage must be chosen to survive crashes and restarts."
- By default a stream has one replica and uses file storage (deno narrative). "By default, a stream will have one replica and use file storage."
- Setting MaxMsgs to 10 on a 12-message stream truncates the two oldest messages; first sequence and first timestamp then reflect the third message.
- Limits combine: "Limits can be combined and whichever one is reached, it will be applied to truncate the stream."
- Max age truncation is not instantaneous on config update; messages remain visible until the age elapses ("we still see all the messages.. until a second passes").
- Max age is expressed in nanoseconds in the JS client (deno narrative): "the age is in nanoseconds, so 1000 milliseconds (1 second) converted to nanos."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Interest-based Stream**

- Interest retention is additive to stream limits; with `max-msgs` = 1 and discard-old, each new message deletes the prior one "regardless if any of the consumer subscriptions were available to process the message."
- Stream info on an empty interest stream after 3 publishes shows 0 messages, `last_seq` 3, and `first_seq` one greater than `last_seq`; first_seq "behaves as a sentinel value indicating the stream is empty."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Work-queue Stream**

- Work-queue retention is additive to limits: with `max-msgs` = 1 and discard-old, every new message deletes the prior one regardless of whether any subscription processed it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Pull Consumers**

- Without a durable name a consumer is removed after InactiveThreshold, which defaults to 5 seconds, when not actively consuming. "consumer will be removed after InactiveThreshold (defaults to 5 seconds) is reached when not actively consuming messages."
- The fetch batch size is the maximum number of messages that may be returned, not a guaranteed count.
- A fetch at the end of the stream blocks until the max wait, "which is 5 seconds by default, but this can be set explicitly as an option."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Pull Consumer - Applying Limits**

- Server-enforced pull consumer limits include: max non-acked in-flight messages, max in-flight pull requests (across subscribers), max pull batch size per request, max timeout on a pull request, and max total bytes of a pulled batch.
- MaxAckPending limits un-acked in-flight messages across all subscriptions bound to the consumer; with MaxAckPending=1 a fetch for 3 returns 1 and the next fetch times out with nothing until that message is acked. "This essentially forces serial processing messages for a pull consumer."
- MaxRequestBatch caps the batch size of any one fetch; requesting more than the limit is an error. "This can be used to keep the fetches to a reasonable size."
- MaxWaiting limits the number of fetch requests waiting in parallel; "This prevents building up too many requests that the server will have to distribute to for a given consumer." Extra concurrent fetches beyond the limit error.
- MaxRequestExpires caps the per-fetch max wait "to prevent requests waiting too long for messages"; a fetch with a longer timeout returns immediately with an error, while one equal or less works.
- MaxRequestMaxBytes caps the total bytes of a pulled batch; a FetchBytes over the limit errors.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Push Consumers (legacy)**

- The maximum number of messages a push subscription buffers is set by `MaxAckPending`; "The default is 1,000."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject-Mapped Partitions**

- A single serialized stream is highly performant; to scale out publishing or consumption, create N streams each representing a partition. "The trade-off introduced here is the ability to support concurrent publishes to N streams, while giving up total order across streams."
- Each partition stream binds `events.*.<i>`; published messages are transparently routed and written to the partition stream, and `nats stream report` shows them spread across all streams.
- Synchronous publish (one ack per message) gives quite low throughput; async batch of 100 raises it; 5 concurrent publishers raise it a bit more. "throughput and latency will highly depend on the quality of the network, and the resources available on the servers."
- The NBE benchmark numbers came from a GitHub Actions runner with 2 CPU cores and 7GB memory hosting 3 servers and 5 R3 streams plus the CLI; "true performance will suffer in comparison to a production setup."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Object-Store Intro**

- The server's default max payload is "about 1MiB"; a 10MiB object works because the client "automatically splits data into multiple chunks and stores it" as multiple stream messages and reassembles on read.
- (java narrative) Chunk size defaults to 128K and is configurable (32K shown); "Setting chunk size is important to consider ... if you know you are on a connection with limited bandwidth or your server has been configured to only accept smaller messages."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first stream**

- Stream names are case-sensitive and cannot contain dots, `*`, `>`, spaces, or slashes. "They can't contain dots, `*`, `>`, spaces, or slashes, so a subject like `orders.created` won't work as a name."
- Default stream config: Replicas 1, Storage File, Retention Limits, Discard Policy Old, Duplicate Window 2m0s, all Maximum limits (Messages, Per Subject, Bytes, Age, Message Size, Consumers) unlimited.
- A new stream is empty and the first message published gets sequence 1.
- Duplicate Window default is 2 minutes: for that long after a message is stored, the server turns away a second message carrying the same `Nats-Msg-Id` header.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publishing**

- Stream sequence numbers start at 1, only increase, and are never reused. "Sequence numbers start at `1` and only increase. The server gives each new message the next number and never reuses one."
- Retrying without a `Nats-Msg-Id` can store the message twice; the duplicate window is two minutes by default, so a retry arriving after that also stores a second copy. "Don't retry a bare publish."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reading back the stream**

- Default consumer limits: Outstanding Acks maximum 1,000 (MaxAckPending); Waiting Pulls maximum 512.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Filtering what you consume**

- Default consumer config shown: Pull Mode true, Deliver Policy All, Ack Policy Explicit, Ack Wait 30.00s, Replay Policy Instant, Max Ack Pending 1,000, Max Waiting Pulls 512.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Delivery and acknowledgment**

- Ack Wait default is 30 seconds; an unacked message is redelivered after it with an incremented delivery count.
- MaxAckPending (default 1,000) caps how many messages a consumer delivers before they're acked.
- For strict in-order processing set MaxAckPending to 1: the consumer delivers one message at a time and a redelivery always comes back before anything new. "That ordering guarantee costs throughput ... so use it only when order actually matters."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Ack responses and redelivery**

- AckWait is the redelivery timer and defaults to 30 seconds.
- MaxDeliver caps delivery attempts per message; default is -1 meaning no limit, so a message can be redelivered forever.
- With `--max-deliver=5`, a message that fails five times stops being delivered; without a term path it's dropped after the fifth attempt.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Pull consumers in depth**

- Two pull request fields bound a pull: `batch` (max messages returned) and `expires` (how long the server holds the pull open).
- A raw fetch with `expires` zero never times out; the server holds it until the batch fills. Client libraries default to about 30 seconds.
- MaxAckPending set too low limits throughput: a limit of 10 against a batch of 100 delivers ten then stops until acks arrive. "Keep it at or above your batch size. The default is 1000; lower it only when you know the in-flight count you want."
- A batch set too large uses more memory than expected because `batch` counts messages, not bytes; most clients offer a `max_bytes` option to bound a pull by size, and whichever limit is hit first ends the pull.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling a consumer**

- When a worker dies before acking, the server hands the message to another worker after AckWait (30 seconds by default).
- MaxAckPending (default 1000) is the ceiling on delivered-but-unacked messages across the whole consumer, shared by all workers: five workers get 1000 between them, not 1000 each. "The cap is shared across the whole consumer, not per worker"
- A low MaxAckPending starves a large set of workers: set to 3, ten workers leave seven idle. "Set the cap to at least your worker count, with room to spare."
- A crashed worker holds its message until AckWait (30s default) because the server can't tell a crash from slow work. "Set `AckWait` to your normal processing time: too short redelivers while a healthy worker is still working, too long leaves real failures stuck."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Ordered consumers**

- An ordered consumer is an ordinary server consumer configured as: AckPolicy none, memory storage, one replica, inactivity threshold of five minutes, start at the requested point.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Priority groups**

- A consumer uses exactly one priority group today; naming more than one is accepted but only the first takes effect.
- The pin timeout (`--pinned-ttl`) must sit comfortably above the pull's `expires`; the server's default pin timeout is two minutes, so keep `expires` under a minute. "The server's default timeout is two minutes; keep `expires` under a minute and the whole cycle fits."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Shaping the stream**

- A seven-day MaxAge does not guarantee seven days of history: a traffic spike can hit MaxBytes first and discard messages only hours old. "Set MaxBytes for your busiest traffic, not your average, if the age window matters to you."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Surviving node loss**

- R=3 is the production floor: three copies across three servers tolerate one server failure with no data loss and no manual recovery. "This is R=3, and it's the production floor."
- R=5 tolerates two simultaneous failures and is the maximum a stream supports. "Most production streams run R=3; R=5 is for state you can't afford to re-derive."
- R=3 is roughly three times the storage and write traffic of R=1; every write still goes through one leader, so a higher count lowers peak write throughput.
- Setting an even replica count: R=2 still has a single point of failure (one of two can't form a majority, writes block); R=4 tolerates only one loss like R=3 while paying for a fourth copy. "Use odd counts: R=3 for the production floor, R=5 for state you can't re-derive."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Advanced publishing**

- Atomic batch defaults: capped at 1,000 messages per batch and at most 50 batches in flight per stream; both are operator-configurable server limits, not fixed protocol caps.
- A sequence gap or over-limit atomic batch is rejected with an error `PubAck`; a batch that goes ten seconds without a message is dropped with no error reply, only a `stream_batch_abandoned` advisory. "Treat the final `PubAck` as the only proof the batch committed."
- An atomic batch can be abandoned: a gap or over-size (1,000 default) batch errors; ten seconds idle drops it silently with only an advisory. "don't assume a half-sent batch landed."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reading messages directly**

- A batched Direct Get streams matching messages over one request; each carries a `Nats-Num-Pending` header that reaches 0 on the last message. A batch is bounded by a count or byte budget (`batch`, `max_bytes`, `multi_last`).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Per-message TTL**

- `SubjectDeleteMarkerTTL` can leave a delete marker in place of an expired message, but only when the expired message was the last one on its subject; on an active subject with newer messages no marker is placed.
- The TTL must be at least one second; a sub-second or zero `Nats-TTL` is rejected with invalid-TTL error (`err_code` 10165) and nothing is stored.
- A valid `Nats-TTL` on a stream that hasn't opted in is rejected with TTL-disabled error (`err_code` 10166); no message stored. The server never quietly drops the header.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Stream and consumer policies**

- `async` persist mode is only accepted on a file-storage stream with a single replica, and an `async` stream refuses atomic batch publishing.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next**

- Checklist: Set Ack Wait longer than your slowest handler, with headroom, to avoid a redelivery storm.
- Checklist: Keep `MaxAckPending` at or above your batch size so it doesn't throttle throughput.
- Checklist: Pair `batch` with `max_bytes` so a single pull is bounded by size as well as count.
- Checklist: Size `MaxAckPending` to at least your worker count, with headroom; the cap is shared across the whole pool.
- Checklist: Tune `AckWait` to real processing time so a crashed worker's message recovers without redelivering honest work.
- Checklist: Keep each pull's `expires` comfortably under `--pinned-ttl` so a pinned client renews in time.
- Checklist: Size `MaxBytes` for your peak, not your average, when the age window matters; either limit can fire first.
- Checklist: Set `SubjectDeleteMarkerTTL` only when consumers must learn a value expired, and keep it at or below your shortest TTL.
- Checklist: Use odd replica counts: R=3 for the production floor, R=5 for state you can't re-derive.
- Checklist: Treat the final `PubAck` as the only proof an atomic batch committed; a sequence gap, an oversized batch, or a ten-second idle drops the whole batch.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subjects & wildcards**

- Subjects cost almost nothing: the interest graph holds an entry only once something subscribes, so a system can use millions of subjects without slowing the server. "a system can use millions of them without slowing the server down, because matching walks the token tree rather than scanning every subscription."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publish-subscribe**

- Default max payload is 1 MB (`max_payload`, 1048576 bytes), announced to every client on connect. "By default the server caps it at **1 MB**"
- An official client checks the payload against `max_payload` before sending and fails the call with `nats: maximum payload exceeded`, leaving the connection up; the server backstops with `-ERR 'Maximum Payload Violation'` and closes the connection.
- Publishing over the limit fails the publish; keep payloads under the limit and pass a reference for anything large. "Publishing over the limit fails the publish."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Request-reply**

- A client doesn't open a subscription per request: it subscribes once to `_INBOX.<connection>.*` and reuses it, so thousands of concurrent requests cost one subscription. "thousands of concurrent requests cost one subscription, not thousands"
- The server limits a single protocol line (subject plus reply subject) to 4 KB by default (`max_control_line`).
- Replies are at-most-once; every request carries a timeout (CLI default five seconds), sized to cover the responder's work plus the network round-trip.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Message headers**

- The server checks header block plus body combined against `max_payload` (the same 1 MB ceiling); a large header block leaves less room for the body. "Headers count against the payload limit."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject mapping**

- A weighted mapping lists destinations with weights 0 to 100; the server picks one per message at random in proportion. Weights totaling less than 100 leave the remainder on the original subject.
- Each weight must be 100 or less and the weights for one source must total 100 or less, or the server rejects the config.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connecting**

- Servers listen on port 4222 by default; the default connect URL is `nats://127.0.0.1:4222`.
- PING/PONG defaults match on both sides: a PING every two minutes, and the connection is declared dead after two unanswered PINGs. "a PING every two minutes, and the connection is declared dead after two unanswered PINGs."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connection lifecycle**

- Publishes made while disconnected go into a bounded reconnect buffer, 8 MB by default, flushed in order on reconnect; a publish that would overflow it returns an error. "That buffer is bounded (8 MB by default)"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Core NATS)**

- Checklist: Ask the server for `max_payload` and keep payloads under it; pass a reference for anything large.
- Checklist: Budget headers into `max_payload`; keep bulk data in the payload, not the headers.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Clustering & Replication Deep Dive**

- A single server isn't enough to see the replication mechanism: RAFT needs a majority, so it only appears once three servers are talking. "RAFT needs a majority, so the mechanism only appears once three servers are talking."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Forming a cluster**

- The `Routes` count in `nats server list` counts route connections, not peers: each link to a peer is a pool of connections (three by default) plus a dedicated system-account route. "each link to a peer is a small pool of connections (three by default) plus a dedicated system-account route"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Raft and leaders**

- The leader sends a heartbeat to followers by default about once a second; followers stay followers as long as it arrives. "by default about once a second"
- A candidate becomes leader on a quorum of votes, a majority `(N+1)/2`; for three peers that's two.
- A three-peer group keeps a leader as long as two peers are up; lose two and the survivor can't reach a majority and the group goes leaderless. This is the consensus math behind odd server counts: an even count buys no extra majority. "an even count buys no extra majority."
- An election takes seconds: the election timer fires between four and nine seconds after the last heartbeat, deliberately staggered. Don't build a client that treats a brief "no leader" as fatal; retry the write. "An election takes seconds, not milliseconds."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Replication and R=3**

- Three is the minimum replica count for production, and a stream supports at most R=5. "Three is the minimum for production, and a stream supports at most `R=5`."
- JetStream doesn't `fsync` every write; it batches disk syncs on `sync_interval`, which defaults to 2 minutes. Until the next sync an applied write can sit in the OS write cache. "`sync_interval`, which defaults to 2 minutes."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Placement**

- Asking for three replicas when only two servers carry the required tags fails the same way; placement doesn't relax the constraint to fit the replica count.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling and peer management**

- Adding a peer changes the quorum right away: an R=4 group commits once three peers hold a write, not two. A new empty peer can't win an election until the leader's first entries reach it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Clustering)**

- Checklist: Treat a brief "no leader" window during failover as normal; the election timer is 4–9s, so let the client retry instead of failing the write.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first cluster**

- With three servers the full mesh is three routes.
- Plan for an odd server count once you replicate: two servers lose their majority as soon as one is down, and four tolerate only one loss, the same as three, so the extra server adds cost without failure tolerance. For a pure routing cluster any count is fine. "Plan for an even server count."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream in a cluster**

- The meta group decides by majority vote, so a JetStream cluster wants an odd number of servers. Three servers form a majority of two; lose one and streams keep serving; lose a second and no write can reach a majority, so the stream stops accepting messages until a server returns.
- Production clusters run an odd count, typically three or five; a stream keeps at most five copies, so more servers add capacity, not more copies of one stream. "typically three or five — a stream keeps at most five copies"
- R1 is the default replica factor unless you ask for more; R3 is the production floor, and a three-server cluster is exactly enough to hold it. "Three copies is `R3`, the production floor"
- By default a consumer takes its stream's replica count; an R1 consumer on an R3 stream is its own single point of failure, since its position lives on one server and losing it loses the reader's place even though the stream survives.
- An even server count gives no extra protection: four tolerate the same single loss as three at the cost of an extra server; run an odd number, never four or six. "An even server count gives you no extra protection."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Super-clusters**

- The gateway `name` identifies the cluster, not the server, and must match the `cluster {}` name exactly; otherwise the server refuses to start with `cluster name conflicts between cluster and gateway definitions`. A server's own entry in `gateways` is ignored automatically.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leaf nodes**

- The default leaf node port is 7422, a fourth kind of listener separate from the client port (4222), route port (6222), and gateway port (7222). "one port per kind of connection."
- Local clients stay hidden behind the leaf: the hub sees one leaf link no matter how many machines connect to the leaf. "Add a thousand more machines and the hub still sees one leaf link."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Topologies)**

- Checklist: Run an odd server count once you replicate a stream.
- Checklist: Run an odd count (three or five), never an even count; a stream replicates across at most five servers.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Sizing & resources**

- CPU: core NATS routing is cheap; TLS handshakes and JetStream replication are where cycles go. Overprovision CPU by 20–30% above steady state so a node has spare cycles for a rebalance when a peer leaves. "overprovision CPU by 20–30% above steady state"
- Memory holds connections, subscriptions, and memory-storage stream data; file-storage streams live on disk, not RAM. A few hundred light client connections fit in a few hundred megabytes; budget a light publisher at roughly 128 MiB.
- Disk holds file-storage streams and is the resource most likely to run out.
- JetStream spends roughly two file descriptors per stream; the default per-process FD limit is plenty on a small cluster and not on a large one, where the hardened unit raises it to `LimitNOFILE=800000`. "JetStream spends roughly two FDs per stream."
- JetStream memory storage defaults to 75% of system RAM (capped by `GOMEMLIMIT` if set), falling back to 256 MB only when the server can't read system memory. "**Memory storage** defaults to 75% of system RAM"
- JetStream file storage defaults to 75% of disk space available under `store_dir`, falling back to 1 TB only when the platform can't report disk size; on a 10 GiB container volume the default is about 7.5 GiB, not 1 TB.
- At R3 each node stores the full stream once (one copy per node). The Helm chart defaults `max_file_store` to the PVC size.
- Server config sizes the node; account limits (`MaxMemory`, `MaxStore`, `MaxStreams`, `MaxConsumers`) size the tenant, enforced regardless of node disk. Read them live with `nats account info` before sizing.
- On an un-tiered account an R3 stream counts as `replicas × bytes` against `MaxStore`: a 10 GiB R3 stream spends 30 GiB. Forget the multiplier and the third replica fails to place. "a 10 GiB ORDERS stream at R3 spends 30 GiB of the account's `MaxStore`"
- On a tiered account replication is baked into the tier: the reported bytes are usable bytes, so a 10 GiB tier holds a 10 GiB R3 stream.
- `max_connections` defaults to 64K (65,536), is reloadable, and overflow disconnects immediately. `max_subscriptions` per connection defaults to unlimited. `max_payload` defaults to 1 MB and must stay `<= max_pending`.
- Setting `max_file_store` beyond the real disk fails as a publish error mid-stream, not a startup warning; set it to the volume size and watch the real disk with `df -h`. "Setting `max_file_store` beyond the real disk."
- If `max_payload` exceeds `max_pending` the server refuses to start; keep `max_pending >= 10× peak message size` so a burst of large messages can't stall a connection; don't raise `max_payload` in isolation. "`max_payload` larger than `max_pending`."
- FD exhaustion on a big cluster shows as connection refusals that look like a network fault; raise the limit (`ulimit -n 800000`) before the process starts. "File-descriptor exhaustion on a big cluster."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Hardening**

- The hardened unit sets `LimitNOFILE=800000`, far above the default 1024; each stream costs roughly two FDs and gossip plus client sockets add many more. "A large cluster exhausts the default 1024 quickly."
- The server listens on four ports: 4222 clients, 6222 cluster routes, 7222 gateways, 8222 HTTP monitor. The first three carry TLS once configured; the monitor port serves `/varz`, `/healthz` in plaintext and leaks server version, client count, and memory usage.
- `MemoryMax` and `GOMEMLIMIT` don't reserve memory; `max_memory_store` is an accounting limit and `GOMEMLIMIT` a soft GC target. Set `MemoryMax` above expected use (memory-store data plus connection and route buffers plus GC headroom) and `GOMEMLIMIT` somewhat below `MemoryMax`. Example: `max_memory_store: 4Gi`, `MemoryMax=6G`, `GOMEMLIMIT=5500MiB`. "A memory cap set below the working set gets the process OOM-killed under load."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Rolling upgrades**

- `lame_duck_grace_period` defaults to `10s` (how long before it starts kicking clients); `lame_duck_duration` defaults to `2m`, minimum `30s` (total window over which kicks are spread). The grace period must be shorter than the duration. "`lame_duck_duration` (default `2m`, minimum `30s`)"
- The Helm chart defaults `lame_duck_duration` to `30s` and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to `60s`; if you raise the duration, raise the grace period above `lame_duck_duration` plus shutdown overhead or the kubelet SIGKILLs the node mid-drain.
- Stepping the meta-leader down forces a metadata election during which stream and consumer operations (create, update, leadership moves) pause: typically about 5 to 10 seconds with default timeouts if killed outright, or roughly a second if it handed leadership off first. "typically about 5 to 10 seconds with default timeouts if the node was killed outright, or roughly a second if it handed leadership off first."
- On Kubernetes a `PodDisruptionBudget` with `minAvailable: 2` stops Kubernetes voluntarily evicting two of three pods together, so a node drain can never cost the R3 stream its quorum.
- A `lame_duck_duration` shorter than the rebalance kicks clients and exits while the stream is still catching up; measure a real drain first, then set the duration above it with margin rather than the minimum. "A `lame_duck_duration` shorter than the rebalance drops clients early."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Kubernetes**

- The chart wires three probes to `/healthz` on 8222: a startup probe on plain `/healthz` with `failureThreshold: 90` (~900s window for boot plus sync), a readiness probe on `/healthz?js-server-only=true`, and a liveness probe on `/healthz?js-enabled-only=true`.
- Never mix CLI and CRD management of the same stream: by default NACK re-creates a deleted stream on its ~30-second resync but does not revert a manual `nats stream edit`; in `--control-loop` mode it also reverts config drift on about a one-minute cycle. Pick one owner per stream. "Never mix CLI and CRD management of the same stream."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Deployment)**

- Sizing means reading account limits before committing to a PVC, rather than estimating after the disk fills; an R3 stream counts three times against account limits.
- Checklist: Set `max_file_store` to a size the disk can actually hold; test small (`10GB`) and watch `df -h`.
- Checklist: Keep `max_payload` at or below `max_pending`; hold `max_pending` at `>= 10×` peak message size.
- Checklist: Raise the file-descriptor limit before the process starts (`ulimit -n 800000`); a big cluster spends about two FDs per stream plus routes and gossip.
- Checklist: Transfer leadership before killing the meta-leader (upgrading it directly stalls stream ops for about 5 to 10 seconds); do non-leaders first.
- Checklist: Set a PodDisruptionBudget with `minAvailable: 2`; without it an eviction can drain all three pods and lose quorum.
- Checklist: Set `MemoryMax` above the node's real peak usage (memory store plus buffers plus GC headroom).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Authentication basics**

- The `authorization.timeout` field is how long the server gives a client to finish authenticating; default 2 seconds. Plain numbers are seconds; duration strings need quotes (unquoted `1m` parses as a number, not a minute).
- `nats server passwd` defaults to bcrypt cost 11 (`$2a$11$` prefix) and refuses passwords shorter than 10 characters.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Operator mode**

- `--defaults` on user add bakes a 1 MiB (1,048,576) max payload limit into each user JWT and no permissions (the user can publish/subscribe anywhere in its account).
- Generated full resolver config uses `allow_delete: true`, `interval: "2m"`, `limit: 1000`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Decentralized authentication**

- Expiry belongs to the minted credential, not the stored user; `--expire 720h` on `nats auth user credential` makes the user JWT lapse after 30 days.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth callout**

- Auth callout requires NATS Server 2.10.0 or later; it is disabled in FIPS-140 mode and can't be configured there.
- A client's own connect deadline also defaults to about two seconds, so with both defaults the client usually reports `i/o timeout` rather than an auth error; if the callout timeout is shorter than the client deadline, the client sees `Authorization Violation`. The reason lives only in the server log.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Encryption & TLS**

- `tls.timeout` is the handshake budget in seconds; default `2`, enough for a healthy network. Too short and a slow client can't finish; too long and a stalled handshake holds a slot open.
- For migration, `handshake_first` accepts `"auto"`/`"auto_fallback"` (fall back to plaintext `INFO` if no TLS bytes arrive within 50 ms) or a duration like `"300ms"` for a custom fallback delay.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connecting**

- The connect timeout caps how long a single dial may block before trying the next URL; default two seconds in most clients, five in Rust, twenty in JavaScript. "Two seconds is enough for a healthy network"
- `max_payload` is the largest single message the server accepts, one megabyte by default; the client enforces it locally so an oversized publish fails before it leaves the client.
- Pitfall: An oversized message fails the publish, not the connect. Don't treat that error as a connection problem; keep messages under `max_payload` (1 MB default), and for large bodies store the blob elsewhere and publish a reference. "for large bodies store the blob elsewhere and publish a reference"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reconnection**

- Base reconnect wait (`ReconnectWait`) defaults to two seconds. Go, Java, Python, JS use the same wait every sweep by default; Rust and .NET grow the wait each attempt by default.
- Default jitter: up to 100 ms on plaintext and up to 1 s on TLS in Go, Java, and JavaScript (TLS handshakes cost more, so spread retries wider); C# up to 100 ms regardless of TLS; Python and Rust add no jitter.
- The `nats` CLI connects with unlimited retries and a delay that starts at 500 ms and grows to a 20-second cap, each step randomized between half and one-and-a-half times its value.
- `MaxReconnect` is tracked per server, not per outage (Go, Java, JS, Python): a server that uses up its count is dropped from the pool and the connection gives up once none are left; Go and Python reset a server's count on successful connect. Defaults: 60 in Go/Java/Python, 10 in JavaScript, unlimited in Rust and C#.
- The reconnect buffer holds outbound publishes during RECONNECTING and flushes them in order on reconnect; default 8 MB in Go and Java, 2 MB in Python; Rust applies backpressure on a bounded queue instead.
- Pitfall: A full reconnect buffer stalls or drops your next publish (8 MB Go/Java, 2 MB Python). Back off publishing and let the buffer drain once the link returns instead of hammering publish in a loop.
- Pitfall: A stale connection on an overloaded server can go undetected for minutes. The client declares the link stale once outstanding pings exceed `MaxPingsOut`; with defaults (two-minute ping interval, one minute in Rust; two allowed outstanding pings) detection waits for the third unanswered ping, up to about six minutes (three in Rust).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Drain & Shutdown**

- The drain timeout bounds the subscription phase; if handlers don't finish in time, drain discards the remaining messages and proceeds to flush and close, surfacing `ErrDrainTimeout` (nats.go). The pending-publish flush has its own hardcoded five-second bound in nats.go; in nats.java the `drain()` timeout covers the final flush too.
- The default drain timeout is 30 seconds in nats.go, but size it to your slowest handler's latency rather than a round number. "Size the timeout to your handler latency rather than to a round number."
- Go `Flush()` has a fixed ten-second timeout; `FlushTimeout()` takes a bound you pick. C# has no flush (`PingAsync()` is the same round trip). Rust's `client.flush()` resolves when buffered writes reach the socket, without waiting for PONG, so it confirms bytes left the client, not server receipt.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Slow Consumers**

- Default pending limits are generous: 500,000 messages and 64 MB in Go (similar in Python and Java); Rust defaults to 65,536 messages; C# to a 1,024-message channel; JavaScript leaves the buffer unbounded and never drops client-side (its slow-consumer option only raises a status).
- Size the pending limit to roughly the handler's latency times the subject's peak rate. Too tight drops messages the handler could have caught up on; too loose wastes memory on a backlog it never catches up on. "A limit sized to roughly the handler's latency times the subject's peak rate"
- Pitfall: The default limits are a backstop rather than a workload-specific tuning. Always set pending limits on a subscription that does real per-message work, sized to handler latency and peak rate.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Request-Reply Resilience**

- The retry loop must be bounded: cap the attempts (five is a reasonable default) and add jitter so a fleet of requesters doesn't retry in lockstep. "five is a reasonable default"
- Pitfall: A timeout shorter than the responder's real latency makes every busy moment look like a failure. Measure the responder's latency and set the timeout to two or three times its p99. "set the timeout to two or three times its p99"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TLS & Auth**

- nats.go, nats.js, nats.net, and nats.java close the connection when the same auth error repeats twice in a row (opt-out `IgnoreAuthErrorAbort`/`ignoreAuthErrorAbort`); the abort applies regardless of the retry budget. nats.py and nats.rs have no abort rule and keep cycling until `max_reconnect_attempts` (60 default) / `max_reconnects` (unlimited default) runs out.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where Next (Resilient Clients)**

- Checklist: Keep messages under the server's `max_payload` and store large bodies elsewhere; an oversized publish fails before it's sent and isn't a connection problem.
- Checklist: Set `MaxReconnect` to `-1` on a long-lived service in Go, Java, Python, and JavaScript (bounded defaults); Rust and C# already retry forever.
- Checklist: Handle a full reconnect buffer and back off publishing; the buffer is bounded (8 MB Go/Java, 2 MB Python) and the overflowing publish fails (Go `ErrReconnectBufExceeded`) or blocks (Rust).
- Checklist: Lower the ping interval under heavy load to catch a wedged connection in seconds, not the ~six minutes the defaults take (two-minute interval, third unanswered ping closes; Rust pings every minute, so ~three).
- Checklist: Always set pending limits on a subscription that does real per-message work; the defaults (500,000 messages, 64 MB in Go) are a backstop.
- Checklist: Measure the responder's p99 and set the request timeout to two or three times it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Monitoring & Observability Deep Dive**

- The monitoring port listens on `:8222` by default once enabled.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Monitoring endpoints**

- Since 2.10 routes are pooled: each peer contributes several route entries (a pool of three plus a dedicated system-account route), so a default three-node cluster shows eight entries on one node, four per peer.
- Pitfall: An unscoped `/jsz` is slow at scale. `/jsz?accounts=true&streams=true&consumers=true` walks every entity and can time out a scrape on a node with thousands of consumers, yielding no data. Don't fetch the whole tree on a schedule; scope with `?acc=` and page with `?offset`/`?limit`.

- Example Prometheus scrape config uses `scrape_interval: 15s` against the exporter target.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Profiling the server**

- For CPU profiles over the system account, the CLI's `--timeout` is the sampling window (default `5s`); the server rejects a window longer than 15 seconds. A longer capture must come from `prof_port`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first bucket**

- History is how many prior values the bucket keeps per key; the default is 1 (only the current value). "One means the bucket holds only the current value of a key and forgets the rest. That's the default"
- History depth can go as high as 64 and no higher. "The depth can go as high as 64, but no higher"
- A key may contain only letters, digits, and `-`, `/`, `_`, `=`, and `.`, with no leading or trailing dot and no two dots in a row. "`a..b` is rejected even though `a.b` is fine"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — History and revisions**

- History depth caps at 64; values written before a history-depth raise are already gone because depth 1 dropped each prior write.
- History holds the prior revisions of a single key up to the depth; it's not an audit log of the whole bucket and doesn't grow without bound. "once a key has more revisions than the depth allows, the oldest one is removed"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TTL and limits**

- Per-key TTL needs nats-server 2.11 or newer, the release that added limit markers; on an older server enabling markers is rejected and the timed create fails.
- Three bucket limits matter most: max bucket size (total bytes across all keys and kept revisions), max value size (largest single value), and history depth.
- History depth caps at 64 and doubles as a per-key cap: the most messages any single key may hold.
- Limits reject, they do not make room for an oversized value; a put over max value size or that would exceed max bucket size returns an error and leaves existing values in place.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Key-Value)**

- Checklist: size the bucket for the working set, not the average; at its byte limit the bucket rejects the next put instead of dropping old values.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Chunking**

- The default chunk size is 128 KB. "The default chunk size is **128 KB**."
- At the 128 KB default, a 3 MB file lands in roughly 24 chunks.
- Chunk size is configurable per put; the 128 KB default is "a reasonable middle for most files, and most of the time you leave it alone."
- A chunk size at the extremes causes problems: too small wastes storage on per-message framing overhead and slows puts/gets; too large exceeds the server's `max_payload` (1 MB by default) or a smaller stream max message size and the put fails outright.
- Don't tune chunk size to chase a benchmark; if you must raise it, keep each chunk under `max_payload`. "the 128 KB default fits almost every file and stays well under the default payload limit"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Metadata and links**

- Metadata is held in the one trailing metadata message, so it adds no extra storage cost and no extra read cost.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Object Store)**

- Checklist: leave chunk size at its default unless you have a reason; too small floods the stream, too large can exceed the stream's max message size.
- Checklist: expect a soft delete to mark deleted and purge chunks but not reclaim disk until the purge completes; size the backing stream accordingly.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Backup & Recovery Deep Dive**

- Memory streams can't be snapshotted, so file storage is required for any stream you want to back up.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Stream backup and restore**

- The server keeps a window of unacknowledged snapshot chunks in flight: 8 MiB by default, which is 64 of the default 128 KiB chunks.
- If no chunk ack arrives for about five seconds the backup aborts; windowed backpressure keeps a large stream from overwhelming a slow disk or high-latency link.
- Flow control can time out on slow disks or distant links (`408 No Flow Response`); the fix is smaller chunks and a smaller window (e.g. `--chunk-size 64k --window-size 1m`).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mirrors as a DR tool**

- `Lag: 0` means the mirror holds every upstream message; any number above zero is the data you'd lose if the primary vanished now.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Backup & Recovery)**

- Checklist: reduce `--chunk-size` and `--window-size` on a slow disk or high-latency link before the flow-control timeout aborts the snapshot.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connect MQTT devices to NATS**

- NATS implements MQTT v3.1.1 and supports QoS 0, 1, and 2; a device requesting MQTT v5 is rejected at connect with CONNACK return code 1, "unacceptable protocol version".
- Before 2.10, a `.` in an MQTT topic was rejected; the `//` encoding was added in 2.10.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first MQTT client**

- MQTT gets its own listener on port 1883 (the conventional MQTT port), separate from the client port 4222.
- A message published by a NATS client always arrives at an MQTT subscriber as QoS 0, whatever QoS the subscription asked for, because a NATS publish carries no QoS.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topics and subjects**

- Characters the server refuses in topics: space, tab, newline, carriage return, form feed, and DEL. The space has never been accepted on any version because it would break the NATS wire protocol control line.
- MQTT `sensors/#` also matches the parent `sensors` while NATS `sensors.>` doesn't, so the server creates two NATS subscriptions (`sensors.>` and `sensors`) for that filter. A filter of just `#` converts to `>` and needs only one.
- A subscription ending in `#` counts twice against `max_ack_pending`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — QoS, sessions, and retained messages**

- QoS 0: at most once, nothing stored, no ack. QoS 1: at least once, stored until PUBACK, duplicates possible. QoS 2: exactly once via a four-packet handshake, most round trips and most state.
- `ack_wait` (redelivery timeout for unacked QoS 1/2 messages) defaults to 30 seconds; redelivered messages are flagged as duplicates (DUP).
- `max_ack_pending` caps in-flight QoS 1 and 2 messages per subscription; it defaults to 1024 with valid range 0 to 65535, and `0` means "use the default" (1024).
- The total `max_ack_pending` across all of a session's subscriptions can't exceed 65535; a subscription that would exceed it is refused with `0x80` in the SUBACK. A `#` subscription counts twice.
- At the default 1024, a session has room for 63 plain subscriptions, or 31 if they all end in `#`; the check is strict, so the subscription that would reach the cap exactly is refused.
- Duplicate client IDs with reconnect logic evict each other in a loop; the server records the client ID as flapping and refuses to hand the session over again for about a second, which slows the cycle without stopping it.
- Only one message is retained per topic; a new retained publish replaces the previous one. Retention is per topic name, not per filter, so a wildcard subscriber receives the retained message for every matching topic.
- Raising `max_ack_pending` without counting subscriptions: the per-session total is capped at 65535 and every `#` subscription costs double; new subscriptions fail with `0x80`, easy to misread as a permissions problem.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth and clustering (MQTT)**

- `allowed_connection_types` values: `STANDARD`, `WEBSOCKET`, `LEAFNODE`, `LEAFNODE_WS`, `MQTT`, `MQTT_WS`, `IN_PROCESS`; a browser-based MQTT client needs `MQTT_WS` rather than `MQTT`. Omitting the option allows every type (the default). Aliases: `connection_types`, `clients`.
- Two limits: a listener-scoped username or token can't be combined with a top-level `users` list, and `no_auth_user` doesn't work in operator mode.
- MQTT state streams are replicated automatically once JetStream is clustered; the replica count is derived from the number of addresses in the server's own `routes` list, clamped between 1 and 3, not from how many servers the cluster has.
- A server listing two routes brings its MQTT streams up at `R=2`, not `R=3`; list all peers in `routes` or set `stream_replicas: 3` explicitly. Asking for more replicas than the cluster can satisfy makes the streams fail to create, surfacing as MQTT clients unable to connect.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (MQTT)**

- Only MQTT v3.1.1 is supported; a client requesting v5 is rejected at connect.
- Checklist: count subscriptions against `max_ack_pending`; at the default of 1024 a session fits 63 subscriptions (31 if they end in `#`) before the 65535 per-session cap.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connect over WebSocket**

- Six of the seven Tier 1 clients implement WebSocket (Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Java, Rust, C#/.NET); the C client has no WebSocket transport.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first WebSocket connection**

- nats.js `wsconnect()` fills in a port you leave out and never picks 4222: `ws://host` -> port 80; `wss://host` -> port 443; bare `host` -> `wss://host:443`; `nats://host:4222` -> `ws://host:4222` (scheme dropped, port kept). "Write the scheme and the port every time."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Browsers and origins**

- The origin match is exact on scheme, host, and port and is a string comparison, not name resolution: `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` are different origins; a mismatch yields `403 Forbidden`.
- A URL with no port means port 80 for `http://` and 443 for `https://`, so `https://ops.acme.example` and `https://ops.acme.example:8443` are different origins; serving on both means listing both.
- `compress: true` (alias `compression`) offers the `permessage-deflate` extension, negotiated per connection; clients that don't ask get uncompressed connections at no cost.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TLS and proxies**

- `no_tls: true` is correct only when the proxy-to-server hop is a network you trust: a private subnet, a service mesh, or the same host.
- A NATS connection is idle between messages; a proxy that closes idle connections after 60 seconds will close a working subscription. Set the proxy idle timeout longer than the server's WebSocket ping interval (`ping_interval` in `websocket {}` from 2.12, server-wide ping interval before).
- `handshake_timeout` bounds reading the request, the TLS handshake, and writing the response; a value tuned on a laptop can reject real clients behind a slow proxy under load.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leaf nodes over WebSocket**

- A leafnode URL without a port gets `:7422` appended whatever its scheme, so `wss://nats.acme.example` quietly dials the leafnode port and fails; write the port explicitly on every remote URL.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (WebSocket)**

- Checklist: set the proxy's idle timeout longer than the server's WebSocket ping interval.
- Checklist: size `handshake_timeout` against the proxy's latency under load.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — What is NATS?**

- NATS optimizes for a small single binary, low latency at high message rates, and secure defaults; it runs from one server on a laptop up to clusters spanning regions.
- Performance: millions of messages per second, sub-millisecond latency, small memory footprint (typically ~15MB).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subjects**

- Keep subjects reasonable: limit to ~16 tokens and under 256 characters total.
- The subject interest graph is in-memory and dynamic: NATS builds a routing table only for subjects with active subscribers, kept entirely in RAM.
- Subjects are essentially free: creating new subjects has virtually no overhead and NATS handles millions of unique subjects.
- Wildcard subscriptions use efficient trie-based matching.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publish-Subscribe**

- Core NATS is at-most-once delivery without persistence; for guaranteed delivery use JetStream.
- NATS has a default max message size of 1MB (configurable). "For large data, consider using object stores or passing references."
- NATS handles millions of subscriptions efficiently; use wildcards to reduce subscription overhead when possible.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue Groups**

- When a worker leaves, NATS stops routing to it within milliseconds.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Getting Started**

- The default NATS client port is 4222 and the HTTP monitoring port is 8222.

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to build a NATS Supercluster | Rethink Connectivity Episode 5**

- Replicated JetStream assets (R3, even R5) survive node loss; the replica count is a trade-off against the performance characteristics you want. "you can make an R3 or even an R5 and it's just going to be dependent on your performance characteristics that you want for your system" (~03:50)
- Three clusters is the recommended shape for the redundancy you need; a 3x3 super cluster shows 6 outgoing and 6 incoming gateway connections per cluster (18 total), meaning a full gateway mesh. "in order to achieve the amount of redundancy that we need it would be good to have three clusters... six outgoing gateway six incoming gateways there's a total of 18" (~13:00)

- Once a local responder reappears, super cluster geo-affinity routes all local requests to the local instance rather than the remote cluster, reducing latency (all 10 subsequent requests hit the east instance). "NATS clusters have geo affinity to make sure your traffic is handled as closely to the requester as possible" (~13:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Mutually Trusted NGS Credentials**

- NGS free accounts had limits too low for the setup, specifically message size and leaf node connection count; developer plans allow leaf node connections and a decent payload size. "the limits of the free accounts are too low, specifically the message size and the number of allowed leaf node connections" (~06:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS Leafnodes**

- Routes (clusters) assume good signal-to-noise, low RTT and decent bandwidth, i.e. a single region or availability zone; stretching a cluster coast-to-coast or across continents does not work well, and NATS was originally the same as Kubernetes or Kafka in this respect. "they don't like to be stretched from east coast to west coast or to Asia Pacific to Europe, and to be frank NATS was the same way with its initial clustering algorithms" (~02:50)
- Requests via a local leaf node returned noticeably faster than direct requests to NGS because TLS and key-exchange costs are amortized once on the leaf connection. "it seemed very fast, right, because we've amortized all of the cost of TLS and all of the complexities around the key exchange" (~16:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Andrew Gracey on Two Node K3S**

- Edge customers demand two-node systems for three reasons: reusing existing active/passive hardware, physical constraints (space, power, cooling), and economics where a third node adds ~50% cost, especially with GPUs. "that additional 50% cost all of a sudden prices you out of the hardware refresh" (~03:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Replace Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis and more w/NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity Ep 10**

- With R3, JetStream picks three available nodes; losing one node still allows reads and writes, losing two still allows reads, losing all three is disaster-recovery territory. "if a second node goes down you can actually still read from that stream" (~06:08)
- Synadia Cloud requires max bytes to be set on every stream so a tenant cannot exhaust the service. "it does require that I set max bytes on all of my streams" (~15:21)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to configure NATS JetStream streams | Rethink Connectivity Ep 11**

- Limits drive stream behaviour: max messages, max bytes (required on Synadia Cloud), max age (per-message TTL for retention like 30 or 365 days), max messages per subject, max message size, max consumers. "limits drives a lot of behavior inside of the stream" (~07:08)
- Deduplication uses the Nats-Msg-Id header with a sliding window that defaults to two minutes and is configurable. "by default this duplicate window is going to be two minutes" (~14:15)
- Use replication factors of 3, 5 or 7; with R3, one node offline still handles writes and two nodes offline still handles reads; default is R1. "you're going to want to use multiples of like three five seven" (~18:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Build Priority Background Jobs & Dead Letter Queues with NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity ep 12**

- Put a message-count cap on queues (example 20,000) for monitoring and SLA purposes. "these queues have some sort of limit on them ... you might want to set kind of a cap on this" (~08:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared: Part 1 | Rethink Connectivity**

- For market data with ~100,000 instruments you would not create 100,000 Kafka topics; you use one topic per exchange with the instrument as key, and then filtering for one instrument means the broker sends everything to a client that discards most of it. "you're transferring all the data over the network to somewhere else where you are discarding most of it" (~15:16)
- JetStream maintains indexes on subject names inside streams, so getting the first or last message for nasdaq.microsoft is a single fast operation, not a scan; filtering happens server-side and only matching messages are transmitted. "internally JetStream maintains indexes on those subject names that are contained into the streams" (~16:16)
- Kafka's throughput comes from batching and a deliberately simple write path aimed at throughput, not latency; Kafka latencies are measured in milliseconds. "latencies in Kafka typically measures in milliseconds" (~34:41)
- Core NATS and even JetStream latencies are measured in microseconds: one-way or two-way in the 100–200 µs range over a network, under 100 µs one-way on a fast network. "over this network you're talking 1 to 200 microsecond ranges ... with fast network below 100 microseconds" (~34:41)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared Pt 2: Consumers | Rethink Connectivity**

- Direct get of the last or first message for an exact subject is how KV works; it is a get, not a query, and over loopback runs in the tens of microseconds. "the order of magnitude is tens of microseconds when going over loopback" (~15:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream for Key-Value Store Tech Preview**

- Max-messages-per-subject limits keep N historical values per subject (e.g. 100 per device) instead of a global total, so busy writers do not push out idle ones. "keep a hundred historical values per device rather than keep a thousand messages in total" (~00:00)
- KV workloads are read-heavy; APIs were added to make reads in that scenario very fast. "kv tend to be very read heavy operations so you will write few times but very often read" (~05:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Mirror Streams Explained — One-Way Replication Made Simple**

- Mirrors tolerate a temporarily unreachable origin and retry after roughly 10 to 20 seconds. "the mirror waits about 10 to 20 seconds before retrying" (~03:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers**

- Co-locating a stream near the data source (per region/neighbourhood) reduces collection latency and improves availability compared with publishing across the country. "whatever the granularity ... to make a stream accessible to that's going to obviously reduce latency of collection ... provide availability" (~10:11)
- A single stream cannot exceed the throughput of the disk it writes to, so ingest rate alone may force you to split into multiple streams. "you can't obviously exceed past the throughput of your disk ... it might be necessary from a purely physical technical perspective that you actually have to break up the ingestion" (~13:17)
- A sourcing stream that aggregates tens, hundreds or thousands of origin streams needs correspondingly large disk. "if you're sourcing data from tens hundreds thousands of streams ... you're probably going to need a fairly beefy amount of disk space" (~23:32)
- Every R3 stream adds load; a per-dwelling stream model multiplies replication cost, so size streams to hardware I/O limits rather than administrative units. "once you say let's have an R3 ... immediately the load on the system increases with each and every stream" (~27:36)
- Do not plan on 100k or a million consumers, one per entity; you will never deploy that many client applications, so pick a wildcard granularity your app can handle in order. "nobody's running 100,000 a million containers ... the middle ground can be having a client application that can apply a wild card at the level of granularity" (~63:23)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.10 Webinar**

- Compression does not degrade ingest throughput because the active block being appended to is left uncompressed; a block is compressed asynchronously only once it is full. "the active block that is actually being written to appended to is basically not compressed and only once the message block is done and filled up then it actually gets asynchronously compressed" (~03:03)
- The new storage format cut restart/recovery of a 2.1 TB, 300-million-message stream from roughly 15 minutes on 2.9 to 1.1 seconds on 2.10, because 2.9 scanned and checksummed every block. "2.1 terabytes in size with 300 million messages ... roughly 15 minutes to actually restart the stream ... with 2.10 it takes 1.1 seconds" (~05:05)
- Before 2.10 any two servers shared one TCP route connection, so a very active account could cause head-of-line blocking for other accounts sharing it. "any two pairs of servers only had a single TCP connection between them ... there can be some unintentional unfairness or head of line blocking" (~19:22)
- Max stream replicas remain five in 2.10; in a stretch cluster those replicas can sit in different regions. "the max stream replicas continue to be five yep but now you can place those replicas in servers that go across completely different regions" (~26:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- The NATS unit-test suite ran 117 hours of tests in a single day through parallel jobs; "unit" tests spin up whole clusters and dozens of servers. "the NATS test suite ran 117 hours worth of unit tests in a single day" (~10:11)
- Users put and delete hundreds of millions of KV keys, producing streams with data at the head and tail and a huge deleted gap in the middle; this "interior deletes" state dominated Raft snapshots. "the state snapshot for the messages we're retaining and deleting ends up being really big because it's tracking more information about things that we no longer want to keep" (~26:29)
- KV was released as a convenience API and a year later a user ran a 10 TB KV store spanning the globe; it worked but needed to work better. "how about 10 terabytes key value store span across the whole globe will it work too yeah the thing is it worked it's just we needed it to work better" (~30:33)
- Users who learn a system scales to 2 TB then "put one more zero at the end"; supporting that is the ongoing 2.11 focus over new features. "it's so easy to just put one more zero at the end not so easy to support that one more zero" (~68:11)

- Pull consumers now match or beat push performance (use-case dependent) with better client resource utilization because the client controls flow, so client buffers can be much smaller at the same throughput. "the buffer on the client side can be much smaller while having the same throughput" (~16:19)

- Host reports an early bench on an M1 Mac at roughly 48 gigabits per second for the simplest single-server pub/sub setup (unverified anecdote). "I think I was getting ridiculous numbers like 48 gigabits per second or something crazy" (~07:23)
- A single client can push on the order of 10 million messages per second if you try very hard, somewhat less on the subscriber side; persistent layers cannot match this. "you can get like 10 million messages per second if you try very hard on single client, a little bit less on subscriber side" (~20:37)

- The server keeps core, JetStream, KV and Object Store in one process on purpose: splitting into services would add operational complexity and inter-service latency that would make current performance unreachable. "it would be impossible to reach the current performance limits of NATS JetStream and KV and Object Store if it was not all in one package" (~17:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03S3: NATS 2.11 Release**

- Per-message TTL is implemented with a timed hash wheel so very large numbers of expiries can be tracked with little memory. "it actually uses an exotic data structure called a timed hash wheel ... track an awful lot of key expiries without actually using too much memory" (~15:21)
- The server's subject interest handling uses an in-house adaptive radix tree (with node-size tweaks learned from real customer subject hierarchies) and modified Patricia trees for the interest graph. "the adaptive radix tree implementation actually has a couple of slight tweaks that differ from the paper" (~16:23)
- KV was introduced (KubeCon Valencia) as a small experiment for IoT caches; users now load millions of keys, so 2.11 is the first release adding default soft limits and safe defaults to features. "now we are at I don't know millions of keys ... this is the first release where we started adding default limit soft cuts" (~30:40)
- Batch get responses are capped (the speaker recalls 64 messages, and a byte limit) after which you paginate with another request. "maximum amount of messages or maximum amount of bytes that can be sent back before you need to paginate in some way, 64 messages I think" (~33:45)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS tools and benchmarking with JNM! NATS Community Office Hours (Reupload)**

- The whole NATS server with JetStream ships as a single ~12 MB binary; Kafka-experienced conference attendees did not believe it until shown. "everything in a single 12 MB binary ... They don't believe it actually at first" (~02:03)
- Synadia publishes no official throughput numbers because distributed-system results depend on network, traffic, disk and cloud variability; they ship a tool to run in your own environment instead. "three kinds of lies in the software business: big lies, small lies, and benchmarks" (~38:47)
- On a ~3-year-old M1 Ultra Mac Studio over loopback, a single publisher with no subscribers reached about 5 million 128-byte msgs/s (~600 MB/s); at 1 MB messages it did about 3,700-4,000 msgs/s but 3.6-3.8 GB/s. "it's 5 million messages a second, they're 128 bytes ... 3.8 gigabytes per second" (~42:54)
- Loopback numbers show what the software can do with near-infinite bandwidth; real deployments are lower purely because of the network, so a faster network gives faster numbers on the same machines. "buy a faster network, you'll get faster numbers with the same machines" (~44:55)
- A publish-only bench with no subscribers is artificially high because the server drops messages with no interest; with four core subscribers each message is copied four times and it is still very fast. "no one is subscribing ... the server says there's no interest for the message and subject, they're dropping there" (~46:59)
- On the same local setup, consuming with explicit acks ran up to about 200,000 msgs/s while an ordered consumer reached about 650,000 msgs/s from a file-backed stream. "up to 200,000 per second with explicit acks ... with an ordered consumer we're in 650,000 per second" (~62:24)
- A community member hit Windows desktop kernel networking throttling before NATS itself throttled, at roughly 5-6 million core msgs/s. "he throttled the Windows kernel before NATS actually hit that throttling point" (~68:28)
- With a subscriber attached, JetStream publish throughput dropped from about 139k to about 84k msgs/s in the demo, with the consumer side being the limiting factor. "with no one listening you got 139 ... with someone listening, 84" (~70:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Benchmark Core NATS & NATS JetStream using the NATS CLI tool**

- Single-threaded synchronous request/reply on a 2021 Intel MacBook Pro over loopback did about 7,500 round trips per second, i.e. ~133 µs average process-to-process round trip through NATS. "7,500 about ... that's a 133 about microseconds an average of a round trip" (~04:04)
- Core pub/sub with one publisher and one subscriber (each on its own connection) reached about 3.9-4.2 million 128-byte msgs/s, roughly 500 MB/s, on the laptop. "we got 3.9 million and we got 4.2 and now we get 4 million" (~07:07)
- With one publisher and 10 subscribers (fan-out), the aggregate was about 5.3 million msgs/s: the publisher at ~500k msgs/s and each subscriber at ~480k msgs/s. "the publisher probably shot about 500,000 per second and the subscribers are for 480 thousands" (~08:09)
- With 128-byte messages the bottleneck is CPU (per-message overhead), not bandwidth; raise the message size to measure bandwidth-bound throughput. "you're going to be CPU bound rather than bandwidth bound as your limit" (~09:09)
- Two publishers, four subscribers with larger messages showed the server receiving ~26k msgs/s and sending ~103k msgs/s, about 2 GB/s aggregate on the laptop. "it's receiving 25,000 messages per second, around 26,000, and sending out 103 or so ... two gigabytes per second" (~10:11)
- Synchronous JetStream publishing is bounded by round-trip time like any request/reply; raise throughput with many synchronous clients or with batching (async publish with a batch size). "the way to increase throughput in those situations is to either have a lot of clients ... or start using batching" (~14:16)
- Publish batch size 10 gives a dramatic improvement, 100 another large one, 1000 only a little more: diminishing returns set in around a batch of 100. "you start getting to where you have a diminishing return of increasing the batch size" (~14:16)
- Two publishers with the default batch of 100 reached nearly the same rate as one publisher with batches of 1000. "we get pretty close to the maximum that we saw with batches of a thousand, except in this case we have two guys just using batches of 100" (~15:17)
- Ten ephemeral ordered push consumers each reading 700,000 messages from a memory stream on the laptop totalled roughly 1.2-3 million msgs/s delivered (7 million messages in total). "1.2 whatever three million messages ... this is distributing seven million messages total" (~20:21)
- A single pull consumer with batch 1 and per-message ack uses little CPU and is slow; batch 100 gives a huge improvement, and adding more pullers scales further (from ~210k msgs/s on the laptop). "going from 210 to, if I had more than just a single laptop ... would obviously be able to scale a lot further" (~23:26)
- File storage publishes slower than memory, but reading back from disk is still fast: a push consumer delivered 4 × 400,000 messages in about 4 seconds (~400k msgs/s) on the laptop. "retrieving from disk is still quite fast ... about 400,000 per second" (~26:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS: Ordered, Scalable Stream Processing**

- Size the elastic work-queue buffer (cap by bytes or message count) to more than a few seconds of processing: when the cap is hit, sourcing is suspended for up to a few seconds before it resumes, and a too-small buffer starves workers. "keep it above a few seconds worth of processing" (~14:14)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Pull Consumer Priority Groups: Overflow, Pinned & Prioritized**

- Keep the priority timeout comfortably above pull expiry, because the pin resets only when the pinned client issues a new pull within the window; default timeout is 2 minutes, which pairs with pulls expiring in a minute or less. "The default timeout is 2 minutes, which pairs nicely with polls that expire in a minute or less" (~06:04)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Atomic Batch Publishing | NATS 2.12**

- A batch is rejected if the batch id exceeds 64 characters, if sequence numbers have gaps, or if the stream uses async persist mode; as of 2.12.1 duplicate messages in a batch also fail validation. "A batch ID over 64 characters, gaps in your sequence numbers, or running on a stream with async persist mode" (~02:03)
- Limits: up to 1,000 messages per batch, 50 batches in flight per stream, 1,000 batches per server, and a batch is abandoned after 10 seconds of inactivity; all are configurable in server config. "you can have up to a thousand messages per batch. Each stream can have 50 batches in flight at once. Each server can have a thousand batches total" (~02:03)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — We need to talk about Microservices... (And how NATS.io can simplify things)**

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The ONE feature that makes NATS more powerful than Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ & Redis**

- Max ack pending caps outstanding unacked deliveries; the default is 100. "by default this is actually set to 100" (~15:18)
- Demo: processing ~31,620 messages one at a time with max ack pending 1 against Synadia Cloud was slow; with the default it finished the whole batch quickly while still acking each message individually. "we've processed the entire batch of 31,000 messages we are all caught up" (~30:31)
- Reporting consumer: ephemeral, headers only, max request batch 1000, ack none, deliver by start time (7 days ago), filter subject orders.us.*.shipped. "max request batch we're going to bump this up to a thousand" (~32:34)

"a lot of times just the chatter that's going back and forth on one of these systems actually brings the system down" (~24:40)
- Account limits (max connections, max leaf connections, bandwidth, exports/imports) are enforced globally and instantly: an 11th connection against a limit of 10 is denied anywhere in the world, and a revoked user is disconnected within about 10 ms globally.
