- Export type follows the messaging pattern: a stream export is one-way publish/subscribe (exporter publishes, importers subscribe); a service export mirrors request/reply and flows both ways.
- The boundary stays closed by default and opens one named subject at a time; an account's `exports` array is the complete list of what leaves it. "you can read an account's `exports` array and know the complete list of what leaves it"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Operator mode**

- Operator mode removes the user list from the server: an operator signs each account, an account signs its users, and the server (trusting only the operator) verifies signatures at connect time. "No user lives in the server config."
- NKey IDs start with `O` (operator), `A` (account), `U` (user); anything starting with `S` (`SO`, `SA`, `SU`) is a seed — roughly the private key — so be very careful. "If you ever see an ID which starts with an `S` ... then _be very careful_"
- The recommended resolver type is the full nats-based resolver (server keeps every account JWT in a local directory; new ones delivered over NATS). Memory, cache, and URL resolvers also exist, but `nats auth` can only push to a full resolver.
- The shift from config mode: the server holds one trusted key, not a list of users.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Decentralized authentication**

- Use decentralized auth when each team should manage its own users without touching the server; the server needs only a way to tell a real user from a forged one (a signature check), not knowledge of every user in advance.
- Decentralized auth scales because a signature check works for a user the server has never seen; no config entry has to exist before the user connects.
- The clean way to assign permissions in operator mode is a scoped signing key: an account signing key with a role name and a fixed permission set; every user issued by that key gets exactly those permissions. "the clean way to assign them is a **scoped signing key**"
- Bearer tokens are a convenience for browser and websocket clients that have nowhere safe to keep a seed; they reduce the credential to a single document that must never leak.
- Use operator signing keys, keep at least one offline, and expose only one operator signing key to risk; then migrate between signing keys of the existing operator instead of between operators. "keep at least one off-line, and only keep one operator signing key exposed to risk"
- Pitfall: Signing users with the account's identity key. It works, but permissions then live on each user and whoever holds the account seed can issue a user with any permissions; a scoped key pins permissions up front so a leaked signing key can only issue users with the chosen scope (ADR-14).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth callout**

- Auth callout delegates the authentication decision to an external NATS service when the source of truth for identity lives in a system NATS can't read (OIDC, LDAP, custom credential service).
- Run the auth service in its own dedicated account (the `account` field) holding nothing else, so no other user can subscribe to request traffic; the callout service can bind clients to any authorized account, so it should be isolated anyway (ADR-26 recommendation). "run `auth-svc` in its own dedicated account"
- The callout libraries recommend dropping requests for bad credentials, because the added delay slows brute-force guessing. "The callout libraries recommend dropping for bad credentials"
- Auth mode selection: static config list → centralized authentication; a trust chain you control with `nats auth` → operator mode; verdict must come from a system NATS doesn't own → auth callout. "Auth callout is for when the verdict must come from a system NATS doesn't own."
- Use the x25519 `xkey` option to encrypt the request and response so credentials on `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH` are sealed even from a leaked subscription; reach for it whenever the wire carries secrets.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Encryption & TLS**

- Per-link TLS independence is deliberate: a laptop client and an inter-datacenter gateway have different threat models, so each link gets its own configuration.
- `verify_and_map: true` requires and verifies the client certificate, then reads an identity out of it as the NATS user: email SANs first, then DNS SANs, then URI SANs, then the subject DN (RFC 2253). A SAN is used only if it matches a user; otherwise it falls back to the subject.
- `verify_and_map` includes everything `verify: true` does plus the mapping, so don't set both. Use plain `verify` only when an external system already maps certificates to users. "Reach for plain `verify` only when an external system already maps certificates to users"
- Some disk controllers handle encryption at rest at the block layer at high performance without server CPU cost; evaluate carefully whether having nats-server do the encryption is right for your deployment. "carefully evaluate if having the nats-server do the encryption itself is the right solution"
- Keep the at-rest key out of the config file via an environment variable (`key: $JS_KEY`).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Security)**

- Four questions define a connection's security posture: account (whose traffic), user (who are you), permissions (which subjects), TLS (is the wire protected). "If you can answer those four questions for a connection, you understand its security posture."
- Centralized auth: user list in server config, change via config reload (`nats-server --signal reload`, no restart); right for one server and a handful of users. "It's the right tool for one server and a handful of users."
- Decentralized auth: operator signs accounts, accounts sign users, server trusts only the operator; adding a user touches no server config; right for many tenants or when teams issue their own credentials.
- Checklist: Prefer a wildcard matching the user's real subject space over an enumerated allow-list.
- Checklist: Match the export type to the data flow: `stream` for one-way, `service` for request/reply.
- Checklist: Sign users with a scoped signing key, not the account root seed.
- Checklist: Run the auth service in its own account, and reach for `xkey` when the wire carries secrets.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Resilient Clients Deep Dive**

- Resilience isn't new application code; it's the connection configured to survive faults: detect a break, buffer while broken, recover without losing the application's place, shut down without losing in-flight work.
- The connection is a state machine: DISCONNECTED, CONNECTING, CONNECTED, RECONNECTING, DRAINING, CLOSED; every fault is a transition. A server dying moves CONNECTED to RECONNECTING; a clean shutdown moves to DRAINING then CLOSED.
- A resilient client: opens with a name, a server pool, and a sane connect timeout; reconnects with backoff and jitter and flushes buffered publishes on rejoin; wires all events to one place and feeds state to a readiness probe; drains on SIGTERM; bounds subscriber memory with pending limits; distinguishes absent responder from slow responder; presents credentials over CA-validated TLS.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connecting**

- Name every connection (e.g. `order-svc`) so it's identifiable in `nats server report connections` and server logs; by default a connection is anonymous.
- The server pool is the list of URLs the client may connect to; with several URLs the client tries them until one answers — failover at connect time.
- Turn randomization off (`NoRandomize`/`dont_randomize`/`retain_servers_order`) only when you deliberately want a preferred-server order; most applications should leave it on so a restart of every instance doesn't overload one server. "Most applications should leave it on"
- Pool and timeout complement each other: one unreachable server costs one timeout, then the client moves to the next URL.
- Handle connect failures at the boundary, branching on whether the client could reach any server in the pool, instead of letting them surface deep in the application.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reconnection**

- Reconnect is on by default in every client; leave it on. Turning it off makes the connection close on the first disconnect, which is rarely what a service wants. "Leave reconnect on"
- In production the common reason no server answers at startup is ordering after a deploy (the client restarts faster than servers); opt in to retry-on-failed-first-connect (`RetryOnFailedConnect`, `waitOnFirstConnect`, `retry_on_initial_connect`, `RetryOnInitialConnect`, Java `connectReconnectOnConnect`) so the service sits in RECONNECTING instead of crash-looping.
- Backoff: after trying every URL once with none answering, the client pauses before the next sweep; without it a client would spin a tight dial loop against a pool that isn't ready.
- Jitter exists so a thousand clients that lost the same server don't retry in lockstep and overload the remaining server.
- For a long-lived service set `MaxReconnect` to `-1` (unlimited) in clients that default to a bounded count so a long outage never closes the connection. "For a long-lived service, unlimited is what you want."
- Under heavy load, lower the ping interval (and `MaxPingsOut` where exposed) so a wedged link is detected in seconds instead of minutes.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connection Events**

- Disconnect is recoverable: log it, count it in a metric, let the reconnect loop work. Closed is final: no further events, no publish succeeds; the process must exit for a supervisor to restart it, or an alert must reach an operator. "Closed — exit or alert."
- A status poll is a snapshot that races the state machine. Poll to report state (dashboards, metrics, readiness probes); react through events. "Poll to report state; react through events."
- Readiness check mapping: Ready while CONNECTED; Not ready while RECONNECTING (route work elsewhere, keep the process up — killing it throws away the reconnect buffer); Dead on CLOSED (closed observer exits, supervisor replaces). "RECONNECTING heals on its own; killing the process over it throws away the reconnect buffer."
- Force reconnect drops the current connection on purpose and runs the normal reconnect path; use it to rebalance long-lived connections that piled onto the server that stayed up longest after a rolling restart.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Drain & Shutdown**

- Close is right only for a connection you no longer care about (failed health check, test, error path where work is already lost); for a planned shutdown use drain. "For a planned shutdown, use drain instead."
- Call drain from the process's SIGTERM handler and wait for the connection to report CLOSED before exiting.
- Drain is the last thing your shutdown does, after the application has stopped producing. "drain is the last thing your shutdown does, after the application has stopped producing"
- The default drain timeout is 30 seconds in nats.go, but size it to your slowest handler's latency rather than a round number. "Size the timeout to your handler latency rather than to a round number."
- Draining a single subscription unsubscribes, lets the handler finish that subscription's buffered messages, and leaves the connection and other subscriptions open; the canonical use is rotating one queue-group member out while the group keeps consuming.
- Drain already ends with a flush, so a drained shutdown needs no flush of its own; call flush at checkpoints drain doesn't cover (after a burst of publishes before treating the batch as sent; before a close on an error path).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Slow Consumers**

- Size the pending limit to roughly the handler's latency times the subject's peak rate. Too tight drops messages the handler could have caught up on; too loose wastes memory on a backlog it never catches up on. "A limit sized to roughly the handler's latency times the subject's peak rate"
- When one subscriber genuinely can't keep up, the real answer is usually more subscribers sharing the load via a queue group, not a bigger buffer; pending limits protect each member. "the real answer is usually not a bigger buffer but more subscribers sharing the load"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Request-Reply Resilience**

- The `_INBOX` prefix is configurable (`inboxPrefix`, `CustomInboxPrefix`); when a user's subscribe permissions don't cover `_INBOX.>`, grant subscribe on a dedicated prefix and have the client set it.
- No-responders is the most useful failure NATS gives you because it's fast and certain; without it a request to an unlistened subject would block for the full timeout. "the no-responders signal is the most useful failure NATS gives you, because it's fast and certain"
- Retry differently per failure: a timeout means someone is there, so a short bounded fast retry; no responders means nothing is listening, so exponential backoff to give the responder time to register. "Use a short, bounded retry for a timeout and an exponential backoff for no responders."
- The retry loop must be bounded: cap the attempts (five is a reasonable default) and add jitter so a fleet of requesters doesn't retry in lockstep. "five is a reasonable default"
- A retried request is a duplicate; make it idempotent by keying every request by a business ID (e.g. `order_id`) and having the responder remember recently seen IDs and return the cached reply. It's a discipline on both ends, not a new message.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TLS & Auth**

- An expired or revoked credential ends in CLOSED (nats.net: `Failed`) in the abort-rule clients; the closed handler is what tells the application it needs fresh credentials or a restart.
- The dependable way to pick up rotated credentials is a credential callback invoked on every connect and reconnect attempt (`UserJWT(userCB, sigCB)`, JS authenticator function, `user_jwt_cb`/`signature_cb`, Java `AuthHandler`, Rust `with_auth_callback`, .NET `AuthCredCallback`).
- A secure connect fails two distinct ways — CA validation (untrusted server cert) and authorization (wrong/expired/revoked creds) — handle them as separate cases at the connect boundary.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where Next (Resilient Clients)**

- The one model: a connection is a state machine (DISCONNECTED, CONNECTING, CONNECTED, RECONNECTING, DRAINING, CLOSED), every fault is a transition, and each option shapes one edge. "That model is the floor for running any NATS client in production."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Services**

- The Services framework (`micro` in Go/Python, `service`/`services` in JS/Java/Rust/C#) formalizes a request-reply responder into a named, versioned handler the server can discover, that reports stats, and that load-balances across copies. No new infrastructure: a service is still request-reply underneath.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Endpoints and groups**

- Most services never need a queue-group override; the default `"q"` already load-balances all instances of a service. Reach for an override only when a subset of endpoints should load-balance separately. "Most services never need this."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Discovery**

- Discovery is broadcast, not load-balanced: the discovery verbs are not in a queue group, so a `$SRV.INFO.<Name>` request reaches every instance and every one replies. A caller waits a short deadline and collects however many responses arrive. "Discovery is broadcast, not load-balanced"
- When you know an instance id, address the third level to get exactly one reply with no deadline loop.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Observability**

- Return a service error for bad input, an unavailable downstream dependency, or a business rule rejecting the request; a handler that responds normally instead leaves `num_errors` at zero and hides the problem.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling**

- Horizontal scaling means running more instances with the same `Name`, `Version`, and endpoint; you don't register instances or configure a load balancer. The default queue group `"q"` is the entire scaling story. "That queue group is the entire scaling story."
- Because the endpoint leaves the queue group as part of the stop, there's no window where a request lands on a queue group whose only member vanished; roll a new version by starting fresh instances then stopping old ones one at a time.
- Durable state (a count that must not reset, a queue of work that outlives the process) doesn't belong in the instance; put it behind JetStream.
- Instances are disposable; make stopping one safe with a graceful stop that drains in-flight work and hands new requests to survivors.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Services)**

- Four pieces: the service (named, versioned, auto-ID, discovery subscribed, stats tracked), endpoints and groups (`{prefix}.{endpoint}`), the `$SRV` discovery verbs, and the default queue group `"q"` that scales it with no coordinator and no config.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Monitoring & Observability Deep Dive**

- Monitoring is observation: where the numbers live, which ones say something's wrong, and how to put them in front of a person before a customer notices; the fix belongs to the Operate chapters.
- Four lenses: numbers come from the monitoring endpoints (`:8222`), lag comes from consumer state, surprises come from advisories, history comes from the exporter; profiling is the escalation when all four agree a node is unhealthy but none says why.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Monitoring endpoints**

- On `/varz`, `connections` is the live client count, `total_connections` is the count since start (only goes up), and `slow_consumers` is the number of clients the server has disconnected for not keeping up — on a healthy node it stays at `0`.
- `/connz?sort=pending&limit=10` returns the ten connections with the most data queued — the clients most likely to fall behind.
- Route health is presence, not raw count: group `/routez` by `remote_name` and confirm each peer is still there; a vanished peer or a climbing `rtt` is the first sign a node dropped off the mesh.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream health**

- Lag is a computed number: `lag = stream.last_seq − consumer.delivered.stream_seq`; a pull consumer reports the same value directly as `num_pending` (Unprocessed Messages). "lag = stream.last_seq − consumer.delivered.stream_seq"
- A healthy consumer keeps lag near zero and `num_redelivered` near zero. Lag climbing while `last_seq` climbs means orders arrive faster than they're processed; `num_redelivered` staying high or growing means workers keep taking orders and failing to ack. "A healthy consumer keeps lag near zero and `num_redelivered` near zero."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Advisories & events**

- A flapping leader showing up as repeated leader-elected advisories is worth watching; the advisory reports the fact, not the election mechanics.
- Subscribe to `$SYS.ACCOUNT.*.CONNECT` to watch clients across every account come and go without polling `/connz` on a timer.
- The fix for transient advisories is to point a stream at the advisory subjects; a stream is always subscribed and stores what it captures. "point a stream at the advisory subjects"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Prometheus & dashboards**

- `nats server check` is the alerting side: it compares a metric to a threshold you set and returns OK / WARNING / CRITICAL in a format Prometheus, Nagios, or a script can read; a dashboard needs a person watching, a check fires on its own.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Profiling the server**

- Reach for a profile when `/varz` shows a heap growing with no matching traffic change or a pinned core with nothing on the dashboards explaining it; profiling is a development and support tool, not day-to-day monitoring.
- `--name`, `--host`, `--cluster`, and `--tags` limit which servers answer a profile request; asking the whole system is wasteful on a large cluster.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Monitoring)**

- The four lenses: numbers come from endpoints (`:8222`, no history, no subscription); lag comes from consumer state (`LastSeq` − `delivered.stream_seq`, plus `num_ack_pending` and `num_redelivered`); surprises come from advisories (transient, learned only if subscribed when fired); history comes from the exporter (`:7777`) with Prometheus storing, Grafana charting, and `nats server check` alerting.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Key-Value Store**

- Compare-and-swap is the mechanism for safe concurrent decrements so "two concurrent sales never lose a write".
- A watch delivers the current value of every key as a snapshot, then live updates as values change.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Watching**

- A watch delivers the current value of every matching key as an initial snapshot, then streams every later change. "One call gives you both halves: the state of the bucket now, and the changes from now on."
- Use the end-of-initial-data signal to hold a "loading" state until the snapshot is complete, or to mark a cache as warm before switching to incremental updates.
- A watch is live state, not a point read; don't open a watch, read the first entry, and close it to fake a get. "you pay for a consumer and a snapshot to get one value get would have handed you directly"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — History and revisions**

- Optimistic concurrency via compare-and-swap uses no locks: read the revision, write on the condition the revision hasn't changed, retry on rejection.
- Use the read-modify-write with update whenever the new value depends on the old one (decrement, increment, status transition).
- Do not use put for a read-modify-write; put is unconditional and overwrites a concurrent writer's value. "Use put to set a key to a given value, and update to change it from the value it currently holds."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TTL and limits**

- Key-value values are meant to be small; large values belong in the Object Store.
- Size the bucket for the working set you need to hold, not the average, and cap max value size above the largest value you legitimately store.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Under the hood**

- Reach for purge when you must actually remove old values (for size, or because they were sensitive), not just hide them.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Key-Value)**

- Key-value values are small and capped; the object store is for large values reassembled from multiple messages on read (a file, a build artifact, anything multi-megabyte).
- A bucket can be sourced from or mirrored into another bucket via a subject transform from `$KV.SRC.>` to `$KV.DST.>` (e.g. regional `EU_INVENTORY` sourcing `INVENTORY`).
- Checklist: wrap every update in a re-get-and-retry loop; a stale-revision update is rejected, not queued.
- Checklist: use update (CAS), not put, for any read-modify-write like a decrement.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Object Store**

- Key-Value keeps small structured values with full revision history per key; Object Store keeps large chunked files and only the latest metadata per object. "Use key-value when you want many small values that you read, overwrite, and audit; use the object store when you want whole files that you put and fetch."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Chunking**

- Don't tune chunk size to chase a benchmark; if you must raise it, keep each chunk under `max_payload`. "the 128 KB default fits almost every file and stays well under the default payload limit"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Metadata and links**

- Reading metadata (`info`) doesn't fetch the bytes; use it as a low-cost index over the bucket and read bytes only when needed.
- Metadata describes only the current object; each re-put replaces it. For a full revision history per name use the Key-Value store.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Watching and listing**

- An object watch delivers only `ObjectInfo` metadata, never chunk bytes; the KV watch delivers values directly because values are small. "the rule for objects is that watch tells you what changed and get returns the bytes"
- The two-step pattern: watch to learn what changed, then get the bytes you actually want.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Object Store)**

- Key-value is the sibling store for "small structured values and a full revision history per key"; go there when you need versioning of a value, and for the per-key watch the object store doesn't have.
- Checklist: use watch to learn what changed, then a separate get for bytes.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Backup & Recovery Deep Dive**

- Protecting a NATS platform means protecting three things, none of which protects the others: a snapshot (recovery point), a mirror (recovery time), and identity (JWTs, nkeys, creds, server config).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Stream backup and restore**

- Name snapshot directories by date; a snapshot is a point in time.
- If you need a second copy under a new name, restore to the original name first, then mirror or source it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mirrors as a DR tool**

- Lag and Last Seen are your RPO; a mirror at `Lag: 0` gives RPO of zero messages. Read them before you trust a mirror in a failover, and watch `Lag` continuously rather than once.
- Mirror is for site failure (promote, short RTO, no loss if lag was zero); snapshot is for wrong data (deleted, purged, corrupted; bounded RPO, restore-length RTO). You need both.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Disaster recovery**

- Decide which tool per failure class ahead of time, not under pressure during an outage.
- Whole cluster gone: promote the mirror. "promotion is minutes, a restore is hours."
- Accidental delete or purge: recover from the mirror (usually the freshest intact copy since it survives an upstream delete) or restore the snapshot as the older fallback.
- Corrupt or wrong messages (bad publisher): restore a known-good snapshot or purge the bad range; the bad data replicated to the mirror too.
- Consumer lost its position: restore a `--consumers` snapshot; only the snapshot captured the saved delivery position.
- Official promotion order: free the mirrored stream's subjects, drop the mirror config, bind subjects to the promoted stream, then redirect publishers and consumers.
- A DR mirror is normally placed in its own JetStream domain (a leaf node) or an independent cluster, rather than sharing one meta group that spans both sites.
- For logical corruption, stop the publishers first so no new bad data races in, then purge the corrupt range or restore a snapshot that predates it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Config and JWT backup**

- Encrypt the backup with `--key` pointing at a curve seed file (`nats auth nkey gen curve`); store the curve seed somewhere other than the backups. "keeping an archive and its key in the same place is a single point of failure"
- Date each identity backup: an older backup restores the previous operator after a key rotation, and a server rebuilt from it trusts a chain nobody signs anymore.
- Run the identity backup on a schedule like the snapshot (a daily cron line).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connect MQTT devices to NATS**

- `nats-server` speaks MQTT natively on its own listener; there's no bridge process and no second broker to run.
- MQTT support exists to keep an existing device investment; use it when endpoints already speak MQTT or can only ever speak MQTT.
- For a greenfield deployment, prefer NATS end to end. "One technology from device to cloud gives you a single security model and one set of observability tools. The NATS clients are efficient enough for constrained hardware."
- A standalone MQTT broker scales by making one node bigger; `nats-server` scales by adding servers (clusters, superclusters, leaf nodes), which carry MQTT traffic like everything else.
- Where a broker's persistence stops at a last-value cache per topic, device traffic on NATS lands in JetStream streams with retention limits, replay, and consumers written later.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first MQTT client**

- Capture device traffic in a normal stream (e.g. `DEVICES` on `sensors.>,fleet.>`) so a QoS 0 reading, gone once delivered, and a QoS 1 reading, which only reaches subscribers that exist at the time, are still readable by a consumer written later.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topics and subjects**

- Treat anything that isn't printable as unusable in topics; strip whitespace from free-text fields before they reach a topic.
- To learn the subject a topic lands on, publish one message and read the subject off a `nats sub ">"` rather than working it out by hand.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — QoS, sessions, and retained messages**

- A message published by a NATS client and delivered to an MQTT subscriber is always QoS 0. "When a device genuinely needs the delivery guarantee, the message has to originate from an MQTT publisher at QoS 1 or 2."
- If traffic starts on the NATS side and delivery matters, keep the durability on the NATS side in a stream rather than expecting MQTT redelivery.
- A redelivered message is a genuine duplicate; handlers that matter should be idempotent.
- Lower `max_ack_pending` if you need more subscriptions per session; like `ack_wait`, a change applies only to new subscriptions.
- The clean session flag clears stored state and makes the session last only as long as the connection. "A device with no durable subscriptions should set it; one that wants messages buffered while it's offline shouldn't."
- The will topic converts to a subject by the same rules, so device liveness is visible to NATS subscribers too.
- Pair the will with RETAIN so the "offline" marker persists as the topic's retained value for dashboards that subscribe later.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth and clustering (MQTT)**

- Permissions for MQTT users are written against converted subjects; a subscribe list for a device using `fleet/#` carries both `fleet.>` and `fleet`.
- `no_auth_user` on the MQTT listener is the answer when device firmware can't send credentials: it maps credential-less MQTT connections onto one top-level user's permissions.
- A bearer JWT lets anyone holding it connect as that user; treat it like a password and put TLS in front of it.
- A leaf node close to devices can serve MQTT without running JetStream itself; the standalone JetStream check doesn't apply once the server has a `leafnodes` configuration.
- `js_domain` selects the JetStream domain MQTT stores its state in; set it to the leaf's local domain so sessions and retained messages stay on the leaf and local devices keep working when the hub link is down. The domain is part of the session's storage identity, keeping sessions in different domains from colliding.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (MQTT)**

- Leaf nodes suit devices well: a leaf on a factory floor or in a vehicle gives local MQTT clients a nearby server that needs only outbound connectivity to the hub, so they keep working when the cloud link is down.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connect over WebSocket**

- If neither the browser nor the HTTP-only-edge case applies, keep using `nats://`. "It's one less moving part, and a plain TCP connection avoids the WebSocket framing overhead."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Browsers and origins**

- `same_origin: true` requires the `Origin` to match the host the request arrived on; it suits page and NATS endpoint on one hostname and gets in the way as soon as they differ. Set both options and a request must pass both; leave both unset (default) and any origin is accepted.
- `allowed_origins` answers "may this web page open a connection using a visitor's browser?", not "may this connection reach my subjects?"; permissions do the latter and apply to browser and non-browser connections alike. Configure both.
- Browser credential approach 1: in operator mode, the browser presents a bearer-user JWT (no nonce signature required); the page holds only a token that expires, never a signing key.
- Browser credential approach 2: the HTTP server sets an `HttpOnly` cookie the page's scripts can't read; the browser attaches it to the handshake and the NATS server reads it via `jwt_cookie`.
- Use the cookie pattern when your web application already has a login; the session cookie is a credential the browser transmits automatically and JavaScript can't exfiltrate.
- For a genuinely public, read-only dashboard, `no_auth_user` names a user unauthenticated WebSocket connections bind to; give it subscribe permission on exactly the subjects shown. It doesn't work in operator mode.
- Restrict browser credentials with `allowed_connection_types: ["WEBSOCKET"]` so they don't also work from a shell on 4222; a WebSocket leaf node uses `LEAFNODE_WS`.
- Compression trades CPU on both ends for bytes on the wire; "it's a measurement rather than a default — compare CPU and throughput on your own traffic before turning it on broadly."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TLS and proxies**

- The more common shape behind an existing edge: the ingress holds the certificate and the NATS listener runs plaintext (`no_tls: true`) on an internal network.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (WebSocket)**

- Reaching for WebSocket is often nothing to do with browsers: where an HTTP ingress or load balancer is the only path into the network, the WebSocket listener is what gets published, and a leaf node uses it exactly as a client does.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Learn**

- The docs have three layers: Concepts (short primers, read first if new), Learn deep dives (one subsystem each, one running scenario, at most two new concepts per page), and Reference (exhaustive, versioned catalog, not a teaching resource).
- Core NATS is the foundation every other chapter builds on; if you're new to NATS start there, and go straight to JetStream if you're here for persistence.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — What is NATS?**

- Location transparency: applications don't need to know where other services are; NATS handles service discovery, load balancing, and fault tolerance.
- Accounts isolate messaging domains within one server or cluster, supporting secure multi-tenant deployments, team isolation, and SaaS platforms.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subjects**

- Good practice is alphanumeric characters plus `-` and `_` for readability.
- Hierarchy design: start general and get specific (`app.region.service.entity.action`, e.g. `myapp.us-east.users.profile.update`).
- Keep subjects reasonable: limit to ~16 tokens and under 256 characters total.
- Establish naming conventions early and stick to them; design hierarchies that work well with wildcard subscriptions.
- Well-designed hierarchies enable fine-grained access control per user/account, efficient JetStream stream filtering, clean import/export between accounts, and logical organization for monitoring.
- The `>` wildcard enables wire taps and monitoring of everything under a prefix.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publish-Subscribe**

- Pub/sub is ideal when multiple services need to react to the same event: event broadcasting, data distribution, fan-out notifications, audit logging.
- Fan-out is one publisher to multiple subscribers (event notification); fan-in is multiple publishers to one subscriber (aggregation).
- NATS handles millions of subscriptions efficiently; use wildcards to reduce subscription overhead when possible.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Request-Reply**

- Timeouts are crucial in request-reply to prevent indefinite waiting; all clients support configurable timeouts.
- With multiple responders and no queue group, all services receive the request and all can respond (scatter-gather), useful for gathering data from multiple sources, aggregating results, or querying replicas for consensus.
- With queue groups, only one service receives the request and responds, giving automatic load distribution, horizontal scalability, and built-in failover.
- Timeout strategy: too short may miss valid responses, too long blocks unnecessarily; add buffer for network round-trip; implement retry logic for transient failures.
- Error handling: always handle timeouts, check for no responders, validate responses before processing.
- Service design: idempotent operations (requests might be retried), lightweight processing (long operations should be async), health checks, graceful shutdown (drain pending requests).
- Performance: reuse connections for multiple requests; modern clients reuse inbox subjects; batch related requests when possible.
- Choose request-reply for synchronous communication, service discovery via no-responders detection, load balancing with queue groups, and RPC-style APIs. Use pub/sub for fire-and-forget, multiple consumers, event streaming, and decoupled systems.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue Groups**

- Queue groups enable horizontally scalable services without a service mesh or API gateway; service code needs no knowledge of other instances, leader election, or coordination.
- Queue groups coexist with regular subscribers on the same subject. "Use queue groups for operational work that needs to happen exactly once, and regular subscribers for observational tasks (audit logging, monitoring, analytics)."
- Queue group naming follows subject-like conventions: service-based (`api.auth.workers`), environment-based (`prod.order-processors`), version-based (`service.v1.workers`).
- Duplicates come only from publisher retries, so make processing idempotent if the publisher may resend.
- Worker design: drain messages before stopping, handle failed messages, monitor worker health.
- Scaling: start small, monitor metrics (queue depth with JetStream, processing time), scale based on load, then automate.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream**

- JetStream extends decoupling to time: publisher and subscriber no longer need to be online at the same moment.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Security**

- Operator mode scales to multi-tenant or large deployments because accounts issue and revoke their own users independently; you choose a resolver model for the server to locate account information.
- Auth callouts delegate the authentication decision to an application-defined NATS service returning a signed JWT; useful for external identity providers (OIDC, LDAP) or custom logic.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topologies**

- NATS scales by composing servers; the same binary and client APIs work across every shape, so you change the deployment topology, not your application.
- Reach for a cluster for high availability, more throughput than one server, production deployments, rolling upgrades without downtime, and JetStream replication.
- Super-clusters fit multi-region or multi-cloud deployments and global services with regional locality; queue groups prefer local workers automatically (geo-affinity).
- Real deployments combine all shapes: clusters across regions via gateways, each fanning out to leaf nodes at edge sites, with the same client code everywhere.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — The NATS Ecosystem**

- Clients come in three tiers: Tier 1 (Synadia-maintained, track new server features at release), Tier 2 (Synadia-maintained, may lag), community (third-party). "If a tier 1 client is available for your language, prefer it."

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Achieve MASSIVE Scale with NATS Clustering | Rethink Connectivity Episode 4**

- Clustering is the answer when you need more scalability or redundancy than a single server gives; a super cluster is a "cluster of clusters" that can live in different regions and clouds. "clusters of clusters called super clusters... these clusters can live in different locations and regions and clouds" (~01:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to build a NATS Supercluster | Rethink Connectivity Episode 5**

- Nodes of a single cluster are assumed to live in the same data center or availability zone; a super cluster spans geographies and even different public clouds (e.g. GCP, AWS, Azure mixed). "nodes in a single cluster are kind of assumed that they live in the same data center or the same availability zone... a super cluster spans not only different geographies but different public clouds" (~01:10)
- Clients connect to the geographically nearest cluster and still reach clients on other clusters transparently. "you can have clients connect to different clusters based on where they are geographically and they can start talking with clients that are connected to other clusters" (~14:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to set up Decentralized Authentication/Authorization in NATS | Rethink Connectivity Episode 6**

- The operator is the entity running the system at the infrastructure level, e.g. a platform team or the company running NATS as a utility across an organization. "you're operating a NATS cluster across an entire organization as a utility and so your company name Acme Corp would be your operator" (~03:10)
- Because user JWTs are not stored server-side, users can be minted without updating the system, and creation of accounts/users happens entirely out of band of NATS (only account JWTs must be pushed). "you could actually mint user JWTs without having to update it in the system... the creation process actually happens outside of NATS" (~06:09)
- Exports are typed as either a service (request/response) or a stream (access to data); the import can alias the subject locally so the importer chooses its own naming. "there's either a service or a stream, a service is kind of a request response... a stream is access to data" (~22:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extend your NATS Cluster with Leaf Nodes | Rethink Connectivity Episode 7**

- Hub-and-spoke: cloud cluster as hub, each store/factory/site as a leaf node running local services, which gives better performance and isolation than having every site connect straight to the cloud. "instead of everything connecting to the cloud we actually get better performance and better isolation by separating these two things out" (~03:00)
- Running a responder locally on the leaf lets requests be served locally with sub-millisecond latency and never leave for the hub; kill it and requests transparently fall back to the hub responder. "it didn't actually ever hit the NGS cloud because it can see that there's somebody who's able to respond... if I kill this service... it's just going to go back to Oregon" (~17:40)
- A leaf-local stream that sources the hub stream with a subject filter (e.g. `orders.store1.*`) yields a real read replica with sequences, not just a cache, and local gets become much faster. "it's not just a cache, it's a real read replica of a stream" (~22:00)
- Layer decentralized auth on top so a leaf node's credentials only permit sourcing specific subjects from the hub stream, giving partners scoped access to a global data store. "you can only source from this subject on this stream... a global data store that can only be accessed in certain ways" (~24:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Dynamic Permissions with Scoped Signing Keys | Rethink Connectivity Episode 8**

- A scoped signing key is a signing key given a role and a permission template; every user signed with it inherits those permissions, which acts as role-based authorization inside an account. "you give it a role and then you can give it a template and every time a user is signed with that signing key they get those permissions out of the box" (~04:40)
- Because permissions live on the signing key, updating the key changes permissions for already-issued users without reconnecting or reissuing credentials. "they don't have to reload, they don't have to reconnect, they don't have to get new user JWTs" (~10:00)
- A DM subject design `chat.dm.{org}.{receiver}.{sender}` with allow-pub on `chat.dm.{org}.*.{name}` and allow-sub on `chat.dm.{org}.{name}.*` lets users send to anyone but only read DMs addressed to them. "they can listen in on any DMs directed to them... but they can only publish on things that they should be able to send" (~14:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Connect ANY Auth System to NATS.io with Auth Callout**

- Any external system (Active Directory, OAuth, OIDC, your own database) can be plugged in; the auth service is a normal NATS connection, so it can also use KV/object store as its user database with no separate backend. "you might not even need to have your own database, you could have a database powered by KV that has all of your user permissions in it" (~06:30)
- Pattern: client does Google OIDC first, passes the Google-signed JWT unchanged as the NATS token; the auth service verifies Google's signature and mints NATS user claims from the Google claims. "it's not a NATS JWT... it's exactly what Google handed back to us, we're just going to give that to the NATS server when we connect" (~10:00)
- Emails are not subject-safe, so base64-encode them into a user ID before using them as a subject token or KV key. "we don't want to use the email just as it is but what we can do is we could base64 encode this email so it's safe enough for subjects" (~21:00)
- Permissions minted per user: read JetStream API info, chat-messages stream info, create/operate consumers on it, read the workspace KV, but publish only to `chat.<channel>.<own user id>`, which makes authorship verifiable. "they can only post on behalf of their own user ID... we kind of use this as a mechanism to verify who has posted what" (~24:00)
- The auth service also upserts the user's profile (name, email, photo) into a KV bucket on each login; clients watching that bucket update instantly, giving zero-touch onboarding. "all the chat applications were watching that key value store so they also updated their profile info before I even jumped into chat" (~28:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Superclusters in Kubernetes: Cross-Cloud Geo-Affinity for High Availability and Low Latency**

- A service in the services framework is declared with a name, version/description and endpoints that bind a handler to a full subject such as `math.numbers.add`; the Python `nats micro` module is one of many language implementations. "I'm using the NATS micro module and I'm going to add a service... declare the service name... and then add an endpoint" (~03:30)
- With a super cluster spanning AWS us-east-1 (EKS) and Azure (AKS), requests from the east were served by an adder service running only in the west when the east instance was removed, giving cross-cloud failover with no noticeable delay to the caller. "the NATS cluster in US East 1 is talking to a NATS cluster in Azure running on the other side of the country and that has an adder service deployed" (~08:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Building an Interactive Whiteboard with NATS Websockets | Rethink Connectivity Episode 3**

- A browser app can use NATS as its whole backend: pub/sub for multiplayer and JetStream for persistence, with only front-end code written. "I'm just writing front end code and I'm using NATS for all the back end stuff" (~01:00)
- Rooms map to subject tokens (`whiteboard.<roomId>`), giving simple multi-tenancy per whiteboard. "I can create a subject like whiteboard dot room id... we're kind of multi-tenant" (~06:50)
- Draw locally first for responsiveness, tag each message with a random per-player id, and on receipt ignore your own messages so only other players' strokes are applied. "if the data's id is not equal to this id then we can call draw raw" (~11:00)
- Persistence is added by creating a stream on `whiteboard.*` and switching the subscription to a JetStream ordered consumer; each page load creates a fresh ephemeral consumer and replays the whole stream. "every time this thing refreshes it creates a new consumer and pulls in all the data via the stream" (~14:00)
- The stream is created with `--allow-rollup` and `--no-deny-purge` so a "clear" message published with the `Nats-Rollup: sub` header replaces all prior messages on that subject, keeping replay cheap for new consumers. "when I send this message clear all of the messages before them so next time a consumer connects it's not getting all of those messages" (~15:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Mutually Trusted NGS Credentials**

- One credential set can work in NGS and self-hosted servers if you accept that the account configuration is identical in both environments. "you are okay with your account configuration in either environment be identical, then this video is for you" (~01:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | Bearer Tokens in NATS**

- Their model: organizations sign bearer JWTs to delegate authorization; a verified token creates an ephemeral in-memory user for the duration of the connection, with no operator/account/user configuration on the server. "if the token is verified an ephemeral user is created in memory for the duration of the connection" (~03:20)
- One JWT can carry both application permissions and the NATS permissions claim, so a single token serves the app and NATS. "if you generate and sign a JWT that has other application permissions... it's very nicely in line with a single token" (~06:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS Leafnodes**

- Architecture endorsed: a central server/cluster/super cluster with many leaf-node spokes that absorb inbound web/mobile client connections. "a very legitimate architecture of a single server cluster or super cluster that then has lots of hub and spokes to actually take on all of the inbound clients" (~06:00)
- Run leaf spokes as a small cluster rather than a singleton; each server solicits its own connection to the hub and self-heals independently, so there is no leader election or single point of failure. "every single one of those NATS servers has configured it exactly the same way to solicit a connection to the NATS super cluster... there is no single point of failure" (~08:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Replace Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis and more w/NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity Ep 10**

- Core NATS is a pub/sub model where the cluster brokers communication between two live clients; this covers pub/sub, request/reply, fan-in and fan-out. "a NATS cluster is really brokering communication between two live clients" (~01:03)
- This behaviour is called temporal coupling: both parties must be online for the logic to work. "they are coupled in the sense that they both need to be online for them to work" (~02:03)
- Core NATS is recommended for RPC and microservices; stream processing and distributing large datasets for one-at-a-time processing need temporal decoupling, which is JetStream. "fantastic for RPCs and for microservices ... stream processing ... that's when we start getting into temporal decoupling" (~02:03)
- Consumers are described as windows into a stream; a consumer may take all data or a filtered subset by subject. "consumers are like windows into a stream" (~07:10)
- Use create-or-update for streams so re-running the program keeps the server config matching the code. "we want to be able to run through it and make sure if we make any updates to the config of the stream that it matches" (~14:20)
- Consumers live server-side; many clients can consume from one consumer and are naturally load balanced, unlike Kafka where partitioning and consumer groups are needed. "I could have a lot of clients consuming from one consumer and they're naturally load balanced" (~20:28)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to configure NATS JetStream streams | Rethink Connectivity Ep 11**

- A stream is a single primitive that can be configured to express many distributed-systems patterns: distributed queue, key-value store, object store, append-only log. "you can have multiple different kind of patterns supported ... replace a whole swath of different tools" (~01:02)
- Max messages per subject set to 1 keeps only the last message per subject; the KV store's history setting is driven by this option. "this is actually in use inside of our key value store where you can set a history" (~08:09)
- Interest retention suits multiple consumers each picking messages for different reasons where persistence after processing does not matter. "you have kind of multiple consumers that are using ... but you also want to keep this acting very much like a queue" (~11:11)
- A work-queue stream behaves like RabbitMQ or any durable queue: message goes in, gets processed, gets deleted. "works very similar to like a RabbitMQ or any other kind of durable queue system" (~12:13)
- Choose discard new when you absolutely must not lose data and would rather fail publishes at the limit. "you would rather start rejecting API calls in order to not lose data" (~13:15)
- Republish is for cases needing millions of consumers, where consumer machinery costs hardware; the stream republishes a core NATS notification when a message is persisted. "once you get into the use case where you might need like millions of consumers ... might not be worth the added cost" (~15:15)
- Republish can be configured headers-only to minimise bytes on the wire; suited to monitoring and logging that is not mission critical. "you could also make this very performant over the wire where it's just sending the bare minimum" (~16:17)
- A mirror is a one-to-one twin of a stream in another cluster; reads are served from the mirror while writes are forwarded to the origin stream to keep global consistency. "all reads will be served from this mirror but all writes will actually be forwarded to the source" (~21:22)
- Sources aggregate and filter many streams into one, and the sourcing stream may also ingest its own subjects; a good use is aggregating leaf-node edge streams into one cloud stream. "aggregate them all into one mega stream in the cloud" (~22:23)
- Allow rollup lets a specially-headed message replace everything before it on the whole stream or one subject, useful for derived or computable state. "it will persist that message that just came through and it will delete everything before it" (~24:25)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Build Priority Background Jobs & Dead Letter Queues with NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity ep 12**

- A worker/job queue is one of the most common queuing patterns (RabbitMQ, Sidekiq, Celery); JetStream can be shaped into this durable-queue form. "Jet Stream can kind of be molded and shaped into all kinds of different expressions of distributed systems" (~00:00)
- JetStream has no built-in priority semantics; priorities are expressed through subject-based addressing (e.g. jobs.high.*, jobs.low.*) with separate worker pools sized differently. "NATS JetStream doesn't have priority semantics built in ... you can have priority semantics by using our subject based addressing" (~02:03)
- Dead-letter queues are deliberately not a first-class JetStream feature; they are a specific pattern expressible through configuration without code. "we wanted to be able to express it but not necessarily bake it into JetStream as a core thing" (~05:05)
- JetStream advisories report which messages hit max failed deliveries; you can capture these into a stream to build your own dead-letter queue. "we have some JetStream advisories that you could listen to and actually insert into a queue" (~06:06)
- Suggested job subject hierarchy: jobs.<priority>.<job-type>, e.g. jobs.high.send-welcome-email. "the first token is going to be the priority ... the second one will be kind of like the job's ID" (~07:07)
- For a work queue, use discard policy "new" so a backed-up queue rejects new jobs rather than deleting old ones. "if my queue gets backed up I don't want to start deleting old messages ... I want to start actually rejecting" (~08:08)
- Set a max age (example 7 days) on the work-queue stream so dead messages that exhausted retries eventually expire rather than backing up forever. "I'm okay having a sort of lifetime to my dead messages" (~09:10)
- Exponential-backoff retry logic like a webhook system is pure JetStream consumer configuration, not code. "you could do all of this straight inside of JetStream without really having to write much code" (~18:26)
- The advisory includes stream, consumer and stream sequence; use `nats stream get <stream> <seq>` to fetch the original failed message, which stays in the stream until its max age. "we also get the stream sequence which is really important here" (~28:36)
- DLQ handling can be automated (delete known-safe failures) or human-in-the-loop, including a UI over the DLQ stream. "we can have kind of a human in the loop kind of intervention" (~29:38)
- The whole priority job queue with DLQ was about 80 lines, mostly configuration, positioned as a replacement for RabbitMQ, Celery or Sidekiq. "we had like 80 lines of code and most of that was configuration too" (~31:39)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared: Part 1 | Rethink Connectivity**

- Subject-based addressing lets you address individual messages or ranges in a stream directly, e.g. get orders.eu.12345 or query orders.us.*. "you can address individual messages or series of messages directly in the stream" (~10:09)
- A sensor taxonomy like sensor.<type>.<id>.<event> or with region tokens supports queries like "all temperature sensors" or "all sensors in us-east". "give me all the sensor data for sensors located in region us-east" (~11:12)
- A JetStream consumer is like a database view on a stream: it can filter and can be shared by many client applications. "you can look at a consumer ... as essentially like a view on a stream" (~18:19)
- Deterministic partitioning can be added in JetStream via server-side subject mapping that hashes chosen subject tokens and inserts a partition-number token, so foo.bar always lands on the same partition. "inserts a token in the subject that has a partition number" (~21:23)
- Discard-new plus max-messages-per-subject gives database-like constraints usable for distributed locking or gating: a second publish to a subject at its limit fails in the ack. "using a stream for distributed locking logic gating things like that" (~26:26)
- JetStream supports CRUD-style concurrency control: insert only if no message exists on the subject, and compare-and-set updates by expecting the last sequence on the subject. "I'm expecting the current last message on that subject to be sequence number 37 ... if it has been changed then that operation fails" (~29:29)
- Rollup is an atomic controlled update that replaces all prior messages on a subject with one summarising message. "replace them with just one message ... that's one atomic operation in JetStream" (~32:35)
- JetStream can also batch via asynchronous publishes for much higher write throughput; batching trades away real-time latency, and NATS leaves that trade-off to the engineer. "you can use asynchronous operations to get much higher write throughputs by doing batching" (~33:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared Pt 2: Consumers | Rethink Connectivity**

- JetStream distributes messages among client applications attached to a consumer evenly and according to demand, so you can scale clients up and down freely. "the consumer will automatically evenly and according to demand distribute the messages between those consuming applications" (~04:06)
- For edge devices on flaky 5G, deliver-last-per-subject avoids replaying five stale "beep" commands after reconnect; the consumer policy encodes business intent. "it probably doesn't want to beep five times ... give me the last message per this particular subject" (~13:16)
- Analogy: a durable is a view on a table; an ephemeral is a query whose result set you iterate again on restart. "ephemeral it's just simply a query over which you iterate the result set" (~19:22)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Move over Kafka! Let's try NATS JetStream**

- Pull fetches with timeouts let you scale down workers when the queue drains. "it allows you to essentially scale down workers as they time out and there's no messages left in the queue" (~08:07)
- KV watch notifies on key updates, a powerful primitive for distributed systems. "being able to know when certain values get updated" (~10:08)
- Stream sourcing builds a stream from one or more other streams, with its own ownership, location and retention rules, including per-source start sequence and subject filters (e.g. orders.eu plus returns.eu into archive-eu). "a stream that gets its data from one or more other streams with all of its own rules around ownership location and retention" (~11:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Comparing and contrasting NATS and Kafka | RethinkConn '22**

- With subject-based addressing the key or unique ID is naturally part of the subject, can be a composite of many tokens, and can include fields you will filter on when consuming. "you can use as many tokens as you need for making up the key so like a composite key" (~06:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | JetStream**

- A stream is a log; multiple services consume it with each having a unique view (position, ack state, push or pull, acks or not); a consumer describes how a set of related services consumes. "each have a unique view over that data that can be in different places within the data" (~07:13)
- Pull consumers let 20–40 worker services each ask for the next message when ready, replacing round-robin or least-weighted routing; a worker can ack, refuse work, or ask for more time. "you can scale up horizontally by having 20 or 30 or 40 of these worker services" (~09:15)
- Streams can be created by the microservice on startup, by CI/CD via the CLI's unattended mode, or by the Terraform provider for teams using a remote JetStream. "stand up a JetStream just for the purpose of that single CI run" (~14:21)
- A dead-letter-queue equivalent: configure max delivery attempts (e.g. 10) and JetStream publishes an event with the message content when exceeded. "configure messages only let me try ten times ... then we will publish an event saying that message's bad" (~16:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Getting Started with NATS JetStream: Streams, Storage, and Data Lifecycle**

- Route a response to different subjects by classification (answers.significant vs answers.throwaway) so consumers can filter per subject later. "If it's less than one, I will publish it to answers.throwaway" (~06:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Why NATS Consumers Just Work (And How to Use Them in 15 Minutes)**

- Three pods pulling on one durable consumer were load balanced automatically and roughly evenly, with variance explained by node speed or distance from the data. "that's automatic load balancing built in because each pod is pulling whenever it's ready" (~10:13)
- Ephemeral consumers suit one-off fire-hose reads of a stream or subject. "useful if you ever want to just pull fire hose of all the data that's stored in a stream" (~15:18)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream for Key-Value Store Tech Preview**

- The backing stream can be replicated to other clusters in a supercluster as read replicas; read-only workers read locally and never talk to the origin, while writes go to the origin with a small replication delay. "if they know they're only ever going to read they never have to communicate to london" (~06:09)
- The Go client offers an in-memory bucket cache: it starts a watcher, loads the whole bucket, marks ready, serves reads from memory, and writes invalidate the key until the watcher refreshes it. "before you need it even your cache will already be up to date" (~07:10)
- Leader election and concurrency control (e.g. only 10 of 1,000 instances allowed to run) were flagged as upcoming JetStream capabilities. "out of a thousand possible instances that needs to run only 10 at a time are allowed to run" (~09:13)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Mirror Streams Explained — One-Way Replication Made Simple**

- Use mirrors for geographic distribution, fan-out from one origin to many mirrors serving millions of clients, and cross-account or cross-domain replication. "One origin stream can feed multiple mirrors, perfect for fan-out topologies that serve millions of client connections" (~02:00)
- With the mirror direct attribute, clients read directly from mirror replicas instead of being routed to the origin, spreading read load. "With mirror direct clients can read directly from the mirror replicas instead of being routed back to the origin" (~02:00)
- Because deletes are independent on each side, mirrors can serve as independent backups. "Deletes on one side don't affect the other. This makes mirrors useful as independent backups" (~06:06)
- Mirrors are the tool for one-way replication across regions and unreliable networks without full synchronisation; they work best with standard (limits) retention. "they work best with standard retention policies" (~09:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers**

- Put the discriminating data (e.g. dwelling ID, room) in the subject, not buried in the payload or header, because consumer filtering works only on subjects. "definitely expose that bit of data in the subject so you can discriminate ... the degree of subscription filtering on the consumer side is all based on the subject" (~06:30)
- Design the subject hierarchy for the consumption side: publishers can publish anywhere, but subscribers must be able to differentiate with wildcards. "when you're modeling your subject hierarchy it's really frankly for the consumption side" (~07:06)
- Choose one stream vs many based on access patterns: how much ordering you need across entities, how co-located streams should be, and ingest rate. "the choice of one stream versus many streams really kind of comes down to how collocated do you want those streams to be and also frankly the rate of ingest" (~12:16)
- Publishers only care about the subject, not the physical stream; subject mapping and stream sourcing let you route to the right underlying stream and change the stream topology over time. "on the publisher side all you care about is what subject you're publishing to not concretely the stream behind the scenes" (~16:23)
- A sensor should be authorized to publish only to its own dwelling-ID-prefixed subject pattern, which doubles as a sort key over the data. "it should only in theory be authorized to publish to say a guid dot something or a pattern" (~20:30)
- Stream sourcing multiplexes many origin streams into one aggregate stream asynchronously, like a materialized view; origin streams stay lightweight and highly available while the sourcing stream can have different retention. "I'm going to multiplex all of the data from all of these source streams ... and I'm going to funnel it all into one stream" (~22:32)
- Split workflows with two consumers on the same stream: one for real-time analytics and one archiving to external object storage; the aggregate can be short-retention while origins retain. "I have two consumers one for the real-time analytics and one for persisting out to stable object storage" (~25:35)
- Start with the simplest setup, a single stream, if throughput, reachability and latency allow; only add streams when requirements force it. "if we can get by with a single stream that can handle everything that's the simplest thing to operate" (~28:37)
- Use an R1 consumer for short-lived, one-off, process-lifetime consumption to avoid replication overhead; use replicated durables for resumable long-running work. "you can opt for saying I only want a single replica consumer ... if it's not going to be a long lived durable consumer" (~43:58)
- An ordered consumer is a bundle of defaults: R1, no acks, client-side reset/retry on gaps, minimal server state, more work on the client. "ordered consumer ... an R1 no acknowledgement it handles if there are dropped messages it actually retries and resets itself internally" (~47:03)
- Batch fetching amortizes network overhead: one round trip for ten messages beats ten round trips. "you lose the network overhead of fetching one at a time pack a load of stuff together" (~56:14)
- Two application instances bound to the same consumer get different batches (load balancing), not copies of the same data. "they're getting individual batches because now the server is assuming okay you're trying to actually parallelize the work" (~59:16)
- Any number of workers can bind to one consumer for Lambda-style fan-out parallelism. "the consumer will happily basically load balance across and deliver across any number of instances" (~60:19)
- To retain order per entity, create a filtered consumer at the granularity you need (e.g. per dwelling subject). "you apply a subject filter and then that consumer will basically only deliver the relevant data" (~61:20)
- Max ack pending of 1 has historically been the recommended way to retain perfect order with a shared consumer. "you can define this max ack pending ... you probably should do this if you want to truly retain perfect order" (~64:26)
- 2.10 logical partitioning: on ingest the stream deterministically appends a partition-number token derived from the subject; consumers filter with wildcards plus a concrete partition ID to get total order within a bucket. "it's deterministic so given the same input subject it's going to derive the same partition ID" (~66:30)
- Emulate exclusive consumption today with a KV-based lease/lock: multiple instances, one acquires the lock with a TTL and is the active participant. "I have a KV bucket ... leasing ... only one basically acquires a lock ... you can have a TTL" (~72:38)
- A mirror can live on slower disks with compression and long retention as an archive while the origin is pruned or compacted. "your mirror stream that is literally for archival ... on slower disks you could apply compression to that stream" (~75:43)
- For latency-sensitive alerting, co-locate the workload with the origin stream (even on a Raspberry Pi at the edge) rather than on the async sourced/mirrored copy, because sourcing and mirroring are asynchronous with retries and partitions. "collocate your application workload to where the origin stream is ... sourcing things mirroring things that's all asynchronous" (~79:48)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.10 Webinar**

- Auth callout exists so identity and permissions can be managed in an external IdP (SAML, Active Directory, OAuth) while NATS still enforces per-connection permissions and limits. "where you manage those permissions where you manage how those users are defined don't necessarily need to be in NATS itself" (~15:19)
- The recommended scope of a cluster is a region (AZ-level fault tolerance); a supercluster spans regions. A "stretch cluster" spreads one cluster (e.g. 9 or 13 nodes) across regions to get multi-region stream replicas. "the scope of a cluster is typically regional a super cluster can span multiple regions ... we've been calling it the pattern as a stretch cluster" (~23:25)
- Because a multi-filter consumer is a single server-side source, relative delivery order across the filtered subjects matches stream order, unlike the old workaround of two unsynchronized consumers. "the relative order for all messages being delivered by that consumer are now in the order that you would expect from the original stream" (~29:34)
- A stream subject transform can append a deterministic partition token computed from a wildcard token, e.g. events.* -> events.{{wildcard(1)}}.{{partition(5,1)}}; ordered pull consumers then bind to events.*.0 through events.*.4. "give me five partitions and compute that relative to the first wild card" (~32:37)
- An OAuth-to-NATS bridge can store the IdP user claims in a KV bucket keyed by session ID; the client presents the session ID as its token and the callout service looks it up to mint the user JWT. "the key value bucket is the link between setting a token through my auth callout callback flow and then your auth callout service being able to observe this token" (~51:00)
- Put NATS permissions and target account in IdP app metadata claims so users are managed in one place and the callout service maps them to a NATS user JWT. "you can define permissions anything that is relevant for your NATS user ... and you can manage it in one place" (~45:57)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- A stretch cluster is the regular clustering mechanism pushed across zones, regions or data centers (e.g. one nine-node cluster instead of three three-node clusters joined as a supercluster). "the alternative is that you just have a nine node cluster and it's the fact that it scales out of a specific location is what we refer to as the stretch clustering" (~42:42)
- In a supercluster each JetStream Raft group is bounded to one cluster, so persistence performance does not suffer from inter-region latency while global connectivity remains. "each JetStream group is only bounded to this specific cluster in a super cluster so ... persistence with JetStream does not suffer because you have more regions" (~43:43)
- Choose a stretch cluster when regulation requires data replicated consistently across regions and you accept higher-latency persistence; mirroring/sourcing across a supercluster gives similar reach but with secondary, eventually available copies. "you can achieve something similar with super clusters but then you need to include some mirroring and sourcing ... the guarantees around when the data will be available its consistency is a little different" (~44:45)
- The callout service can consult LDAP, OIDC, a file or SQLite and can generate permissions dynamically per session, e.g. by time of day. "maybe at this time of day for this particular user ... they have this degree of permission at this time" (~52:52)
- Built-in MQTT lets embedded or industrial devices that will never speak anything else join a NATS backend without extra bridging infrastructure. "those clients might be embedded or they might be industrial and they don't ever stand a chance of talking anything that's not MQTT" (~57:58)
- Stream-level transforms let you change subjects for API changes without breaking clients, and aggregate identical subjects from many factories or leaf nodes without compromising your subject architecture. "it allows you to even handle switching subjects for API changes without any breaking changes" (~62:02)
- Transforms on sources/mirrors solve subject-namespace collisions when bridging systems by rewriting subjects on the fly. "subject namespace collisions ... you can now just rewrite these on the fly so that you don't have to worry about whether you're polluting one namespace with another" (~65:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP07: Going off piste; KV patterns with NATS.io (pt1)**

- Byron's first NATS use was pub/sub fan-out to notify many things instead of HTTP hacks, then NATS Streaming for ETL pipelines: extract, transform, publish to a stream, fan out to consumers that load other systems. "taking data out transforming it throwing it into a stream and then I was able to fan out effectively consume from that stream and plop it in other systems" (~04:09)
- David's first NATS use (2015) was connecting distributed syslog-ingestion instances east-west so they funnelled through one head-end, to avoid ten systems each hammering core internet infrastructure, with failover if one machine died. "the last thing I want is 10 systems basically doing a denial of service attack onto core internet infrastructure" (~08:14)
- Because a KV bucket is a stream, watchers let you subscribe to puts, updates and deletes as a change stream over time. "it's inherently a stream under the hood so ... you can watch changes over time" (~12:23)
- The server can reject one of two concurrent writes to the same key, which gives you a distributed mutex across processes without slapping a local mutex on. "the server has the ability to basically prevent both concurrent writes to happen at the same time" (~12:23)
- If you are protecting one resource from more than a couple of workers, reconsider the design slightly. "if you're protecting one resource from more than maybe a couple of worker systems maybe you want to readdress your design ever so slightly" (~13:25)
