- A lease adds a time element: set a TTL on the lock key so competitors retry until it expires and someone else acquires it; the TTL bounds how long any holder can own the resource. "you can set a TTL on keys ... this key will eventually expire after a certain number of seconds" (~15:29)
- Simplest distributed lock: every worker races to create the key with its node ID as the value, then reads back to see who won; losers stand down. "there's a race all of the machines try and write the key and the one that writes it ... they all go and do a read and go oh I'm not the one that won" (~17:32)
- The lock holder can use the revision of its last write to update the key, extend the TTL or record progress for a long-lived job. "the one that won now has a revision of the last write so we can go back and even update it maybe increment the TTL" (~18:34)
- A "witness" process watches the lock key and heartbeats; when the worker's heartbeat disappears it deletes the key and signals a job restart. "as soon as the heartbeat disappears ... they go back and actually delete the key and then maybe issue another signal saying restart job" (~19:36)
- A semaphore generalizes the mutex: a pool of N resources that workers acquire and release, depleting and refilling over time. "more generalized from a mutex is a semaphore where you can have maybe a pool of resources that everyone is trying to compete for" (~20:37)
- Gaming use case: limited video-render farm capacity for ghost-lap replays, SAN write cycles and CDN upload rate/connection limits are all natural semaphore gates. "you'd only have limited resources to generate those videos ... there would be a queue" (~22:40)
- Batch data pipelines need a shared, distributed record of the last processed offset; store it as a KV key so a pool of workers can grab a job and its offset instead of using a local file or SAN. "you could maintain a key the last offset ... you just have a pool of workers just grab a job grab the last offset" (~28:46)
- For multi-patient analytics, relative order of events per patient is the unit of parallelism. "as long as you keep the relative order of events that occur to a patient that's your unit of parallelism" (~28:46)
- A lock key need not be boolean: store a state-machine value (acquired, in progress, next state) so a witness can detect a stalled transition, reset it and let another worker retry. "it doesn't have to be a binary true false mutex you can have a state machine almost in a way" (~29:49)
- Retry-on-stall requires idempotent downstream processing; rely on natural or primary keys across systems to model it. "there's many downstream things like idempotency you have to be aware of" (~30:49)
- Storing job state in KV rather than a database gives you real-time watching of state changes and an external witness that can intervene. "you don't have that benefit of really watching the state changes over time" (~31:50)
- Keys are subjects with a token hierarchy, so you can model a DAG of job states as a key hierarchy and watch a subtree; the watch history doubles as a write-ahead log for free. "because keys are under the hood just subjects and you have a token hierarchy you can model a DAG as a hierarchy naturally and then you can watch a sub tree" (~33:53)
- Distribute policy (e.g. firewall rules) by having each host run a local agent that watches a KV bucket and realises its own desired state, instead of a central orchestration pool. "there's a local agent running you watch the KV store and then it programmed its own IP tables stuff" (~34:55)
- Distributed leaky-token-bucket rate limiting: claim tokens in batches (e.g. 100), not one at a time, because per-token round trips cost more than the work being gated. "there's no point going to a token bucket going give me one token give me one token ... it's like give me a 100 tokens" (~38:59)
- Batch token claims can starve one worker; fairness systems sometimes have to be unfair to some participant. "you might starve one system out but that's the problem with fair systems" (~38:59)
- Three k3s servers continuously try to acquire a lease on a KV key for leader election; that is the same mechanism they use with etcd. "these three k3s servers that at a minimum all trying to acquire a lease on the KV bucket" (~42:02)
- Application-level leader election, quorum and leasing can be built on NATS KV even though the bucket has its own Raft leader underneath. "I need a leader election I need quorum I need leasing and unleasing you can use NATS KV to do that" (~44:05)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03: Escaping the HTTP Mindset with NATS.io**

- HTTP was designed to serve web pages, not for inter-service or intra-process communication, and most teams adopt it for services without questioning whether its semantics fit. "HTTP was designed as a protocol to serve the web... it was never designed to be inter-process communication" (~03:06)
- HTTP is appropriate as a well-understood "sentinel" mechanism at the edge (browser, front door), with NATS used for the component-to-component middle. "HTTP is great as like a sentinel mechanism that everyone understands at the edge" (~04:08)
- Using NATS as the communication mechanism between modules from the start gives location transparency: modules can live in one monolith or be split and distributed without changing how they talk. "those modules all connect to NATS... you don't have to know physically where they're located" (~09:14)
- Microservice "size" should be defined by DDD bounded context, not lines of code; a bounded context is a starting deployable unit but does not have to equal a single deployable. "bounded context does not equate to a single deployable unit either" (~14:21)
- Keep business capabilities and deployment units as separate dimensions of thought; only split further when part of a system must scale or ship on a different cadence. "decoupling the business logic... from the deployment unit and keeping those as separate dimensions of thought" (~15:23)
- Data and schema are the real contract regardless of transport; everything else is an implementation detail, and an orchestrating service only needs the data contract of what it calls. "data and schema at the end of the day are king and queen" (~16:23)
- The Enterprise Integration Patterns "routing slip" (a predetermined multi-step workflow carried with the message) is a way to make orchestration implicit over NATS, including parallel steps. "he has this message slip pattern... you basically have a predetermined workflow" (~18:25)
- Choreography (event-driven: publish an event, interested components react and may raise further events) and orchestration are a spectrum, not an either/or, chosen per component. "there's a spectrum and I think it depends on what your component is needing to do" (~26:34)
- Choreography decouples function invocation but not data: changing an event schema still breaks downstream subscribers, so data contracts must still be coordinated. "it still couples on the data side going back to schema and data, you can't get around that" (~27:34)
- HTTP cannot broadcast or publish to unknown receivers, which is why teams add a broker or SQS; NATS natively supports request-reply, request-reply-many (scatter/gather), fire-and-forget pub/sub, and persistent streams. "you can do request reply, request reply many... you can publish fire and forget... and then you also have persistent streams" (~28:36)
- Versioning/AB testing pattern: publish to a liberal subject, put the required version in a header, and let responders filter on headers; a new version just subscribes to the same subject. "put the required version in the header on a subject... you literally just pub it to a subject and then you do a scatter-gather response" (~30:37)
- Version can be placed either as a subject token (v1/v2, strict: only responders on that version answer) or in a header (permissive); both are available and the choice sets granularity. "you can even apply a v1 v2 in the subject itself... or you can say I'm going to be a little bit more permissive" (~32:41)
- Scatter-gather and "talk to many instances" come for free in NATS, whereas service discovery still limits HTTP callers to one component at a time. "you still are limited to talking to one component at a time... that just kind of comes for free for NATS" (~31:38)
- Design principle from the host: remove lookups and coordination steps (service catalogs, version tables) because each lookup adds fragility; let the system self-organize via subjects and headers. "remove the fragility by removing choice, allow the system to self-organize" (~36:45)
- NATS can be taken all the way to the front end (browser NATS client with its own auth), so HTTP is only needed at the authentication step. "the only time you use REST or HTTP... is maybe at the point of authentication" (~34:44)
- Observed call graphs in microservice systems are wide but shallow (hub-and-spoke), with few independent east-west calls beyond one or two hops. "the call stack's quite shallow, it might be wide but it's really quite shallow" (~22:31)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02: Monolith to Modular Monolith with NATS.io**

- For a certain scale of application and team, a monolith is the right deployment unit; microservices are not an end goal but a response to organizational coordination pain or a component needing to scale differently. "for a certain scale of application and a certain scale of team monolithic applications are the right choice" (~02:02)
- Load balancing is a native server primitive in NATS: subscribers forming a queue group get messages distributed at random across members with no extra software or external dependency. "the NATS server will distribute those messages across at random to those various members in that group without any additional software" (~07:06)
- Define a subscription as a queue group from day one even if it has a single member; adding instances later scales out transparently because new members just join the group. "you might only have one member of that group right now... from day one you can design this knowing that this is a potential point of distribution" (~11:13)
- Modular monolith path: divide functionality inside one monolith along boundaries and route the internal calls over NATS, so a second monolith instance can be stood up with the right subscriptions to scale horizontally. "internal communication for your monolith can begin to be over NATS" (~13:14)
- Use DDD bounded contexts as the boundaries; within a bounded context keep direct function calls, and put NATS only across boundaries that may be deployed separately later. "within a bounded context you can do function calls all day... but across boundaries those are potentially going to be deployed separately" (~15:18)
- The trade-off of NATS across module boundaries is a small added latency versus in-process calls, accepted in exchange for the ability to split, distribute, and scale later without rewriting. "if you can incur a tiny tiny extra little bit of latency... especially between the service boundaries" (~15:18)
- In Go the NATS server can be embedded directly in the application with no exposed TCP port, or an external server can broker the internal communication as a starting point. "you can even embed the NATS server directly into your application... you don't have to even expose any TCP connection" (~16:19)
- Hot paths in a monolith are the early candidates for extraction; a less-busy instance can serve them and they often have a different development cadence from stable integration components. "it's a good way of identifying early candidates of what can be extracted and removed" (~17:21)
- Embedding NATS in each modular-monolith instance and connecting instances effectively builds a cluster gradually. "connecting that instance to another modular monolith, you build a cluster out effectively in slow-mo" (~18:21)
- NATS used from day one covers messaging, streaming, and KV, acting as a framework for connectivity needs rather than a point tool. "if you just started with NATS from day one it'll serve all your application needs... you can do streaming and KV" (~20:25)
- Agreeing on a payload schema (protobuf, JSON schema) over NATS lets teams with different skills (C++ game engine vs. .NET monetization) keep their own language; NATS's client coverage makes polyglot splits natural. "each team gets to use their beloved language" (~22:29)
- Inventory example: the game watches a KV bucket key for the player, the transaction service updates that key, and the game gets the change notification without polling the database. "watching the KV inventory from the game with the C++ client... no database dips required" (~24:33)
- Polling a database for updates can be inverted into streaming state transitions or KV watchers, which is more responsive and optimized for that use. "if you invert that and you can just stream it out and you can model your state transitions in that way, that can be very powerful" (~26:36)
- Even without a distributed-systems problem, NATS is a useful lightweight starting point because it keeps the option to break off components open. "if you don't have that problem NATS can still be very very useful to you as a starting point" (~27:37)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP04: A Service Mesh Pattern for NATS.io**

- Networking "service function chaining" (steering packets sequentially through IDS, proxy, WAF via VLANs) is not what an application-level service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) does; the host retracts the conflation from the prior episode. "I completely conflated all of that with service meshes" (~04:05)
- What an application service mesh provides today: mTLS with certificate rotation, sidecar injection, service discovery, load balancing, circuit breaking, and black-box tracing. "TLS cert rotation, sidecar injection, service automatic service discovery, a little bit of tracing" (~10:11)
- Service mesh exists mainly because HTTP/gRPC systems have no built-in load balancing or service discovery; those are point-to-point protocols. "HTTP and gRPC based systems... there is no inherent load balancing that is built in" (~15:18)
- Canary / A-B traffic split (80/20) is done in NATS with weighted subject mapping: the public subject maps to .v1 and .v2 subjects by weight and versioned handlers subscribe to those. "a weighted mapping of saying this is the input subject... it gets mapped to a .v1 and a .v2" (~20:24)
- HTTP ingress pattern: a thin proxy maps HTTP method + path to a subject, carries HTTP headers as NATS headers, and does a NATS request on the caller's behalf. "you map basically the method and the path to a subject and then you can encode anything in the body or... in the headers" (~22:29)
- A KV bucket can act as a scheduler substitute: keys hold a minimum service count and workers on VMware, Hyper-V, or Kubernetes claim keys semaphore-style. "we could be using a KV bucket on NATS to say minimum number of services five and you could have some keys that can be claimed" (~30:40)
- Anycast HTTP gateways in multiple regions all bridging to one NATS system yields one globally deployed service set where the nearest responder answers. "one set of services running globally and the nearest one responds to that gateway" (~36:45)
- All of this (global availability, canary, load balancing) needs no network overlay, VXLAN, or encapsulation; it runs over plain IP via NATS. "there's no network mesh required underneath, there's no encapsulation, there's no VXLAN" (~38:47)
- Autoscaling can be self-organizing: when a gateway times out with no responder it can publish on an infrastructure subject and a listener claims and adds a responder; idle gateways can trigger scale-down. "nothing on Bob's responded, increase the license count maybe and then something listening says... I'm going to make that claim" (~39:48)
- Service chaining (responder hands the payload to the next responder, only the gateway waits for the final reply on its inbox) is possible with NATS subjects, relevant mainly for telco and industrial IoT. "handing a payload off to a system and just forgetting about it... only the proxy waits for the response from the last responder" (~43:51)
- Chained handoffs need strong contracts between teams and probably a write-ahead log to track where the baton is. "I think you need a write ahead log just to keep a track of... passing a baton around different services" (~42:51)
- Webhooks and HTTP-only integrations are the key use case for a declarative HTTP-to-NATS proxy; Byron hints a supported one is in progress and it would also support streaming, not just request/reply. "as long as you can configure this declaratively to make an HTTP call for an integration then I'm good" (~48:57)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP05: Exploring Powerful Client-side Features and Abstractions in NATS.io**

- Client design goal: shared orientation points (same verbs and nouns, same structure) across languages, but each client stays idiomatic; identical APIs everywhere is only something NATS engineers think users want. "we don't also want to fall into the trap to make each client the same" (~04:05)
- The services (micro) API is a purely client-side abstraction combining three server capabilities: the interest graph, subject-based routing, and queue groups; no server changes and no JetStream involved. "interest graph with subject based routing and the queue groups, those are the three elements" (~33:45)
- Services get discovery, ping, stats, per-instance addressing, and load balancing out of the box; service instances are stateless and scale by simply running more instances. "you get more instances by just running more instances of the service, you don't need anything to manage it" (~65:19)
- Service discovery via the services API is not a static registry: an instance is discoverable while connected and disappears immediately when offline, with no de-registration or timeout. "it's not a static register either... the second it goes offline then... it's not there" (~31:43)
- Setting max messages per subject to 1 yields a stream that keeps only the latest message per subject, which spawned new non-KV use cases. "thanks to that you can have infinite application of messages if you set it to one" (~37:48)
- The underlying KV/Object stream can be used directly with normal stream operations if the abstraction's API is not enough; recurring workarounds become API candidates. "if this workaround looks like a pattern in the whole community then it will be considered as part of the API" (~59:09)
- The services API doubles as an on-ramp: users who know HTTP handlers can write a request/reply service without understanding asynchronous messaging, then learn NATS top-down. "you don't have to grasp the whole asynchronous messaging stuff, it allows you to slowly get into it" (~66:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Micro-services with auto discovery, observability and load balancing. | Rethink Connectivity Ep 9**

- The NATS services API is a set of conventions baked into client libraries (Go `micro` package, JS/TS, Rust, Java) rather than a framework, proxy, or extra tooling. "the NATS service API is a set of conventions that is baked into a lot of our client libraries" (~01:01)
- A service declared with the API is instantly discoverable, observable via per-instance stats, load-balanced across instances, and can publish its request/reply schemas for client code generation. "you can also get the request and the reply schemas directly from these services just by talking to them" (~00:00)
- Handler errors are returned with a code and description carried as headers (a 400-style code for malformed input); a payload can optionally be attached. "return a 400... I'm okay just having the error be embedded as a header" (~10:11)
- Discovery is a one-to-many request: one request on the control subject gets a reply from every running instance, so no stateful service registry exists; the query reaches the services themselves. "these services aren't necessarily registering themselves with some stateful service discovery engine" (~16:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS as a ServiceMesh**

- If you are asking whether you need a service mesh, you probably do not; meshes carry a lot of complexity and the team must be able to support it. "if you're asking that question you probably don't need one" (~03:03)
- Service-mesh feature list to compare against: discovery, distributed caching, load balancing, retry/timeout, circuit breaking, authn/authz, canary/blue-green rollouts, traffic shifting, mirroring, mTLS, metrics, tracing. "discovery, distributed caching, load balancing, retry timeout circuit break, there's authentication" (~02:03)
- With NATS you do not need to know where a service is or its name; you need to know the subject hierarchy and whether a subscriber exists for request/reply. "I don't need the name of the service, I need to know what subject" (~07:09)
- Tracing is not built into the server; the nats-io "not.go" reference shows carrying an OpenTracing span as a binary prefix on the message payload, stripped by the receiver (worked C# → Go). "you basically shove that on the front of your message data... you chop that piece off" (~15:18)
- Load balancing in NATS is queue subscriptions (register the client with a queue name, effectively round-robin); locality-aware balancing comes from gateways, superclusters, and leaf nodes where closer subscribers get the message. "register your client with the queue name, that's how you load balance" (~17:20)
- Weighted load balancing was on the NATS roadmap at the time (later shipped as weighted subject mapping). "does a roadmap on a weighted load balancer" (~18:21)
- Traffic mirroring/shadowing in NATS is done by deploying the new version subscribing to the same subject (or wildcard) so it receives the same requests; permissions and accounts must allow it. "deploy a newer version and then listen for the same subject" (~20:24)
- Derek Collison: NATS covers both services (request/reply) and streaming; the constraint of meshes being built inside a deployment platform like Kubernetes is what NATS considers too restricting. "the constraint that it has to be built inside of a deployment platform like Kubernetes sometimes can be too restricting" (~25:28)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP01S3: Going back to basics with core NATS!**

- Understanding core NATS is the foundation; JetStream, KV, Object Store and the service API are all layered on it, so learn core first. "if you understand core NATS you will be fine with JetStream, Object, Key Value and whatever other abstractions we built on top of it" (~03:20)
- Everything in NATS is pub/sub: request/reply is pub/sub with a reply inbox, JetStream is request/reply, KV is JetStream. "request reply is pub sub with reply subject, JetStream is request reply which is pub sub, key value is JetStream which is again pub sub" (~22:40)
- Request/reply solves a whole class of timeout ambiguity: if the network is functional, NATS tells you immediately that nobody is listening instead of a timeout of unknown meaning. "you very quickly get an answer that nobody is there, maybe the service is down" (~11:27)
- For publisher-side reliability in core NATS, assume anything can fail and require an acknowledgement/response; use request/reply plus timeouts and retries where you need to know the message arrived. "you always need to retry and hopefully be prepared for the worst cases" (~14:31)
- Periodic signalling (an aggregate or heartbeat every 10 seconds) is a lightweight core-NATS way to know a system is alive without JetStream. "you might want a response back every 10 seconds to say here's an aggregate or here's the last thing that we received" (~16:32)
- Pull consumers already use heartbeats; a core-NATS app can adopt just the heartbeat idea ("once in 10 seconds let me know you're alive") without the rest of the guarantees. "in your specific use case you might not need all of those guarantees ... just one in 10 seconds just let me know" (~18:34)
- Start with core NATS; move to JetStream only when you find yourself reinventing consensus or replicated persistence. "at the moment you start feeling that you're reinventing the wheel of consensus or persistence ... then probably JetStream" (~21:38)
- It is easier to add guarantees incrementally (core → JetStream for specific subjects) than to start with JetStream everywhere and later remove guarantees. "it's much easier to just start adding this than do everything for JetStream and then say okay when I can resign from the guarantees" (~23:41)
- Because subjects decouple producers from storage, an app publishing sensor updates over core NATS can later have those subjects captured by a stream without changing the app. "you can just seamlessly switch to those subjects being captured by JetStream and the app doesn't even need to know" (~24:42)
- Strategy shift: core clients focus on reliability and low-level protocol bindings with unopinionated patterns; opinionated/experimental abstractions go to the separately versioned Orbit umbrella project. "switch the focus and the client to focus on reliability, basically low-level NATS protocol binding ... and then to create separately versioned libraries elsewhere" (~32:52)
- One connection preserves publish ordering across all publishers in the application, and subscribers see that same ordering. "with one connection you also preserve publish ordering" (~38:59)
- NATS has three "planes" (API: core/JetStream; security; topology); starting with all of them at once (JetStream over clustered leaf nodes with auth callout) piles on complexity, so start with a single server, one connection, and add features as they solve problems. "start with probably simple single server ... run an app with one connection ... make it use more features from there on" (~45:08)
- The scale path is incremental: core → JetStream, single server → cluster → leaf nodes/edge, unsecured → multi-tenancy with accounts. "you can scale it really easily from core NATS to JetStream, from single server to cluster, from cluster to leaf nodes" (~46:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02S3: Orbit - The NATS Client Extensions**

- Orbit is a line in the sand: existing client features stay, and every new client-side abstraction built on streams/consumers (like KV, Object Store and the service API are) lands in Orbit instead of the client. "every new abstraction built on top of ... will land in Orbit, so it's like a line in the sand to not break the clients" (~19:21)
- Contributing to Orbit only requires knowing the public client API, not client internals, which lowers the barrier compared with the large client codebases. "the only knowledge necessary being I know how to use the client, not the machinery of the client itself" (~25:29)
- Orbit never talks the wire protocol directly; it builds on the highest available client abstraction and drops at most one layer down to publish/subscribe. "never wire protocol ... we try to use as high level abstraction from the client in Orbit as possible" (~34:41)
- Typed JetStream request helpers (with typed errors and success responses) are being exposed in Go so users can build their own admin APIs on top. "allow people to build their own additional like admin API ... which is actually now exposed in the Orbit of Go" (~34:41)
- Request-many sends one request and collects multiple responses with pluggable stop strategies: expected message count, stall/jitter timeout since the last message, and others; it is a core-NATS extension built on pub/sub. "one of them being how many messages you expect, the other being the jitter, how long you expect to wait for the next message" (~35:41)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03S3: NATS 2.11 Release**

- Tracing is opt-in per message via a trace-destination header (an inbox); each hop sends a trace message back to that inbox, and the CLI wraps this as `nats trace <subject>`. "you provide an inbox and every step of the message ... will send back a trace message to the inbox that you specified" (~06:07)
- Overflow lets a client set a threshold (pending messages or pending acks) above which it starts receiving; e.g. three same-region clients serve normally and clients in another availability zone only pull when the primaries are too busy, minimizing cross-region cost without losing availability. "they will start getting messages only if the primary ones will get too busy" (~25:33)
- Pinning makes one client of many on a consumer receive all messages; the server uses TTLs to detect it stopped pulling and fails over to another client, replacing hand-rolled orchestration of a single active worker. "you can say that client A will get all the messages and the server has mechanisms and TTLs to find out that this client is no longer getting messages and the other one will take over" (~26:34)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS tools and benchmarking with JNM! NATS Community Office Hours (Reupload)**

- JetStream-enabled leaf nodes at the edge give store-and-forward: publishes are stored locally and guaranteed to be mirrored or sourced to the hub when connectivity returns, within milliseconds if the link is up. "it still is stored locally by the stream at the edge and reliably forwarded" (~06:08)
- Guaranteed delivery is not enough for a queue; you need guaranteed processing, e.g. a message whose database insert fails because the database is down for 10 minutes should be redelivered later, not block the partition. "it's not just the guaranteed delivery, you also want to do guaranteed processing" (~09:11)
- Terminate (term) is for messages that are themselves bad; unlike nak, it stops redelivery so a poison message does not loop forever. "the message itself is bad ... you can terminate the message" (~11:15)
- Kafka-style request/reply is CQRS (submit to one topic, poll another later); NATS offers interactive request/reply with geo-affinity where you learn within a timeout that nobody can process the request and can decide whether to resubmit. "I send a request, if there's no one able to process at this point I want to know about this in whatever timeout is" (~13:18)
- With CQRS-style requests, re-publishing after 30 seconds without an answer risks duplicating the work. "if you don't get an answer within 30 seconds and you publish another request, you're going to possibly duplicate the work" (~14:18)
- `nats bench` doubles as a load generator via a sleep between publishes (e.g. 200 µs), and multiple bench instances can be combined for steady load plus bursts. "you can also use it to generate load, generate traffic ... you can set the duration here" (~45:56)
- Benchmark JetStream publish and consume separately before combining them, because together they compete for CPU and you cannot tell which limits the other. "when you do the both together you don't know which one is limiting the other" (~52:04)
- Consumer decision tree: multiple apps sharing a stream or needing resumable position → durable; otherwise ephemeral, and among ephemerals the ordered consumer should be the default. "Ordered consumer should be your default go-to" (~59:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Benchmark Core NATS & NATS JetStream using the NATS CLI tool**

- Run benchmarks on your own target environment (machines, network, pods) rather than trusting published numbers; the CLI is the tool for that. "run benchmarks on your own target environments to see what kind of actual realistic performance you will get" (~00:00)
- Ephemeral consumers suit one app instance getting its own copy of the data at its own pace, disappearing when the app quits; durable consumers are shared by many instances and distribute messages between them like a queue. "a durable consumer essentially acts as a queue for distribution purposes" (~18:19)
- Pull consumers let you specify a batch, which matters because downstream processing (e.g. writing to a database) also needs batching to keep up with the message rate. "if you end up writing one by one to for example a database without batching things then you would never be able to keep up" (~21:22)
- Pull consumers are the horizontal-scaling primitive: add more instances for throughput, or use bigger batches on fewer, faster machines. "pull consumers ... allow you to scale out horizontally" (~22:23)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS: Ordered, Scalable Stream Processing**

- Ordinary NATS load balancing is non-deterministic, so two messages on the same subject can land on different workers and lose per-key order. "ordinary load balancing in NATS is non-deterministic. Two messages on the same subject can land on two different workers" (~01:00)
- Partitioned consumer groups route every message sharing a partition key to the same worker while different keys run in parallel; it is the Kafka consumer group model built from two JetStream pieces. "If that sounds like Kafka consumer groups, that is the same model built in NATS from two JetStream pieces" (~01:00)
- Pinning gives a single active worker with hot standby and no separate leader election system. "a single active worker with a hot standby and no separate leader election system to run" (~03:02)
- Handlers should be idempotent because a rare double delivery during failover is possible. "That is why your handlers should be idempotent" (~03:02)
- Vocabulary: the stream holds data, a group is a kind of work over the stream, a group's work is split into partitions, and each partition is owned by a member (a consumer plus its worker and standbys); one stream can feed many groups. "a single stream can feed many groups, each reading it independently" (~09:07)
- The fix for a known hot key is custom partition-to-member mapping (dedicate a member to the hot partition), not more partitions. "the fix isn't really adding more partitions. It's custom mapping" (~12:10)
- Key-to-worker affinity also yields a high local cache hit rate for slow external lookups; that use does not need max_ack_pending=1, so a worker can keep several messages in flight. "this doesn't need max act pending equals one. You only need key to worker affinity, not serial processing" (~15:16)
- Static groups have the lowest latency and fewest resources; elastic costs a duplicate copy of your messages in the hidden work queue. "at the cost of a duplicate copy of your messages" (~16:17)
- Rule of thumb: static when membership is known and stable; elastic when membership changes, when you can't transform the stream, or when several groups share one stream. "reach for static when membership is known and stable, reach for elastic when membership changes" (~16:17)
- Partitioning is useful even without strict ordering (max_ack_pending=1), e.g. for local caching. "If you don't require this ordering, you can still use this partitioning. There's other reasons such as optimizing local caching" (~30:34)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Pull Consumer Priority Groups: Overflow, Pinned & Prioritized**

- Priority groups replace leader election, lock services, and coordination code for "send all work to one client, fail over instantly" and "drain locally first, spill to another region" patterns. "There's no leader election, no lock service, and no coordination code for you to write and maintain" (~01:00)
- Overflow suits regional routing: local clients handle the common case and cross-region traffic is paid for only when locals genuinely fall behind. "you only pay for cross-region traffic when there's genuinely too much work for the locals to keep up" (~02:00)
- Overflow vs prioritized trade-off: overflow's threshold keeps assignments stable but lets backlog build; prioritized hands over with zero delay and no threshold, at the cost of flip-flopping between clients or regions. "Prioritized hands work over with zero delay and no threshold at all. And the trade-off is some flip-flopping" (~04:02)
- Tiers can be stacked with prioritized: US East priority 0, US West priority 1, EU West priority 2 only sees traffic when both US regions are quiet. "Put EU West at priority two, so it only ever sees traffic when both US regions are quiet" (~05:02)
- Pinned client fits jobs that must not run in parallel (billing run, stateful migration): HA without duplicate processors or a separate lock service. "You get high availability without running duplicate processors and without standing up a separate lock service" (~05:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Distributed Counters in NATS — Global Totals Without Locks**

- NATS 2.12 adds a distributed counter to JetStream: enable a stream flag, publish signed deltas as headers, and every replica converges to the same total without consensus or locks, even with out-of-order arrival. "every replica converges to the same total without consensus, without locks, even with messages arriving out of order" (~01:01)
- Multi-region aggregation: regional counters publish to their own subjects, a continental stream sources them with subject transforms, and a global stream sources the continental ones. "A continental stream sources both with subject transforms, and a global stream sources the continental ones" (~03:03)
- Resetting a replicated counter means publishing a matching negative delta; purge alone will not propagate across sources. "resetting a replicated counter means publishing a matching negative delta. Purge alone won't propagate across sources" (~04:03)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Delayed Message Scheduling in NATS — One-Time, Cron, and Subject Sampling**

- Subject sampling (2.14) republishes the latest message from a source subject on a schedule, e.g. the latest reading every 5 minutes from a sensor emitting hundreds per second. "you can capture just the latest reading every 5 minutes, reducing noise for downstream analytics without touching the sensor code" (~03:03)
- Set Nats-Schedule-TTL so generated messages expire and consumers can discard stale deliveries, e.g. after a restart replays past-due schedules; this requires allow_message_ttl on the stream. "You can set a NATS schedule TTL to give generated messages an expiration, so consumers can detect and discard stale deliveries" (~03:03)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Per-Message TTL — Fine-Grained Expiration for JetStream Messages**

- Named uses: session state that auto-expires without cleanup jobs, distributed cache entries with natural TTLs, per-key KV TTLs. "You can auto expire sessions without cleanup jobs" (~01:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Expected Sequence Headers — Optimistic Concurrency Control Explained**

- Expected sequence headers give optimistic concurrency control: multiple processes work in parallel without locks and conflicting writes are detected and rejected rather than prevented. "It'll detect and reject conflicting rights instead of just outright preventing them" (~00:00)
- Track the sequence returned in each pub ack and use it as the expected value for the next publish. "You track the return sequence and use it for the next publish" (~07:09)
- Per-pattern lets you supply a wildcard pattern (e.g. events.order.1.>) so related subjects for one entity share sequence tracking while other entities stay independent; use it for event sourcing where entity events span multiple subjects. "order.1.created and order.1.shipped can share the same sequence tracking while order two anything stays independent" (~08:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Consumer Pausing | NATS 2.11**

- Named uses: deployments and migrations, emergency maintenance, debugging production issues, rate limiting downstream services. "Deployments and migrations, emergency maintenance, debugging production issues, or rate limiting downstream services" (~01:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Atomic Batch Publishing | NATS 2.12**

- Nats-Expected-Last-Sequence (or the per-subject variant) on the first message of a batch gives optimistic locking: the batch fails if the stream moved while it was built, and you retry with fresh data. "This header is only allowed on the first message of a batch" (~02:03)
- A batch can span multiple subjects in one stream, so messages fanned out to warehouse, payment, and notification consumers commit together. "Different messages going to different consumers but all committed together" (~06:05)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS: Orbit – Extending NATS Clients with Richer Capabilities**

- Request-many (one request, many replies) landed in Orbit rather than the clients because the termination strategies are opinions. "there are quite a few strategies you can terminate the responses and those felt like opinions" (~06:16)
- JetStream retry strategies could not go into clients because banking and vehicle use cases differ too much; they land in Orbit as quality-of-life additions. "retrying is quite often in JetStream is tricky and very opinionated ... impossible to have one solution" (~13:26)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Two-Node Engine with David & Byron**

- Use case: making two identical simple services (e.g. two web servers) highly available with a floating IP and no load balancer, in constrained or remote systems. "without requiring a low balancer" (~02:04)
- External integration works through a "transitioning" KV key: the FSM sets it during a transition, your code (any NATS client) does its work, then updates the key so the engine finishes the transition. "once your code has completed you then update this NATS KV value this transitioning key value and the engine will basically carry on" (~03:04)
- Without a preemption flag the engine latches into the failed-over state, so restoring the configured leader is a deliberate step, avoiding disruptive preemptive restoration in mission-critical stacks. "we might not want the disruption of a preemptive restoration" (~06:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — We need to talk about Microservices... (And how NATS.io can simplify things)**

- The core design shift for microservices on NATS is location transparency: stop asking "who do I talk to" (IP, DNS) and ask "what do I want to talk about" (a subject). "shifting from this who do I talk to to what do I want to talk about really is a fundamental shift" (~03:04)
- Services are addressed by subjects such as math.add, payments.create, search.add_index; the only location a client needs is the NATS server it connects to. "you just need to know the NATS server that you connect to and then you just want to know what you want to talk about" (~04:04)
- An API gateway's two jobs (aggregating many service endpoints behind one endpoint, and a single auth layer) are things the NATS server already does by brokering subjects between clients. "NATS actually just naturally does this ... NATS is the broker between those subjects" (~05:04)
- Load balancing between service instances is built in via queue groups, with no reverse proxy or separate service-discovery process needed. "NATS has load balancing just built in out of the box with a feature called queue groups" (~06:04)
- Queue groups work across clusters and superclusters: a request is first served by a responder in the local cluster and only goes outside if none exists, which gives geo load balancing plus automatic regional failover. "it's going to first try to see if there is anything that can respond ... in its local cluster and if not it's going to search outside" (~06:04)
- The NATS server has no concept of a registered service; service discovery is pure convention built on request/reply to $SRV.PING, where every subscribed instance self-reports. "the NATS server actually doesn't have a concept of services ... we just use convention" (~08:08)
- The `micro` service library exists in many client libraries and lets you declare a service with name, version, endpoints and arbitrary metadata (e.g. description, request/response schema). "we have a little library called micro and it's in many of our client libraries already" (~09:11)
- Self-reported schemas in service metadata could replace a schema registry if adopted as an organizational convention. "maybe you don't need a schema registry if all of the microservices are self-reporting their own schemas by convention" (~10:12)
- The `micro info` response is itself load balanced: whichever instance answers reports its own ID. "this is the ID of the actual instance that decided to respond ... it's actually load balancing the info response" (~12:14)
- Requests to an endpoint served by three micro instances are split fairly evenly between them without any extra configuration. "they've been split fairly evenly between the three nodes" (~13:16)
- Canary deployments are done with weighted subject mappings (server config, or per-account under JWT auth) so callers keep using the same subject. "you might want to route a certain percentage of traffic ... to a V1 versus a V2 and still not have to update any of the clients" (~15:20)
- A "log tap" pattern: services publish structured logs to core NATS (not JetStream) on subjects that carry instance, level, region; any subscriber can filter them in real time. "because it's subject based addressing you can key off of the instance of the service or the log level" (~18:23)
- The speaker does not suggest NATS replace a log store outright; treat the log tap as a debugging "break the glass" switch and keep the default level at error so you don't flood the server. "I've set the log level ... to actually just show me errors that way I'm just not slamming the NATS server with all of my logs" (~19:24)
- The same log subjects can be captured into a stream on demand (nats stream add with subjects math.log.>) for later analysis. "I can even put this into a JetStream if I wanted to" (~20:26)
- Monitoring uses scatter-gather: one stats request fans out to every instance and each responds with its own counters, which can feed a Prometheus-style scrape without an index of URLs. "you can get this very very easily without having to have some sort of index of all of the URLs" (~22:27)
- Authorization in NATS is subject based: JWT claims list which subjects a user may publish or subscribe to, with wildcards, so service-to-service permissions are as fine grained as subjects. "all of the permissions are also driven by subjects" (~26:30)
- One credential authenticates a service to every other service and to the data stores, giving a single unified security model. "one credential to access all of those things" (~26:30)
- Dynamic configuration: services read config from a KV bucket and watch for changes, so log level or other settings change live without restarting pods. "these apps that don't need to be restarted ... they could live update" (~27:32)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — JetStream KV: A fascinating alternative to Redis...**

- Watching keys replaces polling and restarts for configuration: "many many companies" use KV as a configuration-management layer with apps watching for changes. "instead of your applications having to poll ... you can just have them watch for changes" (~04:02)
- Create fails if the key already exists and, combined with TTL, is the primitive for leader election, distributed locks and leases. "the create command ... will fail if that key already exists ... we can use this in combination with TTLs to do very cool things like leadership elections" (~11:08)
- A KV mirror is an automatic read replica: NATS serves reads from the closest mirror and forwards writes to the origin leader with no application change. "NATS is smart enough to serve up requests from the closest mirror ... all of the writes are going to go through the leader" (~18:14)
- Sourcing with subject filters "demuxes" a large central KV into smaller regional or per-business-unit buckets near the consuming apps. "I can source all of this data and just filter on the stuff that I care about" (~19:16)
- The inverse, "muxing", sources many edge KVs (e.g. on Raspberry Pis) into one central cloud KV; subject remapping while sourcing lets each edge key space be rewritten into the aggregate. "you can now do remapping as soon as you're sourcing into these streams" (~21:17)
- Batch get across related keys (user.id, user.name, user.email) fetches a "row" of fields in one request, approaching Redis/DynamoDB semantics. "you can actually use a batch get to get all of those fields in one request" (~23:21)
- Leader election recipe: bucket with a ~3 s TTL; non-leaders loop every second calling Create on key "leader"; the leader renews with Update using its last revision, and an Update error means leadership was lost. "we want the key value store to be able to tell us hey you're working on outdated information and you are no longer the leader" (~30:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The ONE feature that makes NATS more powerful than Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ & Redis**

- Three consumer archetypes: event-sourcing (durable, explicit ack, max-ack-pending 1, all subjects), reporting (ephemeral, start-time, filter), lookup (ephemeral, filter by ID, last-per-subject). "we probably want ... durable we want our acks to be explicit and our max ack pending to one" (~03:03)
- Ephemeral consumers are cleaned up by the server after an inactivity threshold and are very fast to create, which makes ad hoc queries, reporting and browser sessions scalable. "consumers are very very fast to spin up ... ephemeral consumers are actually possible to do in a very scalable way" (~09:11)
- Recommendation: consolidate related data into one stream (e.g. one orders stream with the whole lifecycle) rather than a topic per event type, and rely on filter subjects. "we usually recommend people try to consolidate a lot of things to one stream" (~10:12)
- Max ack pending 1 gives strict in-order processing but is very slow; try to avoid it unless a downstream state machine truly needs strict ordering. "I would actually recommend trying to see if you can get away without having a max ack pending of one" (~25:26)
- Rule of thumb: if you are just inserting events into a database with indexed timestamps, you do not need strict ordering; only decision-making state machines do. "a lot of people think that they need ordering but often ... they're just putting them in a database" (~25:26)
- Last-per-subject suits change-data-capture style reads where only the latest state per subject matters. "give me all the last updated events from all of the orders" (~19:23)
- Replay policy "original" reproduces the original inter-message timing, useful for replaying sessions or debugging spikes; "instant" delivers as fast as flow control allows. "play back the messages in the same timings that they were originally done in" (~20:24)
- Debugging in production: create an ephemeral debug consumer with any configuration without touching or reconfiguring the stream. "the stream is the stream and the consumers are all the consumers" (~21:24)
- Preserving full ordering while scaling out requires partitioning, called out as a separate topic. "maintain complete ordering here and scale these out via partitioning" (~29:30)
- Lookup: ephemeral consumer filtered on orders.*.<orderID>.* with deliver-last gives the current status; last-per-subject gives the full status lifecycle in order. "we could actually use deliver last as well if we just wanted the last status update for this particular order" (~37:39)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Give your Go app superpowers with an Embedded NATS Server**

- Go applications can import nats-server/v2 and run the server in process; benefits are no separate NATS distribution and the option to bypass the network stack entirely. "we can actually bypass the network interface altogether and directly talk to NATS in process" (~00:00)
- Target use cases: modular monoliths, offline-first desktop apps, applications-as-infrastructure that auto-mesh or leaf-node to each other, and environments with no network such as Wasm in the browser. "what if you're building something like a modular monolith or a offline first desktop application" (~02:03)
- With in-process connections you keep multi-tenancy, JetStream, KV and Object Store while "literally just pushing bytes around inside of the application". "we're not going through the network layer we're literally just pushing bytes around inside of the application" (~04:05)
- A single NATS protocol becomes the unified RPC layer whether the peer is in process, on the same box, or across the world; this keeps separation of concerns in a monolith and eases later extraction into microservices. "you have this single protocol that you use to be able to communicate with things" (~06:06)
- An embedded server can leaf-node to a remote/cloud NATS server so JetStream data written locally syncs to the cloud, with control over whether the network is used. "we might want to sync that over to the cloud on a remote NATS server ... we can actually do that with leaf nodes" (~05:06)
- A request from the cloud account reaches the in-process responder through the leaf node and the reply is forwarded back, so in-process connections remain fully reachable across the topology. "even though you're using in-process connections you could still reach in and all the NATS stuff kind of works" (~23:24)
- Publishes into the cloud account on the embedded stream's subjects are captured by the embedded stream because the subscription crossed the leaf connection. "this is again sending it to Synadia Cloud but this is actually being picked up by the embedded NATS server" (~24:26)
- Backing up the local stream to the cloud is a mirror created in the cloud with "import from a different JetStream domain" set to the embedded domain; this is the offline-first sync pattern. "we just created essentially an offline first application ... NATS kind of forwards all that data once we get connected again" (~25:29)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Stream processing: the easy way (with NATS and Benthos)**

- Positioning: NATS plus Benthos is offered as a third option between a bespoke program and a heavyweight stateful stream processor such as Flink or Spark. "either you go and write a bespoke program ... or you opt into a heavyweight stream processing tool a stateful stream processor" (~00:00)
- Benthos is a stateless source→pipeline→sink processor; because it holds no state it scales horizontally and relies on sources/sinks for state, which JetStream provides. "benthos really doesn't need to store any state about what it's doing it can remain completely stateless" (~02:04)
- JetStream streams or KV can sit on the source side, the sink side, or as intermediate state between pipeline stages. "you can have JetStream whether it's a stream or a KV end up on either the source or the sink side ... and then things like NATS KV store some intermediate state" (~04:05)
- With NATS as communication and persistence layer, you run as many stateless Benthos processes as needed without a Flink cluster to babysit. "you're not babysitting like a Flink cluster ... you're really just using this configuration based data processing pipeline" (~05:06)
- Bridging (e.g. Kinesis→JetStream) lets you pull a field out of the payload and use it as the JetStream subject to get subject indexing. "pull something out of its payload and use that as a subject inside of JetStream so you get all that really nice fun indexing" (~07:07)
- The Kinesis→JetStream bridge was about 11 lines of YAML and moved 123,000 rating events into the stream. "we have 123,000 events coming into the ratings" (~12:12)
- Benthos's transactional model covers source and sink being offline so messages are not dropped, without Benthos storing state. "if either one of these things are offline benthos has a really great transactional model to make sure ... messages aren't dropped" (~13:13)
- Enrichment pipeline: S3 CSV input → HTTP lookup (OMDb) in a branch processor → write to a NATS KV keyed by media ID, so a rate-limited API is called once per record instead of on every read. "I don't want to have to look up that poster every time especially since I have an API key that has a rate limit" (~17:17)
- Lightweight analytics does not always need a stateful stream processor; the speaker scopes this to lightweight pipelines, not terabyte-scale stateful jobs. "you don't always need to have a big stateful stream processor in order to do a lot of work" (~23:26)
- The analytics pipeline reads the ratings stream, looks up media in KV and customers in SQLite (results stored as message metadata, not payload), and updates a media_ratings KV with count and rolling average. "we want to update a new key value store called media ratings" (~25:27)
- Scaling to many Benthos instances without KV write contention has two options: partition on the source side, or use optimistic concurrency control so concurrent writers to the same key serialize instead of overwriting. "one is to partition on the source side ... the other one is to use optimistic concurrency control" (~25:27)
- The custom nats_kv_update template does get → mutate → write back with OCC so writers on the same media ID "do a single file line" and apply sequentially. "we're using our optimistic concurrency control to make sure that clients who are processing the same rating ... are not stomping on each other" (~29:33)
- Error handling is delegated to NATS: on any processor error the output NAKs the JetStream message so redelivery/retries come from the consumer rather than from Benthos logic. "if anything's errored then make sure you nack on the NATS side so we can do any sort of retries" (~30:35)
- Backup/tiered-storage pattern: JetStream input → batch 1,000 (max ack pending set to 10,000) → tar + gzip → S3 with a timestamped path; sending message-by-message to S3 is called out as inefficient. "you don't want to just send a message by message over to S3 that's going to be really inefficient" (~33:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS Surveyor**

- Derek Collison: service latency in a global supercluster is four-dimensional (responder processing time, responder-to-server distance, requester-to-server distance, server-to-server distance), and Surveyor reports all four in real time; single-number latency is "too limiting". "service latency is not a single dimension it's actually four dimensions" (~19:34)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Transcending microservices with NATS | RethinkConn '22**

- Microservices are not a free lunch; adopt them only for a real need such as multiple geographies, data sovereignty, multi-cloud, acquisitions, or extending to the edge. "we certainly don't want to advocate for people to move to microservices for the heck of it" (~02:02)
- Leaky service addressability and point-to-point service interactions create a "Death Star" web of services that needs load balancers and service discovery layered in; pub/sub with end-to-end communication removes those layers. "you have to add all these layers in between like load balancers and service discovery" (~11:13)
- Goals of the NATS design: decentralized zero trust, provider agnosticism, location transparency, many-to-many communication, and one uniform connective layer. "I want to send a message I want to receive that message no matter where you are in the world" (~12:13)
- The many separate stacks (RPC, message queue, durable job queue, append-only log, KV) all reduce to sending, receiving, or asking a question; one substrate can replace them. "we're either sending or receiving data or we're asking it a question" (~13:15)
- A "request many"/broadcast roll call every 5 seconds fans out one request to 60+ browser clients worldwide, each replying, and the replies are aggregated. "this is actually using a request many broadcast ... every five seconds" (~16:16)
- HTTP cannot do fan-in/fan-out roll calls (one request, many responders); NATS pub/sub patterns apply to microservices, not just queues and jobs. "you can't just ping a URL and have a roll call come back via HTTP" (~17:17)
- Native HTTP/REST from the browser can be bridged to NATS with simple shims; treat HTTP as a ports-and-adapters layer on the perimeter, with NATS connecting everything behind it. "there's very very simple shims that can be deployed to do a nice translation directly from native HTTP requests into a NATS message" (~25:28)
- Best practice for web clients: a backend exchanges the app's identity token (e.g. OIDC/Google) for a freshly minted NATS user JWT with a short expiration, reissued as needed. "issuing JWTs on the fly as bearer tokens with very short windows for expiration" (~28:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Seamless evolution across geos and clouds | RethinkConn '22**

- Scale and latency are usually treated as non-functional requirements, but in practice they are functional: the system has to work and respond in time; topology becomes a design lever once the technology lets you place services anywhere. "if you actually care about latency or scale it actually becomes arguably a functional requirement" (~00:00)
- With freedom of topology you can place services for data sovereignty or co-locate them with clients for ultra-low latency (e.g. factory floors), and topology directly affects network latency. "topology also impacts your network latency overall if you can place services in the right location" (~03:02)
- Deploying a NATS-connected app is minimal configuration: a container plus replica count on any hosting provider, and it connects and communicates. "How do you deploy a NATS app via Kubernetes? And it's like a three-line YAML file" (~10:11)
- Adding a second service instance in another region gave load balancing and intelligent routing for free; clients nearer the East Coast got much lower RTTs because requests stopped hopping to Los Angeles. "load balancing happens for free. And intelligent routing happens for free" (~11:12)
- Service instances share a queue group; by default NATS randomly selects one member to service a request. "NATS is going to randomly select, by default ... an instance to service that request" (~12:22)
- NATS is deliberately payload-agnostic (strings, base64, JSON, BSON, protobuf); schema validation will not be a core feature but an opt-in add-on, and can be built today with subject mapping and conventions routing traffic through a validating service. "Is it going to be in core NATS and a core feature? Probably not" (~18:27)
- Clients and services were flipped from NGS nodes to a local leaf node without changing the application; 24 leaf nodes on Fly.io extended NGS and services reconnected to their local leaf node. "24 leaf nodes all extending the NGS cluster deployed all over the place" (~24:34)
- With a regular account and no admin access you can extend a SaaS supercluster with your own leaf nodes; or leaf-node a single-region self-hosted system into NGS so edge traffic uses NGS's global footprint. "you can leaf node your system into NGS and have ... everything at the edge talking to NGS" (~25:37)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Where are we now and where to next? | RethinkConn '22**

- Most customers adopt NATS to attack one of four macro problems: speed of innovation, time to market, total cost of ownership, and vendor lock-in. "speed of innovation, time to market, total cost of ownership and vendor lock-in" (~02:03)
- One deployment gives streams, KV, and object store from edge to cloud; an app written on a laptop moves to cloud or edge by changing one URL. "I have to change one URL and the same thing can run in the cloud, on the edge, wherever" (~03:04)
- Scaling services is not a configuration issue: launching more instances into a queue group scales up, and APIs exist to scale down without losing data. "scalability isn't a configuration issue ... it's just launching more instances" (~05:08)
- Most users do not need 20 million messages per second, but that headroom means smaller machines that do not need re-provisioning for years. "a lot of users may not necessarily need 20 million messages a second ... I can do a lot more with less" (~05:08)
- Operators use accounts as guard rails: a fixed number of connections, subscriptions, and HA JetStream assets per account prevents the noisy-neighbor problem and lets teams work in their own sandbox. "set up an account with a specified number of connections, subscriptions, number of high availability assets ... that development team won't exceed that" (~06:08)
- Layer model: communications is the grid where data can go, security is the switches deciding where it is allowed, and persistence (streams, KV, object store) sits on top. "communications is like a power grid ... security are your switches" (~08:10)
- Experimental service API: write a service in a few lines and get health endpoints, statistics, and eventually command and control. "that service would have health endpoints ... I could poll it for statistics" (~11:14)
- Service mesh was built to solve point-to-point, location-based addressing; NATS lacks that flaw, so discovery (a no-op once connected), load balancing, traffic management, and canary testing come built in without Kubernetes. "service mesh ... was built to solve a fundamental design flaw which was point-to-point location-based addressing" (~17:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Versioning and canary deployments with subject mapping | RethinkConn '22**

- Subject mapping converts a published subject into a different subject before delivery; this replaces API gateways or load balancers for versioning and canaries. "takes the input subject name and converts it to a different subject name that is then routed to a subscriber" (~01:02)
- Version subjects internally (e.g. greeter.v1) but expose an unversioned public subject and map it, so version numbers stay out of the public API. "maybe you don't want to necessarily expose the version number as part of your public subject names" (~02:03)
- Weighted mappings do traffic shaping for canaries: route 90% to stable v1 and 10% to v2, then raise the weight until v2 takes all traffic. "90 of the time route it to the stable V1 version ... only 10 of the traffic actually goes to V2" (~03:04)
- Use permissions to keep versioned subjects internal: services may subscribe to v1/v2/v3 subjects while clients may publish only to the unversioned public subject. "restricts the clients to be able to publish only to that non-versioned subject" (~05:06)
- Subject mapping on a leaf node connection lets a site publish to a plain local subject (inventory) that is remapped to a namespaced hub subject (inventory.storeID), so the site needs less knowledge about itself. "inventory dot store ID to just be mapped to inventory and so the locality has to know less information about itself" (~06:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extending stateful services to the edge | RethinkConn '22**

- Stateful services usually push state to a pristine central database, which adds another network hop and a system you must protect as the source of truth. "you have the service deployed, it has to talk to typically a database which is another network hop" (~01:04)
- Edge compute (workers, edge functions) still suffers central-store latency; the next problem is moving data close to compute at the edge, and large localized clusters holding data are not a great answer. "I still have the same latency problems in a lot of ways" (~03:05)
- To get Redis-like tight RTTs from a JetStream KV, run leaf nodes near the application with local read replicas; you gain lower RTT and continued reads when the leaf node is disconnected from the hub. "when that leaf node gets disconnected from the hub it can still function and it can still read from its config" (~09:14)
- A mirror can have a completely different configuration from its origin: the origin was file-based, R3, limits retention, while the leaf mirror was R1, memory storage, work-queue retention. "when I created my mirror I said I only want one replica ... memory and I want it to be a work queue retention" (~11:17)
- Reverse direction: small edge boxes (e.g. Raspberry Pis) use tight retention and store-and-forward via sourcing/mirroring into a hub stream with near-unlimited retention. "retention policy is pretty tight and we do a store and forward over to the hub in the cloud" (~11:17)
- Many clients fetching from one shared consumer bound to the local mirror compete for messages; unacknowledged messages get redelivered (delivery count rises) once the end is reached. "it's starting to now redeliver unless you're acknowledging the messages" (~13:20)
- Mirrors act as digital twins (same messages elsewhere); sourcing muxes many leaf streams into one central "mega stream" for processing pipelines, or demuxes a central stream out to leaf nodes/accounts filtered by subject or wildcard. "we can also demux data ... you get a replica of this data but only a portion of it" (~15:22)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Using JetStream KV for dynamic microservice configuration | RethinkConn '22**

- A KV bucket held live configuration (server URL, subject mapping target, feature flags) that all 55 web apps and every leaf node watched; one put fanned out a watch event to all of them. "with one little push to a KV they all received this watched event that this value has been changed" (~02:03)
- Leaf nodes and clients reacted to the watched key by dynamically unsubscribing and resubscribing to the newly specified server. "those are dynamically unsubscribing and then resubscribing to the server that I specify" (~02:03)
- Browsers acted as queue-group members of a V3 service; requesters got responses from members in their own cluster (e.g. GCP vs AWS), demonstrating closest-responder routing. "it really does do that location transparency and intelligent routing" (~05:10)
- Prefer KV-backed dynamic configuration with locked-down permissions over environment variables, files, or Kubernetes config management; it allows hot reload without restarting services. "you can hot reload their configuration ... without having to restart them" (~06:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking connectivity from cloud to edge | RethinkConn '22**

- Distributed systems have only two interactions: asking and answering questions (microservices/SOA) and making and processing statements (event and data streaming, telemetry). "they can ask and answer questions ... and they can make and process statements" (~04:07)
- Event and data streaming exists mainly to let systems answer microservice questions better, with more data to personalize responses. "event and data streaming are generally used to allow systems to better answer these questions" (~04:07)
- Stateless edge functions (Lambda, edge functions, Wasm) are fine, but once an edge function needs state that lives across the globe the experience is still poor; this is the unsolved problem. "once that edge function really needs data it needs state, it becomes kind of a different story" (~08:10)
- Kubernetes made multi-cloud approachable for compute; a similar technology is needed to treat all infrastructure the same across edge providers, clouds, geos, and your own edge (stores, factories, cars, satellites, ships, medical devices). "the ability to treat all infrastructure the same, any edge provider, any cloud provider across any geos" (~09:12)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Lightweight relational databases at the edge | RethinkConn '22**

- Streams and KV are built into the server, but different data models are needed to query data; the proof of concept projects a raw stream into a relational table for edge workloads. "how can we take a raw stream and actually represent that as a table in a relational database" (~01:01)
- For edge friendliness the PoC uses embedded SQLite on disk, with DuckDB planned for OLAP-style queries; drivers can be extended to other databases. "let's use existing databases that work well there so this is actually using SQLite embedded" (~03:02)
- Creating a table creates a consumer on the same-named stream and subscribes; default columns are the sequence, subject, timestamp, headers (as JSON), and the raw data blob, because nothing more can be inferred from an opaque payload. "create a table, create a consumer and then subscribe" (~04:02)
- Declaring the payload encoding as JSON lets you map explicit JSON fields (id, name, preferences) to real columns and choose a key column as primary key. "you can actually define explicit columns to augment the table" (~06:05)
- Without a declared key the table is append-only, so retries produce duplicate rows keyed by sequence; with a key it behaves like a KSQL-style table where a new message for the same key updates the row in place. "we didn't append a new customer record, we actually updated the record in place" (~09:08)
- Intended architecture: mirror streams down to edge devices and run the projection process locally, joining across tables in a real database; the process resumes populating after disconnect and reconnect. "the nsql process can get disconnected from the server and then you reconnect and then it just keeps resuming" (~11:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Using NATS JetStream as a Kine backend for k3s | RethinkConn '22**

- Multiple edge k3s clusters (NYC, LA, Chicago) each used their own KV bucket on one shared NATS server at the distribution center. "run three clusters but back them all to the same NATS server" (~06:11)
- Extending to the cloud was done by reconfiguring the distribution-center server as a leaf node into NGS; store inventory then appeared in a cloud web app without VPN access. "reconfigure my NATS server here and have it point to NGS as a leaf node" (~07:13)
- The pattern generalizes to multiple distribution centers, NATS at the store level, store-to-store communication, and feeding data down from the top rather than only up from the edge. "you can feed in data from the top as opposed to pushing it all up through the bottom" (~11:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Service monitoring with Helix and Surveyor | RethinkConn '22**

- Recent server versions let an account import its own export, so latency tracking also covers requests made inside the same account. "I can import my own export ... so I can also get latency tracking for things that are happening inside my account" (~16:19)
- This gives client-to-server-to-responder-and-back RTT plus client location metadata, which is hard to get from HTTP or a load balancer. "this kind of gives you information that you can't even get very easily with HTTP itself or with a load balancer" (~17:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Short break and Q&A! | RethinkConn '22**

- Derek predicts that within 2–5 years all software will be designed this way: globally observable, managed via KV-driven configuration, regardless of cloud, edge provider, or own infrastructure. "as we approach 2 to 5 years out, all software will be designed like this" (~01:00)
- Subject naming rule of thumb: organize by the groups and hierarchies you want to filter on; subscribers can wildcard in and need not know the full subject, but publishers must know exactly what they publish to. "your subscribers don't really have to know the full subject ... but your publishers do" (~04:04)
- Across import/export mappings the system can inject the caller's true account (as trusted by the system, not as claimed) into the subject delivered to the service; the NGS usage service works this way so every tenant calls the same subject but the service receives NGS.usage.<account>. "map in his true account as understood by the system and deliver that to Jeremy as part of the subject" (~06:06)
- Zero trust framing: even with permission to use a service, the importer decides whether to share the bare minimum or full identity; JetStream itself is built on these same primitives. "by default it's just the bare minimum, but you can opt in" (~10:10)
- A memory-only close cluster can ingest 200–400k messages/s and be mirrored out worldwide, trading a small loss on catastrophic failure for very high ingest. "cluster memory only 2 3 400,000 ingest per second, and then they're mirrored out" (~13:15)
- Future vision: because NATS is inherently observable, the system could autonomously spin up services and data mirrors where requests originate (e.g. Japan) based on threshold modeling, instead of doing it manually. "we could make this totally autonomous" (~15:18)
- The "last mile" interface is a target pattern: a web app using only normal HTTP (fetch, GET/POST, event sourcing) while a thin service leverages NATS behind it. "what does a world look like where the web app just has normal HTTP stuff" (~17:22)
- For active-active or east/west failover use sources, not mirrors: sources can pull from many streams, have their own subjects, and accept direct writes, e.g. orders.east and orders.west each sourcing the other. "you're going to not use mirrors, you're going to use sources" (~18:23)
- Combine sources with subject mapping so a client publishing to "orders" is mapped to orders.west locally; on failover to east the mapping there routes "orders" to orders.east. "orders goes to order.east" (~19:23)
- KV's advantages over Redis are intricate replication (mirrors/sources) and fine-grained authentication/authorization over who accesses what. "trying to configure Redis to do that is tough" (~24:29)
- Subject mapping can transparently shard a KV across e.g. 10 buckets, each independently replicated, while clients simply get and put keys unaware of topology. "through that subject mapping construct, to transparently shard" (~25:31)
- Clients should stay simple and be agnostic to topology changes (servers, asset placement, number of mirrors/sources), which is why adding mirrors required no client restart. "the client should be very simple, and they should be agnostic to any of the topology changes" (~25:31)
- KV supports compare-and-set, unlike memcached; community members use KV for distributed locks and counting semaphores at global scale. "uses KVs as distributed locks and gaining counting semaphores at a global scale" (~26:33)
- For tens or hundreds of millions of observers of persistent state, the "hybrid structure" is a stream or KV configured to republish events over core NATS, with enough info in each republished event to detect a lost message. "it can be told to republish events. And the republish events have enough information to understand if an endpoint is lost" (~30:39)
- A NATS-only chat app can have a back end that only mints user JWTs, adding stateless claims such as OIDC info; retries and exponential back-off constructs let job services run on NATS alone. "I have no back end except NATS" (~31:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Derek Collison RethinkConn 2025 Keynote and Closing Remarks**
