- Synadia's stack is layered connectivity first, then data, then workloads, which is the reverse of stacks that start with workloads and bolt on networking and security. "we started with intelligent connectivity, then move to data and then workloads. This is the exact opposite of most approaches" (~00:50)
- Fleet data flows use "source muxing" (aggregating every fleet member's data into cloud streams/KV) and "demuxing" (pulling individual members' data back out on the cloud side). "source muxing and demuxing... we can collect data from all of the fleet items and collect them within the cloud" (~03:00)
- Edge AI data-collection pattern: apps store data locally and NATS mirrors it to the cloud, self-healing after outages, so the app never handles transport. "data is stored locally and then the NATS system takes over and mirrors that into the cloud. It self-heals itself" (~04:20)
- Customers use east-west signaling between edge locations to check whether an anomaly seen in one site is appearing in others. "start to use east west signaling for things like anomalies" (~04:35)
- Push-vs-pull sizing argument: if inference runs at 1M requests/s and pulls context, the RAG layer must also serve 1M request-replies/s; pushing data changes to all inference endpoints avoids that. "whenever this data changes, just let all of the inference endpoints know so that they don't even have to ask" (~05:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia CEO Derek Collison Keynote**

- Modern distributed systems are fundamentally about reducing latency to access services and data. "modern distributed systems are a case study in reducing latency to access of services and data" (~00:50)
- A common customer deployment: a KV synchronously replicated in one region (possibly across all three major clouds in that region) with asynchronous digital twins transparently served on get; twins can come and go and the system adapts. "a key value store that is synchronously replicated in a single region but could be across all three major cloud providers... that also has asynchronous digital twins that are transparently accessed" (~03:40)
- The microservices abstraction is seeing explosive growth because most systems are dominated by service interactions. "explosive growth in our microservices abstractions" (~05:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia Roadmap with Byron Ruth**

- Per-message TTL lets you re-up a TTL to emulate an LRU cache or lease without writing a new value revision, saving bandwidth and latency. "re-up a TTL to actually emulate an LRU cache... without the need to actually put a new version of the value" (~01:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: After event Q&A with Derek on Zoom**

- For delayed/embargoed delivery, Derek's earlier TIBCO trading designs used per-endpoint RTT so embargoed messages arrived simultaneously for fairness; NATS already tracks every link's RTT, so an embargo-style TTL is feasible. "NATS systems already track every single link RTT all the time" (~22:30)
- The KV LRU will refresh a key's TTL on every get, but only when enabled on the bucket, never by default. "every time you do a get refresh the TTL on that message individually... it's not going to be by default" (~24:00)
- A planned processing callout works like subject mapping plus auth callout: an account marks subjects for callout and a microservice may transform, deny or pass each message, enabling schema validation, PII enforcement and ETL. "just like the auth call out there can be a microservice... they're allowed to transform it, deny it, or just let it pass through" (~25:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Introducing Synadia Insights: Catch the NATS Failures Nothing Else Reports**

- The detection rule is to compare each consumer's delivered stream sequence with the stream's first sequence; the moment the stream floor crosses the consumer position, everything between has been deleted. "Red is the log book's floor... Orange is analytics bookmark... Eventually, red crosses orange and that crossing is the moment" (~12:00)
- Insights is one binary that scrapes cluster state over the system account each minute with 13 requests, the first a broadcast that discovers every server, and publishes replies to a JetStream stream so the indexer can catch up after a restart. "It asks over NATS on the system account. 13 requests. The first is a broadcast that discovers every server" (~15:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Event-Driven Systems Need a Security Gateway — Meet Synadia Protect for NATS**

- An event gateway applies API-gateway-style policies to subjects, and covers both request-reply and pub/sub, with operational policies such as throttling plus content policies. "secure subjects or channels of communication and apply policies to those channels much like you did with APIs in a restful gateway" (~03:20)
- Enforcement order for a message: TLS on the connection, publish/subscribe permissions on the subject, schema validation of the payload, then content validation. "first of all, you secure the channel, you apply certificates... Then... permissions... schema validation... content" (~06:20)
- A fleet of gateways split by domain is kept in sync by a config server that gateways reach over NATS, never point-to-point, and rule bundles are stored in a JetStream stream. "The gateway itself talk through NATS to the actual config server. So there's no direct point-to-point connection" (~12:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking Connectivity - Hyper-Connectivity & The Intelligent Edge**

- Queue groups load-balance globally and NATS finds the closest responder; if latency trombones to the cloud, move the service into the edge site. "you could just pick up that service and you could put it in your Edge site and get much quicker latencies" (~14:10)
- A roll-call request where every connected client answers demonstrates scatter-gather that HTTP can't do. "you can't do this with HTTP but you can do this with NATS" (~16:20)
- JetStream aims to solve about 80% of distributed persistence problems with one configurable streams-and-consumers model: queues, append-only logs, replays, roll-ups and compaction. "we want to try to solve like 80 percent of the distributed computing problems... streams and consumers" (~19:00)
- Sourcing lets edge servers' local streams store-and-forward into one larger cloud stream (mux), or one cloud stream filter down into leaf-local streams with only relevant data (demux). "you can have one big stream in the cloud that then filters down into a stream inside of... an edge location that is data that's only relevant to them" (~20:40)
- Leaf node uses: hub-and-spoke extension, bridging partner or OEM NATS systems, store-and-forward where a leaf-local stream is sourced or muxed by the hub, and command-and-control for fleets. "you'll have a stream inside of a leaf node... configure the hub to say... I want to replicate that stream maybe inside of a bigger stream" (~26:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — A New Way of Thinking | NATS 2.0 and Connectivity**

- Services scale by running more or fewer endpoints, with no load balancers, sidecars or proxies. "to scale them up you just run more of them there's no load balancers there's no sidecars there's no proxies" (~08:10)
- An importer chooses where an imported subject appears in its own namespace, which removes the brittle multi-week subject-topology design sessions of older messaging systems and leads to short two-token subjects like kv.get. "when you import something you get to pick where it shows up" (~16:50)
- Because everything is pub/sub underneath, any exported service is observable from day one without adding a sidecar, proxy or framework. "in order to do that you already had it when you started you're not now deploying with a sidecar or a proxy" (~19:40)
- Leaf nodes exist because groups resist being forced onto a shared utility; they let a team keep its own servers (sub-microsecond local latency sometimes) while bridging transparently into the shared supercluster. "leaf nodes is our answer to that it allows you to have your cake and eat it too" (~26:20)
- Derek runs an unsecured local server bound only to 127.0.0.1 as a leaf into Synadia's supercluster for instant local tooling. "no security except for the fact that it's only running on 127.0.0.1" (~28:10)
- If requests from Asia are hitting west-coast responders, deploying responders in Asia makes the system route there automatically with no load balancers or cloud configuration. "you just deploy these service responders in Asia the system automatically will route request from Asia directly to those" (~29:30)
- Built-in service observability: export a service, sample e.g. 50% of requests to a subject in your account, and get service time, responder RTT, requester RTT and internal NATS latency per sample, across a supercluster. "here's how long the service itself took here's the responder RTT the request RTT and the internal NATS latency" (~36:20)
- Gap detection without a streaming layer: each message carries the sender's unique ID and a +1 sequence; the receiver stores last sequence per sender and reacts on a gap, which is how NATS servers coordinate internally. "every time I send a message I send a unique identifier and a sequence number that's always plus one" (~42:00)
- Moving an existing request/response API onto NATS is often a ten-minute exercise; the real gain is lockdown without code, scaling without load balancers, global requesters and built-in observability. "a lot of times it can be as easy as a 10 minute exercise" (~45:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - PowerFlex Solves Intermittent Connectivity at the Edge w/ NATS - RethinkConn 2025**

- Streams are split into named "domains" (e.g. orders); every edge site has the same set of streams and they source into the cloud. "every single edge site has these same streams and they're sourcing from one another" (~04:05)
- Instead of sourcing each edge stream individually to the cloud, they bucket all edge streams into a single upload stream and source that once, which was more efficient (designed with Synadia). "we bucketed all the edge sourcing streams into one upload stream and then uploaded all of those with one sourcing to the cloud" (~05:05)
- Auth is decentralized JWT/NKeys: one account spans hub and leaf nodes; each customer gets a unique NKey user issued by one signing key, with permissions scoped via wildcards. "each customer through signing keys gets a unique NKey for authentication but managed with one signing key and permissions and wildcards" (~16:20)
- They maintain a spec repo (CloudEvents + AsyncAPI) with CI that generates typed event payload and publisher libraries for Python, TypeScript, and Rust. "it takes the spec and it generates event payloads and even publishers into libraries" (~17:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - MachineMetrics on Industrial IoT & Predictive Analytics w/ NATS at RethinkConn 2025**

- The winning design idea was decoupling where data is produced from where it is consumed, so compute can move freely. "allows us to basically decouple where data is consumed and where we have our compute" (~02:01)
- JetStream work queues with shared consumers let one piece of service code scale up and down without changes. "the consumer model just makes it so easy to scale services up and down really with just one piece of code" (~07:07)
- Their migration bridge copies the tail of the Kinesis stream into NATS, so consumers move to NATS first and producers can later publish directly on the leaf node. "we take the end of that Kinesis stream and copy it into NATS... it gives us this nice way to gradually switch over" (~11:13)
- They pick NATS over Redis for internal brokering when they need stronger pub/sub or exactly-once guarantees. "it might make sense to use NATS over something like Redis just to get better pub sub guarantees" (~09:12)
- Biggest lesson: subject and payload shape matter enormously and must be designed deliberately, so they built internal libraries that hide connection setup and subject construction from developers. "the shape of the data whether that be subjects or payloads is very very important and you need to be very intentful" (~11:13)
- Goal of edge compute is location freedom: a service shouldn't have to be designed up front for edge or cloud, only constrained by resources. "we don't have to think first and foremost about where it's going to end up on the edge or in the cloud" (~14:17)
- They issue short-lived NATS credentials through their own APIs so clients and edge devices get location-specific credentials that refresh. "we issue short-term NATS credentials through our APIs so that clients as well as edge devices can have location-specific credentials" (~21:27)
- Front ends can read KV and NATS data directly, skipping the traditional React → Node API → DB path. "we can skip that middleman and have access to so much data" (~22:28)
- Planned use of Object Store to distribute small WASM compute modules to edge devices instead of pulling large OCI images. "a piece of code that could live in a NATS object store and that can be distributed everywhere automatically... we're talking kilobytes, not 100 megabytes" (~24:31)
- Decentralized auth gives one account per customer plus mapping back into an account they own; scoped signing keys issue users and revocation is an administrative change that propagates. "an account per customer, but then be able to map things back into an account that we own" (~27:36)
- Payload schemas: developer libraries encapsulate the domain model, generate subjects, and use CloudEvents as the envelope, with message ID used for deduplication. "we use cloud events as the envelope format... deduplicating data on that through message ID" (~31:43)
- The domain-model library is written in Rust and compiled to TypeScript with wasm-bindgen, giving code completion for complex subject hierarchies. "we translate that Rust into TypeScript using wasm-bindgen" (~32:43)
- They plan to automate account/user provisioning via the Synadia Control Plane REST API and react to change-data-capture events flowing over NATS. "now that you can do that through the REST APIs in the Synadia control plane, it is considerably easier" (~35:45)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS at the Edge with F1 Arcade**

- Each venue runs NATS as a leaf node talking to local services; they wrote a custom NestJS transport to get type-safe subjects. "one of our venues with NATS as a leaf node... we actually have a custom NestJS transport which we've used to give us type safety in our subjects" (~05:07)
- Mirror streams are used to add observability and replication without touching the core messaging path. "the ability to replicate and observe JetStreams using things like mirror streams allows us to add on observability without impacting that core messaging" (~05:07)
- Plan: connect all venue leaf nodes to a centralized cluster hosted with Synadia. "plans to connect our venues which are essentially leaf nodes to a centralized cluster with Synadia" (~06:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Lightning Talk - ACI Worldwide at RethinkConn 2025**

- Application symbolic destinations are mapped onto NATS subjects, streams, and consumers; internal command messages use subject filtering; a predefined subject hierarchy is used. "All usage is based on Base24-EPS symbolic destination that's mapped to NATS constructs like subjects, streams, and consumers" (~02:08)
- Their congestion control ("network overload management") reads stream characteristics such as pending count and max messages to drive selective message rejection. "leveraging some stream characteristics like num-pending and max messages. From here, we derived a configurable application selective message rejection algorithm" (~02:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Franco Sabini from Fineco Bank on NATS**

- KV changed their design habits most: previous caching products each had drawbacks, now KV is the default answer for new projects. "the key values changed a lot... every time we have a new project we always think oh yeah that could be a key value" (~08:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Jaxon Repp from HarperDB on NATS and distributed databases**

- HarperDB uses NATS pub/sub between database nodes at the table level to replicate writes so any node can accept writes. "we use NATS in between each node to pub sub at a table level what data moves and where" (~02:05)
- JetStream replaced hand-written queueing, connectivity checks, and retry logic for disconnected replication; it became a black box that just delivers. "all of that is taken care of by NATS so it became less our code and more a black box" (~04:08)
- Every HarperDB node is both a hub and runs leaf nodes, so a severed network (e.g. shop-floor firewall) leaves each side fully functional; on reconnect it converges as one system. "every node is a hub and runs leafs as well... if the network is severed to completely maintain all the functionality" (~05:11)
- They are using NATS for inter-node status chatter to route writes away from an overwhelmed node to another that can persist and relay later. "I'm going to route it over to another node that I know has that data" (~07:13)
- Table-level replication choice lets a node be a fast local single-instance database while selectively replicating subsets (e.g. threshold events) globally. "the ability at a table level to replicate data or not allows us to... rely on very very fast local transactions" (~09:16)
- Lesson: lean into JetStream's built-in features instead of keeping a parallel bookkeeping list of what was sent; trust was built through testing over time. "the first iteration was okay but we send it there but we still hold on to the list" (~13:19)
- NATS as a pluggable module was the first step toward HarperDB's fully componentized architecture (REST, MQTT, WebSocket endpoints as modules). "NATS was that first step in our evolution toward a truly componentized architecture" (~12:18)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Nathan Mellis from Modzy on NATS as a foundational building block**

- All model inference is asynchronous: inputs go into a NATS queue, Modzy spins up the model, drains the queue, then shuts the model down, so expensive GPU models only run when there is work. "it will spin up that model it will drain the queue and then shut the model down" (~02:04)
- The theme of their NATS adoption is topologies: clusters for HA, superclusters for multi-cloud/hybrid across geographies, leaf nodes at the edge. "the ability to do super clusters enables you to do multicloud or hybrid" (~07:09)
- A leaf node exposes a portion of the subject/JetStream space to an otherwise independent edge, enabling push-based self-updating configuration to ~10,000 devices without polling. "those changes can get automatically pushed down to 10,000 devices which can then all reconfigure themselves" (~08:10)
- Request/reply over a supercluster beats HTTP/gRPC for hybrid cloud: a request unanswered locally percolates out to the supercluster, avoiding per-region service deployments and a service mesh. "if the cluster that you're in knows how to answer it it will answer it if it doesn't that'll get percolated out to your super cluster" (~11:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Simple Solutions for Complex Problems - How Workiva uses NATS as a Microservices and RPC transport**

- Delivery guarantees have many definitions (handed to transport, enqueued, processing started, finished), each with different costs; guaranteed ordered exactly-once is expensive and, by some definitions, impossible. "guaranteed ordered exactly once delivery they're really expensive to provide and depending on your definition they might be impossible" (~04:09)
- Design around replayability, idempotence, and commutativity so you stop needing guaranteed, exactly-once, ordered delivery from the transport. "if we can think about idempotence... we don't care about exactly once delivery and if we can think about commutativity... we don't care about ordered delivery" (~05:09)
- Delivery is not processing; business-level guarantees must be built in the business layer because infrastructure can't provide them. "if you need business level guarantees you really have to build those into the business layer because the infrastructure can't provide that" (~06:10)
- Stronger guarantees can be layered on top (STAN was cited as a layer on NATS) but cannot be removed from below, so pushing guarantees into the base makes everyone pay. "we can always build stronger guarantees on top... we can't remove those from below" (~07:10)
- Workiva uses NATS as a service bus: pub/sub, RPC, async messaging; all web traffic passes a gateway that proxies to NATS; queue groups give load balancing between service instances. "the fact that NATS has queue groups queuing built in gives us a really simple way to do balancing" (~16:19)
- Raw pub/sub with hand-agreed encodings decouples services but couples teams; they generate cross-language pub/sub APIs from an IDL (Frugal, a Thrift extension) so developers think in services, not topics. "pub/sub is meant to decouple services but when it's done in that way it kind of couples the teams" (~18:19)
- Subjects are derived from IDL: prefix (with variables such as user) + scope name + operation name, so developers never hand-build subjects. "the topic name is comprised of the prefix plus the scope name plus the operation name" (~20:23)
- RPC over NATS: service instances form a queue group, a client publishes to it, one instance answers with an inbox, and the client sends requests on that inbox; no service discovery or sockets, so connections are cheap to set up and tear down, with heartbeats for health. "there's no service discovery involved there's no sockets that we're creating it's literally just a matter of publishing" (~21:28)
- Deployment: each VM ("drone") runs a local NATS daemon clustered with the others; services talk to localhost and cluster membership JSON is pulled from S3 at startup to set up routes. "each drone also has a NATS daemon running on it and those daemons are clustered together" (~22:28)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | Pub Sub on the Power Grid**

- Duke Energy's Open Field Message Bus (OpenFMB), ratified by the North American Energy Standards Board, uses NATS pub/sub so grid devices publish their state instead of being polled by central SCADA. "having the devices tell us what the current state is and also that they're listening for control messages" (~08:12)
- Compute is pushed to nodes at the grid edge so control loops (solar dips → battery compensates) run locally while data still flows back to the central office. "we want to distribute compute resources out at the edge of the electric grid" (~07:12)
- Back-office enterprise systems become clients of the field message bus rather than holding direct connections to end devices. "instead of having the direct connection all the way to the end devices they wind up becoming clients of the field message buses" (~09:13)
- Feeder-level bus and microgrid bus must be bridged carefully because a customer-owned microgrid exposes only capabilities, not internal components; the feeder sends rules (e.g. absorb 100 kW in an hour). "we're gonna have to build that bridge connectivity between both of those NATS buses and we've got to be careful" (~21:35)
- Cell gateways (Sierra Wireless) with idle compute run Docker and an OpenFMB app that polls the meter locally at 1 Hz and publishes over NATS; end-to-end dashboard latency was about 1.5 s, dominated by polling and Grafana refresh. "about a second and a half later you would see the graph change and part of that is the polling rate" (~25:41)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Partner Talk - NATS on Akamai Cloud - RethinkConn 2025**

- NATS was used as a GraphQL resolver for both queries and subscriptions via a sidecar/protocol adapter alongside the server. "we were using NATS as a GraphQL resolver for both queries as well as subscriptions" (~05:07)
- Speaker frames these route latencies as the worst-case bound for data consistency in a stretched cluster (e.g. writing into LA becomes consistent globally in under a third of a second). "you can achieve consistency on your data if you're writing into Los Angeles... in a little bit under one-third of a second" (~09:13)
- A fan-out job over NATS makes every cluster node run an MTR traceroute to customer IPs and return per-hop latency, used to pick regions for a P95 latency target. "each node in the cluster will run an MTR basically a traceroute to those IP addresses and then using NATS as well they'll return what the latency was" (~14:21)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Go Beyond Kubernetes Native Events with NATS**

- Sveltos, a Kubernetes fleet manager, uses NATS so its event framework can react to events from outside the cluster (user login, onboarding), not only Kubernetes resources. "I needed something to be able to watch for those events happening outside of the cluster" (~02:08)
- NATS can be per-cluster (one per tenant) or one central server that receives all events and lets Sveltos distribute them. "user can have NATS deployed in a single cluster and all the events are pushed to that NATS server and from there distributed everywhere" (~05:13)
- Users choose core NATS for prototyping and switch to JetStream in production when events must not be lost. "if they don't want to lose an event they want to make sure that the events is delivered then they have to go with JetStream" (~10:20)
- Requested pattern: NATS in each managed cluster forwards events to a NATS server in the management cluster, which forwards on to external clients. "they are all forwarded to the management cluster and from the management cluster there is another NATS server which forwards" (~11:23)
- Schema handling is delegated to users: Sveltos expects CloudEvents envelopes over NATS and leaves payload contents to the publisher. "the content for Sveltos is a cloud event and it's up to the user what they want to put in the cloud event" (~13:25)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Connectors – Seamlessly Integrate NATS with Other Systems**

- Before connectors, integrating NATS with databases or legacy systems meant writing your own bridge application. "Basically, you would be on your own and write a little application to communicate and to send the messages over" (~00:00)
- The connectors framework is built on top of workloads (Nex), so a connector can run in the cloud, on-prem, or at the edge. "we build the connectors framework on top of workloads. And this allowed us to basically run your connector anywhere" (~01:02)
- A connector has exactly one responsibility, getting data into or out of NATS, with only per-message transformations; it deliberately is not a full data pipeline. "A connector should have one responsibility. It's getting data into NATS or getting data out of NATS" (~01:02)
- Pipelines are composed by chaining: inlet → NATS → workload transforms → NATS → ... → outlet; messages hop between components over NATS subjects. "this goes on and on and on until at some point you want to write that information back to an existing system" (~02:03)
- Runtimes are language-agnostic executors that run connectors as workloads; any language works if it conforms to the connector specification, and all are managed by the same tooling. "a runtime... can be written in any language as long as it is conformed to the connector specification" (~03:05)
- Inlet = external source into NATS (demo: MongoDB change stream scoped to a database and collection, published to a subject); outlet = NATS to external system (demo: MongoDB insert). "The kind of connector that we want to create is called an inlet" (~06:09)
- An outlet that reads from a subject should use a queue group so multiple connector instances don't process the same message. "I will also add a queue just to make sure that if we have multiple instances of our connector... you won't get multiple instances that will be processing the same message" (~11:15)
- Two transformer types: a mapping script, or a service transformer that calls out to a NATS service and uses its response. "a service transformer which allows us to call out to a different service on NATS" (~09:14)
- Filtering is done in a mapping by emitting a tombstone (drop) for messages that don't match (demo: temperature > 35 °C). "If it isn't, we will drop a tombstone, which is as much as saying we're not interested in this message anymore" (~13:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Workloads - Distributed cloud-to-edge compute with NATS Execution Engine**

- Because NATS built the connectivity layer first and the data layer on top, Nex inherited security, replication, KV, and Object Store for free instead of re-implementing networking, firewalls, and security. "Nex inherited security. Nex inherited replication of data. It inherited KV. It inherited object store" (~03:12)
- Nex was re-architected to decouple the control plane (nex core) from agents ("nexlets"), which are built entirely on the NATS micro services framework, so agents can be written in any client language that supports micro. "they've been built completely on top of the NATS micro construct... we can build nexlets to extend Nex on any NATS client that supports micro" (~04:14)
- When agents or workloads start, nodes mint credentials in real time scoped to the subjects those workloads need; a workload in account A can't talk into account B unless intended. "the nodes are actually minting credentials real time that are scoped to the subjects that those things need to talk to" (~08:19)
- Three nexlet deployment types: embedded (Go, compiled into a single binary), local (child process, any language, suits Rust-native Firecracker/microVM tooling), and remote (compiled agent shipped anywhere and kept alive by systemd, extending Nex to the far edge). "we've created a way that you can compile a nexlet, make it aware that it will be connecting remotely, you ship it to wherever you want" (~10:19)
- Workload kinds: services (restart if they die), jobs, and functions (kept warm, invoked by a trigger message on a subject, run, then shut down). "as soon as it gets a valid request, it spins up your workload, runs it and shuts it down" (~11:19)
- Nexlets declare their own start-workload request schema at registration; the node validates incoming requests against it before forwarding. "upon registering with the node upstream you say this is what my start workload request looks like... anytime a workload request comes in, we actually validate it" (~12:22)
- The demo agent's start request is a NATS Object Store reference; the agent pulls the binary from the object store, saves it locally, and runs it. "The agent's then going to go pull the binary, save it locally, and then start it" (~15:24)
- Synadia managed workloads run a Nex cluster ("nexus") in every NGS region; placement uses tags exactly like JetStream placement, so re-tagging moves a workload between clouds with near-zero downtime. "placement feels the same as JetStream... If you want a workload from AWS to Azure, you just tag it and it moves it for you" (~17:28)
- The multi-cloud demo app shares state through a KV store so workloads can be stopped and started elsewhere without losing state. "The state of this app pulls from a KV store... so it's all sharing state centralized" (~22:39)
- JavaScript functions in Synadia Cloud run as Deno isolates (the earlier v8go binding looked unmaintained), with KV and pub/sub exposed as global functions. "we landed on Deno isolates in our cloud offering" (~27:47)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Migrating from NATS Streaming to JetStream**

- Max messages per subject gives per-subject retention within one stream. "On a per subject basis, you can say for any given subject, I only want three messages, five messages." (~16:57)
- Optimistic concurrency via expected stream or per-subject sequence lets concurrent publishers be serialized. "You can actually specify the expected sequence number of the stream at publish time." (~17:58)
- Republish rebroadcasts every stream write to a core NATS subject for lightweight fan-out. "The stream internally on the NATS server is actually rebroadcasting that message out to a core NATS subject." (~17:58)
- Data migration algorithm: create a stream per channel, republish channel messages, map old channel sequence to new stream sequence (optionally stored in a header), then create consumers with an explicit start sequence from the mapping. "You need to map the sequence number from the message in a channel to the new sequence number that gets created in the stream." (~48:39)
- No KSQL on the roadmap; the demonstrated alternative materializes streams into SQLite tables at a leaf node so edge apps query a native database. "Deploy a leaf node or a small little relational database at an edge location... able to source data from streams, materialize it locally." (~56:48)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS KubeCon Tutorial on Twitch**

- NATS 2.x vocabulary frames usage as streams (sequence of data broadcast to consumers) and services (request-reply), both built on subjects with `*` single-token and `>` tail wildcards. "We talk more about NATS in terms of streams and services." (~05:07)
- For queue groups across a supercluster, the server prefers a local queue subscriber and otherwise forwards to another cluster chosen by RTT, giving lowest-latency load balancing. "It is going to be able to determine, based on the RTT, which is the appropriate load balancer node." (~19:33)
- The "NATS adaptive edge architecture": a central cloud supercluster with edge clusters attached by a single leaf-node connection, so edge sites keep communicating locally while consuming cloud-only services. "A centralized supercluster... and you can connect your edge devices or your local superclusters on the edge with a single leaf node connection." (~22:38)
- The chat demo splits an admin account (credential provisioning) from a user account so subject namespaces don't cross-talk. "We have separated these subject namespaces so that you can have as less as possible cross-talking." (~35:58)
- Dynamic credential provisioning: connect with near-permissionless default creds, request upgraded creds from a provisioner service, then close and reconnect with the new JWT. "We request upgraded credentials based on a username we give and the API will either grant us the new credentials or... an error." (~46:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Zen of High Performance Messaging with NATS by Waldemar Quevedo Salinas**

- Request-reply is built from pure pub/sub using an ephemeral random inbox subscription with an UNSUB limit of one message; the first reply wins. "It does so by having this ephemeral subscription, inboxes." (~09:17)
- NATS replaces the point-to-point "death star" of microservice connections with one always-on connection per service, avoiding separate discovery and load balancing when sub-millisecond latency matters. "It becomes this whole death star microservices kind of thing." (~19:36)
- Periodic heartbeats on `service.<name>.heartbeats` plus a wildcard subscription give simple liveness and discovery. "You can leverage these heartbeats to create some sort of discovery as well." (~24:45)
- Queue groups distribute messages randomly, not round-robin, among members. "One of these messages will be balanced randomly among the different service nodes... it's not round-robin." (~25:48)
- NATS "does not assume the audience": several queue groups and plain subscribers on the same subject each get a copy independently. "You can have multiple distribution queues from the same subjects." (~26:51)
- By definition the first reply to a request is the lowest-latency responder. "The first message that you get back from a request in NATS is the one with the lowest latency." (~26:51)
- To confirm availability, first request "anyone there?", have the service reply with its own inbox, then talk to that inbox directly. "This other service could reply back with its own inbox and then we use that inbox... to communicate directly." (~29:55)
- Designing for replay, safe retries, and tolerance of reordering yields more resilient systems than relying on exactly-once or ordered delivery from the transport. "If we can design our system so that you can safely retry the requests that can be better than having exactly-once delivery." (~31:57)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — SCaLE 13x Derek Collison  NATS A new nervous system for distributed cloud platforms**

- HTTP is loved as an interface but is point-to-point; NATS targets 1:N, 1-of-N, cascading request-reply, and subject-based routing instead of IP+port routing. "HTTP... only goes so far right it's usually point-to-point." (~04:06)
- The "ask everyone, take the first best answer" pattern (as Google search does across shards) was built into NATS from day one; on JMS/RabbitMQ style systems the requester's CPU spikes linearly with responder count. "You can see massive spikes all day long... linearly proportional to how many responders are out there." (~09:14)
- Design principle "don't assume the audience": later observers (logging, metrics) must be able to see any message, which publish-based queuing prevents. "Don't assume who's going to actually be watching it or looking at it." (~12:16)
- Cloud Foundry and Apcera's scheduler use scatter/first-reply: every node decides if it can run a job and delays its reply proportionally to memory pressure or co-location, so the first reply is the best placement. "They actually determine how long they're going to wait before they respond based on things like memory pressure." (~21:26)
- Auto-pruning of the interest graph: `UNSUB <sid> <max>` sets a circuit breaker propagated across the cluster, so a requester of 10,000 responders receives maybe 6–7 replies instead of discarding all 10,000 client-side. "Your client library might see six, seven, maybe... most messaging platforms you have to throw away all 10,000 on the client." (~36:55)
- NATS suits control planes built on idempotent state transitions and compensating transactions rather than transactional messaging. "Idempotent means I can keep sending it as many times as I want and the state transitions always consistent on the other side." (~41:02)
- Avoid "positive chatter" on a control plane: non-helping responders should stay silent rather than replying "I can't help", because such traffic grows with N. "If you can't help me I don't want you to say a word." (~53:25)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Native MQTT Support in NATS Server**

- A local NATS server with MQTT can leaf-node into NGS; `connect.ngs.global` attaches to the geographically closest cluster. "The connect.ngs.global URL will connect it to the closest cluster in NGS." (~06:10)
- Queue groups across a supercluster prefer the member local to where data enters; when that member stops, messages fail over to the member connected in Japan. "As soon as we do that then the new messages are automatically routed to the other member." (~07:11)

## USECASE: Application scenarios (190 claims)


**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Leaf Nodes**

- "Leaf nodes are useful in IoT and edge scenarios and when the local server traffic should be low RTT and local unless routed to the super cluster." Queue semantics are honored "by serving local queue consumers first."
- Leaf nodes bridge servers you control with third-party managed servers (e.g. NGS) "to inexpensively connect geographically distributed servers or small clusters."

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — JetStream on Leaf Nodes (domains)**

- Leaf nodes can "provide a local NATS network even when the connection to a hub or the cloud is down"; JetStream supports this via "independent JetStream islands" (domains).

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — MQTT**

- Use NATS as a drop-in MQTT server to connect existing MQTT endpoints to a remote NATS cluster/supercluster.

**Source class: Legacy NATS docs (nats-io/nats.docs) — Developing with JetStream**

- Streaming is ideal when: producers/consumers are highly decoupled and may be online at different times; a historical record/replay is required; the last message is needed for initialization while the producer may be offline; consumers are unknown a priori "This is often a false assumption"; data outlives the application; consumers need their own pace; decoupled flow control; exactly-once.
- Core NATS is ideal as "the fast request path for scalable services where there is tolerance for message loss or when applications themselves handle message delivery guarantees": tightly coupled request-reply with app-handled timeouts; last-value-only data with frequent updates (stock ticker, control plane, telemetry); low message TTL; consumer set known and live; control plane messages.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-43: JetStream Per-Message TTL**

- Motivation: KV tombstones "forever clog up the buckets with noise"; server-applied limits could leave short-TTL tombstones to notify KV watchers; some messages (schema/type hints) need infinite retention inside a stream with MaxAge.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-48: TTL Support for Key-Value Buckets (updates ADR-8)**

- Goals built on per-message TTL: notify watchers of MaxAge-deleted keys, "Improve Purge so that old subjects can be permanently removed, removing the need for costly compacts", and "Creating keys with a custom lifetime." KV calls these Limit Markers.

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-50: JetStream Batch Publishing**

- Atomic use case: a KV user record spanning 5 keys (address) "Performing updates on these related keys is not safe today as writes might fail after a first update resulting in an address line in one city but a post code in another."

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-51: JetStream Message Scheduler**

- Use cases: delayed publish (`@at <RFC3339>`), recurring publish (`@hourly`, cron, `@every 1m`), and subject sampling (`Nats-Schedule-Source` republishes the last message on a subject on a schedule; wildcards not supported; falls back to the schedule's own body if the source has no message).

**Source class: NATS ADRs (nats-io/nats-architecture-and-design) — ADR-54: KV Codecs (updates ADR-8)**

- Motivating cases: keys with characters invalid in subjects (spaces, dots), filesystem-path keys, end-to-end encryption, app-specific encodings.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Use Cases (category)**

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Regional and Cross Region Streams (Supercluster)**

- Use a supercluster of three regional clusters plus one dedicated cross-region cluster when you need streams that survive a regional failure by spreading replicas across three regions. "The use case is for streams that are resilient to regional failures by having replicas spread out across three different regions."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Regional and Cross Region Streams (Cluster)**

- An alternative to the supercluster layout is a single nine-node cluster stretched across three regions with three AZs each; regional and cross-region placement is then done with tags rather than clusters. "Rather than a supercluster, this relies on a nine node cluster spread out across three regions and three availability zones each."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Replace cluster nodes**

- The rotate-nodes procedure exists to replace the underlying hardware of existing cluster nodes with minimal or no downtime. "The original use case was to replace the underlying hardware of existing nodes in a cluster. The goal is to minimize or remove the need for downtime."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Integrations (category)**

- The integrations category collects examples of third-party systems wired to NATS (currently Debezium).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Change Data Capture via Debezium**

- Change data capture on a database streams granular change events to other parts of the system as data changes; Debezium handles the database-specific capture and Debezium Server can sink directly into a NATS stream. "stream granular change events to other parts of the system as data changes."
- For Postgres, Debezium registers itself as a logical-replication target, converts the raw change to a standard event model, and publishes to a NATS stream named `DebeziumStream` by default. "it publishes to the configured NATS stream, by default, called `DebeziumStream`."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Work-queue Stream**

- Work-queue retention is for "queuing up messages that are intended to be processed once and only once."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Core NATS Deep Dive**

- At-most-once is the right fit when each message is superseded by the next: a live price, a current temperature, a cache invalidation.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publish-subscribe**

- At-most-once suits telemetry you sample, cache invalidations, and live dashboard feeds; it is not enough for an order that must be packed exactly once.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topologies Deep Dive**

- The growth path: single server for a developer laptop; a cluster (three servers joined by routes) to survive a server outage; a super-cluster joined by gateways when traffic arrives from a second region; a leaf node when a site needs NATS on-site with only outbound network access.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Single server**

- One server is the right tool for development (a laptop or a CI run), for NATS on the device itself (edge hardware or embedded in-process), and for a small single-instance service.
- A device server often later dials out to a central system as a leaf node, but on its own it's still a single server.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Topologies)**

- A single server is for development and small workloads; in production it's a single point of failure. A cluster is the shape you run in production. A super-cluster is how a deployment spans regions. A leaf node is how NATS reaches the edge.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TTL and limits**

- Per-key TTL suits values that should clean themselves up: a flash-sale price, a short-lived session token, a time-boxed lock flag.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Metadata and links**

- Links are useful when two names should resolve to the same bytes, or a stable name serves as an entry point for a changing set of files.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connect MQTT devices to NATS**

- MQTT support exists to keep an existing device investment; use it when endpoints already speak MQTT or can only ever speak MQTT.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (MQTT)**

- Sparkplug B is ordinary MQTT traffic to the server; nothing in NATS interprets it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connect over WebSocket**

- A browser can't open a TCP socket, so WebSocket is the only way a page reaches NATS at all.
- The other case is infrastructure that only speaks HTTP: a cloud HTTP load balancer or CDN routes HTTP only, so exposing NATS behind one means exposing the WebSocket listener; the same applies to a leaf node reaching a hub behind that edge.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leaf nodes over WebSocket**

- The reason is usually on the hub side: the leafnode port isn't published through an HTTPS ingress but the WebSocket listener is.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — What is NATS?**

- Use cases: agentic AI (agent-to-agent communication, event streams for LLM inference, multi-region GPU inference routing with scale-to-zero), real-time data streaming (IoT telemetry, market data, log/metrics aggregation), microservices (service mesh data plane, event-driven, CQRS/event sourcing), edge computing (edge-to-cloud, intermittent networks, constrained environments), command and control (RPC, config management, orchestration).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Welcome to NATS**

- NATS is described as "a simple, secure and high-performance open source messaging system for cloud native applications, IoT messaging, and microservices architectures."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publish-Subscribe**

- Pub/sub is ideal when multiple services need to react to the same event: event broadcasting, data distribution, fan-out notifications, audit logging.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue Groups**

- Common uses: background job processing, API request handling across service instances, event processing pipelines, batch operations.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topologies**

- Use a single server for local development and demos, embedded use inside another application, small services where one node is enough, and quick experiments.
- Leaf nodes suit edge and IoT deployments, on-prem services bridging to a cloud cluster, hub-and-spoke architectures, and multi-tenant isolation where each tenant runs its own leaf.

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to set up Decentralized Authentication/Authorization in NATS | Rethink Connectivity Episode 6**

"extending a hub in a hub and spoke topology... bridging two NATS systems... connectivity at the edge" (~03:30)

"planes trains automobiles things that move around these are all really good candidates" (~04:40)

"collocate your application workload to where the origin stream is ... sourcing things mirroring things that's all asynchronous" (~79:48)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- Leaf nodes were not designed for IoT use cases, but that became their main purpose. "the leaf nodes being used for those IoT use cases in the first place because they were not designed for it and now it is their main purpose" (~17:18)
- KV was released as a convenience API and a year later a user ran a 10 TB KV store spanning the globe; it worked but needed to work better. "how about 10 terabytes key value store span across the whole globe will it work too yeah the thing is it worked it's just we needed it to work better" (~30:33)
- MQTT QoS 2 was added because applications such as Home Assistant rely on it, making MQTT an entry point for moving workloads onto NATS. "one of the big projects that comes to mind is Home Assistant that uses MQTT integration relies on QoS 2" (~56:58)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP07: Going off piste; KV patterns with NATS.io (pt1)**

- David's first NATS use (2015) was connecting distributed syslog-ingestion instances east-west so they funnelled through one head-end, to avoid ten systems each hammering core internet infrastructure, with failover if one machine died. "the last thing I want is 10 systems basically doing a denial of service attack onto core internet infrastructure" (~08:14)
- Relying on real-time clocks and NTP for synchronizing events across VMs with time-sliced CPUs fails; David used NATS signals and then Streaming so a system that missed a signal could catch up. "NTP would fail me sometimes ... it really is important when events needed to be synchronized" (~10:17)
- Gaming use case: limited video-render farm capacity for ghost-lap replays, SAN write cycles and CDN upload rate/connection limits are all natural semaphore gates. "you'd only have limited resources to generate those videos ... there would be a queue" (~22:40)
- Distribute policy (e.g. firewall rules) by having each host run a local agent that watches a KV bucket and realises its own desired state, instead of a central orchestration pool. "there's a local agent running you watch the KV store and then it programmed its own IP tables stuff" (~34:55)
- Kine (the k3s etcd-replacement layer) gained a community-contributed NATS KV backend, so k3s can run with NATS instead of etcd or SQLite; the original was single-node, and HA three-node k3s over NATS was later built. "somebody contributed NATS as an alternate backend within the Kine abstraction layer" (~40:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP05: Exploring Powerful Client-side Features and Abstractions in NATS.io**

- For IoT or CPU/memory-constrained devices, pull with a low pending limit avoids being flooded by a push consumer until flow control kicks in. "you can just lower how many things can be pending... without this compromise of now the server can flood me with messages" (~17:22)
- KV was pitched (KubeCon Valencia, ~2.8) as "for simple use cases", but within 18 months it was in use as a Kubernetes persistence layer replacing etcd and for large key counts. "key value being able to be used as a Kubernetes persistence layer instead of etcd" (~39:51)
- KV was motivated by leaf-node and factory-floor topologies where you want as little extra infrastructure as possible; JetStream users get a KV for free. "factory floor where you want to have as little infrastructure and tools installed as possible" (~39:51)
