- Subscriptions bound to a consumer "cannot independently define their own subject to filter on"; the filter lives on the consumer.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue Push Consumers (legacy)**

- As of NATS server v2.8.4, ephemeral queue push consumers are not supported; the server does not track them and auto-cleans up when no subscriptions are bound. If you create a durable and your program crashes before deleting it, check for it on startup.
- With a group of subscriptions each receives a different subset; messages can be processed out of order, there is no correlation between message order and subscription creation order, and "it is possible that not all subscriptions will necessarily get a message."
- Helper-created queue push consumers are deleted when any subscription unsubscribes or drains.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Migration to new JetStream API**

- In the legacy API the only way to continuously receive messages is push consumers; `Subscribe()` "leads to complications because it implicitly creates and manages underlying consumers."
- Unsubscribing a legacy `Subscribe()` subscription deletes the underlying consumer it created; `AddConsumer` "is the only way to create a consumer in the legacy API which will not be deleted when the subscription is unsubscribed."
- Legacy push subscriptions hide complexity and need many options; "when using push consumers, there is no simple way to rate limit the message delivery, which leads to slow consumer errors."
- Legacy pull consumers "are greatly limited in functionality since it is only possible to pull a specific number of messages, without any optimization or coordination between pulls," making them inefficient versus push.
- Because all legacy `Subscribe*` methods return the same `Subscription` interface, "it is very easy to encounter runtime errors by e.g. calling `NextMsg` on a subscription created with `PullSubscribe` or `Subscribe`."
- "deleting a stream will also delete all consumers on that stream."
- (deno) "Durable consumers are not deleted, will consume resources forever if not managed."
- (deno) With legacy push on streams with huge message counts, missing options caused "slow consumers, or ... a consumer that cannot be horizontally scaled."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject-Mapped Partitions**

- Synchronous publish (one ack per message) gives quite low throughput; async batch of 100 raises it; 5 concurrent publishers raise it a bit more. "throughput and latency will highly depend on the quality of the network, and the resources available on the servers."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Confirmed Message Ack**

- A standard ack does not wait for server confirmation; "If server is experiencing high load, or the connection is severed before the ack is received, the ack can be lost, leading to a redelivery."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Object-Store Intro**

- When reading via a readable stream, an error can occur mid-read, so "when you think you are done reading, you must check if there was an error" and discard staged data on error.
- Destroying an object store means "the data is gone forever."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Core Publish-Subscribe**

- A published message is not delivered when the subscriber has no active connection (temporarily offline) or when a network interruption drops the message.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first stream**

- Replicas 1 means the stream lives on one server and goes down with it; fine on a laptop, risky in production. "If that server goes down, the stream goes down with it."
- Unlimited defaults grow forever: with `--defaults` the stream keeps every message until the disk fills, and a full disk takes the server down. "a production stream needs at least one limit so old orders age out before the disk does."
- A stream name is permanent; there is no rename, and the server rejects any update that changes the name with `stream configuration name must match original`. "The only way to 'rename' `ORDERS` is to delete it and create a new stream, which loses every order already stored."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publishing**

- Ignoring the `PubAck`: code that discards it can't tell a stored message from a lost one; plain `nats pub` prints `Published N bytes` whether or not a stream captured the subject. "That line doesn't prove the message was stored."
- Retrying without a `Nats-Msg-Id` can store the message twice; the duplicate window is two minutes by default, so a retry arriving after that also stores a second copy. "Don't retry a bare publish."
- Treating "published" as "delivered": a `PubAck` means the stream stored the message, not that a consumer processed it. "Keep business outcomes separate from the publish."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reading back the stream**

- An ephemeral consumer keeps no position you can return to; it is removed once it goes idle, and a reconnect then starts over from the beginning. "an ephemeral one is removed once it goes idle, and a reconnect then starts over from the beginning."
- Re-running a caught-up reader waits: with nothing new to deliver, the read command waits for the next message instead of returning.
- Replaying a huge stream from the beginning: Deliver All on a stream holding millions of messages takes time and moves a lot of data. "Read the whole history only when you want it."
- Reusing a durable name with a different config returns "consumer already exists"; the server won't silently reconfigure a consumer a reader is using. Edit the consumer or pick a new name.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Filtering what you consume**

- A filter that matches nothing is accepted silently: a typo like `orders.shiped` creates a valid consumer that never receives anything, with no error and no warning. "Don't assume an empty pull means the stream is empty"
- Expecting a filter to delete from the stream: a filter narrows one consumer's view and never removes messages. "Don't use a filter to prune a stream."
- Overlapping filters inside one consumer fail: if one filter subject covers another (e.g. `orders.>` next to `orders.shipped`), create fails with `consumer subject filters cannot overlap`; partial overlap where neither covers the other is accepted.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Delivery and acknowledgment**

- Forgetting to ack looks identical to a crashed reader: the message is redelivered after Ack Wait, and with the default unlimited delivery limit that repeats forever. "Always ack on the success path."
- Acking the same message twice does nothing useful; some clients (Go, Python) reject it locally with "message was already acknowledged", others ignore or resend it, and the server ignores the duplicate. "Ack each delivery exactly once, in one place in your handler."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Ack responses and redelivery**

- A plain nak redelivers immediately, which is rarely what you want for a temporary failure. "A plain nak redelivers immediately. That's rarely what you want."
- Setting a backoff replaces AckWait: the first entry becomes the ack deadline for the first delivery. "Pick a `--backoff-min` at least as long as normal processing takes, or a slow job trips redelivery while it's still running."
- AckPolicy `all` lets one ack retire every earlier message; it only fits a consumer that processes strictly in order (MaxAckPending 1), otherwise acking message 10 also retires a failed message 7 waiting for redelivery. "silent data loss."
- A plain nak retries with no delay, tying up one worker on one message. "Don't send a bare nak for a temporary failure." A consumer backoff won't help; it spaces AckWait timeouts, not naks.
- A poison message with no term path uses every attempt until MaxDeliver gives up, holding up the messages behind it.
- MaxDeliver drops a message with no dead-letter: the message stays in the stream but leaves the consumer's pending list silently. "JetStream has no built-in dead-letter queue." Catch it via the `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<stream>.<consumer>` advisory.
- AckWait shorter than real processing time causes double work: the server redelivers a message still being handled, so two workers run the same order. Raise AckWait or send in-progress during long jobs.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Pull consumers in depth**

- An empty fetch is normal: after `expires` the server replies `408 Request Timeout` (a no-wait fetch with no messages gets `404 No Messages`), and clients report an empty batch (CLI exits non-zero). "A worker that treats an empty fetch as a failure fails on a quiet stream."
- A raw fetch with `expires` zero never times out; the server holds it until the batch fills. Client libraries default to about 30 seconds.
- MaxAckPending set too low limits throughput: a limit of 10 against a batch of 100 delivers ten then stops until acks arrive. "Keep it at or above your batch size. The default is 1000; lower it only when you know the in-flight count you want."
- A batch set too large uses more memory than expected because `batch` counts messages, not bytes; most clients offer a `max_bytes` option to bound a pull by size, and whichever limit is hit first ends the pull.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling a consumer**

- MaxAckPending too low leaves workers idle; too high leaves a big in-progress backlog that all redelivers at once if many workers die together.
- A redelivered order can arrive at a second worker and run twice; key side effects by a business ID such as `order_id`. A redelivery shows in the message's delivery count.
- A low MaxAckPending starves a large set of workers: set to 3, ten workers leave seven idle. "Set the cap to at least your worker count, with room to spare."
- A crashed worker holds its message until AckWait (30s default) because the server can't tell a crash from slow work. "Set `AckWait` to your normal processing time: too short redelivers while a healthy worker is still working, too long leaves real failures stuck."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Ordered consumers**

- Ordered consumers give up per-message acks (not for exactly-once work), sharing (each reader creates its own), and parallelism (single-threaded, in order).
- Using an ordered consumer for work that must be processed once: it can't mark individual messages handled. "use a named consumer with explicit ack and let redelivery cover failures."
- Expecting to share progress across processes: two processes reading with ordered consumers both read the whole stream; they don't split it.
- Counting on the position to survive: memory storage, one replica, and a short inactivity threshold make the cursor disposable; after a crash a long-running job starts over.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Priority groups**

- One group per consumer: passing two groups is accepted but only the first is used. "To split work by region or tier now, run separate consumers on the same stream, each with its own group."
- The pin does not give one client sole ownership: the server can switch the pinned client while it still believes it holds the pin. "If the same message must never be processed twice, use explicit acks and handlers that are safe to run more than once, not the pin alone."
- A quiet pinned client keeps the pin until the timeout, parking every other client; keep each pull's `expires` comfortably under the pin timeout so the client renews in time.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Pausing a consumer**

- A deadline in the past does nothing: the server leaves the consumer running. Pause with a duration like `1h` instead.
- Pausing does not stop publishers: new messages count toward the stream's limits, and a long pause on a tight `MaxMsgs`/`MaxBytes` stream can drop the oldest messages before the consumer reads them. "Size the stream for the longest pause you expect, or keep pauses short."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Shaping the stream**

- Without a limit, a stream grows until it fills the disk and takes the server down with it.
- Discard Old discards the oldest message silently with no warning to the publisher; switch to Discard New to reject the publish (`maximum bytes exceeded` / `maximum messages exceeded`) instead. Discard New still leaves MaxAge in force, so remove or raise the age limit too if you must keep history.
- A seven-day MaxAge does not guarantee seven days of history: a traffic spike can hit MaxBytes first and discard messages only hours old. "Set MaxBytes for your busiest traffic, not your average, if the age window matters to you."
- Whole-stream limits don't balance across subjects: a high-volume subject counts toward the same ceiling, so Discard Old can discard a shipped order to make room for a created one. Add `MaxMsgsPerSubject` when each subject needs its own limit.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Retention policies**

- Set retention at creation and leave it there; the server allows exactly one live change, swapping Limits and Interest in either direction; anything involving WorkQueue is locked.
- Even the allowed Limits→Interest swap applies to stored messages immediately: the server removes any message every consumer has acked and any message on a subject no consumer is interested in, including history you meant to keep.
- Interest can fill the disk: a stalled consumer holds up cleanup for every message it owes an ack on, so the stream grows until its limits. "Interest retention still needs limits set, and it makes watching consumer health more important."
- Retention to or from WorkQueue is locked after creation; the edit is rejected with `stream configuration update can not change retention policy to/from workqueue`. "Create a new stream with the policy you want and move the data."
- WorkQueue rejects consumers that overlap: a second unfiltered consumer fails with `multiple non-filtered consumers not allowed on workqueue stream`; overlapping filters fail with `filtered consumer not unique on workqueue stream`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Altering stream state**

- `purge` empties the stream; `rm` destroys it including config and every consumer. "don't type `rm` for that, and read the confirmation prompt before answering it."
- A deleted sequence is gone, not renumbered: code that assumes messages run 1..N with no holes breaks. "don't work out 'the next message' as `count + 1`, and don't read a message count as the highest sequence."
- A purge can't be undone: on a stream that matters set `DenyPurge` so a stray call can't wipe it, and keep a mirror if the data is worth recovering.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Surviving node loss**

- R=1 means the stream exists on exactly one server with no fault tolerance: lose that server and you lose every message and every consumer's position.
- Trusting R=1 in production: no recovery after disk loss because there was no second copy. "Before you trust a stream with real orders, check its replica count rather than assuming it."
- Setting an even replica count: R=2 still has a single point of failure (one of two can't form a majority, writes block); R=4 tolerates only one loss like R=3 while paying for a fourth copy. "Use odd counts: R=3 for the production floor, R=5 for state you can't re-derive."
- Reading failover from a single-server demo proves nothing about fault tolerance; prove failover on a real cluster.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Advanced publishing**

- The async order trap: a failed publish is re-sent after later messages were stored, so the retry takes a higher sequence and lands after messages you sent next.
- An async publish you never check is a lost write. "Firing publishes without reading the acks gives up the only guarantee a JetStream publish offers."
- An async publish you never check is a lost write; collect and check every ack, and add `Nats-Expected-Last-Subject-Sequence` if order matters.
- An atomic batch can be abandoned: a gap or over-size (1,000 default) batch errors; ten seconds idle drops it silently with only an advisory. "don't assume a half-sent batch landed."
- `AllowAtomicPublish` and async persistence don't mix: a stream with `PersistMode: async` rejects atomic publishing because atomicity depends on the synchronous write path; fast-ingest batches are fine on such a stream.
- Fast-ingest `gap: ok` loses data on purpose; use it only when a hole is acceptable, otherwise `gap: fail` or an atomic batch.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mirrors and sources**

- Treating a mirror as writable: a publish routes to the origin stream; forcing with `Nats-Expected-Stream: <mirror>` is rejected with `expected stream does not match` (error 10060). "publish to the upstream `ORDERS` and let the mirror copy the message on its own."
- Treating mirror contents as real-time: a mirror is eventually consistent and `Lag` climbs during write bursts. "Don't assume a message in `ORDERS` is already in `ORDERS-ARCHIVE` the instant it lands."
- Combining `filter_subject` and `subject_transforms` on one source or mirror entry is rejected; a transform filters and renames in one step, so pick one.
- Cross-domain config fails silently: the consumer API and flow-control subjects must be service exports, the delivery subject a stream export; a wrong type doesn't error, the mirror just never catches up.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reading messages directly**

- Direct Get is not read-after-write coherent: a replica or mirror can trail the leader, so a just-published message may not appear on a direct read for a beat. "When you must see your own most recent write, read the leader with `nats stream get`."
- Direct Get off makes the read hang: with `allow_direct` unset no server answers and the request times out with nothing returned.
- A direct read can be stale; don't use it for read-after-write checks such as confirming a publish landed. "keep Direct Get for high-volume or far-away reads that tolerate a little lag."
- A direct batch isn't a subscription: it returns matching stored messages and stops; use a consumer to follow the stream as it grows.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject mapping and transforms**

- A transform that drops a token a consumer filters on collapses distinct subjects into one, so a consumer can no longer filter by type. "Keep every token a downstream filter needs in the destination."
- Republish is not a consumer: it's plain core NATS, fire-and-forget, no storage, no acks, no replay; a subscriber that's down misses what was republished. "use a consumer when a reader has to catch up on what it missed."
- A republish destination that overlaps the stream's own subjects is rejected as a cycle (error 10052); use a separate subject space, and watch for loops spanning two streams in one account, which the server can't always catch.
- Editing a transform doesn't rewrite what's already stored; to re-namespace existing data, copy it into a new stream that sources from the old one with the transform applied.
- A partition count is fixed once consumers depend on it: changing `partition(3, …)` to `partition(4, …)` can hash the same key to a different bucket and silently change a consumer's coverage. "Pick the bucket count up front"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Per-message TTL**

- Turning `AllowMsgTTL` on cannot be reversed; the server refuses to turn it back off.
- A TTL header on a stream that never opted in fails the publish; it does not store the message without a TTL instead. "Don't publish a TTL message and walk away on a stream you haven't confirmed opted in."
- A short TTL deletes the message whether or not a consumer read it; a consumer holding a message doesn't pause its TTL. "Do size the TTL to outlast the lag of your slowest healthy consumer."
- Turning `AllowMsgTTL` on can't be undone; the stream keeps the feature for life. "Don't flip it on to test something and expect to undo it."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Stream and consumer policies**

- Changing a fixed policy means recreating the object: storage edit fails with `stream configuration update can not change storage type`; deliver policy update fails with `deliver policy can not be updated`. Recreating a consumer loses the saved position.
- Expecting `new` to skip the backlog on every restart: a deliver policy applies once at creation; a durable created with `new` keeps a saved position and resumes from it, backlog included. "Don't use it hoping each reconnect jumps to live traffic."
- Two features answer to "last per subject"; check which feature a flag or value belongs to before copying it.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subjects & wildcards**

- Spaces, tabs, and line breaks are never allowed in a subject; stick to letters, digits, `-`, and `_` inside a token.
- Subjects beginning with `$` belong to the server (`$SYS`, `$JS`, `$KV`, `$O`, `$SRV`); don't publish application messages under `$`.
- The `_INBOX` prefix is reserved for client-generated reply subjects; don't pick `_INBOX` names or publish business messages there.
- `>` only works as the last token; use `*` for a free token in the middle. "`>` only works as the last token."
- Publishing "to a wildcard" produces no error: the `*` is taken as a literal character and the message lands on the literal subject `orders.*.created`, reaching wildcard subscribers but not exact-subject subscribers. "Publishers can't publish \"to a wildcard.\""
- An over-broad `orders.>` pulls every message at every depth including subjects created later; subscribe to the narrowest pattern that covers your need so unwanted traffic stays off the wire. "An over-broad `orders.>` pulls more than you want."
- Whitespace in a subject is read as a wire boundary; a client that skips the check (nats.py's `publish`) writes the space into the PUB line and the server silently misroutes. "Whitespace is never allowed in a subject."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Publish-subscribe**

- Publishing over the limit fails the publish; keep payloads under the limit and pass a reference for anything large. "Publishing over the limit fails the publish."
- A short-lived publisher that exits right after publish can quit before the buffered message reaches the server; flush (or drain) before exit. "Exiting before the publish leaves the client drops it."
- Echo is on by default, so a connection that both publishes and subscribes to the same subject receives its own messages and can loop. "A connection receives the messages it publishes."
- A subscriber that can't keep up builds a server-side backlog; past a threshold the server logs `Slow Consumer Detected` and closes its connection, other subscribers unaffected. "A slow subscriber gets cut off."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Request-reply**

- A request without a timeout can wait forever; pass a deadline on every `request()`. "A request without a timeout can wait forever."
- Don't treat no responders as a hang; branch on it separately: no responders means nothing is deployed, a timeout means deployed but slow. "Treating no responders as a hang."
- A plain `request()` returns the first reply and silently discards the rest; when more than one service may answer, gather explicitly by count or deadline. "Assuming exactly one reply."
- Slow work inside a responder serializes every request behind it; keep the reply path fast or run several instances in a queue group. "Doing slow work inside the responder."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue groups**

- Core NATS is at-most-once: if the picked member dies after delivery, the message is gone and the server won't retry with another member; work that must survive a worker crash belongs in a JetStream work queue.
- A typo in the queue group name makes a second group with no warning, and each message goes to one member of each group, double-handling the work. "A typo in the queue group name makes a second group."
- Don't expect ordering or an even split from a queue group; work that must be strictly ordered for a customer belongs on a single subscriber. "Don't expect ordering or an even split."
- Make a member's work safe to repeat (idempotent by `order_id`), because a slow or briefly cut-off member can still be doing work the publisher assumes was lost. "Make a packer's work safe to repeat."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scatter-gather**

- Scatter-gather works only when responders are not in a queue group; every responder must subscribe plainly.
- Taking only the first reply: `nats request` defaults to `--replies 1`, discarding the other quotes silently. "Taking only the first reply."
- A hand-rolled gather with no deadline blocks forever if a provider is down; bound the wait. "No deadline, so you wait for replies that never come."
- Don't read the gathered set as ranked; arrival order isn't priority and a short set isn't an error. "Reading the gathered set as ranked."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Message headers**

- Keep the `Nats-` prefix out of your own header keys; NATS reserves it for system headers.
- Reading a header key with the wrong case returns an empty value and no error; settle on one spelling convention across services. "Reading a key with the wrong case."
- The server checks header block plus body combined against `max_payload` (the same 1 MB ceiling); a large header block leaves less room for the body. "Headers count against the payload limit."
- Headers are for small metadata (an ID, a content type, a flag); large or structured data belongs in the payload. "Putting real data in headers."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Subject mapping**

- A subscriber still on the pre-map subject receives nothing, because the server moved the message before matching interest.
- A mapping quietly changes who receives what; before mapping a subject services already use, check what subscribes to it and keep a share on the original if needed. "A mapping quietly changes who receives what."
- Weights under 100 keep the rest on the source subject; they don't drop it. "Weights under 100 keep the rest, they don't drop it."
- A partition count is part of the subject contract: raising `partition(3, ...)` to `partition(4, ...)` reshuffles which bucket an id hashes to; pick the bucket count once, up front. "A partition count is part of the subject contract."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connecting**

- Opening a new connection per message repeats the whole handshake each time; open one connection at service start and reuse it. "Opening a new connection per message."
- A client that publishes and subscribes on one subject receives its own messages with echo on (the default). "A client that publishes and subscribes on one subject receives its own messages."
- A short-lived program that exits immediately after publish can quit before the write buffer reaches the server; flush before exit. "Exiting before buffered publishes are sent."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connection lifecycle**

- The reconnect buffer lives in client memory and dies with the process; treat it as a short-term hold over a brief outage, not durable storage. "Trusting the reconnect buffer as a delivery guarantee."
- Connection callbacks run on the client's own thread; blocking one with a database write or slow HTTP call stalls other callbacks and in some clients the connection's processing. Keep handlers to a log line or a channel signal. "Doing real work inside a connection callback."
- Infinite reconnect can hide a wrong address or auth refusal as silent healthy-looking retries; log the drop and every failed attempt. "Letting infinite reconnect hide a dead configuration."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Debugging delivery**

- A `>` tap on a production account receives every message and can get cut as a slow consumer; scope it and don't leave it running. "A `>` tap on a production account receives every message in it."
- A trace is its own fresh message, not proof about a past publish. "A trace is its own message, not proof about a past publish."
- The monitoring port is unauthenticated by default; anyone reaching `:8222` can read subjects and connections. Don't expose it on a shared or public network. "The monitoring port is unauthenticated by default."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Forming a cluster**

- Every server that should join must set the exact same `cluster.name`; a mismatched name is rejected with `Rejecting connection, cluster name ... does not match ...` and the odd server forms a separate cluster.
- A mismatched `cluster.name` forms two clusters that look like one until a message fails to cross; confirm all rows show the same name before trusting the cluster. "A mismatched `cluster.name` forms two clusters."
- Pointing `routes` at the client port (4222) never forms the mesh; always point at a peer's route port. "Pointing `routes` at the client port (4222) never forms the mesh."
- One seed is enough for gossip, but list two or three seed routes so formation survives any one seed being down at boot; don't rely on a single seed in production. "One seed is enough, but list two or three anyway."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Raft and leaders**

- An election takes seconds: the election timer fires between four and nine seconds after the last heartbeat, deliberately staggered. Don't build a client that treats a brief "no leader" as fatal; retry the write. "An election takes seconds, not milliseconds."
- Stepdown moves leadership off the current server but the election still picks the successor; `--preferred` is a request, not a guarantee. Read `nats stream info` afterward to learn who won. "Stepdown moves leadership, but the election still picks the successor."
- The meta leader and a stream leader are different groups; losing one doesn't lose the other. Check `nats server report jetstream` for meta, `nats stream info` for the stream. "The meta leader and a stream leader are different groups."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Replication and R=3**

- `sync_interval: always` costs performance cluster-wide, even for streams that don't need it; weigh before turning it on everywhere.
- R=1 has no copy: no second peer, no quorum; if that server's disk is lost the data is lost with no failover. Only R>=3 survives a node loss; don't run real orders at R=1. "`R=1` has no copy."
- A follower read can be stale; don't assume any peer is current just because the write was acked. "A follower may lag, so a follower read can be stale."
- A `PubAck` proves quorum, not full replication; if you need every copy current (before taking a server down), verify each replica shows `current` in `nats stream info` first. "A `PubAck` proves quorum, not full replication."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Placement**

- Tags are an intersection; a missing tag fails the placement rather than falling back to any server. Read tags back from servers first, then place against exactly what they advertise. "Tags are an intersection; a missing tag fails the placement."
- Don't build an operational assumption like "the leader is always n1-east" on where the group first landed; after a leader dies the next election picks from survivors. "You can't name a leader at placement time."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling and peer management**

- Don't stack membership changes before the replacement catches up; a second change can drop the peers holding the data below the majority and the group stops committing. Make one change, wait for a named leader and a caught-up replacement, then the next. "Don't stack membership changes before the replacement catches up."
- If `stream info` shows `no leader` after a change, stop: you've lost quorum and the fix is to restore a peer, not make another change.
- A freshly added peer isn't safe until its lag is zero; it can't win an election or serve a read while catching up, and killing another server mid-catchup can stall the group. "A freshly added peer isn't safe until its lag is zero."
- Removing the only peer needs `--force` (`removing the only peer on a stream will result in data loss`), and even forced the server answers `peer remap failed`; change the count with `nats stream edit --replicas` instead. "Removing the only peer needs `--force`, and forcing it doesn't move the data."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Single server**

- A single server can't hold a replicated stream: asking for three replicas answers `replicas > 1 not supported in non-clustered mode`; redundancy is a cluster's job, don't treat the error as a config typo to override. "Reaching for redundancy too late."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first cluster**

- Misspelling a cluster name raises no error; the odd server forms its own cluster. Catch it with the rejection line in the log or a cross-server publish test. "Misspell a cluster name."
- The cluster port accepts routes, which are trusted links carrying every account's traffic plus the system account; left reachable with no authorization, anyone with the cluster name can join as a server and read or inject messages across accounts. Bind it to a private interface, firewall it, and in production require route credentials or TLS. "Expose the cluster port to the world."
- Plan for an odd server count once you replicate: two servers lose their majority as soon as one is down, and four tolerate only one loss, the same as three, so the extra server adds cost without failure tolerance. For a pure routing cluster any count is fine. "Plan for an even server count."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream in a cluster**

- By default a consumer takes its stream's replica count; an R1 consumer on an R3 stream is its own single point of failure, since its position lives on one server and losing it loses the reader's place even though the stream survives.
- An R1 stream on a cluster still has no HA; the cluster around it changes nothing. Audit replica counts (`nats stream find --replicas=1`) and raise the streams that matter to R3; `nats server check stream --peer-expect=3` exits non-zero when under-replicated. "An R1 stream on a cluster still has no HA."
- An even server count gives no extra protection: four tolerate the same single loss as three at the cost of an extra server; run an odd number, never four or six. "An even server count gives you no extra protection."
- All three replicas in one failure domain defeat R3: three copies survive one loss only if the servers can fail independently; spread across one rack or one availability zone a single power or network event takes all three. "All three replicas in one failure domain defeat R3."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Super-clusters**

- Stretching one cluster across regions works but every server holds a route to every other and route traffic flows freely across the slow, expensive link.
- Don't grow a cluster across regions with routes; join two independent clusters with a `gateway {}` block so only interested traffic crosses. "Reaching for routes to span regions."
- A typo in a `gateways` entry name never connects and logs `Failing connection to gateway "wset", remote gateway name is "west"` on every retry, but the super-cluster still forms through the other side's reverse connection and gossip, so a working cross-region publish doesn't prove the config is right. "Mismatched gateway names."
- Geo-affinity only keeps traffic home when a local queue subscriber exists; centralize all workers in one region and every other region's messages cross the gateway as steady-state load. Place a queue subscriber for each workload in every region that produces that work. "Chatty cross-region traffic without local workers."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leaf nodes**

- A leaf dials out: put the `remotes` block on the egress-only side and `leafnodes { listen }` on the side that accepts connections; reversing them means nothing connects. "Treating the leaf like an inbound connection."
- A leaf enabling JetStream while sharing the hub's system account extends the hub's JetStream rather than running its own, so a stream created on the leaf may land on the hub; give the leaf its own JetStream domain for a distinct local store. "Expecting JetStream to span the leaf without a domain."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Putting it together**

- Each layer adds operational cost; a super-cluster stood up "to be safe" is two regions to keep healthy before you have a second region's traffic. Add the next layer only when the current one runs out of room; adding early gives no benefit. "Building the whole stack before a limit forces it."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Sizing & resources**

- The container hazard is setting `max_file_store` larger than the volume, or a shared/thin-provisioned volume where "available" overstates safe use: the node accepts writes it can't store and the publish crossing the real boundary fails. Pin `max_file_store` to what the volume can hold.
- Setting `max_file_store` beyond the real disk fails as a publish error mid-stream, not a startup warning; set it to the volume size and watch the real disk with `df -h`. "Setting `max_file_store` beyond the real disk."
- If `max_payload` exceeds `max_pending` the server refuses to start; keep `max_pending >= 10× peak message size` so a burst of large messages can't stall a connection; don't raise `max_payload` in isolation. "`max_payload` larger than `max_pending`."
- FD exhaustion on a big cluster shows as connection refusals that look like a network fault; raise the limit (`ulimit -n 800000`) before the process starts. "File-descriptor exhaustion on a big cluster."
- Operator-mode account limits live in the account JWT the resolver holds; raising `MaxStore` or `MaxStreams` means editing and pushing the JWT, not a server reload or restart. "JWT account limits change only when the account JWT does."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Config management**

- Include paths are relative to the config file, not your shell; use absolute paths when in doubt and validate before trusting. "Include paths are relative to the config file, not your shell."
- Don't SIGHUP a node while JetStream is moving replicas or handing off Raft leadership; wait for the cluster to settle. "A reload during a rebalance can interrupt a leadership transfer."
- Lowering a store limit on reload changes the ceiling, not the contents: existing messages stay but new writes fail until an admin trims the stream under the limit. Raise limits freely; lower them only after checking current storage. "Lowering a store limit on reload does not evict data already stored."
- An expired certificate fails every new connection and every client reconnect at the TLS handshake; rotate well before expiry and track the expiry date. "Rotating a TLS certificate late fails every new handshake."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Hardening**

- A common hardening mistake is securing clients and shipping a cluster whose inter-node Raft traffic, including replicated stream data, is still unencrypted.
- On Kubernetes don't bind the monitor to `127.0.0.1`: kubelet probes connect to the pod IP, so the pods never go ready. Keep the chart's default bind and restrict with a NetworkPolicy.
- `ProtectSystem=strict` blocks writes outside `ReadWritePaths`, not reads; the JetStream `store_dir` (and pid/ports-file directories) must sit inside `ReadWritePaths` or the server can't come up. "`ProtectSystem=strict` blocks writes outside `ReadWritePaths`, not reads."
- `MemoryMax` and `GOMEMLIMIT` don't reserve memory; `max_memory_store` is an accounting limit and `GOMEMLIMIT` a soft GC target. Set `MemoryMax` above expected use (memory-store data plus connection and route buffers plus GC headroom) and `GOMEMLIMIT` somewhat below `MemoryMax`. Example: `max_memory_store: 4Gi`, `MemoryMax=6G`, `GOMEMLIMIT=5500MiB`. "A memory cap set below the working set gets the process OOM-killed under load."
- The monitor port exposed to the internet leaks operational detail useful for reconnaissance; don't leave `http:` bound to `0.0.0.0`. "The monitor port exposed to the internet leaks operational detail."
- Denying cluster port 6222 globally without allowing it between nodes means route handshakes never complete and each node comes up as an orphan; allow 6222 explicitly from the cluster subnet, then deny elsewhere. "A firewall blocking cluster port 6222 leaves nodes unable to form quorum."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Rolling upgrades**

- A `lame_duck_duration` shorter than the rebalance kicks clients and exits while the stream is still catching up; measure a real drain first, then set the duration above it with margin rather than the minimum. "A `lame_duck_duration` shorter than the rebalance drops clients early."
- Restarting the meta-leader without draining leaves no metadata leader until the election timeout fires (about 5 to 10 seconds) and every stream and consumer operation stalls; draining transfers leadership in roughly a second. Always enter lame-duck first and always do non-leaders first. "Upgrading the meta-leader without draining it stalls stream ops until a new leader is elected."
- A node drain, cluster autoscaler, or careless `kubectl delete` can take two or three pods together; set a PDB with `minAvailable: 2` and don't rely on doing steps slowly by hand. "Evicting pods without a PDB can drain all three at once."
- A reconnect storm comes from abrupt kills or a duration so short the spread collapses, not from lame-duck mode, which staggers closes precisely to spread reconnects. Roll one node at a time and let it rejoin before starting the next. "A reconnect storm comes from abrupt kills, not from lame-duck."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Kubernetes**

- A pod stuck Pending is usually an unbound volume (no default storage class); the fix is to confirm a storage class exists, not delete and retry the pod. "A pod stuck Pending is usually an unbound volume."
- A ConfigMap edit does not reload the server by itself; the chart's `nats-server-config-reloader` sidecar (enabled by default) sends the SIGHUP, and without it a change sits inert until the pod restarts. "A ConfigMap edit does not reload the server by itself."
- Readiness (`js-server-only=true`) deliberately skips stream, consumer, and meta-assignment checks, so a pod catching replicas up still reports ready and serves clients; plain `/healthz` (startup probe) is the strict one, hence `failureThreshold: 90`. Override via the chart's container `merge`/`patch`; there's no named `failureThreshold` value. "Replica catch-up shows up in the startup probe, not readiness."
- Never mix CLI and CRD management of the same stream: by default NACK re-creates a deleted stream on its ~30-second resync but does not revert a manual `nats stream edit`; in `--control-loop` mode it also reverts config drift on about a one-minute cycle. Pick one owner per stream. "Never mix CLI and CRD management of the same stream."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Authentication basics**

- Splitting auth data into separate files with `include` buys only a little headroom; treat it as buying time before moving away from centralized configuration. "treat it only as buying time before you move away from centralized configuration"
- Token auth is a single shared secret with no username, set server-wide on the `authorization` block; it can't be per-user, making it usable for quick internal setups but little else. "usable for quick internal setups but little else"
- CLI trap: `--user` doubles as a token field; a lone `--user` with no `--password` is sent as a token and can mask a misconfiguration against a token-configured server.
- The server treats strings starting with `$` as potential hash indicators; don't use plaintext passwords starting with a dollar sign. "don't use plaintext starting with a dollar sign"
- bcrypt protects only the config file at rest because the client still sends plaintext over the wire; pair it with TLS. "bcrypt protects only the config file at rest. Pair it with TLS"
- Pitfall: Running with no authentication in production. A server with no `authorization` block admits every connection; give every server at least one user list. "on a shared network anyone who can reach the port can publish and subscribe, so don't ship it"
- `no_auth_user` admits unauthenticated connects as a named user even when a user list exists; set it only on purpose.
- Pitfall: Leaving plaintext passwords in a deployed config. Don't treat the startup warning as noise; store the bcrypt hash on any server someone else can read.
- Pitfall: Committing credentials to git. A `nats.conf` with a password (even a bcrypt hash) is a secret; once in history, rotating is the only real fix. Reference an env var or secret store and gitignore the real config. "rotating the password is the only real fix, because the old value lives in every clone"
- Pitfall: Putting the password in the connection URL. `nats://user:pass@host` leaks into shell history, process listings, and logs; store it in a named context instead.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Authorization**

- An empty allow list is not a lock-down: `publish: []` parses as no list, so the user can publish anywhere. To block all publishes write `publish: { deny: [">"] }`.
- A denied request looks silent: the publish is denied, no responder sees it, and the requester just times out. Every JetStream API call is a request, so a locked-down user running `nats stream info` fails with `context deadline exceeded` rather than a permission error.
- With `nats auth user edit`, each `--pub-allow`/`--sub-allow` flag replaces the entire list, so always pass the complete set of subjects.
- Pitfall: A subscribe deny silently breaks request-reply. `subscribe: { deny: [">"] }` blocks the inbox subscription; adding `allow: ["_INBOX.>"]` next to it doesn't help because deny beats allow. Replace the deny with the allow. "Adding `allow: ["_INBOX.>"]` next to the deny doesn't help — deny beats allow"
- In the broken subscribe-deny state the CLI request waits out its timeout and exits 0 with no error; the denial shows only in the server log as `Subscription Violation`.
- Pitfall: An allow-list that forgets a needed subject closes it off too; a missing entry is a silent block. Prefer the wildcard matching the user's real subject space over an enumerated list you must remember to grow. "Prefer the wildcard that matches the user's real subject space over an enumerated list"
- Pitfall: An over-broad `>` grants every subject on the server, including the `$JS.API.>` control plane when JetStream is on. Scope each user to the subject prefix it actually uses. "`orders.>` for `order-svc`, never `>`"
- Pitfall: A deny can be invisible under a wildcard subscription. A literal subscribe to a denied subject is rejected loudly, but a wildcard subscription overlapping the deny is accepted and the server filters denied subjects out at delivery time with no error, no gap marker, and no server-log line. "If a subscriber seems to miss messages, check its deny lists before suspecting the publisher."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Accounts and multitenancy**

- Pitfall: `no_auth_user` can reopen access you intended to close. Pointing it at a user in `$G` lands every anonymous client in the global account again. Name a deliberately narrow user, never a wide-open account. "Do name a deliberately narrow user, and don't point it at a wide-open account."
- `no_auth_user` can't be introduced or changed by config reload (`config reload not supported for NoAuthUser`; old config stays active), `nats-server -t` doesn't catch a `no_auth_user` naming a missing user, and the server rejects `no_auth_user` together with a trusted operator.
- Pitfall: The system account has no user, so server events are unreachable. Declaring your own `accounts` block still creates `$SYS` but with no user; declare a `SYS` account with a user and set `system_account: SYS`. "with no user inside it you can't connect there"
- Pitfall: A shared subject name doesn't mean shared delivery. Two accounts using `orders.shipped` never exchange a message; connecting tenants is a deliberate export/import act. "Don't reach for a matching name to connect tenants."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Cross-account**

- In operator mode, both changed account JWTs must be pushed after adding an export/import; until then the share silently doesn't exist, because JWT mode has no startup check to catch a mismatch.
- Pitfall: An export with no import is silent; an import with no export stops the server. Config-mode error: `Error adding stream import "orders.shipped": stream import not authorized`. In operator mode the failure is silent instead. "An export nobody imports isn't an error ... An import with no matching export is loud"
- Pitfall: Service and stream are not interchangeable. A service import with no responder running in the exporting account returns `No responders are available` immediately (exit 0, no timeout).
- Pitfall: A renamed import is not the original subject. Subscribe to the name the import lands on (after `prefix:`/`to:`), not the name the exporter published.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Operator mode**

- Building the trust chain by hand is error-prone; one wrong seed produces a JWT the server silently rejects at connect time. Use `nats auth` (or nsc).
- The `nats auth` store holds every private key in the trust chain (JWTs under `stores`, seeds under `keys` in `$XDG_DATA_HOME/nats`); run the tool on a trusted machine and never on the server. "which is why you run the tool on a trusted machine and never on the server"
- Bearer JWTs are an explicit opt-in exception; avoid them unless needed for WebSocket connections. "You should avoid them unless you need them for WebSockets connections."
- A credentials file is a secret: treat it like a password, readable by the one client that uses it and nothing more.
- Pitfall: Editing an account without pushing it. `nats auth account edit` changes only the local JWT; the server keeps validating against its copy so the edit silently has no effect. Push after every account change and confirm with `account query`. "Push after every account change"
- Pitfall: System account missing under a nats-based resolver. The server exits at boot with `using nats based account resolver - the system account needs to be specified in configuration or the operator jwt`; bites when the operator JWT was built by hand or by a tool that didn't set one.
- Pitfall: Leaking the `.creds` file. It carries the private seed; anyone holding it can connect, with no password to guess and no list to revoke against. Never bake it into an image, log it, or commit it; give it `0600` and mount it to the one client that needs it. To cut off a leak, revoke the user and re-push the account.
- Pitfall: Credential expiration. Expiring credentials reduce compromise impact without a signing-key rotation, but you then have a set of objects to monitor for expiration.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Decentralized authentication**

- Bearer tokens are a convenience for browser and websocket clients that have nowhere safe to keep a seed; they reduce the credential to a single document that must never leak.
- Rotating operators (after operator key compromise) is technically possible by adopting accounts into the new operator gradually, but it is not easy and there are no tooling affordances for it.
- Pitfall: Losing the operator seed. It is the only thing that can sign accounts; back the operator up before building on it (`nats auth operator backup`), encrypt with `--key`, store offline. An unencrypted backup holds the operator seed in cleartext.
- Pitfall: Pasting a seed where a public key belongs. Config and JWT fields only take public NKeys (`O...`, `A...`, `U...`); a pasted `S...` seed must be rotated. "Treat every `S`-prefixed string like a password."
- Pitfall: Signing users with the account's identity key. It works, but permissions then live on each user and whoever holds the account seed can issue a user with any permissions; a scoped key pins permissions up front so a leaked signing key can only issue users with the chosen scope (ADR-14).
- The CLI (v0.4.0) can't edit a scope in place; the only way is to remove the key and re-add the role, which creates a new key and locks out every user signed by the old one at the next push. "Treat key removal as mass revocation, not as an edit."
- Pitfall: Not planning for credential expiry. A user JWT minted by `nats auth user add` never expires, so a leaked creds file is valid until revoked. The only expiry control in v0.4.0 is on the credentials file (`--expire`). Pair a short expiry with a renewal step.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth callout**

- `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH` carries every connection attempt with whatever the client presented (token, password, NKey) readable — base64 is encoding, not encryption — so anything that can read the subject can harvest credentials. "Anything that can read this subject can harvest other clients' credentials."
- Pitfall: The auth service is a single point of failure. If it's down or slow, the server waits out `authorization.timeout` (default two seconds) and rejects the client. Set `timeout` deliberately, run more than one instance, keep OIDC/LDAP lookups fast. "Run more than one instance so a single slow one doesn't stall logins"
- Pitfall: Adding application users to `auth_users`. Every user there skips the callout and connects with no external check; list only the auth service. "Adding an application user here to 'save a round trip' silently exempts it from authentication."
- Two more mistakes: leaving the callout in the global account `$G`, and skipping `xkey` so credentials cross `$SYS.REQ.USER.AUTH` in the clear.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Encryption & TLS**

- Pitfall: TLS on without `verify` is encryption, not authentication. Any client that trusts your CA connects without presenting a certificate until you add `verify: true` or `verify_and_map: true`. "TLS on without `verify` is encryption, not authentication."
- Pitfall: `verify_and_map` needs the certificate subject to name a real user. A typo or wrong attribute fails with `Authorization Violation`. Don't hand-type the DN; read it with `openssl x509 -noout -subject` and paste it.
- Pitfall: Cluster and gateway certificates need both `serverAuth` and `clientAuth` key usages. Route/gateway TLS is always mutual and each node presents its one cert as both server and client; a `serverAuth`-only cert fails the route handshake — the most common cluster-TLS failure. "the most common cluster-TLS failure"
- Pitfall: Certificates rotate on disk, not in the server. Cert/key/CA files are read once at startup; overwriting does nothing until `nats-server --signal reload` (or SIGHUP), and even then existing connections keep the certificate they handshook with; only new connections get the rotated one.
- Pitfall: `handshake_first: true` locks out every legacy client. Migrate with a duration value (`handshake_first: "300ms"`) that accepts both kinds of client, and flip to `true` only after the last client has opted in.
- Pitfall: A wrong at-rest key hides streams; it doesn't destroy them. `Error decrypting our stream metafile: unable to recover keys` means the wrong key; restart with the right one and the stream returns.
- Don't keep running with `prev_key` set after rotation; leaving the old key in place keeps a retired secret live.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Security)**

- Checklist: Scope each user to its actual subject prefix — never grant `>`.
- Checklist: Point `no_auth_user` at a deliberately narrow user, never a wide-open account.
- Checklist: Never rely on a shared subject name to bridge accounts; use an explicit export/import.
- Checklist: Configure the server with the operator JWT (public material only), never a private seed.
- Checklist: List only the auth service in `auth_users`; every other user must go through the callout.
- Checklist: Add `verify` (or `verify_and_map`); TLS alone encrypts but doesn't authenticate the client.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connecting**

- A failed connect isn't always a dead socket: the server can accept TCP and then reject with `-ERR` (e.g. `maximum connections exceeded`), so a retry loop around connect needs a wait between attempts.
- Pitfall: One URL is a single point of failure at connect time. Don't hardcode one URL for a production client; pass the whole pool. "Don't hardcode one URL for a production client."
- Pitfall: A one-URL configuration that depends on discovery fails where discovery is off (`no_advertise`) or where advertised addresses aren't reachable. Configure every server you want the client to rely on, and treat discovered servers as additions.
- Pitfall: A blocked dial with no timeout hangs the startup; a service hanging on startup looks dead rather than slow. Set a deliberate connect timeout and pair it with a pool.
- Pitfall: An oversized message fails the publish, not the connect. Don't treat that error as a connection problem; keep messages under `max_payload` (1 MB default), and for large bodies store the blob elsewhere and publish a reference. "for large bodies store the blob elsewhere and publish a reference"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Reconnection**

- Pitfall: A bounded retry limit gives up on a long outage (rolling upgrade, long partition) and moves to CLOSED, never returning. Set `MaxReconnect` to `-1` and watch the reconnect-error callback so the outage is visible.
- Pitfall: Retry on a failed first connect hides a bad address; the service sits in RECONNECTING forever. Keep the reconnect-error callback wired and alert on a service still RECONNECTING after the deploy finishes.
- Pitfall: A zero wait or a jitter-free delay overloads the remaining server: zero spins a CPU loop; no jitter makes a fleet retry in lockstep. Keep a non-zero wait and keep the jitter. "Keep a non-zero wait, and keep the jitter"
- Pitfall: A full reconnect buffer stalls or drops your next publish (8 MB Go/Java, 2 MB Python). Back off publishing and let the buffer drain once the link returns instead of hammering publish in a loop.
- Pitfall: A stale connection on an overloaded server can go undetected for minutes. The client declares the link stale once outstanding pings exceed `MaxPingsOut`; with defaults (two-minute ping interval, one minute in Rust; two allowed outstanding pings) detection waits for the third unanswered ping, up to about six minutes (three in Rust).

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Connection Events**

- A status poll is a snapshot that races the state machine. Poll to report state (dashboards, metrics, readiness probes); react through events. "Poll to report state; react through events."
- Treat a force reconnect as a real disconnect (in-flight requests may be rejected; the reconnect buffer covers the gap with the same limits), and don't fire it across a whole fleet at once — stagger it. "a synchronized mass reconnect is the load spike that reconnect jitter exists to prevent"
- Pitfall: A status poll used as a trigger races the state machine. Recovery logic gated on polling acts on stale state and re-implements what events deliver in order.
- Pitfall: No closed observer means permanent failure goes unnoticed; the service sits with a dead connection while its process reports healthy. Wire the closed event everywhere, even with unlimited retries. "The closed event is the one that demands an action, and it's the one most often left unwired."
- Pitfall: Connection events and async errors are different signals. Events report state transitions; the async error callback reports problems while CONNECTED (e.g. slow consumer). Count them separately: rising disconnects point at network/servers, rising async errors point at your application.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Drain & Shutdown**

- In Go, `Drain()` returns immediately and drains in the background; returning from `Drain()` is not the signal that draining finished. Register a `ClosedHandler` and wait on it; exiting on `Drain()`'s return loses the work drain was meant to save.
- C# has no per-subscription drain; disposing a subscription drops messages still on their way. Set `DrainSubscriptionsOnDispose` (default `false`; bounded by `DrainPingTimeout`, five seconds default) on any C# service whose subscriptions do real work.
- Pitfall: Publishing after you call drain. Drain can't be reversed; a "shutting down" event emitted after `Drain()` either slips through or fails with a draining error, and you can't count on either. Drain last.
- Pitfall: A drain timeout shorter than your slowest handler discards in-flight work every deploy. Measure the slowest handler and set the timeout above it with margin.
- Pitfall: Assuming a core drain acks your JetStream messages. Drain winds down the connection; it does not acknowledge a consumer's messages. Ack explicitly before the connection closes or JetStream redelivers to the next client. "It does not acknowledge a JetStream consumer's messages for you."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Slow Consumers**

- The default caps are sized for a typical workload, not yours; a high-rate subject or large messages can fill 64 MB in seconds. "The defaults serve as a backstop rather than a workload-specific tuning."
- The async error callback is the single place the client reports asynchronous problems not tied to one API call (slow consumer, permission violation, protocol error). In Go a connection with no callback discards these reports; Rust, JS, C# likewise unless wired; Java and Python fall back to a default logger.
- Pitfall: The default limits are a backstop rather than a workload-specific tuning. Always set pending limits on a subscription that does real per-message work, sized to handler latency and peak rate.
- Pitfall: An unwatched async error callback hides every dropped message. Always set one and log the slow-consumer error visibly. "a quiet drop is worse than a crash because you don't even know it happened"
- Pitfall: Don't confuse the local drop with the server-side disconnect; watch the async-error rate and the disconnect rate separately, since each points at a different fix.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Request-Reply Resilience**

- Pitfall: Treating a timeout and no-responders as the same failure wastes a fast-retry opportunity on a slow responder and floods an unlistened subject. Branch on the error.
- Pitfall: A timeout shorter than the responder's real latency makes every busy moment look like a failure. Measure the responder's latency and set the timeout to two or three times its p99. "set the timeout to two or three times its p99"
- Pitfall: An unbounded retry loop pins a CPU and never reports the problem. Cap attempts, add jitter, and stop with a clear signal (log and let the caller decide).
- Pitfall: A non-idempotent retry that double-acts (e.g. reserves stock twice when only the reply was lost). Key every request by `order_id` and de-dupe on the responder.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TLS & Auth**

- The creds file is the whole identity and a secret: anyone holding it can connect as that user; load it from disk or an environment variable, never paste it into source.
- Pitfall: Do not hardcode credentials in source. A pasted JWT or password gets committed and can't be rotated without a redeploy; load from a path or env var and never commit a `.creds` file.
- Pitfall: Do not skip server verification in production. Skip-verify/insecure TLS accepts an impostor server with a self-signed certificate. Always supply the CA. "An encrypted link provides no protection if the server on the other end can't be trusted."
- Pitfall: An unmonitored credential expiry drops a live connection. The server arms a timer at the JWT's expiry, sends `-ERR 'User Authentication Expired'`, closes the connection, and rejects each reconnect; most clients then abort and land in CLOSED. Refresh credentials ahead of expiry via callback or rotated file.
- Pitfall: Rotate the creds file by opening a fresh connection, not in place. A live connection keeps the identity it authenticated with; overwriting the file changes nothing until the next connection cycle. Open a new connection with new creds and drain the old one.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first service**

- Pitfall: Validate the request body; never let bad input crash the handler. The framework doesn't validate payloads; on parse failure respond with a service error (`Nats-Service-Error` + `Nats-Service-Error-Code` headers, code always safe to parse as a number, `400` for bad input) so the caller sees "bad request" rather than a hang. "Don't assume the payload is well-formed."
- Pitfall: A service `Name` and `Version` are validated at creation. `Name` allows letters, digits, hyphens, underscores (no dots or spaces); `Version` must be valid SemVer; an invalid value fails `AddService` outright.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Endpoints and groups**

- Pitfall: Disabling the queue group turns an endpoint into broadcast — every instance receives every request and the caller gets one reply per instance. Never disable it on an endpoint that responds; do not disable it to "make sure a request is handled". "never disable it on an endpoint that responds"
- Pitfall: Endpoints are immutable once added: no remove, rename, or subject change on a running service; metadata is fixed at creation. Decide endpoint names and subjects deliberately before going live, the way you pick a stream name. To change shape, stop and start a replacement.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Discovery**

- Pitfall: Discovery is broadcast: a single reply is not the whole answer. A plain request returns the first response and silently hides the rest, so five instances appear as one. Wait a deadline and collect every reply, as the CLI does.
- Pitfall: `$SRV` is a reserved subject prefix; do not publish to it yourself. Publishing under `$SRV` collides with the framework's machinery and corrupts what callers discover. Keep your subjects under your own prefixes.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Observability**

- Pitfall: A service error arrives as headers, not as a failed call. A caller that only checks "did I get a reply" reads every service error as success. Check `Nats-Service-Error-Code` on every response; do not treat a returned message as proof the request succeeded.
- Pitfall: Stats are per instance, and `Reset()` zeroes them. `$SRV.STATS.<Name>` returns one `stats_response` per instance; sum across IDs yourself (the server keeps no aggregate), and don't assume counters only ever grow — `Reset()` zeroes them and resets `started`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Scaling**

- Disabling the queue group (`WithEndpointQueueGroupDisabled`) is broadcast, not scaling: useful for fan-out work, wrong for load balancing. Keep it on when you want to scale.
- `Stop()` returns before background processing finishes; don't exit the process the moment it returns — drain the connection or wait on the `DoneHandler` until in-flight work completes. "don't exit the process the moment it returns"
- Pitfall: Instances don't share memory — protect external state. Each instance keeps its own counter/cache/"remaining stock" and they drift. Keep handlers stateless; push shared state into a database or a JetStream stream/KV bucket. "Keep handlers stateless"
- Pitfall: A blocking handler stops its instance from serving other requests; handlers run synchronously on the service's connection. The queue group masks it by routing to peers, but if every instance blocks the whole service stalls. Keep handlers fast, move long work off the request path, add instances.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Monitoring endpoints**

- Pitfall: Alert on `connections`, not `total_connections`. A client in a reconnect loop barely moves `connections` but inflates `total_connections`; alerting on the lifetime counter pages someone for a number that was always going to grow. Alert on `connections` for capacity, watch `slow_consumers` for dropped clients.
- Pitfall: An unscoped `/jsz` is slow at scale. `/jsz?accounts=true&streams=true&consumers=true` walks every entity and can time out a scrape on a node with thousands of consumers, yielding no data. Don't fetch the whole tree on a schedule; scope with `?acc=` and page with `?offset`/`?limit`.
- Pitfall: The monitoring port is unauthenticated by default. Anyone who can reach `:8222` can read `/connz` and see users, subjects, and traffic; don't expose it to the open internet. "The monitoring port is unauthenticated by default."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — JetStream health**

- Pitfall: Crashed workers show up as rising lag with nobody fetching. `num_pending` climbs whether or not any client fetches, so it's ambiguous alone; the signature of crashed workers is lag rising while `num_waiting` is `0` and `delivered.stream_seq` stops advancing. Read all three together.
- Pitfall: In-flight is not lag. `num_ack_pending` counts messages a worker holds; `num_pending` counts messages no worker has taken. Rising in-flight means a stuck handler; rising lag means not enough handlers. "rising in-flight means a stuck handler, rising lag means not enough handlers"
- Pitfall: A filtered consumer's lag counts only its subjects. Empty pending on a filtered consumer doesn't mean the stream is empty; compare it against the stream's per-subject counts, not `last_seq`.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Advisories & events**

- Pitfall: Advisories are transient — published exactly once and not stored in any stream. Don't rely on a watching human or ad-hoc subscription; capture advisories in a durable destination that is always subscribed.
- Pitfall: A `max_deliver` advisory is the only built-in signal a message was dropped. Subscribe to `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.>` or capture it in a stream; otherwise poison messages disappear silently.
- Pitfall: A leader-elected advisory reports a flap, not its cause. Treat it as a symptom; don't diagnose the election from the advisory body alone.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Prometheus & dashboards**

- Pitfall: A node-local health check passes even with no quorum. `/healthz?js-enabled-only=true` returns `200` even when the cluster has lost the quorum that keeps a stream writable, because it never looks past the local server. Don't wire it as your only JetStream alert; add `/healthz?js-meta-only=true`, which turns `503` when the cluster loses quorum. "Do not wire a node-local check as your only JetStream alert."
- Pitfall: A check with no threshold never fires. `nats server check consumer` defaults don't know your SLA; without `--unprocessed-critical` it sits at OK while lag climbs. Always set explicit thresholds (the example pins `--unprocessed-critical 100`). "A silent check looks like coverage while providing none, which makes it worse than having no check."
- Pitfall: The exporter keeps no time series. It only converts format; Prometheus stores history. Don't treat the exporter alone as monitoring; run both.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Profiling the server**

- Pitfall: The profiling port has no authentication; anyone who can reach it can pull a goroutine dump showing subjects and internal state. It binds to the same `host` as the client port (default `0.0.0.0`, every interface) with no separate profiling host. Leave `prof_port` unset in production or restrict it by firewall/network policy; prefer the authenticated system-account route. "Leave `prof_port` unset in production"
- Pitfall: Turning on `prof_port` costs a restart (not reloadable), meaning a rolling restart mid-incident that may lose the state you're chasing. Reach for `nats server request profile` first.
- Pitfall: Block profiling is empty until you enable it; `prof_block_rate` must be above zero. It is reloadable, so raise it with SIGHUP, take the profile, and drop it back to zero — block sampling slows the server down.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first bucket**

- A get returns an entry rather than a value, and a missing key is signaled distinctly from an empty one; don't treat a missing key as "the count is zero". "an empty value is a value, and a missing key is the absence of one"
- Bucket and key names are validated. A bucket name may contain only letters, digits, dash, and underscore, and can't be empty.
- A colon is not allowed in a key (`ord:8w2k` is rejected client-side before sending); use an underscore or dash instead.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Watching**

- Don't stop reading at the boundary signal; a loop that treats the nil entry as end-of-stream quits before every live change. "when an entry is nil, skip it and keep looping. Do not break."
- A watch is live state, not a point read; don't open a watch, read the first entry, and close it to fake a get. "you pay for a consumer and a snapshot to get one value get would have handed you directly"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — History and revisions**

- A rejected update is dropped rather than queued, and you must retry; a fire-and-forget update silently loses the write on conflict. "Don't assume an update succeeded; check the result, and on a revision mismatch, re-get the key and try again"
- Do not use put for a read-modify-write; put is unconditional and overwrites a concurrent writer's value. "Use put to set a key to a given value, and update to change it from the value it currently holds."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TTL and limits**

- A per-key TTL is set at create, and only at create; neither put nor update takes a TTL, and rewriting the key appends a value with no TTL so the key stops expiring. "Use delete-then-create to change a TTL, not put or update."
- Limits reject, they do not make room for an oversized value; a put over max value size or that would exceed max bucket size returns an error and leaves existing values in place.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Under the hood**

- Delete does not remove history; only purge does. "If you delete `widget-blue` to scrub a wrong count and assume the bad value is unrecoverable, it's sitting one `nats kv history` away."
- Do not operate the backing stream directly: don't hand-edit `KV_INVENTORY` config and don't publish to `$KV.INVENTORY.>` with raw `nats pub`, because raw publishes lack the CAS, `KV-Operation`, and `Nats-Rollup` headers.
- A key has to be a legal subject token because it becomes the last token of `$KV.INVENTORY.<key>`; a colon or double dot is rejected.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Where to go next (Key-Value)**

- Checklist: use the key-value API, never raw `nats pub` to `$KV.INVENTORY.>` or hand edits to `KV_INVENTORY` config.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first object**

- A digest mismatch means do not use the bytes; `ErrDigestMismatch` means retry the get, and a repeated mismatch means the object is damaged and should be put again.
- Getting a missing object is an error, not empty bytes; treat "not found" as a real branch. "don't ship the order on the assumption that an absent invoice is an empty one"
- Don't assume a put "worked" without a get confirming it round-trips.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Chunking**

- A chunk size at the extremes causes problems: too small wastes storage on per-message framing overhead and slows puts/gets; too large exceeds the server's `max_payload` (1 MB by default) or a smaller stream max message size and the put fails outright.
- Always check the get result before you use the bytes; re-put from the source on failure rather than shipping a partial file.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Metadata and links**

- A link is a snapshot rather than a live reference; deleting the target leaves the link dangling (`ErrObjectNotFound`), and renaming the target breaks it too. "Do verify the target exists with `info` before you depend on the link, and re-create the link after you delete or rename its target."
- `UpdateMeta` changes name, description, headers, and metadata, not chunk size or link; a new chunk size or link target is silently discarded. "To change the chunk size, delete the object and put it again. To change a link target, delete the link and add a new one."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Watching and listing**

- Watch delivers metadata, not the bytes; a service that tries to read a large payload off the watch finds only metadata and breaks.
- An empty bucket is an empty result, not an error; don't conflate "no objects" with "the bucket is missing".
