**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Under the hood (Object Store)**

- A soft delete does not reclaim disk the instant you call it; the purge frees bytes as the stream cleans up. "Don't delete a large object and immediately assert the disk is smaller."
- A re-put after a delete is a new object identity, not a restored history. "Don't reach for the object store when you need the *previous* version after an overwrite; that history lives in the Key-Value Store."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Stream backup and restore**

- Memory streams cannot be snapshotted; the backup fails with `memory streams do not support snapshots`. Set `Storage: File` on any stream you want to back up.
- The stream name cannot change on restore; the server rejects with `stream name may not be changed during restore`.
- Flow control can time out on slow disks or distant links (`408 No Flow Response`); the fix is smaller chunks and a smaller window (e.g. `--chunk-size 64k --window-size 1m`).
- `--no-consumers` silently drops consumer state; the restore rebuilds the stream with no consumers and nothing warns you.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Mirrors as a DR tool**

- A mirror's configuration is fixed once the stream exists; you can't re-point a running mirror or change what it copies. Changing it means delete and recreate, after which messages re-replicate.
- Don't let a healthy mirror be your reason to stop taking snapshots.
- Don't reach for R3 as DR: a corrupt write replicates across all three R3 replicas just as it lands in a mirror.
- A mirror is not a backup; don't run a mirror instead of snapshots. "Pair them: the mirror for site failure, the snapshot for bad data."
- Read `Lag` before you trust the copy; replication is eventually consistent, not synchronous. "Diagnose the link before a failover, never during one."
- A mirror's config is effectively locked after creation; settle upstream, site, and subjects upfront.
- Avoid a Work Queue upstream under a mirror: the mirror's hidden internal consumer is a direct consumer that bypasses the work queue's subject-overlap check, so a worker and the mirror can both receive the same message. Use a `Limits` upstream instead.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Disaster recovery**

- Never promote a mirror before lag reaches zero, or with a stalled lag you've consciously accepted; tail messages in flight are lost and new writes land on top of the gap.
- R3 replication will not save you from a mistake; an accidental delete or bad publish replicates to all three copies at once.
- Stop publishers before purging corrupted messages; otherwise new corrupt data arrives behind you and you keep purging against a growing tail.
- An untested snapshot is unverified; a healthy `nats stream info` on the live stream proves nothing about the archive. "Rehearse the restore on a schedule (quarterly is a reasonable minimum)"

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Config and JWT backup**

- The backup file is the whole authority; always pass `--key` and keep the curve seed away from the backups. Restore without the key fails with no recovery path. "Test-restore on a spare machine once so you know the file and the key actually pair up."
- A restored store doesn't refill the server's resolver; the fix is one `nats auth account push` per account, which works only while you still have `server.conf`.
- An un-backed-up operator rotation orphans the archive; tag every backup with the operator version or timestamp and take a fresh backup right after any rotation.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first MQTT client**

- An `mqtt {}` block with no `listen` or `port` disables MQTT silently, with no error and no log line, so always set one.
- Starting without JetStream fails at startup; the requirement applies per account too: an MQTT user whose account has no JetStream is refused at connect. "Enable JetStream on the server, and on the account your MQTT users bind to."
- Pointing an MQTT-over-WebSocket client at 1883 is rejected with `MQTT clients over websocket must connect to the Websocket port, not the MQTT port`; plain MQTT goes to 1883, MQTT over WebSocket goes to the WebSocket listener.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Topics and subjects**

- `*` and `>` are ordinary characters in MQTT and pass through unescaped; if one becomes a whole token in the subject NATS reads it as a wildcard. `fleet/*/telemetry` subscribes to `fleet.*.telemetry`. "Keep `*` and `>` out of topic names unless you mean the NATS behavior."
- Writing permissions as MQTT topics never matches; it fails late: the device connects fine, then its publishes are rejected.
- Granting only `sensors.>` for a `#` subscription: the server returns `0x80` in the SUBACK and tears down the `sensors.>` subscription it had already created, so the device receives nothing at all.
- Assuming a leading or trailing slash is cosmetic: `sensors/temp` and `/sensors/temp` are different subjects. "If some devices in a fleet emit a leading slash and others don't, you have two subject trees, not one."
- Letting free text into a topic: a space closes the connection on publish and fails the SUBACK on subscribe. "Sanitize anything interpolated into a topic."

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — QoS, sessions, and retained messages**

- Expecting QoS 1 to cover NATS-originated messages: they arrive at QoS 0 with no redelivery. "put it in a JetStream stream and have something replay it, rather than relying on the MQTT subscription"
- Sharing a client ID across devices looks like a flaky network. "Give every device its own client ID, and prefer one derived from hardware rather than baked into an image."
- Raising `max_ack_pending` without counting subscriptions: the per-session total is capped at 65535 and every `#` subscription costs double; new subscriptions fail with `0x80`, easy to misread as a permissions problem.
- Assuming a retained message is a message queue: only the last retained value per topic is kept. "Use JetStream when you need the history."
- Testing a will with a clean shutdown discards the will; test with a hard kill or by cutting the network.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Auth and clustering (MQTT)**

- An explicit deny on `$MQTT.sub.>` is still enforced and breaks QoS 1 and 2 subscriptions. "leave those subjects out of your permission lists entirely: don't allow them (unnecessary) and don't deny them (breaks QoS 1)"
- Leaving credentials off the MQTT listener lets any device that can reach port 1883 connect. "Devices sit on networks you control least, so put credentials and TLS on the MQTT listener before it leaves a lab."
- Denying `$MQTT.sub.>` silently breaks QoS 1 and 2 subscriptions while QoS 0 keeps working, so the fleet looks half-broken.
- Forgetting `--bearer` in operator mode: a valid JWT is refused with CONNACK return code 5; both the user and the account must be bearer-enabled.
- Adding a cluster block without `server_name` makes the server refuse to start; set `server_name` on every server from the beginning.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Your first WebSocket connection**

- There is no default WebSocket port; a `websocket {}` block without `port` or `listen` starts the server with no WebSocket listener, no error, and no warning.
- Pointing a client at the wrong listener: `nats://` to the WebSocket port and `ws://` to 4222 both fail, and neither failure names the real problem.
- A `websocket {}` block with no port: the server starts and the listener doesn't exist; check the log for `Listening for websocket clients`.
- A `websocket {}` block with neither `tls {}` nor `no_tls: true` exits at startup.
- A client URL without an explicit port: nats.js fills one in and never picks 4222.
- Shipping `no_tls: true`: it's a development flag, and the `DO NOT USE IN PRODUCTION!` warning is printed once at startup.
- A FIPS-140 build made with Go 1.25 or earlier refuses the whole WebSocket listener (and `ws://`/`wss://` leafnode remotes) because the handshake computes SHA-1 over `Sec-WebSocket-Key`; build with Go 1.26 or later.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Browsers and origins**

- A browser has no filesystem; putting an account seed in front-end code hands it to anyone who opens developer tools.
- Treating `allowed_origins` as access control: it's evaluated only when an `Origin` header is present, so it constrains browsers and nothing else.
- Setting `same_origin: true` when the page and the endpoint are on different hostnames fails, which is the normal case behind an ingress.
- Serving the page from a host you didn't list breaks the handshake for every user with a `403` until the list is updated.
- Putting a seed or credentials file in front-end code: "Anything the page can read, a visitor can read."
- Giving the dashboard user publish permission: a display-only page needs subscribe on `orders.>`; publish rights on a credential that ships to browsers is a much larger surface than needed.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — TLS and proxies**

- Any other `websocket {}` change on reload (`verify_and_map`, `pinned_certs`, `allowed_origins`, timeouts) is rejected, and a rejected field aborts the entire reload, including otherwise-valid changes in the same edit.
- A proxy that drops `Upgrade` and `Connection`: the client reports a connection error, not a protocol error; if `ws://` works directly and fails through the proxy, check this first.
- A proxy idle timeout shorter than the ping interval: connections drop on a timer with no error on either side. "The pattern to look for is disconnects at a suspiciously round interval."
- `no_tls: true` on a hop that isn't private: correct behind a terminating proxy on a trusted network and wrong the moment traffic crosses anything else; there's no warning distinguishing the two.
- Forgetting `advertise` behind NAT: connections succeed and then fail on a later reconnect to an unreachable advertised URL.
- Expecting `wss://` to configure the server: the client scheme and the server `tls {}` block are set independently, and a mismatch fails at the handshake.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Leaf nodes over WebSocket**

- Every URL in a single remote must use the same kind of scheme; mixing `wss://` and `nats://` stops the server at startup (`cannot have a mix of websocket and non-websocket urls`). You can't list the ingress and a direct leafnode port as alternatives.
- A leafnode URL without a port gets `:7422` appended whatever its scheme, so `wss://nats.acme.example` quietly dials the leafnode port and fails; write the port explicitly on every remote URL.
- Reading the scheme as the encryption status: neither the scheme nor the block alone tells you what a link is doing; check both.
- Mixing schemes in one `urls` list refuses to start.
- Pointing the remote at the leafnode port: 7422 speaks the leafnode protocol directly and will not complete a WebSocket handshake.
- Granting `LEAFNODE` to a WebSocket leaf: the value has to match the transport.
- A path-routing proxy that doesn't forward `/leafnode`: route `/` or give the remote the proxy's prefix so the path becomes `/nats/leafnode`.
- Reaching a hub that isn't running a WebSocket listener: a hub with only a leafnode port has nothing for a `wss://` remote to connect to.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Queue Groups**

- Core queue groups never redeliver: a message sent to a worker that crashes mid-processing is lost. For redelivery and durability, use JetStream worker pools.

**Source class: NATS by Example narratives + new docs Learn deep dives — Security**

- NATS doesn't require authentication by default, so production deployments should always configure one of: config-based auth, decentralized auth (operator mode), or auth callouts.

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Achieve MASSIVE Scale with NATS Clustering | Rethink Connectivity Episode 4**

- Username/password in the config file is the simplest but least secure auth flow because the credentials sit in plain text. "this one isn't the most secure because the username and password is in plain text on your config file" (~03:40)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to build a NATS Supercluster | Rethink Connectivity Episode 5**

- Defining accounts and users inline in the server config is not ideal; decentralized JWT auth is the recommended construct for secure clusters and super clusters. "we're defining all of our accounts and all of our users inside of our server config and this might not be ideal" (~04:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extend your NATS Cluster with Leaf Nodes | Rethink Connectivity Episode 7**

- With one giant cloud stream and many (e.g. 2000) stores, having every store fetch messages from the cloud hammers the hub; instead build filtered local read replicas. "everybody's going to be hammering the cloud with requests for orders and you might not want that" (~19:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Dynamic Permissions with Scoped Signing Keys | Rethink Connectivity Episode 8**

- Minting users with permissions baked into the JWT means adding a new feature later requires re-minting and redistributing JWTs, which may be infeasible; scoped signing keys avoid this. "we would have no way of expanding the subjects they're allowed to use unless we re-minted the JWT... that might not be feasible" (~12:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Connect ANY Auth System to NATS.io with Auth Callout**

- Users defined in the server config are the easiest option but do not scale; decentralized JWT auth scales far, needs no config updates and keeps secrets out of config files, but is more complex and cumbersome. "put your users defined inside of a NATS server config which is the easiest approach but isn't super scalable" (~03:00)
- A chat app using a single all-powerful shared NATS user lets anyone impersonate anyone; that is the anti-pattern the callout replaces. "I have a single NATS user that just has permissions to do anything that they want which obviously isn't great" (~09:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Andrew Gracey on Two Node K3S**

- Adding a third "witness" node at the edge increases operational complexity and is an extra point of failure, defeating the cost goal; the risk-versus-TCO balance kills the project for many customers. "now you just increase your cost again and increase the complexity of your solution by adding a third different node" (~04:30)
- Moving the edge control loop to the cloud fails on latency and bandwidth (5G, satellite, DSL downstream links) and on cloud outages; companies that moved control loops to the cloud are moving them back. "imagine trying to run Kubernetes over DSL right, it's not going to happen, there's just not enough bandwidth" (~06:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Replace Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis and more w/NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity Ep 10**

- In core NATS, if a subscriber is offline when a message is published, the server drops it or delivers only to online subscribers; the offline one never gets it. "there's no subscribers so I'm just going to drop the message" (~02:03)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — How to configure NATS JetStream streams | Rethink Connectivity Ep 11**

- Memory storage is ephemeral: if the server goes offline those messages are lost; it is niche and suited to caches or hosts without fast disk writes. "if that server goes offline those messages are going to be lost" (~06:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Build Priority Background Jobs & Dead Letter Queues with NATS JetStream | Rethink Connectivity ep 12**

- In a work-queue stream, a message that exhausted max deliveries stays in the stream until manually acknowledged or deleted, so failures stack up the queue size. "it will stay there in the stream until you either manually acknowledge it or manually delete it" (~05:05)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared: Part 1 | Rethink Connectivity**

- For market data with ~100,000 instruments you would not create 100,000 Kafka topics; you use one topic per exchange with the instrument as key, and then filtering for one instrument means the broker sends everything to a client that discards most of it. "you're transferring all the data over the network to somewhere else where you are discarding most of it" (~15:16)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS & Kafka Compared Pt 2: Consumers | Rethink Connectivity**

- Changing Kafka partition counts does not rebalance data, so teams over-partition up front (e.g. 100 partitions as a high-water mark for max consumers). "you cannot have more than just one single client application per topic partition ... so you over partition" (~05:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Comparing and contrasting NATS and Kafka | RethinkConn '22**

- Kafka topics usually need predefinition; auto-created topics default to one partition and topic creation can trigger re-partitioning across servers. "the default number of partition is one and that's not very useful in Kafka for many cases" (~05:06)
- Filtering in Kafka requires a Kafka Streams process that reads everything and writes filtered sub-streams, storing messages more than once. "so you end up storing the message actually more than once" (~07:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Getting Started with NATS JetStream: Streams, Storage, and Data Lifecycle**

- Memory storage works but is not durable; use file storage for disk durability. "If you used the storage memory mechanism ... it would store data in memory. I don't want that" (~08:08)
- Default limits are unlimited, meaning data piles up with no cleanup; set limits so NATS cleans up automatically. "my maximums are all set to be unlimited, which means I'm just going to keep on piling data on without any data cleanup. That's not great" (~09:09)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Why NATS Consumers Just Work (And How to Use Them in 15 Minutes)**

- An ephemeral consumer does not track progress: it is created with a generated name, disappears when done, and re-running re-delivers everything (92 rows became 184). "I'm creating a new consumer that isn't tracking state ... 92 throwaway answers twice" (~15:18)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Mirror Streams Explained — One-Way Replication Made Simple**

- Filter subject and subject transform cannot be combined on a mirror. "you can't use filter subject and subject transform together. You got to pick one" (~02:00)
- Mirroring a work-queue origin is only partially supported and not resilient over intermittent links like leaf nodes; interest-based origins are unsupported with undefined behaviour. "if you're using interest-based retention, don't try it. Mirror streams don't officially support that" (~03:02)
- The server does not verify the mirror is caught up before promotion, so unreplicated messages are lost. "the server won't verify if the mirror is fully caught up, so any unreplicated messages will be lost" (~07:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP09: Grokking NATS.io Streams and Consumers**

- Avoid the design where everything must synchronously deluge into one single stream; prefer origin streams plus async sourcing. "rather than saying I have this one single stream that everything basically has to deluge into synchronously" (~25:35)
- A client that processes too slowly on a fast delivery path becomes a slow consumer and the server disconnects it. "the server is not going to be happy ... you're a slow consumer of this data so I'm going to disconnect you" (~48:05)
- Push consumers deliver to an inbox subscription as fast as the publish side sends, which can overwhelm applications and forced developers to think about flow control and max ack pending. "that can overwhelm applications ... that whole push-based model even though it sounded nice in theory I think actually confused quite a few people" (~53:11)
- Do not plan on 100k or a million consumers, one per entity; you will never deploy that many client applications, so pick a wildcard granularity your app can handle in order. "nobody's running 100,000 a million containers ... the middle ground can be having a client application that can apply a wild card at the level of granularity" (~63:23)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS 2.10 Webinar**

- Before 2.10 any two servers shared one TCP route connection, so a very active account could cause head-of-line blocking for other accounts sharing it. "any two pairs of servers only had a single TCP connection between them ... there can be some unintentional unfairness or head of line blocking" (~19:22)
- Partition mapping stays stable unless you edit the partition count; changing it moves subjects between buckets, though strategies exist to handle that. "unless you're messing around with the partition count and editing those things" (~34:41)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP06: The journey and features of the NATS.io 2.10 release**

- Raft consensus traffic is itself carried over NATS between cluster nodes; with a single TCP route per server pair, application traffic and consensus traffic could block each other, and one account could effectively deny service to another. "what we don't want to happen is that application traffic gets stuck behind consensus traffic ... you don't want one to be able to cause a denial of service effectively to another" (~34:36)
- Before 2.10 users needing several non-wildcard subsets (e.g. factories 1-5 of 10) had to create many consumers, which costs the server and forces the client to re-order across consumers. "people needed to create many consumers to get this one specific stream of data which is not only not perfect from optimization point of view for the server ... you have to handle the order" (~60:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP07: Going off piste; KV patterns with NATS.io (pt1)**

- Relying on real-time clocks and NTP for synchronizing events across VMs with time-sliced CPUs fails; David used NATS signals and then Streaming so a system that missed a signal could catch up. "NTP would fail me sometimes ... it really is important when events needed to be synchronized" (~10:17)
- If you are protecting one resource from more than a couple of workers, reconsider the design slightly. "if you're protecting one resource from more than maybe a couple of worker systems maybe you want to readdress your design ever so slightly" (~13:25)
- A KV lock is advisory: nothing locks the data out, so correctness depends on workers honouring the lock in code; NATS is not a magic firewall. "it's down to the developer to adhere to the lock nothing's going to actually lock the data out ... NATS isn't some kind of magic firewall" (~18:34)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03: Escaping the HTTP Mindset with NATS.io**

- HTTP was designed to serve web pages, not for inter-service or intra-process communication, and most teams adopt it for services without questioning whether its semantics fit. "HTTP was designed as a protocol to serve the web... it was never designed to be inter-process communication" (~03:06)
- Sticking an HTTP proxy in front of every decomposed component is the default reflex and the wrong one for service-to-service traffic. "what do people do? oh well we'll stick a HTTP proxy in front of everything" (~02:05)
- Starting with in-process function calls and later distributing means rewriting all the communication logic; that rewrite is the pain NATS-first design avoids. "now you have to completely rewrite all of your logic, all of your communication mechanisms, so it's very painful" (~10:16)
- Programs embrace async primitives internally, then fall back to synchronous HTTP between components; NATS lets you break that synchronous point-to-point mindset. "we think about HTTP and service calls between components and then we're right back into synchrony land" (~19:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02: Monolith to Modular Monolith with NATS.io**

- A load balancer or proxy is another software component to deploy, manage, and learn, separate from the application, and it drags in network, firewall, and TLS-offload concerns. "it's another thing that you would have to manage and deploy and learn... independent of your actual application" (~07:06)
- Starting with in-process method calls and later distributing pushes teams to add RabbitMQ for queues and Kafka for streaming, each a new technology, dependency, and operational burden. "you start bringing in all these things and it's like more technologies to learn more dependencies... more operational overhead" (~19:23)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP04: A Service Mesh Pattern for NATS.io**

- Service meshes inject a sidecar container per pod (Envoy for Istio); it is convenient for the developer but adds compute, cost, and complexity for operators as the fleet scales. "the people that actually are paying the bills to run extra compute... that's where it gets a little interesting" (~09:11)
- Automation and mesh layers make an application's operational behaviour opaque because logic is split between code and layer-specific DSLs and config files. "you begin to lose insight as to how your application runs because the logic and the know-how is split" (~17:20)
- Service meshes fall apart in heterogeneous estates (Kubernetes plus VMware, Hyper-V, bare Linux, mainframes, telco packet-centric environments) because they are Kubernetes-centric. "is it Kubernetes centric at that point and is everything else a satellite" (~18:21)
- Chained handoffs need strong contracts between teams and probably a write-ahead log to track where the baton is. "I think you need a write ahead log just to keep a track of... passing a baton around different services" (~42:51)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP05: Exploring Powerful Client-side Features and Abstractions in NATS.io**

- The original JetStream API mimicked core NATS Subscribe so closely that users jumped into JetStream without learning it and did not realize a consumer is a server-side construct, producing surprises. "people didn't even realize that the consumer's a server-side construct" (~06:07)
- Historically the Go client was the role model that other clients copied (callbacks everywhere even where iterators are idiomatic); the new approach decides per language how close to stay. "we have this role model Go client and then others are following it and we never discussed how close they should be" (~09:10)
- Auto-ack in the old subscribe-style API looked simpler but raised cognitive load because users could not tell whether messages were acked, and behaviour differed between clients. "even if the code looks simpler the cognitive load was bigger" (~14:18)
- For client-side abstractions (KV, Object Store, services) the server cannot validate compatibility, so a bucket written from Rust can silently not work from Go unless the clients are cross-tested. "server will not help you here because it's just an abstraction layer" (~40:51)
- Transactional multi-key updates in KV were requested; the team says it is a wide change across the ecosystem and especially the server, not a workaround, and not coming soon. "don't expect it to be very soon but that's something you would love to have but it has to be done right" (~49:58)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS as a ServiceMesh**

- If you are asking whether you need a service mesh, you probably do not; meshes carry a lot of complexity and the team must be able to support it. "if you're asking that question you probably don't need one" (~03:03)
- Do not use constant sampling for tracing; it locked the speaker's machine up. "make sure... that you don't do constant sampling like I did and lock your machine up" (~16:18)
- Circuit breaking is the one mesh feature the speaker had not found in NATS. "circuit breaker, I haven't seen that in NATS yet" (~23:27)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP01S3: Going back to basics with core NATS!**

- People skip core NATS and go straight to JetStream "because we need persistence"; the speakers consider this a mistake. "sometimes people don't know where to start or they even skip core NATS entirely and go straight to JetStream" (~03:20)
- A persistence layer (JetStream) is heavyweight and "stores everything"; with core NATS you can be selective about what gets stored. "every persistence layer is pretty heavy, it just stores everything if you use JetStream, while here you can be way more selective" (~11:27)
- Start with core NATS; move to JetStream only when you find yourself reinventing consensus or replicated persistence. "at the moment you start feeling that you're reinventing the wheel of consensus or persistence ... then probably JetStream" (~21:38)
- The clients deliberately do not add generic request retry logic: a built-in retry is an opinion that suits ~90% of use cases but is wrong for the other 10% (e.g. transactional systems needing immediate failure). "for 90% of use cases yeah it should retry but it will then make very bad user experience for those 10%" (~29:46)
- Stacked retries across layers (front end retries, back end retries, next back end retries) can bring a whole system down; a single enforced retry opinion is dangerous. "based on timing it would just bring the whole system down" (~30:50)
- Connection pooling is a frequent request from database-minded users; the answer is to start with one connection and keep it unless you have a very specific reason. "you should start with one connection and unless you are something very specific use case you should keep that one connection" (~37:58)
- Pooling is deliberately not provided because users would default to it out of habit and then be confused by lost ordering. "if we give pooling to the users everybody would start with pooled connections and half of the people will be confused why I lost the order" (~42:05)
- Cloud I/O is often burstable: things look fine for hours and then throughput drops with no change in NATS; network/IO is usually the first bottleneck. "in the cloud environment when the I/O is burstable quite often, it looks fine for a few hours and then suddenly drops" (~49:14)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP02S3: Orbit - The NATS Client Extensions**

- In the past, features were merged into individual clients as users asked; every such feature soon triggered "why is it not in the other language", so now every new tier-one feature must pass a parity check agreed by all maintainers. "every new feature added to tier one client has to go through the parity check" (~09:15)
- Language-agnostic client APIs that look identical across languages end up feeling foreign in every language; NATS prefers idiomatic clients and steers users to per-language examples. "it felt very weird for me as a Gopher, like it didn't feel like Go" (~12:16)
- Bundling JetStream, KV and Object Store in one client with a single version makes breaking changes practically impossible under semver, even for APIs marked experimental. "it feels like we never can break anything, we can mark a specific API experimental but how does it matter" (~16:20)
- Maintainers are conservative about exposing client internals because each exposed piece becomes something that can break during client evolution; needs are now justified by concrete Orbit usage. "we are always very careful with exposing any internals because it makes evolving the client even harder" (~31:36)
- The service API being placed in the clients is regretted because its API was frozen immediately; if built today it would live in Orbit. "we were actually not very happy that the service API was in the clients because we very quickly felt that we couldn't break the API" (~40:51)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — EP03S3: NATS 2.11 Release**

- KV was introduced (KubeCon Valencia) as a small experiment for IoT caches; users now load millions of keys, so 2.11 is the first release adding default soft limits and safe defaults to features. "now we are at I don't know millions of keys ... this is the first release where we started adding default limit soft cuts" (~30:40)
- Consumers are server-side state; many small operations via consumers eat server resources, whereas batch get creates no server state and is fire-and-forget. "the biggest difference is that batch get does not create state on the server, it just gives you what you asked for and it's done" (~34:46)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS tools and benchmarking with JNM! NATS Community Office Hours (Reupload)**

- With CQRS-style requests, re-publishing after 30 seconds without an answer risks duplicating the work. "if you don't get an answer within 30 seconds and you publish another request, you're going to possibly duplicate the work" (~14:18)
- Cloud burstable instances and general-purpose EBS (gp2/gp3) show good numbers for short tests but throttle after roughly 20 minutes of sustained JetStream writes; io1/io2 volumes cost more but are not throttled. "you'll get like maybe 20 minutes worth of good traffic and all of a sudden it'll throttle you way down" (~40:52)
- Benchmarks shorter than a few seconds are unreliable; make runs longer to get a proper number. "if the benchmark takes tenths of a second or less ... you may want to make it a little bit longer" (~48:01)
- Do not benchmark on laptops: thermal throttling kicks in after about 30 seconds at full clock; if you must, run 20-30 s tests then wait 20-30 s to cool. "on a laptop you got about 30 seconds and then at full speed ... your clock speed is going to be throttled down" (~49:02)
- In a cluster, bench publisher and subscriber connect to random servers; landing on the same server gives better numbers than being on different servers (extra route hop), so run several times or pin to one server for consistency. "if you happen to have your pub and your sub connecting to the same server you're going to get better numbers" (~54:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Benchmark Core NATS & NATS JetStream using the NATS CLI tool**

- Sub-second benchmark runs show noticeable variation; use runs of 30 seconds to a minute or more (increase the message count above the 100,000 default) for sustained numbers. "you would want to do benchmarks that run for more than a fraction of a second, you know 30 seconds a minute or more" (~05:06)
- Laptops throttle CPU frequency as temperature rises during benchmarks; let them cool between runs and do multiple runs, dropping outliers and averaging. "do more than one benchmark, more than one run ... that allows you to eliminate the outliers" (~11:12)
- Changing storage type between runs requires deleting the existing bench stream first (`nats stream rm benchstream -f`), otherwise the old config is reused. "simply remember to remove the stream, that's the simplest thing" (~25:26)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Partitioned Consumer Groups in NATS: Ordered, Scalable Stream Processing**

- Pinning is affinity plus failover, not a distributed lock; a client may briefly still think it is pinned after the server moved on, and buffered messages cannot be pulled back. "Pinning is affinity and failover. It is not a distributed lock" (~03:02)
- Client-side per-key threading breaks under redelivery: a failed earlier message can be redelivered after a later one for the same key was already processed. "if buy fails and gets redelivered later, it comes back after pay was already processed and the order breaks again" (~06:04)
- max_ack_pending=1 serializes unrelated keys behind each other and makes the single worker a single point of failure; a second worker becomes load balancing, not standby. "With max ack pending equal to one, only one worker can be active at a time, so there's no safe way to add a hot standby" (~08:05)
- With more partitions than members, a hot partition sharing a member with a quiet one starves the quiet key. "if a hot partition lands on the same member as a quiet one, that quiet key starves waiting in line behind the flood" (~12:10)
- Static group membership is fixed at creation; changing the mapping means deleting and recreating the group, so custom mapping suits a known hot key, not a moving one. "static membership is fixed at creation. To change the mapping, you delete and recreate the group" (~13:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Pull Consumer Priority Groups: Overflow, Pinned & Prioritized**

- A message can briefly be processed by two clients during failover overlap, so handlers must be idempotent; pinning is affinity and failover, not a distributed lock, and buffered messages cannot be revoked. "pinning is affinity and failover, not a distributed lock ... messages already in its buffer can't be revoked" (~06:04)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Distributed Counters in NATS — Global Totals Without Locks**

- Caveats: once allow_message_counter is on it cannot be turned off; counter streams cannot be mirrors (use sources); limits retention is required; no discard new, no per-message TTLs, no Nats-Rollup header. "Once you turn allow message counter on, you can't turn it off. Counter streams can't be mirrors. Use sources instead" (~03:03)
- Resetting a replicated counter means publishing a matching negative delta; purge alone will not propagate across sources. "resetting a replicated counter means publishing a matching negative delta. Purge alone won't propagate across sources" (~04:03)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Delayed Message Scheduling in NATS — One-Time, Cron, and Subject Sampling**

- Before 2.12 there was no native way to hold a message for later; NAK-with-delay on a consumer was a workaround that did not scale. "You could use NACK with delay on a consumer, but that was a workaround and it didn't scale" (~01:01)
- The stream must opt in with allow_message_schedules; once enabled it cannot be disabled, and it cannot be enabled on source or mirror streams. "Once you enable it, you cannot disable it on that stream. It also cannot be enabled on source or mirror streams" (~03:03)
- Cron schedules with a time zone are exposed to DST transitions (skipped hour on spring forward, double fire on fall back); use UTC. "Sticking with UTC avoids this entirely" (~03:03)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS JetStream Expected Sequence Headers — Optimistic Concurrency Control Explained**

- Per-subject tracks each distinct subject separately, so order.1.created and order.1.shipped cannot share tracking; publishing to a new subject with expected 1 fails because its last sequence is 0. "events.order.1 shipped is a different subject with no prior messages. Its last sequence is zero, not one" (~07:09)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Atomic Batch Publishing | NATS 2.12**

- Without atomic batching each publish is independent, so a connection drop after the third of five related messages leaves a partial write. "your connection drops after the third? Well, you have a partial right. Your data is inconsistent" (~01:01)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS: Orbit – Extending NATS Clients with Richer Capabilities**

- Opinionated defaults (e.g. timeouts) in the core clients are regretted over time because NATS use cases are too varied (cars on bad networks vs cloud) for one sensible default. "every opinion that we try to land in the client, it's just matter of time, we will regret it" (~02:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — We need to talk about Microservices... (And how NATS.io can simplify things)**

- The speaker does not suggest NATS replace a log store outright; treat the log tap as a debugging "break the glass" switch and keep the default level at error so you don't flood the server. "I've set the log level ... to actually just show me errors that way I'm just not slamming the NATS server with all of my logs" (~19:24)
- The speaker explicitly does not argue against relational databases; the JetStream stores are proposed only where distributed scale-out is the need. "SQL databases and relational databases have their own use cases ... I'm not going to fight anybody on that" (~29:35)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — JetStream KV: A fascinating alternative to Redis...**

- The KV does not have all of Redis's operations; the value slot is currently opaque ("dumb") with no value-based semantics. "the NATS key value store right now is kind of dumb when it comes to the types of values" (~09:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The ONE feature that makes NATS more powerful than Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ & Redis**

- Alternatives give a firehose and expect client-side filtering, which at high scale is slow and inefficient; JetStream filters before sending over the wire. "the alternatives kind of just give you a firehose of messages and expect you to filter them out on the client side" (~04:04)
- Push consumers send as fast as the server can, making flow control hard for slow consumers even with the built-in flow control and heartbeats; they suit monitoring / most-real-time cases. "it still gets a bit challenging to reason about flow control" (~06:06)
- Max ack pending 1 gives strict in-order processing but is very slow; try to avoid it unless a downstream state machine truly needs strict ordering. "I would actually recommend trying to see if you can get away without having a max ack pending of one" (~25:26)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS Connect Live! | NATS Surveyor**

- Enterprise pain motivating Surveyor: opening Prometheus scrape ports across data centers and securing exporter connections is slow and complex; the speaker never got a Prometheus port opened in a three-year enterprise stint. "my very first task was open a port for Prometheus and I left three years later having never achieved that goal" (~03:06)
- Trade-off: Surveyor uses the system it monitors as transport, so a split brain or outage blinds it; it is not the be-all of monitoring and additional node-level monitoring is still needed. "we are using the thing that we're monitoring as a transport for monitoring ... so you also need some additional monitoring" (~07:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Transcending microservices with NATS | RethinkConn '22**

- Microservices are not a free lunch; adopt them only for a real need such as multiple geographies, data sovereignty, multi-cloud, acquisitions, or extending to the edge. "we certainly don't want to advocate for people to move to microservices for the heck of it" (~02:02)
- A perimeter-based security model (everything inside a VPC, cloud-specific IAM) breaks down once systems span clouds and the edge; NATS' cloud-agnostic security model is meant to replace it. "having this notion of a perimeter-based security model really breaks down it doesn't work anymore" (~08:10)
- Leaky service addressability and point-to-point service interactions create a "Death Star" web of services that needs load balancers and service discovery layered in; pub/sub with end-to-end communication removes those layers. "you have to add all these layers in between like load balancers and service discovery" (~11:13)
- The demo used a single shared bearer JWT embedded in the web app; one bad actor can ruin it for everyone, so this is demo-only, not best practice. "one bad actor could ruin the whole bunch" (~27:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Where are we now and where to next? | RethinkConn '22**

- JetStream was designed assuming a few thousand durable consumers, but users want 30–40 thousand, so large consumer sets need optimization work. "we've seen users want 30, 40 thousands so we're going to be doing some work optimizing for large consumer sets" (~10:13)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Extending stateful services to the edge | RethinkConn '22**

- Stateful services usually push state to a pristine central database, which adds another network hop and a system you must protect as the source of truth. "you have the service deployed, it has to talk to typically a database which is another network hop" (~01:04)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Effective debugging using the NATS CLI | RethinkConn '22**

- `nats server list` is an unopinionated snapshot of what can be seen now; it does not flag right or wrong, so the operator must know what to look for, e.g. a missing node or changed route/gateway counts after a network outage. "it's not going to flash any warnings at you ... you need to bring your own knowledge" (~03:04)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Using JetStream KV for dynamic microservice configuration | RethinkConn '22**

- Prefer KV-backed dynamic configuration with locked-down permissions over environment variables, files, or Kubernetes config management; it allows hot reload without restarting services. "you can hot reload their configuration ... without having to restart them" (~06:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking connectivity from cloud to edge | RethinkConn '22**

- Stateless edge functions (Lambda, edge functions, Wasm) are fine, but once an edge function needs state that lives across the globe the experience is still poor; this is the unsolved problem. "once that edge function really needs data it needs state, it becomes kind of a different story" (~08:10)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Using NATS JetStream as a Kine backend for k3s | RethinkConn '22**

- When restoring mirrored buckets as primary buckets, edit the backup to remove the mirror configuration first, or you recreate them as mirrors. "I have to go into these backups and just remove this mirror" (~09:17)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Service monitoring with Helix and Surveyor | RethinkConn '22**

- Decentralized auth with nsc is deliberately unopinionated about where JWTs are stored, which causes ergonomic friction; nsc is a utility for a decentralized design, not a management UX. "because it's decentralized there's some like ergonomic issues that naturally come up with it" (~02:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Short break and Q&A! | RethinkConn '22**

- JetStream KV has no value-based constructs (push, pop, Redis data-type semantics); it is a payload per key, like memcached, so tightly Redis-typed workloads will not map. "the NATS key value store does not have any kind of like value-based constructs in it" (~23:28)
- Core NATS servers handle millions of connections, but making millions of devices each a JetStream consumer raises real state and persistence questions. "if you're saying we want to have millions and millions of devices, and we all want them all to be consumers of a JetStream ... there's some real things to figure out" (~29:38)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Synadia Roadmap with Byron Ruth**

- Server-side filtering is subject-level only (per-token wildcards); filtering on headers or message body is not supported by the server and will not be; a message-processing callout to an external service is the planned way. "if you wanted to filter based on headers or the message body... that's not supported in the server and it won't be" (~04:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: After event Q&A with Derek on Zoom**

- A recurring adoption problem is that people skip the basics and start with advanced topics. "folks seem to start on chapter 20 instead of chapter 1" (~35:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Introducing Synadia Insights: Catch the NATS Failures Nothing Else Reports**

- A stream with a message-count limit discards the oldest messages while consumer positions have no limit, so a stopped consumer whose position falls below the stream's first sequence silently loses every message in between, with no error, log line or alert. "The logbook has a limit. The bookmarks do not." (~03:00)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Rethinking Connectivity - Hyper-Connectivity & The Intelligent Edge**

- Poll-based semantics don't scale when millions of devices hit a central place, so push had to be a native pattern. "poll based semantics does not scale when you have millions of devices all trying to hit some centralized place" (~08:50)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — A New Way of Thinking | NATS 2.0 and Connectivity**

- Most distributed systems work well with low RTT and high bandwidth but degrade on long RTTs; at large scale the coordination chatter alone can bring a system down even with little data flowing, which the supercluster gateway design (optimistic sends with interest-graph pruning) was built to avoid. "a lot of times just the chatter that's going back and forth on one of these systems actually brings the system down" (~24:40)
- When not to use NATS: don't rip and replace working HTTP, gRPC, Kafka or MQ investments; use NATS for new greenfield work. "don't replace what you have... use NATS to do new greenfield type of implementations" (~47:20)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - PowerFlex Solves Intermittent Connectivity at the Edge w/ NATS - RethinkConn 2025**

- They used core NATS fire-and-forget for transactional data in parking garages with bad internet, then moved that traffic to JetStream. "We were using fire and forget for things that shouldn't be fire and forgot about" (~03:04)
- The main operational friction is that JetStream requires stream setup per site, so commissioning each new customer means creating new streams. "every time we get a new customer and we have to commission a new site, we have to add new streams. That's maybe the biggest hiccup" (~10:14)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Customer Story - MachineMetrics on Industrial IoT & Predictive Analytics w/ NATS at RethinkConn 2025**

- They chose not to rip and replace Kinesis wholesale (too large a project for a small team); new development defaults to NATS/JetStream/KV. "let's just replace Kinesis with NATS for all our data ingestion is a massive project" (~09:12)
- Biggest lesson: subject and payload shape matter enormously and must be designed deliberately, so they built internal libraries that hide connection setup and subject construction from developers. "the shape of the data whether that be subjects or payloads is very very important and you need to be very intentful" (~11:13)
- Decentralized auth is worth learning thoroughly before use; it is the tricky part and they are reworking their auth model with Synadia. "it's certainly a topic to spend some time making sure that you understand thoroughly" (~27:36)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS at the Edge with F1 Arcade**

- The previous stack was MQTT plus Redis with a hand-rolled queuing system; Redis went down under load testing at the largest venue despite being adequately provisioned, and messaging lacked observability. "Redis despite being adequately provisioned would go down when running our load testing suite" (~04:05)
- Migration required replacing WebSockets, HTTP calls, and MQTT with NATS; settling subject names and learning streams/consumers/acks is a real learning curve. "nailing down subject names... is something you're just going to have to work through" (~07:11)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Franco Sabini from Fineco Bank on NATS**

- The trigger to leave TIBCO Rendezvous was a sysadmin mandate against multicast protocols, which also don't work well on-prem-to-cloud. "a very strong request from our system administrators not to use multicast protocols anywhere in our environment" (~03:06)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Jaxon Repp from HarperDB on NATS and distributed databases**

- Raw WebSockets and then SocketCluster gave no delivery guarantee and created network storms at scale; a database must guarantee delivery, so they moved to JetStream while it was still in beta. "if there's one thing that a database is responsible for is guaranteeing delivery of data" (~03:07)
- Throughput was never a problem for fire-and-forget, but enabling fully acknowledged, exactly-once writes is where they hit throughput limits and back pressure. "as soon as we enable guaranteed delivery... that's when we push up against things" (~06:12)
- Lesson: lean into JetStream's built-in features instead of keeping a parallel bookkeeping list of what was sent; trust was built through testing over time. "the first iteration was okay but we send it there but we still hold on to the list" (~13:19)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Synadia RethinkConn 2024: Nathan Mellis from Modzy on NATS as a foundational building block**

- Their previous queue took many resources, was hard to configure, and could only be used one way; NATS replaced it over several months. "it took up a lot of resources it was hard to configure and you could only use it pretty much one way" (~05:07)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Simple Solutions for Complex Problems - How Workiva uses NATS as a Microservices and RPC transport**

- Raw pub/sub with hand-agreed encodings decouples services but couples teams; they generate cross-language pub/sub APIs from an IDL (Frugal, a Thrift extension) so developers think in services, not topics. "pub/sub is meant to decouple services but when it's done in that way it kind of couples the teams" (~18:19)
- A NATS daemon on every VM doesn't scale to hundreds of nodes; they'd move to a floating cluster or NATS on a subset of machines, which the service abstraction makes painless. "we don't really want to be running a NATS cluster of like hundreds of nodes" (~24:30)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Go Beyond Kubernetes Native Events with NATS**

- Kafka was rejected as too heavy and operationally noisy to deploy on 100 clusters; NATS via the Helm chart was deployed to all staging clusters in ~5 minutes. "I could have used Kafka but it's very heavy. It consumes a lot of resources. It's not really that straightforward to set it up" (~03:08)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Connectors – Seamlessly Integrate NATS with Other Systems**

- A connector has exactly one responsibility, getting data into or out of NATS, with only per-message transformations; it deliberately is not a full data pipeline. "A connector should have one responsibility. It's getting data into NATS or getting data out of NATS" (~01:02)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Workloads - Distributed cloud-to-edge compute with NATS Execution Engine**

- Packing everything into one binary bloated builds, made build tags confusing, and slowed debugging; that drove the rearchitecture toward "nothing but NATS" using Orbit and micro. "we had packed everything into a single binary, and it was starting to get really bloated" (~04:14)
- Live demo hit the account's connection limit when many viewers connected, locking the presenter out. "There's so many of y'all on this. You took up all my connections" (~20:35)
- Firecracker was the original sandbox but doesn't run on Windows, is hard on macOS, and in cloud only GCP allows nested virtualization without expensive bare-metal instances, so it was dropped from the happy path. "the only cloud it ran in without problem was GCP because it was the only one that allowed nested virtualization" (~26:45)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — Migrating from NATS Streaming to JetStream**

- Streaming's reconnection behavior needed large documented caveats and was a known pain point. "There's like these big caveats and these big explanations about how to properly do reconnection." (~10:49)
- A stream bound to `*` or `>` captures every publish in the account; always scope streams under a single-token prefix. "That would be a problem. So, in practice, what you typically do is create a stream that has a single token prefix." (~31:18)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — NATS KubeCon Tutorial on Twitch**

- Never enable debug and trace logging in production; throughput drops by at least half. "The performance drops at least half when you have this logging." (~26:42)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — The Zen of High Performance Messaging with NATS by Waldemar Quevedo Salinas**

- Benchmarking with a tight publish loop plus a subscription in the same client makes that client a slow consumer: the server grows its pending buffer, then disconnects it to protect itself. "The NATS server is protecting itself." (~15:25)
- NATS is not meant for a new connection per request; keep one persistent connection as a dial tone. "NATS is not a system where you have to create a new connection for each one of the requests." (~20:37)
- A request timeout is ambiguous: no responder, dropped request, slow responder, or responder crash mid-processing, so callers must handle errors deliberately. "We need to be more careful when how to do error handling in these cases." (~28:53)

**Source class: Talks and videos (YouTube transcripts) — SCaLE 13x Derek Collison  NATS A new nervous system for distributed cloud platforms**

- Expecting the messaging system to guarantee delivery once handed a message is often an anti-pattern; store-and-forward has a place for batch work, but the app must handle failure. "A lot of times it's almost an anti-pattern to expect that once I give it to the messaging system it's going to take care of everything." (~17:21)
- Avoid "positive chatter" on a control plane: non-helping responders should stay silent rather than replying "I can't help", because such traffic grows with N. "If you can't help me I don't want you to say a word." (~53:25)
